design_detail: Narrative, non-systematic review (the authors' own description) of human studies of sleep in people who use alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids: self-reported and polysomnographic sleep during use, early abstinence and later abstinence, links between sleep and relapse, and medicines tried for sleep problems. PubMed, Ovid Medline and Web of Science searched with drug and sleep terms, plus reference lists; no dates, selection criteria or numbers of studies given. 222 references.
can_establish: What sleep changes the cited literature (up to about 2015) describes during and after regular use of each of the four drugs, as summarized by the authors, which medicines had been tried for those sleep problems, and the authors' framework linking slow-wave and REM sleep to relapse.
cannot_establish: How common or how large each sleep change is in people who use these drugs (no systematic selection, pooling or appraisal; most figures are single studies quoted without sample sizes); whether sleep problems cause relapse (the studies cited are associations); whether any sleep medicine helps in withdrawal (trials cited are few and not appraised); or anything about occasional use, since nearly all cited studies concern people with use disorders.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited studies are mostly polysomnographic and questionnaire studies of people with alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioid use disorders in inpatient or outpatient treatment, compared with healthy sleepers or with their own baseline, and a few placebo-controlled medicine trials.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond the search terms; psychotherapy for sleep was deliberately left out.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors. The cocaine section rests largely on studies from the senior author's laboratory (eight of 222 references, including Morgan et al. 2010 on modafinil); the opioid section draws heavily on methadone-maintenance samples; few studies of occasional use or of women are cited.

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies: diagnosed alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioid use disorder; laboratory administration in some acute studies; methadone or buprenorphine treatment.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as summarized: acute administration studies of THC (10, 20 or 30 mg) and of opioids; methadone maintenance (one cited study links doses above 120 mg a day to poorer sleep); trazodone 50 mg at night in methadone-maintained patients; amitriptyline against lorazepam in opioid withdrawal (amounts printed without units); buprenorphine and methadone tapered over two to three weeks in one study and buprenorphine tapers of one, two or four weeks in another. Abstinence periods studied range from the first night to several years.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed systematically; one cited methadone-maintenance study found nicotine and benzodiazepine use associated with poorer sleep, and about half of methadone-maintained patients reported using illicit drugs or medicines to help sleep.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Central to the review: findings are organized by early abstinence (acute withdrawal) and late abstinence (subacute withdrawal), which the review does not define in days for all drugs.

comparison.controls: Healthy sleepers, or the same people at baseline or at other points of abstinence, in the cited studies; placebo in the cited medicine trials.
comparison.matching: Not described; the review notes that differences in how controls were recruited and matched for age may explain inconsistent REM findings in alcohol studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that sleep problems predict later substance use (described as bidirectional) and that depression shortens REM latency, both of which confound abstinence comparisons; premorbid sleep is rarely measured.

outcomes.instruments: Self-report (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire, Sleep Disorders Questionnaire, Insomnia Severity Index); polysomnography (sleep latency, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, slow-wave sleep, REM sleep and latency, wake after sleep onset); actigraphy; sleep-disordered breathing measures.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised. For cocaine the review argues that self-reports become unreliable in abstinence ('occult insomnia'), with polysomnography worsening while self-rated sleep improves.
outcomes.operationalization: Table 2 summarizes the direction of objective changes in early and late abstinence relative to healthy sleepers, with question marks for insufficient or conflicting data.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the cited studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled. Figures as cited: clinical insomnia in 35 to 70% of people with alcohol use disorder against about 15 to 30% in the general population; sleep difficulties in 32 to 76% of people in cannabis withdrawal, strange dreams lasting up to about six weeks in some studies; total sleep time around the third week of cocaine abstinence as low as 300 to 330 minutes, and slow-wave sleep at three weeks half that of age-matched healthy sleepers; more than three-quarters of methadone-maintained patients reporting sleep complaints; signs of central sleep apnoea in 30 to 90% of patients on long-term opioid therapy, in a dose-dependent way.
analysis.selective_reporting: Non-systematic selection; the authors' own cocaine studies are described in detail, while conflicting results in other sections are noted briefly (for example REM in alcohol use disorder).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized, regular use of each of the four drugs is followed in abstinence by objectively poorer sleep (longer time to fall asleep, shorter sleep, less slow-wave sleep), lasting weeks to months and for alcohol sometimes years, with drug-specific patterns of REM change; alcohol and cannabis help falling asleep at first but lose this effect with regular use; self-reported sleep problems and some objective measures predict relapse in several studies; and the medicine trials cited give mixed or negative results for relapse even when sleep improves.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion speaks of overwhelming evidence of chronic sleep alterations common to all four drugs and proposes that medicines targeting slow-wave and REM sleep may be more useful than usual sleep medicines, which could be counterproductive. Gaps: (1) ‘overwhelming’ is asserted without a systematic search, counts or appraisal; (2) the relapse link is drawn from associations and offered as a mechanism; (3) modafinil is called the best present candidate for cocaine use disorder largely on the authors' own studies, while its effects on clinical outcome are described as mixed; (4) Table 2 marks most early-abstinence alcohol cells as insufficient or conflicting while the text describes clear changes. The review does label much of the mechanism as hypothesis.

timeline.event: Morgan et al. placebo-controlled study of modafinil and sleep in chronic cocaine use, from the senior author's laboratory and cited here as reference 147
This narrative review.

replication.where_it_stands: A useful map of the sleep literature for four drugs up to about 2015, but not a systematic summary; figures should be taken from the primary studies it cites. Its cocaine section overlaps with Morgan et al. (2010), which another reader holds, and should not be counted as independent of it.

funding.funder: NCATS CTSA grant UL1 TR000142 (NIH) and the NIH Roadmap for Medical Research; NIDA DA-011744 (P. T. Morgan); Connecticut Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors at Yale. The senior author's laboratory produced several of the cocaine studies the review relies on.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with meta-analysis of polysomnographic studies in abstinence from each drug, appraising control matching (age, depression, other drugs) and reporting effect sizes by time since last use; and randomized trials of sleep treatments in early abstinence measuring both sleep and relapse.

domains.note: Databases are named but there are no dates, criteria or numbers; the authors call the review non-systematic.
No appraisal; findings are cited without sample sizes or designs in most places.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The cocaine section, including the recommendation of modafinil, rests largely on the senior author's laboratory; the other sections cite mainly other groups.
The slow-wave and REM framework for relapse and the medicine recommendations are presented partly as hypothesis and partly as conclusion.

domains.domain: Balance of sleep-promoting and sleep-disrupting effects across drugs
domains.note: Acute sleep-promoting effects of alcohol and cannabis, tolerance to them, and the benefit of opioids for pain-related sleep problems are reported alongside the harms.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' checklist is used; two domains are high, so the overall judgment is high. The review may be cited for its map of the sleep literature and as a second-hand source for the direction of sleep changes in abstinence, labelled as such; numbers should be taken from the cited primary studies, and it should not be cited for the size of any effect, for causation of relapse, or for the effectiveness of any sleep medicine.

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the paper as a narrative, non-systematic review of human clinical studies found in PubMed, Ovid Medline and Web of Science plus reference lists.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, as summarized: alcohol shortens sleep latency in healthy people, but in alcohol use disorder sleep latency is prolonged during drinking and in acute and post-acute withdrawal, total sleep time is reduced, slow-wave sleep is deficient for months and possibly years, REM rebounds after stopping (with inconsistent findings), and sleep is fragmented from the second night of abstinence onwards; clinical insomnia is reported by 35 to 70% of people with alcohol use disorder against about 15 to 30% of the general population.
key_findings.locator: Alcohol › Subjective measurements; Objective measurements (Sleep latency, Total sleep time, Slow-wave sleep, Rapid eye movement, Objective sleep quality); Table 2

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, as summarized: self-reported insomnia and longer sleep latency in early abstinence predicted relapse in several studies, with mixed results for other objective measures.
key_findings.locator: Alcohol › Relationship between subjective measurements and clinical outcomes; Relationship between objective measurements and clinical outcomes

key_findings.finding: Medicines for sleep in alcohol use disorder, as summarized: gabapentin largely positive in trials; quetiapine improved wake after sleep onset and insomnia in one placebo-controlled trial with mixed effects on drinking; trazodone improved sleep measures but in a large placebo-controlled trial was associated with less abstinence during treatment and more drinking after it; ramelteon and agomelatine only in case series; benzodiazepines often avoided because of dependence and overdose risk with alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Alcohol › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, as summarized: short-term use eases falling asleep, but regular use brings tolerance; in withdrawal, sleep difficulties are reported by 32 to 76% of people, strange dreams typically start within days of stopping and can last weeks, and polysomnography shows longer time to fall asleep, more waking, less total and slow-wave sleep and REM rebound; returning to cannabis, alcohol or other sedatives to sleep is commonly observed.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis › Subjective measurements, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Objective measurements, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Cannabis, as summarized: withdrawal sleep problems improve with oral THC or resumed cannabis use; zolpidem, mirtazapine, gabapentin and quetiapine improved some sleep measures, but none conclusively reduced relapse; valproate, lithium, nefazodone and bupropion showed no definite benefit.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis › Pharmacotherapy options targeting sleep abnormalities, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Cocaine, as summarized: the first days to a week after stopping bring hypersomnia, bad dreams and fatigue; over the following weeks self-rated sleep improves while polysomnography worsens to insomnia-like levels (total sleep time around the third week as low as 300 to 330 minutes; slow-wave sleep at three weeks half that of age-matched healthy sleepers; low REM in weeks two and three), a pattern the authors call occult insomnia, linked to poorer sleep-dependent learning.
key_findings.locator: Cocaine › Subjective measurements, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Objective measurements (Total sleep time; Slow-wave sleep; Rem); Table 2

key_findings.finding: Opioids, as summarized: acute opioid use reduces REM and slow-wave sleep and increases waking; in the first week of abstinence from heroin total sleep time, slow-wave and REM sleep are reduced and sleep latency and waking increased compared with healthy sleepers, and in the first three weeks sleep latency is prolonged and efficiency reduced; after six weeks to six months of abstinence from methadone slow-wave and REM sleep rebound above baseline.
key_findings.locator: Opioids › Objective measurements, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Subjective measurements, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Opioid treatment, as summarized: more than three-quarters of people in methadone maintenance report sleep complaints and about half use illicit drugs or medicines to help sleep; long-term opioid therapy is associated with central sleep apnoea (signs in 30 to 90% of patients, dose-dependent); buprenorphine treatment in 70 patients was associated with mild to severe sleep-disordered breathing.
key_findings.locator: Opioids › Opioids and sleep disordered breathing, 1st paragraph; Methadone, 1st paragraph; Buprenorphine, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Medicines for sleep in opioid withdrawal or treatment, as summarized: trazodone did not improve subjective or objective sleep in methadone-maintained patients; amitriptyline and lorazepam did not differ on most sleep measures in a randomized double-blind study of 27 people with withdrawal insomnia; methadone and electrostimulation were not effective for insomnia in withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Opioids › Methadone, 1st paragraph; Buprenorphine, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks all early-abstinence alcohol cells as insufficient or conflicting data, while the text states that sleep latency is prolonged and total sleep time reduced during acute withdrawal.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table and the text disagree; neither gives the underlying numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: The cannabis objective-measurements section refers to Table 1 (a glossary) for withdrawal changes that are summarized in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-reference error.

reporting_issues.issue: The amounts of amitriptyline and lorazepam in the cited withdrawal-insomnia trial are printed without units.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study conditions cannot be read from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The review uses stigmatizing labels rather than person-first language for people in the cited studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error in the evidence; quotations from the review need person-first rewording (METHODS §9).

design_detail: Exploratory systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA; no registered protocol) of psychological changes and adverse effects from 1 day to 1 month after classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT, 5-MeO-DMT, mescaline, ayahuasca) in adults, from studies of any design that measured outcomes with standardized published instruments before and after use. MEDLINE and Web of Science searched from 1950 to 17 August 2021, English and German. 48 studies (52 publications), 1774 participants; results summarized by counting studies reporting a statistically significant increase, decrease, other change or no change in each of 19 outcome domains.
can_establish: Which psychological changes and adverse effects studies up to August 2021 reported in the month after a classic psychedelic, in which outcome domains changes were reported most consistently, how often adverse after-effects were looked for, and what kinds were reported.
cannot_establish: How large the changes are (no effect sizes or pooling); whether they are caused by the drug rather than expectation, setting, selection or regression to the mean (71% of studies lacked a standardized placebo-controlled double-blind design); how often after-effects occur in recreational use, where preparation and aftercare are usually absent (the authors say the results cannot be generalized there); how often adverse effects occur (only about half the studies said they looked, mostly without standard checklists); and whether post-session support changes the after-effects (the authors state this has not been tested).

sample.recruitment: MEDLINE via PubMed and Web of Science Core Collection to 17 August 2021, plus reference lists; 3973 publications screened after removing duplicates, 1918 excluded on title and abstract and 2003 on full text (Results › Study selection and sample characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human adults, clinical or nonclinical, any study type with baseline and pre–post analysis of standardized published psychological instruments between 1 day and 1 month after use; all reports of subacute adverse effects in any form. Excluded: studies that ended the acute experience with antipsychotics by default, microdosing, projective tests, book chapters, poster abstracts, case reports, reviews, comments and follow-ups not clearly timed; languages other than English and German.
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 6 to 315 (mean 38, median 18); 7 publications from 1958 to 1971 (86% LSD), none from 1972 to 1998, 45 from 1999 to 2021 (mostly psilocybin or ayahuasca); 35% clinical samples (depression, cancer-related distress, addiction and others), 65% healthy or unselected convenience samples. 83% of studies had at least one follow-up within two weeks.
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Laboratory trials and observational studies of ceremonies, both with preparation and aftercare; English and German only; only statistically significant results counted. Observational studies were mostly of ayahuasca (60%) and controlled studies mostly of psilocybin and LSD (86%), so substance and design are confounded.

exposure.measurement: Administration in laboratory or clinical studies, or self-selected use in ceremonies and retreats (observational studies).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1): LSD 50 to 450 µg by mouth (one study 75 µg intravenously; one 3 µg/kg); psilocybin 0.143 to 0.4 mg/kg or 10 to 32 mg; ayahuasca by volume with stated DMT content where known; 5-MeO-DMT 17 to 61 mg inhaled; mescaline 0.5 g injected; doses not reported in several observational studies. Mostly single sessions, some with two to six sessions. Follow-up 1 day to 1 month after the session.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; observational ceremony studies did not control other substance use.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: outcomes were measured 1 day to 1 month after a session.

comparison.controls: Each person's own baseline in all studies; a control group in 24 of 48 studies (placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectation, motivation and selection into ceremonies or trials were not assessed; floor effects for anxiety and suicidality in healthy samples are noted by the authors.

outcomes.instruments: Standardized published scales in 19 domains (for example depression, anxiety, mood, wellbeing and life satisfaction, mindfulness, personality and attitudes, social effects, spirituality, creativity, psychosis, mania, cognitive performance, complaints); adverse events in any form reported by the studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Only standardized and published instruments were accepted, which the authors use as their outcome-level safeguard against bias.
outcomes.operationalization: Each study's result in each domain was coded as increase, decrease, other change or no change according to the statistical significance of pre–post differences (or drug-by-time interactions); trends were ignored.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; significance as reported by the primary studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; most outcomes are self-reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. Results are counts of studies reporting significant change per domain (Figure 2, an image, and Supplementary Tables S1 to S3, not read). Text figures: changes were most consistent (70 to 90% of studies investigating the domain, more than 450 participants) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing and life satisfaction; and social effects. No changes in manic or psychotic symptoms or cognitive performance (few studies). Adverse events: 25 studies (52%, 550 participants) said whether they assessed them; 11 (297 participants) reported none and 14 (253 participants) reported 52 headaches, 6 cases of insomnia or sleep disturbance, 6 of tension, 3 of exhaustion, 3 of visual distortion, 2 each of fatigue, migraine, nausea, difficulty concentrating and vivid dreams, and single cases including severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse to methamphetamine use and a psychiatric disturbance lasting a week.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only statistically significant findings were counted (vote counting), so non-significant results and their direction are lost; the authors discuss possible publication bias and selective reporting in a field with high public interest.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the median study had 18 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 48 mostly small studies, many of them uncontrolled, the changes reported in the month after a classic psychedelic were mostly towards less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness, with no group-level worsening of psychopathology. Adverse after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked: mostly headaches, then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with rare severe events.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the results support narrative reports of a subacute afterglow comprising potentially beneficial changes, and that subacute adverse events were mild to severe with no serious adverse events. The authors are careful elsewhere: they state that the findings summarize effects observed under favourable conditions, should not be taken as the average expected effect, and cannot be generalized to recreational use. Remaining gaps: (1) vote counting of significant pre–post changes cannot show that the drug caused them; (2) ‘no serious adverse events’ sits beside a severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse and a week-long psychiatric disturbance, and half the studies did not say whether they looked; (3) the comparison of subacute side effects with those of SSRIs is not based on data.

timeline.event: Pahnke and colleagues' description (JAMA, 1970) of the psychedelic afterglow lasting about two weeks to a month, quoted in this review's introduction.
Müller et al. pooled analysis of flashback phenomena after LSD and psilocybin in six controlled trials, which reports a later-weeks after-effect not covered by this review's outcome domains
This review: the first systematic review restricted to the subacute window, by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic map of subacute effects of psychedelics in the papers read for this card. It shows where changes have been reported, not how large or how causal they are; a meta-analysis cited in its introduction combined subacute with long-term effects and is not separable from it.

funding.funder: Article processing charge funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (491192747) and the Open Access Publication Fund of Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin; no other funding stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no potential conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin and the Psychedelic Substances Research Group at Charité, Berlin.

what_would_settle_it: Placebo-controlled trials, and prospective studies of people using psychedelics outside research, with daily ratings of mood, sleep, headache and distress over the month after use using a standard adverse-effect checklist and a validated afterglow instrument, reporting effect sizes for both benefits and harms.

Each of two authors extracted half the studies and cross-checked the other's, with consensus on disagreements; the sheet was piloted on five studies.

domains.note: 2003 full texts were excluded; no list of excluded studies with reasons is given in the article.

Vote counting of significant results.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooling.

domains.note: The authors state that 72% of studies lacked control, blinding or standardization, that observational findings need confirmation, and that results reflect favourable conditions.
Differences between domains, floor effects, substances, settings and follow-up windows are discussed.
No meta-analysis; publication bias and selective reporting are discussed in the limitations.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding of the article charge and the absence of conflicts are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are 'no' (2 protocol, 4 search, 7 excluded studies, 9 risk of bias), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. This is partly a consequence of the review's exploratory aim, which the authors state, and their interpretation is cautious. It may be cited for the inventory of studies and outcome domains, for the direction of reported changes as counts of studies, for the list of reported adverse after-effects with the caveat that half the studies did not say whether they looked, and for the authors' statement that the results reflect favourable settings; it should not be cited for the size or causation of any afterglow effect or for its frequency in recreational use.

key_findings.finding: 48 studies (52 publications) with 1774 participants were included: 16 psilocybin, 16 ayahuasca, 10 LSD, 2 5-MeO-DMT, 3 several psychedelics and 1 mescaline; 17 clinical and 31 nonclinical samples; sample sizes 6 to 315 (median 18); follow-up 1 day to 1 month.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study selection and sample characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 2, All studies row

key_findings.finding: 14 of 48 studies (29%) had a standardized treatment with placebo control and double-blind allocation, 19 (40%) a standardized treatment without control or blinding, and 15 (31%) no standardization (observational); controlled studies were mostly of psilocybin and LSD (86%), observational studies mostly of ayahuasca (60%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph; Table 2, footnote a

key_findings.finding: Changes were reported most consistently (in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured them, each domain with more than 450 participants) for depression, stress and grief; mindfulness, acceptance and emotion regulation; personality, values and attitudes; wellbeing and life satisfaction; and social effects. Mindfulness data came only from healthy or unselected samples, and mindfulness and wellbeing data mostly from observational studies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No study reported group-level worsening of psychopathology, and none found increases in suicidality, manic or psychotic symptoms or decreases in cognitive performance, although few studies assessed these outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Only 25 of 48 studies (52%, 550 participants) said whether they assessed adverse events. Of these, 11 (297 participants) reported none and 14 (253 participants) reported subacute adverse events: 52 headaches (usually lasting no more than a day or two), 6 cases of insomnia or sleep disturbance, 6 of tension, 3 of exhaustion, 3 of visual distortion, 2 each of fatigue, migraine, nausea, difficulty concentrating and vivid dreams, and single cases including severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse to methamphetamine use, a post-traumatic stress flashback with tinnitus and panic, and a psychiatric disturbance lasting a week.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of four studies that collected complaints with a standardized list, three found no change and one an increase in complaints one day after use that had gone at one week.
key_findings.locator: Results › Synthesis of results › Subacute effects of psychedelics, Figure 2 footnote d

key_findings.finding: Most subacute effects were seen in all three follow-up windows, most consistently between 3 and 14 days; results at 1 to 2 days were the most variable; increases in creativity were limited to the early windows.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the results come from laboratory studies and ceremonies with preparation and aftercare, cannot be generalized to recreational use, may be biased by selective reporting, and should be read as a summary of effects observed under favourable conditions, not as the average expected effect.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

(2016) with 243 participants, but the LSD total (362) and the overall total (1774) in Table 2 match the Table 1 rows only if that study contributes no participants (editors' arithmetic: the other LSD studies, counting the repeated Schmid sample once, sum to 362).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the 243 is a misprint or the totals omit that study; the total participant count is uncertain by up to 243.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion state that no serious adverse events were reported, while the adverse-event list includes a severe anxiety exacerbation with relapse to methamphetamine use and a psychiatric disturbance lasting one week.
reporting_issues.consequence: Depends on the definition of serious; claims should name these events rather than repeat that none was serious.
