design_detail: Pooled descriptive analysis of flashback phenomena in all six double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized crossover trials of LSD or psilocybin in healthy volunteers run by one research group in Basel up to April 2021. Flashbacks were recorded as adverse events at sessions and asked about once at an end-of-study visit; participants who reported them were followed up by email in May 2021. Frequencies are descriptive; there is no comparison with a no-drug condition.
can_establish: How many healthy, screened trial participants reported flashback-like experiences after LSD or psilocybin when asked at the end of a controlled study, what those experiences were like (sense, length, frequency, feeling, timing) and whether any met DSM-5 criteria for hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD).
cannot_establish: Whether the drug caused the reported experiences (no estimate of how often similar experiences occur without a drug; an earlier psilocybin analysis found similar rates before and after dosing); frequencies in people who use LSD or psilocybin outside research, with psychiatric histories, frequent use or other drugs; flashbacks starting after the end-of-study visit in people who reported none (only those with flashbacks were followed up); and the true rate of HPPD (a zero count in 142 people is compatible with a rate up to about 2%).

sample.recruitment: All participants of the six LSD or psilocybin trials conducted by the Basel group as of April 2021 (NCT01878942, NCT02308969, NCT03019822, NCT03321136, NCT03604744, NCT03912974); four enrolled participants dropped out before receiving a study drug (Methods › Studies included in analysis; Results › Subject characteristics).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 25 to 65 (25 to 50 in one trial), German-speaking, willing to avoid illicit drugs during the study. Excluded: personal or first-degree family history of seizures or of psychotic or major psychiatric disorder, cardiac or neurological disorders, more than ten prior illicit drug uses (cannabis excepted) or any illicit use in the previous two months, pregnancy or nursing, interfering medicines.
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.7 (SD 9.0); 74 women and 68 men; previous hallucinogen use in 30.3% (mean 2.2 occasions), MDMA in 40.1%, other stimulants in 34.5%, cannabis in 78.9% (Results › Subject characteristics; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Follow-up was sought only from the 13 who reported flashbacks: one could not be reached and another gave incomplete information. Whether all participants who dropped out after a session (at least two of the 13) had a full end-of-study visit is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers with little previous drug experience and no psychiatric history, likely with positive attitudes towards psychedelics, as the authors note; people who had had bad after-effects before may have been less likely to enrol.

exposure.measurement: Randomized administration of LSD, psilocybin or comparators under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions in six crossover trials; every participant also had placebo sessions.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: LSD 0.025 to 0.2 mg by mouth (capsules, or a solution in ethanol), 213 administrations, 1 to 5 per person; psilocybin 15 to 30 mg by mouth (capsules of 5 mg), 103 administrations, 1 or 2 per person. The two single-dose LSD trials used 0.1 mg (n = 24 in Table 1) and 0.2 mg (n = 16 in Table 1); one trial compared LSD 0.1 mg with d-amphetamine 40 mg and MDMA 125 mg; one compared LSD 0.025 to 0.2 mg and LSD with ketanserin; one gave psilocybin 25 mg after pretreatment with escitalopram (20 mg in Table 1; the person in Table 2 had two 10 mg doses) or placebo; one compared LSD 0.1 and 0.2 mg with psilocybin 15 and 30 mg. Flashbacks counted if more than 24 hours after a dose. End-of-study visit a mean of 39.8 days (SD 37.2, range 2 to 193) after the last session; follow-up a mean of 31.2 months (SD 28.6, range 3.3 to 86.8) after that visit.
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drugs prohibited during the trials; alcohol and caffeine avoided the evening before and on session days. Three of the 13 people with flashbacks had also received a non-hallucinogenic study drug (escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: the outcome is recurrence of drug-like experiences after the acute effects had ended.

comparison.controls: None for the flashback outcome. Placebo sessions existed within each crossover trial, but flashback reports could not be attributed to a placebo condition and no no-drug rate is given.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tendency to unusual perceptual experiences, migraine, tinnitus and anxiety, proposed risk factors for HPPD, were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Open questions about any flashback phenomena at each session and at the end-of-study visit, with description of quality, quantity, impairment and timing; email follow-up asking about further flashbacks, frequency, impairment and triggers; ICD-10 (F16.7) definition of flashbacks and DSM-5 criteria for HPPD applied by the authors.
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated questionnaire; the authors note that heightened awareness of ordinary perceptual experiences may explain some reports.
outcomes.operationalization: Flashback: recurrence of drug-like experiences after the acute effects had ended (the study's time threshold is recorded in the exposure field). HPPD: persisting flashback phenomena with clinically significant distress or impairment (DSM-5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; by the end-of-study visit participants were usually unblinded to the substances received across the trial.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive percentages without confidence intervals: 13 of 142 (9.2%) reported flashback phenomena; 7 of 90 after LSD only (7.8%), 2 of 24 after psilocybin only (8.3%), 4 of 28 after both (14.3%); 2 of 142 (1.4%) distressing; 0 of 142 met DSM-5 criteria for HPPD. Simulated probability of observing no case of HPPD in 142 people: 24.0% for a true incidence of 1%, 5.7% for 2%, 1.3% for 3%, 0.3% for 4%, 0.1% for 5%. Editors' calculation: with zero events in 142, the one-sided 95% upper limit for the rate is about 2.1% (3 divided by 142).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The six parent trials are registered; this pooled analysis of flashbacks has no registered protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 13 cases are tabulated individually (Table 2), which limits selective reporting.
analysis.power: The authors note that 142 people are too few to assess a rare condition such as HPPD.

interpretation_gap.results_show: About 1 in 11 healthy, screened trial participants who received LSD and/or psilocybin reported some flashback-like experience when asked at the end of the study, mostly a single, brief visual change in the days after the last session, felt as neutral or pleasant. Two (1.4%) found it distressing, one of whom then had panic attacks and left the study; one person had brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months. No one reported impairment of daily life and no one met criteria for HPPD.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the phenomenon common, occurring in up to 9.2% of healthy subjects, and the paper concludes that flashbacks are not a clinically relevant problem in controlled studies with healthy participants. Gaps: (1) 9.2% is the overall rate, not an upper limit (14.3% among those given both drugs), and without a no-drug comparison the rate cannot be attributed to the drugs, as the Discussion itself acknowledges; (2) ‘not clinically relevant’ sits beside one participant who developed panic attacks after a flashback and dropped out, and another who dropped out after a very difficult session followed by distressing flashbacks; (3) the Discussion says both distressing cases resolved within a week of drug administration, although one began 17 days after psilocybin; (4) the absence of HPPD in 142 people cannot exclude a rate of up to about 2%.

timeline.event: Studerus et al. pooled analysis of psilocybin studies in 110 healthy participants, finding spontaneous altered states in about 10% both before and after dosing (as cited by this paper).
Vizeli and Liechti pooled analysis of MDMA studies in 131 healthy participants from the same group, with flashback-like experiences in 9% (6.5% beyond 24 hours), as cited by this paper.
This pooled analysis of LSD and psilocybin trials.
Evens et al. systematic review of subacute effects of psychedelics, which lists headaches, sleep problems and single distressing events among after-effects in the month after use

replication.where_it_stands: Consistent with earlier pooled analyses of controlled studies (psilocybin; MDMA, from the same group) in which roughly one in ten participants reported flashback-like or spontaneous altered experiences, much lower than the 15 to 75% quoted from naturalistic studies. None of these analyses compares with a no-drug rate, and all concern screened volunteers.

funding.funder: Open access funding by the University of Basel. The contributing trials were supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation (grant 32003B_185111 to M. E. Liechti), Mind Medicine, Inc., and the University of Basel.
funding.declared_conflicts: M. E. Liechti is a consultant for Mind Medicine, Inc.; the statement says this party had no role in financing, planning or conducting the present study or publication (the sentence's subject is ambiguous between Liechti and the company). The other authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: The analysis was done by the group that ran all six trials; one funder of the contributing trials is a company that employs the senior trial investigator as a consultant.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people taking LSD or psilocybin within and outside research settings, with a standardized flashback and HPPD questionnaire given before dosing (to establish the no-drug rate) and at fixed times for at least a year afterwards to everyone, including people with psychiatric histories or frequent use.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Appropriate for the paper's stated target, healthy participants of controlled studies; not representative of people who use LSD or psilocybin outside research.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: All participants of all the group's LSD and psilocybin trials up to April 2021.
Enough to describe a frequency near 9%; too small to estimate a rare condition such as HPPD, as the authors note.

domains.domain: 4. Subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Trial-by-trial demographics, drug histories and visit intervals in Table 1.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Whether every participant, including those who left after a session, had an end-of-study visit is not stated.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used to identify the condition
domains.note: ICD-10 and DSM-5 definitions applied to answers to open questions; no validated instrument.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The interval from last session to the end-of-study visit ranged from 2 to 193 days; follow-up was offered only to those who reported flashbacks.
Percentages without confidence intervals; the simulation of the chance of observing no HPPD case is appropriate.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Coverage of the end-of-study visit is not stated; 12 of 13 responded to follow-up.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Editors' summary of the JBI checklist: moderate risk of bias for the frequency of reported flashbacks in screened trial volunteers, mainly because the question was asked once at very different intervals, without a standard instrument, and follow-up covered only those who reported flashbacks, which could undercount late or forgotten experiences; the lack of a no-drug comparison could overcount them. The paper may be cited for the frequency and character of flashbacks reported by healthy, screened participants of controlled LSD and psilocybin trials and for the absence of HPPD in 142 such people (with its upper limit); it should not be cited for rates in recreational use or as showing that the drugs cause the reported experiences.

key_findings.finding: 142 healthy participants (146 enrolled; 4 left before any drug) from six double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trials: 90 received LSD only, 24 psilocybin only and 28 both; 74 women; mean age 31.7; previous hallucinogen use in 30.3%.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Studies included in analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results › Subject characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: At the end-of-study visit, 13 of 142 (9.2%) reported flashback phenomena: 7 of 90 after LSD only (7.8%), 2 of 24 after psilocybin only (8.3%) and 4 of 28 after both (14.3%); 10 of the 13 were women.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Flashbacks were visual in 11 of 13 (with auditory, cognitive or self-disintegration features in 3) and purely emotional in 2; they lasted seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%), hours in one case; 53.8% happened once; in all but two cases they were limited to the week after the last drug administration; more than half occurred while relaxing or around falling asleep or waking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Flashbacks were neutral or positive for 10 of 13 and distressing for 2 (1.4% of all 142); one was not documented. No one reported impairment of daily life. One distressing case followed an exceptionally difficult session after which the participant left the study; the other was a single episode during escitalopram pretreatment 17 days after psilocybin, followed by panic attacks, after which the participant left the study.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Two participants had more than five episodes: one about 20 brief visual flashbacks within a short period after dosing, and one about 30 brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months, which had stopped about ten months before follow-up; at follow-up (mean 31.2 months later; 12 of 13 responding) she was the only one reporting recurrence after the end-of-study visit.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Flashback phenomena at follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: No participant met DSM-5 criteria for HPPD. The simulated chance of seeing no case among 142 people was 24.0% if the true incidence were 1%, 5.7% at 2% and 1.3% at 3%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder, 1st paragraph; Methods › Hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: zero events in 142 gives a one-sided 95% upper limit of about 2.1% for the rate.

key_findings.finding: Three of the 13 people with flashbacks had also received escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA in the trials; the authors note that rates in naturalistic studies (15 to 75%) are much higher, and that a pooled MDMA analysis by the same group found flashback-like experiences in 9% (6.5% beyond 24 hours).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations the sample size (especially for HPPD), varying doses and substances, likely positive attitudes and prior drug experience of participants, follow-up only of those who reported flashbacks at different intervals, and exclusion of people with mental disorders.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 25 participants for the psilocybin-and-escitalopram trial, while the Methods and Table 1 give 24; the abstract's four groups add up to 143, not 142.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the denominators used for the percentages (24 for psilocybin only) follow Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods assign the two single-dose LSD trials their sample sizes the other way round from Table 1 (the lower-dose trial has 24 participants in Table 1 and 16 in the text).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the doses and sizes are recorded in the exposure field as in Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that both distressing cases resolved spontaneously within a week of drug administration, but the Results describe one as starting 17 days after psilocybin and being followed by panic attacks.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion understates one distressing case; the Results text should be followed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes flashbacks as occurring in up to 9.2% of healthy subjects, while 14.3% of those who received both drugs reported them.
reporting_issues.consequence: 9.2% is the overall rate, not an upper limit.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 112 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9166883 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, funding and conflict-of-interest statements and reference list read; no figures; no supplementary material)

design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA cited as the reporting guideline; no protocol or registration mentioned) of studies in which a measure taken before a classic psychedelic (psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca or DMT, mescaline) was reported to predict an acute drug effect. One database (PubMed): 42 searches crossing six drug terms with seven predictor terms, filtered to English, human studies and 1994 onward; the search date is not reported (manuscript received 8 January 2021). Two authors screened 1635 records; 10 articles met the criteria and 4 more were added from outside sources (for example reference lists or papers published after the search), 14 in all. The synthesis is narrative, organised by drug and then by 'states' and 'traits' (Tables 1 and 2): no pooled estimates, no tabulated effect sizes, no formal risk-of-bias assessment. The inclusion rule required that a pre-drug measure was predictive of an acute effect, so only reported associations were tabulated, never predictors tested and found null.
can_establish: Which pre-drug states, traits and biological measures had been reported, in 14 studies published before early 2021, as associated with acute effects of classic psychedelics, in which direction, and in what kinds of designs and samples: a map of reported associations and a pointer to the primary studies.
cannot_establish: How strong or consistent any predictor is (no effect sizes were pooled, and studies reporting no association were excluded by the inclusion rule); whether any predictor causes a better or more difficult experience; how the experience was measured in each study (the review names no instruments); or that the state predictors highlighted in the abstract were measured before the drug, since four of the 14 studies, including both sources of those states, are marked retrospective, with the 'baseline' states reported after the experience.

sample.recruitment: Literature search of PubMed only: two authors independently ran 42 searches crossing six drug terms (ayahuasca, LSD, lysergic acid diethylamide, mescaline, psilocybin, n,n-dimethyltryptamine) with seven predictor terms (predict, correlate, associate, pre-drug, individual difference, baseline, risk factor), filtered to English, human and 1994 to present (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph). Primary-study samples (Table 1): healthy volunteers in laboratory studies (Lebedev 2015, Lewis 2020, Carhart-Harris 2015, Terhune 2016, Stenbaek 2020, Studerus 2012); expert Buddhist meditators on a retreat (Smigielski 2019); long-term AIDS survivors in open-label group therapy (Stauffer 2020); people experienced with ayahuasca (Bouso 2013); and unselected people (Table 1's term): an analysis of reports posted on Erowid (Bienemann 2020), retrospective surveys of people who had used psilocybin (Carbonaro 2016; Russ 2019a and 2019b; how they were recruited is not stated in the review) and a prospective survey of people planning to take a psychedelic (Haijen 2018).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed articles in which classic psychedelic drugs were used and a pre-drug measure predicted an acute effect. Excluded: book chapters, case reports and reviews. Discrepancies were resolved by evaluating the study together with several team members (Methods › Selection Criteria, 1st paragraph). The 1994 limit is justified as the start of modern US administration studies; the English-language limit is not justified.
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 10 to 1993 (the review's printed mean and SD cannot be reproduced; see reporting issues); median publication year 2018. Examples from the text: 1993 respondents to an online survey of challenging experiences with psilocybin mushrooms (78% men, 89% white); 10 healthy volunteers given LSD intravenously in one laboratory (one woman; on average 65 previous LSD experiences), the same 10 analysed in two articles; 15 volunteers (two women) and 55 volunteers (22 women) in psilocybin imaging studies; 38 expert meditators (39 in Table 1); 18 long-term AIDS survivors, almost all older men, in open-label group therapy; 261 volunteers (100 women) from 23 pooled laboratory studies (Results › Drugs, all subsections).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Attrition within primary studies is mentioned only for Haijen et al. (2018).
sample.selection_effects: One database, English only, no grey literature, trial registries or systematic citation searching; the 4 extra articles were added ad hoc. The inclusion rule admitted only studies reporting a predictive association, so null findings were excluded by design (the authors name the file-drawer problem). Nine of the 14 articles come from two research groups: six include R.L. Carhart-Harris as an author (Carhart-Harris 2015, Terhune 2016, Lebedev 2015, both Russ 2019 articles, Haijen 2018) and three F.X. Vollenweider (Studerus 2012, Lewis 2020, Smigielski 2019) (editors' check of the reference list). The two LSD articles share one sample of 10.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used; the review does not name the instruments. Predictors are classed in Table 1 as states (S) or traits (T); age is classed as a state. Four studies are marked retrospective (Table 1, footnote a): Bienemann 2020 (an analysis of negative psilocybin reports posted to Erowid), Carbonaro 2016 (a survey of people who had used psilocybin about their most challenging experience) and Russ 2019a and 2019b (samples Table 1 calls unselected). The review does not say how the Carbonaro or Russ respondents were recruited; its Limitations paragraph mentions online crowd-sourcing only as a general feature of retrospective designs. In the two Russ studies the 'baseline' states (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion, deservingness, spiritual motivation) were therefore reported after the experience.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated in Table 1: psilocybin by mouth at fixed or weight-adjusted amounts in laboratory and clinical studies, or 'varied' (unknown) in the naturalistic and online studies; LSD 40-80 µg intravenously in one laboratory sample; psilocybin 2 mg intravenously in one study; ayahuasca 100 mL by mouth in one study. Dose was not used as a moderator in the synthesis.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Two tabulated predictors are other drug histories (cannabis and alcohol consumption, from Studerus 2012); drugs taken alongside the psychedelic in the naturalistic studies are not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.

comparison.controls: Variation in each predictor within each study's drug condition. Six of 14 studies had a control condition (placebo or a drug-naive group), which the review uses as a mark of quality, but the predictor analyses themselves are between-person associations under the drug.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed. Dose, setting, drug identity and purity varied, uncontrolled, within the naturalistic and online studies; the review names these as limitations study by study but does not treat them as possible confounders of the tabulated associations.

outcomes.instruments: Not named. Outcomes are listed as constructs in Table 1, for example mystical experience, challenging experience, dread, ego dissolution, oceanic boundlessness, visionary restructuralization, 'bad trip', acute impairment of executive function, suggestibility, stimulus-colour consistency and intensity of the emotional experience. Some are not acute effects: well-being after use (Haijen 2018, Table 1) and spiritual change and long-term positive change (Russ 2019b; Table 2 and Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; the review does not say which questionnaires were used, when they were rated or by whom.
outcomes.operationalization: A study entered if a pre-drug measure was reported as related to an acute effect. Table 1 gives only the sign of each association; the text quotes correlations for some studies (see effect sizes). 'Positive' and 'adverse' reactions are the primary studies' constructs, never defined by the review.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at review level, where no tests were run; 76 is the editors' count of predictor-outcome associations tabulated in Table 1, each reported as significant by its primary study. The primary studies' own multiplicity handling is not reported; 19 of the 76 come from one study (Studerus 2012), which tested many predictors against many outcomes, so chance findings are likely among them.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two authors screened records; how data were extracted, and by whom, is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled or tabulated. Correlations and other effect sizes quoted in the text: Russ 2019b (n = 143) surrender r = 0.72 and absorption r = 0.61 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation r = 0.64 and confusion r = 0.58 with dread, age r = -0.23 with dread; Stauffer 2020 (n = 18, open label) attachment anxiety r = 0.53 with mystical-type experience and attachment avoidance r = 0.62 with challenging experience; Carbonaro 2016 (n = 1993) age r = -0.06 and history of hallucinogen use r = -0.05 with difficulty of the experience; Carhart-Harris 2015 (n = 10) conscientiousness r = 0.89 with change in suggestibility and imagery ability r = 0.72 with change in imagery; Terhune 2016 (same 10 people) absorption r = -0.67 with stimulus-colour consistency; Bouso 2013 (n = 24) lifetime ayahuasca use r = -0.62 with executive impairment; Bienemann 2020 (n = 346) sex and 'bad trip' reports V = 0.20, called small. Editors' calculation: correlations of -0.05 and -0.06 correspond to under 0.4% of shared variance.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA is cited (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph). The supporting information, a spreadsheet of the same results organised by outcome, is a download and was not opened.
analysis.selective_reporting: Built into the design: the inclusion rule admits only predictors reported as predictive, so the review cannot show predictors that were tested and not found (the authors acknowledge the file-drawer problem in Limitations). The abstract and Conclusion present absorption as a predictor of positive and mystical-type experiences and omit that, in the one prospective naturalistic study, absorption was also associated with challenging experiences (Table 1 and Table 2 show it; in Haijen 2018's Table 7 the coefficients were 0.215 for challenging and 0.347 for mystical-type experience).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Eight of the 14 samples have 55 or fewer participants (editors' count from Table 1: 10, 10, 15, 16, 18, 24, 39 and 55).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 14 mostly small or retrospective studies, the trait absorption was reported as positively associated with mystical-type or oceanic experiences in four (Studerus 2012, both Russ 2019 articles, Haijen 2018), but in the only prospective naturalistic study (Haijen 2018) absorption was also positively associated with challenging experiences and visual effects. The state predictors in the abstract (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion) come from two retrospective online studies by the same team. A positive 'set' the day before (fewer challenging experiences), clear intentions (more mystical-type experience) and recreational intentions (fewer challenging experiences) come from one prospective study. Acceptance rests on one study of 38 or 39 expert meditators, and each biological predictor on a single study of 15, 16 or 55 people. In the largest study, age and history of hallucinogen use correlated with difficulty at r = -0.06 and -0.05.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says people high in absorption, openness and acceptance and in a state of surrender were more likely to have positive and mystical-type experiences, and the Conclusion that such people “may represent ideal candidates for psychedelic therapy”. Gaps: (1) the state predictors were reported after the experience in their only two sources, yet are presented as baseline predictors; (2) absorption's association with challenging experiences in the one prospective study is left out of the abstract and Conclusion; (3) the 'ideal candidates' statement rests on healthy volunteers and people using psychedelics on their own, not on therapy outcomes in patients; (4) the abstract infers that people become slightly less sensitive after repeated use, and the Discussion that overuse may blunt benefits, from between-person correlations that equally fit selection (people who had difficult experiences may stop using); (5) the abstract and Conclusion call the anterior cingulate predictor a volume, while the cited study measured cortical thickness; (6) the Future Directions section speculates about changing baseline traits before treatment, which no included study tested. The Limitations paragraph is frank about small, open-label and self-selected samples, but those limits do not reach the abstract.

timeline.event: Studerus et al. pooled 23 psilocybin laboratory studies (261 volunteers) to find predictors of response; the review includes it and calls it an earlier overview that was not systematic and covered one laboratory and one drug.
Haijen et al. prospective online study of people planning to take a psychedelic; the review's only prospective naturalistic source of set and intention predictors.
Russ et al., two retrospective online studies (183 and 143 people), one titled a replication and extension of the Studerus 2012 model; the sole sources of the review's state predictors.
This review.
Studerus et al. applied the pooled-laboratory predictor approach to MDMA (194 volunteers).
Vizeli et al. applied it to LSD (213 volunteers) and cite this review.

replication.where_it_stands: The first systematic review of pre-drug predictors of acute psychedelic effects, by its authors' account, mapping a small and early literature. Because it admits only positive findings, does not appraise or weight studies by design and contains sign errors in its tables, claims should cite the primary studies (Haijen 2018 for set and intentions measured before use; the Basel pooled laboratory analyses for mood and personality measured before dosing) and use this review as a pointer, not as evidence that a predictor is consistent or strong.

funding.funder: No funding for the review is stated. Effort for Dr. Davis was provided by Tim Ferriss, Matt Mullenweg, Craig Nerenberg, Blake Mycoskie and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation; the statement says the funders had no role in study design, data analysis, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr. Davis is a board member of Source Research Foundation; the statement says this organization was not involved in the design or execution of the study or in the interpretation or communication of findings.
funding.affiliations_note: Four authors in the Department of Psychology, Central Michigan University; A.K. Davis at the College of Social Work, The Ohio State University, and the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. No review author is an author of an included study (editors' check of the reference list).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered individual-participant meta-analysis of prospective studies, in laboratories, clinics and naturalistic settings, in which states, traits and intentions are measured before the drug with validated instruments, the experience is rated with the same questionnaires (for example MEQ30, CEQ, 5D-ASC) at a fixed time, every predictor tested is reported whether or not it was significant, and models allow for dose, drug, setting and prior experience.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Components stated broadly: humans given classic psychedelics, any pre-drug measure, any acute effect; a comparator does not apply to a question about predictors. The outcome is defined only as 'an acute effect', and non-acute outcomes were nevertheless included.
No protocol or registration mentioned.

Chapters, case reports and reviews were excluded; no reason is given for admitting every other design, including analyses of posted online reports and retrospective surveys, alongside placebo-controlled studies.

One database (PubMed) with stated keywords; English only without justification; no grey literature, registries, systematic reference-list searching or expert contact; search date not reported; 4 of 14 articles added ad hoc. Partial yes requires at least two databases.
Two authors independently searched and assessed the 1635 records; discrepancies were resolved with several team members (Methods › Selection Criteria; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph).
Extraction is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded full texts or reasons; the flow diagram (Figure 1) is an image and could not be viewed in this reading.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives population, drug, dose and route, sample size, control condition, predictor, outcome and direction, with retrospective designs flagged; settings, instruments, timing of measurement and effect sizes are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool or stated method. The prose names limitations study by study (sample size, open label, retrospective design, uncontrolled dose and setting, self-selection), unevenly, and calls some studies methodologically rigorous without stating criteria. A close call against partial yes, which would need confounding and selection bias assessed across the studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
Narrative synthesis only.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations paragraph discusses designs in general, but the abstract and Conclusion present predictors from retrospective online studies (the state predictors) and from single small studies (acceptance, the brain measures) as if equivalent to prospectively measured ones.

The conflicting sex findings are discussed with alternative explanations, but not why absorption relates to both mystical and challenging experiences, nor differences between laboratory and naturalistic designs, outcomes or drugs.
No quantitative synthesis. The file-drawer problem is named in Limitations, and the inclusion rule itself (only predictive associations) selects on positive results.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Support for one author and his board membership are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13 are not met (no protocol, a one-database English-only search, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment, and conclusions that do not account for study design), so confidence is critically low by the AMSTAR 2 rule. Beyond the AMSTAR items, the inclusion rule admits only positive associations, so the review cannot speak to consistency, and its tables contain sign errors and an impossible summary statistic (reporting issues). The review may be cited as a map of predictors reported up to early 2021 and as a pointer to primary studies; it should not be cited as evidence that any predictor is consistent or strong, for the claim that preparation-related states predict experiences (their sources are retrospective), or for the 'ideal candidates for therapy' conclusion.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed only, 42 searches (six drug terms by seven predictor terms), English, human, 1994 to present, search date not reported; two authors assessed 1635 records; 10 articles met the criteria and 4 were added from outside sources, 14 in all.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Methods › Selection Criteria, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Included studies: 10 on psilocybin, 2 on LSD (both from the same 10 participants), 1 on ayahuasca, 1 on psychedelics in general; sample sizes 10 to 1993; 6 of 14 with a control condition; 4 with a retrospective design; median publication year 2018.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Selection, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 and footnote a; Results › Drugs › LSD, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Absorption was tabulated with more mystical-type experience, ego dissolution, oceanic boundlessness and visionary restructuralization and less dread, and also with more challenging experience and visual effects (Haijen 2018) and less stimulus-colour consistency (Terhune 2016); sources Studerus 2012, Russ 2019a and 2019b, Terhune 2016 and Haijen 2018. In Russ 2019b (n = 143, retrospective) absorption correlated r = 0.61 with mystical-type experience.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (absorption row); Table 1 (Haijen rows); Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 6th paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: All state predictors named in the abstract (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion), with deservingness and spiritual motivation, come from Russ 2019a (n = 183) and Russ 2019b (n = 143), both marked retrospective. In Russ 2019b surrender correlated r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, and preoccupation r = 0.64 and confusion r = 0.58 with dread.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (Russ rows, footnote a); Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Discussion › States, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: From the one prospective naturalistic study (Haijen 2018; 212 to 654 participants across time points): a positive 'set' just before use went with fewer challenging experiences, clear intentions with more mystical-type experience and visual effects, and recreational intentions with fewer challenging experiences; the review notes attrition and varied substances, doses and settings as limits.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psychedelics Not Otherwise Specified, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (set, clear intention and recreational intention rows); Discussion › States, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 prints the sign for set and challenging experience as positive, contradicting Table 2 and the text (reporting issues); the text also attributes to set associations that Haijen 2018 reports only for clear intentions.

key_findings.finding: Openness was tabulated with fewer adverse experiences (Russ 2019a) and more oceanic boundlessness and mystical experience (Smigielski 2019); acceptance with mystical experience in Smigielski 2019 only, a placebo-controlled study of expert Buddhist meditators on a retreat (38 in the text, 39 in Table 1; 15 women).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (openness and acceptance rows); Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 7th paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sex: only Bienemann 2020, an analysis of 346 negative psilocybin reports posted to Erowid, found 'bad trips' more often reported by women (V = 0.20, called small); three studies with adverse-reaction measures found no sex difference, and the review judges sex not a robust predictor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Age and previous use: in Carbonaro 2016 (n = 1993; 78% men, 89% white), age r = -0.06 and history of hallucinogen use r = -0.05 with difficulty of the experience; in Studerus 2012 age went with less impaired control and cognition and previous psychedelic use with less disembodiment and visionary restructuralization; in Bouso 2013 (n = 24) lifetime ayahuasca use correlated r = -0.62 with executive impairment under ayahuasca. The review infers that older and more experienced people have generally less intense effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 8th and 10th paragraphs; Results › Drugs › Ayahuasca, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 4th paragraph; Discussion › States, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Biological predictors, each from one study: lower serotonin 2A receptor binding with longer peak effects, faster comedown and higher mystical-type ratings (Stenbaek 2020, n = 16, no control); lower executive-network node diversity with more ego dissolution (Lebedev 2015, n = 15, two women, placebo-controlled); right rostral anterior cingulate thickness with spiritual experience and insightfulness (Lewis 2020, n = 55).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Authors' stated limitations: many studies open label, small or homogeneous; self-selection in retrospective online designs; most relationships unreplicated; possible unpublished null results (file drawer).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The review gives the sample sizes as ranging from 10 to 1993 with a mean of 108.75 and SD of 91.95. From Table 1 the mean is 237.5 (SD 517) taking Haijen 2018 as 212, or 269.1 (SD 529) taking it as 654, and with one value of 1993 among 14 studies and a mean of 108.75 the SD could not be below about 523 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed summary cannot be correct for the studies in Table 1; quote sample sizes from the table, not from the summary.

reporting_issues.issue: Signs disagree between tables: for Haijen 2018, set and challenging experience is positive in Table 1 but negative in Table 2 and in the text; for Lebedev 2015, executive-network node diversity and ego dissolution is negative in Table 1 and in the text but positive in Table 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Table 2; Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2, the summary most readers will use, carries a reversed sign for node diversity, and Table 1 a reversed sign for set; use the text and the primary studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives openness and well-being in Haijen 2018 as negative, whereas Haijen 2018 (read in this session; Table 6) reports openness positively associated with well-being at baseline (B = 1.500, p = 0.002) and two weeks after (B = 1.273, p = 0.030). Table 1 also leaves the direction blank for history of psychedelic use and well-being, which Table 2 gives as negative.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's openness entry for Haijen is reversed; well-being after use is also outside the review's own scope of acute effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The text summarises Haijen 2018 as finding that clear intentions and a positive set were both conducive to mystical-type experiences and visual effects and decreased challenging experiences; in Haijen's Table 7, set was associated only with lower challenging-experience scores (beta -0.324; with mystical-type experience 0.014, p = 0.835) and clear intentions only with mystical-type experience and visual effects (with challenging experience -0.134, p = 0.088).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drugs › Psychedelics Not Otherwise Specified, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Haijen 2018 directly for which state predicted which outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The anterior cingulate predictor is called 'rACC volume' in the abstract, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion and Conclusion, but 'thickness' in Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 3rd paragraph, and in the cited study's title; the Discussion (Traits, 1st paragraph) cites it as reference 54 (Haijen) instead of 45 (Lewis).
reporting_issues.consequence: The biomarker should be described as cortical thickness, from Lewis et al. (2020).

reporting_issues.issue: Lewis 2020 is called a placebo-controlled study in the text, but Table 1 marks it as having no control condition; Smigielski 2019 has 39 participants in Table 1 and 38 in the text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 3rd and 7th paragraphs; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of 6 controlled studies may be 7; check the primary studies before describing their designs.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the psilocybin doses in Studerus 2012 as 115-315 mg/kg, a unit implausible for humans and unlike the µg/kg used for Smigielski 2019 in the same table; µg/kg is probably meant (not checked against Studerus 2012, which was not read).
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not take doses from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: The paragraph on Stenbaek 2020 reports that lower serotonin 2A binding went with higher mystical-type ratings, then gives an explanation in which greater receptor availability leads to more intense effects, the opposite direction, without comment.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the binding finding should be taken from the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller mismatches between Table 1, Table 2 and the text: alcohol consumption goes with complex imagery in Table 1 but visual effects in Table 2; preoccupation and adverse experience (Russ 2019a) is in Table 1 but not Table 2; spiritual change appears only in Table 2; age is classed as a state; a sentence on Russ 2019b cites reference 44 (Lebedev) where 46 (Russ 2019a) is meant; and Table 2's openness row cites reference 54 (Haijen 2018) with 46 and 48, although none of the outcomes listed there (adverse experience, oceanic boundlessness, mystical experience) comes from Haijen 2018, whose openness entry in Table 1 concerns well-being.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Tables 1 and 2; Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The tables cannot be used interchangeably; check each entry against its primary study.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8033773 (DOI 10.1021/acsptsci.1c00014 confirmed on the page): abstract, all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, the Figure 1 legend, the funding and competing-interest notes and the reference list; Figure 1 (the flow diagram) is an image and the figure image was not viewable in this reading; the supporting-information spreadsheet was not opened. No correction, comment or reply is linked on the page. Haijen et al. (2018), PMC6225734, was read in the same session and is used for reporting issues 3 and 4.

disagreements.first_pass: Limitations, 1st paragraph
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269 (confirmed, locator detail): the Limitations heading sits under the Discussion (Discussion > Limitations, 1st paragraph).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: the PMC page's heading levels, read in the tab of AI reader 280, put Limitations (h3) under Discussion (h2).

disagreements.first_pass: Whatever each primary study used; the review does not name the instruments. Predictors are classed in Table 1 as states (S) or traits (T); age is classed as a state. Four studies are marked retrospective (Table 1, footnote a): Bienemann 2020 (an analysis of negative psilocybin reports posted to Erowid), Carbonaro 2016 (an online survey about the most challenging psilocybin experience) and Russ 2019a and 2019b (online samples). In the two Russ studies the 'baseline' states (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion, deservingness, spiritual motivation) were therefore reported after the experience.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed: the card's exposure field calls both Russ 2019 studies 'online samples'; the review never says so for those studies, and the only basis in the review is the general Limitations remark about retrospective designs using online crowd-sourcing.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading the saved PMC copy: Table 1 calls the Russ and Carbonaro samples unselected; the text says only that Carbonaro et al. surveyed people who used psilocybin and that both Russ studies were retrospective; 'online' appears only in Discussion › Limitations as a general remark. Corrected here (also for Carbonaro 2016, to which the same applies) and in sample.recruitment; the claim's anchor and statement were corrected in patch 280.

disagreements.first_pass: Literature search of PubMed only: two authors independently ran 42 searches crossing six drug terms (ayahuasca, LSD, lysergic acid diethylamide, mescaline, psilocybin, n,n-dimethyltryptamine) with seven predictor terms (predict, correlate, associate, pre-drug, individual difference, baseline, risk factor), filtered to English, human and 1994 to present (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph). Primary-study samples (Table 1): healthy volunteers in laboratory studies (Lebedev 2015, Lewis 2020, Carhart-Harris 2015, Terhune 2016, Stenbaek 2020, Studerus 2012); expert Buddhist meditators on a retreat (Smigielski 2019); long-term AIDS survivors in open-label group therapy (Stauffer 2020); people experienced with ayahuasca (Bouso 2013); and unselected people reached online or through reports posted online (Bienemann 2020, Carbonaro 2016, Russ 2019a and 2019b, Haijen 2018).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed (same point as for exposure.measurement): 'online' is not stated in the review for the Russ studies.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after the same check; recruitment now described in the review's own terms.

disagreements.first_pass: Smaller mismatches between Table 1, Table 2 and the text: alcohol consumption goes with complex imagery in Table 1 but visual effects in Table 2; preoccupation and adverse experience (Russ 2019a) is in Table 1 but not Table 2; spiritual change appears only in Table 2; age is classed as a state; and a sentence on Russ 2019b cites reference 44 (Lebedev) where 46 (Russ 2019a) is meant.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed: Table 2's openness row cites ref. 54 (Haijen 2018) alongside 46 and 48, although none of the outcomes listed there (adverse experience, oceanic boundlessness, mystical experience) come from Haijen; a further citation mismatch in the same family as reporting issues 1 to 4 and 8.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in the saved PMC copy (Table 2 openness row: refs 54, 46, 48; Table 1 Haijen rows: openness with well-being). Added to the ninth reporting issue (smaller mismatches) rather than as a new issue; its consequence is unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: Built into the design: the inclusion rule admits only predictors reported as predictive, so the review cannot show predictors that were tested and not found (the authors acknowledge the file-drawer problem in Limitations). The abstract and Conclusion present absorption as a predictor of positive and mystical-type experiences and omit that, in the one prospective naturalistic study, absorption was equally associated with challenging experiences (Table 1 and Table 2 show it).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269 (interpretation-gap note, not a key finding): 'absorption was equally associated with challenging experiences' overstates slightly; in Haijen 2018 the coefficient was 0.215 for challenge against 0.347 for mystical-type.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted as a factual wording error, not a change of judgment: 'equally' replaced by 'also', with the two coefficients from Haijen 2018's Table 7 (saved PMC copy). The interpretation-gap rating is unchanged.

design_detail: Prospective, web-based observational study with opportunity sampling. Adults who planned to take a psychedelic on their own initiative signed up at a study website and completed five online surveys: about 1 week before (traits, intentions, well-being), within 1 day before (state of mind, the 'set' items), about 1 day after (drug taken, self-estimated dose, setting, and the acute experience) and 2 and 4 weeks after the planned date (well-being). Set, setting and intention items written by the authors were reduced to principal components. Predictors of the acute experience were modelled together in a multivariate linear regression of standardized variables; well-being over time in linear mixed models. No control group; the drug, amount, purity, setting and company were the participants' own choices.
can_establish: Whether, among people who had already decided to take a psychedelic and who completed the surveys, a state of mind rated the day before, and intentions and traits rated a week before, were associated with how mystical, challenging or visually intense they rated the experience about a day later, with the predictors and the self-estimated dose adjusted for one another.
cannot_establish: That preparation, mood or intentions cause a better or less difficult experience (observational, with the dose estimated after the experience and drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs taken not in the model); that the experience caused the rise in well-being (no control group, 68% lost by four weeks, baseline well-being below population norms, so regression to the mean is possible); or anything about the people who dropped out, who were not compared with completers.

sample.recruitment: Opportunity sample: online advertisements on Facebook, Twitter, email newsletters and online drug forums (two Reddit forums on LSD and on psychedelics) linking to the study website; participants gave the expected date of their experience and were sent timed survey links by email (Materials and methods › Participant recruitment and dissemination of the study, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: aged 18 or over, good comprehension of English, an intention to take in the near future a drug the authors list as a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, LSD or 1P-LSD, ayahuasca, DMT or 5-MeO-DMT, salvia divinorum, mescaline, iboga or ibogaine). No exclusion criteria are stated; psychiatric history was asked about but did not exclude.
sample.demographics: Baseline (n = 654): 485 men (74.2%), 165 women (25.2%), 4 other; age 28.9 (SD 10.4); 39.1% students; 49.7% with a bachelor's or postgraduate degree (editors' sum); 30.4% from the United States, 19.6% the United Kingdom, 9.2% Denmark; 214 (32.7%) reported having ever been diagnosed with a psychiatric illness; 62 (9.5%) had never used a psychedelic and 404 (61.8%) had used one 6 or more times (editors' sum). Day-after survey (n = 379): LSD or 1P-LSD 183 (48.3%), psilocybin 109 (28.8%), ayahuasca 42 (11.1%), DMT or 5-MeO-DMT 12 (3.2%), mescaline 10 (2.6%), other 23 (6.1%) (Tables 1 and 2).
sample.attrition: 654 at baseline, 535 one day before (81.8%), 379 about one day after (58.0%), 315 at two weeks (48.2%) and 212 at four weeks (32.4%) (editors' percentages). Reasons for dropping out were not collected and completers were not compared with dropouts; the authors say they intend to do so. The acute-experience regression appears to rest on about 198 people (editors' inference from the error degrees of freedom). Of the day-before items, the first ten were answered by 535 people, 'strong expectations' by 386 and 'clear intention' by 326 (Table 3, footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people planning a psychedelic experience, reached through social media and drug forums; the authors report the sample was positively biased towards psychedelic use and more so towards therapeutic use (Figure 2, an image not viewed), and that completing every survey may have favoured well-prepared, motivated people (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph). 90.5% had used psychedelics before. With 42% lost before the experience was reported and no comparison of completers and dropouts, the associations describe completers only; if people who had difficult experiences were less likely to report them, the challenging-experience findings would be biased in an unknown direction.

exposure.measurement: About a week before (survey 1): absorption (Modified Tellegen Absorption Scale, 25 scored items); openness and emotional stability (Ten-Item Personality Inventory, two items per trait); trait anxiety (six-item short form of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory); suggestibility (Short Suggestibility Scale, 21 items); stubbornness (Stubborn Opinionatedness scale, 16 items); number of lifetime psychedelic uses; a self-rating of being highly experienced with psychedelics; and ten motives rated from 'not at all' to 'very much', reduced to three components: 'spiritual connection' (spiritual, religious, nature, therapeutic), 'recreation' (fun or party, social, curiosity) and 'emotional' (to escape or to confront difficult emotions; medicinal). Within a day before (survey 2): 12 visual-analogue items written for the study, reduced to 'set' (feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious, in a good mood, ready to surrender, not preoccupied with duties), 'setting' (a good feeling about the people who will be present and about the environment) and 'clear intentions' (strong expectations and a clear intention). About a day after (survey 3): the drug taken, a self-estimated dose, and whether the setting was a retreat or designed with a therapeutic aim, combined into one yes-or-no 'therapeutic environment' variable (Materials and methods › The surveys; Tables 3 and 4; Discussion › Set, setting, and drug dose…, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not controlled. Dose was estimated by the participant after the experience, in five response categories the survey anchored to LSD equivalents (low, up to 50 µg; moderate, up to 100; high, up to 200; very high, up to 300; extremely high, over 300); at the day-after survey 39 (10.3%) chose low, 144 (38.0%) moderate, 135 (35.6%) high, 37 (9.8%) very high and 24 (6.3%) extremely high (Table 2). Route was not recorded. At the two- and four-week surveys, 88 and a further 29 participants reported more than one psychedelic experience during the study (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: the paper does not say whether alcohol, cannabis or other drugs were taken with the psychedelic. Having more than one psychedelic experience during the study was among the candidate covariates for the well-being models, which kept only significant covariates; it is not in the final models.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (naturalistic use). How recently participants had last used a psychedelic before baseline is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Predictors are compared across participants within the cohort; well-being is compared within participants over time and with published population norms for the Warwick-Edinburgh scale (mean 50.7, 95% CI 50.3 to 51.1).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. In the acute-experience regression all 16 predictors were entered together (lifetime uses, self-rated experience, five traits, three intention components, set, setting, clear intentions, self-estimated dose, therapeutic environment). Covariates for the well-being models were chosen by statistical significance from age, sex, employment, education, lifetime uses, further psychedelic experiences during the study and four attitude items.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not in the acute-experience model: drug type (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca and others differ in duration and character), psychiatric history (32.7% reported a diagnosis), age and sex. Not measured: the actual amount and purity, other drugs taken, who was actually present and what they did, and preparation practices.

outcomes.instruments: Acute experience, self-rated online in survey 3, sent one day after the planned experience (the Introduction says within a few days after): the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30, total score), the Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ, total score), and a 'visual effects' score the authors built from three subscales (elementary imagery, complex imagery, audio-visual synaesthesia) of the Altered States of Consciousness rating scale (OAV or 11D-ASC). Well-being: Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS, 14 items) at baseline and at two and four weeks (Materials and methods › Survey 3 › Measures; Survey 1 › Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated questionnaires for the acute experience and well-being; a population norm for the WEMWBS (England and Scotland) is used for comparison. The set, setting, clear-intention and motive items were written for this study; their only structural check is the principal component analysis (set and setting: KMO 0.800, three components explaining 54.33% of variance; intentions: KMO 0.695, 55.14%). The visual-effects composite is specific to this study. Openness and emotional stability rest on two items each.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Challenging experience' is the CEQ total and 'mystical-type experience' the MEQ total, both continuous, rated by the participant about a day after; no threshold for a 'bad trip' or a 'complete' mystical experience is used. The predictors set, setting and clear intentions are component scores from items rated within a day before taking the drug; intentions and traits were rated about a week before. Dose and therapeutic environment were reported after the experience.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; alpha 0.05 for every test. Four outcomes (MEQ, CEQ, visual effects, WEMWBS), with 48 predictor coefficients in Table 7 (16 predictors by 3 outcomes), 15 in Table 5 and 57 in Table 6 (19 predictors by 3 time points), and t-tests on 18 variables comparing people whose well-being fell with the rest (editors' counts).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: all measures were self-reported online by participants who knew what they had taken and in what circumstances. Completion at the intended times could not be verified, and the day-before survey could be filled in on paper and transferred later (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Acute experience (Table 7; standardized coefficients with all predictors adjusted for one another; R2 0.342 for MEQ, 0.324 for CEQ, 0.211 for visual effects). Challenging experience: set beta = -0.324 (SE 0.070, p < 0.001); recreation intentions -0.224 (SE 0.081, p = 0.006); setting -0.137 (SE 0.075, p = 0.070); clear intentions -0.134 (p = 0.088); absorption 0.215 (SE 0.082, p = 0.010); self-estimated dose 0.219 (SE 0.077, p = 0.005); trait anxiety 0.140 (p = 0.211); therapeutic environment 0.021 (p = 0.813). Mystical-type experience: absorption 0.347 (SE 0.076, p < 0.001); dose 0.285 (SE 0.071, p < 0.001); clear intentions 0.180 (SE 0.072, p = 0.013); spiritual connection 0.153 (p = 0.054); set 0.014 (p = 0.835); lifetime uses -0.144 (p = 0.086). Visual effects: dose 0.327 (p < 0.001); absorption 0.227 (p = 0.003); clear intentions 0.155 (p = 0.033). Openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, lifetime uses, self-rated experience and therapeutic environment were associated with none of the three. Well-being (WEMWBS): 49.0 (95% CI 48.3 to 49.7) at baseline, 52.6 (51.8 to 53.4) at two weeks, 51.8 (50.6 to 53.0) at four weeks; quadratic trend F(154) = 23.20, p < 0.001 (editors' calculation: +3.6 and +2.8 points, in shrinking samples). MEQ by time interaction F(232) = 3.03, reported p < 0.050; MEQ coefficient on WEMWBS 0.948 at baseline (p = 0.083), 2.287 at two weeks (p < 0.001) and 1.608 at four weeks (p = 0.015). CEQ was negatively associated with WEMWBS at every time point, baseline included (B = -1.435, -1.975, -1.252), with no interaction with time. In the full model (Table 6) only trait anxiety and lifetime uses interacted with time, and the MEQ coefficients were -0.258, -0.102 and 0.002.
analysis.covariates: Acute-experience model: the 16 predictors adjusted for one another. Well-being models: lifetime uses and the self-rated experience item, retained because they were significant among the candidate covariates listed under comparison.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. Hypotheses are stated in the Introduction (well-being higher at two weeks than at baseline; mystical-type experience predicting the change); the analyses of predictors of the acute experience are exploratory. Many more measures were collected and are to be reported elsewhere (Materials and methods › The surveys, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 'key measures of interest' are reported, with the rest deferred to future papers; covariates were selected by significance; the visual-effects composite and the set, setting and intention components were built in this sample. The correlation matrix is in a supplement (a Word file) that was not read.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The acute-experience regression has 16 predictors on about 198 complete cases.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people who completed the surveys, feeling comfortable, open, prepared, unanxious and in a good mood within the day before (the 'set' component) was associated with lower challenging-experience scores about a day after (beta -0.32), as were recreational or social intentions (beta -0.22); clear intentions and expectations were associated with higher mystical-type and visual scores (beta 0.18 and 0.16); trait absorption and self-estimated dose were associated with higher scores on all three measures, mystical and challenging alike. Set was not associated with mystical-type experience, and a retreat or therapeutic setting with none of the acute measures. Mean well-being rose from 49.0 to 52.6 at two weeks while the sample fell from 654 to 315, with no comparison group; mystical-type ratings were associated with that rise in the smaller model (interaction p about 0.050), not once traits, intentions, set and setting were added.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says absorption and higher doses 'promoted' all aspects of the experience and that a positive set and recreational intentions decrease the likelihood of a challenging experience; the Discussion says the principle that psychedelics enhance well-being even in healthy people “appears to be supported by the present study's data”, and the Strengths section that the prospective design makes causal inference easier; the Conclusions say baseline traits explained the greatest proportion of the variance in well-being change. Gaps: (1) causal verbs for observational associations, with the dose estimated after the experience and drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; (2) without a control group, and with heavy attrition and a baseline below the population norm (those whose well-being rose had lower baseline scores, the pattern regression to the mean produces), the well-being rise cannot be attributed to the drug; (3) no partition of variance by type of predictor is reported, so the 'greatest proportion' statement has no supporting statistic; (4) the mystical-type effect on well-being highlighted in the abstract did not survive the fuller model, which the Discussion acknowledges; (5) the primary interaction is at p = 0.050, not below it. The Implications section turns these associations into practical recommendations for therapeutic use.

timeline.event: Leary et al.: apprehension before psilocybin correlated negatively with the pleasantness of the experience (described in this paper's Introduction).

Studerus et al. pooled 23 psilocybin laboratory studies: absorption and feeling well beforehand predicted peak experiences; younger age, emotional excitability beforehand and a PET scanner predicted challenging experiences (as described in this paper's Introduction).
This study.
Aday et al. systematic review: this study is its only prospective naturalistic source of set and intention predictors (its Table 1 misprints two of this study's signs).
Studerus et al., MDMA pooled laboratory analysis: anxious-depressed mood measured just before dosing predicted higher acute anxiety scores.
Vizeli et al., LSD pooled laboratory analysis: anxiety rated just before dosing predicted acute anxiety; the authors call this consistent with the present study.

replication.where_it_stands: Still the main prospective study of set, intentions and setting in self-directed psychedelic use found for this page. Its central acute finding, a better state of mind the day before going with fewer challenging experiences, agrees in direction with laboratory analyses that measured mood before dosing (Studerus 2012 for psilocybin, as described here; Studerus 2021 for MDMA; Vizeli 2024 for LSD), which is why the status is partial: those are conceptual replications in controlled settings with other instruments. No study has repeated the naturalistic prospective design with the same measures, and the well-being findings have no comparison group. The authors describe the design as never before used in psychedelic research (Discussion › Strengths, 1st paragraph, as of 2018); where the claims call it the only prospective study, they mean among the sources read for this page, not in the literature as a whole.
