The reviewer FB declared to the handling editor a past co-authorship with several of the authors (MK, LR, DN, RL, RC-H).
funding.affiliations_note: Psychedelic Research Group and the Computational, Cognitive and Clinical Neuroimaging Laboratory, Imperial College London; S. Russ at Dickinson State University, whose work inspired the set items. Handling editor N. Andrews; reviewers F.S. Barrett and E. Nalivaiko. The study website recruits for further online studies by the same group.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered prospective cohort, recruited from the same sources, that measures set and intentions with validated instruments before use, records the substance (confirmed by drug checking where possible), amount, other drugs and setting at the time rather than afterwards, follows dropouts as well as completers, and includes a comparison group who do not take a psychedelic; and randomized trials of preparation, for example a structured preparation session against none, in clinical or laboratory settings with challenging-experience scores as a prespecified outcome.

domains.note: Predictors were adjusted for one another and for self-estimated dose, but not for drug type, psychiatric history, age or sex, and other drugs taken were not measured; drug type in particular plausibly affects both preparation and challenging-experience scores. Covariates for the well-being models were selected by significance.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Set and intentions were measured before use, a strength, but with unvalidated items; openness and emotional stability with two items each; completion times unverifiable. For dose the risk is high: it was estimated after the experience, when intensity may colour the estimate (the authors say so).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: Self-selected, experienced, positively disposed sample from social media and drug forums; entry did not depend on the outcome, but the sample is atypical.

What sitters or companions did during the experience, and any redosing or other drugs, were not recorded; for well-being, 88 and a further 29 participants had additional psychedelic experiences during follow-up.

58% reported the experience and about 30% of the baseline sample entered the acute-experience regression; 32% remained at four weeks; no analysis of dropouts. Mixed models assume data missing at random, which is doubtful if difficult experiences affected continuation.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Validated questionnaires, but self-rated about a day later by people who knew their own preparation and intentions; the same person rated set and outcome, so a shared optimistic or anxious style could inflate associations.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Unregistered and exploratory for the acute predictors; many measures collected and only some reported; components and a composite built in the sample; no correction for multiple tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because of unadjusted confounding (drug type, psychiatric history, unmeasured other drugs) and heavy, unanalysed attrition, with further concerns about a retrospectively estimated dose and shared self-report of predictors and outcomes. The prospective timing of the set and intention measures is a real strength over retrospective surveys. The source can be cited for the association, among people completing the surveys, between a better state of mind the day before (and recreational or social intentions) and lower challenging-experience scores, and between clear intentions and higher mystical-type scores, always as associations; and for the finding that absorption and self-estimated dose went with more intense experiences of every kind. It should not be cited for causal effects of preparation, for an effect of a therapeutic or retreat setting (the null finding rests on a loosely defined yes-or-no item), or for psychedelics raising well-being.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: five online surveys, about 1 week before, within 1 day before, about 1 day after, and 2 and 4 weeks after a self-chosen psychedelic experience; completed by 654, 535, 379, 315 and 212 people. Setting questions (retreat, therapeutic design, party-type setting, number of people present, someone looking after the participant) were asked in survey 3, but their distribution is shown only in Figure 3 (an image not viewable in this reading; values not extracted).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Survey 3 › Measures, 1st paragraph; Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Baseline sample (survey 1, n = 654; Table 1): 485 men (74.2%), mean age 28.9 (SD 10.4); 214 (32.7% of 654; 36.0% of the 595 who answered) reported a past psychiatric diagnosis; 62 (9.5%) had never used a psychedelic and 189 (28.9%) had used one more than 21 times. Drug at the day-after survey (n = 379; Table 2): LSD or 1P-LSD 183 (48.3%), psilocybin 109 (28.8%), ayahuasca 42 (11.1%), DMT or 5-MeO-DMT 12 (3.2%), mescaline 10 (2.6%), other 23 (6.1%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Table 2

key_findings.finding: The 'set' component (31.12% of item variance) loaded on feeling comfortable (0.765), open (0.708) and well prepared (0.648), on feeling anxious (-0.635), being in a good mood (0.619), being ready to surrender (0.583) and being preoccupied with work or duties (-0.392); 'setting' (12.49%) on a good feeling about the group and the main person looking after the participant and about the environment; 'clear intentions' (10.72%) on strong expectations and a clear intention. All rated 0-100 within a day before use.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and footnote; Results › Principle component analysis: set and setting, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Challenging experience (CEQ total, self-rated about a day after) was lower with a better set the day before (beta = -0.324, SE 0.070, p < 0.001) and with recreational or social intentions rated a week before (beta = -0.224, SE 0.081, p = 0.006); the setting component showed a non-significant trend (beta = -0.137, p = 0.070). Higher with absorption (beta = 0.215, p = 0.010) and self-estimated dose (beta = 0.219, p = 0.005). Model R2 0.324.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predicting challenging experiences, 1st paragraph; Results › Predicting acute psychedelic experience measures, 1st paragraph; Table 7 (challenging experience panel); Results › Predicting visual effects, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mystical-type experience (MEQ30 total) was higher with absorption (beta = 0.347, p < 0.001), self-estimated dose (beta = 0.285, p < 0.001) and clear intentions (beta = 0.180, p = 0.013), with a trend for spiritual-connection intentions (beta = 0.153, p = 0.054); set was unrelated (beta = 0.014, p = 0.835). Visual effects were higher with dose (0.327), absorption (0.227) and clear intentions (0.155, p = 0.033). R2 0.342 and 0.211.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predicting mystical-type experiences, 1st paragraph; Results › Predicting visual effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 7 (mystical-type and visual panels)

key_findings.finding: No statistically significant association (p < 0.05) with any acute measure in the model of about 198 people: openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, number of lifetime uses (closest: mystical-type experience −0.144, p = 0.086), self-rated experience, and being in a retreat or therapeutically designed setting (challenging experience beta = 0.021, p = 0.813), a variable the authors formed by grouping two yes-or-no questions asked after the experience (a psychedelic retreat; a setting designed with a therapeutic objective). The authors caution that retreats were grouped with therapeutic settings and that the term was not defined for participants.
key_findings.locator: Table 7; Materials and methods › Survey 3 › Measures, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Set, setting, and drug dose as predictors for acute psychedelic experience measures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Trait-variables as predictors for the acute psychedelic experience measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Well-being (WEMWBS) averaged 49.0 (95% CI 48.3 to 49.7) at baseline, below the population norm of 50.7 (50.3 to 51.1), then 52.6 (51.8 to 53.4) at two weeks and 51.8 (50.6 to 53.0) at four weeks; quadratic trend F(154) = 23.20, p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in well-being scores, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Means at each time point come from shrinking samples (654, 315, 212) with no control group.

key_findings.finding: Well-being fell at two weeks in 85 people and was unchanged or higher in 194 (editors' calculation: 30.5% fell); the groups did not differ in mystical-type or challenging-experience scores, only in baseline well-being, which was lower in those whose well-being rose (reported as F(277) = 6.95, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Splitting participants based on change in well-being, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: For 1 and 277 degrees of freedom F = 6.95 gives p = 0.009 (editors' calculation); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: In the model with acute measures only, mystical-type experience interacted with time on well-being (F(232) = 3.03, reported p < 0.050): coefficients 0.948 at baseline (p = 0.083), 2.287 at two weeks (p < 0.001), 1.608 at four weeks (p = 0.015). Challenging experience went with lower well-being at every time point, baseline included (B = -1.435, -1.975, -1.252), without interacting with time. More lifetime uses went with lower well-being at two weeks (B = -1.378, p = 0.010).
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute psychedelic experience measures predicting well-being changes, 1st paragraph; Table 5

key_findings.finding: In the full model, only trait anxiety (interaction F(172) = 3.93) and lifetime uses (F(106) = 6.11) interacted with time; mystical-type experience no longer predicted well-being (B = -0.258, -0.102, 0.002). Feeling good about the setting and people the day before went with higher well-being at two weeks (B = 1.206, p = 0.037) and spiritual-connection intentions with higher well-being at every time point (B = 1.428, 1.365, 1.872).
key_findings.locator: Results › Traits, set and setting, intentions and acute psychedelic experience measures predicting well-being changes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: survey timing could not be confirmed; the sample may favour well-prepared, motivated people; attrition reasons were not collected; dose was reported after the experience and may reflect its intensity; well-being is a loosely defined construct.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Lifetime number of psychedelic uses correlated negatively with the change in well-being from baseline to two weeks (printed as r(279) = −0.23, p < 0.001): people with more earlier experience improved less; the authors link this to their higher baseline well-being (printed as r(654) = 0.21 with lifetime uses).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Bivariate. The bracketed numbers are sample sizes rather than degrees of freedom (see the reporting issue on r(653)). Consistent with the lifetime-uses by time interaction in the full model (Table 6: two weeks −2.215, SE 0.673, p = 0.001).

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of people whose well-being fell with the rest is described as an independent t-test but reported as F(277) = 6.95, p < 0.001; for 1 and 277 degrees of freedom (t = 2.64) the p value is 0.009 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Splitting participants based on change in well-being, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The baseline difference is real but weaker than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The primary test that mystical-type experience predicts the change in well-being is reported as F(232) = 3.03, p < 0.050; with a three-level time factor (2 and 232 degrees of freedom) p = 0.050 (editors' calculation), at rather than below the threshold.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Acute psychedelic experience measures predicting well-being changes, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline link between mystical-type experience and well-being change is borderline even before the full model removes it.

reporting_issues.issue: F statistics are printed with a single degrees-of-freedom value (for example F(181), F(154), F(172), F(106)); for Table 7 the F values equal the squared t values, so they are 1-df tests, and the error df of 181 with 16 predictors implies about 198 complete cases.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predicting acute psychedelic experience measures to Predicting visual effects; Table 7
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sample for the acute-experience findings is about 198, not the 379 who reported the experience; the paper does not say so.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists 214 (32.7%) ever diagnosed with a psychiatric illness and 381 (67.3%) never diagnosed; 381 is 58.3% of 654, the rows sum to 595, and 67.3% is simply 100 minus 32.7 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: 59 people with no answer are unaccounted for; the share with a diagnosis is 32.7% of all or 36.0% of those answering.

reporting_issues.issue: The intention to confront difficult emotions is reported to correlate with the CEQ at r(653) = 0.22, but the CEQ was collected only at survey 3 (379 respondents), so neither the n nor the df can be 653; elsewhere r(654) is printed for a correlation on 654 people, whose df would be 652.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Acute psychedelic experience measures as predictors for change in well-being, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample behind that correlation is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say lifetime uses were not related to baseline well-being (B = 0.392, p = 0.479 in Table 6; -0.030, p = 0.958 in Table 5), while the Discussion says more lifetime use went with higher baseline well-being (r = 0.21, p < 0.001); the models also contain the closely related self-rated-experience item.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Traits, set and setting…, 1st paragraph; Tables 5 and 6; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The bivariate and adjusted associations disagree without comment, so neither should be cited alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say all variables were standardized, but the well-being models have intercepts near 50 (Tables 5 and 6), so their outcome is in raw WEMWBS points and their coefficients are points per standard deviation of the predictor (editors' reading); only Table 7 is fully standardized.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and methods › Statistical analyses, 7th paragraph; Tables 5 to 7
reporting_issues.consequence: The coefficients in Tables 5 and 6 and in Table 7 are on different scales.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions say baseline traits explained the greatest proportion of the variance in well-being change, but no variance explained by type of predictor is reported for the well-being models; Table 6 gives coefficients only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement has no supporting statistic in the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of 'classic psychedelic' drugs that qualified for entry includes salvia divinorum and iboga or ibogaine, not usually classed as classic psychedelics; Table 2 has no rows for them (23 'other'). The lifetime-use categories '6-20 times' and 'more than 21 times' leave 21 uses unassigned.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analyses pool all drugs.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6225734 (DOI 10.3389/fphar.2018.00897 confirmed on the page): abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 7 rendered as text with footnotes, figure legends, author contributions, conflict-of-interest and funding statements, article notes and reference list; Figures 1 to 4 are images and the figure images were not viewable in this reading (setting data in Figure 3 and attitudes in Figure 2 not extracted; Figure 4 values are given in the text); the supplementary Word file (correlation matrix) was not opened. No correction, comment or reply is linked on the page.

disagreements.first_pass: Sample: 74.2% men, mean age 28.9 (SD 10.4); 32.7% reported a past psychiatric diagnosis; 9.5% had never used a psychedelic and 28.9% had used one more than 21 times. Drug at the day-after survey (n = 379): LSD or 1P-LSD 48.3%, psilocybin 28.8%, ayahuasca 11.1%, DMT or 5-MeO-DMT 3.2%, mescaline 2.6%, other 6.1%.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, targeted check of the claim anchor built from this finding (cl_xc_mindset_before, anchor 1): the men and diagnosis shares are of the 654 at baseline, not the 379; Table 1's diagnosis rows sum to 595 (36.0% of those answering).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed against Table 1 (demographic data collected at the first time point, total 654) and Table 2 (total 379) in the saved PMC copy. The finding now names each denominator and gives the counts, so the two samples cannot be mixed again; no number changed.

disagreements.first_pass: Not associated with any acute measure: openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, number of lifetime uses, self-rated experience, and being in a retreat or therapeutically designed setting (challenging experience beta = 0.021, p = 0.813). The authors caution that retreats were grouped with therapeutic settings and that the term was not defined for participants.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269 (confirmed, wording): 'not associated' means no coefficient with p below 0.05 in a model of about 198 people (lifetime uses with mystical-type score −0.144, p = 0.086); 'no statistically significant association' would be more exact. For cl_xc_setting_support the same reader noted that the retreat or therapeutic-setting variable came from two separate yes-or-no questions grouped into one variable.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking Table 7, Survey 3 › Measures (1st paragraph: separate yes-or-no items on a retreat and on a therapeutic design) and Discussion › Set, setting, and drug dose…, 4th paragraph (people in a retreat grouped with those reporting a therapeutic setting) in the saved PMC copy. Wording changed, the item structure added, and the Survey 3 locator added.

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed: Discussion, 2nd paragraph: lifetime number of psychedelic uses correlated negatively with the change in well-being, r(279) = −0.23, p < 0.001 (people with more experience improved less), consistent with the lifetime-uses by time interaction in Table 6; relevant wherever the well-being rise is cited.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: found as stated in the saved PMC copy (Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 6, lifetime uses × two weeks −2.215, p = 0.001). Added as a key finding with a note on the bracketed numbers.

disagreements.first_pass: Still the main prospective study of set, intentions and setting in self-directed psychedelic use found for this page. Its central acute finding, a better state of mind the day before going with fewer challenging experiences, agrees in direction with laboratory analyses that measured mood before dosing (Studerus 2012 for psilocybin, as described here; Studerus 2021 for MDMA; Vizeli 2024 for LSD), which is why the status is partial: those are conceptual replications in controlled settings with other instruments. No study has repeated the naturalistic prospective design with the same measures, and the well-being findings have no comparison group.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed: Discussion › Strengths, 1st paragraph: the authors describe the design as never before implemented in psychedelic research (as of 2018); the claims' 'the one prospective study' framing rests on this plus the editors' own knowledge of the literature, which the card could note under replication.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: found as stated in the saved PMC copy. Sentence added; the claims now limit the phrase to the sources read (patch 280).

design_detail: Mixed-methods analysis nested in an open-label, single-arm study of psilocybin with psychological support for treatment-resistant depression at Imperial College London. 19 patients each received oral psilocybin 10 mg and, one week later, 25 mg (study conditions), lying with eye-shades in a furnished room with two therapists while one standardized playlist played from ingestion (one patient who strongly disliked it in the first session heard a different playlist in the second). One week after the 25 mg session each patient gave a semi-structured interview about the music in both sessions. Qualitative part: interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) with counts of how many patients mentioned each theme. Quantitative part: four researchers blind to identity and outcome rated each transcript for music liking, resonance and openness; the averaged ratings were correlated (Pearson, n = 19) with the percentage fall in QIDS-SR16 depression scores recorded at the same one-week time point (the paper does not say it was the same visit), with five principal components of the 11-dimension Altered States of Consciousness scale (11D-ASC), and with a self-rated drug-intensity scale. No control condition; music was never varied or withheld.
can_establish: What these 19 patients said the music did during their psilocybin sessions (welcome and unwelcome influences, with counts), and that patients whose one-week interviews described the music more favourably also reported larger falls in depression scores at that time point and higher scores on an ASC-derived mystical-experience factor.
cannot_establish: That music, or a liked or resonant music experience, caused better outcomes or more mystical experiences (no control condition, music not varied, no adjustment, predictor recorded at the same time point as the outcome and after the acute-experience ratings), that music mediates outcomes (no mediation analysis), or how far the findings apply beyond a small, highly selected trial sample.

sample.recruitment: Patients of the Imperial College London open-label study of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016a, as cited; Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 1st paragraph). How patients were recruited is not described in this paper.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: moderate to severe major depression (21-item HAM-D score of 17 or more) with no improvement despite at least two different antidepressant treatments of at least 6 weeks within the current episode. Excluded: current or previous psychotic disorder, psychotic disorder in an immediate family member, suicide attempt requiring hospitalisation, mania, blood or needle phobia, pregnancy, current drug or alcohol dependence (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Not reported in this paper: age, sex, baseline depression scores and medication status are referred to the parent trial report.
sample.attrition: All 19 patients were interviewed and completed the QIDS at baseline and one week after the 25 mg session (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 4th paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph). The paper does not say whether any patient of the parent study was not interviewed.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers with treatment-resistant depression who entered a psilocybin trial (expectations not measured), treated in a hospital research facility with two therapists and a 4-hour preparation visit that included listening to samples of the session music. The analysed sample equals the interviewed sample; whether it equals the whole trial cohort is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Music experience: three 0–100 visual analogue ratings (liking, resonance, openness; five verbal anchors each), made independently by four researchers blind to patient identifiers and treatment outcomes, from transcripts of interviews held one week after the 25 mg session that covered both sessions; the four raters' scores were averaged per patient (Methods › Ratings for music experience, 2nd paragraph; Correlation analyses, 1st paragraph). The three variables were chosen because they showed a notable polarity in the same transcripts during coding and were then hypothesised as predictors (Methods › Ratings for music experience, 1st paragraph). Drug intensity: the patient's own 0–100 rating of peak drug effects, made after each session (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: synthetic psilocybin (THC-Pharm) formulated into 5 mg capsules, taken by mouth, 10 mg in the first session and 25 mg one week later, by every patient (open label); dosing at 10.30 am after arrival at 9 am, most patients ready to leave about 7 hours after dosing (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). Music: one standardized playlist (mainly contemporary ambient, neo-classical, contemporary classical and traditional or ethnic styles, chosen to limit religious associations), arranged by phases (pre-onset, ascent, peak, descent, return), with the most emotionally evocative pieces at the peak, started at ingestion and played through in-ear headphones and a hi-fi speaker carrying the same signal. One patient who strongly disliked the music in the first session received a different playlist (used at Johns Hopkins University) in the second (Methods › Therapeutic setting; Music selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Playlist design). The full playlist is in the online supplement, which was not opened.
exposure.polysubstance: Current drug or alcohol dependence excluded. Other drug use, and antidepressant or other medication at the time of the sessions, are not reported in this paper.

comparison.controls: None. Single-arm, open-label study: every patient received psilocybin with music; there was no placebo, no music-free condition and no alternative-music arm. The quantitative analysis compares patients who described the music more or less favourably.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Nothing was measured before the sessions about music preferences, personality (for example openness or absorption), expectancy or the relationship with the therapists; baseline depression severity is not reported here and was not used as a covariate.

outcomes.instruments: 16-item Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptoms, self-rated (QIDS-SR16), at screening and one week after the 25 mg session, expressed as percentage reduction from baseline; 11D-ASC completed at the end of the session, reduced by principal component analysis with varimax rotation to five components labelled mystical experience, impaired cognition, audiovisual perception, anxiety and insightfulness; drug-intensity visual analogue scale; semi-structured interview with four open questions about how the music influenced the experience, analysed by IPA (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 1st and 4th paragraphs; The semi-structured interview; Correlation analyses, 1st paragraph; Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: QIDS and the ASC are established self-report scales. The liking, resonance and openness ratings were made up for this study from interview transcripts; agreement between the four raters averaged r = 0.6 (± 0.1, not stated to be an SD) over 18 rater-pair correlations, which the authors call good, and the three ratings correlated r = 0.90 to 0.96 with each other, which the authors read as probably one construct. Mystical experience was not measured with the Mystical Experience Questionnaire; the term labels a component loaded by three ASC dimensions (experience of unity, spiritual experience, blissful state) (footnote 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Clinical improvement: percentage fall in QIDS score from screening to one week after the 25 mg session. A good music experience: high averaged ratings of liking, resonance and openness from the one-week interview. Prediction: a bivariate Pearson correlation in 19 patients, not a model with covariates.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: False discovery rate control (Benjamini–Hochberg) across the correlations, with an adjusted significance threshold stated as p = 0.016 (Results › Predictors…, 2nd paragraph). Two printed p values do not fit their r values at n = 19 (see reporting issues), and one of them bears on whether a result passes that threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The four music-experience raters were blind to patient identifiers and outcomes, but they rated transcripts recorded at the same time point as the outcome questionnaire, in which patients could describe how they were doing. Depression and ASC scores were self-rated by patients who knew they had received psilocybin (open label).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pearson r, n = 19 (Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph). Percentage fall in QIDS at one week: liking r = 0.60 (p = .006), resonance r = 0.59 (p = .008), openness r = 0.57 (printed p = .001), drug intensity r = 0.004 (p = 0.98). Editors' calculation (Fisher z, n = 19), 95% intervals: liking 0.20 to 0.83, resonance 0.19 to 0.82, openness 0.16 to 0.81, drug intensity -0.45 to 0.46. Mystical-experience component: liking r = 0.61 (p = .006), resonance r = 0.67 (p = .002), openness r = 0.70 (p = .0008), drug intensity r = 0.58 (p = 0.009). Insightfulness component: resonance r = 0.53 (printed p = .016), openness r = 0.59 (p = .007), drug intensity r = 0.65 (p = 0.002), liking r = 0.44 (p = .06). Impaired cognition (r = 0.55, p = 0.01) and audiovisual perception (r = 0.71, p = 0.0006) correlated with drug intensity and with none of the music variables; the anxiety component correlated with none. The music variables correlated with each other at r = 0.9, 0.96 and 0.91 and, by the text, not with drug intensity (values not printed) (Results › Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables). Correlations that were not significant appear only in Figure 4, an image that was not viewable in this reading; their values were not extracted.
analysis.covariates: None: bivariate correlations only. Baseline depression severity, the overall quality of the acute experience and expectancy were not adjusted for.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration, protocol or analysis plan is cited in this paper. The three music predictors were derived from the coding of the same interviews and then hypothesised as predictors (Methods › Ratings for music experience, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Correlations that were not significant are not given as numbers in the text (only in the Figure 4 image), including those of the music variables with the anxiety, impaired-cognition and audiovisual components and with drug intensity. The Introduction hypothesizes that music promotes mystical experiences, which in turn predict outcome, but the correlation of the mystical-experience component with the fall in depression is not reported, so that pathway was not tested in the paper.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. With n = 19 the 95% interval for r = 0.60 runs from about 0.20 to 0.83 (editors' calculation). Whether the music correlations differ from the drug-intensity correlation was not tested formally; the abstract contrasts a significant with a non-significant correlation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 19 patients of an open-label trial, more favourable descriptions of the music, rated from interviews held at the one-week visit, went with larger falls in self-rated depression at that same one-week time point (r about 0.6, with wide intervals) and with higher mystical-experience and insightfulness component scores from questionnaires completed at the end of the session; self-rated drug intensity did not correlate with the change in depression. In the interviews, 18 of 19 patients described welcome and 10 of 19 unwelcome influences of the music.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the nature of the music experience significantly predictive of reductions in depression, unlike drug intensity, and concludes that music plays a central therapeutic function (Abstract). The Discussion says the findings indicate that an interaction between drug and music promotes positive outcomes (Discussion › Music experience predicts experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph) and that outcomes “suffered” when the music was dissonant, disliked or resisted (Discussion › Implications for the use of music in psychedelic therapy, 1st paragraph); the Conclusions speak of a central mediating role for music. No mediation was tested, music was never varied or withheld, nothing was adjusted, and the predictor was recorded at the same time point as the outcome and a week after the ASC ratings it is said to predict, so patients who had improved may have recalled and described the music more warmly. The Limitations concede that, without a placebo condition, causal inference is problematic and that the data were mainly qualitative (Limitations and future directions, 1st paragraph).

timeline.event: Parent study: open-label feasibility study of psilocybin with psychological support for treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016a, as cited for the clinical outcomes; not read for this card).

Correction (10.1007/s00213-018-4886-8, Psychopharmacology 235:1623, read): the article became open access under a CC BY 4.0 licence on 19 March 2018, and the co-author listed as Christopher Timmerman should be Christopher Timmermann. No data or conclusions changed.

Strickland et al. (2021): randomized comparison of musical genres in psilocybin sessions, named in the project's BeforeDuring evidence map as the one randomized comparison of music (not read for this card).

Nader (2025), opinion article written in response to this paper (10.3389/fpsyt.2025.1652568, read for this card): argues that music may act as a confounder that displaces the patient's own psychological material, states that no controlled research compares music with silent settings and calls for randomized comparisons; it also raises a possible conflict of interest of the first author as head of a company providing music for psychedelic therapy. No new data.

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication of the correlation is listed in the project's evidence map (2026-10-31). Whether music, or a particular kind of music experience, changes the outcome of psychedelic therapy has not been tested by randomizing music against silence; Nader (2025) states that no controlled research makes that comparison.

funding.funder: No funding section in the article. The conflict-of-interest statement names the Beckley Foundation as one of the sponsors of the study. The Methods state that Imperial College London's Joint Research and Compliance Office sponsored and approved the study, that the National Institute for Health Research Clinical Research Network adopted it, and that the NIHR/Wellcome Trust Imperial Clinical Research Facility approved the site (Methods › Approvals; Compliance with ethical standards).
funding.declared_conflicts: Amanda Feilding is the director of the Beckley Foundation, one of the sponsors of the study; David Nutt is an advisor for the Beckley Foundation (Compliance with ethical standards › Conflict of interest). No other interests declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Psychedelic Research Group and C3NL at Imperial College London, the School of Psychology at Sussex University, and the Beckley Foundation. The first author's earlier studies of LSD and music are cited in the Introduction. The paper does not say who designed the playlist, who conducted the interviews or who coded them. Nader (2025) states that the first author is CEO of a company providing music for psychedelic therapy; the 2018 paper declares no such interest, and Nader does not date the role. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison within a psilocybin trial of music against silence (and of a fixed playlist against one adapted to the patient), with the music experience rated on the session day before any outcome is known, outcome raters blind to condition, adjustment for baseline severity and for the intensity and quality of the acute experience, a pre-registered analysis plan and follow-up beyond one week.

domains.note: No adjustment. The music ratings correlate strongly with the mystical-experience component (r 0.61 to 0.70); a generally good or bad session, expectancy, the relationship with the therapists or baseline severity could drive both how the music is remembered and how mood changes, and the paper itself cites its group's report that the quality of the acute experience predicts outcome (Roseman et al., 2017). Drug intensity, one self-rated item, is the only alternative examined, and only in separate bivariate correlations.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: The exposure was rated from interviews held one week after the 25 mg session, at the same time point as the outcome questionnaire and after any improvement had happened, so current mood and outcome can shape how the music is recalled and described. The three ratings were derived from the same transcripts, are not validated and agreed only moderately between raters (average r 0.6). Raters were blind to outcome, but the transcripts could reveal how patients were doing.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: All 19 interviewed patients were analysed, but the paper does not say whether the parent study enrolled others who were not interviewed; a small, highly selected volunteer sample.

The playlist was changed for one patient after strong dislike in the first session, and the therapists checked in every 30 to 60 minutes and could give psychological support depending on how the session was going; these responses are neither described per patient nor analysed.
QIDS completed by all 19 at both time points; every transcript rated by all four raters.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: QIDS is self-rated in an open-label study by the same patients whose interview supplied the exposure, at the same time point, which invites a common-method correlation; the outcome is only one week after the last session.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registered analysis plan; predictors chosen from the qualitative coding; principal component analysis of 11 ASC scales in 19 patients; non-significant correlations shown only in a figure; the hypothesized link between mystical experience and outcome not reported; two printed p values do not match their r values.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Mixed-methods study: the quantitative part (correlations of the music experience with outcome) is appraised with ROBINS-E as the round's brief asks, and the qualitative part is described, not rated. Its qualitative method has strengths (independent coding by at least two researchers, an interview guide printed in full, theme counts across all patients) and limits (one interviewer for 18 of 19 interviews, no reflexive account of the team's stake in music, no saturation account, quotations held in a supplement that was not read). Two ROBINS-E domains are high, and each could by itself produce the reported association: confounding by the overall quality of the session, and an exposure recorded after, and alongside, the outcome. ROBINS-E rates the result very high when several domains are high in ways that substantially lower confidence. The card may be cited for what these 19 patients said the music did (welcome and unwelcome influences, with counts) and for the correlations as a hypothesis, stated with their intervals and the timing of measurement. It should not be cited as showing that music, or a liked or resonant music experience, improves the outcome of psilocybin therapy, or that music mediates its effects.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: 19 patients with treatment-resistant depression, open label, oral psilocybin 10 mg then 25 mg one week apart (study conditions); QIDS at screening and one week after the 25 mg session; 11D-ASC at the end of the session; drug-intensity rating after each session; music interview one week after the 25 mg session, covering both sessions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants; Experiment overview and procedures, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; The semi-structured interview, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Interviews (mean 1,048 words, SE 133) yielded four groups of themes: welcome influences of the music in 18 of 19 patients (95%), unwelcome influences in 10 of 19 (53%), appreciated music styles or playlist features in all 19, and unappreciated styles or features in 11 of 19 (58%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Welcome influences: intensification of the experience in 17 of 19 (of emotion 15 of 17, of imagery 9 of 17, general 8 of 17); guidance in 15 of 19 (a sense of being on a journey 11 of 15, support 11 of 15, music matching the emotional state 6 of 15, continuity and direction 5 of 15); calming in 10 of 19; openness to the music-evoked experience in 7 of 19, of whom 6 described being open to challenging experience as important and therapeutic.
key_findings.locator: Results › Welcome influences: intensification, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Welcome influences of the music: guidance, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Welcome influence of the music: calming; Welcome influences of the music: openness to music-evoked experience

key_findings.finding: Unwelcome influences: music intensifying emotions patients did not want, such as fear or sadness (5 of the 10 with unwelcome influences), discomfort (5 of 10) and irritation (4 of 10); resistance to the music-evoked experience in 9 of 19 (47%); a sense of misguidance in 6 of 19 (32%), mostly music felt as dissonant with the unfolding experience (4 of 6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Unwelcome influences of the music: intensification; resistance to music-evoked experience; misguidance

key_findings.finding: Music styles and playlist: all 19 named styles they appreciated (ethnic styles 8 of 19; voices without lyrics or with foreign-language lyrics 7 of 19; neo-classical or classical 7 of 19); 17 of 19 appreciated the playlist design (selection 12 of 17, ordering matched to drug effects 9 of 17, the mere presence of music 6 of 17). 11 of 19 disliked some styles, with no single theme above 30%; 6 of 19 disliked aspects of the playlist design, 2 of them preferring their own music.
key_findings.locator: Results › Appreciated music styles and playlist features: music styles; playlist design; Unappreciated music styles and playlist features: music styles; playlist design

key_findings.finding: Percentage fall in QIDS at one week correlated with interview-rated music liking (r = 0.60, p = .006), resonance (r = 0.59, p = .008) and openness (r = 0.57, printed p = .001), but not with self-rated drug intensity (r = 0.004, p = 0.98); n = 19. Editors' calculation (Fisher z), 95% intervals: 0.20 to 0.83, 0.19 to 0.82, 0.16 to 0.81 and -0.45 to 0.46.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The printed p = .001 for openness does not fit r = 0.57 with n = 19 (about .011 by the editors' calculation); see reporting issues. The music ratings come from interviews at the same time point as the QIDS outcome (one week after the 25 mg session).

key_findings.finding: The mystical-experience component of the ASC correlated with music liking (r = 0.61), resonance (r = 0.67), openness (r = 0.70) and drug intensity (r = 0.58); insightfulness with resonance (r = 0.53), openness (r = 0.59) and drug intensity (r = 0.65) but not liking (r = 0.44, p = .06); impaired cognition (r = 0.55) and audiovisual perception (r = 0.71) only with drug intensity; the anxiety component with none of the variables. FDR-adjusted significance threshold stated as 0.016.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Figure 4 legend
key_findings.note: The resonance–insightfulness correlation (printed p = .016) gives about p = .020 at n = 19 (editors' calculation), above the stated threshold. The ASC was completed at the end of the session and the music ratings a week later, so the music variable cannot have been measured first.

key_findings.finding: The four raters' agreement on the music ratings averaged r = 0.6 (± 0.1, not stated to be an SD) over 18 correlations, which the authors call good; the three music ratings correlated r = 0.9, 0.96 and 0.91 with each other, and the authors note they probably represent one construct; self-rated drug intensity correlated with none of the three (values not printed).
key_findings.locator: Results › Inter-rating reliability and discriminative validity of music experience variables; Discussion › Music experience predicts experience and therapy outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state as limitations that there was no placebo condition, which makes causal inference problematic, and that the data were mainly qualitative, so the magnitude of the themes could not be studied; they present the study as giving the patients' perspective and as generating hypotheses.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and future directions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sessions took place in a furnished therapy room in a clinical research facility (medical equipment removed or hidden, adjusted lighting, cushions, plants, art); patients lay on a bed with eye-shades, two therapists checked in about every 30 to 60 minutes, and a preparation visit of about 4 hours included listening to samples of the session music with eye-shades on.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Therapeutic setting; Experiment overview and procedures, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The fall in depression correlates with openness at r = 0.57 with a printed p = .001, while the larger correlations with liking (r = 0.60) and resonance (r = 0.59) have p = .006 and .008. With the same n = 19, r = 0.57 corresponds to p of about .011 (editors' calculation, t with 17 df).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed value overstates the strength of the openness result; at about .011 it would still pass the stated FDR threshold of 0.016, so the conclusion is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Resonance correlates with insightfulness at r = 0.53 with a printed p = .016, equal to the stated FDR threshold; with n = 19, r = 0.53 corresponds to p of about .020 (about .018 even at r = 0.535) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Predictors in music experience for psilocybin experience and therapy outcomes, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: By the paper's own threshold this association may not be significant; the statement that resonance predicts insightfulness is weaker than written.

reporting_issues.issue: The percentage reduction in QIDS is defined as ((baseline − post-treatment) / baseline) multiplied by −100, which makes an improvement negative; with the positive correlations reported, this formula would mean that a better music experience went with less improvement, the opposite of the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a sign slip in the formula; the direction of the main result has to be taken from the text, since Figure 4 could not be viewed.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance is described in two ways: the text gives an FDR-adjusted threshold of 0.016, while the Figure 4 legend marks p < 0.05 and p < 0.001 after FDR correction.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Predictors…, 2nd paragraph; Figure 4 legend)
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot tell which threshold each marked correlation passed.

reporting_issues.issue: The ASC was completed at the end of the session and drug intensity after each session, but the paper does not say which session's scores entered the correlations, whereas the music ratings refer to both sessions together.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Experiment overview and procedures, 4th paragraph; The semi-structured interview)
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlations may pair measures from different sessions; the time order of exposure and outcome is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor slips: the Figure 3 legend calls the ASC dimensions acoustic features; in the unwelcome intensification cluster the percentages are labelled as of the cluster but use the 10 patients with any unwelcome influence as denominator; the resistance section refers to Table 6 as listing the themes of the cluster intensification.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Figure 3 legend; Results › Unwelcome influences of the music: intensification; resistance to music-evoked experience)
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the main findings; the size of the unwelcome intensification cluster is not stated.

design_detail: Mixed-methods online survey (Qualtrics), pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/35kbs) and approved by the University of Bristol School of Psychological Science ethics committee (116995). Quantitative part (rated with ROBINS-E): 163 adults with at least two lifetime uses of a classic psychedelic or an analogue, recruited through university societies and online psychedelic communities, each recalled, in one sitting, their first and their most recent psychedelic experience outside research or therapy and above a microdose: time since, substance, place, intention, which listed harm-reduction practices they used (before, during, during 'myths', after), the Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ; 24 of its 26 items asked) and the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI). They then rated each practice's importance for a safe experience from −10 to +10. A practice's Harm Reduction Score is its mean importance rating in the sample; a person's Participant Harm Reduction Score for an occasion is the sum of the Harm Reduction Scores of the practices they reported using then. Analyses: repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t test (first versus most recent), Pearson correlations of the score with CEQ and EBI, and an unplanned descriptive comparison of party settings with other settings. Qualitative part (described, not rated): inductive three-stage thematic analysis of 61 free-text comments, mainly by the senior author with the first author.
can_establish: Which places, intentions and listed practices 163 self-selected, mostly male, experienced people who use psychedelics recalled for their first and most recent experiences, how they rated the importance of each practice for safety, and whether people who recalled using more practices rated as important also recalled more emotional breakthrough and, for the first experience, fewer challenging experiences.
cannot_establish: Whether any practice prevents challenging experiences or brings about emotional breakthrough (retrospective, unadjusted correlations of about 0.2 between ratings made at one sitting, with the predictor weighted by the same respondents' importance judgments and including practices after the experience); whether people adopt more harm reduction as they gain experience (a first experience recalled a median 42 months later is compared with a recent one recalled after a median 2 months, among people who kept using); or how common any practice is among people who use psychedelics generally.

sample.recruitment: Opportunistic: advertisements through relevant university societies and online psychedelic communities led to the Qualtrics survey; an optional link allowed entry to a prize draw for a £50 voucher (Methods › Participants; Procedure).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over; at least two lifetime uses of a classic psychedelic (LSD, psilocybin, DMT, mescaline) or an analogue or derivative (for example 2C-B); fluent in English. Neither the first nor the most recent experience could have been in a research study or a professional therapy setting, or a microdose (self-defined; no definition was given). Three attention checks; many respondents were excluded for failing them (numbers and details in the supplement, not read).
sample.demographics: Mean age 27.5 (SD 8.06), median 26, mode 20, range 18 to 56; 13 aged 40 or over; 120 men, 35 women, 8 non-binary. Estimated lifetime psychedelic uses: mean 28.4 (SD 45.2), median 11.5, mode 20, with 16 people estimating 100 to 300 uses. Education and the substances ever used are in supplementary Table S1 (not read).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). The number who started, the number excluded and item non-response are given only in the supplement (not read); every analysis uses 163.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected through university societies and psychedelic communities and largely male. Requiring two or more lifetime uses excludes people who stopped after their first experience; the authors note possible survivor bias towards people with fewer unpleasant early experiences and a lower propensity to harm (Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 2nd paragraph). The first-versus-recent comparison is therefore made only among people who continued to use psychedelics.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported checklist of harm-reduction practices for each recalled experience, compiled by the authors from trusted online harm-reduction resources, the published literature and discussion with colleagues (the list and its sources are in supplementary Table S3, not read), grouped as before, during, during 'myths' (anecdotal beliefs and practices generally advised against for inexperienced people, such as being alone in a dark place, included partly to make respondents read the list carefully) and after. Importance for a safe experience was rated once for every practice, after both experiences had been reported, from −10 (detrimental) through 0 (no effect on safety) to +10 (extremely helpful). The Participant Harm Reduction Score sums the sample-mean importance of the practices a person used, so it mixes how many practices were used with how important the sample judged them. One practice, arranging a time to take the dose, had no importance scores because of a methodological error.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured for either experience: no amount, route or redosing record (the authors suggest that people using for the first time may have taken smaller amounts; Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 4th paragraph). Substance on the first and most recent occasion: LSD 47% and 33%, psilocybin 41% and 36%, 2C-B 4% and 6%, DMT 2% and 6%, mescaline 1% and 1%, other 6% and 18% (Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Some participants reported using other psychedelics or non-psychedelic drugs on the same occasion (Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph); not quantified in the main text or analysed. Smoking cannabis was one of the listed 'myth' practices; the authors call its effects equivocal.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective survey). Time since the first experience: mean 67.52 months (SD 78.33), median 42, mode 24; since the most recent: mean 8.68 months (SD 20.76), median 2, mode 1 (Table 1).

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant's first versus most recent experience. For the correlations, people with higher versus lower Participant Harm Reduction Scores. For setting, experiences at a party, club or festival (24 first, 12 most recent) versus all other places, descriptively only.
comparison.matching: None; no covariates in any analysis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental health, personality and amount taken were not measured; substance, place and intention were measured but not used as covariates, nor were the number of earlier experiences at the time of the most recent one or the time since each experience. Intentions changed strongly between occasions (curiosity 72% to 20%; spiritual pursuits 20% to 46%; processing difficult emotions 9% to 32%), and the authors themselves suggest intention and amount may explain differences between the experiences.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not measured beyond the mention of polydrug use on some occasions.

outcomes.instruments: CEQ (Barrett et al., 2016): seven subscales (isolation, grief, physical distress, fear, insanity, paranoia, death), items rated 0 to 5; 2 of the 3 insanity items were not asked because of an experimenter error, so 24 items were used; subscale scores are item means expressed as a percentage of the maximum; Cronbach's alpha 0.96 (first) and 0.95 (most recent). EBI (Roseman et al., 2019): six statements rated 0 to 100; alpha 0.92 and 0.93. Both were rated by the participant for each recalled experience, in the same sitting as the practice checklist.
outcomes.validity_norms: Both are validated questionnaires developed from internet surveys of people who used psychedelics. The shortened CEQ was not re-validated; the authors report internal consistency and an overall mean (17) similar to earlier studies. Neither has been validated for recall years after the experience.
outcomes.operationalization: A positive experience is a higher EBI score and a negative one a higher CEQ score, which the authors call proxies; they note that challenging experiences are not always negative and may precede breakthrough, and the two scores correlated positively (r = 0.39 first, 0.37 most recent). Harm itself (injury, need for help, lasting difficulties) was not measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni for the post hoc comparisons after the ANOVA only. 15 counts the inferential tests printed in Results (3 ANOVA effects, 4 reported Bonferroni contrasts, the CEQ subscale ANOVA, the EBI paired t test, 2 EBI–CEQ correlations and 4 correlations of the Participant Harm Reduction Score with EBI and CEQ); 5 of them test the pre-registered hypotheses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: every measure is a self-rating by a participant who knew which practices they had reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Participant Harm Reduction Score, mean (SD): first 40.06 (18.90), most recent 48.68 (18.81); main effect of occasion F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001 (printed partial eta squared 0.012; 0.15 from the F and df, editors' calculation). Bonferroni contrasts, most recent higher: before-use practices t = −9.63, p < 0.001; after-use t = −3.28, p = 0.03; during t = −1.47, p = 1; during-myths t = −0.04, p = 1. EBI: first 27.77 (26.46), most recent 39.18 (29.91), t(162) = 4.42, p < 0.001, d = 0.35 (equal to t divided by the square root of n, a paired dz; 0.40 when the difference is divided by the average SD, editors' calculation). CEQ: 17.14 (18.06) and 17.29 (17.06), no meaningful difference in any subscale. Correlations of the Participant Harm Reduction Score (n = 163; 95% CIs by Fisher z, editors' calculation): with EBI r = 0.24 on both occasions (0.09 to 0.38), p = 0.002; with CEQ, first experience r = −0.21 (−0.35 to −0.06), p = 0.006; most recent r = −0.15 (−0.30 to 0.00), p = 0.061. Shared variance 2% to 6% (editors' calculation).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Pre-registered on OSF (https://osf.io/35kbs/; DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/35KBS). The authors say they followed the registered analysis plan and flag the exploratory analyses (the EBI–CEQ correlation; the party-setting comparison, described as unplanned). Measurement deviations: 2 of the 3 CEQ insanity items were not asked, and one practice had no importance scores. The registration itself was not read for this card.
analysis.selective_reporting: The prevalence and importance score of each practice appear only in Figure 1 (an image that could not be viewed in this reading) and supplementary Table S3 (not read); the text describes only some practices. Four of the possible post hoc contrasts are reported. The abstract does not say that the CEQ correlation for the most recent experience was not statistically significant, or that the score includes practices used after the experience.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation is reported. Editors' calculation: 163 people give 80% power at two-sided alpha 0.05 to detect a correlation of about 0.22, so the most recent CEQ correlation (−0.15) could not be expected to reach significance; the authors call the party-setting analyses underpowered and ran no tests on them.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 163 self-selected experienced people who use psychedelics, recalling a first experience a median of three and a half years earlier and a recent one a median of two months earlier, the importance-weighted sum of practices used was higher for the recent experience, for practices before and after use but not during it. EBI was higher for the recent experience and CEQ was the same. The weighted practice score correlated weakly with EBI (r = 0.24 on both occasions) and with lower CEQ for the first experience (r = −0.21) but not significantly for the recent one (r = −0.15, p = 0.061). Experiences in party settings (24 first, 12 recent) had lower practice scores and higher CEQ, descriptively and untested; EBI was lower in party settings for the first experience only.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion reads the correlations as "some preliminary evidence that harm reduction practices may reduce negative and enhance positive experiences" (Discussion, 2nd paragraph) and as lending credibility to the importance ratings, although the score is built from those same ratings. The abstract and conclusion say the research helps to understand how engagement in harm reduction may increase with experience, a reading that rests on a recalled within-person comparison spanning years, with no allowance for recall, intention or amount. The abstract describes the CEQ association as strongest for the first experience rather than absent for the most recent one. The limitations paragraph says party settings were associated with lower EBI, which Table 2 shows only for the first experience (most recent: 41.56 in party settings versus 39.00 elsewhere), with no test run. Against this, the wording is hedged throughout, and the authors name survivor bias, forgetting, the missing CEQ items and the underpowered setting analysis.

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of the most difficult experience with psilocybin mushrooms, and Barrett et al.'s Challenging Experience Questionnaire, used here as background and measure (as cited).
Carhart-Harris et al. on the importance of context, cited for the dependence of psychedelic effects on set and setting
Haijen et al. prospective study, cited as earlier evidence that intentions, setting and readiness to confront difficult emotions predict CEQ and EBI scores
Roseman et al. validate the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory used here (as cited).
Gashi et al. interviews with experienced people who use psychedelics on turning bad trips into valuable experiences (as cited).
This survey.
Simonsson et al. quota-stratified US survey: respondents linked their most challenging experience to no preparation, a negative mindset or no psychological support, also by retrospective self-report
Piercey et al. mini review cites this survey as the main outcome evidence for protective strategies with classical psychedelics and misstates parts of it (see that card)
Wood, McAlpine and Kamboj mixed-methods study of strategies for resolving challenging experiences, also retrospective

replication.where_it_stands: No replication with this list and score. Later studies on the same question (Simonsson et al., 2023; Wood et al., 2024) are also retrospective self-report, and a validated protective-strategies scale (Mian et al., 2023, as cited by Piercey et al., 2024) had not yet been tested against challenging experiences. Whether practices measured before use change the experience has not been tested prospectively.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people planning a psychedelic experience outside research or therapy that records planned practices, intentions, place and company beforehand, then the practices actually used and the amount, and the CEQ and EBI within days, analysing practices one by one rather than as an importance-weighted sum, with adjustment for prior experience, intention and amount, and with any importance ratings taken from an independent panel.

domains.note: No covariates at all. Intention (which shifted sharply between occasions), amount, substance, place, prior experience and mental health could each drive both the practices recalled and the CEQ and EBI ratings.

Recalled checklist (first experience a median of 42 months earlier) of an unvalidated list, weighted by importance ratings given by the same respondents after recalling both experiences, and including practices after the experience that cannot have shaped it.

Self-selected from psychedelic communities; requiring two or more uses excludes people who stopped after a difficult first experience (survivor bias, acknowledged), which bears directly on the first-experience correlations; many excluded on attention checks, with numbers only in the supplement.

Practices after the experience (a rest day, talking with someone, creative and mindful pursuits) and later meaning-making, which the authors suggest may change memories of the experience, could alter how it was rated.
Exclusions and non-response reported only in the supplement; two CEQ items missing for everyone; one practice without importance scores.
CEQ and EBI rated retrospectively, years later for most first experiences, in the same sitting as the practice checklist and by the same person; CEQ short of 2 of its 26 items.

Pre-registered hypotheses and labelled exploratory analyses, but practice-level data only in an image and the supplement, four of the possible post hoc contrasts reported, and the registration not read for this card.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that harm-reduction practices make psychedelic experiences better or less difficult, the correlations are at very high risk of bias: nothing was adjusted, the score is weighted by the same respondents' importance judgments and includes practices after the experience, everything was recalled at one sitting (for first experiences, years later), and people who stopped after a difficult first experience could not take part. The qualitative part is a reasonable catalogue of views from 61 comments, with two authors coding, but no reflexivity or saturation account, and it describes beliefs, not effects. Cite the paper for what this self-selected group of experienced people recalled and how they rated practices (for example, being with trusted friends common and rated important; an unintoxicated sitter uncommon and rated low; testing rated important but seldom done), for the shift in place and intention between first and recent experiences, and, as hypothesis-generating, for weak correlations of a weighted practice score with emotional breakthrough (r = 0.24) and, for first experiences only, with fewer challenging experiences (r = −0.21). Do not cite it for any practice preventing challenging experiences, for harm reduction increasing with experience as a measured change, or for party settings causing worse experiences.

key_findings.finding: 163 participants after exclusions, recruited through university societies and online psychedelic communities: mean age 27.5 (SD 8.06), median 26, mode 20, range 18 to 56, 13 aged 40 or over; 120 men, 35 women, 8 non-binary. Estimated lifetime psychedelic uses: mean 28.4 (SD 45.2), median 11.5, mode 20; 16 people estimated 100 to 300 uses.

key_findings.note: In the PMC rendering the mode and median age and the mode number of uses are typeset as citation links to references 20 and 26 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Time since the first experience: mean 67.52 months (SD 78.33), median 42, mode 24; since the most recent: mean 8.68 months (SD 20.76), median 2, mode 1. Substance, first and most recent: LSD 47% and 33%, psilocybin 41% and 36%, 2C-B 4% and 6%, DMT 2% and 6%, mescaline 1% and 1%, other 6% and 18%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, time and drug rows; Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Place of the first and the most recent experience: at home (including temporary residences such as hotels, holiday cottages and student dormitories) 41% and 57%; a trusted friend's house 31% and 18%; in nature 11% and 12%; a festival 7% and 4%; a club 5% and 5%; a ceremonial setting 0% and 2%; a house or outdoor party 3% and 0%; at school 1% and 0%; unclear 1% and 2%. Where two places were given, the first was counted.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, location rows and footnote; Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Intentions (more than one allowed), first and most recent experience: curiosity 72% and 20%; fun 66% and 57%; spiritual pursuits 20% and 46%; self-enlightenment 19% and 41%; exploring therapeutic properties 15% and 37%; processing difficult emotions 9% and 32%; artistic inspiration 9% and 25%; no intention 4% and 1%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, intention rows; Results › Characteristics of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Participant Harm Reduction Score (sum of the sample-mean importance of the practices used): first experience 40.06 (SD 18.90), most recent 48.68 (18.81); repeated-measures ANOVA, main effect of occasion F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001; occasion by time interaction significant; Bonferroni contrasts higher for the most recent experience for practices before use (t = −9.63, p < 0.001) and after use (t = −3.28, p = 0.03), not during use (t = −1.47, p = 1) or for the during-myths (t = −0.04, p = 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, Harm Reduction Score row
key_findings.note: The printed effect sizes and one df in this paragraph are inconsistent (see reporting issues); cite F(1,162) = 28.32 with the means.

key_findings.finding: Experience scores: EBI first 27.77 (SD 26.46), most recent 39.18 (29.91), paired t(162) = 4.42, p < 0.001, d = 0.35; CEQ (percent of maximum) first 17.14 (18.06), most recent 17.29 (17.06), with no meaningful difference in any of the seven subscales. EBI and CEQ were positively correlated (exploratory): r = 0.393 (first) and 0.369 (most recent), both p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 2, EBI and CEQ rows

key_findings.finding: Pre-registered associations: the Participant Harm Reduction Score correlated with EBI at r = 0.24 (p = 0.002) for both experiences and with CEQ at r = −0.21 (p = 0.006) for the first experience; for the most recent experience the CEQ correlation was r = −0.15 (p = 0.061). Editors' 95% intervals (Fisher z, n = 163): 0.09 to 0.38; −0.35 to −0.06; −0.30 to 0.00.
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Unplanned descriptive comparison, no tests: first experience in a party, club or festival setting (n = 24) versus elsewhere (n = 139): practice score 21.95 (SD 12.61) vs 43.20 (18.57), CEQ 19.27 (18.02) vs 16.77 (18.10), with the difference mainly in the isolation subscale (29.44 vs 17.36), EBI 20.38 (24.16) vs 29.05 (26.71). Most recent experience, party (n = 12) versus elsewhere (n = 151): practice score 26.23 (12.25) vs 50.46 (18.10), CEQ 31.46 (24.02) vs 16.16 (15.96), all subscales numerically higher, EBI 41.56 (23.56) vs 39.00 (30.31).
key_findings.locator: Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Table 1 implies 14, not 12, most recent experiences at a festival or club (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Individual practices as described in the text: ensuring one was comfortable with one's surroundings had the highest importance score of all practices and was reported more often for the most recent experience; most participants were with trusted friends on both occasions (high score), while few had an unintoxicated trip sitter (low score); few tested their drugs although testing scored high, while many obtained drugs from a reputable source, especially for the most recent experience; most allowed a rest day and spoke to someone afterwards, the two highest-scoring after-use practices; about 35% reported being in a dark room, a practice scored close to zero. Practices reported more often for the most recent experience also included setting a purpose, measuring the dose and arranging a time to take the drug.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Results › Theme 2 Importance of the drug, 2nd paragraph; Subtheme 3.2 Darkness versus light, 1st paragraph; Subtheme 3.3 Tripping alone versus in company, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Percentages and scores for each practice are only in Figure 1 (an image that came back blank on screenshot because the browser pane was hidden; figure image not viewable) and supplementary Table S3 (not read).

key_findings.finding: More than 70% of participants, for both the first and the most recent experience, reported at least one of the practices the authors classed as myths; relatively many reported smoking cannabis, isolating themselves from others to focus on negative thoughts and problems, and being in a dark room, the last two being practices that harm-reduction websites suggest only for more experienced people.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Qualitative analysis (61 free-text comments; three themes): (1) profound positive experiences, with comments that the survey missed benefits and that not every hard trip is a bad one; (2) the importance of the drug: practices depend on the substance, some comments voiced substance-specific beliefs that the authors say are not, to their knowledge, evidence-based (about cannabis with LSD as against psilocybin, and about eating or fasting before particular substances), testing was seen as important for pills or powders from unknown sources and less so for mushrooms, especially home-grown, a trusted source was seen as making testing unnecessary, and the amount taken was described as among the most important safety factors; (3) set and setting, which participants described largely as creating safe, calm spaces and reducing stress and anxiety.
key_findings.locator: Results › Qualitative analysis of free-text responses, 1st paragraph; Theme 1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Theme 2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Theme 3, 1st paragraph (block quotations not counted as paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: Qualitative subthemes on set and setting: many participants said their set-and-setting practices aimed to improve the experience rather than to make it safer, and distinguished practices that reduce harm from those that improve the experience; they proposed adding being in a good mood beforehand, clearing the mind through meditation or mindfulness, having no commitments that day and limiting phone and social media use before and during the experience; the effect of darkness was said to depend on other circumstances (frightening when alone, disorienting at a club); participants were ambivalent about using alone and about sober sitters (a sober person without psychedelic experience may make communication harder), preferred companions who are deeply trusted or experienced, and thought a support person matters more for first-time use than later.
key_findings.locator: Results › Subtheme 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Subtheme 3.2, 1st paragraph; Subtheme 3.3, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph (block quotations not counted as paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: Measurement problems stated by the authors: 2 of the 3 CEQ insanity items were not asked (experimenter error), so that subscale had one item; one practice (arranging a time to take the dose) had no importance scores (methodological error).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures › Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ), 1st paragraph; Harm reduction practices, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a self-selected, largely male sample from psychedelic forums and organizations, with possible survivor bias; many exclusions on attention checks; recall and forgetting, especially for the first experience and for practices before and after it, with post-trip meaning-making possibly changing memories; CEQ and EBI used as proxies for negative and positive experiences; the missing CEQ items; and an underpowered, exploratory setting analysis.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths, limitations and future directions, 2nd to 5th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The ANOVA paragraph is garbled: the main effect of occasion, F(1,162) = 28.32, is printed with partial eta squared 0.012, while F and df give 0.15 (editors' calculation); the same sentence then attaches F(3,486) = 563.82, partial eta squared 0.78, the values of a three-df effect (apparently the main effect of time, which the authors call not meaningful), to the statement that scores were higher for the most recent experience.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither printed effect size can be cited for the occasion effect; cite F(1,162) = 28.32, p < 0.001 with the means from Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The occasion by time interaction is printed as F(3,162) = 24.76 with partial eta squared 0.133; in a 4 × 2 within-person design with 163 people the error df is 486, and 0.133 is what F = 24.76 gives with (3, 486); with (3, 162) it would be 0.31 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Harm reduction practices used during first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Misprinted df; the effect size matches (3, 486). No change to the conclusion.
