design_detail: Cross-sectional online survey of US adults recruited on the Prolific panel, 1 to 9 October 2021, with quotas on sex, five age bands and five ethnic groups to mirror the US adult population (N = 2,822). Analyses use the 613 respondents who reported ever using any of seven classic psychedelics (ayahuasca, DMT, LSD, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro, psilocybin). All measures are retrospective self-report at one sitting: three items on challenging experiences (frequency, impairment of functioning, length of impairment) adapted from a meditation adverse-effects survey; a modified 11-item Meditation-Related Adverse Effects Scale (MRAES-MBP) for enduring effects attributed to psychedelics; a gladness item; the 26-item Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ) for the respondent's most challenging lifetime experience; and checklists, for that experience, of set-and-setting factors the respondent associated with it, of what helped, of medications in use at the time, of thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the following days or weeks, and of help-seeking. Multiple linear regression (CEQ score) and logistic regression (any harm thought or attempt), with the 11 medication variables entered together in one model and the 10 set-and-setting variables together in another; no other covariates are stated. Appraised with ROBINS-E because the paper's analytic results, and the claims the before-and-during page will draw from it, are exposure-outcome associations; the prevalence figures are described with their sampling limits in the sample and key-findings fields.
can_establish: How often people in this quota-stratified opt-in online panel of US adults (October 2021) who had ever used a classic psychedelic reported challenging experiences, impairment, enduring symptoms they attributed to psychedelics, harm thoughts or attempts and help-seeking after their most challenging experience, and which retrospectively reported circumstances and medications went with higher CEQ scores and with harm thoughts or attempts among them.
cannot_establish: That any circumstance or medication caused a more difficult experience or harm (one retrospective survey in which the circumstances are respondents' own attributions recorded together with the outcome, with no demographic, psychiatric or use-history covariates); national prevalence in a probability-sample sense (an opt-in panel matched on three characteristics only); whether the actions respondents said helped did help; or anything about when the experiences happened, which substance or amount was taken, or how often people had used psychedelics.

sample.recruitment: Prolific Academic online panel, 1 to 9 October 2021; quota stratification on sex (2 groups), age (18-27, 28-37, 38-47, 48-57, 58+) and ethnicity (White, Mixed, Asian, Black, Other) to reflect the US adult population. Recruitment materials did not mention psychedelics (materials in the supplement). Payment of 2.20 US dollars; approval by the University of Wisconsin-Madison institutional review board (Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over and currently resident in the US. No exclusion criteria, attention checks or data-quality exclusions are reported, and the number who started but did not finish is not given.
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article; key demographics of the 613 are in Supplemental Table 1 (a PDF supplement, not read). The article gives no age, sex, education, psychiatric history or number of lifetime psychedelic uses for the analysed group.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). Non-completion, exclusions and item non-response are not reported; every table states 613 observations.
sample.selection_effects: An opt-in commercial panel with demographic quotas, not a probability sample; the authors note it may not be representative on other characteristics such as socioeconomic status (Discussion, 4th paragraph), yet the abstract calls it nationally representative. Lifetime use in the sample was 21.7% (613 of 2,822, editors' calculation). The paper does not compare this with a national survey, but it planned the sample from a published US prevalence estimate (its reference 17, by the same first author), expecting about 395 people with lifetime use among about 2,800 respondents, about 14.1% (editors' calculation); the panel gave about one and a half times that, which suggests that the opt-in panel over-represents people who have used psychedelics, or that use had risen (Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph). People who died, are institutionalized or are not online panel members cannot appear. The 362 respondents who said they had never had a challenging experience still answered the CEQ and every most-challenging-experience checklist, so Table 2 and the regressions pool people with and without challenging experiences.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported checklist of lifetime use of seven classic psychedelics. For the most challenging experience: a multiple-choice list of set-and-setting factors the respondent judged to be associated with it (modified from Carbonaro et al., 2016; options in the supplement) and a checklist of 11 medication categories in use at the time. All recalled at one sitting with no biological verification; the date of, and time since, the experience were not asked or not reported (Materials and Methods › Measures › Most challenging, difficult, or distressing experience, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: no amount, number of lifetime uses, route or date, and no record of which substance was taken on the most challenging occasion (respondents only named which psychedelics they associated with challenging experiences). 'Dose was too large' is a factor the respondent chose, not a measured dose.
exposure.polysubstance: 'Combining with other drug' was one of the factors respondents could attribute their experience to (4.4%). Use of alcohol, cannabis or other drugs was not measured as a covariate. Smoking cannabis (18.4%), drinking alcohol (8.8%) and taking another drug (3.6%) appear among the actions respondents reported as helpful during the experience (Table 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective survey of past experiences).

comparison.controls: Within the 613 people with lifetime use, respondents who did not tick a given factor or medication. The prevalence figures have no comparison group: the enduring-symptom items were not asked about periods without psychedelics, and no one without psychedelic use answered them.
comparison.matching: None. Each regression is mutually adjusted only within its block (medications entered together; set-and-setting factors entered together, Table 3 and Table 4 notes); no demographic, psychiatric, personality or use-history covariate is described, although the abstract and discussion call the models covariate-adjusted.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history (including the conditions for which lithium and other mood stabilizers are prescribed), personality traits that the authors cite as predictors of challenging experiences (neuroticism, Barrett et al., 2017), age at the experience, substance and amount, number of previous experiences, other drug use and socioeconomic position: none measured or used.

outcomes.instruments: CEQ (Barrett et al., 2016): 26 items rated 0 (none) to 5 (extreme) for the self-selected most challenging lifetime experience, Cronbach's alpha .97; how the total was scored is not stated. Frequency of challenging experiences (5 options), impaired ability to function (5 options) and length of impairment (6 options), adapted from items used by Goldberg et al. (2021) for meditation. Modified 11-item MRAES-MBP: enduring effects 'as a result of classic psychedelics' rated on a 5-point duration scale (never to more than 1 year), asked of everyone with lifetime use. Gladness item rated 1 to 6. Thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after the most challenging experience (4 items); sought medical, psychiatric or psychological assistance (yes or no); a checklist of helpful actions derived from Carbonaro et al. (2016).
outcomes.validity_norms: The CEQ was developed for psilocybin mushroom experiences; the frequency, impairment and duration items and the MRAES-MBP come from meditation research, and no validation for psychedelic experiences is reported. No norms and no comparison group.
outcomes.operationalization: A challenging experience is any answer other than 'Never' on the single frequency item. Degree of difficulty is the CEQ score for the respondent's most challenging experience, completed also by respondents who said they had never had one. 'Overall risk of harm' is any of the four harm thoughts or attempts in the following days or weeks. Each measure was rated once, retrospectively, by the respondent, at an unknown interval after the experience.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 42 counts the coefficient tests in Tables 3 and 4 (21 predictors against 2 outcomes; 2 could not be estimated in Table 4); descriptive prevalences are not counted. Editors' calculation: at a Bonferroni threshold of .00125 for 40 estimable tests, the lithium (p = .041 and .016), other mood stabilizer (.018, .015), no preparation (.010), disagreeable physical environment (.029), no psychological support for harm (.011) and major life event for harm (.022) results would not remain; only results printed as p < .001 might.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: respondents rated both the circumstances and the outcome themselves, knowing both.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3 (CEQ, standardized beta, n = 613): no psychological support .25 (p < .001), dose too large .24 (p < .001), negative mindset .14 (p < .001), major life event before the experience .13 (p < .001), no preparation .09 (p = .010), disagreeable physical environment .09 (p = .029), disagreeable social environment .04 (p = .263), disagreeable music .05 (p = .192), combining with other drug -.06 (p = .099); lithium .11 (p = .041), other mood stabilizers .10 (p = .018), MAOIs .09 (p = .068), SSRIs .03 (p = .431). No intervals, unstandardized coefficients, R-squared or CEQ distribution. Table 4 (any harm thought or attempt, 41 events, adjusted odds ratios with 95% CI): negative mindset 4.56 (2.10 to 9.94), no psychological support 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42), major life event 2.93 (1.17 to 7.35), no preparation 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45), dose too large 1.60 (0.66 to 3.88), disagreeable physical environment 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35), disagreeable social environment 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = .051), disagreeable music 2.67 (0.87 to 8.21); lithium 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65; 8 people exposed), other mood stabilizers 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34; 16 exposed), SSRIs 2.11 (0.61 to 7.37); St John's wort and haloperidol dropped. The printed p values agree with the intervals (editors' check on the log scale). Prevalences are printed without intervals; editors' 95% Wilson intervals: impairment longer than one day 55/613, 9.0% (7.0 to 11.5); any harm thought or attempt 6.7% (5.0 to 8.9); sought assistance 2.6% (1.6 to 4.2); severe impairment 4.6% (3.2 to 6.5).
analysis.covariates: None beyond mutual adjustment within each block of predictors; unadjusted estimates are in Supplemental Tables 2 and 3 (not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or preregistration is mentioned; the introduction describes the aims as exploratory. The data-availability sentence of the author manuscript still carries the journal-submission placeholder instead of a location for the data and Stata syntax.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports that 59.1% never had a challenging experience but not that 57.1% reported at least one enduring symptom they attributed to psychedelics, or that 6.7% reported harm thoughts or attempts. Unadjusted analyses and the sample's demographics are only in the supplement. The CEQ's scoring and distribution are not reported. The discussion does not mention that smoking cannabis and drinking alcohol were among the actions respondents reported as helpful, or the borderline inverse association of a disagreeable social environment with harm.
analysis.power: A priori: 395 people with lifetime use would give 80% power to detect a small R-squared increase at alpha .05 in linear regression (G*Power); about 2,800 respondents were sought to reach that number, from a published prevalence estimate (reference 17), and 613 were obtained (Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph). Not addressed for the logistic models: 41 events for 9 and 10 predictors (about 4 events per predictor), with 8 people exposed to lithium, which yields an interval of 1.78 to 279.65.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In an opt-in panel matched to the US on sex, age and ethnicity, 59.1% of 613 people with lifetime classic psychedelic use said they had never had a challenging experience, 4.6% reported severe impairment of functioning, 9.0% (printed 8.9%) impairment lasting more than a day, 57.1% at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they attributed to psychedelics, 6.7% thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the following days or weeks, and 2.6% help-seeking. Among the same respondents, attributing their most challenging experience to no psychological support, a dose they judged too large, a negative mindset, a major life event, no preparation or a disagreeable physical environment went with higher retrospective CEQ scores, and negative mindset, no psychological support and a major life event with higher odds of harm thoughts or attempts; lithium (8 people) and other mood stabilizers (16 people) were associated with both outcomes, with very wide intervals.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes the data as nationally representative of the US adult population and the models as "covariate-adjusted regression models" (Abstract), whereas the sample is an opt-in panel matched on three characteristics and the models adjust each predictor only for the others in its block. The discussion says the findings strengthen support for safety guidelines and judges it prudent for clinical trials and for legalization initiatives to follow current guidelines strictly until more is known (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), and proposes calming exercises such as mindfulness as preparation because 'trying to calm the mind' was the action most often reported as helpful (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), which is a self-report of helpfulness, not a test. The lithium interpretation draws on seizure reports, an outcome this survey did not measure, and does not consider that people taking lithium or mood stabilizers may differ in psychiatric history. Against this, the abstract uses associational language throughout, and the limitations paragraph states that no causal inference is possible, that representativeness covers only sex, age and ethnicity, and that self-report is open to bias (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of challenging experiences with psilocybin mushrooms (self-selected respondents), the source of this study's set-and-setting and helpful-action lists; the authors describe their own associations as consistent with it (as cited).
Barrett et al. develop the Challenging Experience Questionnaire used here (as cited).
Haijen et al. prospective study of predictors of responses to psychedelics, cited here for states and traits that predict challenging experiences
Nayak et al. analysis of online experience reports linking lithium co-use with seizures, cited for the lithium interpretation (as cited; seizures were not measured in this survey).
Simonsson et al. population-based survey of psychedelic-related seizures from an overlapping author group, also cited for the lithium interpretation (as cited).

This survey: prevalence of challenging experiences among people with lifetime use in a quota-stratified US panel, and cross-sectional associations with self-attributed set-and-setting factors and medication co-use.
Wood, McAlpine and Kamboj mixed-methods study of strategies for resolving challenging experiences, which cites this survey

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication. The set-and-setting pattern agrees with earlier self-selected surveys as the authors say, but all such evidence is retrospective and self-attributed; whether preparation, support or mindset measured before use predicts the difficulty of an experience needs prospective designs such as Haijen et al. (2018). The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations rest on 8 and 16 people and are confounded by indication; they are a signal for pharmacovigilance, not an estimate.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people planning to use a classic psychedelic outside a laboratory, measuring mindset, preparation, recent life events, intended setting and support, medications and psychiatric history before use, and rating the experience with the CEQ within days, with analyses adjusted for substance, amount, personality and psychiatric history; for lithium and mood stabilizers, systematic pharmacovigilance or case-series data that record the indication and the acute effects.

domains.note: No control for confounding beyond mutual adjustment of exposures within each block. The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations are open to confounding by the conditions these drugs treat; the set-and-setting associations by personality, psychiatric history, substance and amount. None was measured.

Exposures are respondents' own attributions of their most challenging experience to listed factors, recalled at an unknown interval and reported together with the outcome; 'dose was too large' is a judgment, not a dose; medication use at the time is recalled.
Opt-in panel; the respondent chooses which experience counts as the most challenging; people with and without any challenging experience are analysed together.

Actions taken during the experience (changing location, help from friends, cannabis, alcohol) and later help-seeking could change both the CEQ rating and harm thoughts; they were not considered in the models.
Non-completion, exclusions and item non-response are not reported; every analysis has 613 observations.

CEQ and harm items rated retrospectively by the same person who reported the exposures, for an experience of unknown date; the CEQ was also completed by respondents who said they had never had a challenging experience; the frequency and impairment items gave inconsistent counts (see reporting issues).
No preregistration; 42 coefficient tests without correction; unadjusted results relegated to the supplement; no R-squared or CEQ distribution.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence of what predicts a difficult experience, the associations are at very high risk of bias: the predictors are respondents' retrospective attributions recorded with the outcome, nothing was measured before use, and no confounder was adjusted for. The prevalence figures are more useful but must carry their labels: an opt-in panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity only, unvalidated items borrowed from meditation research that gave inconsistent counts, and no comparison group for the enduring symptoms. Cite the paper for the proportions in this sample (for example 59.1% never had a challenging experience; 2.6% sought help) and, as hypothesis-generating, for the pattern that people who blame a negative mindset, lack of support or a recent life event report harder experiences. Do not cite it for any factor causing or preventing difficult experiences, for the effectiveness of what respondents said helped, or for a risk estimate for lithium or mood stabilizers.

key_findings.finding: Of 2,822 US adults recruited on Prolific with quotas on sex, age and ethnicity, 613 (21.7%, editors' calculation) reported ever using a classic psychedelic; all analyses are in these 613.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Frequency of challenging, difficult or distressing experiences with classic psychedelics: never 59.1% (362), rarely 23.3% (143), occasionally 13.1% (80), regularly 3.6% (22), frequently 1.0% (6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1, frequency rows

key_findings.finding: Impaired ability to function: severely 4.6% (28), moderately 8.2% (50), somewhat 16.0% (98), not at all 32.6% (200), no difficulties 38.7% (237). Length of impairment: 1 day or less 33.8% (207), a few days to 1 week 4.4% (27), over 1 week to 1 month 1.1% (7), over 1 month to 1 year 2.3% (14), over 1 year 1.1% (7); longer than one day 55 people, printed as 8.9% (9.0% by editors' calculation, 95% Wilson interval 7.0 to 11.5).
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1, impairment and length rows
key_findings.note: The two impairment items do not agree: 176 people reported some impairment of functioning but 262 gave an impairment length (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 57.1% (350) reported at least one of the modified MRAES-MBP symptoms lasting at least a few days that they attributed to classic psychedelics: feeling anxious 36.1% (221), difficulty sleeping 27.9% (171), difficulty thinking or making decisions 24.0% (147), feeling disconnected from everything 23.7% (145), feeling cut off from other people 20.1% (123). Asked of all 613, including those reporting no challenging experience; no comparison with periods or people without psychedelic use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1, symptom rows; Materials and Methods › Measures › Challenging, difficult, or distressing experiences, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 78.6% agreed, from slightly to strongly, that they were glad to have used classic psychedelics (482 of 613, editors' sum: slightly agree 23.2%, agree 28.2%, strongly agree 27.2%); 21.4% disagreed to some degree, 5.9% strongly.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, gladness rows

key_findings.finding: Challenging experiences were most often associated with LSD (24.0% of the 613; 31.5% of those who had used LSD), then tryptamines (ayahuasca, DMT, psilocybin: 15.3%; 19.7%) and phenethylamines (mescaline, peyote, San Pedro: 4.1%; 14.7%). Number of occasions of use of each substance was not measured.
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1; footnote 2

key_findings.finding: Factors respondents associated with their most challenging experience (multiple choice, n = 613): no preparation 29.7% (182), negative mindset 15.7% (96), no psychological support 15.5% (95), disagreeable social environment 15.0% (92), disagreeable physical environment 14.5% (89), dose was too large 13.2% (81), major life event before the experience 6.9% (41), disagreeable music 4.9% (30), combining with another drug 4.4% (27).
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph; Table 2, set and setting rows
key_findings.note: 41 of 613 is 6.7%, not 6.9% (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Actions respondents reported as helpful during their most challenging experience (multiple choice, n = 613, helpfulness self-rated and not tested): trying to calm the mind 41.9% (257), changing location 27.4% (168), asking a friend for help 20.2% (124), changing the social environment 20.2% (124), smoking cannabis 18.4% (113), changing the music 16.2% (99), changing the environment in another way 12.6% (77), drinking alcohol 8.8% (54), using the body to shift the experience 7.8% (48), taking another drug 3.6% (22).
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph; Table 2, helpful interventions rows

key_findings.finding: In the days or weeks after the most challenging experience, 6.7% (41) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others: thoughts of hurting oneself 4.6% (28), thoughts of hurting others 2.6% (16), attempts to harm oneself 1.5% (9), attempts to harm others 0.7% (4); 2.6% (16; 95% Wilson interval 1.6 to 4.2, editors' calculation) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological assistance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph; Table 2, risk-of-harm and sought-assistance rows

key_findings.finding: 11.3% (69) reported using at least one listed medication at the time of their most challenging experience: SSRIs 5.2% (32), other mood stabilizers 2.6% (16), SNRIs 1.8% (11), other serotonergic medicines or supplements 1.8% (11), tricyclic antidepressants 1.5% (9), lithium 1.3% (8), other antipsychotics 1.1% (7), methadone or buprenorphine 1.1% (7), MAOIs 0.8% (5), haloperidol 0.8% (5), St John's wort 0.5% (3).

Medications entered together: lithium .11 (p = .041), other mood stabilizers .10 (p = .018); no other medication associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 2nd paragraph; Table 3 and its note

Lithium 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65; 8 exposed) and other mood stabilizers 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34; 16 exposed); St John's wort and haloperidol were dropped from the model.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the associations cannot show causality because of the cross-sectional design, that Prolific allowed stratification on sex, age and ethnicity only, so the sample may not be representative on other characteristics such as socioeconomic status, and that self-report is open to bias.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Impairment lasting longer than one day is given as 8.9% (abstract, results, discussion), the sum of the rounded row percentages (4.4 + 1.1 + 2.3 + 1.1); the counts in Table 1 give 55 of 613, 9.0%.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Table 1, length of impairment rows

reporting_issues.issue: The three challenging-experience items give inconsistent counts: 362 said they had never had a challenging experience but only 237 chose 'not applicable, I have not had difficulties' on the impairment item; 176 reported some impairment of functioning (somewhat, moderately or severely), yet 262 reported an impairment length (207 of them 1 day or less).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1, frequency, impaired ability to function and length of impairment rows

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion describe the regressions as covariate-adjusted, but the table notes state only that the medication variables and the set-and-setting variables were each entered simultaneously; no demographic, psychiatric or use-history covariate appears anywhere.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Materials and Methods › Measures › Statistical Analyses; Table 3 note; Table 4 note
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may assume the associations, notably those for lithium and mood stabilizers, were adjusted for confounders; they were adjusted only for the other predictors in the same block.

design_detail: Mixed-methods study in two parts, both online (Qualtrics), approved by the University College London Research Ethics Committee and explicitly not pre-registered. Study 1 (qualitative, described here and not rated): written answers to four open questions from 16 attendees of psilocybin retreats at four collaborating centres in the Netherlands and Mexico, selected for reporting both distress during ceremonies and significant personal transformation; inductive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke) with two researchers coding independently in NVivo. Its themes, with the literature, were used to write a new 26-item inventory of responses to challenging experiences (ReCiPE). Study 2 (quantitative, rated with ROBINS-E): a self-selected online survey advertised through social media, research groups and forums to people who had used a classic psychedelic; of 869 completers, 555 reported a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported experience and 529 were analysed. Each strategy was rated not tried, tried and not helpful, somewhat helpful or substantially helpful, then scored 1 if tried and judged helpful; exploratory factor analysis (WLSMV on tetrachoric correlations, Geomin rotation); Pearson correlations of ReCiPE factor counts and CEQ subscales with the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI); and a multiple regression of EBI on the CEQ and ReCiPE factors that correlated with it. All ratings are retrospective self-report by the same person, in some cases years after the experience.
can_establish: What kinds of responses 16 retreat attendees who reported both difficulty and transformation described using during challenging psilocybin ceremonies; and, among 529 self-selected people recalling a challenging psychedelic experience, how many said they tried each of 26 strategies and found it helpful, how those judgments grouped, and how the number of strategies judged helpful and the kind of challenge went with retrospectively rated emotional breakthrough.
cannot_establish: Whether any strategy shortens, eases or resolves a challenging experience or brings about emotional breakthrough (helpfulness is the respondent's own retrospective judgment, scored only when the strategy was judged helpful, and correlated with an outcome rated by the same person at the same time; no comparison, manipulation or prospective measurement); how often these strategies are used or helpful among people who use psychedelics in general; or whether the findings hold in clinical, ceremonial or recreational settings specifically (setting, substance and amount are not analysed).

sample.recruitment: Study 1: attendees of psilocybin retreats at four collaborating centres in the Netherlands (8) and Mexico (8), contacted by email if they had agreed to research contact (Methods › Study 1 › Participants and recruitment). Study 2: online survey advertised to people with psychedelic experience through targeted social media, research groups and forums (Methods › Study 2 › Participants and recruitment). n_total counts the 16 plus the 529 analysed.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both studies: aged 18 or over, proficient in English, prior psychedelic experience, electronic consent. Study 1 additionally: prior psilocybin retreat attendance and self-reported significant personal transformation together with distress or difficulty during ceremonies. Study 2: at least one experience with psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline; experiences limited to MDMA, ketamine or other non-classic psychedelics excluded, combined use allowed; only those reporting distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported experience completed the CEQ and ReCiPE.
sample.demographics: Study 1: mean age 45; 9 women, 7 men; 13 with no religious affiliation; 15 with graduate or postgraduate education; retreats of 3 to 7 days with up to 3 ceremonies; median 6 months since attendance. Study 2 (n = 529): 243 men (45.94%), 256 women (48.39%), 30 non-binary or other (5.67%); mean age 37.71 (SD 10.88). Substance, setting, time since the experience and lifetime psychedelic experience were collected but are reported only in Supplementary Material S.VI (a docx file, not read).
sample.attrition: Study 2: 26 of the 555 who reported a challenge (4.7%) were not analysed, without a stated reason; the regression's degrees of freedom imply 527 cases. The number who started the survey but did not complete it is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Both samples self-selected. Study 1 was chosen for reporting transformation, so its accounts describe challenges that ended well, as the authors note. Study 2 was recruited where people interested in psychedelics gather and, by the authors' account, consisted mainly of experienced people from Western cultures who may have developed effective coping over time (Discussion, 9th paragraph). The main text does not say how respondents chose which experience to report.

exposure.measurement: ReCiPE, a new 26-item inventory written from the Study 1 themes and the literature: for each strategy, not tried, tried and not helpful, tried and somewhat helpful, tried and substantially helpful. For factor analysis, correlations and regression the answers were turned into a binary score (1 = tried and judged somewhat or substantially helpful), so a factor 'score' is the number of strategies judged helpful, not how often or how much a strategy was used (Methods › Study 2 › Measures › Responses to challenging psychedelic experiences). Kinds of challenge were measured with the CEQ subscales. The scale is in the supplement (cited as S.II in the Methods and S.V in the Results).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. Substance and time since the experience were collected (reported in supplement S.VI only); amount, route and setting of the reported experience are not reported in the article. Study 1 concerned psilocybin retreat ceremonies, with amounts not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Combined use with non-classic psychedelics was allowed in Study 2 but not recorded in the article. One ReCiPE item asks about taking another drug or drinking alcohol during the challenge: 12.1% of the 529 tried it and judged it helpful; it did not load on any factor.

comparison.controls: None. Associations are within the 529 people who reported a challenge; no group without the strategies or without a challenge was compared on the same measures.
comparison.matching: None; the regression contains no covariates other than the CEQ and ReCiPE factors.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality and habitual emotion regulation (which the authors name as possible explanations), psychiatric history, prior psychedelic experience, setting (therapeutic, ceremonial or recreational), substance and amount, presence and behaviour of others, and time since the experience: not used in any analysis.

outcomes.instruments: Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI; Roseman et al., 2019): 6 items on a 0 to 100 visual analogue scale, averaged; single factor explaining 71.4% of variance, Cronbach's alpha .918 in this sample. Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ; Barrett et al., 2016): 26 items, 0 to 5, seven subscales (fear, grief, physical distress, insanity, isolation, death, paranoia), alpha at least .928; an added trauma-reliving item was not analysed. ReCiPE alphas: total .801; Acceptance and Reappraisal .726 without its weakly loading item (.718 with it, as kept), Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction .731 without its two weakly loading items (.716 with them, as kept), Social Support and Disclosure .786.
outcomes.validity_norms: The EBI and CEQ are published validated scales; the ReCiPE is new, its three-factor structure is preliminary and chosen partly on interpretability, the fit indices are described only as passing thresholds without values, and the authors say it needs further validation with an interval scoring scheme (Discussion, 10th paragraph). The EBI was chosen as outcome because it suits a mixed non-clinical group.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Emotional breakthrough' is the mean EBI score for the reported experience, rated by the respondent at the time of the survey. 'Helpful strategy' is the respondent's own judgment of helpfulness, made at the same time, about a strategy used during the same experience.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; alpha .05 throughout. 62 counts the 55 correlations in Table 3 and the 7 regression coefficients in Table 4.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report).

analysis.effect_sizes: Correlations with EBI (Table 3, n = 529): Acceptance and Reappraisal r = 0.50, Social Support and Disclosure 0.27, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction 0.18; CEQ grief 0.41, death 0.20, physical distress 0.10, fear -0.14; insanity -0.07, isolation -0.03, paranoia -0.08 (not significant). Fear correlated with fewer acceptance (r = -0.20) and sensory (-0.14) strategies judged helpful; grief with more acceptance (0.19) and social-support (0.24) strategies. Regression (Table 4): F(7, 519) = 50.93, adjusted R-squared 0.399 (R-squared change 0.407); standardized beta: grief 0.37, acceptance and reappraisal 0.33, death 0.17, social support and disclosure 0.07 (p = .041), fear -0.24 (all others p < .001); physical distress -0.02 (p = .693) and sensory regulation 0.02 (p = .527) not significant. Editors' calculation from t multiplied by SE in Table 4: unstandardized coefficients of about 7.0 EBI points per unit of CEQ grief, -4.5 per unit of fear, 2.6 per unit of death, 4.1 per acceptance strategy judged helpful and 1.2 per social-support strategy. No covariates.
analysis.covariates: None. The regression predictors were the variables that correlated significantly with the EBI.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The Methods state that neither study was pre-registered (Methods, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Predictors entered the regression only if they correlated significantly with the outcome, which inflates the variance explained and the coefficients. The fit indices of the factor solutions, the per-item frequencies (Figure 1, an image, and supplement S.VII), and the substance, setting and timing of the reported experiences (supplement S.VI) are not in the text. The text says unstandardized coefficients and their intervals were reported, but Table 4 has no unstandardized column.
analysis.power: Not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Retreat attendees described four families of responses to difficult ceremonies (inner responses, embodied practice and engagement with the environment, interpersonal responses, and responses from facilitators). In 529 self-selected people recalling a challenging experience, letting go or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%) were the strategies most often tried and judged helpful; anger or aggression (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling the experience to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%) the least. Respondents who judged more acceptance-and-reappraisal and social-support strategies helpful, and who reported more grief- and death-type and less fear-type challenge, rated their emotional breakthrough higher, all measured at one retrospective sitting.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract stays mostly with associational wording but says the findings offer insights for "enhancing safety in both clinical and non-clinical settings", and no safety outcome was measured. The discussion opens by saying the research examined the effectiveness of strategies (Discussion, 1st paragraph), whereas it measured self-judged helpfulness; it says the correlations confirm that breakthrough involves adopting more helpful strategies (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), a causal reading of cross-sectional data in which helpfulness may itself reflect how the experience ended; and it proposes that ACT-based preparation could reduce a direct effect of fear on breakthrough and raise an indirect effect through acceptance (Discussion, 8th paragraph), mediation language without any mediation analysis. The text also interprets the standardized coefficients as unstandardized slopes (a rise of 0.37 in breakthrough per unit of grief), which understates the implied unstandardized slope of about 7 points (Results › Multiple regression, 3rd paragraph). The limitations paragraphs are frank about self-selection, retrospective recall and the new scale, and the discussion notes that set and setting could explain the associations.

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of challenging experiences with psilocybin mushrooms and Barrett et al.'s Challenging Experience Questionnaire, both used here as background and measure (as cited).
Roseman et al. validate the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory used as this study's outcome (as cited).

Simonsson et al. quota-stratified US survey, cited here: 'trying to calm the mind' was the action most often reported as helpful during the most challenging experience (41.9% of 613), a pattern in line with the acceptance strategies most often judged helpful here
This study: first version of the ReCiPE, with a preliminary three-factor structure and cross-sectional associations with emotional breakthrough.

replication.where_it_stands: A first, exploratory instrument-development study. No independent sample has tested the ReCiPE's structure, and no study has measured strategies during or immediately after sessions, or manipulated them (for example through preparation that teaches acceptance), to test whether they change how a challenging experience unfolds.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article. The competing-interests declaration notes that R.G.M is supported by the Wellcome Trust.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: the authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Research Department of Clinical, Educational and Health Psychology and the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London. Study 1 participants came through four collaborating retreat centres, with which one author liaised (author contributions); the centres and any arrangement with them are not named. The discussion's recommendations on preparation cite the second author's own scale of psychedelic preparedness and digital preparation intervention (refs 30 and 88). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of preparation that teaches acceptance and reappraisal skills against an attention-matched control, in people about to take part in a psilocybin session in a clinical or retreat setting, with challenge (CEQ) and breakthrough (EBI) rated within a day and strategy use recorded during or right after the session by participants and by blinded observers; together with an independent confirmatory factor analysis of the ReCiPE.

domains.note: Study 2 regression has no covariates: setting, substance, amount, prior experience, personality and habitual emotion regulation could all drive both the strategies judged helpful and emotional breakthrough, as the authors acknowledge for set and setting.

New, preliminarily validated inventory; the score counts only strategies judged helpful, a retrospective judgment that is likely shaped by how the experience ended, which is close to the outcome itself.
Self-selected through psychedelic forums, research groups and social media; only people reporting a challenge were analysed; the way the reported experience was chosen is not described.

What others did during the experience (facilitators, friends, therapists) and any later integration work could affect both strategy judgments and breakthrough ratings; not recorded except as ReCiPE items.
26 of 555 respondents with a challenge were not analysed and the regression has 527 cases, without explanation or a stated method for missing data.
EBI rated retrospectively, sometimes years later, by the same person who judged the strategies, with knowledge of both.

Not pre-registered; regression predictors chosen because they correlated significantly with the outcome; factor solution chosen partly on interpretability; printed intervals inconsistent with the estimates.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a cross-sectional exposure-outcome study (ROBINS-E) for Study 2; Study 1 is described, not rated. Study 1 is a reasonable catalogue of responses, with two independent coders and attributed quotations, but it rests on 16 highly educated retreat attendees chosen for transformative outcomes, written answers without follow-up questions, and no reflexivity or saturation account; it says nothing about frequency or effect. In Study 2, the associations between strategies judged helpful and emotional breakthrough are at very high risk of bias: no confounders were adjusted for, both measures are retrospective ratings by the same person, the strategy score depends on a helpfulness judgment that partly reflects the outcome, and the regression was built from significant correlations. Cite the paper for the strategies people described and for the share of this self-selected sample who said they tried each strategy and found it helpful, labelled as self-judged; not for any strategy being effective, and not for the regression coefficients as effect sizes.

key_findings.finding: Study 1: 16 psilocybin retreat attendees (8 Netherlands, 8 Mexico; retreats of 3 to 7 days with up to 3 ceremonies; median 6 months since attendance; mean age 45; 9 women; 15 with graduate or postgraduate education) wrote about challenging episodes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 1: qualitative analysis › Participant characteristics

key_findings.finding: Study 1 themes of responses to difficult ceremonies: inner responses (accepting and observing; self-talk and reassurance; interrogating or commanding the challenge; interpretation and meaning-making; journaling); embodied practice and engagement with the environment (intentional breathing; opening the eyes and moving around rather than lying still, one participant having been encouraged to stay lying with an eye mask; sensory engagement with the surroundings and the ceremony; leaving the ceremony; sleep); interpersonal responses (avoiding others; asking for help; disclosure); and facilitator responses (touch and reminders to breathe; listening; reassurance, which one participant found unhelpful when it was evasive; rhythm and sound; introducing new elements).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 1: qualitative analysis › Thematic analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Study 2: of 869 survey completers, 555 reported distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported psychedelic experience and 529 were analysed: 243 men (45.94%), 256 women (48.39%), 30 non-binary or other (5.67%); mean age 37.71 (SD 10.88).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 555 of 869 is 63.87%, not the printed 64.24% (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Share of the 529 who tried a strategy and judged it somewhat or substantially helpful: letting go, accepting or surrendering 84.5%; observing the mind and not fighting it 77.3%; closing the eyes, lying or sitting down 73.9%. Least often: directing anger or aggression at the experience 9.4%, trying to fall asleep 9.7%, assertively telling it to stop or go away 10.6%, taking another drug or consuming alcohol 12.1%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend
key_findings.note: These percentages are of all 529 and combine how often a strategy was tried with how often it was judged helpful. Per-item counts for not tried and tried-but-not-helpful are only in Figure 1 (figure image not viewable; values not extracted) and supplement S.VII (not read).

key_findings.finding: Respondents judged on average 11.25 strategies helpful (SD 4.78; mode 10) of 26: Acceptance and Reappraisal 5.25 (SD 2.39) of 11, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction 3.82 (SD 2.41) of 10, Social Support and Disclosure 2.17 (SD 1.80; mode 0) of 5.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 3rd paragraph; Reliability, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory factor analysis of the binary ReCiPE favoured three factors (two-factor solution fit poorly; three and four factors fit similarly, three chosen as more coherent with fewer cross-loadings): Acceptance and Reappraisal, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction, Social Support and Disclosure; factor correlations 0.330, 0.118 and 0.217. Telling the experience to stop, trying to sleep and taking another drug or alcohol loaded below 0.4 on every factor but were kept, so Factor 1 counts 11 strategies (letting go, observing the mind, questioning the challenge, telling it to stop, directing anger or aggression at it (0.43), interpreting sensations as meaningful, journaling, focusing on breathing, closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (cross-loading), asking forgiveness, calling on spirits or a deity), Factor 2 ten (including trying to sleep and taking another drug or alcohol) and Factor 3 five. Alphas: total .801; Factor 1 .726 without telling it to stop (.718 with it, as kept), Factor 2 .731 without its two weakly loading items (.716 with them, as kept), Factor 3 .786.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Factor analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2; Reliability, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Correlations with the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (Table 3 prints no n; 529 were analysed and the regression used 527): Acceptance and Reappraisal r = 0.50, Social Support and Disclosure 0.27, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction 0.18; CEQ grief 0.41, death 0.20, physical distress 0.10, fear -0.14; insanity, isolation and paranoia not significant. Fear went with fewer acceptance strategies judged helpful (r = -0.20); grief with more acceptance (0.19) and social-support (0.24) strategies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Correlations; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Regression of emotional breakthrough on four CEQ and three ReCiPE factors: F(7, 519) = 50.93, p < .001, adjusted R-squared 0.399; standardized beta grief 0.37, acceptance and reappraisal 0.33, fear -0.24, death 0.17 (all p < .001), social support and disclosure 0.07 (p = .041); physical distress -0.02 (p = .693) and sensory regulation and physical interaction 0.02 (p = .527) not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Multiple regression, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4 and its note
key_findings.note: Printed intervals and the text's reading of the coefficients are inconsistent with Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Neither study was pre-registered; the regression's predictors were the variables that correlated significantly with emotional breakthrough; no covariates were included; alpha .05 throughout.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study 2: online survey › Data analysis, 1st paragraph and Multiple regression

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: both samples self-selected; mainly experienced people from Western cultures who may have developed effective coping; retrospective reports, some of experiences years earlier; Study 1 selected for transformative outcomes; varied settings and motives in Study 2; the ReCiPE is new and its binary scoring loses information; direct clinical applicability limited.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 9th, 10th and 11th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: 555 of 869 completers is printed as 64.24%; 555/869 is 63.87% (64.24% would correspond to a denominator of about 864).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but it suggests an unreported exclusion before the 869 or a different denominator; the flow from survey starts to the analysed 529 is not fully described.

reporting_issues.issue: The regression's F(7, 519) implies 527 cases, while the analysed sample is 529; no missing-data handling is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two cases are unaccounted for; minor for the estimates, but the sample flow cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 prints standardized betas beside standard errors and t values that belong to unstandardized coefficients (for fear, -0.24 with SE 0.81 and t = -5.50, which implies B of about -4.5), and lists the intercept (29.33) in the beta column. The text then reads the standardized betas as unstandardized slopes (a rise of 0.37 in breakthrough for each unit of grief) and says unstandardized coefficients were reported, though no such column exists.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's interpretation of slope sizes is wrong by more than an order of magnitude: the implied unstandardized slope for grief is about 7 EBI points per CEQ unit (editors' calculation from t and SE).

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% interval printed for Acceptance and Reappraisal (0.16 to 0.26) does not contain its own estimate (beta = 0.33); the intervals for death (0.07 to 0.19 around 0.17), grief (0.28 to 0.42 around 0.37) and fear (−0.30 to −0.14 around −0.24) are lopsided. None can be reproduced from Table 4 (editors' calculation gives about 0.25 to 0.41 for acceptance by rescaling the interval of B).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed intervals cannot be used; the significance of these predictors is not in doubt (t = 8.29, 4.45 and 9.78), but their precision should be quoted from Table 4's t values, not from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The location of the ReCiPE is given as Supplementary Material S.II in the Methods and as S.V in the Results; S.II is also cited for the qualitative findings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; readers looking for the scale must check both sections of the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The factor named Acceptance and Reappraisal is a count of 11 strategies judged helpful that, besides letting go, observing the mind and reappraisal items, includes two confrontational responses, assertively telling the experience to stop (item 4, loading 0.17, kept) and directing anger or aggression at it (item 5, 0.43), as well as journaling, focusing on breathing, closing the eyes or lying down (cross-loading), asking forgiveness and calling on spirits or a deity. The abstract reports the factor's association with emotional breakthrough under its label, and the Discussion links it to acceptance-based preparation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 and its note; Results › Study 2: online survey › Factor analysis, 2nd paragraph; Reliability, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Discussion, 4th and 8th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The r = 0.50 and beta 0.33 belong to a mixed count, not to acceptance alone; cite them as the 11 strategies the authors grouped as acceptance and reappraisal, naming what the group includes.
