design_detail: Retrospective review of the 70 deaths in Liverpool that the national programme on Substance Abuse Deaths (np-SAD, a register fed by coroners) reported as drug-related deaths (DRDs): 57 deaths that occurred in 2004 (np-SAD annual report) and 28 DRD inquests completed in January to June 2005 (np-SAD surveillance report), with double counting removed (85 listed, 70 kept; 15 duplicates by editors' arithmetic). For each death the authors read Liverpool coroner's and Drug and Alcohol Action Team (DAAT) records and linked the person (initials, date of birth, sex) to the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System and to drug-related criminal-justice databases (Drug Arrest Referral 2003/04 and Drug Interventions Programme 2004/05 in the Methods; Table 1 and its footnote 3 give contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06, reporting issue 9). Deaths are compared across np-SAD's own three categories, 'drug abuser/dependent' (38; called here the problem-drug-use group), 'non-drug abuser/dependent' (21; here the group without problem drug use) and 'unknown' (11), with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and a Mann-Whitney U test. One results paragraph and one table; no multivariable analysis. Liverpool was chosen because np-SAD reported it had the highest number of DRDs in 2004. The Discussion adds an argument, from cited sources, that the national, np-SAD and European definitions all leave out deaths from injection-related infections. The authors call the study preliminary.
can_establish: What the local drug-related-death count that np-SAD supplied for performance monitoring contained in one city over about 18 months: how many deaths np-SAD itself placed outside its problem-drug-use category, how old they were, what toxicology found, how many were deaths from drug toxicity, how many were of non-residents, and how many of the people had been in contact with drug treatment or drug-related criminal-justice services as found by record linkage.
cannot_establish: How many drug-related deaths any definition misses (only deaths already in the count were examined, so the undercounting argument about infections rests on cited sources); how the same deaths would be counted under the narrower national or European definitions (never applied to the 70); whether the pattern holds outside Liverpool or after 2005 (one high-count city); or which drug caused any death (toxicology is presence only, the share of deaths tested is not reported, and who decided 'death from drug toxicity', and how, is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: every death np-SAD reported as a DRD for Liverpool in two of its publications (Methods). np-SAD's wider definition, used for the local performance figures, counts 'relevant deaths' in which psychoactive substances were implicated, whether or not controlled under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and with or without a post-mortem, or in which there was a history of drug abuse, or in which controlled drugs were present at post-mortem (Background, 2nd paragraph, citing np-SAD's surveillance report). Information on each person came from Liverpool DAAT and coroner records and from the two linked monitoring systems (Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: all 57 deaths np-SAD's annual report gave for Liverpool in 2004 and all 28 DRD inquests its surveillance report gave for January to June 2005, minus double counts. No exclusions are described. The study period is given as 1 January 2004 to 30 June 2005 in the abstract and Table 1 title, but the two source lists use different time bases (deaths occurring in 2004; inquests completed in the first half of 2005).
sample.demographics: Men 45 of 70 (64.3%): 24 (63.2%) in the problem-drug-use group, 13 (61.9%) in the group without problem drug use, 8 (72.7%) unknown, p=0.924. Median age at death 42.36 years (IQR 33.28 to 51.35): 38.23 (32.39 to 44.07), 53.59 (44.13 to 65.81) and 41.15 (29.99 to 52.21). Resident in Liverpool 55 (78.6%): 27 (71.1%), 18 (85.7%), 10 (90.9%), p=0.338. Known history of alcohol abuse 22 (31.4%): 10 (26.3%), 7 (33.3%), 5 (45.5%), p=0.569 (Table 1). Ethnicity, employment, living situation, manner or intent of death and psychiatric history are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 11 deaths (15.7%) were in np-SAD's 'unknown' category because the information was not available (Methods); they appear in Table 1 but are left out of every comparison.
sample.selection_effects: One city, chosen because np-SAD reported it as the area of the UK with the highest number of DRDs in 2004, so not a representative area. A death enters only if a coroner reported it to np-SAD; how completely Liverpool coroners reported is not described. The two source lists mix year of death with year of inquest, so the 70 are not the deaths of a defined period. 15 of the 70 (21.4%, editors' arithmetic) were not Liverpool residents, so the city's count partly reflects where people died or were investigated rather than where they lived.

exposure.measurement: The grouping variable is a register classification, not measured drug use. np-SAD assigns its categories from coroners' information (Table 1, footnote 1): 'drug abuser/dependent' requires a known history of drug abuse and at least one of four criteria: (1) reported by the coroner as known to use illicit drugs; (2) prescribed substitute medication for drug dependence; (3) a non-prescribed illicit drug present at post-mortem; (4) other information in the coroner's report suggesting a history of drug abuse. 'Non-drug abuser/dependent' means none of the four was met; 'unknown' means the information was not available (Methods). The Methods say the 70 were 'categorised accordingly', while the footnote says np-SAD made the classification, so whether the authors re-applied the criteria is not fully clear (the Abstract and the Results attribute the categories to np-SAD). Toxicology is reported as drugs known to have been detected, which did not necessarily contribute to the death (Table 1, footnote 2); laboratory, specimens, screening panels and the number of deaths tested are not stated. Service contact was found by matching initials, date of birth and sex to the treatment and criminal-justice databases; the accuracy of the matching is not assessed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported. Toxicology is given only as presence or absence of heroin/morphine, methadone, alcohol and cocaine, without concentrations.
exposure.polysubstance: Detected at post-mortem, problem-drug-use group against group without problem drug use: heroin/morphine 22 (57.9%) vs 3 (14.3%), methadone 12 (31.6%) vs 1 (4.8%), cocaine 16 (42.1%) vs 0, alcohol 15 (39.5%) vs 11 (52.4%) (Table 1). Combinations are not tabulated. The text says the toxicity deaths in the group without problem drug use mostly involved antidepressants, antipsychotics and opioid analgesics, without counts (Results; Discussion, 1st paragraph). The authors note that heroin and morphine cannot be told apart at post-mortem (Results).

comparison.controls: A comparison inside the count: the 38 deaths np-SAD placed in its problem-drug-use category against the 21 it placed outside it. There is no second register, no enhanced review of the deaths, and no re-count of the same 70 deaths under the narrower national (Drug Strategy) or European definitions.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the main question. For the group comparison: causes of death other than drug toxicity, intent (suicide, accident, undetermined), prescribed medicines, mental-health history and whether a post-mortem or toxicology was done are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Being outside the problem-drug-use category means only that none of np-SAD's four criteria was recorded. In that group alcohol was detected in 11 of 21 (52.4%), 7 (33.3%) had a known history of alcohol abuse, heroin/morphine was detected in 3 and methadone in 1 (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: From coroner and DAAT records and the two linked databases: sex, residence in Liverpool, detection of heroin/morphine, methadone, alcohol and cocaine, known history of alcohol abuse, drug treatment contact and drug-related criminal-justice contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06, death from drug(s) toxicity, and age at death (Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: None reported: toxicology methods are not described and the record linkage was not validated.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Death from drug(s) toxicity' includes toxicity from prescribed drugs (Table 1, footnote 4); who decided it (the coroner's conclusion, the pathologist's cause of death, or the authors reading the records) and on what criteria is not stated, and manner or intent is not recorded. 'Recent' contact means a matched record in the 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06 data year. A DRD is whatever np-SAD counted under its wider definition; the paper does not report the ICD-10 codes or causes of the 25 deaths that were not from drug toxicity.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 11 comparisons in Table 1 (10 chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and one Mann-Whitney U test), each at p<0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts, percentages and p-values only; no intervals or effect sizes. Editors' calculations (Wilson 95% intervals): deaths outside the problem-drug-use category 21 of 70, 30.0% (20.5 to 41.5), or 21 of the 59 with known status, 35.6% (24.6 to 48.3); deaths from drug toxicity 45 of 70, 64.3% (52.6 to 74.5); deaths not from drug toxicity 25 of 70, 35.7% (25.5 to 47.4). Toxicity deaths 90.5% in the group without problem drug use against 50.0% in the problem-drug-use group, a difference of 40.5 percentage points (Newcombe 95% interval 15.9 to 57.1; editors' calculation). Median age difference 15.4 years (z=3.942, P<0.001). Every printed p-value reproduces with Fisher's exact test or the uncorrected chi-square test on the Table 1 counts (editors' recalculation), and every percentage and total in Table 1 is consistent with its counts.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported, though available in the records the authors read: the causes of the 25 deaths that were not from drug toxicity (19 in the problem-drug-use group), the drugs responsible for the 45 toxicity deaths, intent, how many deaths had a post-mortem or toxicology, and how many of the 70 would have been counted under the national or European definitions.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The group without problem drug use has 21 deaths and the unknown group 11, so percentages carry intervals of about plus or minus 10 to 20 points.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of the 70 deaths np-SAD reported as DRDs for Liverpool (deaths in 2004 and inquests completed in the first half of 2005), np-SAD placed 38 in its problem-drug-use category, 21 outside it and 11 as unknown. The 21 were older (median 53.6 against 38.2 years), none had linked treatment or criminal-justice contact (against 31.6% and 18.4% of the problem-drug-use group), heroin/morphine, methadone and cocaine were detected less often, and 19 of them (90.5%) died of drug toxicity, against 19 of 38 (50.0%) in the problem-drug-use group. Half of the problem-drug-use deaths in the count were therefore not deaths from drug toxicity; what they died of is not reported. 15 of the 70 were not Liverpool residents.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the national monitoring system “includes deaths of people who are not drug abusers” (Abstract, Conclusion); this is supported in the register's sense, but the group means only that none of np-SAD's four criteria was recorded by the coroner, not that the person never used drugs (alcohol was found in 52% of them). The abstract presents their different post-mortem drug profiles and absent service contact as findings; both are partly built into the classification, because a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem or substitute prescribing places a death in the problem-drug-use category, so 0% cocaine outside it is expected by construction and 0% treatment contact partly so, which the paper does not say. The abstract adds that the compact definitions fail to include deaths attributable to drug misuse, such as those from blood-borne viruses; this is not a result of the study (it examined only deaths already counted and has no data on infection deaths) but an argument from the definitions and cited figures (16% of deaths among drug-treatment clients in the North West of England due to infections, from the first author's earlier study; hepatitis C in nearly half of people who inject drugs in the UK; an estimated 4% progressing to severe cirrhosis, from a modelling study of people who inject drugs in Scotland, with no time frame) (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The Discussion calls the investigation preliminary. The conclusion that the true burden of drug-related mortality is unknown is an argument consistent with the data, not a measurement.

timeline.event: Webb et al. analysed cause and manner of death in drug-related deaths recorded by coroners in England and Wales in 2000, including deaths recorded as overdose that had another cause (on the project's drug-deaths list; not read for this card).
This study: composition of np-SAD's Liverpool drug-related-death count, 2004 to mid-2005.

A study of ketamine deaths notified to the same coroner-fed register (NPSAD) describes its inclusion criteria as still covering deaths with only a drug history or a controlled drug present at post-mortem (as recorded on card sc_corkery_2021, written by another reader).

Chen et al. compared Office for National Statistics data with National Programme on Substance Use Mortality data for opioid-related deaths in England and Wales (title as listed; read by another reader in this round).

replication.where_it_stands: No repetition in another area is reported in the paper. The project's reading list for this topic (search-logs/DrugDeaths_DOI-LIST.md, section 1, Known gaps) names this paper and Goldberger et al. (2013) as the only peer-reviewed comparisons of drug-death definitions its PubMed search found, and found no recent paper comparing the European, ONS 'drug poisoning' and 'drug misuse', Scottish and US definitions side by side. The study remains a single-city, single-period illustration that a wide register definition adds deaths outside drug services' reach; its undercounting argument has to be supported from studies that link people who use drugs to all their deaths.

funding.funder: The investigation into drug-related deaths in Liverpool was funded by the Department for Public Health, Liverpool Primary Care Trust (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors from the Centre for Public Health, Liverpool John Moores University, whose staff manage the monitoring systems used for the linkage (Acknowledgements); one from Liverpool Primary Care Trust, the funder; one from the Liverpool Drug and Alcohol Action Team, the kind of body whose performance the DRD figures were used to monitor. The conclusion (the figures include deaths outside DAATs' reach) bears on that body's performance assessment. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount; the counts and categories are np-SAD's.

what_would_settle_it: Apply np-SAD's wider definition, the national (Drug Strategy and ONS) definition and the European definition to the same complete set of deaths in several areas and years, from full coroner files, recording for each death the cause and manner, whether a post-mortem and toxicology were done and what they found, and service contact by validated linkage; and, for the undercount, link a cohort of people in drug treatment to all their death registrations to count the deaths from infections and other causes that no drug-related-death definition captures.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The frame is np-SAD's own list of Liverpool DRDs, which is exactly the target when the question is what the performance figures contained; but it is one city, chosen for having the highest count, and built from two lists with different time bases (year of death, year of inquest).
Every death on both lists was included and double counts removed; no sampling.

The whole local count, but small: 21 of 70 outside the problem-drug-use category is 30.0% with a 95% interval of about 20.5% to 41.5% (editors' calculation), and the group comparisons rest on 21 deaths.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives sex, residence, age, four toxicology findings, alcohol history, service contact and toxicity deaths by category, but not causes or manner of death, the drugs responsible for the toxicity deaths, or how many deaths had a post-mortem or toxicology.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 70 appear in Table 1, but the 11 deaths with unknown status (15.7%) are left out of every comparison, and the coverage of toxicology and of the linkage is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: np-SAD's criteria for its categories are stated, but they depend on what each coroner's file happened to record; 'death from drug toxicity' is not defined and who decided it is not stated; the linkage on initials, date of birth and sex was not validated, so contacts may be missed.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: np-SAD counts deaths with or without a post-mortem, and the paper does not say how many of the 70 had toxicology or which substances were screened, so 'not detected' cannot be separated from 'not tested'; coroners' files vary in content.

Fisher's exact, chi-square and Mann-Whitney tests suit small groups and every printed p-value reproduces (editors' recalculation), but no intervals are given, 11 tests are uncorrected, and the toxicology and contact comparisons are partly built into the classification.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Records of all reported deaths; no response was required. Missing classification is covered under item 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for record-linkage and certificate studies, because the study describes the composition of a death count (no exposure-outcome question that ROBINS-E could address). For what np-SAD's Liverpool figures contained, the study is direct: it reads the count itself and np-SAD's own categories, so the composition (21 of 70 deaths outside the problem-drug-use category; 25 of 70 not deaths from drug toxicity; 15 of 70 of non-residents) can be cited with its small numbers and its single city and period. Confidence is lower for the group comparisons, because the toxicity classification is undefined, toxicology coverage is unknown and the toxicology and service-contact differences are partly circular. It may be cited for: np-SAD's wider definition as described in 2007; the composition of one local count used for performance monitoring; and, attributed to the authors as an argument, that the national, np-SAD and European definitions of the time left out deaths from injection-related infections. It may not be cited as a measurement of undercounting (no deaths outside the count were examined), for other places or later years, or for which medicines caused the toxicity deaths (no counts given).

key_findings.finding: Of 70 deaths np-SAD reported as drug-related for Liverpool, it placed 38 (54.3%) in its 'drug abuser/dependent' category, 21 (30.0%) in 'non-drug abuser/dependent' and 11 (15.7%) as unknown.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, row n
key_findings.note: Percentages are editors' arithmetic from Table 1; the text says half were in the first category.

key_findings.finding: The 70 deaths came from two np-SAD publications: 57 deaths that occurred in Liverpool in 2004 (annual report) and 28 DRD inquests completed in Liverpool in January to June 2005 (surveillance report), with double counting removed (85 listed, so 15 duplicates by editors' arithmetic).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Definitions in force: the UK Drug Strategy definition counts a death whose underlying cause is poisoning, drug abuse or drug dependence and in which a drug controlled under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 is involved (16,088 such deaths in England and Wales, 1993 to 2004, from ONS); the local performance figures came from np-SAD's wider definition, which also counts psychoactive substances not controlled under the Act, deaths with or without a post-mortem, deaths with a history of drug abuse and deaths with controlled drugs present at post-mortem. The European and England and Wales definitions are described as similar and compact.
key_findings.locator: Background, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: np-SAD's rule for its problem-drug-use category: a known history of drug abuse plus at least one of: reported by the coroner as known to use illicit drugs; prescribed substitute medication for dependence; a non-prescribed illicit drug present at post-mortem; other information in the coroner's report suggesting drug abuse. Deaths meeting none are classed as not drug abuser/dependent, and deaths without the information as unknown.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 1, footnote 1

key_findings.finding: The group without problem drug use was older at death: median 53.59 years (IQR 44.13 to 65.81) against 38.23 (32.39 to 44.07) in the problem-drug-use group, about 15 years, z=3.942, P<0.001 (Mann-Whitney U); all 70: median 42.36 (33.28 to 51.35).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, row age at death

key_findings.finding: Death from drug(s) toxicity, including toxicity from prescribed drugs: 19 of 38 (50.0%) in the problem-drug-use group, 19 of 21 (90.5%) in the group without problem drug use (p=0.002), 7 of 11 (63.6%) unknown, 45 of 70 (64.3%) overall. So 25 of the 70 counted deaths (35.7%; 19 in the problem-drug-use group) were not deaths from drug toxicity (editors' arithmetic); their causes are not reported. The text says the toxicity deaths outside the problem-drug-use group mostly involved antidepressants, antipsychotics and opioid analgesics, without counts.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, row death from drug(s) toxicity and footnote 4
key_findings.note: Who decided that a death was from drug toxicity, and on what criteria, is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Drugs detected at post-mortem (not necessarily contributing to death), problem-drug-use group against group without problem drug use: heroin/morphine 22 (57.9%) vs 3 (14.3%), p=0.001; methadone 12 (31.6%) vs 1 (4.8%), p=0.022; cocaine 16 (42.1%) vs 0, p<0.001; alcohol 15 (39.5%) vs 11 (52.4%), p=0.339. All 70: heroin/morphine 27 (38.6%), methadone 13 (18.6%), cocaine 19 (27.1%), alcohol 31 (44.3%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, toxicology rows and footnote 2; Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The share of deaths with toxicology is not reported, so these are minimum proportions; the illicit-drug differences are partly built into np-SAD's classification (criterion 3).

key_findings.finding: Linked service contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06: drug treatment 12 of 38 (31.6%) and drug-related criminal justice 7 of 38 (18.4%) in the problem-drug-use group; none in the group without problem drug use (p=0.005 and p=0.043) or in the unknown group; 12 of 70 (17.1%) and 7 of 70 (10.0%) overall. Matching used initials, date of birth and sex.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, contact rows and footnote 3; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 55 of the 70 deaths (78.6%) were of Liverpool residents, so 15 (21.4%, editors' arithmetic) of the deaths in the city's count were of people living elsewhere: 27 (71.1%) residents in the problem-drug-use group, 18 (85.7%) in the group without problem drug use, 10 (90.9%) unknown, p=0.338.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, row resident in Liverpool

key_findings.finding: Example of a death in the count: a person over 90 with coronary heart disease who died of myocardial insufficiency with contributory carbamazepine toxicity, classed outside the problem-drug-use category.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that the np-SAD, England and Wales and European definitions all exclude deaths from bacterial and viral infections, often transmitted by injecting, and cite (not from this study) 16% of deaths among drug-treatment clients in the North West of England due to infections, hepatitis C in nearly half of people who inject drugs in the UK, and an estimated 4% progressing to severe, potentially fatal cirrhosis (no time frame given); they propose adding deaths from blood-borne infections to the international definition.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; references 9 and 11
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; the 16% comes from the first author's own earlier study, and the 4% from a modelling study of people who inject drugs in Scotland (reference 11, Hutchinson et al., 2005), which the authors apply to the UK and Europe. This study has no data on infection deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says the proportion of DRDs with recent treatment or criminal-justice contact was 31.6% and 18.4%; Table 1 shows these are the proportions in the problem-drug-use group (12 of 38, 7 of 38), while among all 70 DRDs they are 17.1% and 10.0%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim about service contact among all counted deaths must use 17.1% and 10.0%; the printed figures are nearly twice the whole-count figures (31.6/17.1 and 18.4/10.0 are both about 1.85, editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says heroin/morphine was detected in half of the problem-drug-use group; Table 1 gives 22 of 38 (57.9%). The text also says half of the DRDs were in that group (38 of 70, 54.3%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the table values.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Table 1 title give the period as 1 January 2004 to 30 June 2005, but the 70 deaths combine deaths that occurred in 2004 with inquests completed in January to June 2005; deaths in early 2005 without a completed inquest by June are absent, and deaths before 2004 with inquests in early 2005 could be included.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Abstract, Methods; Table 1 title
reporting_issues.consequence: The 70 is not a count of deaths in a defined period and cannot be turned into a rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say how many of the 70 deaths had a post-mortem or toxicology, which laboratory or specimens were used, or which substances were screened, although np-SAD counts deaths with or without a post-mortem.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Background, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, footnote 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The detection percentages are minimums over an unknown tested denominator, and 'not detected' cannot be separated from 'not tested'.

reporting_issues.issue: 'Death from drug(s) toxicity' is defined only as including prescribed drugs; who decided it (coroner, pathologist or the authors) is not stated, intent is not recorded, and the causes of the 25 deaths not from drug toxicity are not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1, footnote 4; Results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 90.5% against 50.0% contrast cannot be checked against a stated rule, and what np-SAD's wider definition added beyond toxicity deaths cannot be seen.

reporting_issues.issue: The Background lists among np-SAD's 'relevant deaths' those in which there is a history of drug abuse, without saying which causes of death count as relevant, and Table 1 shows that 25 of the 70 counted deaths were not deaths from drug toxicity; the Discussion says the np-SAD definition excludes deaths from bacterial and viral infections. The paper does not reconcile the two or say whether any of the 25 non-toxicity deaths were infection deaths.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Background, 2nd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Which non-toxicity deaths the wide definition counted, and whether infection deaths were among them, is unknown; the claim that np-SAD excludes infection deaths should be attributed to the authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparisons of illicit-drug detection and service contact between np-SAD's categories are partly circular: a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem and substitute prescribing are among the criteria that place a death in the problem-drug-use category. The paper does not acknowledge this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 0% cocaine outside the problem-drug-use category is expected by construction (a non-prescribed illicit drug at post-mortem is criterion 3). The 0% treatment and criminal-justice contact are partly so: substitute prescribing is criterion 2, and other treatment or drug-related arrests count only if the coroner's file records them (criteria 1 and 4), whereas the linkage looked beyond that file. None of these is an independent finding; the age and toxicity-death differences are not affected in this way.

reporting_issues.issue: Whether the authors re-applied np-SAD's criteria or used np-SAD's own assignments is ambiguous (Methods: categorised accordingly; Table 1 footnote 1: the classification is made by np-SAD), though only mildly, since the Abstract and the Results also attribute the categories to np-SAD. Minor typographical points: the abstract reads 'cv. 31.6%', and the p-value column heading says 'not a drug user/dependent' where the row label says abuser.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Abstract, Results
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the categories should be cited as np-SAD's.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name the criminal-justice sources as Drug Arrest Referral (2003/04) and its successor, the Drug Interventions Programme database (2004/05), while the Table 1 row covers contact in 2003/04, 2004/05 or 2005/06 and footnote 3 names the Arrest Referral Scheme in 2003/04 and the Drug Interventions Programme in 2004/05 and 2005/06; the Methods give no years for the treatment database, whose Table 1 row covers the same three years.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 1, contact rows and footnote 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the years from Table 1 and its footnote (2003/04 to 2005/06).

design_detail: Analysis of US national death-certificate data: the Mortality Multiple Cause micro-data files of the National Vital Statistics System (National Center for Health Statistics), 1999–2015, for all 50 states and the District of Columbia. All deaths with an underlying cause of unintentional drug poisoning (ICD-10 X40–X44) were classed by their contributory T codes as opioid-related (any of T40.0–T40.4 or T40.6, with or without other drugs), non-opioid-related (other drug codes only) or unspecified (T50.9 only). For each state and year, unspecified deaths were then 'reallocated' to opioids in proportion to the opioid share among deaths with a named drug, and reported and reallocated 2015 state mortality rates and ranks were compared. Suicides (X60–X64), assaults (X85) and deaths of undetermined intent (Y10–Y14) were excluded. There was no linkage to toxicology or investigation records and no validation of the reallocation.
can_establish: How many unintentional overdose deaths in the US in 1999–2015 were certified with no drug named, how that share differed between states (from none in Washington DC to 50.8% in Pennsylvania in 2015), and how much state opioid mortality rates and rankings would change if unspecified deaths involved opioids as often as deaths with a named drug in the same state and year.
cannot_establish: How many unspecified deaths actually involved opioids, or were caused by them (the reallocation is an assumption the authors call rather strong, never checked against toxicology or case records); whether certified opioid-related deaths were caused by opioids (an opioid code counts a death as opioid-related whatever other drugs were coded); deaths certified as suicide or of undetermined intent; or why certificates lacked a drug (testing, certifier, resources were not measured).

sample.recruitment: Registry: every death certificate filed with the vital statistics offices of the 50 states and the District of Columbia, as coded by the National Center for Health Statistics into the multiple-cause micro-data files, 1999–2015 (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: deaths with an underlying cause of unintentional drug poisoning, ICD-10 X40–X44, with all contributory T codes. Excluded: drug-poisoning deaths of other intent, namely suicide (X60–X64), assault (X85) and undetermined intent (Y10–Y14) (Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported. No age, sex or race breakdown is given; the authors list comparing the age, race, sex and geography of deaths with and without a named drug as future work (Strengths and Weaknesses, 1st and 4th paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (complete registrations). 313 deaths had no drug T code at all; how they were handled in the reallocation is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Restricting to unintentional deaths leaves out overdose deaths certified as undetermined intent, whose share varies by state; the authors note that states with more undetermined deaths are less affected by their reallocation (Strengths and Weaknesses, 2nd paragraph). Within the unintentional deaths, which deaths lack a named drug depends on each jurisdiction's testing and certification, which the study did not measure.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count: the certifier (a coroner or medical examiner) records the drugs on the death certificate; the National Center for Health Statistics assigns the underlying cause (X40–X44 for unintentional drug poisoning) and the contributory T codes from what was recorded, under WHO rules (Introduction, 2nd paragraph). 'Opioid-related' means at least one of T40.0 (opium), T40.1 (heroin), T40.2 (other opioids, i.e. opioid pain relievers), T40.3 (methadone), T40.4 (other synthetic narcotics, e.g. fentanyl) or T40.6 (other and unspecified narcotics); 'unspecified' means T50.9 as the only drug code. T50.9 is also used for drugs with no specific code, such as bath salts, which the authors judge affects only a tiny proportion of deaths (Methods, 2nd paragraph). No toxicology data were used, and the paper does not report what was tested in what share of deaths.
exposure.polysubstance: An opioid-related death may also carry non-opioid codes; by Table 1, 115,192 of the 255,527 opioid-related deaths (45%) also had a non-opioid drug code, and 100,650 (39%) also carried T50.9 (editors' calculation from Table 1 rows). Each death is counted once, in the opioid category if any opioid is coded. Opioid subtypes are not mutually exclusive: opioid pain relievers 41.5%, heroin 25.4%, methadone 20.3%, other and unspecified narcotics 14.4%, synthetic opioids other than methadone 14.2%, opium 0.01% (Results, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: No external comparison: reported counts and rates are compared with the same counts after reallocation. In the Discussion, the states most affected are compared qualitatively with Ruhm's corrected state rates (different method, all intents) and with Warner et al.'s classification of state death-investigation systems.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Characteristics that could make unspecified deaths differ from specified ones (age, sex, race, place, toxicology availability, certifier type and experience, jurisdiction size) were not measured; the authors name them as reasons the key assumption may fail.

outcomes.instruments: Counts and percentages of unintentional overdose deaths by state and year in each drug category; reported and reallocated 2015 opioid-related mortality rates per 100,000 population, state ranks, percentage change in rate and change in rank (Table 2). Analysis in SAS 9.4.
outcomes.validity_norms: The opioid category is only as valid as the drug information certifiers write and coders translate, which is the problem studied; reallocated deaths are model estimates, not observations, with no validation.
outcomes.operationalization: Reallocated opioid deaths = unspecified deaths in a state-year multiplied by the opioid share of specified deaths in that state-year (Methods, 4th paragraph). The paper also describes the share as opioid-related among all overdose deaths (same paragraph, Table 2 footnote, Figure 3 legend); the published numbers match the specified-death version (reporting issue 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive counts and rates; no hypothesis tests except an unreported comparison of unspecified shares by state death-investigation system, said to be not significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only, with no confidence or uncertainty intervals. 1999–2015: 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths, 58% opioid-related, 20% non-opioid, 22% unspecified. Opioid-related deaths rose from 5,868 (1999) to 29,383 (2015), +401%; non-opioid from 3,005 to 7,505, +150%; unspecified from 2,255 to 7,227, +220%, peaking at 8,145 in 2011. Unspecified share of unintentional overdose deaths about 20% in 1999 and 16% in 2015 (editors' calculation, 2,255 of 11,128 and 7,227 of 44,115, ignoring deaths with no drug code). 2015: unspecified above 35% in 5 states (Pennsylvania 50.8% highest), below 5% in 17, none in Washington DC. Reallocation: more than 70,000 deaths for 1999–2015 (9 in Vermont to 11,152 in Pennsylvania), at least 72% of the 97,159 unspecified deaths (editors' calculation); 5,662 in 2015 (sum of Table 2), raising the national 2015 count from 29,383 to about 35,045 (+19%, editors' calculation). 2015 state rates rose by less than 1% in 5 states and by over 50% in 5 (Pennsylvania 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000, +103%).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No sensitivity analysis of the reallocation assumption (for example by age, sex, place or certifier) and no uncertainty around reallocated counts. The comparison of unspecified shares by death-investigation system in 2015 is reported only as not significant, without numbers or a test.
analysis.power: Not applicable (complete registrations); small state-year counts make some state proportions unstable, which is not discussed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US death certificates, 22% of unintentional overdose deaths in 1999–2015 named no drug, with very large differences between states. If those deaths involved opioids as often as deaths with a named drug in the same state and year, about 70,000 more deaths would count as opioid-related over 17 years (5,662 in 2015, about a fifth more than reported), and the 2015 opioid death rate would double in Pennsylvania and rise by more than half in four other states, while barely changing in states that name drugs on nearly every certificate.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say "Potentially 70 000 opioid-related, unintentional overdose deaths" from 1999 through 2015 "have been missed", and the abstract that states may be "greatly underestimating" opioid deaths. Gaps: (1) the 70,000 is the product of an assumption the authors themselves call rather strong and did not test; no unspecified death was checked against toxicology or case records, so the true number could be higher or lower; (2) the method can only add opioid deaths, and the paper does not consider the other direction, deaths counted as opioid-related because an opioid was coded among several drugs (45% of opioid-related deaths also had a non-opioid code, editors' calculation); (3) the Discussion takes agreement with Ruhm's corrections on which states are most affected as support that the states were correctly identified, but both analyses use the same certificates, so agreement shows robustness to the method, not accuracy; (4) the abstract gives the wrong end value for unspecified deaths (29,383 instead of 7,227); (5) the Discussion reads Kentucky's 1999–2015 rise of 43% in opioid-related drug codes and fall of 28% in unspecified reporting as suggesting that state-based efforts can improve drug-specific reporting, but this is a before-and-after change in one state, with no comparison state and no dates for the efforts, and the paper does not say whether the figures are percentage points or relative changes (Discussion, 4th paragraph). The body is more careful than the conclusion: it says 'could be categorized' and 'potentially', and states its assumptions in a limitations section.

timeline.event: Warner et al. (Academic Forensic Pathology): states with centralized medical examiner systems specified drugs on 92% of drug-intoxication certificates against 62% for decentralized county coroner systems, as quoted in this paper's Discussion.
Slavova et al., 'Drug overdose deaths: let's get specific': variation in unspecified drug reporting across 11 states in 2010, which this paper's Discussion describes in the first person (ref 11)
Ruhm (Population Health Metrics): statistical adjustment of drug-poisoning deaths, 1999–2012 (ref 9).

Ruhm (Addiction): corrected national opioid-involved deaths 1999–2015, all intents, by regression prediction; largest corrections in 2011 for any opioid and 2015 for heroin and synthetic opioids, as summarized in this paper (ref 15)

Horon et al.: in Maryland, linking toxicology and scene investigation to certificates found 1,052 more heroin-related deaths in 2012–2015 (card sc_horon_2018); an external check by record linkage in one state

Lowder et al. (American Journal of Public Health), as summarized by Gutkind et al.: 86.8% of unspecified overdose deaths in Marion County, Indiana, 2011–2016, were opioid-positive in toxicology, more than this paper's assumed share.

Slavova et al., review of methodological complexities in counting opioid overdose deaths, with Buchanich among its authors, relays this paper's estimate of about 70,000 unaccounted-for deaths (card sc_slavova_2019); not independent support.
Gutkind et al. scoping review includes this study among the national analyses of unspecified deaths (card sc_gutkind_2025)

replication.where_it_stands: The direction is supported: every correction method and every state or county linkage study summarized by Gutkind et al. (2025) found more opioid-involved deaths than the certificates alone. Agreement with Ruhm's corrections on the most affected states is partial replication on the same national certificates, not an independent check, and the 2019 review by Slavova et al., which relays the 70,000 estimate, has Buchanich among its authors. The size of the national correction remains a model estimate; no national validation against toxicology exists in the papers read for this round. The share of unspecified certificates fell after 2015 (8% of overdose deaths in 2018, per Gutkind et al.), so these 1999–2015 corrections should not be carried forward to later years.

funding.affiliations_note: University of Pittsburgh Graduate School of Public Health (two authors: Buchanich in the Department of Biostatistics; Burke, the school), Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine (Department of Preventive Medicine; Balmert), and the Office of the Medical Examiner of Allegheny County, Pittsburgh (Williams; the article gives the office, not his role), in Pennsylvania, the state with the highest share of unspecified certificates in 2015. Buchanich is a co-author of the 2019 review by Slavova et al. (card sc_slavova_2019).

what_would_settle_it: A national or multi-state sample of overdose deaths certified with no named drug, linked to their post-mortem toxicology and investigation files, with the drugs found compared with the drugs in specified deaths from the same jurisdictions and years; this would test the reallocation assumption directly and show whether unspecified deaths involve opioids more often, less often or as often as specified ones, separately for coroner and medical-examiner systems.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All US death registrations is the right frame, but restricting to deaths certified as unintentional leaves out overdose deaths of undetermined intent, whose share varies by state.
A census of registered deaths, not a sample.
438,607 deaths nationally; some state-year counts are small, but the main estimates are national and state totals.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Data source, years, codes and categories are described in detail; no demographic description of the deaths and no account of each state's testing or certification practice.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All registered unintentional overdose deaths are analysed; the handling of 313 deaths with no drug code is not stated but cannot matter at this scale.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Opioid involvement is identified from certificate codes, whose completeness is the problem studied, and for unspecified deaths from an untested proportional assumption with no toxicology or case-record validation.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Drug specification depends on each jurisdiction's testing and certifier (coroner or medical examiner, centralized or not), which varies widely by state, as the paper itself shows.

Counts, percentages and rates are appropriate and Table 2's rates are internally consistent; but reallocated counts carry no uncertainty interval or sensitivity analysis, the denominator of the key proportion is described two ways, and one system comparison is reported only as not significant.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Death registration is complete; missing drug information is the subject of the study and is covered under items 6 and 7.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths from a national register (round brief, certificate studies). The tabulated shares of certificates naming no drug, by state and year, are a census of coded data with low risk of bias for what they describe: what certificates say, not what was in the body. The headline estimate, about 70,000 missed opioid deaths, rests on an untested assumption and on certificate codes whose quality varies by jurisdiction, so its risk of bias is high, in a direction that cannot be predicted; overall high, because that estimate is what the paper is cited for. Citable for: the number and share of unintentional overdose deaths certified with no drug named, 1999–2015, by state; the state range in 2015; how far state rates and ranks depend on unspecified certificates; a proportional-reallocation estimate of the possible undercount, labelled as such. Not citable for: the number of opioid deaths actually missed, or opioids as the cause of the reallocated deaths.

key_findings.finding: From 1999 through 2015 there were 438,607 unintentional drug-overdose deaths (ICD-10 X40–X44) in US death records: 255,527 (58%) opioid-related, 85,608 (20%) non-opioid-related, 97,159 (22%) with no drug named (T50.9 only) and 313 with no drug code.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 and its footnote f

key_findings.finding: Opioid-related unintentional overdose deaths rose from 5,868 in 1999 to 29,383 in 2015 (+401%); non-opioid-related from 3,005 to 7,505 (+150%); deaths with no drug named from 2,255 to 7,227 (+220%), with a peak of 8,145 in 2011.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract gives the 2015 value for unspecified deaths as 29,383, the opioid figure (reporting issue 1). Editors' calculation: the unspecified share of unintentional overdose deaths was about 20% in 1999 and 16% in 2015.

key_findings.finding: Among opioid-related deaths, the opioid codes recorded were opioid pain relievers 41.5%, heroin 25.4%, methadone 20.3%, other and unspecified narcotics 14.4%, synthetic opioids other than methadone 14.2% and opium 0.01% (not mutually exclusive).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: An opioid-related death could also carry other drug codes: by Table 1, 115,192 of 255,527 opioid-related deaths (45%) also had a non-opioid code, and 100,650 (39%) also had T50.9 (editors' calculation from the Table 1 rows).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (rows with opioid-related 'Yes'); Methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In 2015 the share of unintentional overdose deaths with no drug named exceeded 35% in 5 states (in descending order Pennsylvania, Louisiana, Alabama, Indiana, Mississippi), was below 5% in 17 states, was 0% in Washington DC and highest in Pennsylvania (50.8%). The opioid-related share ranged from 36.0% (Hawaii) to 97.0% (New Hampshire).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (values from Figure 2, an image, as stated in the text)

key_findings.finding: Between 1999 and 2015 the percentage of unspecified deaths fell in 35 states (by 0.2% in Louisiana to 42.2% in North Dakota) and rose in 16 (by 0.2% in New Mexico to 12.8% in New Jersey); the paper does not say whether these are percentage points or relative changes. The opioid-related percentage fell in 9 states (by 0.1% to 16.9%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Reallocating unspecified deaths in proportion to the opioid share of specified deaths in the same state and year added more than 70,000 potential opioid-related deaths for 1999–2015 (from 9 in Vermont to 11,152 in Pennsylvania); California, Florida and Pennsylvania each gained more than 5,000, reaching 30,813, 25,144 and 20,521; counts more than doubled in Alabama, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi and Pennsylvania.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Methods, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: more than 70,000 of 97,159 unspecified deaths is at least 72%.

key_findings.finding: In 2015, reallocation added 5,662 deaths to the 29,383 reported (sum of Table 2; the Discussion says more than 5,600). State rates changed by less than 1% in Connecticut, Washington DC, New Hampshire, Maine and Rhode Island and rose by more than 50% in Alabama (+94%), Indiana (+85%), Mississippi (+55%), Louisiana (+99%) and Pennsylvania (9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000, +103%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Table 2; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ranks: West Virginia highest before and after reallocation (31.2 and 31.6 per 100,000), South Dakota lowest; 8 states unchanged; Indiana, Louisiana, New Jersey and Pennsylvania rose at least 10 places (Indiana 34th to 15th); Oklahoma, South Carolina, Utah, Virginia and Washington fell 7 places.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: The text says 17 states rose in rank; Table 2 shows 15 (16 if Idaho's sign is corrected) (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Of the 5 states with the highest unspecified shares, 3 had hybrid coroner–medical examiner systems (Alabama, Mississippi, Pennsylvania) and 2 decentralized county coroner systems (Indiana, Louisiana); in 2015 states with centralized medical examiner systems had lower unspecified shares than the other three system types, but the differences were not significant (no figures given).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' stated assumptions: unspecified deaths involve opioids in the same proportion as specified deaths in the same state and year (called rather strong), and certifiers report drug information in the same way across their jurisdiction; drug reporting may depend on the extent of toxicology testing, post-mortem redistribution, certifier experience and jurisdiction size. Only unintentional deaths were examined, so states with more undetermined-intent deaths are less affected.
key_findings.locator: Strengths and Weaknesses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Even complete reporting loses detail in coding: ICD-10 has a fixed set of drug-class codes, so new drugs such as fentanyl analogues fall under T40.4, and toxicology may not detect newly emerging synthetic opioids, which then never reach the certificate.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says unspecified overdose deaths rose 220% 'from 2255 to 29 383'; the Results give 2,255 to 7,227 (7,227/2,255 is the stated +220%), and 29,383 is the 2015 opioid-related count.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's end value is wrong; cite 7,227 from the Results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods define the reallocation denominator as 'specified drug overdose deaths (any death coded as T30.6-T50.9)': T30.6 is not a drug code, and a range ending at T50.9 would include the unspecified deaths. The next sentence, the Table 2 footnote, the Figure 3 legend, the Abstract › Methods and Strengths and Weaknesses (1st paragraph) instead describe the opioid share of all unintentional overdose deaths.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 4th paragraph; Table 2 footnote a; Figure 3 legend; Abstract › Methods; Strengths and Weaknesses, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The published numbers fit the specified-death denominator: Pennsylvania's 1,307 reallocated against 1,268 reported implies an unspecified share of 50.8%, exactly the share the Results give, whereas the all-deaths version would imply 103% (editors' check). Nationally, the opioid share of deaths with a named drug (255,527 of 341,135, 74.9%) applied to the 97,159 unspecified deaths gives about 72,800, which fits 'more than 70,000', whereas the all-deaths share (58.3%) gives about 56,600 (editors' calculation; the paper reallocated by state and year). Readers should describe the method as reallocation by the opioid share of deaths with a named drug.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend assigns T36.0–T39.9 and T40.5–T50.8 to 'opioid-related' and T40.0–T40.4 to 'non–opioid-related', the reverse of the Methods (and omits T40.6).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figure 2 legend; Methods, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling error in the legend; the Methods' definitions should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the ranks of 17 states rose after reallocation; Table 2's change-in-rank column has 15 positive values. Idaho's change is printed as −2, although its rank columns go from 45th to 43rd, a rise of 2; with that corrected, 16 states rose (editors' count).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 6th paragraph; Table 2 (Idaho row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the number of states whose rank rose from Table 2's rank columns (16), or avoid the count.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the 5 states with the most reallocated deaths (California, Florida, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas) accounted for 46.4% (15,247 of 32,860) of reallocated deaths. This matches neither period: for 1999–2015 the total is over 70,000 and Pennsylvania alone gained 11,152 while California and Florida each gained over 5,000; for 2015 the total is 5,662 and the top five are Pennsylvania, Florida, California, Indiana and New Jersey (editors' check against Table 2).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph; Results, 4th paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The 46.4% concentration figure cannot be traced to the paper's own data and should not be cited; in 2015 the five states it names account for 2,674 of the 5,662 reallocated deaths (47.2%, editors' check), close to but not the printed share.

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote c of Table 1 describes underlying cause X42 as poisoning by psychodysleptics (hallucinogens) only, yet the Results say most opioid-related deaths were coded X42.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 footnote c; Results, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The footnote's label is incomplete; it does not affect the counts, which are classified by T codes.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion attributes corrected opioid and heroin death rates for 2014 by state to ref 9, whose title covers drug-poisoning deaths in 1999–2012.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison is probably with another Ruhm paper; it cannot be checked from the citation as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say whether the 2015 state rates in Table 2 are crude or age-adjusted, and names no population source; the column heading gives rates per 100,000 population. The populations the rates imply are of whole-state size (editors' calculation: 261 deaths at 5.37 per 100,000 gives about 4.86 million for Alabama, and 1,268 at 9.90 about 12.8 million for Pennsylvania), which fits crude rates.
reporting_issues.consequence: Compare these rates only with each other; they should not be set beside age-adjusted state rates, such as CDC's published rates.
