design_detail: National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) statistical report, National Vital Statistics Reports vol. 75, no. 1 (5 March 2026, pp. 1 to 13), updating the 2011 to 2016 report in the same series. Data: the 2017 to 2023 National Vital Statistics System (NVSS) mortality files for US residents who died in the United States, linked to the literal text of death certificates, retrieved from NCHS's live database on 6 April 2025. A death enters the overdose count when its ICD-10 underlying cause is X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (homicide) or Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent); a death enters a drug's count when that drug is mentioned in any of three certificate text fields (Part I causes, Part II contributing conditions, how the injury occurred), found by NCHS software (the Drugs Mentioned with Involvement, DMI, method) and assumed to be involved unless the surrounding words say otherwise. Deaths with several drugs are counted under each. Outputs: annual counts and percentages for the top 15 drugs (Table A), age-adjusted rates for 16 drugs with joinpoint trend tests (Table; Figures 1 to 4), the three commonest other drugs found with each of the top 10 drugs in 2023 (Table B), and the top 10 drugs by intent in 2023 (Table C). No toxicology data and no external validation. Filed as evidence-report with the editors' evidence-report checklist, as the round brief directs for statistics by public bodies.
can_establish: How many US drug overdose deaths in 2017 to 2023 (as defined by the four ICD-10 underlying-cause ranges) had each specific drug written on the death certificate, at minimum, how those counts and age-adjusted rates changed, which drugs were written together, and how the drugs named differed by recorded intent.
cannot_establish: How many deaths each drug caused (a mention is taken as involvement, and in multi-drug deaths the contribution of each drug cannot be told apart), how many deaths involving a drug were missed (the counts are minimums, toxicology practice is unseen and varies), how far trends reflect better reporting rather than real change (specificity rose from 87.7% to 96.0%), or anything about drug deaths outside these codes (chronic effects, adverse effects of therapeutic doses, deaths with other underlying causes).

sample.recruitment: Registry: all death certificates in the NVSS mortality files for 2017 to 2023 for US residents who died in the United States (NCHS codes data from 57 jurisdictions, mostly states), linked to literal text and retrieved on 6 April 2025 from a live database that continues to receive updates after the final files close, so counts may differ from other published sources (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Data and Methods › Data source and study population, 1st to 3rd paragraphs). n_total is the editors' sum of the seven annual totals in Table A.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: underlying cause X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14, which reflect acute intoxication. Excluded: deaths from chronic exposure to drugs (such as liver toxicity), adverse effects of therapeutic or prophylactic doses, and deaths of non-residents or abroad (Data and Methods › Data source and study population, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported in this report (no breakdown by sex, age or race). Manner across the period: unintentional 87% to 93%, suicide 4% to 7%, undetermined 3% to 5%, homicide 0.2% (Data source and study population, 1st paragraph). 2023: 98,497 unintentional, 4,711 suicide, 2,926 undetermined, 218 homicide (Table C; Results › by intent, 1st paragraph); these add to the 2023 total of 106,352 (editors' arithmetic).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Counts of 1 to 9 deaths are not shown and rates based on fewer than 20 deaths are not shown (Analysis, 3rd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: A death can enter a drug-specific count only if the certifier (usually a medical examiner or coroner for overdose deaths) wrote that drug on the certificate; whether toxicology was done, what was tested and how results were interpreted vary by jurisdiction, decedent and year (Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, bulleted list). Deaths without a named drug or drug class cannot enter any drug's count: 12.3% of overdose deaths in 2017 and 4.0% in 2023 had no ICD-10 multiple-cause code in T36.0 to T50.8 (about 8,700 and 4,300 deaths, editors' arithmetic from the percentages and annual totals). Drug deaths coded to other underlying causes are outside the overdose total by definition.

exposure.measurement: Drug involvement = a mention in the literal text written by the medical certifier, searched by the DMI software across Part I, Part II and the how-injury-occurred field (Introduction, 2nd paragraph). A mentioned drug is assumed involved unless contextual terms indicate otherwise (for example 'not drug related', or 'methicillin' within the name of an infection) (Identifying drug mentions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Search terms include generic and brand names, street names, abbreviations, metabolites and misspellings; the updated list was applied to the whole period, so numbers can differ from earlier reports (3rd paragraph). Terms map to 'principal variants' linked to the FDA's unique ingredient identifiers, and these to 'referent drug groups' defined with FDA and NCHS expertise; for example the fentanyl group includes analogues (carfentanil), precursors and metabolites (norfentanyl) (4th and 5th paragraphs). The full term and group list is in a supplementary spreadsheet, not read. NCHS sees no toxicology.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; certificates record no amounts, and none are reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Every death is counted under every drug mentioned, so drug counts are not mutually exclusive: the top-15 counts sum to 1.47 times the total overdose deaths in 2017 and 1.69 times in 2023 (editors' arithmetic, Table A). Concomitant drugs were analysed for the top 10 drugs of 2023 (Table B); alcohol, nicotine and other non-drug substances were not included as concomitant substances (Analysis, 4th paragraph). The report states that for multi-drug deaths the text cannot show whether one drug or a combination caused the death (Discussion › Data considerations, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: No external comparison (no toxicology, enhanced surveillance or second register). Internal measure of reporting quality: the share of overdose deaths with at least one ICD-10 multiple-cause code in T36.0 to T50.8 (a drug or drug class named), 87.7% in 2017 to 96.0% in 2023. Comparisons are across years and across intent categories.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Counts and percentages of overdose deaths with each referent drug mentioned; age-adjusted death rates (direct method, 2000 US standard population; 2010-based postcensal population estimates for 2017 to 2020 and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2024, estimate series on the blended base for 2021 to 2023); joinpoint regression (version 5.0.2, weighted least squares on log rates, up to two joinpoints, overall alpha 0.05); pairwise comparisons of rates between years by methods described elsewhere (Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: The DMI method is described in earlier NCHS reports; this report does not validate mentions against toxicology or case review.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Drug overdose death' = acute intoxication as underlying cause (the four ICD-10 ranges). 'Involving' a drug = the drug mentioned anywhere in the three text fields, including Part II, unless context negates it. 'Concomitant drug' = another specific drug mentioned on the same certificate.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across drugs: 16 drug-specific joinpoint trend analyses (Table), each with its own overall alpha of 0.05 for model selection, plus pairwise year comparisons whose number is not stated. Ranks were not tested for significance (Tables A and C, footnote 1).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (automated text search).

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts, percentages, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 standard population and annual percent changes; no intervals. Totals: 70,715 (2017) to 108,790 (2022), up 53.8%, then 106,352 (2023); up 50.4% from 2017 to 2023 (both checked, editors' arithmetic). Fentanyl: 27,542 deaths (38.9%) in 2017 to 73,944 in 2022 and 73,297 (68.9%) in 2023; rate 8.8 (2017), 21.8 (2021, about 29% a year), 22.7 (2022), 22.3 (2023). Methamphetamine: 9,438 (13.3%) to 34,167 (32.1%); rate 3.0 to 9.7 (2021, about 37% a year), then 10.4 (2023, stable). Cocaine: 15,050 (21.3%) to 31,700 (29.8%); rate 4.7 to 9.3, about 14% a year. Heroin: 16,085 (22.7%) to 4,071 (3.8%); rate 5.1 to 1.2, falling about 6% a year in 2017 to 2020 and about 35% a year in 2020 to 2023. Xylazine: 12 deaths (2017; rate not shown) and 102 (2018, rate 0.0) to 6,096 (5.7%, rate 1.9) in 2023, about 61% a year from 2018. Oxycodone rate 1.9 to 1.2 (down 36.8%, trend not significant); morphine 1.5 to 0.7 (significant fall from 2021); methadone, hydrocodone, clonazepam, diazepam and alprazolam without significant trend; gabapentin 0.6 to 1.3 (2021, about 27% a year), then stable at 1.2; amphetamine 0.5 to 1.3 (2021, about 28% a year); bromazolam 151 deaths (0.1) in 2021 to 1,734 (0.5) in 2023 (Results; Table A; Table). All Table A percentages reproduce from their counts and annual totals, and the counts agree between Table A and the rates table (editors' check of all 105 Table A cells).
analysis.covariates: Age adjustment only; no breakdown or adjustment by sex, race, region or jurisdiction.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Routine statistical report; methods follow earlier NCHS reports in the series.
analysis.selective_reporting: The report gives the share of deaths with a T36.0 to T50.8 code (drug or drug class) but never the number with at least one specific drug identified by the DMI search, although its abstract and Table A describe results among deaths with at least one specific drug mentioned. No results by jurisdiction are given, although the Discussion names jurisdictional variation in investigation and certification as a main limitation. The rate denominators change from 2010-based postcensal estimates (2017 to 2020) to the July 1, 2024, blended-base series (2021 to 2023) without comment on the trend analyses.
analysis.power: Not applicable (national census of registered deaths); small counts are suppressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US overdose deaths defined by ICD-10 underlying cause, the drugs most often written on certificates in 2017 to 2023 were fentanyl (first every year; 68.9% of overdose deaths in 2023), methamphetamine and cocaine; heroin mentions fell steeply; xylazine, gabapentin and bromazolam rose; fentanyl was written with most other top drugs (99.0% of xylazine deaths, 48.3% of oxycodone deaths); and the drugs named differed by intent (fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine in unintentional deaths; diphenhydramine, oxycodone and bupropion in suicides). All counts are minimums of deaths with a drug mentioned, and naming of drugs became more complete over the period.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report keeps to 'involved' and 'mentioned', states that counts are minimums and that the text cannot show which drug caused a multi-drug death, and warns that better reporting may explain part of some increases (Discussion › Data considerations, 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs). Gaps: (1) the fentanyl rate change from 2022 to 2023 is described as stabilising (Abstract), as a decrease to 22.3 (Results), and as a decrease that was not statistically significant (Discussion › Findings, 3rd paragraph), while the Table and Figure 2 footnotes say the 2023 rate was lower than the 2022 rate at p<0.05; (2) the Discussion says the fentanyl rate almost tripled from 2017 to 2021, while the Table gives 8.8 to 21.8, about 2.5 times (editors' arithmetic); (3) the Discussion says oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, clonazepam and diazepam had little to no decreases, while the oxycodone rate fell 36.8% by the report's own figure and hydrocodone from 0.9 to 0.6: these trends were not statistically significant, which is not the same as small; (4) the improvement from 87.7% to 96.0% is described in the Discussion and in the notes to the rates table and Figures 1 to 4 as reporting of at least one specific drug in the literal text, while the Methods and Table A define it as a T36.0 to T50.8 code, which can be a drug class; (5) the Discussion attributes the fall in overdose suicides from 5,086 (2016) to 4,711 (2023) to opioid-class drugs using a 2016 figure from the previous report, whose search-term list differs, although the report warns that numbers may differ from earlier reports for that reason; (6) the Discussion lists methamphetamine among drugs with steep increases between 2017 and 2023, while the Results and the Table's footnote give a significant rise only from 2017 to 2021 (3.0 to 9.7) and call the rate stable from 2021 (9.7) to 2023 (10.4).

timeline.event: Trinidad et al., NCHS: the literal-text method for characterising drug involvement in deaths (National Vital Statistics Reports 65(9); ref 7; listed as report R4 on the project's drug-deaths list).
Warner et al., NCHS: drugs most frequently involved in overdose deaths, 2010 to 2014 (ref 21; report R5 on the project's list).
Hedegaard et al., NCHS: the same analysis for 2011 to 2016, which this report updates (ref 10).
This report: 2017 to 2023, with an expanded search-term list applied to the whole period.

replication.where_it_stands: The current national NCHS series turning certificate text into drug-specific counts. Its counts are minimums of deaths with a drug written on the certificate, not of deaths caused by it, and their completeness depends on toxicology and certification practices that NCHS does not see. Studies on this project's drug-deaths list measure that gap from outside the certificate (for example Slavova et al., 2015, on state variation in naming the drug; Buchanich et al., 2018, on incomplete certificates; Horon et al., 2018, comparing certificates with enhanced surveillance); claims about how much drug-specific counts are understated should cite them, not this report.

funding.funder: Not reported. The report is a National Center for Health Statistics publication (National Vital Statistics Reports); no funding statement is printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (no competing-interests statement).
funding.affiliations_note: The authors' affiliations are not printed beside their names; the report's back matter lists NCHS and its Divisions of Vital Statistics and of Analysis and Epidemiology, and the acknowledgements thank NCHS reviewers and Information Technology Branch staff (two of them contractors) who ran the DMI processing. Margaret Warner and Bruce Goldberger are thanked for expertise and guidance; Goldberger, a forensic toxicologist, co-chaired the 2013 SAMHSA consensus panel on definitions (card sc_goldberger_2013). No commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: Link a national sample of overdose death certificates, including those naming no drug, to their full toxicology reports and investigation files, and measure by jurisdiction, year and drug how often a drug found and judged contributory is missing from the certificate text, how often a mentioned drug was incidental, and how often heroin is recorded as morphine; repeating this over time would separate real trends from improvements in reporting.

domains.note: For a statistics report this concerns case ascertainment: every registered death of a US resident in the United States with one of the four stated ICD-10 underlying-cause ranges, with exclusions and the data extraction date stated. The definition itself leaves out drug deaths coded to other underlying causes, which the report states.

Read as appraisal of the data source: the report measures the specificity of drug reporting each year and lists the limitations of certificate text (toxicology practice, interpretation, metabolites, choice of drugs to list, software space limits), but does not validate mentions against toxicology or case review, gives no jurisdiction-level quality measures and cannot separate causal from co-present drugs.

Read as stated rules for counting and reporting: the ICD-10 codes, the DMI rules (mention means involvement unless context negates; term mapping and referent groups), multiple counting, the joinpoint settings and the suppression thresholds are all stated; the full term list is in a supplement. The reliability threshold is worded both as 20 or more and as more than 20 deaths.
A federal statistical agency's routine report by its own staff; no funding or interests statement is printed, and no commercial interest is apparent.
Review by named NCHS staff in other divisions and the Office of the Director, and data-file quality checks by the Division of Vital Statistics; no external peer review is described.

The Conclusions are descriptive and the caveats (minimum counts, improved reporting, no attribution within multi-drug deaths) are clear, but the Discussion contradicts the Table and Figure 2 on the significance of the 2022 to 2023 fentanyl fall, overstates the 2017 to 2021 fentanyl rise, calls non-significant falls of about a third 'little to no decreases', describes a drug-or-class code measure as specific-drug reporting, compares 2023 suicides with a 2016 figure built with a different term list, and lists methamphetamine among steep increases from 2017 to 2023 although its rate was stable from 2021.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Filed as design evidence-report with the editors' evidence-report checklist, as the round brief directs for statistics by public bodies; the six domains are read for a statistics report rather than an evidence synthesis (case ascertainment for search and selection; appraisal of the data source; stated counting rules). As a count of what US certificates say, the report is complete, transparent and internally consistent in its tables (every Table A percentage and the counts shared between tables reproduce). Its limits are those of certificate text, which it states plainly, and a handful of discussion statements that go beyond or against its own tables. It may be cited, attributed to NCHS, for the ICD-10 definition of overdose deaths used in US statistics, for how drug-specific counts are built from certificate text (mention taken as involvement; multi-drug deaths counted under each drug), for the minimum numbers and rates of deaths with each drug mentioned, for the concomitant-drug percentages and for the drugs named by intent, and for the growth in drug-specific reporting from 87.7% to 96.0%. It may not be cited for deaths caused by a drug, for the size of any undercount, for the significance of the 2022 to 2023 fentanyl change without noting the report's conflicting statements, or as showing that the drugs listed with fentanyl contributed to the deaths.

key_findings.finding: Overdose deaths were defined by ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (homicide) and Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent), which reflect acute intoxication; deaths from chronic drug exposure (such as liver toxicity) and adverse effects of therapeutic or prophylactic doses were excluded; only US residents who died in the United States were included. Across 2017 to 2023 the manner was unintentional in 87% to 93% of these deaths, suicide 4% to 7%, undetermined 3% to 5%, homicide 0.2%.
key_findings.locator: Data and Methods › Data source and study population, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: In 2023 the undetermined share was 2,926 of 106,352, 2.75% (editors' arithmetic), within the stated 3% to 5% only after rounding.

key_findings.finding: Why certificate text is searched: ICD-10 drug codes are broad. Fentanyl, Demerol, tramadol, nitazenes and Suboxone all fall under T40.4 ('other synthetic narcotics', usually published as synthetic opioids other than methadone), and oxycodone falls under T40.2 ('other opioids') with drugs such as codeine and morphine, so code-based data cannot track specific drugs.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The literal text is written by the medical certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner for overdose deaths; NCHS searches three fields of the US standard certificate: Part I causes, Part II significant contributing conditions, and how the injury occurred.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Counting rule: a drug mentioned in the text is assumed to be involved in the death unless contextual words indicate otherwise (for example 'not drug related'). Search terms cover generic and brand names, street names, abbreviations, metabolites and misspellings, mapped to principal variants (linked to FDA unique ingredient identifiers) and grouped into referent drug groups chosen with FDA and NCHS expertise; the fentanyl group includes fentanyl analogues such as carfentanil, precursors and metabolites such as norfentanyl. The updated term list was applied to all years, so numbers can differ from earlier reports.
key_findings.locator: Data and Methods › Identifying drug mentions and involvement of the drug in the death, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Deaths involving more than one drug are counted in every relevant drug's count, percentage and rate (a death with cocaine and heroin is in both). In consequence the 15 drug-specific counts in Table A sum to 103,675 against 70,715 deaths in 2017 (1.47 times) and 179,965 against 106,352 in 2023 (1.69 times).
key_findings.locator: Analysis, 1st paragraph; Table A
key_findings.note: Sums and ratios are editors' arithmetic from Table A.

key_findings.finding: NCHS states that the drug-specific numbers and rates may be undercounts and should be read as minimums, because a drug may have been involved without being written on the certificate.
key_findings.locator: Analysis, 5th paragraph; Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Specificity of drug reporting: the share of overdose deaths with at least one ICD-10 multiple-cause code in T36.0 to T50.8 rose every year: 87.7% (2017), 92.0%, 93.8%, 94.4%, 95.2%, 95.8%, 96.0% (2023). NCHS says this improvement could influence the observed trends, that some increases may be partly due to better reporting but large increases are unlikely to be explained by it alone, and that better reporting could obscure real declines.
key_findings.locator: Data and Methods › Measuring the percentage of specific drugs on death certificates; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sources of error named by NCHS, in both directions: whether toxicology is done and what is tested vary by jurisdiction, decedent and year; interpretation depends on the tests ordered and the investigation; shared metabolites can misattribute drugs (morphine mentions may reflect heroin, underestimating heroin and overestimating morphine); some certifiers list a single lethal drug while others list several, and some say electronic registration software limits the space for drugs; rarely mentioned drugs may be missing from the term list.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 3rd paragraph, bulleted list and 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: For multi-drug deaths, the literal-text analysis cannot determine whether one drug or a combination caused the death.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Overdose deaths rose from 70,715 in 2017 to 108,790 in 2022 (53.8%) and were 106,352 in 2023. Fentanyl ranked first every year: 27,542 deaths (38.9%) in 2017, 73,944 in 2022, 73,297 (68.9%) in 2023. Methamphetamine rose from 9,438 (13.3%) to 34,167 (32.1%), from fourth to second; cocaine from 15,050 (21.3%) to 31,700 (29.8%); heroin fell from 16,085 (22.7%, second) to 4,071 (3.8%, seventh); xylazine entered the top 15 in 2021 (3,501) and was fourth in 2023 (6,096, 5.7%); bromazolam entered in 2023 (1,734, 1.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Most frequently mentioned drugs, bulleted list; Table A

key_findings.finding: Age-adjusted rates per 100,000: fentanyl 8.8 (2017) to 21.8 (2021), about 29% a year, then 22.7 (2022) and 22.3 (2023); heroin 5.1 to 1.2, falling about 6% a year in 2017 to 2020 and about 35% a year in 2020 to 2023; methamphetamine 3.0 to 9.7 (2021, about 37% a year), then 10.4; cocaine 4.7 to 9.3 (about 14% a year); xylazine 0.0 (2018) to 1.9 (about 61% a year); oxycodone 1.9 to 1.2 (down 36.8%, not significant); morphine 1.5 to 0.7 (significant fall from 2021).
key_findings.locator: Results › Age-adjusted rates, Selected opioids, Fentanyl and xylazine and Selected stimulants bullets; Table, with footnotes 1 to 8
key_findings.note: Table footnote 4 and the Figure 2 legend say the 2023 fentanyl rate was lower than the 2022 rate at p<0.05; the Discussion says this fall was not significant (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Drugs written together in 2023 (Table B): fentanyl was the commonest other drug for 9 of the top 10 drugs, from 99.0% of xylazine deaths (6,033 of 6,096) and 81.9% of heroin deaths to 57.4% of methadone and 48.3% of oxycodone deaths (2,002 of 4,142), and 76.0% of cocaine and 66.5% of methamphetamine deaths. Among fentanyl deaths, cocaine was written in 32.9%, methamphetamine 31.0% and xylazine 8.2%. Alcohol, nicotine and non-drug substances were not counted as concomitant drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug overdose deaths in 2023 involving multiple drugs, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table B; Analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Drugs by intent in 2023 (Table C): unintentional deaths (98,497) most often mentioned fentanyl 71.9%, methamphetamine 33.9% and cocaine 31.0%; suicides (4,711) diphenhydramine 14.7%, oxycodone 10.3%, bupropion 9.8%, fentanyl 9.7%, acetaminophen 8.0%; undetermined-intent deaths (2,926) fentanyl 63.2%, cocaine 32.5%, methamphetamine 13.9%. The 218 homicides are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most frequently mentioned drugs ... by intent of death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table C

key_findings.finding: Overdose suicides fell from 5,086 in 2016 to 4,711 in 2023 while the overall suicide rate rose; NCHS attributes the fall to fewer opioid-class mentions, including oxycodone 648 (12.7%) to 485 (10.3%) and hydrocodone 472 (9.3%) to 315 (6.7%), with morphine leaving the top 10.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The 2016 figures come from the previous report (ref 10), built with an older search-term list (reporting issue 5).

reporting_issues.issue: The fentanyl rate change from 2022 (22.7) to 2023 (22.3) is described in three ways: stabilised (Abstract), decreased (Results), and decreased but not statistically significant (Discussion › Findings, 3rd paragraph); the Table footnote 4 and the Figure 2 legend state that the 2023 rate was lower than the 2022 rate at p<0.05.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Abstract; Results › Fentanyl and xylazine; Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Table, footnote 4; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether fentanyl-involved deaths fell significantly in 2023 cannot be settled from the report; claims should give the rates and note the conflict.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the fentanyl rate almost tripled between 2017 and 2021; the Table gives 8.8 and 21.8, a ratio of about 2.5 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Table
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the rates, not the description.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, clonazepam and diazepam as having little to no decreases, while the Results give a 36.8% fall in the oxycodone rate (1.9 to 1.2) and the Table shows hydrocodone 0.9 to 0.6 and diazepam 0.7 to 0.5; these trends were not statistically significant.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Results › Selected opioids; Table
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-significant trend should not be cited as no change.

reporting_issues.issue: The specificity measure is defined in the Methods and the Table A note as at least one ICD-10 code in T36.0 to T50.8 (a drug or drug class), but the Discussion and the notes to the rates table and Figures 1 to 4 describe the same 88% to 96% as reporting of at least one specific drug in the literal text. The number of deaths with at least one specific drug found by the DMI search is never given, although the Abstract and Table A describe their results among such deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion compares overdose suicides in 2023 (4,711) with 2016 (5,086) and the opioid figures of 2016 from the previous report, although the report says its updated term list makes numbers differ from earlier reports, and attributes the fall to opioid-class drugs although deaths can count under several drugs.

reporting_issues.consequence: The 2016 to 2023 comparison is not on a consistent method; cite it as approximate.

design_detail: Consensus statement of a panel convened and funded by the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA, Center for Substance Abuse Treatment), published in the Journal of Addictive Diseases (issue July 2013, online 27 September 2013). Who wrote it: 2 co-chairs (a forensic toxicologist, University of Florida; an epidemiologist, University of Texas at Austin), 10 members (forensic toxicologists, two of them heading commercial toxicology laboratories; three medical examiners or forensic pathologists; a past president of the International Association of Coroners and Medical Examiners; an emergency physician and medical toxicologist; a state drug epidemiologist) and 13 ex officio members (Food and Drug Administration 4, Drug Enforcement Administration 2, SAMHSA 3, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention including the National Center for Health Statistics 2, National Institute on Drug Abuse 1, and the project director at the contractor JBS International, who is the corresponding author) (Appendix A). On what evidence: a MEDLINE and Embase search, 1970 to 2012, English language, plus US, Canadian and UK official guidelines and government reports; the panel wrote a preliminary report that was circulated to unnamed experts for review (Methods). No search terms, yield, selection criteria or consensus procedure are reported, recommendations are not graded, and the statement cites 19 references (8 journal articles; 11 reports, manuals, handbooks, guidelines or classifications). Content: recommendations in four areas (scene investigation; toxicological testing, with a nine-point standard; case definitions of drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected deaths and of 'drug', each mapped to vital-statistics categories; determination and documentation of causality on the death certificate), four constructed cases, and a glossary (Appendix B). Filed as narrative-review with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for consensus papers. No data.
can_establish: What a SAMHSA-convened US panel of forensic toxicologists, medical examiners and federal agency staff recommended in 2013 as standard definitions for drug-related deaths (drug-caused, drug-poisoning, drug-detected), how it mapped them onto ICD-10 vital-statistics categories, how it advised medical examiners and coroners to test, judge causality and word death certificates, and which sources of error in drug-death counts it names.
cannot_establish: How often deaths are wrongly attributed to, or missed for, any drug, or whether the standards make counts more accurate or more consistent: the statement reports no data, does not describe what its literature search found or how consensus was reached, grades none of its recommendations, and its four cases are constructed examples.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (consensus statement). SAMHSA convened a panel of medical examiners, coroners, toxicologists, epidemiologists and other public health officials to examine the research literature and current practice (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). The impetus came from SAMHSA expert meetings in 2003, 2007 and 2010, which concluded that medical examiners and coroners did not use common definitions for deaths caused by opioids (Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; the cited reports, refs 1, 3 and 4, are SAMHSA reports on methadone-associated mortality).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MEDLINE and Embase, 1970 through 2012, for research articles and clinical guidelines on death classification and case definitions; English-language articles; official guidelines from the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom; relevant government reports (Methods). No search terms, counts or inclusion criteria are given.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: US-only panel weighted towards forensic toxicology, medical examiner offices and regulatory agencies (FDA, DEA). No member is listed from drug treatment services or from organisations of people who use drugs, and death-certificate coding is represented only by one NCHS epidemiologist (ex officio), although the Introduction says panel members had backgrounds in addiction medicine, opioid pharmacology, methadone maintenance treatment and medical education (Introduction, 3rd paragraph). The motivating concern was methadone-associated mortality, and the Conclusions frame the definitions around separating deaths caused by methadone from deaths in which it was contributing or merely present.

exposure.measurement: Not a study. The statement's recommendations on establishing drug involvement: a full scene investigation with photographs, collection of drug evidence and a history from family or bystanders; prescription-monitoring records for deaths involving controlled prescription drugs (prescription history, use without a prescription, tolerance); contact with local opioid treatment programmes in methadone or buprenorphine cases (Scene Investigation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs); a nine-point toxicology standard (Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 6th paragraph and numbered standards 1 to 9); and certification from a synthesis of circumstances, medical and substance-use history, drug source and autopsy findings rather than laboratory values alone (Determination and Documentation of Causality, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; no amounts are given. The statement recommends that investigators inventory drugs found at the scene, and that the route be recorded, where known, in the 'how injury occurred' field of the certificate (Scene Investigation, 1st paragraph; Determination and Documentation of Causality, 16th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: All drugs judged physiologically significant should be listed individually in Part I of the certificate, by their role in the death rather than their lethality; drugs that did not contribute should not be recorded (they still count as drug-detected); each drug in a mixed intoxication is to be judged alone and in combination, by similarity of mechanism and known additive or synergistic effects; 'multidrug intoxication' and 'polypharmacy' are discouraged; attention is drawn to opioids combined with benzodiazepines, other opioids and alcohol (Determination and Documentation of Causality, 4th, 5th, 7th and 8th paragraphs; Appendix B, Drug Poisoning). The definition of 'drug' excludes alcohol and tobacco, while the toxicology standard includes testing for alcohol.

comparison.controls: None; no data are reported.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable. The 'outcomes' are definitions and their stated vital-statistics equivalents: drug-caused death parallels the NCHS category of drug-induced deaths (ICD-10 underlying-cause codes listed in NCHS's annual 'Deaths: Final Data'); drug-poisoning death parallels the drug subset of poisoning, underlying cause X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) and Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent); 'drug' corresponds roughly to T36 to T50; drug-detected death maps to no ICD-10 codes (Case Definitions).
outcomes.validity_norms: The definitions were not tested in this paper for agreement between certifiers or for their effect on counts.
outcomes.operationalization: Drug-caused death: certified as resulting from exposure to a drug, alone or with other substances, whatever the intent; includes acute toxicity, chronic drug effects, adverse reactions, legal executions, terrorist events and mental and behavioural disorders due to drugs; excludes infections resulting from drug use (for example from injecting) and congenital anomalies. Drug-poisoning death (proposed subcategory): certified as due to acute exposure, the lay concept of an overdose, whatever the intent; excludes chronic effects, adverse effects of a correct drug properly given, executions, terrorism and mental and behavioural disorders. Drug-detected death: a drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and trauma deaths; excludes deaths in which toxicology was done before death in hospital. For the first two, toxicology is usually but not always required: in rare cases circumstantial evidence may suffice when testing was unavailable or omitted (Case Definitions).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None: the statement contains no data.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol and no consensus method (voting, Delphi or other) is described; the external reviewers of the preliminary report are not named and their input is not summarised.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable in the usual sense. What the literature search found, and which sources support which recommendation, is not reported; Case 4 omits the drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected classification lines given for Cases 1 to 3.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A set of definitions, laboratory and certification recommendations and four constructed cases, agreed by a SAMHSA-convened panel and reviewed by unnamed experts, with no data on how drug deaths were being classified or on how much the standards would change the counts.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say that “Concise, scientifically accurately, universally accepted” case definitions like those presented can address a critical distinction (Conclusions); read as describing the panel's own definitions, no evidence of acceptance is offered for definitions the statement itself proposes, though the sentence can also be read as what such definitions could do once adopted. They say the definitions address the distinction between deaths caused by methadone and deaths in which methadone is a contributing factor or merely present, but the definitions fold contributing drugs into 'drug-caused' and separate only caused from detected, and they apply to all drugs, not methadone. The claim that adoption will improve the quality of data is untested. Case 1 presents a determination of death by multidrug intoxication as highly compelling when the concentrations are described as low-toxic, resting on the history, an assumed tolerance and metabolism during a coma of unknown length (Determination and Documentation of Causality, 13th to 15th paragraphs); this shows that, under the panel's approach, attribution can rest on circumstances rather than on the measured levels, a point the statement does not discuss as a source of over-attribution. The Introduction's description of panel members' backgrounds (addiction medicine, methadone maintenance treatment) does not match the Appendix A list.

timeline.event: National Association of Medical Examiners position paper on certifying cocaine-related deaths (Stephens et al., 2004; ref 19), cited for listing only the contributing drug.
This SAMHSA consensus statement.
Review of methodological complexities in counting opioid overdose deaths, with Goldberger among its authors (card sc_slavova_2019, this reader).

National Association of Medical Examiners position paper on investigating, diagnosing and certifying deaths related to opioids and other drugs (read by another reader in this round; an earlier opioid-only version is dated 2014 in the project's list).

replication.where_it_stands: A consensus document, not a study, so replication does not apply. The project's reading list names it with Beynon et al. (2007) as the only peer-reviewed comparisons of definitions its PubMed search found (search-logs/DrugDeaths_DOI-LIST.md, section 1, Known gaps). Whether its definitions were adopted, and whether they changed counts, has to be shown by later studies (for example the medical examiners' position paper and studies of certification practice on the same list); this statement cannot show it.

funding.funder: Funding support from the Center for Substance Abuse Treatment of the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, US Department of Health and Human Services. The paper states that SAMHSA had no role in data collection, analysis or manuscript preparation, and that all panel members had access to the data, took part in its interpretation and approved the manuscript; the views are those of the panel and not necessarily of SAMHSA or the Department (author notes).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest or competing-interests statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: SAMHSA convened and charged the panel; a SAMHSA medical officer (Center for Substance Abuse Treatment) served as Government Project Officer and is the third author, and three SAMHSA staff were ex officio members, which sits awkwardly beside the statement that SAMHSA had no role in manuscript preparation. The corresponding author is the project director at the contractor (JBS International). Two panel members headed commercial toxicology laboratories (Drugscan, Inc.; NMS Labs), whose services a comprehensive testing standard would extend; ex officio members came from FDA and DEA. Flags for closer reading, not reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Give the same set of complete death-investigation files to several medical examiners and coroners and measure their agreement on drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected categories and on the drugs named, before and after training in these standards; and compare drug-death counts in jurisdictions that adopted the standards with those that did not, against an independent enhanced review of each death.

domains.note: Databases and years are named, but there are no search terms, yield, selection criteria or link from the evidence to each recommendation; 11 of the 19 references are reports, manuals, handbooks, guidelines or classifications.
No source is appraised and no recommendation is graded; the toxicology standard and the causality rules are given without supporting studies.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The case for standardisation rests on SAMHSA's own earlier meetings (refs 1, 3, 4); a co-chair's paper (ref 5) and a panel member's book (ref 14) are cited; otherwise the evidence is the panel's own expertise.

Recommendations are labelled as the panel's, but none says whether it rests on evidence or on judgment; Case 1 presents a circumstantial determination with low-toxic concentrations as highly compelling; the Conclusions' sentence on 'universally accepted' definitions like those presented can be read as claiming acceptance for the panel's own.

domains.domain: Balance of panel membership and of attention to over- and under-attribution of deaths to drugs
domains.note: The statement names undercounting (immunoassay gaps, no standard thresholds, non-specific certificate wording, morphine and heroin confused) and overcounting (incidental findings, detected against caused, unreported sampling site), but gives no guidance on recording uncertainty, and its worked cases favour attribution in the ambiguous case. Treatment services and people who use drugs are not represented, despite the Introduction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a consensus statement; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, as the round brief directs, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domains (search and appraisal, both high). The statement can be cited, attributed to the SAMHSA consensus panel, for its definitions of drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected deaths and of 'drug', for the ICD-10 equivalents it gives, for its recommendations on toxicology, certificate wording and listing every contributing drug, for the coding consequence of wording (acute intoxication terms coded as poisoning, X42 with T40.5 for cocaine, against 'use' or 'abuse' coded to F14), and for the sources of error it names in both directions. It cannot be cited for any quantity (how often deaths are misattributed or missed), for the adoption or effect of its standards, or for its toxicology claims as established findings, since none is supported by cited studies in the text.

key_findings.finding: SAMHSA convened the panel after expert meetings in 2003, 2007 and 2010 concluded that medical examiners and coroners did not appear to use common definitions for deaths caused by opioids, and that their definitions might differ from those used on death certificates; the panel's charge was to separate deaths caused by a drug from deaths in which the drug was detected but was not a major cause of or contributor to death.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract

key_findings.finding: Evidence base and process: MEDLINE and Embase, 1970 through 2012, English-language research articles and clinical guidelines, plus US, Canadian and UK official guidelines and government reports; the panel wrote a preliminary report that was circulated to experts for review, and their input was incorporated. Panel: 2 co-chairs, 10 members and 13 ex officio members from FDA, DEA, SAMHSA, CDC/NCHS, NIDA and the contractor.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Appendix A

key_findings.finding: Sources of undercounting named in toxicology: immunoassays vary in what they detect, and many do not detect oxycodone and hydromorphone; laboratories use no standard detection threshold; the panel says the lack of standard practice may lead to underreporting of prescription opioids in the deceased. Standards of routine toxicology vary across death-investigation systems; the commonest approach is an immunoassay screen of urine with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmation.
key_findings.locator: Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Measured concentrations vary with the sampling site, route, chronicity of use, time from use to sampling and from death to sampling, and collection method; peripheral (iliac or femoral) blood is the most reliable, yet the site is often not reported, and heart blood, subclavian blood, body-cavity fluid, spleen squeeze or embalming-contaminated blood may all be reported simply as 'blood', which the panel calls an avoidable source of error.
key_findings.locator: Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nine-point standard of forensic toxicology practice: record the sampling site and use peripheral vessels where possible; collect and test admission blood and urine, as opposed to autopsy specimens, where applicable and available; test comprehensively for prescription, illicit and over-the-counter drugs and alcohol; emphasise urine for detection; use an immunoassay screen of defined sensitivity with supplementary assays for drugs with poor cross-reactivity; measure free and total drug in blood, ideally with glucuronide metabolites; test other tissues where blood may be compromised by post-mortem artefact; use similar cut-offs for confirmatory GC-MS and LC-MS; use validated, controlled methods.
key_findings.locator: Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 6th paragraph and numbered standards 1 to 9

key_findings.finding: Drug-caused death: a death certified as resulting from exposure to a drug, alone or with other substances, whatever the intent (unintentional, suicide, homicide, undetermined); includes acute toxicity, chronic drug effects, adverse drug reactions, legal executions, terrorist events and mental and behavioural disorders due to drugs; excludes infections resulting from drug use and congenital anomalies. It parallels the NCHS category of drug-induced deaths, which also includes adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use.
key_findings.locator: Case Definitions › 1. Drug-Caused Death, Concept, Includes, Excludes and Equivalent Category

key_findings.finding: Drug-poisoning death (proposed subcategory): a death certified as due to acute exposure to a drug, meant to match the lay concept of an overdose, whatever the intent; includes acute toxicity from recreational use, drugs given or taken in error, drugs prescribed to another person and overdose in a medical setting; excludes infections, congenital anomalies, chronic effects, adverse effects of a correct drug properly given, executions, terrorism and mental and behavioural disorders. Equivalent: an ICD-10 underlying cause of X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14.
key_findings.locator: Case Definitions › 1-a. Drug Poisoning Death

key_findings.finding: Drug-detected death: a drug found on post-mortem testing whatever its role, including natural and trauma deaths (for example motor vehicle crashes, suffocation) and all drug-caused and drug-poisoning deaths; excludes deaths whose toxicology was done before death by hospital staff; maps to no ICD-10 codes. The panel notes it is simpler for medical examiners and coroners to report because it can be drawn from their own laboratory database without cut-points.
key_findings.locator: Case Definitions › 2. Drug-Detected Death

key_findings.finding: 'Drug': any compound used for diagnosis, treatment or prevention, for relief of pain, to control a physiological or pathological condition, or for the feeling it causes; includes illicit drugs (heroin, cocaine, hallucinogens), prescription and over-the-counter drugs, biological substances and inhaled solvents; excludes alcohol, tobacco and noxious substances eaten as food, such as hallucinogenic mushrooms; corresponds roughly to ICD-10 T36 to T50.
key_findings.locator: Case Definitions › 3. Drug

key_findings.finding: Causality is to be judged from circumstances, medical and substance-use history, drug source and autopsy, not laboratory values alone, including whether the pre-terminal events fit the drug's action and whether the person was likely tolerant; the panel singles out accumulation of long half-life drugs such as methadone in the first days of treatment, and overdose after tolerance has fallen during a period without the drug (for example in prison or hospital). Competing natural or external causes and mixed intoxications complicate certification.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Certificate rules: list every drug judged physiologically significant individually in Part I, by its role rather than its lethality, and conditions that contributed but did not cause the underlying cause in Part II; list a drug in Part I when the certifier concludes it caused death even without toxicology; leave non-contributing drugs off the certificate; name individual drugs rather than 'drug intoxication' or 'polypharmacy', because certificates are the source of national mortality statistics; record the parent drug, and specify heroin rather than morphine when 6-acetylmorphine or the circumstances point to heroin.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 5th to 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Wording decides the code: acute cocaine intoxication, acute cocaine toxicity, toxic effects of cocaine, cocaine poisoning and cocaine overdose are all coded as poisoning, X42 with T40.5, whereas cocaine use, cocaine abuse, cocaine snorting and cocaine addiction are coded to F14 (mental and behavioural disorders due to cocaine). The panel advises 'toxicity', 'intoxication' or 'poisoning' for acute deaths, 'use', 'abuse', 'dependence' or 'disorder' only when substance use itself is meant as the cause, and avoiding 'overdose', which lacks a specific meaning.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 10th to 12th paragraphs; Appendix B, Drug Poisoning (Overdose)

key_findings.finding: Case 1: a 40-year-old man with a history of substance use disorder who used drugs with friends, went to sleep and could not be woken the next day, with pulmonary congestion and oedema at autopsy and toxicology showing low-toxic concentrations of oxycodone and diazepam, is certified as acute intoxication by oxycodone and diazepam (drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected). The panel reasons that he was expected to be opioid-tolerant and would have metabolised much of the drug during the coma, so the circumstances are highly compelling even though the concentrations are not classically lethal; diazepam is listed because it contributed to respiratory depression.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 13th to 16th paragraphs (Case 1)
key_findings.note: The attribution rests on circumstances and assumed tolerance and metabolism, not on the measured concentrations; the comment also invokes ethanol, which the case does not report finding.

key_findings.finding: Case 2: a 45-year-old woman treated for years with opioid analgesics for fibromyalgia, prescribed methadone 4 days earlier, with a methadone concentration toxic to a non-tolerant person and no other findings, is certified as acute intoxication by methadone with chronic pain in Part II, and described as not tolerant to the drug's effects.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 17th and 18th paragraphs (Case 2)

key_findings.finding: Case 3: a 22-year-old man shot in the head while selling cocaine, with a lethal concentration of a drug on toxicology, is certified as death from gunshot wounds: not drug-caused and not drug-poisoning, but drug-detected; the panel keeps the drug off the cause-of-death statement and says drug-detected counts still matter for statistics on illicit drug use.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 19th to 21st paragraphs (Case 3)

key_findings.finding: Case 4: a 52-year-old man with hypertension who collapsed after smoking crack cocaine, with a hypertensive-type intracerebral haemorrhage and alcohol and alprazolam also found, is certified as intracerebral haemorrhage due to acute cocaine toxicity, with hypertension in Part II and an accidental manner (the non-natural manner preferred when intoxication exacerbates natural disease); only cocaine is listed, as alprazolam likely did not contribute.
key_findings.locator: Determination and Documentation of Causality, 22nd and 23rd paragraphs (Case 4)

key_findings.finding: Who decides: medical examiners are described as appointed, professionally trained forensic pathologists who certify cause and manner of death; coroners as elected or appointed officials with widely varying qualifications who, if not physicians, must use coroners' physicians for autopsies. Manner options on the US certificate: natural, accidental, homicide, suicide, pending investigation, could not be determined.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Medical Examiner and Coroner; Appendix B › Death Certification

key_findings.finding: Scene investigation: inspect the whole scene, photograph it, collect all evidence of possible exposure to drugs, take a history from family members or bystanders, and inventory the drugs to determine or estimate the amount taken; in deaths involving controlled prescription drugs, request the person's records from the state prescription drug monitoring programme, where one exists, for prescription history and evidence of use without a prescription, which the panel says help to judge tolerance, and to find the health care providers who hold the medical history; in methadone or buprenorphine deaths, contact local opioid treatment programmes to learn whether the person received the drug from them, where the jurisdiction allows it.
key_findings.locator: Discussion and Recommendations › Scene Investigation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The panel asks that toxicology measurements also be judged on whether they can distinguish acute from chronic drug use, for example by measuring free and glucuronidated metabolites, which current bench-top liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry makes more feasible, and says that collecting such data on drug-related deaths may give indicators for judging future cases.
key_findings.locator: Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: No reference is cited in that paragraph.

reporting_issues.issue: The drug-detected definition contradicts itself: its laboratory criterion says evidence of the drug must be found on post-mortem toxicology, then allows the definition to be met on circumstantial evidence when testing was unavailable; it says it includes all drug-caused and drug-poisoning deaths, yet excludes deaths whose only toxicology was done in hospital before death. Its circumstantial-evidence sentence even ends by speaking of certifying the death as a drug poisoning death, apparently carried over from definition 1-a.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Case Definitions › 2. Drug-Detected Death, Laboratory Criteria, Includes and Excludes
reporting_issues.consequence: A drug-caused death certified without post-mortem toxicology, or after hospital testing only, is in one category and out of the other, so drug-detected counts are not a superset of drug-caused counts as stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The definition of 'drug' includes hallucinogens among illicit drugs but excludes hallucinogenic mushrooms as noxious substances eaten as food, and excludes alcohol, while the toxicology standard tests for alcohol and the Case 1 comment refers to ethanol although none is reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Case Definitions › 3. Drug; Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, standard 3; Case 1 comment
reporting_issues.consequence: Under these definitions deaths involving psilocybin-containing mushrooms or alcohol alone would not count as drug deaths; claims should state the definitions' boundaries rather than treat 'drug death' as self-evident.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says panel members had backgrounds in addiction medicine, opioid pharmacology, methadone maintenance treatment and medical education, but the Appendix A list shows forensic toxicologists, medical examiners, a coroners' association past president, a medical toxicologist, epidemiologists and agency staff, none described as working in addiction treatment. The nearest are two ex officio members from SAMHSA's Division of Pharmacologic Therapies (Center for Substance Abuse Treatment), listed with federal agency titles; the Introduction also says the panel included representatives of organisations committed to the safety and effectiveness of opioid addiction treatment.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Appendix A
reporting_issues.consequence: The panel's composition should be described from Appendix A, not from the Introduction.

reporting_issues.issue: The funding note says SAMHSA had no role in data collection, analysis or manuscript preparation, although SAMHSA convened and charged the panel, a SAMHSA medical officer served as Government Project Officer and is an author, and three SAMHSA staff were ex officio members; no competing-interests statement is printed for any panel member. The same note says all panel members had access to the data, although the statement reports none.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, author notes; Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Appendix A
reporting_issues.consequence: The agency's role should be described as convening, funding and co-authoring; interests of members from commercial laboratories and regulators are undeclared.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 2 calls a woman treated for years with various opioid analgesics not tolerant to the drug's effects (methadone, started 4 days earlier) without saying why that history gave no tolerance; the induction-period risk described in the 2nd paragraph of the causality section (long half-life drugs such as methadone accumulating in the first days of treatment, before tolerance develops) fits the case but is left implicit. Case 1 infers tolerance from a history of substance use disorder and uses assumed tolerance and metabolism during a coma to support attribution despite low-toxic concentrations.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Determination and Documentation of Causality, 2nd and 13th to 18th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Tolerance is inferred from history, not measured: assumed present in Case 1 and absent in Case 2, and in both the inference supports attribution; the cases illustrate the panel's reasoning, not a tested rule.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 4 omits the drug-caused, drug-poisoning and drug-detected classification lines given for Cases 1 to 3, although it is the case that most tests the definitions (a drug precipitating death from natural disease); it also says toxicology indicated acute cocaine intoxication, a judgment the statement elsewhere says laboratory values alone cannot make.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Determination and Documentation of Causality, 22nd and 23rd paragraphs; 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: How the panel would count a cocaine-precipitated haemorrhage under its own categories is left to inference.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions describe a three-way distinction between deaths caused by methadone and deaths in which it is contributing or merely present, but the definitions provide two (drug-caused, which includes contributing drugs, and drug-detected) and cover all drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the definitions themselves, not the summary in the Conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors: 'SAMSHA' (Introduction, 1st paragraph), 'a certain opioids' (Abstract), 'listed as a the cause of death', 'Terms such as such as', 'scientifically accurately', 'Coroners Medical Examiners', 'causes about death' and 'did not contribute the death' (Case 4 comment); the panel is called the Consensus Panel and the Expert Panel interchangeably.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Introduction; Case Definitions › 2; Determination and Documentation of Causality; Conclusions
reporting_issues.consequence: None on content.

reporting_issues.issue: Standard 2 of the toxicology standard asks for admission blood and urine to be collected and tested, as opposed to autopsy specimens, where applicable and available, while the drug-detected definition requires evidence of the drug on post-mortem toxicology and excludes deaths whose toxicology was performed before death by hospital staff; the statement does not say whether a drug found only in admission specimens, tested after death by the medical examiner's laboratory, makes a death drug-detected.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Toxicologic Testing and Analysis, numbered standard 2; Case Definitions › 2. Drug-Detected Death, Laboratory Criteria and Excludes
reporting_issues.consequence: How such deaths are counted is left to each office, so drug-detected counts can differ with laboratory practice as well as with the deaths themselves.

design_detail: Scoping review (following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, with JBI scoping-review guidance cited) of US studies published 2013–2022 that quantified misclassification of opioid involvement in drug-overdose deaths: deaths certified with no named drug ('unspecified'), how that share varied by place and by the medicolegal death investigation (MDI) system (coroner or medical examiner, centralized or decentralized), how many unspecified deaths involved opioids, and whether the specific opioid (heroin, fentanyl) was named. PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus were searched in October 2022 with MeSH terms; English and US only; two reviewers screened independently; data were extracted by each reviewer and consolidated into three tables; no risk-of-bias appraisal and no pooling, by design. 17 studies were included, all described as repeated cross-sectional surveillance analyses with data from 1999 to 2019: national analyses of the multiple-cause-of-death files of the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS), one of the CDC State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS, 38 states and Washington DC), one comparing poison-centre and death-certificate data, and state or county record-linkage or case-review studies (Maryland, Florida, Kentucky twice, Marion County Indiana, San Francisco, New York City, Allegheny County Pennsylvania). Read as the PubMed Central author manuscript (NIHMS2046083) of the article published in Annals of Epidemiology.
can_establish: Which US studies published 2013–2022 measured how far death certificates miss or misname opioid involvement, what each reported as the review summarizes it, and the range of those results: national corrections putting opioid-involved deaths about 20–35% above reported counts in 1999–2015, a share of overdose deaths with no named drug that fell from about a quarter around 2008–2010 to 8% in 2018 and differed widely by state, more unspecified certificates where coroners rather than medical examiners certify, and additional opioid-positive or heroin-related deaths found whenever toxicology or scene data were linked.
cannot_establish: The true size of the undercount (no appraisal or pooling, and the national range comes from three analyses by one author with one approach on the same national files); whether opioids caused the additional deaths found by toxicology linkage (several included studies counted an opioid found in post-mortem toxicology); how often deaths are wrongly put down to opioids or to the wrong opioid (the review asks only about underestimation); whether coroner systems cause more unspecified certificates (cross-sectional associations between jurisdictions); or anything about other countries, other drugs, or deaths after 2019.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Database search in October 2022 of PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus, combining MeSH terms for coroners and medical examiners, opioid-related disorders, the opioid epidemic, opiate overdose, drug overdose, death certificates, suicide and cause of death; reference lists of the included studies were checked and added nothing (Methods › 1; Results › 1). The included studies used death certificates in the national multiple-cause-of-death files and records of state or county medical examiners and coroners (toxicology, death-scene notes), with data years from 1999 to 2019.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed studies in English, conducted in the US, published 2013–2022, covering MDI systems, death certificates or overdose surveillance methods. The start year was chosen to cover the rise of synthetic opioid deaths. Excluded: trend descriptions that did not quantify misclassification; descriptions of one data source or method without a quantified comparison with another dataset; work that was not peer-reviewed; studies of risk factors or disparities in drug-related mortality; qualitative studies, commentaries, opinions, case reports and editorials (Methods › 1. Search Strategy and Data Sources).
sample.demographics: By the editors' reading of Tables 1–3: 9 studies used national data (7 the NVSS multiple-cause-of-death files, 1 SUDORS for 38 states and Washington DC, 1 the National Poison Data System against the Drug-Involved Mortality data built from certificate literal text) and 8 used state or county data (Maryland; Florida; Kentucky, two studies; Marion County, Indiana; San Francisco; New York City; Allegheny County, Pennsylvania). Ruhm 2017 appears in both Table 1 and Table 2, so the tables hold 18 rows for 17 studies.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases, English only, US only, a 2013–2022 publication window, no grey literature (so reports of public bodies enter only through journal papers), and search strings given as MeSH headings without the strings used in Web of Science and Scopus; the authors call their terms not exhaustive. Inclusion required a quantified comparison with another source, and the question is framed as underestimation, so the set is built to find missed opioid deaths; no study was sought on deaths wrongly attributed to opioids. Three of the national estimates are by one author (Ruhm 2016, 2017 and 2018) analysing overlapping years of the same national files. Reasons for the 24 full-text exclusions are given only in Figure 1, an image that could not be viewed (screenshot blank).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. In the included studies the 'exposure' is the data source or the certification setting: a death certificate with or without a named drug (multiple-cause ICD-10 coding in the NVSS files), the jurisdiction's MDI system, and linkage with post-mortem toxicology, death-scene investigation notes, prescription-monitoring data or a second register. Opioid involvement among unspecified deaths was estimated in three ways, as the tables describe them: statistical prediction or imputation from deaths with a named drug (Ruhm's three studies), proportional reallocation (Buchanich 2018), and linkage or case review in which an opioid or a heroin marker (6-monoacetylmorphine, a morphine-to-codeine ratio, scene evidence) found at investigation counted the death as opioid- or heroin-involved.
exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed by the review. It does not say how each included study counted deaths with several drugs; the Discussion (4th paragraph) notes that polysubstance and stimulant-involved deaths may pose further documentation problems and calls for studies of their misclassification.

comparison.controls: Within the included studies: counts from death certificates compared with corrected counts (prediction, imputation, reallocation) or with counts after linkage to toxicology, scene investigation or a second register (Florida Medical Examiners Commission data; SUDORS; poison-centre data); coroner jurisdictions compared with medical-examiner jurisdictions.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). For the comparisons of MDI systems, the authors name differences in resources for toxicology and scene investigation, training and the timeliness of reports as possible explanations; only Denham et al. (2022), as tabulated, adjusted for individual, county and state characteristics.

outcomes.instruments: An extraction table per study (aim, design, inclusion criteria, exposure, outcome, covariates, analytic method, key findings), filled by each of two reviewers and consolidated (Methods › 2. Review and analysis). No appraisal instrument.
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither the included studies nor the reference sources they used (toxicology panels, scene notes, case review) were appraised; the authors state that a scoping review does not include a risk-of-bias assessment.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Misclassification' means an opioid-involved death certified with no named drug ('unspecified': a certificate on which no specific drug was identified, per the table notes) or a death in which the specific opioid was not named, judged against a correction method or a second source. In several state and county studies a death was counted as opioid- or heroin-involved because the substance or its marker was found in post-mortem toxicology; the review reports these as additional opioid-related or heroin-related deaths.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently and met to resolve discrepancies; each extracted data, then the two compared and consolidated them.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling; figures as the review reports them. National corrections: Ruhm 2018, corrected counts 21–35% above reported counts for any opioid and 20–35% for heroin or synthetic opioids across 1999–2015, corrected rates 12.5 and 7.4 per 100,000 against reported 10.3 and 6.2; Ruhm 2017, corrected opioid-involved rates 24% and heroin rates 22% above reported rates in 2014; Buchanich 2018, about 72% of unspecified unintentional overdose deaths in 1999–2015 estimated opioid-related, about 70,000 deaths reallocated. Share of overdose deaths with no named drug: about 25% in 2008–2010, 15–20% in 2014–2016, 8% in 2018; from 0% (Washington DC) to 63.8% (Louisiana) in 2008. Coroner against medical-examiner counties (Denham 2022): odds of an unclassified overdose death OR 1.77 (95% CI 1.08 to 2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32 to 6.46) in 2018. Linkage: Florida 8,633 more opioid-related deaths (34% of the NVSS count, 2003–2017); Maryland 1,052 more heroin-related deaths (given as 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths, 2012–2015); Marion County 86.8% of unspecified deaths opioid-positive, opioid-involved share from 34.2% to 86.0% (642 more cases); Kentucky 44 more potentially heroin-related deaths (2%) in 2013–2014, and in 2015 4.7% heroin-positive deaths certified as unspecified and 6% more fentanyl-positive deaths; heroin deaths up 21% in San Francisco (text), 17% in New York City, and from 171 to 245 in Allegheny County.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Covariates of the included studies are listed in the tables: individual, county and state characteristics in Denham 2022 and in Ruhm's models; 'not applicable' or 'not listed' for most linkage studies.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The review states that it followed PRISMA-ScR.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's national figure rests on one author's three analyses and is stated as an underestimate of 20–35% (see interpretation gap). Additional deaths found by toxicology linkage are reported as opioid- or heroin-related without separating presence from cause. The overcounting direction appears in one sentence of the Discussion, and the reclassifications that lowered counts attributed to morphine and codeine (Allegheny County) are reported only as heroin gains.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Seventeen unappraised US studies with data from 1999 to 2019, all repeated cross-sectional analyses of death records. Three national analyses by one author put corrected opioid-involved counts 20–35% above reported counts across 1999–2015 (24% in 2014); a fourth reallocated about 72% of unspecified unintentional deaths as opioid-related by assuming they matched specified deaths. The share of overdose deaths with no named drug fell from about a quarter around 2008–2010 to 8% in 2018 and ranged from 0% to 63.8% between states in 2008. Three studies found more unspecified certificates in coroner than in medical-examiner jurisdictions (in one, adjusted OR 1.77 in 2014 and 3.87 in 2018). Every state or county linkage study found additional deaths with an opioid or heroin marker, or reclassified deaths to heroin, when toxicology or scene data were added.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says opioid involvement "was underestimated nationally by 20–35%" (Abstract › Results; the Conclusion says "by as much 20–35%"). Gaps: (1) corrected counts 20–35% above reported counts mean reported counts were about 17–26% below the corrected ones (editors' calculation: 1 − 1/1.20 and 1 − 1/1.35), and the range is one author's year-by-year estimates under one model, not agreement among independent studies; (2) the Results say coroner counties were four times more likely to record an unspecified death, which restates one study's 2018 odds ratio of 3.87 as a likelihood (the 2014 odds ratio was 1.77) when 8–19% of deaths were unspecified, so the ratio of probabilities would be smaller; (3) deaths found by toxicology linkage are called opioid-related or heroin-related although several studies counted an opioid found, a limitation the Discussion itself states (drug screening can mark a death as drug-involved when the drug did not contribute, 5th paragraph); (4) the recommendations to train coroners, change their qualifications and add resources rest on cross-sectional associations between jurisdictions, and the suggestion that elected coroners may hesitate to certify opioid deaths for fear of consequences for constituents' families is not examined by any included study; (5) against this, the scoping design and the absence of appraisal are stated plainly, and the limitations name the language, database and date limits; (6) the Discussion calls the national 20–35% consistent with studies at the state level (refs 40 and 41), but Horon's 26% is additional heroin-related deaths as a share of all overdose deaths, not a rise over a reported heroin count, and Quast's 34% compares Florida's medical-examiner records with the national files for Florida; neither is a model correction like Ruhm's, so the agreement is between different measures.

timeline.event: Warner et al. (Academic Forensic Pathology): state differences in completeness of manner and drug specification on certificates, 2008–2010; included in this review (Table 1).
Ruhm (Population Health Metrics): statistical adjustment of drug-poisoning deaths, 1999–2012; included (Table 2).
Ruhm (American Journal of Preventive Medicine): corrected state opioid and heroin mortality rates, 2008–2014; included (Tables 1 and 2).
Ruhm (Addiction): corrected national opioid-involved deaths, 1999–2015; source of the 20–35% range; included (Table 2)
Buchanich et al.: unspecified unintentional overdose deaths reallocated, 1999–2015; included (Table 2; card sc_buchanich_2018)
Horon et al.: enhanced surveillance against standard certificates for heroin deaths, Maryland 2012–2015; included (Table 2; card sc_horon_2018)
Denham et al.: coroner county systems associated with higher odds of unclassified overdose deaths, 2014 and 2018; included (Table 1).

Drake and Ruhm (American Journal of Preventive Medicine), cited in the Introduction and Discussion: almost 6% of overdose deaths listed no specific drug category in 2020; published after the search and not an included study.
This review (online December 2024): by its authors' account the first synthesis of the literature on misclassification of fatal opioid overdose.

replication.where_it_stands: The only review of opioid misclassification in US death data that its authors know of. Its national figure rests on Ruhm's three analyses, which share author, data and approach, so the 20–35% range is one estimate repeated, not replication. Buchanich 2018 and Horon 2018, also read for this round, are inside it: claims must not cite the review and those studies as independent support. Deaths after 2019, other countries, stimulants and the overcounting direction are outside its scope.
