what_would_settle_it: A national validation study that samples drug-poisoning deaths at random across coroner and medical-examiner jurisdictions, certified with and without a named drug, re-investigates each with full quantitative toxicology, scene and history review by forensic pathologists blind to the certificate and using one standard case definition, and reports both how many opioid-caused deaths the certificates missed or misnamed and how many certified opioid deaths the review would not attribute to opioids.

domains.note: Three databases, dates, explicit criteria, duplicate independent screening and PRISMA-ScR reporting; but English and US only, no grey literature, search strings given only as MeSH headings, a 2013–2022 window, and exclusion reasons only in an image that could not be viewed.
No appraisal of the included studies or of their reference sources, by design; toxicology presence, scene review and statistical prediction are reported side by side as findings of misclassification.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 17 included studies is by the review's authors, as far as the reference list shows.

The Results report the studies' figures, with the citation and number errors listed under reporting issues; the Discussion and Conclusion add recommendations (coroner training and qualifications, resources) and an explanation (elected coroners' hesitation) that no included study tested.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on undercounting against overcounting (overcounting under-represented)
domains.note: The question, search and synthesis concern underestimation only; deaths wrongly put down to opioids appear in one Discussion sentence, and reclassifications that lowered morphine and codeine counts are reported only as heroin gains.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a scoping review (METHODS §5.3), and it is not rated as a systematic review. It maps the US literature transparently and says it does not appraise, but its figures are unappraised second-hand summaries, its national range comes from one author's repeated analyses, and its frame looks only for missed opioid deaths. Citable for: which US studies measured opioid misclassification in 2013–2022 and what they reported, as pointers to the primary studies (whose own figures should be cited from their full texts); the fall in unspecified certificates to 8% by 2018 and the state range in 2008, as second-hand figures; the association of coroner systems with more unspecified certificates in three studies. Not citable for: a national undercount of 20–35% as an established fact, causation of the additional deaths found by toxicology, the effect of coroner training, or the overcounting direction.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed, Web of Science and Scopus searched in October 2022 for US studies in English published 2013–2022; 117 records after duplicates, 76 excluded at title and abstract, 24 at full text, 17 included; reference lists of included studies added none; no risk-of-bias assessment because the review is a scoping review.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 1. Search Strategy and Data Sources, 1st paragraph; Methods › 2. Review and analysis, 1st paragraph; Results › 1. Sample and Study Characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Exclusion reasons are only in Figure 1 (PRISMA diagram), an image: figure image not viewable. The Discussion (6th paragraph) says removing duplicates eliminated 66% of all imported records, which would put the records imported at about 340 to 350 (editors' calculation from the 117 left); only Figure 1 could confirm it.

key_findings.finding: The share of overdose deaths with no specific drug on the certificate fell from about 25% in 2008–2010 to 15–20% in 2014–2016 and 8% in 2018. Per Table 1: 19.3% in 2014 and 8% in 2018 (Denham 2022); 25.4% in 2008 and 19.5% in 2014 (Ruhm 2017); 24.4% in 2010 to 14.6% in 2016, 20.3% overall (Tote 2019).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2. Misclassification of Cause of Death, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The share of unspecified overdose deaths ranged from 0% in Washington DC to 63.8% in Louisiana in 2008; South Carolina fell from 39.8% (2008) to 6.0% (2014), a drop of 33.8 percentage points; Southern states had higher shares than the Northeast and West (Ruhm 2017).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.1 Geographic Variation in Unspecified Drug-related Overdose Deaths, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Three studies found lower shares of unspecified overdose deaths where medical examiners rather than coroners certify, and centralized medical-examiner systems lower than decentralized ones. In Denham 2022, coroner systems had higher odds of an unclassified overdose death, OR 1.77 (1.08 to 2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32 to 6.46) in 2018; unclassified deaths fell by 72% in medical-examiner counties and 43% in coroner counties between 2014 and 2018; odds were lower where the certifier is a pathologist, violent deaths are investigated, coroners must be trained, or the system is centralized.
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.1.1 Variation by Medicolegal Death Investigation (MDI) System, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Denham et al. 2022 row)
key_findings.note: The text's 'four times more likely' restates the 2018 odds ratio; these are cross-sectional associations between jurisdictions.

key_findings.finding: National corrections from NVSS data: corrected counts 21–35% above reported counts for any opioid and 20–35% for heroin or synthetic opioids, 1999–2015, with corrected rates of 12.5 and 7.4 per 100,000 against reported 10.3 and 6.2, and 23.1% of overdose deaths with no drug specified (26% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015) (Ruhm 2018); corrected opioid-involved rates 24% and heroin rates 22% above reported rates in 2014 (Ruhm 2017).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.1 Misclassification of opioid involvement at the national level, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Ruhm C 2018 and Ruhm C 2017 rows)
key_findings.note: All three national prediction or imputation studies are by one author on the same national files; the year of the corrected rates is not given in the table.

key_findings.finding: Buchanich 2018: assuming unspecified unintentional overdose deaths involve opioids in the same proportion as specified ones, about 72% of unspecified deaths in 1999–2015 were estimated opioid-related; about 70,000 deaths were reallocated, the review's table adds 'over 50% in 5 states' without saying whether counts or rates rose, and state rankings changed for all but 8 states.
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.1, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Buchanich et al. 2018 row)
key_findings.note: Checked against the primary paper (card sc_buchanich_2018): it reports more than 70,000 reallocated of 97,159 unspecified deaths and does not print 72%, which is that ratio; its rate increases above 50% in 5 states are for 2015, and its counts more than doubled in the same five states over 1999–2015.

key_findings.finding: State and county linkage: Florida local records found 8,633 more opioid-related deaths than the NVSS files (34% of the NVSS count, 2003–2017; Quast 2020); Maryland enhanced surveillance found 1,052 more heroin-related deaths (given as 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths, 2012–2015; Horon 2018); in Marion County, Indiana, 86.8% of unspecified deaths were opioid-positive and adding toxicology raised the opioid-involved share from 34.2% to 86.0% (642 more cases; Lowder 2018).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.2 Misclassification of opioid involvement at the state and county level, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Quast, Horon, Lowder rows)
key_findings.note: Checked against the primary paper (card sc_horon_2018): 1,052 of 3,957 overdose deaths is 26.6%, the overdose total is not defined there, and the additional deaths met a broader definition that partly counts heroin markers present in toxicology. Lowder's 642 added cases were recoded because an opioid was found in toxicology, and the table's 'doubled' is a 2.5-fold rise (reporting issue 9).

key_findings.finding: Kentucky: in 2013–2014 a quarter of overdose certificates named no drug although 89% of those deaths had post-mortem toxicology, and 44 more deaths (2%) were classed as potentially heroin-related by morphine-to-codeine ratio; in 2015, 88% had toxicology, 4.7% of overdose deaths were heroin-positive but certified as unspecified, 2.3% more were heroin-positive with heroin not listed, and 6% more were fentanyl-positive (58% of these had no drug listed, 42% other drugs).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.2.2, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Slavova et al. 2017 rows, refs 44 and 45)

key_findings.finding: Specific opioids, national (O'Donnell 2022, SUDORS, 38 states and Washington DC, 2018–2019): 44.2% of probable and 52.6% of suspected heroin deaths listed only morphine on the certificate, and reclassification raised the share of heroin deaths from 80.2% to 93.3%; fentanyl was detected in 73.6% of deaths, and 1% was likely pharmaceutical fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.3.1 Misclassification of heroin- and fentanyl-involvement at the national level, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (O'Donnell et al. 2022 row)
key_findings.note: The share of fentanyl deaths classed as illicitly manufactured fentanyl is 37.1% in the text and 89.3% in Table 3 (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Specific opioids, county studies: in Allegheny County 2008–2010, 66% of 112 unintentional deaths with morphine but not heroin listed met criteria for heroin, and after review heroin deaths rose from 171 to 245 while morphine deaths fell from 132 to 41 and codeine deaths from 34 to 5 (Mertz 2014); in New York City 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication (71%) were attributed to heroin, raising heroin deaths by 17% (Gill 2016); in San Francisco an expanded definition added 20 heroin deaths to 152 (Hurstak).
key_findings.locator: Results › 2.3.2 Misclassification of heroin-involvement at the state and county level, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (Mertz, Gill, Hurstak rows)
key_findings.note: The text gives the San Francisco increase as 21%; 20 on 152 is 13% (reporting issue 4). The New York City 17% rise cannot be checked from the review, which gives no base count of heroin deaths.

key_findings.finding: Poison-centre against death-certificate data, 2010–2015 (Mallama 2019): the death-certificate-based Drug-Involved Mortality data held 61 deaths for each one in the National Poison Data System (the table says drug-related overdose deaths; the study's aim concerns opioid-involved fatal cases); multi-substance cases were 77% in the poison-centre data against 58.6%, and suicide 54% against 10% for commonly dispensed opioids.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (Mallama et al. 2019 row); Results › 2.3.1, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states the opposite direction once: drug screening can mark a death as drug-involved when the person used the drug before death but it did not contribute, and incomplete scene notes can wrongly mark a death as not drug-involved; it endorses autopsy, scene investigation, prescription-monitoring checks and quantitative toxicology, as recommended by the National Association of Medical Examiners and a SAMHSA expert panel.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: English only, three databases, no grey literature, search terms not exhaustive, included data only through 2019, and possible COVID-19 reporting lags from 2020; the authors suggest content saturation because reference lists added no studies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: more resources for toxicology and scene investigation, training or changed qualifications for coroners, and data integration; the Discussion notes CDC's SUDORS was funded in 12 states in 2016 and 47 states and Washington DC by 2019, and that heroin deaths may still have been underestimated within it in 2018–2019.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: Results › 2, 1st paragraph cites refs 40 and 41 (Maryland and Florida studies) among the nine national studies and omits refs 38 and 39 (the SUDORS and poison-centre studies); the same paragraph lists 40 and 41 again among the eight state or county studies. By the tables, the national studies are refs 17 and 32–39 and the state or county studies refs 31 and 40–46.
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts (9 and 8) are right, but the printed citations cannot be used to tell which studies are national; Horon 2018 is a Maryland study, not a national one.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref 47 (Robinson, 'County coroners and their role in the heart of the opioid epidemic', per the reference list) is cited as if it were an included study in Results › 2, 1st paragraph (31,40–47), Results › 2.2.2 (31,44–47) and Discussion, 1st paragraph (40,41,44–47); the 17 included studies are refs 17 and 31–46.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader may count a piece outside the included set among the evidence for the state and county findings; the findings themselves come from refs 31 and 40–46.

reporting_issues.issue: For O'Donnell 2022, the text says 37.1% of fentanyl deaths were probable or suspected illicitly manufactured fentanyl, while Table 3 gives 89.3%, with 1% pharmaceutical and 9.7% unknown (summing to 100%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.3.1, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (O'Donnell et al. 2022 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither figure should be cited from this review; the primary paper is needed.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says including toxicology reports and case narratives increased the number of heroin deaths identified in San Francisco by 21%, while Table 3 gives 152 deaths by the standard definition and 20 more by the expanded one, an increase of 13% (editors' calculation, 20/152).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.3.2, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (Hurstak et al. row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The 21% cannot be reproduced from the review's own table; check Hurstak et al. (2018) before citing either figure.

reporting_issues.issue: For Kentucky 2015, the text says an additional 4.7% and 6% 'of unspecified deaths' involved heroin and fentanyl; Table 2 gives 4.7% of overdose deaths (heroin-positive but unspecified) and says 42% of the 6% additional fentanyl-positive deaths had other drugs listed, so they were not unspecified.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.2.2, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Slavova et al. 2017, ref 45 row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator is all overdose deaths, not unspecified deaths, and the figures are toxicology-positive deaths, not deaths certified as caused by heroin or fentanyl.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › 2.2.1 says three studies (refs 33, 36, 37) used multiple imputation; Table 2 describes Ruhm 2016 and Ruhm 2018 as predictions from probit models fitted to deaths with a named drug, and only Ruhm 2017 as multiple imputation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 2.2.1, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (Ruhm rows)
reporting_issues.consequence: A labelling inconsistency; all three approaches assume that unspecified deaths resemble specified deaths with the same recorded characteristics, an assumption the review does not discuss.

reporting_issues.issue: The limitations paragraph describes checking the reference lists of the included studies as a 'forward search'; reference-list checking is backward searching, and no search of later citing papers is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of likely content saturation rests on backward checking only.

design_detail: Commentary in Public Health Reports (2015) by epidemiologists from the University of Kentucky and ten state or city health departments, writing as members of the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) Overdose Subcommittee, with an illustrative descriptive analysis of 2010 US multiple-cause-of-death (MCOD) data from CDC WONDER for 11 volunteer jurisdictions (Kansas, Kentucky, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York City, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Utah, Washington) and the United States. Four indicators per jurisdiction: the age-adjusted overdose death rate (ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85, Y10 to Y14); the age-adjusted rate with at least one opioid-analgesic code (T40.2 to T40.4); the age-adjusted rate with T40.6 ('other and unspecified narcotics'); and the crude rate with T50.9 ('other and unspecified drugs') as the only drug code. The indicator values are shown only in a single figure (an image); the text quotes some of them. The work grew out of the CSTE subcommittee's testing of the poisoning-surveillance indicators proposed by the Safe States Alliance Injury Surveillance Workgroup (ISW7). Filed as cross-sectional with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for certificate studies, because the evidence the site would use is the certificate-data comparison; the commentary's arguments and recommendations are recorded separately on this card.
can_establish: That in 2010 US death-certificate data about a quarter of overdose deaths carried no specific drug code, that how often certificates named a drug or drug class differed widely between jurisdictions, and how certifiers' wording maps to ICD-10 codes (a named opioid analgesic to T40.2 to T40.4, 'opioid' alone to T40.6, 'drug overdose' alone to T50.9), which makes drug-specific rates hard to compare between jurisdictions.
cannot_establish: How many of the unspecified deaths involved opioid analgesics, heroin or any other drug (no death was re-examined and no undercount is estimated); whether the type of death-investigation system causes the differences (the system-type percentages are second-hand and unadjusted, and the 11 jurisdictions' systems are not described); or whether the pattern held after 2010 or outside these volunteer jurisdictions.

sample.recruitment: Registry: 2010 MCOD files compiled from death certificates, as made available on CDC WONDER (accessed 16 January 2015) (7th paragraph; Figure, footnote b). Jurisdictions: epidemiologists from 11 jurisdictions volunteered, with members of the CSTE Overdose Subcommittee, to analyse the ISW7 mortality indicators (6th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Overdose deaths: ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (assault), Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent). Drug-specific indicators by multiple-cause T codes as listed in the design detail (7th paragraph and indicator list). The 'unspecified only' indicator counts deaths with T50.9 and no other code in T36 to T50.8.
sample.demographics: Not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Under NCHS rules, rates based on fewer than 10 deaths were suppressed (New York City 'unspecified only'; Kansas and Oklahoma T40.6) and one rate based on fewer than 20 deaths was judged unreliable (North Carolina T40.6); all four were left out of the figure (Figure, footnote a).
sample.selection_effects: The 11 jurisdictions volunteered and were not chosen to represent US states; their death-investigation systems are not described. One year of data (2010), analysed in 2015. Ten of the eleven named authors work in the health departments of jurisdictions they describe; the first author is at the University of Kentucky College of Public Health (Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center), and Kentucky had the highest overdose rate and the highest unspecified-only rate quoted in the text.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. The variable of interest is how specifically drugs were named, measured through the ICD-10 multiple-cause codes that NCHS assigns from the certificate text using automated coding software (3rd paragraph). The certifier (coroner or medical examiner) determines the cause of death and completes the certificate; the commentary explains that a named opioid analgesic is coded T40.2 to T40.4, 'opioid' alone T40.6, and 'drug overdose' with no drug T50.9 (3rd and 4th paragraphs). Toxicology is not examined.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Indicators are not mutually exclusive: a death with an opioid-analgesic code can also carry T40.6 or other codes; only the T50.9 indicator is restricted to deaths with no other drug code (7th paragraph and indicator list).

comparison.controls: Comparison between 11 jurisdictions and the United States on the four indicators; no comparison with toxicology, enhanced surveillance or medical examiner and coroner records. The comparison by type of death-investigation system (centralized state medical examiner against coroner, hybrid and county medical examiner systems) is quoted from earlier work (Warner et al., 2013), not computed here.
comparison.matching: None; overall rates are age-adjusted, but the 'unspecified only' rate is crude because CDC WONDER could not age-adjust that query directly.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Jurisdiction characteristics that could explain differences in specificity (investigation system, toxicology practice and funding, caseload, certifier training) are not described or measured.

outcomes.instruments: Age-adjusted rates per 100,000 population (overdose; opioid analgesics T40.2 to T40.4; 'other and unspecified narcotics' T40.6) and a crude rate (T50.9 only), from CDC WONDER queries of 2010 MCOD data (7th paragraph and indicator list).
outcomes.validity_norms: ICD-10 coding by NCHS software is standard; the indicators come from the ISW7 consensus recommendations, which the subcommittee was testing (5th and 6th paragraphs). Agreement of the codes with toxicology is not assessed.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Unspecified' = an overdose death whose only drug code is T50.9; 'opioid analgesic death' = any T40.2 to T40.4 code (T40.2 other opioids, T40.3 methadone, T40.4 other synthetic narcotics); 'other and unspecified narcotics' = T40.6 (4th and 7th paragraphs). Undercounting is inferred from non-specificity; it is not measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Rates only, without intervals or tests. United States, 2010: 38,329 overdose deaths, age-adjusted 12.3 per 100,000; 16,651 with an opioid analgesic listed (5.4); 9,429 with only 'other and unspecified drugs' (3.0), which is 24.6% of all overdose deaths and agrees with the 'about 25%' quoted from earlier work (editors' arithmetic); opioid-analgesic deaths were 43.4% of the total (editors' arithmetic). Jurisdictions, as quoted in the text: highest overdose rate Kentucky 23.6; highest opioid-analgesic rate Oklahoma 13.6, where only 28 deaths (4%) lacked a specific drug category, so that even if all 28 involved opioid analgesics the rate would rise by less than 1.0; 'unspecified only' rates Kansas 4.2, Michigan 4.8, Kentucky 7.4, Massachusetts and Maryland 0.2 each; T40.6 rates Massachusetts 3.4 and Maryland 1.7 (2nd, 8th and 9th paragraphs). Quoted from Warner et al. (2013): certificates listing specific drugs 92% in states with centralized state medical examiner systems, 62% in decentralized coroner systems, 73% in hybrid systems, 71% in decentralized county or district medical examiner systems (2nd paragraph). The remaining jurisdiction values are in the figure, which could not be viewed.
analysis.covariates: Age adjustment for three of the four indicators only.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Commentary; no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text quotes the values that illustrate its argument; the full set is only in the figure. No indicator is given for heroin (T40.1), although the opening paragraph says heroin-related deaths are also undercounted.
analysis.power: Not applicable; several jurisdiction rates were suppressed or unreliable because of small counts.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2010, a quarter of US overdose deaths had no specific drug code, and jurisdictions differed widely in how often certificates named a drug, a drug class or only 'narcotics': Oklahoma left 4% unspecified, while Kansas, Michigan and Kentucky had unspecified-only rates of 4.2 to 7.4 per 100,000, and Massachusetts and Maryland had few unspecified deaths but many coded only as 'other and unspecified narcotics'. A jurisdiction's drug-specific rate therefore partly reflects how specifically its certifiers write.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The opening paragraph says classification methods may be leading to a substantial undercount of opioid-analgesic and heroin-related deaths, and the 8th paragraph concludes that opioid-analgesic involvement in Kansas, Michigan and Kentucky was “significantly underestimated” (8th paragraph). These are inferences, hedged in the text (possible, even likely; not unreasonable to believe; further study is needed): no death was re-examined, no estimate of the undercount is made, heroin is not analysed, and 'significantly' is not a statistical result. The system-type contrast (92% against 62% to 73%) is relayed from earlier work as the 'degree of underestimation', although it measures specificity, unadjusted. The practical conclusion, to compare jurisdictions on total overdose rates rather than drug-specific rates and to use drug-specific trends only where specificity is stable, follows directly from the data.

timeline.event: Warner, Paulozzi, Nolte, Davis and Nelson, state variation in certifying manner of death and drugs involved (Academic Forensic Pathology; ref 2), the source of the 25% and system-type figures; not indexed in PubMed according to the project's list.
SAMHSA consensus panel's uniform definitions, cited in the commentary as a recommendation not yet consistently adopted (card sc_goldberger_2013, this reader).
This commentary: 2010 data for 11 jurisdictions.
Buchanich et al., the effect of incomplete death certificates on estimates of unintentional opioid-related overdose deaths, 1999 to 2015 (title as listed; read by another reader in this round).
NCHS report: the share of US overdose deaths with at least one drug or drug-class code (T36.0 to T50.8) rose from 87.7% in 2017 to 96.0% in 2023 (card sc_garnett_2026, this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive illustration, not a study to be replicated. The problem it illustrates, that unspecified certificates hide drug involvement unevenly across jurisdictions, is the subject of later studies on this project's list that re-assign or correct unspecified deaths (for example Buchanich et al., 2018; Ruhm, 2018, by their listed titles; not read for this card). National specificity improved after 2010: in the NCHS data, 12.3% of overdose deaths in 2017 and 4.0% in 2023 had no drug or drug-class code (Garnett et al., 2026), against about a quarter in 2010 here; whether the variation between jurisdictions narrowed is not shown in that report.

funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (no competing-interests statement).
funding.affiliations_note: First author at the University of Kentucky College of Public Health (Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center); the other ten at the health departments of New York City, North Carolina, Kansas, Utah, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Oklahoma, Washington and Oregon, i.e. the jurisdictions analysed; group authorship by members of the CSTE Overdose Subcommittee. The acknowledgements thank Leonard Paulozzi (CDC) for mentorship and review of the manuscript and Margaret Warner (CDC), an author of the earlier work quoted, for advice on MCOD files. what_would_settle_it: For a sample of overdose deaths coded only T50.9 or T40.6 in several jurisdictions, retrieve the medical examiner or coroner files and toxicology reports, record which drugs were found and judged contributory, and estimate by jurisdiction and investigation system how many opioid-analgesic, heroin and other drug deaths the certificates missed, as the commentary itself proposes.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Complete national vital-statistics data for each jurisdiction and the United States, but the 11 jurisdictions volunteered and are not a sample of US states.
All registered overdose deaths of 2010 in each jurisdiction; no sampling.
National figures rest on 38,329 deaths, but several jurisdiction rates were suppressed (fewer than 10 deaths) or unreliable (fewer than 20), and Oklahoma's unspecified count was 28.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The 11 jurisdictions' death-investigation systems, toxicology practice and death counts are not described, although the argument turns on how certification practice differs.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All deaths enter the indicators, but four jurisdiction rates were omitted from the figure under NCHS suppression and reliability rules.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The condition is the coding itself (overdose by underlying cause; drug specificity by multiple-cause T codes), identified with standard ICD-10 definitions on national data.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Codes are assigned nationally by the same NCHS software; what varies between jurisdictions is the certifier's wording, which is the subject of the paper rather than a measurement flaw.

Standard CDC WONDER rates with NCHS suppression rules, but no intervals, a crude rate set beside age-adjusted rates, and in-text comparisons (more unspecified than opioid-analgesic deaths in Kansas and Michigan) whose basis, counts or rates, is not stated.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Registered deaths; no response involved.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for certificate studies; the paper is a commentary, so its arguments are recorded under the interpretation gap rather than scored. As a description of how specifically 2010 US certificates named drugs, nationally and in 11 jurisdictions, the data are complete and coded uniformly, but the jurisdictions volunteered, their systems are not described, most values sit in a figure (not viewable in this reading) and there are no intervals. It may be cited for: the 2010 national figures (38,329 overdose deaths; 16,651 with an opioid analgesic coded; 9,429 with only unspecified drugs); the way certifier wording maps to ICD-10 codes; the jurisdiction values quoted in the text; and the CSTE subcommittee's advice that jurisdictions be compared on total overdose rates rather than drug-specific rates. It may not be cited for the size of any undercount, for heroin, or for the effect of investigation-system type, which is second-hand and unadjusted.

key_findings.finding: United States, 2010: 38,329 drug overdose deaths on death certificates (age-adjusted 12.3 per 100,000); an opioid analgesic was listed as contributing in 16,651 (5.4 per 100,000); a further 9,429 (3.0 per 100,000) were associated only with 'other and unspecified drugs'.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: 9,429 is 24.6% and 16,651 is 43.4% of 38,329 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Quoted from earlier work (Warner et al., 2013): about 25% of US overdose deaths had no drug specified on the certificate, and the share of overdose certificates listing specific drugs was 92% in states with a centralized state medical examiner system, against 62% with decentralized coroners, 73% with hybrid county coroner and medical examiner systems, and 71% with decentralized county or district medical examiners.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the years covered and any adjustment are not stated in this commentary.

key_findings.finding: Who decides and who codes: coroners or medical examiners determine the cause of death and complete the certificate; NCHS codes the text to ICD-10 with software that automates and standardizes coding. A death is an overdose death when its underlying cause is X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14; T36 to T50 codes identify drug classes.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Wording decides the code: naming an opioid analgesic (for example hydrocodone, methadone or tramadol) gives a code in T40.2 to T40.4; writing 'opioid' alone gives T40.6, 'other and unspecified narcotics'; writing simply 'drug overdose' gives T50.9, 'other and unspecified drugs', and the opioid's contribution disappears from the coded data.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The analysis came from the CSTE Overdose Subcommittee's volunteer testing, in 11 jurisdictions with 2010 certificate data, of the mortality indicators proposed in the Safe States Alliance ISW7 consensus recommendations for poisoning surveillance (April 2012); the subcommittee found limitations in how overdose deaths are counted locally.
key_findings.locator: 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Four indicators from 2010 MCOD data on CDC WONDER: age-adjusted overdose death rate; age-adjusted rate with at least one T40.2 to T40.4 code; age-adjusted rate with T40.6; and the crude rate with T50.9 as the only drug code (crude because CDC WONDER could not age-adjust that query directly).
key_findings.locator: 7th paragraph and indicator list

key_findings.finding: Kentucky had the highest age-adjusted overdose death rate (23.6 per 100,000). Oklahoma had the highest opioid-analgesic rate (13.6), partly because only 28 of its overdose deaths (4%) lacked a specific drug category; even if all 28 involved opioid analgesics its rate would have risen by less than 1.0 per 100,000. 'Unspecified only' rates were relatively high in Kansas (4.2), Michigan (4.8) and Kentucky (7.4), and in Kansas and Michigan more overdose deaths were attributed to 'other and unspecified drugs' than to opioid analgesics.
key_findings.locator: 8th paragraph; Figure
key_findings.note: The other jurisdiction values are in the figure image, which was not viewable in this reading (the browser pane was hidden and the screenshot came back blank); no value was estimated from it.

key_findings.finding: Massachusetts and Maryland each had few deaths with no drug or class specified (0.2 per 100,000), but substantial rates coded only as 'other and unspecified narcotics' (3.4 and 1.7 per 100,000), which the authors suggest could be opioid analgesic, heroin or cocaine deaths described vaguely as 'opioids' or 'narcotics'.
key_findings.locator: 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Rates suppressed under NCHS rules (fewer than 10 deaths): New York City 'unspecified only', Kansas and Oklahoma T40.6; North Carolina T40.6 unreliable (fewer than 20 deaths); all omitted from the figure.
key_findings.locator: Figure, footnote a

key_findings.finding: The subcommittee workgroup advises that ranking jurisdictions by drug types named on certificates may mislead, that jurisdictions be compared on total overdose rates, and that drug-specific trends within a jurisdiction remain useful only while the degree of specification does not change markedly from year to year; it suggests checking medical examiner, coroner and toxicology records to identify the drugs in nonspecifically coded deaths.
key_findings.locator: 10th and 11th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The commentary cites two 2013 recommendations: that of the National Association of Medical Examiners and American College of Medical Toxicology expert panel, that certifiers list all substances responsible for a fatal overdose on the certificate, and the SAMHSA consensus panel's uniform standards and case definitions for opioid-related deaths. Until these are consistently adopted, the authors write, epidemiologists need to know the quality and limits of their jurisdiction's certificate data, check the completeness and accuracy of the codes where possible, and read counts and rates with caution where the share of deaths with unspecified drugs is considerable; they add that NCHS and some states were working to improve how drugs are specified and that vital-statistics registrars should work with medical examiners and coroners on it.
key_findings.locator: 11th and 12th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The jurisdiction-level indicator values are given only in a figure image; the text quotes a selection (the examples that support the argument).
reporting_issues.consequence: Values not quoted in the text could not be extracted in this reading and cannot be checked from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'unspecified only' indicator is a crude rate while the other three are age-adjusted, and the statement that Kansas and Michigan had more deaths attributed to unspecified drugs than to opioid analgesics does not say whether it compares counts or these differently computed rates.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 7th paragraph and indicator list; 8th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-indicator comparisons within a state should be cited with that caveat, or as counts from the source data.

reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; indicator list
reporting_issues.consequence: The commentary supports a claim about non-specific certificates, not a measured heroin or opioid undercount.

reporting_issues.consequence: Recorded as not reported.

design_detail: Narrative review in Current Epidemiology Reports (2019; Topical Collection on Injury Epidemiology) by six authors: four from the University of Kentucky (biostatistics, the Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center, pharmacy practice and science, preventive medicine and environmental health, health management and policy), one from the University of Pittsburgh (biostatistics) and one from the University of Florida (Department of Pathology, Immunology and Laboratory Medicine: Goldberger, a co-chair of the 2013 SAMHSA consensus panel according to that statement's Appendix A, card sc_goldberger_2013, a role this review does not state). It describes how US drug overdose deaths are investigated by medical examiners and coroners, certified, transmitted by state vital-statistics offices and coded to ICD-10 by NCHS (with a flowchart, Fig. 1), then the analytic problems this creates (unspecified drugs, abrupt changes in specification or testing, variation in undetermined intent, delays, the changing meaning of 'prescription opioid' codes once illicit fentanyl arrived), and the tools proposed to correct them (cause-of-death text analysis, statistical reallocation of unspecified deaths, toxicology markers, enhanced multi-source surveillance). No search strategy or selection criteria; 95 references, 11 marked as of major importance in the text citations (the reference list prints the mark beside 5 of them), 12 written by the review's own authors (4 of the 11). Filed as narrative-review with the editors' checklist.
can_establish: How the US system that produces drug-overdose death counts works and where, according to the authors and the sources they cite, it loses or distorts information on which drugs were involved; which correction methods had been proposed by 2019 and what they estimated.
cannot_establish: The size of any undercount or misattribution as a pooled or appraised estimate (no search, appraisal or synthesis; the estimates are relayed from single studies, several by the authors), or how far deaths are wrongly attributed to opioids, which the review barely addresses.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Sources chosen by the authors: peer-reviewed studies, position and consensus papers (NAME, SAMHSA, OSAC), NCHS and CDC reports and data (CDC WONDER), federal survey and policy reports, and one personal communication.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and centred on US opioid deaths. Several key empirical statements come from the authors' own work: the CSTE commentary (Slavova et al., 2015), the SAMHSA panel (Goldberger et al., 2013), the reallocation estimate (Buchanich et al., 2018), and Kentucky studies on benzodiazepine listing, gabapentin testing and enhanced surveillance. The over-attribution side (deaths wrongly put down to opioids) is hardly represented.

exposure.measurement: Not a study. The review describes drug involvement as recorded on certificates (Part I causes; contributing conditions) and coded by NCHS to ICD-10 multiple-cause T codes, and the post-mortem toxicology that underlies it, for which the authors say the US has no nationally accepted best practices, standards or guidelines (The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: The review sets the recommendation that drugs not contributing to death be left off the certificate beside Gill's statement that, because a single drug's role can rarely be separated in multi-drug intoxications, it is customary to list all drugs above trace amounts (7th paragraph of that subsection), without reconciling them. It reports a Kentucky study (by the authors' group) in which benzodiazepines were less often listed as contributing drugs than fentanyl, heroin, methadone or cocaine (Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; the review discusses ICD-10 underlying-cause and multiple-cause codes, cause-of-death text analysis, toxicology markers (6-acetylmorphine, morphine-to-codeine ratio, 4-ANPP, norfentanyl) and adjusted rates from cited studies.

outcomes.operationalization: Overdose death = ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14; drug involvement = T36 to T50 multiple-cause codes; a death whose only drug code is T50.9 typically had no drug or drug class written on the certificate (Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis. Figures relayed from cited sources: certificates listing specific drugs, by investigation system, centralized medical examiner 92%, decentralized medical examiner 71%, hybrid 73%, coroner 62% (Warner et al., 2013); South Carolina's prescription-opioid (T40.2 to T40.4) rate 4.7 per 100,000 in 2013 and 9.3 in 2014 while specificity rose from 57.7% to 94.4%; Kentucky gabapentin prevalence among overdose decedents 2.9% (2013) to 17% (2014) after routine testing began; undetermined intent 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah against 8% nationally (Warner et al., 2013), and in 2016 from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland); T40.4 as a share of T40.2 to T40.4 deaths in 2016 under 20% in Nevada and Utah and over 80% in New Hampshire and Massachusetts; about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths possibly unaccounted for in 1999 to 2015 (Buchanich et al., 2018); 2015 opioid-involved rate 12.46 per 100,000 after adjustment against 10.31 reported, 21% higher (Ruhm, 2018); benzodiazepines listed as contributing on certificates in 67% (alprazolam) and under 40% (clonazepam, diazepam), against fentanyl 89%, heroin 88%, methadone 81%, cocaine 77% (Kentucky; denominator not stated in the review); certificates naming specific drugs or classes 75% (2011) to 85% (2016) (Hedegaard et al.); 75% of medical examiner and coroner offices always requesting testing for opioids other than heroin or fentanyl and 51% to 75% always requesting testing for fentanyl and heroin (2017 NFLIS survey); 32% of offices with computerized, networked systems (2017 survey).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Narrative review; no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review gives the undercounting side in detail and the over-attribution side (incidental drugs listed, attribution without lethal concentrations, post-mortem interpretation) almost none. The statement that about 20% of overdose certificates name no specific drug is given without a source.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A descriptive account of how US overdose death data are produced, with relayed evidence that drug specificity on certificates varies by jurisdiction and over time, that changes in recording or testing practice can produce artefactual jumps (South Carolina 2014; Kentucky gabapentin 2014), that intent coding varies widely, that some drugs are less often listed than others when detected, and that statistical reallocation suggests opioid involvement was undercounted (about 70,000 deaths in 1999 to 2015; 21% in 2015).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions stay close to this: certificates are the foundation of surveillance, variation in certification can bias rates, text analysis improves specific-drug quantification, enhanced surveillance has potential, and uniform national standards are unlikely soon in a fragmented system. Gaps: (1) the abstract says text analysis tools improve quantification of specific opioid rates, while the body says they cannot reach the roughly 20% of certificates naming no specific drug; (2) the reallocation and adjusted-rate estimates are relayed with only a one-sentence caveat (assumptions reasonable but difficult to verify), one of them from a co-author; (3) a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 is presented as a strong and probable indicator of heroin from cited studies without appraisal; (4) the South Carolina explanation rests on personal correspondence; (5) the framing is one-directional (undercounting), with no discussion of how often listed drugs did not contribute, although the review itself reports the custom of listing every drug above trace amounts.

NCHS report: overdose certificates with a drug or drug-class code rose to 96.0% by 2023 from 87.7% in 2017 (card sc_garnett_2026, this reader), continuing the 75% (2011) to 85% (2016) series this review quotes.

replication.where_it_stands: A 2019 map of the problems, still useful as an orientation and as a pointer to primary studies. Its figures should be cited from the primary sources after they are read. National specificity has since improved further (96.0% with a drug or drug-class code in 2023, Garnett et al., 2026), so the 'about 20% unspecified' figure is out of date; the questions it raises about jurisdictional variation, testing practice and intent coding are addressed by later studies on the project's list.

what_would_settle_it: For the undercount: link a national sample of overdose deaths, including those coded only T50.9 or T40.6, to full toxicology and medical examiner or coroner files and measure drug-specific omission by jurisdiction and system type. For the other direction, which the review leaves open: in the same linked sample, have independent forensic reviewers judge which listed drugs contributed, and measure how often drugs on certificates were incidental.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; 95 references chosen by the authors.

No formal appraisal; a few limitations are named (the adjustment assumptions are difficult to verify), but survey figures, the heroin ratio and the NAME recommendations (called evidence-based) are relayed without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 12 of 95 references and 4 of the 11 flagged as of major importance are by the review's authors, including the reallocation estimate, the benzodiazepine-listing and gabapentin-testing findings, and one of the three recommendation papers the review names (the SAMHSA panel, co-chaired by a co-author).

Most statements are attributed and hedged, but the 'about 20% unspecified' figure is unsourced and sits awkwardly with the 85% (2016) specificity figure quoted later, and the South Carolina explanation rests on personal correspondence.

domains.domain: Balance of attention to undercounting and to over-attribution of deaths to opioids
domains.note: Under-represented: over-attribution. Undercounting is covered in depth; the other direction appears only in relayed recommendations, none quantified: the SAMHSA panel's distinction between drug-caused and drug-detected deaths (MDI subsection, 4th paragraph), the rule that non-contributing drugs be left off the certificate beside Gill's remark on listing all drugs above trace amounts (7th paragraph), and NAME's call to interpret toxicology in the context of the circumstances (3rd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review; the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain (no systematic search). The review is careful and well sourced as orientation, and most statements are attributed, but it pools and appraises nothing, relies in part on the authors' own work, and covers mainly one direction of error. It may be cited for the description of the US investigation, certification and coding pathway (who certifies, who codes, which codes), for the named sources of distortion (unspecified certificates, abrupt changes in specification or testing, variation in undetermined intent, delays, the T40.4 problem once illicit fentanyl spread), and as a pointer to primary studies. Its numbers (system-type percentages, South Carolina, Kentucky gabapentin, 70,000 uncounted deaths, 21% adjustment, benzodiazepine listing, survey shares) are second-hand and should be cited from the primary sources once read; the claim stays at draft if it rests on this review alone (METHODS §5.3).

key_findings.finding: Overdose mortality data are produced by several agencies and actors, with no single agency having quality-control oversight of the whole process (investigation, certification, registration, coding, surveillance; Fig. 1).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 is a flowchart image; its legend was read, the image itself was not viewed (the browser pane was hidden, and a screenshot taken earlier in this session came back blank).

key_findings.finding: Who decides: medicolegal death investigations are opened under state law for unexplained, sudden or unnatural deaths, including suspected overdoses; the officers are medical examiners or coroners, who vary in how they are selected (appointed or elected) and in professional credentials, and who complete the medical part of the certificate (underlying cause, causal chain, other significant conditions, manner).
key_findings.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths › The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Toxicology: the authors state that the US has no nationally accepted best practices, standards or guidelines for post-mortem toxicology and that many jurisdictions do not test all suspected overdose deaths for novel substances including fentanyl and its analogues; a 2017 national survey of offices reported that only 75% always request testing for opioids other than heroin or fentanyl and only 51% to 75% always request testing for fentanyl and heroin.
key_findings.locator: The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand (NFLIS 2017 medical examiner/coroner office survey, ref 34); the survey's response rate is not given.

key_findings.finding: Listing drugs: drugs physiologically significant in causing death should be listed individually, preferably by generic name, in Part I, and drugs that did not contribute should not be recorded; the review also quotes Gill that in multi-drug intoxications a single drug's role can usually not be separated, so it is customary to list every drug found above trace amounts.
key_findings.locator: The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Who codes: after filing with the state office of vital statistics, a limited set of fields is sent to NCHS, which codes the cause-of-death text to ICD-10: one underlying cause and up to 20 contributing-cause codes. Phrases such as overdose of drug, toxic effect, intoxication, drug taken inadvertently, lethal amount, wrong drug given in error or wrong dose taken accidentally are coded as drug poisoning even in treatment settings; the underlying cause falls in X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14, with T36 to T50 codes for drugs.
key_findings.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths › Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Opioid codes are broad: T40.0 opium, T40.1 heroin, T40.2 other opioids (oxycodone, codeine, hydrocodone, oxymorphone and morphine together), T40.3 methadone, T40.4 other synthetic narcotics, T40.6 other and unspecified narcotics ('opioid', 'opiate'); a death whose only drug code is T50.9 typically had no drug or drug class written on the certificate.
key_findings.locator: Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quoted from Warner et al. (2013): states with centralized medical examiner systems averaged 92% completeness in listing drugs, against decentralized medical examiner 71%, hybrid 73% and coroner 62% systems; 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah were classed as undetermined intent against 8% nationally. In 2016 the undetermined share still ranged from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data › Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 1st and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Artefactual jumps: South Carolina's age-adjusted prescription-opioid (T40.2 to T40.4) death rate went from 4.7 per 100,000 in 2013 to 9.3 in 2014, mainly because the share of drug-poisoning certificates listing specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% after the state vital-statistics office began collecting drug names for all deaths in January 2014; routine gabapentin testing in Kentucky from July 2014 raised gabapentin prevalence among overdose decedents from 2.9% to 17%. The authors warn that gradual procedural improvements produce smaller, harder-to-detect shifts.
key_findings.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The South Carolina explanation is from personal correspondence with the state office.

key_findings.finding: Delays and provisional undercounting: ICD-10 R99 (unspecified causes) is used as the underlying cause for injury deaths until investigation ends, and an NCHS study found an inverse relationship between the share coded R99 and the share coded drug poisoning; the lag to certificate availability is much longer for overdose deaths than for natural deaths or suicides, usually because of toxicology delays.
key_findings.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 5th paragraph; Statistical Adjustment for Undercounting, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The meaning of 'prescription opioid' codes changed with illicit fentanyl: CDC had used T40.2 to T40.4, and Seth et al. proposed dropping T40.4 because synthetic-opioid deaths were likely due to illicitly made fentanyl; in 2016 T40.4 made up under 20% of T40.2 to T40.4 deaths in Nevada and Utah but over 80% in New Hampshire and Massachusetts.
key_findings.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Text analysis of certificates can identify specific opioids that ICD-10 groups together (an NCHS and FDA tool), but cannot help for the approximately 20% of overdose certificates that name no specific drug.
key_findings.locator: Identifying Specific Opioids by Cause-of-Death Text Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No source is given for the 20%; the review later quotes NCHS figures of 85% specified in 2016.

key_findings.finding: Statistical correction: Buchanich et al. reallocated unspecified unintentional overdose deaths in proportion to opioid involvement among specified deaths, by state and year, and estimated about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths unaccounted for in 1999 to 2015; Ruhm's model-based adjustment gave a 2015 opioid-involved rate of 12.46 per 100,000 against 10.31 reported (21% higher). Ruhm's adjusted state rates for 2008 to 2014 differed from reported rates by widely varying percentages that reflected each state's share of unspecified deaths. The authors call the assumptions reasonable but difficult to verify, and add that models could include characteristics of the investigation systems (jurisdiction type, toxicology protocols), but such information is not readily available.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Adjustment for Undercounting, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand; Buchanich is a co-author of this review.

key_findings.finding: Toxicology markers proposed for enhanced surveillance: heroin's specific metabolite 6-acetylmorphine is often undetected because of rapid metabolism to morphine; cited studies treat a morphine-to-codeine concentration ratio above 1 as a strong and probable indicator of heroin; 4-ANPP indicates illicitly made fentanyl or analogues; heroin metabolites can proxy a short survival time, and absent norfentanyl may indicate rapid death after fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Drugs found but not listed: in a Kentucky study (the authors' group) that linked certificates with post-mortem toxicology, benzodiazepines were less often listed as contributing drugs on certificates, 67% for alprazolam and under 40% for clonazepam and diazepam, against fentanyl 89%, heroin 88%, methadone 81% and cocaine 77% (the review does not state the denominator, presumably decedents in whom each drug was detected); in a multi-jurisdiction study, the region with the lowest gabapentin prevalence was the only one not testing every potential overdose for gabapentin. The authors recommend reporting the type of toxicology testing (screening or confirmatory; routine or on request).
key_findings.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: That the Kentucky study linked certificates with post-mortem toxicology is taken from the title of reference 62, not from the review's sentence.

key_findings.finding: Enhanced surveillance: CDC funded 32 states in 2016 to 2017 for Enhanced State Opioid Overdose Surveillance, with at least 60% of the September 2017 supplemental funding mandated for medical examiners and coroners, including comprehensive toxicology; its reporting system (SUDORS) covers only unintentional opioid overdose deaths.
key_findings.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Specificity trend and capacity: NCHS reported that overdose certificates identifying specific drugs or drug classes rose every year, 75% (2011), 76%, 78%, 81%, 83%, 85% (2016); a 2017 survey found only 32% of responding medical examiner and coroner offices had computerized, networked systems. The authors conclude that the fragmented system makes uniform national standards unlikely in the near future.
key_findings.locator: Death Certificates Remain the Core of Population-Based Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Three papers set out recommendations for certifying opioid-related deaths, as the review relays them: the National Association of Medical Examiners position paper, which the review calls evidence-based (a complete scene investigation; a comprehensive toxicology panel with results interpreted in the context of the circumstances of death; every responsible substance listed by generic name; deaths from misuse of opioids without apparent intent of self-harm classed as accidents, keeping 'undetermined' for the rare cases where the evidence supports more than one intent); the SAMHSA consensus panel (scene investigation, a standard of practice for forensic toxicology and guidance on documenting the cause of death, distinguishing 'drug-caused' from 'drug-detected' deaths, and noting that non-uniform classification affects the quality of incidence and prevalence data); and the Organization of Scientific Area Committees MDI subcommittee (three essential initiatives: standardized drug-related death investigation, more drug-death surveillance by medical examiners and coroners, and their access to death certificates and other information for quality control and analysis).
key_findings.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths › The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Relayed, not appraised; the SAMHSA panel was co-chaired by a co-author of this review (card sc_goldberger_2013).

key_findings.finding: Relayed from the first author's 2015 commentary: the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists Overdose Subcommittee advised that practitioners know the quality and limits of their jurisdiction's certificate data, check the completeness and accuracy of the codes where possible and read counts and rates with caution where the share of unspecified deaths is considerable, that jurisdictions be compared on total drug overdose death rates, and that drug-specific trends remain useful only while the degree of drug specification does not vary markedly from year to year.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data › Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The same advice is a key finding of card sc_slavova_2015.

reporting_issues.issue: The review twice says about 20% of US overdose certificates name no specific drug, without a source, while it later quotes NCHS figures of 85% of certificates identifying specific drugs or drug classes in 2016 (15% without).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Identifying Specific Opioids by Cause-of-Death Text Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Death Certificates Remain the Core, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the dated NCHS series (and its 'drug or drug class' definition), not the unsourced 20%.

reporting_issues.issue: The recommendation to leave non-contributing drugs off the certificate and Gill's report that listing every drug above trace amounts is customary are placed side by side without reconciliation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-specific counts may include drugs that were present but did not contribute; the review does not estimate how often.

reporting_issues.issue: The South Carolina explanation for a doubling of the prescription-opioid death rate rests on personal correspondence, and the survey shares of offices requesting toxicology are given as 75% and '51–75%', a range for a single survey figure, without response rates; the two figures also imply that offices 'always' request testing for other opioids more often than for fentanyl and heroin, which the review leaves unexplained.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methodologic Considerations, 3rd paragraph; The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Use these as illustrations; the primary sources are needed for precise figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors: 'undermined intent' for undetermined (Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph); misspellings in reference annotations ('discusse', 'etimates', 'involed', 'acurate', 'commision'); and the description of Kentucky's enhanced surveillance by Hargrove et al. is cited as reference 84, an NCHS provisional-counts page, while Hargrove et al. is reference 45.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph; Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 6th paragraph; references 3, 45, 49, 84, 87
reporting_issues.consequence: None on content.
