design_detail: Narrative review by a clinical pharmacologist of what can be inferred about drug concentrations and effects during life from samples taken after death: qualitative tests (false positives and false negatives), quantitative analysis, lethal doses and concentrations, tolerance, changes with sampling site and time after death (post-mortem redistribution), the relation between concentrations before and after death, whether a drug's properties predict redistribution, and how a lethal concentration could in principle be defined. The author states that it rests on a systematic search (EMBASE 1974 to June 2007; Medline 1950 to June 2007; text words for post-mortem redistribution), reference lists and a personal collection, but gives no inclusion criteria, counts or appraisal. One table of approximate pharmacokinetic values and heart-to-femoral (central-to-peripheral) post-mortem blood ratios for 32 drugs (ratios from Leikin and Watson 2003), with the author's own correlations; five figures (two scatter plots, three schematic). Read with the editorial in the same issue by J. M. Ritter, the journal's Editor-in-Chief (Br J Clin Pharmacol 2008;66(4):427–429; DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2125.2008.03293.x; PMC2561124), which endorses the review.
can_establish: The mechanisms by which drug concentrations measured after death can differ from those during life, illustrated with the cases, small series and animal experiments published up to mid-2007, and the argument, and the study design it proposes, for defining a lethal concentration.
cannot_establish: How large or how frequent post-mortem changes are for any drug in routine casework (no systematic synthesis or appraisal; the examples are single cases, small series and animal studies), or how well post-mortem concentrations separate deaths caused by a drug from other deaths (no such comparison is made); its own correlations rest on approximate published ratios without uncertainty and cannot be reproduced from its table.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence cited includes single autopsy cases; Rouzioux's 10 cases (1980); Milroy and Forrest's 111 methadone deaths; Jones and Holmgren's 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning; a few dozen paired samples taken before and after death; animal experiments in rats, rabbits and swine; and Leikin and Watson's table of heart-to-femoral ratios.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Search stated: EMBASE 1974 to June 2007 for autopsy with drug blood level, Medline 1950 to June 2007 for autopsy with tissue distribution, both also for post-mortem and redistribution as text words, plus reference lists and a personal collection. No inclusion criteria, numbers screened or included, or language limits are given (Search strategy).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author to illustrate the problems of interpretation, including well-known criminal cases (Shipman, Palmer, Litvinenko) and single cases. Large datasets comparing deaths caused by a drug with other deaths are mentioned in one paragraph (Druid and Holmgren 1997; Reis et al. 2007) without their results.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). The concentrations discussed come from whole blood after death (femoral, heart or other sites), from tissues and fluids, and from plasma or serum during life.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; the review stresses that after death the dose taken cannot be established.
exposure.polysubstance: Raised as a further difficulty: more than one drug is commonly implicated in a death, and interactions between drugs, or between a drug and ethanol, make interpretation harder still (Importance of tolerance, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The review proposes the comparison that would be needed: deaths in which a drug is found assigned to drug-induced or not drug-induced without knowledge of the measured concentrations, then the two concentration distributions compared.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review names tolerance, hypersensitivity (a sub-therapeutic penicillin concentration can kill a person with anaphylaxis), pharmacogenetic variation and hidden causes of sudden death such as arrhythmia as factors that blur any relation between concentration and death.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data collection). The author's own analysis correlates the heart-to-femoral ratio with the volume of distribution (r = 0.247, P > 0.1) and with the octanol–water partition coefficient (r = 0.035, P > 0.1), using approximate ratios from Leikin and Watson (2003) and handbook values (Table 1; Figures 1 and 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The author notes that the published ratios carry no stated uncertainty, which he calls 'undoubtedly very large'.
outcomes.operationalization: Extent of post-mortem redistribution = heart (central) to femoral (peripheral) blood concentration ratio, with a ratio above 3.0 taken as marked redistribution.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (two descriptive correlations).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Second-hand figures as cited (see key findings). The author's correlations: r = 0.247 with volume of distribution and r = 0.035 with the partition coefficient, both P > 0.1. Editors' recalculation from Table 1: r = 0.22 with volume of distribution (31 drugs with a value), 0.09 with the raw and 0.35 with the log partition coefficient (32 drugs; p about 0.05 for the latter); a correlation of 0.247 from about 31 drugs has a 95% interval of about −0.12 to 0.55 (Fisher z), so the data do not exclude a moderate relationship.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable to a narrative review; the choice of examples is the author's.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the correlations rest on about 31 drugs, too few to exclude a moderate correlation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The cited evidence shows, case by case, that post-mortem concentrations can differ from those measured during life: in the few human cases with both, post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios for drugs run from 1.0 (salicylate) to 17.66 (chloroquine), depending on drug, site and time, and two carbon monoxide deaths had concentrations about 25–30% lower after death; that heart blood exceeds femoral blood by about 1.4 to 4 times for 32 drugs (approximate published ratios); that quoted 'lethal' ranges are very wide and overlap (methadone ranges between 60 and 4500 µg/L across sources; MDMA 40–8500 µg/L); that tolerance shifts the relation between concentration and effect (ethanol in 693 poisoning deaths ranged about threefold); and that qualitative results can be falsely positive or falsely negative. It contains no study comparing concentrations in deaths caused by a drug with those in other deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that post-mortem changes make the assumptions of clinical pharmacology largely invalid and interpretation difficult or impossible, and that compilations of lethal concentrations are misleading; the Conclusion that there is "no reliable or obvious connection" between concentrations in life and after death. These are fair readings of most of the examples, though a few show little change after death (salicylate 1.0 and paracetamol 1.5 in single cases; little redistribution of moclobemide, as cited). The examples rest on single cases, small series and animal studies without appraisal, and the review does not weigh the large comparisons of drug deaths against other deaths that it mentions. Its proposed remedy (assigning deaths independently of concentration, then comparing) is stated as a requirement, not tested. Ritter's editorial endorses the review without qualification and says post-mortem measurements are not at present useful in establishing the cause of death, while hoping that measurements in appropriate tissues at defined intervals may become so.

timeline.event: Holt and Benstead find different digoxin concentrations in three post-mortem blood samples from one body (as summarized in the review).

Rouzioux reports 10 cases: in 8, post-mortem left-ventricular concentrations were 2.58 to 17.66 times those during life; in 2 carbon monoxide deaths, 25–30% lower (as summarized). The review's later list of this author's ratios includes an imipramine case at 1.39, below this range (see reporting issues).
Koren and MacLeod name post-mortem redistribution in a rat study of digoxin (as summarized).
Pounder and Jones call post-mortem drug redistribution a toxicological nightmare (cited as reference 7).
Druid and Holmgren compile femoral-blood concentrations of drugs in fatal and control cases from Swedish data (mentioned in the review without results).

Leikin and Watson, 'what the dead can and cannot tell us': source of the heart-to-femoral ratios in Table 1 and of the suggestion that drugs with a volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are candidates for redistribution.
This review, with Ritter's endorsing editorial in the same issue (DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2125.2008.03293.x).

Launiainen and Ojanperä cite the review in their introduction and report post-mortem femoral-blood medians above therapeutic plasma ranges for 46 of 129 drugs in 57,903 Finnish autopsy cases (read in this round).
Borra et al.: review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: A frequently cited statement of the case against reading post-mortem concentrations as if they were concentrations during life, endorsed by the journal's editor. Later database work (for example Launiainen and Ojanperä 2014) supports its central point with large numbers. Its figures are second-hand and should be cited from the primary sources; claims resting only on this review stay at draft and say that their figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC full text has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no competing-interest statement appears in the PMC full text. The author thanks five colleagues for discussions and suggestions.
funding.affiliations_note: West Midlands Centre for Adverse Drug Reactions, City Hospital, and Department of Clinical Pharmacology, University of Birmingham. The author's own book on forensic pharmacology is reference 1; the review relies on others' studies. The accompanying editorial is by the journal's Editor-in-Chief, J. M. Ritter (role stated in the editorial's author information on PMC; Department of Clinical Pharmacology, King's College and St Thomas' Hospitals, London), and carries no funding or conflict statement either. Received 16 February 2008, accepted 19 May 2008.

what_would_settle_it: The study the review itself calls for: a large series of deaths in which a drug was found, each assigned to drug-induced or not drug-induced by assessors blind to the measured concentrations, with standardized femoral sampling at recorded intervals after death, comparing the two concentration distributions (and, for a subset, paired samples from before and after death) to estimate how far they overlap.

domains.note: Databases, years and index terms are stated, which is more than most narrative reviews give, but there are no inclusion criteria, counts or flow, and a personal collection was added; the choice of examples is the author's.

No formal appraisal; the author does name some weaknesses (published ratios without uncertainty, few animals and time points, unpaired samples in the swine study), but the cited case-level figures are taken at face value, and several citations appear mismatched (references 68, 75 and 82).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The evidence is from other investigators; the author cites his own book and one classification paper.

The schematic figures are labelled as schemes and the proposed design is clearly a proposal, but the abstract and Conclusion state the inferences more absolutely than single cases and small series can support, and three of the author's own calculations are misreported (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether post-mortem concentrations can be interpreted
domains.note: The review assembles evidence of uncertainty; large controlled compilations that compare concentrations in drug deaths with those in other deaths (Druid and Holmgren; Reis et al.), the side that could show where femoral concentrations do discriminate, are mentioned without their results.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain. The review is careful and its direction is consistent with later large studies, but its evidence is illustrative rather than systematic and several of its own numbers are misreported. Citable for: the mechanisms by which post-mortem concentrations differ from those during life (redistribution from lungs, heart muscle, gut and bladder; post-mortem generation of ethanol and GHB; hydrolysis of morphine conjugates; changes in protein binding and pH); that heart blood commonly exceeds femoral blood; that qualitative tests can be falsely positive or negative; that quoted lethal ranges overlap widely; that tolerance shifts concentration–effect relations; and the argument that lethal concentrations can only be defined by comparing deaths assigned without knowledge of concentrations. Not citable, except through the primary sources, for any specific ratio or range; and not for the claim that volume of distribution does not predict redistribution, which rests on a correlation that cannot be reproduced from the review's own table.

key_findings.finding: Scope and method: a review of what can be inferred about pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics during life from data obtained after death, based on EMBASE (1974 to June 2007) and Medline (1950 to June 2007) searches with stated index terms, text words for post-mortem redistribution, reference lists and a personal collection.
key_findings.locator: Introduction; Search strategy

key_findings.finding: Qualitative results can mislead in both directions. False positives: immunoassays detecting endogenous digoxin-like substances in renal failure; standard analyses that do not distinguish active R-methadone from almost inactive S-methadone; ethanol and GHB generated after death; contamination from soil, burial containers or lithium-heparin tubes. False negatives: specific tests not done (polonium in the Litvinenko case after negative radiation screens); drug gone before death (paracetamol by the time of death from liver failure; paraquat weeks after ingestion). Opiates can be detected in urine after eating poppy-seed cake. A positive test does not establish that a substance caused death, nor a negative one that it did not.
key_findings.locator: Qualitative post-mortem analysis, 2nd paragraph; False-positive results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; False-negative results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: A Swiss study is cited as finding that the medical history plays an important role in interpreting post-mortem data in about 70% of cases; accounts documented before death are favoured because bias and deception can affect histories taken afterwards.
key_findings.locator: The medical history, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quantitative analysis: drug assays commonly have accuracy and precision standard deviations above 10% of the mean; almost all post-mortem analysis is of whole blood whereas reference values in life are mostly from plasma or serum, and the whole-blood-to-plasma ratio varies by drug even in life (0.5 for phenytoin, 2 for maprotiline); femoral venous blood is thought least susceptible to post-mortem change; sedimentation, clotting, haemolysis, putrefaction and contamination can make blood results unhelpful and cavity fluids meaningless.
key_findings.locator: Quantitative post-mortem analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Approximate heart-to-femoral post-mortem blood ratios for 32 drugs (from Leikin and Watson 2003) range from 1.4 (phenytoin) to 4 (chlorpromazine, midazolam); for example amitriptyline 3.1, oxycodone 3.1, propoxyphene 3.5, haloperidol 3.6, morphine 2.2, codeine 1.8, dextroamphetamine 2, ketamine 1.6, diazepam 1.6. In 11 cases with fentanyl, the ratio ranged from 0.89 to 3.2 (mean 1.6).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced from the properties of a drug?, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand, approximate values without uncertainty, as the author says; cite the primary source for any single ratio.

key_findings.finding: The author reports a weak relation between the heart-to-femoral ratio and the volume of distribution (r = 0.247, P > 0.1) and none with the octanol–water partition coefficient (r = 0.035, P > 0.1), and that the ratio exceeds the volume of distribution in L/kg for 15 of 33 drugs; he notes that other authors have already concluded that volume of distribution cannot be the sole determinant of redistribution (reference 81, a study of three beta-blockers in rabbits), and concludes that it does not indicate an upper limit for the divergence between samples taken before and after death.
key_findings.locator: Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced from the properties of a drug?, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, footnote; Figures 1 and 2, captions
key_findings.note: Not reproducible from Table 1 (editors' calculation: r = 0.22 with volume of distribution; 0.09 or 0.35 with the raw or log partition coefficient; ratio above volume of distribution for 9 of 31 drugs); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Ratios of post-mortem to ante-mortem concentrations in the few human cases with both: imipramine 4.85, 1.39, 9.94 and 7.60 and chloroquine 17.66 and 14.6 (Rouzioux); post-mortem femoral to ante-mortem serum amitriptyline 3.6, 4.3 and 12, imipramine 3.0 and 6.0; chloroquine ante-mortem serum to post-mortem peripheral 0.7, with heart to peripheral 2.9; MDMA 1.1 to 6.6 and MDA 1.5 to 13.3; single cases of dosulepin 11.7, propoxyphene 8.3, amitriptyline 3.9, methadone 2.6, propranolol 1.9, paracetamol 1.5, salicylate 1.0; diltiazem 1.7.
key_findings.locator: Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Single cases and very small series with varying sample timing, cited second-hand. Rouzioux's imipramine ratio of 1.39 lies below the range of 2.58 to 17.66 that the review gives earlier for 8 of the 10 cases in the same work (Site-related and time-related differences, 1st paragraph); sampling site or timing may differ but is not stated (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Published lethal concentrations overlap widely: quoted ranges of 40–8500 µg/L for MDMA and 60–3100 µg/L for methadone; for methadone in post-mortem blood, Milroy and Forrest found quoted ranges of 220–3040, 200–4500, 320–3980, 1000–2000 and 100–2500 or 100–2600 µg/L, and 84–2700 µg/L in their own 111 cases; in 25 of their cases with arm and leg blood, the author computes a median difference of 72 (printed as µmol/L; interquartile range 20–200).
key_findings.locator: Extrapolation from post-mortem concentrations to ante-mortem concentrations
key_findings.note: The unit of the arm–leg difference is probably misprinted; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Tolerance: for opioids there is little or no separation between therapeutic and toxic concentrations, and receptor downregulation in regular use shifts concentration–response curves; amounts that would kill people without tolerance are tolerated by people who use heroin habitually. Ethanol: a 'lethal' concentration above 500 mg/100 mL has been quoted, yet one patient was still talking above 1500 mg/100 mL; in 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning, post-mortem concentrations averaged 356 mg/100 mL, with a spread (printed as a 95% confidence interval) of 185 to 526 mg/100 mL, about threefold between people. More than one drug is commonly implicated in a death.
key_findings.locator: Importance of tolerance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Making deduction from post-mortem drug concentrations, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mechanisms of post-mortem change: diffusion from the stomach (ethanol), bladder (a single case with femoral diphenhydramine and dihydrocodeine an order of magnitude above heart blood), lungs (lipophilic basic drugs such as amitriptyline, chlorpromazine and methadone, raising left-ventricular and aortic concentrations) and heart muscle (digoxin); in rabbits, MDMA in heart blood rose mainly by redistribution from lung tissue; hydrolysis of conjugates raises apparent free morphine; serum potassium rises from about 3.5 mmol/L before death to 18 at 1 hour and 25 at 24 hours after death. Calculating a body burden from a post-mortem concentration and a volume of distribution measured in life should be abandoned.
key_findings.locator: Site-related and time-related differences in post-mortem concentrations, 4th paragraph; Transfer across barriers, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Redistribution of absorbed drug, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Influence of volume of distribution, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Animal studies: in swine given intravenous morphine, the heart-to-femoral ratio for free morphine was about 0.5 at 30 minutes after death and 1.0 at 120 minutes; in rats dying within 10 minutes of a diamorphine overdose, lung morphine was nearly 10 times heart-blood morphine. Morphine metabolite ratios vary up to 40-fold between living patients, so deductions from post-mortem metabolite ratios are uncertain. A ratio of 1 between heart and femoral blood does not show that the post-mortem concentration equals the concentration before death.
key_findings.locator: Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposed standard for defining a lethal concentration: assign a series of deaths in which the drug is found to drug-induced and not drug-induced groups without knowledge of the measured concentrations, then compare the distributions; broad overlap is expected, so there is no clear lethal concentration. Conclusion: concentrations after death cannot generally be read back to concentrations before death, lethal concentrations are extremely difficult to define, post-mortem concentrations have been over-interpreted, and good evidence should be required before lethal concentrations are defined.
key_findings.locator: Making deduction from post-mortem drug concentrations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 5 caption; Conclusion

key_findings.finding: Ritter's editorial (same issue) endorses the review: death makes the assumptions of clinical pharmacology largely invalid, compilations of lethal concentrations are unreliable, clinical pharmacologists without forensic training should hesitate to give expert opinions on post-mortem data, and post-mortem drug measurements are not at present useful in establishing the cause of death, though measurements in appropriate tissues at defined intervals might become so.
key_findings.locator: Beware drawing inferences from drug analyses in post-mortem samples, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The correlations cannot be reproduced from Table 1, whose footnote gives the same coefficients as Figures 1 and 2: from the 31 drugs with a volume of distribution, r = 0.22 (printed 0.247); from the 32 drugs with a partition coefficient, r = 0.09 for the raw value (Table 1 footnote) or 0.35 for its logarithm (Figure 2), printed 0.035 with P > 0.1. The text's ratio above the volume of distribution for 15 of 33 drugs is 9 of 31 in Table 1 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and footnote; Can the extent of post-mortem redistribution be deduced..., 2nd paragraph; Figures 1 and 2, captions
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the figures use a different, unlisted set of 33 drugs or the values are misreported; with the log partition coefficient the Table 1 data give a correlation of 0.35 (p about 0.05), so the statement that drug properties show no relation to redistribution should not be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: For 693 deaths from acute alcohol poisoning, 185 to 526 mg/100 mL is called the 95% confidence interval around the mean of 356; it is the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations (implied SD 87), a range of individual values. The confidence interval of the mean would be about 350 to 363 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Importance of tolerance, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The point made (about threefold variation between people) is correct for the range of values; only the label is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The arm–leg difference in methadone concentration in 25 cases is given as a median of 72 µmol/L (interquartile range 20–200 µmol/L), while the series' concentrations are given as 84–2700 µg/L. At methadone's molar mass of about 309 g/mol, 72 µmol/L is about 22 mg/L, about eight times the highest concentration in the series (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Extrapolation from post-mortem concentrations to ante-mortem concentrations
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit is probably µg/L; the size of the arm–leg difference should be taken from Milroy and Forrest (2000), not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 68, cited for post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios of MDMA (1.1 to 6.6) and MDA (1.5 to 13.3), is Elliott and Burgess (2005) on urine analysis in suspected drink spiking, whose title does not suggest such data. Reference 75, a study of morphine concentrations by collection site in heroin overdose victims, is cited among animal experiments on morphine (the porcine study is reference 78), and reference 82, on the redistribution of selected psychiatric drugs in post-mortem cases, is cited for animal experiments showing little redistribution of moclobemide. References 6 and 83 are the same paper listed twice.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; References 6, 68, 75, 78, 82 and 83
reporting_issues.consequence: The MDMA and MDA ratios cannot be traced to their source from this review, and part of the animal evidence it cites for morphine and moclobemide is cited to papers whose titles describe human deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes its search as systematic and the problems as systematically reviewed, but it reports no selection criteria, numbers of records or synthesis method.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is a narrative review with a documented search and must not be appraised or cited as a systematic review.

reporting_issues.issue: Rouzioux's series is given two ways: 8 of 10 cases with post-mortem left-ventricular concentrations 2.58 to 17.66 times those in life (Site-related and time-related differences, 1st paragraph), and later post-mortem to ante-mortem ratios for four imipramine cases (4.85, 1.39, 9.94 and 7.60) and two chloroquine cases (17.66 and 14.6), one of which (1.39) lies below that minimum.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Site-related and time-related differences in post-mortem concentrations, 1st paragraph; Relationship between concentrations measured before and after death, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sampling site or timing behind the two sets of figures may differ but is not stated; neither range should be cited from this review without Rouzioux (1980, reference 44).

design_detail: Record-review comparison of two case definitions of a heroin-related death, applied to the same records of Maryland's statewide Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) for overdose deaths in 2012–2015. Standard approach: the death certificate's cause-of-death section contains the word 'heroin'. Enhanced surveillance (a protocol developed by the state Vital Statistics Administration, the OCME, the Maryland Poison Center and the Behavioral Health Administration): every OCME record with an intoxication-type cause-of-death term was reviewed (cause of death, toxicology results, scene-investigation notes) and counted as heroin-related if (1) heroin was on the certificate, (2) toxicology found 6-monoacetylmorphine, (3) toxicology found quinine with morphine or free morphine, or (4) the certificate named morphine or no specific substance and scene notes suggested heroin; deaths whose scene notes suggested prescription morphine were not counted. The enhanced count contains the standard count by construction. Descriptive counts, percentages and 95% confidence intervals by year, age, race or ethnicity and gender; no statistical tests.
can_establish: How many more Maryland overdose deaths in 2012–2015 met a broader protocol definition of heroin-related death (certificate wording plus toxicology markers and scene evidence) than had heroin written on the certificate, how that gap changed over the four years, and in which age, sex and racial or ethnic groups certificates named heroin least often.
cannot_establish: That the 1,052 additional deaths were caused by heroin (two of the four criteria count heroin markers found in toxicology whatever the certifier concluded; no independent reference standard was used, and who reviewed the records, or whether a second reviewer checked them, is not reported); whether any certificate naming heroin was wrong (the comparison can only add deaths); how the protocol would perform in other states or with later toxicology; or the size of the national undercount.

sample.recruitment: Records: the Maryland OCME, which must investigate every death in the state from violence, suicide or casualty, or that occurs in a suspicious, unexpected or unusual manner; cause-of-death information for 2012–2015 was provided by the OCME to the Vital Statistics Administration, which compiles the state's overdose statistics (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Standard approach: certificates of overdose deaths whose cause-of-death section includes 'heroin'. Enhanced approach: all OCME records whose cause of death includes any of poisoning, intoxication, toxicity, inhalation, ingestion, overdose, exposure, chemical, use, combined effects, combined toxic effects or effects (Methods, 3rd paragraph). The definition of the 3,957 'total overdose deaths' (intent, codes, whether alcohol-only deaths count) is not stated beyond a reference to the state's report on drug- and alcohol-related intoxication deaths (ref 7).
sample.demographics: Of the 2,182 deaths heroin-related by enhanced surveillance (Table 3): 1,680 men, 501 women; 1,505 non-Hispanic White, 623 non-Hispanic Black, 26 Hispanic, 25 other; aged under 25: 237, 25–34: 566, 35–44: 447, 45–54: 592, 55 or older: 339. No demographics are given for the 3,957 overdose deaths.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. One decedent of unknown age, 3 of unknown race and 1 of unknown gender are left out of the subgroup rows of Table 3.
sample.selection_effects: One state with a centralized, statewide medical examiner system, 2012–2015. The protocol was designed and applied by the agencies that certify the deaths and compile the official counts. The undefined denominator of overdose deaths limits comparison of the shares with other places.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count and who decided. Standard: an OCME medical certifier wrote the cause of death, described as the certifier's best medical opinion that may vary among certifiers (Methods, 1st paragraph); the count is a text search of that section for 'heroin'. Enhanced: the study team reviewed each record against the four criteria (the paper does not say who reviewed, how many reviewers, whether they were blind to the certificate, or how often they agreed). What was tested: a 'toxicology screen' recording 6-monoacetylmorphine, morphine or free morphine, and quinine, which the authors describe as a common heroin adulterant (Methods, 5th paragraph); the panel, the specimens and the share of deaths tested are not reported. Scene evidence counted as strongly suggesting heroin included reports that the person was known to use heroin and was found with drug paraphernalia, or that heroin use was witnessed on the day of death.
exposure.polysubstance: Not separated. A death counted as heroin-related whatever other drugs were present or written on the certificate, and no breakdown of co-occurring drugs is given. 55 of the additional deaths had a substance other than heroin or morphine as the certified cause; the authors concede the certifier may have judged heroin present but not directly related to the death (Discussion › Limitations).

comparison.controls: The same records classified two ways. Because criterion 1 of the enhanced approach is the standard approach, the enhanced count can only equal or exceed it. No independent reference standard (for example blinded review by forensic pathologists) was used for either approach.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Reasons certifiers did not write 'heroin' (time from use to specimen, route, chronic use, quality of analysis, morphine as heroin's breakdown product) are discussed in the Introduction, not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Counts and percentages of heroin-related deaths by approach and year (Table 1); sources of identification for the additional deaths (Table 2); the number of enhanced-approach deaths with heroin on the certificate, with percentage and 95% confidence interval, by year, age, race or ethnicity and gender (Table 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither approach was validated against an independent standard; no inter-rater reliability is reported for the judgments made from scene notes.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Heroin-related' means heroin written in the cause-of-death section (standard) or meeting any of the four criteria (enhanced). The paper uses the same words for both, although criteria 2 and 3 rest on substances found in toxicology rather than on a judgment that heroin caused the death.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests; subgroup differences are described from percentages and confidence intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The review was done within the agencies that produce the counts, and the chief medical examiner is a co-author.

analysis.effect_sizes: Heroin-related deaths 2012–2015: 1,130 by certificates against 2,182 by enhanced surveillance (1.93 times as many, editors' calculation), 28.6% against 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths. By year: 2012, 179 against 392 (22.4% and 49.1% of 799); 2013, 221 against 464 (25.8% and 54.1% of 858); 2014, 309 against 578 (29.7% and 55.5% of 1,041); 2015, 421 against 748 (33.4% and 59.4% of 1,259). Share of enhanced-approach deaths with heroin on the certificate: 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9) overall, rising from 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 58.2% under age 25 falling to 41.9% at 55 or older; non-Hispanic White 53.5%, non-Hispanic Black 47.0%; men 56.8%, women 35.1%; non-Hispanic Black women 25.9% (18.5 to 33.3); Hispanic men 77.3% (17 of 22); Hispanic women 0 of 4. Of the 1,052 additional deaths, the certificate named morphine for 804 (76.4%), no specific substance for 193 (18.3%) and another substance for 55 (5.2%); toxicology showed 6-monoacetylmorphine in 136, morphine with quinine in 892, and morphine or free morphine in 998 (overlapping). Editors' calculation: the 1,052 additional deaths are 26.6% of all 3,957 overdose deaths, and certificates named heroin in 52% of protocol-defined heroin deaths.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; no ethics approval was needed because the study involved only deceased individuals (Human Participant Protection).
analysis.selective_reporting: No breakdown of the additional deaths by the criterion, or combination of criteria, that qualified them; Table 2's sources overlap and do not sum to 1,052, and one of its rows conflicts with the text (reporting issue 1).
analysis.power: Not applicable. Subgroup intervals are wide for Hispanic and 'other' groups (22 to 26 deaths), and there is none for Hispanic women (4 deaths).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Applying a broader protocol to the same Maryland medical-examiner records, 2,182 overdose deaths in 2012–2015 met at least one heroin criterion, against 1,130 with 'heroin' written on the certificate. Most of the 1,052 extra deaths had morphine certified as the cause together with scene evidence of heroin, toxicology markers (6-monoacetylmorphine in 136; morphine with quinine in 892) or both. The share of protocol-defined heroin deaths that the certificates named rose from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015 and was lowest for people aged 55 or older (41.9%), women (35.1%) and Black women (25.9%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says certificates "may underestimate the contribution of heroin", which the data support. The Limitations go further: the enhanced approach "almost certainly provides a more accurate count", asserted without any reference standard. Gaps: (1) the enhanced definition contains the standard one, so 'nearly double' measures how much broader it is, not how often certificates are wrong, and the design cannot detect certificates that name heroin wrongly; (2) two criteria rest on toxicology presence, and the 55 deaths certified as due to another substance were counted even though the certifier may have judged heroin present but not causal, so 'heroin-related' in the enhanced count partly means 'heroin present'; (3) the Discussion's statements that certificates underestimate heroin deaths among older people, women and Black people, and that enhanced counts were substantially higher among Hispanic women, rest on percentages without tests and, for Hispanic women, on 4 deaths; (4) the Public Health Implications suggest that recent rises in deaths attributed to heart disease might be missed overdose deaths, with no data in the paper; (5) the linked editorial (Galea and Vaughan, 2018) repeats the finding as showing that enhanced surveillance can better identify heroin, without noting the missing reference standard; (6) the Discussion (8th paragraph) presents the rise in the share named on certificates, from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, as a sign that the recommendations are being implemented in Maryland, without any data on when or how they were implemented, so a trend over time is read as an effect.

timeline.event: SAMHSA consensus panel recommends uniform standards and case definitions for opioid-related deaths (ref 10, cited with ref 11 in the Discussion, 6th paragraph, for the need for standardized methods); the recommendations summarized in the 7th paragraph, including naming the parent drug rather than the metabolite when evidence supports it, are attributed to SAMHSA experts but printed with ref 12, the 2015 Maryland Vital Statistics Annual Report, presumably meant as ref 10

Mertz, Janssen and Williams (Journal of Forensic Sciences): heroin under-represented among unintentional overdose deaths in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, when morphine was certified (ref 6); a similar county case review.

Slavova et al., 'let's get specific': in 2010 the overdose death rate attributed to other and unspecified drugs ranged from 0.2 to 7.4 per 100,000 across 11 jurisdictions (US 3.1), as cited in this paper's Discussion (ref 4)

Galea and Vaughan, issue editorial in the American Journal of Public Health (doi 10.2105/AJPH.2018.304422, PMC5944893), linked from this article: summarizes it as showing that standard certificates may underestimate heroin deaths and that enhanced surveillance can better identify them; no critique of the method.
Buchanich et al.: national reallocation of unintentional overdose deaths with no named drug; a different approach to undercounting, on national certificates (card sc_buchanich_2018)

Gutkind et al. scoping review: summarizes this study as 1,052 additional heroin-related deaths, 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths in Maryland 2012–2015, and places it beside county reviews in New York City (heroin deaths +17%), San Francisco and Allegheny County and a 38-state SUDORS analysis that all found heroin under-named on certificates (card sc_gutkind_2025)

replication.where_it_stands: The direction agrees with case reviews elsewhere summarized by Gutkind et al. (2025): heroin is under-named on certificates, mostly because morphine is written instead. The size varies widely (about 17% more heroin deaths in New York City and 13–21% in San Francisco, as Gutkind et al. report them, against nearly double here), and none of the studies read for this round checks either approach against an independent standard, or in both directions. Maryland's own certificates named heroin more often each year of the study (45.7% to 56.3%), which the authors link to the recommendations being implemented, without data on implementation.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement appears on the PMC page.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement appears on the PMC page.
funding.affiliations_note: At the time of the study, Horon, Singal and Sharfstein were with the Maryland Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, Baltimore, which compiles the state's overdose statistics; Fowler is the chief medical examiner of the State of Maryland, whose office wrote the certificates evaluated; correspondence to Sharfstein at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. The study evaluates the authors' own agencies' data with a protocol those agencies developed; recorded as a flag for closer reading. By the CONTRIBUTORS note (author information), Fowler contributed to the study's conceptualization and design, to data collection and to revision, and Horon to conceptualization and design, data collection, analysis and interpretation, so the certifying office took part in designing the comparison as well as in supplying the records.

what_would_settle_it: Blinded review of a random sample of both groups of Maryland records (the 1,130 certificates naming heroin and the 1,052 added deaths) by forensic pathologists outside the office, using a written causal standard and the toxicology concentrations and scene evidence, reporting agreement with each approach in both directions; repeated in states with coroner systems.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The statewide medical examiner must investigate unexpected and unusual deaths, so its records are the right frame for Maryland overdose deaths.
All records with intoxication-type cause-of-death terms, 2012–2015; no sampling.
3,957 overdose deaths and 2,182 protocol-defined heroin deaths; small subgroups (Hispanic, other; 4 Hispanic women) are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics of the heroin-related deaths and the setting are described; the definition of the 3,957 overdose deaths and the toxicology panel are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Every record was reviewed; 5 decedents with unknown age, race or gender are left out of subgroup rows only.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: 6-monoacetylmorphine is a specific heroin marker and morphine with quinine a presumptive one; but the protocol was never validated, scene-note judgments are subjective, and criteria 2 and 3 count presence, not a judgment of cause.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One written protocol, but who applied it, whether reviewers were blind to the certificate and how consistently it was applied are not reported; the standard approach depends on individual certifiers' wording, which the authors say varies.

Counts, percentages and 95% confidence intervals are appropriate and re-derive from the tables; Wald-type intervals are given for subgroups of 22 to 26 deaths, no interval for 4, and subgroup differences are interpreted without tests.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths from a state register compared under two case definitions (round brief, certificate studies). The comparison is in effect a check of the certificates' sensitivity against a broader definition, but the broader definition is not a validated reference: it includes the certificates by construction, rests partly on presence in toxicology and on unblinded scene-note judgments, and was built and applied by the agencies that produce the counts. Counts and percentages are internally consistent, apart from one table row. Citable for: in Maryland 2012–2015, certificates named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths while 2,182 met a protocol combining certificate wording, toxicology markers and scene evidence; most missed cases had morphine written as the cause; certificates named heroin less often for older people, women and Black women; the share named rose from 45.7% to 56.3%. Not citable for: heroin as the cause of all 2,182 deaths, the accuracy of certificates that name heroin, or undercounting outside Maryland.

key_findings.finding: Maryland 2012–2015: death certificates naming heroin identified 1,130 heroin-related overdose deaths; enhanced surveillance identified 2,182, nearly double; that is 28.6% against 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths.
key_findings.locator: RESULTS, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Total row)

key_findings.finding: By year, certificates against enhanced surveillance: 2012, 179 (22.4% of 799) against 392 (49.1%); 2013, 221 (25.8% of 858) against 464 (54.1%); 2014, 309 (29.7% of 1,041) against 578 (55.5%); 2015, 421 (33.4% of 1,259) against 748 (59.4%). Overdose deaths, heroin-related deaths and the heroin share all rose over the period by both approaches.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; RESULTS, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Enhanced-surveillance criteria: heroin on the certificate; 6-monoacetylmorphine in toxicology; quinine with morphine or free morphine in toxicology; or morphine or no specific substance on the certificate plus scene notes suggesting heroin. Deaths with scene notes suggesting prescription morphine were not counted. The protocol was developed by the Vital Statistics Administration, the OCME, the Maryland Poison Center and the Behavioral Health Administration.
key_findings.locator: METHODS, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Of the 1,052 additional deaths, the certificate named morphine, alone or with other substances, for 804 (76.4%), gave no specific substance (for example narcotic or opioid intoxication) for 193 (18.3%) and named another substance for 55 (5.2%). Every record certifying morphine had scene evidence suggesting heroin.
key_findings.locator: RESULTS, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives 1,042 for morphine certified with scene evidence; the text's 804 is consistent with 804 + 193 + 55 = 1,052 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Sources for the additional deaths (overlapping): toxicology showed 6-monoacetylmorphine in 136 records, morphine with quinine in 892, and morphine or free morphine in 998.
key_findings.locator: RESULTS, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Among the 2,182 protocol-defined heroin deaths, the certificate named heroin in 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9), rising from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015; by age, 58.2% under 25, 58.0% at 25–34, 54.6% at 35–44, 47.0% at 45–54 and 41.9% at 55 or older.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (Total, Year of death, Age group rows); RESULTS, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: By sex and race or ethnicity, the certificate named heroin in 56.8% of deaths of men and 35.1% of women; non-Hispanic White 53.5%, non-Hispanic Black 47.0%; non-Hispanic White men 57.9%, women 39.4%; non-Hispanic Black men 52.9%, women 25.9% (18.5 to 33.3); Hispanic men 77.3% (17 of 22), Hispanic women 0 of 4.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (Race/ethnicity, Gender, Race/ethnicity and gender rows); RESULTS, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: With enhanced surveillance the largest number of heroin-related deaths was at ages 45–54 (592) rather than 25–34 (566), whereas by certificates the peak was at 25–34 (328 against 278 at 45–54).
key_findings.locator: DISCUSSION, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (Age group rows)

key_findings.finding: Who certifies: the OCME must investigate all Maryland deaths from violence, suicide or casualty, or that are suspicious, unexpected or unusual; the cause of death it writes is the certifier's best medical opinion and may vary among certifiers. The authors judge the office's approach possibly conservative in attributing deaths to heroin.
key_findings.locator: METHODS, 1st paragraph; DISCUSSION, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Why certificates miss heroin, as the authors give it: certifiers may write a nonspecific cause such as narcotic intoxication or drug overdose; time from use to specimen, route, chronic use and quality of analysis make identification hard; heroin itself is rarely detected because of its short half-life, so its breakdown products morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine are found and morphine intoxication may be written.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (untitled), 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' own limitation, in the overcounting direction: some deaths counted by enhanced surveillance may not have been heroin-related, including some certified as morphine intoxication, and some of the 55 deaths certified as due to another substance, where the certifier may have judged heroin present but not directly related; they judge these few.
key_findings.locator: DISCUSSION › Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recommendations cited from SAMHSA experts: list every physiologically significant drug, name the parent drug rather than the metabolite when toxicology or scene findings support it (for example heroin rather than morphine), avoid the terms 'overdose' and 'use' on certificates, and evaluate whether toxicology can distinguish chronic from acute use.
key_findings.locator: DISCUSSION, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: The paragraph's citation is reference 12, the 2015 Maryland Vital Statistics Annual Report; the SAMHSA consensus panel paper (Goldberger et al. 2013) is reference 10, cited with reference 11 in the paragraph before, so the citation is probably misnumbered (reporting issue 5).

reporting_issues.issue: The text twice gives 804 additional records that certified morphine as the cause (76.4% of 1,052, with 193 and 55 making up the rest), while Table 2 gives 1,042 in its row for morphine listed as the cause on the certificate with supporting scene evidence.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, RESULTS, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: 1,042 would leave only 10 of the 1,052 additional deaths without morphine on the certificate, contradicting the 193 and 55 in the text; use 804.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's third toxicology row reads 'morphine or free morphine and supporting evidence from scene investigation' (998), while the text describes the 998 as records showing morphine or free morphine, with no scene condition. Neither matches the four criteria in the Methods, in which morphine in toxicology counts only with quinine, or through a certificate naming morphine or no substance plus scene notes. The abstract likewise names morphine 'alone' as a major factor.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; RESULTS, 2nd paragraph; METHODS, 4th paragraph; Abstract › Results
reporting_issues.consequence: How many additional deaths each criterion qualified, alone or together, cannot be reconstructed; morphine in toxicology without quinine, 6-monoacetylmorphine or scene evidence was not, by the Methods, enough to count a death.

reporting_issues.issue: The denominator of 3,957 'total overdose deaths' is not defined (intent, ICD-10 codes, whether alcohol-only intoxications are included); the Methods cite the state report on drug- and alcohol-related intoxication deaths for the cause-of-death terms.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 28.6% and 55.1% shares, and Gutkind et al.'s restatement of the additional deaths as 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths, have an undefined denominator; the counts of heroin deaths are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The article carries no funding statement and no conflict-of-interest statement on the PMC page; the authors include the state's chief medical examiner and officials of the health department whose data are evaluated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, whole article; Author information

reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, DISCUSSION, 6th and 7th paragraphs; References 10 to 12
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misnumbered citation; the recommendations should be traced to Goldberger et al. (2013; reference 10, card sc_goldberger_2013), not to the state report.

reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, RESULTS, 3rd paragraph; Table 3, column headings
reporting_issues.consequence: They measure the certificates' sensitivity against the broader definition. The card's findings use the right denominator; the paper's wording should not be copied into claims.
