design_detail: Retrospective descriptive analysis of Finland's national post-mortem toxicology database (one laboratory: Department of Forensic Medicine, Hjelt Institute, University of Helsinki): 57,903 medico-legal autopsy cases of all causes with comprehensive drug analysis completed between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2010. For the 129 drugs detected at least 50 times in femoral venous blood, Table 2 gives the number of cases, the limit of quantification, the mean, median and 90th, 95th and 97.5th percentile concentrations (from findings with a numerical value), the percentage of the drug's cases certified as a fatal poisoning with that drug as the main finding (forensic pathologists' death certificates: ICD-10 cause of death with the drug's ATC code as the external cause), and an ad hoc 'PM blood/plasma relationship' comparing each median with the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical compilation (Schulz et al. 2012): 1 if the median lies within the range, otherwise the median divided by the nearer limit. The Discussion compares the medians with Swedish post-mortem data and Linnet's 2012 review. Filed as cross-sectional with the JBI prevalence checklist because it describes the distribution of a measurement in a defined population; METHODS §5.3 would also allow it as a registry description without an instrument.
can_establish: How drug concentrations in post-mortem femoral venous blood were distributed in Finnish medico-legal autopsy cases of all causes in 2000–2010, measured in one accredited laboratory; how often each drug's cases were certified as fatal poisonings by that drug; and how each drug's median compares with the therapeutic range in plasma given by a clinical compilation.
cannot_establish: The concentration at which a drug causes death (the distributions mix poisonings with other deaths and are not split by cause), why a median exceeds the therapeutic plasma range (post-mortem redistribution, the difference between whole blood and plasma, overdose and tolerance cannot be separated in this design), how concentrations change with the time between death and sampling, or how far the distributions apply outside Finland or to deaths not selected for toxicology.

sample.recruitment: Registry: every medico-legal autopsy case in Finland with comprehensive post-mortem drug analysis completed between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2010, from the one laboratory that performs all Finnish post-mortem toxicology (Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st paragraph; Data refining, 1st paragraph). Police inquire into sudden or unexpected deaths and may order a medico-legal investigation by a forensic pathologist, which always takes place when a death is not known to be caused by disease, or is known or suspected to involve an accident, crime, suicide, poisoning, occupational illness, medical procedure or war, or occurs outside medical care or is otherwise sudden or unclear. Of about 50,000 deaths a year, about 11,000 have a medico-legal autopsy and over 6,500 (over 13% of all deaths) a toxicological analysis, ordered by the forensic pathologist.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Drugs detected at least 50 times in post-mortem femoral blood, counting findings below the limit of quantification reported as positive; distribution statistics were calculated from findings with a numerical value only. Because methods and limits changed, benzodiazepines and nifedipine come only from the 53,095 cases analysed by GC-ECD, and phenobarbital, phenytoin, ibuprofen, indometacin, ketoprofen, levetiracetam, meprobamate, naproxen, oxcarbazepine, theophylline and warfarin only from the 23,385 cases analysed by GC-MS (Data refining, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Table 1: 75% male (43,458); mean age 54.6 years (SD 17.1; median 56); median age 55 for men and 59 for women (p<0.001, Mann–Whitney); blood alcohol at or above 0.2‰ in 24,879 cases (43%), median 1.8‰. No breakdown by cause or manner of death, or by other drugs present.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The number of positive findings below the limit of quantification, left out of each drug's percentiles, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: The cases are deaths selected by police and pathologists for medico-legal investigation and toxicology (about 13% of all deaths in Finland), three quarters of them men. Fatal drug poisonings are about 8%, and all fatal poisonings about 15%, of toxicologically investigated cases (Discussion, 6th paragraph), but for 36 drugs more than 10% of the drug's cases were poisonings attributed to it, up to 59% for dextropropoxyphene, so for those drugs the median is not a level found in deaths unrelated to the drug, as the authors say. Leaving out findings below the limit of quantification moves each distribution upwards by an amount that is not reported. The dataset averages about 5,260 cases a year (57,903 over 11 years), fewer than the more than 6,500 toxicological analyses a year that the paper describes for the laboratory without dating the figure (Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st paragraph); whether the difference reflects growth over time or cases left out of the femoral-blood dataset (for example, without femoral blood or without comprehensive drug analysis) is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Concentration in femoral venous blood taken at autopsy, on average five days after death, with bodies kept at 3–5 °C; samples preserved with 1% sodium fluoride, stored at 4 °C and analysed mostly within 12 days of arrival. About 200 drugs quantified in blood: dual-column GC-NPD for acidic and neutral drugs (replaced by GC-MS in February 2007), GC-ECD for benzodiazepines (replaced by GC-NCIMS in March 2010), dual-column GC-NPD for basic drugs, with GC-MS and LC-MS/MS for confirmation; urine screened by immunoassay and LC-TOF-MS. Laboratory accredited since 1997; validation data are in an online supplement (a PDF, not opened) (Materials and methods › Toxicological analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no data on amounts taken, timing, route, or long-term against single use.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled: each drug's distribution includes every case in which it was found, whatever else was present (blood alcohol in 43% of all cases). The authors cite an earlier study of their own finding significant pharmacokinetic interactions rare (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

comparison.controls: No control group. Each median is compared with the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical compilation (Schulz et al. 2012; for fentanyl Winek et al. 2001; for ropivacaine Dollery 1999); the Discussion compares medians with Swedish post-mortem data (Jones and Holmgren 2009; Druid and Holmgren 1997; Reis et al. 2007) and with Linnet's 2012 review.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cause and manner of death other than poisoning by the drug, the interval to sampling for individual cases, the condition of the body, chronic against acute use, tolerance and each drug's distribution between whole blood and plasma are not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Concentration distributions in mg/L (mean, median, 90th, 95th and 97.5th percentiles); fatal poisoning attributed to the drug as the main finding, from death certificates on which the forensic pathologist recorded the ICD-10 cause of death and the drug's ATC code as the external cause; the 'PM blood/plasma relationship'; the midpoint of each drug's volume of distribution from the literature.
outcomes.validity_norms: Analytical methods described with references, validation data in the unread supplement. The attribution of a death to a drug is the certifying pathologist's judgment; no criteria are stated, and pathologists had each case's measured concentrations (the authors note only that they did not have these published distributions).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Normal' post-mortem concentration = the median of all quantified findings in all-cause autopsy cases; 'possible overdose levels' = the upper percentiles; relationship = 1 for a median within the therapeutic plasma range, otherwise the median divided by the lower limit (below the range) or the upper limit (above it).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive statistics for 129 drugs. The only tests are a Mann–Whitney comparison of age by sex and an inspection of the relationship against volume of distribution, reported without a statistic.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Analysts and certifying pathologists knew the case; the authors note that the pathologists did not have these distributions when they certified.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only; no confidence intervals. Median post-mortem femoral blood concentration against the therapeutic plasma range: within (relationship 1) for 61 of 129 drugs (47%), below for 22 (17%), above for 46 (35.7%; printed 35%). Highest relationships: hydroxychloroquine 100, promazine 24, levomepromazine 16, dextromethorphan 10, dextropropoxyphene 8.7, metformin 5.5, paroxetine 4.7, amlodipine 4.5, melperone 4.0, citalopram 3.6. Lowest: desmethyldiazepam 0.13 (0.5 by the stated rule), lidocaine 0.27, dixyrazine, ethylmorphine and glimepiride 0.33, ketoprofen 0.34, oxazepam 0.35. If the single approximate therapeutic values were handled as they are for dixyrazine and ketoprofen, risperidone would fall below the range and tizanidine and 4-methylaminophenazone above it, giving 58, 23 and 48 drugs (editors' calculation). No correlation coefficient is given for the relationship against volume of distribution.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The volume-of-distribution analysis is described without its plot or a statistic; the comparison with the Swedish medians (Figure 2) is only an image, which was not viewable. Per-drug mixes of causes of death, numbers of findings below the limit of quantification and shares of cases with other drugs present are not reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Per-drug N ranges from 7 (phenobarbital) and 9 (indometacin) to 22,125 (caffeine); 16 drugs have fewer than 50 cases, for which the 95th and 97.5th percentiles rest on very few values.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 57,903 Finnish medico-legal autopsy cases with toxicology (2000–2010), the median quantified femoral-blood concentration lay within the therapeutic plasma range for 61 of 129 drugs, below it for 22 and above it for 46, by up to 100-fold (hydroxychloroquine). For 36 drugs more than 10% of cases were fatal poisonings attributed to that drug; for buprenorphine and methadone the median lay within the therapeutic plasma range although 45% and 43% of their cases were certified as poisonings by them, and the paper does not give the poisoning cases' concentrations separately. Medians agreed with the Swedish all-cause data for most of the 20 drugs in common, with exceptions (dextropropoxyphene, codeine, amphetamine), and with the 'other cause of death' groups of two further Swedish studies except for dextropropoxyphene and moclobemide.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say the study shows that using clinical therapeutic ranges would "commonly lead to misjudgement of a normal PM concentration as a lethal level". The paper compared medians with therapeutic ranges, not with toxic or lethal ranges; its one worked example, amlodipine, has a median (0.07 mg/L) above the therapeutic range but below the quoted toxic threshold (0.088 mg/L). Medians are called 'normal' post-mortem concentrations although they include fatal poisonings and leave out findings below the limit of quantification (the authors themselves say the normal level is probably lower than the median for 36 drugs), and upper percentiles are said to indicate possible overdose levels although they come from the same mixed population. Relationships above 1 for basic drugs are attributed largely to post-mortem redistribution, which this design cannot separate from the blood-to-plasma difference, overdose or tolerance. The Conclusions also suggest, from good agreement with earlier Swedish studies for common drugs, that post-mortem reference concentrations are applicable on an international basis, and give the sample as 59,903 cases.

timeline.event: Pounder and Jones, and Prouty and Anderson, describe post-mortem drug redistribution (cited in the Introduction).

Druid and Holmgren: concentrations of 83 drugs in post-mortem femoral blood from single- and multi-substance poisonings and from other deaths without incapacitation by drugs (as summarized in the Discussion).
Reis et al.: post-mortem and therapeutic reference concentrations of 15 antidepressants (as summarized in the Discussion).
Ferner: concentrations measured after death cannot generally be read back to concentrations before death, and lethal concentrations are hard to define (cited in the Introduction).
Jones and Holmgren: distributions of the 25 most frequent drugs in 24,876 Swedish post-mortem femoral blood samples of all causes of death, the approach this study extends.

Linnet: review comparing post-mortem concentration intervals in the non-intoxicated state with therapeutic serum levels (upper-limit ratios 0.13 to 11.3, median 1.5, for 57 compounds, as summarized in the Discussion).
This study (online 23 July 2013): 129 drugs in 57,903 Finnish autopsy cases.
Ketola and Kriikku: meta-analysis of tissue-to-femoral-blood concentration ratios (on the reading list; not cited by this paper and not read by this reader).
Borra et al.: review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: Its medians agree with the Swedish all-cause database for most of the drugs in common and with the 'other cause of death' groups of Druid and Holmgren and of Reis et al. for most drugs, with named exceptions; the reading list counts it among the Nordic forensic databases that document overlap between concentrations in deaths and in living people for medicines. Cite it for the distributions in Finnish all-cause autopsy cases, for how often post-mortem medians exceed therapeutic plasma ranges and for the share of each drug's cases certified as poisonings; not for lethal or toxic thresholds.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC full text has no funding statement or acknowledgements.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC full text.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors are at the Department of Forensic Medicine, Hjelt Institute, University of Helsinki, the laboratory that performs all post-mortem toxicology in Finland and holds the database analysed; several of the cited method papers are the group's own. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND). Received 4 March 2013, accepted 6 June 2013, online 23 July 2013, issue April 2014.

what_would_settle_it: A database study reporting, for each drug, separate concentration distributions for deaths certified as poisoning by that drug and for deaths with a clearly unrelated cause (for example trauma), handling findings below the limit of quantification by appropriate methods, recording the interval from death to sampling, and with paired samples taken before and after death in a subset to separate redistribution from the difference between whole blood and plasma.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.note: All Finnish medico-legal autopsy cases with toxicology over 11 years suit the stated aim (all causes of death), but toxicology is ordered for a selected 13% of deaths, and the frame does not match the use the paper makes of the medians as levels in deaths unrelated to the drug.

domains.domain: 2. Study participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: A census of the database for the period, restricted by analytical method for some drugs for uniform limits of quantification.
Very large overall, but 16 drugs have fewer than 50 quantified cases (7 for phenobarbital, 9 for indometacin), too few for stable upper percentiles.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The Finnish system, laboratory, interval to autopsy, storage and methods are described; causes of death, other drugs present and numbers below the limit of quantification are not given per drug.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Positive findings below the limit of quantification count towards the 50-detection rule but are left out of the percentiles, in numbers not reported, which raises every distribution by an unknown amount.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used for identification of the condition
domains.note: Accredited single-laboratory chromatographic methods on femoral blood (validation in an unread supplement); the attribution of fatal poisoning is the certifying pathologist's judgment without stated criteria.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: One laboratory and one sampling site, but methods changed in 2007 and 2010 (handled partly by restricting some drugs to one method), and the interval from death to sampling varied without analysis.

Medians and percentiles suit skewed data, but there are no intervals, the 'relationship' is an ad hoc ratio applied inconsistently to single approximate values, the volume-of-distribution analysis has no statistic, and some cells are impossible (quetiapine).

domains.domain: 9. Response rate adequate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Laboratory records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence for a descriptive database study. The measurements are of high technical quality (one accredited laboratory, femoral blood, preserved samples, a census of 11 years); the risk of bias lies in what the distributions are taken to represent: they mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out findings below the limit of quantification, ignore the time to sampling and are set against plasma ranges by an ad hoc ratio, and several cells are misprinted. Editors' summary: moderate. Citable for: median post-mortem femoral blood concentrations in all-cause Finnish autopsy cases exceeded the therapeutic plasma range for 46 of 129 drugs, by large factors for several basic drugs (promazine 24, levomepromazine 16, dextromethorphan 10); for buprenorphine and methadone the medians lay inside the therapeutic plasma range although 45% and 43% of cases were certified as poisonings by them; and the per-drug distributions with their N and share of poisonings. Not citable for: lethal or toxic thresholds; 'normal' levels for the 36 drugs with more than 10% poisonings; the quetiapine row; or redistribution as the cause of any particular ratio.

key_findings.finding: How a case entered the data and who decided the cause: Finnish police inquire into sudden or unexpected deaths and may order a medico-legal investigation by a forensic pathologist, who decides on toxicology; all analyses are done in one accredited laboratory (over 6,500 cases a year, over 13% of all deaths). The forensic pathologist later issues the death certificate with cause and manner of death, coded in ICD-10 with the ATC code of any drug named as the external cause, and these data are joined to the toxicology database. 'Fatal poisoning' in this paper means a certificate naming that drug as the main finding.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data refining, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 57,903 autopsy cases with comprehensive post-mortem drug analysis, 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2010: 75% male (43,458), mean age 54.6 years (SD 17.1), median age 55 for men and 59 for women (p<0.001); blood alcohol at or above 0.2‰ in 24,879 (43%), median 1.8‰. Fatal drug poisonings were about 8%, and all fatal poisonings about 15%, of toxicologically investigated cases.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overview; Table 1; Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sampling and analysis conditions: femoral venous blood taken at autopsy, on average five days after death, bodies at 3–5 °C; samples with 1% sodium fluoride stored at 4 °C, analysed mostly within 12 days; about 200 drugs quantified by gas-chromatographic methods that changed in 2007 and 2010; drugs detected at least 50 times included, with findings below the limit of quantification counted as detections but left out of the percentiles.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Toxicological analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data refining, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Median post-mortem femoral blood concentration against the therapeutic plasma range: within it for 61 of 129 drugs (47%), below it for 22 (17%) and above it for 46 (35.7%; printed 35%). The largest ratios of median to upper therapeutic limit: hydroxychloroquine 100, promazine 24, levomepromazine 16, dextromethorphan 10, dextropropoxyphene 8.7, metformin 5.5, paroxetine 4.7, amlodipine 4.5, melperone 4.0, citalopram 3.6.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, last column; Data refining, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Four printed ratios depart from the stated rule (desmethyldiazepam, risperidone, tizanidine, 4-methylaminophenazone); applied consistently, the counts would be 58, 23 and 48 (editors' calculation). Several printed ratios also differ slightly from the printed medians (amlodipine 4.7, metformin 6.0 and paroxetine 4.8 by the stated rule), probably because they were computed from unrounded medians; the order and the counts are unchanged, so ratios are cited as printed (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: For 36 of the 129 drugs, more than 10% of cases were fatal poisonings attributed to that drug as the main finding; the highest shares were dextropropoxyphene 59%, buprenorphine 45%, methadone 43%, dixyrazine, doxepin and promazine 42%, melperone 32%, amitriptyline 27%, codeine and levomepromazine 23%. The authors state that for these 36 drugs the normal post-mortem concentration is probably lower than the median.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, proportion of fatal poisonings; Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 1, which lists the 36 drugs, is an image that was not viewed; the count of 36 was confirmed from Table 2 (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Opioids (N; median; 97.5th percentile in mg/L; therapeutic plasma range; % of cases certified as poisoning by the drug): buprenorphine 671; 0.0012; 0.022; 0.0005–0.005; 45%. Methadone 207; 0.40; 2.2; 0.1–0.5; 43%. Codeine 1,903; 0.16; 5.1; 0.03–0.25; 23%. Tramadol 1,581; 0.90; 21; 0.1–1; 18%. Fentanyl 419; 0.0058; 0.061; 0.001–0.01; 12%. Oxycodone 1,259; 0.10; 1.7; 0.005–0.1; 8%. Morphine 1,094; 0.07; 1.1; 0.01–0.1; 4%. Every one of these medians lies within the therapeutic plasma range. The authors state, from their earlier studies, that for strong opioids such as buprenorphine and methadone the post-mortem concentration plays a limited role in assessing the cause of death, and that the same is partly true for amphetamine and other drugs to which tolerance develops.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows 13, 26, 42, 71, 79, 87 and 119; Discussion, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: The fentanyl range is from Winek et al. (Table 2, footnote e); the other therapeutic ranges are from Schulz et al.

key_findings.finding: Other drugs (N; median; 97.5th percentile in mg/L; therapeutic plasma range; % certified as poisoning by the drug): amphetamine 565; 0.28; 6.2; 0.02–0.1; 12%. Methamphetamine 51; 0.18; 25; up to 0.1; 10%. MDMA 57; 0.30; 4.0; 0.1–0.35; 0%. Tetrahydrocannabinol 347; 0.002; 0.024; 0.005–0.01; 0%. Ketamine 118; 0.50; 6.3; 1–6; 1%. Alprazolam 940; 0.05; 0.40; 0.005–0.05; 13%. Diazepam 7,404; 0.09; 0.8; 0.1–2; 0%. Pregabalin 380; 8.0; 96; 2–5; 12%. Gabapentin 135; 11; 157; about 0.5–6; 8%. Dextromethorphan 54; 0.40; 2.8; 0.01–0.04; 15%. Caffeine 22,125; 3.0; 13; 4–10; 0%.
key_findings.note: These are post-mortem concentrations in deaths of all causes, measured in one laboratory, not amounts taken; methamphetamine's mean (1.7 mg/L) and 97.5th percentile (25 mg/L) rest on 51 cases, and its therapeutic range is printed as '-0.1', with no lower limit, read here as up to 0.1 mg/L.

key_findings.finding: By drug class: most neutral and acidic drugs (benzodiazepines, anti-epileptics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, paracetamol) had medians within or below the therapeutic plasma range, especially extensively plasma-bound drugs such as benzodiazepines and warfarin, with exceptions in Table 2 (for example phenazepam 2.1, gabapentin 1.8 and pregabalin 1.6); basic drugs commonly had ratios above 1, which the authors think is largely due to post-mortem redistribution. The Discussion states that antidepressants other than fluoxetine (1) ranged from 1.2 (sertraline) to 4.7 (paroxetine) and that antipsychotics were either 1 (six named) or from 1.8 (clozapine) to 24 (promazine); Table 2 contradicts both statements (trazodone 0.57; dixyrazine 0.33; mesoridazine, at 1, is not among the six named), so by Table 2 the ranges are 0.57 to 4.7 for antidepressants and 0.33 to 24 for antipsychotics. No marked correlation was found between the ratio and the midpoint of the volume of distribution (no statistic given).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, rows 35, 69 and 120
key_findings.note: The classes of trazodone (an antidepressant) and of dixyrazine and mesoridazine (phenothiazine antipsychotics) are the editors' classification; the paper does not tabulate drug classes.

key_findings.finding: Against Swedish all-cause data (Jones and Holmgren 2009), medians were very close for most of the 20 drugs in common, with exceptions: dextropropoxyphene 2.6 against 0.8 mg/L, codeine 0.16 against 0.05 and amphetamine 0.28 against 0.5, which the authors attribute partly to different limits of quantification and different patterns of use. Against the 'other cause of death' groups of Druid and Holmgren (1997) and Reis et al. (2007), medians agreed except for dextropropoxyphene (2.6 against 0.2) and moclobemide (1.9 against 0.6).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2 caption (twenty drugs in common; image, values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Worked example: amlodipine's post-mortem median of 0.07 mg/L (313 cases, 3% certified as poisonings by it) would, if a driver killed in a traffic accident had this level, easily be misread as serious intoxication against clinical plasma references (therapeutic 0.003–0.015 mg/L; toxic from 0.088 mg/L), although it is the median of these cases.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; Table 2, row 6
key_findings.note: The example's median lies below the quoted toxic threshold, so it illustrates misreading against therapeutic, not lethal, ranges.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions give the sample as 59,903 cases; the abstract, Methods, Results and Table 1 give 57,903.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error; cite 57,903.

reporting_issues.issue: The quetiapine row is internally impossible: mean 0.62 mg/L, median 0.90 mg/L, 90th percentile 13 mg/L and 95th percentile 30 mg/L. If a tenth of values were at least 13 mg/L the mean would be at least 1.3 mg/L, and if a twentieth were at least 30 mg/L it would be at least 1.5 mg/L (editors' check); the mean also lies below the median, as in only one other row (phenobarbital, 7 cases).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one value in the row is misprinted; the printed ratio (1.8) equals the median divided by the upper therapeutic limit (0.90/0.5), so the misprint more likely lies in the mean or the percentiles than in the median. The row should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Desmethyldiazepam's relationship is printed as 0.13, but by the stated rule its median (0.10 mg/L) divided by the lower therapeutic limit (0.2 mg/L) is 0.5; the printed 0.13 equals the median divided by the upper limit (0.10/0.8 = 0.125), which suggests the wrong limit was used. Single approximate therapeutic values are handled inconsistently: dixyrazine (median 0.10 against about 0.3) and ketoprofen (1.3 against about 3.7) get ratios below 1, while risperidone (0.004 against about 0.006) and tizanidine (0.02 against about 0.015) get 1, as does 4-methylaminophenazone (15 against 10 for the parent drug).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2, rows 3, 28, 35, 58, 104 and 117; Data refining, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline counts (61 within, 22 below, 46 above) would be about 58, 23 and 48 with the rule applied consistently (editors' calculation); the qualitative conclusion is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Drugs were selected if detected at least 50 times, yet 16 drugs in Table 2 have N below 50, down to 7 (phenobarbital) and 9 (indometacin); the table does not say whether N counts detections or quantified findings.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2, cases column; Data refining, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: N probably counts quantified findings within the method-restricted subsets, but readers cannot tell; upper percentiles from fewer than 50 values should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: men and women sum to 57,886, 17 fewer than the 57,903 total, while the footnote mentions 15 unidentified bodies without age; blood-alcohol counts by sex sum to 24,878 against 24,879; the all-cases blood-alcohol SD (1.16‰) cannot be produced from the male (1.11) and female (1.12) SDs with near-equal means, which pool to about 1.11 (editors' calculation; the age SDs pool correctly).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; sex is unknown for some cases and one summary statistic is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The relationship between the ratio and the volume of distribution is reported as showing no marked correlation, but no coefficient, plot or table of volumes is given (the figures show only the 36 drugs with over 10% poisonings and the Swedish comparison).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The negative finding cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's class ranges are contradicted by Table 2: antidepressants other than fluoxetine are said to range from 1.2 (sertraline) to 4.7 (paroxetine), but trazodone's ratio is 0.57; antipsychotics are said to be 1 or from 1.8 (clozapine) to 24 (promazine), but dixyrazine's is 0.33, and mesoridazine (1) is left out of the six antipsychotics named at 1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, rows 35, 69 and 120
reporting_issues.consequence: Class ranges should be cited from Table 2 (0.57 to 4.7 for antidepressants, 0.33 to 24 for antipsychotics), not from the Discussion.

reporting_issues.issue: Several printed ratios cannot be reproduced from the printed medians and therapeutic ranges: amlodipine 0.07/0.015 = 4.7 (printed 4.5), metformin 6/1 = 6.0 (5.5), phenazepam 0.09/0.04 = 2.25 (2.1) and betaxolol 0.10/0.05 = 2.0 (1.9), with smaller differences for paroxetine (4.8 against 4.7) and ketoprofen (0.35 against 0.34) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably computed from unrounded medians; no drug changes category, so the counts stand, but ratios should be cited as printed and not recomputed from the table.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 275 (blind second reading) and AI reader 285 (adjudication)

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of surveillance records of drug poisoning deaths with death dates in 2019–2021 in nine US states (Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina, Washington, Wisconsin). Suicides and deaths of undetermined intent came from the restricted-access file of the CDC's National Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS); unintentional overdose deaths came from the State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS), obtained through state data-sharing agreements. The authors combined the two systems because, as they state, each of the three manners is held in only one of them. Exposure: the county's death investigation system, coded 'coroner' for any 'Non-Medical Examiner Death Investigation System' in a CDC listing and otherwise medical examiner. Outcome: manner recorded as undetermined intent, against suicide or unintentional. Five logistic regressions, all with year fixed effects: (1) system only; (2) plus state fixed effects; (3) plus county population band, poverty, unemployment and rurality; (4) plus indicators that an autopsy, an opioid test and an alcohol test were recorded, a suicide note was recorded and an investigator's narrative was available; (5) plus age, sex and race. Read as the PubMed Central author manuscript (NIHMS2209286) of the article published online before final editing on 13 August 2026.
can_establish: Whether, within the same state and year, drug poisoning deaths in counties served by coroners were recorded as of undetermined intent more often than deaths in counties served by medical examiners, in nine convenience-sampled US states in 2019–2021, and how far that association changed with adjustment for county characteristics, recorded investigation steps and the decedents' age, sex and race.
cannot_establish: Which recorded manner was correct (no death was re-reviewed and there is no reference standard), whether the extra undetermined deaths in coroner counties are concealed suicides or concealed unintentional overdoses, whether a county that changed its system would change its classifications (a between-county cross-section, with system type taken from a later listing), or whether the association holds outside the nine states; with state fixed effects the estimate draws only on states that have both kinds of county, which the text does not name.

sample.recruitment: Surveillance registries: every drug poisoning death recorded as suicide or undetermined intent in the NVDRS restricted-access file and every unintentional drug overdose death in SUDORS for the nine states, death dates 2019–2021, any age (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). The states were a convenience sample, chosen also for their variation in investigation systems, because individual-level SUDORS data are not available to researchers nationally; NVDRS data were restricted to the same states (Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: drug poisoning deaths of any age recorded as undetermined intent, suicide or unintentional, in the nine states, 2019–2021. Not stated anywhere in the paper: the case definition or ICD-10 codes that make a death a 'drug poisoning death' in either system; whether the manner variable is the death certificate's or the investigator's report (the paper speaks of coroners and medical examiners classifying intent and of data abstractors); whether homicides and pending cases were excluded (implied by the three categories); whether any death appeared in both systems and how duplicates were handled; whether both systems covered every county of each state in every year; and whether 'county' means the county of death, of injury or of residence.
sample.demographics: Table 1: mean age 43.0 years (SD 13.5); 38,177 male (68.9%; the text says just over 69%); White 70.2%, Black 26.1%, American Indian 2.1%, Asian 1.1% (race counts overlap, see reporting issues; no Hispanic-ethnicity variable is shown although Methods mention race/ethnicity). Coroner-county deaths against medical-examiner-county deaths (editors' percentages from Table 1 counts): White 79.5% vs 65.6%, Black 18.0% vs 30.1%, male 66.6% vs 70.0%, in counties under 25,000 people 4.3% vs 1.4% and over 250,000 52.4% vs 75.0%; mean rurality index 2.3 vs 1.7, poverty 14.3% vs 12.8%, unemployment 5.6% vs 5.8%.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (all recorded deaths). Model 5 includes 55,423 deaths, 7 fewer than models 1–4, without explanation (Table 2).
sample.selection_effects: Nine states chosen for convenience and for their mix of systems. Indiana uses only county coroners and North Carolina only a centralized medical examiner (Results, 2nd paragraph), so once state fixed effects are included such states contribute nothing to the coroner contrast; the per-state counts that would show which states carry it are only in Figure 1, an image that was not viewable. Because the three manners come from two different surveillance systems, any difference between NVDRS and SUDORS in coverage or completeness by type of county would shift the undetermined share directly; the paper does not discuss this. The period overlaps the COVID-19 pandemic, which the authors say strained death-investigation offices (Discussion, 12th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: County death investigation system from a CDC listing of state medical examiner and coroner organizations (reference 22, dated 30 August 2024, accessed 22 January 2025): an indicator set to 1 (coroner) for any 'Non-Medical Examiner Death Investigation System', otherwise medical examiner (Methods, 3rd paragraph). The listing post-dates the 2019–2021 deaths; changes of system during the period, mixed county arrangements and the qualifications of individual coroners (the Background notes that some states require coroners to be physicians) are not addressed. 18,232 deaths (32.9%) occurred in coroner counties.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: the exposure is a county's system type. No drug-specific data are analysed; whether an opioid or an alcohol toxicology test was recorded as performed (regardless of its result) enters only as a covariate.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: the drugs involved in each death are not analysed. Opioid and alcohol testing enter only as indicators that a test was recorded, with 'no' and 'unknown' both coded 0 (Methods, 3rd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Drug poisoning deaths in counties with a medical-examiner system (37,198), compared within the same state and year once state and year fixed effects are included (models 2–5).
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment. County: population band (under 25,000; 25,000–250,000; over 250,000, chosen to match a Bureau of Justice Statistics survey of offices), annual poverty rate, annual unemployment rate, 2023 rurality index (1–9). Investigation: autopsy (full or partial), opioid test recorded, alcohol test recorded, suicide note recorded, investigator narrative available. Decedent: age, sex, race. State and year fixed effects (Methods, 3rd, 4th and 6th paragraphs).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Office funding, staffing and caseload (the authors say they could not measure funding), certifiers' qualifications and training, the scope of toxicology panels and the drugs found, the decedents' psychiatric and substance-use history and other recorded circumstances, and pandemic strain on offices (Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs). Some of these (resources, qualifications) are part of what a 'system' is rather than confounders of it.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable: drugs involved are not analysed in either group.

outcomes.instruments: Manner of death as held in NVDRS (suicide, undetermined intent) or SUDORS (unintentional), as classified in the death investigation by a coroner or medical examiner and abstracted into the surveillance systems; the paper does not say which source document the manner field reflects.
outcomes.validity_norms: No reference standard: the study compares how deaths were recorded, not whether the recorded manner was correct. The data come from two systems with separate abstraction, combined by manner.
outcomes.operationalization: Binary: undetermined intent (1) against suicide or unintentional (0). Who decided: the coroner or medical examiner who certified the death; the investigator's choice is the outcome itself.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: one outcome, five nested specifications of the same model, all reported; no correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (routinely recorded classifications).

analysis.effect_sizes: Odds ratios with 95% CIs from logistic regression (R 4.4.1). Coroner against medical examiner: model 1 (year fixed effects only) 0.32 (0.29–0.35); model 2 (plus state fixed effects) 1.79 (1.43–2.27); model 3 (plus county controls) 1.52 (1.20–1.95); model 4 (plus investigation controls) 1.61 (1.26–2.06); model 5 (plus age, sex and race; n=55,423) 1.60 (1.25–2.05). Crude shares recorded as undetermined (editors' calculation from Table 1): 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) in coroner counties against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%) in medical-examiner counties, crude odds ratio 0.32 (0.29 to 0.35, Woolf interval), matching model 1. Other model 5 odds ratios: autopsy 1.27 (1.12–1.44); suicide note 0.46 (0.28–0.73); no investigator narrative 0.52 (0.30–0.92); opioid test recorded 1.14 (1.00–1.29); alcohol test recorded 1.00 (0.86–1.17); male 0.77 (0.71–0.83); age per year 0.99 (0.99–1.00); population over 250,000 against under 25,000 0.61 (0.42–0.89); unemployment per percentage point 0.94 (0.90–0.99); rurality per index step 0.96 (0.93–1.00); poverty 1.01 (1.00–1.02). No absolute differences (predicted probabilities or marginal effects) are reported.
analysis.covariates: Year fixed effects in every model; state fixed effects from model 2; county population band, poverty, unemployment and rurality from model 3; autopsy, opioid test, alcohol test, suicide note and narrative availability from model 4; age, sex and race in model 5 (Methods, 6th paragraph; Table 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the sequence of models is set out in Methods (6th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: All five models are in Table 2, including model 1, whose reversed association the authors attribute to Maryland; the abstract reports only models 2 and 5. No sensitivity analysis excluding Maryland, by state or by year is reported, and no model with suicide or unintentional classification as the outcome.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The paper does not say whether the standard errors allow for clustering of deaths within counties; the exposure varies only between counties, so intervals computed as if the 55,430 deaths were independent would be too narrow. The number of counties, and of coroner counties in states with both systems, is not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within states and years, drug poisoning deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as undetermined intent rather than suicide or unintentional (OR 1.79 with state and year fixed effects; 1.52 to 1.61 with further adjustment; lowest lower confidence limit 1.20). Pooled across the nine states without state adjustment the association ran the other way (OR 0.32; 3.1% undetermined in coroner counties against 8.9% in medical-examiner counties), which the authors attribute to Maryland. The share recorded as suicide was, crudely, higher in coroner counties (6.5% against 5.1%; editors' calculation), and suicide classification was not modelled. No classification was checked against a re-review.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives OR 1.79 as the association without saying that it is the within-state estimate, and omits the reversed pooled estimate. The Discussion (2nd paragraph) calls model 2 the model without control variables and states that coroner-county deaths have "at least 52% increased odds", treating the smallest point estimate as a floor when the lowest confidence limit is 1.20. The Discussion (9th paragraph) and Conclusions infer that suicide may be underreported in coroner counties because undetermined deaths may conceal suicides; the study did not examine suicide classification, and the possibility that undetermined deaths conceal unintentional overdoses is not discussed. The reading of the autopsy association (investigators order an autopsy when uncertain) is the authors' interpretation of a cross-sectional association. Several associations are also described with causal verbs: unemployment 'reduced the odds' (Results, 5th paragraph), an autopsy 'raised the odds' (Results, 6th paragraph), each year of age 'reduced the odds' (Results, 7th paragraph) and a suicide note 'reduced the odds' by 54% (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Against this, the abstract's conclusion is hedged (system type 'may be an important factor') and the limitations are stated plainly: convenience sample, unmeasured funding, unknown tests coded as not done, the pandemic.

timeline.event: Breiding and Wiersema: variability of undetermined manner of death classification in the US (cited as reference 6, with Warner et al. 2013, for Maryland's high undetermined rates).
Warner et al., Academic Forensic Pathology: state variation in certifying manner of death and the drugs involved in drug intoxication deaths (reference 5).
Rockett et al. propose a 'drug self-intoxication' death category for NVDRS (reference 16); SUDORS later added unintentional overdose deaths.
Tote et al.: coroner systems associated with higher rates of incomplete toxicology reports in overdose deaths, 2010–2016 (reference 23, as summarized in this paper).
Denham et al.: coroner county systems associated with a higher likelihood of unclassified drug overdoses than medical-examiner systems (reference 35, title as cited).

Zaychik: state transitions from coroner to medical-examiner systems and drug-mortality data (not cited by this paper; paired with it on the reading list, which summarizes it as finding no improvement; not read by this reader).
This study: within-state association between coroner systems and undetermined-intent classification of drug poisoning deaths in nine states.

replication.where_it_stands: A single cross-sectional study of nine states with no direct replication. It sits beside studies cited in its Discussion that link coroner systems with fewer drugs named in overdose deaths (Denham et al., 2022) and with suicide reporting (Fernandez and Jayawardhana, 2025), and with Zaychik (2024) on the reading list. Cite it for the within-state association between system type and the recorded undetermined share, with the reversed pooled estimate beside it; not for misclassification of suicide or of any other manner, which it did not measure.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse of the National Institutes of Health, award R21DA059189; the funders had no role in design, conduct, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing, review or the decision to submit. The acknowledgements thank nine state health agencies that shared data, and the CDC for their funding of Indiana's OD2A work.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report there are no competing interests to declare.
funding.affiliations_note: Emergency Medicine and the Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, Chicago; School of Social Work, University of Maryland, Baltimore. An NVDRS disclaimer states that the findings are the authors' and not the official position of the CDC or the participating states. Ethics approval: Northwestern University IRB STU00219548.

what_would_settle_it: A blinded re-review, by one panel applying one written standard, of a random sample of drug poisoning deaths recorded as undetermined, suicide and unintentional in coroner and medical-examiner counties of the same states would show whether coroner counties misclassify and in which direction; comparing counties before and after a change of system, against counties that did not change, would test whether the system itself changes classification.

domains.note: State and year fixed effects, county population band, poverty, unemployment and rurality, and age, sex and race were adjusted. The pooled estimate reverses once state is adjusted (0.32 to 1.79), which shows how strongly differences between areas drive the contrast; within states, unmeasured differences between coroner and medical-examiner counties (local drug supply, the circumstances of the deaths, local practice) remain possible, as the authors say.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: System type from a CDC listing dated 2024 and accessed in January 2025, applied to deaths in 2019–2021; every non-medical-examiner arrangement is coded as one category; whether the county is that of death, injury or residence is not stated. Errors of this kind are probably unrelated to the outcome and would tend to weaken the contrast.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Convenience sample of states. Unintentional deaths come from SUDORS and the other two manners from NVDRS; the paper does not report whether the two covered the same counties and years or whether duplicates were removed, and any difference by type of county would change the undetermined share directly. The within-state contrast rests on states with both systems, not named in the text.

Autopsy, toxicology testing and narrative availability are steps taken by the investigating office after the death and are partly consequences of the system; adjusting for them (models 4 and 5) estimates a different quantity, but the estimates with and without them are close (1.52 against 1.61 and 1.60).

'No' and 'unknown' testing are coded together; race counts do not add up to the total; 7 deaths drop out of model 5 without explanation; the investigator narrative is missing for 4.2% of coroner-county and 1.4% of medical-examiner-county deaths (editors' percentages); missing manner or county is not reported.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: The outcome is the manner as recorded, which is what the study sets out to compare; whether the recorded manner was correct is outside its question. Abstraction by two systems is a minor source of error.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol. All five models are reported, but the abstract omits the reversed pooled estimate, and no sensitivity analysis (excluding Maryland, by state, by year) is reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E, the tool for observational studies of exposures, with the county's system type as the exposure. Five domains raise some concerns and none is high: the within-state estimate is stable across three adjusted specifications (1.52 to 1.61), and the main weaknesses (a later system listing, two surveillance systems combined by manner, unmeasured county differences) could bias it in either direction or towards the null. Separately from bias, the precision may be overstated, because the paper does not say whether the standard errors allow for deaths being clustered within counties. Citable for: within the same state and year in nine US states in 2019–2021, drug poisoning deaths investigated in coroner counties were recorded as undetermined intent more often than those in medical-examiner counties (adjusted OR about 1.5 to 1.6), while pooled without state adjustment the direction was reversed; and for how often autopsy and opioid and alcohol testing were recorded. Not citable for: how many suicides are hidden among undetermined drug deaths, which system classifies correctly, or the effect of changing a county's system.

key_findings.finding: How a death entered the count: drug poisoning deaths with death dates in 2019–2021, any age, in nine states, recorded as suicide or undetermined intent in the NVDRS restricted-access file or as unintentional overdose in SUDORS. No ICD-10 codes or case definition are given for either system; the manner is the classification made in the death investigation by a coroner or medical examiner and abstracted into the surveillance data. The comparison is between county system types; no death was re-reviewed.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Background, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: The absence of a case definition is the editors' observation from the full text; the list of codes may be in the systems' own documentation, which the paper does not cite.

key_findings.finding: 55,430 drug poisoning deaths: 48,463 recorded as unintentional (87%), 3,887 as undetermined intent (7%) and 3,080 as suicide (6%); 18,232 (33%) occurred in coroner counties and 37,198 in medical-examiner counties.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Without state adjustment, coroner counties had lower odds of an undetermined classification: model 1 (year fixed effects only) OR 0.32 (95% CI 0.29–0.35); 558 of 18,232 coroner-county deaths (3.1%) and 3,329 of 37,198 medical-examiner-county deaths (8.9%) were recorded as undetermined (editors' percentages). The authors attribute the reversal to Maryland, a centralized medical-examiner state with unusually high undetermined rates.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 1; Table 2, model (1)
key_findings.note: Per-state counts are in Figure 1, an image that was not viewable, so Maryland's share of the undetermined deaths could not be checked.

key_findings.finding: Within states (state and year fixed effects), coroner counties had higher odds of an undetermined classification: model 2 OR 1.79 (1.43–2.27); with county population band, poverty, unemployment and rurality (model 3) 1.52 (1.20–1.95); adding autopsy, opioid-test, alcohol-test, suicide-note and narrative indicators (model 4) 1.61 (1.26–2.06); adding age, sex and race (model 5, n=55,423) 1.60 (1.25–2.05).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th to 7th paragraphs; Table 2, models (2) to (5)

key_findings.finding: Recorded investigation steps in model 5: autopsy OR 1.27 (1.12–1.44); suicide note 0.46 (0.28–0.73); no investigator narrative available 0.52 (0.30–0.92); opioid test recorded 1.14 (1.00–1.29); alcohol test recorded 1.00 (0.86–1.17). The authors read the autopsy association as investigators ordering autopsies when uncertain, and the suicide-note association as greater certainty.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, model (5); Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Results, 6th paragraph (model 4 values)
key_findings.note: Results, 6th paragraph prints the model (4) values (autopsy 1.29, no investigator narrative 0.52, suicide note 0.46); the model (5) values given here are from Table 2, and the Discussion's 5th paragraph restates them (autopsy 1.27; a suicide note with 54% lower odds).

key_findings.finding: What was tested and in what share of deaths: an autopsy (full or partial) was recorded for about 67% (37,346 printed; the two system columns sum to 37,436), an opioid toxicology test for 79% and an alcohol test for 76%; a suicide note for 2.1%; no investigator narrative for 2.3%. By system (editors' percentages from Table 1): autopsy 67.1% in medical-examiner and 68.4% in coroner counties; opioid test 79.3% and 79.6%; alcohol test 84.5% and 58.6%; no narrative 1.4% and 4.2%. 'No' and 'unknown' were both coded as not tested.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Methods, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The indicators record whether a test was reported as done, not its result or the drugs screened.

key_findings.finding: Crude shares recorded as suicide: 1,194 of 18,232 deaths (6.5%) in coroner counties and 1,886 of 37,198 (5.1%) in medical-examiner counties (editors' calculation from Table 1). Suicide classification was not modelled.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, suicide row

key_findings.finding: County and decedent covariates in model 5: population over 250,000 against under 25,000 OR 0.61 (0.42–0.89); unemployment per percentage point 0.94 (0.90–0.99); rurality per index step 0.96 (0.93–1.00); poverty 1.01 (1.00–1.02); male against female 0.77 (0.71–0.83), 23% lower odds; age per year 0.99 (0.99–1.00); no race category associated (for example Black 1.03, 0.95–1.12).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th and 7th paragraphs; Table 2, model (5)
key_findings.note: Results, 5th paragraph prints the model (3) values (unemployment 0.93, rurality 0.96, population over 250,000 0.62); the values given here are model (5) of Table 2, and Results, 7th paragraph gives the age result and the 23% lower odds for men.

key_findings.finding: Exposure coding: system type from a CDC listing (reference 22, accessed January 2025), coroner meaning any 'Non-Medical Examiner Death Investigation System'. Indiana relies only on county coroners and North Carolina has a centralized medical-examiner system.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 3rd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph; reference 22

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a convenience sample of states that may not generalize; 'no' and 'unknown' tests coded together although some tests may have been done; other confounders may remain, and funding of offices could not be measured; sex as recorded may not distinguish sex from gender; the 2019–2021 period overlapped the COVID-19 pandemic, which strained death-investigation offices.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 37,346 autopsies in the whole sample, but the medical-examiner (24,969) and coroner (12,467) columns sum to 37,436; the printed standard deviation (46.8) fits 37,436 slightly better than 37,346 (46.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a transposition of digits; the autopsy share is 67.4% or 67.5%, which does not change any conclusion.

reporting_issues.issue: The note to Table 2 assigns ***, ** and * to the 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001 levels, the reverse of the usual key, and the intervals contradict it: for example, opioid test recorded in model 4 is 1.15* with a 95% CI of 1.01–1.31, which cannot be significant at 0.001, while the coroner estimate of 1.79*** has an interval far from 1. Likewise rurality in model (5), printed 0.96* with an interval of 0.93–1.00, cannot be significant at 0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stars follow the usual key (*** p<0.001); read significance from the confidence intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion (4th paragraph) says model (3) adds the autopsy and toxicology-test indicators; Results (6th paragraph) and Table 2 add them in model (4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Model numbers in the Discussion cannot be used as printed; take them from Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion (2nd paragraph) describes the 1.79 estimate as obtained without control variables, but model 2 includes state and year fixed effects; the model without them (model 1) gives 0.32. The same paragraph reads the smallest point estimate (1.52) as a floor (at least 52% increased odds), although the lowest lower confidence limit across the models is 1.20.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader of the Discussion would not learn that the unadjusted association runs the other way, nor that the adjusted estimates are compatible with an odds ratio as low as 1.20.

reporting_issues.issue: Race counts in Table 1 sum to 55,758 overall (37,537 in medical-examiner and 18,221 in coroner counties) against 55,430 deaths (37,198 and 18,232): categories overlap in medical-examiner counties (339 more race entries than deaths), and at least 11 coroner-county deaths have none (a net figure: more, if categories also overlap there). Methods mention race/ethnicity, but no ethnicity variable is shown.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1, race rows; Methods, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: How race was coded in model 5 is unclear (editors' sums); the null race associations cannot be interpreted precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: Text against table: suicide notes are described as slightly under 2% of investigations (Table 1: 1,148 of 55,430, 2.07%), and decedents as just over 69% male (38,177 of 55,430, 68.9%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding slips with no effect on the analysis; cite the table counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods define the unemployment rate as the percentage of the labor force who were employed, while the formula given divides the unemployed by the labor force.
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording error; the formula is the standard unemployment rate.

reporting_issues.issue: Year fixed effects appear in all five models of Table 2 but are not described in Methods, which mention only state indicators; model 5 drops 7 deaths (55,423) without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor gaps in the description of the analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The Key Messages describe the data as a novel data linkage, but Methods describe combining records from two systems by manner; no record linkage, de-duplication or check of county coverage between NVDRS and SUDORS is described.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Key Messages; Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any death could appear twice, or whether a system covered fewer counties, cannot be judged from the paper.
