design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys (fieldwork 2001–2005; probability household samples, nationally representative in most countries, regional or urban-only in China, Colombia, Japan, Mexico and Nigeria; 85,088 respondents) using the WHO CIDI 3.0 with retrospective ages of first use of tobacco, alcohol, cannabis and other illicit drugs. Outputs: cumulative use by age 29 by country and age cohort; discrete-time survival models (person-years to 29) of initiating a later drug after an earlier one, by country and cohort, and pooled across countries with an interaction between earlier-drug use and its prevalence; the prevalence of three 'gateway violations'; and pooled discrete-time survival models of dependence onset with violations, number of drugs used, age of onset and early mental disorders as predictors.
can_establish: How the order of first use of tobacco or alcohol, cannabis and other illicit drugs, as recalled by adults in 17 countries in 2001–2005, varied across countries and birth cohorts; whether the association between using an earlier drug and starting a later one was stronger or weaker where the earlier drug was more common; and whether out-of-order initiation went with later dependence.
cannot_establish: Whether using one drug causes use of another: no individual-level common causes are modelled, the instrumental-variable logic (prevalence varying for reasons unrelated to individual risk) is assumed rather than tested, and country or cohort prevalence is an ecological variable confounded with culture, law, drug markets and survey methods; the true timing of first use (ages recalled, often decades later); or precise country estimates where use was rare (several rest on fewer than 20 people and many models did not converge).

sample.recruitment: General population: probability household samples of adults, nationally representative except China (Beijing and Shanghai), Colombia and Mexico (urban areas, about 73–75% of the population), Japan (four metropolitan areas) and Nigeria (21 of the 36 states, about 57% of the population); France sampled from telephone numbers and the Netherlands from postal registries. Face-to-face interviews by trained lay interviewers; all respondents completed Part I, and Part II (said to contain the substance-use assessment) went to everyone with a core disorder and about 25% of the others, weighted back to the population. Weighted average response rate 69.9%, from 45.9% (France) to 87.7% (Colombia) (2. Method › 2.1 Sample; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults 18 and over in most countries (16+ New Zealand, 20+ Japan, 21+ Israel, 18–65 Colombia and Mexico) (Table 1). Survival analyses restricted to person-years up to age 29 for comparability across cohorts (2.3 Analysis methods). Table 1 also lists a Part II subsample aged 44 or under (39 or under in Nigeria, China and Ukraine) whose use in this paper is not explained.
sample.demographics: Four age cohorts at interview (18–29, 30–44, 45–59, 60+); the sex and age composition of each sample is not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); non-response ranged from 12.3% to 54.1% by country.
sample.selection_effects: Response was below 60% in Belgium, France, Germany, Japan and the Netherlands; coverage was regional or urban in five countries; people outside private households are outside the sampling frame. Older cohorts' reports of use before 29 depend on survival to interview and on long recall. Countries where a drug was rare contribute very few people who used it, so their country-level estimates are fragile.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported ever use and age at first use, recalled at interview: tobacco (even a puff), alcohol (any drink), cannabis, cocaine, and other drugs from a reference list (heroin, opium, glue, LSD, peyote or any other); 'other illicit drugs' combine cocaine and these drugs and exclude prescription drugs. Age of first tobacco use was not assessed in Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Japan and New Zealand, where violations involving tobacco were defined by a different rule (2.2 Measures; 2.2.1). Background prevalence of each earlier drug (by country, and in the Results by country and cohort) is the moderator in the pooled models.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not used: exposure is any use. Age of onset of regular use was asked but not analysed (4.1 Limitations, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the paper: the order of first use across drug classes. Dependence models include tobacco and alcohol use and the number of illicit drug classes used as a time-varying covariate.

comparison.controls: Survival models compare person-years after with person-years before first use of the earlier drug within each country; pooled models compare countries or cohorts with different prevalence; dependence models compare people who started in the usual order with those who did not.
comparison.matching: None. Country models control for person-year and sex; pooled interaction models for gender, age cohort and country; dependence models for sex, age cohort, early-onset internalizing and externalizing disorders, age at onset and years since onset of use, tobacco and alcohol use, number of illicit drugs, the violations and country (2.3 Analysis methods; Table 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Individual propensities (behavioural disinhibition, family history, conduct problems before first use), peer and family drug use and individual access to drugs are not in the initiation models (early mental disorders enter only the dependence models); the national or cohort-level factors behind prevalence (culture, religion, law, markets) are not measured, as the authors note.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable: the analysis concerns sequences of drug use.

outcomes.instruments: WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview version 3.0, fully structured and lay-administered, for DSM-IV dependence (alcohol, nicotine, drugs) and early-onset internalizing and externalizing disorders, with retrospective ages of onset (2.2 Measures). Nicotine dependence was not assessed in ten countries and drug dependence in six (Table 5, notes 5 and 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical calibration of the CIDI 3.0 is cited (Kessler et al., 2004). The authors acknowledge recall error in ages of first use and possible cross-national differences in willingness to report, which they tried to reduce with piloting, community endorsement, non-directive probing and self-completion of sensitive questions by literate respondents (4.1 Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Initiation: first use of any amount of the later drug class by 29. Violations: (1) cannabis before both alcohol and tobacco; (2) other illicit drugs before both alcohol and tobacco; (3) other illicit drugs before cannabis; a less strict version (before either alcohol or tobacco) is in supplementary tables. Dependence onset: onset of the full DSM-IV syndrome (2.2.1; Table 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (α=0.05, two-tailed). 10 counts the outcome types (initiation of cannabis and of other illicit drugs, three violations, five dependence outcomes); across 17 countries, four cohorts and the pooled models the paper reports well over 400 estimates and tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: structured lay interviews; sensitive questions self-administered by literate respondents.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled interactions (discrete-time survival across countries, adjusted for gender, age cohort and country): alcohol or tobacco initiation × prevalence of alcohol or tobacco use, for later initiation of other illicit drugs, OR 32.7 (95% CI 8.3 to 129.0); cannabis initiation × cannabis prevalence, for later other illicit drug initiation, OR 0.3 (0.2 to 0.6); no significant interaction for alcohol or tobacco and later cannabis (no estimate printed). The scale of the prevalence variable is not stated. Country examples (Table 3): cannabis and later other illicit drugs, total, USA OR 137.1 (94.8 to 198.3), New Zealand 118.0 (83.3 to 167.2), Netherlands 62.5 (9.6 to 406.5); at ages 18–29, Netherlands 7.4 (1.8 to 30.4) against USA 107.1 (57.9 to 198.1) and Spain 160.1 (36.8 to 695.9). Proportion of people using other illicit drugs by 29 who had not used cannabis first (Table 4, total): Japan 83.2%, Nigeria 77.8%, South Africa 59.2%, Mexico 48.4%, Colombia 33.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, USA 11.4%. Dependence (Table 5, pooled): violations largely unrelated (for example cannabis before tobacco and alcohol, alcohol dependence OR 0.6, 0.3 to 1.0), except other illicit drugs before cannabis and alcohol dependence (1.6, 1.1 to 2.3); number of drug classes used strongly related (classes: cannabis, cocaine, prescription drugs, other drugs; drug dependence among people who used cannabis: 2 classes 6.1, 3 classes 15.4, 4 classes 35.7, against 1); later age of onset of use protective (ORs 0.2 to 0.7, unit not stated); each early internalizing disorder 1.3 to 1.7 and each early externalizing disorder 1.2 to 1.7.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of survey data; no registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Country-level rates for two of the three violations, the less strict definition and supplementary dependence models are only in a supplement (a Word file, not read); chi-square statistics for Table 5 are 'available upon request'; many country cells are omitted because models did not converge.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Estimates for rare drugs rest on very few people (Table 4's n column, people with the violation: Japan 13 of 16 who used other illicit drugs, Nigeria 7 of 8, Belgium 9, Israel 5), and many odds ratios have intervals spanning two to four orders of magnitude (for example Israel 18–29, cannabis and later other illicit drugs, 3650.6, 209.0 to 63,756.4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In nearly every country with enough people who used drugs, starting an earlier drug in the usual sequence was followed by much higher odds of starting a later one, but the strength of the association varied across countries and cohorts. In pooled models the association of cannabis with later other illicit drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while the association of alcohol or tobacco with later other illicit drug use was stronger where alcohol or tobacco were more common. Starting out of order was more common where the earlier drug was rare (Japan, Nigeria, from a handful of respondents). Out-of-order starts were largely unrelated to later dependence, while the number of drug classes used, an earlier start and early mental disorders were related to it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the gateway pattern 'at least partially reflects unmeasured common causes rather than causal effects', and that preventing specific gateway drugs may not by itself greatly reduce later drug use; the Conclusions say violations are not associated with dependence. Gaps: (1) variation of an association with national prevalence fits common causes, but also differences in drug markets, laws and measurement between countries and a changing make-up of the people who use a drug as it becomes common; the instrumental-variable reasoning is assumed, not tested, as the Limitations concede; (2) the two significant interactions point in opposite directions, and only the cannabis one fits the deviance-marker reasoning of the Introduction (a rarer drug marking higher-risk people), yet the Discussion counts both as support for environmental influences without addressing the contrast; (3) the prevention implication rests on cross-sectional associations, with no analysis of a change in prevalence within a country over time; (4) the Japan and Nigeria proportions rest on 16 and 8 people who used other illicit drugs (13 and 7 of them with the violation); (5) 'not associated with dependence' overstates the pooled results, where one violation was associated with alcohol dependence (OR 1.6). The Conclusions themselves speak of suggestive evidence.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the sequence this paper tests across countries.

Weiss et al.: in hospitalised patients the association of cocaine use with mood disorder weakened as cocaine use became more common, the analogy on which this paper's prevalence logic rests (as described in the Introduction).
Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a common-factor model reproduces the gateway pattern (cited for the common-cause explanation).
Wells & McGee, New Zealand Mental Health Survey: violations uncommon, more common in recent cohorts and not associated with dependence (as cited); the survey is one of the 17 pooled here.
Degenhardt et al., US National Comorbidity Survey Replication: same findings (as cited); also one of the 17 surveys pooled here.
This study: 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys.
Vanyukov et al. cite this study's Japan figures against the gateway hypothesis, combining age groups (see that card).

replication.where_it_stands: The cross-national description that the order of first use varies with how common each drug is, cited in the round's reading list as showing that the order varies between countries. No independent replication of the prevalence-interaction finding is named in the reading list or in the paper (the earlier New Zealand and US analyses use two of the same surveys). Its causal reading is weak by design, and the reading list notes that no study separates causal, common-liability and availability explanations in one design. Later uses of its numbers should keep the small numbers behind the Japan and Nigeria figures.

funding.funder: Not reported: the author manuscript on PMC contains no acknowledgments, funding or role-of-funder statement (the published version was not read).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: 23 authors from the WMH survey consortium (National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, Sydney; Harvard Medical School; national institutes and universities in the participating countries); the first author's group also wrote the earlier US analysis it cites (Degenhardt et al., 2009).

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts in several countries recording first use of each drug as it happens, with individual measures of liability before any use and of local availability and price, analysed with explicit instruments (for example abrupt changes in tobacco taxes or in cannabis law and supply) to test whether shifts in use of an earlier drug change use of later drugs beyond what liability and opportunity predict.

domains.note: Initiation models control only person-year and sex (country models) or gender, cohort and country (pooled models); the individual propensities that form the competing explanation under test are not modelled, and the moderator (country or cohort prevalence) is ecological and confounded with culture, law, drug markets and survey methods.

Ages of first use recalled, up to decades later; how onsets in the same year were ordered is not stated; age of first tobacco use was not asked in eight countries, so violations involving tobacco were defined differently there; 'other illicit drugs' lump cocaine with heroin, inhalants and hallucinogens.
Probability household samples with response rates of 45.9% to 87.7% (below 60% in five countries), regional or urban coverage in four countries and Part II subsampling corrected by weights.
Not relevant to the question.

Key measures were not assessed in several countries (tobacco onset, nicotine dependence, drug dependence), many country cells are missing because models did not converge, and item non-response and its handling are not described.

Initiation of the later drug and dependence onset are also recalled; willingness to report illicit use differs across countries, as the authors acknowledge, which bears directly on cross-country comparisons.

Hundreds of estimates without correction; parts of the violation results and the sensitivity analyses are only in the supplement; the scale of the pooled interaction terms is not given; Table 5 test statistics are available only on request.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a test of whether using one drug causes use of another, the risk of bias is high: individual-level common causes are not addressed, the key moderator is ecological, and all timing is recalled. As a description of how the order of first use and its associations vary across countries and cohorts, the study is stronger: large probability samples with a common instrument and fieldwork procedures, though with variable response, regional coverage in some countries and very few people who used rare drugs. Cite it for the cross-national variation in the order of initiation and for the pooled associations with dependence as associations; not as evidence that the gateway pattern is non-causal.

key_findings.finding: Seventeen WHO World Mental Health surveys (seven developing and ten developed countries), 85,088 adults in total (2372 in the Netherlands to 12,992 in New Zealand), fieldwork 2001–2005, weighted average response rate 69.9% (45.9% France to 87.7% Colombia).
key_findings.locator: 2. Method › 2.1 Sample, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Use by age 29 varied widely: alcohol lowest in South Africa (40.6%), Lebanon (52.8%), Nigeria (55.6%) and Israel (55.7%); tobacco low in South Africa (32.4%) and Nigeria (16.1%); cannabis very low in Nigeria (2.8%), Japan (1.6%) and China (0.3%) against a cross-country median of 9.8% and about 40% in the USA (40.9%) and New Zealand (40.1%); in Japan other illicit drugs (2.4%) were more common than cannabis. Most countries showed higher use in younger cohorts.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results › 3.1 Cross-national and cohort differences in drug use, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: With few exceptions, using a drug earlier in the sequence predicted starting a later one by 29 (country odds ratios mostly between about 10 and several hundred), but the strength varied: for cannabis and later other illicit drugs at ages 18–29, OR 7.4 (1.8 to 30.4) in the Netherlands against 107.1 (57.9 to 198.1) in the USA and 160.1 (36.8 to 695.9) in Spain.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Cross-national and age cohort differences in associations…, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Pooled across countries, the association of cannabis initiation with later other illicit drug initiation was weaker where cannabis use was more common (interaction OR 0.3, 0.2 to 0.6), whereas the association of alcohol or tobacco initiation with later other illicit drug initiation was stronger where alcohol or tobacco use was more common (OR 32.7, 8.3 to 129.0); no significant interaction for alcohol or tobacco and later cannabis.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Cross-national and age cohort differences in associations…, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The scale of the prevalence variable is not given, so the size of the interaction odds ratios cannot be interpreted; covariates gender, age cohort and country.

key_findings.finding: Starting other illicit drugs before cannabis was most common where cannabis was rare (Japan 83.2%, Nigeria 77.8%) and uncommon where cannabis was common (USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%); starting other illicit drugs before both alcohol and tobacco was reported for 52.5% in Japan and 51.8% in Nigeria against 0.6% in Germany, 0.2% in New Zealand and 0.0% in Ukraine; 16.3% of people in South Africa who used cannabis had used neither alcohol nor tobacco before it.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Cross-national and cross-cohort differences in violations…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4
key_findings.note: The Japan and Nigeria proportions in Table 4 rest on 16 and 8 people who used other illicit drugs by 29 (Table 2), of whom 13 and 7 started them before cannabis (Table 4's n column); the violation rates involving alcohol and tobacco come from supplementary tables (not read), and in Japan, Germany and New Zealand age of first tobacco use was not asked, so those rates use a different definition.

key_findings.finding: In pooled models of dependence onset, violations of the sequence were largely unrelated to dependence on any drug (one exception: other illicit drugs before cannabis and alcohol dependence, OR 1.6, 1.1 to 2.3), whereas the number of drug classes used (drug dependence among people who used cannabis: 6.1, 15.4 and 35.7 for 2, 3 and 4 classes against 1), an earlier start (age of onset ORs 0.2 to 0.7) and early internalizing (1.3 to 1.7 per disorder) and externalizing disorders (1.2 to 1.7) were related.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Cross-national and cross-cohort differences in violations…, 3rd paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: The 'number of illicit drugs used' counts prescription drugs as one of its four classes (cannabis, cocaine, prescription drugs, other drugs; Table 5, note 4), unlike 'other illicit drugs', which exclude prescription drugs; the 6.1, 15.4 and 35.7 therefore include prescription drug use as a class.

key_findings.finding: Women had lower odds than men of alcohol dependence among people who drank (OR 0.4, 0.3 to 0.5) and of drug dependence among people who used cannabis (0.7, 0.5 to 0.8), with no significant difference for nicotine (1.0), cocaine (0.9) or other illicit drug dependence (0.8, 0.6 to 1.0).
key_findings.locator: Table 5, row Female
key_findings.note: General-population samples; ages of first use and of dependence onset were recalled at a single interview; adjusted for age cohort, early mental disorders, age of onset and years since onset, other substance use, number of drugs, violations and country. The paper does not discuss these sex differences. The odds are per person-year of dependence onset among people who had used each drug (discrete-time survival), pooled across countries, and the countries differ by outcome: tobacco dependence was not assessed in 10 of the 17 countries and drug dependence not in 6 (Table 5, notes 5 and 6).

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that ages of first use are recalled with error (tending to rise with repeated assessment, though the order is reported to stay stable), that willingness to report may differ across countries, that country is a coarse unit, and that no instrumental variable was measured.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion › 4.1 Limitations, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the evidence is suggestive that initiation is not constant across contexts, that the sequence is not immutable, and that age of onset and degree of exposure to any drug, rather than the order, predict dependence.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion › 4.2 Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the cumulative use of 'tobacco or alcohol' is lower than that of alcohol alone for the USA at 18–29 (96.0% vs 96.2%; n 1316 vs 1318) and Ukraine at 18–29 (99.4% vs 99.7%; n 297 vs 298), which is impossible for a union.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 (United States and Ukraine, 18 to 29)
reporting_issues.consequence: Small; the 18–29 percentages are projected estimates, which may explain the percentages but not the counts. It suggests the combined rows were computed separately and should not be added up by hand.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 marks as significant an odds ratio of 1.0 with interval 1.0 to 1.0 (Belgium, 60 and over, cannabis and later other illicit drugs) and an odds ratio of 14.7 whose interval includes 1 (0.9 to 236.7; Belgium, 30–44, alcohol or tobacco and later other illicit drugs); in Table 4, New Zealand's age-association χ2 of 28.6 is not marked significant while smaller values elsewhere are.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 (Belgium rows); Table 4 (New Zealand row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The significance markers are not reliable cell by cell; degenerate estimates from sparse data are presented alongside the others.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled interaction odds ratios (32.7 and 0.3) are given without the scale of the prevalence variable, and the Methods describe the moderator as prevalence within each country while the Results speak of countries/cohorts.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2.3 Analysis methods, 2nd paragraph; 3.2, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the direction of the interactions can be used; their size cannot be interpreted or compared.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say substance use was assessed in Part II, but Tables 2 to 4 use Part I samples for Colombia, Mexico, Israel, South Africa and New Zealand, and Table 1 lists no Part II sample for Israel or South Africa. Table 2 is headed n=54,068, while the samples its footnotes name sum to 54,307 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2.1 Sample, 2nd paragraph; Tables 1 and 2 (footnotes 1 and 2)

reporting_issues.issue: The n column of Table 4 is not defined; its values look like the number of people with the violation rather than the denominator (Japan 13, against 16 who used other illicit drugs by 29 in Table 2), and the Japan estimate for ages 18–29 (77.3%) carries a standard error of 52.4 points.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline proportions for Japan (83.2%) and Nigeria (77.8%) rest on about 16 and 8 people who used other illicit drugs; they show that the order can differ, not its population rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity definition is described as cannabis use 'before either alcohol or cannabis use', which should presumably read alcohol or tobacco, and Table 2's oldest cohort is headed '<= 60' while Table 3 and the Methods use 60 and over.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2.2.1 Order of onset and violations of the gateway progression, last paragraph; Table 2 header
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling errors; the less strict definition is clear from the Limitations (no use of one or the other of alcohol and tobacco).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the number of early-onset mental disorders an important moderator of the risk of developing dependence, but Table 5 enters early internalizing and externalizing disorders only as predictors, with no interaction terms.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should call early-onset disorders predictors of dependence onset (associated with it), not moderators.

reporting_issues.issue: The note on sample design under Table 1 says that nine of the 15 surveys were based on nationally representative household samples, while the paper pools 17 countries and Table 1 marks 12 samples as nationally representative.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the note appears to describe a different set of surveys. Coverage should be taken from Table 1's rows (not nationally representative: China, Colombia, Japan, Mexico and Nigeria).

design_detail: Literature review with a documented search but narrative synthesis, funded through NIDA Clinical Trials Network node grants and acknowledging the support of the Network's Gender Special Interest Group. Medline and PsycInfo were searched for English-language articles from January 1975 to September 2005 with listed terms, and reference lists were checked; 2,474 Medline and 636 PsycInfo records were screened on title and abstract for relevance by three authors, leaving 280 relevant articles (11.8% randomized trials, 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental trials, 31.2% prospective cohorts). The text discusses adult studies from 1990–2005 on treatment entry, retention, outcome, and women-only against mixed-gender treatment. Excluded: epidemiology of women's substance use, adolescents, criminal-justice populations, nicotine treatment, and studies with substance outcomes as secondary outcomes; pregnancy studies are in the supplement only. No eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no appraisal of the included studies and no pooling; the study-level table is an online supplement that was not read. Classed as a narrative review rather than a systematic review for these reasons, although the authors describe the review as systematic and critical.
can_establish: What the published literature to September 2005 on adult women in substance use treatment contained (mostly observational, 11.8% randomized) and what its larger studies showed about gender differences in entering treatment, staying in it and its outcomes, with the primary studies to consult.
cannot_establish: The size of any gender difference (nothing is pooled); whether women-only or gender-specific programmes cause better outcomes (few randomized comparisons, with mixed results); anything about adolescents, pregnant women, criminal-justice populations or nicotine treatment (excluded); or findings after 2005.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (literature review). Medline and PsycInfo, January 1975 to September 2005, English only, with reference-list searching (1.1 Search Method).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Relevance to treatment entry, retention or outcome in women, from women-only samples or gender comparisons in mixed samples; literature reviews, meta-analyses and theoretical papers also included. Excluded: general characteristics and epidemiology, adolescents, pregnant women (supplement only), criminal-justice populations, nicotine, and studies where substance outcomes were secondary (1. Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: English only; PsycInfo restricted to subject headings; screening by relevance without stated criteria or duplicate decisions. Almost all outcome and retention data come from people who entered treatment, so they describe women and men in treatment, not everyone with a disorder; the review notes that treatment-entry findings depend on the time since onset and on how treatment is defined.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. For the gender differences in treatment entry, the review names the sample: population surveys (NLAES 1992, described as a retrospective cohort analysis of one cross-sectional survey, so onset and treatment were reported after the fact; the 1999 and 2002 national household surveys, past-year treatment; a three-country survey with a broad definition of help-seeking) and clinical or community cohorts (an 8-year prospective follow-up of initially untreated drinkers; HMO and programme cohorts). For the faster progression of women to treatment stated in the Introduction, the samples, timing measures and adjustments are not described.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from use of multiple drugs as a gender-specific predictor of outcome in one cited study.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women in mixed-gender samples; within-women comparisons by characteristics; women-only against mixed-gender programmes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies (for example the Addiction Severity Index, self-reported abstinence, relapse, sessions attended, length of stay, completion); not standardized across studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors note that retention and completion are defined in many different ways (dichotomous session or day thresholds, continuous length of stay, completion of a planned course), which hampers comparison (3. Characteristics Associated with Substance Abuse Treatment Retention and Completion, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Recovery outcomes are taken as each study defined them, for example abstinence in the past 30 days at a 6- or 7-month follow-up, relapse, days abstinent, or decreases in drinking over five years; time windows range from 12 weeks to five years and nearly all participants had treatment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited; none pooled. Ever treated for alcohol use disorders in NLAES 1992 (7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence): 23% of men vs 15.1% of women; cumulative probability of treatment by 30 years after onset .424 vs .356; no difference in the first 8 years; men 13%–20% more likely between 8 and 25 years. Past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence (1999 household survey, 32,628 people): 12.5% of women vs 12.1% of men. Retention in large multi-programme data sets: very few gender differences (for example men 20% less likely than women to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care among 10,010 patients). Abstinence at 6 months in older adults: 79.3% of women vs 54% of men, not significant after adjustment for length of stay.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text discusses studies from 1990 to 2005 selected from the 280 without a stated rule; the full study-by-study results are only in the supplement. Results are otherwise reported in both directions, including null and unfavourable findings for women-only treatment.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level; the authors note that few outcome studies had samples large enough to test gender by race, ethnicity or age.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one national US survey, women with alcohol use disorders were less likely than men to have ever been treated, a gap that appeared only more than eight years after onset and was absent in the most severe cases; past-year and broadly defined help-seeking showed no gender difference, and for illicit drugs one national survey found none. Small clinical studies of retention disagree; large multi-programme data sets show few gender differences, which where present favour women. Most outcome studies find no gender difference and those that find one mostly favour women. Randomized comparisons of women-only with mixed-gender treatment are few and mixed, and the one comparing outcomes favoured a hospital mixed-gender programme on abstinence over the women-only programme, which did not differ from two community mixed-gender programmes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that a convergence of evidence shows women are less likely over the lifetime to enter treatment, and that once in treatment gender is not a significant predictor of retention, completion or outcome. Gaps: (1) the lifetime treatment-entry conclusion rests chiefly on one survey of alcohol use disorders (Dawson, 1996) together with sex ratios in treatment facilities; for illicit drugs the population data cited show no gender effect, and the alcohol gap depends on time since onset and severity; (2) the Introduction states as established, without counter-evidence, that women progress faster from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence (the sentence before gives the label of a most reproducible finding to women's vulnerability to adverse medical and social consequences, and the paragraph's last sentence folds faster progression into that vulnerability), citing six studies, among them treatment samples and Dawson (1996), whose results as described in section 2.3 do not show earlier treatment entry for women; (3) 'not a significant predictor' summarizes mostly observational studies of people already in treatment, with varied outcome definitions, and is not an equivalence result. The authors are otherwise careful: they call the evidence base the very earliest stage, say women-only treatment is not necessarily more effective, and describe the subgroup interventions as early-stage.

timeline.event: Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager describe telescoping in women in treatment (cited in the Introduction).
Dawson's analysis of NLAES 1992: lifetime alcohol treatment 23% of men vs 15.1% of women with alcohol abuse or dependence (as described in this review).
Project MATCH telescoping study, cited in the Introduction for faster progression in women.

Randomized comparison of a women-only day programme with three mixed-gender programmes; the only difference favoured a hospital mixed-gender programme on total abstinence, with no difference from the two community programmes (Kaskutas et al., 2005, as described in this review).
This review.
General-population analysis of two US surveys: men had higher hazards of dependence and of treatment, and the full telescoping pattern was not found.
The same group's update (search terms reused): women and men do not substantively differ in treatment outcomes, smoking cessation excepted.

replication.where_it_stands: Its central conclusions (no substantive gender difference in retention or outcome once in treatment; women-only settings not by themselves more effective) were restated by the same group in 2018 (mchugh_2018). Its telescoping statement predates the general-population test (keyes_2010), which did not find the full pattern.

what_would_settle_it: For treatment entry, a prospective population cohort with linked treatment records recording when men and women first meet criteria and first receive treatment; for treatment effects, the trial the authors propose: one standard treatment delivered in men-only, women-only and mixed-gender groups with randomization, standard outcome definitions and enough women to test interactions with age, race and co-occurring disorders.

domains.note: Two databases, dates, terms, reference lists and record counts are reported and screening was by three authors; but English only, relevance was the only stated criterion, duplicate decisions are not described, and the studies discussed were chosen from the 280 without a stated rule.

No formal appraisal, though designs and sample sizes are given, larger representative studies are weighted over small clinical ones, and some limits are named (broad help-seeking definitions; small samples; non-random assignment to programmes).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Several studies central to the entry, retention and outcome sections are the authors' own (Green et al.; Greenfield et al.; Hien et al.).
Suggested explanations are marked as such ('may', 'it has been suggested'), and the summaries state the limits of the evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on gender differences in treatment entry, retention and outcome
domains.note: Findings in both directions are given, including null results and a trial favouring a mixed-gender programme; only the Introduction's statement on faster progression in women omits counter-evidence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives some concerns, set by the partly systematic selection, the absence of appraisal and reliance on the authors' studies. AMSTAR 2 was not used because the review has no eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no assessment of the included studies and no synthesis method, and its study-level table is in an unread supplement. The review may be cited for the state of this literature to 2005, for its summary that gender did not predict retention or outcome among people in treatment, and as a guide to the primary studies (Dawson, 1996, for lifetime treatment entry; the large multi-programme retention studies; the randomized programme comparisons), whose figures should be cited from the primary papers where possible. Its Introduction's statement on faster progression in women should not be cited without the sample caveat.

key_findings.finding: Search: Medline and PsycInfo, January 1975 to September 2005, English only, with reference lists checked; 2,474 Medline and 636 PsycInfo records, screened by three authors for relevance, gave 280 relevant articles, 90% from 1990 or later (43.9% of those since 2000). 11.8% were randomized trials, 7.9% non-randomized or quasi-experimental trials and 31.2% prospective cohorts.
key_findings.locator: 1.1 Search Method; 1.2 Search Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states that women advance more rapidly than men from use to regular use to first treatment for alcohol, opioid and cannabis dependence and arrive with equal severity despite fewer years of use and smaller quantities, citing mainly treatment-sample studies (Piazza et al., 1989; Randall et al., 1999; Hernandez-Avila et al., 2004) together with Dawson (1996); it adds that age of initiation is roughly equal between the sexes in younger cohorts.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: No sample type, timing measure or adjustment is described for these studies; see reporting issue 2 on Dawson (1996).

key_findings.finding: Women are under-represented in treatment relative to their share of disorders: men to women 3.3:1 in US alcohol treatment facilities in 1991 against 2.7:1 for alcohol use disorders in the population; 2.3:1 in US facilities in 2002 against 1.9:1 for past-year alcohol dependence and 1.5:1 for illicit drug dependence (2003 NSDUH); in Australia 2:1 for high-risk drinking against 3:1 to 10:1 in alcohol services. Women with problem drinking more often seek help in non-specialist settings, especially mental-health services.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Gender Disparities among Participants in Substance Abuse Treatment; 2.2 Gender Disparities in Choice of Treatment Service Sectors

key_findings.finding: Lifetime treatment entry in a general-population sample (NLAES 1992; 7,359 people with alcohol abuse or dependence; retrospective cohort analysis): 23% of men and 15.1% of women had ever been treated (physician, counsellor, Alcoholics Anonymous, other professional or treatment facility); cumulative probability of treatment by 30 years after onset .424 in men and .356 in women; no gender difference up to 8 years after onset; men 13%–20% more likely to start treatment between 8 and 25 years after onset; no gender difference among the most severely dependent; the male-to-female ratio fell from 1.75:1 with one symptom to 1.24:1 with 15 symptoms (Dawson, 1996).
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Gender Disparities in Treatment Entry and Ever Receiving Treatment, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Shorter windows and broader definitions show no gender difference in treatment entry: past-year alcohol treatment among people with alcohol dependence 12.5% of women vs 12.1% of men (1999 household survey, 32,628 people; specialty care 5.7% vs 4.3%, non-specialty 6.8% vs 7.7%); no difference in services over 8 years among 230 women and 236 men who were untreated at the start; gender not associated with past-year use of substance-use services (2002 NSDUH); no gender difference in ever seeking help in a three-country survey that counted telling any professional or attending self-help (50–85% help-seeking). Among 248 inner-city women in Puerto Rico with cocaine or heroin dependence, 36.6% had ever been treated.
key_findings.locator: 2.3, 1st, 4th, 5th and 6th paragraphs; 2.7 Summary

key_findings.finding: Documented barriers for women include pregnancy and fear of losing custody or of prosecution, childcare, economic barriers, co-occurring mood, eating, anxiety and post-traumatic disorders, trauma histories, lack of partner or family support, stigma, and lower perceived need for treatment.
key_findings.locator: 2.4 Specific Barriers to Treatment Entry for Women, 1st–5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Retention: up to 50% of people in treatment drop out within the first month; small clinical studies disagree (five found more dropout in women, two less, one a complex pattern, others none); large multi-programme data sets show very few gender differences, for example 10,010 patients in 96 programmes (men 20% less likely to stay 90 days in outpatient drug-free care) and 26,047 patients in 87 Los Angeles programmes (where differences appeared, women more often completed), and in the Alcohol and Drug Services Study (4,689 adults, 1,239 women) gender was not associated with completion after adjustment.
key_findings.locator: 3. Characteristics Associated with Substance Abuse Treatment Retention and Completion, 1st paragraph; 3.1 Gender Differences in Treatment Retention, 1st, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Programme features: in the Alcohol and Drug Services Study, women-only facilities or on-site childcare were not associated with completion but were positively correlated with length of stay; in a randomized trial, women who kept one or two children with them in residential treatment stayed significantly longer, a result confirmed in a quasi-experimental study.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Program-Related Characteristics Associated with Treatment Retention in Women, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Outcomes: many studies find few or no gender differences; where differences appear, women generally do better. Examples: 567 women and 506 men treated for methamphetamine use, greater improvement in women in family and medical problems at 3 and 9 months; a Dutch trial of 34 women and 29 men with crack cocaine dependence, longer abstinence in women; older adults in outpatient alcohol treatment, 79.3% of women vs 54% of men abstinent in the past 30 days at 6 months, a difference that disappeared after adjusting for length of stay, although women had no heavy-drinking days in the past month at 6 months against an average of four for men; five-year follow-up of treatment and community samples, women more likely to decrease drinking; a meta-analysis of seven brief-intervention studies in primary care, no gender difference.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Substance Abuse Outcomes versus Predictors of Outcomes, 1st–5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In an HMO outpatient programme, women who completed treatment were more than nine times as likely as other women to be abstinent for 30 days at 7-month follow-up, men who completed about three times as likely as other men.
key_findings.locator: 4.4 Effects of Treatment Retention and Completion on Substance Abuse Outcomes, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Co-occurring psychiatric disorders generally predict poorer outcomes in both sexes, with sex-specific patterns that vary between studies; 30–50% of people with bulimia and 12–18% with anorexia had a concurrent alcohol or drug use disorder, and no treatment outcome studies for this combination existed.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Co-occurring Psychiatric Disorders and Substance Abuse Outcomes Following Treatment, 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In a nine-site quasi-experimental study, 1,023 women with co-occurring disorders and histories of violence in integrated, trauma-informed services improved more in PTSD symptoms and drug use and problem severity at six months than 983 women in usual care.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 History of Victimization, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Women-only against mixed-gender treatment: a meta-analysis (Orwin et al., 2001) found single-gender treatment effective, most strongly for pregnancy outcomes, with small improvements in alcohol and drug use, but few of its studies compared women-only with mixed-gender programmes. Randomized comparisons: no difference in refusal or 25-day attrition (Condelli et al., 2000); higher retention in a women-only day programme for women with prenatally exposed infants (Strantz and Welch, 1995); in Kaskutas et al. (2005), the only significant difference was higher total abstinence in a hospital-based mixed-gender programme, which cost twice as much per week, than in the women-only programme, which did not differ from the two community-based mixed-gender programmes (small sample; the review concludes that women may be equally well served by high-quality mixed-gender and women-only day programmes). Non-randomized comparisons were null (Bride, 2001; Copeland et al., 1993) or favoured women-only programmes on days in treatment and completion (Grella, 1999).
key_findings.locator: 5. Gender-Specific Versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Services, 1st paragraph; 5.2 Comparisons of Women-Only versus Mixed-Gender Treatment Settings, 1st–6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Preferences: in a study of women's treatment needs that the review calls quasi-experimental (Swift and Copeland, 1996), women who had attended women-only programmes generally endorsed them; 42% of the women surveyed had no strong feelings for or against mixed-gender programmes, while 11% felt uncomfortable or unsafe in them, 10% found male clients arrogant or sexist and 6% felt harassed or dominated.
key_findings.locator: 5.3 Potential Effective Elements in Women-Only Treatment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: about 12% of studies were randomized and the evidence base is at its earliest stage; women with substance use disorders are less likely than men to enter treatment over the lifetime; gender is not necessarily a predictor of retention, completion or outcome once treatment begins; changing a programme to women-only does not by itself change outcomes, while interventions for specific subgroups of women show promise in small or non-randomized studies.
key_findings.locator: 6. Summary of Findings and Implications, 1st–4th and 6th paragraphs

design_detail: National register-based adoption study (Archives of General Psychiatry 2012; read as the NIH author manuscript). 18,115 Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 (12,783 by age 5), linked through personal identity numbers to 78,079 biological parents and siblings they were not raised with and 51,208 adoptive parents and siblings they were raised with, in 9 national registers covering 1961–2009. The outcome is the study's register-defined 'drug abuse' (DA): drug-use-disorder or drug-psychosis diagnoses (alcohol and tobacco excluded) in hospital, outpatient, primary-care and death records, convictions under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse (convictions only for alcohol-related crimes, or for drug trafficking or possession, excluded), or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids. Analyses: DA rates in relatives of adoptees and parents with and without DA; a 'genetic' risk index built from biological relatives and an 'environmental' risk index built from the adoptive family (each the predicted probability from a logistic regression in the same sample, cut into deciles); and a gene × environment interaction on the scale of raw probabilities. No heritability percentage is estimated.
can_establish: That in Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 with register information on a biological parent, a DA record was more common when biological parents or siblings they were not raised with had DA, alcohol problems, psychiatric hospitalization or convictions, and also when the adoptive home included an adoptive sibling with DA or was disrupted by divorce or a parent's death; that is, factors passed on from biological relatives and factors of the rearing home both predict DA, which a design in intact families cannot separate.
cannot_establish: A heritability percentage (none is estimated); that the biological-relative association is purely genetic (prenatal exposure, care before placement and selective placement are reduced but not excluded); that the gene × environment interaction holds on a multiplicative (odds) scale, which was not reported; or that the figures apply outside Swedish adoptions of the 1950s to 1990s with a biological parent in the registers, or outside its register definition of drug abuse.

sample.recruitment: Registry: all people born 1950–1993 who had been adopted, with information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, from the Multi-Generation Register (the paper does not say 'born in Sweden'; requiring register information on a biological parent in practice limits the sample to children whose biological parents were in the Swedish registers), linked to the hospital discharge (1964–2009), prescribed drug (2005–2009), mortality (1961–2009), outpatient (2001–2009), primary health care (2001–2007, Stockholm and middle Sweden only), crime (1973–2007) registers and censuses (Methods; Sample).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: adoptions by biological relatives or by an adoptive parent living with a biological parent; biological siblings reared with the adoptee. Age at first cohabitation with adoptive parents (AFCAP), estimated from 5-yearly censuses and therefore an upper bound, at most 10 years (main cohort) or 5 years (sensitivity cohort) (Sample).
sample.demographics: Adoptees 52.2% male; mean (SD) age at last available information 46.2 (8.5) years; mean AFCAP 4.4 years (Results › General description; Table 2). Biological parents had more DA (5.8% vs 1.0%), psychiatric hospitalization (18.8% vs 3.1%), alcoholism hospitalization (15.9% vs 0.9%), convictions (41.3% vs 9.4%), low education (76.5% vs 42.8%) and maternal divorce (38.7% vs 6.8%) than adoptive parents (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable as such (register follow-up). Emigration, death and the different years each register covers are not handled as time at risk; logistic regression treats DA as ever or never.
sample.selection_effects: Only adoptions with register information on a biological parent (in practice, children whose biological parents were in the Swedish registers; the paper does not say 'domestic adoptions'); adoptive families were selected for placement and carry little risk (1.0% DA in adoptive parents), so the range of adoptive-home environments is narrow. Selective placement was modest (the two risk indices correlated +0.11; a +0.14 educational correlation between biological and adoptive parents in earlier Swedish work). At least 70.9% lived with their adoptive parents by age 5 (an estimate from 5-yearly censuses), so up to about 3 in 10 may have been placed later; the authors say children were usually removed from their mothers shortly after birth and spent the time before placement in nursery or foster homes (Methodological limitations, 2nd–3rd paragraphs).

exposure.measurement: Register records of relatives: DA (same definition as the outcome), hospitalization for alcoholism (ICD-8 291, 303; ICD-9 291, 303; ICD-10 F10) or psychiatric illness, any criminal conviction, education (low or high, by the 75th percentile within birth decade), divorce, death, medical hospitalization, maternal age. Adoptive-family variables were counted from first cohabitation until the adoptee was 20; biological-relative and adoptive-sibling variables over their whole lives (Genetic risk score; Environmental risk score).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (family history as exposure).
exposure.polysubstance: DA covers all drugs other than alcohol and tobacco together (ICD-10 F11–F16, F18–F19 and their ICD-8 and ICD-9 equivalents); no results by drug.

comparison.controls: Adoptees whose biological (or adoptive) relatives had no DA record; relatives of adoptees without DA.
comparison.matching: None; birth year controlled in all analyses after the description; sex and AFCAP in the risk-index models.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mothers' substance use during pregnancy, the care adoptees received before placement, and the criteria by which agencies matched children to adoptive homes were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Register-defined DA: ICD-8 304; ICD-9 292 and 304; ICD-10 F10–F19 except F10 and F17, in hospital discharge, mortality, outpatient and primary-care registers; convictions under crime codes 5011 and 5012 (crimes related only to alcohol, or to drug trafficking or possession, excluded); or collection of prescribed hypnotics and sedatives (ATC N05C, N05BA) or opioids (N02A) averaging more than 4 daily doses over 12 months, cancer patients excluded (Outcome variable).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation against interviews. The 820 adoptee cases came from discharge (527), crime (313), outpatient (264), prescribed drug (118) and primary care (8) registers, with overlap; between-register odds ratios of registration ranged from 5.6 (prescription vs crime) to 118.0 (discharge vs outpatient) (Table 1). The authors compare Sweden's register prevalence with a Norwegian survey's 3.4% lifetime DSM-III-R abuse or dependence (Methodological limitations, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Ever having a DA record in any of the registers up to 2009; the authors say the construct may be broader than DSM-IV dependence and can include false negatives (no contact with services) and false positives (arrest or treatment without a use disorder; high-dose opioids for chronic pain).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (one outcome; many predictors, selected for the risk indices at P<.10).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Register entries were made independently of the study and of relatives' records.

analysis.effect_sizes: DA in adoptees 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8) vs 2.9% in all Sweden for the same birth years. Adoptees of biological parents with vs without DA 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62), χ²(1)=39.4; none, one or both biological parents with DA 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%, χ²(2)=44.0; biological father 9.9%, mother 8.2%. Biological full siblings 10.7% vs 6.1%, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67); adoptive parents 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80), P=.15; adoptive siblings 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65) (Results; Table 3; χ² values read from the page's MathJax source). Risk indices, OR per decile: genetic 1.13 (1.10–1.16), environmental 1.10 (1.07–1.12); jointly with sex, AFCAP and birth year 1.12 (1.09–1.15) and 1.09 (1.06–1.12); male sex 1.44 (1.24–1.66) (Table 5). Probability scale (Table 6): genetic 0.0049 and environmental 0.0036 per decile, male +0.0151; with the interaction, genetic 0.0028, environmental 0.0015 (−0.0006 to 0.0036), interaction 0.0005 (0.0001–0.0008), P<.05. Editors' calculation from Table 6: each environmental decile adds about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest genetic decile and about 0.6 points at the highest (0.0015 + 9×0.0005).
analysis.covariates: Birth year (after the descriptive analyses); sex and AFCAP in the risk-index models. The relative-pair odds ratios do not say what they were adjusted for or how several siblings of one adoptee were handled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The gene × environment test and its probability scale are described as an a priori aim (Statistical analysis); no protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The sensitivity analysis in adoptees placed by age 5 (n=12,783) is reported only as an unchanged broad pattern, without numbers; the interaction on the logistic scale is not reported; the risk indices were built and tested in the same sample, with predictors chosen at P<.10.
analysis.power: Not reported; large cohort, but only about 1% of adoptive parents had DA, so the adoptive-parent comparison is imprecise (OR 1.55, 0.86–2.80).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Moderate familial associations in both directions of the adoption design: odds ratios of about 1.4 to 2.1 for DA in biological relatives not reared together, and about 2 for adoptive siblings reared together; a non-significant, imprecise association with adoptive parents' DA; data-derived risk indices from the biological and adoptive families each predicting DA; and a positive interaction between them on the scale of absolute risk.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that DA is strongly influenced by genetic risk factors and that adverse environments are more pathogenic in people at high genetic risk; the Comment calls the result a replication of the strong genetic contribution found in twin studies (1st paragraph). No heritability was estimated, and the genetic index includes biological parents' education and divorce, so it captures whatever passes from biological parents (genes, prenatal environment, care before placement, selective placement), not genes alone. The authors say they could "rule out" intrauterine effects because risk was greater with affected fathers than mothers (Comment, 3rd paragraph), but the rates were 9.9% and 8.2% with overlapping intervals (7.2–12.1 and 6.3–10.5) and no test of the difference is reported. The conclusion that social influences shared with adoptive siblings are more potent than transmission from adoptive parents (Comment, 5th paragraph) compares a significant with a non-significant result; the adoptive-parent interval (0.86–2.80) contains the sibling estimate, and only 1.0% of adoptive parents had DA. The interaction holds on the probability scale chosen a priori; the paper does not show whether it holds on the odds scale, where two risk factors that multiply each other's odds produce an interaction of this kind on the probability scale.

timeline.event: US adoption studies of 197 adoptees whose parents were selected from hospital and prison records for alcohol problems, drug use or antisocial behaviour (Cadoret et al., 1995, 1996, as described in this paper): consistent with a genetic contribution.

Twin study of DSM-III-R drug abuse and dependence in 3,372 male twin pairs (Tsuang et al., 1996, as cited): one of four population twin studies from Australia and the US that the authors say they replicate.
Heritability in the genomics era: what a heritability figure does and does not mean (Visscher et al., 2008); not yet appraised

246 adoptive adolescent same-sex sibling pairs resembled each other for substance use disorders (Buchanan et al., 2009, as described in this paper): consistent with the shared-environment finding, which some adult twin studies did not show.
Narrative review of the genetic epidemiology of substance use disorders, without heritability estimates; appraised in this batch

replication.where_it_stands: The association with biological relatives not reared together agrees with the earlier twin and adoption studies the authors cite; the substantial association with adoptive siblings, read as shared environment, differs from some adult twin studies that found little shared environment for lifetime drug use disorders (Comment, 5th paragraph). Later Swedish register work by the same group was not read in this round.

funding.funder: Grant RO1 DA030005 from the National Institute of Drug Abuse; grants 2008-3110 and 2008-2638 from the Swedish Research Council; a project grant from ALF, Lund, Sweden. The sponsors had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation or the manuscript (Acknowledgments › Funding/Support; Role of the Sponsors).
funding.declared_conflicts: Financial Disclosure: None reported (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: Virginia Institute for Psychiatric and Behavioral Genetics, Virginia Commonwealth University; Center for Primary Health Care Research, Lund University; Stanford Prevention Research Center. The interaction scale follows the first author's earlier methods paper (Kendler & Gardner, 2010, as cited). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Adoption and twin designs analysed together in the same register population with drug-specific, validated outcomes, time-to-event models that account for register coverage, emigration and death, risk indices built in one half of the data and tested in the other, the gene × environment interaction reported on both the probability and odds scales, and direct data on prenatal exposure and age at placement; ideally repeated in another country and in later birth cohorts.

domains.note: The adoption design removes genetic confounding of rearing-environment effects and rearing confounding of biological-relative effects, but prenatal exposure, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 possibly placed after age 5) and selective placement remain; the father-versus-mother argument against prenatal effects is not tested.

Relatives' DA, psychiatric and criminal histories come from registers with different coverage periods, so older relatives and earlier decades are measured differently; misclassification is probably non-differential.

National register of adoptions with near-complete identity linkage; the requirement of information on at least one biological parent (which in practice limits the sample to children whose biological parents were in the Swedish registers) limits generality more than it biases the associations.
Not relevant to family-history exposures.

Outpatient, prescription and primary-care registers cover only 2001–2009 (primary care only Stockholm and middle Sweden), so ascertainment differs by birth cohort; emigration and death are not handled; missing biological fathers are not described.

Broad register construct mixing diagnoses, convictions for crimes the register codes as related to drug abuse (codes 5011 and 5012; alcohol-only, trafficking and possession convictions excluded) and long-term high-volume prescriptions, not validated against interviews; families with criminal or psychiatric records may also be more visible to police and services.
Risk indices built and tested in the same data with predictors chosen at P<.10; the age-5 sensitivity analysis reported without numbers; the odds-scale interaction not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the familial associations (biological relatives not reared together; adoptive siblings reared together) the national adoption design is strong and the outcome, though broad, is recorded independently of the study, so the main concerns are residual prenatal and pre-placement effects, a heterogeneous register outcome and cohort-dependent ascertainment. The risk-index and gene × environment results are weaker: data-derived indices, no validation and a scale-dependent interaction. The study may be cited for odds ratios of DA in biological and adoptive relatives of Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993, with the register definition stated; it may not be cited for a heritability percentage, for a purely genetic interpretation of the biological-relative association, or for gene × environment interaction without naming the probability scale.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 18,115 Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 (12,783 by age 5), with 78,079 biological parents and siblings and 51,208 adoptive parents and siblings; adoptees 52.2% male, mean (SD) age at last information 46.2 (8.5) years, mean age at first cohabitation with adoptive parents 4.4 years; follow-up in registers 1961–2009.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Sample; Results › General description, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: DA, as defined from registers, was recorded in 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8) of adoptees (820 people) against 2.9% in all of Sweden for the same birth years; the 820 cases came from hospital discharge (527), crime (313), outpatient (264), prescribed drug (118) and primary care (8) registers, with overlap.
key_findings.locator: Results › General description, 1st paragraph; Methods › Outcome variable, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Among adoptees, DA rose across birth decades (1950–59 to 1980–93: 4.1%, 4.6%, 5.0%, 6.5%) while the national rate stayed between 2.8% and 3.1% with no trend; birth year was controlled in later analyses.
key_findings.locator: Results › General description, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adopted-away children of biological parents with DA had DA in 8.6% vs 4.2% when neither biological parent had DA (OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.66–2.62; χ²(1)=39.4, P<.001); with none, one or both biological parents affected, 4.2%, 8.2% and 11.9% (χ²(2)=44.0, P<.001); with an affected biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: χ² values are inline MathJax on the PMC page and were read from its math source.

key_findings.finding: Biological siblings not reared with the adoptee: full siblings of adoptees with DA had DA in 10.7% vs 6.1% (OR 1.84, 1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3% (OR 1.41, 1.19–1.67).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Rearing family: adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with DA had DA in 6.8% vs 4.5% (OR 1.55, 0.86–2.80, P=.15; only 1.0% of adoptive parents had DA); genetically unrelated adoptive siblings of adoptees with DA had DA in 6.2% vs 3.2% (OR 1.95, 1.43–2.65, P<.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, 2nd paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Risk indices (deciles of predicted probability): 'genetic' index from biological parents and siblings (DA, alcoholism, psychiatric hospitalization, convictions, low education, divorce, maternal age) OR 1.13 per decile (1.10–1.16); 'environmental' index from the adoptive family (parental divorce, death, alcoholism, convictions, medical hospitalization, maternal age; adoptive siblings' DA and hospitalizations) OR 1.10 (1.07–1.12); jointly 1.12 and 1.09; male sex OR 1.44 (1.24–1.66); the two indices correlated +0.11.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predictors of genetic and environmental risk, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Tables 4 and 5
key_findings.note: The authors' lowest-to-highest decile odds ratios (3.39 and 2.59) use ten steps; with deciles coded 0 to 9 the contrast is 1.13^9≈3.0 and 1.10^9≈2.4 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the multivariable models that built the indices, DA in adoptees was predicted by biological parents' DA (OR 1.44, 1.11–1.85), alcoholism (1.36), psychiatric hospitalization (1.26) and convictions (1.22), and by adoptive siblings' DA (1.76, 1.16–2.67), the adoptive mother's divorce (1.31, 1.03–1.68) and an adoptive parent's death (1.37, 1.08–1.73); biological siblings' DA added nothing once parents were in the model (1.02, 0.60–1.72).
key_findings.locator: Table 4, multivariate columns

key_findings.finding: Gene × environment on the probability scale: interaction coefficient 0.0005 per decile × decile (95% CI 0.0001–0.0008, P<.05); with it, the environmental main effect fell to 0.0015 (−0.0006 to 0.0036). Each environmental decile thus added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest genetic decile and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation).
