design_detail: Critical analysis in the history and philosophy of science. The authors outline a feminist philosophy of science framework (science embedded in the communities that produce it; methods built on men; men's experience treated as the universal standard) and apply it to selected 'key source publications' on telescoping: Jellinek's surveys of Alcoholics Anonymous members (1946, 1952), the 1952 WHO expert committee report, Lisansky (1958), James (1975), Mulford (1977), Piazza et al. (1986, 1989), and later studies of other drugs and gambling. Includes a count of the articles citing Piazza et al. (1989) in Web of Science and PubMed, and one figure redrawn from Piazza et al. (1989). No search strategy, inclusion criteria, appraisal tool or quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: Where the telescoping idea came from (stage models built from recalled drinking histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous, with women's data set aside), how small and clinically selected the samples were in which it was first described, how often the 1989 paper is cited as a general rationale rather than tested, and the conceptual objections to making men the reference group.
cannot_establish: Whether women's drinking or drug use actually progresses faster than men's (the empirical studies are neither searched for systematically nor appraised nor pooled); whether any biological or social mechanism produces such a difference (the authors say none has been demonstrated); or whether abandoning the term would improve research or care (a normative proposal, not a tested one).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (critical narrative review). The studies discussed are described with their samples: Jellinek's mailed questionnaire to Alcoholics Anonymous members (98 men analysed); James's mailed questionnaire to women in Alcoholics Anonymous (89 women); Mulford's patients at Iowa community alcoholism centres (3,132 men, 395 women); Piazza's women in residential treatment and Alcoholics Anonymous (41 women, 1986) and people from treatment programmes and self-help groups (33 women, 105 men, 1989); and a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men for cannabis (Khan et al., 2013; a NESARC general-population analysis by its reference title) (History of Telescoping Research).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the authors chose the publications, described in the abstract as drawn from international and US peer-reviewed journals published from 1952 onwards (the text also uses Jellinek's 1946 survey).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and serves the conceptual argument. Nearly all the foundational evidence comes from treatment programmes and self-help groups, where people who reach treatment are, by construction, the people being timed; the authors state that the progressive-disease model behind telescoping leaves out people who recover without treatment or return to non-problem drinking.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. In the studies described, landmark ages (first drink, first drunkenness, first alcohol-related problem, first treatment admission) were recalled by people in treatment or self-help groups and reported in questionnaires; none is described as recorded as it happened. The review does not say what, if anything, the later studies adjusted for.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from James's (1975) questions on the timing of tranquilizer use relative to drinking.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (James's respondents reported a mean of three years' continuous abstinence, range 1–19).

comparison.controls: The paper's central point: in telescoping research men are the reference group and women are compared on landmarks defined from men's drinking histories.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (no new data).

outcomes.instruments: As described for the cited studies: Jellinek's 36-item questionnaire mailed through the AA Grapevine; the Iowa Alcoholic Intake Schedule, validated among men (Mulford); James's women-specific questionnaire (39 items from Jellinek and Glatt plus 85 written from recovering women's experiences); Piazza's questionnaire on landmark ages.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors' critique is that landmarks, criteria and instruments were developed and validated in men and then applied to women.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping as described by Piazza et al. (1989): a later onset of drinking in women but a shorter interval from landmark to landmark, especially from first alcohol-related problem to first treatment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, none pooled. Piazza et al. (1989): women began drinking about 2 years later and first became intoxicated about 3 years later than men, entered treatment at the same age, and had a mean interval from first problem to first treatment 4.3 years shorter. Mulford (1977): women arrived for treatment about 2 years after their first attempt to quit, men about 3 years. Khan et al. (2013): time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women. Citation count: 75 of 103 articles citing Piazza et al. (1989) used telescoping only as a rationale.
analysis.selective_reporting: The empirical studies for and against telescoping receive one paragraph; methodological explanations other than gender bias (recalled onset ages; who reaches treatment and when) are not discussed. Biological sex differences in alcohol effects are presented with single citations as possible mechanisms, without appraisal.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A historical account showing that the stage model behind telescoping came from recalled drinking histories of men in Alcoholics Anonymous (98 men analysed by Jellinek, 15 women set aside), that the 1989 telescoping paper rested on 33 women and 105 men from treatment and self-help settings, that later and larger samples, including a general-population analysis of alcohol, gave discrepant results, while a national general-population survey of cannabis use disorder (NESARC, by its reference title) is described as finding a 2.5-year shorter interval in women, and that most papers citing the 1989 study use it as background rather than test it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that telescoping research carried gender bias in its conventions, methods and language, and that the term "telescoping" and the "masculine" framework "should be discarded" (Conclusions, 3rd paragraph). This is a normative recommendation drawn from a conceptual and historical critique, and the paper presents it as such. Gaps: (1) the argument about biased origins does not by itself show that the timing difference is absent; the empirical question is handled in one paragraph that cites studies on both sides without appraising them; (2) the statement that telescoping may occur only in people who go on to a clinical diagnosis is attributed to the general-population analysis of Keyes et al. (2010) but not examined; (3) biological differences (body water, alcohol metabolism, liver disease, heart disease, brain atrophy in women) are presented as possible mechanisms on single citations, beside the authors' own statement that no mechanism has been demonstrated; (4) the claim that the victim narrative was clinically counterproductive is put as a possibility without evidence.

timeline.event: Jellinek's analysis of a questionnaire mailed through the AA Grapevine: about 10% response, 98 men analysed, 15 women excluded as too few and too different (as described by Marks and Clark).
WHO expert committee report: phases of alcoholism in women less clear-cut and development often more rapid (as quoted by Marks and Clark).
Lisansky first uses the phrase 'telescoped development' for women's alcoholism (as described by Marks and Clark).
James's women-specific questionnaire (89 women in Alcoholics Anonymous; 29 with complete data): 8 of 26 Jellinek symptoms at a different stage in women (as described by Marks and Clark).
Mulford, Iowa community alcoholism centres (3,132 men, 395 women): women reached treatment sooner after a first attempt to quit (as described by Marks and Clark).
Piazza, Vrbka and Yeager define telescoping in 33 women and 105 men from treatment programmes and self-help groups (as described by Marks and Clark).
Project MATCH treatment-sample study, placed by Marks and Clark among studies with discrepant results (see reporting issues).
General-population analysis of two US surveys finds no full telescoping pattern.
National cannabis analysis (Khan et al., 2013; a NESARC general-population survey by its reference title): time to cannabis use disorder 2.5 years shorter in women (as described by Marks and Clark).
This critique recommends discarding the term telescoping.

replication.where_it_stands: A conceptual critique, not an empirical test. It documents that the telescoping construct was built on men's recalled histories in clinical and self-help samples and that the general-population test for alcohol did not find the full pattern, while it describes a general-population survey of cannabis use disorder (Khan et al., 2013; NESARC by its reference title; timing measure and adjustment not given) as finding a shorter time in women; it does not settle whether progression differs by sex. The review by McHugh et al. (2018) is the broader evidence summary on this round's list.

funding.funder: Role of Funding Source: National Institute on Drug Abuse, T32 DA035200 to K.R. Marks; the funder had no role in design, data collection or analysis, or preparation and submission of the manuscript (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no conflict of interest to declare (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Department of Behavioral Science, University of Kentucky. Clark is a co-author of one cited qualitative study (Cooper et al., 2014); no other reliance on the authors' own work.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review of telescoping studies that separates treatment samples from general-population samples and recalled from prospectively recorded timing; and a prospective general-population cohort, designed from the start to test sex and gender differences in course, with landmarks and measures validated in both women and men and analysed by race, class and age as well as gender.

domains.note: Key publications chosen by the authors; no search strategy, dates or criteria, apart from an undated citation count in Web of Science and PubMed.

Samples, response rates and the male basis of the instruments are described for the historical studies, but the empirical tests of telescoping (Piazza 1989, Khan 2013, Keyes 2010 and others) are not appraised for recall of onset ages or for selection into treatment.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One cited study has a co-author of this review (Cooper et al., 2014).

The recommendation to discard the term is clearly normative, and the authors say no mechanism has been demonstrated; but biological mechanisms are listed on single citations and the clinical harm of the victim narrative is asserted without evidence.

domains.domain: Balance between the conceptual critique and the empirical evidence on timing
domains.note: Studies that found telescoping and studies that did not each get a sentence; explanations other than gender bias (recalled onset ages, timing of treatment entry) are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high, set by the absence of a systematic search. The review is useful and explicit about its aim: it may be cited for the history of the concept (Jellinek's male AA samples, the exclusion of women's data, the small treatment and self-help sample of 1989), for the argument that men were the reference group, and for the observation that most citing papers use telescoping as a rationale. It should not be cited as evidence that telescoping does or does not occur; the primary studies, read directly, carry that question.

key_findings.finding: Jellinek's stage model came from a 36-item questionnaire mailed to Alcoholics Anonymous members through the AA Grapevine in about 1945: about 10% responded, data were analysed for 98 men, and the 15 women's data were excluded as too few and too different from the men's (the differences were not specified). The later replication in over 2,000 participants was also confined to men in Alcoholics Anonymous. Ages at each point were recalled.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: A 1952 WHO expert committee report described the phases of alcoholism in women as less clear-cut and their development as often more rapid; Lisansky used the phrase 'telescoped development' in 1958 and warned that stereotypes could shape research on women's drinking.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Foundational Background, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Mulford (1977), a treatment sample from Iowa community alcoholism service centres (3,132 men, 395 women), using an interview validated among men: women arrived for treatment about two years after their first attempt to quit drinking, men about three years.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: James (1975) built a women-specific questionnaire (39 items from Jellinek and Glatt plus 85 written from recovering women's experiences) and mailed it through the AA Grapevine: 15% response, 89 women, mean age about 45, mean continuous abstinence 3 years (range 1–19). In the 29 women with complete data, 8 of the 26 Jellinek symptoms fell at a different stage than in Jellinek's men; the comparison was descriptive, not statistical.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Piazza et al. (1986) re-analysed 18 Jellinek symptoms in 41 women from residential treatment and Alcoholics Anonymous and concluded that Jellinek's model described women's alcoholism; the women-specific questions were not used.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Piazza et al. (1989), widely credited with defining the term telescoping (the phrase 'telescoped development' had been used by Lisansky in 1958; key finding 1): 33 women and 105 men recruited from treatment programmes and self-help groups answered a questionnaire on ages at first drink, first drunkenness, first alcohol-related problem and first treatment admission (recalled). Men and women entered treatment at the same age; women started drinking about 2 years later and were first intoxicated about 3 years later; the mean interval from first problem to first treatment was 4.3 years shorter in women, who reported as many symptoms over a shorter time.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 5th paragraph; Figure 1 (redrawn from Piazza et al., 1989)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image; a screenshot of the tab came back blank, so the figure image was not viewable and no values were read from it.

key_findings.finding: Similar findings were reported for other drugs and gambling; for example, in a national sample of 1,217 women and 3,297 men, time from first cannabis use to cannabis use disorder was 2.5 years shorter in women (Khan et al., 2013). Larger and more diverse samples gave discrepant results, with fewer telescoping effects in some cohorts; the authors summarize Keyes et al. (2010) as finding no telescoping in the general population and suggest it may occur only in people who go on to a clinical diagnosis. They state that the mechanism has not been demonstrated.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The reference list gives Khan et al. (2013) as a NESARC analysis of gender differences in cannabis use disorders (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 130:101–108), that is, a US general-population survey; the text says only that participants were recruited nationally, and gives no timing measure or adjustment.

key_findings.finding: Of 103 peer-reviewed articles citing Piazza et al. (1989) in a Web of Science and PubMed search, 75 did not study telescoping but cited it as a rationale or context for sex and gender differences in general.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: The date of the citation search is not given.

key_findings.finding: Proposed biological mechanisms (hormones, metabolism, subjective drug effects) and social ones (stronger social consequences and disapproval for women, the role of mothers, partners' drug use and loss of a partner) are listed; the authors state that a causal relation between any of them and telescoping has not been demonstrated.
key_findings.locator: History of Telescoping Research › Empirical Research, 8th and 9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors identify gender bias in three places: the progressive-disease conventions drawn from male AA convenience samples, which leave out people who recover without treatment; landmarks, criteria and instruments validated in men, with men as the reference group (had women been the reference, men's longer course might have been called 'magnification'); and comparative language such as 'accelerated progression' and 'a more severe form of alcoholism'.
key_findings.locator: Bias in Telescoping Research, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: discard the term telescoping and the 'masculine' framework; design studies from the outset to test sex and gender differences rather than run underpowered post hoc comparisons; describe group differences in descriptive rather than comparative language; and study how sex and gender intersect with race, class, age, education and culture.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions › Feminist Philosophy as a Transformative Framework for Future Directions, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

design_detail: Critical narrative review of sex differences (biological) and gender differences (socially determined roles), using the NIH Office of Research on Women's Health definitions, across substance use disorders: biology (metabolism, subjective effects, ovarian hormones, neuroimaging), US epidemiology (mainly 2015 National Survey on Drug Use and Health figures), course of illness including telescoping, consequences and co-occurring disorders, treatment seeking, treatment outcome, gender-specific treatment, and pregnancy. Search terms were adapted from the authors' group's 2007 review (greenfield_2007), whose methods are not repeated; treatment papers were limited to 2007 to April 2017, and government survey reports and earlier 'seminal' papers were added; 517 papers were reviewed for relevance. No inclusion criteria, appraisal tool, flow diagram or pooling. Focus on human studies; preclinical work referred elsewhere.
can_establish: What the authors' group, updating its 2007 review, judged the main human findings on sex and gender differences in substance use disorders to be as of April 2017, with US prevalence figures from national surveys and pointers to the primary studies on telescoping, treatment entry, treatment outcome and gender-specific treatment.
cannot_establish: The size or certainty of any sex or gender difference (no systematic selection, no appraisal of the cited studies, no pooling); whether differences are caused by sex, by gender or by who reaches treatment (the cited designs rarely separate them); or whether the selection of studies is complete.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Literature found with search terms adapted from Greenfield, Brooks et al. (2007), plus US government survey publications for prevalence and earlier papers chosen as seminal for biology, aetiology and pregnancy (Introduction, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond date limits: treatment papers published 2007 to April 2017; papers before 2007 allowed for aetiology and pregnancy. The databases are not named in this paper (the reader is referred to the 2007 review). The text nonetheless cites some treatment studies from before 2007 (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own, from 517 papers reviewed for relevance by unstated criteria. Many findings on women's greater impairment, comorbidity and faster progression come from treatment samples, which the review itself warns may over-represent women with more severe disorders (Course of Illness, 1st paragraph). Several treatment studies discussed are the authors' own.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. For sex and gender comparisons the review does not say, study by study, whether samples were treatment or general-population samples (except for telescoping, where it contrasts the two), how the timing of first use, problems and treatment was measured (recalled or recorded as it happened), or what was adjusted for.
exposure.polysubstance: Named as an understudied area in women (Discussion, 6th paragraph); not otherwise addressed.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women, and women with women by subgroup (pregnant, postpartum, with co-occurring disorders), as in the cited studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The review notes that prospective studies measuring differences before drug exposure are needed to tell sex differences in biology from consequences of use (Biological Sex Differences, 8th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies; not described in the review.
outcomes.operationalization: Sex as biological difference and gender as socially determined roles that vary across cultures and over time (NIH Office of Research on Women's Health); telescoping as faster progression from initiation to problems and from problems to treatment seeking.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited; none pooled. US 2015 (NSDUH, ages 12 and older), women vs men: past-month alcohol use 47.4% vs 56.2%; binge drinking 20.5% vs 29.6%; heavy drinking 4.2% vs 8.9%; alcohol use disorder 4.1% vs 7.8%; past-month illicit drug use 7.9% vs 12.5%; illicit drug use disorder 2% vs 3.8%; adults' prescription drug misuse 2.2% vs 2.7%. Ages 12–17: alcohol 9.9% of girls vs 9.6% of boys, binge drinking 5.8% in both, illicit drugs 8.8% in both. Treatment received among people needing it (2015): 10.4% of women vs 11.1% of men. Trials: COMBINE (N=1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (N=653, 40% women) found no gender differences in outcome; smoking cessation meta-analysis of 32 trials (N=14,389, 51% women). Mortality in clinical-trial participants with substance use disorders relative to the general population: about 5-fold in women and 3-fold in men, difference not significant.
analysis.selective_reporting: Gender-specific treatment is presented as supported, but the evidence summarized for women-only against mixed-gender programmes in general is mostly observational (programme comparisons), randomized support is cited only for programmes designed for particular groups of women, and the authors' own larger randomized trial found the women-focused group as effective as mixed-gender counselling, not better; null findings (Bride, 2001) are explained by programme features. Biological findings are described as consistent where they rest on few studies.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level; the review notes that many neuroimaging studies did not test sex differences or were underpowered, and that trials stratify by gender but rarely analyse it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A broad summary in which: women in the US use alcohol and illicit drugs less than men but the gap is closing or absent in adolescents; women start using later on average; faster progression in women (telescoping) has been reported mainly in treatment samples and was not found in a general-population analysis (keyes_2010); women in treatment report more functional impairment and more anxiety, depression and trauma; women are less often treated for alcohol use disorder but treatment entry for drug use disorders is more equal; most large trials show no gender difference in outcome or retention, smoking cessation being the exception, and most of the medicine-specific differences listed go against women; women-only programmes are associated with better outcomes in observational comparisons, while the authors' own larger trial found equivalence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that adverse medical, psychiatric and functional consequences are often more severe in women and that men and women do not substantively differ in treatment outcomes; the Discussion infers that much of the historical gender gap in prevalence may have been social and cultural rather than biological. Gaps: (1) the 'more severe consequences' statement rests largely on treatment samples, to which the review's own caution about telescoping (women in treatment may have more severe disorders) applies equally but is not applied; (2) the abstract's statement that gender contributes to initiation and course is causal in form, while the support is associations, including an ecological association between gender-role traditionality and the size of the gender gap across countries; (3) the statement that men and women do not differ in likelihood of use once access is controlled is generalized from three cited studies; (4) the telescoping paragraph lists replications but cites, for marijuana, a paper whose reference-list title concerns alcohol dependence (see reporting issues). The wording is otherwise hedged ('may', 'suggest'), and the Discussion is explicit about gaps and under-representation of women in trials.

timeline.event: Project MATCH telescoping study, cited by McHugh et al. as a replication of telescoping in alcohol.
The authors' group's earlier review of treatment entry, retention and outcome in women, whose search terms this review reuses.
General-population analysis of two US surveys, cited as failing to replicate telescoping.
NESARC transition analysis, cited for greater nicotine and lower cannabis dependence liability in women.
Becker, McClellan and Reed (2017) review, cited for the explanation that telescoping appears in treatment samples but not in population surveys.
Marks and Clark critique the telescoping concept as rooted in gender bias.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely used overview that updates greenfield_2007; for each question its claims need the primary studies. On telescoping it gives both sides and the treatment-versus-population explanation; on treatment outcome its conclusion of no substantive difference (apart from smoking cessation) matches the 2007 review.

funding.funder: Role of Funding Sources: NIDA grants UG1 DA015831 (Greenfield and McHugh) and K23 DA035297 (McHugh); NIDA had no further role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Under Author Disclosures, the Conflict of Interest statement says that all other authors declare no conflicts of interest; no declaration for any particular author precedes it in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Division of Alcohol and Drug Abuse, McLean Hospital, and Department of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School. The authors (notably Greenfield and McHugh) wrote several of the treatment studies discussed, including the COMBINE gender analysis, a prescription-opioid trial analysis and the Women's Recovery Group trials of their own women-focused group therapy; recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: For telescoping and consequences, prospective general-population cohorts of women and men that record use, problems and treatment as they happen and measure sex (including hormonal status) and gender (roles, access, stigma) separately; for treatment, trials powered in advance for sex-by-treatment interactions; and systematic reviews with explicit criteria and appraisal for each question.

domains.note: Search terms and date limits are given and 517 papers were reviewed, but the databases are not named here, no inclusion criteria or flow are reported, prevalence sources and 'seminal' older papers were chosen by the authors, and pre-2007 treatment studies appear despite the stated limit.

No formal appraisal; some limits are named (cross-sectional imaging cannot show causality; underpowered imaging; women under-represented in disulfiram trials; survey items missing childcare barriers), but most findings are given without design or sample.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The treatment sections lean on the group's own work (the 2007 review, COMBINE and prescription-opioid analyses, the Women's Recovery Group trials).
Mostly hedged, but some statements are made as settled on few studies (greater intoxication in women from gastric enzyme and body water; no sex difference in use once access is controlled).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against sex and gender differences
domains.note: Telescoping is presented with both sides; for gender-specific treatment, the equivalence result of the authors' own larger trial and null programme comparisons are under-weighted relative to observational benefits.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high, set by the unsystematic selection. The review is useful as a map: it may be cited for the US prevalence figures it reports from named national surveys (better cited to the surveys themselves), for the statement that telescoping has been found mainly in treatment samples and not in a population-based analysis, and as pointers to primary studies. It should not be the sole support for any claim about the size or cause of a sex or gender difference; claims should rest on the primary studies or on systematic reviews.

key_findings.finding: Methods: a critical review using search terms adapted from the authors' 2007 review (methods not repeated here), with treatment papers limited to 2007 through April 2017, added US government survey reports and earlier seminal papers for aetiology and pregnancy; 517 papers were reviewed for relevance. Sex is defined as biological difference and gender as socially determined roles.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (untitled opening section), 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Alcohol: women have lower gastric alcohol dehydrogenase activity and lower total body water than men, giving higher blood alcohol concentrations and greater intoxication after the same amount (as cited: Baraona et al., 2001; Chrostek et al., 2003). Sex differences in the metabolism of other drugs have not been consistently shown; some evidence suggests faster nicotine metabolism and higher peak plasma cocaine in women.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Stated as settled on two citations; the project's reading list flags that the gastric-enzyme explanation was contested (Ammon et al., 1996), which this review does not mention.

key_findings.finding: Subjective drug effects show no consistent sex difference: some laboratory studies found none, others greater effects in men or in women. In two laboratory studies (as cited), women gave higher abuse-liability ratings at the lowest doses tested of THC (5 mg; no route given) and d-amphetamine (8–10 mg), and men at the higher doses tested (15 mg THC; 16–20 mg d-amphetamine); one study found greater THC effects in men than women only among people who did not use cannabis often.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Doses are the laboratory study conditions as cited, not guidance of any kind.

key_findings.finding: Menstrual-cycle findings are inconsistent (greater liking in the follicular than luteal phase in some studies, none in others); given progesterone has more consistent effects, reducing cue-induced cocaine craving and nicotine craving, and was associated with less cocaine relapse in postpartum women (one trial) and less nicotine relapse in a small pilot.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Neuroimaging: many studies did not detect, did not test, or were underpowered to test sex differences; cross-sectional volume differences cannot show causality; single studies report higher striatal dopamine release in men than women after stimulants, alcohol and nicotine. The authors add that these differences may reflect gender as well as sex, and that prospective studies are needed to tell pre-existing differences from effects of use.
key_findings.locator: Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 5th–8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: US prevalence, 2015 NSDUH (ages 12 and older), women vs men: past-month alcohol 47.4% vs 56.2%; binge drinking (4+ drinks for women, 5+ for men) 20.5% vs 29.6%; heavy drinking 4.2% vs 8.9%; alcohol use disorder 4.1% vs 7.8%; past-month illicit drug use 7.9% vs 12.5%; illicit drug use disorder 2% vs 3.8%. Ages 12–17: alcohol 9.9% of girls vs 9.6% of boys, binge drinking 5.8% in both, illicit drugs 8.8% in both, prescription drug misuse 2.3% vs 1.7%. Adults' prescription drug misuse 2.2% vs 2.7%.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Prevalence and Incidence, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Trends: the gender gap in substance use disorders is narrowing; binge drinking among US women over 60 rose 3.7% a year (1997–2014) with no change in men; heroin use rose 100% in women vs 50% in men (2002–2013); past-year cannabis use rose more in men (+4.4% vs +2.7%; 16.9% vs 10.1% in 2014). Across countries (WHO World Mental Health Surveys), less traditional gender roles go with a smaller gap; men have more access to drugs, and in three cited studies the chance of use did not differ by sex once access (opportunity) was controlled.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Prevalence and Incidence, 1st, 2nd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Telescoping: women on average start using later (Greenfield et al., 2010; keyes_2010); faster progression in women has been reported for alcohol (Diehl et al., 2007; Randall et al., 1999), marijuana, cocaine (Haas and Peters, 2000, in drug-involved offenders) and prescription opioids, but not for heroin (Lewis et al., 2014; Stoltman et al., 2015), and a large population-based analysis of alcohol (Keyes et al., 2010) did not find it. Citing a 2017 review, the authors explain the discrepancy by sample: telescoping has been found mainly in women already in treatment, who likely have more severe disorders, and not in population surveys; a subset of women may progress rapidly.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The review does not say how timing was measured or what was adjusted for in the studies it lists.

key_findings.finding: Dependence liability varies modestly by gender: greater for nicotine and lower for cannabis in women than men (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011; Wagner and Anthony, 2007); heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine use follow a chronic course of persistent regular use in both sexes (one cited cohort), and treatment, especially early and sustained, is associated with a better course in both.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No definition of chronic course or remission and no description of the cited cohorts are given.

key_findings.finding: Consequences: women in treatment report more severe impairment in employment, family and social, medical and psychiatric functioning and poorer quality of life; men report more legal problems (mixed). Mortality among women with alcohol use disorders was four times the general population in one 1983 follow-up; prescription-opioid overdose deaths rose 400% in women vs 265% in men since 1999; among people in substance use disorder treatment (the cited source is, by its title, a pooled analysis of 22 Clinical Trials Network trials), mortality was about 5-fold the general population in women and 3-fold in men, a difference that was not significant.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Adverse Consequences and Co-occurring Psychiatric Disorders, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Co-occurring disorders: anxiety and depressive disorders are more common in women with substance use disorders, conduct disorder and antisocial personality disorder in men; women more often report trauma and PTSD beginning before the substance use disorder and more often use substances to relieve negative feelings.
key_findings.locator: Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Adverse Consequences and Co-occurring Psychiatric Disorders, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Treatment seeking: some studies find women reach treatment sooner after first use and after onset; in 2015, 10.4% of an estimated 7.9 million US women who needed treatment for an alcohol or drug use disorder received it, against 11.1% of men; under-use is most marked among women with alcohol use disorder; men more often receive specialized addiction treatment and women more often mental-health care. Gender was not associated with past-year treatment use for illicit drug use disorders (Compton et al., 2007, a NESARC analysis by its reference title), and women were 46.8% of 2014 admissions for primary prescription-opioid use disorder.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Treatment outcome: most large randomized trials found no gender difference in outcome, for example COMBINE for alcohol dependence (N=1,226, 31% women) and a prescription-opioid trial (N=653, 40% women). The exception is smoking cessation, with worse outcomes in women; in a meta-analysis of 32 trials (N=14,389, 51% women) varenicline worked as well in both sexes against placebo, with women benefiting more relative to nicotine replacement and bupropion. Behavioural treatments and mutual-help groups worked similarly in women and men; the efficacy of disulfiram for alcohol use disorder in women is unknown because women were, for example, 1.2% of trial participants.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 2nd–5th paragraphs; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Retention: an aggregation of 24 NIDA Clinical Trials Network trials (N>11,000) found no difference in retention by gender, and an analysis of over 1.7 million US treatment episodes found no difference in completion except that women less often completed detoxification.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Gender-specific treatment: across 43 programmes, women in women-only programmes had better drug-use outcomes than women in mixed-gender programmes despite greater severity; other comparisons found modest benefits; a programme that switched to single-gender groups without other changes found none. The authors' own Women's Recovery Group gave greater reductions at 6 months in a small closed-group trial, and in a larger rolling-group trial was as effective as mixed-gender counselling. Women-only treatment is also associated with less criminal activity and incarceration after treatment (two cited studies, designs not described), and several randomized trials are cited as supporting gender-specific treatment for particular groups of women: women with children, women with co-occurring psychiatric disorders and women in the criminal justice system.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy: from NSDUH (CBHSQ, 2016), past-month illicit drug use 4.7%, tobacco 13.9%, alcohol 9.3% and any substance 21.7% of pregnant women; about 3.6% of pregnant women meet criteria for alcohol use disorder and 1.6% for a drug use disorder (cited to Vesga-Lopez et al., 2008, not to NSDUH); only 8.7% of pregnant women with substance use disorders receive specialized treatment (Terplan et al., 2012); 6.8% of treatment facilities offer childcare (SAMHSA, 2017).
key_findings.locator: Substance Use in Pregnancy, 1st paragraph; Treatments for Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the narrowing gender gap over three decades suggests much of the historical difference may have been social and cultural rather than biological; sex differences robust in animal models are much less so in humans; most large trials stratify by gender but do not analyse it; in a review of structural neuroimaging studies, almost three-quarters did not evaluate sex differences.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Gender differences in response to particular medicines (as cited): nicotine replacement worked better in men in a large randomized study (Perkins and Scott, 2008); varenicline worked better in women in one meta-analysis (McKee et al., 2016) and, in another, as well in both sexes against placebo but with more benefit for women relative to nicotine patch and bupropion; with naltrexone for smoking, men cut down more and women gained less weight; women responded worse to disulfiram for cocaine dependence (DeVito et al., 2014); naltrexone findings for alcohol dependence were mixed (men responded better under some dosing; no difference in COMBINE); no gender difference with buprenorphine or methadone; women did worse than men with buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine dependence, although buspirone did not beat placebo in either sex.
key_findings.locator: Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Outcome, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Most of the differences listed go against women (nicotine replacement, smoking reduction with naltrexone, disulfiram for cocaine, buspirone for cannabis and for cocaine); varenicline and smaller weight gain with naltrexone are in women's favour. The abstract's and Discussion's summary of no substantive difference apart from smoking cessation leaves them out.

reporting_issues.issue: Telescoping in marijuana is cited to 'Khan, Okuda, et al., 2013', whose reference-list entry is a NESARC paper on gender differences in lifetime alcohol dependence; the cannabis paper is Khan, Secades-Villa et al. (2013), cited correctly elsewhere in the review.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph; References
reporting_issues.consequence: The marijuana telescoping evidence should be traced to the cannabis paper; whether the alcohol paper, a general-population analysis, reports telescoping is not stated and would bear on the treatment-versus-population explanation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conflict of Interest statement says that 'all other authors' declare no conflicts, but no declaration by any author precedes it in the author manuscript (the Author Disclosures heading is followed only by Contributors).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Author Disclosures › Conflict of Interest
reporting_issues.consequence: Declared interests cannot be fully recorded from this version; the published version should be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Treatment papers are said to be limited to 2007–April 2017, but the treatment sections cite earlier studies (Linehan et al., 1999; Najavits et al., 1998; Orwin et al., 2001; Bride, 2001).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Introduction (untitled), 2nd paragraph; Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Gender-Specific and Gender-Responsive Treatments, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated selection rule was not followed, which confirms that selection was by judgment.

reporting_issues.issue: Blanco et al. (2013) is cited both for women reaching treatment sooner after onset and for no gender difference in treatment entry for prescription-opioid use disorder; the review does not say whether these refer to speed and to probability respectively.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Treatment of Substance Use Disorders in Women › Treatment Seeking, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about women's speed of entry into treatment need the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Keyes et al. (2010) is cited for 'other studies' not finding telescoping across cohorts, right after being cited as the population-based analysis; the reference list also gives Seedat et al. (2009) twice as 2009a and 2009b with identical details; small editing slips ('malesmen', 'sex gender differences').
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Gender Differences in Substance Use Disorders › Course of Illness, 1st paragraph; Biological Sex Differences in Substance Use, 2nd and 7th paragraphs; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the general-population evidence against telescoping cited here is one analysis, not several.

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol use in pregnancy is given as 9.3% 'including 4.6% and 0.8% with heavy use', without saying what the two figures measure.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript), Substance Use in Pregnancy, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The two sub-figures cannot be cited without the NSDUH source.

design_detail: Registered report (Stage 1 in-principle acceptance 25 January 2022 through Peer Community In Registered Reports; materials, code and data on OSF) of an online randomized between-participants vignette experiment, 2 × 2 × 2: health condition ('drug use' vs 'health concern'), label ('chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem') and attributional judgment (high treatment stability: in a treatment programme and committed to success, vs low: has visited a doctor and the condition could get worse or improve). 1,613 adults read one vignette about 'Alex' for at least 60 s, then completed the Stigma and Attribution Assessment (five subscales), the Personal and Perceived Public Stigma Measure (total) in random order, and a Financial Discrimination Task (rewards and punishments of 0 to 100 pence given to Alex's answers on a sham learning platform). Each research question was tested with Welch t-tests plus equivalence tests (two one-sided tests, bounds d ±0.20, α=.01); questions 2 and 3 were analysed within the drug-use arm only. Designed to explain why Kelly et al. (2021) and Rundle et al. (2021) disagreed about the brain-disease label.
can_establish: That in this online sample of adults who said they had no substance use or psychiatric diagnosis and knew of none in a close relative, describing a person's difficulty as drug use rather than a health concern caused large or nearly large increases in self-reported social distance, perceived danger and public stigma (d 0.78 to 0.95), and that calling the drug use a 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than a 'problem' caused stronger agreement that it was genetic or disease-based, after a single short vignette.
cannot_establish: How people who use drugs are actually treated by the public, clinicians or services (one hypothetical allocation task, no real behaviour); how people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis, or a close relative with one, respond (they were not eligible); or whether the label or the treatment framing has small effects on social distance, danger, optimism or public stigma, which the study could not tell apart from zero or from trivial (inconclusive results).

sample.recruitment: Online volunteers recruited through university research-participation schemes (SONA), Prolific and social media (Twitter, LinkedIn), paid in course credit or £5.00 per hour; country of residence not stated in the article (Method › Design and Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over and confirming that they did not have, and did not know a close relative with, a past or current substance use or psychiatric diagnosis. Excluded after recruitment: 9 of 1,622 (6 failed attention checks, 2 withdrew data, 1 implausible response time); for each research question, people who failed that question's manipulation check: 53 (3.29%) for RQ1, 32 (3.78%) for RQ2, 102 (11.96%) for RQ3 (Method › Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph; Results).
sample.demographics: Largest age band 18–25 years (36.5%); 55.9% women; 77.1% White; fuller demographics only in a supplement (File S2), not read.
sample.attrition: Single session; 0.6% excluded overall; manipulation-check exclusions per research question as above, not broken down by condition.
sample.selection_effects: A convenience sample of students and online panel members, mostly young, that deliberately excludes people with a substance use or psychiatric diagnosis in themselves or a close relative (people who used drugs without such a diagnosis were not excluded by this criterion); vignette judgments by such a sample may differ from those of clinicians, employers or the wider public.

exposure.measurement: Randomized vignette condition (assigned by the Inquisit software). The vignette (an image in the article, read on screen): Alex has serious trouble at home and work because of increasing drug use, or a health concern; is now in a treatment programme, or has visited a doctor; learns from staff that the condition is best understood as a chronically relapsing brain disease, or as a problem; and is committed to doing all they can to succeed after treatment, or is told the condition could get worse but could improve with treatment.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (vignette experiment). No drug is named in the vignette.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The authors chose not to vary the substance (footnote 1); four questionnaire items in the drug-use arm refer to opioid addiction.

comparison.controls: The other level of each factor: health concern vs drug use (RQ1, all participants); 'problem' vs 'chronically relapsing brain disease' (RQ2, drug-use arm); high vs low treatment stability (RQ3, drug-use arm).
comparison.matching: Randomization; balance of characteristics across conditions is not reported in the article.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Participants' prior beliefs about addiction and contact with people who use drugs were not measured as moderators.

outcomes.instruments: Stigma and Attribution Assessment (Kelly et al., 2021; 22 items, 1–6 agreement; subscales social distance, perceived danger, prognostic optimism, blame attribution, need for continued care; α in this sample printed as .88, .79, .70 and .69, four values for five subscales, so which subscale lacks one is unclear); Personal and Perceived Public Stigma Measure (Rundle et al., 2021; 23 items, 1–4; total score, subscale α .70 to .91); Financial Discrimination Task (Jones et al., 2022): rewards for Alex's three correct and punishments for three incorrect answers, 0 to 300 pence each (Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scoring direction differs by subscale: higher scores mean more danger and more need for continued care, but less social distance, more blame and more prognostic optimism (Measures; Table 1 note). The three blame items attribute the condition to the disease process (for example that Alex's opioid addiction is genetic in origin), so a higher blame score means stronger agreement with a genetic or disease cause (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). The financial task is a hypothetical, indirect measure of discrimination.
outcomes.operationalization: Stigma as self-reported attitudes on the subscales and total; discrimination as lower rewards and larger punishments in the task. Each difference classified as meaningful (significant at α=.01 and interval outside d ±0.20), equivalent (not significant and interval inside ±0.20) or inconclusive.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Conservative α of .01 for 8 outcomes × 3 research questions; no further correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-completed online measures; participants knew the vignette they had read but not the comparison; the hypotheses were non-directional.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cohen's d with intervals labelled 99% CI (Results; see reporting issues). RQ1, drug use vs health concern: social distance d=.87 [.74, .99], perceived danger .78 [.66, .90], public stigma .95 [.82, 1.07], blame −.35 [−.47, −.23] (all meaningful); prognostic optimism −.06 [−.18, .06] (equivalent); continued care .09 [−.03, .21] (inconclusive); reward −.03 [−.14, .09] (equivalent); punishment .14 [.02, .26] (inconclusive). RQ2, brain disease vs problem: blame .54 [.38, .71] (meaningful); continued care .01 (equivalent); social distance −.20 [−.36, −.03], prognostic optimism −.07, danger −.11, public stigma −.18 [−.34, −.02], reward .15 (inconclusive); punishment .007 (equivalent). RQ3, low vs high stability: social distance −.23, danger .19, blame −.11, prognostic optimism −.17 [−.35, −.004], continued care .11, public stigma .31 [.14, .48], reward −.13 (all inconclusive); punishment −.02 (equivalent). Table 1 (an image, read on screen) gives means and SDs: for example public stigma 50.59 (8.86) vs 42.15 (8.99) in RQ1 and 49.62 (8.89) vs 51.20 (8.78) in RQ2; blame 8.61 (2.63) vs 7.22 (2.51) in RQ2; punishment 62.05 (59.59) vs 53.96 (54.18) pence in RQ1. Editors' check: the RQ2 d values recomputed from Table 1's means and SDs match the text (blame 0.54, public stigma −0.18, social distance 0.20 in magnitude).
analysis.covariates: None (two-group comparisons per research question; interactions between factors not tested).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Stage 1 protocol accepted in principle on 25 January 2022 (PCI RR, https://osf.io/4vscg); all manipulations, measures and exclusions said to be reported; PCI RR bias-control Level 6. The Stage 1 protocol and supplements (Table S1, Files S2 and S3) were not read, so deviations could not be checked; restricting RQ2 and RQ3 to the drug-use arm is stated in the Results without saying whether it was planned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All research questions and all eight outcomes are reported for each, including null and inconclusive results; exploratory analyses with wider equivalence bounds are only in File S3.
analysis.power: Planned 1,578 participants for 90% power to detect equivalence within d ±0.20 at α=.01 (2,804 would have been needed for ±0.15, beyond the funding). Because RQ2 and RQ3 used only the drug-use arm, the smallest cells (392 and 362) allowed equivalence bounds of only ±0.28 and ±0.30 (Method › Design and Participants, 2nd–3rd paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Large effects of calling the person's difficulty drug use rather than a health concern on self-reported social distance, danger and public stigma (d about 0.8 to 0.95) and a smaller effect on the blame subscale (d −0.35); the brain-disease label raised agreement that the condition is genetic or disease-based (d 0.54), with small, inconclusive differences on the other measures, social distance and public stigma being slightly lower with the label (printed intervals −0.36 to −0.03 and −0.34 to −0.02, which do not include zero; at 99% the public-stigma interval would reach zero); in the financial task, slightly larger punishments with the drug-use description (d 0.14, 0.02 to 0.26; p = .005), which the study's rule classes as inconclusive, and otherwise equivalent or inconclusive differences; the treatment-stability framing was inconclusive on every self-report measure and on rewards, and equivalent on punishments.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports "Greater (genetic) blame" with the brain-disease label. The blame items state that the condition is genetic or disease-caused, and the authors' own Discussion reads the label as possibly absolving personal blame by shifting it to brain pathology (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); a reader of the abstract alone could take the result to mean more stigmatizing blame. Whether the contrast drawn with Kelly et al. (2021), who reported lower blame with this label, reflects a real difference or the scoring direction of the same subscale is not settled in the paper. The conclusion that labels affect discrete elements of stigma rests mainly on the health-condition contrast, in which the questionnaire wording also differed (items naming opioid addiction in the drug-use arm only). The suggestion that attitudes do not translate reliably into discrimination rests on one hypothetical financial task with equivalent or inconclusive results and passes over the RQ1 punishment difference, which was significant at the study's α (p = .005) though classed as inconclusive; the proposal that addiction is a functional attribution was not tested. The authors label inconclusive results as such.

timeline.event: Randomized study of two commonly used terms for people with substance-related conditions (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010), on the label side of the same question; not yet appraised

Kelly et al. (2021), 3,635 participants, opioid-dependence vignettes with six labels: 'chronically relapsing brain disease' went with lower blame but lower prognostic optimism and higher danger and need for continued care (as described in this paper).
Rundle et al. (2021), 872 participants: public stigma highest for alcohol use disorder; endorsement of a disease model not associated with public stigma (as described in this paper).
This registered report: large stigma effects of naming drug use, greater genetic or disease attribution with the brain-disease label, other label effects inconclusive.

replication.where_it_stands: Two of the three large vignette studies (Rundle et al., 2021, and this one) compared a described drug or alcohol problem with other health conditions and found that it drew more self-reported stigma; Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison condition, although these authors count it as agreeing (Introduction, 6th paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph). The three disagree on what the brain-disease label does to blame, danger and optimism, partly because they used different measures and vignettes. None measured real-world treatment of people who use drugs.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no known conflicts of interest to declare (Acknowledgements).

The Financial Discrimination Task was developed by members of the team (Jones et al., 2022). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered experiment, powered for differences of about d 0.15 in each comparison, that crosses the labels with the full factorial and samples clinicians, employers and members of the public as well as people with lived experience, uses wording-matched questionnaires and a blame measure that separates personal blame from biological attribution, and adds real decisions (for example referrals or allocation of actual resources) with follow-up.

domains.note: Assignment by the Inquisit software to eight conditions; concealment inherent in online assignment; balance of characteristics across conditions is in a supplement not read.

People who failed the manipulation check for a question were excluded from that analysis (3.3% to 12%), a per-protocol analysis; numbers by condition are not given, and the treatment-stability check asked about the setting (treatment programme or doctor) rather than perceived stability.
9 of 1,622 excluded (0.6%), for stated reasons.

Self-reported attitudes after an explicit vignette, open to demand effects; questionnaire wording differed between the drug-use and health-concern arms (opioid addiction named in four items in one arm); the blame subscale measures genetic or disease attribution, so its label invites misreading; internal consistency .69 to .91.
Registered report with all outcomes reported; provisional, because the Stage 1 protocol was not compared here, and the restriction of RQ2 and RQ3 to the drug-use arm is not stated as planned.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted, pre-registered randomized experiment with transparent equivalence testing and reporting of null and inconclusive results. Concerns are the per-protocol exclusions on manipulation checks, the questionnaire wording that differed between arms for the health-condition comparison, and a blame subscale whose name does not match what it measures. It may be cited for the large effect of describing a condition as drug use (rather than a health concern) on self-reported social distance, danger and public stigma in a non-clinical online sample, and for the brain-disease label increasing genetic or disease attribution, described as such; it may not be cited for effects on real discrimination or on clinicians, or as showing that the brain-disease label increases or reduces stigma overall.

key_findings.finding: 1,613 adults (1,622 recruited; 9 excluded) from university research-participation schemes (SONA), Prolific and social media were randomized to one of eight vignette conditions; largest age band 18–25 years (36.5%), 55.9% women, 77.1% White; people with their own or a close relative's substance use or psychiatric diagnosis were not eligible.
key_findings.locator: Method › Design and Participants, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Procedure

key_findings.finding: Describing Alex's difficulty as drug use rather than a health concern (819 vs 741) produced greater self-reported social distance (d=.87, 99% CI as printed .74 to .99), perceived danger (d=.78, .66 to .90) and public stigma (d=.95, .82 to 1.07), and lower scores on the blame subscale (d=−.35, −.47 to −.23); prognostic optimism was equivalent (d=−.06) and continued care inconclusive (d=.09). Means: public stigma 50.59 vs 42.15; perceived danger 17.37 vs 13.32; social distance 18.84 vs 23.76 (lower = more distance).
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 1, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ1 columns
key_findings.note: Table 1 is an image, read on screen. The intervals labelled 99% match 98% intervals (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In the financial task, describing the condition as drug use left rewards unchanged within the equivalence bounds (d=−.03, equivalent; 248.11 vs 249.72 pence) and went with slightly larger punishments (62.05 vs 53.96 pence; d=.14, .02 to .26; Table 1: Welch t(1557.96)=2.81, p=.005), a difference significant at the study's α of .01 but classed as inconclusive because its interval also overlaps the ±0.20 equivalence bounds.
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 1, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ1 Reward and Punishment rows
key_findings.note: Table 1 is an image: t and p as read on screen by the second reader; the first reader's means and SDs (62.05, 59.59; 53.96, 54.18) reproduce them (editors' recomputation).

key_findings.finding: Within the drug-use arm, the label 'chronically relapsing brain disease' rather than 'problem' (392 vs 423) raised blame-subscale scores, whose items attribute the condition to genetic or disease causes (d=.54, .38 to .71; means 8.61 vs 7.22); need for continued care was equivalent (d=.01); social distance (d=−.20, −.36 to −.03), prognostic optimism (−.07), danger (−.11) and public stigma (−.18, −.34 to −.02) were inconclusive; on the means, the brain-disease label went with slightly less social distance (19.46 vs 18.38, higher = less distance) and slightly lower public stigma (49.62 vs 51.20).
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 2, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ2 columns; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The label did not reliably change the financial task: rewards inconclusive (d=.15), punishments equivalent (d=.007).
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 2, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within the drug-use arm, framing treatment as likely to succeed (high stability) or as an uncertain course (low stability) (383 vs 362) produced only inconclusive differences on every self-report measure (for example public stigma d=.31, .14 to .48, higher with low stability; social distance d=−.23) and on rewards; punishments were equivalent. 102 participants (11.96%) failed this manipulation check.
key_findings.locator: Results › Research Question 3, 1st paragraph; Table 1, RQ3 columns
key_findings.note: Besides the outlook, the two versions differ in setting: in the 'likely to succeed' (high-stability) version Alex is now in a treatment programme, in the 'uncertain' version Alex has visited a doctor, and the manipulation check asked about this setting (Method › Manipulation and Attention Checks; vignette image).

key_findings.finding: Power: 1,578 participants were planned for 90% power to show equivalence within d ±0.20 at α=.01 (2,804 for ±0.15 was beyond the funding); with RQ2 and RQ3 restricted to the drug-use arm, the detectable equivalence bounds were ±0.28 and ±0.30.
key_findings.locator: Method › Design and Participants, 2nd–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that problematic substance use is among the most stigmatized health conditions (agreeing with Kelly et al., 2021 and Rundle et al., 2021), that the brain-disease label's effects remain mixed, that aggregated and multidimensional stigma measures lead to different conclusions, and propose that addiction works as a functional attribution, used to assign or displace responsibility depending on context (a proposal, not tested here).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Conclusions
key_findings.note: 'Agreeing with Kelly et al., 2021' is the authors' reading: as the Introduction (4th and 6th paragraphs) describes them, only Rundle et al. (2021) compared an alcohol use disorder with other conditions, and Kelly et al. (2021) had no comparison health condition.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals labelled 99% CI match 98% intervals: for example, for public stigma in RQ3 (d=.31, groups of 362 and 383) a 99% interval is about .12 to .50 and a 98% interval .14 to .48, the printed values; the same holds for all 24 printed intervals, 8 outcomes in each of the 3 research questions (editors' calculation from the Table 1 means, SDs and group sizes, normal approximation to the standard error of d; done independently by the second reader and the adjudicator). A 98% interval is what a two one-sided tests procedure at α=.01 produces.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Method › Analytic Strategy; Results, all three research questions
reporting_issues.consequence: The intervals are narrower than labelled; at 99% the RQ2 public-stigma interval would include zero. The meaningful/equivalent/inconclusive classifications reported do not change.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints p<.01 for the RQ2 public-stigma Welch test, t(806.59)=−2.55, which corresponds to p≈.011 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Table 1, RQ2 Public stigma row
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; consistent with the 99% interval including zero; the result is classified inconclusive in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: 102 manipulation-check failures for RQ3 are given as 11.96% of the drug-use arm, but that arm had 847 participants (392 + 423 + 32 from RQ2), so 102 is 12.0%; 11.96% implies 853.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Results › Research Questions 2 and 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic inconsistency.

reporting_issues.issue: Signs and degrees of freedom are inconsistent in places: for social distance the sign of d in the text is opposite to the sign of t in Table 1 for RQ1 and RQ2, for RQ3 the t is positive although the low-stability mean is lower (18.14 vs 19.38); the RQ3 punishment t is printed as 0.21 although the low-stability mean is lower (62.21 vs 63.16) and d is −.02, so it should be −0.21; two RQ3 rows give different degrees of freedom for the two tests of the same comparison (742.93 and 742.82; 753.49 and 735.49).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the direction of each effect has to be read from the means, remembering that a lower social-distance score means more distance.

reporting_issues.issue: In the drug-use arm, four questionnaire items refer to Alex's opioid addiction (they were edited to remove the term for the health-concern arm), although the vignette itself mentions only drug use, not opioids or addiction.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Measures › Stigma and Attribution Assessment; vignette (image) under Vignette Development
reporting_issues.consequence: The RQ1 comparison varies the questionnaire wording as well as the vignette, which affects at least the blame subscale; the RQ2 and RQ3 comparisons, within one arm, are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: Two descriptive slips: the text calls the 36.5% aged 18–25 'the majority' (it is the largest age group, not a majority), and it says all Stigma and Attribution Assessment subscales had acceptable internal reliability (above .70) in this sample, while one printed alpha is .69 and only four alphas are printed for five subscales.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML: Method › Design and Participants, 3rd paragraph; Method › Measures › Stigma and Attribution Assessment, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sample is less dominated by young adults than 'the majority' suggests, and one subscale's reliability is borderline or unreported.
