design_detail: Narrative review (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 2017; read as the NIH author manuscript) of the neurobiology and genetic epidemiology of substance use disorders across alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, cocaine and opioids: twin and family studies (described in words, without estimates), candidate-gene and genome-wide association studies (Tables 2 to 5 list GWAS hits for alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, and cocaine and opioid phenotypes), gene–environment interplay, epigenetics (methylation, microRNA, histone modification, much of it from animal studies), phenome-wide association studies and treatment prospects. The abstract's Methods say only that the literature was reviewed: no databases, dates, criteria or appraisal. Table 1 lists the DSM-5 criteria.
can_establish: How these authors summarized, as of 2017, the direction of twin and family findings (initiation influenced by genes and by shared and unique environment; regular use and dependence more strongly genetic, with shared environment fading after adolescence; liability partly shared across substances), the weak and poorly replicated record of individual genetic variants, and examples of environments that change the size of genetic influence.
cannot_establish: Any heritability figure for any substance use disorder (none is reported; the only twin variance figure is a range of 11–74% for smoking abstinence), the completeness of the evidence (no systematic search), or that genetic influence works mainly through the dopamine system (the genome-wide studies it reviews did not single out dopamine genes).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Studies chosen by the authors; Tables 2 to 5 list genome-wide association results with each study's design, sample size, ancestry and best markers.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: No search or selection criteria. The twin evidence is cited without the populations, birth cohorts, sexes or diagnostic methods of the studies, so the reader cannot tell which countries and eras the statements describe. The GWAS tables cover samples mostly of European ancestry, with some African, Dutch, Japanese, Korean and Han Chinese samples, as labelled in the tables.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: twin-model variance components; genotyped variants (single markers, gene-based tests, polygenic risk scores); methylation and gene expression. Phenotypes range from lifetime use and age at first use to dependence diagnoses and symptom counts (Tables 2 to 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed as a source of shared liability (3.2) and as a source of phenotypic heterogeneity that weakens association studies (6, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Varies across cited studies (identical vs fraternal twins; cases vs controls in association studies; some opioid GWAS used people who used opioids without dependence as controls, Table 5 footnotes).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed for the cited studies.

outcomes.instruments: Cited outcomes: substance initiation, regular use, dependence (DSM criteria, symptom counts), cigarettes per day, age at first use, alcohol consumption trajectories, smoking abstinence; gene expression and methylation measures.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors name phenotypic heterogeneity (different measures reflecting different stages of use disorder) as a cause of non-replication (6, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Genetic influence: variance attributed to additive genetic effects in twin models, or associations of variants with a phenotype; environment: shared and unique environmental variance in twin models, or measured exposures in gene–environment studies.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no synthesis); the GWAS tables use the cited studies' thresholds (genome-wide significance, or the best markers up to p≤5×10⁻⁶).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates and no twin heritability estimates. Quantities given: polygenic risk scores explained less than 1% of variance in alcohol dependence (Kapoor et al., 2016; Salvatore et al., 2014) and in age at onset of regular drinking (Vink et al., 2014) (4.1, 3rd paragraph); twin studies attribute 11%–74% of the variance in smoking abstinence to additive genetic influences (8 studies cited; 7, 3rd paragraph); a cannabis GWAS meta-analysis of more than 32,000 participants from 13 sites found no single-marker association with lifetime use but gene-based associations with NCAM1, CADM2, SCOC and KCNT2 (4.2, 2nd paragraph). Tables 2 to 5 give per-marker p-values and, where available, effect sizes; many effect-size cells are blank (printed as a question mark).
analysis.selective_reporting: Selection of studies is the authors'; null and non-replicated findings are acknowledged in section 6 and for OPRM1 (4.4) and cocaine (4.3), but the abstract keeps the dopamine emphasis.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors name low power of single-site association studies as a limitation (6, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Qualitative statements about twin findings without numbers; candidate-gene associations that often failed to replicate; genome-wide studies with few replicated hits outside alcohol-metabolizing genes and nicotinic receptor genes; polygenic scores explaining under 1% of variance; a cocaine GWAS with no genome-wide significant dopamine-pathway genes; a null meta-analysis for the much-studied OPRM1 variant in opioid dependence; epigenetic findings that are largely from animals or did not replicate in genome-wide studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that substantial genetic influences on SUD are "particularly important within the dopaminergic system" and that epigenetic studies indicate drug-specific changes in gene expression; the Conclusions say genes regulating the dopamine system have been found to be important (7, 1st paragraph). The body's own evidence is weaker: the cocaine GWAS found no dopamine-pathway genes (4.3), the OPRM1 meta-analysis was null (4.4), few nicotine associations replicated and results of different designs do not converge (6, 1st paragraph), and genome-wide methylation studies did not replicate candidate-gene methylation results (5.2, 4th paragraph). Animal and human findings are interleaved without labels (for example on D2 receptors, 4.1, 1st paragraph, and ghrelin, 7, 1st paragraph). The word substantial is not given a number anywhere in the review.

timeline.event: Heritability in the genomics era: concepts and misconceptions (Visscher et al., 2008), on what a heritability figure does and does not mean; not yet appraised

National Swedish adoption study of registered drug abuse (Kendler et al., 2012): odds ratios of drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, with no heritability estimate; not cited by this review (an editors' cross-reference); appraised in this batch
Common liability to addiction and the gateway hypothesis (Vanyukov et al., 2012); appraised in this round (card sc_vanyukov_2012)
Meta-analysis of twin and adoption studies of the heritability of alcohol use disorders (Verhulst, Neale & Kendler, 2015; on the Alcohol list, not yet appraised).
Multivariate genome-wide association meta-analysis of over 1 million people for liability shared across substance use disorders (Hatoum et al., 2023; on the General list, not yet appraised).

replication.where_it_stands: The review is a 2017 overview of directions, not a source of numbers. Heritability figures for drug use disorders must be taken from primary twin or adoption studies and their meta-analyses, each with its population and era, and read with Visscher et al. (2008) on what such figures mean. The Swedish adoption study appraised in this batch (Kendler et al., 2012) gives odds ratios of drug abuse in biological and adoptive relatives, not a heritability figure, and is not cited by this review.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC author manuscript has no funding, contributors, acknowledgments or conflict-of-interest section. The publisher's version may carry these statements; it was not read.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Virginia Commonwealth University (epidemiology; psychology), University of New England (Australia), Northwestern University. Some cited work is the authors' own: the only twin neuroimaging example (Prom-Wormley et al., 2015), the gene–environment reviews (Dick & Kendler, 2012), work on drug-induced plasticity (Bowers et al., 2010) and the twin-consortium paper cited for shared environment fading in adulthood (Maes et al., 2017). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review and meta-analysis of twin and adoption estimates for each drug use disorder that reports, for every estimate, the population, birth cohort, sex and diagnostic method, tests the twin model's assumptions and looks for change across eras; and well-powered, multi-ancestry genomic studies with independent replication.

domains.note: The Methods say only that the literature was reviewed; no databases, dates or criteria.

No appraisal of the twin, association or epigenetic studies; twin findings are summarized without estimates or sample descriptions; the GWAS tables contain apparent copying errors (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only twin neuroimaging example is the first author's study, the gene–environment section leans on reviews by a co-author, and the 3.1 statement that shared environment no longer matters for regular use or dependence in adulthood cites first Maes et al. (2017), a twin-consortium paper with Prom-Wormley and Dick among its authors, whose reference entry lacks a title; most of the evidence is from other groups.
The abstract and Conclusions give the dopamine system a primacy that the reviewed genome-wide evidence does not show; animal and human findings are interleaved without labels.

domains.domain: Balance of genetic and environmental explanations, and of replicated and unreplicated findings
domains.note: Replication failures and environmental moderation are acknowledged (5.1; 6), but the limits of twin and adoption designs (shared-environment assumptions, the populations and eras sampled, what a heritability figure means) are not discussed; this side is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review has no search or appraisal, gives no heritability estimates, and its abstract claims a dopamine emphasis that the body's own summary of genome-wide studies does not support. It may be cited for its qualitative account of twin findings (initiation vs progression; shared environment fading after adolescence; shared and substance-specific liability), for the statement that individual variants have small effects and replicate poorly, and as a pointer to gene–environment examples, always as second-hand. It may not be cited for any heritability figure or for the primacy of dopamine genes.

key_findings.finding: The review reports no twin or adoption heritability estimate for any substance use disorder; twin findings are given only in words (section 3), and Table 1 is the DSM-5 list of criteria. The only twin variance figure in the review is that additive genetic influences account for 11%–74% of the variance in smoking abstinence across 8 cited twin studies.
key_findings.locator: 3. Twin and Family Studies, 3.1–3.3; Table 1; 7. Conclusions and Future Directions, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The wide 11–74% range for one smoking outcome illustrates how much twin estimates vary between studies; the populations behind it are not described.

key_findings.finding: As summarized from twin studies: initiation of tobacco, alcohol or cannabis use is influenced by genetic and by shared and unique environmental factors; additive genetic influences are larger for progression (regular use and dependence); shared environment is no longer significant for regular use or dependence in adulthood but remains significant in adolescence; genetic influence on regular use and dependence remains after allowing for genes specific to initiation.
key_findings.locator: 3. Twin and Family Studies › 3.1 Genetic and Environmental Effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: As summarized: twin studies point to genetic and environmental factors shared across substances as well as factors specific to each; for initiation the shared factors are mainly environmental, for use and dependence mainly genetic and unique environmental, and the shared influences appear stable over time.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Genetic and Environmental Influences on SUD Across Multiple Substances, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Polygenic risk scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence in two studies and in age at onset of regular drinking in a third; two studies found associations with dependence rather than initiation for both alcohol and tobacco.
key_findings.locator: 4. Genetic Association Studies › 4.1 Alcohol and Nicotine, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cannabis: four GWAS found no genome-wide significant association with cannabis use disorder; a meta-analysis of more than 32,000 participants from 13 sites found no single-marker association with lifetime cannabis use but gene-based associations with NCAM1, CADM2, SCOC and KCNT2.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Cannabinoids, 2nd paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Table 4 also lists Sherva et al. (2016) with genome-wide significant markers for a cannabis dependence symptom count, which the text does not mention (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cocaine: although candidate-gene studies focused on dopamine-pathway genes, a GWAS of cocaine dependence found no genome-wide significant association for dopamine-pathway genes. Opioids: the frequently reported OPRM1 A118G association with opioid dependence was not confirmed by a meta-analysis.
key_findings.locator: 4.3 Cocaine, 1st paragraph; 4.4 Opioids, 1st paragraph; Table 5

key_findings.finding: The authors list why genetic associations replicate poorly: small effects of each variant, low power of single-site studies, different measures of use disorder, genetic heterogeneity, discovery and replication samples of different ancestry, and subtypes of use disorder; few nicotine-dependence associations have replicated and results of different designs do not converge.
key_findings.locator: 6. Limitations of SUD Genetic Epidemiology Studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Environment changes the size of genetic influence, as summarized: genetic influence on late-adolescent alcohol use is higher in urban areas, in communities with more migration and with more older adolescents and young adults; genetic influence on adolescent smoking is greater with low parental monitoring; the risk linked to a CHRNA5 variant was lower with high parental monitoring; a smoking polygenic score mattered more after more traumatic events and less in neighbourhoods with high social cohesion.
key_findings.locator: 5.1 Gene-Environment Interplay, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Epigenetics, as summarized: candidate-gene methylation studies report weak differences between affected and unaffected groups, with inconsistent direction for OPRM1; genome-wide methylation studies generally do not replicate the candidate-gene results, alcohol results have not replicated, and none existed for cannabis or opioids; much of the microRNA and histone evidence comes from rats, cell cultures and post-mortem studies.
key_findings.locator: 5.2 Epigenetic Influences, 3rd–7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors note that policy changes and changing social norms reduced smoking initiation in the United States, and that how genetic variants bear on such population changes is unclear.
key_findings.locator: 7. Conclusions and Future Directions, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (author manuscript): 4.2 Cannabinoids, 2nd paragraph; Table 4, Sherva rows

reporting_issues.issue: Many effect-size and effect-allele cells in Tables 4 and 5 are printed as a question mark, and Table 2 has a malformed marker identifier (ra62338789).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables cannot be used to compare effect sizes across studies.

design_detail: Theoretical narrative review, the lead article of a Drug and Alcohol Dependence supplement (vol. 123, Suppl. 1), contrasting the 'gateway hypothesis' (a sequence of first use from tobacco or alcohol to cannabis to other illicit drugs) with the concept of a common liability to addiction (a single latent, largely heritable trait behind the risk of all drug addictions). It draws on genetic, psychometric, neurobiological, epidemiological and evolutionary arguments and ends with untested evolutionary hypotheses. No search strategy, selection criteria, appraisal or synthesis of data; one conceptual figure; no tables.
can_establish: The case made by the group that developed the common-liability concept and its measurement for why the usual order of first drug use need not reflect causal stages, and pointers to the twin, psychometric, cross-national and genetic studies it cites in support.
cannot_establish: Whether one drug's use raises the risk of using another, or by how much (no new data, no systematic search, no appraisal of the cited studies); whether common liability explains the order of initiation better than a causal or an availability explanation (designs that found associations surviving familial control are not discussed); any heritability figure, population or era (none is given); or anything about the evolutionary hypotheses, which are offered as proposals.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: no search or selection method is described; the authors chose the literature.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated.
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The cited evidence for common liability is drawn largely from twin and psychometric studies, about a fifth of all references include one of the authors, and the central developmental evidence (the transmissible liability index, pubertal maturation and deviant peers) is the group's own. Studies that found the association between early cannabis use and later drug use surviving co-twin control or extensive adjustment, named in this round's reading list (Lynskey et al., 2003; Fergusson et al., 2006), are not cited.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review). The paper treats the order of first use of tobacco or alcohol, cannabis and other illicit drugs as the gateway 'exposure', and the latent common liability, indexed by the group's transmissible liability index (TLI) built from psychological indicators measured before drug use, as the alternative.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the paper: co-occurrence of use and of use disorders across drugs, explained by a shared liability.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the paper's argument is that pre-drug characteristics (behavioural disinhibition, externalizing problems, pubertal timing) carry much of the risk, but it reports no data of its own on them.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Addiction is treated as compulsive drug seeking and use, distinguished from physiological dependence; liability is a latent quantitative trait with a diagnostic threshold, below which it is 'propensity' and above which 'severity' (Section 3.1).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported. The few numbers are cited from other sources: from the 2007 US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, lifetime use among people aged 18–49 of marijuana by about half, cigarettes by 70% and alcohol by 90%, and cocaine by almost a quarter of those aged 35–49 (Section 3.2.2, 2nd paragraph); from Degenhardt et al. (2010), cannabis use by 4.5% and other illicit drug use by 4.8% of 18–29-year-olds in Japan, where 83.2% of people who used other illicit drugs had not used cannabis first (Section 2, 6th paragraph; see reporting issues). Genetic statements (moderate to high heritability; little drug-specific genetic variance; heritability rising with age) carry no estimates. The review also says that more than 50% of people with an addiction have other psychopathology, citing Regier et al. (1990), an Epidemiologic Catchment Area report by its reference title, with no population or years given; its wording names the people by a label the site does not use (3.4.4, 8th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence is selected to support one side; the qualifications in the gateway literature are quoted as evasions rather than weighed, and evidence of residual associations after familial control is not discussed.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: An argued critique of the gateway concept (stages defined circularly, frequent reversals of the order, dependence of the order on how common each drug is, no mechanism separate from drug use itself) and a case for a common liability resting on cited twin evidence of shared genetic risk across drug use disorders, psychometric evidence that symptoms for different drugs lie on one dimension, and the group's own developmental studies; no new data and no appraisal of the cited studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says initiation sequencing is 'variable and opportunistic rather than uniform and developmentally deterministic', and the Conclusions call common liability 'parsimonious and empirically proven' and the gateway hypothesis 'redundant', possibly hindering research and intervention. Gaps: (1) 'empirically proven' is stated for a latent construct supported by correlational twin and psychometric evidence that the paper summarizes without estimates or appraisal; (2) the paper treats common liability and gateway effects as mutually exclusive, but a shared liability does not rule out an additional causal effect of earlier use, and the designs that test this (co-twin control, cohorts with extensive adjustment) are not discussed; (3) the claim that causality is 'readily refuted' by atypical sequences misreads a probabilistic claim, since a drug can raise the risk of using another without the order being invariant; (4) the gateway concept is presented in its deterministic form while its proponents' stated qualifications are dismissed as hedging; (5) the closing statement that 'the papers in this special issue' support the conclusion names none of them.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the origin of the gateway sequence criticised here.
Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a common-factor model reproduces the gateway pattern; cited as support for common liability and opportunity.
Lynskey et al.: co-twin control study of early cannabis use and later drug use, named in this round's reading list among designs that kept an association after adjustment; not cited by this review.
Tarter et al. (the review's own group): predictors of marijuana use before and after licit drug use; cited as evidence of reversals of the sequence.
Degenhardt et al., WHO World Mental Health Surveys: the order of first use varies with each drug's prevalence across 17 countries; cited here for the Japan figures (see reporting issues).
This review (online January 2012).

Irons, Iacono & McGue (Iacono is a co-author of this review), Minnesota twins (read in this round): drinking by 14 associated with more drug classes used at 24 within MZ pairs discordant for early drinking, which a liability shared by co-twins cannot by itself produce.

replication.where_it_stands: A position paper by the main proponents of common liability and the reading list's liability source on the gateway question. Its critique of the gateway concept is reasonable as argument, but it does not engage the designs that found associations persisting after control for familial factors, and later co-twin evidence on early drinking (Irons et al., 2015) found within-MZ-pair associations with later drug use. The reading list notes that no study separates the causal, common-liability and availability explanations in one design; the two explanations may both hold.

funding.funder: Role of funding source, as printed: NIDA had no role in the analysis, preparation and writing of the report or in the decision to submit it. No grant numbers are given in the author manuscript; a disclaimer states that the views are the authors' and not those of NIDA or any sponsoring organization.
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Pittsburgh (most, including the first author), Rockefeller University, Johns Hopkins, the University of Minnesota, Washington University and Virginia Commonwealth University, and one from NIDA's Division of Epidemiology, Services and Prevention Research. The review is the lead article of a special issue and promotes its authors' concept and instrument (the transmissible liability index); recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that separates the three explanations in one design: for example a genetically informative cohort with drug use recorded as it happens, measuring liability before any use, local availability of each drug, and the order of first use, with MZ twins discordant for early cannabis use, and testing whether early use of one drug predicts later use of another beyond both shared liability and opportunity.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

No appraisal: cited findings are stated as established, including figures that rest on a handful of respondents (the Japan figures) and a claim of a negligible true association between cannabis and other drug use attributed to Earleywine (2002) without data.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 30 of the 145 references (21%) include one of the authors (one of them, Walden et al., 2004, with Iacono's name printed as 'Lacono'), and the developmental and measurement evidence for common liability (transmissible liability index, pubertal maturation, deviant peers) is the group's own; the genetic-correlation evidence comes mostly from other groups.

The evolutionary section is presented as proposals and testable hypotheses, but it runs on from the evidence without a clear break, uses value-laden groupings (it lists homosexuality with suicide and celibacy among behaviours said to need a Darwinian explanation), and the Conclusions call common liability empirically proven.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a causal gateway effect
domains.note: Evidence that associations between earlier and later drug use survive co-twin control or extensive adjustment is not cited; the gateway concept is presented in its strongest deterministic form.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This is an advocacy review by the proponents of one explanation, without search or appraisal and with the opposing evidence largely absent. It may be cited for the argument against reading the order of first use as causal stages, for its definitions of common liability, and as a pointer to the twin and psychometric studies it relies on (which must be read themselves); not for the size of any genetic or gateway effect, for heritability figures, or for the claim that common liability is proven.

key_findings.finding: The authors define the gateway hypothesis as a sequence of first use from tobacco or alcohol to cannabis to other illicit drugs, and common liability as a non-specific liability to all drug addictions regardless of the order of initiation; they note that the gateway hypothesis addresses only initiation, not the development of use disorders.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 6th paragraph; 2. Gateway hypothesis, 1st and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that gateway 'stages' are defined circularly (the stage is identified by the drug and the drug by the stage), that no mechanism separate from drug use is specified, and that its proponents avoid explicit causal claims while implying that earlier drugs are required for progression.
key_findings.locator: 2. Gateway hypothesis, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Reversals of the sequence are described as common, citing studies in which a substantial share of people started with illicit drugs or used other drugs before cannabis, and the cross-national WHO surveys (Degenhardt et al., 2010) for Japan, where cannabis was used by 4.5% and other illicit drugs by 4.8% of 18–29-year-olds and 83.2% of people who used other illicit drugs had not used cannabis first.
key_findings.locator: 2. Gateway hypothesis, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The Japan figures combine age groups and rest on very few respondents in the source (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Against a gateway role of alcohol and tobacco the authors cite a study titled in the reference list as a Mendelian-randomization test, in which aldehyde dehydrogenase deficiency was related to lower rates of drinking but did not predict lower rates of other drug use (Irons et al., 2007), and a school-based randomized prevention trial (by its reference title) after which early protection against or delays in tobacco onset did not reduce later involvement with cannabis or other illegal drugs (Furr-Holden et al., 2004); no numbers are given.
key_findings.locator: 2. Gateway hypothesis, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cited evidence for a common liability: high genetic correlations between liabilities to different drug addictions with virtually no drug-specific genetic variance (Kendler et al., 2003), apart from a licit versus illicit grouping (Kendler et al., 2007); symptoms of different drug use disorders lying on one dimension; and a statistical model in which correlations of cannabis and other drug use are accounted for by common liability and opportunity (Morral et al., 2002). No estimates, populations or eras are given.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.1 Empirical support for the common addiction liability concept; 1. Introduction, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state, citing twin studies, that variation in starting drug use owes much to shared and non-shared environment, whereas variation in use disorders is predominantly genetic with no detectable shared-environment effect, and that heritability grows with age (Hicks et al., 2007); when the review cites Hicks et al. (2007) again, it is for a combined antisocial-behaviour and drug-dependence construct whose heritability grows with age "at least in males"; no figures or samples are given.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2 Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 3.4.4 Drug abuse and (anti)social behavior, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' transmissible liability index, built from psychological indicators measured before drug use, was higher in boys who later developed cannabis use disorder than in boys who used cannabis without developing it (Kirisci et al., 2009, the authors' own study); no numbers are given.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2 Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that any sensitization by cannabis to other drugs would be shared by all drugs and so could not single out cannabis as a gateway, and that the probability of starting with a given drug follows its prevalence and availability, making the sequence opportunistic.
key_findings.locator: 3.2.2 Ontogenesis of the liability phenotype, 6th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The only data the review cites against cannabis sensitization is Ellgren et al. (2004) (3.2.2, 6th paragraph). The review does not say what kind of study it was; its reference title (dopamine levels and behaviour after cannabinoid exposure during adolescence, in a pharmacology journal) describes an experiment that reads as an animal study, so any use of the point must check that paper and label it.

key_findings.finding: On language, the authors argue that any new label for addiction will acquire the negative connotations of the old ones because illicit behaviour evokes negative reactions, and that addiction, though a disorder, results from voluntary norm-violating behaviour and is "subject to moral judgment regardless of the term used".
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: An opinion, with no data; relevant to the encyclopedia's question on words and stigma as an example of one position.

key_findings.finding: The evolutionary section proposes, as hypotheses, that drugs act on an evolved common reward metric as a false fitness signal, and that people with a low amplitude of affective states in safe modern environments seek larger changes, including through drug use and risky or antisocial behaviour.

key_findings.finding: The Conclusions call common liability parsimonious and empirically proven, the gateway hypothesis redundant and of uncertain utility, and warn that presenting the sequence as a theory may be misread causally and hinder research and intervention.

reporting_issues.issue: The Japan example pairs prevalences for 18–29-year-olds (cannabis 4.5%, other illicit drugs 4.8%) with the all-ages proportion of people using other illicit drugs who had not used cannabis first (83.2%). In the source (Degenhardt et al., 2010, read in this round), the prevalences rest on 4 respondents each, the 83.2% on about 13 of 16 respondents of all ages, and the 18–29 proportion is 77.3% with a standard error of 52.4 points. The Japanese survey sampled people aged 20 and over in four metropolitan areas (Degenhardt et al., 2010, Table 1), so the '18–29' band is 20–29 there and the figures are not national.

reporting_issues.consequence: The figure presented as 'a staggering 83.2%' is an all-ages estimate from a handful of people; it illustrates that the order can differ where cannabis is rare, but cannot carry weight as a population estimate.

design_detail: Perspective (the authors call it an opinion piece) arguing that the effects of classic psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin, DMT/ayahuasca) depend on context, meaning 'set' (expectations and other psychological factors brought to the experience) and 'setting' (the environment). It proposes a 2×2 drug × context design to test this and previews, in one figure, preliminary results of the authors' own prospective web survey (psychedelicsurvey.com): two predictor models in 266 people who completed surveys 1 week before, 1 day before, 1 day after and 2 weeks after a psychedelic experience they had planned. No literature search, no selection criteria and no methods section for the survey; the authors say it will be reported more fully elsewhere.
can_establish: What this research group argued in 2018 about context and psychedelic effects, the experiment it proposed to test the argument, and that in its preliminary survey self-rated readiness, intention and trust, rated before the experience, went with the self-rated quality of the experience afterwards.
cannot_establish: That context causes better or worse psychedelic outcomes (nothing in the paper manipulated context), how large any context effect is, or how robust the survey associations are (no full methods, named outcome measures, sample description or model details are given, so the full report has to be read instead); as an opinion piece it is not evidence for empirical claims on its own (METHODS §3.2).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable to the argument (narrative perspective). Survey: people who planned to take a psychedelic entered the date of the planned experience on a study website and were sent surveys at four time points (PDF p. 4, left column, last paragraph); how they were recruited, how many enrolled and which psychedelics they took are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Literature: none stated; sources were chosen by the authors and include books, newspaper articles and conference talks. Survey: nothing reported beyond planning to take a psychedelic.
sample.demographics: Not reported for the survey sample.
sample.attrition: Not reported: only the 266 who completed all four surveys are described; the number who started is not given (Figure 3 legend, PDF p. 5).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people who plan their psychedelic use in advance and volunteer for an online study; the authors themselves expect biases such as extensive prior experience with psychedelics and positive attitudes towards them (PDF p. 4, right column, 1st full paragraph). Analysing only people who completed all four surveys can drop those whose experience went badly or who stopped responding. Most of the experimental evidence offered for the hypothesis comes from the authors' own laboratory.

exposure.measurement: Survey, self-report. Readiness (four items, for example feeling ready to surrender to whatever happens and feeling open to the experience), intention (two items: having a clear intention, and having strong expectations) and trust (two items on the relationship with the people who will be present or look after the person) are all worded about the upcoming experience, so they were rated before it (Figure 3 legend, PDF p. 5). How and when 'therapeutic setting' and 'drug dose' were measured is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Survey: the dose variable is not described (substance, units and how dose was estimated are not given). Doses mentioned in the running text are cited from other studies.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported for the survey and not addressed in the argument.

comparison.controls: None. The survey models are associations within one self-selected sample; nobody was assigned to a different context. Placebo arms of other trials are discussed only as cited evidence (Griffiths et al., 2016; PDF p. 3).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Survey: personality, psychiatric history, previous psychedelic experience and baseline well-being are not reported as measured or adjusted for in the models shown; the authors name previous experience and attitudes as likely biases.

outcomes.instruments: Survey: a 'peak' experience (described by the authors as effectively synonymous with a mystical-type experience), a 'challenging' experience, and psychological well-being 2 weeks after the experience. The questionnaires used for each are not named in this paper (PDF pp. 4–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: A good experience is the peak (mystical-type) construct and a difficult one the challenging-experience construct, both rated after the experience; the longer-term outcome is well-being 2 weeks later, a period the authors themselves say may be too short for integration after a challenging experience (PDF p. 4, right column, 2nd full paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported; how many candidate predictors were tested before the factors shown in Figure 3 were kept is not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report online).

analysis.effect_sizes: Only the coefficients printed in Figure 3 (PDF p. 5; read on a 300-dpi crop). Peak experience: intention β = 0.26 (p < 0.01), therapeutic setting β = 0.26 (p = 0.013), drug dose β = 0.2 (p = 0.04), readiness β = 0.16 (p = 0.076, drawn as a trend); peak experience to well-being at 2 weeks β = 1.96 (p < 0.001). Challenging experience: readiness β −0.46 (p < 0.01), intention β −0.25 (p = 0.02), trust β −0.37 (p < 0.01); challenging experience to well-being β −1.12 (p < 0.005). The model type, whether the β are standardized, sample size per model and confidence intervals are not reported. The β symbol is transcribed from the figure, not a statement that these are standardized coefficients. The different magnitudes alone do not establish coefficient type; do not compare paths as if they shared a known standardized scale.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned for the survey; the perspective itself has none.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only preliminary models are shown, without methods. The text mentions 'additional measures' in the project, including an emotional breakthrough measure said to have been applied 'to good effect', but no results for them are shown (PDF p. 4, right column, 2nd full paragraph).
analysis.power: Not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No experiment on context is reported. The only data are preliminary associations in a self-selected online sample of 266 survey completers: intention rated before the experience, a self-reported therapeutic setting and a higher self-reported dose went with more peak-type experiences, and lower readiness, intention and trust went with more challenging experiences; peak experiences went with larger gains in well-being 2 weeks later and challenging experiences with smaller gains.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The central hypothesis is that the therapeutic action of psychedelics is "fundamentally reliant on context" (PDF p. 1), and the abstract presents the survey as new findings on contextual determinants of the experience. The text itself concedes that few controlled studies have tested the relationship (PDF p. 3) and that controlled studies isolating contextual variables have not been done (PDF p. 4). Specific gaps: (1) the text says the same factors that predict a peak experience, plus trust, protect against a challenging one, but the challenging-experience model in Figure 3 contains only readiness, intention and trust, not setting or dose; (2) readiness is listed as predictive of a peak experience although the figure shows it as a trend (p = 0.076); (3) the link between challenging experience and well-being is called a predictor in one paragraph and a trend in the next, while the figure draws it as significant (p < 0.005); (4) the suggestions that a favourable context explains improvement in the control arms of recent trials, that neglected context may account for the rare reported harms, and that 5-HT2A-driven plasticity makes psychedelic effects exceptionally sensitive to context are offered as the authors' view, without data in the paper.

timeline.event: Ludwig et al. (1969), a clinical study of LSD treatment in alcoholism, cited here as the one exception to the absence of controlled tests of context (PDF pp. 3–4); its design is not described in this paper.

Haijen et al., 'Predicting responses to psychedelics: a prospective study', from the same group: a prospective web survey with surveys before and after a planned psychedelic experience, apparently the fuller report announced here (this paper does not name it). The project's card for it records 654 participants at the first survey, so its sample and models differ from the preliminary Figure 3; cite it rather than this figure.

Kaelen et al., 'The hidden therapist', cited here (in the text as Kaelen et al., 2017) for the finding that patients' relationship to the music in psilocybin therapy predicted the quality of the experience, which in turn predicted outcome.

Strickland et al.: randomized within-person comparison of two music genres during psilocybin sessions in 10 people in a smoking-cessation pilot, a small test of one contextual element; no detectable difference in mystical or challenging experience.
Estric et al.: systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials of classic psychedelics; set and setting were described inconsistently, and no included trial compared different sets or settings.

replication.where_it_stands: The hypothesis that context drives psychedelic outcomes remains largely untested by experiment: up to December 2023 no trial of a classic psychedelic for a psychiatric disorder (substance use disorders excluded) had compared settings (Estric et al., 2025). Randomized evidence on single elements is sparse: a comparison of two music genres in 10 people (Strickland et al., 2021) and, as Strickland et al. describe it, a study that randomized 75 healthy volunteers to different doses and amounts of preparation and support, with preparation and support varied together (Griffiths et al., 2018). The predictive associations previewed here should be taken from the full report by the same group (Haijen et al., 2018).

funding.funder: As printed under Funding: RCH is supported by the Alex Mosley Charitable Trust and has served as an advisor for Compass Pathways; the authors thank two named people for their work on Psychedelicsurvey.com and the people who completed the survey (PDF p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest (PDF p. 6). The first author's advisory role for Compass Pathways is stated under Funding, not under conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Six authors from the Psychedelic Research Group, Imperial College London, one from the Istituto Superiore di Sanità, Rome. The article was written by the first author. Compass Pathways is named in Estric et al. (2025, reference list) as the company that received the US FDA breakthrough designation for psilocybin therapy. Most of the experimental evidence offered for the hypothesis is the group's own. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized factorial trial of the kind the paper proposes, crossing drug or placebo with an enriched or a plain context (for example music or none, preparation or none), with outcomes and analysis registered in advance, assessors blind to condition where possible, and follow-up long enough to see whether context changes clinical outcomes and the rate of difficult experiences.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; an opinion piece citing sources chosen by the authors, including books, newspaper articles and conference talks.

Cited studies are not appraised: outcomes of 1950s–60s LSD therapy are called impressive and reassuring, and worse outcomes when context was neglected are supported partly by a book on military experiments, without any assessment of design or bias (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only new data are the group's own unpublished survey, and the experimental support (music, autobiographical memory scripts, suggestibility, music in psilocybin therapy, quality of the experience predicting outcome) is mostly from the group (PDF p. 3).

The main thesis is labelled a hypothesis and the lack of controlled tests is acknowledged, but several inferences are presented as logical or likely (context explaining control-arm improvement; neglected context explaining rare harms), and the text overstates Figure 3 in three places.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether context or the drug's pharmacology drives outcomes and harms
domains.note: The opposing practical view (cost and complexity) and evidence that challenging experiences can be beneficial are mentioned, and dose is acknowledged as a reliable predictor; under-represented is evidence that effects or harms occur largely regardless of context, which the paper does not examine.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument applies to an opinion piece (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. Selection is unsystematic, cited studies are not appraised and the supporting evidence is largely the authors' own. The preliminary survey figure cannot be appraised from this paper because no methods are given, so claims about predictors of a good or difficult experience should cite the full report (Haijen et al., 2018), not this figure. The paper may be cited for the authors' hypothesis, their proposed 2×2 design, their statement that controlled tests of context were lacking in 2018, and their own report of anxiety in scanner settings; under METHODS §3.2 it is not evidence for empirical claims on its own.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that, although set and setting are widely assumed to matter, few controlled studies had tested the relationship between psychedelics and context, and that controlled studies designed to isolate key contextual variables had not been carried out, apart from a dose-response study, retrospective analyses and Ludwig et al. (1969).
key_findings.locator: Running text (no section headings): p. 3, right column, 1st paragraph; p. 4, left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page

key_findings.finding: Preliminary survey: people who planned to take a psychedelic received surveys 1 week before, 1 day before, 1 day after and 2 weeks after the planned experience; the models in Figure 3 are based on 266 people who completed all four surveys.
key_findings.locator: p. 4, left column, last paragraph (continuing in the right column); Figure 3 legend, p. 5
key_findings.note: No recruitment numbers, attrition, sample description or substances taken are reported. Figure 3 gives example predictor items, but does not name the outcome questionnaires or give full measurement details.

key_findings.finding: Peak (mystical-type) experience model: intention (β = 0.26, p < 0.01), a therapeutic setting (β = 0.26, p = 0.013) and drug dose (β = 0.2, p = 0.04) predicted a peak experience; readiness (β = 0.16, p = 0.076) is drawn as a trend-level path. A peak experience predicted higher well-being 2 weeks later (β = 1.96, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Figure 3, upper model
key_findings.note: Values read from the figure on a 300-dpi crop. Model type, whether β are standardized, measures, covariates and confidence intervals are not reported; setting and dose were self-reported in an uncontrolled sample. The β labels are as printed; their magnitude does not settle standardization, so the paths cannot be compared on an assumed common standardized scale.

key_findings.finding: Challenging experience model: lower readiness (β −0.46, p < 0.01), lower intention (β −0.25, p = 0.02) and lower trust in the people present (β −0.37, p < 0.01) predicted a challenging experience; a challenging experience went with smaller gains in well-being 2 weeks later (β −1.12, p < 0.005). Therapeutic setting and dose do not appear in this model.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3, lower model
key_findings.note: Read from the figure on a 300-dpi crop; same reporting limits as the upper model.

key_findings.finding: The readiness, intention and trust items are worded about the upcoming experience, so these predictors were rated before the drug was taken; the intention score combines having a clear intention with having strong expectations for the experience.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: The authors report that higher doses did not strongly predict a challenging experience in this sample, and that the sample is likely biased, for example towards extensive previous experience with psychedelics and positive attitudes towards them.
key_findings.locator: Right column, 1st full paragraph

key_findings.finding: Scanner settings: the authors report transient anxiety on at least two occasions in about 100 psychedelic scanning sessions (MRI and MEG), which in retrospect they think may have reflected negative set as much as the imaging setting; they cite Studerus et al. (2012) for confined neuroimaging settings increasing the likelihood of challenging experiences, and suggest music, scanner-experienced participants and better briefing and integration for future imaging studies.
key_findings.locator: p. 3, right column, last paragraph, continuing at the top of p. 4, left column

key_findings.finding: As the authors describe modern psychedelic trials, they provide extensive psychological preparation over several visits, a managed environment (low lighting, selected music, pleasing décor, priming) and typically two mental health professionals as sitters or guides who prepare, support and help integrate; the authors note this level of support is unusual in mental health care and question its feasibility in time and cost.
key_findings.locator: Right column, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposed test: a 2×2 design crossing a psychedelic or placebo with an enriched or un-enriched context (for example music or no music, low or bright lighting, psychotherapy or none, priming or none); the authors propose running it at low doses for safety, and even suggest a cross-cultural comparison.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4 and legend; see also p. 4, left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page

key_findings.finding: The authors propose that serotonin 2A receptor signalling and the plasticity associated with it make the psychedelic experience exceptionally sensitive to context; this is presented as a hypothesis, with no new data.
key_findings.locator: Left column, paragraph on comprehensive approaches to drug action (2nd paragraph starting on the page)

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that the improvement seen in control conditions of recent double-blind psilocybin trials (Griffiths et al., 2016) is most likely a favourable-context effect mediated by positive expectancy and exceptional care; this is their view, not a tested finding.
key_findings.locator: Left column, 1st paragraph starting on the page

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that the factors predicting a peak experience, plus being with well-trusted people, protect against a challenging experience (p. 4), but the challenging-experience model in Figure 3 contains only readiness, intention and trust, not therapeutic setting or dose (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not show that setting or dose protected against challenging experiences; the same paragraph says dose did not strongly predict them.

reporting_issues.issue: Readiness is listed in the text among factors predictive of a peak experience (p. 4), but Figure 3 shows it at p = 0.076 with a broken (trend-level) line.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readiness should not be cited from this paper as a significant predictor of a peak experience.

reporting_issues.issue: The link between a challenging experience and well-being at 2 weeks is described as a predictor of a reduced well-being effect in one paragraph and as a trend relationship in the next (p. 4, right column), while Figure 3 draws it as a significant path (β −1.12, p < 0.005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Its strength cannot be settled from this paper; use the full report.

reporting_issues.issue: The text refers to the long-term outcomes shown in Figure 4 (p. 4), but those outcomes are in Figure 3; Figure 4 is the proposed 2×2 design.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor cross-reference error.

reporting_issues.issue: The in-text citation Kaelen et al., 2017 (p. 3), for the finding that patients' relationship to music predicted the quality of the experience, has no entry in the reference list, which lists Kaelen et al. (2018), 'The hidden therapist' (p. 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 2018 paper (kaelen_2018) is presumably meant.

reporting_issues.issue: The conflicts statement declares no potential conflicts, while the Funding section states that the first author has served as an advisor for Compass Pathways.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader relying on the conflicts statement would miss a commercial advisory role; both are recorded as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The survey results are shown without methods: no recruitment or response numbers, attrition, sample description, named measures, model specification, coefficient type or intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model calculations and risk of bias cannot be independently reconstructed here; claims should rest on the full report. The β symbol and the sizes of the coefficients do not establish that they share a standardized scale.
