design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA-guided; no protocol or registration reported) of how 'set' (participant selection, preparation, integration) and 'setting' (monitors, environment, end of session) were described in clinical trials of classic psychedelics in people with psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders. PubMed and Web of Science to 12 September 2022, rerun on 6 December 2023, plus reference lists; English or French. 27 articles on 25 trials (13 randomized, 12 open-label) of psilocybin (16), ayahuasca (5), LSD (2) and 'DMT' (2, one of which is a 5-MeO-DMT formulation); 761 participants by the Results (763 in the abstract). Each trial was scored for whether it reported 16 predefined sub-domains (Table 2) and its practices were described (Table 3); the trials were not appraised and their outcomes were not synthesized.
can_establish: What 25 published clinical trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders (to December 2023) reported about participant selection, preparation, monitors, environment, music and end-of-session procedures, and how completely they reported it.
cannot_establish: Whether any element of set or setting changes therapeutic outcomes or the risk of a difficult experience (no included trial compared settings, the trials were not appraised and no outcomes were synthesized); what trials did but did not report (the score measures reporting); and practice outside clinical trials, in healthy volunteers, in addiction treatment, or with MDMA or ketamine, all of which were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed and Web of Science (drug names LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, N,N-dimethyltryptamine, ibogaine or mescaline, combined with setting, therapeutics, psychotherapy or psychiatry) to 12 September 2022, rerun with the same strategy on 6 December 2023, plus manual search of reference lists (PDF p. 2, Methods › Data source and research strategy). Figure 1 (PDF p. 3): 3,045 PubMed and 1,867 Web of Science records (4,912); 1,282 removed for lacking an English or French abstract, 3,322 on title and 71 as duplicates; 237 abstracts screened, 47 full texts assessed, 15 articles included, and 12 more added after the update.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed clinical trials in English or French, with a title and abstract, in participants with a psychiatric diagnosis. Excluded: reviews, meta-analyses and expert opinion; healthy volunteers (47 at abstract stage); addiction treatment and withdrawal; articles on the population of an already included study without a new or modified protocol (23 at full text); MDMA and ketamine, as not classic psychedelics (PDF pp. 2–3, 17).
sample.demographics: Trial sizes 6 to 233; one trial (Goodwin et al., 2022) contributes 233 of the 761 participants (31%, editors' arithmetic). 12 of 25 trials in the USA only, all ayahuasca trials in Brazil. Mainly depression: 7 unique trials in the eight-article list for major depressive episodes (Carhart-Harris 2021 and Murphy 2022 describe one trial), 2 recurrent, 5 treatment-resistant, 6 depression or anxiety with a life-threatening illness; one each in OCD, social anxiety, body dysmorphic disorder, anorexia nervosa and bipolar II depression (PDF p. 4; Table 1, pp. 5–6). Women 422 of 761 (55%) by the editors' sum of Table 1.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Trials only, of classic psychedelics, in psychiatric patients without substance use disorders; two databases, English or French, no registries or grey literature. Trial participants were heavily screened: 13 trials excluded anyone with occasional or regular use of an illicit psychoactive substance other than alcohol, 7 a history of alcohol dependence, and the ayahuasca trials anyone who had taken ayahuasca before (once in four trials, twice in one); two trials allowed no more than 10 previous hallucinogen experiences, and one required previous tolerated use of an indole psychedelic (PDF p. 7). Features were scored as reported in articles, supplements and protocols, so a practice done but not described counts as absent.

exposure.measurement: Presence or absence of 16 set-and-setting sub-domains as described in each trial's article, supplements and protocols, scored out of 16 per trial, plus a narrative description of each trial's practices (Tables 2 and 3). Who did the scoring, and whether it was checked by a second reviewer, is not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Trial doses are listed in Table 1 as trial conditions (PDF pp. 5–6) and are not reproduced here. Session length in Table 3 ranges from 2 h (intravenous DMT) to 12 h (LSD), mostly 6–8 h for psilocybin and 4 h for ayahuasca (PDF pp. 11–15).
exposure.polysubstance: Trial rules on medicines and other substances before sessions, as listed by the review (PDF p. 7, Results › Drug interactions; numbers of trials are the editors' tally of the studies cited): washout of antidepressants and other psychotropic medicines, most often at least 2 weeks before the first dose (13 trials), with other schedules elsewhere; no cannabis for 24 h before each session (4 trials); alcohol and other psychoactive drugs strongly discouraged for 24 h before each session (3 trials) or stopped for 2 weeks during full-time hospitalization (3 ayahuasca reports); no food supplements in the week before (2 trials); no tyramine-rich foods for 24 h before and 12 h after ayahuasca because of its monoamine-oxidase-inhibiting content (1 trial); caffeine withheld for 24 h (1 trial) or taken as usual on the morning (2 trials); no nicotine from 2 h before until questionnaires about 7 h after psilocybin (1 trial). None of these rules was evaluated.

comparison.controls: Not applicable: no included trial compared settings; the review compares how completely trials reported each feature.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level.

outcomes.instruments: Six predefined domains, refined into 16 sub-domains during full-text reading: participant selection (general health, drug interactions, exclusion criteria); pre-session interventions (information on effects, therapeutic-alliance meeting, advice on the attitude to adopt); post-session meeting; monitors (specific training, presence and number during the session, prior meeting with the participant); environment (pleasant environment, safe environment, control of visual distractors, control of sound distractors); end of session (debriefing, safe return home) (PDF pp. 2–3; Table 2, p. 10).
outcomes.validity_norms: The domains were based on earlier publications, including safety guidelines for hallucinogen research (Johnson et al., 2008) and Carhart-Harris et al. (2018); no validation or inter-rater reliability of the score is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: A sub-domain counts as present if the trial described it anywhere in its article, supplement or protocol; no description counts as missing. The total out of 16 measures completeness of reporting, not quality of practice or any effect on outcomes.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Number of the 25 trials reporting each sub-domain (Table 2, PDF p. 10): general health, drug interactions and exclusion criteria 25 (100%) each; information on effects 21 (84%); therapeutic-alliance meeting 19 (76%); advice on attitude 18 (72%); post-session meeting 20 (80%); specific monitor training 13 (52%); monitor present during the session 18 (72%); prior meeting of monitors and participant 18 (72%); pleasant environment 17 (68%); safe environment printed as 20 (80%), although the column has 21 ticks (84%; editors' count on the rendered page and the text layer); control of visual distractors 16 (64%); control of sound distractors 19 (76%); debriefing 19 (76%); safe return home 20 (80%). Median total 14 of 16, range 6 to 16; 3 trials reported all 16 (PDF pp. 16, 18).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the 16 sub-domains were refined during full-text reading (PDF p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Figure 1 gives the flow of the first search only; the December 2023 update, which supplied 12 of the 27 articles, has no flow numbers. No list of excluded studies.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 25 trials (27 articles) to December 2023, every trial reported health screening, checks for drug interactions and exclusion criteria, while reporting of other set-and-setting features varied: monitor training 52%, visual distractors 64%, pleasant environment 68%, advice on attitude 72%, monitor present 72%, therapeutic-alliance meeting 76%, sound control 76%, debriefing 76%, post-session meeting 80%, safe return home 80%, information on effects 84% (Table 2). The median trial reported 14 of 16 features; only 3 reported all 16. No included trial compared different sets or settings.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion, that differences in set and setting limit comparability and reproducibility and that harmonization would help, is supported. The discussion goes further: that therapeutic effects in trials with minimal set and setting "suggests that psychedelics have a therapeutic effect independently of the context" (PDF p. 17). The trials cited for this (three ayahuasca reports and two labelled DMT) are all open-label without a control group, were not appraised, and scored low on a measure of reporting rather than practice (the authors themselves think missing training information is a reporting omission, p. 17); no included trial varied context. The same paragraph then suggests that set and setting optimized for mystical-type experiences might give a better effect, which no included trial tested, and the Results state that a two-interview preparatory phase maximized the experience and the therapeutic effects in one trial (p. 8), although preparation was not varied there. The abstract's figures also differ from the Results (763 vs 761 participants; psilocybin 47%, against 16 of 25 trials).

timeline.event: Carhart-Harris et al., perspective on the importance of context: one of the publications used to predefine the review's domains (PDF p. 2).
Kaelen et al., 'The hidden therapist': cited in the discussion as a study specifically relating the subjective experience of music to the psychedelic experience (PDF p. 17).
Haijen et al., prospective study cited in the discussion as agreeing that emotional breakthrough and mystical experience predict lower depression scores (PDF p. 17).

Strickland et al.: randomized comparison of two music genres during psilocybin sessions in a smoking-cessation pilot (n = 10), a comparison of settings that falls outside this review's scope because addiction trials were excluded.

Golden et al., rapid scoping review of setting with wider designs (healthy volunteers, naturalistic and quasi-experimental studies): none of its 29 empirical studies overlaps with this review's (PDF p. 18).
Seybert et al., systematic review scoring psychedelic trials against the TIDieR reporting checklist, cited as using a similar method (PDF p. 18).

replication.where_it_stands: A systematic map of set-and-setting reporting in psychiatric trials of classic psychedelics to December 2023. It shows inconsistent reporting and no trial comparing settings; evidence that particular elements matter remains correlational within trials (therapeutic alliance in Murphy et al., 2022, and music in Kaelen et al., 2018, as the review cites them), plus one small randomized comparison of music genre in an addiction trial outside its scope (Strickland et al., 2021). Its participant total may count some ayahuasca participants more than once (see reporting issues).

funding.funder: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship and/or publication of the article (PDF p. 18).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest (PDF p. 18).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, CHU Nîmes and University of Montpellier; CH Thuir; Department of Biostatistics (BESPIM), CHU Nîmes; University of Santiago de Compostela; CIBERSAM, Madrid (PDF p. 1). None of the review's authors appears among the listed authors of the included trials in the reference list.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials that vary one element of set or setting at a time (for example music or none, one or two monitors, a decorated or a standard room, more or less preparation) under otherwise identical psychedelic treatment, with registered outcomes including difficult experiences; and a reporting standard for psychedelic trials (a TIDieR extension or a Delphi consensus, as the authors propose) so that reviews can compare what trials actually did.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with a psychiatric disorder, substance use disorders excluded), intervention (a classic psychedelic in a clinical trial) and outcome (16 set-and-setting sub-domains) are specified; no comparator is needed for the descriptive aim.
No protocol or registration is mentioned, and the sub-domains were refined during full-text reading (PDF p. 2).
Restriction to peer-reviewed clinical trials is explained (to prioritize robust designs), and its cost, the exclusion of more experimental designs, is acknowledged (PDF p. 18).

Two databases with the keywords given and reference lists searched, and the exclusion of grey literature is justified; but the English-or-French limit is not justified (1,282 records were dropped at the first step for lacking an English or French abstract), and there was no registry search or expert contact. A close call with partial yes, which requires justified publication restrictions.

Titles and abstracts of the first search were screened independently by two reviewers, but the update, which supplied 12 of the 27 articles, was screened by one reviewer and cross-checked by another (PDF pp. 2, 18).
Study characteristics were collected by one of two reviewers; who scored the 16 sub-domains, and whether the scoring was checked, is not stated (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons are counted in Figure 1 for the first search only; no list of excluded full texts.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, drug, dose, indication, sex split, design and sessions, adverse effects and main outcome for each trial, and Table 3 gives detailed set-and-setting practice.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of the trials; the 16-item score measures completeness of reporting, not bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No data synthesis was planned, given the descriptive aim (PDF p. 4).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion infers a therapeutic effect independent of context from five open-label, uncontrolled ayahuasca and DMT reports without considering their risk of bias (PDF p. 17).

Variation in practice, the review's outcome, is described and discussed (two approaches to the room, fewer monitors in recent trials, less developed set and setting in ayahuasca and DMT trials); no outcome results were synthesized, so there is no outcome heterogeneity to explain.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No conflicts and no funding declared (PDF p. 18).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 applies because this is a systematic review by design, although the tool was built for reviews of effects and this review maps reported practice. Five critical items are not met (no protocol, a restricted search, no list of excluded studies, no appraisal of the trials, risk of bias ignored when inferring an effect), which gives critically low confidence. Practically: the counts of what the 25 trials reported can be checked against Tables 2 and 3 (one column total is off by one) and can be cited as a description of these published trials and of how inconsistently set and setting are reported; they cannot be cited for what trials in general did, for whether any element of set or setting changes outcomes (no included trial compared settings and none was appraised), or for the authors' inference that psychedelics work independently of context.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 4,912 records from PubMed (3,045) and Web of Science (1,867) to 12 September 2022; after removing 1,282 without an English or French abstract, 3,322 on title and 71 duplicates, 237 abstracts were screened and 47 full texts assessed; 15 articles were included, and the December 2023 update added 12 (no flow numbers given), for 27 articles on 25 trials.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data source and research strategy (p. 2); Figure 1 (p. 3); Results › Study selection (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The database counts (3,045 and 1,867) and the exclusions by step (1,282, 3,322, 71) are printed only in Figure 1, an image without a text layer; read on the rendered page. The Results text gives 4,912, 4,675 removed, 237, 190, 32, 15 and 12.

key_findings.finding: The 25 trials: 13 randomized (6 against placebo, 2 against an active comparator or active placebo, 1 against a waiting list, 4 comparing doses) and 12 open-label; 16 psilocybin, 5 ayahuasca, 2 LSD and 2 labelled DMT; sizes 6 to 233, 761 participants; 12 in the USA only, all ayahuasca trials in Brazil; five trials reported at least one serious adverse event, from hypotension and bradycardia to suicidal ideation in 5 participants.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1 (pp. 5–6)
key_findings.note: One of the two trials labelled DMT (Reckweg et al., 2023) is a vaporized 5-MeO-DMT formulation according to its title in the reference list (p. 20). The abstract gives 763 participants.

key_findings.finding: Participants' drug histories in the trials: 13 trials excluded anyone with occasional or regular use of an illicit psychoactive substance other than alcohol, 7 excluded a history of alcohol dependence, the ayahuasca trials excluded previous ayahuasca use, two trials allowed no more than 10 previous hallucinogen experiences, and one (Moreno et al., 2006) required previous well-tolerated use of an indole psychedelic.
key_findings.locator: Results › Selection process for participants, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Trial rules before sessions, as listed: antidepressant and other psychotropic washout, most often at least 2 weeks before the first dose (13 trials); no cannabis for 24 h before each session (4 trials); alcohol and other psychoactive drugs strongly discouraged for 24 h before (3 trials); no food supplements in the preceding week (2 trials); no tyramine-rich food for 24 h before and 12 h after ayahuasca because of its monoamine-oxidase inhibitor content (1 trial); caffeine withheld for 24 h (1 trial) or taken as usual (2 trials); no nicotine from 2 h before until about 7 h after psilocybin (1 trial). None of these rules was evaluated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug interactions (one paragraph)
key_findings.note: The review lists the studies for each rule without counting them; the numbers of trials are the editors' tally of the studies it cites (the 13 for the 2-week washout counts Carhart-Harris et al., 2021, and Murphy et al., 2022, as one trial).

key_findings.finding: Preparation: information on effects was given in 21 trials and not mentioned in 4; in 19 trials clinicians met participants beforehand to build trust, in one to four meetings of about 2 h each on days other than the session (6–8 h in all in one trial); advice on attitude centred on openness and letting go; two trials (three articles) used a structured approach based on acceptance and commitment therapy; in 4 trials participants visited the session room beforehand.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pre-session interventions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The text lists three studies for the acceptance-and-commitment approach, but two of them (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021; Murphy et al., 2022) are articles on one trial. Gasser 2014 appears in both the one-interview and two-interview lists, so the per-number allocation is internally inconsistent; Table 3 describes two preparatory sessions.

key_findings.finding: Monitors: training was described in 13 trials (52%), often only as specific training; 12 trials kept two monitors in the room throughout and one had four; five trials published in 2023 used a single monitor per participant; some trials stressed male–female monitor pairs, while others rejected them.
key_findings.locator: Results › Monitor training and presence during the session, 2nd paragraph (p. 9); Table 2 (p. 10); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Environment and music, as the review describes them: trials either disguised the hospital room (living-room style, decorated, flowers or plants; sofa, recliner or bed) or left the hospital setting unchanged (4 trials); 11 trials asked participants to wear an eye mask throughout and 1 to close their eyes; the running text says 16 played a predefined playlist through headphones (Table 3 instead describes stereo speakers for Carhart-Harris 2016) and one alternated music and silence without headphones; two trials allowed no music (dos Santos et al., 2021, music and films not allowed; D'Souza et al., 2022, no music and no decoration). The authors judge the choice between disguising and decorating the room to have been made arbitrarily, without evidence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Session environment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 9); Table 3, dos Santos and D'Souza rows (p. 13); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Food on session days, as recorded in Table 3 and never evaluated: a light or low-fat breakfast or a light snack (Moreno 2006, Grob 2011, Griffiths 2016, Palhano-Fontes 2019, Davis 2021, Sloshower 2023); a light meal and fruit or light snacks available during the session (Goodwin 2022, Lewis 2023); a meal provided (Reckweg 2023, timing not stated) or a light meal that participants could share with therapists and, if appropriate, family at the end of the session (Aaronson 2023); and, in the anorexia nervosa trial, a standardized breakfast introduced partway through the study to avoid hypoglycaemia (Peck 2023).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Session protocol column

key_findings.finding: End of session: an end-of-session debrief in 9 trials according to the text (19 in Table 2); 24 h of in-hospital observation in 6 trials; 12 trials ensured that participants did not drive within 24 h (staying in hospital, a taxi, or collection by a relative or close person), and one required a phone call on arrival home.
key_findings.locator: Results › End-of-session procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Completeness: median 14 of 16 sub-domains reported (range 6 to 16), only 3 trials reported all 16, and reporting was least complete for monitor training (52%), control of visual distractors (64%) and a pleasant environment (68%); ayahuasca and DMT trials scored lowest (6 to 12 in Table 2).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 10); Results › Overall quality of description of set and setting domains and sub-domains in the studies (p. 16); Discussion, 7th paragraph (starts on p. 17; the passage on all 16 items is on p. 18)

key_findings.finding: The authors found no study comparing the efficacy of psychedelics in different sets and settings and state that it is unclear how important context is for a therapeutic effect.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 763 participants; the Results give 761, which matches the editors' sum of Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 761 (Results, Table 1).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says psilocybin was over-represented at 47%, but psilocybin trials are 16 of 25 (64%) and contribute 596 of 761 participants (78%; editors' arithmetic from Table 1); no basis for 47% is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite 47%; it may be a figure left from the first set of 15 articles, but the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the databases were searched until 12 December 2023, while the Methods give 12 September 2022 for the first search and 6 December 2023 for the update.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the Methods dates.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the column 'care to create a safe environment' has 21 ticks (all trials except Schneier 2023, Holze 2023, Goodwin 2023 and Reckweg 2023) but its total is printed as 20 (80%). The 25 row totals, which agree with their ticks, sum to 314, one more than the sum of the printed column totals (313).
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' count, confirmed on the rendered page and on the text layer: 21 of 25 (84%). The abstract's statement that a safe environment was consistently present rests on this column.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says an end-of-session debrief was organized in nine trials (p. 16), while Table 2 counts debriefing in 19 (76%) (p. 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two counts probably use different definitions (Table 2 may include discharge assessments), but the paper does not explain; cite either only with its definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that all studies were conducted in a hospital facility (p. 9), but Table 3 describes one trial in a room in a private practice office (Gasser et al., 2014, p. 11) and one in an outpatient office (Sloshower et al., 2023, p. 14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Not every included trial took place in a hospital.

reporting_issues.issue: Reckweg et al. (2023) is counted as a DMT trial (text and Table 1), but its title in the reference list describes a vaporized 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine formulation (GH001), that is 5-MeO-DMT.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only one trial (D'Souza et al., 2022) concerns DMT itself; the 5-MeO-DMT trial belongs to a different drug page.

reporting_issues.issue: Three ayahuasca reports use the same single-dose protocol in the same Brazilian inpatient setting: Osório et al. (2015, titled a preliminary report), Sanches et al. (2016) and Zeifman et al. (2021, titled results from an open-label trial); Zeifman's row has the same sex split as Sanches's (14 women, 3 men) and refers to Sanches for adverse effects. The review counts them as three trials and adds their participants, without saying whether they overlap, although it excluded 23 other articles for reporting an already included population.
reporting_issues.consequence: If the Osório and Zeifman samples are within Sanches's, up to 23 of the 761 participants are counted twice and the ayahuasca evidence comes from three trials, not five; not settled by the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion attributes both a survey of nearly 2000 people who had used psilocybin mushrooms (11% reporting that they had put themselves or others at significant physical risk) and an adverse event rate under 1% among 250 trial participants to the same reference, Carbonaro et al. (2016), which the reference list gives as a survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the trial figure cannot be identified from this review; do not cite it from here.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller text–table mismatches: the discussion says almost two-thirds of trials described post-session interviews (p. 18), but Table 2 gives 20 of 25 (80%); it says most trials insisted on male–female monitor pairs (p. 17), while the Results say monitor gender was only occasionally specified (p. 9); the text's list of 16 psilocybin trials names Lewis 2023a and 2023b separately and omits Aaronson 2023, which Table 1 lists as a psilocybin trial (p. 4); the text speaks of 27 included studies where it means articles (p. 4). The list labelled eight major-depressive-episode studies also includes Carhart-Harris 2021 and Murphy 2022 separately, although the review groups them as one trial (seven unique trials).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables, not the discussion's summaries, should be cited for counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The pre-session paragraph lists Gasser 2014 under both one and two preparatory interviews. It also mixes grouped articles and trials when listing interview numbers; Table 3 describes two preparatory sessions for Gasser.
reporting_issues.consequence: The allocation of trials by number of preparatory interviews cannot be taken as a consistent mutually exclusive count. No primary-trial schedule is corrected from the review alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name a reviewer for extracting study characteristics but do not state who scored the 16 set-and-setting sub-domains, whether that scoring was duplicated or checked, or how disagreements were handled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers can recount Table 2’s printed ticks; they cannot assess independent checking of the underlying coding or reconstruct it reliably without reviewing the 27 source articles and their supplements/protocols. This is a reporting limitation, not evidence that every score is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The running text says 16 studies played a predefined selection through headphones and includes Carhart-Harris 2016 in that list, whereas Table 3 describes that trial’s music as played through high-quality stereo speakers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the count as the review’s reported summary and retain the device inconsistency; the primary study would have to be checked to settle it. This does not resolve whether music changes outcomes.

design_detail: Record-linkage study of two Norwegian sources of drug deaths, notifications 2007–2009. Source 1: the Cause of Death Registry (CDR): physicians' death certificates coded in ICD-10, with drug-induced deaths selected by the EMCDDA definition (underlying cause F11–F12, F14–F16 or F19; or X41, X44 or Y11 with T43.6 as the first contributing cause; or X42, X44, Y12 or Y14 with any of T40.0–T40.9 as the first contributing cause; or the suicide codes X61 or X64 with T43.6, or X62 or X64 with T40.0–T40.9). Source 2: the police registry of drug deaths: unnatural deaths that physicians must notify to the police, investigated by local police, reported to the National Criminal Investigation Service and selected by local and central police as drug overdoses or drug deaths, without ICD codes and with drug information in one non-standardized spreadsheet column. Persons were matched on the national personal identification number, then manually (same date of death, sex, age, concordant cause and place of death) against CDR deaths with an F, X or Y underlying cause; 11 were matched manually. Four groups (police registry without a CDR match; police registry with a CDR cause outside the definition; both; CDR/EMCDDA only) were compared with chi-square tests, and CDR-only against both with logistic regression. Single author.
can_establish: How far Norway's Cause of Death Registry (under the EMCDDA definition) and the police registry counted the same people as drug deaths in 2007–2009, and how the people counted by only one source differed in age, sex, certified cause, first-listed drug, autopsy and place of death.
cannot_establish: Which source was right about any discordant death (no reference standard or case review); why deaths were missing from either source (the reasons offered are not measured); how many drug deaths both sources missed; or whether deaths in the 'morphine/codeine' group came from medicines rather than heroin certified as morphine.

sample.recruitment: Registers: notifications for 2007–2009 from the Norwegian Cause of Death Registry (EMCDDA definition) and from the police registry of drug deaths (pp. 75–76).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: CDR: Norwegian residents only, deaths meeting the EMCDDA definition, counted by year of death (delayed certificates are added later and are said to be few). Police registry: all unnatural deaths regardless of residency, selected by the police as drug deaths (p. 75).
sample.demographics: 929 persons: 725 men (78%) and 204 women (22%). Mean age 42.7 years (95% CI 41.4 to 44.0) in the CDR/EMCDDA-only group against 35.3 (34.3 to 36.2) in both registries (p. 76; Table 1, p. 77).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 33 police-registry persons could not be matched: 39% were not Norwegian citizens and the rest had missing or erroneous ID numbers.
sample.selection_effects: Two registers with different rules (residency, definition, who reports and selects), so non-overlap mixes differences in definition, reporting and investigation. Table 1 takes cause, drug and place of death from the CDR for matched persons; the police registry's own drug information is used only for the 33 unmatched (Table 1, footnotes a–c). National police figures were published only until 2009.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. CDR: physicians must issue a death certificate for the deaths they encounter; the CDR codes it in ICD-10, applying ICD-10 rules that can adjust the certificate's information, and the EMCDDA selection uses only the underlying and the first contributing cause (pp. 75, 77–78). Police registry: physicians must notify the police of unnatural deaths, including use or suspected use of narcotics; the police decide whether an autopsy is performed, generally when the cause is uncertain or unknown and the death sudden and unexpected, with no obligation when narcotics are suspected as the cause; local police investigate (previous knowledge of the person, evidence at the scene, witnesses, health and emergency personnel), add autopsy information if it is available before submission, and local and central police select the deaths they label drug overdoses or drug deaths (p. 75). What was tested: autopsy in 715 of 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths (Table 2), 431 of 455 in both registries and 284 of 367 CDR/EMCDDA-only (editors' sums from Table 1); toxicology coverage is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported; route of use is not recorded in either source as analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: One drug per person is analysed: the first contributing T-code in the CDR, or the first-mentioned drug in the police registry. The Discussion cites a Nordic study giving a median of 4–5 drugs per fatal poisoning, excluding alcohol (p. 78).

comparison.controls: The two registries compared with each other; neither is a reference standard, and the author states that neither should be considered the correct figure for drug deaths in Norway (p. 78).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (linkage on the personal identification number).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Prescriptions, route of use, treatment and service contact were not available.

outcomes.instruments: Group membership (Fig. 2, p. 76); characteristics by group with chi-square tests (Table 1, p. 77); adjusted odds ratios of being in the CDR/EMCDDA count only rather than in both, for 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths (Table 2, p. 78); a first comparison of all CDR/EMCDDA deaths with all police-registry deaths as differences in proportions with confidence intervals (p. 76); yearly counts 1996–2009 from a published source (Fig. 1, p. 75).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither registry is validated against toxicology or case review.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Drug-induced death': the EMCDDA code selection in the CDR. 'Drug death': the police selection. 'Type of drug': the first contributing T-code (CDR) or first-mentioned drug (police). 'Cause of death' groups: dependence, overdose, suicide, other (CDR underlying cause).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 11 chi-square tests in Table 1, 6 differences in the first comparison and one multivariable model; most p-values are below 0.001.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (register data).

analysis.effect_sizes: Overlap: 455 of 929 (49%) in both; 367 (40%) CDR/EMCDDA only; 74 (8%) in the police registry with a CDR cause outside the definition; 33 (4%) in the police registry without a CDR match. Editors' calculation: the police registry lacked 367 of 822 CDR/EMCDDA deaths (44.6%), and the CDR/EMCDDA count lacked 107 of 562 police-registry deaths (19.0%). CDR/EMCDDA-only against both: mean age 42.7 (41.4 to 44.0) against 35.3 (34.3 to 36.2); dependence or suicide as underlying cause 33% against 8%; heroin as first contributing drug 24% against 67%; among women, morphine/codeine 47% against 16%. Adjusted odds ratios of being CDR/EMCDDA-only rather than in both (n = 822): women 1.05 (0.68 to 1.61); under 25 0.35 (0.20 to 0.64), 25–39 0.65 (0.45 to 0.92), 60 and over 3.77 (0.99 to 14.3), against 40–59; suicide 1.9 (1.09 to 3.36) and dependence/other 10.6 (3.09 to 36.4), against overdose; morphine/codeine 6.89 (4.35 to 10.9), methadone 3.69 (2.29 to 5.96), synthetic opioids 4.63 (2.06 to 10.4), stimulants 2.36 (1.16 to 4.76), none or other codes 1.84 (0.71 to 4.73), against heroin; no autopsy 2.66 (1.42 to 4.98); hospital or other institution 2.61 (1.49 to 4.56), other place 1.02 (0.67 to 1.54), place not reported 0.55 (0.33 to 0.91), against home. First comparison, described as all CDR/EMCDDA against all police-registry deaths (the values reproduce with the 529 police-registry persons who have a CDR record; reporting issue 4), differences in proportion: male 0.014 (−0.014 to 0.041); dying at home 0.016 (−0.032 to 0.064); under 40 years 0.107 (printed CI 0.107 to 0.141); overdose 0.054 (0.032 to 0.076); heroin 0.109 (0.085 to 0.134); autopsy 0.051 (0.031 to 0.071).
analysis.covariates: Table 2 model: sex, age group, cause of death, type of drug, autopsy and place of death together; interaction terms with sex were tested and none was significant.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned; permissions came from the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics, the Office of the Public Prosecutor and the CDR in Statistics Norway (p. 76).
analysis.selective_reporting: The source of the police group's values in the first comparison is not stated; they reproduce from Table 1 only if the police group is the 529 police-registry persons with a CDR record, compared on CDR variables (editors' calculation; reporting issue 4).
analysis.power: Not reported; intervals are wide for small groups (30 persons aged 60 and over; 32 with synthetic opioids).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 929 people registered as drug deaths in Norway in 2007–2009 by the CDR under the EMCDDA definition (822) or by the police (562), 455 (49%) were in both; 367 (40%) were only in the CDR/EMCDDA count; 74 (8%) were in the police registry and in the CDR but with a cause outside the EMCDDA definition; 33 (4%) police-registry deaths had no CDR record (39% not Norwegian citizens, the rest with missing or erroneous ID numbers). Deaths found only in the CDR/EMCDDA count were older and more often certified as dependence or suicide, with morphine/codeine, methadone or synthetic opioids rather than heroin as the first contributing drug, without autopsy, and in hospitals or other institutions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The conclusion that prevention measures based on the two sources will differ is supported descriptively. (2) The Discussion's reasons for non-overlap (health personnel not reporting deaths to the police; the police not treating every drug death as suspicious; ICD-10 coding of certificates; more complete autopsy information in the CDR; different publication times) are proposed, not measured (pp. 76–78). (3) The morphine/codeine group is read as deaths from pharmaceuticals, especially among women and disability pensioners (p. 78); the paper does not consider that some deaths certified as morphine may be heroin deaths, the misclassification measured in Victoria by Stam et al. (2019; card sc_stam_2019), and it has no data on prescriptions, routes of use or service contact, on which its prevention remarks (switching from injecting to smoking, take-home naloxone, substitution treatment) depend. (4) The statement that the CDR figures are more complete rests on size and overlap, not on a reference standard; the author also says neither source gives the correct figure. (5) Figure 1's trends are called surprisingly similar up to 2009, although the police count is lower in every year and the gap is wider from 2002 onwards (read from the figure; values not printed).

timeline.event: Edland-Gryt (ed.), Alcohol and Drugs in Norway 2012 (Table 5.4): yearly CDR/EMCDDA and police counts for 1996–2009, the source of Fig. 1; the police count is lower in every year.
Simonsen et al. (as cited, p. 78): fatal poisonings among people who use drugs in the Nordic countries in 2012, with a median of 4–5 drugs per case excluding alcohol; not read for this card.

Amundsen (as cited, p. 78): people who died of drug-related causes by the CDR/EMCDDA definition fell into three equal-sized socioeconomic clusters (very low socioeconomic status, disability pensioners, people on the edge of the workforce); not read for this card.

Stam et al. (Victoria, 2012–2013; card sc_stam_2019): deaths certified as morphine, or in generic multi-drug terms, were a main source of heroin deaths missing from national coded counts, which bears on how this paper's morphine/codeine group can be read.

Fugelstad et al. (Sweden): mortality-register statistics, including the EUDA specification, compared with toxicology data; by its title, statistics based on death certificates miss one-third of cases. Listed for this page; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: The author knew of no similar linkage of a cause-of-death register with a police register. Other comparisons of register counts with fuller case information, in Victoria (card sc_stam_2019) and New Mexico (card sc_landen_2003), likewise find substantial disagreement in both directions, driven by definitions, certificate wording and reporting routes. A Swedish comparison of register data with toxicology (Fugelstad et al., 2020) is listed for this page but has not been read here.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: There are no conflicts of interest (as printed, p. 79).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health; most of the work was done at the Norwegian Institute of Alcohol and Drug Research, which merged with the Institute on 1 January 2016 (pp. 74, 78–79). what_would_settle_it: Linking both registries to forensic toxicology results for every death, with a blinded review of discordant cases (CDR/EMCDDA-only and police-only) by forensic pathologists, would show which deaths each source misses or wrongly includes and why; the same review of deaths certified as morphine or codeine would show how many were heroin deaths.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The national CDR (all certified deaths of residents) and the national police registry are the frames for drug deaths in Norway; the CDR excludes non-residents.
All notifications for 2007–2009 in both registers; no sampling.
929 persons; some groups are small (33 unmatched; 30 aged 60 and over in Table 2).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The groups are described by sex, age, cause, drug, autopsy and place of death, and both registration processes are described.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 929 persons appear in Table 1; the 33 unmatched have police data only, explained by non-citizenship or ID problems.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The CDR selection uses an explicit code list but only the first contributing cause; the police selection is unstandardized and undocumented; neither is checked against toxicology or case review.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Linkage on the personal identification number is reliable; police drug information is free text; the source of the police group's variables in the first comparison is not stated (they reproduce from Table 1 with the 529 police-registry persons who have a CDR record).

Chi-square tests and logistic regression suit the question, but the first comparison treats the two overlapping registries as independent samples, one interval has its lower limit equal to the estimate, one p-value does not match its chi-square, and Table 1 has sum errors.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Registers, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a linkage of two death registers (round brief, record-linkage studies). The overlap counts rest on reliable identifier linkage of complete national registers and are internally consistent; what the non-overlap means cannot be separated into definition, reporting and investigation, because the police selection is undocumented and no discordant case was reviewed, and the comparative statistics have several reporting errors. Citable for: in Norway in 2007–2009 only 49% of 929 people counted as drug deaths by either source were counted by both; 367 deaths in the CDR/EMCDDA count (44.6% of it) were absent from the police registry; these were older, more often certified as dependence or suicide, more often had opioids other than heroin as the first contributing drug, less often autopsied and more often died in institutions. Not citable for: which source is correct, why deaths were missing, or that the morphine/codeine deaths were from medicines.

Autopsy was more common in both registries, and death in a hospital or other institution more common in the CDR/EMCDDA-only group.

key_findings.finding: Who decides in Norway: physicians must issue death certificates, which go to the CDR (ICD-10 since 1996); physicians must also notify the police of unnatural deaths, including use or suspected use of narcotics; the police decide whether an autopsy is performed, generally when the cause is uncertain or unknown and the death sudden and unexpected, but with no obligation to order one when narcotics are suspected; local police investigate and report to the National Criminal Investigation Service, which published national figures until 2009.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: How the police registry is built: information from previous knowledge of the deceased, evidence found or seized at the scene and witnesses, with autopsy information added if completed and available before submission; drug information is not standardized (one spreadsheet column); local and central police select deaths, including narcotics in the EMCDDA definition, and label them drug overdoses or drug deaths; no ICD codes. The CDR registered only Norwegian residents; the police registered all unnatural deaths regardless of residency.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The EMCDDA definition applied to the CDR counts only the underlying cause and the first contributing cause of death, in fixed pairs: dependence codes F11–F12, F14–F16 or F19 as the underlying cause; accidental poisoning X41, X44 or Y11 as the underlying cause with T43.6 as the first contributing cause, or X42, X44, Y12 or Y14 with any of T40.0–T40.9; self-poisoning X61 or X64 with T43.6, or X62 or X64 with any of T40.0–T40.9. X41 is never paired with a T40 code, nor X42 with T43.6.

design_detail: Review article from the Netherlands Forensic Institute and the University of Groningen on post-mortem redistribution (PMR) of drugs, organized by study design: post-mortem administration to cadavers, animal experiments, repeated post-mortem sampling in human cases, ante-mortem against post-mortem comparisons, and single-time-point ratios (central/peripheral blood, liver/peripheral blood). The search is documented (PubMed and Embase, 18 April 2025, stated strings, dual screening of titles and abstracts, flow diagram): 87 publications were selected and grouped as category A (29, several post-mortem time points), B (7, ante-mortem against post-mortem) and C (51, single time point, several matrices; listed only in the online supplement), and further cross-referenced publications are used. There is no appraisal of the included studies, no presented systematic extraction of effect magnitudes or sample sizes, and the synthesis is narrative. Filed as a narrative review under the editors' checklist because it maps designs and findings without appraising them; it is not rated as a systematic review.
can_establish: Which designs have been used to study post-mortem redistribution and what each can and cannot show, and which findings the authors take as established as of April 2025: redistribution occurs for the compounds studied, starts within minutes in animals, affects cardiac blood earliest and femoral blood as well.
cannot_establish: How large post-mortem changes are for any drug or case (no magnitudes are extracted and the cited studies are not appraised), or whether the case variables it recommends predict redistribution (predictive accuracy is not presented; the proposal rests partly on their own unpresented studies and on associations reported second-hand from other groups).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Publications found in PubMed and Embase on 18 April 2025 and screened by two independent researchers; further cross-referenced and supporting publications were added without a stated method (p. 2, §2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded at screening: reviews; method validation and ex vivo studies; non-toxicology; post-mortem formation or degradation of compounds; case reports and case series of fewer than five subjects; studies that measured no peripheral blood (or blood of unknown origin) and sampled only once. Only femoral blood counted as peripheral blood. Excluded after full reading: non-English language, study design, missing information, bodily material, conference abstracts (p. 2, §2), and, per Fig. 1, quality (p. 3).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, English only, one search date. Case reports and small series were excluded at screening, yet several are cited for findings (for example in the repeated-sampling section, where 7 of the 12 references cited alongside the reported 17-hour mean interval (the underlying aggregation is not specified) are not in Table 1 although they used its repeated-sampling design; two are titled as reports of one or two cases, refs. 76 and 77, and a third, ref. 79, as a single fatal poisoning). The 51 category C publications are not discussed individually and are listed only in the unread supplement, so it cannot be checked which of the studies cited in §§5.3–6.2 were selected. Reviews were excluded, though several are cited (Ferner, Leikin and Watson, McIntyre).

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies: drugs placed in cadavers after death (mostly in the stomach, also trachea or epidural space), drugs given to animals before they were killed, and drugs taken in life by the people whose bodies were studied; concentrations measured in femoral and cardiac blood, lung and liver tissue and vitreous humour at one or more post-mortem times, and in ante-mortem hospital samples.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not extracted; animal doses, routes and survival times are mentioned only as study conditions (for example, 10 days of continuous subcutaneous infusion against a single acute dose of citalopram in rats).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, apart from one rat experiment co-administering nortriptyline with other drugs (p. 5).

comparison.controls: Within-body comparisons over post-mortem time; ante-mortem against post-mortem samples; cardiac against femoral blood (C/P ratio); liver against femoral blood (L/P ratio).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review stresses that dose, route, survival time after the dose, interval from death to sampling and the condition of the body are often unknown in human cases (pp. 5–6).

outcomes.instruments: Post-mortem change in drug concentration between sampling times or against ante-mortem values; C/P and L/P ratios.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors argue that a C/P ratio marks the occurrence but not the extent of redistribution, that a ratio of 1 does not exclude it, and that an L/P ratio says nothing about redistribution in a given case (pp. 6–7).
outcomes.operationalization: Redistribution is taken as a post-mortem change in concentration (a significant change between time points, a post-mortem value differing from the ante-mortem value, or a C/P ratio different from 1), separated as far as possible from post-mortem formation and degradation, which were excluded topics.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None extracted: findings of the cited studies are relayed as significant or non-significant increases or decreases without sizes, sample numbers or specimen details. The one summary figure is the interval from death to first sample in the subset of human repeated-sampling studies where it was available or estimated: mean 17 h, range 1–292 h, across 12 cited references, method of averaging not stated (p. 6). McIntyre's proposed L/P cut-offs (below 5, little or no redistribution; above 20–30, propensity for significant redistribution) are reported and criticized (p. 7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Magnitudes and sample sizes of the cited studies are not given; the category C publications are not discussed individually; the authors' own three C/P studies are summarized as supporting case-based interpretation without their results.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: From a documented two-database search (87 selected publications plus cross-referenced ones), the review reports, without effect sizes or appraisal: redistribution was seen for every compound studied by post-mortem administration to cadavers; in animals, cardiac blood concentrations rose within minutes of death, with lung reservoirs and rapid acidification of blood as proposed mechanisms; in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs (among them fentanyl and methadone) and fell for 6-MAM, risperidone, caffeine and THC; in studies with available or estimated timing, the first post-mortem sample was often taken many hours after death (mean 17 h, range 1–292 h); ante-mortem against post-mortem comparisons carry their own biases; and C/P and L/P ratios at a single time point cannot measure how much redistribution occurred in a case. Case-feature associations with C/P ratios are cited from the authors and other groups, without validated individual-case prediction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract introduces animal studies immediately before discussing early cardiac-blood rises, lung reservoirs and rapid acidification, so it does provide an animal-study cue; it does not separately qualify each mechanism sentence. The body states animal findings cannot easily be extrapolated to humans (p. 2). From cadaver studies the authors infer redistribution is likely for all compounds wherever a gradient exists, beyond the compounds tested. Redistribution before the first human sample is offered as a possible explanation for later absent changes, not demonstrated to have occurred in those cases (p. 6). Recommendations on case variables rest partly on their own three studies without presented results, but the review also cites other groups' C/P associations for methadone, THC and fentanyl. These associations do not establish how much post-mortem redistribution occurred in an individual case. The judgment that case information outweighs cognitive-bias risk is the authors' position, with no measured trade-off presented (p. 7).

timeline.event: Pounder and Jones call post-mortem redistribution a toxicological nightmare; Borra et al. say this still holds 35 years later (ref. 90, p. 7).
Leikin and Watson publish C/P ratios for several drugs, the data set later reanalysed by Ferner and by QSAR studies (ref. 92, p. 7).
Elliott: MDMA and MDA in ante-mortem and post-mortem samples after hospital admission, one of the 7 category B studies (Table 2, p. 4); also summarized by Milroy (2011).
Ferner finds no clear correlation between volume of distribution or lipophilicity and the C/P ratios in Leikin and Watson's data (ref. 91, p. 7).

McIntyre's review proposes the liver/peripheral blood ratio as a marker of redistribution (below 5 little, above 20–30 marked); Borra et al. judge it a marker of a drug's propensity at best (ref. 88, p. 7).

Mantinieks et al.: compilation of post-mortem to ante-mortem concentration ratios, a category B study cited for higher femoral than ante-mortem concentrations of several drugs and higher free morphine after death (Table 2, p. 4; p. 6).

The authors' own three studies (Kamphuis et al., 2021; Emaus et al., 2023; de Groot et al., 2023) relate case variables to C/P ratios of morphine, cocaine, amphetamines and benzodiazepines over ten years of forensic cases (refs. 95–97, p. 7); Tascon et al. (2023) report THC C/P ratios differing by state of decomposition (ref. 99).

replication.where_it_stands: That drug concentrations change after death, earliest and most in cardiac blood but also in femoral blood, is well documented; the review does not establish validated prediction of the size of change for an individual body from drug properties, case features or ratios at one time point, and human repeated-sampling studies are few and usually start many hours after death. Within this library, Launiainen and Ojanperä (2014) give all-cause post-mortem femoral distributions, and Ketola and Kriikku (2019, a meta-analysis of tissue-to-femoral-blood ratios for 50 drugs, per the reading list) address sampling site.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Three authors are at the Netherlands Forensic Institute (L.C.P. Borra, R. van der Hulst, I.J. Bosman), the others at University Medical Center Groningen and the University of Groningen (P.H. Elsinga, H.H. Boersma, D.J. Touw). Section 6.2 bases its proposed list partly on the authors' own three C/P-ratio studies, also citing other groups' associations (refs. 95–97). Received 17 July 2025, accepted 18 October 2025, online 22 October 2025.

what_would_settle_it: The study the authors themselves describe: repeated sampling of femoral and cardiac blood and other matrices in a large series of human bodies from soon after death, with recorded interval since death, temperature, decomposition, resuscitation, trauma, BMI and body position, and with preserved ante-mortem whole-blood samples where they exist, analysed within individuals so that the size of post-mortem change can be estimated for each drug and modelled against those variables.

domains.note: Search strings, date, databases, dual screening and a flow diagram are given, but only two databases and English only, the text and figure disagree on the number excluded, a quality exclusion appears only in the figure, and many cited studies come from outside the selection.

The limitations of each design are discussed carefully, and some specific flaws are named (grouped rather than paired samples in two studies; limited reporting of sample handling), but no study is appraised individually and no sizes are reported.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Most evidence is others', but the forward-looking recommendation (which case variables matter) rests partly on the authors' three C/P studies, cited without their results. Other groups' methadone, THC and fentanyl C/P associations are also cited; no predictive-performance comparison is presented.

The abstract gives an animal-study cue before mechanism sentences, but does not qualify each mechanism separately; universality across compounds is inferred, and case-information benefit outweighing cognitive-bias risk is an authors' judgment rather than a measured comparison.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how much and how predictably femoral blood concentrations change after death
domains.note: Earlier redistribution is offered as a possible explanation for absent later human changes, without a systematic summary of stable human femoral concentrations or effect magnitudes. Stable animal comparisons are acknowledged (for example femoral cocaine in pigs), so the review does not ignore all null findings.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The search is better documented than in most narrative reviews, and the design-by-design reasoning is careful, but the included studies are not appraised, their results are relayed without sizes, part of the evidence comes from outside the selection, and the recommendations rest partly on the authors' own unpresented work. Citable for: the designs used to study redistribution and their limitations; the authors' summary that redistribution occurs in both cardiac and femoral blood; the list of drugs with significant post-mortem rises or falls in femoral blood (as relayed); the interval from death to first sample where timing was available or estimated (mean 17 h, range 1–292 h); the limits of C/P and L/P ratios; the recommended blood-sampling practice. Not citable for: the size of post-mortem change for any drug; lung-reservoir and acidification mechanisms as established in humans; case variables as validated predictors.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that post-mortem drug concentrations do not necessarily reflect concentrations at the time of death, because of post-mortem redistribution and post-mortem degradation and formation of compounds, which makes interpretation a major challenge for forensic toxicologists.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed and Embase searched on 18 April 2025 with stated strings; 793 records screened on title and abstract by two independent researchers against stated exclusion criteria (reviews; method validation and ex vivo studies; non-toxicology; post-mortem formation or degradation; case reports and series under five subjects; single-time-point studies without peripheral blood); 104 read in full, 17 more discarded, 87 selected and grouped as category A (several post-mortem time points), B (ante-mortem against post-mortem) or C (single time point, several matrices including peripheral blood). Only femoral blood counted as peripheral blood. Cross-referenced and supporting publications were also used. The review describes a general consensus that femoral blood is preferred because it is less susceptible to redistribution than peripheral blood from other origins; this is relative susceptibility, not freedom from post-mortem change.
key_findings.locator: §2 Literature search and selection strategy, all paragraphs
key_findings.note: The text says 672 records were excluded at screening, which would leave 121, not 104 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Flow diagram: PubMed 524 and Embase 448 records; 793 after removing duplicates; excluded: reviews 114, method validation or ex vivo study 104, non-toxicology 219, post-mortem formation or degradation 19, case series under 5 subjects 143, no peripheral blood quantification and a single time point 90; 104 remaining; excluded for language, quality or conference abstract 17; 87 included: category A 29, B 7, C 51.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Values read from the rendered figure, which is an image (not in the PDF's text layer). The figure's exclusions sum to 689, consistent with 104 remaining.

key_findings.finding: Tables 1 and 2 list the 29 category A publications (1991–2025) and the 7 category B publications (1999–2021) by year, first author and title only, mixing animal experiments (rats, rabbits, dogs, pigs) with human case studies; the 51 category C publications are listed only in the online supplement.
key_findings.locator: §2, last paragraph (p. 2); Tables 1 and 2 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Studies placing drugs in cadavers show time-dependent diffusion from one high-concentration reservoir (usually the stomach) to nearby fluids and tissues, mainly the spleen and right liver lobe, with early rises in thoracic organs and cardiac blood possibly via the oesophagus or trachea after gastric reflux; human cadaver results generally agree with animal ones. Up to 48 h between administration and sampling sufficed for redistribution, which probably continues afterwards. Because every compound studied redistributed, the authors consider it likely for all compounds wherever a concentration gradient exists, with size, solubility, pKa and lipophilicity affecting direction and extent.
key_findings.locator: §3, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: All reviewed animal studies showed large variability between animals; samples were often taken from different animals at each time point (small fluid volumes, especially in rodents, and repeated sampling breaches the skin and may speed decomposition), and several studies may have been underpowered.
key_findings.locator: §4, 4th paragraph (starts p. 2, continues p. 4 after the figure page)

key_findings.finding: Early redistribution in animals: morphine in rat cardiac blood was significantly above ante-mortem blood 5 minutes after death; morphine in rabbit femoral blood rose immediately after death; citalopram in rat cardiac blood rose by 15 minutes. Blood pH fell significantly within 5 minutes of death and the morphine rise correlated with the pH fall; acidification seems to matter mainly for basic drugs (basic drugs rose considerably in rat cardiac blood, acidic drugs stayed near ante-mortem values). Lung concentrations of basic drugs fell as cardiac blood concentrations rose; removing the lungs reduced, and ligating the large vessels prevented, the cardiac-blood rise; THC rose in rabbit cardiac blood at 2 h while lung THC fell.
key_findings.locator: §4.1.1, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Later changes: a longer post-mortem interval goes with decomposition and easier diffusion, and forensic cases often have longer intervals than the animal studies; time-dependent changes were larger at room temperature than at 4 °C in several animal studies; microorganisms may lower concentrations by bacterial or fungal metabolism, or raise free morphine by hydrolysing morphine-3-glucuronide (free/total morphine rose throughout 96 h in rats), an effect not seen in two human morphine studies.
key_findings.locator: §4.1.2, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Incomplete absorption or distribution at death: in animals killed soon after dosing, residual reservoirs in the gut or peritoneal cavity fed post-mortem rises. After 10 days of continuous subcutaneous citalopram in rats, cardiac blood did not change significantly at 1, 3 and 24 h after death, whereas after a single acute dose, or an extra dose 3 h before death, it tended to rise with time; in pigs killed 5 minutes after a high intravenous cocaine dose, vitreous cocaine was below femoral blood at death and significantly higher 8 h later, while femoral blood did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: §4.2, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Recommended blood sampling: femoral blood from the femoral vein by targeted dissection at autopsy with a sterile syringe, preferably after clamping the vein above the draw site to prevent flux from the iliac vein; cardiac blood from the right atrium or inferior vena cava with the heart in situ; sodium fluoride tubes; storage at −20 °C with few freeze–thaw cycles. The publications reviewed often gave limited information on sample type, collection and storage.
key_findings.locator: §5, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 5) and 3rd paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Human bodies sampled more than once: large variability between drugs and between cases for the same drug. Significant post-mortem rises in femoral blood were reported for amisulpride, chlorpromazine, clozapine, fentanyl, fluoxetine, methadone, mirtazapine, olanzapine, promethazine, quetiapine, sertraline and zuclopenthixol; significant falls for 6-MAM, risperidone, 9-OH-risperidone, caffeine and THC. Where reported or estimated, the interval from death to the first sample averaged 17 h (range 1–292 h), so redistribution before the first sample may explain why some drugs showed no change between samples. Two studies grouped rather than paired cases across time points, which may have underestimated change.
key_findings.locator: §5.1, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Changes are relayed without sizes. A mean first-sampling interval of 17 hours (range 1–292) is reported alongside 12 citations, seven not in Table 1 and including case reports. The underlying interval values, weights and aggregation method are not supplied; this is not established as a pooled estimate from those papers and is not the separate THC study in reference 30.

key_findings.finding: Ante-mortem against post-mortem comparisons cannot separate post-mortem loss from elimination before death, nor attribute rises to redistribution when distribution was incomplete at ante-mortem sampling or drugs were given afterwards; hospital patients may differ from forensic cases (critical illness alters distribution); ante-mortem samples are often plasma or serum and need correcting for the blood/plasma ratio; tubes may lack fluoride or contain gels that absorb drugs. Femoral blood exceeded ante-mortem plasma or serum most often for antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, citalopram, sertraline, paroxetine, mirtazapine), and also for MDMA, MDA, atenolol, verapamil, THC, olanzapine, levetiracetam and metoclopramide; opioids varied in both directions, with significantly higher free morphine after death in two studies.
key_findings.locator: §5.2, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: A single post-mortem time point cannot separate ante-mortem distribution from redistribution. A C/P ratio different from 1 suggests redistribution only on the assumption that cardiac and femoral blood were equal at death; because femoral blood itself changes after death, the ratio marks occurrence rather than extent, and a ratio of 1 does not exclude redistribution.
key_findings.locator: §5.3, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Liver/peripheral blood ratio: McIntyre's proposed model (below 5, little or no redistribution; above 20–30, a propensity for significant redistribution) is judged of limited use, because high liver concentrations mostly reflect uptake before death and a drug's volume of distribution; at best the ratio indicates a drug's propensity and gives no information on redistribution in a particular case.

The authors conclude that the “toxicological nightmare” named 35 years ago still applies: the literature shows redistribution occurs, but evidence linking it to specific variables is often absent, so practical recommendations are difficult. Drug properties explain only part of it: Ferner found no clear correlation between volume of distribution or lipophilicity and the C/P ratios in Leikin and Watson's data, and QSAR studies suggest post-mortem ionization of basic drugs plays a role.
key_findings.locator: §6.1, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Citing their own three studies of C/P ratios (morphine; cocaine; amphetamines and benzodiazepines; ten years of forensic case data), the authors name trauma, attempted resuscitation, BMI, grade of decomposition at autopsy and body position at discovery as promising variables, without giving results; they propose repeated sampling of several matrices in human bodies with stratification by such variables and large samples, and recommend interpreting toxicology with case information, acknowledging a risk of cognitive bias that they judge outweighed by the benefit. The same section also cites other groups reporting significant C/P-ratio differences: methadone by BMI (ref. 98), THC by decomposition state (99) and fentanyl across several case-variable subgroups (100). These are reported associations with a single-time-point ratio, not a validated measure or predictor of the amount of redistribution.
key_findings.locator: §6.2, 1st paragraph; §6.3, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 lists quality among the reasons for the final 17 exclusions, but the text gives language, design, missing information, bodily material and conference abstract, and describes no quality criteria.

reporting_issues.issue: Much of the evidence cited appears to lie outside the 87 selected publications: of the 12 references behind the mean interval of 17 h from death to first sample, 7 are not in Table 1 although they used its repeated-sampling design, and refs. 76 and 77 are titled as reports of one or two cases, a category excluded at screening; the rat studies central to §4.1.1 (Sawyer et al., 1988; Nagasawa et al., 2016) are not in Tables 1–2 either. reporting_issues.consequence: The review's evidence base is not fully defined by its search; whether a given cited study met the criteria cannot be checked from the article.
