design_detail: Comparison of two English and Welsh sources for 2011–2022 without record linkage (privacy restrictions; called a triangulation approach). ONS: published counts of drug poisoning deaths, by date of occurrence (2024 release of 2023 registrations), in which a specific substance is named in a cause-of-death field, found by ONS natural language processing. NPSUM (National Programme on Substance Use Mortality, King's College London): voluntary coroner reports with the cause of death and the full toxicology report, in which the consulting toxicologist evaluates each detected substance's likely involvement. For each opioid and year, NPSUM opioid-related deaths reported by 1 August 2024 were coded as Code 1 (the opioid named as a cause) or Code 2 (an ambiguous drug-related cause, with the toxicologist implicating the opioid), and the ONS count was divided by the Code 1 share to estimate the total, with 95% confidence intervals from the Wilson score interval for that share. Opioids: heroin/morphine, methadone, tramadol, dihydrocodeine, fentanyl and codeine (paracetamol combinations excluded). Spearman correlations (12 yearly values) of the share missed and of the median number of drugs detected at post-mortem with year and with each other. Short report.
can_establish: What the ONS counts of deaths naming specific opioids would become if, in every year, ONS missed deaths with ambiguous certified causes in the same proportion as NPSUM's coroner-reported cases; how that proportion changed over 2011–2022; and how often NPSUM's opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected at post-mortem.
cannot_establish: The actual number of opioid-related deaths ONS missed (no linkage; the estimate rests on NPSUM cases representing all deaths, which was not tested, and NPSUM held only part of the deaths ONS counted); whether the implicated opioids caused the added deaths (they rest on the consulting toxicologist's judgment of likely involvement, not on the coroner's determination); whether polydrug use caused the ambiguous wording (a correlation between two 12-year trends); or any effect of the undercount on funding, policy or deaths; how many deaths ONS counted under an opioid that a toxicologist would not have implicated (the projection treats every death naming the opioid as correct and can only add deaths, so it measures undercounting only); or whether heroin deaths were recorded as morphine (ONS and the programme both count heroin and morphine as one category, heroin/morphine).

sample.recruitment: Registry data: ONS published counts, from all death registrations in England and Wales, and NPSUM, which receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales on deaths related to psychoactive drug use (Methods, p. 2; details in Supplementary Material 2, not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: NPSUM opioid-related death: an opioid cited as a cause of death by the coroner (by name, or with the generic terms 'opioid' or 'opiate'), or an ambiguous drug-related cause (e.g. multi-drug toxicity, polydrug use) with the consulting toxicologist implicating the opioid as causative; opioids identified by NPSUM's codes for substances with opioid-receptor agonist activity; deaths from paracetamol–opioid combinations (co-codamol, co-dydramol) excluded to mirror ONS codeine and dihydrocodeine figures; deaths occurring in 2011–2022 and reported by 1 August 2024 (p. 2). ONS: deaths related to drug poisoning naming the substance, by date of occurrence (p. 2); the ICD-10 definition behind the ONS counts is not restated.
sample.demographics: Not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Deaths occurring in 2011–2022 but reported to NPSUM after 1 August 2024 are not included; the effect on the most recent years is not discussed.
sample.selection_effects: NPSUM depends on voluntary reporting; the main text gives the share of coroners reporting (over 90%) but not the share of deaths. In 2011 NPSUM held 416 heroin/morphine deaths, 294 of them with heroin or morphine named as a cause, against 574 such deaths counted by ONS, so NPSUM held about half of the deaths ONS counted if the definitions match (editors' calculation). The authors note that some coroners routinely cite every implicated substance and others do not (p. 4), so the share of ambiguous wording among reporting coroners may not represent all coroners.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. The coroner determines the cause(s) of death after evaluating the available evidence (police records, emergency services, pathology, toxicology, GP summaries) (p. 2). ONS counts a death as related to a specific opioid only when the opioid is named in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest, identified by natural language processing; with ambiguous causes such as multi-drug toxicity or polydrug use, ONS cannot tell which substances were involved (pp. 1–2). NPSUM additionally counts a death with an ambiguous cause when the consulting toxicologist implicated the opioid as causative in the toxicology report (p. 2). What was tested: post-mortem toxicology, whose screens are not always comprehensive (p. 4); the share of deaths with toxicology and the panels used are not reported. How deaths certified with only 'opioid' or 'opiate' were coded for specific opioids (Code 1 or Code 2) is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: 96.8% (16,101 of 16,628) of the NPSUM opioid-related deaths had multiple drugs detected at post-mortem (p. 3). The median number of drugs detected per year appears only in Figure 1 (for heroin/morphine four in 2011 and six in 2022, abstract). Each opioid is reported separately and no all-opioid total is given; how deaths implicating several opioids were counted is not stated.

comparison.controls: ONS counts (named causes only) against NPSUM-based projections for the same years; individual deaths were not linked.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Differences between coroner areas in wording, toxicology practice and reporting to NPSUM were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Yearly ONS counts and estimated totals with 95% confidence intervals by opioid (Table 1); the share missed ('% underestimate', the share of the estimated total not counted by ONS); the median number of drugs detected at post-mortem (Figure 1); Spearman's ρ, labelled very strong (0.70 or more), strong (0.40–0.69), moderate (0.30–0.39), weak (0.20–0.29) or negligible (0.01–0.19).
outcomes.validity_norms: The projection was not validated against linked records.
outcomes.operationalization: Estimated total = ONS count ÷ (1 − NPSUM share of ambiguous-cause cases). '% underestimate' = (estimate − ONS count) ÷ estimate (2011 heroin/morphine: 239 of 813, 29%); relative to the ONS counts, the heroin/morphine estimates are 42% higher in 2011, 57% higher in 2022 and 51% higher over 2011–2022 (editors' calculation).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; no p-values are reported for the 18 Spearman correlations (six opioids, three correlations each), each based on 12 yearly values.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. NPSUM cases were coded by the programme, whose director is the corresponding author.

analysis.effect_sizes: Heroin/morphine: 2011 ONS 574, NPSUM 416 with 122 (29.3%) ambiguous, estimate 813 (95% CI 767–868), 239 additional (193–294); 2022 ONS 1,264, estimate 1,980 (1,894–2,074 in Table 1; 1,895–2,075 in the Results); 2011–2022 ONS 13,471, estimate 20,323 (Table 1 interval 19,382–21,358), 6,852 additional (Results interval 6,557–7,132), 34%. Totals for 2011–2022, ONS against estimate: methadone 5,752 against 9,444 (39%), tramadol 2,455 against 3,865 (36%), dihydrocodeine 1,201 against 1,854 (35%), codeine 1,886 against 2,859 (34%), fentanyl 599 against 887 (32%). Printed Spearman ρ, share missed with year: heroin/morphine 0.78, methadone 0.85, tramadol 0.74, dihydrocodeine 0.43, fentanyl 0.43, codeine 0.43; median drugs with year 0.90, 0.97, 0.97, 0.81, 0.87, 0.94; share missed with median drugs 0.81, 0.79, 0.78, 0.41, 0.33 and, for codeine, 0.59 described as a decrease. Editors' recomputation from Table 1 of ρ for share missed with year: 0.78, 0.85 and 0.74 as printed for heroin/morphine, methadone and tramadol; 0.41 for dihydrocodeine (0.34 to 0.55 allowing for rounding of the estimates); 0.33 for fentanyl (0.31 to 0.34); −0.47 for codeine. With 12 years, ρ of 0.43, 0.41 and 0.33 corresponds to two-sided p of about 0.16, 0.19 and 0.30 (editors' calculation, t approximation).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the study is stated to follow STROBE (Supplementary Material 1, not read); NPSUM was re-confirmed in August 2024 as not requiring research ethics review because all subjects are deceased (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: NPSUM yearly totals and Code 1/Code 2 counts are given only for heroin/morphine in 2011, so the projections cannot be re-derived for other years or opioids; the medians of drugs detected appear only in Figure 1; no sensitivity analysis of the representativeness assumption (for example by coroner area) is reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. Yearly fentanyl counts are small (22–80 ONS deaths), with wide intervals (2012: estimate 41, 28–83).

interpretation_gap.results_show: If ONS misses deaths with ambiguous causes in the same proportion as coroner-reported NPSUM cases, the 13,471 ONS deaths naming heroin or morphine in 2011–2022 correspond to about 20,323 (34% of the estimate missed), with similar shares for the other opioids. For heroin/morphine, methadone and tramadol the share missed rose over the period, as did the median number of drugs detected, and 96.8% of NPSUM opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected. The confidence intervals cover only the sampling variation of NPSUM's ambiguous share, not the assumption that NPSUM represents all deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says the data 'suggest' systematic underestimation, but the Conclusions say the study 'demonstrates' that ONS underestimated opioid-related deaths for over a decade, 'likely due to coroner reporting practices of polydrug deaths' (p. 5), on the basis of a correlation between two rising 12-year series; the Discussion itself lists other reasons for ambiguous wording (legal sensitivities, simplification for families, a focus on intent) (p. 3). The abstract's 'similar trends' for the other opioids does not hold for codeine, whose share missed fell (Table 1; Figure 1F), and the fentanyl and dihydrocodeine correlations would not be statistically significant (editors' calculation). The statements that the underestimate 'will have led to insufficient resource allocation' and delays in policy (p. 5) and that current resource allocation is almost certainly insufficient (p. 4) are not tested. The claim that the rise in tramadol deaths behind its 2014 scheduling occurred two years earlier (p. 4) is not visible in Table 1, whose estimates rise in the same year as the ONS counts (235 in 2012, 329 in 2013); the 2011 estimate (246) is close to the 2013 ONS count (254), a difference in level, not an earlier rise. The recommendation of drug checking and safe consumption rooms (p. 5) is outside the study's data. The 34% 'underestimate' is the share of the estimate that ONS did not count; relative to the ONS counts the estimate is about 51% higher.

timeline.event: Beynon et al. (card sc_beynon_2007): Liverpool deaths reported as drug-related to a coroner-fed national register (np-SAD) compared across that register's wider definition and narrower official definitions.

Fugelstad et al. (Sweden, online 2017; card sc_fugelstad_2020): death-by-death comparison of certificate-based and toxicology-based counts with an inventory; the certificate-based selection missed about a third of inventory deaths and included about as many deaths the inventory did not count.
Ruhm (card sc_ruhm_2018): US corrections for certificates naming no drug, resting on a similar assumption that deaths without a named drug resemble those with one.
Chief Coroner's Guidance No. 17 on short-form and narrative conclusions (Teague, 2021), cited for how ONS identifies opioid-related deaths from the Record of Inquest.

replication.where_it_stands: A single, unlinked projection by the programme that supplies the correction factor, co-authored by an ONS statistician. Its direction agrees with US studies of certificates naming no drug (cards sc_ruhm_2018, sc_buchanich_2018) and with ONS's own statement, as reported here, that its substance-specific counts are likely underestimates (p. 1). Its size depends on NPSUM's coverage and on whether reporting coroners word their conclusions like other coroners, which only a linkage of ONS and NPSUM records would test. The authors say work on other substances is under way (p. 5).

funding.funder: SC is supported by the China Scholarship Council (Funding, p. 5); no other funding is stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: DM works for the Office for National Statistics. CSC is Director of the National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (Declaration of competing interest, p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: King's College London, Institute of Pharmaceutical Science (Chen, Copeland); ONS Population Health Monitoring Group (Mais); National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (Copeland). The corresponding author directs the programme whose data provide the correction, and the paper calls for every coronial jurisdiction to report to NPSUM and for sustained NPSUM funding, which it says is not currently available (p. 5). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Record linkage of ONS death registrations with NPSUM case files, or a random sample of coroners' files with toxicology, for the same deaths, reporting for each opioid and year how many ONS deaths without the opioid named had it implicated by the toxicologist, together with NPSUM's coverage by coroner area; and a test of whether ambiguous wording rises with the number of drugs detected within coroner areas, not only across years.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The ONS frame covers all registered deaths, but the correction factor comes from voluntary NPSUM reports.

NPSUM cases are a non-random set of voluntary coroner reports whose coverage of deaths is not stated in the main text; for heroin/morphine in 2011 NPSUM held about half of the deaths ONS counted (editors' calculation).
16,628 NPSUM opioid-related deaths and 13,471 ONS heroin/morphine deaths; yearly fentanyl numbers are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Definitions and data sources are given; no demographics, and NPSUM's yearly totals are not given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: NPSUM denominators by year and opioid are not reported, and deaths reported after 1 August 2024 are missing for recent years.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Coroners' named causes are standard; the toxicologist's implication of an opioid in ambiguous cases is a reasoned judgment but not validated, and the coding of generic 'opiate' causes is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Coroners' wording varies, as the authors note, toxicology screens differ, and ONS's language processing and NPSUM's coding are different procedures applied to different sets of deaths.

The intervals ignore the main uncertainty (representativeness); the total intervals disagree between text and table; correlations are printed without signs, some contradict Table 1 and Figure 1, none has a p-value, and correlating two trending 12-year series is read as support for a mechanism.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Reporting to NPSUM is voluntary (over 90% of coroners); the share of deaths reported is not given in the main text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a comparison of two death registers (round brief, certificate studies). The ONS counts are a census of named causes, and the 96.8% of NPSUM opioid-related deaths with several drugs detected is a direct count. The estimates the paper is cited for, however, are projections that assume NPSUM's share of ambiguous-cause deaths applies to all deaths, without linkage, with intervals that exclude that assumption, and with correlation results that are partly irreproducible from the paper's own table; hence high. Citable for: ONS counts deaths as opioid-related only when an opioid is named on the Record of Inquest; in NPSUM's coroner-reported cases, about 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin/morphine deaths had ambiguous causes with the toxicologist implicating the opioid, so ONS opioid-specific counts are likely to be low; nearly all NPSUM opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected. Not citable for: the true number of opioid deaths in England and Wales (20,323 is a projection), polydrug use as the cause of ambiguous certification, or effects on policy or deaths.

key_findings.finding: ONS context cited by the authors (2023 registrations): 5,448 deaths from drug poisoning in England and Wales (0.94% of all deaths), of which 2,551 (46.8%) were opioid-related; age-standardised opioid-related deaths rose from 22.9 per million in 2012 to 43.8 in 2023.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: ONS counts a death as related to a specific opioid only when the opioid is named in a cause-of-death field on the Record of Inquest, using natural language processing; with ambiguous causes such as multi-drug toxicity or polydrug use it cannot determine the substances involved, and ONS acknowledges in its annual reports that its opioid and other substance-specific counts are therefore likely underestimated.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Office for national statistics data (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: NPSUM receives voluntary reports from over 90% of coroners in England and Wales on deaths related to psychoactive drug use, with the coroner's cause of death and the full toxicology report, in which the consulting toxicologist evaluates each detected substance's likely involvement; a death is opioid-related if the coroner cited an opioid (by name or as 'opioid' or 'opiate') or gave an ambiguous drug-related cause while the toxicologist implicated the opioid; paracetamol–opioid combinations were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › National programme on substance use mortality data, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Method: NPSUM deaths for each opioid and year (occurring 2011–2022, reported by 1 August 2024) were split into Code 1 (opioid named as a cause) and Code 2 (ambiguous cause, opioid implicated by the toxicologist), and ONS counts were divided by the Code 1 share (worked example: 123 of 183 named, 67%, so ONS counts are taken to represent 67% of deaths); 95% CIs by the Wilson score interval. Individual deaths could not be linked because of privacy restrictions.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Data analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine, 2011: ONS identified 574 deaths; NPSUM had 416, of which 122 (29.3%) had ambiguous causes; an estimated 239 additional deaths (95% CI 193–294) gives a total of 813 (767–868), a 29% underestimate. 2022: ONS 1,264, estimate 1,980 (95% CI 1,895–2,075), a 36% underestimate.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' check: a Wilson interval for 122/416 reproduces 767–868 and 193–294 exactly; 574 ÷ (1 − 122/416) gives 812, not 813. The abstract gives 765–866 for 2011, and Table 1 gives 1,894–2,074 for 2022 (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine, 2011–2022: ONS recorded 13,471 deaths; a further 6,852 (95% CI 6,557–7,132) were estimated not counted, giving 20,323, an overall underestimate of 34%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1; Discussion › Meaning of the study, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: 'Underestimate' is the share of the estimate that ONS did not count; relative to the ONS count the estimate is 51% higher (editors' calculation). Table 1's interval for the total (19,382–21,358) does not match the Results' interval for the additional deaths (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: Other opioids, 2011–2022 (ONS count against estimate, share missed): methadone 5,752 against 9,444 (39%), tramadol 2,455 against 3,865 (36%), dihydrocodeine 1,201 against 1,854 (35%), codeine 1,886 against 2,859 (34%), fentanyl 599 against 887 (32%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1, Total and % Underestimate columns (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Yearly share missed, first and last year (editors' calculation from Table 1): heroin/morphine 29.4% to 36.2%; methadone 25.7% to 47.0%; tramadol 32.9% to 44.2%; dihydrocodeine 18.4% to 39.6%; fentanyl 21.1% to 26.8% (13.9% to 46.3% between years); codeine 36.5% to 35.5%, with 49.1% in 2015 and 19.5% in 2021.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Figure 1 (p. 3)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation; Figure 1 plots the complementary share captured by ONS, and its codeine panel (F) shows that share rising over time.

key_findings.finding: Printed Spearman correlations: share missed with year, heroin/morphine 0.78, methadone 0.85, tramadol 0.74, dihydrocodeine 0.43, fentanyl 0.43, codeine 0.43; median number of drugs detected with year, 0.90, 0.97, 0.97, 0.81, 0.87 and 0.94; share missed with median drugs, described as a very strong inverse relationship for heroin/morphine (0.81), methadone (0.79) and tramadol (0.78), strong inverse for dihydrocodeine (0.41) and moderate inverse for fentanyl (0.33), while codeine's share missed decreased as the median rose (0.59).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 (p. 3)
key_findings.note: Signs are not printed, and several values or directions conflict with Table 1 and Figure 1 (reporting issues 1–3). Editors' recomputation from Table 1 and the medians read from Figure 1 reproduces all six median-with-year values and the five 'inverse' values in size (all positive), but gives −0.47 (codeine) and 0.33 (fentanyl) for the share missed with year.

key_findings.finding: 96.8% of the NPSUM opioid-related deaths in the study (16,101 of 16,628) had multiple drugs detected at post-mortem toxicology; for heroin/morphine the median number of drugs detected was four in 2011 and six in 2022.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 3); Abstract (p. 1); Figure 1A (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Reasons the authors give for ambiguous wording: increasing polydrug use (their hypothesis), and also legal sensitivities in deaths involving specific prescription drugs, simplification for bereaved families and the public, and, in intentional or undetermined deaths, a focus on intent or mental health rather than pharmacology.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Principle findings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the figures are estimates because the datasets could not be linked and because the share of NPSUM deaths with ambiguous causes is assumed to represent all drug deaths, which coroners' differing practices could bias; toxicology screens are not always comprehensive, so polydrug use and the median number of drugs may be underestimated.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of this and other studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: coroners should list every drug implicated, so that ONS processing recognises each substance; every coronial jurisdiction should report to NPSUM, which would need sustained funding that is not currently available; adopting ICD-11, with more detailed drug-poisoning codes, could improve ONS data.
key_findings.locator: Future work, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Correlation coefficients are printed without signs, and the relationships between the share missed and the median number of drugs detected are called inverse for heroin/morphine, methadone, tramadol, dihydrocodeine and fentanyl, although the share missed and the median both rose. Recomputed from Table 1 and the yearly medians read from Figure 1, these five coefficients reproduce the printed sizes and are all positive (0.81, 0.79, 0.78, 0.39 and 0.33), while codeine's is negative (−0.59, printed 0.59) (editors' calculation; the medians read from the figure also reproduce every printed correlation of the median with year).
reporting_issues.consequence: For five opioids the relationship is positive (more drugs detected, larger share missed), as the abstract implies; the word inverse in the Results should be disregarded and only codeine's relationship read as negative.

reporting_issues.issue: The coefficients printed for the share missed over time do not all fit Table 1: recomputed from it, codeine's is −0.47 (the share missed fell, as Figure 1F shows), not 0.43 within 'increased rates of these underestimations', and fentanyl's is 0.33 (0.31 to 0.34 allowing for rounding of the estimates), not 0.43 (editors' calculation). As printed, the codeine coefficients cannot all hold: if both the share missed and the median rose over time (0.43 and 0.94), their correlation with each other could not be −0.59 (editors' check: the matrix is not a valid correlation matrix).
reporting_issues.consequence: Codeine does not show the rising undercount the abstract attributes to 'similar trends'; cite Table 1's yearly counts rather than the printed coefficients for codeine and fentanyl.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the correlations were computed to see if there were any significant relationships, but no p-values or intervals are given; with 12 years, coefficients of 0.43, 0.41 and 0.33 correspond to two-sided p of about 0.16, 0.19 and 0.30 (editors' calculation), yet they are labelled strong or moderate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the heroin/morphine, methadone and tramadol trends are clearly distinguishable from chance; correlations between two series that both trend over time do not show that one drives the other.

reporting_issues.issue: Intervals for the same estimate differ between places: 2011 heroin/morphine 765–866 in the abstract against 767–868 in the Results and Table 1 (the latter reproduces as a Wilson interval for 122/416, editors' check); 2022, 1,894–2,074 in the abstract and Table 1 against 1,895–2,075 in the Results. The 2011 point estimate (813) is 812 when recomputed from 574 and 122/416 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: For heroin/morphine over 2011–2022, the Results give 6,852 additional deaths with a 95% CI of 6,557–7,132, implying a total of 20,028–20,603, while Table 1 gives 20,323 (19,382–21,358). The Table 1 limits equal the sums of the yearly limits (with 2015's upper limit taken as about 1,803; issue 6) (editors' check), an interval that assumes all yearly errors move together.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two different intervals are given for the same quantity, and neither reflects the main uncertainty (whether NPSUM cases are representative); present 20,323 as a projection without a precise interval.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the 2015 heroin/morphine interval as 1,657–2,803 around an estimate of 1,727, an upper limit far out of line with the other years; about 1,803 makes the yearly upper limits add up to the printed total's 21,358 (editors' check). The 2020 methadone interval is printed as '(; 1128–1290)'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical errors; the 2015 upper limit should be read as about 1,803.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the median number of 'co-administered' drugs, while the Methods measure drugs detected at post-mortem.
reporting_issues.consequence: Detection does not show that the drugs were taken together; describe the figure as drugs detected.

design_detail: Position paper of the National Association of Medical Examiners (NAME) Expert Panel on Evaluating and Reporting Opioid and Other Drug Deaths, published as a Review Article in the American Journal of Forensic Medicine and Pathology (received 4 March, accepted 7 March 2020). It updates the 2014 NAME and American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) position paper on opioid deaths, which had sunset under NAME policy; the CDC financially supported the earlier panel and supported this update. It answers six questions: which deaths need jurisdiction and autopsy; what scene investigation is needed; when to perform toxicology; how to collect specimens and what to test for; how post-mortem concentrations bear on certification; and how to certify cause, manner, how and where the injury occurred. No search, selection criteria, appraisal or grading of evidence is described; 53 references. Who wrote it (p. 152): 16 named authors and panel members (9 MD, 5 PhD, 2 BS), from pathology departments (University of Alabama at Birmingham, University of Washington, Wake Forest School of Medicine), medical examiner offices (Jefferson County, Alabama, for the first author; Cuyahoga, Broward, Hennepin, Dane and Clackamas counties; the Armed Forces Medical Examiner System), two coroner's offices (Boulder County, Colorado; Montgomery County, Ohio), forensic toxicology or laboratory organizations (Department of Forensic Genetics and Forensic Toxicology, National Board of Forensic Medicine, Sweden; NMS Labs; RTI International's Laboratory Quality Assurance and Proficiency Program), emergency medicine and medical toxicology (Rutgers New Jersey Medical School) and the American Medical Association's science and drug policy unit. Filed as a narrative review with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs for position papers of professional bodies.
can_establish: What the NAME expert panel recommended in 2020 for investigating, testing, interpreting and certifying suspected drug deaths in the United States, and the reasons and citations it gave, citable as the panel's position.
cannot_establish: How accurate certification is with or without autopsy, toxicology or these practices, how often deaths are wrongly put down to drugs or missed, or whether following the recommendations improves the counts: no data are analysed, no evidence is graded, and the paper's claim that its 2014 predecessor improved certificate specificity rests on a before–after trend.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (position paper). NAME convened the panel with the CDC's support to review the 2014 paper, the literature published since, and the changing nature of drug deaths (p. 152, Introduction 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or selection criteria; the 53 references were chosen by the panel. The panel followed the same process as the 2014 panel (NAME position-paper guidelines, reference 3), which this paper does not describe.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Practitioners of death investigation and toxicology, plus emergency medicine and medical toxicology and one AMA staff member; no member is listed from a vital-statistics agency or public health surveillance programme, and none as representing people who use drugs (five people are thanked for technical support, without affiliations, p. 158). The cited evidence on autopsy accuracy comes largely from general autopsy-discrepancy studies, some decades old.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The paper's guidance on who decides: the medical examiner or coroner assumes jurisdiction and determines cause and manner; consultation with a forensic pathologist or toxicologist is advised for difficult interpretation (p. 156, Cause of death 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Guidance when several drugs are found: list by generic name every drug judged to have caused or contributed to death, at concentrations sufficient to do so; do not list drugs judged to have played no role; in an example with eight substances detected (alprazolam, 6-acetylmorphine, morphine, codeine, hydrocodone, ethanol, acetaminophen, diphenhydramine) the parent drug heroin is certified rather than its metabolites (pp. 156–157, Cause of death 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Evidence cited for the main recommendations: autopsy-discrepancy and external-examination studies (references 6, 8–15), post-mortem CT studies (16–19), toxicology screening (29–31), specimen handling (23, 35–37), interpretation of concentrations (38–47) and certification guidance from NCHS and CDC (49, 52).
outcomes.operationalization: The panel's working definitions: autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause of death, except delayed deaths due to overdose or suspected overdose, with review from hospital admission to death; toxicology for every decedent meeting any of eight circumstances; a drug is listed when present at a concentration sufficient to have caused or contributed to death in the circumstances; manner 'accident' for misuse without apparent intent of self-harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis. Figures quoted from cited sources: certificate specificity for drugs causing overdose deaths rose from 75% (2012) to 88% (2017) (reference 2, p. 152); overdose deaths 47,055 in 2014 and 70,237 in 2017, with provisional 2018 data 4% below 2017 and 44% above 2014 (references 4 and 5, p. 152); diagnoses in error compared with autopsy in up to 20% to 30% of cases (references 6 and 8–13, p. 153); routine post-mortem CT in an Australian office cut its autopsy rate from 62% to 47% (reference 18, p. 153); in heroin and methadone deaths, the triad of cerebral oedema, pulmonary oedema and bladder distension on CT was 100% specific but 26% sensitive for opioid intoxication (reference 19, p. 153); NAME's standard of at most 250 autopsies per pathologist per year (reference 7, p. 153).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Position paper; the panel's process (NAME position-paper guidelines) is referenced but not described.
analysis.selective_reporting: Evidence is cited for some recommendations and not others; the 20% to 30% error range is supported by general autopsy studies and by a mortality data brief, not by studies of suspected overdose deaths; no study is cited on how accurate the circumstantial rules for attributing deaths to depressants or stimulants are. The preceding autopsy paragraph also cites a drug-toxicity study (reference 15), without a numerical result, for the comparison with external examination.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A practitioners' consensus: autopsy for suspected overdose deaths (with post-mortem CT judged experimental), comprehensive toxicology with blood from the iliofemoral vein preferred and urine and vitreous retained, generic drug names on certificates and amendment once toxicology is interpreted, 'accident' as the usual manner, and caution in reading post-mortem concentrations. The evidence behind it is cited, not appraised.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and introduction call the recommendations evidence-based and “the best evidence-based practices at this time” (p. 152), but no search, appraisal or grading is described, and several recommendations rest on experience (protection of responders, p. 154) or on circumstantial rules (p. 156). The introduction says the 2014 paper accomplished its goal, shown by specificity rising from 75% to 88% after its publication (p. 152): a before–after trend with no comparison. The 20% to 30% error range (p. 153) comes from general autopsy-discrepancy studies (from 1912, 1979, 1980, 1987, 1993 and 2003) and a mortality data brief, not from suspected overdose deaths. The Summary's statement that using the recommendations will improve detection and reporting of opioid-related deaths (p. 157) is a prediction.

timeline.event: First NAME and ACMT panel, supported by the CDC; its paper appeared in Academic Forensic Pathology (2013) and was republished in the Journal of Medical Toxicology (2014) (reference 1, p. 152).
SAMHSA consensus panel's uniform standards and case definitions for opioid-related deaths (not cited by this paper; card sc_goldberger_2013).
Warner and Hedegaard: specificity of drugs on overdose death certificates rose from 75% in 2012 to 88% in 2017 (reference 2, as cited, p. 152).
NCHS reference guide for completing death certificates for drug toxicity deaths (reference 52).
This position paper.

Hancock et al. cite this paper as current NAME best practice and find, at one North Carolina centre, 265 of 2,719 suspected drug deaths (9.75%) with a non-drug final cause after full autopsy, a category whose definition includes negative toxicology, with its components not counted separately (card sc_hancock_2024, this reader).
Smiley-McDonald et al.: in the 2018 census, 11.2% of US offices reported no access to toxicology, and 14.1% were NAME-accredited (card sc_smiley_mcdonald_2025, this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: The professional position cited by later studies on the project's list (Hancock 2024 and Smiley-McDonald 2025). Its autopsy recommendation cites both general discrepancy studies and a drug-toxicity study (Dye 2019, reference 15), alongside the panel's assessment that equivalence of external examination has not been shown. The quoted 20–30% range itself is not a drug-death-specific error rate. Hancock's selected regional series later reports 265 of 2,719 suspected deaths with a non-drug final classification after autopsy; that mixed category does not directly measure how often external examination plus toxicology would misattribute death. The office census describes reported resource and testing access, not verified testing for every death.

funding.funder: No separate funding statement. The text says the CDC provided financial support for the 2013 panel to meet, and that NAME convened this panel with the CDC's support (p. 152).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (p. 152, first-page footnote).
funding.affiliations_note: Two panel members are at laboratory organizations (NMS Labs, Horsham, Pennsylvania; RTI International's Laboratory Quality Assurance and Proficiency Program), and the paper recommends comprehensive toxicology for broad groups of deaths. The first author is an author of three cited works (references 1, 29 and 46). A panel member, Jerri L. McLemore (Department of Pathology, Wake Forest School of Medicine), has the same name and institution as the second author of Hancock et al. (2024). Acknowledged for technical support: Bruce A. Goldberger, Nicole Jones, Margaret Warner, Julie K. O'Donnell and Denise McNally (p. 158). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A multi-office study of suspected overdose deaths in which a certifier records a cause of death from investigation, external examination, toxicology and, where available, post-mortem CT before the autopsy, without seeing its findings, against an independent panel's cause after full autopsy; and an evaluation, against comparison jurisdictions, of whether adopting these recommendations changes the specificity and accuracy of drug-death counts.

domains.note: No search, dates or selection criteria; the panel chose the 53 references, and its process is only referenced (NAME guidelines), not described.
No appraisal or grading; the 20% to 30% error range cites general autopsy-discrepancy studies and a mortality data brief; the circumstantial attribution rules cite one source each.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 53 references include the first author (the 2014 paper and two studies); the main arguments rest on others' work.

Recommendations are not marked as resting on evidence or on judgment; the effect of the 2014 paper is asserted from a trend; responder-safety advice rests on ACMT members' experience; the Summary predicts improvement. Uncertainties are acknowledged elsewhere (no simple way to tell lethal from sublethal concentrations; redistribution unpredictable; tolerance unmeasurable; post-mortem CT experimental).

domains.domain: Balance of attention to deaths wrongly put down to drugs and drug deaths missed
domains.note: Both directions appear: autopsy to find other causes, warnings that a concentration in a published lethal range does not by itself make a drug the cause and that drugs that played no role should not be listed. But the practical rules lean toward attribution when drugs are present (depressants with drowsiness or snoring; stimulants with agitation or sudden collapse; analogues presumed to act like their parents), with no guidance on recording uncertainty about a drug's contribution and no data on how often either error occurs. Wrong attribution to drugs is the under-represented side.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a position paper; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, as the round brief directs, and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domains (search and appraisal, both high). The paper can be cited, attributed to the NAME expert panel, for its recommendations: autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause (except delayed deaths due to overdose or suspected overdose, with review of the hospital course); toxicology for decedents meeting any of eight circumstances; retention of blood, urine and vitreous, with iliofemoral blood preferred and the sampling site labelled; a comprehensive panel reviewed periodically; listing by generic name every drug judged to have caused or contributed, avoiding 'mixed drug intoxication'; amending certificates once toxicology is interpreted; 'accident' for misuse without apparent intent of self-harm; and for its statements of the limits of post-mortem levels (lethal ranges, redistribution, tolerance, dose cannot be back-calculated). It cannot be cited for any error rate, for the effect of the 2014 paper, for the accuracy of its circumstantial attribution rules, or for the safety advice to responders as an established finding.

key_findings.finding: The six recommendations: (1) autopsy gives the best information for interpreting toxicology, circumstances, history and scene, and the panel considers it essential in apparent overdose deaths; (2) scene investigation includes reconciling prescriptions and medication counts and noting paraphernalia or other evidence of intoxicating substances; (3) retain blood, urine and vitreous humour whenever available, with iliofemoral blood preferred to more central sites; (4) a comprehensive toxicology panel including potent depressants, stimulants and antidepressants, with special testing for novel substances present in the community; (5) when death is attributed to a drug or drugs, as cause or contributing factor, list them by generic name in the autopsy report and death certificate; (6) the best manner for an overdose without any apparent intent of self-harm is 'accident'.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, recommendations 1–6

key_findings.finding: History: NAME and ACMT published a joint position paper on opioid deaths in 2014, after a CDC-supported panel of pathologists and toxicologists worked through 2013; that paper sunset under NAME policy, and NAME, with the CDC's support, convened a new panel that followed the same process and answered six questions.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The panel states that the 2014 paper accomplished its goal, shown by certificate specificity for drugs causing overdose deaths rising from 75% in 2012 to 88% in 2017, an improvement that led the CDC to support the update.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: A before–after trend with no comparison; the paper presents no evidence that the 2014 paper caused the change.

key_findings.finding: The panel recommends that a medical examiner or coroner assume jurisdiction and perform, or cause to be performed, an autopsy whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause of death; it states that no peer-reviewed article has shown external examination with strong evidence of illicit drug use to be as accurate as autopsy, and that diagnoses are in error, compared with autopsy, in up to 20% to 30% of cases.
key_findings.locator: Question 1 (which deaths require jurisdiction and autopsy), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The 20% to 30% range cites references 6 and 8–13: general autopsy-discrepancy studies and a mortality data brief, not studies of suspected overdose deaths. Separately, the preceding paragraph cites Dye et al. 2019 (reference 15) for the external-examination comparison in suspected drug toxicity, without a numerical effect. The autopsy recommendation therefore does not rest only on the general discrepancy studies.

key_findings.finding: Post-mortem CT: routine CT as part of preliminary case evaluation in an Australian office cut its autopsy rate from 62% to 47%; in heroin and methadone deaths, cerebral oedema, pulmonary oedema and bladder distension together were 100% specific but only 26% sensitive for opioid intoxication; given few studies, the panel considers post-mortem CT experimental and not ready for routine use in suspected overdose deaths.
key_findings.locator: Question 1, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: As cited (references 18 and 19).

key_findings.finding: Workload: NAME's standard allows at most 250 autopsies per pathologist per year; the panel strongly recommends that offices receive enough funding and staff to autopsy suspected overdose deaths within that standard. NAME's standards allow autopsy to be deferred in delayed deaths after overdose (hospital admission before death), with review of the medical record and any admission blood or urine.
key_findings.locator: Question 1, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Toxicology: history, investigation and autopsy together are an insensitive indicator of drug intoxication; urine screening kits give incomplete evidence, are subject to false positives and are inadequate for establishing a cause of death. The panel recommends toxicology to identify and quantify controlled and illicit substances, and relevant novel drugs, in all decedents with any of: known history of prescription or illicit drug use; evidence of drug use at the scene; autopsy findings suggesting drug use; massive lung oedema and froth with no other explanation; suspected drug smuggling; no unequivocal cause at autopsy; a potential natural cause where a drug may also have contributed; or traumatic deaths.
key_findings.locator: Question 3 (when to perform toxicology), 1st paragraph and list items 1–8

key_findings.finding: Specimens: delay to autopsy, sampling technique and preservation contribute more to inaccuracy than the testing procedures; blood, urine and vitreous should be collected whenever available, with bile and gastric contents also relevant; because of post-mortem redistribution the iliofemoral vein is the best blood source, followed by subclavian, heart or aorta, or any intact vessel, with blood from a body cavity a last resort; each specimen is labelled with its anatomical source and kept at 4°C, blood in fluoride-oxalate (grey-top) tubes.
key_findings.locator: Question 4 (specimen collection and scope), 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Scope: an adequate opioid panel includes buprenorphine (norbuprenorphine), codeine, fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, loperamide, methadone, 6-acetylmorphine, morphine, oxycodone, oxymorphone, tapentadol and tramadol; a full panel adds benzodiazepines, antidepressants, muscle relaxants, sleep aids, ethanol, pain-adjunct medicines, stimulants and prevalent new psychoactive drugs; offices should review the panel's scope periodically.
key_findings.locator: Question 4, 5th to 7th paragraphs and lists

key_findings.finding: Interpreting post-mortem concentrations: they must be read with the circumstances, history, scene and autopsy; published tables of toxicology results are often based on a few cases with little context; a drug can cause death below a reported lethal range, and a concentration within it does not necessarily make the drug the cause; post-mortem concentrations should not be used to calculate the amount taken; redistribution is unpredictable in size and direction and may not occur in every case, but should not be an excuse to avoid deciding; tolerance accounts for part of the overlap between therapeutic and lethal concentrations, and there is no reliable quantitative measure of tolerance before or after death.
key_findings.locator: Question 5 (interpretation of post-mortem concentrations), 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Heroin: the panel treats 6-acetylmorphine in a sample as “sufficient evidence to ascribe intoxication to heroin”; without it, a blood morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 may be considered evidence of heroin use, especially with paraphernalia at the scene. Solid-tissue concentrations are often uninterpretable beyond showing exposure.
key_findings.locator: Question 5, 6th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The 6-acetylmorphine sentence has no attached citation in this paragraph. The following morphine-to-codeine discussion cites references 44–46: their titles describe empirical work in impaired drivers, heroin-related poisoning deaths and heroin toxicity without detected 6-AM. These sources were not read for this card-only adjudication, so their methods or rule accuracy are not appraised here.

key_findings.finding: Certification wording: complete the certificate with the most specific details available and amend it when toxicology results are known and interpreted (filing is sometimes required before they are); list the generic names of all drugs judged to have caused or contributed; avoid 'mixed drug intoxication' or 'polypharmacy' without naming drugs; list the parent drug rather than metabolites; the order of drugs matters little; do not record drugs that played no role, and do not list every detected substance under other significant conditions.
key_findings.locator: Question 6, 1st paragraph (p. 156); Cause of death, 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs (pp. 156–157); Other significant conditions (p. 157)

key_findings.finding: Circumstantial rules for attributing a role: if the decedent seemed drowsy, hard to wake or snored loudly, any central nervous system depressants present were likely to have played a role; if the decedent seemed unusually frantic, complained of burning up, or entered a frenzied state with unusual strength, any stimulants present were likely to have played a role and should be listed as causing death; contraction band necrosis also suggests a stimulant role; cocaine, amphetamines and methadone should be considered as causes when present and the history is of sudden collapse; structurally similar new compounds may be presumed to act like their better-studied parents.
key_findings.locator: Cause of death, 3rd to 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Each rule cites a single source (references 20, 50, 22, 51); no study of their accuracy is cited.

key_findings.finding: Manner of death: suicide requires indication of intent of self-harm, and taking opioids in excess for self-treatment or for their effects is not by itself suicide; assigning 'undetermined' routinely does not serve public health; deaths from misuse of opioids without apparent intent of self-harm should be classed 'accident', with 'undetermined' reserved for rare cases with evidence for more than one manner; 'homicide' should be reserved for intentional exposure to sedate or kill a specific person, not used to help a legal case.
key_findings.locator: Manner of death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: How and where injury occurred: health departments hope for the decedent's relevant medical history, route of administration, source of the drug and formulation (Table 2), without personal identifiers; when the place of use is unknown, the place where the person became unresponsive or was found dead is entered.
key_findings.locator: How injury occurred; Where injury occurred; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Scene safety: the panel says fear that responders could be overcome by touching or inhaling potent opioids such as carfentanil has proved more theoretical than practical, citing ACMT members' emergency experience; nitrile gloves and N95 respirators are described as sufficient protection.
key_findings.locator: Question 2 (scene investigation), 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Experience-based, not a study finding; ACMT's own position statement is cited (reference 27).

key_findings.finding: The panel says its recommendations are based on the best evidence in the medical literature at the time of review and that using them will improve the detection and reporting of opioid-related deaths.
key_findings.locator: Summary

reporting_issues.issue: The 20% to 30% error range for diagnoses made without autopsy is supported by references 6 and 8–13, of which reference 8 is an NCHS data brief on overdose death counts and references 9–11 are general clinical autopsy-discrepancy studies (1912, 1979, 1993).
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be cited as an error rate for drug deaths certified without autopsy.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper presents the rise in certificate specificity from 75% (2012) to 88% (2017) as showing that the 2014 paper accomplished its goal.
reporting_issues.consequence: A causal claim from an uncontrolled trend; the rise cannot be attributed to the paper from this evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The recommendations are described as evidence-based throughout, but no method (search, selection, appraisal, grading, consensus procedure or external review) is described; the panel refers to itself as the 2019 position paper panel (p. 154) in a paper received on 4 March and accepted on 7 March 2020 (p. 152).
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of each recommendation cannot be judged from the paper; they should be cited as the panel's judgment.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction says the joint NAME and ACMT paper was published in 2014, while reference 1 gives Academic Forensic Pathology 2013 with a 2014 republication in the Journal of Medical Toxicology.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the earlier paper exists in two versions.
