design_detail: Swedish record-linkage comparison of drug-related deaths (DRDs) in five datasets, matched death by death on the personal identification number. Three come from the national mortality register (NMR), which is built from the mandatory death certificate: NMR/Sweden (a Swedish specification: any listed drug-related ICD code anywhere on the certificate, underlying or contributory cause; 1994–2012, N = 7,497), its Stockholm-area subset NMR/Stockholm (1985–1996, N = 1,181), and NMR/EMCDDA (the European specification: a listed code as the underlying cause only, from a shorter list; 1997–2012, N = 3,908). The fourth, Toxreg, is built from forensic toxicology alone: deaths in which an illegal drug, or methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl, was found at forensic examination, whatever the certified cause; ages 10–60, or any age if morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine were both found (1994–2012; N = 6,648 in Table I, 6,448 in the text and Figure 2). The reference standard is an inventory of DRDs in the Stockholm area in 1985–1996 (1,061 forensic cases and 151 hospital cases, N = 1,212), each death assessed individually. NMR/Stockholm (12 years) and Toxreg (1994–1996 only) were matched to the inventory, and NMR deaths missing from it were classified by the authors from the certificate. For 1994–2012 the national datasets were compared only with each other (overlap, size, age, sex, annual counts and, by Toxreg's main drug, capture by NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA), without a reference standard.
can_establish: How far, in the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, a certificate-based ICD-code selection and (for 1994–1996) a forensic-toxicology register agreed death by death with an inventory of individually assessed drug-related deaths, in both directions (inventory deaths missing from each source, and deaths in each source that the inventory did not count), and how much three Swedish national selections overlapped and differed in size, age, sex and main drug in 1994–2012.
cannot_establish: How accurate Swedish certificate-based or toxicology-based counts were after 1996 (nothing later was compared with a reference), how accurate the EMCDDA selection is (it was never compared with the inventory), whether the drugs counted in Toxreg caused the deaths (Toxreg counts presence), or anything about other countries; and because the reference inventory counted deaths of people with a personal history of drug use as drug-related whatever the cause, as the paper describes it, the deaths 'missed' by the registers are not all missed drug poisonings.

sample.recruitment: Registers and an inventory; no recruitment. NMR: the causes of death on death certificates, which Swedish law makes mandatory for all deaths, entered into the national mortality register kept by the National Board of Health and Welfare, with attrition of about 1% (p. 2 of the online-first PDF). Toxreg: forensic toxicology results in the registers of the National Board of Forensic Medicine (pp. 3, 7). Inventory: begun as an attempt to estimate the true number of HIV-related deaths in the Stockholm area, first including all known cases of 'lethal injection' and then expanded to all decedents with a personal history of drug use problems (the paper's term is drug abuse) or with illegal drugs present at death; its main sources were examination records of the Stockholm forensic institute and medical records of HIV-related hospital deaths (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: NMR/Sweden and NMR/Stockholm: any code in Table II anywhere on the certificate (ICD-9 for 1994–1996: 292, 304.0–304.9, 305.2–305.3, 305.5–305.7, 305.9, 965.0, 968.5, 969.6, 969.7; ICD-10 from 1997: F11–F16, F18, F19, O35.5, P04.4, T40.0–T40.9, T43.6, Z50.3, Z71.5, Z72.2). NMR/EMCDDA: underlying cause only and a shorter list, without F13, F18, O35.5, P04.4, T40.4 or the Z codes (Table II, p. 4). Table II lists no external-cause codes, and the paper does not say how intent was handled. Toxreg: an illegal drug or methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl found at forensic toxicology, ages 10–60 (any age with morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine), whatever the certified cause (p. 3). Inventory: deaths involving illegal drugs or non-prescribed morphine or methadone, and deaths of people with a personal history of drug use problems; deaths involving prescribed methadone or morphine, including suicide with morphine prescribed for pain, were not counted (p. 3).
sample.demographics: 1997–2012: NMR/Sweden mean age 43 years, 24.4% women; NMR/EMCDDA mean age 40, 16.1% women; Toxreg mean age 37, 16.5% women (p. 5). No demographics are given for the Stockholm inventory or for the deaths each source missed.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registers). NMR attrition about 1% (p. 2); the cause-of-death register covers more than 99% of deaths and the forensic database more than 90% of non-natural deaths below age 65 (p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: The validation rests on one region in 1985–1996, when many deaths of people who used drugs were HIV-related; the authors note fewer HIV deaths, more hepatitis C, older ages, more chronic drug-related organ damage and more prescription-opioid use today (p. 7). Toxreg could be validated only for 1994–1996, cannot capture deaths that were not forensically examined (the hospital cases, 151 in the whole 1985–1996 inventory; how many fell in 1994–1996 is not given) and excludes ages over 60 unless morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine were both found. The periods compared differ: NMR/Stockholm against 12 years of the inventory, Toxreg against 3. Stockholm residents who died elsewhere were outside the inventory's reach (21 of the 30 drug-related NMR deaths it missed).

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. NMR: a physician completes the mandatory death certificate; the National Board of Health and Welfare registers it, and the causes are ICD-coded by the statistical office (pp. 2, 7–8). A death enters NMR/Sweden if any listed code appears anywhere on the certificate, and NMR/EMCDDA only if the underlying cause is a listed code (pp. 2–3; Table II). Toxreg: forensic toxicology alone, the presence of an illegal drug or of methadone, buprenorphine or fentanyl, regardless of the certified cause (p. 3). Inventory: each death was assessed individually as due to drug use or not; who assessed is not stated, and the inventory's sources are described with reference to the first author's 1997 doctoral thesis (ref 20) (p. 3). NMR deaths absent from the inventory were classified by the authors from the causes on the certificate (pp. 3–4). What was tested: 1,061 of the 1,212 inventory deaths (87.5%, editors' calculation) were forensic cases, and 10% of these had a history of drug use but no positive toxicology (p. 5); the toxicology panel, specimens and the share of deaths tested outside the inventory are not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. 'Injection deaths' (accidents or suicides) are mentioned as a manner-of-death group without definition (p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Toxreg and the inventory count each death once, under a main drug chosen by a priority order based on relative toxicity in Nordic drug deaths: heroin or morphine, methadone, buprenorphine, fentanyl, amphetamine, cocaine, other drugs, THC (the inventory without buprenorphine and fentanyl, absent in 1985–1996); other drugs, pharmaceuticals and alcohol are recorded in Toxreg but not analysed (p. 3). The NMR selections count a death once if any listed code appears; the codes do not separate illegal from other drugs, and T40.4 covers drugs as different as buprenorphine, dextropropoxyphene, fentanyl, pethidine and tramadol (p. 7).

comparison.controls: Reference standard: the 1985–1996 Stockholm inventory, for NMR/Stockholm (1985–1996) and Toxreg (1994–1996). For 1997–2012 the national selections are compared only with each other, without a reference.
comparison.matching: Deaths linked one to one on the Swedish personal identification number (pp. 3–4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Why the certificate-based selection missed inventory deaths was not examined death by death, except for the hospital deaths; the inventory's own accuracy and the reliability of its individual assessments are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Share of inventory deaths found in each dataset; deaths in each dataset absent from the inventory, with reasons; values labelled sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value with 95% confidence intervals (p. 5); overlap counts (Figure 2), annual counts (Figure 1), mean age and share of women (p. 5), and the share of Toxreg deaths, by main drug, found in NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA (Table III).
outcomes.validity_norms: The reference inventory is not validated, and its definition of a drug-related death is broader than either register specification: deaths of people with a personal history of drug use problems counted whatever the stated cause (p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Captured = the inventory death appears in the dataset under its ICD-code or toxicology rule. Not drug-related = a dataset death absent from the inventory, unless the authors judged it drug-related from its certificate (pp. 3–4). The paper labels as sensitivity the share of each dataset's deaths that were in the inventory, and as positive predictive value the share of inventory deaths found in the dataset: the reverse of the usual definitions with the inventory as the reference (reporting issue 1).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive proportions with confidence intervals; trends compared by eye (Figure 1), without statistics.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The authors classified the unmatched NMR deaths themselves; the reference inventory is described with the first author's doctoral thesis (ref 20) and Toxreg's method was developed in connection with it (ref 18).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive inventory membership, not validated causal attribution. Stockholm 1985–1996: 761 of 1,212 inventory deaths in NMR/Stockholm (62.8%; 451 absent, editors’ subtraction); 734 of 1,061 forensic cases. The printed hospital share is 28%, but 761−734=27 and 27/151=17.9%, so these statements conflict. NMR includes 419 deaths absent from the inventory; 30 are confirmed inventory omissions. The remaining 389 are not a validated count of falsely attributed drug deaths: only 49 and 7 are separately described, leaving 333 unclassified in the report. The printed NMR total 1,181 differs from 761+419=1,180. With inventory membership as reference, 761/1,212=62.8% is capture and 761/1,180=64.5% is positive predictive value, reversing the paper’s labels. Toxreg 1994–1996: the paper reports 317 of 454 inventory deaths, then calls 317 the Toxreg total and says 43 of those were outside the inventory. That contradiction leaves the overlap/total unresolved; 317/(317+43)=88.1% is only one conditional reconstruction, not verified capture. Its printed interval 84.3–81.2 is internally impossible. National 1994–2012: 4,238 deaths in both NMR/Sweden and Toxreg, 2,210 in Toxreg only (34%), 3,259 in NMR/Sweden only (43%); NMR/EMCDDA and Toxreg shared 2,840 (editors' calculation), with 3,608 in Toxreg only and 1,068 in NMR/EMCDDA only. Table III capture of Toxreg deaths by main drug, NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA: heroin 96% and 90%, THC 23% and 9%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The study is covered by an approval of the Stockholm Regional Ethics Review Board (p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Several breakdowns are not shown, including hospital capture and the reasons for unmatched records. Of 419 NMR records absent from the inventory, 30 are confirmed inventory omissions and only 49 plus 7 others are described; the remaining 333 lack reported classification. They are not thereby validated non-drug deaths. No NMR comparison restricted to 1994–1996 is reported, specificity denominators are absent, and the Toxreg overlap and total are internally contradictory.
analysis.power: Not applicable (complete registers and an exhaustive inventory).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The Stockholm inventory includes deaths of people with a history of drug-use problems regardless of acute poisoning, including 151 hospital deaths mainly related to HIV. NMR held 761 of its 1,212 deaths and 419 absent records; 30 of the latter were confirmed inventory omissions, but most remaining records were not classified individually in the report. Similar totals therefore do not validate causal accuracy. Toxreg’s claimed 317-of-454 overlap conflicts with a later statement that 43 of 317 Toxreg cases were outside the inventory. Nationally, certificate and toxicology selections shared 4,238 of 9,707 deaths in 1994–2012 and differed in age, sex and main drug.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title's 'miss one-third' is arithmetically supported (37% of inventory deaths not captured) but needs three qualifications the abstract does not give: the reference inventory counted deaths of people with a personal history of drug use as drug-related (p. 3), including 151 hospital deaths that were mainly HIV-related, so the missed deaths are not all missed drug poisonings; the selection also held 419 deaths absent from the inventory, but incomplete classification prevents treating all remaining unmatched deaths as false causal attributions; and the figures come from one region in 1985–1996. The Discussion's statement that one-third of certificates for inventory deaths 'did not mention drugs' (p. 7) is an inference, because the missed deaths' certificates were not examined. The Conclusions' 'statistics based on forensic toxicology were more complete' (p. 9) compares 3 years (Toxreg) with 12 (NMR), and the Results pair it with mislabelled statistics, including a Toxreg sensitivity of 88.1% that fits 317/(317+43) only under an assumption contradicted by the stated total of 317. 'DRDs due to poisoning were captured well in all three datasets' (p. 9) has no figure behind it, and NMR/EMCDDA was never compared with the inventory. The conclusion that time trends were 'remarkably consistent' (p. 9) and can be compared between countries rests on visual inspection of Swedish series whose ratios changed over time; no other country was analysed.

timeline.event: Fugelstad, doctoral thesis on drug-related deaths in Stockholm 1985–1994 (ref 20), with which the paper describes the reference inventory's sources.

Eksborg and Rajs (Substance Use & Misuse; ref 18): causes and manners of death in relation to post-mortem tests for illegal drugs; the paper says Toxreg's method was developed in connection with the Stockholm inventory, citing this work.
EMCDDA standard protocol version 3.2 for the drug-related deaths key indicator (ref 10), the source of the European specification used for NMR/EMCDDA.

Amundsen (International Journal of Drug Policy): linkage of Norway's Cause of Death and Police Registries for 2007–2009, reporting lack of overlap between the two sources (by its listed title; read by another reader in this round).

Ruhm (card sc_ruhm_2018) and Buchanich et al. (card sc_buchanich_2018): US national corrections for overdose certificates naming no drug, a different source of undercounting, estimated by assumption rather than linkage.

Chen et al. (card sc_chen_2025): England and Wales, national counts naming specific opioids against projections from coroner-reported cases with toxicology, without linkage; undercounting only is examined.

replication.where_it_stands: The Stockholm validation has not been repeated; the authors describe it as still the only study of its type in the Stockholm area (p. 2). The US and English studies read for this round (cards sc_buchanich_2018, sc_horon_2018, sc_ruhm_2018, sc_chen_2025) estimate undercounting of specific drugs from a second source, a protocol or an assumption, not from an individually assessed inventory, and none measures over-inclusion. The 'one-third missed' applies to Stockholm in 1985–1996 and to an inventory that counted deaths of people with a history of drug use whatever the cause; in the same data the certificate and inventory totals were similar, which does not validate causal attribution. It should not be carried to Sweden today, where the authors expect more chronic and older drug-related deaths (p. 7), or to other countries.

funding.funder: None: the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of the article (Funding, p. 9 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship or publication of the article (Declaration of conflicting interests, p. 9 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Karolinska Institute, Department of Clinical Neuroscience (Fugelstad, Ramstedt); Uppsala University, Section for Forensic Medicine (Thiblin) and Section for Social Medicine (Johansson). The reference inventory is described with the first author's 1997 doctoral thesis (ref 20), the 2016 report cited for Toxreg's coverage is by the first author (ref 14), and Toxreg's method was developed in connection with the inventory (ref 18), so the authors evaluate datasets partly built on their own earlier work; the fourth author's thesis concerns errors in death certificates (ref 6). Flags for closer reading, not reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A new validation in a recent period: all deaths, or a random sample, in one or more regions (including people who died without forensic examination), each assessed by reviewers blind to the register outcome against written definitions that separate drug poisonings from other deaths of people who use drugs, then matched to the certificate-based (Swedish and EMCDDA) and toxicology-based selections, reporting both directions with correctly labelled sensitivity and positive predictive value; ideally repeated in a country with fewer forensic examinations.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Mandatory death certificates and the forensic registers are the right frames, but the validation covers one region in 1985–1996 (Toxreg only 1994–1996), while the headline is applied to national and international statistics of other periods.
An exhaustive inventory and complete register extracts, linked by personal identification number; no sampling.
1,212 inventory deaths (454 in 1994–1996) and 9,707 national deaths.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Datasets and the code lists from 1994 are described; the codes used for 1985–1993, the toxicology panel, who assessed the inventory deaths and how, and the inventory's demographics are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All linked records are counted, but the reasons for about 333 of the 389 remaining unmatched certificate-selection deaths (not all independently classified as non-drug deaths), and for the missed inventory deaths other than hospital cases, are not examined; key breakdowns are 'data not shown'.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The reference inventory assessed each death individually, but it is not validated and its definition counts deaths of people with a personal history of drug use whatever the cause, so 'missed' mixes missed poisonings with deaths the register specifications were not designed to count; Toxreg counts presence, not cause.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Who assessed the inventory deaths, against which written criteria and with what agreement is not reported; the unmatched certificate deaths were classified by the authors, unblinded and without a second reader.

Sensitivity and positive predictive value are interchanged, one interval is impossible and two are narrower than their counts allow, several totals disagree between table, text and figure, the specificity denominators are not given, and trends are compared only by eye.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents; register attrition is about 1%.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The existing high JBI-prevalence judgment is retained. This is a regional inventory/register comparison with different definitions and periods, not an independent validation of causal drug deaths. NMR’s 761/1,212 inventory capture is reproducible, but the hospital percentage, total and summary labels conflict. Most of 389 remaining unmatched NMR records are not individually classified, and Toxreg’s 317-overlap/317-total statements conflict. National overlap 4,238/9,707 is descriptive. Cite those definitions and contradictions; do not cite 88.1% as validated toxicology capture, unmatched records as proven causal false positives, or one-third as today’s missed poisonings in Sweden or elsewhere.

key_findings.finding: In the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, the certificate-based selection (NMR/Stockholm) contained 761 of the 1,212 deaths in the reference inventory (63%). The paper prints sensitivity 64.5% (95% CI 61.7–67.2), specificity 99.9 (95% CI 99.90–99.92) and positive predictive value 62.8 (95% CI 60.4–65.1). By editors' calculation, 451 inventory deaths (37%) were not in NMR/Stockholm.
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Table I (p. 3) for the period
key_findings.note: The labels are interchanged (reporting issue 1): 761/1,212 = 62.8% is the share of inventory deaths captured, and 64.5% fits 761 of the 1,180 NMR/Stockholm deaths (761 matched plus 419 unmatched), the share of certificate-selected deaths that were in the inventory; its printed interval reproduces exactly (editors' calculation). The specificity denominator is not given.

key_findings.finding: Of the 1,061 forensically examined inventory deaths, 734 (69%) were in NMR/Stockholm; by main drug, capture was highest for heroin (80%) and lowest for cocaine (13%), and 81% of 'injection deaths' (accidents or suicides) were captured. Of the 151 hospital deaths in the inventory (described as mainly HIV-positive people who used drugs) only 28% were in NMR/Stockholm, the most important under-coverage (breakdowns: data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: 761 captured overall minus 734 forensic cases leaves 27 hospital deaths (17.9% of 151), not 28% (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: In the other direction, NMR/Stockholm contained 419 deaths absent from the inventory. Judged by the authors from the causes on the certificates, only 30 were drug-related deaths: 21 Stockholm residents who died elsewhere and were not examined at the Stockholm forensic department, and 9 missed for administrative reasons such as forensic records lent or mislaid. Of the remainder, 49 were suicidal bathtub drownings after ingestion of various pharmaceuticals or deaths related to alcohol or pharmaceuticals rather than illegal drugs, and in 7 no cause of death had been found (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors’ subtraction: 419−30=389 remaining unmatched records and 389−49−7=333 without reported classification. These are not validated false drug-death attributions. The NMR and inventory totals are similar, but the printed NMR total 1,181 differs by one from 761+419=1,180.

key_findings.finding: Toxreg’s 1994–1996 paragraph first reports 317 of 454 inventory deaths included, then describes 43 of 317 Toxreg cases as outside the inventory because findings reflected medical treatment. Those statements do not define a consistent overlap and total. Printed statistics are sensitivity 88.1% (95% CI 84.3–81.2), specificity 99.7 (99.6–99.8) and positive predictive value 69.8 (66.1–73.3).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: 317/454=69.8% follows the first overlap statement. 317/(317+43)=88.1% would be a positive predictive value only if 317 were overlap and 43 additional cases; the later stated total of 317 contradicts that assumption. Keep the ambiguity rather than selecting a corrected total or validated capture rate.

key_findings.finding: Toxreg cannot capture inventory deaths with a history of drug use but no positive toxicology, which made up 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases, nor hospital deaths that were not forensically examined; the paper says Toxreg did not capture 'the 151 hospital cases in the inventory' (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › NMR/Stockholm and Toxreg datasets: Agreement with Stockholm inventory, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: NMR is compared over 1985–1996 and Toxreg over 1994–1996. The 151 hospital deaths belong to the longer inventory, and their number in the shorter period is not supplied. The conditional subtraction 454−317=137 relies on the first Toxreg overlap statement; the conflicting later total prevents treating it as a resolved capture estimate.

key_findings.finding: National datasets: NMR/Sweden had 6,591 drug-related deaths in 1997–2012, mean age 43 years, 24.4% women; NMR/EMCDDA 3,908, mean age 40, 16.1% women; Toxreg 6,448, mean age 37, 16.5% women.
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 2 labels Toxreg's 6,448 as the 1994–2012 total (Table I gives 6,648), so the Toxreg figures may cover a longer period than the other two (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: NMR/Sweden and Toxreg, 1994–2012: 4,238 deaths were in both, 2,210 in Toxreg only (34% of Toxreg's 6,448) and 3,259 in NMR/Sweden only (43% of its 7,497); 9,707 deaths were in either.
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: The counts are printed inside Figure 2, an image without a text layer (the text gives only the 34% and 43%); checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: NMR/EMCDDA and Toxreg: 3,608 Toxreg deaths were not in NMR/EMCDDA and 1,068 NMR/EMCDDA deaths were not in Toxreg; by editors' calculation 2,840 were in both (3,908 − 1,068 = 6,448 − 3,608).
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 3rd paragraph (continued on p. 6)
key_findings.note: 2,840 equals the sum of Table III's NMR/EMCDDA column (editors' sum). NMR/EMCDDA starts in 1997 while the 6,448 Toxreg deaths include 1994–1996 (Figure 2), so part of the 3,608 could never be in NMR/EMCDDA (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Share of Toxreg deaths, by Toxreg's main drug, also present in NMR/Sweden and in NMR/EMCDDA: heroin (819 deaths) 96% and 90%; morphine (1,495) 73% and 60%; methadone (688) 79% and 66%; buprenorphine (347) 76% and 66%; fentanyl (157) 72% and 70%; amphetamine (1,381) 56% and 22%; cocaine (122) 43% and 16%; other drugs (122) 36% and 18%; THC (700) 23% and 9%.
key_findings.locator: Table III; Results › Data description: General characteristics, 4th paragraph (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Period not stated; the Toxreg column sums to 5,831, which fits 1997–2012 (reporting issue 6). Because Toxreg counts presence, and includes deaths with cannabis as the only drug whatever the underlying cause (p. 8), a Toxreg death outside the NMR selections is not necessarily a missed drug poisoning. Fentanyl's 114 of 157 is 72.6% (printed 72).

key_findings.finding: Annual counts for 1997–2012 moved in the same direction in all three national datasets; NMR/Sweden and Toxreg were closer to each other than to NMR/EMCDDA, and at about the same level from 2006 apart from a Toxreg peak in 2008. No statistic compares the trends.
key_findings.locator: Results › Data description: General characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 prints no values. Approximate readings from a 300-dpi crop: NMR/EMCDDA about 150 (1997), 200 (2006) and 410 (2012); NMR/Sweden about 360, 330 and 520; Toxreg about 250, 300 and 525. NMR/Sweden was about 50 to 115 above Toxreg each year in 1997–2005, and NMR/EMCDDA rose from about two-fifths to about four-fifths of NMR/Sweden, so the series did not change in proportion. The approximate Toxreg readings for 1997–2012 sum to about 5,830, matching Table III's total.

key_findings.finding: The authors report that, in the comparison with the inventory, the NMR and toxicology datasets captured acute poisonings far better than chronic drug-related conditions, and expect recent data to cover total drug mortality less well because chronic conditions may now be more common; no figures are given beyond the heroin, cocaine, injection-death and hospital-death percentages.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations and strengths, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' summary in both directions: according to the inventory only two-thirds of the deaths in the NMR/Sweden dataset were related to drug use ('abuse-related'), yet the total numbers for Sweden are 'more or less correct'; NMR-based statistics would be a questionable basis for more detailed analyses.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Most useful statistics for international comparisons: numbers or trends?, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The two-thirds comes from NMR/Stockholm in 1985–1996 and is applied here to NMR/Sweden.

key_findings.finding: Coverage of the sources: the cause-of-death register covers more than 99% of deaths and the forensic database more than 90% of non-natural deaths below age 65 in Sweden, including poisonings; attrition from the national mortality register is about 1%.
key_findings.locator: Datasets › Three NMR selections, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Discussion › Limitations and strengths, 2nd paragraph (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: ICD codes do not distinguish illegal from other drugs and some cover dissimilar substances: T40.4 (other synthetic narcotics) covers buprenorphine, dextropropoxyphene, fentanyl, pethidine and tramadol; the ICD specifications record neither other drugs present nor concentrations found at toxicology.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Pros and cons of statistics based on NMRs and forensic toxicology, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Toxreg requires only that a drug be found at forensic examination, so it includes deaths with cannabis as the only drug whatever the underlying cause (excluded by the EMCDDA specification) and some deaths in which a drug was present for reasons other than non-medical use, which the authors call few in their material; it misses drug-related deaths not due to acute intake, such as drug-related organ damage, and excludes ages over 60.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Pros and cons of statistics based on NMRs and forensic toxicology, 3rd and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: In 1994–1996, 43 of about 360 Stockholm-area Toxreg cases (12%) reflected medical treatment (editors' reconstruction, key finding 4).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that basing international comparisons on numbers or rates of drug-related deaths gives misleading results, but that comparing trends is meaningful provided no major change in investigation or certification practice has occurred; no data from other countries were analysed.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 2nd paragraph; Abstract (p. 1)

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that international comparisons of numbers of drug-related deaths based on mortality-register selections are made more problematic by varying forensic practices and by how fully official statistics cover deaths, especially of non-residents, and that this might at least partly explain why the Nordic and Baltic countries, with comparatively many forensic examinations, have higher rates of drug-related deaths than most other European countries. No other country's data were analysed; the suggestion rests on cited work (refs 8, 9) and is not tested here.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Most useful statistics for international comparisons: numbers or trends?, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: With inventory membership as reference, NMR’s 761/1,212=62.8% is capture and 761/1,180=64.5% is positive predictive value, opposite the printed labels. Toxreg’s 317/454=69.8% and 317/(317+43)=88.1% fit the same reversal only conditionally; the text also calls 317 the entire Toxreg total, including 43 outside the inventory.
reporting_issues.consequence: The NMR label reversal is reproducible. For Toxreg, retain both conflicting count statements; do not assert a unique corrected total, validated 88.1% predictive value, or causal miss rate. Inventory membership is not an independent standard for drug-caused death.

reporting_issues.issue: Toxreg's printed sensitivity of 88.1% has a 95% CI of 84.3–81.2: the upper limit lies below both the point estimate and the lower limit. Conditionally, if there were 317 overlap plus 43 extra cases despite the conflicting stated total, a Wilson interval is 84.3–91.0 and an exact interval 84.2–91.2 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical error, probably for about 91; the value is in any case the share of Toxreg cases confirmed by the inventory, not Toxreg's capture (issue 1).

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals printed for the values labelled positive predictive value are narrower than their counts allow: 60.4–65.1 for 761/1,212 (Wilson 60.0–65.5) and 66.1–73.3 for 317/454 (Wilson 65.4–73.9) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the uncertainty of the capture estimates is slightly larger than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The text uses 317 for two different groups: the inventory deaths that Toxreg included (317 of 454) and the Toxreg cases of 1994–1996, of which 43 were not inventory deaths. Both cannot hold; the printed percentages fit 360 Toxreg cases (317 + 43, editors' reconstruction).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of Stockholm-area Toxreg cases in 1994–1996 is not printed; 360 is an inference from the percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: Hospital deaths: 761 inventory deaths were captured overall and 734 of the 1,061 forensic cases, leaving 27 of the 151 hospital deaths (17.9%), but the text says 28% of the 151 (about 42) were in NMR/Stockholm (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the three figures is wrong and the breakdown is 'data not shown'; cite the overall 761 of 1,212.

reporting_issues.issue: Toxreg totals and periods disagree. Table I gives N = 6,648 for 1994–2012; the text and Figure 2 give 6,448, which Figure 2 labels 1994–2012 (4,238 + 2,210 = 6,448). The text sets this total beside 1997–2012 counts for NMR/Sweden (6,591) and NMR/EMCDDA (3,908), and the Methods say the age and sex description covers 1997–2012 (p. 4). Table III's Toxreg column sums to 5,831, and the 1997–2012 Toxreg line of Figure 1 to about the same (editors' sum and approximate reading), so Table III (period not stated) appears to cover 1997–2012, while the comparison with NMR/EMCDDA (3,608 Toxreg deaths not in it) appears to include 1994–1996 Toxreg deaths, which NMR/EMCDDA cannot contain.
reporting_issues.consequence: For 1997–2012 alone, about 2,991 of 5,831 Toxreg deaths (51%) were outside NMR/EMCDDA, rather than 3,608 of 6,448 (56%) (editors' calculation, assuming Table III covers 1997–2012). The mean age and share of women printed for Toxreg may cover a different period from the other two datasets.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I says NMR/Stockholm (1985–1996) is derived from NMR/Sweden, whose period it gives as 1994–2012, and Table II gives codes only from 1994 (ICD-9 for 1994–1996, ICD-10 from 1997), so the selection rules for 1985–1993, most of the validation period, are not printed. The Methods name NMR/Stockholm for the 1997–2012 description that the Results give for NMR/Sweden (p. 4), and the Conclusions refer to the NMR/Sweden dataset for 1985–1996, which is NMR/Stockholm. NMR/Stockholm's 761 matched and 419 unmatched deaths make 1,180, against 1,181 in Table I.
reporting_issues.consequence: The codes behind the headline comparison cannot be checked for 1985–1993, and the dataset names are used interchangeably; attach the validation figures to NMR/Stockholm, 1985–1996.

reporting_issues.issue: Table III's column headings read GMR/Sweden and GMR/Europe for NMR/Sweden and NMR/EMCDDA, its period is not stated, and fentanyl's 114 of 157 is printed as 72% (72.6%). Table II excludes T40.4, which the Discussion says covers buprenorphine and fentanyl, from the EMCDDA selection, yet Table III shows NMR/EMCDDA holding 66% of Toxreg's buprenorphine and 70% of its fentanyl deaths; the paper does not say through which codes these deaths entered.
reporting_issues.consequence: The European selection's code list may be incompletely printed; cite Table III's capture figures as printed, with these caveats.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says about one-quarter of the inventory cases were missing from the toxicology-based dataset; the counts give 137 of 454 (30%) for 1994–1996 (editors' calculation), and Toxreg could not capture the hospital deaths at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: Report the first statement of 317/454 alongside the conflicting 43-of-317 statement. Neither the discussion’s one-quarter claim nor the printed 88.1% establishes a resolved causal miss fraction.

Tables I–III and Figures 1–2 checked on rendered pages (Figure 1 cropped at 300 dpi; its values are approximate readings); proportions and intervals recomputed by script; no supplement. Matching editorial application by ChatGPT407 on 2026-11-10 of genuine independent source-check qualifications (readers416–419); exact field changes and source outputs retained in the DD recovery record. No appraisal labels changed.

disagreements.first_pass: Toxreg cannot capture inventory deaths with a history of drug use but no positive toxicology, which made up 10% of the 1,061 forensic cases, nor the 151 hospital deaths, which were not forensically examined (data not shown).

design_detail: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (no meta-analysis) of deaths, and of injuries with medico-legal relevance, in police and prison custody linked to physical restraint, use-of-force devices and the label 'excited delirium' (ExD; the authors prefer 'acute behavioral disturbance', ABD). PubMed and Scopus, 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025, English or Portuguese, reported against PRISMA 2009; earlier studies admitted from reference lists when 'frequently cited' or 'foundational', plus automated database suggestions, grey literature from official bodies, and two articles added during peer review. 116 included studies by the authors' count (62 rated good, 51 fair, 3 weak), spanning observational studies, case series and reports, forensic reports, experiments in healthy volunteers and animals, and systematic and scoping reviews; narrative, qualitative and opinion articles used as context. Presented as a predefined thematic subset of a broader review of deaths in custody. The review counts no deaths and pools no proportions.
can_establish: What the restraint-and-custody literature since 2010, as selected and summarized by these authors, says about deaths in custody: that 'excited delirium' has no validated diagnostic criteria and works as a diagnosis of exclusion, that autopsy and biomarker findings are non-specific, which mechanisms are proposed, which single-study figures exist, and what the authors recommend for investigation and certification.
cannot_establish: How often drugs cause or contribute to deaths in custody, how often restraint deaths are misclassified or missed in official statistics, or which mechanism operates in a given death: no deaths are counted, no drug proportions or concentrations are reported, the 116 included studies are not identified in the article, and the mechanistic conclusions rest on narrative selection weighted toward reviews from one author group and series of deaths selected on the outcome.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). PubMed and Scopus searched with combinations of keywords and MeSH terms, 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025, English or Portuguese, no restriction by country or legal system; earlier studies from reference screening; automated database suggestions; grey literature and normative documents from international and national forensic, human-rights and public-health bodies; two articles added during peer review 'to broaden the epidemiological scope' (p. 2, Methods, 5th–7th paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Population: people under the direct physical or legal control of police or correctional officers and not free to leave (street arrest, transport, interrogation, imprisonment) who were exposed to deliberate force or coercive measures (high-risk positions such as prone, mechanical restraints, conducted energy devices); routine administrative encounters excluded. Outcomes: deaths in custody of any cause, natural or non-natural, and restraint-related injuries needing forensic examination, medical documentation or judicial investigation. Included designs: observational studies, case series, forensic reports, experimental studies, systematic and scoping reviews. Narrative articles, qualitative studies, official documents, book chapters and reflective papers used as contextual evidence; editorials and commentaries on ExD used only for the conceptual and ethical framework. Excluded: letters without original data, duplicate publications, non-custodial populations except post-release analyses linked to custodial events (p. 2, Methods, 3rd–6th paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Not reported for the review as a whole. The review describes restraint-related deaths in the literature as predominantly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and psychostimulant intoxication, and reports over-representation of racialized minorities among deaths classified as 'legal intervention'; no counts are given (p. 3, section 3.1, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Screening numbers are in the PRISMA 2009 flow diagram in the supplementary material, which was not among the files read.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is only partly reproducible: no search terms are printed, the date and language limits are not justified, pre-2010 sources entered by an undefined rule (for example Stratton et al., 2001; O'Halloran & Frank, 2000; Strote & Range Hutson, 2006; three book chapters), two articles were added at peer review without being named, and the article's 68 references (8 on methods) cannot account for 116 included studies, so the complete included set and possible overlap between primary studies and cited reviews cannot be reconstructed from the main article. The authors state that the primary literature is overwhelmingly observational and retrospective and drawn from secondary sources (autopsy summaries, police use-of-force logs, civil-litigation records), mostly from high-income countries (p. 6, Limitations). Series of deaths are selected on the outcome, and the 229-death series is cited to papers including a study of civil-litigated cases (reference titles, p. 7). The review does not cite the 2018 systematic review of excited delirium by Gonin et al. (on the project's death-counting list).

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies and is not tabulated. Restraint position, compression, devices (conducted energy devices, spit hoods, vascular neck restraint) are taken from police logs, autopsy and investigation reports, litigation records, or experimental protocols in healthy volunteers and animals. Drug exposure appears only as psychostimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine) and phencyclidine 'frequently identified in toxicological analyses' (p. 3), with no proportions, specimens, test panels or concentrations.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No amount or concentration of any drug is reported. The only restraint-duration figure is from one retrospective series (58% of 229 deaths within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint; p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Intoxication is one of several interacting factors (with restraint, exertion, obesity, hyperthermia and heart disease) in the authors' model, but no study's toxicology is summarized; alcohol is not discussed in the text and appears only in the title of one cited Finnish study (ref. 7).

comparison.controls: None at review level. Comparisons cited from single studies: deaths against non-fatal use-of-force encounters in prospective police cohorts (low mortality reported), features of 'excited delirium' against conducted-energy-device exposure, prone against non-prone positions in operational data, healthy volunteers in restraint positions against baseline, and post-mortem computed tomography against autopsy (pp. 3–4).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The cited death series rarely have pre-event health, drug-use or full toxicology data beyond what autopsy and records give, which the authors acknowledge (p. 6, Limitations, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Narrative synthesis by theme: epidemiological and clinical profile; proposed mechanisms; experimental and physiological evidence; conducted energy devices and other techniques; medico-legal investigation. Quality appraisal with NHLBI tools (observational studies), JBI checklists (case reports, qualitative studies, opinion articles), SANRA (narrative reviews) and PRISMA-ScR with JBI guidance (scoping reviews); study-level ratings in Supplementary Table 1, not read (p. 2, Methods, 9th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal tool is named for the volunteer and animal experiments; PRISMA-ScR is a reporting checklist, not an appraisal tool; the 'predefined quality thresholds' used to retain studies for the Results are not stated; quality is summarized only as 62 good, 51 fair and 3 weak (pp. 2, 6).
outcomes.operationalization: Death in custody: any death while under police or correctional control, natural or non-natural. 'Excited delirium' as each source used it; the review reproduces a ten-feature law-enforcement checklist (constant activity, violent or bizarre behaviour, 'superhuman strength', high pain tolerance, no fatigue, rapid breathing, profuse sweating, marked hyperthermia, unresponsiveness to police, being naked or inappropriately clothed) but adopts no definition and no criteria of its own. Drug involvement is not operationalized, and how drug findings were weighed in assigning cause of death is not described for any cited study.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers and full-text disagreements resolved by consensus; who extracted data and who rated quality is not stated (p. 2, Methods, 7th–8th paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled; figures are cited from single studies. Finland: 12 restraint-associated deaths among 21,036 autopsies (0.06%; ref. 7). A retrospective review of 229 deaths: 58% within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint, and verbal respiratory distress (for example 'I can't breathe') documented in at least 20% before cardiac collapse (refs. 24, 29). Ventilatory decreases 'frequently exceeding 28–40%' in prone and hogtie conditions, as summarized in one review (ref. 36). 75 deaths temporally associated with TASER exposure: TASER considered a contributing factor in 27%, typically with physical restraint and intoxication (ref. 51). 944 applications of vascular neck restraint: immobilization in 92.6%, transient loss of consciousness in 23.7%, no deaths directly attributed (ref. 52). 46 investigative reports in Ontario: most deaths classified as accidental or natural (ref. 14) (pp. 3–4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported. The article calls itself a predefined thematic subset of a broader systematic review whose protocol also covered suicide and general mortality, but gives no registration number or citation for that protocol; two articles were added during peer review (p. 2, Methods, 2nd and 5th paragraphs).
analysis.selective_reporting: Results are statements without study counts, so the weight of evidence behind each cannot be seen. Evidence that does not fit the favoured model (low mortality in prospective use-of-force cohorts; operational data on prone positioning; volunteer experiments without hypoxia) is reported but discounted, while the retrospective death series and reviews that support it are not appraised in the text. The pooled analysis cited for the restraint-centred reading (Strömmer et al., 2020, ref. 32) is cited without its published critiques and the authors' replies (de Boer et al., 2023 and 2024; recorded on the project's card sc_strommer_2020).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative account, without counts, of a literature dominated by retrospective death series, case reports, reviews and volunteer experiments: restraint-related deaths are described mostly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and stimulant intoxication; 'excited delirium' lacks validated criteria and specific autopsy or biomarker findings; volunteer studies of prone restraint show reduced lung volumes and more work of breathing without clinically significant hypoxia; one review of 229 deaths (cited to papers including a study of litigated cases) reports rapid collapse after prone restraint; most restraint deaths in one Ontario series of 46 reports were classified as accidental or natural; under-reporting in official vital statistics is asserted from one review without figures.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state that deaths in custody are predominantly multifactorial, the Results that current evidence 'strongly favors' ventilatory compromise and metabolic collapse over stress-induced cardiac death (p. 3), the abstract that volunteer experiments 'should not be used to negate associated risks', and the Limitations that the evidence rests on 'a solid methodological foundation' (p. 6). The mechanistic preference rests mostly on reviews sharing one author (refs. 24, 29, 35, 36) and a pooled case analysis whose critiques are not mentioned (ref. 32); the same experimental literature is described as showing profound reductions in ventilatory capacity on p. 3 and modest ventilatory changes on p. 4; and the 'solid foundation' is a count of quality ratings from tools of different kinds, not an appraisal of the evidence for the causal claims. The Discussion also allows a catecholamine-driven arrhythmic pathway with stimulant intoxication in some deaths (p. 4, section 4.2; p. 5, section 4.3), which the Results section presents as weakened. The recommendations (complete autopsy with toxicology, independent investigation, avoiding prone positioning, replacing ExD with ABD) are expert judgments that the synthesis does not test.

timeline.event: Stratton et al., factors associated with sudden death of people restrained for excited delirium (ref. 34), a pre-2010 source admitted under the review's 'foundational' rule and cited for the restraint model (not read).
Vilke et al., defining review of excited delirium syndrome (ref. 11), cited for the clinical picture and for stimulants found on toxicology (not read).
Gonin et al., systematic review of excited delirium (on the project's death-counting list); not cited by this review.

Strömmer et al., pooled analysis of 168 published cases (ref. 32), cited as converging on a restraint-centred multifactorial reading; its critiques by de Boer et al. (2023, 2024) and the authors' replies, recorded on the project's card, are not cited here.
Steinberg, comprehensive review of prone restraint cardiac arrest (ref. 36), the main source for the PEA/asystole argument and the 28–40% ventilatory figure (not read).
Slocum et al., scoping review seeking inter-specialty consensus on excited delirium syndrome (ref. 62), cited for moving to descriptive terminology (not read).

Steinberg & Frugoli, review of mortality with in-custody prone restraint (ref. 29), and Steinberg, Patel & Frugoli, study of civil-litigated prone restraint deaths (ref. 24): sources for the 229-death figures and the under-reporting statement (not read).
This review (search to 1 September 2025).

replication.where_it_stands: Contested field. This review adds a 2010–2025 search but no counts, pooled estimates or reconciliation of the conflicting evidence, so it is a guide to sources rather than an estimate. How often deaths labelled 'excited delirium' are restraint deaths, drug deaths or both remains open. The review may be cited for the status of the ExD label (no validated criteria, not in DSM or ICD, used as a diagnosis of exclusion), for the non-specificity of autopsy and biomarker findings, for the single-study figures it quotes (as second-hand), and for the authors' recommendations on investigation; not for the frequency or causal role of drugs, nor for one mechanism dominating.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding source, p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declarations of interest: none (p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: First author: Department of Forensic Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto; second author also National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, Coimbra, Portugal (p. 1). AI-assisted tools are declared for translation, language revision and the Fig. 1 conceptual image, not for content, analysis or interpretation; the declaration speaks of a single author for a two-author paper (p. 6).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective, multi-jurisdiction register of every death in police and prison custody, with standardized recording of restraint position and duration, compression, devices used, initial cardiac rhythm, core temperature, blood gases, full toxicology with concentrations, and full autopsy by investigators independent of the custodial authority, compared with a register of non-fatal use-of-force encounters from the same jurisdictions (the authors themselves call for prospective multicentre data with standardized definitions, p. 5).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people under police or prison control exposed to force or coercive measures), interventions (restraint positions, mechanical restraints, conducted energy devices) and outcomes (deaths of any cause; medico-legally relevant injuries) are defined (p. 2), but there is no comparator and the aims (mechanisms, clinical profile, investigation practice) are not framed as PICO questions.
No registration or citable protocol; the review is described as a predefined subset of a broader review whose protocol is not cited, and two unnamed articles were added during peer review (p. 2).
Included and 'contextual' designs are listed but the choice is not explained, and primary studies are synthesized together with reviews that may contain them.

Two databases (PubMed, Scopus) with reference screening, automated suggestions and grey literature, but no search terms or strategy are printed, the language (English, Portuguese) and date limits (2010–2025) are not justified, and pre-2010 studies entered by an undefined 'frequently cited or foundational' rule. The supplement is described as holding the flow diagram and the quality table, not the search.

Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts, with disagreements resolved by consensus (p.2). Whether the same duplicate process covered additions from reference lists, automated suggestions, the foundational rule and peer review is not reported.
Who extracted the data, and whether in duplicate, is not reported.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies with reasons is printed in the main article. The supplement is described as containing a PRISMA flow diagram and quality-assessment table; its full contents were not supplied or read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The article has no table of included studies; the extracted items (authorship, year, design, quality, sample, interventions, findings) may be presented in Supplementary Table 1, which was not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Tools named by design: NHLBI tools for observational studies (which ask about confounding and selection), JBI checklists for case reports, qualitative and opinion articles, SANRA for narrative reviews, PRISMA-ScR with JBI guidance for scoping reviews. No tool is named for the volunteer and animal experiments, PRISMA-ScR is a reporting checklist, the retention threshold is not stated, and study-level ratings are only in the unread supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported; funding is not among the extracted items (p. 2).
Narrative synthesis only.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations name retrospective designs, reliance on autopsy summaries, police logs and litigation records, and possible bias from ties between death-investigation systems and law enforcement, but then call the evidence a solid foundation on the strength of the quality counts. The mechanistic and multifactorial conclusions are drawn without considering selection on death and litigation or reliance on one author group's reviews, while volunteer experiments are discounted for indirectness.

Heterogeneity is named as the reason for not pooling. Conflicting findings (low mortality in prospective use-of-force cohorts and operational data on prone positioning; no hypoxia in volunteers) are explained by the favoured multifactorial model rather than examined for design differences such as selection on the outcome.
No quantitative synthesis; the Limitations acknowledge that publication bias cannot be excluded (p. 6).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No external funding; no conflicts declared (p. 6).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from Supplementary Table 1, which was not read; the overall rating does not depend on it. Four critical items are not met in the article itself: no registered or citable protocol (2), a search without printed terms or justified limits (4), no list of excluded studies (7), and no account of risk of bias when drawing the mechanistic conclusions (13); item 9 is met only in part. Under AMSTAR 2, more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence. The review may be cited for what it reports the literature says about the ExD label, for the non-specificity of autopsy and biomarker findings, for the single-study figures it quotes (second-hand, with their primary sources named), and for the authors' recommendations on investigation; not for how often drugs are involved, for the cause of any death, or for one mechanism dominating.

key_findings.finding: Methods: PubMed and Scopus searched for 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025 (English or Portuguese) under PRISMA 2009, with reference screening, automated database suggestions, grey literature, earlier 'frequently cited or foundational' studies, and two articles added during peer review; two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts; results synthesized narratively because designs, settings (police vs prison), definitions of restraint, diagnostic criteria for ExD, legal frameworks and outcome classifications varied too much to pool.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st and 5th–8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors rated the 116 included studies as good (62, 53.4%), fair (51, 44.0%) or weak (3, 2.6%) and state that only studies meeting predefined quality thresholds were retained for the Results and Discussion; the thresholds are not given.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 9th paragraph (p. 2); Limitations, 3rd paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: The review states that 'excited delirium' lacks validated diagnostic criteria in the official classifications (DSM, ICD) and specific biomarkers, is used in medico-legal contexts to explain deaths in custody, is criticized as deflecting attention from restraint and as racially biased, and, with no pathognomonic autopsy findings, is classified as a diagnosis of exclusion; the authors favour 'acute behavioral disturbance', keep 'ExD' when citing historical concepts and the terms of the original studies, and recommend replacing the label with it where possible.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 1), 4th–5th paragraphs (p. 2); section 3.2, 6th paragraph (p. 3); section 5, 6th paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Drugs: psychostimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine) and phencyclidine are described as 'frequently identified' in toxicological analyses, citing a 2012 defining review and a 2009 book chapter; no proportion, specimen, test panel or concentration is given, and the review does not say how drug findings were weighed in assigning cause of death.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.2, 4th paragraph (p. 3); reference list, refs. 11 and 38 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Profile: deaths involving prone restraint described as predominantly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and psychostimulant intoxication, commonly with handcuffing and body weight on the torso; racialized minorities over-represented among deaths classified as 'legal intervention'. The 3rd paragraph also reports that features of 'excited delirium' were documented in a minority of use-of-force encounters, that an accumulation of features went with hyperthermia (ref. 30), and that police and prehospital literature uses a ten-feature checklist for the picture, so the label is applied to living people in policing and prehospital care, not only in death investigation (editors' reading). No counts are given.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.1, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Counts cited: population-level data from Finland, 12 restraint-associated deaths among 21,036 autopsies (0.06%); a retrospective review of 229 deaths in which 58% occurred within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint and verbal respiratory distress was documented in at least 20% before cardiac collapse. The review also notes that prospective studies in controlled settings occasionally report low mortality.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.1, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand (refs. 7,24,29), not newly verified primary data. The review does not say how a death was classed as restraint-associated or by whom. One of the two sources cited for229 deaths has civil-litigated cases in its title (ref.24), but the selection of the entire229 cannot be established from this review alone.

key_findings.finding: Under-reporting: citing one 2025 review (ref. 29), the authors state that large-scale investigations show persistent under-reporting of restraint-related deaths in official vital statistics, so forensic, police and open-source data must be combined to quantify them; no figures are given.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.1, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); reference list, ref. 29 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Classification: an analysis of 46 investigative reports in Ontario found frequent interplay between physical restraint and individual risk factors such as substance use or comorbidity, with most deaths classified as accidental or natural (ref. 14); the Introduction cites the same source for critics' view that ExD is used to classify restraint deaths as accidental or natural.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 5th paragraph (p. 2); section 3.5, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Who classified the deaths (coroners or inquests) and on what evidence is not stated in the review.

key_findings.finding: Mechanisms: the review favours ventilatory compromise with metabolic acidosis ('prone restraint cardiac arrest') over stress-induced arrhythmic death, because terminal rhythms in prone restraint deaths are reported to be mostly pulseless electrical activity or asystole rather than ventricular arrhythmias (refs. 35, 36); the Discussion still allows that catecholamine surges with stimulant intoxication may precipitate malignant arrhythmias in some deaths and recommends recording the initial heart rhythm to tell the pathways apart.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.2, 1st–3rd paragraphs (p. 3); section 4.2, 6th paragraph (p. 4); section 4.3, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Experiments in healthy volunteers: prone and weighted restraint reduced lung volumes and increased work of breathing without clinically significant hypoxia or major haemodynamic compromise; one review is cited for ventilatory decreases frequently exceeding 28–40% in prone and hogtie conditions; spit hoods produced no clinically significant changes in oxygen saturation or haemodynamics; in simulated encounters, intense exertion produced larger metabolic disturbances than conducted energy devices, chemical sprays or police dogs. The authors hold that volunteer data cannot be extrapolated to custody with agitation, exertion, obesity, stimulant intoxication and prolonged struggle.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.3, 1st–5th paragraphs (p. 3); section 4.2, 4th paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Conducted energy devices: in animal models, repeated or prolonged discharges caused marked acidaemia and apnoea with rapid recovery in most trials and a low risk of ventricular fibrillation; in human volunteers brief discharges raised serum lactate only. In one series of 75 deaths that followed TASER exposure closely in time, those who died were mostly men with frequent cardiovascular disease and stimulant intoxication, and TASER was considered a contributing factor in 27%, typically with physical restraint and intoxication.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.4, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Who judged TASER contributory (pathologists or the study's authors) is not stated in the review.

key_findings.finding: Investigation: conventional autopsy findings were often non-specific for distinguishing mechanical asphyxia from stress-related cardiac death or ExDS; post-mortem computed tomography showed sensitivity comparable to autopsy for major findings; superficial bruising was detected less often in people with darker skin and better with specialized dissection; deaths attributed to ExDS may occur without overt restraint or initially resemble homicide.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.5, 2nd–4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers: HSP70 expression has been found in people with documented cocaine use regardless of any ExD diagnosis, so the review treats such markers as non-specific stress responses; it states that no single pathological or molecular finding establishes causality and that comprehensive toxicological analysis is indispensable for distinguishing intoxication from other mechanisms in deaths initially attributed to ExD.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.1, 4th–5th paragraphs (p. 4); section 4.3, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: timely, independent medico-legal investigation of every death in custody by experienced teams without functional dependence on the custodial authority, with complete autopsy, full toxicology and scene reconstruction (and documentation of initial heart rhythm, blood gases, restraint duration and position); review of restraint protocols with prone positioning avoided or kept brief; replacing ExD with ABD where possible; periodic independent audits.
key_findings.locator: Section 4.3, 3rd paragraph; section 5, 2nd–4th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: two databases only; publication bias cannot be excluded; heterogeneity prevents direct comparison; evidence mostly from high-income countries; primary literature overwhelmingly observational and retrospective, built on secondary records (autopsy summaries, police records of force used, records from civil litigation) that lack standardized clinical variables; ties between some death-investigation systems and law enforcement may bias causal interpretation and reporting of in-custody deaths.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st–3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The review reports 116 included studies, but the article has 68 references, 8 of them on methods (snowballing, review steps, NHLBI, JBI, SANRA and scoping-review guidance); at most 60 could be included studies, and some of those are textbooks, book chapters, a commentary and a philosophy-of-science paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The full set of116 studies cannot be identified from the main article alone. Individual statements do have named citations, but their underlying populations and overlap require checking; the complete included-study list may be in the unread supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Only studies meeting 'predefined quality thresholds' were retained for the Results and Discussion (p. 2), yet the thresholds are not stated and the Limitations count 3 'weak' studies among the 116 included (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which studies were used and whether weak studies inform the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The same experimental literature is described as showing 'profound reductions in ventilatory capacity' (p. 3, following a 'systematic evaluation of experimental data' sentence without its own citation or methods) and 'significant impairments' (p. 3, ref. 36, a single-author review that sets aside earlier readings of the changes as clinically modest), and then as showing 'modest ventilatory changes' (p. 4, refs. 46–47).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the ventilatory effect cannot be taken from this review; the primary experiments must be read.

reporting_issues.issue: The search window is 2010–2025, but many cited sources predate it (for example refs. 27, 34, 51, 53, 59, 60 and book chapters 6, 12, 38), admitted by an undefined 'frequently cited or foundational' rule; the two articles added at peer review are not named.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selection is discretionary and cannot be reproduced.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that 'narrative reviews converge' on a multifactorial explanation of deaths attributed to ExD cites a pooled analysis of published cases (ref. 32) and a philosophy-of-science article (ref. 65), not narrative reviews.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claimed convergence rests on two sources of other kinds; the pooled analysis has published critiques that the review does not mention.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure1 shows an upward arrow beside pH under the label metabolic acidosis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conceptual image label is internally inconsistent; it supplies no measured pH data and should not be used as physiological evidence.
