design_detail: Retrospective single-centre review of the case files of all standard medicolegal autopsies performed in 2016–2021 at the Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Regional Autopsy Center (AHWFBRAC), which provides medicolegal autopsies for 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038) and kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021. Of 6,248 files, 2,956 were included after excluding decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury and intentional (suicidal) overdoses. Each case was classified twice: (1) suspicion of a drug-related death before autopsy, from the preliminary report of death and investigative information (drug paraphernalia at the scene, current or prior substance use disorder, prior overdoses) that the centre's medicolegal death investigators obtained from county medical examiners with standardized questions; and (2) the final cause of death after full autopsy and comprehensive toxicology, as determined by the assigned forensic pathologist. Results are a 2×2 table with sensitivity, specificity and the authors' own false-positive and false-negative rates. Filed as cross-sectional with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case-file and certificate studies; the accuracy statistics are recorded as the paper's.
can_establish: How often, at one regional autopsy centre in 2016–2021, deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug-related ended with a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology (265 of 2,719), and how often deaths not suspected ended with a drug-related cause (115 of 237).
cannot_establish: How many deaths external examination with toxicology but without autopsy would actually have put down to drugs wrongly (the 265 'false positives' include deaths with negative toxicology, which toxicology alone would have flagged, and the split is not reported); whether the final causes were right (the pathologist's determination is the reference, and illicit drugs found were treated as at least contributing unless a catastrophic Adelson class I process was present); or the figures elsewhere, for intentional overdoses, children or deaths with obvious injury, which were excluded. Within the 2,719 suspected deaths, 9.75% is at most an upper bound of unknown distance for extra misattribution if full autopsy were omitted. It does not bound misattribution among all included deaths: the 122 not-suspected/non-drug deaths could include drugs present with another cause, but that split is also unreported.

sample.recruitment: Records: case files of all standard medicolegal autopsies performed at AHWFBRAC from 2016 to 2021 (p. 189, Methods/Materials 1st paragraph; p. 190, Results 1st paragraph). The centre served 33 western North Carolina counties and performed full autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021 while other offices had moved to external examination with toxicology specimens (p. 189, Introduction 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury, and deaths from intentional suicidal overdose of prescription or illicit drugs. Suicidal overdoses were excluded because they were already identified as intentional at referral and because, the authors say, many did not meet the study's criteria for a likely drug-related death (p. 189, Methods/Materials 1st paragraph). The number excluded for each reason is not reported; 3,292 of 6,248 files were excluded in all (editors' arithmetic).
sample.demographics: Not reported. Age and sex were extracted from the files (p. 189, Methods/Materials 2nd paragraph) but are not presented.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (record review). No missing-data handling is reported.
sample.selection_effects: One regional centre; only autopsied deaths enter. Excluding obvious lethal injuries and suicidal drug overdoses changes the case mix relative to all deaths investigated. Only 237 included deaths were not suspected of drug involvement and 387 had a non-drug final cause; exclusions are not counted by reason, so the case mix among the excluded 3,292 files cannot be reconstructed. The authors note that the sample reflects western North Carolina only (p. 192, Discussion 5th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. The classification under test is suspicion of a drug-related death before autopsy, from the preliminary report of death (a brief report available at the time of autopsy) and investigative information gathered by the centre's medicolegal death investigators from county medical examiners with standardized questions; the criteria were drug paraphernalia at the scene (needles, syringes, cut straws, pill crushers, burnt foil, rolled papers, baggies with residue), current or prior substance use disorder, and prior overdoses (p. 189, Methods/Materials 2nd and 3rd paragraphs). How the criteria were combined, who classified each case for the study, and whether that classification was made without knowledge of the final cause are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Substances found in blood or other tissues were tabulated from the toxicology reports (p. 189, Methods/Materials 3rd paragraph); Figure 2 gives the yearly share of drug-related deaths in which heroin, fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine were 'involved' (p. 191). Combinations are not analysed.

comparison.controls: Within-series comparison: deaths suspected and not suspected before autopsy, each set against the final cause after full autopsy and toxicology (Table 1, p. 190). There is no comparison with deaths certified without autopsy and no independent review of the final causes.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Case characteristics that could affect both suspicion and final cause (age, sex, known disease, decomposition, interval to autopsy) are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Final cause of death from the autopsy and toxicology reports, as determined by the forensic pathologist assigned the case (p. 189, Methods/Materials 3rd paragraph; p. 192, Discussion 5th paragraph). Toxicology: specimens sent to a forensic toxicology laboratory that screened for over-the-counter, prescription and illicit drugs by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and gas chromatography with nitrogen-phosphorus detection after base/neutral extraction, and by targeted liquid chromatography with high-resolution (quadrupole-Orbitrap) mass spectrometry, with confirmation and quantitation by LC-MS-MS; point-of-care urine screens were not used (pp. 189–190, Methods/Materials 4th paragraph). Specimen types, sampling sites, the share of cases tested and concentrations are not reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors assume the assigned pathologist's cause of death is correct, and treat illicit drugs present at death as at least contributing to death except when an Adelson class I natural or traumatic process (catastrophic, fatal regardless of other conditions) was found (p. 192, Discussion 5th paragraph; p. 191, Results 2nd paragraph). The reference therefore partly incorporates the investigative information on which the suspicion under test was based, and it counts the presence of illicit drugs as contribution.
outcomes.operationalization: False positive: high suspicion at referral, but toxicology negative, or illicit substances present with other significant non-toxicologic findings that explain the death. False negative: very low or no suspicion at referral, but toxicology showed a drug toxicity as the cause of death without significant autopsy findings (p. 190, Methods/Materials 5th paragraph). Formulas: sensitivity TP/(TP+FN); specificity TN/(TN+FP); false-positive rate FP/all suspected cases (that is, 1 minus the positive predictive value, not 1 minus specificity); false-negative rate FN/all final drug-related cases. The authors note that these definitions are not universal.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: four descriptive proportions and yearly drug shares; no hypothesis test is reported, although drug trends are called significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The classification was made retrospectively from files that contained the autopsy and toxicology reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (p. 190): suspected 2,719 (final drug-related 2,454; not drug-related 265); not suspected 237 (drug-related 115; not 122). Reported: sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%, false-negative rate 4.48%, false-positive rate 9.75% (p. 190, Results 1st paragraph); all four reproduce from Table 1 (editors' arithmetic). No intervals are reported. Editors' calculations (Wilson 95% intervals): false-positive rate as defined, 265/2,719 = 9.75% (8.7 to 10.9); positive predictive value 2,454/2,719 = 90.25% (89.1 to 91.3); share of the 237 deaths not suspected that had a drug-related final cause, 115/237 = 48.5% (42.2 to 54.9); conventional false-positive rate (1 minus specificity), 265/387 = 68.5% (63.7 to 72.9); overall agreement, 2,576/2,956 = 87.1% (85.9 to 88.3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The 265 false positives are not split into deaths with negative toxicology and deaths with drugs present but another cause, although only the second kind would be missed by external examination with toxicology; the alternative causes are given only as examples (p. 191). Age and sex were extracted but not reported, and the exclusions are not counted by reason.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The main proportions rest on 2,719 suspected and 387 non-drug cases; figures for the 237 deaths not suspected are less precise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At one regional centre, 9.75% of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related had a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology. The share within those suspected deaths that external examination with toxicology would have put down to drugs wrongly could be smaller, because the false-positive definition includes negative toxicology; the split is not reported. This does not bound misattribution among initially unsuspected deaths. In the other direction, 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) ended with a drug-related cause.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states only the purpose and gives no results. The Results say investigators could “correctly predict” a suspected drug-related fatality in more than 95% of cases (p. 190, Results 2nd paragraph), but 95.5% is the sensitivity: 90.3% of suspected deaths were drug-related and overall agreement was 87.1% (editors' calculation). The Results and Conclusions present the almost-10% false-positive rate as the share of cases that could have been misclassified if only investigation, toxicology and external examination had been done (p. 190, Results 2nd paragraph; p. 192, Conclusions), which overstates it, since toxicology-negative deaths are included. The Conclusions add that the data are informational and not meant to sway offices toward one practice (p. 192). Rises in fentanyl and methamphetamine are called significant without any test (p. 191, Results 3rd paragraph). The Discussion itself acknowledges that scene investigation, external examination and comprehensive toxicology supported a correct determination in a majority of cases (p. 191, first paragraph), which tempers the emphasis on errors; its own reference classifications are assumed correct.

timeline.event: Nashelsky and Lawrence, accuracy of cause-of-death determination without forensic autopsy (cited as reference 21 among reasons offices use external examinations; not read for this card).

Fryer et al.: in a selected group of high-risk referrals, external examination, toxicology and/or post-mortem CT could cut standard autopsies by two-thirds (reference 20, as summarized in the Discussion, p. 191).
Andrew and Duval: 11% to 13% of suspected drug-related deaths had toxicology that explained nothing and another cause (reference 18, as summarized, p. 191).

Dye et al.: three pathologists given history, scene, external examination and toxicology, without internal findings, classified cause and manner correctly in 75% to 80% of 60 cases selected from 629 (reference 19, as summarized, p. 191; on the project's list as #28, not read).
NAME position paper: autopsy recommended whenever intoxication is suspected as a possible cause of death; cited by this study as current best practice (reference 14).
This study: 265 of 2,719 suspected drug-related deaths (9.75%) had a non-drug final cause after full autopsy at one North Carolina centre, 2016–2021.

replication.where_it_stands: A single-centre study with no direct replication. The two earlier studies it summarizes report broadly similar magnitudes by different designs (11% to 13% with another cause; 20% to 25% misclassified without internal examination), but they are second-hand here. The project list is not an exhaustive census of such studies; the paper itself cites earlier investigations. Read with the NAME position paper (Davis et al., 2020), which recommends autopsy without quantifying the error it prevents.

funding.funder: No funding statement printed.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 189, first-page footnote).
funding.affiliations_note: First author a pathology resident (Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center); second an associate professor, Wake Forest University School of Medicine; third a senior biostatistician in that school's Department of Biostatistics and Data Science (p. 189). The NAME position paper that recommends autopsy for suspected overdose deaths (Davis et al., 2020, p. 152) lists a panel member with the same name and institution (Jerri L. McLemore, Department of Pathology, Wake Forest School of Medicine). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study in several offices in which, for every suspected drug-related death, a certifier records a cause of death from scene investigation, external examination and full toxicology before the autopsy, without seeing its findings, and an independent panel then assigns the cause after full autopsy; reporting separately the deaths with drugs present but another cause, and including intentional overdoses and deaths with injuries.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All autopsies of a regional centre serving 33 counties, but only autopsied deaths in one region; the target, suspected drug deaths certified without autopsy elsewhere, is wider.

All files for 2016–2021 were reviewed, but 3,292 of 6,248 were excluded with no count by reason, and suicidal overdoses were excluded partly because they did not fit the study's own suspicion criteria.
2,719 suspected and 387 non-drug cases give precise main proportions; the 237 deaths not suspected give wider intervals.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: No age, sex, manner of death, interval to autopsy or decomposition by group; the final causes of the 265 false positives are not tabulated.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Table 1 accounts for all 2,956 included cases. Figure 1's regional total for 2016–2021 (2,605, editors' sum) differs from the 2,569 final drug-related cases, without explanation.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Full autopsy with comprehensive toxicology interpreted by a forensic pathologist is the best available reference, but it is assumed correct, it counts illicit drugs present as contributing unless a class I process is found, and the 'false positive' category merges negative toxicology with drugs present and another cause.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: How the suspicion criteria were combined, who classified the cases and whether they knew the final cause are not reported; many pathologists over six years, with no agreement measure.

Counts and proportions reproduce from Table 1, but there are no intervals, the false-positive rate is not the conventional one, the verbal definition of the false-negative rate contradicts its formula, sensitivity is described as prediction accuracy, and trends are called significant without a test.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case-file studies, because the figure the site needs is a proportion: the share of suspected drug deaths that full autopsy assigned to another cause. The paper presents it as test accuracy; a QUADAS-2 reading would flag the same weaknesses (a retrospective classification of suspicion with unknown blinding, and a reference standard that incorporates the investigation behind that suspicion and counts illicit drugs present as contributing). Editors' summary: moderate risk of bias as a description of this series; as an estimate of what external examination with toxicology would misattribute, 9.75% is an upper bound of unknown distance within the 2,719 suspected deaths, not a bound for all misattribution. Citable for: at one North Carolina centre in 2016–2021, 265 of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related (9.75%) had a non-drug final cause after full autopsy and toxicology, including some with negative toxicology; 115 of 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) had a drug-related final cause; the examples of alternative causes; and the rule that illicit drugs found counted as contributing unless a class I process was present. Not citable for: the misclassification rate of certification without autopsy as such, rates in other regions, suicidal drug overdoses or children, or the accuracy of post-mortem drug levels (none are reported).

key_findings.finding: The Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Regional Autopsy Center provides medicolegal autopsies for 33 counties of western North Carolina (population 2,354,038) and performed full autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021, while other offices had adopted external examination with toxicology specimens; the study asked whether external examination with comprehensive toxicology alone missed disease or injury that would change the cause of death.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 6,248 autopsy case files from 2016–2021, 2,956 met the inclusion criteria after excluding decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury, and deaths from intentional suicidal overdose of prescription or illicit drugs.
key_findings.locator: Methods/Materials, 1st paragraph (p. 189); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 190)
key_findings.note: Exclusions are not counted by reason; 3,292 files excluded in all (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Pre-autopsy suspicion came from the preliminary report of death and from information that the centre's medicolegal death investigators obtained from county medical examiners with standardized questions; a likely drug-related death was judged from drug paraphernalia at the scene, current or prior substance use disorder, and prior overdoses.
key_findings.locator: Methods/Materials, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Table 1: of 2,719 deaths suspected before autopsy to be drug-related, 2,454 had a drug-related final cause and 265 did not; of 237 deaths not suspected, 115 had a drug-related final cause and 122 did not (column totals 2,569 drug-related and 387 not; 2,956 in all).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Reported accuracy: sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%, false-negative rate 4.48% and false-positive rate 9.75%, where the false-positive rate is false positives divided by all suspected cases (265/2,719) and the false-negative rate is false negatives divided by all final drug-related cases (115/2,569).
key_findings.locator: Methods/Materials, 5th paragraph (formulas); Results, 1st paragraph (values)
key_findings.note: All four reproduce from Table 1 (editors' arithmetic). No confidence intervals are given; the editors' Wilson 95% interval for 9.75% is 8.7% to 10.9%.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculations from Table 1: positive predictive value of suspicion 90.25% (2,454/2,719); share of deaths not suspected that had a drug-related final cause 48.5% (115/237; 95% interval 42.2% to 54.9%); conventional false-positive rate, 1 minus specificity, 68.5% (265/387); overall agreement 87.1% (2,576/2,956).
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Wilson intervals); none of these figures is printed in the paper.

key_findings.finding: A false positive was defined as a death with high suspicion at referral whose toxicology was negative, or in which illicit substances were present but other significant non-toxicologic findings explained the death; the paper does not report how many of the 265 fell into each kind.
key_findings.locator: Methods/Materials, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Alternative causes found in suspected drug deaths were Adelson class I processes, catastrophic and fatal regardless of other conditions; examples given are pulmonary emboli, a ruptured gastric ulcer, a ruptured berry aneurysm without stimulants in the body, and a compressive subdural haematoma with a manner of homicide.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 190, right column; examples on p. 191)
key_findings.note: Examples only; no counts by cause.

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: the cause of death determined by the assigned forensic pathologist was assumed correct; illicit drugs present at the time of death were taken as at least contributing to death except in deaths with class I natural or traumatic processes; the sample reflects western North Carolina only.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Toxicology screened for over-the-counter, prescription and illicit drugs by GC-MS, GC-NPD and targeted high-resolution LC-MS, with confirmation and quantitation by LC-MS-MS; point-of-care qualitative urine drug screens were not used. Specimen types and sites are not stated and no concentrations are reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods/Materials, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 gives the yearly percentage of drug-related deaths in the region in which each of four illicit drugs was 'involved', 2016 to 2021: heroin 23, 19, 18, 20, 10, 5; fentanyl 10, 29, 44, 51, 54, 77; methamphetamine 13, 16, 25, 23, 30, 40; cocaine 17, 19, 18, 21, 15, 22. The text says fentanyl and, to a lesser degree, methamphetamine increased significantly and cocaine stayed consistent.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2; Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Values are printed as data labels in the figure image (read on a 300-dpi rendering; they are not in the PDF text layer). The denominator of each percentage and the meaning of 'involved' (detected, or listed as a cause) are not stated; no test is reported.

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 gives the yearly number of drug-related deaths at the centre, 2016 to 2021: 316, 336, 369, 334, 530 and 720; and nationally: 63,600, 70,237, 67,367, 62,172, 93,665 and 107,622.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1
key_findings.note: Data labels in the figure image (read on a 300-dpi rendering; not in the text layer). No source is given for the national values; the regional values sum to 2,605 (editors' arithmetic), not the 2,569 final drug-related cases of Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Studies summarized in the Discussion: one found 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths had toxicology that explained nothing and another cause (Andrew and Duval); in another, three pathologists blind to internal findings determined cause and manner correctly in 75% to 80% of 60 cases selected from 629 (Dye et al.); a third found external examination, toxicology and/or post-mortem CT could cut standard autopsies by two-thirds in a selected high-risk group (Fryer et al.).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the primary studies were not read.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the false-positive rate was almost 10%, enough cases to matter for misclassification; that post-mortem CT might reduce the risk if offices had access to it; and that the data are meant as information, not to sway offices toward one practice.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Discussion, 4th paragraph (begins p. 191)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says 2,569 cases were suspected to be drug-related at referral and 387 were not; Table 1 shows 2,719 suspected and 237 not suspected, and 2,569 and 387 are the totals of final drug-related and non-drug causes.
reporting_issues.consequence: Group sizes must be taken from Table 1; the printed rates reproduce only from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The false-negative rate is defined in words as the proportion of negative preliminary findings that were true overdose deaths (115/237 = 48.5%, editors' calculation), but the formula and the printed value use all final drug-related cases as the denominator (115/2,569 = 4.48%). The false-positive rate (265/2,719) is 1 minus the positive predictive value, not 1 minus specificity (265/387 = 68.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels invite misreading. The 4.48% hides that nearly half of the deaths not suspected were drug-related; the 9.75% is not a conventional false-positive rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the investigators correctly predicted a suspected drug-related fatality before autopsy in more than 95% of cases, which is the sensitivity read as overall accuracy; the timing of suspicion is described as 'at autopsy' for the four groups but 'upon referral' in the definitions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Overall agreement was 87.1% and the positive predictive value 90.3% (editors' calculations); the 95% figure should not be cited as prediction accuracy.

reporting_issues.issue: The false-positive category combines deaths with negative toxicology and deaths with drugs present but another cause, and the split is not reported, although the paper presents the whole 9.75% as the deaths that could have been misclassified without autopsy.
reporting_issues.consequence: Within the 2,719 suspected deaths, 9.75% is an upper bound of unknown distance for what external examination with toxicology would misattribute. The paper does not give the split needed to estimate that share, nor does this percentage bound misattribution among the 237 initially unsuspected deaths or outside this selected series.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1's regional counts sum to 2,605, against 2,569 final drug-related deaths in Table 1, and its national counts have no stated source; the 2019 national value (62,172) differs from the 70,630 for 2019 that Smiley-McDonald et al. (2025, p. 542) give from NCHS data, while the 2017 and 2018 values agree with Davis et al. (2020, p. 152) and Smiley-McDonald et al. (2025).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure's numbers should not be cited as official counts; the regional difference may reflect the excluded intentional overdoses or minors, which the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2's trends are called significant with no test, heroin is said to have declined steadily though 2019 (20%) is above 2018 (18%), and the denominators of the percentages are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The yearly shares may be cited as descriptive figures from the figure labels, not as tested trends.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction gives national deaths 'in 2021 alone' (more than 100,000, over 70,000 involving synthetic opioids) from a CDC press release dated 17 November 2021 (reference 12), before the year had ended.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure refers to a 12-month period other than calendar 2021; cite national counts from NCHS reports, not from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states the purpose but reports no results, and the methods do not say how the suspicion criteria were combined or who classified the cases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study cannot be judged from its abstract; the classification step cannot be reproduced.

reporting_issues.issue: The opening Results prose labels 2,569/387 as preliminary groups, but these are Table 1 final-cause column margins. Table 1 preliminary rows and the component counts instead give 2,719 suspected and 237 unsuspected.
reporting_issues.page: p. 190, opening Results and Table 1; p. 192, limitations
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table’s 2×2 and supported row margins. The final assigned cause is assumed correct, not independently validated. The 265/2,719 upper-limit interpretation concerns suspected cases only and is not a direct test of external examination plus toxicology.

design_detail: Compilation that the authors call a meta-analysis: published post-mortem drug concentrations in specimens other than blood and urine, found by keyword searching and reference lists (no database or dates named), combined with results from the authors' laboratory, the national post-mortem toxicology database of the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare (THL), 2000–2018. It covers the 50 compounds (49 drugs and the metabolite norbuprenorphine) most often quantified in non-blood specimens in that database; drugs of abuse without an available or reasonable normal range were excluded, so there is no cocaine, MDMA or cannabinoid, while amphetamine, methamphetamine, morphine, codeine, fentanyl, methadone, oxycodone, buprenorphine, tramadol and several benzodiazepines are included. Summaries: Table 2, each drug's median concentration in each specimen divided by the median femoral-blood concentration reported by Launiainen & Ojanperä (2014), unpaired; Table 3, the median of within-case specimen-to-femoral ratios where a literature source gave both values (paired, literature only); Tables 4–5, ratios or means adopted from sources that reported only aggregates. Across-drug summaries are means, number-weighted means, medians and, in Table 2, medians rescaled so that femoral blood equals 1. No weighting by study, intervals, heterogeneity statistics, risk-of-bias assessment or sensitivity analysis.
can_establish: Descriptive median concentrations in alternative post-mortem specimens relative to femoral blood for the compounds tabulated, from a large compilation of literature cases and laboratory data; and, from the paired within-case data (Table 3), that the available per-drug median ratios span more than tenfold in all ten specimen types. This is between-drug variation, not the spread of ratios within one drug or a prediction for an individual death.
cannot_establish: How far a single case can deviate from a median ratio (no ranges, percentiles or intervals are given); whether ratios differ between poisoning and other deaths or with time since death (neither was classified); whether the literature compiled is complete or representative (no systematic search, no appraisal of sources); or anything about the drugs left out, including cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids.

sample.recruitment: Literature: studies and case reports giving post-mortem drug concentrations in specimens other than blood or urine, found with keywords such as post-mortem, concentration, tissue, matrix and specimen and by following references (PDF p. 4). Own data: THL's national post-mortem toxicology database, with toxicology in about 6,500 deaths a year, requested by the forensic pathologist performing the medico-legal investigation (PDF p. 4), and analyses in 118,990 cases in 2000–2018; for the 50 drugs, 1,442 results in non-blood specimens (PDF p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Drugs: the 50 with the most quantitative results in specimens other than post-mortem blood, urine or vitreous humour in the THL database; drugs of abuse for which a normal range is not available or reasonable were excluded (PDF p. 4). Sources: studies presenting only blood or urine concentrations were excluded (PDF p. 4). No criteria on cause of death, time since death, sampling site, analytical method, language or date; the reference list runs from 1964 (ref. 102, PDF p. 17) to 2018 and includes German-language case reports (e.g. refs 89–91 and 95, PDF p. 16).
sample.demographics: Not reported: the age, sex and cause of death of the compiled cases are not given.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The numbers of records screened and excluded are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Published poisoning cases affect the compilation: in Table 2 the compiled cases' femoral-blood concentrations had a median ratio of 3.35 (mean 10.55) to the reference medians regardless of cause of death, and reached 95.0 for metoprolol and 111.5 for propranolol (PDF pp. 42–43). The authors say some studies focus on intoxications while others ignore cause of death; they could not classify causes, so a numerical majority of poisoning cases is not established (PDF pp. 7–8). The laboratory's own non-blood results come from a service that analyses other matrices when post-mortem blood is not available (PDF p. 5), which the Introduction associates with decomposed, burned or otherwise destroyed bodies (PDF p. 2). Table 2 uses unpaired medians and an external all-cause reference; case selection can therefore contribute to differences attributed to specimens.

exposure.measurement: Concentrations as reported by each source; the analytical methods of the literature sources are not recorded. THL data: liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry with electrospray ionization; samples taken at autopsies performed on average 7 days after death and stored refrigerated until analysis (PDF p. 4). Whether morphine results are free or total (including conjugated) morphine is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Co-administration of other drugs is named as a source of variation but was mostly not reported by the sources and was not analysed (PDF pp. 6, 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (deaths). Time since death was not always given in the sources and can range from a few hours to months (PDF p. 8); THL autopsies took place on average 7 days after death (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: Femoral blood as the reference specimen: in Table 2, the median femoral-blood concentration regardless of cause of death from Launiainen & Ojanperä (2014), listed in Table 1; in Table 3, the femoral-blood concentration measured in the same case.
comparison.matching: Within-case pairing in Table 3 only (4,960 results from literature sources).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cause of death and post-mortem interval were not always given, preventing classification by cause; co-administration, possible intoxication, metabolism and genetic background, age, diseases and circumstances during death were mostly not given. Sampling site and procedure could vary from case to case; no frequency is supplied for these variations (PDF pp. 7–8).

outcomes.instruments: Ratio of the drug concentration in other blood (such as cardiac blood), vitreous humour, skeletal muscle, liver, kidney, brain, heart, lung, spleen and bile to that in femoral blood, by drug (Tables 2–5); across-drug summaries as mean, number-weighted ('adjusted') mean, median and, in Table 2, median rescaled so that femoral blood equals 1 ('adjusted median') (PDF pp. 43–44).
outcomes.validity_norms: Femoral blood is treated as the reference matrix. The Table 2 denominators are medians across all causes of death, while the numerators come mostly from poisoning case literature; rescaling to femoral blood equal to 1 assumes the same case-mix inflation for every specimen, which is not tested.
outcomes.operationalization: A specimen is judged more useful for quantitative interpretation the closer its median ratio is to that of femoral blood; the recommended order of specimens when femoral blood is unavailable is presented as following from this (PDF p. 7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests). A correlation of the ratios with volume of distribution, half-life and log P was examined, but neither the method nor the data are shown (PDF p. 6).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; duplicate screening or data extraction is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Medians across the per-drug medians of paired within-case ratios (Table 3, PDF p. 44), with the number of results: other blood 1.27 (576), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), muscle 0.99 (385), liver 5.06 (1,697), kidney 2.86 (401), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), bile 5.52 (537); number-weighted means 1.52, 0.53, 1.09, 8.67, 3.99, 2.33, 4.52, 9.90, 10.35 and 66.99. Unpaired rescaled medians (Table 2, PDF p. 43): other blood 1.57, vitreous humour 0.30, muscle 0.54, liver 6.30, kidney 4.12, brain 2.21, heart 2.50, lung 4.86, spleen 2.66, bile 8.37. Between drugs (Table 3): liver from 0.95 (pregabalin, 3 results) to 54.29 (sertraline, 29); vitreous humour from 0.03 (sertraline, 11) to 1.59 (fentanyl, 6); other blood from 0.90 (hydroxyzine, 6) to 14.61 (chloroquine, 2). No ranges, percentiles or confidence intervals are given for any drug or specimen.
analysis.selective_reporting: The correlation with pharmacokinetic parameters is reported only as data not shown (PDF p. 6); no per-case or per-source values or spreads are given. The authors call the unpaired Table 2 their main result (PDF p. 6) rather than the paired Table 3.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Many drug–specimen cells rest on one to three results (for example, in Table 3, heart for morphine and spleen for fentanyl, one result each); the authors call such ratios only suggestive (PDF p. 8).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across drugs, the paired data put the median specimen-to-femoral ratio near 1 for muscle (0.99) and other blood (1.27), at about half for vitreous humour (0.45), near 2 for brain (1.84) and heart (2.03), and between 2.9 and 5.5 for kidney, lung, spleen, liver and bile, with tenfold or larger differences between drugs in all ten specimen types; how far individual cases scatter around these medians is not reported. These are ranges across the available drug-specific medians, not within-drug ranges.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract and Conclusions present a meta-analysis and group vitreous humour with specimens whose concentrations are similar to femoral blood, slightly lower (PDF pp. 2, 8), although the across-drug summary was about a half (paired) to a third (unpaired) of femoral blood. The recommended order (other blood, muscle, vitreous humour, brain, heart, spleen, kidney, liver, bile; PDF pp. 2, 7, 8) is linked to closeness to femoral blood without a defined distance metric or predictive validation, and omits lung despite tabulating it. On a multiplicative scale, brain 1.84 and heart 2.03 are closer to 1 than vitreous 0.45 (1/0.45 = 2.22); on an absolute-difference scale vitreous is closer. The editors' multiplicative comparison therefore does not uniquely disprove the order. The authors call unpaired Table 2 the main result and paired Table 3 very similar (PDF p. 6); across-drug summaries resemble each other, but drug-level comparisons can differ more than tenfold (codeine other blood: 6.4/0.4 = 16 from Table 2 against paired median 1.16 in Table 3). The Introduction's aim of distinguishing normal and fatal concentrations in alternative specimens (PDF p. 3) could not be pursued because cause of death could not be classified (PDF p. 8). The list of drugs with the highest ratios (PDF p. 7) can partly reflect how far literature cases' femoral blood exceeded the external reference.

timeline.event: Pounder & Jones, four-case series showing several-fold site differences in post-mortem blood; one of this compilation's doxepin sources (ref. 180).

Leikin & Watson's narrative review lists possible transformation or redistribution for 99 entries (98 distinct labels), with numeric parentheses for 82 including a nicotine/cotinine annotation. For 17 of 24 shared labels its value exceeds 1.10 times this compilation's other-blood/femoral median, while 3 are below 1/1.10 times it and 4 fall between those bounds. The matrices and source sets differ: other blood is not only cardiac, and Leikin's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral. This is a descriptive cross-source comparison, not a paired replication or validated correction.
Launiainen & Ojanperä, source of the femoral-blood medians regardless of cause of death that form the Table 2 denominators and Table 1 (not read by this reader).
Borra et al., a review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: A widely usable lookup of typical specimen-to-femoral ratios for medicines, of which the paired Table 3 is the better-founded part. It gives no spread for any ratio, does not separate poisoning from other deaths and excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids. The femoral-blood reference study it depends on (Launiainen & Ojanperä 2014) and the 2026 review (Borra et al.) are on the reading list.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective multi-centre post-mortem study taking femoral blood and each alternative specimen in the same consecutive deaths, recording cause of death, time since death and storage, analysed with one validated method, and reporting for each drug the full spread of within-case ratios (for example a 90% prediction interval) separately for poisonings and other deaths; and the same for cocaine, MDMA, cannabinoids and newer synthetic drugs, which this compilation excludes.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 is applied by analogy, because the paper presents itself as a meta-analysis of literature data (as with Strömmer 2020, senior decision 74); items written for reviews of interventions are read for a compilation of concentration ratios. All seven critical items are unmet, which gives critically low confidence. This is a judgment on how far the pooled ratios can be trusted as unbiased summaries, not on the paper's usefulness: it is a large, transparent table of typical values. Citable for: typical (median) ratios of drug concentrations in alternative post-mortem specimens to femoral blood, preferably the paired values of Table 3 with their numbers of results; the wide variation between drugs; the authors' recommended order of specimens, as their recommendation. Not citable for: the ratio to expect in an individual case, differences between fatal and non-fatal concentrations, drugs not included (cocaine, MDMA, cannabinoids), or the recommended order as an evidence-based ranking.

key_findings.finding: The compilation comprises 10,993 analytical results from 5,375 post-mortem cases in 388 studies, including results from the authors' laboratory database (2000–2018), for 50 commonly used drugs in femoral blood, other blood (such as cardiac blood), vitreous humour, muscle, liver, kidney, brain, heart, lung, spleen and bile.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; also Material and Methods, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Where a literature source gave the femoral-blood concentration of the same case, the authors calculated within-case ratios and then per-drug medians. The median across those drug-specific medians was: other blood 1.27, vitreous humour 0.45, muscle 0.99, liver 5.06, kidney 2.86, brain 1.84, heart 2.03, lung 3.69, spleen 4.25 and bile 5.52 (number of results 576, 356, 385, 1,697, 401, 565, 185, 187, 71 and 537). The authors report 4,960 results; the printed N columns sum to that figure, including one oxazepam brain result with no printed ratio. These across-drug summaries are not medians of one pooled set of all individual cases.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion, 6th paragraph (PDF p. 6); Table 3, rows Median and Adjusted mean (PDF p. 44)

key_findings.finding: Unpaired comparison: each specimen's median concentration divided by the reference median femoral-blood concentration (reference 7, Launiainen & Ojanperä), then rescaled so that femoral blood equals 1, gave other blood 1.57, vitreous humour 0.30, muscle 0.54, liver 6.30, kidney 4.12, brain 2.21, heart 2.50, lung 4.86, spleen 2.66 and bile 8.37. Before rescaling, femoral blood in the compiled cases had a median ratio of 3.35 (mean 10.55) to the reference medians.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows mean, median and adjusted median; Results and discussion, 5th paragraph (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: The text gives brain as 2.11 (PDF p. 6); the table's 2.21 matches 7.42 divided by 3.35 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Ratios vary widely between drugs (Table 3, number of results in brackets): liver from 0.95 (pregabalin, 3) and 1.25 (tramadol, 11) to 54.29 (sertraline, 29) and 41.00 (lidocaine, 41); vitreous humour from 0.03 (sertraline, 11) and 0.15 (amitriptyline, 20) to 1.59 (fentanyl, 6) and 1.44 (oxycodone, 8); muscle from 0.16 (codeine, 14) to 7.24 (clozapine, 1); other blood from 0.90 (hydroxyzine, 6) to 14.61 (chloroquine, 2); bile up to 616.67 (buprenorphine, 19) and 1094 (norbuprenorphine, 13). Ephedrine (1 result) shares the vitreous minimum of 0.03 with sertraline. Across the available drug-specific medians, maximum/minimum exceeds ten in every specimen type; several extremes rest on one or two results and no within-drug spread is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Opioids, paired medians (Table 3, number of results in brackets): morphine other blood 1.26 (53), vitreous humour 0.40 (120), muscle 1.00 (135), liver 2.11 (339), kidney 4.39 (43), brain 0.51 (205), lung 1.60 (40), bile 38.69 (158); codeine other blood 1.16 (12), vitreous 1.00 (20), muscle 0.16 (14), liver 2.11 (61), bile 5.52 (46); fentanyl other blood 1.15 (33), vitreous 1.59 (6), liver 6.18 (120), heart 5.12 (14), bile 3.51 (20); methadone other blood 1.17 (13), muscle 0.73 (11), liver 5.00 (46), brain 1.82 (19), bile 5.94 (14); oxycodone other blood 1.19 (16), vitreous 1.44 (8), liver 1.66 (30), bile 5.64 (14); buprenorphine liver 11.42 (8), bile 616.67 (19).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Morphine, Codeine, Fentanyl, Methadone, Oxycodone and Buprenorphine
key_findings.note: Whether morphine values are free or total morphine is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Amphetamines and benzodiazepines, paired medians (Table 3, number of results in brackets): amphetamine other blood 1.43 (6), vitreous humour 1.11 (3), muscle 0.75 (5), liver 3.50 (51), brain 1.70 (25); methamphetamine other blood 1.50 (9), vitreous 0.89 (4), muscle 1.09 (9), liver 3.48 (63), kidney 2.27 (17), brain 2.64 (34); diazepam other blood 0.95 (11), muscle 0.56 (9), liver 3.70 (22); alprazolam other blood 1.23 (2), vitreous 0.26 (2), liver 4.88 (15).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows Amphetamine, Methamphetamine, Diazepam and Alprazolam

key_findings.finding: Drugs of abuse for which a normal range is not available or reasonable were excluded; the 50 compounds (49 drugs and norbuprenorphine) include amphetamine, methamphetamine, opioids and benzodiazepines but no cocaine, MDMA or cannabinoid.
key_findings.locator: Material and Methods, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 1 (PDF p. 41)

key_findings.finding: The authors report no apparent correlation between the ratios and volume of distribution, half-life or log P in any specimen, and conclude that these parameters cannot predict tissue-to-femoral ratios; the data are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: When femoral blood is unavailable, the authors recommend this order of specimens for quantitative analysis: other blood, muscle, vitreous humour, brain, heart, spleen, kidney, liver, bile. Liver remains suitable for screening but is not recommended for quantitation, bile ratios are high and hard to interpret, and in probable fatal intoxication all available specimens should be measured.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs (PDF p. 7); Conclusions, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 8); also Abstract (PDF p. 2)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: cases could not be classified by cause of death because it was not always given; time since death was not always given and can range from hours to months; co-ingestion, metabolism and genetic background, age, disease and circumstances of death were mostly unreported; some drug–specimen cells have few results, making those ratios only suggestive; sampling site and procedure varied between cases.
key_findings.locator: Limitations (one paragraph, PDF p. 7, continuing on PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Compounds with the highest mean ratios regardless of specimen, for which the authors advise caution in judging possible intoxication: buprenorphine, chloroquine, propranolol, orphenadrine, metoprolol, norbuprenorphine, clozapine, zopiclone, chlorpromazine, verapamil, hydroxyzine, oxazepam, temazepam, trimipramine and diltiazem.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion, 8th paragraph
key_findings.note: The metric is not defined and verapamil is listed twice. For several of these drugs the literature cases' own femoral blood was far above the reference median in Table 2 (propranolol 111.5, metoprolol 95.0, chloroquine 24.6; PDF p. 42 and 43), so the high ratios partly reflect case selection.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the rescaled median for brain as 2.11, while Table 2 gives 2.21.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value is consistent with the brain median of 7.42 divided by the femoral median of 3.35 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Table 3 says its data are also included in Table 2, but Table 3 has rows for ephedrine and moclobemide, which appear in neither Table 1 nor Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The caption overstates the overlap: Tables 2 and 3 cover slightly different compound sets (ephedrine and moclobemide replace bisoprolol and warfarin in Table 3), so their across-drug summaries do not refer to identical sets. This does not by itself show that the within-case ratios are wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the paired ratios of Table 3 very similar to those of Table 2 (PDF p. 6), but for single drugs the unpaired Table 2 implies very different ratios: codeine other blood 6.4 and femoral blood 0.4 in Table 2, but a paired median of 1.16 in Table 3; codeine muscle 1.6 and femoral blood 0.4, but a paired 0.16; methamphetamine vitreous humour 23.6 and femoral blood 3.8, but a paired 0.89 (4 results in each table).
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-level ratios should be taken from Table 3 with its numbers of results, not from Table 2 (editors' calculation of the Table 2 contrasts: about 16, 4 and 6 times femoral blood); the across-drug summaries of Table 2 carry the same case-mix problem.

reporting_issues.issue: Sources disagree for the same drug and specimen without comment: amitriptyline vitreous humour 2.1 (mean of 40 cases, Table 4) against 0.15 (median of 20 results, Table 3), and amitriptyline liver 2.5 (Table 4) against 13.77 (Table 3); the text notes only that the Table 4 liver value is surprisingly low.
reporting_issues.consequence: Between-source heterogeneity is large and unexamined; single-drug values rest on whichever sources happened to be found.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists quetiapine with a post-mortem femoral-blood mean of 0.62 mg/L and a median of 0.9 mg/L, a median above the mean, which is unusual for concentration data; the protein-binding column, headed in per cent, prints fractions (for example 0.94).
reporting_issues.consequence: The fractional protein-binding values do not match the percentage heading. A mean below a median is mathematically possible, so the quetiapine pair alone does not establish a transcription error; it remains worth checking against Launiainen & Ojanperä 2014 because the reference median sets its Table 2 denominators. No corrected value is inferred from the present manuscript.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list uses the number 392 twice (Jantos & Skopp 2013 on methadone; Houts et al. 1998, Courtroom Toxicology), and Table 5 cites 392 for both methadone and paracetamol; the 388 studies of the Abstract cannot be matched to the numbered list, which mixes background and data sources.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sources behind individual table cells can only be traced approximately.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints N = 0 with no ratio for ephedrine other blood and oxazepam kidney, and N = 1 with no ratio for oxazepam brain.
reporting_issues.consequence: N = 0 with an empty ratio can simply mean no observations; the positive oxazepam brain count without a value is an unresolved reporting omission. The N columns sum to the reported 4,960, but that does not supply the missing ratio or establish a corrected count.

disagreements.first_pass: Published cases are mostly fatal poisonings: in Table 2 the femoral-blood concentrations of the compiled cases had a median ratio of 3.35 (mean 10.55) to the reference medians, which were medians regardless of cause of death, and reached 95.0 for metoprolol and 111.5 for propranolol (PDF pp. 42–43); the authors acknowledge that the literature centres on intoxications (PDF pp. 7–8). In Table 2 each specimen's median comes from a different set of cases, so the unpaired ratios mix differences in case selection with differences between specimens.

The authors say some studies focus on intoxications while others ignore cause of death; they could not classify causes, so a numerical majority of poisoning cases is not established (PDF pp. 7–8). disagreements.first_pass: The Abstract and Conclusions present a meta-analysis and group vitreous humour with the specimens whose concentrations are similar to femoral blood, slightly lower (PDF pp. 2, 8), although its typical concentration was about a half (paired) to a third (unpaired) of femoral blood. The recommended order (other blood, muscle, vitreous humour, brain, heart, spleen, kidney, liver, bile; PDF pp. 2, 7, 8) is said to follow from closeness to femoral blood, but in ratio terms brain and heart are closer than vitreous humour in both tables (editors' calculation: Table 3, brain 1.84-fold and heart 2.03-fold above against vitreous 2.2-fold below), and lung, also tabulated, is left out. The authors call the unpaired Table 2 the main result and the paired Table 3 very similar (PDF p. 6); across drugs the summaries are similar, but drug by drug they can differ more than tenfold (codeine, other blood: 16 times femoral blood in Table 2 against a paired median of 1.16 in Table 3; editors' calculation). The Introduction's aim of understanding the difference between normal and fatal concentrations in alternative specimens (PDF p. 3) could not be pursued, because cause of death could not be classified (PDF p. 8). The list of drugs with the highest ratios (PDF p. 7) partly reflects how far the literature cases' own femoral blood exceeded the reference medians.
disagreements.reviewer: Own review qualifies a metric-dependent criticism; second reader agrees substantial gap, which is retained.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 405 (ChatGPT, OpenAI; adjudicator): The Abstract and Conclusions present a meta-analysis and group vitreous humour with specimens whose concentrations are similar to femoral blood, slightly lower (PDF pp. 2, 8), although the across-drug summary was about a half (paired) to a third (unpaired) of femoral blood. The recommended order (other blood, muscle, vitreous humour, brain, heart, spleen, kidney, liver, bile; PDF pp. 2, 7, 8) is linked to closeness to femoral blood without a defined distance metric or predictive validation, and omits lung despite tabulating it. On a multiplicative scale, brain 1.84 and heart 2.03 are closer to 1 than vitreous 0.45 (1/0.45 = 2.22); on an absolute-difference scale vitreous is closer. The editors' multiplicative comparison therefore does not uniquely disprove the order. The authors call unpaired Table 2 the main result and paired Table 3 very similar (PDF p. 6); across-drug summaries resemble each other, but drug-level comparisons can differ more than tenfold (codeine other blood: 6.4/0.4 = 16 from Table 2 against paired median 1.16 in Table 3). The Introduction's aim of distinguishing normal and fatal concentrations in alternative specimens (PDF p. 3) could not be pursued because cause of death could not be classified (PDF p. 8). The list of drugs with the highest ratios (PDF p. 7) can partly reflect how far literature cases' femoral blood exceeded the external reference. Source check: PDF pp. 2–8; Tables 2–3; a405/ketola_calculations.json.

design_detail: Record-linkage comparison of two state sources of poisoning deaths among New Mexico residents in 1995–1998. Source 1: vital statistics mortality files (death certificates; underlying cause coded in ICD-9 by nosologists trained by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) in the state Office of Vital Records and Health Statistics; includes residents who died in another state). Source 2: the database of the statewide Office of the Medical Investigator (OMI), searched by OMI 'Manner of Death' codes that investigators assign when entering the death-certificate information developed by pathologists. Records were linked manually and deterministically (date of death, then age, sex, race or ethnicity and name; then allowing 1 day, 1 year and slight spelling differences), and unmatched poisonings were looked for among non-poisoning deaths in the other source. Three categories were counted four ways (vital statistics; OMI; both; either): all poisoning (ICD-9 305, E850–E869, E950–E952, E962, E980–E982), unintentional illicit drug overdose (E850.0, E854.2, E855.2, E858.8) and unintentional heroin overdose (E850.0, E858.8), the last two with and without E858.8, the code for accidental poisoning by 'other drugs' used when a certificate names drugs of different types. NCHS public-use multiple-cause files for 1995–1998, which could not be linked to individual records, showed which drug codes accompanied E858.8 in New Mexico and the US. Age-adjusted rates (1940 US standard) for 1989–1998. Descriptive; no reference standard and no statistical tests.
can_establish: How far two New Mexico sources agreed on which deaths of residents were poisonings, unintentional illicit drug overdoses and unintentional heroin overdoses in 1995–1998, why the discordant poisoning deaths differed (out-of-state deaths, deaths not reported to the medical investigator, certificate wording and coding rules), and how much the multi-drug code E858.8 changes subcategory counts.
cannot_establish: Which source was right about any discordant death (no independent review); the true number of heroin deaths (ICD-9 has no heroin-specific code and the OMI heroin category is not defined in the paper); how many deaths both sources missed; how far including E858.8 overcounts heroin deaths beyond the 55.6% that matched OMI morphine deaths; or whether the results hold under ICD-10 (in use from 1999) or in states without a centralized medical examiner.

sample.recruitment: Records: New Mexico vital statistics mortality files and the OMI database; all poisoning deaths of New Mexico residents occurring in 1995–1998 (pp. 274–275).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Deaths of New Mexico residents, including out-of-state deaths in vital statistics. The OMI may investigate all sudden, unexplained, suspicious, violent or unattended deaths in New Mexico except within certain tribal and federal jurisdictions (Indian reservations and military installations), where it is often invited (p. 274). 'Poisoning' covers all agents, not drugs only: the definition takes ICD-9 305, E850–E869, E950–E952, E962 and E980–E982, and the authors describe poisoning as involving agents as diverse as carbon monoxide, alcohol, prescription drugs and drugs such as heroin and cocaine (Introduction, 3rd paragraph, and Materials and Methods › Definitions, 1st paragraph, p. 274); 7 of the 17 OMI poisonings coded as other injuries in vital statistics were fire-related (p. 276).
sample.demographics: Poisoning death rates 1995–1998: highest at ages 35–44 (33.5 per 100,000 person-years), then 25–34 (28.1); White Hispanic 20.8, White non-Hispanic 12.5, Native American 8.1 (lowest); men 22.2 against women 7.8 (sex and race or ethnicity rates age-adjusted). Intent: 78.3% unintentional, 21.2% suicide, 0.3% homicide, 0.2% undetermined (p. 275).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). The 24 out-of-state deaths among the discordant vital-statistics poisonings were not reviewed further.
sample.selection_effects: One state with a centralized medical examiner, which the authors expect to capture more injury deaths than non-centralized medical examiner or coroner systems; deaths on tribal and federal land fall outside OMI jurisdiction unless it is invited. The authors work for the agencies that produce both sources.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. Vital statistics: the certifier's two-part cause-of-death section, coded by nosologists under explicit rules: 'use' or 'abuse' on the certificate gives ICD-9 305 (nondependent abuse of drugs); 'overdose', 'intoxication', 'toxicity' or 'poisoning' gives an external-cause E-code; a single drug in part I is coded as that drug even if part II lists others; several drugs of one type in part I are coded as that type (e.g., codeine, heroin and morphine as opiates, E850.0 when accidental); drugs of different types in part I are coded as E858.8 when accidental; drug plus alcohol is coded by the drug, alcohol alone in part I as alcohol; a natural condition in part I with a drug in part II is coded as the natural condition unless it is a direct sequel of drug use (p. 274). OMI: for all deaths suspected to be due to drugs, toxins or poisons a full autopsy and toxicological evaluation is carried out by policy (Toxicology Bureau of the New Mexico Scientific Laboratory Division; screening findings confirmed, e.g., by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry; antemortem specimens obtained when the person died after hospitalization), and pathologists consult the toxicologists (p. 274). The share of deaths actually autopsied and tested is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the question: accidental poisonings naming drugs of different types are coded E858.8, which hides the drugs in underlying-cause data. Multiple-cause codes 965.0 (opiates and related narcotics), 968.5 (surface and infiltration anaesthetics, including cocaine) and 969.7 (psychostimulants, including amphetamines) were used to see what lay behind E858.8.

comparison.controls: The two sources compared with each other. Percentages are of the deaths found in either source ('captured by either database'), not of an independent reference.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (record linkage on identifiers).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths).

outcomes.instruments: Counts by year and in total for each source, both and either (Tables 1–3, pp. 276–277); review of discordant poisoning deaths (p. 276); shares of E858.8 deaths matched to OMI drug codes (p. 276); multiple-cause code frequencies (pp. 276–277); age-adjusted rates (Figure 1, p. 276).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither source is validated; OMI Manner of Death codes were developed for data retrieval, and the OMI definitions of illicit drug and heroin overdose are not given.
outcomes.operationalization: Categories as in the design; a death is 'captured' by a source if it is in that source's category, among deaths in either source's category.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; who linked and reviewed the records is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Poisoning: vital statistics 1,046 and OMI 1,046 of 1,105 deaths in either source (94.7% each); both 987 (89.3%). Discordant vital-statistics poisonings (59): 24 out of state; of the other 35, 13 (37.1%) not reported to the OMI, 15 (42.8%) OMI natural deaths coded 305 in vital statistics, 2 miscoded as non-poisoning by the OMI, 3 undetermined-intent poisonings classed otherwise by the OMI, 2 unintentional injuries of unspecified cause in the OMI. Discordant OMI poisonings (59): 4 (6.8%) not found in vital statistics, 1 revised OMI certificate not recoded, 17 (28.8%) coded as other injuries, 37 (62.7%) coded as natural deaths, 16 (43.2%) of these as heart disease (ICD-9 420–429). Illicit drug overdose with E858.8: vital statistics 609, OMI 526, both 494, either 640 (95.2%, 82.2%, 77.2%); without E858.8: vital statistics 339, both 277, either 480 (70.6%). Heroin overdose with E858.8: vital statistics 537, OMI 360, both 351, either 537 (100%, 67.0%, 65.4%); without E858.8: vital statistics 273, both 216, either 416. E858.8 deaths matched to an OMI death with a drug code for morphine, cocaine and/or methamphetamine: 72%; to an OMI illicit drug overdose with a morphine code: 55.6%. E858.8 deaths with multiple-cause code 965.0, 968.5 and/or 969.7: 90% New Mexico, 88% US; with 965.0: 85% and 83%. Editors' calculations: the number of E858.8 deaths is not printed; Tables 2 and 3 imply 270 and 264; Table 3's union omits 9 OMI-only heroin deaths (reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Rates age-adjusted to the 1940 US standard population; no other adjustment.
analysis.selective_reporting: Discordant illicit drug and heroin deaths are not reviewed case by case as the poisoning deaths were; the number of E858.8 deaths and the OMI heroin definition are not given.
analysis.power: Not applicable (counts).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Linking New Mexico vital statistics and medical examiner (OMI) records for residents' poisoning deaths in 1995–1998, each source alone held 1,046 of the 1,105 deaths found in either (94.7%), and 987 (89.3%) were in both. Discordance ran both ways: of 59 vital-statistics poisonings not classed as poisonings by the OMI, 24 were out-of-state deaths, 13 were never reported to the OMI and 15 were OMI natural deaths that vital statistics coded to nondependent abuse of drugs (ICD-9 305, the code the coding rules give when 'use' or 'abuse' is written on the certificate; the certificates' words are not reported); of 59 OMI poisonings not classed as poisonings in vital statistics, 37 had been coded as natural deaths (typically with poisoning mentioned only in part II of the certificate) and 17 as other injuries. Subcategory counts hinge on E858.8: with it, vital statistics held 95.2% of illicit drug and 100% of heroin deaths found in either source, the OMI 82.2% and 67.0%; without it, vital statistics held 70.6% of illicit drug deaths (as printed).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract says each source alone captured smaller percentages of illicit drug and heroin deaths; this holds for the OMI and, for vital statistics, only without E858.8 (reporting issue 5). (2) 'Captured' measures overlap with the union of two imperfect definitions, not accuracy: ICD-9 has no heroin-specific code, as the authors concede (p. 278); the vital-statistics heroin definition (E850.0 or E858.8) admits other opiates and mixtures; and 44.4% of E858.8 deaths did not match an OMI illicit drug overdose with a morphine code (editors' calculation from 55.6%), so the union contains deaths that were not heroin deaths and the OMI's 67.0% understates its completeness by an unknown amount. (3) The recommendation to include E858.8 in illicit drug and heroin definitions (p. 278) trades undercounting for overcounting; by the paper's own figures 10–12% of E858.8 deaths are not due to illicit drugs, and more are not due to heroin, which the Discussion does not weigh. (4) 'Illicit drugs' in the multiple-cause analysis are codes 965.0, 968.5 and 969.7, which by the paper's own descriptions include opiates and related narcotics, surface and infiltration anaesthetics and psychostimulants, so the 90% and 88% are upper bounds for illicit drugs. (5) The Results' statement that all three New Mexico rates were substantially higher than the US poisoning rate after 1993 does not fit Figure 1 for heroin (reporting issue 6).

timeline.event: Soslow and Wolf (Massachusetts, ref 10) and, in 1994, Dijkhuis et al. (ref 9): cited for medical examiner records capturing an inadequate share of poisoning and injury deaths (p. 274); not read for this card.

Moolenaar et al. (ref 11): New Mexico carbon monoxide deaths 1980–1988, medical examiner against national mortality data; cited for New Mexico's centralized medical examiner capturing most injury deaths (p. 274); not read for this card.
Hoppe-Roberts et al. (ref 6): poison control centre reports capture only 5% of poisoning deaths, as cited (p. 274); not read for this card.
Ossiander: textual cause-of-death data used to study drug poisoning deaths; listed for this page, not read for this card.

Horon et al. (Maryland, 2012–2015; card sc_horon_2018): certificates naming heroin identified 1,130 overdose deaths against 2,182 found by a protocol adding toxicology markers and scene evidence from the medical examiner's records.

Stam et al. (Victoria, 2012–2013, ICD-10; card sc_stam_2019): the largest shortfall of heroin-coded deaths against coronial records was under X44, accidental poisoning by other and unspecified drugs (69 against 98), a comparable non-specific code.

replication.where_it_stands: The problem identified here, multi-drug poisonings coded to a non-specific code that hides the drugs involved, recurs under ICD-10 in Victoria (card sc_stam_2019), and heroin deaths remain hard to identify from certificates alone in Maryland (card sc_horon_2018). The ICD-10 linkage of medical examiner and vital statistics records the authors called for is not among the papers read for this card.

Recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Linking medical examiner case files, with their toxicology results, to ICD-10 underlying- and multiple-cause records for the same deaths, with blinded pathologist review of samples in both directions (deaths coded as heroin or illicit-drug poisoning that were not, and deaths with heroin evidence that were not so coded), would measure the accuracy of each definition rather than their overlap.

domains.note: Statewide vital statistics (including out-of-state deaths of residents) and the statewide medical examiner database are the right frames for residents' poisoning deaths.
All poisoning deaths in both sources, 1995–1998; no sampling.
1,105 poisoning deaths; 640 illicit drug and 537 heroin deaths in either source.

domains.note: Nosologists follow explicit NCHS rules and the OMI has autopsy and confirmed-toxicology policies, but the linkage was manual with no error rate, and the multiple-cause records could not be linked.
Counts and percentages are appropriate and mostly consistent, but union columns in Tables 2 and 3 are internally inconsistent (one value impossible) and no uncertainty is given.

domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a comparison of death counts from two registers (round brief, record-linkage studies). The poisoning comparison is careful (manual linkage and case-by-case review of discordant deaths in both directions); the illicit drug and heroin comparisons rest on non-specific ICD-9 codes, an undefined OMI category and union columns with arithmetic errors. Citable for: in New Mexico in 1995–1998 vital statistics and medical examiner records each held about 95% of residents' poisoning deaths found in either; deaths were lost from vital-statistics poisoning counts when they were coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning only in part II of the certificate, and added when deaths the medical examiner classed as natural were coded 305, the code the rules give for 'use' or 'abuse' on the certificate (the certificates' words are not reported); 'poisoning' here covers all agents, including alcohol and carbon monoxide; the multi-drug code E858.8 holds a large share of illicit drug and heroin deaths in underlying-cause data. Not citable for: the accuracy of either source, the true number of heroin deaths, or the 70.6% figure without its caveat.

key_findings.finding: Poisoning deaths of New Mexico residents, 1995–1998: 1,046 in vital statistics, 1,046 in OMI records, 987 in both and 1,105 in either; each source alone held 94.7% and both together 89.3% of the deaths in either. By year, either source: 255, 249, 289 and 312; deaths rose by all four approaches each year from 1996 to 1998.

key_findings.finding: Only vital statistics held New Mexico residents who died in another state: 24 poisoning deaths over the 4 years.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 59 poisoning deaths in vital statistics not classed as poisonings by the OMI, 24 occurred out of state and were not reviewed; of the other 35, 13 (37.1%) were never reported to the OMI; 15 (42.8%) were natural deaths in the OMI database (e.g., cirrhosis, sepsis, heart disease) that vital statistics attributed to nondependent drug abuse (ICD-9 305); 2 were miscoded as non-poisoning by the OMI; 3 were undetermined-intent poisonings in vital statistics classed differently by the OMI; 2 were unintentional injuries of unspecified cause in the OMI.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Of 59 OMI poisoning deaths not classed as poisonings in vital statistics, 4 (6.8%) were not found in vital statistics; 1 had a revised OMI certificate that was not recoded; 17 (28.8%) were coded as other injury deaths (6 unintentional fire-related deaths, 1 fire-related suicide); 37 (62.7%) were coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning mentioned in part II but not part I of the certificate; 16 (43.2%) of these were coded as heart disease (ICD-9 420–429).
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Unintentional illicit drug overdose deaths: with E858.8, vital statistics 609, OMI 526, both 494, either 640, so vital statistics held 95.2% and the OMI 82.2% of the deaths in either; without E858.8, vital statistics 339, both 277, either 480, so vital statistics held 70.6%.

key_findings.finding: Unintentional heroin overdose deaths: with E858.8, vital statistics 537, OMI 360, both 351, either 537, so vital statistics held 100% and the OMI 67.0%; without E858.8, vital statistics 273, both 216, either 416.

key_findings.finding: Of vital-statistics deaths coded E858.8, 72% matched an OMI death with a drug code for morphine, cocaine and/or methamphetamine, and 55.6% matched an OMI illicit drug overdose with a drug code for morphine.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (starts on p. 275; the 72% sentence is on p. 276) and 4th paragraph (p. 276)
key_findings.note: The number of E858.8 deaths is not printed; both percentages fit 270 deaths (e.g., 150/270 = 55.6%; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: In NCHS multiple-cause data, 90% of New Mexico resident deaths and 88% of US deaths with underlying cause E858.8 also carried code 965.0 (opiates and related narcotics), 968.5 (surface and infiltration anaesthetics, including cocaine) and/or 969.7 (psychostimulants, including amphetamines); 85% and 83% carried 965.0. The authors conclude that 10–12% of E858.8 deaths are not due to illicit drugs.

key_findings.finding: Coding rules that decide whether and how a drug death is counted in vital statistics: 'use' or 'abuse' on the certificate gives ICD-9 305; 'overdose', 'intoxication', 'toxicity' or 'poisoning' gives an external-cause code; several drugs of one type in part I are coded as that type, drugs of different types as E858.8 (accidental) or the corresponding suicide, homicide or undetermined codes; drug plus alcohol is coded by the drug; a natural condition in part I with a drug only in part II is coded as the natural condition unless it is a direct sequel of drug use.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Definitions, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The OMI investigates sudden, unexplained, suspicious, violent or unattended deaths statewide except within certain tribal and federal jurisdictions; for all deaths suspected to be due to drugs, toxins or poisons it carries out a full autopsy and toxicological evaluation, with screening results confirmed (e.g., gas chromatography or mass spectrometry) and antemortem specimens obtained for people who died after hospitalization.

key_findings.finding: Timeliness: the OMI typically reported in-state poisoning deaths within 3 months of death; underlying-cause vital statistics were typically available within 1 year after the calendar year, with classification more consistent under explicit coding rules; NCHS public-use multiple-cause data about 2 years after.

The authors note that no ICD-9 or ICD-10 code corresponds exactly to unintentional heroin overdose.

key_findings.finding: New Mexico rates of poisoning, unintentional illicit drug overdose and unintentional heroin overdose rose in 1989–1998 (Figure 1, age-adjusted to the 1940 US population); poisoning in New Mexico was above the US poisoning rate throughout. Values are not printed and were not extracted.
