key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the NCHS multiple-cause files could not be linked to the linked medical examiner and underlying-cause records; the study used ICD-9 data, ICD-10 being used from 1999 deaths, so a similar ICD-10 study is needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2, excluding E858.8: the 1998 union ('VS or OMI', 108) is smaller than the vital-statistics count for the same year ('VS only', 109), which is impossible for a union. Editors' calculation with the OMI counts from the left half of the table: the 1995 and 1996 unions (123, 121) are reproduced, but 1997 and 1998 would be 134 and 210, and the total 588 rather than 480.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's 70.6% (339 of 480) depends on the inconsistent total; with 588 the vital-statistics share without E858.8 would be about 58%. The direction of the conclusion (excluding E858.8 loses many deaths) is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3, including E858.8: the union of the two sources equals the vital-statistics count (537), although 9 OMI heroin deaths (360 − 351; 5 in 1995, 2 in 1996, 2 in 1997) were not in the vital-statistics count (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 100% and 67.0% are computed on a denominator that leaves out OMI-only heroin deaths; with them the shares would be 98.4% and 65.9% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: One-death discrepancies in the union columns (editors' calculation): Table 2 (with E858.8) gives a 1997 union of 151 and a total of 640, where the columns give 152 and 641; Table 3 (without E858.8) gives a 1997 union of 91 and a total of 416, where the columns give 92 and 417.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages change by less than a tenth of a point.

reporting_issues.issue: The vital-statistics columns imply different numbers of E858.8 deaths in the two tables, although both definitions include every unintentional E858.8 death (editors' calculation): 609 − 339 = 270 in Table 2 against 537 − 273 = 264 in Table 3; by year, 45 against 43 in 1995 and 72 against 68 in 1997.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one vital-statistics count is wrong by up to 6 deaths; the number of E858.8 deaths, the denominator of the 72% and 55.6%, is never printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that for illicit drug and heroin overdose deaths each source alone captured smaller percentages than for poisoning (94.7%); with E858.8 included, Tables 2 and 3 give vital statistics 95.2% and 100%. The Results also describe either source as capturing 5.4% more poisoning deaths than either alone (editors' calculation: 59 more deaths are 5.6% of 1,046 or 5.3% of 1,105).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement holds only for the OMI, and for vital statistics only when E858.8 is excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the New Mexico rates of poisoning, illicit drug overdose and heroin overdose were all substantially higher than the US poisoning rate after 1993; in Figure 1, read enlarged (no values printed; years from the axis), the heroin overdose rate lies below the US poisoning rate in 1994 and at about the same level in 1996 and 1997, and the illicit drug overdose rate is at about the US level in 1994.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the New Mexico poisoning rate was clearly above the US rate in every year after 1993; the figure also compares New Mexico subcategories with total US poisoning, which are not like for like.

design_detail: Narrative review (journal section: Review), presented as part of the Canadian Association of Poison Control Centres symposium at the North American Congress of Clinical Toxicology, October 2000 (p. 47), on interpreting drug concentrations measured after death: redistribution and differences between sampling sites, whole blood against serum, alternative specimens (vitreous humour, skeletal muscle, bile, adipose tissue, organs), production and loss of analytes after death, false-positive immunoassays after haemolysis, embalming and storage, ending with nine questions for the toxicologist. Nine tables list drugs in which redistribution probably does not occur (20 entries), possible post-mortem transformation or redistribution (99 entries, 98 distinct labels, 82 with numeric parentheses including the ambiguous nicotine/cotinine annotation), recommended tissues for some poisonings, bile and blood concentration pairs, single post-mortem blood levels for five psychotropic drugs, analytes open to false-positive urine immunoassay, autopsy findings linked to toxins, embalming effects and storage problems. No search method, selection criteria or appraisal; 90 references from 1975 to 2002.
can_establish: Which factors a physician toxicologist and a poison-centre pharmacist considered necessary in 2003 for interpreting a drug concentration measured after death, the checklist they proposed, and pointers to the literature on each factor.
cannot_establish: The size or frequency of any effect described (ratios and thresholds come without case numbers, ranges or per-drug sources), whether the literature was selected completely or fairly, or how reliable any listed fatal level or heart-to-peripheral ratio is for a given death.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or criteria stated; 90 references (1975–2002) chosen by the authors: case reports and series, animal studies, analytical-method papers, reviews and textbooks.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence selection is the authors'. By the titles of the works cited, several statements rest on animal or single-case evidence: the timing of morphine redistribution on two rat studies and one human study (refs 5–7), diffusion from the stomach into the liver on a rat model (ref. 16, which the text labels as an animal model), and the vitreous-to-blood ethanol range on a dog study of fluoxetine and one road-death case (refs 36 and 53). The heart-to-peripheral ratios are cited collectively (refs 14, 15 and 20–33) without saying which source, or how many cases, gave each value.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (review).
exposure.polysubstance: Co-ingested drugs are named as one reason deaths from newer antidepressants and antipsychotics are hard to recognize (p. 50); not otherwise addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (review). The review stresses comparison with a blood sample taken just before or at death and between several post-mortem sampling sites (p. 48).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The review lists tolerance and dosing interval among the clinical information needed to interpret a level (p. 52, question 4) but offers no way to establish tolerance after death.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios (Table 2, p. 49), tissue concentration thresholds (Table 3, p. 50), bile and blood concentration pairs (Table 4, p. 51), single post-mortem blood levels presented as associated with psychotropic deaths (Table 5, p. 51), analytes open to false-positive immunoassay (Table 6, p. 51).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validity data; the tabulated values come without case numbers, ranges (except cocaine and imipramine in Table 2) or per-drug sources.
outcomes.operationalization: Potential for redistribution is equated with a high heart-to-peripheral ratio (p. 48), and drugs with an apparent volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are called candidates for redistribution (p. 50, no source cited).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without sources per value. Heart-to-peripheral ratios (Table 2, p. 49): amphetamine 2.0, methamphetamine 2.4 (listed separately as D-methamphetamine 2.1), MDMA 2.65, MBDB 2.5, paramethoxyamphetamine 1.6, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3, morphine (heroin) 2.2, codeine 1.8, oxycodone 3.1, pethidine 2.1, ketamine 1.6, phencyclidine 1.8, gamma-hydroxybutyrate 2, diazepam 1.6, alprazolam 1.5, flunitrazepam 3, midazolam 4, doxepin 5.5, strychnine 15, hydrochlorothiazide 23; alfentanil, methylfentanyl, remifentanil, sufentanil and tetrahydrocannabinol are listed without a ratio. Whole blood against serum: 12–18% for ethanol and a factor of 1.6 for cannabinoids; vitreous humour ethanol 0.9–1.3 times blood; ethanol produced by putrefaction usually about 0.05 g%, developing over 3–10 days (p. 50).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The tables give single values without the spread or number of cases behind them. A cited study whose title reports a lack of predictable site-dependent differences for cocaine, benzoylecgonine and cocaethylene (ref. 23, p. 54) is not discussed, while Table 2 gives cocaine a ratio of 1.5 to 2.3 (p. 49).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A catalogue, drawn from cited literature, of reasons a drug concentration measured after death may not reflect the concentration at death: redistribution (heart blood higher than peripheral blood for many basic drugs), whole blood against serum, production or loss of analyte after death, false-positive immunoassays after haemolysis, embalming and storage; with tabulated ratios, thresholds and levels whose evidence base is not shown.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion is cautious: extrapolating an autopsy result to the state before death may not always be possible, and limited knowledge of change after death can lead to incorrect assumptions (pp. 52–53). Within the text, certainty is sometimes raised beyond what is shown: the drugs of Table 1 are said to have been demonstrated not to change (p. 47) while the table's own title says redistribution probably does not occur (p. 48); Table 5 gives single blood levels said to be directly associated with psychotropic deaths (p. 50), without site, number of cases, spread or co-ingestants, which sits uneasily with the review's own message; and the volume-of-distribution threshold and the statement that cocaethylene would not be formed after death are given without a source (p. 50). For one drug the listed level falls below a typical post-mortem value: olanzapine 0.160 mg/L here (p. 51), while Ketola & Kriikku (2019) list a median femoral-blood concentration of 0.2 mg/L regardless of cause of death (their Table 1, PDF p. 41; editors' cross-check).

timeline.event: Pounder & Jones, four-case series showing several-fold differences in drug concentrations between blood sampled from different vessels after death (read in this batch); this review cites Pounder's 1993 book chapter instead.

Ketola & Kriikku compile paired within-case ratios with numbers of results. Across 24 shared labels with numeric values, Leikin's value is more than 1.10 times the Ketola other-blood/femoral median for 17, below 1/1.10 times it for 3, and between those bounds for 4 (editors' comparison). Examples are morphine 2.2 against 1.26, methamphetamine 2.4 against 1.50, oxycodone 3.1 against 1.19 and diazepam 1.6 against 0.95. Other blood is not exclusively cardiac and Leikin's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral; different source sets and populations mean this is not a paired replication or a universal correction factor.
Borra et al., a review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: The factors the review lists remain the frame used for interpreting post-mortem toxicology. Its single heart-to-peripheral values can be compared with later compilations that give case-result counts: Ketola & Kriikku's within-case medians are lower for most shared labels under the editors' stated comparison. The matrices and source sets differ, however, so this describes disagreement between compilations rather than a validated replacement or correction for an individual death.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Leikin: Evanston Northwestern Healthcare OMEGA, Glenbrook Hospital, Glenview, Illinois; Watson: South Texas Poison Center, Department of Surgery, University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio (p. 47). Five of the 90 references are the authors' own (refs 4, 9, 27, 35 and 83). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with an explicit search and appraisal of studies that measured the same drug in blood at or just before death and at several post-mortem sites, reporting for each drug the number of cases and the spread of ratios; and, for tables of fatal levels, studies comparing concentrations in deaths attributed to a drug with deaths from other causes in which the same drug was present, by sampling site.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.
No appraisal; animal, single-case and human series evidence are mixed without labels in places (morphine timing; vitreous ethanol range), and tabulated values carry no case numbers.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Five of 90 references are the authors' own; the central points rest on others' work.

Uncited generalizations (volume of distribution above 3 L/kg; cocaethylene not formed after death), Table 1 described in the text as demonstrated although its title says probably, and single fatal levels presented as direct associations; the conclusion itself is cautious.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how predictable site differences are
domains.note: Single heart-to-peripheral values per drug are offered as guides; evidence of between-case variation and unpredictability is under-represented (a cited cocaine study titled as finding no predictable site differences is not discussed).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain. The review is a clear practitioner's guide with a cautious conclusion, but its selection is unsystematic and its tables give values without per-value source attribution, case counts or distributions (some entries are ranges, and Table 2 is cited collectively). Citable for: the list of factors that can make a post-mortem concentration differ from the concentration at death (sampling site and redistribution, whole blood against serum, production or loss after death, false-positive immunoassays after haemolysis, embalming, storage) and the authors' nine-question checklist, as the authors' expert view. Not citable for: any specific heart-to-peripheral ratio, tissue threshold or fatal level as an established value; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Comparing a post-mortem concentration with therapeutic and toxic ranges from the living assumes the concentration does not change during and after death; the authors call this assumption incorrect for many substances and say post-mortem change must be considered for all but a few drugs, listed in Table 1 (20 entries, including alcohols, carbon monoxide, carbamazepine, hydrocodone, lorazepam, mirtazapine and zopiclone) under the title of drugs in which redistribution probably does not occur.
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph (p. 47, left column continuing in right column); Table 1 (p. 48)

key_findings.finding: Interpretation ideally rests on a consistent relationship between the concentration at a specific site at death (usually venous plasma or serum) and the post-mortem concentration; dose, time of intake before death, route, tolerance and whether steady state was reached all affect the concentration–effect relationship, and most such relationships come from trough levels at steady state during therapy.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph, beginning 'The goal of interpreting' (p. 47, right column, continuing on p. 48, left column)

key_findings.finding: Redistribution can be fast: thiopental and pentobarbital concentrations rose significantly in the first 4 hours after death (ref. 4); morphine rose within the first few minutes when compared with samples from before or around death, but no rise was seen when the first sample was taken 3 hours or more after death (refs 5–7). Because the rate of redistribution is generally unknown, post-mortem samples should be compared with one taken immediately before or at death, and from multiple sites.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'To expand our understanding' (left column, continuing at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: By their titles (p. 53), refs 5 and 7 are studies in rats and ref. 6 a study in humans; the text does not say so.

key_findings.finding: Proposed mechanisms: passive diffusion along concentration gradients as tissue breaks down, with fluid shifts, pH, volume of distribution and the body's condition; stomach, liver, bladder and lungs as sources; gravity-dependent blood flow; in supine bodies, rapid diffusion of basic drugs from the lungs into the left heart chambers; and diffusion from the myocardium into heart blood, which the authors call debatable. Ethanol from the stomach can contaminate pericardial blood, but only after large amounts (400 ml of 10% ethanol), with minimal contamination of femoral vein samples (ref. 18).
key_findings.locator: Paragraphs beginning 'The assumption that death results' and 'Recent studies have demonstrated' (right column)

key_findings.finding: Heart-to-peripheral blood ratios are offered as a measure of the potential for redistribution, with high ratios meaning heart or pericardial samples may overstate concentrations. Table 2 lists possible transformation or redistribution: 99 entries and 98 distinct labels, of which 82 have numeric parentheses (including Nicotine (Cotinine-3), which does not unambiguously assign 3 to nicotine itself). Examples are amphetamine 2.0, methamphetamine 2.4 (D-methamphetamine 2.1), MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3, morphine (heroin) 2.2, codeine 1.8, oxycodone 3.1, ketamine 1.6, phencyclidine 1.8, gamma-hydroxybutyrate 2, diazepam 1.6, alprazolam 1.5, midazolam 4 and doxepin 5.5. Sixteen labels have no numeric value, including tetrahydrocannabinol, nitrazepam, pentobarbital, lidocaine, quetiapine and several fentanyl analogues; venlafaxine 1.6 appears twice.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The cardiac to peripheral blood level' (p. 48, right column); Table 2 (p. 49)
key_findings.note: No case numbers, ranges (except cocaine and imipramine) or per-drug sources; the table is cited collectively to refs 14, 15 and 20–33 (p. 50).

key_findings.finding: Whole blood, the usual post-mortem matrix, differs from the serum or plasma used clinically: the review reports a 12–18% difference for ethanol and a factor of 1.6 to calculate plasma cannabinoid concentrations from whole-blood values (refs 34, 35); clotting, fluid movement and cellular changes after death alter the blood sampled. These are second-hand statements, not conversion factors validated here for every case.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'A primary difficulty' (left column)

key_findings.finding: Drugs with an apparent volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are called candidates for redistribution (no source given); transformation of parent drug to metabolites after death is described as rare (nitrobenzodiazepines); ethanol produced by putrefaction in decomposed bodies is usually about 0.05 g% and takes 3 to 10 days to develop; and cocaethylene is said not to be expected to form after death by this mechanism (no source given).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'An analysis of the drugs' (left column)

key_findings.finding: Alternative specimens: skeletal muscle (especially the lateral dome of the diaphragm) as a stable matrix for qualitative detection; bile for identifying drugs concentrated in the liver; drugs in adipose tissue reflecting distribution before death; vitreous humour often the only other matrix allowing quantitative interpretation, with vitreous ethanol 0.9 to 1.3 times blood and lagging behind it, and vitreous useful for 6-acetylmorphine, benzodiazepines and electrolytes.
key_findings.locator: Paragraphs beginning 'Alternative matrices' and 'The vitreous humor' (left column, the second continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Recommended tissues (Table 3, cited collectively to refs 41–47) include brain or cerebellum for heroin, with a cerebellum-to-blood morphine ratio of about 1 when death occurs within 1 hour of administration and 3.5 when it occurs within 2 to 48 hours, and 6-acetylmorphine in cerebrospinal fluid detecting 46% more heroin-related cases than blood. These footnote statements have no individual citation or denominator; Jenkins & Lavins 1998 (ref. 41) is a probable source for the CSF figure by its title, not independently validated here. Other listed advice includes fentanyl liver concentrations over 69 µg/kg associated with overdose; vitreous potassium to estimate the post-mortem interval (hours = 7.14 × potassium − 39.1); and a lidocaine kidney-to-liver ratio below 1 after absorption from the trachea during intubation and above 1 after intravenous treatment.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and its footnotes a and b (right column)

key_findings.finding: About 3% of all deaths are listed by medical examiners as of unknown cause, and up to 10% of sudden deaths among people with long-term heavy drinking may be of unknown cause; a blood beta-hydroxybutyrate level over 2500 µmol/L may indicate alcoholic ketoacidosis as the cause of death (ref. 56).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Another example of postmortem blood results' (right column)

key_findings.finding: Table 5 lists single post-mortem blood levels that the authors present as directly associated with psychotropic-related deaths: fluoxetine 0.63, paroxetine 0.4, sertraline 1.5, olanzapine 0.160 and trazodone 9 mg/L (refs 57–59).
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Death due to newer antidepressant' (p. 50, right column); Table 5 (p. 51)
key_findings.note: Single values without sampling site, number of cases, spread or co-ingestants.

key_findings.finding: Haemolysis after death can raise lactate dehydrogenase, lactic acid and protein in serum and urine, which can make urine immunoassays falsely positive for amphetamines, barbiturates, opiates, cocaine metabolite, propoxyphene and benzodiazepines (Table 6; refs 60, 61); C-reactive protein appears not to change after death (ref. 62).
key_findings.locator: Table 6 (p. 51); paragraph beginning 'Due to postmortem hemolysis' (p. 52, left column)
key_findings.note: How often this happens and with which assays is not stated; ref. 61 concerns the EMIT drugs-of-abuse assay, by its title (p. 55).

key_findings.finding: Nine questions the toxicologist must address before judging a drug's role in a death: whether several sites were sampled and where; whether the drug is known or suspected to redistribute; whether data define the concentration–toxicity relationship; whether clinical information on the exposure (for example tolerance, dosing interval) is adequate; whether the concentration was clinically sufficient to cause, prevent or be directly involved in the death; whether autopsy findings typical of the overdose exist; whether the body was embalmed; whether the analyte needs special storage; and whether pills in the stomach contain active drug or are drug-free wax matrices.
key_findings.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Thus, it is clear' and questions 1–9 (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: The review's listed advice on embalming (Table 8) includes possible raised amitriptyline and lowered nortriptyline (65% conversion in 24 h), slightly lowered liver fentanyl, reduced blood ethanol and benzodiazepines and raised methanol, with no apparent effect on morphine; the text says formaldehyde at 5 to 20% methylates tricyclic amines. Its storage table (Table 9) lists 6-acetylmorphine as stable at −20 °C, morphine and its metabolites degrading at 4 °C but not at −20 °C, gamma-hydroxybutyrate potentially raised in citrate-buffered blood, and LSD needing protection from light and heat. These are second-hand entries without study-specific storage duration, matrix or individual support for the 6-acetylmorphine assertion; they do not establish unlimited stability.
key_findings.locator: Question 7 and Table 8 (p. 52); Table 9 (p. 53)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: even when a concentration is available from an autopsy sample, interpreting it and extrapolating it to the state before death may not always be possible; the drug's post-mortem stability and potential for redistribution must be built into the interpretation, and further animal research and multiple-site, timely ante-mortem and post-mortem measurements are needed.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion (p. 52, right column, continuing on p. 53)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says post-mortem changes have been demonstrated not to occur for the drugs of Table 1, while the table's title says redistribution probably does not occur in them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 should be cited as the authors' judgment that redistribution is probably absent, not as demonstrated.

reporting_issues.issue: In one sentence, putrefactive ethanol is usually in the range of 0.05 gm%, although concentrations of up to 0.2 mg% are infrequently found; the second unit makes the upper value lower than the usual one.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper value is probably 0.2 g%; as printed (0.2 mg%, 250 times lower than 0.05 g%; editors' calculation) it cannot be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4's title gives a bile-to-blood ratio in mg/L, but its entries are pairs of concentrations (for example heroin (morphine) 32–0.43, cocaine 0.7–0.2); colchicine appears twice with different blood values (2.9–0.6 as Cochicine, 2.9–0.06 as Colchicine). Table 2 lists venlafaxine twice and methamphetamine and D-methamphetamine with different ratios (2.4, 2.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 4 entries are best read as single example concentration pairs without source or case number, not as ratios; the duplicates suggest the tables were not checked closely.

reporting_issues.issue: References 52 (adipose tissue) and 62 (C-reactive protein) are two different papers printed with the same citation, Forensic Sci Int 2001;121:157–160.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two supporting statements cannot be traced as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that limited knowledge of post-mortem change can lead to incorrect assumptions cites ref. 81 (in vitro production of gamma-hydroxybutyrate in urine samples), while ref. 83 (Watson & McKinney, on the practical interpretation of post-mortem concentrations) is listed but never cited in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; probably a numbering slip, with the statement meant to cite ref. 83, by the second author.

reporting_issues.issue: The vitreous-to-blood ethanol range of 0.9 to 1.3 is cited to refs 36 and 53, which by their titles are a study of fluoxetine and norfluoxetine in dogs and a single road-death case.
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be traced to a study comparing vitreous and blood ethanol across many cases; it needs a primary source before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives cocaine a heart-to-peripheral ratio of 1.5 to 2.3, while ref. 23, cited among the sources for site differences, is titled as reporting a lack of predictable site-dependent and time-dependent differences for cocaine, benzoylecgonine and cocaethylene; the text does not discuss it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cocaine ratio, and single ratios generally, may suggest more predictability than the cited evidence supports.

reporting_issues.issue: Nitrazepam appears both in Table 1 (redistribution probably does not occur) and Table 2 (transformation or redistribution may occur), without a Table 2 ratio. Table 9 separately says it degrades with heat, light or bacteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: The categories need not conflict: transformation and redistribution are different processes. The review does not identify which Table 2 process applies to this entry, and Table 1 cannot be used to claim absence of all post-mortem change.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 footnote a reports 46% more heroin-related cases detected using CSF 6-acetylmorphine than blood but attaches no individual source, denominator or description of the blood test. The surrounding text cites refs 41–47 collectively.
reporting_issues.page: p. 50, Table 3 footnote a; p. 55, ref. 41
reporting_issues.consequence: Jenkins & Lavins 1998 is a probable source by title, not confirmed by this reading. Retain the percentage only as an explicitly second-hand review statement pending primary-source verification.

Sixteen labels have no numeric value, including tetrahydrocannabinol, nitrazepam, pentobarbital, lidocaine, quetiapine and several fentanyl analogues; venlafaxine 1.6 appears twice. design_detail: Descriptive analysis of the literal cause-of-death text on death certificates (SuperMICAR files of the Washington State Department of Health) for the 7,817 poisoning deaths of Washington State residents in 2003–2010: ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X49, X60–X69, X85–X90 or Y10–Y19, all intents, drugs and other substances, with 42 deaths from complications of medical care excluded. The text of Part I, Part II and the how-the-injury-occurred box was combined, parsed into words and phrases, spelling-corrected with a module built for the study and matched to a drug-word list (537 words) built by manual adjudication; each drug word was given an ICD-10 injury code and a category (prescription, illicit, either, over-the-counter, alcohol, nonspecific, common, disease, unknown). Outcomes: counts of deaths naming each substance, co-mentions, counts by underlying-cause code, by intent and by injury code, and age-specific and age-adjusted (US 2000 standard) rates by sex and year. No toxicology, no validation of the text processing, no statistical tests. A methods paper ('Practice of Epidemiology').
can_establish: Which substances certifiers in Washington State named on poisoning death certificates in 2003–2010, how often, in which combinations and under which ICD-10 codes, and therefore how much substance detail ICD codes alone would have lost (for example, oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone and 'opiate' all fall under T40.2).
cannot_establish: Whether the named substances caused the deaths (a word anywhere in the cause-of-death text, Part II or the injury description counted); how complete certifiers' naming was (no toxicology); how accurate the text processing was (no error rate or second coder); whether a drug had been prescribed to the person (categories are by type of drug, so methadone and morphine count as prescription drugs whatever their source); or anything outside Washington State, whose certificates named a specific drug far more often than the national average (93% against 75% in 2008–2010, cited from ref 28).

sample.recruitment: Registry: all deaths of Washington State residents in 2003–2010 in the Washington State Department of Health death data, with the SuperMICAR text, which the state began using in 2003 (pp. 884–885).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: underlying cause in the ICD-10 poisoning categories X40–X49, X60–X69, X85–X90 and Y10–Y19, all intents, poisoning by drugs and by other substances such as alcohol and carbon monoxide. Excluded: complications of medical or surgical care (Y40–Y59, 42 deaths), deaths classified as due to drug or alcohol dependence, and poisonings from adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 885; Results, 1st paragraph, p. 886).
sample.demographics: Median age 46 years for deaths naming a prescription drug, 43 for an illicit drug, 43 for both and 45 for neither (p. 887). Age and sex appear only as rates in Figures 2–5. Washington State population 6,126,885 in 2003 and 6,724,540 in 2010 (p. 886).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (complete registrations).
sample.selection_effects: One state whose certificates usually name a specific drug (93% of drug poisoning certificates in 2008–2010, as cited from ref 28); the results depend on what certifiers wrote, which the author notes may not be consistent across counties or states (p. 892). Deaths whose underlying cause was coded to drug or alcohol dependence are outside the 7,817.

exposure.measurement: How a substance entered the count, and who decided: the certifier writes the cause-of-death text; with SuperMICAR, vital statistics staff key in the text verbatim without making coding decisions, and the program generates the multiple- and underlying-cause ICD codes under WHO rules (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 885). For this study the author combined the text of Part I, Part II and the injury description, so a substance named anywhere in these fields counted as named, or 'involved', for that death, once per death (pp. 885–886; Table 1 footnote). The injury codes in Tables 3–5 are the author's assignment of one ICD code to each drug word (p. 886). No toxicology data were used, and what was tested at death is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Many certificates named more than one substance; each was counted once per death (Table 1 footnote), and co-mentions are tabulated for the 10 most named substances (Table 2). Under ICD rules, a death with drugs of different categories in Part I is coded X44 (p. 887), and two drugs with the same code written on one line receive a single code (p. 891).

comparison.controls: The certificate text compared with what the ICD-10 codes could show for the same deaths (Tables 3 and 5). No external reference.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths).

outcomes.instruments: Counts of deaths naming each substance (Table 1), co-mention counts (Table 2), the most named substances by underlying-cause code (Table 3), by intent (Table 4) and by injury code (Table 5); age-specific and age-adjusted death rates per 100,000 by sex and year for the five most named substances and for prescription, illicit, both or neither (Figures 2–5). SAS 9.2 and R 2.12.2; word lists and code on the author's GitHub (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: The text processing was not validated (no comparison with manual review, no error rate); misspellings were frequent, the 537 drug words appearing in 442 misspelled forms (p. 891).
outcomes.operationalization: Named or 'involved' = the word appears in the certificate text. Prescription = a drug normally obtained through a prescription or used in a clinic; illicit = normally obtained on the street and usually illegal; either = may denote both, such as 'opiate' (Appendix Table 1, p. 894). In Tables 3–5 'opiate' was counted only when no specific opiate was named.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive counts and rates; no tests or intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; unmatched words were adjudicated by hand by the study team (p. 886).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive counts; no confidence intervals. Methadone was named for 2,149 deaths (27.5%), alcohol 1,446, opiate 1,240 (15.9%; 676 of these also named a specific opiate), cocaine 1,174, oxycodone 1,047, methamphetamine 681, morphine 648, diphenhydramine 574, hydrocodone 563, heroin 539 (Table 1). At least one prescription-category drug was named in 5,454 deaths (70%), an illicit drug in 2,162 (28%), and a term that could be either in a further 198 (3%). Age-adjusted rates for deaths naming only prescription drugs were 3–5 times those for deaths naming only illicit drugs or both (Figure 4, no values printed). Methadone was named in 894 X42 and 1,042 X44 deaths, oxycodone in 281 and 584 (Table 3). T40.2 (other opioids) covered 2,725 deaths, most often naming oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, opiate, hydromorphone and codeine (overlapping counts); T40.4 covered 521 (fentanyl 198, tramadol 153, propoxyphene 141) (Table 5).
analysis.covariates: None; age-adjusted rates by the direct method, US 2000 standard population (p. 886).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned; exempt from institutional review board review because only nonliving subjects were involved (p. 886).
analysis.selective_reporting: Figures give rates without numbers or intervals; the category assigned to each drug word is not printed (the lists are on GitHub, not read); how negations or qualifying context in the text (for example a drug ruled out) were handled is not described.
analysis.power: Not applicable (complete registrations).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In Washington State poisoning deaths in 2003–2010, the certificate text named specific substances that ICD codes merge: 21 of the 25 most named, by the author's count, share an injury code with other substances, and opioids such as oxycodone, morphine and hydrocodone can only be separated in the text. Methadone was the most named substance, and certificates named prescription-category drugs in 70% of deaths and illicit drugs in 28%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that prescription drugs 'were involved in more deaths than were illicit drugs' in both sexes and at all ages (abstract, p. 884; Discussion, p. 893) depends on classifying methadone (2,149 deaths) and morphine (648) as prescription drugs whatever their source; the author concedes that morphine is also a metabolite of heroin and was counted without qualification (p. 892), and the Discussion counts diphenhydramine among the most named prescription drugs while describing it as an over-the-counter ingredient (p. 891). 'Involved' means named anywhere in the certificate text, including Part II and the injury description, not judged causal. The Results' suggestion that prescription drugs 'were not replacing illicit drugs' (p. 887) is read from aggregate rate trends. The abstract's statement that only 4 of the 25 most named substances have unique ICD codes leaves out carbon monoxide, which has its own code in Table 5. The accuracy of the text processing is assumed rather than measured.

timeline.event: Washington State begins using SuperMICAR, which stores the certifier's text alongside the ICD codes (p. 884).
Warner et al. (Academic Forensic Pathology; ref 28): state variation in naming drugs on certificates, cited for Washington's 93% against 75% nationally in 2008–2010 and fewer than 50% in some states.
Trinidad et al., NCHS report on using literal text from the death certificate to characterize drug involvement (named on this project's drug-deaths list as report R4; not read).

Garnett et al., NCHS report for 2017–2023 (card sc_garnett_2026): national drug-specific overdose counts from the same three certificate text fields searched by NCHS software, because ICD-10 codes are too broad to track specific drugs.

replication.where_it_stands: A methods demonstration rather than a finding to replicate. The approach later became routine at national level: NCHS counts drugs named in the same three certificate fields (card sc_garnett_2026). Like this paper, such counts are minimums of drugs written on certificates, not of drugs that caused the deaths, and they depend on testing and certification practice; where many certificates name no drug, the text shows less, as the author notes (p. 892).

funding.funder: Washington State Department of Health; no external funding (Acknowledgments, p. 893).
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflict of interest: none declared (Acknowledgments, p. 893).
funding.affiliations_note: Sole author at the Washington State Department of Health, Olympia, whose death records are the data; the word lists and code are public on the author's GitHub (p. 886). Recorded as context, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Validation of text-derived drug counts against independent toxicology and investigation files for a random sample of the same deaths, reporting how often a named drug was detected and judged contributory and how often a detected drug went unnamed, with a second coder to measure text-processing errors; and classification of methadone, morphine and other opioids by source (prescribed to the person, diverted, illicit) from investigation records rather than by type of drug.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All poisoning deaths of Washington State residents, 2003–2010, by underlying cause.
A census of registered deaths.
7,817 deaths; counts for rarely named substances are small but are not the paper's focus.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Counts by intent and the state population are given; age and sex appear only as rates in figures, and the certifier system and toxicology practice in Washington are not described.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 7,817 records were processed; only the 42 deaths from complications of medical care were excluded, by design.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Transparent text matching with public code, but not validated against manual review or toxicology; the handling of negations is not described; any mention counts as involvement.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same algorithm was applied to every record, but what certifiers write varies, for example between heroin and morphine and in the use of scene evidence across counties (p. 892).
Counts and directly age-adjusted rates are appropriate, but no intervals are given, figures print no values, and a few counts disagree slightly between text and tables.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths from certificate data (round brief, certificate studies). The counts of substances named on certificates are a census of the text with low risk of bias for what certifiers wrote, given unvalidated but transparent processing. The prescription-against-illicit comparison carries more risk, because the categories are by type of drug (methadone, morphine and apparently diphenhydramine count as prescription drugs) and 'involved' means mentioned, not causal; hence moderate overall. Citable for: which substances Washington certificates named in 2003–2010 and how often; that ICD-10 injury codes group many drugs (T40.2 alone covered 2,725 deaths, most often naming oxycodone, morphine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, codeine or unspecified 'opiate') and that deaths naming methadone or oxycodone were coded X44 more often than X42; that literal text recovers this detail. Not citable for: drugs as causes of death, how drugs were obtained, or the national picture.

key_findings.finding: There were 7,859 poisoning deaths of Washington State residents in 2003–2010: 5,850 unintentional, 1,461 suicides, 11 homicides, 495 of undetermined intent and 42 from complications of medical or surgical care, which were excluded, leaving 7,817. The state population was 6,126,885 in 2003 and 6,724,540 in 2010.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Deaths were included by underlying cause in the ICD-10 poisoning categories X40–X49, X60–X69, X85–X90 and Y10–Y19 (all intents, drugs and other substances); deaths classified as due to drug or alcohol dependence and poisonings from adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use were not included.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Who wrote and who coded: the certifier writes the cause-of-death text; with SuperMICAR, vital statistics staff key the text in verbatim without making coding decisions, and the program produces the multiple- and underlying-cause ICD codes under WHO rules. The text is stored for each Part I line, for Part II and for the injury description, which the study combined and parsed.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Text processing: words were spelling-corrected with a module built for the study and matched against a drug-word list and a nondrug-word list built by manual adjudication (every word was adjudicated by hand for the first year of data); by the end there were 537 drug words and 4,335 nondrug words, and the drug words appeared in 442 misspelled forms; brand names were converted to generic names; each drug word was given an ICD-10 injury code and a category.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 891)

key_findings.finding: Substances named most often (number of deaths; each substance counted once per death): methadone 2,149 (27.5%), alcohol 1,446, opiate 1,240, cocaine 1,174, oxycodone 1,047, methamphetamine 681, morphine 648, diphenhydramine 574, hydrocodone 563, heroin 539, citalopram 533, diazepam 468, alprazolam 412, amitriptyline 397, acetaminophen 395, carbon monoxide 394, hydromorphone 269, fluoxetine 243, trazodone 227, cyclobenzaprine 220, venlafaxine 220, quetiapine 199, fentanyl 198, sertraline 192, bupropion 169.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: 'Opiate' was written on 1,240 certificates (15.9%), and 676 of these also named a specific opiate; the only illicit drugs among the 25 most named substances were cocaine, methamphetamine and heroin.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 5 gives 543, not 564 (1,240 − 676), deaths naming 'opiate' without a specific opiate (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Most frequent co-mentions (Table 2): opiate with cocaine 333 deaths, methadone with cocaine 320, alcohol with opiate 299, methadone with alcohol 278, opiate with heroin 265, methadone with oxycodone 239, alcohol with oxycodone 233, alcohol with cocaine 217, opiate with morphine 206, methadone with diazepam 204; each of the 10 most frequent pairs includes methadone, alcohol, cocaine or opiate.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (printed landscape); Results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The ranking of pairs is the editors' reading of Table 2, which lists for each of the 10 most named substances its 10 most frequent partners.

key_findings.finding: At least one prescription-category drug was named in 5,454 deaths (70%), an illicit drug in 2,162 (28%), and in a further 198 (3%) a term that could be either, such as 'opiate'. Age-adjusted rates for deaths naming only prescription drugs were 3–5 times those for deaths naming only illicit drugs or both; prescription-drug death rates rose in 2003–2008 and then began to fall while illicit-drug death rates stayed constant, which the author reads as prescription drugs not replacing illicit drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph; Figure 4 (p. 889)
key_findings.note: The categories follow Appendix Table 1, by type of drug rather than by how it was obtained; methadone and morphine count as prescription drugs and diphenhydramine appears among them (reporting issue 2). Figure 4 prints no values.

key_findings.finding: Women had lower rates than men for each of the five most named substances except oxycodone, where rates were similar, and lower rates for deaths naming only illicit drugs, both or neither, while prescription-drug death rates were as high among women as among men. Rates peaked at ages 40–49, except that among women the rates for oxycodone and alcohol were highest at 50–59 and the prescription-drug rate slightly higher at 50–59. Median age: 46 years (prescription), 43 (illicit), 43 (both), 45 (neither).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Figures 2, 4 and 5 (pp. 888–889)
key_findings.note: Comparisons rest on rates drawn in figures without values, intervals or tests; in Figure 4 the men's prescription-drug line lies somewhat above the women's in most years (editors' reading of the figure).

key_findings.finding: Rates of deaths naming methadone or cocaine peaked in 2006; deaths naming oxycodone may have started to decline in 2009; the methamphetamine rate stayed fairly constant.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Figure 3 (p. 888)

key_findings.finding: Underlying-cause coding: deaths naming methadone were coded X44 (unintentional, other and unspecified drugs) more often than X42 (unintentional, narcotics and psychodysleptics), 1,042 against 894, and those naming oxycodone 584 against 281, because X44 is used when drugs from different categories are named in Part I. X42 had 2,308 deaths and X44 2,708; X64 (suicide, other and unspecified drugs) had 650, most often naming diphenhydramine (141) and acetaminophen (138).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph (p. 887); Table 3 (p. 890)

key_findings.finding: By intent (Table 4): unintentional deaths most often named methadone (1,941), alcohol (1,181), cocaine (1,085) and oxycodone (870); suicides named carbon monoxide (288), alcohol (196), acetaminophen (175) and diphenhydramine (148); deaths of undetermined intent named methadone (121), alcohol (69), cocaine (53) and oxycodone (48), and shared their top six substances with unintentional deaths while also including diphenhydramine and acetaminophen.
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th paragraph; Table 4 (p. 891)

key_findings.finding: Within injury codes (the author's assignment of codes to words; Table 5), T40.2 'other opioids' covered 2,725 deaths, of which the most commonly named substances were oxycodone (1,047), morphine (648), hydrocodone (563), opiate without a specific opiate (543), hydromorphone (269) and codeine (148), counts that overlap (they sum to 3,218, editors' sum); T40.4 covered 521 (fentanyl 198, tramadol 153, propoxyphene 141); T42.4 benzodiazepines 1,311 (diazepam 468, alprazolam 412); T43.2 other antidepressants 1,516; T45.0 680 (diphenhydramine 574, doxylamine 94). T40.1 (heroin, 539), T40.3 (methadone, 2,149), T40.5 (cocaine, 1,175 deaths, 1,174 naming cocaine) and T51.0 (ethanol, 1,446) each correspond to one substance.
key_findings.locator: Table 5; Results, 9th paragraph (p. 890)

key_findings.finding: ICD coding conventions lose detail: two drugs with the same code written on one line of the certificate receive a single code (for example fentanyl and tramadol, both T40.4), while one drug named on two lines is coded twice, so code counts cannot tell two drugs from one drug named twice.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 884); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 891)

key_findings.finding: Context cited from another study (ref 28), not this study's data: specific drugs were named on 93% of drug poisoning death certificates in Washington State in 2008–2010 against 75% nationally, and on fewer than 50% in some states. The author notes that heroin and morphine were counted without qualification although morphine is a heroin metabolite, and that certifiers' use of scene evidence may not be consistent across counties or states.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author concludes that in Washington State in 2003–2010 prescription drugs were associated with more poisoning deaths than illicit drugs, in both sexes and at all ages, and that many of the most named drugs share ICD codes with other drugs and cannot be identified from the codes alone.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 12th and 13th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: 'Opiate' was named on 1,240 certificates, 676 of which also named a specific opiate, leaving 564 that named only 'opiate'; Table 5 counts 'opiate' 543 times under the rule that it counted only when no specific opiate was named.
reporting_issues.consequence: A difference of 21 deaths that the paper does not explain; which words counted as a specific opiate is not defined in either place.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists diphenhydramine among the most often named prescription drugs and calls its presence a surprise, while describing it as an ingredient of many over-the-counter allergy drugs and sleep aids; Appendix Table 1 has a separate over-the-counter category, and the category given to each drug word is not printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The prescription total (5,454, 70%) may include drugs available without prescription; cite the prescription-against-illicit comparison with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion say only 4 of the 25 most named substances (methadone, alcohol, cocaine, heroin) have an ICD code that identifies them; carbon monoxide, 16th in Table 1 with 394 deaths, has its own code in Table 5 (T58).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the point stands (most of the top substances share codes), but 20 rather than 21 of the 25 lack a substance-specific code if carbon monoxide is counted, as Table 1 counts it.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says oxycodone's code T40.2 is shared 'with all opioids other than opium, methadone, and heroin', but the Introduction and Table 5 place fentanyl, tramadol and propoxyphene under T40.4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use Table 5 for which opioids share which code.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the top drugs named among suicides were acetaminophen and diphenhydramine, but Table 4 lists carbon monoxide (288) and alcohol (196) before acetaminophen (175) and diphenhydramine (148); alcohol is counted as a drug elsewhere (Table 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor wording: carbon monoxide was the substance most often named on suicide certificates, alcohol second.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper never reports how many of the 7,817 certificates named no specific drug: Appendix Table 1 has a 'nonspecific' word category and Figures 4–5 show a group naming neither a prescription nor an illicit drug only as rates. The only completeness figure, specific drugs named on 93% of Washington drug-poisoning certificates in 2008–2010 against 75% nationally, is cited from another study (ref 28).
reporting_issues.consequence: How much of Washington's certificate text could not be resolved to a drug is not measured here; cite the 93% as second-hand. The point that text cannot recover a drug that was never written rests on the author's reasoning (p. 892), not on a count.

design_detail: Descriptive case series of four medico-legal autopsies of suspected drug overdose deaths. Blood was drawn separately (needle puncture after ligation or cross-clamping) from up to 11 vessel sites: pulmonary vein and artery, thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava above and below the renal veins, subclavian and femoral veins; also mixed cardiac blood (case 3) and portal venous blood (case 2), with cerebrospinal fluid, vitreous humour, bile, urine, solid organs and gastrointestinal contents. Drugs: doxepin (case 1); amobarbital, secobarbital and pentobarbital (case 2); clomipramine and flurazepam taken with chloral hydrate (case 3); imipramine, with lidocaine given in hospital (case 4). The only measurement in life is one hospital blood sample in case 4. Concentrations are reported descriptively; no statistics.
can_establish: That in four selected overdose deaths, concentrations of tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and flurazepam differed several-fold between blood samples taken from different vessels of the same body, usually highest in central vessels and lowest in subclavian or femoral veins (not in case 1), and that in the one case with a sample from life, every post-mortem blood sample, femoral included, was higher than that sample.
cannot_establish: How often or by how much such differences occur in deaths generally (four cases chosen to illustrate, no denominator); whether the differences arose after death rather than before it (no body was sampled at intervals after death; diffusion out of organs is the authors' inference); whether they apply to other drugs, including illicit drugs, or to deaths after ordinary amounts; or that any death after therapeutic doses has been misread as an overdose (no such case is studied).

sample.recruitment: Medico-legal autopsies: suspected drug overdoses identified before autopsy so that an extended protocol (many tissues and fluids, multiple blood samples) could be followed (p. 254, Materials and Methods). The office, period and number of eligible or sampled cases are not stated; the authors were at the University of Dundee and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, Edmonton, Alberta (p. 253).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond suspected drug overdose identified before autopsy (p. 254).
sample.demographics: Case 1: man aged 23, 175 cm, 70 kg. Case 2: man aged 38, 180 cm, 87 kg, found dead in a remand-centre cell and described as known to inject oral pharmaceutical preparations. Case 3: woman aged 24, 165 cm, 64 kg. Case 4: man aged 47, 177 cm, 92 kg (pp. 254–259). No significant pre-existing natural disease at autopsy in any case.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The cases were presented to illustrate the dramatic extent of the phenomenon (Abstract and Introduction, p. 253), so they are likely to be among the most striking; how many deaths were sampled with this protocol, and why these four were published, is not reported. All four were deaths after large ingestions (cases 1, 3 and 4 described as suicidal overdoses), three with unabsorbed drug still in the stomach or bowel (cases 1–3). The drugs are tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and flurazepam; the findings may not carry over to other drugs, including illicit drugs, or to deaths after ordinary amounts.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem concentrations by gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection (doxepin, imipramine, clomipramine and their desmethyl metabolites), high-performance liquid chromatography with UV detection at 214 nm (the three barbiturates) and gas chromatography with electron-capture detection (flurazepam, desalkylflurazepam); internal standards, a 5-point calibration before each set of samples, all specimens run in duplicate, independent in-house quality controls with each run (p. 254). No limits of detection, precision or recovery are given. Lidocaine (case 4) and trichloroethanol (case 3) results are reported without a described method, and the screening used to establish which drugs were present is not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amounts taken are unknown. Described as suicidal overdoses of doxepin (case 1), of chloral hydrate, clomipramine and flurazepam (case 3) and of imipramine (case 4); in case 2 the stomach held a ruptured condom with granular debris, and no cause or manner of death is stated (pp. 254–259). Unabsorbed drug: tablet debris and two intact capsules in the duodenum (case 1, p. 254); 746, 993 and 903 mg of amobarbital, secobarbital and pentobarbital in the stomach contents (case 2, Table 2, p. 257); 2,400 mg of clomipramine and 9 mg of flurazepam in the stomach contents (case 3, Table 3, p. 258). Case 4 had gastric lavage with charcoal in hospital (p. 259).
exposure.polysubstance: Case 2: three barbiturates together. Case 3: chloral hydrate (its metabolite trichloroethanol measured only in mixed cardiac blood, 247 mg/l, and liver, 342 mg/kg), clomipramine and flurazepam. Case 4: lidocaine given intravenously in hospital (pp. 257–259). Case 1 is reported as doxepin and its metabolite only (p. 254). Ethanol is not reported for any case.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (deaths). Interval from death to autopsy sampling: case 1, 17 h after the body was found and 40 h after he was last known alive; case 2, 30 h after discovery and an estimated 36 h after death; case 3, an estimated 24–48 h after death; case 4, 7.25 h after death and 9.25 h after the hospital sample (pp. 254–259). Body position and storage before autopsy are not reported.

comparison.controls: No comparison group and no deaths from other causes. Comparisons are within each body (blood from different vessels, tissues and fluids) and, in case 4 only, with one hospital blood sample drawn on admission, about 1 h before cardiac arrest (p. 259).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Concentrations at the moment of death are unknown in all four cases. Case 4 has a separate sample from life: the text puts it about one hour before cardiac arrest, while the reported intervals imply about two hours before death. Arrest and death are not interchangeable. Further absorption after that sample cannot be excluded. One post-mortem sampling occasion per person is described; repeated post-mortem sampling is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Drug and metabolite concentrations in mg/l (blood and fluids), mg/kg (tissues) and mg (gastrointestinal contents) (Tables 1–4, pp. 256–260); blood concentrations by vessel plotted in Figures 1–4 (pp. 255–259); Figure 5 sets case 4 organ concentrations beside blood from nearby vessels (p. 260).
outcomes.validity_norms: No assay validation data are reported; there are no reference values for site differences.
outcomes.operationalization: Site dependence is shown as the spread of concentrations across blood samples from one body. That the spread is an artefact arising after death is the authors' inference from its size and pattern (pp. 260–262), not a change measured over time.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive values; no statistical tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Not material to instrumental assays, but the four cases were chosen for publication with their results known.

analysis.effect_sizes: Printed ranges (pp. 255–259): case 1, doxepin 3.6–12.5 and desmethyldoxepin 1.2–7.5 mg/l; case 2, amobarbital 4.3–25.8, secobarbital 3.9–25.3 and pentobarbital 5.1–31.5 mg/l in systemic blood, with portal venous blood at 40.9, 42.8 and 48.3 mg/l; case 3, clomipramine 4.0–21.5 and desmethylclomipramine 1.7–8.1 mg/l, mixed cardiac blood 15.3 and 4.1 mg/l, flurazepam 0.15–0.99 mg/l with mixed cardiac blood 0.51 mg/l; case 4, imipramine 4.1–18.1 and desipramine 1.0–3.6 mg/l against 2.3 and 0.6 mg/l in the hospital sample, lidocaine 0.9–1.4 mg/l. Editors' calculation, highest to lowest systemic-blood value within one body (excluding the separately reported portal values): doxepin 3.5-fold; amobarbital 6.0-, secobarbital 6.5- and pentobarbital 6.2-fold; clomipramine 5.4-fold; flurazepam 6.6-fold; imipramine 4.4-fold; lidocaine 1.6-fold. Case 4 post-mortem imipramine was 1.8 to 7.9 times the hospital value (4.1/2.3 and 18.1/2.3); the femoral veins, read from Figure 4 at 300 dpi, were about 5.0 and 5.6 mg/l, about 2.2–2.4 times it. In case 1 the femoral vein, read from Figure 1, was about 5.0 mg/l, about 0.4 times the pulmonary venous value and above the pulmonary artery (3.6) and thoracic aorta (4.4). Figure5 is a qualitative organ/blood comparison; its apparent femoral-bar inconsistency with Figure4 is noted separately, so the approximate femoral values above are taken from Figure4 rather than substituted from Figure5.
analysis.selective_reporting: Desalkylflurazepam was assayed (p. 254) but no result is reported; flurazepam blood values are given only as a range with the highest and lowest sites (p. 257). Whether other deaths were sampled with this protocol and not reported is unknown.
analysis.power: Not applicable (four cases).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four selected overdose deaths, blood concentrations of tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and flurazepam differed about 3.5- to 6.6-fold between systemic vessels of the same body (not including case 2 portal values) (editors' calculation), usually highest in the pulmonary vessels or in the inferior vena cava and lowest in subclavian or femoral veins; in case 1 the lowest doxepin value was in the pulmonary artery. In case 4 every post-mortem blood sample exceeded a hospital sample taken about an hour before cardiac arrest. Lidocaine, given in hospital and hardly concentrated in organs other than muscle and cerebral cortex, varied only 1.6-fold across the same samples (editors' calculation).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract says the data suggest diffusion of drug out of solid organs into blood and states that the lowest levels were found in peripheral vessels (p. 253); the Discussion calls diffusion from solid organs the major factor while conceding that the cause is unresolved and probably multifactorial (pp. 261–262). The mechanism is inferred, not observed: no body was sampled at intervals after death, and the authors judge incomplete distribution in life insufficient as a full explanation, but explicitly allow it as a contributor. They do not measure its relative contribution; substantial unabsorbed drug remained in the gut in cases1–3, and further absorption after the hospital sample in case4 cannot be excluded. The warning that an artefactually raised level after therapeutic doses may be misread as a lethal overdose (p. 262) cites a conference paper (ref. 14), not these overdose cases. The Abstract's peripheral-lowest generalization does not hold for case 1.

timeline.event: Jones & Pounder, a single detailed case study of site dependence of drug concentrations in post-mortem blood (ref. 9 of this paper; not read by this reader).

Leikin & Watson's review tabulates approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs (doxepin 5.5, imipramine 1.8 to 2.2, clomipramine 1.9), without case numbers or per-drug sources; it cites Pounder's 1993 book chapter, not this paper.

Ketola & Kriikku compile paired within-case ratios from the literature, with this paper among the doxepin sources: median ratio of other blood (such as cardiac blood) to femoral blood 1.27 across drugs, doxepin 1.61 (26 results).
Borra et al., a review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: Site dependence of post-mortem blood concentrations has since been compiled across many drugs (Leikin & Watson 2003; Ketola & Kriikku 2019, both read in this batch), with central-to-femoral ratios usually smaller than the several-fold differences shown in these selected cases and varying widely between drugs and between cases. Neither later source settles how much of the difference arises after death rather than from incomplete distribution before death.

funding.funder: No funding statement. The Acknowledgements thank three named technical staff for the large number of drug determinations (p. 262).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article (1990).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Dundee, and Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, Edmonton, Alberta (p. 253). Two sources cited for key points are the authors' own: the 1987 case study (ref. 9) and Jones's 1988 conference paper on site-dependent differences (ref. 14). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated sampling of the same vessels from shortly after death until autopsy, in consecutive rather than selected deaths with known drug intake and, where possible, a blood level taken at or just before death, including deaths after ordinary therapeutic or recreational amounts, with body position and storage temperature recorded. This would separate change after death from uneven distribution before death and show how often a level is raised enough to change the conclusion about cause of death.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Four autopsies of suspected overdoses chosen to illustrate the phenomenon; no frame (office, period, eligible deaths) is stated.
Selection to illustrate; how many deaths were sampled with the protocol and why these four were reported is not stated.
Four cases: enough to show that several-fold differences occur, not how often or how large they usually are.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, body size, autopsy findings and intervals from death to autopsy are given; the office, period, body storage and position, and who decided cause and manner of death are not; case 2 has no stated cause or manner.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All four cases are reported, but not every measured result (desalkylflurazepam; flurazepam by site), and whether other sampled deaths were left out is unknown.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Site-specific blood from ligated or cross-clamped vessels and chromatographic assays with internal standards, calibration, duplicates and quality controls; no validation data, and the condition of interest (change after death) is inferred from the pattern, not measured over time.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Same sampling technique throughout, but the set of sites differs between cases (one or both subclavian and femoral veins; mixed cardiac blood only in case 3; portal vein only in case 2) and death-to-sampling intervals range from 7.25 h to an estimated 48 h.
Descriptive concentrations only; no estimate to which statistics would apply.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Autopsy cases, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI items are applied to a small case series without a comparison group, as the round brief directs (the project's JBI instrument is the prevalence checklist; items 8 and 9 do not apply). The measurements appear careful (separately ligated vessels, duplicate assays with quality controls), so the concentrations are credible as measured; the risk lies in selection (four illustrative cases, no denominator) and in the inference about cause (no serial sampling), which together make the editors' summary high. Citable for: several-fold differences in tricyclic antidepressant, barbiturate and flurazepam concentrations between blood drawn from different vessels of the same body, usually central higher than femoral; and, in one case, every post-mortem sample including femoral blood above a sample taken in hospital before death. Not citable for: how often or by how much this happens in deaths generally, the mechanism, illicit drugs, or deaths after therapeutic doses being misclassified as overdoses (not studied here).

key_findings.finding: Case 1 (suicidal doxepin overdose; autopsy 17 h after the body was found and 40 h after he was last known alive): blood doxepin 3.6–12.5 mg/l and desmethyldoxepin 1.2–7.5 mg/l across nine vessel sites; highest in the pulmonary vein, the other sites varying over a small range; pulmonary artery 3.6 and 1.8 mg/l, thoracic aorta 4.4 and 1.6 mg/l.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 1 (5208), 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd continuing on p. 255); Fig. 1 (p. 255)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 1 at 300 dpi (approximate): femoral vein doxepin about 5.0 mg/l and subclavian about 5.1 mg/l, both above the pulmonary artery (3.6) and thoracic aorta (4.4). The lowest desmethyldoxepin bar is about 1.5 mg/l, not the printed 1.2 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Case 2 (man found dead in a remand-centre cell, ruptured condom and granular debris in the stomach; autopsy 30 h after discovery and an estimated 36 h after death): systemic blood amobarbital 4.3–25.8, secobarbital 3.9–25.3 and pentobarbital 5.1–31.5 mg/l, highest in the inferior vena cava above the renal veins and lowest in the right femoral vein; portal venous blood 40.9, 42.8 and 48.3 mg/l; of the solid organs only the liver concentrated the drugs (61, 74 and 89 mg/kg).
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 2 (5202), 2nd paragraph (p. 255, continuing on p. 256); Fig. 2 (p. 256); Table 2 (p. 257)
key_findings.note: The lowest site (right femoral vein) is read from Figure 2, whose bars there match the printed minima (about 4.4, 4.0 and 5.1 mg/l at 300 dpi).

key_findings.finding: Case 3 (suicidal overdose of chloral hydrate, clomipramine and flurazepam; autopsy an estimated 24–48 h after death): clomipramine 4.0–21.5 and desmethylclomipramine 1.7–8.1 mg/l across vessels, highest in the pulmonary artery and vein and lowest in the femoral veins; mixed cardiac blood 15.3 and 4.1 mg/l. Flurazepam 0.15–0.99 mg/l, highest in the inferior vena cava below the renal veins and lowest in the subclavian and femoral veins; mixed cardiac blood 0.51 mg/l.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 3 (5269), 2nd paragraph (p. 257, continuing on p. 259); Fig. 3 (p. 258)

key_findings.finding: Case 4 (suicidal imipramine overdose treated in hospital with gastric lavage, charcoal and intravenous lidocaine; autopsy 7.25 h after death): a blood sample drawn on admission, about 1 h before cardiac arrest, held imipramine 2.3 and desipramine 0.6 mg/l and no lidocaine; post-mortem blood held imipramine 4.1–18.1 and desipramine 1.0–3.6 mg/l, lowest in the subclavian and femoral veins, high in the aorta and the inferior vena cava above the renal veins, highest in the pulmonary vein. Lidocaine ranged 0.9–1.4 mg/l in the same samples. Editors' calculation: every post-mortem sample exceeded the hospital value, by 1.8- to 7.9-fold.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 4 (5061), 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 4
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 4 at 300 dpi (approximate): left and right femoral veins about 5.0 and 5.6 mg/l imipramine, about 2.2–2.4 times the hospital value. The stated intervals place the hospital sample about 2 h before death (autopsy 9.25 h after the sample and 7.25 h after death).

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the printed ranges, highest to lowest systemic-blood concentration within one body, excluding the separate portal values: doxepin 3.5-fold (case 1); amobarbital 6.0-, secobarbital 6.5- and pentobarbital 6.2-fold (case 2); clomipramine 5.4- and flurazepam 6.6-fold (case 3); imipramine 4.4-fold and lidocaine 1.6-fold (case 4).
key_findings.locator: Results › Cases 1–4

key_findings.finding: Tricyclic antidepressants were concentrated in liver and lung: case 1 doxepin 62 mg/kg in liver, 73 and 26 mg/kg in the left and right lungs and 70 mg/kg in renal cortex, against 7.5–10.8 mg/kg in skeletal muscle; case 4 imipramine 136 mg/kg in liver and 100 mg/kg in lungs, against 16–24 mg/kg in skeletal muscle. In case 4, the relative concentrations in organs broadly paralleled those in blood from each organ's associated vessels.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 256); Results › Case 4, 2nd paragraph (p. 259); Table 4 and Fig. 5 (p. 260)

key_findings.finding: Unabsorbed drug remained in the gut in cases 1–3: tablet debris and two intact capsules in the duodenum (case 1); 746, 993 and 903 mg of amobarbital, secobarbital and pentobarbital in the stomach contents with further amounts along the small bowel (case 2); 2,400 mg of clomipramine and 9 mg of flurazepam in the stomach contents (case 3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Case 1, 1st paragraph (p. 254); Table 2 (p. 257); Table 3 (p. 258)

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that arterial–venous differences in life and the variable make-up of post-mortem blood cannot fully explain differences this large, while explicitly allowing incomplete distribution in life as a contributory factor (in their earlier case they found no correlation between drug concentration and haemoglobin content), and propose diffusion after death along concentration gradients from organs holding high concentrations, especially liver and lung, into nearby vessels; they state that the cause remains unresolved and is probably multifactorial.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 260, continuing on p. 261), 2nd, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 261)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that a post-mortem blood concentration may differ several-fold from the true concentration at death; that after therapeutic doses an artefactually raised level could be misread as a lethal overdose (citing ref. 14); that predicting the dose taken from post-mortem blood is invalid for some drugs (citing ref. 5); and that databases of post-mortem blood concentrations lose reference value when the sampling site is unknown. Their Discussion limits the several-fold differences to some, not all drugs; lidocaine given in hospital varied much less in case4.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th (last) paragraph (p. 261, continuing on p. 262)

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract states that the lowest levels were found in peripheral vessels such as the subclavian and femoral veins, but in case 1 the lowest doxepin concentration (3.6 mg/l) was in the pulmonary artery and the femoral vein (about 5.0 mg/l, read from Figure 1) exceeded several central sites; the Results themselves say the case 1 samples other than the pulmonary vein varied over a small range.
reporting_issues.consequence: The central-high, peripheral-low pattern held in three of four cases; it should not be cited as universal even within this series.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract and Results give 1.2 mg/l as the lowest desmethyldoxepin blood concentration in case 1, but no bar in Figure 1 lies below about 1.5 mg/l (enlarged crop of the figure; the pulmonary artery bar at 1.8 matches the text).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a sample is missing from the figure or a value is misprinted; the metabolite's spread would be about 5-fold rather than 6.3-fold if the minimum is 1.5 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Materials and Methods describe an assay for desalkylflurazepam, but no result for it is reported; lidocaine (case 4) and trichloroethanol (case 3) results are reported without any described method.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the lidocaine values, which show little site variation, rest on an undescribed assay.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 4's hospital sample is described as drawn about 1 h before cardiac arrest, while the stated intervals (autopsy 9.25 h after the sample and 7.25 h after death) place it about 2 h before death; the course in between and its bearing on the comparison are not discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absorption from the gut may have continued after the sample was drawn, so the excess of post-mortem over hospital values cannot be attributed wholly to change after death. Cardiac arrest and death are different endpoints, so one hour before arrest versus two hours before death is not by itself a contradiction; the intervening course is not described.

reporting_issues.issue: The office, period and number of deaths sampled with the protocol are not reported, the four cases were chosen to illustrate the phenomenon, and case 2's cause and manner of death are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The series shows that large site differences occur, not how often; how the deaths were classified cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure5's schematic femoral-vein imipramine bar appears near 9 mg/l, whereas Figure4's left/right femoral bars are about5.0 and5.6 mg/l (all approximate readings). The text gives no explanation for the schematic's selected/combined femoral value.
