design_detail: Analysis of US national death-certificate data, the CDC Multiple Cause of Death files for 1999–2015 (with county of residence, which the public-use files lack), covering all drug poisoning deaths of US residents: ICD-10 underlying cause X40–X44, X60–X64, X85 or Y10–Y14 (all intents). Opioid involvement = any of T40.0–T40.4 or T40.6 among the multiple causes; heroin/synthetic opioid involvement = T40.1 or T40.4. For deaths whose only drug code was T50.9 (unspecified drugs, medicaments and biologicals), involvement was imputed: year-specific probit models were fitted to deaths with at least one drug category specified, with demographic, day-of-week, place-of-death and 2010 county covariates, and their predicted values were applied to the unspecified deaths. Reported and corrected counts, rates per 100,000 (mid-year US population) and changes since 1999 are compared by year (Tables 1 and 2). No toxicology or case records; no confidence intervals. A short 'Data Notes' article; details and Stata do-files are in the Supporting Information (not read).
can_establish: How much national counts and rates of opioid-involved and heroin/synthetic-opioid-involved drug poisoning deaths in 1999–2015 change if deaths certified with no named drug are assumed to involve these drugs with the probability predicted from deaths with a named drug and similar recorded characteristics, and how that assumption changes the size and the percentage growth of the trend.
cannot_establish: How many deaths with no drug named actually involved opioids (no such death was checked against toxicology or investigation records); whether opioids caused the deaths counted as opioid-involved (a T code counts involvement, whatever other drugs were present); how uncertain the corrected figures are (no intervals were computed); deaths in which other drugs were named but an opioid was missed; or deaths wrongly counted as drug-related or as opioid-involved (the method can only add involvement).

sample.recruitment: Registry: all deaths of US residents in the CDC Multiple Cause of Death files, 1999–2015 (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 1339); the correction needs county of residence, which the public-use mortality files do not contain (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 1342).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Drug poisoning deaths by ICD-10 underlying cause: X40–X44 (unintentional), X60–X64 (suicide), X85 (assault) and Y10–Y14 (undetermined intent) (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 1340; Table 1 note). Deaths coded to other underlying causes are outside the count by definition.
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article: the model covariates are listed, but no distribution of the deaths is given (the Supporting Information was not read).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (complete registrations).
sample.selection_effects: Which deaths have no drug named depends on testing and certification practice, which varies by place and over time, the paper's premise: 23.1% of drug poisoning deaths had no specific drug, from 26.0% (2008) to 17.2% (2015) (p. 1340). The covariates listed in the Table 1 note do not include state or the type of death-investigation system, so differences in certification practice enter the model only through demographic, place-of-death and county variables.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided: certifiers (the Discussion refers to medical examiners and coroners) write the causes on the death certificate, and the drugs listed as immediate or contributory causes appear as ICD-10 T codes in the multiple-cause files (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 1340). Reported counts use only these codes and attribute no drug to deaths whose only drug code is T50.9 (Methods, 3rd paragraph). Corrected counts add imputed involvement for those deaths, using predicted values from year-specific probit models fitted to deaths with at least one drug category specified (Methods, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1 note, p. 1341); whether the predicted probabilities were summed or used to classify each death is not stated in the article. No toxicology data were used; what was tested at death, and in what share of deaths, is not reported, and the Discussion notes that budgets are likely to limit testing and autopsies (p. 1343).
exposure.polysubstance: A death counts as opioid-involved if any opioid code is present, whatever other drugs are coded; heroin and synthetic opioids (T40.4, which includes fentanyl and other synthetic opioids) are grouped because recent increases in synthetic-opioid deaths are driven largely by non-prescription use, as the paper states. Only deaths with no drug specified are adjusted, so deaths naming other drugs while an opioid involved went unnamed remain uncorrected; the author says the corrected estimates therefore still understate (pp. 1342–1343).

comparison.controls: Reported (certificate-only) counts and rates against corrected (imputed) ones for the same deaths; a simpler 'naive' correction, dividing reported rates by the share of deaths with at least one drug specified, as a check of the method (p. 1342). No external reference such as toxicology or case review.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Characteristics that might make unspecified deaths differ from specified ones beyond the covariates (toxicology availability, certifier type, jurisdiction) were not measured; the missing-at-random assumption is stated (p. 1343).

outcomes.instruments: Annual counts and rates per 100,000 (mid-year US population from the World Bank via FRED, ref 12) of any-opioid-involved and heroin/synthetic-opioid-involved drug poisoning deaths, reported and corrected, with absolute and percentage change since 1999 (Tables 1 and 2). Stata version 15.
outcomes.validity_norms: Corrected counts are model predictions without validation; reported counts are only as complete as certificates and their coding.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Opioid-involved' = an opioid T code on the certificate (reported) or imputed (corrected): involvement, not cause.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive estimates, no hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals (stated as a limitation, p. 1343). Any opioid: reported 8,050 (1999) and 33,091 (2015); corrected 10,232 and 39,999. Heroin/synthetic opioids: reported 2,675 and 19,884; corrected 3,421 and 23,857. Corrected/reported ratio, editors' calculation from Table 1: any opioid 1.209 (2015) to 1.357 (2008); heroin/synthetic 1.200 (2015) to 1.346 (2008). Rates per 100,000 in 2015: any opioid 10.31 reported, 12.46 corrected; heroin/synthetic 6.20 and 7.43. Change 1999–2015: any opioid +25,041 reported against +29,767 corrected (311.1% against 290.9%); heroin/synthetic +17,209 against +20,437 (643.3% against 597.4%). Deaths added by the correction, editors' calculation from Table 1: any opioid 2,182 (1999), at most 7,859 (2011), 6,908 (2015); heroin/synthetic 746 (1999) to 3,973 (2015). For 2015, the 6,908 added deaths are about 77% of the roughly 9,000 deaths with no drug specified (17.2% of the 52,404 drug poisoning deaths given in the Introduction), close to the 76% opioid share among deaths with a drug specified (33,091 of about 43,400), so the imputation was close to proportional reallocation (editors' calculation).
analysis.covariates: In the imputation model (Table 1 note, p. 1341): sex; race (white, black, other non-white); Hispanic origin; marital status; education (four levels); seven age categories; day of week; place of death (hospital in-patient, hospital out-patient or emergency department, dead on arrival, home, other); interactions between sex and race/ethnicity; and 2010 county characteristics (poverty rate, education shares, share of households headed by females, median income, population per square mile and its square, physicians per 1,000).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The yearly shares of unspecified deaths and the full adjustment procedure appear only in the Supporting Information (Table S1 and Stata do-files; not read). How predicted values were turned into counts is not stated in the article. No sensitivity analysis of the missing-at-random assumption (for example by state, intent or certifier type) is reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable (complete registrations).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Imputing opioid involvement for deaths certified with no named drug raises national opioid-involved counts by 21–35% a year as printed (20.9% in 2015 to 35.7% in 2008 by editors' calculation from Table 1; 6,908 deaths in 2015: 33,091 to 39,999) and heroin/synthetic-opioid counts by 20–35% (19,884 to 23,857 in 2015); it increases absolute growth since 1999 and can lower percentage growth, because the 1999 base also rises. The estimates have no stated uncertainty and were not checked against any external source.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the official 2015 figure an undercount, "with the actual number being approximately 39 999": a single model prediction presented as the actual number, to the last death, although the paper computed no confidence intervals (p. 1343). The conclusion that imputation is "likely to provide more accurate estimates" (abstract), and the Discussion's statement that the estimates would be considerably more accurate even if the missing-at-random assumption fails (p. 1343), are asserted without any check against toxicology or case records. The abstract's largest differences, 'in 2011 for any opioids (5677 deaths and 1.7 per 100 000)', are differences between corrected and reported change since 1999; the number of deaths the correction added in 2011 was 7,859 (editors' calculation from Table 1). The method only adds involvement: deaths wrongly certified as drug-related or as opioid-involved are named as a limitation (p. 1343) but play no part in the corrected figures. The paper consistently says 'involved', which does not mean caused.

timeline.event: Slavova et al., 'Drug overdose deaths: let's get specific' (ref 6): cited among earlier recognitions that certificates often name no drug.
Ruhm (Population Health Metrics; ref 8): statistical adjustment of drug poisoning deaths, 1999–2012, an earlier correction by the same author.
Ruhm (American Journal of Preventive Medicine; ref 9): geographic variation in opioid and heroin mortality rates; the correction method here follows this earlier research.

Buchanich et al. (card sc_buchanich_2018): proportional reallocation of unintentional overdose deaths with no named drug, 1999–2015, about 70,000 potential opioid-related deaths; a different method on the same national certificates, compared with Ruhm's state corrections in its Discussion.
Slavova et al. review of methodological complexities (card sc_slavova_2019) relays this paper's 2015 rates (12.46 corrected against 10.31 reported).

Gutkind et al. scoping review (card sc_gutkind_2025): its national figure rests on Ruhm's three analyses, which share author, data and approach; a county linkage study it summarizes (Lowder et al., 2018) found opioids in the toxicology of 86.8% of unspecified overdose deaths in Marion County, Indiana.
Garnett et al., NCHS report for 2017–2023 (card sc_garnett_2026): the share of overdose deaths with at least one specific drug code rose from 87.7% (2017) to 96.0% (2023).

replication.where_it_stands: The direction is consistent across methods: proportional reallocation (Buchanich et al., 2018) and the state and county linkage studies summarized by Gutkind et al. (2025) also find more opioid involvement than certificates show, and one county's toxicology found opioids in 86.8% of unspecified deaths, more than the roughly 77% this model implies nationally for 2015 (editors' calculation), though presence in toxicology is a different measure. The size of the national correction remains a model estimate, repeated by one author on overlapping data, without validation or uncertainty. Certificates named a specific drug far more often after 2015 (NCHS: 87.7% of overdose deaths in 2017, 96.0% in 2023), so these 1999–2015 corrections should not be extended to later years.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article has no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declaration of interests: none (p. 1343).
funding.affiliations_note: Frank Batten School of Leadership and Public Policy, University of Virginia (sole author). The method follows the author's own earlier adjustment studies (refs 8, 9, 14); the scoping review on card sc_gutkind_2025 notes that its three national correction studies are by this author on overlapping data, so they are not independent replications.

what_would_settle_it: A national or multi-state random sample of deaths certified with T50.9 as the only drug code, linked to post-mortem toxicology and investigation records, measuring how often opioids (and heroin or fentanyl) were present and judged contributory, compared with the model's predicted probabilities for the same deaths; with uncertainty intervals for the corrected national counts and sensitivity analyses by state and death-investigation system.

domains.note: All drug poisoning deaths of US residents, all intents, 1999–2015, from the national multiple-cause files.
A census of registrations, not a sample.
568,699 drug poisoning deaths.

domains.note: Codes, data source and covariates are described; the deaths themselves are not described, and the yearly shares of unspecified deaths and the procedure's details are only in the Supporting Information.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths from national certificates (round brief, certificate studies), as on card sc_buchanich_2018. The reported counts are a census of what certificates say, with low risk of bias for that. The corrected counts, which are what the paper is cited for, depend on the assumption that deaths with no drug named resemble deaths with a named drug and the same recorded characteristics; this was not tested against toxicology and carries no stated uncertainty, and the direction of any resulting bias is unknown. Citable for: the share of US drug poisoning deaths with no drug specified in 1999–2015 (23.1%; 26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015); reported counts; model-based corrected counts, labelled as estimates (for example about 40,000 rather than 33,091 opioid-involved deaths in 2015); and the point that such corrections raise absolute growth and can lower percentage growth. Not citable for: the actual number of opioid-involved deaths, opioids as the cause of the added deaths, or years after 2015.

key_findings.finding: Of 42,170,818 deaths of US residents in 1999–2015, 568,699 were drug poisonings; 23.1% of these had no specific drug identified (only T50.9), from a high of 26.0% in 2008 to a low of 17.2% in 2015, with a steady fall after 2008 and no clear pattern before.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The yearly shares are in Supporting Information Table S1, not read; the Methods give one-sixth to one-quarter depending on the year (Methods, 2nd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Counting rules: a drug poisoning death has an ICD-10 underlying cause of X40–X44, X60–X64, X85 or Y10–Y14 (all intents); opioid involvement means T40.0–T40.4 or T40.6 among the multiple causes; heroin/synthetic opioid involvement means T40.1 or T40.4. Synthetic opioids (most importantly fentanyl) are grouped with heroin because, while fentanyl has legal uses, recent increases in deaths are driven largely by non-prescription consumption, as the paper states citing ref 11.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 note (p. 1341)

key_findings.finding: Correction: year-specific probit models, estimated by maximum likelihood on overdose deaths with at least one drug category identified, predicted opioid (and, in a separate model, heroin/synthetic opioid) involvement from sex, race, Hispanic origin, marital status, education, seven age groups, day of week, place of death, sex–race/ethnicity interactions and 2010 county characteristics; the predicted values were used to impute involvement for deaths with only unspecified drugs. Reported counts attribute no drug category to those deaths.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1 note

key_findings.finding: Corrected counts were 21–35% higher than reported for any opioid and 20–35% higher for heroin/synthetic opioids in every year: in 1999, 8,050 and 2,675 deaths reported against 10,232 and 3,421 corrected; in 2015, 33,091 and 19,884 against 39,999 and 23,857. Rates per 100,000 in 2015: 10.3 and 6.2 reported, 12.5 and 7.4 corrected.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (p. 1341); Table 2 (p. 1342)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: the corrected/reported ratio for any opioid ranged from 1.209 (2015) to 1.357 (2008), i.e. up to 35.7% (editors' calculation; the paper prints 21–35%), and for heroin/synthetic opioids from 1.200 (2015) to 1.346 (2008). Table 2 gives the 2015 corrected rates as 12.46 and 7.43; the Discussion rounds the first to 12.4 (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Deaths added by the correction each year (editors' calculation from Table 1): any opioid 2,182 in 1999, rising to a maximum of 7,859 in 2011 and 6,908 in 2015; heroin/synthetic opioids 746 in 1999 rising to 3,973 in 2015.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (# of Deaths columns)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation. For 2015, the 6,908 added deaths are about 77% of the roughly 9,000 deaths with no drug specified (17.2% of the 52,404 drug poisoning deaths given in the Introduction, p. 1339), close to the opioid share among deaths with a drug specified (33,091 of about 43,400, 76%): the model's imputation was close to proportional reallocation.

key_findings.finding: Growth 1999–2015: corrected counts rose by 29,767 (any opioid) and 20,437 (heroin/synthetic) against 25,041 and 17,209 reported; corrected rates by 8.8 and 6.2 per 100,000 against 7.4 and 5.2. The largest gap between corrected and reported growth was for 1999–2011 for any opioid (5,677 deaths and 1.7 per 100,000) and for 1999–2015 for heroin/synthetic opioids (3,228 deaths and 1.0 per 100,000); the author attributes the difference to more complete reporting after 2011 offsetting any-opioid growth, while heroin/synthetic-opioid deaths rose fast enough after 2011 to more than offset better reporting.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (p. 1341)
key_findings.note: 5,677 and 3,228 are differences between corrected and reported change since 1999, not the number of deaths added in 2011 (7,859) or 2015 (3,973) (editors' calculation; reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Percentage growth can be slower after correction because the 1999 base was 27% (any opioid) and 28% (heroin/synthetic) higher: 1999–2015, 291% corrected against 311% reported for any opioid; from 2007 to 2015 corrected counts grew 61% and 287% and corrected rates 51% and 265%, against 79% and 332% (counts) and 68% and 306% (rates) reported; such comparisons depend on the base year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 1340); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1342)
key_findings.note: Table 1 gives 23,857/6,140 = +288.6% for corrected heroin/synthetic count growth from 2007 to 2015 (editors' calculation), not 287% (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: A simpler 'naive' correction gave similar, not identical, results: specific drug involvement was identified for 74.7% of overdose deaths in 2011, and dividing that year's reported rates (7.31 and 2.25 per 100,000) by 0.747 gives 9.79 and 3.01, against 9.83 and 2.99 from the full procedure, which needs county of residence, absent from the public-use files.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the author: only deaths with no drug specified are adjusted, so with drug 'cocktails' the corrected estimates still understate drug-specific rates; drug mentions may be wrong (heroin use attributed to morphine or codeine); T40.6 (unspecified narcotics) and T40.4 (fentanyl with other synthetic opioids) lack specificity; drug deaths may be attributed to non-drug causes or the reverse; the correction assumes information is missing at random given the covariates; and no confidence intervals were computed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author argues that training and standardization of medical examiners and coroners might improve the completeness and accuracy of certificates, but that budgets are likely to limit expensive testing and autopsies, which give the most accurate information, so corrections will remain necessary for trends, which would otherwise partly reflect changes in reporting accuracy.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give the correction as 21–35% for any opioid, and the abstract as 20–35% for both groups, in every year; by Table 1 the any-opioid correction reached 35.7% in 2008 (26,567 against 19,582) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: cite the printed 21–35% for any opioid, or the yearly counts; a range of 21–36% must be labelled as the editors' calculation (20.9% in 2015 to 35.7% in 2008).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract places the largest differences 'in 2011 for any opioids (5677 deaths and 1.7 per 100 000)' and in 2015 for heroin/synthetic opioids (3,228 deaths). The Results show these are differences between the corrected and reported change since 1999; by Table 1 the correction added 7,859 deaths in 2011 and 3,973 heroin/synthetic deaths in 2015 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may cite 5,677 as the 2011 undercount; it is not. Cite the yearly differences from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Corrected heroin/synthetic count growth from 2007 to 2015 is printed as 287%, but Table 1 gives 23,857/6,140 = 288.6% (editors' calculation). The Discussion gives the 2015 corrected any-opioid rate as 12.4 per 100,000, while Table 2 gives 12.46 and the Results 12.5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor rounding or transcription slips; cite the table values.

design_detail: Secondary analysis, by six RTI International staff, of the public-use file of the US Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) 2018 Census of Medical Examiner and Coroner Offices (CMEC), which RTI had collected for BJS by mail, web and telephone from June 2019 to March 2020, with 2018 as the reference year. 1,648 of 2,037 offices responded (80.9%): 1,341 on the long form and 307 on a shortened form of critical items. Most toxicology analyses use the 1,320 long-form offices that answered question C12i on how they primarily provide toxicology (internally, externally, no access, not necessary); some items use up to 1,648 offices. BJS hot-deck imputations for item non-response are included. Office-level answers only: the census did not ask how many deaths were tested. Analyses are percentages, medians and chi-square tests; logistic regressions and correlation matrices are named in the methods but no results from them are shown.
can_establish: What US medical examiner and coroner offices reported in 2018 about access to toxicology testing, who decided which cases were tested, drug screening and laboratory confirmation, accreditation, forensic toxicologist staffing and salaries, specimen-retention schedules, computerized case records and participation in SUDORS and FARS, by type of toxicology access and by population served.
cannot_establish: How many deaths, or suspected overdose deaths, were tested, on which specimens or with what panel (not asked; the authors state the number is unknown); whether the offices' answers were accurate (single self-reported items, with misclassification the authors document); or how access and practice changed after 2018. Offices reporting no access may have cases processed through an autopsy provider or state medical examiner; the 11.2% is not a share of deaths untested.

sample.recruitment: Census of all US medical examiner and coroner offices (about 2,000; 2,037 in the response-rate denominator), BJS 2018 CMEC, collected by RTI International for BJS from June 2019 to March 2020 by mail, web and telephone, with telephone follow-up for missing or doubtful answers (p. 543, Materials and methods, 1st paragraph and 2018 CMEC data collection). Public dataset obtained from the National Archive of Criminal Justice Data, ICPSR 38251 (p. 543; p. 549, Data availability).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Toxicology analyses restricted to long-form respondents who answered C12i (n = 1,320); the paper says no short-form data were used (p. 543, Measures; p. 547), yet recordkeeping and national-data items are reported for 1,647 to 1,648 offices (p. 544, Measures continued; p. 546).
sample.demographics: Offices by population served: small 550, medium 575, large 195 of 1,320. Median population served 19,186 for offices without access to toxicology and 38,719 for those with access; 154 long-form offices reported zero to four deaths (p. 544, Results, 1st paragraph). Context from the BJS report: about 80% of offices were within a coroner system (p. 544, Determination of toxicology testing need), and only 16 states have centralized offices, most offices being local, with a national median annual budget of $68,000 (p. 542, Introduction 3rd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one-time census). 389 offices did not respond; item non-response ranged from 0.0% (E1) to 5.6% (A9), handled by BJS hot-deck imputation, which the analysis keeps (p. 543).
sample.selection_effects: Respondents are offices, each answered by one person whose role is not reported. Non-responding and short-form offices are not described, and the toxicology items cover 1,320 of 2,037 offices (64.8%, editors' arithmetic). The analysts work for the organization that collected the census for BJS.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. Office characteristics come from single self-reported census items (p. 543, Measures): C12i primary toxicology provision (four options; not all possible routes); A5 population served; B1 and B3 total and personnel budget; A6 and A7 accreditation; A8d and A8e forensic toxicologists and analysts or chemists on the payroll on 31 December 2018; A9d salary range; A12 and A13 ABFT certification; C14e which staff decide which cases receive toxicology (check all that apply); D9 to D11 change of testing strategy during the opioid epidemic, drug screening and laboratory confirmation; E1 and E2 computerized case management; E3b written retention schedule for toxicology specimens; F8b and F8f participation in SUDORS and FARS.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Comparisons between the four toxicology-provision categories and between office sizes; the 2004 census is quoted once for computerized case management.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Differences between categories (caseload, coroner or medical examiner office, state system, rurality) are not adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: The census items listed under exposure. Descriptive percentages and medians, and chi-square tests whose statistic is printed as χ without degrees of freedom (pp. 544–546); SPSS 28.0.1.1 and R 4.2.1 (p. 544, Data analysis).
outcomes.validity_norms: Unvalidated self-report. The authors discuss possible misclassification or misunderstanding of C12i: of 230 offices that reported no access to or no need for toxicology, 43 later said toxicology decisions were not performed by the office, while 187 (about 14% of offices) named staff who made them; and 97 of 227 such offices answered the laboratory-confirmation question D11 (p. 548, Discussion 7th and 8th paragraphs). They also note respondents may have counted drug screens as toxicology, or may have answered about rare circumstances; the responses alone do not prove classification error.
outcomes.operationalization: Access to toxicology = internal or external provision on C12i. Drug screening = yes to D10 (screening at the death scene, external examination or autopsy); confirmation = yes to D11 (routine laboratory confirmation after screening) (p. 546, Table 3 notes). A forensic toxicologist is defined as performing case interpretation; an analyst or chemist does not (p. 544, Results 2nd paragraph). C12i describes the office’s primary provision route; other providers and rare testing remain possible. C14e percentages count offices selecting each staff role, with multiple selections allowed; they do not measure the share of deaths decided by that role.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; seven chi-square tests are printed and several further comparisons are described as significant or as data not shown.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reported primary toxicology provision among 1,320 offices (Table 1, p. 544): internal 78 (5.9%), external 1,012 (76.7%), no access 148 (11.2%), not needed 82 (6.2%). Access 96.4% of large and 75.1% of small offices (χ = 29.88, P < 0.001); of the 78 internal offices, 39 large, 23 medium, 16 small. Strategy changed because of the opioid epidemic 57.4% (761/1,326); drug screening 53.9% (715/1,326); routine confirmation 95.1% of screening offices (674/709) (p. 545). By category (Table 3, p. 546): changed strategy 73.1% internal, 58.2% external, 46.9% no access, 51.2% not needed (χ = 8.08, P = 0.004); screening 57.7, 55.7, 45.9, 39.5 (χ = 5.11, P = 0.024); confirmation 95.6, 96.1, 87.7, 93.8 (χ = 8.89, P = 0.003). Accreditation (Figure 1, p. 545): NAME 14.1% overall, 42.7% internal, 12.0% external, 11.6% no access, 17.5% not needed; IACME 13.4%, 14.3%, 13.1%, 16.6%, 10.0%; 73 offices (about 5.6%) accredited by both or expecting to be. Who decides which cases are tested (Figure 2, p. 545): coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall, 41.0% internal, 67.5% external; autopsy pathologist 27.0%, 60.3%, 27.5%; death investigator 24.4%, 16.7%, 25.5%. Computerized case management 44.8% (Table 4: 69.2, 49.6, 31.1, 26.8; χ = 46.61, P < 0.001); toxicology-specimen retention schedule 45.3% (79.5, 49.2, 30.4, 20.7; χ = 74.94, P < 0.001) (p. 546). SUDORS 25.3%, FARS 30.5% (p. 546). Staff: 211 full-time and 9 part-time forensic toxicologists (p. 544). Editors' calculation, treating responding offices as a sample (Wilson 95% intervals): internal 5.9% (4.8 to 7.3); no access 11.2% (9.6 to 13.0); no access or not needed 17.4% (15.5 to 19.6); screening 53.9% (51.2 to 56.6); confirmation 95.1% (93.2 to 96.4). All role percentages are office-level, check-all-that-apply responses, and C12i identifies a primary route only.
analysis.covariates: None. Logistic regressions and correlation matrices are named in the methods (p. 544) but no results are reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of a public dataset; no protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Several results are 'data not shown' (size breakdown of internal offices, offices with few deaths, networked case systems, accreditation by both bodies, SUDORS and FARS by category); salaries in offices with external toxicology are called significantly lower with no test shown.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the internal-toxicology category has 78 offices and the salary medians rest on 58 to 62 offices.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2018, 82.6% of 1,320 responding US medical examiner and coroner offices reported access to toxicology, almost all through external laboratories; 11.2% reported no access and 6.2% no need. Small offices had access less often than large ones (75.1% against 96.4%). Coroners or other non-physicians were the staff role selected most often by responding offices on a check-all-that-apply question; this is not a share of case decisions. About half the offices screened for drugs at the scene, external examination or autopsy, and 95.1% of those routinely confirmed in a laboratory. Fewer than half had a specimen-retention schedule (45.3%) or a computerized case system (44.8%). The census does not record how many deaths were tested. The reported primary-route category “no access” can coexist with testing through another provider, as the authors explain.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract matches the tables. The Discussion overstates or misstates several figures: four out of five offices with access changed their testing strategy (p. 547; Table 3 gives 73.1% internal and 58.2% external, 57.4% overall); 47% of offices had a computerized case system, 12 percentage points above the 35% of the 2004 census (p. 547; Results and Table 4 give 44.8%); NAME accreditation 14.3% (p. 547; Figure 1 gives 14.1%); overdose deaths rose 36% from 67,367 in 2018 to 105,700 in 2023 (p. 547; the rise is 56.9%, editors' arithmetic); and about 294 deaths per forensic toxicologist (p. 547), a ratio the authors themselves qualify by saying the number of suspected overdose cases that are tested is unknown (p. 548). The Conclusion that offices are adapting to the drug market rests on a single yes-or-no item about changed strategy.

timeline.event: Earlier BJS census of medical examiner and coroner offices (Hickman et al.): 35% of offices had a computerized case system (as cited, p. 547). Zaychik (2024, p. 2) cites the same census: offices serving over 250,000 people performed toxicology in drug intoxication deaths in 57% of cases, smaller offices in 34%.
Kentucky coroners' survey on the toxicology-testing mandate (cited as reference 21).
NAME position paper recommending comprehensive toxicology and autopsy in suspected overdose deaths (cited as reference 22).
BJS report on the 2018 census, Medical Examiner and Coroner Offices, 2018 (Brooks; reference 2), which this paper extends with items not published there.

Lundberg et al. (JAMA): in five states with decentralized systems, opioid laboratory tests were unavailable in about half of 74,751 injury-death investigations and in 1 in 10 unintentional overdose investigations (reference 32, as summarized, pp. 543 and 547).
This paper: toxicology capability of US offices in 2018 from the census public file.

replication.where_it_stands: The only national description of toxicology capacity in US medical examiner and coroner offices on the project's list, for 2018; no later census is reported. It describes what offices said they could do, not how many deaths were tested; death-level evidence on missing toxicology comes from studies such as Lundberg et al. (2025, as summarized here) and, for one state, from the Kentucky coroner survey (Quesinberry et al., 2019).

funding.funder: Supported in part by the Forensic Technology Center of Excellence (award 15PNIJ-21-GK-02192-MUMU), awarded by the National Institute of Justice, Office of Justice Programs, US Department of Justice; funding also provided in part by RTI International. The original 2018 CMEC data collection was performed under Cooperative Agreement 2017-MU-CX-K052 from the Bureau of Justice Statistics to RTI International (pp. 548–549, Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement printed. The Acknowledgments state that the opinions are the authors' and do not necessarily reflect those of the US Department of Justice (p. 548).
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors are at RTI International, which collected the census for BJS; two (Smiley-McDonald, Ropero-Miller) are credited with funding acquisition (p. 548, Author contributions). Several cited works are by the same authors (references 1, 28, 29, 36, 41, 42). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount; the data are public (ICPSR 38251).

what_would_settle_it: A death-level national sample: for a representative sample of US deaths certified as, or suspected to be, drug overdoses in one year, record from case files whether toxicology was done, on which specimens and with what panel, and compare the drugs named on the certificate with those found; repeated in the next census year to measure change.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All US medical examiner and coroner offices (2,037).
A census; no sampling.
1,320 offices for the main figures; the internal-toxicology category (78) and the salary medians (58 to 62 offices) are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Offices are described by toxicology provision, size and budget, but not by coroner or medical examiner type, state or caseload in the toxicology tables, and the respondent's role is unknown.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Toxicology items cover 1,320 of 2,037 offices; short-form and non-responding offices are not compared; denominators change from item to item (1,310 to 1,648) and the paper contradicts itself on whether short-form records were used.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Single self-reported items, not validated; the authors discuss possible misclassification or misunderstanding of C12i, but also rare-use and other-provider explanations. Figure 1’s accreditation patterns do not independently prove response errors.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One questionnaire, but three modes (mail, web, telephone), skip patterns not always followed on paper forms, and imputed values included.

Percentages reproduce from their counts, but there are no intervals, chi-square tests lack degrees of freedom, regressions named in the methods are not reported, and the Discussion contains several arithmetic errors.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: 80.9% of offices responded, but only 1,341 (65.8% of 2,037, editors' arithmetic) on the long form that carried the toxicology items; item non-response was imputed, the short-form offices were not.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI prevalence checklist, because the paper describes how common practices and capacities were among US offices in one census year. Editors' summary: moderate risk of bias. The census frame and response are strong; the limits are single self-reported items with possible response misclassification, toxicology items covering about two-thirds of offices, shifting denominators, and errors confined mostly to the Discussion. Citable for, as offices' own reports for 2018: toxicology provision (5.9% internal, 76.7% external, 11.2% no access, 6.2% not needed, of 1,320); access by office size (96.4% large, 75.1% small); the staff roles selected by offices on a check-all-that-apply item (coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall); drug screening (53.9%) and routine laboratory confirmation (95.1% of screening offices); NAME (14.1%) and IACME (13.4%) accreditation; specimen-retention schedules (45.3%) and computerized case systems (44.8%); SUDORS (25.3%) and FARS (30.5%) participation; and the authors' statement that the number of suspected overdose deaths tested is unknown. Not citable for: the share of deaths tested, the Discussion's 'four out of five', 47%, 36% and 294-cases-per-toxicologist figures, or any change after 2018.

key_findings.finding: The 2018 CMEC reached 1,648 of 2,037 offices (80.9%): 1,341 (81.4% of respondents) on the long form and 307 (18.6%) on a shortened form; data were collected by RTI International for BJS from June 2019 to March 2020 by mail, web and telephone, about calendar 2018.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods, 1st paragraph; 2018 CMEC data collection, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 1,320 offices that answered how they primarily provide toxicology, 78 (5.9%) had an internal toxicology function, 1,012 (76.7%) used external toxicology services, 148 (11.2%) reported no access to toxicology and 82 (6.2%) said they did not need it; 230 (17.4%) therefore had no access or no need. These office categories do not count untested deaths; testing through another provider remains possible.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results, MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Large offices (serving 250,000 or more; n = 195) were most likely to have access to toxicology (96.4%) and small offices (24,999 or less; n = 550) least likely (75.1%); population served was significantly related to access (χ = 29.88, P < 0.001). Of the 78 offices with internal toxicology, 39 were large, 23 medium and 16 small. Median population served was 19,186 for offices without access and 38,719 for those with access.
key_findings.locator: Results, MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The text gives 23 of 78 as 29.4% (editors' arithmetic: 29.5%). Degrees of freedom are not printed.

key_findings.finding: Responding offices reported 211 full-time and 9 part-time forensic toxicologists on staff in 2018 (data from 1,647 offices); 10% of offices employed forensic toxicologists and 7.8% forensic analysts or chemists; most offices employed no ABFT-certified staff.
key_findings.locator: Results, MEC characteristics by toxicology capabilities, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The authors say this undercounts toxicology professionals in external laboratories and consultants (p. 547, Discussion 3rd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Median total budgets were $1,350,000 for offices with internal toxicology, $95,878 with external services, $30,657 with no access and $20,000 for offices not needing toxicology; median minimum and maximum forensic toxicologist salaries in offices with internal toxicology were $64,024 and $112,312.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 544)
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives n = 1,320 for budgets, 834 for personnel budgets, 62 and 58 for the salary medians; the text gives n = 1,317 and n = 58.

key_findings.finding: Fewer than one in six offices were accredited by NAME or IACME: NAME 14.1% of all offices (42.7% with internal toxicology, 12.0% external, 11.6% no access, 17.5% not needed) and IACME 13.4% (14.3%, 13.1%, 16.6%, 10.0%); 73 offices (about 5.6%) were accredited by both or expected to be by the end of 2018.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 544); Figure 1 (p. 545)
key_findings.note: Figure values are printed data labels in the image (read on a 300-dpi rendering; not in the text layer). The Discussion gives NAME 14.3% (p. 547).

key_findings.finding: Coroner/non-physician was the role most often selected by offices as responsible for deciding which cases received toxicology (64.7% of responding offices, check all that apply, n = 1,340); by Figure 2, coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall, 41.0% in offices with internal toxicology and 67.5% with external; autopsy pathologist 27.0%, 60.3% and 27.5%; death investigator 24.4%, 16.7% and 25.5%. About 80% of offices were within a coroner system according to the BJS report.
key_findings.locator: Results, Determination of toxicology testing need (p. 544); Figure 2 (p. 545)
key_findings.note: Figure 2 values are printed data labels in the image (read on a 300-dpi rendering). The 'Total' bars are not the weighted average of the two groups shown (editors' arithmetic), and n = 1,340 exceeds the 1,320 who answered C12i.

key_findings.finding: 57.4% (761 of 1,326) of offices said their toxicology testing strategy changed because of the rise in drug-related deaths and the opioid epidemic; 53.9% (715 of 1,326) performed drug screening tests at the death scene, external examination or autopsy; 95.1% (674 of 709) of those routinely confirmed screens with laboratory toxicology. By category (Table 3): changed strategy 73.1%, 58.2%, 46.9% and 51.2%; screening 57.7%, 55.7%, 45.9% and 39.5%; confirmation 95.6%, 96.1%, 87.7% and 93.8% (internal, external, no access, not needed).
key_findings.locator: Results, Forensic toxicology testing strategy (p. 545); Table 3 (p. 546)

key_findings.finding: 44.8% of offices had a computerized case management system and 45.3% a retention schedule for toxicology specimens (n = 1,648); by category, 69.2% and 79.5% with internal toxicology, 49.6% and 49.2% external, 31.1% and 30.4% no access, 26.8% and 20.7% not needed (χ = 46.61 and 74.94, both P < 0.001).

key_findings.finding: Participation in national drug data collections was low: 25.3% of offices took part in CDC's State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System (SUDORS; n = 1,647) and 30.5% in NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS; n = 1,648). key_findings.note: Editors’ arithmetic: if the quoted category percentages are within-category shares, the maximum within the 1,320 C12i offices is about 16.4% for SUDORS and 21.1% for FARS. The category denominator is not fully explained, and its intended meaning cannot be recovered here.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the annual number of suspected overdose cases that receive toxicology testing is unknown, even in offices with in-house testing, and that data from at least two states indicate testing is not done at the level needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins p. 547, right column; statement on p. 548)

key_findings.finding: The authors' context figure: dividing 67,367 drug overdose deaths in 2018 by the toxicologist count gives about 294 cases for each forensic toxicologist to interpret within the death investigation system.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 67,367/220 (the paper's 211 full-time plus 9 part-time) = 306; 67,367/230 (the BJS count quoted in the same paragraph) = 293. The ratio assumes all overdose deaths are interpreted by toxicologists employed by offices, whereas most offices use external laboratories.

key_findings.finding: Second-hand, from a study of five states with decentralized systems: opioid laboratory tests were unavailable in about half of injury-death investigations (51% of 74,751 in the Discussion) and in 1 in 10 unintentional overdose death investigations.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 542, continues p. 543); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 547)
key_findings.note: As summarized from reference 32 (Lundberg et al., JAMA 2025); the Discussion calls it a 2021 CDC study, which is its data year.

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors give: the census was voluntary, with 63 questions of which 8 were specific to toxicology; respondents did not always answer every question and skip patterns on paper forms were not always followed; the toxicology-provision question depended on respondents' interpretation (some may have counted drug screens), and answers to later questions led the authors to discuss possible misclassification or misunderstanding for about 14% of offices, while also allowing rare-use explanations.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample definitions conflict: the paper says no short-form data were used (pp. 543, 547), but refers to 'the full 1648 long form sample' and to 1,647 offices answering A8d 'on the CMEC long form' (p. 544), while the long form had 1,341 respondents (p. 543); the response-rate denominator is 2,037 on p. 543 and 2,036 on p. 547.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which offices enter the 1,647 to 1,648 totals (staff counts, computerized systems, retention schedules, SUDORS and FARS); they appear to include short-form or imputed records.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says four out of five offices with access to toxicology changed their testing strategy, but Table 3 gives 73.1% (internal) and 58.2% (external), and 57.4% overall.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Table 3, not the Discussion.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives 47% of offices with a computerized case system, 12 percentage points above the 35% of the 2004 census, against 44.8% in the abstract, Results and Table 4; NAME accreditation 14.3% against 14.1% in Figure 1; and it calls the 73 offices accredited by both bodies 5.6% 'of these accredited' offices, whereas the Results give them as about 5.6% of all offices.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the Results values; the 2004 comparison is about 10 points, not 12 (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: Context arithmetic: overdose deaths are said to have risen 36% from 67,367 in 2018 to 105,700 in 2023 (p. 547) and by an additional 35% after 2018 (p. 542); from 67,367 to 105,700 is a 56.9% rise (36.3% is the rise divided by the 2023 figure), and from 70,630 in 2019 it is 49.7% (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: These trend percentages should not be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The category-participation wording leaves its denominator unclear: it reports 20.8%/26.9% for external-toxicology offices and 2% or less for the other C12i categories (n = 1,320), alongside overall participation of 25.3%/30.5% using 1,647/1,648 offices. These are different analysis bases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed category rates cannot be safely reconciled or reinterpreted without the raw tabulation or author clarification. The difference from the overall rates alone does not demonstrate an error, because the overall sample is larger; retain the overall figures with their stated bases.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2's 'Total' bars (pathologist 27.0%, coroner 64.7%, investigator 24.4%) are not the weighted averages of the internal and external groups (about 29.8%, 65.6% and 24.9%, editors' arithmetic), and the stated n = 1,340 exceeds the 1,320 offices that answered the toxicology-provision question, although the text says only offices requesting toxicology are shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The full and subgroup bars may use different respondents; unequal weighted averages alone do not prove a figure error. Report 64.7% as the published office-level response, with multiple staff roles allowed and the sample-description uncertainty retained; it is not a share of deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods name logistic regressions and correlation matrices, but none is reported; chi-square statistics are printed as χ without degrees of freedom; external-toxicology offices are said to pay significantly lower salaries with no test shown. The Discussion reports about 300 offices with five or fewer deaths per year, whereas the Results report 154 long-form offices with zero to four deaths: the thresholds and potentially the samples differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the descriptive percentages and the seven printed chi-square tests can be checked. The low-caseload figures are not necessarily contradictory; the paper does not supply a cross-tabulation to reconcile them.

reporting_issues.issue: Offices reporting no access to toxicology were accredited by IACME more often (16.6%) than offices with external access (13.1%), and offices reporting no need were accredited by NAME more often (17.5%) than offices with external access (12.0%) (Figure 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Accreditation and an office’s primary toxicology route are different measures; these patterns alone do not demonstrate misclassification. Retain the authors’ possible-response-interpretation caveat, including testing through other providers and rare circumstances.

disagreements.first_pass: JBI prevalence checklist, because the paper describes how common practices and capacities were among US offices in one census year. Editors' summary: moderate risk of bias. The census frame and response are strong; the limits are single self-reported items with documented misclassification, toxicology items covering about two-thirds of offices, shifting denominators, and errors confined mostly to the Discussion. Citable for, as offices' own reports for 2018: toxicology provision (5.9% internal, 76.7% external, 11.2% no access, 6.2% not needed, of 1,320); access by office size (96.4% large, 75.1% small); who decides which cases are tested (coroner or non-physician 64.7% overall); drug screening (53.9%) and routine laboratory confirmation (95.1% of screening offices); NAME (14.1%) and IACME (13.4%) accreditation; specimen-retention schedules (45.3%) and computerized case systems (44.8%); SUDORS (25.3%) and FARS (30.5%) participation; and the authors' statement that the number of suspected overdose deaths tested is unknown.
