design_detail: Record-review comparison of two counts of heroin-related deaths for deaths occurring in Victoria, Australia, from 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2013. Reference count (the authors' 'gold standard'): closed coronial cases in the National Coronial Information System (NCIS) returned by a broad search (heroin in the certified cause of death, parts 1a, 1b, 1c, 2 or 3; heroin in the NCIS field for the object (primary or secondary) that caused death, alone, with other drugs or as a keyword; heroin as a keyword in police, pathology and coronial reports; heroin, heroin and morphine, or morphine alone in toxicology reports; 9,060 records), each judged with the authors' previously published attribution model (Stam et al., 2017, ref 30), which weighs toxicological evidence (6-acetylmorphine, the morphine-to-codeine ratio, or morphine alone) and investigative evidence (circumstances, scene, clinical and pathological findings). Comparison count: deaths registered in Victoria in the national mortality data of the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) to which Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) mortality coders assigned the heroin code T40.1 as an associated cause, with underlying cause X42, X44, X62, X64, X85, Y12 or Y14 (and F11 or F19 for deaths before 2013). The ABS codes held in the NCIS for each reference case were then used to classify missed cases by underlying-cause code (Table 1) and by how the coroner's finding attributed the death (Table 2). Counts and percentages only; no statistical tests.
can_establish: How many deaths in Victoria in 2012–2013 that met the authors' heroin-attribution model in closed coronial records did not carry the heroin code T40.1 in national mortality data, and at which steps they were lost: the coroner's wording, attribution to morphine or to generic drug toxicity, coding, and deaths never coded at all.
cannot_establish: That all 243 reference deaths were caused by heroin (the reference is the authors' own model, not validated here; 63 of the 243 had no 6-acetylmorphine detected; who applied the model, and whether blind to the codes, is not reported); how often national data wrongly add heroin deaths (only 4 such deaths, among records the search returned, were identified); whether the shortfall holds after 2013, when the ABS revision process changed, or outside Victoria; or why the 20 uncoded deaths were never coded (inferred by elimination).

sample.recruitment: Records: closed NCIS coronial cases for deaths in Victoria in 2012–2013, which typically held an autopsy and toxicology report, a police narrative and the coronial finding; national mortality data held by the AIHW, coded by the ABS (PDF pp. 5–7).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Reference: records returned by the four search strategies (9,060), duplicates removed, kept when the model judged the toxicological and investigative evidence sufficient to attribute the death to heroin; heroin overdose deaths and deaths from misadventure or impairment secondary to acute heroin intoxication were included; deaths in which heroin use was judged coincidental were excluded. Comparison: open and closed cases, registered in Victoria (not by residence), dated by date of death, with the codes listed above (PDF pp. 5–7, 9–10).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex or other characteristics of the 243 deaths, and no breakdown by year.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). How many of the 9,060 records failed which criterion is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One state over two years, chosen so that coronial investigations would be finalized. The reference search covered closed NCIS cases only, while the comparison count included open and closed cases; heroin deaths still open at the search would be missing from the reference (how many cases were open is not stated). The reference includes 8 misadventure deaths from heroin intoxication, while the national comparison count required a drug-poisoning (or, before 2013, F11 or F19) underlying cause; 20 reference deaths had another underlying cause and so could not enter the national count as defined (key finding 13). The model was built by the same team (ref 30). One co-author is at the ABS Mortality Data Centre, whose coding is evaluated, and two at the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine (PDF p. 1).

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. Reportable deaths (unexpected, accidental, suspicious or of unknown cause) go to the coroner for medico-legal investigation (police, toxicology and pathology reports) and are first registered with the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, which passes them to the ABS; after the coroner's formal finding the certified cause of death reaches the NCIS; ABS mortality coders assign ICD-10 codes from both sources and the ABS supplies the AIHW (PDF p. 4; Figure 1, PDF p. 21). Reference count: the authors applied their model to NCIS records (PDF pp. 5–6); how many reviewers, whether they were blind to the ABS codes held in the NCIS, and their agreement are not reported. 'Attributed to heroin' meant heroin named, alone or with other drugs, in the certified cause of death or in the NCIS object-that-caused-death field (PDF p. 8). What was tested: NCIS cases typically held an autopsy and toxicology report (PDF p. 6); the share of the 243 with toxicology is not reported; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180 (74%, editors' calculation).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not separated. The model attributes deaths to heroin alone or in combination with other drugs; 11 deaths were attributed to both heroin and morphine; the drugs found with heroin are not reported. Deaths certified as mixed or combined drug toxicity, with heroin listed only in the NCIS object field, were among those the coding missed (PDF pp. 11–12).

comparison.controls: The same deaths counted two ways: the reference count (NCIS records judged with the authors' model) against the national coded count (T40.1 assigned by ABS coders, reported by the AIHW). All 165 AIHW deaths were among the NCIS search results; 161 were among the 243 and 4 were excluded by the model. Neither count was checked against an independent standard.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Reasons heroin may go unidentified (rapid conversion to 6-acetylmorphine and then morphine; a long interval between use and death, including resuscitation and hospital admission; post-mortem redistribution and instability of 6-acetylmorphine, also in frozen samples) are described from the literature, not measured (PDF p. 5).

outcomes.instruments: Counts by ICD-10 underlying-cause code, AIHW against reference (Table 1, PDF p. 19); counts by attribution group with the number coded T40.1 (Table 2, PDF p. 20); time from death to case closure for the 20 uncoded deaths (PDF p. 10); a published national report for the same period (PDF p. 9).
outcomes.validity_norms: The attribution model is cited (ref 30) and not re-validated here; its strength-of-evidence categories are not reported for the 243 deaths.
outcomes.operationalization: Reference 'heroin-related death': judged by the model on toxicological and investigative evidence, including deaths with morphine alone in toxicology. 'Identified by the ABS': T40.1 as an associated cause. 'Missed': a reference death without T40.1.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reference 243 against AIHW 165: 78 fewer in the national data, that is 32.1% of 243 (the paper's 'underreported by 32%') and 47.3% of 165 (the paper's '47% greater'; editors' calculation). 161 of 243 reference deaths (66%) had T40.1; 82 (34%) did not; 4 T40.1 deaths were excluded by the model. By attribution group, coded T40.1: heroin toxicity 146 of 180 (81%); heroin and morphine 8 of 11 (73%); morphine or another opioid 5 of 39 (13%); generic drug toxicity 0 of 5; misadventure 2 of 8 (25%). Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, 154 (81%) were coded T40.1 and 37 were not (3 of these coded T40.2 only). Of 44 drug-toxicity deaths not attributed to heroin, 5 (11%) were coded T40.1. By underlying cause, AIHW against reference: X44 69 against 98 (the largest difference), X42 75 against 79, Y14 10 against 12, Y12 4 against 5, F11 1 against 3, X64 6 against 6; 20 reference deaths had another underlying code and 20 none. Editors' calculation: taking the coroner's own attribution as the reference, coding missed 37 of 191 heroin-attributed deaths (19%).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; approved by the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine Research Advisory Committee (RAC 030/14) and the Department of Justice and Regulation Human Research Ethics Committee (CF/15/2853) (PDF p. 8).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's shares of missed deaths (40%, 30%, 24%) cannot be reproduced from the tables; the 20 uncoded deaths are not broken down by attribution group; the model's evidence categories, the deaths' demographics and the national-data extraction date are not reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable (counts).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In Victoria in 2012–2013, 243 deaths met the authors' heroin-attribution model in closed coronial records, against 165 deaths with the heroin code T40.1 in national mortality data (161 of them among the 243; 4 judged coincidental by the model). Of the 82 reference deaths without T40.1, 37 had heroin named by the coroner, mostly in wording the coding did not pick up (3 were coded T40.2 only); 39 were certified as morphine, another opioid or generic drug toxicity; 6 were misadventure deaths; and 20 deaths, cutting across these groups, had no ICD-10 code at all.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract and Conclusion say heroin deaths were "underreported by 32%" and the Discussion that the actual number was 47% greater than 165 (PDF pp. 2, 13, 15); both treat the authors' unvalidated model as the true count, although 63 of its 243 deaths had no 6-acetylmorphine detected and who applied it is not reported. (2) The abstract gives late registration as the cause of 24% of missed deaths; the Results present it as the most reasonable explanation once closure time was excluded, without registration dates or closure times for coded deaths (PDF p. 10). (3) The abstract's 40% and 30% shares cannot be reproduced from the tables (reporting issue 1). (4) The Discussion asserts over-reporting of morphine-related deaths (PDF pp. 13–14), but no count of national morphine deaths is given; what is shown is that 34 deaths certified as morphine or another opioid were judged heroin-related by the model and lacked T40.1. (5) The Discussion says variability in a secondary report was demonstrated, from one national figure (220 deaths) whose derivation is not examined. The overcounting direction is measured only as the 4 coded deaths the model excluded.

timeline.event: Mertz, Janssen and Williams (Journal of Forensic Sciences, ref 24): a re-examination of unintentional overdose deaths in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, found heroin-related deaths attributed to morphine and codeine toxicity and deaths missed through inconsistent certification, as Stam et al. describe it (PDF p. 13); not read for this card.
Stam, Gerostamoulos, Dietze et al. (Forensic Science International, ref 30): the attribution model used here as the reference count; not read for this card.
Ruhm (Addiction, ref 36): cited here for underreporting of opioid-related deaths through incomplete death certification to an extent similar to this study (PDF p. 14).

Horon et al. (Maryland, 2012–2015; card sc_horon_2018): certificates named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths while 2,182 met an enhanced-surveillance protocol of certificate wording, toxicology markers and scene evidence; most of the additional deaths had morphine certified as the cause.
Darke's commentary (doi 10.1111/add.14520) and Robertson's letter (doi 10.1111/add.14627) on this paper, linked in PubMed; not among the files read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: In Victoria, as in Maryland (card sc_horon_2018) and, as described here, Allegheny County, deaths certified as morphine or in generic multi-drug terms are the main source of shortfall in heroin-specific counts, and here also the wording of the coroner's finding (heroin only in the NCIS object field) and deaths never coded. None of these studies checks its reference count against an independent standard, and the overcounting direction is measured here only as 4 deaths. The commentary and letter published with this paper have not been read.

funding.funder: NCS (the first author) was supported by an Australian Government Research Training Program Scholarship; the research received no other specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (PDF p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed in the accepted manuscript: no other authors declare any actual or potential conflict of interest (PDF p. 2). No declaration for any author precedes this sentence (reporting issue 6).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Monash University (Department of Forensic Medicine; Department of Community Emergency Health and Paramedic Practice; Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine), the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, Ambulance Victoria, and the Mortality Data Centre of the Australian Bureau of Statistics (Moran), whose coding is evaluated (PDF p. 1). The reference model is the team's own (ref 30). Recorded as flags for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Blinded review of a random sample of Victorian coronial cases, both those coded T40.1 and those the model calls heroin-related without it, by forensic pathologists outside the team using written criteria and reporting their agreement, followed by a repeat comparison of coronial records with final ABS data for deaths after the change in the ABS revision process.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The NCIS holds the coronial records of reportable deaths, the right frame for heroin deaths; only closed cases were searched, while the national count included open cases.
All records returned by four broad search strategies (9,060) were assessed; no sampling.
243 reference deaths; some groups are small (5 generic, 8 misadventure, 11 heroin and morphine).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The reporting, coding and revision process is described with a diagram; no age, sex or year breakdown of the deaths is given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 243 deaths appear in both tables; the 20 uncoded deaths are not assigned to attribution groups.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The reference combines a specific marker (6-acetylmorphine) with weaker ones (morphine-to-codeine ratio, morphine alone) and investigative evidence in a published model, but the model is the authors' own and not validated here; 63 of 243 had no 6-acetylmorphine.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Who applied the model, how many reviewers, whether they were blind to the ABS codes held in the NCIS, and their agreement are not reported.
Counts and percentages agree with the tables, but the abstract's 40% and 30% shares cannot be reproduced, and no uncertainty is given for the shortfall.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths compared under two definitions (round brief, certificate studies). The comparison is in effect a check of the national heroin code's sensitivity against the authors' own attribution model, which is reasonable (toxicology plus investigative evidence from full coronial files) but unvalidated and applied by unnamed reviewers who could see the codes. The counts are internally consistent; the abstract's breakdown of missed deaths is not. Citable for: in Victoria in 2012–2013, the national heroin code T40.1 was missing from 82 of 243 deaths that met the authors' model in coronial records, and the national count (165) was 78 lower; 37 of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin were not coded as heroin, mostly because of how the cause was worded; most deaths certified as morphine, another opioid or generic drug toxicity were not coded as heroin; 20 deaths had no code at all. Not citable for: heroin as the cause of all 243 deaths, the accuracy of the national count in later years or other states, or the 40% and 30% breakdown.

key_findings.finding: Victoria, deaths in 2012–2013: 243 heroin-related deaths in closed coronial (NCIS) records by the authors' model, against 165 deaths with the heroin code T40.1 in AIHW national mortality data; 78 fewer in the national data. The abstract and Conclusion express this as heroin deaths 'underreported by 32%' (78 of 243); the Discussion as an actual number 47% greater than 165 (78 of 165).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results and Conclusions; Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Conclusion
key_findings.note: The two percentages share the numerator 78 and differ in denominator (editors' calculation: 78/243 = 32.1%, 78/165 = 47.3%). 78 is a net difference: 82 reference deaths lacked T40.1 and 4 coded deaths were excluded by the model.

key_findings.finding: Of 9,060 NCIS records returned by the search, 243 met the model's criteria: 235 heroin toxicity deaths and 8 deaths from misadventure as a result of heroin intoxication; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180.
key_findings.locator: Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: So 63 reference deaths (26%) rested on the morphine-to-codeine ratio or morphine alone with investigative evidence (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: All 165 AIHW heroin deaths were among the NCIS search results. Of the 243 reference deaths, 161 had T40.1; 4 more deaths with T40.1 were excluded because the model judged heroin use coincidental rather than a direct contributor; 82 reference deaths had no T40.1 and so were not counted as heroin-related in the AIHW and ABS data.
key_findings.locator: Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 2nd paragraph; Results › Discrepancies in the assigned classification and coding › Comparison of the cases assigned the heroin-specific ICD-10 code of T40.1

key_findings.finding: By ICD-10 underlying-cause code, AIHW against reference counts: X42 (accidental poisoning by narcotics and psychodysleptics) 75 against 79; X44 (accidental poisoning by other and unspecified drugs) 69 against 98, the largest difference (29); Y14 10 against 12; Y12 4 against 5; F11 1 against 3; X64 6 against 6; X62 0 against 0; another underlying code, 20 reference deaths; no code at all, 20 reference deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: The AIHW column includes the 4 deaths the model excluded, so row differences are net; the text calls the X44 difference 29 missed cases.

key_findings.finding: 20 reference deaths had no ICD-10 code for either the underlying or the associated cause. Time from death to case closure for them: median 15.5 months (IQR 6 months), range 10 to 30 months. The authors conclude closure time was not the cause and judge it most reasonable that the deaths were reported late at initial registration and so never assessed for coding by the ABS.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No registration dates and no closure times for coded deaths are reported; the explanation is reached by elimination.

key_findings.finding: Reference deaths by how the coroner's finding attributed the death (heroin named in the certified cause of death or in the NCIS object field), with the number coded T40.1: heroin toxicity 146 of 180 (81%); heroin and morphine toxicity 8 of 11 (73%); morphine or another opioid 5 of 39 (13%); generic drug toxicity naming neither 0 of 5 (0%); misadventure from heroin intoxication 2 of 8 (25%); total 161 of 243 (66%).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Identified causes of variation in the classification and coding, definition of attribution; Results › Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, alone or with other drugs, 154 (81%) were coded T40.1 and 37 were not. In 3 of the 37 heroin was stated in the cause of death but only the generic opioid code T40.2 was assigned. Most of the rest were missed because of how the cause was worded: generic terms such as mixed or combined drug toxicity, with the contributing drugs listed only in the NCIS object field; morphine in the cause-of-death field with heroin listed only as the object; or a complication such as hypoxic brain injury listed first, in the setting of heroin use or toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st and 2nd paragraphs and the list that follows
key_findings.note: The number of deaths of each kind is not reported. The 20 deaths with no code at all (late registration, key finding 4) are not broken down by attribution group, so some of the 37 may never have been coded rather than missed through wording; the paper's 'vast majority' through wording is the authors' judgement, not shown in numbers. If the abstract's 30% (about 25 of 82) refers to these deaths, roughly a dozen of the 37 would be late registrations (editors' inference).

key_findings.finding: Of 44 drug-toxicity deaths not attributed to heroin in the certification (39 morphine or another opioid, 5 generic drug toxicity), 5 (11%) were nevertheless coded T40.1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: The abstract's breakdown of missed deaths: 40% from attribution to morphine toxicity or non-specific drug-toxicity certification; 30% attributed to heroin but with irregular certification; 24% from late initial registration with the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, after which the ABS did not assess them for coding. The Discussion repeats the 40% and 30%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Not reproducible from the tables (reporting issue 1): Table 2 puts 39, 37 and 6 of the 82 missed deaths in these groups (48%, 45% and 7%), and the 20 uncoded deaths (24% of 82) cut across them (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The only published secondary report found for the period that used ABS data and covered Victoria (Australia's Annual Overdose Report 2016) gave 220 heroin-related deaths nationally for 2012 and 2013.
key_findings.locator: Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Why heroin may be missed, as the authors describe from the literature: heroin is rapidly converted to 6-acetylmorphine and then to morphine, so morphine found after death may come from heroin or from morphine itself; after a long interval between use and death, including resuscitation and hospital admission, 6-acetylmorphine may not be detected; 6-acetylmorphine redistributes after death and is unstable in stored samples, including frozen ones; multiple drug use is common.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Heroin-related deaths and study period, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: How the counts are produced in Australia: reportable deaths go to the coroner and are first registered with the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, which informs the ABS; after the coroner's formal finding the certified cause reaches the NCIS; ABS mortality coders assign ICD-10 codes from both sources; the ABS reports to the AIHW. ABS data are preliminary when first published, revised the next year and final after the second year; cases still open at first coding are revised as the NCIS receives information.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: The authors' stated limitation: since 2012–2013 the ABS revision process has changed; before, only the underlying cause was revised, while associated-cause toxicity codes are now also revised when more information becomes available.
key_findings.locator: Limitations

key_findings.finding: The two counts were not defined alike. The national comparison count took deaths with T40.1 as an associated cause only when the underlying cause was a drug poisoning (X42, X44, X62, X64, X85, Y12, Y14) or, before 2013, F11 or F19, while the reference also included 8 deaths from misadventure as a result of heroin intoxication. Of the 82 reference deaths without T40.1, 20 had another underlying-cause code, outside the national definition, and 20 had no ICD-10 code at all; the other 42 had a poisoning or F11 underlying cause (editors' calculation from Table 1: 203 reference deaths in those rows, 161 of them coded T40.1). How the 8 misadventure deaths and the 20 uncoded deaths are distributed across these groups and the attribution groups of Table 2 is not cross-tabulated.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Heroin-related deaths from the AIHW and ABS, bullet list (p. 7); Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 1st paragraph (p. 9); Results › Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 1 (p. 19)
key_findings.note: Part of the 78-death net shortfall therefore reflects the difference in definitions and late registration, not miscoding of deaths the national count was designed to capture (editors' reading).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's shares of missed deaths (40% attributed to morphine or certified as non-specific drug toxicity; 30% attributed to heroin with irregular certification; 24% late registration) state no denominator and cannot be reproduced from Tables 1 and 2. Of the 82 reference deaths without T40.1, Table 2 places 39 in the morphine, other-opioid or generic groups, 37 in the heroin-attributed groups and 6 among misadventure deaths, while the 20 uncoded deaths (20 of 82 = 24%) are not assigned to these groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 40% and 30% would fit 82 missed deaths only if the 20 uncoded deaths were first removed from the attribution groups (about 33 and 25 deaths; editors' calculation), which the paper does not show. Claims should cite the table counts, not the abstract's shares.

reporting_issues.issue: The shortfall is given three ways: 78 fewer deaths (net), heroin deaths 'underreported by 32%' (78 of 243) and an actual number 47% greater than 165 (78 of 165); meanwhile 82 reference deaths lacked T40.1 and 4 coded deaths were excluded by the model. The per-code differences in Table 1 (e.g., 29 for X44) are also net, because the AIHW column contains the 4 excluded deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say which figure they use: the heroin code was missing from 82 of 243 reference deaths (34%); the national count was 78 (32%) lower than the reference count; 4 coded deaths were judged not heroin-related.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say two (25%) of the eight misadventure deaths were specifically attributed to heroin in the cause-of-death certification, whereas Table 2's figure for that row, 2 (25%), is the number assigned T40.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: How many misadventure deaths named heroin on the certificate is unclear; 2 of 8 is certain only as the number coded T40.1.

reporting_issues.issue: The same number, 180, is given for deaths in which 6-acetylmorphine was detected (Results, 1st paragraph) and for deaths attributed to heroin toxicity alone (Results; Table 2); attribution is not cross-tabulated by 6-acetylmorphine detection.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether coroners' attribution to heroin followed 6-acetylmorphine detection, and how many deaths in each attribution group rest on weaker markers, cannot be determined.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give 220 heroin-related deaths nationally for 2012–2013 from Australia's Annual Overdose Report 2016, and the Discussion calls this a demonstration of variability in a secondary report, without explaining how the figure was derived or how it relates to Victoria's 165 (AIHW) and 243 (reference) deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: The national figure is lower than Victoria's own reference count; the paper does not establish why, so it should not be cited as a measure of national underreporting.

reporting_issues.issue: The accepted manuscript's conflict-of-interest declaration reads that no other authors declare a conflict, but no declaration for any author precedes it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A declared interest may be missing from this version; the version of record should be checked before the funding field is finalized.

verification.source_read: Accepted manuscript PDF, 21 pages (title page, abstract, text, references, Table 1 on PDF p. 19, Table 2 on PDF p. 20, Figure 1 on PDF p. 21); all pages read, every number checked on the rendered pages; no supplement; pages differ from the version of record (Addiction 114(3):504–512), so anchors give the PDF's own page. Darke's commentary (doi 10.1111/add.14520) and Robertson's letter (doi 10.1111/add.14627) were not among the files and were not read.

disagreements.first_pass: (none)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 328 (second reader) (missed): definitional mismatch: the national count took T40.1 only with a poisoning (X42/X44, X62/X64, X85, Y12/Y14) or F11/F19 underlying cause, so the 8 misadventure deaths could enter it only if coded as poisonings; part of the 78-death net gap is definitional rather than misrecording; they probably sit among the 20 deaths with another underlying-cause code, but this is not cross-tabulated. Editor's lead: 8 of 243 were misadventure deaths outside the national definition; the 20 uncoded deaths were late registrations.

Added as key finding 13; where the 8 misadventure deaths sit is left open, as the paper does not say (2 of the 8 were coded T40.1, Table 2).

design_detail: Online randomized between-participants experiment with a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design (the authors call it a cross-sectional online study with a randomised design). UK adults from the Prolific research panel (June 2022) each read one of eight simulated BBC-branded news stories about a death reported at an inquest, adapted from a real BBC online report about an ecstasy death in 2019, varying the decedent's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 years, had used the drug 'once or twice'; or 43 years, had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy/MDMA or heroin), each with a matching face photograph from the Chicago Face Database. Primary outcome: a bespoke 9-item measure of stigma towards the depicted person; second outcome: a 6-item measure of support for harm-reduction policies; both answered once, straight after the story and attention checks. Primary analysis: 2 × 2 × 2 MANOVA on the two outcomes; exploratory four-step hierarchical regressions on participant characteristics (demographics, political orientation and conservatism, belief in a just world, empathic perspective-taking, drug knowledge, general stigma, familiarity, having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death). Not pre-registered. Ethics approval from Liverpool John Moores University (22/PHI/010).
can_establish: That among UK adults on an online panel reading one simulated news report of a drug-related death, a male, an older (43, 15 years of regular use) and a heroin decedent drew higher self-reported stigma towards the person depicted than a female, a younger (21, had used the drug once or twice) and an ecstasy decedent (by the editors' calculation about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations), and that the older version drew slightly higher stated support for harm-reduction policies (about 0.1 standard deviation), with the descriptive age difference concentrated in the ecstasy stories. The exact test attached to that comparison is unclear (see reporting issues).
cannot_establish: Whether these differences last beyond the survey or change behaviour, votes or policy (one short story read once, a new outcome measure answered immediately); whether age itself or the use history attached to it (once or twice against 15 years of regular use) produced the age effects (they were manipulated together); how real news, with its own photographs and framing, works; or that participant traits in the exploratory regressions (just-world belief, empathy, politics) cause stigma (observational, with about 30% of participants missing from those models by the editors' calculation).

sample.recruitment: Online research panel (Prolific, UK) in June 2022: members were invited by email with a one-line topic description (how people respond to drug-related news stories), the time needed and the payment (a small monetary reward managed by the panel), and gave consent on a Qualtrics survey (p. 3, Methods › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Living in the UK and aged over 18, from panel profiles checked by screening questions (p. 3). 1280 recruited; 32 clicked the link but did not proceed, leaving 1248 (97.5%). Completing the survey in under 5 minutes (half the pilot median of 10) would have led to exclusion, and none did; attention checks on the story's gender, age and drug withdrew no one (p. 5, Procedure).
sample.demographics: Mean age 45.7 (SD 15.4); 51.0% women; 57.4% with a degree or above; 86.7% White/White British; median household income band £25,000–49,900; voting preference left 62.6%, centre 13.3%, right 24.2%; lifetime use of any drug 53.5%, cannabis 51.0%, MDMA/ecstasy 16.6%, heroin/methadone 3.8%; 79.2% had seen a drug-related death in the media and 52.2% harm reduction in the media (Table 1, p. 6).
sample.attrition: Of 1280 recruits, 32 did not proceed beyond the survey link; the exact randomisation stage for these non-completers is not specified. Under the usual model and intercept conventions, the reported degrees of freedom imply 1238 in the factorial analysis, 1240 in Table 1's one-way test and 868 in each final regression (69.6% of 1248). Counts and reasons for these analysis-specific omissions are not given. The paper does state that certain familiarity and general-stigma responses were recoded as missing (p. 5); this does not account for the omissions quantitatively.
sample.selection_effects: A commercial online panel of people who chose to take part for payment; matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only, with degree holders (57% against 42% in the UK) and people preferring left-wing parties (63% against 39% at the 2019 general election) over-represented (p. 9). Findings apply at most to UK adults on such panels.

exposure.measurement: Random allocation to one of eight story versions. The changed text was the name and pronouns (Jane or John), the stated age and use history (21 and 'once or twice', or 43 and regularly for 15 years) and the drug (ecstasy, MDMA in the coroner's sentence, or heroin); the image showed a White person with a neutral expression, described as matched on rated age (21 or 24 years) and attractiveness; Flesch Reading Ease 63 for all stories; piloted with departmental colleagues (pp. 3–4; Fig. 1). In the published example (young, ecstasy) the brother who speaks at the inquest is 26; in the template's older version he is 48. Comprehension checks on the story's gender, age and drug followed the story.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: a single written news story, read once.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable to the stimulus (one drug named per story). Participants' own drug use was recorded (Table 1) and not used in the analyses.

comparison.controls: Factorial contrasts within the experiment: female against male decedent, younger against older, ecstasy against heroin; there is no story-free or neutral comparison condition.
comparison.matching: Randomization. The authors state that measured covariates were balanced across groups (Table 1) without reporting tests; editors' check: women made up 44.9% to 62.6% of the eight groups, chi-square 11.5, df 7, p about 0.12, compatible with chance.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparison. Empathy and just-world beliefs may have been measured before the story (Limitations) or after it (Procedure); see reporting issues.

outcomes.instruments: Stigma towards the depicted person (primary): a bespoke nine-item measure with blame, anger and pity items adapted from the Attribution Questionnaire (AQ-9), one controllability and one responsibility item, and four social-distance items after McGinty et al.; each 1–9, total 9–81, higher meaning more stigma; Cronbach's α=.81 (pp. 3–4). Support for harm reduction: a culturally adapted version of the measure of Wild et al. (2021), six items (general harm-reduction programmes, government funding for harm reduction, drug checking services, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone, opioid agonist therapies), each 1–5, totalled; α=.88 (p. 4). Covariates: political conservatism (four items, α=.78), the empathic perspective-taking scale of the Interpersonal Reactivity Index (α=.75), the Global Belief in a Just World Scale (seven items, α=.88), a Level of Familiarity scale (11 items, α=0.74), general stigma towards people with substance use problems (four items, α=.80), self-rated drug knowledge, own drug use, and having seen media coverage of harm reduction and of families affected by a drug-related death (pp. 4–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The stigma measure is new; only internal consistency is reported. Item-level results are in Supplementary S2, not read.
outcomes.operationalization: Stigma is the total of the nine items; the pity item and the social-distance items are worded so that a higher answer means less stigma, and their reverse-scoring is not described. Support for harm reduction is the total of six policy ratings given after general descriptions of each approach, presented separately from the story. A criminal-justice diversion item was collected for a separate analysis and excluded (p. 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: alpha .05 for all tests (p. 5). The MANOVA tests the two outcomes jointly; the univariate follow-ups, the interaction probe and two four-step regressions with up to 17 predictors are uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-reported outcomes. Participants saw only their own story and were told the study was about responses to drug-related news stories (p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD) and univariate F(1,1230) (p. 5): stigma, male against female decedent 45.6 (12.1) against 43.4 (12.6), F=11.1, p<.001; older against younger 46.7 (11.8) against 42.3 (12.7), F=40.5, p<.001; heroin against ecstasy 46.9 (11.5) against 42.1 (12.8), F=50.1, p<.001. Harm-reduction support: age F=4.5, p=.035 (printed 22.98 against 23.57, the first being the younger group by the editors' check against Table 1); gender F=.0, p=.802; drug F=.0, p=.922; age × drug interaction F(2,1229)=4.9, p=.007, the authors describe greater support for the older ecstasy story and print F(1,1230)=4.8, p=.029 beside it (22.7 against 23.89, younger first); it is unclear whether this F is a univariate age-by-drug interaction or a within-ecstasy age contrast. Editors' calculations (standardized mean differences with pooled SD, approximate 95% intervals using assigned Table 1 group sizes, which exceed the inferred complete-case analysis sample): stigma heroin against ecstasy d≈0.39 (0.28 to 0.51), older against younger d≈0.36 (0.25 to 0.47), male against female d≈0.18 (0.07 to 0.29); harm-reduction support older against younger d≈0.12 (0.01 to 0.23), ecstasy stories older against younger d≈0.24 (0.08 to 0.39); partial eta squared from the F values 0.009 (gender), 0.032 (age) and 0.039 (drug) for stigma and 0.004 (age) for harm-reduction support. Exploratory regressions: stigma final R²=.569 (F17,850=65.9); harm-reduction support final R²=.379 (F printed as 3247; about 32.5 by the editors' recalculation from R²) (p. 7).
analysis.covariates: None in the MANOVA (covariates judged balanced). The regressions entered the story factors, then age, sex, education and household income, then political orientation, political conservatism, belief in a just world and empathic perspective-taking, then support for harm reduction (stigma model only), drug knowledge, general stigma, familiarity and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death (p. 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the protocol was not pre-registered and that the findings should be considered exploratory (p. 9).
analysis.selective_reporting: Item-level analyses are only in Supplementary S2 (not read), yet the Discussion draws on them (older decedents rated more responsible and in control, with more blame and anger; p. 8). Hypotheses were stated in advance in the paper, but without registration the choice of total scores, the MANOVA and the regression steps cannot be checked against a plan; a diversion-programme item was collected for another analysis.
analysis.power: The authors report a priori planning for a medium MANOVA effect (f=0.25, power 0.95), with a minimum sample of 54 (p. 3). This calculation does not establish power for every smaller univariate effect, interaction or subgroup contrast; those analyses have different requirements and the complete-case counts are not directly reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among UK online-panel adults, one simulated news story was followed by differences in reported stigma for gender, age bundled with use history, and drug: descriptive d values about 0.18–0.39, with partial eta squared about .009–.039. Partial eta squared is not the share of all outcome variance. Harm-reduction support showed a small reported age main effect (d about .12), with the descriptive age difference concentrated in ecstasy stories. The F=4.8 printed beside the ecstasy comparison has an unclear test label; gender and drug main effects on support were not statistically detected. The study measured immediate attitudes, not behaviour or policy changes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the sample a "nationally representative sample (UK)" (p. 1), while it was matched on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented degree holders and left-wing voters (p. 9). The abstract and conclusions describe associations, appropriately cautious for an exploratory experiment, but the conclusions then advise campaigners and media producers on framing and images (p. 10) from one exposure measured immediately. The discussion suggests that reporting more opioid deaths, to match the mortality profile, may lead to higher stigma (p. 8), an extrapolation from one heroin story. It reports greater support after older than younger heroin deaths (p. 9), contradicting the results, the abstract and the next sentence of the discussion (ecstasy) and Table 1 (no age difference among the heroin stories); and it lists having seen media accounts of a family affected by a drug-related death among predictors of higher support (p. 9), while Table 3 and the results show that predictor was not significant. The age manipulation also changed the use history (once or twice against 15 years of regular use), the brother's age, and possibly the photograph's apparent age, so 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'; the authors note the use-history explanation themselves (p. 9).

timeline.event: Forsyth's quantitative study of drug-fatality reports in the popular press, cited here as showing that UK press reports over-represented young women and ecstasy deaths; not read.
Kelly & Westerhoff randomized clinicians to two terms for a person with a substance-related condition (on the project's language-and-stigma list; not read for this card).
Forsyth: of 18 alleged mephedrone deaths named in online news, the most linked were later reported not to involve the drug causally (card sc_forsyth_2012).
Pennington et al.: registered-report vignette experiment on labels and models of problematic substance use and stigma, about a living person (card sc_pennington_2023).
This study: first experiment, by the authors' account, on how news depictions of a drug-related death affect public stigma and support for harm reduction.

replication.where_it_stands: The authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug-related deaths. Related vignette experiments concern labels for living people (Kelly & Westerhoff, 2010; Pennington et al., 2023). The findings are exploratory (not pre-registered) and await a pre-registered replication with real news items, separate manipulation of age and use history, delayed outcomes and a behavioural measure.

funding.funder: Not reported: the paper has ethics and interest declarations but no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work (p. 10, Declarations of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Public Health Institute and School of Psychology, Liverpool John Moores University; School of Psychological Sciences, University of Bristol; Faculty of Health Sciences and Sport, University of Stirling (p. 1). The lead author's earlier experiments on messaging about drug consumption rooms and on representations of people who use drugs are cited in support; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered randomized experiment in a probability sample, using real published news reports varied one feature at a time (decedent gender, age apart from use history, drug, ethnicity, framing and images), with a validated stigma measure, a behavioural or policy-choice outcome, and follow-up after days or weeks.

domains.note: The paper reports online random allocation to eight conditions but does not detail sequence generation or concealment. Table 1's sex distribution is compatible with chance (editors' calculation: chi-square about 11.5, 7 df, p about .12), although some other table cells are inconsistent. The existing low judgment is retained.

Participants were presented with their allocated story and attention questions followed it. The authors report no withdrawals for the attention checks or completion-time rule; this is not a reported count of correct answers. No departures from allocation are described.

The usual interpretation of the main-analysis degrees of freedom implies about 10 of 1248 (0.8%) omitted, without counts or reasons reported. Their impact is not established from the small proportion alone. The exploratory regressions imply 868 analysed, about 30% fewer than the full sample. The existing low main-outcome judgment is retained; missingness in the regressions remains a separate limitation.

Self-reported attitudes answered immediately after the story by participants who knew the topic; a new stigma measure with internal consistency only and undescribed reverse-scoring; demand effects possible, though each participant saw one condition.
Not pre-registered; two outcomes analysed jointly, item-level results in a supplement, an extra item collected for another paper; the authors call the findings exploratory.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A large randomized experiment with little missing data for the main analysis and an open statement that it is exploratory. Concerns are the absence of registration, a new outcome measure without validity data, outcomes measured once straight after one simulated story, the bundling of age with use history, and several reporting errors (Table 1 cells, a regression F, harm-reduction means printed in reverse order, discussion statements that contradict the results). It may be cited, as an experiment, for the direction and approximate size of differences in self-reported stigma towards a depicted decedent by gender, age with use history and drug, and for the very small differences in stated support for harm-reduction policies, in UK adults on an online panel. It may not be cited for effects on real behaviour, on policy or over time, for the effect of age apart from use history, or for participant traits causing stigma.

key_findings.finding: UK adults (n=1280) were recruited from the Prolific panel in June 2022 and randomized to one of eight simulated news stories; thirty-two clicked the survey link but did not proceed, leaving 1248 (97.5%). Eligibility: living in the UK, aged over 18; the sample was matched to the UK adult population on sex, age and ethnicity. An a priori calculation for a medium effect (f=0.25, power 0.95) gave a minimum of 54.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Design; Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The stories were adapted from a BBC online report of an ecstasy death in 2019, kept its branding and length, and varied the decedent's gender (Jane or John), age with use history (21 years and 'once or twice', or 43 years and regular use for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin), with a White, neutral-expression face from the Chicago Face Database matched on rated age (21 or 24 years) and attractiveness; Flesch Reading Ease 63; piloted with departmental colleagues.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Materials › Stimuli, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 3); Fig. 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: In the Fig. 1 example (Jane, young, ecstasy; read on the rendered page, the figure being an image) the brother at the inquest is 26; in the printed template (older version, p. 3) he is 48, a change not marked as manipulated text.

key_findings.finding: Outcomes: stigma towards the depicted person on a bespoke nine-item measure (blame, anger and pity adapted from the AQ-9; controllability; responsibility; four social-distance items), each 1–9, total 9–81, higher meaning more stigma, α=.81; support for six harm-reduction policies (general programmes, government funding, drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone, opioid agonist therapy) on an adapted version of the measure of Wild et al. (2021), each 1–5, totalled, α=.88.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4) and 2nd paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Procedure: demographic questions, then randomization to a story, comprehension checks on the story's gender, age and drug (no one withdrawn), the primary outcome, then the remaining questions; a completion time under 5 minutes (half the 10-minute pilot median) was the exclusion rule and excluded no one. Ethics approval: Liverpool John Moores University Research Ethics Committee, reference 22/PHI/010.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: MANOVA on stigma and harm-reduction support: main effects of gender (Wilks' Λ=.99; F2,1229=9.1, p<.001), age (Λ=.93; F=45.2, p<.001) and drug (Λ=.94; F=36.9, p<.001); gender × age (F=.1, p=.869) and gender × drug (F=2.3, p=.099) not significant; age × drug significant (Λ=.99; F=4.9, p=.007); gender × age × drug not significant (F=.1, p=.926).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Stigma towards the depicted person was higher for male than female decedents (mean 45.6, SD 12.1, against 43.4, SD 12.6; F1,1230=11.1, p<.001), for older than younger decedents (46.7, SD 11.8, against 42.3, SD 12.7; F=40.5, p<.001) and for heroin than ecstasy deaths (46.9, SD 11.5, against 42.1, SD 12.8; F=50.1, p<.001).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: d≈0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; partial eta squared 0.009, 0.032 and 0.039.

key_findings.finding: The authors report higher harm-reduction support for older stories (F(1,1230)=4.5, p=.035), printing the means in younger-first order: 22.98 (SD 5.09) and 23.57 (4.78). Gender (F=.0, p=.802) and drug (F=.0, p=.922) main effects were not detected. They describe the age pattern in the ecstasy stories, printing 22.7 (5.4) and 23.89 (4.67) with F(1,1230)=4.8, p=.029. The article does not clearly distinguish whether that last F tests the univariate age-by-drug interaction or a simple age effect within ecstasy stories.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Weighting the rounded Table 1 means by assigned group size gives older 23.6 versus younger 23.0, older ecstasy 23.9 versus younger ecstasy 22.7, and heroin about 23.3 in both ages. Approximate descriptive d is .12 overall and .24 within ecstasy. Under a common within-cell error model using all assigned group sizes, a conditional reconstruction gives F about 5.4 for age-by-drug and 10.1 for the ecstasy age contrast. Allowing ±.05 for every printed cell mean and SD gives broad bounds about 3.8–7.4 and 8.4–12.0 respectively. Ten main-analysis cases appear omitted, and complete-case summaries, raw data and supplements are unavailable. The reconstruction suggests an interaction label, but does not establish the exact test or corrected F. Independent reader417 reproduces approximately F=5.43 for the interaction and F=10.07 within ecstasy from the assigned-group summaries, but Table 1 covers 1,248 while residual df=1,230 implies 1,238 analysed under the full eight-cell model. These are conditional reconstructions and cannot identify the exact printed test.

key_findings.finding: By condition, mean stigma ranged from 38.6 (Jane, young, ecstasy) to 50.1 (John, old, heroin) (F7,1232=14.67, p<0.001) and harm-reduction support from 22.4 to 24.0. Whole sample: mean age 45.7 (SD 15.4), 51.0% women, 57.4% with a degree, 86.7% White/White British; lifetime use of any drug 53.5%, cannabis 51.0%, MDMA/ecstasy 16.6%, heroin/methadone 3.8%; 79.2% had seen a drug-related death in the media.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Exploratory regression for stigma, final step (R²=.569; F17,850=65.9, p<.001): male (B=1.959), older (B=4.826) and heroin (B=4.665) decedents, stronger belief in a just world (B=.222), lower empathic perspective-taking (B=-.227), lower support for harm reduction (B=-.717) and higher general stigma towards people with substance use problems (B=1.347) went with higher stigma, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death with lower stigma (B=-1.518, p<.05); political orientation, conservatism, drug knowledge and familiarity were not significant. The story factors alone gave R²=.068; the later steps added .016, .234 and .251.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory regression for harm-reduction support, final step (R²=.379): older decedent (B=.675, p<.05), empathic perspective-taking (B=.095), drug knowledge (B=.178) and familiarity (B=.135) went with more support; older participant age (B=-.018), right-wing against left-wing orientation (B=-1.486), political conservatism (B=-.485) and general stigma (B=-.389) with less; having seen coverage of a family affected by a drug-related death was not significant (B=-.192, SE .344). The story factors alone gave R²=.007.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results, 6th paragraph (p. 7, continuing on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the protocol was not pre-registered, so the findings should be considered exploratory; empathic perspective-taking and just-world beliefs were presented before the stimuli and may have primed responses; photographs came from a face database rather than the kinds used in news; a single written story may not reflect how people now consume news; decedent ethnicity was not varied. Degree holders (57% against 42% in the UK population) and people preferring left-wing parties (63% against 39% at the 2019 general election) were over-represented but balanced across groups.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations (single paragraph)

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that rebalancing news reports towards the commoner opioid deaths may raise stigma towards decedents; report from item-level analyses (Supplementary S2) that older decedents were rated more responsible for, and more in control of, their deaths and drew more blame and anger; and suggest that the longer use attached to the older decedent may explain the greater support for harm reduction.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 8) and 5th paragraph (p. 8, continuing on p. 9)
key_findings.note: The item-level analyses are in a supplement not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The harm-reduction means are printed in the reverse order of the comparison named: 'older compared to younger' is followed by 22.98 against 23.57, and 'older ecstasy decedent compared to younger' by 22.7 against 23.89; the group-size-weighted Table 1 means show the first number is the younger group in both (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction stated in words (older higher) is right; anyone reading the numbers in printed order would reverse it.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says support was greater after older than younger heroin deaths, while the results, the abstract and the following sentence of the discussion place the age difference in the ecstasy stories, and Table 1 shows no age difference among the heroin stories (23.3 against 23.3, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The heroin statement is an error; cite the ecstasy interaction.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion lists having seen media accounts of a family affected by a drug-related death among predictors of higher harm-reduction support, while Table 3 (B=-.192, SE .344, not significant) and the results say it was not a significant predictor.
reporting_issues.consequence: That statement in the discussion is unsupported by the paper's own analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The harm-reduction regression is reported as F16,851 = 3247; with R²=.379, 16 predictors and 851 residual degrees of freedom, F is about 32.5 (editors' calculation; the stigma model's F of 65.9 recomputes correctly).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the model remains significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Analysis-specific sample sizes are not explicitly reported. Under standard intercept/model assumptions, the factorial degrees of freedom imply 1238 analysed, Table 1's one-way test 1240 and each final regression 868 (69.6% of the stated 1248). Some missing-value recodes are described, but their counts and the reasons for each model's omissions are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only about 0.8% are implied missing from the main factorial analysis, but the direction and impact of that missingness are unknown. The regressions use a substantially smaller inferred sample whose comparability with the full sample is not established.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 contains inconsistent cells. Using the displayed group sizes, the printed White/White British percentages average about 83.0%, versus the stated overall 86.7%; replacing condition 2's 56.5% with 86.5% would give 86.7%, but is not a uniquely established correction. Cannabis lifetime use exceeds any-drug use in condition 3 (59.7% versus 52.3%). Centre/right preferences average about 14.8%/22.5%, versus printed overall 13.3%/24.2%; swapping the two condition 8 cells gives about 13.2%/24.1%, closer but not exact. Variable-specific denominators are not documented.
reporting_issues.consequence: The balance table needs clarification; likely transcription problems and any variable-specific missingness cannot be disentangled here. The authors state that covariates were balanced, but present no balance-test results. No inferred cell replacement is adopted as source data.

reporting_issues.issue: The order of measures is described inconsistently: the Procedure puts demographics before randomization and the remaining questions after the outcome, while the Limitations say empathic perspective-taking and just-world beliefs were presented before the stimuli.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether these covariates could have been changed by the story (if measured after) or could have primed the responses (if before).

reporting_issues.issue: The step-3 participant-sex coefficients conflict with the stated male-versus-female coding and prose direction: Table 2 B=1.603 accompanies a statement about female participants having higher stigma; Table 3 B=-.967 accompanies a statement about male participants having higher support. design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of one year of a coroner-fed register (the authors call it a retrospective cohort study): accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths (NP-SAD) in 2000. NP-SAD holds deaths in which a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, or in which the person had a history of drug dependence or misuse; coroners report voluntarily, supplying demographics, prescribed medication, place and circumstances of death, substances found post mortem, the coroner's verdict and the cause of death as on the death certificate, with a description of the circumstances. Deaths with a suicide verdict, an open verdict where suicidal or homicidal intent was clear, no verdict, or too little information for a causal judgement were excluded. Two researchers independently assigned each remaining death to one of six categories of cause (direct overdose, traumatic accident, toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition, toxicity with a drug-related medical condition, acute infection, acute non-traumatic physical event) using, in order, the certificate's cause of death, the coroner's verdict, the drugs implicated, the drugs found post mortem and the coroner's report; a medical consultant specialising in addiction confirmed the categories. Agreement was measured with phi; categories were described by sex, age, employment, living arrangement, place of death and recorded history of drug misuse with 'prevalence ratios', and drugs implicated in the cause of death and found post mortem were tabulated by category. No comparison with official statistics or ICD codes.
can_establish: How the 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000 divided, on these researchers' reading of the coroners' returns, between direct drug toxicity and other mechanisms (aspiration and other acute events, toxicity with a medical condition, injuries, infections), and which drugs coroners named as implicated in, or reported as found after, the deaths in each category.
cannot_establish: How many deaths official statistics counted wrongly as drug poisoning, or missed (no comparison with ONS records or ICD codes was made); any risk by sex, age, employment, living arrangement or drug (no population denominators: the 'prevalence ratios' compare numbers of deaths); whether a drug not reported was absent or untested (negative results were not recorded); or how complete NP-SAD was (coroners reported voluntarily and coverage is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Register: accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to NP-SAD, St George's Hospital Medical School, in 2000; coroners reported voluntarily (p. 68, section 2.1; p. 73).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: A drug-related fatality was defined, after Quaglio et al. (2001) and Van Haastrecht et al. (1994), as accidental overdose in cases of recent drug use under circumstances that did not suggest other causes of death; deaths were excluded as intentional or not known for a suicide verdict, an open verdict with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, no verdict, or information insufficient for a causal judgement (p. 68, section 2.2). The number of records screened and excluded is not reported.
sample.demographics: 828 men (79.8%) and 209 women; 84.3% under 45; mean age 37.7 years; 61.5% unemployed; a history of drug misuse or dependence recorded for 755 (72.8%), not for 194, unknown for 88; died at their home address 615, in hospital 305, elsewhere 117 (p. 69, section 3.3; Table 1, p. 70).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Missing values are not acknowledged: occupation is given for 1,008, living arrangement for 970 and age group for 1,035 of the 1,037 deaths (editors' sums from Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: A voluntary, coroner-fed register whose coverage is not stated; accidental deaths only; the categories are the researchers' reading of coroners' returns, which differ in detail. The Introduction notes that counts differ by source (605 coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse and 1,296 NP-SAD drug-related deaths in 2000; 2,943 ONS drug-poisoning deaths in 1999). All authors worked for NP-SAD.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered the count, and who decided: the coroner reported it to NP-SAD with the verdict and the certified cause of death; NP-SAD's inclusion rule is stated above; the two researchers (LW and SC) independently identified accidental cases and assigned the category, and a medical consultant specialising in addiction (FS) confirmed them (pp. 68–69). Drugs 'implicated' are those named in the cause of death; drugs 'found post mortem' are as reported by coroners (pp. 71–72). What was tested: no toxicology panel, specimen or share of deaths tested is reported; NP-SAD records positive findings only, so whether a substance not reported was absent or not tested is unknown, and there was no standardized toxicological testing or reporting at inquest (p. 73). Alcohol is recorded only when present or implicated together with other drugs (p. 73).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the tables: each drug is counted wherever it was implicated or found, alone or in combination, so rows overlap; alcohol appears only with other drugs. Sole-drug figures are given only in the text (e.g., methadone the sole drug implicated in 4% of direct overdoses) and cannot be checked against a table.

comparison.controls: No external comparison. Deaths are compared across the six categories; each 'prevalence ratio' divides the percentage of a category's deaths in one subgroup (e.g., women) by the percentage in a reference subgroup (e.g., men) within the same category.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). The population of people who use drugs from which the deaths arose, by sex, age or employment, is unknown, so no risk can be computed.

outcomes.instruments: Category of cause of death (six categories defined on pp. 68–69); agreement between the two researchers (phi); Table 1 demographics by category with prevalence ratios (p. 70); Table 2 drugs implicated by category (p. 71); Table 3 drugs found post mortem by category (p. 72).
outcomes.validity_norms: The categories are the authors' own and not validated against any reference; agreement phi 0.77 overall and 0.64 for acute infection.
outcomes.operationalization: Direct overdose: death directly related to an episode of toxicity, including its physiological consequences (respiratory depression, pneumonia, anoxia, renal failure, multiple organ failure). Traumatic accident: injury from behaviour related to intoxication (e.g., road traffic accident, drowning, electrocution). Non-drug-related and drug-related medical condition: toxicity superimposed on a pre-existing condition mentioned as a contributing cause (e.g., asthma, epilepsy, heart disease; or hepatitis B or C, endocarditis, cirrhosis). Acute infection related to an episode of drug use (e.g., septicaemia, acute endocarditis, necrotising fasciitis). Acute physical event: e.g., aspiration of gastric contents, postural asphyxia or hypothermia, where intoxication likely impaired self-protection.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 50 prevalence ratios in Table 1 are flagged only by whether their 95% CI lies above or below 1; no intervals are printed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the researchers classified deaths from the full coroners' returns.

analysis.effect_sizes: Categories: direct overdose 802 (77%); acute physical event 74 (7%); drug-related medical condition 72 (7%); non-drug-related medical condition 40 (4%); traumatic accident 31 (3%); acute infection 18 (2%). Agreement (phi): 0.77 overall; direct overdose 0.85; traumatic accident 0.92; acute event 0.88; medical conditions 0.72; acute infection 0.64 (agreement on 11 of 18). Heroin/morphine implicated in 424 (53%) and found in 488 (60.8%) of direct overdoses; implicated in 11 of 18 acute infections (61%), 33 of 72 drug-related medical conditions (46%), 42 of 74 acute physical events (57%) and 9 of 31 traumatic accidents (29%). Alcohol implicated in 232 (29%) and found in 316 (39.4%) of direct overdoses; implicated in 15 (48%) and found in 17 (54.8%) traumatic accidents. Cocaine implicated in 35 (4%) and found in 74 (9.2%) direct overdoses; implicated in 8 (26%) traumatic accidents. Editors' sums across all categories, implicated against found: heroin/morphine 528 against 601; alcohol 300 against 397; hypnotics and sedatives 129 against 291; cocaine 56 against 105; amphetamines 19 against 41. Prevalence ratios are ratios of within-category percentages (e.g., women 20.3% and men 79.9% of direct overdoses give 0.3; editors' check), so they describe the make-up of each category, not risk.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sole-drug figures appear only in the text; the numbers screened and excluded are not given; confidence intervals for the prevalence ratios are not printed; no breakdown of drug by medical condition supports the statements on infections and on amphetamines and heart disease.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Several ratios rest on very small numbers, e.g., the drug-related medical condition ratio of 30.0 for ages 25–34 against 15–24 compares 30 deaths with 1 (editors' calculation from Table 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000, the researchers placed 802 (77%) in direct overdose, the default category when nothing suggested otherwise (a recorded default classification; an upper-limit interpretation is conditional on other classifications being correct, not a validated bound on true causes), and 235 (23%) in five other categories: 74 acute physical events (mostly aspiration of gastric contents), 72 toxicity with a drug-related medical condition, 40 toxicity with another medical condition, 31 traumatic accidents and 18 acute infections. Drugs named as implicated in the deaths were fewer than those reported as found post mortem (e.g., cocaine implicated in 56 deaths and found in 105, editors' sums).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract presents the 23% as the "'masked' manner of death in cases typically recorded as overdose" (p. 67), but no comparison with official statistics, ICD codes or how these deaths were certified was made, and 112 of the 235 are by the authors' own definitions drug toxicity superimposed on a medical condition. (2) The abstract and Results speak of higher or lower risk by sex, age, employment, living arrangement and history of drug misuse, but the prevalence ratios compare numbers of deaths within each category, with no population denominators; the Results (25–34-year-olds at highest risk in all categories) and the Discussion (risk decreasing from age 25 for overdose, trauma, acute events and infections) also read the same table in opposite ways (pp. 69, 72). (3) The abstract's statements that heroin/morphine use carries further risks from acute infection and from HIV, HBV or HCV, and that amphetamine use was most associated with cardiovascular death, rest on counts of drugs implicated within small categories (11 of 18 acute infections; amphetamines in 6 of 40 non-drug-related medical-condition deaths) without any cross-tabulation of drug by condition. (4) The Discussion reads methadone's 13% share of direct overdoses as support for reduced mortality in treatment, which a share of deaths cannot show. (5) The Discussion's suggestions (recovery-position education, take-home naloxone, fear of prosecution delaying first aid) are not tested by these data. (6) The design is called a retrospective cohort study; it is a cross-sectional series of deaths.

timeline.event: Brettle et al. (as cited, p. 68): among pre-AIDS deaths of HIV-positive people who injected drugs, 45% were direct accidental overdoses and 24% of drug-related deaths were associated with an underlying drug-related medical condition.

Counts by source quoted in the Introduction (p. 67): coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse rose from 573 to 605 in 2000 (Allen, 2001); NP-SAD recorded 1,296 drug-related deaths in 2000; ONS reported 2,943 deaths in England and Wales in 1999 with drug poisoning as the underlying cause (ONS, 2001).
Gossop et al. (as cited, p. 73): the cause of death on death certificates is often imprecise or ill-founded, and routine recording of all substances found by toxicology could improve accuracy.

Beynon et al. (card sc_beynon_2007): of 70 deaths that np-SAD reported as drug-related for Liverpool (2004 to mid-2005), 25 were not deaths from drug toxicity (that card's arithmetic); np-SAD's definition is wider than the UK Drug Strategy definition used for national statistics.

Chen et al. compared ONS data with data of the National Programme on Substance Use Mortality (NPSUM); by its title, opioid-related deaths in England and Wales have been systematically underestimated. Listed for this page; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: That a substantial share of deaths in the coroner-fed register were not direct toxicity deaths is consistent with the Liverpool review of np-SAD deaths (card sc_beynon_2007), which found about a third were not drug-toxicity deaths. Neither study compared its categories with how the same deaths were counted in ONS statistics, so the size of any overcount in official drug-poisoning figures remains unmeasured by these papers. The comparison of ONS and NPSUM counts (Chen et al., 2025) addresses the opposite direction and has not been read here.
