what_would_settle_it: Linking the same coroner-reported deaths to their ONS mortality records (underlying cause and all codes) and to complete toxicology results, including negative ones, with two blinded pathologists classifying the mechanism of death, would show how many deaths counted as drug poisoning in official statistics had another mechanism and how many drug-related deaths official statistics missed; statements about risk would also need population denominators.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: NP-SAD was fed voluntarily by coroners; its coverage of drug-related deaths in England and Wales in 2000 is not stated.
All accidental cases were meant to be included, but the number of records screened and excluded under the four exclusion rules is not reported.
1,037 deaths overall; the non-overdose categories are small (18 to 74), so their breakdowns are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 describes the deaths in each category by sex, age, employment, living arrangement, place of death and recorded history of drug misuse.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All deaths are categorised, but missing values for occupation (29), living arrangement (67) and age (2) are not acknowledged.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The categories have written definitions, but they overlap (pneumonia under direct overdose, aspiration pneumonia under acute events), the stated case definition conflicts with including injury and medical-condition deaths, and no external reference was used.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Two independent raters and a confirming consultant, phi 0.77 overall and 0.64 for acute infection; how disagreements were resolved is not described, and coroners' returns vary in detail and lack negative toxicology.

Ratios of within-category percentages are presented as risks, without population denominators, printed intervals or correction; several ratios and percentages in Tables 1 and 2 do not match their own counts.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Coroners reported voluntarily; the proportion of coroners or eligible deaths reported is not given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a description of deaths in a register by category (round brief, certificate and register studies). The frame's completeness and the exclusions are not reported, the categories are the researchers' unvalidated reading with moderate agreement, and the comparative statistics are inappropriate for the risk statements made from them; several table values are internally inconsistent. Citable for: among 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to NP-SAD in 2000, the researchers judged 77% direct overdoses and 23% other mechanisms (aspiration and other acute events, toxicity with medical conditions, injuries, infections); drugs reported as found after death outnumbered those named as implicated (e.g., cocaine 105 against 56); alcohol was found in nearly 40% of these deaths. Not citable for: overcounting in official statistics, any risk by sex, age, employment or drug, or associations of particular drugs with particular conditions.

key_findings.finding: Of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported by coroners in England and Wales to NP-SAD in 2000, the researchers classed 802 (77%) as direct acute overdose; the remaining 23% were 31 traumatic accidents (3%), 40 toxicity with a non-drug-related medical condition (4%), 72 toxicity with a drug-related medical condition (7%), 18 acute infections (2%) and 74 acute non-traumatic physical events (7%).
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Causes of death, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (column headings)
key_findings.note: The five non-overdose categories total 235 deaths (editors’ calculation). Direct overdose was the default when nothing suggested otherwise (p. 68). A ceiling/floor interpretation is the editors’ conditional inference assuming the other classifications were correct; the authors do not establish validated bounds on true causes.

key_findings.finding: Conditions named by coroners within categories: aspiration of gastric contents in 42 cases of direct aspiration asphyxia and 22 of aspiration pneumonia, 6 postural asphyxia, 1 hypothermia; road traffic accidents in 11 traumatic deaths, others from drowning, falls, electrocution and railway accidents; across the two medical-condition categories, 21 pre-existing cardiac conditions, 6 cardiac arrests indirectly associated with substance misuse, 13 pneumonia or bronchopneumonia, 2 epilepsy, 5 renal disease, 6 asthma, 16 chronic infections or illnesses (including HIV), and liver disease in 39 (hepatitis B and C, cirrhosis, fatty liver); acute infections were specified in 20 cases (necrotising fasciitis, septicaemia, endocarditis).
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Causes of death, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: 20 cases with acute infection specified against 18 deaths in the acute infection category; the difference is not explained. The 13 pneumonia cases are printed in words (Thirteen).

key_findings.finding: Agreement between the two researchers who independently identified and categorised the deaths (phi): 0.77 overall; 0.85 direct acute overdose; 0.92 traumatic accident; 0.88 acute event; 0.72 drug-related and non-drug-related medical conditions; 0.64 acute infection, where they agreed on 11 of 18 cases. A medical consultant specialising in addiction confirmed the categories.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Case categorisation, last paragraph; 3.1 Concordance ratings

key_findings.finding: Who and what decided the category: a hierarchy of evidence, in order, of the cause of death on the death certificate, the coroner's verdict, the drugs implicated, the drugs found post mortem and additional information in the coroner's report. Direct overdose included deaths from the physiological consequences of toxicity (respiratory depression, pneumonia, anoxia, renal failure, multiple organ failure); the two medical-condition categories were toxicity superimposed on a pre-existing condition mentioned as a contributing cause.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Case categorisation

key_findings.finding: Case definition: a drug-related fatality was accidental overdose in cases of recent drug use under circumstances not suggesting other causes; deaths were excluded for a suicide verdict, an open verdict with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, no verdict, or too little information for a causal judgement. NP-SAD includes deaths with a psychoactive substance directly implicated, or of people with a history of drug dependence or misuse; coroners supply circumstances, substances found post mortem, the verdict and the certified cause of death.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 The NP-SAD database; 2.2 Case identification

key_findings.finding: The deaths were mostly of men (79.8%), people under 45 (84.3%), unemployed people (61.5%) and people with a recorded history of drug misuse or dependence (72.8%); mean age 37.7 years.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Causes of death and demographic characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Prevalence ratios reported as differences in risk: women against men, traumatic accident 0.1, acute physical event 0.2, drug-related medical condition 0.2, non-drug-related medical condition 0.4, acute infection 0.5; ages 25–34 against 15–24, drug-related medical condition 30.0, acute infection 10.0, direct overdose 2.3; over 45 against 15–24, traumatic accident 0.1.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Causes of death and demographic characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: Each ratio divides two percentages from the same category column of Table 1 (e.g., women 20.3% and men 79.9% of direct overdoses give 0.3); they describe the make-up of each category's deaths, not risk (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine was implicated in 424 (53%) direct overdoses and found post mortem in 488 (60.8%); it was the drug most often implicated in acute infections (11, 61%), drug-related medical conditions (33, 46%) and acute physical events (42, 57%), and was implicated in 9 (29%) traumatic accidents.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Substances implicated in death and cause of death, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, recorded only when present or implicated with other drugs, was implicated in 300 deaths across all categories: 232 (29%) direct overdoses and 15 (48%) traumatic accidents; it was found post mortem in 316 (39.4%) direct overdoses and 17 (54.8%) traumatic accidents, and in nearly 40% of all deaths.
key_findings.locator: 3.4, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Table 3; 4. Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 73)

key_findings.finding: Cocaine was implicated in 35 (4%) direct overdoses, 2% as the sole drug, and found post mortem in 74 (9.2%); it was implicated in 8 (26%) traumatic accidents, once as the sole drug. The Discussion gives cocaine as implicated in 54 deaths and found in 105.
key_findings.locator: 3.4, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Table 3; 4. Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 73)
key_findings.note: Table 2 sums to 56 deaths with cocaine implicated (editors' calculation; reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Ecstasy was implicated in 15 (2%) direct overdoses, 6 (1%) as the sole drug, and found post mortem in 20 (2.5%); it was implicated in 7 (23%) traumatic accidents, once as the sole drug.
key_findings.locator: 3.4, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Methadone was implicated in 107 (13%) direct overdoses, 4% as the sole implicated drug (not sole detection), and found post mortem in 112 (14.0%); it was implicated in 19 (26%) drug-related medical-condition deaths. Other opiates (e.g., co-proxamol, dihydrocodeine) were implicated in 106 (13%) direct overdoses and 9 (23%) non-drug-related medical-condition deaths; amphetamines in 11 (1%) direct overdoses and 6 (15%) non-drug-related medical-condition deaths.
key_findings.locator: 3.4, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Table 3
key_findings.note: Methadone in acute physical events is printed as 20 (19%) in Table 2 and as 19% in the text; 20 of 74 is 27% (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Counts of drug deaths differ by source, as the Introduction reports: coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse rose 5% in 2000, from 573 to 605 (Allen, 2001); NP-SAD recorded 1,296 drug-related deaths in 2000; ONS reported 2,943 deaths in England and Wales in 1999 with drug poisoning as the underlying cause. The authors attribute the differences to differing data collection and recording.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors note that there was no standardized system of toxicological testing and reporting at inquest and no statutory requirement for coroners to give detailed information; NP-SAD returns rely on toxicology and death-certificate information; and because negative findings are not recorded, it is unclear whether substances not reported were absent or not tested for.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 6th (last) paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heroin/morphine was implicated in over half of all the accidental deaths; of the direct overdose deaths, over half had heroin/morphine among the drugs implicated, and the Discussion says a third of 'those direct overdose cases' died after taking only heroin/morphine. No table gives sole-drug counts, and whether the third refers to all direct overdoses or to those with heroin/morphine is not clear.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: A third of all 802 direct overdoses would be about 267 deaths, a third of the 424 with heroin/morphine implicated about 141 (editors' calculation); neither can be checked against a table.

reporting_issues.issue: The case definition (accidental overdose under circumstances that did not suggest other causes of death; deaths deemed overdoses when nothing suggested otherwise) conflicts with the categorisation, which places 23% of the included deaths in other categories, including injuries and acute infections.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 1,037 voluntarily reported deaths have unclear completeness and cannot measure errors in official overdose statistics. The 802 direct-overdose and 235 alternative classifications are observed record-based assignments. Calling 77% a ceiling and 23% a floor assumes other assignments were correct; it is a conditional editorial inference, not an authors’ finding or validated bound on true causes.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's prevalence ratios are ratios of within-category percentages (women 20.3% against men 79.9% gives 0.3 for direct overdose), but the text reads them as risks. The women's direct-overdose ratio (0.3) carries the footnote for a 95% CI above 1.0. Printed ratios that do not match their own percentages (editors' calculations): in the no-fixed-abode row 0.8, 0.6, 0.6 and 0.4 are about ten times the ratios of the printed percentages (e.g., 6.7/85.9 = 0.08); the history-of-misuse ratio for drug-related medical conditions is printed 0.9 against 9.7/88.9 = 0.1, while the text gives 1.1; the employed ratio for traumatic accidents is printed 1.1 against 48.4/51.6 = 0.9.
reporting_issues.consequence: None of the risk statements by sex, age, employment, living arrangement or history of drug misuse can be cited; the table supports only descriptions of who died in each category.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that the 25–34 age group has the highest risk of death in all categories, but Table 1 gives a higher ratio for 35–44 than for 25–34 in non-drug-related medical conditions (15.0 against 12.0); the Discussion reads the same table as showing risk decreasing from age 25 for direct overdose, traumatic accidents, acute events and infections.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's age statements contradict each other and its table; the age figures can be cited only as numbers of deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: Printed percentages that do not match their counts (editors' calculations): in Table 2, the acute physical event column (other opiates 7 printed as 5%, against 9%; methadone 20 as 19%, against 27%; anti-psychotics 4 as 4%, against 5%; alcohol 21 as 27%, against 28%) and cocaine in acute infections (2 printed as 1%, against 11%), while the text uses 19% for methadone in acute events; in Table 3, 9 of 40 printed as 22.0% (22.5%) and amphetamines 1 of 74 as 3.0% (1.4%); in Table 1, men and women add to 100.2% for direct overdose and 100.4% for acute events.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the counts, recomputing percentages; whether methadone was implicated in 20 or about 14 acute-event deaths cannot be settled from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: In several cells a drug is implicated in more deaths than it was found in post mortem: heroin/morphine in acute physical events (42 against 41), methadone in acute physical events (20 against 17), ecstasy in acute physical events (2 against 0), anti-psychotics in non-drug-related medical conditions (1 against 0), GHB (2 against 1) and anti-Parkinson drugs (3 against 2) in direct overdoses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either drugs were named as implicated without being reported as found (possible when toxicology was not reported) or the tables contain transcription errors; the paper does not say which.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives cocaine as implicated in 54 deaths; the six category counts in Table 2 add up to more (editors' sum: 35 + 8 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 5 = 56).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the contrast with 105 deaths in which cocaine was found holds either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the acute physical event category asphyxiation (7%), although it includes 22 aspiration pneumonias and 1 hypothermia, describes the data as from the United Kingdom although they cover England and Wales, and calls the design a retrospective cohort study; agreement was measured with phi rather than a chance-corrected statistic, and how disagreements between the two raters were resolved is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the category as acute non-traumatic physical events (mostly aspiration), the setting as England and Wales, and the design as a cross-sectional series of deaths.

design_detail: Ecological controlled before–after (difference-in-differences) analysis of US vital statistics (CDC Compressed Mortality Files: underlying cause of death, coded in ICD-8 for 1968–1978 and ICD-9 for 1979–1998), aggregated by state. Intervention: a state's switch from a coroner, justice-of-the-peace or mixed system to a medical examiner system, with dates from Hanzlick and Combs (1998). Of nine states that switched between 1970 and 1996, seven were analysed (West Virginia, Arizona and New Mexico 1976; New Jersey 1978; Massachusetts 1983; New Hampshire 1986; Alaska 1996); Delaware and Florida (1970) were dropped for lack of pre-switch years. Each was paired with one control state that stayed coroner or mixed, chosen for proximity and visually similar pre-switch trends in the outcome (Ohio, Idaho, New York, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Indiana, Montana). Outcome: the yearly share of solid and liquid poisoning deaths (drugs and other substances) whose underlying-cause code was non-specific. Ordinary least-squares model with a group indicator, a before/after indicator and their interaction, fitted on all years (N = 429 state-years), on 7 years before to 10 after the switch (N = 236) and on 7 before to 5 after (N = 176). Single author, public-policy department. Filed as registry (vital-statistics data) and appraised with ROBINS-I as a non-randomized comparison of an intervention, as the round brief directs.
can_establish: Whether, in seven US states that adopted medical examiner systems between 1976 and 1996, the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code fell more after the switch than in seven matched states that kept coroner or mixed systems, within the precision these data allow.
cannot_establish: Whether medical examiner systems name drugs more specifically on certificates in the ICD-10 era (the outcome uses underlying-cause codes only, includes non-drug poisonings and ends in 1998); whether reform has no effect (the intervals include falls of 10 to 14 percentage points from a baseline near one half); or whether individual certifiers matter more than systems, for which the paper offers only anecdotes.

sample.recruitment: Registry: CDC Compressed Mortality Files, county-level underlying cause of death 1968–2016, of which 1968–1998 were analysed at state level (p. 2, Section 2, Materials and methods, 1st paragraph; footnote 2, p. 4). Switching states from Hanzlick and Combs (1998) (Table 1, p. 2); controls from states that stayed coroner or mixed throughout (pp. 2–3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Nine states switched in 1970–1996; Delaware and Florida (1970) were excluded because only two pre-switch years exist, and controls were matched on geographic proximity and approximately parallel pre-switch trends in the outcome, searching further afield when no neighbouring state matched (pp. 2–3, Section 2, 3rd paragraph). Four state-year values above 1.00 were removed; none lay within a decade of a switch (p. 3, Section 2, 6th paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (aggregate state data). The numbers of poisoning deaths behind each state-year share are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Alaska has only two post-switch years, 1997 and 1998 (p. 4, Results 1st paragraph and footnote 2).
sample.selection_effects: Seven switches, all before 1999, in states the author says already had many characteristics of medical examiner states (p. 5, Discussion 6th paragraph). Controls were picked by the author from visual similarity of trends, without a stated rule. Whether control states had county-level switches of their own (said to have continued into the 1990s, p. 2) is not checked. Two switches replaced physicians (Massachusetts: physician coroner; New Hampshire: locally appointed physician), so the lay-coroner contrast that motivates the study does not apply to them.

exposure.measurement: The intervention is the state's switch to a medical examiner system, dated from Hanzlick and Combs (1998) (Table 1, p. 2). Previous systems: justices of the peace (West Virginia, Arizona), coroner (New Mexico, New Jersey), physician coroner (Massachusetts), locally appointed physician (New Hampshire), magistrate coroner (Alaska). Resulting systems: centralized medical examiner (West Virginia, New Mexico, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Alaska) or decentralized medical examiner (Arizona, New Jersey). Control states' systems are described only as coroner or mixed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (one underlying-cause code per death).

comparison.controls: Seven control states that kept coroner or mixed systems, one per switching state.
comparison.matching: Pairs (Table 2, p. 3): New Hampshire–Ohio, New Mexico–Idaho, New Jersey–New York, Massachusetts–Pennsylvania, Arizona–Nevada, West Virginia–Indiana, Alaska–Montana, chosen by proximity and by the pre-switch trend of the outcome, on the assumption that this controls for other relevant variables. A synthetic control was considered and rejected because the literature identifies no predictors of certificate specificity (pp. 3–4, Section 2.1, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. State characteristics the author names as possible common causes or mediators (population density, political culture, regulatory structure, autopsy facilities, certifiers' training, staff carried over from the old system) are not measured (pp. 4–5, Discussion 3rd to 6th paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: Share (u/t) of solid and liquid poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code, by the ICD codes of Table 3 (pp. 3–4). Non-specific (u): ICD-8 E859.9, E869, E950.3, E950.9, E980.3, E980.9; ICD-9 E858.9, E866.9, E950.5, E950.9, E980.5, E980.9. All (t): accidental poisoning by drugs and medicaments (ICD-8 E850–E859; ICD-9 E850–E858) plus the suicide and undetermined-intent solid and liquid poisoning codes (E950.0–E950.9, E980.0–E980.9).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated. Because the older codes cannot separate drug overdoses from other solid or liquid poisonings, all were included (p. 3, Section 2, 5th paragraph); multiple-cause data, needed for the drug-specification measures of the cross-sectional studies, exist only from 1999 (p. 3, Section 2, 4th paragraph). The ICD-9 revision of 1979 separated 'other specified' from 'unspecified' substances and produced sharp falls in the share in switching and control states alike (p. 4, Results 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Improved data quality = a smaller non-specific share after the switch, relative to the control state (the interaction term).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None needed for one outcome; the same interaction was estimated in three overlapping windows, all non-significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (coded vital statistics).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 4 (p. 5): difference-in-differences estimate −0.02 (SE 0.04) in the all-years model, −0.03 (0.05) with 10 post-switch years and −0.02 (0.06) with 5; none significant. Before/after ('Year') coefficients −0.23, −0.18 and −0.14 (all p < 0.05), attributed to the ICD-9 change; group coefficients −0.04, −0.01, −0.01; intercepts 0.53, 0.50, 0.50; R² 0.29, 0.20, 0.11; residual standard error 0.19 to 0.20; N 429, 236, 176. The author calls the estimates a 2%–3% impact on rates (p. 4); on the proportion scale they are 2 to 3 percentage points. Editors' calculation (estimate ± 1.96 SE): 95% intervals −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07 and −0.14 to 0.10, compatible with falls in the non-specific share of up to 10 to 14 percentage points from about 0.50, and with rises of up to 6 to 10 points. These normal intervals are conditional calculations from rounded standard errors. The paper states no allowance for repeated state-years; it does not establish a corrected interval or how a different error model would change width.
analysis.covariates: None. No state or calendar-year fixed effects; ordinary least-squares standard errors, with no stated allowance for repeated observations of the same state.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol. The second stated objective, quantifying the change, was dropped because no change was found (p. 2, Section 1.2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Estimates for each pair are not reported, although Figure 1 suggests the pairs differ: after the switch New Jersey stays well above New York, while New Mexico, West Virginia and Massachusetts lie below their controls (values not extracted). All three pooled models are reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With seven switching states and the intervals above, moderate effects could not be excluded (editors' reading).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In seven state switches between 1976 and 1996, the non-specific share of poisoning deaths' underlying-cause codes did not fall detectably more than in seven matched states (estimates −0.02 to −0.03, SE 0.04 to 0.06); the intervals include sizeable improvements as well as small deteriorations.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the research finds no evidence that system-level reform is associated with better drug-related mortality data, which is accurate as a statement of non-significance. The Discussion goes further, saying reform “did not result in improved public health data” on drug-related mortality (p. 4, Discussion 1st paragraph), and the Conclusion says reform was not associated with the expected increase (p. 6), reading absence of evidence as evidence of absence. The outcome is called drug-related mortality data, but it includes non-drug poisonings, uses underlying-cause codes only and ends in 1998. The recommendation to focus on individual certifiers and offices rather than systems (abstract; p. 6, Conclusion) rests on unsourced anecdotes, not on analysis.

timeline.event: Hanzlick and Combs, history and trends of medical examiner and coroner systems: the source of the switch dates (reference 14).

Warner et al. (cross-sectional): drugs specified on 92% of certificates in centralized medical examiner states, 71% in decentralized medical examiner states, 73% in hybrid states and 62% in coroner states (reference 3, as cited, p. 2).
Fernandez (working paper): states that changed to a medical examiner system reported suicides more accurately, using longitudinal data (reference 4, as cited, pp. 2 and 4).
This study: no detectable change in the non-specific share of poisoning underlying-cause codes after seven state switches, 1976–1996.

Smiley-McDonald et al.: in the 2018 census, about 80% of US offices were within a coroner system, and coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which cases received toxicology (card sc_smiley_mcdonald_2025, this reader).

Lundberg et al.: within the same state and year, drug poisoning deaths in coroner counties were recorded as of undetermined intent more often than in medical examiner counties (nine states, 2019–2021; card sc_lundberg_2026).

replication.where_it_stands: The only longitudinal test of system reform for poisoning or drug-death data on the project's list. It does not overturn the cross-sectional associations (Warner et al., 2013, as cited; Lundberg et al., 2026), because its outcome, era and precision differ from theirs. Whether a switch to a medical examiner system changes how specifically drugs are named on certificates in the ICD-10 era remains untested.

funding.funder: No specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (p. 6, Funding; repeated under Declaration of competing interest).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author reports no competing interests (p. 6, Conflicts of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Public Policy and Political Economy, University of Texas at Dallas; current affiliation National Knowledge and Research Center for Emergency Preparedness, University of Haifa (p. 1). No interest in either kind of system is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: A difference-in-differences or synthetic-control study of recent county or state switches from coroner to medical examiner systems in the ICD-10 era, using multiple-cause data on whether certificates name specific drugs (T36–T50.8 against T50.9 alone), toxicology completeness and undetermined intent, with state and year fixed effects, standard errors clustered by jurisdiction, controls chosen by a stated rule and enough switching units to exclude a change of a few percentage points.

domains.note: A pooled two-group comparison with no covariates and no state or calendar-year fixed effects; controls matched only by visual pre-trend; parallel pre-switch trends are not tested and look doubtful for New Hampshire–Ohio and Alaska–Montana (Figure 1); the 1979 ICD-9 revision, which produced the largest changes in the data, falls inside the all-years model and inside the windows of five of the seven pairs (all but New Hampshire, whose window begins in 1979, and Alaska).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Seven of nine switching states (two dropped for too few pre-switch years); one control per state chosen by the author without a stated rule; four state-years removed for values above 1.00.

Switch dates from a 1998 secondary source; heterogeneous switches (justices of the peace, lay coroners, physician coroners or appointed physicians to centralized or decentralized medical examiners); control states' own systems and any county-level switches within them are not documented.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: The author notes that staff, facilities and oversight may have carried over, so some switches may have been changes of title only (p. 4); how fully each switch was implemented is unknown.
Complete vital statistics; four state-years removed outside the 10-year windows; the all-years N (429) is one fewer than expected (430), without explanation.

Underlying-cause codes only; non-drug poisonings included; the numerator contains accidental non-drug codes (E869, E866.9) that the denominator lacks, so the share is not a true proportion; the coding scheme changed during the study. Error of this kind probably affects switching and control states alike and would push the estimate toward no difference.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; the analysis windows and the controls were chosen by the author; all three pooled models are reported, but pair-specific results are not.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I, because the paper estimates the effect of an intervention (switching to a medical examiner system) without randomization. Two domains are serious: confounding, from a pooled model without fixed effects and a coding revision inside most windows; and outcome measurement, from a measure that mixes non-drug poisonings, uses underlying causes only and is not a true proportion. Apart from bias, the estimates are imprecise, and the paper states no allowance for repeated state-years. A different error structure could alter precision, but neither its implementation nor its effect on interval width is established here. Citable for: in seven state switches from 1976 to 1996, no detectable change in the non-specific share of poisoning underlying-cause codes relative to matched states, with intervals that cannot exclude a fall of 10 to 14 percentage points; the code lists used; the sharp fall in non-specific coding at the 1979 ICD-9 revision. Not citable for: 'medical examiner systems do not improve drug-death data', effects in the ICD-10 era, effects on the naming of specific drugs, or the claim that individual certifiers matter more than systems.

key_findings.finding: The research question: does switching from a coroner to a medical examiner system improve public health data on drug-related mortality? The author notes that cross-sectional studies had linked data quality to system type, and that no longitudinal study had tested this for drug deaths.
key_findings.locator: Section 1.2, Research question and objectives, 1st paragraph; Section 1.1, Background, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Nine states switched to medical examiner systems between 1970 and 1996 (Table 1): Delaware 1970 (coroner with state medical examiner to centralized), Florida 1970 (justices of the peace to decentralized), West Virginia 1976 (justices of the peace to centralized), Arizona 1976 (justices of the peace to decentralized), New Mexico 1976 (coroner to centralized), New Jersey 1978 (coroner to decentralized), Massachusetts 1983 (physician coroner to centralized), New Hampshire 1986 (locally appointed physician to centralized) and Alaska 1996 (magistrate coroner to centralized).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Section 2, Materials and methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Delaware and Florida were excluded (only two pre-switch years); the remaining seven were paired with controls chosen for proximity and parallel pre-switch trends in non-specific poisoning (Table 2: New Hampshire–Ohio, New Mexico–Idaho, New Jersey–New York, Massachusetts–Pennsylvania, Arizona–Nevada, West Virginia–Indiana, Alaska–Montana).
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 2, continues p. 3); Table 2 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Because multiple-cause data exist only from 1999 and the older codes cannot isolate drug overdoses, the outcome is the share of all solid and liquid poisoning deaths (drug and non-drug) whose underlying-cause code is non-specific, with the codes listed in Table 3.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 3); Table 3 (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: After shares were calculated for the fourteen states over 31 years, four state-year values above 1.00 were removed; the author states that all non-specific codes are included in the all-poisoning category and that it is not clear why this occurred; none of these values lay within a decade of a switch.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 3 itself lists E869 (ICD-8) and E866.9 (ICD-9) among the non-specific codes but not among the all-poisoning codes, which would allow values above 1.00 (editors' reading of Table 3).

key_findings.finding: The model was Y = β0 + β1·Year + β2·Group + β3·Year×Group, with Year a before/after indicator and the interaction as the effect, fitted on all observations, on 7 years before and 10 after, and on 7 before and 5 after the switch; the author considers the two windowed models better measures of the switch's effect.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, Materials and methods, 7th and 8th paragraphs (the one-line paragraph introducing the equation, and the paragraph after it)

key_findings.finding: Difference-in-differences estimates were −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (SE 0.05) and −0.02 (SE 0.06) in the all-years, 10-year and 5-year models (N 429, 236, 176), none statistically significant; the before/after coefficients were −0.23, −0.18 and −0.14 (p < 0.05), which the author attributes to the ICD-9 change.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Table 4 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of 95% intervals: −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10. The windowed Ns reproduce only if the switch year is included in each window (7 + 1 + 10 and 7 + 1 + 5 years, with Alaska and Montana contributing 10 years each); the all-years N is one fewer than 14 × 31 − 4 = 430 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 descriptively shows sharp falls in both members of the first four state pairs, which the author attributes to the ICD-9 revision. A comparable fall in Massachusetts precedes its system switch. The pairs have differing levels and trajectories, but the plots are not formal state-specific reform-effect estimates or a test of effect heterogeneity.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Figure 1 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Values not extracted from the figure. Read on a 300-dpi rendering: after the switch, New Jersey stays well above New York, while New Mexico, West Virginia and Massachusetts lie below their controls; New Hampshire lies above Ohio before and after.

key_findings.finding: A county-level analysis was intended but abandoned because counts of unspecified drug deaths are too low at county level.
key_findings.locator: Section 2.1, A note on synthetic controls, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Second-hand figures in the Background: in a frequently cited study, drugs were specified on 92% of death certificates in centralized medical examiner states, 71% in decentralized medical examiner states, 73% in hybrid states and 62% in coroner states (Warner et al., reference 3); and a 2004 report found that offices serving more than 250,000 people performed toxicology in drug intoxication deaths in 57% of cases, against 34% in offices serving fewer.
key_findings.locator: Section 1.1, Background, 4th and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: As cited (references 3 and 9: Warner et al. 2013, Academic Forensic Pathology; the BJS census report for 2004); not read.

key_findings.finding: Context in the Introduction and Background: medical examiners or coroners certify unnatural or unusual deaths, about 20% of US mortality; a 2009 National Academy of Sciences report counted 2,342 separate death investigation jurisdictions; the author classes current states as 17 centralized medical examiner, 6 decentralized medical examiner, 19 hybrid and 14 coroner.
key_findings.locator: Section 1, Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Section 1.1, Background, 2nd paragraph (p. 2)
key_findings.note: The four state counts sum to 56, without explanation (editors' arithmetic); Smiley-McDonald et al. (2025, p. 542) give 16 states with centralized offices.

key_findings.finding: Discussion examples of state practice: in New Mexico, 88.8% of drug poisoning deaths filed in 2013–2017 carried T50.9 (other and unspecified drugs) but only 2.9% carried T50.9 alone, because certifiers there add T50.9 to specifically named drugs in case other drugs were missed; Maryland recorded 85% of drug deaths as of undetermined intent, against 1% to 30% in most states (Warner et al.).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph
key_findings.note: The New Mexico figures have no cited source.

key_findings.finding: Anecdotes offered for the role of individual officials: after a board-certified forensic pathologist was elected coroner of Montgomery County, Pennsylvania, in 2007, use of T50.9 in drug deaths fell by over 60 percentage points within two years, and Franklin, Ohio, saw a similar fall after the 2008 election of a forensic pathologist as coroner.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph
key_findings.note: No source is cited for either figure.

key_findings.finding: The author's conclusion: the longitudinal analysis failed to confirm the cross-sectional association; system reform was not associated with the expected improvement; specific, likely narrow mechanisms focused on individual certifying officials and offices should be identified instead of system-wide regulation.
key_findings.locator: Section 5, Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 contradicts the statement that all non-specific codes are included among all poisoning codes: the non-specific list includes E869 (ICD-8) and E866.9 (ICD-9), accidental poisoning by other or unspecified solid or liquid substances, while the all-poisoning list includes only accidental poisoning by drugs (E850–E859; E850–E858).
reporting_issues.consequence: The share can exceed 1.00, as it did in four state-years the author could not explain; accidental non-drug poisonings enter the numerator only, adding measurement error that may vary between states and over time.

reporting_issues.issue: The all-years model has N = 429, one fewer than 14 states × 31 years minus 4 removed values (430); the windowed Ns (236, 176) reproduce only if the switch year is counted inside each window, which the methods do not say (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the analysis cannot be reproduced exactly from the description.

reporting_issues.issue: The model description calls Group a county indicator and the Results refer to control and experimental counties, although the analysis is by state; the before/after indicator is named Year; the sentence defining Y is incomplete ('either the rate of unspecified drug deaths').
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take the analysis for county-level; it is state-level throughout.

reporting_issues.issue: The estimates −0.02 to −0.03 are described as a 2%–3% impact on rates; on the proportion scale they are 2 to 3 percentage points, about 4% to 6% of a baseline share near 0.50 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the estimate is understated in relative terms; either way it is imprecise.

reporting_issues.issue: Standard errors are ordinary least squares on 176 to 429 state-years from 14 states, with no stated allowance for repeated observations of the same state.
reporting_issues.consequence: The true uncertainty is probably wider than the printed standard errors, which strengthens the point that moderate effects cannot be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The Montgomery County and Franklin falls in T50.9 use (over 60 percentage points) and New Mexico's 88.8% and 2.9% are given without sources.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be checked and should not be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The title, abstract and conclusion speak of drug-related mortality data, but the measure includes non-drug solid and liquid poisonings (for example arsenic, strychnine, lye, corrosives and agricultural chemicals in Table 3) and uses underlying causes only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The result concerns the specificity of poisoning codes in 1968–1998, not how specifically certificates named drugs.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's title says 1968–2016 but its source is from 1998; the Background's state counts (17, 6, 19, 14) sum to 56.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; switches after 1998, if any, would not appear in the source.

design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of the 1992 National Longitudinal Alcohol Epidemiologic Survey (NLAES; 42,862 US adults, the survey analysed for alcohol in grant_1997). Among the 6,447 respondents who had used drugs from any of ten classes nonmedically at least 12 times (lifetime drug use as defined in the paper), the weighted prevalence of lifetime DSM-IV drug abuse without dependence and of lifetime drug dependence, each aggregated across drugs, was tabulated by recalled age at first drug use (13 or younger to 21 or older), overall and by sex and race; logistic regression estimated the change in odds per year of later onset, adjusted for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current vs former use.
can_establish: That in a 1992 US household sample of adults who had used a drug nonmedically at least 12 times, those who recalled starting younger more often met criteria for a lifetime DSM-IV drug use disorder (adjusted odds about 4% to 5% lower per year of later onset), and that about 39% of this group had met criteria for drug abuse or dependence at some time.
cannot_establish: Whether early drug use causes later drug use disorders (cross-sectional, recalled onset, family drug history not measured; conduct problems and psychopathology not adjusted for, with their survey measurement status not established here); which drug the onset and the disorder concerned (both aggregated across drug classes); or what share of everyone who ever tries a drug develops a disorder (people who used fewer than 12 times were not in the analysis).

sample.recruitment: General-population household sample: NLAES 1992, sponsored by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, fieldwork by the US Bureau of the Census; noninstitutionalized adults aged 18 and older in the contiguous US and the District of Columbia; oversampling of Black and young adult (18–29) respondents; about 92% of selected households and 97% of selected respondents took part (p. 165, Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Lifetime drug use was defined as having used drugs in any of ten classes nonmedically at least 12 times (whether per class or in total is not specified): sedatives, tranquilizers, opioids other than heroin, amphetamines, cocaine and crack, cannabis (including THC and hashish), heroin, methadone, hallucinogens, and other drugs such as inhalants and solvents; nonmedical use = without a prescription, in greater amounts, more often or longer than prescribed, or for another reason (pp. 165–166, Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Lifetime drug use in the whole sample (weighted): men 19.5%, women 12.0%, Black 12.3%, nonblack 16.0%, total 15.6% (Table 1, p. 167). Age, education and income of the 6,447 are not reported, nor their numbers by sex and race.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview). Missing data are not reported; nor is the number of people at each onset age.
sample.selection_effects: Household survivors only: deaths, institutions and homelessness are outside the frame, which plausibly leaves out some people with early onset and severe disorders. The 12-use threshold selects people beyond experimentation, so the 40% figure in the paper describes them, not everyone who ever tried a drug.

exposure.measurement: Age at first drug use, recalled at the interview. Test-retest kappas for drug-specific onset ages were 0.68 (heroin), 0.69 (sedatives), 0.77 (cocaine) and above 0.92 (tranquilizers, amphetamines, other opioids, cannabis) (p. 166, 4th paragraph). How the overall onset age was derived from the drug-specific questions is not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. Duration of drug use was a covariate but is not defined in this paper.
exposure.polysubstance: Drug classes were aggregated: the drug first used may differ from the drug of the disorder; no drug-specific analysis was done (the authors suggest one, p. 171). Alcohol and tobacco use were not adjusted for; family history of alcoholism was.

comparison.controls: People with later recalled onset of drug use: prevalence tabulated for each year from 13 or younger to 21 or older (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 168–169); regression per year of later onset, with onset entered as a continuous term (pp. 169–170).
comparison.matching: None. Adjusted for age group (18–29 as reference, 30–44, 45–64, 65 and older), sex, race (Black vs nonblack), family history of alcoholism in first-degree relatives, duration of drug use, and current vs former use (p. 167, Statistical Analysis; Table 4, p. 170).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of drug use disorders was not measured (p. 166); conduct problems, psychopathology, childhood adversity, peers, and age at first drink or first cigarette were not used. Current vs former use may itself follow from the disorder.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS: DSM-IV drug abuse (at least one of four abuse criteria in any one year: continued use despite social or interpersonal problems, recurrent hazardous use, failure to fulfil major role obligations, recurrent drug-related legal problems) and dependence (at least three of seven criteria in any one year), derived for each drug and combined into any drug abuse and any drug dependence; clustering and duration criteria; lifetime = past year or before; the two diagnoses mutually exclusive (abuse = without lifetime dependence) (p. 166, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Test-retest kappas 0.79 (past year) and 0.73 (lifetime) for any drug abuse or dependence (p. 166, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence; lifetime drug abuse among people without lifetime dependence, with abuse criteria that include recurrent drug-related legal problems.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two outcomes, each also estimated in four subgroups).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (structured lay interview).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 4 (p. 170): age at onset of drug use, beta −0.05 (SE 0.01; p printed as < .00003) for abuse and −0.04 (SE 0.01; < .01) for dependence. Other coefficients, abuse and dependence: male 0.39 and 0.03 (not significant); Black −0.55 and −0.02 (not significant); family history of alcoholism 0.26 and 0.71; duration of drug use 0.01 and 0.05; former vs current use −0.59 and 0.18; age 30–44 0.02 and −0.51, 45–64 −0.28 and −0.77, 65 and older −0.54 and −4.10 (vs 18–29). Editors' conversion: per-year odds ratios about 0.95 for abuse (approximate 95% CI 0.93–0.97) and 0.96 for dependence (0.94–0.98), that is, 4.9% and 3.9% lower odds per year; the betas are printed to two decimals, so these are rough.
analysis.covariates: Age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism (first-degree relatives), duration of drug use, current vs former use (p. 167).
analysis.selective_reporting: Subgroup models are reported only as percentage reductions (with 'not significant' for dependence in Black respondents), without estimates or intervals; no unadjusted estimates; model sample sizes not given.
analysis.power: Not reported; 97 to 121 Black respondents with a disorder (unweighted), which the authors suggest may explain the null result in that group (p. 171).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people who had used a drug at least 12 times, lifetime drug abuse fell from 28.9% (onset at 13 or younger) to 11.1% (21 or older, a total that conflicts with its subgroups) and lifetime dependence from 33.6% to 13.6%, dependence being nearly flat (11% to 15%) for onset at 17 or later. After adjustment, odds were about 5% (abuse) and 4% (dependence) lower per year of later onset. About 20% had lifetime abuse and 19% dependence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls early onset a significant predictor of the later development of drug abuse and, by a slip, of lifetime alcohol dependence, and gives the per-year reductions as 4% for abuse and 5% for dependence (p. 163); the Results call onset a major contributor to the development of drug abuse and dependence (p. 170); the Discussion calls age at first drug use "a powerful predictor of lifetime drug abuse" in every subgroup and of dependence except in Black respondents (p. 171), and closes by calling early onset a powerful predictor of very serious long-term consequences (p. 172); 40% of all people who use drugs are said to go on to abuse or dependence (pp. 164, 171–172). The authors also ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors reduces risk, and whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker (p. 171). Gaps: (1) 'powerful' describes adjusted odds about 4% to 5% lower per year, with dependence flat after 17; (2) the abstract reverses the abuse and dependence figures and names alcohol instead of drug dependence; (3) 'subsequent development' and 'contributor to the development' are causal readings of a cross-sectional association with recalled onset; (4) the 40% applies to people who had used a drug at least 12 times and includes abuse defined partly by legal problems; (5) subgroup statements come without estimates or tests.

timeline.event: Robins and Murphy, young Black men (location not given here): earlier drug use went with greater risk of later problems, as cited by the authors (p. 165).

Robins and Przybeck, St Louis adults aged 18 to 35 with DSM-III criteria: the earlier drug use began, the greater the risk of abuse and dependence, as cited by the authors, who criticize the restricted sample and older criteria (pp. 164–165).

Labouvie, Bates and Pandina: 15-year-old males followed for 13 years; age at onset of drug use did not predict drug-related problems at 30, as cited by the authors, who discount it (men only, a single 3-year window, an aggregate problem measure) (p. 164).
Alcohol counterpart in the same survey: odds of lifetime dependence 14% lower per year of later first drink (read in this round).
This study: NLAES, people who had used a drug at least 12 times; adjusted odds about 5% (abuse) and 4% (dependence) lower per year of later onset.

replication.where_it_stands: The drug counterpart of the alcohol study shows a weaker per-year association, and the only prospective study of age at first use and later drug problems the authors discuss found no prediction (Labouvie et al., 1997). Later prospective and twin tests named on the project's General list (Odgers et al., 2008; Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2016) were not read for this card. Whether early drug use causes later disorders remains open, as the authors acknowledge.

funding.funder: No funding or acknowledgment statement. Both authors were at the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (Division of Biometry and Epidemiology), which sponsored the NLAES (pp. 163, 165).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Government researchers analysing their institute's own survey; no commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure conduct problems, family drug problems and other liabilities before any drug use and record use and disorders drug by drug as they happen; comparisons of twins or siblings who differ in age at first use of a particular drug; and long-term follow-up of prevention trials that succeed in delaying first use.

domains.note: Adjusted for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism and duration of drug use; family history of drug disorders, conduct problems, psychopathology, childhood adversity and other substance use were not measured or not used; adjustment for current vs former use may itself be affected by the disorder.
Recalled onset; drug-specific reliabilities from 0.68 to above 0.92, but how the overall onset age was derived is not described, and recall may differ between people with and without a disorder.

Household survivors with good response; deaths, institutions and homelessness, plausibly related to both early onset and severe disorder, are outside the frame; the 12-use threshold defines who counts as having used drugs.
Lifetime diagnoses; treatment after onset cannot remove a past diagnosis.
Missing data and the numbers at each onset age are not reported.
Structured lay interview with fair to good reliability (0.73 lifetime); disorders aggregated across drugs and recalled in the same interview as the onset age; abuse partly defined by legal problems.
No unadjusted estimates; subgroup results given as percentages or as not significant, without estimates or intervals; the abstract misreports the main figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The gradient in Tables 2 and 3 is a reasonable description of what US adults who had used a drug at least 12 times reported in 1992, from a large probability sample with a standard interview, although one total in Table 2 conflicts with its subgroups. As evidence that early drug use causes drug use disorders it is weak: the exposure was recalled in the same interview as the outcome, the main competing explanations were not adjusted for; only family drug history is explicitly said to be unmeasured, the drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked, and one covariate may follow from the outcome. Cite it for the cross-sectional association in this group (lifetime dependence 33.6% for onset at 13 or younger against 11% to 15% for onset at 17 or later; adjusted odds about 4% to 5% lower per year) and for the share with abuse (20.1%) or dependence (18.6%) among people who had used a drug at least 12 times; do not cite the abstract's per-year figures (reversed), the 11.1% abuse total for onset at 21 or older (inconsistent with its subgroups), or the paper as showing that delaying first drug use prevents drug use disorders.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime drug use (nonmedical use of drugs in any of ten classes at least 12 times) was reported by 15.6% (SE 0.2) of the weighted NLAES sample: men 19.5%, women 12.0%, Black 12.3%, nonblack 16.0%; 6,447 respondents, about 16% of the sample.
key_findings.locator: Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 1st paragraph (starting p. 165); Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (p. 167)

key_findings.finding: Among people with lifetime drug use so defined, 20.1% (SE 0.6) had lifetime drug abuse without dependence (men 22.6%, women 16.3%, Black 13.9%, nonblack 20.7%) and 18.6% (SE 0.6) lifetime drug dependence (men 18.8%, women 18.4%, Black 18.1%, nonblack 18.7%). Editors' sum: 38.7% with either diagnosis, the basis of the paper's statement that 40% of people who use drugs develop abuse or dependence.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 167); Results, 1st paragraph (pp. 167–169)
key_findings.note: The 40% applies to people who had used a drug at least 12 times, not to everyone who ever tried a drug.

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of lifetime drug abuse without dependence by recalled age at first drug use, total (SE): 13 or younger 28.9% (1.9); 14, 21.5% (2.2); 15, 24.3% (1.9); 16, 25.1% (1.7); 17, 20.3% (1.7); 18, 17.7% (1.5); 19, 18.0% (2.4); 20, 13.6% (2.0); 21 or older 11.1% (0.9). Men had higher prevalence than women at every onset age (for example 30.8% vs 25.5% at 13 or younger; 17.9% vs 6.0% at 20).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and Figure 1 (p. 168); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 169)
key_findings.note: The total for onset at 21 or older (11.1%) is lower than all four subgroup values (11.7% to 13.9%), which is impossible for a weighted total (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Weighted prevalence of lifetime drug dependence by recalled age at first drug use, total (SE): 13 or younger 33.6% (1.9); 14, 26.8% (2.4); 15, 25.4% (1.9); 16, 17.7% (1.3); 17, 15.1% (1.4); 18, 15.0% (1.5); 19, 13.4% (1.9); 20, 11.4% (1.8); 21 or older 13.6% (1.2). Men and women had similar values at most ages (33.8% vs 33.2% at 13 or younger; 13.2% vs 14.1% at 21 or older); in Black respondents prevalence went from 28.9% to 17.8%, irregularly.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 169); Figure 2 (p. 170)
key_findings.note: Editors' sums of Tables 2 and 3 (mutually exclusive diagnoses): either disorder 62.5% for onset at 13 or younger, about 35% at 17, about 25% at 20 and at 21 or older. The 21-or-older sum includes the internally inconsistent 11.1% abuse total and is not a resolved combined-disorder estimate.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current vs former use, age at onset of drug use had beta −0.05 (SE 0.01) for lifetime abuse and −0.04 (SE 0.01) for lifetime dependence; the authors give these as 5% and 4% lower odds per later year of onset. Family history of alcoholism had beta 0.26 (abuse) and 0.71 (dependence); male sex 0.39 (abuse) but 0.03 (dependence, not significant). Editors' conversion: odds ratios of about 0.95 and 0.96 per year.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starting p. 169); Table 4 (p. 170)

key_findings.finding: By subgroup, the odds of lifetime abuse fell 4% (men), 6% (women), 5% (nonblack) and 2% (Black) per year of later onset, and the odds of dependence 5% (men), 2% (women) and 4% (nonblack); in Black respondents onset was not significantly related to dependence. No estimates, intervals or tests of subgroup differences are given.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (starting p. 170)
key_findings.note: The paragraph says alcohol abuse where drug abuse is meant (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: The authors cite their earlier NLAES report that 76% of onsets of drug use occurred before 19, and a prospective study (Labouvie et al., 1997; males aged 15 followed for 13 years) in which age at onset did not predict drug-related problems at 30, which they discount (men only, one 3-year window, an aggregate measure).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors ask whether the delay of drug use itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors reduces the risk of later disorders, whether early onset is a modifiable risk factor or a marker of disorders that would develop anyway, and whether delaying onset could have unintended effects; they call for prospective studies from childhood beyond young adulthood.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Family history of drug use disorders was not measured; family history of alcoholism among first-degree relatives was used as a control instead (kappas 0.65 to 1.00 by type of relative).
key_findings.locator: Drug use, abuse and dependence assessment, 5th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the per-year reductions as 4% for drug abuse and 5% for dependence, the reverse of Table 4 (beta −0.05 for abuse, −0.04 for dependence), the Results (p. 170) and the Discussion (5% and 4%, p. 171).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Table 4: about 5% lower odds per year for abuse and about 4% for dependence.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements name alcohol where drugs are meant: the abstract says early drug use predicted lifetime alcohol dependence (p. 163); the Results speak of the trend in alcohol dependence (p. 169) and of the odds of lifetime alcohol abuse in subgroups (p. 171); and they list duration of drinking among the covariates (p. 169), whereas the Methods and Table 4 say duration of drug use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording errors; the tables show that all analyses concern drug use disorders.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 and Figure 1 the total prevalence of abuse for onset at 21 or older (11.1%, SE 0.9) is lower than every subgroup value (men 13.9%, women 11.7%, Black 12.6%, nonblack 13.0%), which is impossible for a weighted total of these groups; the Results repeat the 11.1% (p. 169).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the total or the subgroup values for this onset group are wrong; the end point of the abuse gradient is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The n in the column heads of Tables 2 and 3 are the numbers of people with abuse (1,273) or dependence (1,232), not the denominators, and the Results give n = 1,273 for both abuse and dependence (p. 168); the number of people at each onset age is never given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of each cell can be judged only from its standard error.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4, the dependence coefficient for age 65 and older (−4.10, SE 1.31) gives p of about .002, not < .0005 as printed; the SE of 0.72 for male sex (dependence) is out of line with the SEs of the other sex, race, family-history and use-status coefficients (0.07 to 0.15) and may be a misprint; several p values cannot be checked because the betas and SEs are printed to two decimals (for example duration of drug use for abuse, 0.01 with SE 0.01, printed p < .043) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the onset coefficients are not affected, but the table is not fully reliable.

reporting_issues.issue: Duration of drug use, a covariate, is not defined, and how the overall age at first drug use was derived from the drug-specific onset questions is not described; whether people with dependence were part of the reference group of the abuse model is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure and a key covariate are not fully specified; if people with dependence were in the abuse model's reference group, the abuse estimate would be diluted.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes the 20% with abuse and 19% with dependence as shares of those who have ever used drugs, and the Discussion as shares of all persons who use drugs (pp. 164, 171–172), whereas the Methods count only people who used drugs at least 12 times (p. 166). The Discussion also says abuse was more prevalent in nonblack than Black respondents at each onset age (p. 171), but at onset 14 Table 2 shows 30.3% vs 20.7% the other way (the Results say at most ages, p. 169).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 40% must be cited with the 12-use definition; the race statement should follow the table.

design_detail: Narrative review in the Current Opinion format of research on using several substances, said to cover work published mainly in the preceding 18 months: definitions and the DSM-5 changes, reasons for use, prevalence and latent-class patterns, psychiatric and physical health correlates, imaging and neuropsychology, and prevention and treatment. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal of the cited studies; 71 numbered references, those judged of special or outstanding interest annotated by the authors. University of Queensland group; published July 2014.
can_establish: How polysubstance use was defined and measured in research of about 2012–2014, which latent-class patterns those studies reported, and where the authors judged the evidence on harms, prevention and treatment to be thin as of 2014.
cannot_establish: Prevalence in any population beyond the cited sources (figures are second-hand and mix national surveys with student, clinical and rave samples); whether using several substances causes the mental-health, physical-health or cognitive differences described (the review summarizes associations without formal appraisal or a design inventory); or the size of any effect.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited sources include 2013 surveys from the USA, UK, Australia, Denmark and Latin America, student surveys (US and Brazilian college students), clinical and treatment samples, studies of club and rave attenders, and small imaging studies (pp. 270–272).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; the review examines key research published mainly over the previous 18 months (p. 270).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen and annotated by the authors. At least 8 of 71 references name a review author among their listed authors (refs 13, 22, 23, 32, 33, 41, 66, 68; several lists end in et al.), including the Australian latent-class studies that supply several prevalence figures and correlates (refs 22 and 23, both marked of outstanding interest) and the treatment-sample latent-class study of people using cannabis (ref. 41, also marked of outstanding interest).

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: lifetime use, use in the past 1 to 12 months, or simultaneous use (several substances on the same occasion), mostly by self-report in surveys, grouped by latent class analysis (p. 270).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors note that most population research recorded only frequency of use, not diagnostic criteria or severity (p. 270), and call for profiles that include frequency and severity (p. 273).
exposure.polysubstance: The topic of the review. Simultaneous use is described as hard to capture in surveys because of the number of possible drug pairs, and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples (p. 270).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the imaging study described in most detail tested people after 1 month of abstinence (ref. 51, p. 272).

comparison.controls: As in the cited studies: latent classes using no or few substances; healthy controls or alcohol-dependent-only groups in imaging studies; patients using no other illicit substances in the treatment sample (pp. 271–272).
comparison.matching: Not described for any cited study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. Pre-existing differences and socioeconomic disadvantage (which the review lists as a correlate of polysubstance use, p. 270) are not considered as alternative explanations for the health and cognitive associations.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: psychological distress, anxiety and depression symptoms, generalized anxiety and major depressive disorder diagnoses, psychotic symptoms, sexual risk behaviour, infectious disease, overdose, magnetic resonance spectroscopy metabolites, grey-matter volume, neuropsychological tests and prevention outcomes (pp. 271–273).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised. The authors note that the reliability of clinical assessment of the DSM-5 severity index was not yet known (p. 270) and that neuroimaging studies may lack power (p. 272).
outcomes.operationalization: Wide-ranging (extended-range) polysubstance use defined by latent-class membership in each cited study; health harms defined by the cited studies' measures.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without appraisal: rave attenders up to 75% using several substances, average five drugs at the last rave (ref. 12, p. 270); limited-range use reported by 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime, ref. 23) to 34% before age 16 (ref. 18); extended-range use 2% at 12–17 vs 13.5% at 18–29 (refs 22, 23); a sedative-and-alcohol cluster with last-year prevalence 1.3% among young Australian adults (ref. 22) (p. 271). US National Survey on Drug Use and Health: non-medical prescription drug use 6.3% in the past year and 2.7% in the past month; pain relievers 4.8%, tranquillizers 2.1%, stimulants 1.2%, sedatives 0.3%; 14.4–15.5% at 18–25, 7.8–8.7% at 12–17, 3.8–4.8% at 26 and older; lifetime non-medical benzodiazepine use 7.5% in US high-school seniors (refs 34, 35; p. 271). Danish national sample: odds ratio 27 (95% CI 14.85–49.15) for long-term benzodiazepine misuse in people with long-term opioid use and chronic pain compared with individuals without chronic pain (ref. 6, p. 272).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; adjustment in the cited studies is not described.
analysis.selective_reporting: The study-selection process is not reported. Null behavioural differences between people using several substances and controls are reported in the body (p. 272) but are absent from the abstract and the conclusion, which state cognitive deficits as established.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors say low statistical power may affect the neuroimaging studies (refs 61, 63; p. 272).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A descriptive account of recent studies: definitions of polysubstance use vary (lifetime, recent, same occasion); latent-class studies find limited, moderate and extended ranges of use; extended-range use is more common in young adults, in men and in club, rave, treatment-seeking and other high-risk samples; extended-range classes report more distress, anxiety, depression and sexual risk; some imaging studies find metabolite and grey-matter differences, while several find no behavioural difference from controls and another reports large differences on standard tests outside the scanner; prevention evidence is weak.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion opens: "It is clear that individuals who use multiple substances are at elevated risk" of comorbid psychiatric and other health conditions, and adds that they have more pervasive cognitive deficits that place them at risk of poorer treatment outcomes (p. 273); the abstract likewise lists deficits in cognitive functioning. Gaps: (1) the latent-class associations are summarized without a formal appraisal and do not by themselves establish a causal effect, so 'risk of developing' is causal wording the designs cannot support; (2) the imaging section reports both null behavioural differences (refs 55–58) and large differences on standard tests outside the scanner (ref 62), before concluding that polysubstance use is clearly associated with deficits in brain function and cognition (p. 272); (3) no study of treatment outcomes by cognitive status is described; (4) a contrast between age groups in two samples,without described within-person follow-up,is read as a risk of expanding use over time,and a comparison after 1 month of abstinence as suggesting that cocaine may be more injurious than alcohol (pp. 271–272); (5) socioeconomic disadvantage and pre-existing differences are not weighed as explanations.

timeline.event: Fernández-Calderón et al., cluster analysis of polysubstance use in underground rave attenders (ref. 12): source of the up-to-75% figure.

Quek et al. and White et al. (review authors' group), latent class analyses of Australian national samples of young adults and adolescents (refs 22, 23): sources of the 2%, 13.5%, 18% and 1.3% figures.
Connor et al., latent class analysis of 826 people referred for cannabis treatment (ref. 41, size from the reference annotation): wide-ranging class with more psychopathology.
This review.

Liu et al., review of polysubstance use in cocaine research: alcohol and cannabis use alongside cocaine common in every sample; human imaging studies seldom excluded people who drink or use cannabis (as summarized on the project's card sc_liu_2018).

replication.where_it_stands: Citable for definitions, the variety of ways polysubstance use is measured, the latent-class pattern of limited, moderate and extended ranges, and the authors' view (2014) that research on prevention and treatment for polysubstance use was underdeveloped. Prevalence figures and health associations should be cited from the primary surveys or from the systematic reviews of latent-class studies on the project's list (Tomczyk et al., 2016, adolescents; LeComte et al., 2025, adults; not yet appraised).
