funding.declared_conflicts: There are no conflicts of interest (as printed, p. 273).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research and Discipline of Psychiatry, The University of Queensland, and the Alcohol and Drug Assessment Unit, Princess Alexandra Hospital, Brisbane. Several cited Australian studies, and the treatment-sample latent-class study, are by the authors' group and are highlighted by them as of outstanding interest. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Standard definitions of concurrent and simultaneous polysubstance use applied in repeated national surveys; panel studies following the same people from adolescence to young adulthood (latent transition analysis) to observe changes in range of use; prospective cohorts measuring mental health and cognition before multiple-substance use begins, with adjustment for socioeconomic disadvantage and earlier difficulties; and randomized trials comparing concurrent with sequential treatment of several substance problems.

domains.note: No search methods,dates or selection criteria are reported beyond a focus on the previous 18 months; the authors chose and annotated the evidence.

No study-by-study appraisal and designs are seldom named (two age-group samples are called panel designs); convenience samples (rave attenders) sit beside national surveys. Some limitations are named: low power in neuroimaging, weak methods in prevention research, unknown reliability of the DSM-5 severity index.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 8 of 71 references are by review authors, including the Australian prevalence and correlate studies and the treatment-sample latent-class study, which the authors mark as of outstanding interest.

Causal and certain wording from cross-sectional associations (risk of developing comorbid conditions; alcohol use increases the risk of experimenting with smoking; limited-range use may increase later expansion; cocaine may be more injurious than alcohol), and a conclusion of clear cognitive deficits next to null behavioural findings.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on harms of polysubstance use
domains.note: Studies finding no behavioural difference from controls are reported but dropped from the abstract and conclusion; explanations other than harm from the substances (socioeconomic disadvantage, pre-existing differences, selection into clinical samples) are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain. The review is a useful map of definitions, measurement approaches and latent-class patterns as of 2014, but its selection methods are not described, part of its evidence is the authors' own, and its conclusions use causal and certain language the cited designs cannot support. Citable for: definitions and measurement issues, the latent-class pattern, and the authors' 2014 view that prevention and treatment research for polysubstance use was underdeveloped. Not citable for: prevalence figures or health and cognitive harms as established facts; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Polysubstance use is defined broadly as using more than one drug over a defined period, at the same time or at different times, for therapeutic or recreational purposes; in prevention and treatment it usually means several illicit drugs but can include licit and prescription drugs used non-medically.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Historical DSM polysubstance dependence (use of three or more substances other than caffeine and nicotine with no single substance dominating, dependence criteria met for the substances as a group but not for any one) was removed in DSM-5, where substance use disorders are diagnosed by substance and graded on a severity continuum from 2 (mild) to 11 (severe) criteria; most population research records only frequency of use, not criteria or severity.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 269, continuing on p. 270)

key_findings.finding: Measures of polysubstance use in 2013 surveys were based on lifetime use (refs 18, 23, 24, 26), use in the past 1 to 12 months (refs 19–22, 25–27) or simultaneous use on the same occasion (refs 22, 26); simultaneous use is hard to capture in surveys and has mostly been studied in smaller high-risk samples (club or bar patrons, clinical populations).
key_findings.locator: Prevalence and the Current Patterns of Multiple Substance Use, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The review also says that, in older groups, people reporting past-year polysubstance use were very likely to report same-occasion use (ref22,p271). Thus some national survey work assessed it; the measurement difficulty is not an absence of all such data.

key_findings.finding: Latent class analyses typically find a limited-range class (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate-range class (adding amphetamine derivatives) and an extended-range class (adding non-medical use of prescription drugs and other illicit drugs); Figure 1 is a conceptual diagram, not to scale.
key_findings.locator: Prevalence and the Current Patterns of Multiple Substance Use, 2nd paragraph (p. 270, continuing on p. 271); Figure 1 (p. 271)

key_findings.finding: Among teenagers, limited-range use was most common, reported by 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime, ref. 23) to 34% before age 16 (ref. 18). Extended-range use was 2% at 12–17 years and 13.5% at 18–29 years (refs 22, 23), which the review calls panel survey designs and reads as limited-range use in adolescence possibly increasing the risk of expanded use in young adulthood.
key_findings.locator: Prevalence section, 3rd paragraph and 5th paragraph (right column) (p. 271); annotations to references 22 and 23 (p. 274)
key_findings.note: The reference annotations describe refs 22 and 23 as nationally representative samples of young adults and of adolescents respectively and say nothing of following the same people over time; the annotation of ref. 22 gives 13.2% for polydrug use, against 13.5% in the text.

key_findings.finding: US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (ref. 34): non-medical prescription drug use 6.3% in the past year and 2.7% in the past month in people aged over 12 (as printed); pain relievers 4.8%, tranquillizers 2.1%, stimulants 1.2%, sedatives 0.3%; higher at 18–25 years (14.4–15.5%) than at 12–17 (7.8–8.7%) or 26 and older (3.8–4.8%). Lifetime non-medical benzodiazepine use was 7.5% in a national sample of US high-school seniors (ref. 35).
key_findings.locator: Prevalence section, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Women and men: some evidence that polysubstance use involving non-medical prescription drugs is higher in young adult women than men (refs 19, 26); young adult men (about 18–35 years) are at higher risk of extended-range use (refs 22, 26, 27, 39); other correlates are being single, having low education and being employed (refs 21, 22). A small cluster of sedative and alcohol use had last-year prevalence of 1.3% among young Australian adults (ref. 22).
key_findings.locator: Prevalence section, 4th and 5th paragraphs (right column) (p. 271); annotations to references 19 and 26 (p. 274)
key_findings.note: Both sources for the sex difference are student samples by their annotations (US first-year college students, ref. 19; Brazilian college students, n = 12,544, ref. 26), measured by self-report; adjustment is not described. The annotation of ref. 26 says 18–34-year-old men were the most likely to report polydrug use.

key_findings.finding: Settings: up to 75% of rave attenders used several substances, with an average of five drugs at the last rave attended (ref. 12, a cluster analysis of underground rave attenders); polysubstance use in club and dance venues is described as widespread and far higher than in other venue types (refs 25, 28).
key_findings.locator: Reasons for Use, 2nd paragraph (p. 270, right column); Prevalence section, 5th paragraph (p. 271)

key_findings.finding: Health correlates from latent class analyses: classes with wide-ranging use report more psychological distress (refs 22, 23) and more anxiety and depression symptoms (ref. 31); people who drink and also use illicit drugs are more likely to have generalized anxiety and major depressive disorder (ref. 40); in a treatment-seeking cannabis sample the wide-ranging class had more depression, anxiety, manic excitement and positive psychotic symptoms than patients using no other illicit drugs (ref. 41); latent class studies also link polysubstance use with sexual risk behaviour and infectious disease (refs 42, 43).
key_findings.locator: Comorbid Psychopathology and Health, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepines with opioids: in a Danish national sample (ref. 6), people with long-term opioid use and chronic pain had an odds ratio of 27 (95% CI 14.85–49.15) for long-term benzodiazepine misuse compared with individuals without chronic pain; people using both drug classes are described as at higher risk of non-fatal and fatal overdose (ref. 48), comorbid conditions and forensic problems (ref. 7).
key_findings.locator: Comorbid Psychopathology and Health, 2nd paragraph (p. 271, continuing on p. 272)
key_findings.note: The comparison group is described only as individuals without chronic pain; whether they also used opioids cannot be told from the review.

key_findings.finding: Imaging: after 1 month of abstinence, people dependent on alcohol and on one or more stimulants (mostly cocaine) had lower N-acetylaspartate, creatine, myo-inositol and choline-containing metabolites in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex than people dependent on alcohol alone, who did not differ from controls; N-acetylaspartate correlated with visuospatial and working-memory performance (ref. 51). Abstinent people using several substances had less grey matter in the right temporal pole and medial frontal lobe (ref. 50). In neither metabolite study were the abnormalities related to severity of use.
key_findings.locator: Imaging and Neuropsychology Studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Several of these imaging studies, and recent studies of inhibitory control (ref. 57) and decision-making (ref. 58), found no difference in behavioural performance between people using several substances and controls; large differences were reported on standard tests given outside the scanner in another study (ref. 62), in which only severity of cocaine use was related to brain metabolism.
key_findings.locator: Imaging and Neuropsychology Studies, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Prevention and treatment: school and community programmes to reduce youth substance use show modest efficacy, with small short-term effects and poor longer-term outcomes (refs 64–66); pervasive methodological weaknesses prevent conclusions about prevention aimed at adults who use several substances (ref. 67); there is limited evidence on whether treating several substance problems at once works better than treating them one after another; personality-targeted prevention has reported promising results at 24 months (ref. 71).
key_findings.locator: Prevention, Treatment, and Further Research, 1st paragraph (p. 272, continuing on p. 273) and 2nd paragraph (p. 273)

key_findings.finding: Energy drinks with alcohol: experimental studies at low doses of caffeine and alcohol did not find increased short-term behavioural effects or a higher perceived level of intoxication (refs 15, 16); a commentary (ref. 17) argues that laboratory doses are lower than those drunk in real settings and calls for research independent of industry funding.
key_findings.locator: Reasons for Use, 3rd paragraph (p. 270); annotations to references 15–17 (p. 274)
key_findings.note: The annotations to refs 15 and 16 state that their authors acknowledged a conflict of interest with an energy-drink company; ref. 15 is described as a double-blind four-arm crossover trial in 52 volunteers.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that people who use several substances are at elevated risk of comorbid psychiatric and other health conditions and have more pervasive cognitive deficits that place them at risk of poorer treatment outcomes, and that prevention and treatment approaches for polysubstance use are underdeveloped compared with those for single substances.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: The contrast of extended-range use at 12–17 years (2%) and 18–29 years (13.5%) is attributed to panel survey designs, but the two cited sources (refs 22, 23) are annotated as nationally representative samples of different age groups, with no follow-up of the same people described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures compare age groups in two samples; they do not show that adolescents' limited-range use expands later, which the paragraph infers.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 13.5% for extended-range use at 18–29 years (refs 22, 23), while the annotation to ref. 22 gives a polydrug-use prevalence of 13.2% in young Australian adults.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two figures may describe different quantities; the primary paper is needed before either is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 26 is cited for higher polysubstance use involving non-medical prescription drugs in young women than men, but its annotation reports that 18–34-year-old men were the most likely to report polydrug use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not necessarily contradictory (different outcomes), but the support for a sex difference rests on two student samples and cannot be checked from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Danish odds ratio (27, 95% CI 14.85–49.15) compares people with long-term opioid use and chronic pain against individuals without chronic pain, without saying whether the comparison group used opioids; the outcome is called long-term use of benzodiazepines abuse.
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast actually estimated cannot be identified from the review; ref. 6 must be read before the figure is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The US survey prevalence is given for people aged over 12, and the age-group figures are ranges (for example 14.4–15.5% at 18–25) without saying what the ranges span (years, drug types or estimates).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be quoted precisely without the source report (ref. 34).

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites refs21–22 for being single, lower education and employment as correlates; the annotation to ref22 lists male sex, lower education and higher income. Whether these are different model contrasts or selective summaries cannot be resolved from the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary ref22 report is needed before treating these lists as one verified adjusted pattern.

design_detail: Science report, three printed pages (pp. 912–914) without section headings. Two school-based panels in New York State: (i) a two-phase random sample representative of public secondary school students in 18 schools, surveyed with self-administered classroom questionnaires in fall 1971 (T 1) and spring 1972 (T 2), 5–6 months apart, 5,468 students linked across the two waves by self-generated identification codes; (ii) senior-class members of the same schools, re-contacted by mail and telephone 5–9 months after graduation (T 3, winter 1972–73; n=985). At each wave students reported ever use and past-month use of 14 legal and illegal substances, and at T 2 and T 3 use during the interval. Lifetime use at the start of an interval placed each student on a seven-step cumulative (Guttman) scale (none; legal drugs only; cannabis; pills; psychedelics; cocaine; heroin), cross-tabulated against the scale step reached by use during the interval (Table 1); students who had used only legal drugs were split by the legal drugs they currently used (Table 2); a four-stage diagram gives transition probabilities (Fig. 1). Results are weighted percentages only: no statistical tests, intervals or covariate adjustment; survey weighting accounts for selection and school response.
can_establish: The order in which New York State public high-school students of 1971–73 took up beer or wine, cigarettes or hard liquor, cannabis and other illicit drugs, and the share at each step who started the next one within 5–9 months, in that place and era.
cannot_establish: That using a drug at one step causes progression to the next (the contrasts are unadjusted percentages that a shared propensity, age, peers or the order in which drugs are offered could produce), or that the same order holds in other places and later cohorts, which the author himself says is probably culturally determined (p. 914).

sample.recruitment: School-based classroom survey: a two-phase random sample representative of public secondary school students in New York State (18 schools); the seniors' panel re-contacted after graduation by mail and telephone (p. 912, running text, 3rd paragraph; References and Notes, note 4, p. 914).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Students in sampled schools and homerooms who returned usable questionnaires (8,206 at T1, 7,250 at T2); the panels are those who could be linked across waves. No other criteria are stated (note 4, p. 914).
sample.demographics: High-school students aged 14 to 18 (Fig. 1 legend, p. 912). The breakdown by sex, grade, race and family education is said to have been analysed but is not reported (p. 914, running text, 10th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Only 66% of fall students could be matched in spring and 60% of spring seniors after graduation; the post-graduation follow-up had a 69% response rate. Unmatched students included a higher proportion of people who used drugs; the correction for unmatched cases weighted the panel to reproduce T 1 marihuana use in the full cross-sectional sample, in addition to each wave’s selection-probability and school-response weights (note 4, p. 914). The column Ns of Table 1 add up to 4,588, not 5,468 (editors' sum; see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Public-school students present in class: pupils absent on the survey days, those who had left school and private-school students are not covered. The anonymous linkage failed for a third of students, disproportionately those using drugs, and the weighting corrects only one marker of this loss. The results describe New York State public schools in 1971–73.

exposure.measurement: Self-administered questionnaire at each wave: ever use and use in the past 30 days of 14 substances, and at T2 and T3 use in the interval since the previous survey (p. 912, running text, 3rd paragraph). The starting position is the step of the cumulative scale reached by lifetime use at the earlier wave.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured beyond ever use, past-month use and use in the interval: no amounts, frequency or routes.
exposure.polysubstance: The scale is itself a cumulative count of drug classes used. 'Pills' combine stimulants, depressants and tranquilizers (p. 912, running text, 4th paragraph); whether medically prescribed use was excluded is not stated.

comparison.controls: Students at lower steps of the scale at the start of the same interval (no drug ever; legal drugs only), and, for the legal drugs, groups defined by which legal drugs they were currently using (Table 2, p. 913).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measures of temperament, conduct problems, school performance, family or peer drug use, or local availability of drugs are reported; the groups compared differ in age and grade as well as in drug history.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: By construction the groups differ in which drugs they had already used; no other drug-use differences are reported.

outcomes.instruments: The highest scale step reached by drug use during the follow-up interval, classified independently of the starting pattern (Table 1, p. 913); use of each drug class during the interval (Table 2, p. 913). Fig. 1 probabilities come from the high-school panel, with students who started several drugs within one interval assigned an order in proportion to students who started only one of them (Fig. 1 legend, p. 912; note 9, p. 914).
outcomes.validity_norms: For the cumulative scale in the earlier cross-sectional survey, reproducibility .98 and scalability .64, above the conventional lower limits of .90 and .60 (p. 912; note 7, p. 914). Self-reports were not validated.
outcomes.operationalization: Progression is a move to a higher step during the interval and regression a move to a lower one; an 'error' is a pattern in which a drug was used without all the drugs ranked below it (Table 1 footnote, p. 913).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests, standard errors or intervals are reported; all results are percentages.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-administered questionnaires).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only (Tables 1–2, Fig. 1). Starting cannabis within 5–6 months: 27% of baseline exclusive-legal-drug students currently using beer/wine,cigarettes and hard liquor in the past 30 days (N≥342) against 2% of students who had used no drug (N≥467) (Table 2). Moving beyond cannabis: 26% of students whose lifetime use had reached cannabis (N=558) against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs (N=2,911) and 1% of students who had used no drug (N=482) (Table 1; abstract). Editors' calculation, ignoring weighting and clustering and using printed minimum N labels, so not design-valid uncertainty intervals: approximate 95% intervals 22–32% for the 27%, 1–3% for the 2% and 22–30% for the 26%; risk ratios about 13.5 (27% against 2%) and 6.5 (26% against 4%).
analysis.covariates: None. The author states that the sequences were similar in both cohorts, in all grades, in both sexes and across family education and race, but these data are not presented (p. 914, running text, 10th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The seniors' version of Table 1 is not shown apart from a single figure (16% moving beyond cannabis, p. 913); the grade, sex, family-education and race comparisons on which the abstract's consistency claim rests are not presented.
analysis.power: Not reported. Several starting groups are small: the cocaine and heroin columns of Table 1 hold 40 students each, and two seniors' columns of Table 2 hold 8 and 5, so their percentages are imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over 5–6 months, students who had used no drug rarely took up cannabis (1–2%), students who had used beer or wine, cigarettes and hard liquor took it up more often (27%), and about a quarter of students whose use had reached cannabis went on to another illicit drug, mostly pills or psychedelics, against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs. Steps were occasionally skipped: 1% of students who had used no drug used pills without the lower steps, and 2% of legal-drug-only students used pills or psychedelics out of order. These are unadjusted percentages in a panel that lost a third of students, more of them people using drugs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the legal drugs 'necessary intermediates' between non-use and marihuana and marihuana a 'crucial step' towards other illicit drugs (abstract, p. 912), wording that reads as causal and as without exception. The body also calls cannabis a crucial step and stage (p 913,left column); these statements sit beside the qualifications that a drug does not invariably lead to the next, many students stop or go back, the number of stages depends on the classification, and the stages are probably culturally determined, which only comparative studies can settle (p. 914, 11 th paragraph; note 3). The abstract's statement that the sequence holds in each high-school year rests on data not presented (p. 914, 10 th paragraph). The abstract names LSD, amphetamines or heroin as the drugs reached, but of the 26% most moved to pills (12 points) or psychedelics (9 points), and heroin accounted for about 2 points (Table 1, p. 913). The order of first use among students who started two drugs within one interval was not observed (note 9; Fig. 1 legend).

timeline.event: This study: New York State school panels, 1971–73.

Wagner & Anthony, US household surveys 1991–94: earlier alcohol or tobacco use went with an earlier first chance to try marijuana and with starting it once offered; marijuana use with an earlier chance to try cocaine and with starting it (see that card).

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: in US household surveys 1982–94, 16 per 1,000 young people started a hard drug before marijuana; a model with a shared propensity and no gateway effect reproduced the ordering (see that card).
Lynskey et al., Australian twins born 1964–71: most people who used both cannabis and other illicit drugs reported starting cannabis first; 17 of 622 reported another drug first (see that card).

Degenhardt et al., 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys: the order of first use varied with how common each drug was; other illicit drugs before cannabis were most common where cannabis was rare (as recorded on that card).
Vanyukov et al.: narrative review by proponents of common liability arguing that the stage sequence need not reflect causal steps (see that card).

replication.where_it_stands: The order described here (legal drugs, then cannabis, then other illicit drugs) is reported again in US household surveys and in Australian twins among the papers read for this round (Wagner & Anthony, 2002; Morral et al., 2002; Lynskey et al., 2003), while cross-national surveys show that the order varies across countries and cohorts alongside differences in how common drugs are (Degenhardt et al., 2010, as recorded on its card). The descriptive sequence is replicated in settings like this one; whether it reflects a causal step, a shared propensity or the order in which drugs are offered remains open, and the reading list notes that no single design separates the three explanations.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse research grant DA-00064 (References and Notes, note 12, p. 914).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author: Biometrics Research, New York State Psychiatric Institute, and School of Public Health and Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University (p. 914).

what_would_settle_it: A cohort followed from before any drug use, recording first offers and first use of each drug as they happen (in months, not recalled intervals), with propensity measured at baseline (conduct problems, family and peer use), analysed so that the order of opportunities and a shared liability are separated from any effect of the earlier drug, and repeated in places where cannabis is not the most available illicit drug.

domains.note: No covariate adjustment for confounding. Students at different steps differ in age, grade, peers, family background and propensity to use drugs, none of which enters the comparisons; a shared liability or the order in which drugs are offered would produce the same pattern.
Self-reported ever use in a classroom questionnaire with broad classes ('legal drugs', 'pills'); the cumulative scale fits well, but individual reports were not checked.
Only 66% of students were linked across waves (60% of seniors), unmatched students used drugs more, and the weighting corrects only T1 marihuana prevalence (note 4, p. 914).
None relevant.
Table 1 accounts for 4,588 of the 5,468 panel students (editors' sum); how the remainder (non-cumulative starting patterns, missing answers or weighting) was handled is not described.

Use during the interval is self-reported; for students who started several drugs within one 5–6-month interval the order was not observed, and for legal drugs it was assigned by assumption (note 9; Fig. 1 legend).
The seniors' table and the grade, sex, family-education and race analyses are not shown; Fig. 1 and Table 2 disagree on two values (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged as evidence that using one drug leads to the next (the gateway question), the study has no control for confounding at all, and a third of the panel was lost selectively. As a description, it is a well-sampled two-wave panel showing the order of first use and short-term transition rates in New York State public schools in 1971–73. Citable for that order, for the transition percentages with their denominators, and for the author's own caveat that the stages are probably culturally determined; not citable as evidence that legal drugs or cannabis cause later drug use, nor for the size of any such effect.

key_findings.finding: Two New York State school panels: 5,468 students linked between fall 1971 and spring 1972 (5–6 months) and 985 graduated seniors re-contacted 5–9 months after graduation; usable questionnaires were obtained from 8,206 students at T1 and 7,250 at T2.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 3rd paragraph (p. 912, middle column); References and Notes, note 4 (p. 914)

key_findings.finding: Linkage by self-generated codes matched 66% of fall students in the spring and 60% of spring seniors after graduation (post-graduation response rate 69%); unmatched students included more people who used drugs, and each wave was weighted for school and homeroom selection probabilities and school response; the additional linkage-loss correction weighted the T 1–T 2 panel to reproduce T 1 marihuana use in the full cross-sectional sample.
key_findings.locator: References and Notes, note 4

key_findings.finding: In the earlier cross-sectional survey, lifetime use fitted a seven-step cumulative scale (none; legal drugs; cannabis; pills; psychedelics; cocaine; heroin) with reproducibility .98 and scalability .64, against conventional minima of .90 and .60.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 4th paragraph (p. 912, right column); References and Notes, note 7 (p. 914)

key_findings.finding: Of 482 students who had used no drug by fall 1971, 62% used none in the next 5–6 months, 36% used legal drugs only, 1% used legal drugs and cannabis, and 1% used pills without the lower steps (out of order); none used cannabis without legal drugs.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column (i); running text, 7th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs, 79% stayed at legal drugs, 10% used no drug in the interval, 7% added cannabis, 2% reached pills with a complete cumulative pattern including cannabis, and 2% reached pills (1%) or psychedelics (1%) out of order, which the author reads as going to other illicit drugs without cannabis (2–3% in each cohort).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column (ii); running text, 8th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Of 558 students whose lifetime use had reached cannabis but no further, 26% moved beyond cannabis within 5–6 months (16% among graduated seniors, not tabulated). Highest step reached in Table 1: pills 12% (9% in cumulative order plus 3% out of order), psychedelics 9% (5% plus 4%), cocaine 2% (out of order), heroin 2% (1% plus 1%); 19% used only legal drugs in the interval and 56% stayed at cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column (iii) and footnote; running text, 8th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: The printed cells beyond cannabis sum to 25% (editors' sum), within rounding of the stated 26%. Approximate 95% interval for 26% of 558: 22–30% (editors' calculation, ignoring weighting and clustering).

key_findings.finding: No student who had used an illicit drug by T1 used no drug at all in the interval; regression went to lower illicit steps or to legal drugs. Out-of-order patterns rose with the starting step: 1% (none), 2% (legal), 11% (cannabis), 12% (pills), 18% (psychedelics), 28% (cocaine) and 34% (heroin). Of the 40 students at the heroin step, 42% used heroin in the interval, 23 of those percentage points without some lower-step drugs.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 6th paragraph (begins p. 912, right column; continues p. 913, left column); Table 1

key_findings.finding: Starting cannabis between fall 1971 and spring 1972, by current legal-drug pattern at T 1 among baseline exclusive-legal-drug students (past 30 days;never-any-drug group separate): never used any drug 2% (N≥467); used legal drugs but not currently 5% (N≥694); beer or wine only 4% (N≥731); cigarettes only 16% (N≥70); cigarettes plus beer or wine 16% (N≥356); hard liquor plus beer or wine 11% (N≥429); all three 27% (N≥342). Starting other illicit drugs in the same groups: 1%, 2%, 2%, 7%, 6%, 4% and 11%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, New York State total high school panel sample (T1 to T2)
key_findings.note: Approximate 95% intervals 22–32% for the 27% and 1–3% for the 2% (editors' calculation, ignoring weighting); risk ratio about 13.5 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Graduated seniors, spring 1972 to winter 1972–73: starting cannabis 6% of those who had used no drug (N≥62), 11% after beer or wine only (N≥103), 18% after cigarettes plus beer or wine (N≥16), 18% after hard liquor plus beer or wine (N≥206) and 29% after all three (N≥91); other illicit drugs 2%, 2%, 6%, 2% and 4%. The columns with N≥8 and N≥5 are largely or wholly empty.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, graduated seniors panel sample (T2 to T3)

key_findings.finding: Among the legal drugs, most students who started one began with beer or wine; exclusive starts with cigarettes or hard liquor were rare (5% and 2% in the high-school cohort, base not stated). Students using beer or wine took up hard liquor two to three times as often as cigarettes (33% against 14%; seniors 41% against 14%); 68% of students using cigarettes and beer or wine took up hard liquor, against 21% of students using hard liquor and beer or wine taking up cigarettes. The author states that no student in either cohort went from beer or wine to illicit drugs without hard liquor or cigarettes, and describes the associations of tobacco and hard liquor with starting marihuana as independent and additive (no test shown).
key_findings.locator: Running text, 9th paragraph (begins p. 913, left column; ends p. 914, left column); Table 2; References and Notes, note 8 (p. 914)

key_findings.finding: Fig. 1 (high-school panel, ages 14 to 18) gives stage probabilities: no use to beer or wine .28; beer or wine to hard liquor .32 and to cigarettes .08; hard liquor to cigarettes .21; cigarettes to hard liquor .68; marihuana .16 from the hard-liquor path, .27 after both and .11 from the cigarettes path; marihuana to other illicit drugs .26. Students who started more than one drug within the interval were placed in order by assumption.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 and legend (p. 912); References and Notes, note 9 (p. 914)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of the rendered figure. The two marihuana values for the single-legal-drug paths appear transposed relative to Table 2 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The author states that the patterns were strikingly similar in both cohorts, in all grades, in both sexes and independent of family educational background and race, but the data are not presented.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 10th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: The author's caveats: a drug does not invariably lead to those higher in the sequence, many students stop at a stage and many regress, the number of stages depends on how drug behaviours are classified, and the stages are probably culturally determined, a question only comparative and cross-cultural studies can answer.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 11th paragraph (left column); References and Notes, note 3

key_findings.finding: Methodological point made by the author: since each stage is a cumulative pattern, people at a stage should be compared with those who reached the preceding stage, not with the whole population, or characteristics of the earlier stage will be misattributed to the later drug.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 12th (last) paragraph (left column)

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 places .16 on the marihuana path after hard liquor and .11 on the path after cigarettes, whereas Table 2 (T1 to T2) gives 11% starting cannabis after hard liquor plus beer or wine and 16% after cigarettes plus beer or wine. The figure's .21 and .68 match those same two Table 2 columns, so the two marihuana values appear transposed in the figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which legal drug went with more cannabis initiation should be taken from Table 2 (cigarettes); Fig. 1 should not be cited for that comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The column Ns of Table 1 sum to 4,588 against a stated panel of 5,468 (editors' sum), with no explanation (non-cumulative starting patterns, missing answers or weighted Ns could account for it). The text's figure of 82% of students who had used legal drugs cannot be derived from Table 1, where 4,106 of 4,588 (89.5%, editors' calculation) had at least used legal drugs by T1; its base is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators behind the percentages are uncertain, and up to 16% of the panel is unaccounted for in the main table.

reporting_issues.issue: In the abstract, the group in which 1% moved to other illicit drugs is printed with a garbled label (a 'nondrug' group qualified by marihuana); Table 1 shows the 1% refers to students who had used no drug at T1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the figure should be attributed to students who had used no drug, from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Students who took up cannabis and another illicit drug within the same 5–6-month interval appear in Table 1 as following the cumulative order, although the order in which they started the two drugs was not observed; the paper describes an ordering assumption only for legal drugs (note 9) and for Fig. 1 (legend).
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the evidence that cannabis precedes other illicit drugs is assumed rather than observed; how large that part is cannot be told from the paper.

disagreements.first_pass: Science report, three printed pages (pp. 912–914) without section headings. Two school-based panels in New York State: (i) a two-phase random sample representative of public secondary school students in 18 schools, surveyed with self-administered classroom questionnaires in fall 1971 (T1) and spring 1972 (T2), 5–6 months apart, 5,468 students linked across the two waves by self-generated identification codes; (ii) senior-class members of the same schools, re-contacted by mail and telephone 5–9 months after graduation (T3, winter 1972–73; n=985). At each wave students reported ever use and past-month use of 14 legal and illegal substances, and at T2 and T3 use during the interval. Lifetime use at the start of an interval placed each student on a seven-step cumulative (Guttman) scale (none; legal drugs only; cannabis; pills; psychedelics; cocaine; heroin), cross-tabulated against the scale step reached by use during the interval (Table 1); students who had used only legal drugs were split by the legal drugs they currently used (Table 2); a four-stage diagram gives transition probabilities (Fig. 1). Results are weighted percentages only: no statistical tests, intervals or adjustment.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract calls the legal drugs 'necessary intermediates' between non-use and marihuana and marihuana a 'crucial step' towards other illicit drugs (abstract, p. 912), wording that reads as causal and as without exception. The running text is more cautious: a drug does not invariably lead to the next, many students stop or go back, the number of stages depends on the classification, and the stages are probably culturally determined, which only comparative studies can settle (p. 914, 11th paragraph; note 3). The abstract's statement that the sequence holds in each high-school year rests on data not presented (p. 914, 10th paragraph). The abstract names LSD, amphetamines or heroin as the drugs reached, but of the 26% most moved to pills (12 points) or psychedelics (9 points), and heroin accounted for about 2 points (Table 1, p. 913). The order of first use among students who started two drugs within one interval was not observed (note 9; Fig. 1 legend).

disagreements.first_pass: The order described here (legal drugs, then cannabis, then other illicit drugs) is reported again in US household surveys and in Australian twins among the papers read for this round (Wagner & Anthony, 2002; Morral et al., 2002; Lynskey et al., 2003), while cross-national surveys show that the order depends on how common each drug is (Degenhardt et al., 2010, as recorded on its card). The descriptive sequence is replicated in settings like this one; whether it reflects a causal step, a shared propensity or the order in which drugs are offered remains open, and the reading list notes that no single design separates the three explanations.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of four independent cross-sectional US household surveys (National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse 1991, 1992, 1993 and the 1994a subsample that kept the old questions), pooled. Ages (whole years) of first alcohol or tobacco use, of the first chance to try marijuana and cocaine, and of first use of each, all recalled at interview, were rearranged into person-year records. Discrete-time survival methods: unadjusted cumulative probability curves (Figs. 1–2), and survival regressions within risk sets defined by census tract or city block group and survey year, with sex, race/ethnicity and age group as covariates and earlier drug use as a time-varying exposure, giving relative risks of (a) a first opportunity and (b) first use once an opportunity had occurred. A supplementary analysis drops people whose first use fell in the same year as their first opportunity ('rapid transition') as a check on active drug-seeking. Marijuana analyses use ages 12–18 (n=26,015); cocaine analyses ages 12–25 (n=44,624).
can_establish: That among US household residents aged 12–25 interviewed in 1991–94, those who reported earlier alcohol or tobacco use also reported an earlier first chance to try marijuana and more often started it once they had the chance, and that reported marijuana use went with an earlier first chance to try cocaine and with starting cocaine once offered, after conditioning on neighbourhood, survey year, sex, race/ethnicity and age group.
cannot_establish: That earlier drug use causes later opportunities or later use: no individual propensity (temperament, conduct problems, family or peer drug use) was included as a covariate in the described analysis, the timing comes from ages recalled in whole years with same-year events of uncertain order, and the opportunity itself is a self-defined, recalled event that was not validated.

sample.recruitment: Household survey: multistage area-probability samples of the US noninstitutionalized civilian population; persons with no fixed address, institutionalized persons and military personnel are outside the frame; response rates 84.2% (1991), 82.5% (1992), 79.2% (1993) and 85.3% (1994) (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 12–18 for marijuana analyses (n=8,976, 8,179, 7,617 and 1,243 by survey year) and 12–25 for cocaine analyses (n=15,546, 14,766, 12,338 and 1,974); 1994 data from the 1994a subsample asked the old questions on opportunity (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 2nd–3rd paragraphs). Exclusions for missing answers are not described.
sample.demographics: Marijuana sample (Table 1): 13,044 male and 12,971 female; 11,463 non-Hispanic White, 6,798 non-Hispanic Black, 6,290 Hispanic, 1,016 Asian/Pacific Islander and 448 American Indian; 11,641 aged 12–14, 3,760 aged 15 and 10,614 aged 16–18; 49% had used alcohol or tobacco and 14% marijuana (editors' calculation). Cocaine sample (Table 2): 21,297 male and 23,327 female; 18,708 aged 19–25; 27% had used marijuana and 8.1% cocaine (editors' calculation) (p. 921).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); survey non-response 15–21%.
sample.selection_effects: Household samples miss people without a fixed address, in institutions or in the military, and people who died young; the authors argue that including the most heavily involved would strengthen the associations (p. 923, Discussion, 2 nd paragraph). No use of sampling weights is described, so national generalization and design-based precision of these respondent associations are uncertain.

exposure.measurement: Standardized self-report (interview or questionnaire with procedures to encourage complete and accurate reporting): ages at first use of alcohol, tobacco, marijuana and cocaine, even once; alcohol/tobacco onset is the earlier of the two; there was no question on the first opportunity to try alcohol or tobacco (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: first use only.
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol and tobacco combined into one onset variable; cocaine opportunity analyses stratified by alcohol/tobacco history and marijuana history; other drugs were not considered.

comparison.controls: Respondents in the same risk set (census tract or block group and survey year) who had not yet used the earlier drug at each year of age, earlier use being coded 0 until the event and 1 afterwards (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 7th paragraph; p. 920, 8th paragraph).
comparison.matching: Conditioning on neighbourhood and survey year by stratified risk sets, plus covariate adjustment for sex, race/ethnicity and age group at interview; for cocaine, also age at first marijuana use (pp. 919–920, Materials and Methods, 4th, 7th and 8th paragraphs).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No individual measures of propensity: temperament, conduct or school problems, family drug use and peer drug use were not included. The neighbourhood strata address area-level availability, policing and disorder only.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: For marijuana outcomes the comparison is people who had not used alcohol or tobacco by that age; for cocaine outcomes, people who had not used marijuana, within strata of alcohol/tobacco history.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported age at the first chance to try marijuana and cocaine (if the respondent had wanted to) and at first use of each, in whole years (p. 919, Materials and Methods, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the opportunity questions is reported; the authors note there is no gold standard for either age (p. 923, Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Opportunity = reported age of the first chance; transition = first use at or after the opportunity; 'rapid transition' = first use within the same year as the first opportunity (difference under 1 year), excluded in the drug-seeking check (p. 920, Materials and Methods, 9th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; most reported p values are below 0.001.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report).

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted relative risks from discrete-time survival regression: first chance to try marijuana, alcohol/tobacco use against none, about 3 (95% CI 2.8 to 3.3); starting marijuana once offered, about 7 (5.7 to 9.5), and 8.9 (5.7 to 14.1) after excluding same-year transitions; first chance to try cocaine against people who had used none of the three, 1.9 (1.7 to 2.1) after alcohol or tobacco only, 4.6 (3.8 to 5.6) after marijuana only and 7.6 (6.9 to 8.4) after both; starting cocaine once offered, marijuana against no marijuana, 15 (11.3 to 19.8), and 20.4 (10.2 to 40.7) after excluding same-year transitions (pp. 920, 923). Cumulative probabilities (unadjusted curves): a chance to try marijuana by 18 for about three in four people who had used alcohol or tobacco against one in four of others (text; about 70% and 25% on Fig. 1 A); a chance to try cocaine by 25 of 13%, 26%, 51% and 75% across the four alcohol/tobacco and marijuana groups. Crude lifetime odds ratios in Tables 1–2 (63.8 for marijuana after alcohol or tobacco; 100.8 for cocaine after marijuana) are not time-ordered.
analysis.covariates: Sex, race/ethnicity, age group at interview and survey year; risk sets defined by census tract or block group; for cocaine, age at first marijuana use and strata of alcohol/tobacco history.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-survey estimates are said to be essentially comparable but are in appendix tables available on request or on a website (not read). Several relative risks are printed only as approximate multiples (about three, about seven, 15), and whether each is adjusted is not always stated.
analysis.power: Not reported; the samples are large, but the transition analyses are restricted to people who reported an opportunity, and the number of people without earlier drug use who had an opportunity is not given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US household residents aged 12–25 (1991–94), reported earlier use of alcohol or tobacco went with about a threefold higher rate of a first chance to try marijuana and, once offered, about a sevenfold higher rate of starting it; reported marijuana use went with 4.6- to 7.6-fold higher rates of a first chance to try cocaine and, once offered, a 15-fold higher rate of starting it. Both transition associations held (8.9 and 20.4) when same-year transitions were dropped. All rest on ages recalled in whole years, conditioning on neighbourhood, survey year, sex, race/ethnicity and age group, with no measure of individual propensity.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion presents the results as new evidence on a possibly causal association and as the first epidemiologic support for two separate mechanisms, one acting on opportunity and one on use once offered (p. 923, Discussion, 1st paragraph), and speculates, labelled as such, that parental supervision works by reducing opportunities (p. 924, 7th paragraph). The data locate the associations at two points in the sequence; they do not show why they arise, and a shared individual propensity would produce both. The abstract's statement that the associations did not arise solely from drug-seeking rests on dropping same-year transitions, which removed 73% of people who used cocaine and, as the authors note, also people who took up an unbidden offer at once under peer pressure (p. 923; p. 924, Discussion, 5th paragraph). The text's three in four by age 18 is about 70% on Fig. 1A.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the sequence these analyses elaborate (see that card).
This study: four US household surveys, 1991–94.

Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a model calibrated to US household surveys of 1982–94 (overlapping these data) in which a shared propensity and the order of first opportunities, with no gateway effect, reproduce the gateway phenomena (see that card).
Lynskey et al.: within Australian twin pairs, early cannabis use went with later other drug use; access to other drugs through cannabis contacts is among the mechanisms they propose (see that card).
Degenhardt et al., 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys: the order of first use varied with how common each drug was (as recorded on that card).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no independent replication of the opportunity analyses appears in the sources read for this card; the authors build on their group's earlier analyses of US and Panamanian surveys (references 11–15, not read). Morral et al. (2002) used overlapping US survey data to show that a shared propensity together with the order of opportunities can reproduce the gateway pattern, which fits these results but does not distinguish a causal from a shared-liability explanation. Later studies were not searched by this reader.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse R01 award (grants DA 09897 and DA 09897-04S2) and Mexico's National Council on Science and Technology (CONACyT) (scholarship 110421 and repatriation grant 000358) (Acknowledgments, p. 924).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Bloomberg School of Public Health, Johns Hopkins University; the first author also at the Instituto Nacional de Psiquiatría, Mexico (p. 918).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records offers and first use as they happen (in months rather than recalled years), measures individual propensity before any use, and compares people who reach a first opportunity for a later drug with and without prior use of the earlier one; ideally with variation in opportunity that does not depend on the person, such as changes in local availability.

domains.note: Neighbourhood (census tract or block group), survey year, sex, race/ethnicity and age group were conditioned on, but no individual propensity (temperament, conduct problems, family or peer drug use) was included as a covariate in the described analysis, and such factors plausibly drive both earlier use and later opportunities and use.
Ages of first alcohol, tobacco and marijuana use recalled in whole years by people aged 12–25; events in the same year have an unknown order and were handled by censoring at the tie.
Household frame without homeless, institutionalized or military people; response 79–85%; no sampling weights described.
None relevant.
Exclusions for missing answers and the number of people censored at tied events are not reported; the counts of 12–18-year-olds differ between Tables 1 and 2 (see reporting issues).

The opportunity is a self-defined, recalled event without validation; people who used an earlier drug may notice, define and remember offers differently from people who did not, in a direction that cannot be predicted.
Per-survey results are only in appendix tables not published with the article; several estimates are printed as approximate multiples without stating the model.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The analysis adds a step that stage studies lacked (whether an earlier drug goes with being offered the next one, or with accepting it once offered) and conditions on neighbourhood, but it rests on recalled whole-year ages and has no measure of individual propensity, so it cannot separate an effect of prior use from a shared liability. Citable for the conditional rates and adjusted relative risks as associations in US household residents aged 12–25 in 1991–94, and for the finding that the associations persisted when same-year transitions were excluded; not as evidence that alcohol, tobacco or marijuana use causes later opportunities or later use.

key_findings.finding: Four independent US household surveys (1991, 1992, 1993 and the 1994a subsample) with response rates of 84.2%, 82.5%, 79.2% and 85.3%; marijuana analyses used 26,015 respondents aged 12–18 (8,976, 8,179, 7,617 and 1,243) and cocaine analyses 44,624 aged 12–25 (15,546, 14,766, 12,338 and 1,974).
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Respondents reported, in whole years, the age at first use of each drug and the age at which they first had a chance to try marijuana or cocaine had they wanted to; no opportunity question was asked for alcohol or tobacco. Events reported at the same age had an uncertain order; such respondents contributed person-years only up to the year of the tie.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Relative risks came from discrete-time survival regression within risk sets defined by census tract or city block group and survey year, meant to limit confounding by neighbourhood drug availability, police presence and disorder, adjusted for sex, race/ethnicity and age group, with earlier drug use and opportunity coded as time-varying. As a check on drug-seeking, people whose first use came in the same year as their first opportunity were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 6th–9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: By age 18, an estimated three in four people who had used alcohol or tobacco had had a chance to try marijuana, against one in four of those who had not; adjusted relative risk of a first marijuana opportunity about 3 (95% CI 2.8 to 3.3), with comparable estimates in the four surveys (appendix tables not published with the article).
key_findings.locator: Results › Accounting for the opportunity to try marijuana, 1st paragraph (p. 920); Fig. 1, part A (p. 922)
key_findings.note: On a 300-dpi crop of Fig. 1A, the curve for people who had used alcohol or tobacco ends at about 70% at age 18 and the other at about 25% (first reader's reading); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Once offered marijuana, an estimated 85–90% of people who had used alcohol or tobacco started using it, with a median lag of 1 year, against under 25% within 6 years (under 20% within 5 years) of those who had used neither.
key_findings.locator: Results › Marijuana use, given a marijuana exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph (p. 920); Fig. 1, part B (p. 922)
key_findings.note: The 85–90% has no stated time horizon; on Fig. 1B the curve is about 88% at 5 years and approaches 100% by about 13 years, the long tail resting on few people (first reader's reading).

key_findings.finding: Survival regression: people who had used alcohol or tobacco were about seven times as likely to start marijuana once offered (95% CI 5.7 to 9.5), in pooled data and in each survey; excluding same-year transitions, adjusted relative risk 8.9 (95% CI 5.7 to 14.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Marijuana use, given a marijuana exposure opportunity, 2nd paragraph; Results › Do these observed findings depend on seeking out marijuana exposure?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Estimated cumulative probability of a chance to try cocaine by age 25: 13% in people who had used no alcohol, tobacco or marijuana; 26% after alcohol or tobacco without marijuana; 51% after marijuana without alcohol or tobacco; 75% after marijuana and alcohol or tobacco. Median age at first cocaine opportunity 17 after marijuana with alcohol or tobacco, against 23 after marijuana without them. The association with alcohol/tobacco history differed across strata (chi-square 10.89, 1 df, p<0.001), so analyses were stratified.
key_findings.locator: Results › From marijuana use to cocaine exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph (p. 920) and 2nd paragraph (begins p. 920, continues between the tables on p. 921 and on p. 923); Fig. 2, part A (p. 922)

key_findings.finding: Adjusted relative risk of a first chance to try cocaine, against people who had used none of the three: 1.9 (95% CI 1.7 to 2.1) after alcohol or tobacco without marijuana; 4.6 (3.8 to 5.6) after marijuana without alcohol or tobacco; 7.6 (6.9 to 8.4) after both.
key_findings.locator: Results › From marijuana use to cocaine exposure opportunity, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Once offered cocaine, an estimated 50% of people who had used marijuana started within 2 years, and most eventually did; for people who had not used marijuana the estimates were small at 2 years and under 10% many years later. Relative risk 15 (95% CI 11.3 to 19.8); the association did not differ by alcohol/tobacco history (chi-square 1.77, 1 df, p>0.18).
key_findings.locator: Results › From marijuana use to cocaine use, given a cocaine exposure opportunity, 1st paragraph (p. 923); Fig. 2, part B (p. 922)
key_findings.note: On Fig. 2B (adjusted for alcohol/tobacco use) the curve for people who had used marijuana is about 55% at 2 years and levels off near 75% (first reader's reading).

key_findings.finding: 73% of people who used cocaine reported first use at the same age as their first cocaine opportunity; excluding them, people who had used marijuana remained more likely to start cocaine once offered (adjusted relative risk 20.4, 95% CI 10.2 to 40.7).
key_findings.locator: Results › Do these observed findings depend on seeking out cocaine exposure opportunities?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2, part C (p. 922)

key_findings.finding: Lifetime status at interview (not time-ordered): marijuana use in 28.4% of 12- to 18-year-olds who had used alcohol or tobacco against 0.6% of those who had not (crude odds ratio 63.8, 95% CI 51.2 to 79.5); cocaine use in 28.6% of 12- to 25-year-olds who had used marijuana against 0.4% (100.8, 84.4 to 120.3), and in 16.4% after alcohol or tobacco against 0.9% (20.9, 18.2 to 23.9).
key_findings.locator: Tables 1 and 2
key_findings.note: Editors' recomputation from the printed counts reproduces these as crude, unweighted odds ratios.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: reorganizing cross-sectional data into sequences invites bias; the household frame misses the most heavily involved; reports may differ in completeness between people who did and did not use drugs, with no gold standard for either age; and excluding same-year transitions also removed people who accepted an unbidden offer at once under peer pressure.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 923); 5th paragraph (p. 924)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says an estimated three in four people who had used alcohol or tobacco had had a chance to try marijuana by 18, but on Fig. 1A their curve ends at about 70% (read from a 300-dpi crop), clearly below the 75% line.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite about 70% (or about seven in ten) from the figure, against about one in four for people who had not used alcohol or tobacco.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the race/ethnicity rows add up to 44,660 respondents (41,061 without cocaine use), against 44,624 (41,025) in every other block of the same table (editors' sums).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor (36 respondents); one race/ethnicity cell is misprinted. The race/ethnicity odds ratios are consistent with their own rows.

reporting_issues.issue: Several relative risks are printed only as approximate multiples (about three, about seven, 15) with intervals to one decimal, and the text does not always say whether an estimate comes from the adjusted model.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should cite the interval or say 'about'; the exact point estimates cannot be recovered from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Exclusions for missing answers and the number of respondents censored at tied ages are not reported. The 12- to 18-year-olds number 26,015 in Table 1 but 25,916 in the age rows of Table 2 (editors' sum), with more 12- to 14-year-olds in Table 2 (11,655 against 11,641) and fewer at 15 (3,740 against 3,760) and 16–18 (10,521 against 10,614).
reporting_issues.consequence: Losses to missing data and ties are unknown; censoring at ties removes people whose earlier and later events fell in the same year, which could bias the estimates in either direction.

reporting_issues.issue: The surveys use a multistage area-probability design, but no sampling weights or design-based variance estimation is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Generalization of these respondent associations to the weighted US population is uncertain, and the confidence intervals may be too narrow if the survey design was not accounted for.
