design_detail: Two-step individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis of 18 record-linkage cohorts from the Mortality After Release from Incarceration Consortium (MARIC): cohorts of everyone released from incarceration during each study period (none built on a health condition or offence type), linked to national or state death registers. 1,471,526 people released 1980–2018 in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 10,534,441 person-years; 75,427 deaths. Each cohort team applied a common statistical analysis plan and returned aggregate counts, person-time, crude mortality rates (CMRs) and age- and sex-adjusted Cox hazard ratios; the central team pooled them by random-effects meta-analysis (Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation for confidence intervals), pooled incidence rate ratios (IRRs) between periods after release, ran univariable meta-regression on sex, age and region, and ran sensitivity analyses (excluding time reincarcerated; restricting to the ten cohorts that could separate deaths in custody from release-day deaths; leave-one-out). Analyses by time since release used the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day (Figure 2 caption, p. 1785). Rates only: there is no general-population comparison.
can_establish: Crude death rates, causes as coded in death registers, and timing of death after release from incarceration in these 18 mostly high-income cohorts (the analyses by time since release in the 16 of them that could give deaths by day); how rates differ by time since release, sex, age and region; and that release-day estimates are probably inflated, at least in part, by deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths (the authors' reading of their data, pp. 1781, 1784, 1786).
cannot_establish: How far these rates exceed those of the general population (no standardized mortality ratios or comparison group), why deaths cluster soon after release (tolerance, drug use, treatment and the drug supply were not measured), which drugs were involved (the poisoning category combines alcohol and other drugs, of unintentional and undetermined intent, with no toxicology), or how accurate and comparable cause-of-death coding was across eight countries and four decades.

sample.recruitment: Registry. Correctional release records linked with national or state death registers. The MARIC consortium (30 cohorts; 1,502,007 adults released 1980–2018 in 12 mostly high-income countries) was assembled from a literature search in March 2016 and colleagues' suggestions; 29 of its 30 cohorts had linked incarceration data with death registers. The 18 cohorts analysed here, 98% of the consortium, are those of unselected releases: USA 5 (Washington, New York, Pennsylvania, North Carolina ×2), Australia 5 (Western Australia ×3, New South Wales, Queensland), Canada 3 (Ontario ×2, British Columbia), New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and Brazil (Mato Grosso do Sul) 1 each (p. 1780; Table 1, p. 1782).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohorts: unselected samples of everyone released during the study period (cohorts built on a specific health condition or previous criminal-justice involvement excluded); reasons for each cohort's inclusion or exclusion are in appendix pp 4–7 (not read). Individuals excluded if not released during the study period or if the recorded release date was after the recorded date of death. Follow-up starts at release from the first incarceration in the study period (index incarceration); for 'any incarceration' analyses all later post-release time at risk is added, minus time reincarcerated (p. 1781, Data analysis, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: 88.3% men (sex recorded by corrections as male or female); median age at release 26–36 years by cohort (age for the Brazilian cohort from a subset of 2393 only); median follow-up 3.1–18.1 years by cohort, range 0–24 years; one cohort (Rosen, North Carolina) men only (Table 1, p. 1782). Race and ethnicity were not analysed (p. 1786).
sample.attrition: Loss to follow-up (emigration, failed linkage, deaths outside the registers' coverage) is not discussed. Two cohorts (Binswanger; Cunningham and King) could not provide some cause-specific data or deaths by day; 640 deaths had a missing cause (Table 2 footnotes, p. 1784; Figure 2 legend, p. 1785).
sample.selection_effects: Almost entirely high-income countries (one Brazilian cohort); cohorts exist only where release records could be linked to death registers. The index release was often not a person's first (earlier records unavailable), and risk is said to rise with each release. The authors suggest US cohorts may be less selected because incarceration thresholds are lower there ('inverse selection'). Cohort crude rates range from 236 per 100,000 person-years (Lim, New York, 244,274 people) to 1183 (Fazel and Chang, Sweden). Three Western Australian cohorts (Giles 2005–2014, Preen A 1994–2003, Preen B 1985–2008) overlap in place and period; whether any person or death appears in more than one cohort is not addressed in the main text (Table 1; Figure 1).

exposure.measurement: Release from incarceration, with release and reincarceration dates, from correctional records. Deaths and underlying causes from linked national or state death registers, grouped from ICD-9 or ICD-10 underlying-cause codes into a two-level, mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive system (code list in appendix p 8, not read) (pp. 1780–1781).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. No drug use, treatment in custody (including opioid agonist treatment), sentence length or pre-release health data were analysed; only age, sex, region and time since release.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured. The 'alcohol and other drug poisoning' category (unintentional and undetermined intent) does not separate drugs, alcohol or combinations, and no toxicology is reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not measured. Time since release is the only proxy for a break in use; tolerance and drug use before or after release were not recorded.

comparison.controls: Internal only: periods after release (days 2–14 daily, weeks 3–12 weekly, weeks 13–52, week 53 onward, total follow-up), sex, age groups and regions; index release against any release. No general-population comparison and no standardized mortality ratios.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Hazard ratios adjusted for age and sex only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Substance use disorders, mental illness, treatment, prior incarcerations, sentence length, race and ethnicity were unavailable or not analysed (Limitations, p. 1786).

outcomes.instruments: All-cause and cause-specific mortality from the death-register underlying cause (ICD-9 or ICD-10). Table 2 categories: maternal, nutritional and infectious (HIV; respiratory infections; tuberculosis; maternal; other); non-communicable (cardiovascular; cancer; liver; chronic respiratory; diabetes; other); injuries (alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional and undetermined intent; suicide; interpersonal violence; transport; other); other and ill-defined (intermediate and immediate causes; ill-defined or unknown); missing cause.
outcomes.validity_norms: The validity and comparability of cause-of-death certification and coding across countries and decades are not assessed. Inspection of release-day data suggested that in some cohorts deaths in custody might have been coded as occurring on the day of release; ten cohorts could separate the two definitively, eight could not (pp. 1781, 1786); the authors call the day-1 spike probably at least partly an artefact (p. 1784).
outcomes.operationalization: A drug death here is a death whose underlying cause is coded to alcohol and other drug poisoning of unintentional or undetermined intent; where intentional self-poisoning was classed is not stated in the main text (code list in appendix p 8). The Discussion calls these 'overdose deaths' (p. 1784). Who certified causes, whether autopsy or toxicology was done, and in what share of deaths, are not reported. Primary analyses start observation on day 2 (the first full 24 hours after release) because of the release-day coding problem.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 24 rows of Table 2 (all-cause, categories and subcategories) are each estimated overall and, mostly in the appendix, by period after release, sex, age group and region; statements of significance (for example men's higher cardiovascular and transport death rates) are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (registry outcomes). Cohort teams applied the common analysis plan; one named author accessed and verified the data and performed all meta-analyses (Contributors, p. 1787).

analysis.effect_sizes: Per 100,000 person-years, random-effects pooled CMRs with 95% CIs. All-cause after the index release 725 (625–831), I² 100% in the text and Figure 1, 98.8% in Table 2; men 731 (630–839), women 660 (560–767), meta-regression p=0.330; cohort CMRs 236 to 1183. Days 2–7: all-cause 1612 (1048–2287), I² 91.1%; more than 1 year: 737 (636–844). IRR of the first week against week 2 1.5 (1.2–1.8), I² 26.0%; against weeks 3–4 2.0 (1.5–2.6), I² 53.0%; against weeks 9–12 2.2 (1.6–3.0), I² 70.5%. Days 2–7 by cause: alcohol and other drug (AOD) poisoning 657 (332–1076), I² 89.0%; suicide 135 (36–277); cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). Whole follow-up: AOD poisoning 146 (103–197), I² 99.7%, 16,126 deaths; cardiovascular 102 (85–119); cancer 74 (61–88); suicide 67 (49–87); interpersonal violence 50 (32–72); transport 43 (33–56); all injuries 371 (310–438); non-communicable diseases 261 (220–306). Days 2–7 by region: Europe 2762 (1832–3872), USA 934 (389–1703). AOD poisoning by region: Europe 292 (258–329), Brazil 16 (12–22). Sensitivity: excluding reincarceration time (16 cohorts) 720 (605–845); ten cohorts able to separate custody deaths, overall 693 (557–845) and release-day CMR 826 (0–3455) against 4036 (887–8940); days 2–7 after any release 2460 (1516–3618); leave-one-out 701 (604–805) without the Swedish cohort and 762 (690–838) without the New York cohort. Absolute: 14,671 of 16,126 (91.0%) AOD poisoning deaths occurred more than 4 weeks after release. No prediction intervals; no standardized mortality ratios.
analysis.covariates: Crude rates are unadjusted. Cox hazard ratios from univariable models and multivariable models with age and sex only, pooled by random effects; reported in the appendix (p 31) and summarized as no association between sex and all-cause mortality.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A study protocol was published (Borschmann et al., 2020, Int J Popul Data Sci 5:1145; not read) and the statistical analysis plan is available on request (p. 1787). The article itself states that aggregation of weeks after the first two was decided post hoc and that observation was started on day 2 after inspection of release-day data (p. 1781); whether other analyses depart from the protocol cannot be judged without it.
analysis.selective_reporting: Most stratified results (age, cause by region, cause by period) are only in the appendix, which was not read. The Summary reports the first-week peak but not that 91.0% of the poisoning deaths occurred more than 4 weeks after release, nor the release-day coding artefact; both are in the main text.
analysis.power: Large overall (75,427 deaths), but estimates for single days and for days 2–7 have wide intervals (all-cause 1048–2287; AOD poisoning 332–1076), and the daily estimates in Figure 2A overlap widely with each other and with later periods.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the 16 cohorts that could give deaths by day (the time-period analyses leave out New Zealand's only cohort and one Washington cohort), crude death rates were highest on days 2–7 after release (all-cause 1612 per 100,000 person-years; alcohol and other drug poisoning 657), fell over the following week, and then stayed roughly level at about 700–860 per 100,000 from week 3 onward (Figure 2A, read approximately). Across all 18 cohorts, poisoning was the leading cause over the whole follow-up (146 per 100,000; 21.4% of deaths), but 91.0% of poisoning deaths occurred more than 4 weeks after release (the paper does not say from which release). Rates differed greatly between cohorts (236 to 1183) and regions (I² near 100%). Release-day estimates were probably inflated, at least in part, by deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths (the authors' reading of their data).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says the markedly elevated death rate in the first week underscores an urgent need for coordinated transitional care to prevent post-release deaths from suicide and overdose (p. 1779). The first-week peak is supported, but: most poisoning deaths happened later, as the authors themselves say when noting that acute prevention would prevent only a small minority (p. 1784); the comparison with the general population that the Background invokes is not made in this study; the poisoning category identifies neither opioids nor any other drug; and nothing about tolerance, drug use or treatment was measured, so neither the cause of the early peak nor the effect of any intervention is shown. The Results say the all-cause rate 'decreased consistently' to 737 more than a year after release (p. 1783), but Figure 2A shows a plateau after about the first week, with the rate beyond a year slightly above the overall pooled rate of 725. The calls for medications for opioid use disorder and naloxone at release (p. 1786) rest on other evidence.

timeline.event: Pratt et al., population-based cohort of suicide in recently released prisoners (ref. 11), cited among studies showing markedly elevated death rates after release compared with the general population (not read).

Binswanger et al., NEJM, release from prison and the risk of death (ref. 10); a Washington State cohort led by Binswanger is one of the 18 pooled here (Table 1), so the two are not independent (not read).

Kinner et al., estimate of deaths among recently released prisoners in Australia (ref. 18), cited for lower death rates during incarceration, the reason for the reincarceration sensitivity analysis (not read).
Kinner, Forsyth & Williams, systematic review of record-linkage studies of mortality in ex-prisoners: why (good) methods matter (ref. 12; on the project's General list; not read).
MARIC cohorts identified through a literature search (March 2016) and colleagues' suggestions.
Forsyth et al., Australian prospective cohort (ref. 28), cited for a rising risk of death with each subsequent release (not read).
MARIC protocol published (Borschmann et al., Int J Popul Data Sci 5:1145; ref. 15; not read).
This IPD meta-analysis, published with a linked Comment in the same issue (Lancet 2024;403:1727–1729; not among the files read).

replication.where_it_stands: The largest pooled description of death after release from incarceration. It confirms a first-week peak in these cohorts and suggests that earlier day-1 peaks are probably partly a coding artefact. It pools cohorts that were published separately (for example Binswanger's Washington cohort), and earlier meta-analyses of drug-related deaths soon after release (Merrall et al., 2010, on the project's _Tolerance list; not read) may share cohorts with it, so it should not be counted as independent replication of them. It reports crude rates only: the excess over the general population and the role of lost tolerance must come from other studies.

funding.funder: MARIC: Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC; GNT1120004). Bukten and Clausen cohort: The South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority (grant number 2019091) and The Norwegian Research Council (grant number 301535). The paper states that the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (pp. 1779, 1781, 1787).
funding.declared_conflicts: As declared (p. 1787): RB, salary and research support from an NHMRC Emerging Leadership-2 Investigator Grant (EL2; GNT2008073); MJS, Australian Research Council Future Fellowship (project number FT180100075), funded by the Australian Government; SLa, research scholar award from Fonds de recherche du Québec–Santé; JRA, US National Institutes of Health (R01 AI130058); RC, PK and KT, a University of Otago research grant; all other authors, no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Byline authors from the University of Melbourne, the University of Oxford, the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, Curtin University and Griffith University (p. 1779); the collaborators include the cohort investigators, who analysed their own cohorts under the common plan, as the IPD design requires. Data stewards (Washington Department of Corrections, Western Australian Department of Justice, British Columbia, Stats NZ) disclaim endorsement (Acknowledgments, p. 1787). Individual participant data will not be shared. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Linked release cohorts that record, for each release, recent drug use and treatment in custody (including opioid agonist treatment), with toxicology for every post-release death (drugs and concentrations), consistent cause-of-death coding across jurisdictions, reliable separation of deaths in custody from release-day deaths, and standardized mortality ratios against the general population by time since release.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (everyone released from incarceration in unselected cohorts), strata (time since release, sex, age, region) and outcomes (all-cause and cause-specific death) are stated; comparisons are internal, which suits the descriptive aim; there is no general-population comparator.

The article says a protocol was published previously (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the analysis plan is available on request; neither was read. Two departures are declared (aggregation of weeks after week 2 decided post hoc; observation from day 2 after inspecting the data). Whether the protocol set out the search, criteria and a risk-of-bias plan, and whether it preceded cohort identification in 2016, cannot be judged from the article.
Restriction to cohorts of everyone released (not built on a health condition or offence) is explained as a way to increase generalisability (p. 1780).

Cohorts were identified through a 'comprehensive search of the literature' in March 2016 and colleagues' suggestions, with details in the protocol (not read); the article gives no databases, terms or restrictions and reports no update after 2016. The Research-in-context search (MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, English, to 1 February 2023) is a background search, not the cohort search. A search about seven years older than publication rules out 'yes'; partial yes or no depends on the protocol.

How cohorts were screened, and by how many reviewers, is not described in the article; the 18 of 30 consortium cohorts were chosen by a stated rule (unselected releases), with reasons in appendix pp 4–7 (not read).

IPD process: each cohort team applied the common analysis plan to its own data and returned aggregate outputs, and a central author accessed and verified the data (Contributors, p. 1787). Not duplicate extraction in the usual sense, but data produced by one team were checked by another; judged met, a close call.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for cohort inclusion and exclusion are in appendix pp 4–7 (p. 1781), which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives each cohort's country or state, dates, size, sex split, median age, follow-up, person-years and deaths; how each cohort was linked to death records, linkage quality and ICD version are not in the article.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or data-quality appraisal of the cohorts is described in the Methods or listed among the appendix contents; linkage completeness, death-register coverage, cause-of-death certification and coding were not assessed. The release-day artefact was found by inspecting the data, not by a planned appraisal.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of the individual cohorts is not reported, except for the Norwegian cohort (Acknowledgments).

Random-effects pooling of cohort CMRs (Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation for intervals), of IRRs and of log hazard ratios, with meta-regression and leave-one-out analyses. Weaknesses not scored by this item: with I² of 98.8–100% the random-effects weights are almost equal (5.50–5.58% per cohort, Figure 1), so the pooled CMR is close to an unweighted average of very different cohorts and describes no particular population; no prediction intervals; a transformation for proportions is applied to deaths per person-time.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses tested the two data problems the authors identified (deaths during reincarceration: 720 vs 725; deaths in custody coded as release-day deaths, restricting to ten cohorts: 693 vs 725 overall, 826 vs 4036 on the day of release) and the influence of each cohort (leave-one-out, 701 to 762). No analysis examined cause-of-death misclassification.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion treats the release-day artefact carefully, but interprets cause-specific and regional rates (for example the highest AOD poisoning rate in Europe and the lowest in Brazil) through selection and context alone, without considering differences in death certification, toxicology practice and coding of drug deaths and undetermined intent across eight countries and four decades.

I² is reported for each estimate; meta-regression by sex, age and region and leave-one-out analyses were done, and regional differences are discussed (inverse selection in the USA; violence in Brazil; the effect of missing low- and middle-income cohorts).

Not investigated or discussed. In an IPD consortium analysed under one plan, selective publication of results matters less, but which jurisdictions have linkable records and joined the consortium is examined only as the scarcity of low- and middle-income cohorts.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and authors' interests are declared (pp. 1781, 1787).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 2, 4, 5 and 7 can be judged only from the published protocol (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the appendix (pp 4–7), neither of which was read; the overall rating does not depend on them. Three critical items are not met in the article itself: no appraisal of the cohorts' data quality or risk of bias (9), no account of cause-of-death misclassification or coding differences when interpreting cause-specific and regional rates (13), and no investigation of publication or availability bias (15). Under AMSTAR 2, more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence; a reader who set item 15 aside as unsuited to an IPD consortium would still find two. The rating concerns how far the pooled rates are unbiased summaries; it does not question the study's size or internal care (a common analysis plan, sensitivity analyses that exposed the release-day artefact, leave-one-out checks). Cite it for crude rates, causes as coded and timing of death after release in these cohorts, the first-week peak, the 91% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks, and the probable release-day coding artefact; not for excess mortality relative to the general population, for which drugs were involved, or for lost tolerance as the mechanism.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 18 cohorts (98% of the 30-cohort MARIC consortium) of everyone released from incarceration in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA, 1980–2018: 1,471,526 people (1,299,322 men, 88.3%; 172,204 women, 11.7%), 10,534,441 person-years and 75,427 deaths (5.1%).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 1780); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1781); Table 1 (p. 1782)

key_findings.finding: How deaths were counted: by linkage of correctional records with national or state death registers; causes are the underlying cause of death in ICD-9 or ICD-10, grouped into a two-level, mutually exclusive system (codes in appendix p 8); drug deaths are the category 'alcohol and other drug poisoning (unintentional and undetermined intent)'. Who certified causes and whether autopsy or toxicology was done are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design and data sources, 2nd paragraph (p. 1780); Methods › Data analysis, 3rd paragraph (p. 1781); Table 2 (p. 1784)

key_findings.finding: All-cause pooled crude mortality after release from the index incarceration: 725 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 625–831), I² 100% (text, Figure 1) or 98.8% (Table 2); men 731 (630–839), women 660 (560–767), no difference on meta-regression (p=0.330); rates similar up to age 34 and rising with age after that. Cohort rates ranged from 236 (Lim, New York) to 1183 (Fazel and Chang, Sweden).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1781, continuing on p. 1782); Figure 1 (p. 1783); Table 2 (p. 1784)

key_findings.finding: Causes over the whole follow-up: alcohol and other drug (AOD) poisoning was the leading cause, CMR 146 (103–197), I² 99.7%, 16,126 deaths (21.4% of all deaths); then cardiovascular disease 102 (85–119) and cancer 74 (61–88). Injuries accounted for 37,425 deaths (printed as 49.7%), CMR 371 (310–438), including suicide (6199 deaths, 8.2%; CMR 67, 49–87) and interpersonal violence (6361, 8.4%; CMR 50, 32–72); non-communicable diseases 29,731 (39.4%); infectious diseases 3597 (4.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 1782); Table 2 (p. 1784)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 37,425 of 75,427 is 49.6%.

key_findings.finding: Timing: the all-cause CMR was highest on days 2–7 after release, 1612 (1048–2287), I² 91.1%, against 737 (636–844) more than 1 year after release; pooled incidence rate ratios for the first week were 1.5 (1.2–1.8) against week 2, 2.0 (1.5–2.6) against weeks 3–4 and 2.2 (1.6–3.0) against weeks 9–12.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 2's caption (p. 1785) says the Cunningham and King cohort (New Zealand's only cohort) and the Binswanger cohort (Washington) could not provide deaths by day and were excluded from these analyses, and the Results tie 1612 and 737 to Figure 2: the rates by time since release and the rate ratios rest on 16 cohorts in seven countries (editors' count from Table 1).

key_findings.finding: Days 2–7 by cause: AOD poisoning CMR 657 (332–1076), I² 89.0%; suicide 135 (36–277); cardiovascular disease 71 (16–153). AOD poisoning had the highest rate of any cause in the first 2 weeks and the highest point estimate in every period examined, and was the only cause whose rate peaked in the first week; cancer deaths peaked after more than 1 year (77, 63–93).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 1783); Figure 2B (p. 1785)
key_findings.note: From the same time-period analyses (Figure 2B): 16 cohorts in seven countries.

key_findings.finding: Shape of the curve (Figure 2A, all-cause, values read approximately from the plotted points): about 1900 per 100,000 person-years on day 2 and about 1600 on day 3, about 1000–1200 on days 4–8, about 500–800 on days 9–14, and about 700–860 in each period from weeks 3–4 to week 53 onward; the daily intervals are wide and overlap the later periods.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2A
key_findings.note: No values are printed in the figure; read on a 300-dpi rendering, approximate to about ±50. Figure 2 excludes two cohorts (Cunningham and King; Binswanger) without deaths-by-day data.

key_findings.finding: 14,671 (91.0%) of the 16,126 AOD poisoning deaths, which the Discussion calls 'overdose deaths', occurred more than 4 weeks after release; the authors conclude that acute post-release prevention would prevent only a small minority of these deaths and that sustained treatment and harm reduction are needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The share mainly reflects that most person-time lies beyond 4 weeks (median follow-up 3.1–18.1 years by cohort), while the rate per person-year is highest in the first week; both hold at once. The paper does not say whether 'more than 4 weeks after release' counts from the index release or from the most recent release, or whether the release day is included (p. 1784; Methods, p. 1781). The second reader's rough reconstruction from the pooled rates (about 420 such deaths in the first 4 weeks after the index release, against the 1,455 implied) suggests time since each release, but pooled random-effects rates are not crude totals and the appendix was not read, so this is not settled.

key_findings.finding: Release-day coding artefact: inspection of the data suggested that in some cohorts deaths in custody had been coded as deaths on the day of release; ten cohorts could separate the two definitively, eight could not. Restricted to the ten, the release-day CMR fell from 4036 (887–8940) to 826 (0–3455) and the overall CMR was 693 (557–845) against 725. Primary analyses therefore started observation on day 2.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data analysis, 6th–7th paragraphs (p. 1781); Results, 9th paragraph (p. 1783); Discussion, 8th paragraph (p. 1786)
key_findings.note: The 4036 is the release-day rate in the main day-level analysis (at most 16 cohorts) and the 826 the rate in the ten cohorts, so the comparison sets different sets of cohorts side by side, and the 826 has an interval of 0–3455; the authors call the day-1 spike probably at least partly an artefact (p. 1784).

key_findings.finding: Reincarceration: in the 16 cohorts with reincarceration data (1,309,958 people, 8,324,428 person-years, 56,731 deaths), excluding time and deaths while reincarcerated gave an all-cause CMR of 720 (605–845), almost identical to 725. The days 2–7 rate after any release, 2460 (1516–3618), was numerically higher than after the index release, 1612, but not significantly on meta-regression.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Regions: the days 2–7 all-cause CMR was highest in Europe, 2762 (1832–3872), and lowest in the USA, 934 (389–1703), with no regional difference after more than 1 year. Over the whole follow-up, AOD poisoning was highest in Europe, 292 (258–329), and lowest in the Brazilian cohort, 16 (12–22), where interpersonal violence was highest, 299 (281–319); suicide was highest in Australia and New Zealand, 103 (81–128). The authors suggest 'inverse selection' (lower incarceration thresholds in the USA) for the low US rates.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th and 6th paragraphs (p. 1783); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 1785)
key_findings.note: Days 2–7 rates come from the time-period analyses (16 cohorts; Figure 2 caption, p. 1785).

key_findings.finding: Leave-one-out: the largest changes from the primary estimate of 725 came from removing the Swedish cohort, 701 (604–805), and the New York cohort, 762 (690–838).
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph (p. 1783, continuing on p. 1784)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the index release was probably not the first for many people; almost all cohorts were from high-income countries; only age and sex were examined (no race or ethnicity; sex recorded as binary); nothing was known about what happened between release and death; sentence length was not examined; eight cohorts could not separate deaths in custody from release-day deaths.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors call for health assessment at prison reception, care equivalent to the community including medications for opioid use disorder, pre-release planning that includes naloxone for people who have had opioid use disorder, and routine monitoring of post-release mortality; none of these was measured or evaluated in the study.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 1785, continuing on p. 1786)

reporting_issues.issue: Heterogeneity for the same all-cause estimate (725, 625–831) is given as I² 100% in the Results text and Figure 1 and as 98.8% in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both mean near-total between-cohort heterogeneity.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the Brazilian (Liu) cohort's women as 7215 (1.6%) of 62,425, against 55,210 men (88.4%); editors' calculation: 7215 of 62,425 is 11.6%, consistent with the printed share of men.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 column totals for sex and person-time do not equal the sums of the rows: the printed totals are 172,204 women, 1,299,322 men and 10,534,441 person-years, while sample sizes and deaths add up exactly. Editors' calculation from the printed rows (checked on a 300-dpi rendering): 172,564 women and 1,298,962 men, a difference of 360 each way, and 10,534,666 person-years.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small, but the sex split and person-time used in the Summary and Results cannot be reproduced from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the all-cause rate 'decreased consistently' after the first week to 737 (636–844) more than 1 year after release, but Figure 2A shows lower daily rates on days 9–14 (about 500–800) than in weeks 3–4 (about 860) and a level of about 700–860 from week 3 onward; 737 is above the overall pooled rate of 725.
reporting_issues.consequence: The excess is concentrated in roughly the first week rather than declining steadily; the wording overstates a gradient.

reporting_issues.issue: Injury deaths are printed as 37,425 (49.7%) of 75,427 deaths; editors' calculation: the share is 49.6%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding error; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 does not add up exactly, which a footnote attributes to cohorts that could not provide some causes; the denominator for each cause is not given. Editors' calculation: the cause categories sum to 75,417 rather than 75,427, and the infectious subcategories to 3612 against a category total of 3679 (the text's 3597 equals the subcategories without the 15 maternal deaths). The 'other and ill-defined' subcategories (1121 + 2818 = 3939) also fall 3 short of their category total (3942); the non-communicable and injury subcategories add up exactly.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cause-specific rates come from slightly different sets of cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: Follow-up per person is described as ranging from 1 month to 24 years (p. 1780, for the consortium) but as 0–24 years in the Summary and from 0.0 years in every cohort of Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in describing follow-up.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the AOD poisoning category 'overdose deaths' and links it to opioid use disorder treatment and naloxone, but the category includes alcohol poisoning and deaths of undetermined intent and identifies no drug.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be cited as opioid overdose deaths; claims about opioids need other sources.

reporting_issues.issue: Three Western Australian cohorts (Giles 2005–2014; Preen A 1994–2003; Preen B 1985–2008) overlap in place and period; the main text does not say whether any person or death appears in more than one cohort (cohort descriptions are in appendix pp 4–7, not read).
reporting_issues.consequence: If they overlap, some deaths would count twice in pooled estimates; this cannot be settled without the appendix.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Lancet 2024;403:1779–1788, all pages (Summary, Research in context, Methods, Results, Tables 1–2, Figures 1–2, Discussion, collaborators, contributors, declarations, data sharing, acknowledgments and references); tables and figures checked on rendered pages, Table 1 and Figure 2A also at 300 dpi. The online appendix, the published protocol (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the linked Comment (Lancet 2024;403:1727–1729) were not among the files and were not read.

disagreements.first_pass: Crude death rates, causes as coded in death registers, and timing of death after release from incarceration in these 18 mostly high-income cohorts; how rates differ by time since release, sex, age and region; and that deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths inflate day-1 estimates.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed items 1 and 3: the time-period analyses exclude two cohorts (Figure 2 caption, p. 1785); the paper hedges the release-day miscoding ('suggested ... might have', p. 1781; 'probably at least partially an artefact', p. 1784; 'may have been', p. 1786), while the card states it as shown.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking pp. 1781, 1783–1786 on rendered pages: Figure 2's caption excludes the Cunningham and King (New Zealand) and Binswanger (Washington) cohorts, which could not give deaths by day; the three passages hedge the miscoding as the second reader says. Both points added; wording otherwise kept.

disagreements.first_pass: Two-step individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis of 18 record-linkage cohorts from the Mortality After Release from Incarceration Consortium (MARIC): cohorts of everyone released from incarceration during each study period (none built on a health condition or offence type), linked to national or state death registers. 1,471,526 people released 1980–2018 in Australia, Brazil, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, Sweden and the USA; 10,534,441 person-years; 75,427 deaths. Each cohort team applied a common statistical analysis plan and returned aggregate counts, person-time, crude mortality rates (CMRs) and age- and sex-adjusted Cox hazard ratios; the central team pooled them by random-effects meta-analysis (Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation for confidence intervals), pooled incidence rate ratios (IRRs) between periods after release, ran univariable meta-regression on sex, age and region, and ran sensitivity analyses (excluding time reincarcerated; restricting to the ten cohorts that could separate deaths in custody from release-day deaths; leave-one-out). Rates only: there is no general-population comparison.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed item 1: say which cohorts the time-period figures rest on.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: sentence added (Figure 2 caption, p. 1785, checked at 300 dpi).

disagreements.first_pass: Provisional: items 2, 4, 5 and 7 can be judged only from the published protocol (Borschmann et al., 2020) and the appendix (pp 4–7), neither of which was read; the overall rating does not depend on them. Three critical items are not met in the article itself: no appraisal of the cohorts' data quality or risk of bias (9), no account of cause-of-death misclassification or coding differences when interpreting cause-specific and regional rates (13), and no investigation of publication or availability bias (15). Under AMSTAR 2, more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence; a reader who set item 15 aside as unsuited to an IPD consortium would still find two. The rating concerns how far the pooled rates are unbiased summaries; it does not question the study's size or internal care (a common analysis plan, sensitivity analyses that exposed the release-day artefact, leave-one-out checks). Cite it for crude rates, causes as coded and timing of death after release in these cohorts, the first-week peak, the 91% share of poisoning deaths after 4 weeks, and the release-day coding artefact; not for excess mortality relative to the general population, for which drugs were involved, or for lost tolerance as the mechanism.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed item 3 (hedging): the card cites the study for 'the release-day coding artefact'.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted as a wording correction only ('probable'); the AMSTAR 2 judgments and the overall rating (critically low) are unchanged.

design_detail: Between-subjects vignette experiment, called randomized by the authors, in which two versions of a questionnaire were handed out alternately to attendees present at the start of two addiction-focused talks at two mental health/addiction-focused conferences in October 2008 (location not stated). The two vignettes are identical except for the term: Mr. Williams, attending a court-ordered treatment program that requires abstinence from alcohol and other drugs, had two positive urine drug screens and a positive breathalyzer reading a month earlier and a further positive urine screen since, and now awaits the judge; he is described either as 'a substance abuser' or as having 'a substance use disorder' (the term appears twice in each version). Participants rated their agreement (1 to 6) with 32 statements; three subscales were derived by exploratory factor analysis of the pooled answers and compared between versions with independent t-tests at a significance level of .025 per comparison. 728 people were handed a form and 516 completed it (71%). No behaviour or real decision was measured.
can_establish: That among these conference attendees, described as mental health care providers (64.5% with doctoral-level degrees), reading the version that called the man 'a substance abuser' went with slightly more agreement with a mixed set of culpability, punishment and non-medical statements than reading the version that said he had 'a substance use disorder' (subscale means 2.92 vs 2.82 on a 1–6 scale), with no detectable difference in willingness for social contact or in treatment-related items.
cannot_establish: Whether the term changes what clinicians actually do, the care patients receive or their help-seeking; whether the effect holds for other scenarios (one vignette only, a man under court supervision with positive drug tests), other professionals, the public or policy makers; whether the difference is reliably above zero (the printed p of .02 matches an unstated one-sided test, allocation was by alternation and 29% did not take part); or that the terms leave social-contact and treatment judgments unchanged (differences of about d 0.2 were not excluded).

sample.recruitment: Conference attendees present at the start of two addiction-focused talks at two mental health/addiction-focused conferences in October 2008, each with a single stream of presentations; the location of the conferences is not stated; participants were not compensated (Method › Study population and protocol, 1st paragraph, p. 203; Measures, 2nd paragraph, p. 204).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No eligibility or exclusion criteria: all attendees who chose to complete and return the questionnaire (Method › Study population and protocol, 3rd paragraph, p. 204).
sample.demographics: 516 completers: mean age 51; 63.4% women; 81.0% White; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; professional focus (more than one allowed) mood disorders 66.9%, anxiety disorders 59.9%, psychosis 37%, alcohol/drug problems 34.8% (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 205). Professions (psychologist, psychiatrist, social worker and so on) are not reported, nor are characteristics by version.
sample.attrition: 212 of the 728 people handed a form (29%) did not complete it; the authors say they do not know why (Limitations, p. 206). Completion by version is not reported. The perpetrator-punishment test has 504 degrees of freedom, implying 506 analysed, so 10 completers are missing from it without explanation (Results, 3rd paragraph, p. 205).
sample.selection_effects: Attendees of addiction-focused talks at mental health conferences: mostly doctoral-level and White, with a mean age of 51 and only about a third reporting an alcohol or drug focus. The forms, with the term already in the vignette, were handed out before people decided whether to take part, so taking part could follow reading the term; 29% did not take part, for unknown reasons and in unknown proportions by version. The authors themselves caution against generalizing to mental health providers or other groups (Limitations, p. 206).

exposure.measurement: Version of the questionnaire received. The two forms were handed out alternately and sequentially by study staff through the auditoria; the authors describe this as an even and random distribution that removed seating biases (Method › Study population and protocol, 2nd paragraph, p. 204). No other randomization procedure is described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Each version used its term twice in an otherwise identical paragraph (Fig. 1, p. 203); completing the questionnaire took about 20 minutes (p. 204).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The vignette's character was required to abstain from alcohol and other drugs and had positive urine drug screens (drug not named) and a positive breathalyzer reading (Fig. 1, p. 203).

comparison.controls: Attendees who received the version saying that Mr. Williams has (and has had for the past few years) 'a substance use disorder'.
comparison.matching: Allocation by alternation of the two forms. The authors report that the versions did not differ on any measured variable (chi-square and t-tests, ps > .17), but give neither the group sizes nor the characteristics by version (Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph, p. 204).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Participants' prior attitudes towards people who use drugs, their profession, addiction training and personal or family experience of substance use were not measured, or are not reported by version.

outcomes.instruments: 32 statements rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree). By the source column of Table 1, 21 come from the 1996 General Social Survey mental-health module (Pescosolido et al., 1996), 3 from Kloss and Lisman (2003) and 8 from the authors (editors' count; the text says eight were written by the authors and the majority came from the General Social Survey, Measures, 1st paragraph, p. 204). Exploratory factor analysis of all 516 (principal axis factoring, oblique Promax rotation, loading threshold .32) gave three factors explaining 33% of the variance: 'perpetrator-punishment' (14 items, α .80), 'social threat' (4 items, α .86) and 'victim-treatment' (8 items, α .64); one cross-loading item was dropped and five further items loaded on no factor (editors' count from Table 1) (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 205; Table 1, p. 204).
outcomes.validity_norms: The subscales were derived from this sample's own answers and have no external validation; the authors call for their reliability and validity to be confirmed in other samples (Limitations, p. 206). Content (Table 1, p. 204): 'perpetrator-punishment' mixes punishment by the judge (disciplinary action, 200 hours of community service, a jail sentence as a wake-up call, harsher consequences for further use), causes (poor choices, a reckless lifestyle, the way he was raised, God's will), responsibility and avoidability, violence to himself or to others, and referral to a religious leader or a spiritual or natural healer; 'social threat' consists only of willingness to have him as an employee, close friend, neighbour or co-worker; 'victim-treatment' mixes referral to treatment, self-help, family and medication with genetic and chemical-imbalance causes and expected severity. The scoring of the subscales (direction; mean or sum) is not stated; the printed means of 2.82 and 2.92 imply item means on the 1–6 scale, below its midpoint of 3.5.
outcomes.operationalization: Stigma was operationalized as agreement with the 14-item 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale (culpability and punitive or non-medical responses), with willingness for social contact ('social threat') and with endorsement of treatment and biological causes ('victim-treatment'). No behaviour, real decision or patient outcome was measured.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Significance level set at .025 per comparison for the three t-tests, citing Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, 2000) (Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph, p. 205). How .025 follows from that procedure is not explained: applied to three tests at a false discovery rate of .05, it would require the smallest p-value to be at most about .017 (editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-completed questionnaire. Each participant read only one version; what participants were told about the purpose of the study is not reported. The staff handing out the forms knew the alternation.

analysis.effect_sizes: 'Perpetrator-punishment': 'substance abuser' version mean 2.92 (SD 0.57) vs 'substance use disorder' version 2.82 (SD 0.58); t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02; d = 0.20 as printed, called small by the authors (Results, 3rd paragraph, p. 205). Editors' calculations: for t = 2.05 with 504 df the two-sided p is about .041 and the one-sided p about .020, so the printed p matches a one-sided test; d from the printed means and SDs is about 0.17 (0.16 to 0.19 allowing for rounding of the means) and from t and df about 0.18, with an approximate 95% CI of 0.01 to 0.36 assuming two groups of about 253; the mean difference of 0.10 scale points has an approximate 95% CI of 0.00 to 0.20. 'Social threat' and 'victim-treatment': no significant differences (ps > .59), with no means, SDs or test statistics printed. Editors' calculation: with about 253 per group, p > .59 implies |d| below about 0.05, with 95% intervals reaching up to about ±0.22. Subscale intercorrelations: 'social threat' with 'perpetrator-punishment' Spearman r = −.27 (p < .01), described as more willingness for contact going with less agreement with disciplinary measures; 'victim-treatment' unrelated to both (p > .05) (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 205).
analysis.covariates: None (unadjusted independent-samples t-tests); demographic balance checked with chi-square and t-tests (p. 204).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified analysis plan is mentioned. The study was approved by the Partners Healthcare Human Research Committee; consent was given by continuing past the consent page (Measures, 2nd paragraph, p. 204).
analysis.selective_reporting: Group sizes are not reported. Means and test statistics are printed only for the subscale that differed. The hypothesis that the 'substance abuser' term would raise perceived ability to self-regulate (Introduction, 6th paragraph, p. 203) was not tested as its own outcome: of the three self-regulation items from Kloss and Lisman, two entered the 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale and one ('capable of overcoming his problem on his own') was dropped for cross-loading (Table 1, p. 204; Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 205). Item-level differences between versions are not reported. That p = .02 is one-sided is not stated.
analysis.power: Not reported. Editors' calculation: with about 253 per group the study had about 50% power to detect d = 0.2 at a two-sided α of .025 (about 61% one-sided).

interpretation_gap.results_show: One of three factor-derived subscales differed: readers of the 'substance abuser' version agreed slightly more with a mixed set of culpability, punishment and non-medical statements (2.92 vs 2.82 on a 1–6 scale, both below the scale midpoint; d about 0.2). Its printed significance (p = .02) corresponds to an unstated one-sided test; two-sided, p is about .04 (editors' calculation), above the authors' own .025 threshold. No difference was detected in willingness for social contact or in treatment-related items, but differences of about d 0.2 were not excluded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that even among highly trained mental health professionals the two terms evoke "systematically different judgments" and that the 'substance abuser' term may perpetuate stigmatizing attitudes (abstract, p. 202). The Conclusions suggest that national institutes, health care organizations, policy makers and criminal justice systems may wish to reconsider their terms, and argue that less perceived stigma would lead people to seek help sooner (p. 206): help-seeking was not measured. The Limitations suggest the difference might be larger among legislators or policy makers, which was not tested (p. 206). The title and abstract call the study randomized, while the Methods describe forms handed out alternately (p. 204). Against this, the Limitations state plainly that the effect was small and that its translation into real-world decisions or actions is unknown (pp. 205–206), and the Conclusions add an argument that does not depend on the effect's size: the 'abuser' label gives no gain in descriptive precision, so dropping it should do no harm (p. 206).

timeline.event: Kelly's proposal for more precise addiction terminology ('Toward an addiction-ary'), cited as a source of this study's hypothesis (Introduction, p. 203); not read.

This study: 516 conference attendees; a small difference on a culpability-and-punishment subscale between the 'substance abuser' and 'substance use disorder' versions of one vignette, none on social contact or treatment items.

Kelly, Dow & Westerhoff (2010, Journal of Drug Issues), a companion experiment on whether the choice of substance-related terms influences perceived need for treatment, named on the project's reading lists as not found in PubMed; not read.

Pennington et al.: pre-registered online vignette experiment on other labels ('chronically relapsing brain disease' vs 'problem'; drug use vs a health concern) in a non-clinical sample, not on these two terms (card sc_pennington_2023).

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no direct replication of the 'substance abuser' versus 'substance use disorder' contrast appears in the sources read for this card. The project's language-and-stigma list names later word-choice experiments (Ashford, Brown & Curtis, 2018; Goddu et al., 2018) that are not yet appraised; the one appraised later experiment (Pennington et al., 2023) tested other labels in a non-clinical online sample. The study remains a single, small effect in one clinician sample and one scenario.

funding.funder: Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Grant #020753 (title-page footnote, p. 202).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Center for Addiction Medicine, Department of Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital (Harvard Medical School), Boston. The hypothesis draws partly on the first author's earlier proposal for more precise terminology (Kelly, 2004, cited p. 203). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered experiment with computer-generated, concealed allocation and full reporting of group sizes and all outcomes, testing person-first terms against labels across several vignettes (not only a court-supervised relapse) in clinicians and in the public, with decision outcomes (for example sanction and treatment recommendations), two-sided tests and equivalence bounds; and, beyond vignettes, studies of whether the terms used in records or by services change the care actually given or people's help-seeking.

domains.note: Forms were handed out alternately and sequentially (p. 204): the sequence was not random and was known to the staff handing them out, and people held a form, with its term, before deciding whether to take part. The authors report no differences on measured characteristics (ps > .17) but give no group sizes or values. RoB 2 treats allocation by alternation as not concealed.
Each participant read one version and was analysed by the version received; with alternation, neighbouring attendees probably held different versions, and whether any compared them is not reported.

29% of those handed a form did not complete it and 10 completers are missing from the main test; numbers and reasons by version are unknown (pp. 204–206), and willingness to complete an attitude questionnaire may depend on the attitudes it measures.

Self-reported agreement immediately after the vignette. Participants knew the term they had read, and in an audience attending addiction talks the term may have cued socially desirable answers, which the authors suggest may have operated (p. 206). The subscales were built from these data without external validation; 'victim-treatment' α .64.

No protocol or analysis plan; the outcome scales were derived after data collection (from the pooled answers, without reference to version); the printed p = .02 matches an unstated one-sided test; the other two subscales are reported only as ps > .59; the self-regulation hypothesis was not analysed as stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Allocation by alternation and 29% non-participation with an unknown split by version each give high risk under RoB 2, and the result itself is fragile: a difference of 0.10 on a 1–6 scale (d about 0.2) whose printed significance relies on an unstated one-sided test at a threshold that the cited procedure does not yield. The study may be cited for a small difference, in this sample of conference attendees, in agreement with culpability and punishment statements after reading 'substance abuser' rather than 'substance use disorder' in one court-supervision vignette, and for no detectable difference in willingness for social contact or in treatment items. It may not be cited as showing that the term changes clinicians' decisions, patients' care or help-seeking, as showing a large or systematic effect, or as showing that the terms make no difference to social distance.

key_findings.finding: 728 conference attendees were handed one of two questionnaire versions, alternately and sequentially; 516 completed it (71%), taking about 20 minutes; there were no eligibility criteria and no compensation.
key_findings.locator: Method › Study population and protocol, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The two vignettes differ only in the term: Mr. Williams 'is a substance abuser' and 'has been a substance abuser for the past few years', or 'has a substance use disorder' and 'has had a substance use disorder for the past few years'. In both he attends court-ordered treatment requiring abstinence from alcohol and other drugs, had two positive urine drug screens and a positive breathalyzer reading a month ago and another positive urine screen since, and awaits the judge.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 (read on the rendered page)

key_findings.finding: Completers: mean age 51; 63.4% women; 81.0% White; 64.5% with a doctoral-level degree; professional focus mood disorders 66.9%, anxiety disorders 59.9%, psychosis 37%, alcohol/drug problems 34.8%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Factor analysis of the questionnaire items gave three factors explaining 33% of the variance, with a loading threshold of .32: a fourteen-item 'perpetrator-punishment' subscale (α .80), a four-item 'social threat' subscale (α .86) and an eight-item 'victim-treatment' subscale (α .64); the item 'capable of overcoming his problem on his own' was dropped for loading similarly on factors 1 and 3. 'Social threat' and 'perpetrator-punishment' correlated negatively (r = −.27, p < .01); 'victim-treatment' was unrelated to both (p > .05).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 (p. 204)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 1: 32 items in all; 14 + 4 + 8 enter the subscales, one was dropped for cross-loading and five load at least .32 on no factor.

key_findings.finding: On 'perpetrator-punishment', readers of the 'substance abuser' version scored 2.92 (SD 0.57) and readers of the 'substance use disorder' version 2.82 (SD 0.58): t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02, d = 0.20, described by the authors as a small effect.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the two-sided p for t = 2.05 with 504 df is about .041; the printed .02 is the one-sided value, and no one-sided test is stated. d recomputed from the printed means and SDs is about 0.17, and from t and df about 0.18.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences between versions on 'social threat' or 'victim-treatment' (ps > .59); no means, SDs or test statistics are given for these subscales.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 'social threat' subscale consists of four willingness items (as an employee, close friend, neighbour, co-worker; loadings .686 to .848). The two violence items load on 'perpetrator-punishment' (.350 to himself, .434 to others), as do upbringing as a cause (.444), God's will (.378) and referral to a religious leader (.498) or a spiritual or natural healer (.484).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: The Results name as the items most highly correlated with 'perpetrator-punishment' a reckless lifestyle as cause (.69), being responsible for causing the problem (.59), a jail sentence as a wake-up call (.53) and poor choices as cause (.51).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 205); Table 1 (p. 204)
key_findings.note: These figures are the Promax pattern loadings of Table 1 rounded (.691, .586, .525, .506, p. 204), not item–subscale correlations, although the Results call them correlations; in an oblique rotation, pattern loadings are regression weights.

key_findings.finding: The versions did not differ on any measured demographic variable (ps > .17); the significance level for the three subscale t-tests was set at .025 per comparison, citing Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, 2000).
key_findings.locator: Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 204) and 4th paragraph (p. 205)

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: the difference was significant but small; whether differences of any size on these scales translate into real-world decisions or actions is unknown; the 71% response rate was less than ideal and the reasons for non-participation are unknown, so generalization should be cautious; the subscales need confirmation in other samples.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that it may matter how people with substance-related conditions are described, propose 'substance use disorder' or 'substance-related problem or condition' instead of the 'abuser' label, and suggest that institutions, policy makers and criminal justice systems reconsider their terms.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The only significant result is printed as t = 2.05, 504 df, p = .02, and the paper does not say that a one-sided test was used. By the editors' calculation, for these values the two-sided p is about .041 and the one-sided p about .020.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under a two-sided test the difference would not meet the authors' own threshold of .025 per comparison; the evidence for any difference is weaker than the paper presents. The directional hypothesis (p. 203) could justify a one-sided test only if planned, which cannot be checked without a protocol.

reporting_issues.issue: The threshold of .025 per comparison is attributed to Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, 2000), and how .025 was obtained is not explained. By the editors' calculation, that step-up procedure with three tests at a false discovery rate of .05 would require the smallest p-value to be at most about .017.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even the one-sided p of .02 would not pass the cited procedure as usually applied; the claim of significance rests on an unexplained threshold.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of participants in each version is never reported, and the perpetrator-punishment test has 504 df where 516 completed the questionnaire. By the editors' arithmetic, 504 df implies 506 analysed, so 10 completers are missing from the test without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Balance between versions, differential non-completion and the precision of the estimates cannot be checked; the editors' intervals assume two groups of about 253.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed d of 0.20 is larger than the d implied by the printed means, SDs, t and df. By the editors' calculation, d is about 0.17 from the means and SDs and about 0.18 from t and df.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the effect is small on any of these figures, as the authors say; claims should give it as about 0.2 or less.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract call the study randomized; the Methods describe forms handed out alternately and sequentially, with no random sequence described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The allocation was quasi-random (alternation); the study should be described as an experiment with alternating allocation, and its risk of bias rated accordingly.

reporting_issues.issue: The subscale labels do not match their content: 'social threat' contains only willingness for social contact (no threat or violence item), while the two violence items, an external cause (the way he was raised), God's will and religious or spiritual referral load on 'perpetrator-punishment', which the authors interpret as internal causal attribution and culpability.
reporting_issues.consequence: The null result on 'social threat' concerns social distance, not perceived dangerousness; the positive result is a difference on a heterogeneous 14-item composite of punitive, moral and non-medical statements, not specifically on internal attribution.
