design_detail: Systematic review with a thematic (narrative) synthesis and no meta-analysis of studies published from January 2000 to November 2011, in English or Dutch, on health professionals' attitudes towards patients with alcohol or illicit drug use disorders in Western countries, the explanations offered for negative attitudes, and the consequences of those attitudes for healthcare delivery. PubMed, PsycINFO and Embase were searched; 1562 records remained after duplicates were removed and 28 papers were included (Australia 12, UK 7, USA 5, Canada 1, Ireland 1, one eight-country European comparison and one USA–UK comparison), five of which come from two shared samples. The included studies are mostly cross-sectional questionnaire surveys of professionals' self-reported attitudes, with interview and focus-group studies, two implicit association tests and two studies using observation; the review describes no randomized experiment, and the one vignette study (Rao et al., 2009) compared described patient types. Study quality was rated with 11 indicators taken from Buckley et al. (2009); all 28 met at least 7 and were weighted equally. No protocol or registration is mentioned.
can_establish: What 28 papers from 2000–2011 in Australia, the UK, Ireland, North America and seven other European countries (the eight countries of one comparative study include Scotland) reported about health professionals' self-reported attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug use disorders, the explanations those studies offered, and how few of them examined consequences for care.
cannot_establish: How common negative attitudes are (there are no counts or pooled estimates, and several included studies found moderate, neutral or positive attitudes); that negative attitudes cause poorer care or outcomes (the consequence evidence is a handful of qualitative, mixed-methods and cross-sectional studies, one with a null result and one, not discussed, finding better care); whether training improves attitudes (studies of education and training were excluded, and the associations cited are cross-sectional); or anything about Asia, Africa, South America or studies after 2011.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. PubMed, PsycINFO and Embase were searched for articles published from January 2000 to November 2011 in English or Dutch; the PubMed strategy is printed, with very similar versions said to have been used for the other two databases. The strategy combined health-personnel, substance-use-disorder and attitude terms with care-delivery or stigma terms (sets #30 to #33). No grey literature, reference-list, citation or expert searching is described (2.1, p. 24; Table 1, p. 26; Fig. 1, p. 25).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: studies of the attitudes of health professionals (or of professionals together with students) towards patients with alcohol or illicit drug use disorders, and studies of stigma, perception or healthcare delivery as a consequence of these attitudes; reviews, commentaries and letters were excluded. Excluded: attitudes towards specific subgroups (pregnant women, sexual or ethnic minorities, because of double stigma), towards screening and identification, or towards treatments (methadone maintenance, needle and syringe provision, 12-step programs); studies of medical students only; studies from Asia, Africa and South America, excluded at the full-text stage as culturally, historically and socially different; studies of a very specific setting or explicit subgroup (Table 2, p. 26; 2.2, pp. 24–25). Records concerning education, training or students were excluded at screening (34 abstracts and 4 full texts; Fig. 1, p. 25).
sample.demographics: Professional groups (3.2, p. 26): seven papers studied a mix of professions, eight nurses, seven staff of addiction or mental health services, four physicians and one physicians and nurses; five also included patients. Sample sizes in Table 4 range from 8 interviewed professionals (Brener et al., 2010b) to 1,605 nurses (Ford et al., 2008, 2009); Ding et al. (2005) also surveyed 2,864 patients with HIV, and Segal & Dittrich (2001) observed 683 psychiatric emergency visits from 1985–1986 (Table 4, pp. 27–29). Years of data collection are not otherwise given.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Response rates in Table 4, where given, range from 31% (May et al., 2002) to 92% (Saitz et al., 2002); all workshop attendees took part in Strauser et al. (2009); several papers give none (pp. 27–29).
sample.selection_effects: Three databases, of which PsycINFO contributed only 10 records against 1170 from PubMed and 395 from Embase, without comment; a search requiring care-delivery or stigma terms alongside attitude terms; English and Dutch only; 31 records excluded because no abstract or full text was available; 10 full texts excluded because the studies came from Asia, Africa or South America; and exclusion of studies of training, screening and attitudes to treatments. The primary studies drew self-selected respondents, with response rates as low as 31%; the authors note that only motivated professionals take part in such studies (4.1, p. 33).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The target of the attitudes is the patient group each study asked about, in that study's own terms (2.3, p. 25): people who inject drugs (some with hepatitis C or HIV), people who use illicit drugs or opiates, people with alcohol problems, people with a dual diagnosis, cocaine addiction among other conditions, and patients with substance use problems in general (Tables 4 and 5, pp. 27–32).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. Attitudes towards patients with alcohol and with illicit drug problems are combined in the synthesis; the only contrast by substance reported in the text is that regard was especially low for patients who use drugs (Gilchrist et al., 2011; 3.3, p. 26).

comparison.controls: None at review level: comparison was declared not applicable (2.1, p. 24). Within primary studies, attitudes were compared with those towards other patient groups (depression and diabetes, Gilchrist et al., 2011; schizophrenia and forensic patients, Rao et al., 2009; depression and hypertension, Saitz et al., 2002; AIDS, psychosis, depression, cancer and intellectual disability (printed as 'mental retardation'), Strauser et al., 2009; other psychiatric emergency patients, Segal & Dittrich, 2001), between professions or settings, and by contact, experience or training (Tables 4 and 5).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The professional characteristics offered as explanations (contact, experience, training, role support) were measured at the same time as attitudes in the primary studies, so their direction of influence is not established.

outcomes.instruments: The primary studies used the Substance Abuse Attitude Survey (called a Scale in the text; 5 papers), the Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Perception Questionnaire or its drug version (4 papers by the text; Table 5 names the alcohol version for Ford et al., 2008 and 2009, one sample, and the drug version for Albery et al., 2003 and Howard & Holmshaw, 2010), the Medical Condition Regard Scale, the Attitude to Mental Illness Questionnaire with vignettes, the Addiction Beliefs Scale, the Psychiatric Disability Attribution Questionnaire, implicit association tests, quality-of-care indices applied to observed visits, and interviews or focus groups (3.2, p. 26; Table 5, pp. 30–32).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was judged with 11 indicators from Buckley et al. (2009), a review of portfolios in undergraduate medical education: research question, subjects, data collection, completeness of data (attrition under 50%, acceptable response rate), control for confounding, analysis, conclusions, reproducibility, prospective design, ethics and triangulation; a study was of acceptable quality if it met at least 7 (Table 3, p. 26). All 28 passed and were weighted equally; ratings by study are not reported (3.1, 1st paragraph, continued on p. 26).
outcomes.operationalization: The review does not define a negative attitude; it keeps each study's terms and measures (2.3, p. 25). Consequences for healthcare delivery covered patients' perceived discrimination and treatment completion, patients' views of their professionals, patient-reported problems with care, and professionals' accounts of their own practice; one included study measured quality of care from observed visits (Segal & Dittrich, 2001).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles were screened by one reviewer, with a random 10% screened by a second (94% agreement); abstracts and full texts were assessed by two independent reviewers, with disagreements settled by discussion or a third reviewer; data were extracted by one reviewer and verified by a second (2.2 and 2.3, pp. 24–25).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. A thematic synthesis without pooled estimates, effect sizes or counts of studies by direction of finding (2.3, p. 25). The only figures carried from primary studies are descriptive, for example that 23.2% of the patients in Ding et al. (2005), described in Table 5 as HIV and IDU patients, had physicians with negative attitudes towards patients who inject drugs (Table 5, p. 30).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the PRISMA explanation paper (Liberati et al., 2009) is cited only for the PICO approach used to build search terms (2.1, p. 24).
analysis.selective_reporting: The one included study that measured quality of care from observed visits (Segal & Dittrich, 2001: better care for patients with substance use problems than for other psychiatric emergency patients on all four criteria) appears only in Tables 4 and 5 and is not mentioned in the text, including the section on consequences (3.5, pp. 32–33). Studies with positive findings are mentioned as a contrast (3.3, p. 29) without a count of studies in each direction.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples), many studies, mostly cross-sectional self-report surveys and qualitative studies from Australia, the UK and the USA, reported negative attitudes, or lower regard for patients with substance use disorders than for other patients, especially among professionals outside addiction services; five papers' summaries in Table 5 describe moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive attitudes, and a sixth stigma below the criterion for negative stigma. More contact, experience, training and role support went with more positive attitudes in cross-sectional data. On consequences, one mixed-methods study found that clients' perceived staff discrimination predicted dropping out of treatment, one cross-sectional study linked professionals' attitudes to patients' views of them, two qualitative studies described disempowerment and shorter, task-oriented visits, one large survey found no association between physicians' attitudes and patients' reports of their care, and one observational study found better care for patients with substance use problems.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states as findings that negative attitudes "diminished patients' feelings of empowerment and subsequent treatment outcomes" and that a more task-oriented approach results in less personal engagement and diminished empathy, and concludes that negative attitudes are common and "contribute to suboptimal health care" (abstract, p. 23). In the Results these statements rest on one qualitative study of treatment staff and consumers (Curtis & Harrison, 2001) and one qualitative study of 18 district nurses (Peckover & Chidlaw, 2007), and are worded with 'may' (3.5, p. 33); the treatment-completion finding is attributed to the wrong Brener paper (p. 32); the null finding of Ding et al. (2005) is mentioned but not weighed; and the observational study finding better care (Segal & Dittrich, 2001) is not mentioned. That professionals generally had negative attitudes is a narrative judgment without a count. The recommendation of more education and training (4.2, p. 33) rests on cross-sectional associations, after records concerning education or training were excluded at screening (Fig. 1, p. 25). The abstract does end by noting that few studies have evaluated consequences.

timeline.event: Howard and Chung, review of nurses' attitudes towards patients who misuse substances, cited in the Introduction as finding greater acceptance although a minority regarded these patients as immoral and unlikely to recover (p. 24); not read.
This review: 28 papers published 2000–2011 on health professionals' attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug use disorders; few examined consequences for care.
Bielenberg et al., systematic review of stigma interventions for providers who treat patients with substance use disorders (on the project's language-and-stigma list; not read).
Pavone et al., systematic review of interventions to reduce clinician stigma toward people with opioid use disorder (on the project's language-and-stigma list; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The project's language-and-stigma list named this review as its largest gap. It summarizes the literature to 2011 only, from Western countries, and does not quantify how common negative attitudes are; the evidence it gathered on consequences for care was thin and pointed in different directions. The later reviews on the project's lists concern interventions to reduce clinician stigma; none has been appraised for this card, so whether the question of consequences has since been answered is not known from the sources read.

funding.funder: Role of funding source: 'Nothing declared' (p. 33).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (p. 34).
funding.affiliations_note: Tranzo, Tilburg School of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Tilburg University (all four authors); Phrenos Centre of Expertise, Utrecht, and Parnassia Bavo Group, Dijk en Duin Mental Health Center, Castricum (van Weeghel) (p. 23). None of the authors is an author of an included study (editors' check of the reference list, pp. 34–35).

what_would_settle_it: A registered, updated systematic review with appraisal reported study by study, a list of excluded studies and no regional exclusion, which counts and where possible pools attitude findings by profession and patient group; and prospective studies linking clinicians' measured attitudes to the care actually delivered (observed or from records) and to patients' retention and outcomes, adjusting for the patients' severity.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (health personnel), exposure (patients with alcohol or illicit drug use disorders as the target of attitudes) and outcomes (attitudes, healthcare delivery, stigma) are set out with the PICO approach, but the comparison is declared not applicable (2.1, p. 24); judged no, as for other reviews without a comparator in this project.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.

All original studies were eligible, quantitative and qualitative, and reviews, commentaries and letters were excluded (abstract; Fig. 1); a brief reason for including both quantitative and qualitative studies is given, but only in the Discussion (4.1, p. 33).

Three databases, the PubMed strategy printed (Table 1) and a date range justified by the aim of recent evidence; but English and Dutch only without justification (named only as a limitation, 4.1), no grey literature, reference lists, citation searching or experts, records without an abstract or full text excluded (31), and only 10 records from PsycINFO, unexplained. Judged no on the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Abstracts and full texts assessed by two independent reviewers; titles by one reviewer with a random 10% double-screened (94% agreement) (2.2, pp. 24–25).

Extraction by one reviewer, verified by a second, with disparities resolved by discussion and rereading the original studies (2.3, p. 25); judged yes as for other reviews in this project in which a second reviewer checked the extraction.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives counts by reason only; the 27 excluded full texts are not listed.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 gives country, population, sample size, setting and design, and Table 5 instruments and main results; the patient group targeted, years of data collection, several response rates and the direction of each finding are not given systematically.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: An 11-item checklist from a review of educational portfolios (Buckley et al., 2009), with items on confounding, appropriateness of subjects, validity of data collection and completeness or response rate, was applied by two reviewers at full text (Table 3; Fig. 1); but every study passed a 7-of-11 threshold, the same checklist was applied to qualitative studies, and no ratings are reported study by study.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No meta-analysis; thematic synthesis because of heterogeneous populations, designs and settings (2.3, p. 25).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: All studies were weighted equally because all passed the quality threshold (3.1, 1st paragraph, continued on p. 26). The limitations mention self-selection of motivated respondents and social desirability in the primary studies (4.1, p. 33), but the abstract's causal statements about consequences and the recommendation of training are drawn from qualitative and cross-sectional studies without discussing those designs' limits.

Variation in attitudes is related narratively to discipline, contact, experience, training and support (3.3 and 3.4), but studies with positive or neutral findings are listed without explaining why they differ, the null result of Ding et al. (2005) on care is noted without discussion, and the observational study finding better care (Segal & Dittrich, 2001) is not mentioned.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding ('Nothing declared') and conflicts ('No conflict declared') are stated (pp. 33–34).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, no protocol; 4, the search; 7, no list of excluded studies; 13, risk of bias not carried into the conclusions) and a fifth (9) only partly, so confidence in the review as an accurate and comprehensive summary is critically low. The practical consequences: studies may be missing (PsycINFO yielded 10 records; English and Dutch only; 10 eligible full texts excluded by region); the synthesis gives no count of studies by direction and weights a 31%-response survey equally with a 92%-response one; and the conclusions about consequences for care outrun the few, mostly qualitative studies behind them while omitting one contrary observational study. The review may be cited for what the included studies reported, with their designs, and for the observation that few studies published by 2011 examined consequences of professionals' attitudes for care; it may not be cited for how common negative attitudes are, for a causal effect of attitudes on care or outcomes, or for training improving attitudes.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed 1170, PsycINFO 10 and Embase 395 records (1575 combined); 13 duplicates; 1562 titles screened and 1142 excluded; 420 abstracts screened and 365 excluded (31 because no abstract or full text was available, 34 concerning education, training or students); 55 full texts assessed and 27 excluded, 10 of them (37%) as Asian, African or South American studies; 28 included.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1

key_findings.finding: Searches covered articles published from January 2000 to November 2011 in English or Dutch; titles were screened by one reviewer with a random 10% screened by a second (94% agreement), and abstracts and full texts by two independent reviewers.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Search strategy; 2.2 Study selection, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quality was judged with 11 indicators from Buckley et al. (2009), acceptable if at least 7 were met; all 28 included papers met the criteria and were given equal weight; ratings by study are not reported.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Search results, 1st paragraph (continued on p. 26); Table 3 (p. 26)

key_findings.finding: Of the 28 papers, 12 were from Australia, 7 the UK, 5 the USA, 1 Canada and 1 Ireland, with one eight-country European comparison and one USA–UK comparison. Twenty were quantitative (the Substance Abuse Attitude Survey in 5, the Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Perception Questionnaire in 4); five used interviews or focus groups, two implicit association tests and two observation; five also included patients.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 General findings
key_findings.note: The design categories overlap (20 + 5 + 2 + 2 = 29 for 28 papers; the implicit association tests are also quantitative). By the editors' reading of Table 4, the two studies using observation are Segal and Dittrich (2001), who rated the quality of care in observed visits, and Curtis and Harrison (2001), who used participant observation within a qualitative study (pp. 27, 29).

key_findings.finding: Five of the included papers are marked as coming from shared samples: Brener et al. (2007, 2010a), 60 health care workers, and Ford et al. (2008, 2009) with Ford (2011), a survey of 1605 nurses in the Australian Capital Territory (the 2011 paper interprets one open-ended question, with N = 311).
key_findings.locator: Table 4, Brener and Ford rows and footnote

key_findings.finding: The review summarizes that health professionals generally had negative attitudes towards patients with substance use problems. Examples: regard was lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems compared with depression or diabetes, among 866 professionals in 8 European countries, and lowest among physicians outside addiction services (Gilchrist et al., 2011); in six focus groups with 35 health and social care professionals, most preferred that addiction specialists provide the care (McLaughlin et al., 2006); nurses reported low motivation and satisfaction in caring for patients who use illicit drugs (Ford et al., 2008); in a vignette study professionals held more stigmatizing views of active substance use disorder than of other mental illness, and more positive views of recovery than of relapse (Rao et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Attitudes of health professionals, 1st paragraph (p. 26, continued on p. 29) and 3rd paragraph (p. 29); Table 4, Gilchrist et al. (2011) row (p. 28); Table 5, Gilchrist et al. (2011) row (p. 31)
key_findings.note: Table 5's summary of Gilchrist et al. (2011) says both that regard did not differ by gender, age or professional group and that psychologists, social workers and addiction-service staff showed the highest regard and physicians outside addiction services the lowest (p. 31); the primary study is needed to settle which applies. The eight countries are Greece, Spain, Bulgaria, Italy, Slovenia, Slovakia, Poland and Scotland (Table 4, p. 28); Scotland is part of the UK, so the review's countries outside the UK and Ireland number seven.

key_findings.finding: Positive or neutral findings: mental health professionals with generally positive and non-discriminatory attitudes, most rejecting moral stereotypes (Pinikahana et al., 2002), and primary care physicians with positive attitudes (Saitz et al., 2002), reported as a contrast. In Table 5, six of the study summaries describe attitudes as moderate (Giannetti et al., 2002), neutral (Happell & Taylor, 2001), appropriate (an unlabelled row on emergency departments), positive (Pinikahana et al., 2002; Saitz et al., 2002, who also report lower satisfaction) or below the criterion for negative stigma (Strauser et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: 3.3, 2nd paragraph (p. 29); Table 5 (pp. 31–32)
key_findings.note: The count of six is the editors' reading of the Table 5 summaries; the review itself gives no count. Five of the six use the words moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive; the sixth (Strauser et al., 2009) reports stigma below the criterion for negative stigma.

key_findings.finding: Five papers found more positive or different attitudes with more personal or work experience or contact (Brener et al., 2007; Ding et al., 2005; Giannetti et al., 2002; May et al., 2002; Russell et al., 2011). Anaesthesiologists were less positive than physicians who regularly treat these patients and more positive if they had a personal history of addiction (May et al., 2002); forensic psychiatric nurses were more negative than other mental health professionals (Foster & Onyeukwu, 2003).
key_findings.locator: 3.3, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Explanations offered: nurses described violence, manipulation and irresponsibility as barriers to care (Ford, 2011, an open-ended survey question); general practitioners perceived patients with drug problems as manipulative, aggressive, rude and poorly motivated (McGillion et al., 2000); higher perceived controllability of injecting drug use went with more negative attitudes (Brener et al., 2010a); professionals reported low knowledge (four studies); education improved nurses' therapeutic attitude only with at least moderate role support (Ford et al., 2008, 2009).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Explanations for negative attitudes, 1st paragraph (p. 29) and 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 32); Table 5 (p. 30)

key_findings.finding: Consequences for care, quantitative: clients who reported more perceived discrimination by staff and dissatisfaction were less likely to complete treatment (cited in the text as Brener et al., 2010a; Table 5 gives this finding for Brener et al., 2010b, a mixed-methods study of 92 clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney); patients judged their professionals more favourably when the professionals had more positive attitudes (Brener et al., 2007); physicians' negative attitudes were not associated with patients' reported problems with care, dissatisfaction, unmet needs or perceived access (Ding et al., 2005: 2864 patients with HIV, 17.1% currently injecting, and 373 physicians, 75% response).
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Consequences of attitudes on healthcare delivery, 1st paragraph (p. 32, continued on p. 33); Table 4 (p. 27); Table 5 (p. 30)
key_findings.note: The Brener et al. (2007) statement is the review's text (p. 32); Table 5 summarizes that study differently (see reporting issues). The treatment-completion finding belongs to Brener et al. (2010b), not 2010a.

key_findings.finding: Consequences for care, qualitative: clinicians may unwittingly impose their beliefs on patients and impede collaboration (Curtis & Harrison, 2001: 57 participants, 26 of them consumers, in alcohol and other drug services); district nurses described shorter visits, visiting in pairs and a more task-oriented approach (Peckover & Chidlaw, 2007: 18 nurses, 82% response).
key_findings.locator: 3.5, 2nd paragraph (p. 33); Table 4 (pp. 27–28)

key_findings.finding: Segal & Dittrich (2001): 683 observed visits by patients to 9 psychiatric emergency services in California in 1985–1986; patients with substance use problems received better quality of care than other patients on all 4 study criteria, although clinicians' attitudes towards them were not always positive. The study is not mentioned in the text.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 29) and Table 5 (p. 32), Segal and Dittrich rows

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: relevant studies may have been missed; records without an abstract or full text were excluded; only English and Dutch articles were included; the primary studies may suffer selection bias because only motivated professionals take part, and self-report and social desirability limit their quality.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that in most examined studies professionals expressed negative attitudes; that inadequate training, education and support may contribute; that more and longitudinal studies of consequences are needed; and that more education and training and organisational support may improve attitudes and care.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Conclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.5 attributes the finding that clients who perceived more staff discrimination were less likely to complete treatment to Brener et al. (2010a). In Tables 4 and 5 and the reference list, Brener et al. (2010a) is a study of 60 health care workers' attitudes, and the treatment-completion finding belongs to Brener et al. (2010b), titled as a study of perceived discriminatory treatment by staff as a predictor of treatment completion.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim using this finding must cite the primary study as Brener et al. (2010b, Drug and Alcohol Review 29, 491–497), a mixed-methods study of 92 clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney.

reporting_issues.issue: Segal & Dittrich (2001), the only included study that measured the quality of care actually delivered (observed psychiatric emergency visits), found better care for patients with substance use problems; it appears in Tables 4 and 5 but nowhere in the text, including the section on consequences.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's conclusion that negative attitudes contribute to suboptimal care leaves out the one contrary observational result it included; any claim about consequences for care must mention it (with its 1985–1986 data).

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5 the row following Howard and Holmshaw (2010) has no study name and no instrument name; its content (a five-subscale attitude scale; appropriate attitudes and knowledge gaps in emergency departments) matches Kelleher and Cotter (2009), the emergency-department study in Table 4, which otherwise has no row in Table 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader would attribute the emergency-department findings to Howard and Holmshaw; the attribution to Kelleher and Cotter is the editors' inference and should be checked in the primary study before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that patients judged their professionals more favourably when the professionals had more positive attitudes (Brener et al., 2007), but Table 5's summary of that study links clients' favourable views to attending services with more people with hepatitis C, not to the professionals' attitudes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The link between professionals' attitudes and patients' views cannot be confirmed from the review; the primary study must be read before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Happell and Taylor (2001) is cited among studies that established positive effects of training and education on attitudes and perceived knowledge, but Table 5 reports that nurses who did and did not use a liaison service did not differ in attitudes (only perceived knowledge was higher); Ding et al. (2005), also cited, concerns knowledge rather than training in Table 5; and all four cited studies are cross-sectional.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence that training improves attitudes is thinner than the text implies and is associational; the review cannot support a causal claim about training.

reporting_issues.issue: PsycINFO contributed only 10 records, against 1170 from PubMed and 395 from Embase, without comment; in the printed strategy every retrieved record needed a substance-use term and a care-delivery or stigma term: sets #31 and #32 combine the attitude-of-health-personnel term with a care-delivery (#31) or stigma (#32) term, and set #30 needs no attitude term but requires a health-personnel term with both a care-delivery and a stigma term (Table 1, p. 26).
reporting_issues.consequence: Attitude studies in the psychological literature, or indexed without care-delivery or stigma terms, may have been missed; the authors acknowledge only in general terms that relevant studies may not have been found.

reporting_issues.issue: Happell et al. (2002) and Pinikahana et al. (2002), by the same three authors in the same journal and year, both describe crisis assessment and treatment teams in metropolitan Melbourne and rural Victoria and both include 134 registered nurses, but they are not marked as sharing a sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly one more overlapping sample than the review flags; the 28 papers would then represent at most 24 independent samples (25 with the overlaps the review marks).

reporting_issues.issue: Subgroup counts in Table 4 do not add up to the stated totals: Gilchrist et al. (2011) give 866 professionals, broken down as 92, 80 and 81 by setting; Pinikahana et al. (2002) give 173, broken down as 134, 16, 12, 3 and 3 by profession; McLaughlin et al. (2006) give 35, with 9, 14, 3, 3 and 1 by profession plus two unnumbered roles. By the editors' arithmetic the breakdowns sum to 253, 168 and 30.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sample sizes from Table 4 should be checked in the primary studies before they are quoted; for Gilchrist et al. the breakdown may refer to something other than the whole sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The professional groups listed in 3.2 (seven mixed, eight nurses, seven addiction or mental health staff, four physicians, one physicians and nurses) add up to 27, not 28 papers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one paper is unaccounted for in the description of populations.

reporting_issues.issue: Studies of a very specific setting or explicit subgroup were to be excluded (Study selection, p. 25), yet the included papers concern, among others, forensic psychiatric nurses, anaesthesiologists, physicians of patients with HIV who inject drugs, dual-diagnosis care and clients with hepatitis C; no list of exclusions shows how the rule was applied.
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection rule appears under-specified or unevenly applied, which adds to the uncertainty about which studies the review represents.

design_detail: Conceptual narrative review in the journal's 'Fundamental concepts in genetics' series by three quantitative geneticists: definitions of broad- and narrow-sense heritability as ratios of variances (Box 1), common misconceptions (Box 2), history of the term (Box 3), the heritability of IQ (Box 4), heritability of all-or-none traits on the observed and liability scales (Box 5), heritability of new phenotypes (Box 6), estimation designs and their assumptions, why heritability changes, effects of selection and inbreeding, and marker-based estimation. Examples come from livestock, plants, insects, wild animals and human height, IQ, schizophrenia and major depression. No search strategy and no appraisal of the cited studies. No drug-use or addiction phenotype is discussed anywhere in the review.
can_establish: What heritability means as a technical term (a ratio of variances in a particular population for a measurement taken at a particular time or age), what it does not mean (genetic determination, a statement about differences between groups or over time, or about the size of gene effects), and under what conditions an estimate is biased or changes.
cannot_establish: Any heritability figure for drug use or addiction (none is discussed), or how far the twin-design assumptions it describes hold for substance use disorders; its numerical examples are second-hand illustrations, quoted without intervals.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Numerical examples are taken from cited studies, for example IQ correlations summarized from 4,672 MZ and 5,546 DZ twin pairs (Box 4, p. 260).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; examples chosen by the authors to illustrate concepts.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Examples were chosen to illustrate, mostly from agriculture, evolutionary biology and human height and IQ. 14 of the 115 references name one of the three authors as an author (editors' count), including the within-family marker method that the review presents as estimating heritability without the usual assumptions about family resemblance (p. 263).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (conceptual review). The review explains how heritability is estimated: offspring–parent regression, full- and half-sib correlations, the difference between MZ and DZ twin correlations, linear mixed ('animal') models fitted by residual maximum likelihood, Bayesian methods, and marker-based relatedness or identity-by-descent sharing (pp. 256–258, 263).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; the subject of the review is the parameter itself.
outcomes.operationalization: Heritability is defined as the proportion of total phenotypic variance in a population, for a measurement taken at a particular time or age, attributable to variation in additive genetic values (narrow sense, h²) or in all genetic values (broad sense, H²) (p. 255, Definitions; Box 1, p. 256).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Illustrative values as cited (second-hand, without intervals): human height about 0.8 (Box 2, p. 257; p. 264), lowered to 0.6 if the 15-cm sex difference is not removed (p. 258); schizophrenia and major depression, with first-degree relative risks of 9 and 3 and incidences of 1% and 3%, heritabilities of 0.16 and 0.12 on the observed scale against 0.81 and 0.37 on the liability scale (p. 259); IQ twin correlations 0.86 (MZ) and 0.60 (DZ), twin-study estimates 0.5–0.8, and 0.3 (narrow sense) and 0.5 (broad sense) in a meta-analysis that modelled maternal effects (Box 4, p. 260); first-lactation milk yield in dairy cattle from about 25% in the 1970s to about 40% (p. 261); cricket wing dimorphism 0.71 in the laboratory and 0.21 in the field (p. 261); gene expression about 0.3 from MZ twins (p. 264). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (p. 259, approximate): human height in Finland about 0.82 for people born 1947–57 and about 0.72 for people born before 1929.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable; examples were chosen to illustrate.
analysis.power: The review notes that hundreds of observations are needed for a standard error of a heritability estimate below 0.1, and thousands for precise estimates (p. 258).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A conceptual account: heritability is a population- and time-specific ratio of variances that depends on the genetic and environmental variance present; it changes when either changes, when gene–environment correlation changes, with age, and with the method of measurement; a high value does not mean a trait is fixed by genes, says nothing about differences between groups or about changes in the mean over time, and says nothing about the number or size of gene effects; classical twin designs estimate only three variance components and rest on assumptions (equal shared environment for MZ and DZ twins, no gene–environment correlation) that bias heritability upward when they fail.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions present heritability as a key parameter for comparing the relative importance of genes and environment within and across populations, traits and environments (p. 255; p. 264); the conclusions also state its limits: it does not give the size of either variance component, refers to a particular population and environment and not to their differences, and tells nothing about individual genes (p. 264). The review says a heritability in one population does not in theory predict that of another but that in practice heritabilities of similar traits are often remarkably similar across populations and species (p. 256); a claim that heritability figures for addiction cannot be carried across populations needs both halves. Box 4 concludes from twin and family data that a large proportion of within-population IQ variation is associated with additive genetic factors while noting that some of the assumptions cannot be tested (p. 260). The expectation that marker-based within-family estimation will give unbiased heritabilities for contested traits (p. 263) is the authors' forecast for their own method.

timeline.event: Fisher parameterizes the resemblance between relatives; his percentages for human stature correspond to what are now called broad- and narrow-sense heritability (Box 3, p. 258).
Wright uses h for the path from genotype to phenotype; h² becomes the symbol for heritability (Box 3, p. 258).
Lush is thought to be the first to use the term heritability formally (Box 3, p. 258).

Visscher et al.: heritability of height estimated at 0.8 from genome-wide identity-by-descent sharing within sibling pairs, a method free of assumptions about family resemblance (as described, p. 263).

replication.where_it_stands: The review describes the statistical methods for estimating heritability as having more or less converged across species and disciplines while strong, often untestable assumptions remain for human behavioural traits (p. 255), and it lists open questions (why heritabilities have the values they do; why they change little under long selection; p. 264). Its expectation that marker-based methods would give estimates free of family-design assumptions bears on the DNA-based studies of substance use disorders on the same list (for example Hatoum et al. 2023), not read in this round.

funding.funder: Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (grants 389892, 442915 and 443011) and the Australian Research Council (grant DP0770096) (Acknowledgements, p. 266).
funding.declared_conflicts: No competing-interests statement in the PDF.
funding.affiliations_note: Queensland Institute of Medical Research, Brisbane (Visscher, Wray) and Institute of Evolutionary Biology, University of Edinburgh (Hill). Two of the authors' own papers are the marker-based estimation studies the review presents (refs. 56 and 62). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For drug use and addiction specifically: heritability estimates for substance use and substance use disorders made in the same population across birth cohorts and policy or availability regimes, on a stated scale (observed or liability), with designs that do not depend on the equal-environments assumption (adoption, within-family marker sharing), to show how far the figure moves when the environment changes.

domains.note: No search or criteria; examples were chosen by the authors to illustrate concepts.
Box 4 discusses the assumptions behind the IQ twin estimates, but other figures (schizophrenia and depression, milk yield, Finnish height, brain volume) are quoted without appraisal or intervals.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 14 of 115 references are the authors' own, including the marker-based method the review promotes as assumption-free.
Forecasts are marked as such (in the future, with sufficient data), and open questions are listed as unanswered.

domains.domain: Balance of views on the meaning and usefulness of heritability
domains.note: Box 4 (p. 260) sets out two arguments that twin estimates of IQ heritability may be too high (gene–environment correlation, refs. 5 and 90; maternal effects larger for MZ than for DZ twins, ref. 97) and reports the lower meta-analytic estimate that models maternal effects (ref. 98); beyond these, the controversy is summarized rather than argued, and the review argues for the parameter's continued usefulness, so the critical side is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). For the site's purposes this is a conceptual explainer by specialists: its definitions and its list of what a heritability figure does and does not mean do not depend on a systematic search, and they are what claims should cite it for. Its numerical examples are second-hand, quoted without intervals, and two worked examples do not match the review's own formulas (see reporting issues). Cite it for definitions, misconceptions and the reasons heritability changes; do not cite its example figures as evidence about those traits, and do not cite it for any figure about drug use, which it does not discuss.

key_findings.finding: Heritability is defined as a ratio of variances: the proportion of total variance in a population, for a particular measurement taken at a particular time or age, attributable to variation in additive genetic values (narrow sense, h²) or total genetic values (broad sense, H²); it measures with one number the fraction of variation between individuals in a population that is due to their genotypes.
key_findings.locator: Definitions, 1st paragraph; Box 1 (p. 256)

key_findings.finding: Because heritability is a ratio, numerator and denominator both matter: the denominator usually excludes variation due to known fixed effects such as sex, age and cohort; if the 15-cm average height difference between men and women were ignored, the heritability estimate for height would fall from 0.8 to 0.6.
key_findings.locator: Definitions, 2nd paragraph (p. 255); Estimation of heritability, 6th paragraph (p. 258, right column)

key_findings.finding: Heritability depends on the population: genetic variance depends on which alleles segregate, their frequencies, effect sizes and mode of action, and environmental variance also differs between populations, so in theory the heritability in one population does not predict that in another; in practice, heritabilities of similar traits are often remarkably similar across populations and even species. It can also differ between sexes and between early and late life (beef cattle: about 0.3 for weaning weight, 0.4 for market weight).
key_findings.locator: Definitions, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Misconceptions (Box 2): heritability is not the proportion of a phenotype passed on to the next generation (genes, not phenotypes, are passed on); a high heritability does not mean genetic determination, since the environment can change the phenotype (the secular rise in human height coexists with heritabilities of about 0.8), and for height (heritability 0.8, population SD about 7 cm) the SD of offspring around the parents' mean is 5.4 cm; a low heritability does not mean little additive genetic variance; heritability says nothing about the causes of differences between groups or of changes in the mean over time (Flynn effect; US-born white men about 9 cm taller than Dutch men in the mid-19th century, Dutch men now about 5 cm taller); a large heritability does not imply genes of large effect.
key_findings.locator: Box 2

key_findings.finding: The usual partition of phenotypic variance assumes no gene–environment covariance and no gene-by-environment interaction; both are often ignored because they cannot be estimated, and according to the review, ignoring a covariance inflates the genetic variance, and ignoring an interaction inflates the environmental variance.
key_findings.locator: Box 1, last two paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Estimation limits: bias can come from confounding, for example through assortative mating and selection; the sampling variance of a heritability estimate is inversely proportional to the squared relationship of the relatives used and to the number of families, so hundreds of observations are needed for a standard error below 0.1; the classical twin design yields only three statistics (MZ resemblance, DZ resemblance, total variance), so only three variance components can be estimated although many more causes can be postulated; dominance and common-environment variance are confounded in full-sib designs; and the review's example of upward bias is parent–offspring resemblance partly due to common environment (the twin case is in Box 4, p. 260).
key_findings.locator: Estimation of heritability, 4th and 5th paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: Heritability is not constant: it changes when genetic variance changes (selection, inbreeding, migration, mutation), when environmental variance changes, when the correlation between genes and environments changes, with age, and even with the method of measurement (self-reported against clinically measured height). Examples: first-lactation milk yield in dairy cattle from about 25% in the 1970s to about 40%; cricket wing dimorphism 0.71 in the laboratory and 0.21 in field cages (genetic correlation between the environments close to 1); livestock traits more heritable under good husbandry; the heritability of IQ rises with socio-economic status. Empirical evidence for morphometric traits suggests lower heritabilities in poorer environments, but not for traits more closely related to fitness (2nd paragraph).
key_findings.locator: Heritability is not necessarily constant, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 summarizes heritabilities from reviews: on average larger for morphological than for fitness-related traits, and larger in better than in poorer environments; human height in Finland is shown for two birth cohorts, born 1947–57 (better environment) and before 1929 (poorer environment).
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 and legend
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the bar chart at 300 dpi against the axis ticks (approximate): about 0.82 for the 1947–57 cohort and about 0.72 for the pre-1929 cohort. The values are not printed.

key_findings.finding: For all-or-none traits such as disease, heritability depends on the scale: schizophrenia and major depression, with first-degree relative risks of 9 and 3 and incidences of 1% and 3%, have similar heritabilities on the observed 0/1 scale (0.16 and 0.12) but quite different ones on the underlying liability scale (0.81 and 0.37); heritability on the observed scale is always smaller than on the liability scale (at most 0.64, when incidence is 0.5 and liability heritability is 1), and for risk prediction from family history or genotypes the observed scale matters most.
key_findings.locator: Applications, 2nd paragraph (p. 259); Box 5 (p. 262)
key_findings.note: The pairs are not one worked conversion and do not follow from the Box 5 formula (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: IQ (Box 4): twin estimates are consistently 0.5–0.8 across ages (lower in preschool children, about 0.6–0.8 in old age); across many studies the average MZ and DZ correlations were 0.86 and 0.60 (4,672 MZ and 5,546 DZ pairs). Gene–environment correlation may inflate these estimates, and maternal (in utero) effects larger for MZ than DZ twins would bias them upward because equal common environments are assumed; a meta-analysis modelling maternal effects gave 0.3 (narrow sense) and 0.5 (broad sense). The box concludes that a large proportion of within-population IQ variation is associated with additive genetic factors. The box calls the view that a large heritability means intelligence cannot be changed by intervention an incorrect perception (referring to Box 2).
key_findings.locator: Box 4, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Marker-based estimation within families: full sibs share on average 50% of their genome identical by descent with an SD of about 4% (half sibs 25%, SD 3%); relating this variation to phenotypic similarity gave a height heritability of 0.8, in line with twin and family studies, without assumptions about the causes of family resemblance; the authors expect such methods to allow unbiased estimation for contested traits such as IQ and for disease concordance.
key_findings.locator: Heritability in the genomics era › Exploiting variation in relatedness, 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: because heritability is a ratio of variances it does not give the size of either component; it refers to a particular population and environment and not to differences between them; and, as a composite measure, it tells nothing about the actions and interactions of individual genes.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions and further research, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: How a trait is measured changes its heritability: the heritability of the mean of several records differs from that of a single record; with a single-record heritability of 0.10, the mean of 10 records has a heritability of about 0.53 when repeated measures share no environmental component, but only 0.125 when the correlation of repeated measures is 0.8.
key_findings.locator: Heritability and repeated measures (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with the formula that reproduces 0.53 gives 0.122 for the second case (see reporting issues). The printed 0.125 also equals 0.10/0.8 (heritability divided by repeatability), the value approached as the number of records grows, so it may be that limit rather than a rounding of 0.122.

reporting_issues.issue: Box 2 gives the SD of offspring height around the parents' mean as 5.4 cm, from a residual variance of 1 − ½h², whereas the Figure 2 legend gives residual variances about the offspring–midparent regression of 0.98 and 0.68 for h² of 0.2 and 0.8, which equal 1 − ½h⁴; by the editors' calculation the Figure 2 formula would give about 5.8 cm for height. The two describe spread around different quantities (the parents' genetic mean against their measured average), which the review does not distinguish.
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the point made (either value is close to the population SD of about 7 cm); cite the 5.4 cm figure as an illustration, not as a precise value.

reporting_issues.issue: In the repeated-measures example the review prints 0.125 for a repeatability of 0.8; by the editors' calculation, the formula that reproduces its first value (0.53, for a single-record heritability of 0.10 and no environmental repeatability), h²n/[1 + (n − 1)r] with n = 10, gives 0.122 for the second.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial: the printed 0.125 equals 0.10/0.8, the limit as the number of records grows, so it may be that value rather than a rounding of 0.122; no consequence for the claims.

reporting_issues.issue: The schizophrenia and depression example cannot be reproduced from the review's own Box 5 formula: by the editors' calculation, applying it to the printed liability-scale values (0.81 and 0.37) with incidences of 1% and 3% gives observed-scale values of about 0.06 for both, not 0.16 and 0.12. The printed observed-scale values equal 2K(λ − 1)/(1 − K) computed from the printed incidences and relative risks (0.162 and 0.124), and an exact liability-threshold calculation from the same inputs gives about 0.82 for schizophrenia but about 0.51 for depression. The review does not say how either pair was obtained; its note to ref. 19 calls the relationship approximate, while Box 5 states it as an equality.
reporting_issues.consequence: The qualitative point stands (for a rare disorder, observed-scale heritability is much smaller than liability-scale heritability), but the pairs should not be cited as a worked conversion, and Box 5's formula should not be used to convert published heritabilities of substance use disorders between scales.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 69 is garbled: its printed title repeats the opening of ref. 68's Arabidopsis title and ends with expression of PTGER4, while the text cites ref. 69 as a genome-wide association study of Crohn disease in humans.
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the site's claims.
