design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects single-group (proportion) meta-analysis of the share of people with a substance use disorder (alcohol, heroin or several substances) who were in remission at the last follow-up of observational cohorts published 2000–2015 with at least three years of follow-up, or with lifetime cumulative probabilities. 21 cohorts (12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance). Two rates were pooled: a 'standard' rate (people in remission at final follow-up divided by those who reached it) and a 'conservative' rate (the same people divided by everyone at baseline, counting deaths and losses as not remitted). Also reported: annualized remission rates under a constant-rate model (PEARRs), subgroup analyses, univariate meta-regressions and trim-and-fill. No protocol registration is mentioned.
can_establish: The range of remission proportions reported by long-term cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or polysubstance use disorders published 2000–2015, mostly recruited through treatment, and how strongly those proportions depend on how losses are counted and on the length of follow-up.
cannot_establish: A remission rate for people with substance use disorders in general (15 of 21 cohorts were clinical samples, and follow-up ran from 3 to 50 years), the chance of remission within any given period (the pooled proportions mix very different follow-up lengths), whether remission depends on treatment (treatment during follow-up was not analysed), or how often remission occurs among people who never reach treatment (two general-population cohorts only).

sample.recruitment: Database search of Medline, PubMed, EMBASE and PsycINFO, hand search of 19 addiction journals chosen by experts, and reference lists; studies published January 2000 to December 2015, from OECD countries, in English or French (PDF pp. 2–3, Methods › 2.1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies of people with an SUD (abuse or dependence) at baseline, with follow-up of three years or more and two or more data collections, or lifetime remission with cumulative probability estimates; participants at least 18 at final follow-up; remission defined over at least six months. Excluded: cohorts in which not everyone had an SUD at baseline; studies limited to particular groups (homeless people, indigenous peoples, veterans, people with medical conditions such as pregnant women); trials, studies of experimental treatments and of methadone or buprenorphine programmes; for cohorts published several times, all but the longest follow-up (PDF pp. 2–3, Methods › 2.1; Fig. 1, PDF p. 4).
sample.demographics: Across the 21 cohorts: follow-up 3 to 50 years (mean 17, median 13); baseline N 86 to 5,719 (mean 1,018, median 613); mean age 33 at baseline and 48 at last follow-up; on average 70% men in 16 cohorts and only men in the other 5; 34% to 98% White (10 cohorts reporting); unemployment 16% to 86% (10 cohorts); 10% to 89% with co-occurring mental disorders (7 cohorts); 24% to 100% involved in criminal activity (8 cohorts) (PDF pp. 4, 7, Results › 3.1). 13 cohorts were from the US (editors' count from Table 1 and the text).
sample.attrition: Review level: not applicable. Within cohorts, retention ranged from 21% to 96% (mean 67%) counting deaths as losses and from 47% to 98% (mean 80%) excluding deaths (PDF p. 4, Results › 3.1, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Mostly treatment-recruited cohorts: 15 clinical, 4 community and 2 general-population samples (both from the US NESARC survey) (PDF p. 11); all four heroin cohorts were treatment samples, one of them a compulsory, court-ordered treatment programme (Table 1 footnote g, PDF p. 6). The authors expect population samples to show better outcomes (PDF p. 11). Excluding veterans, trials and opioid-agonist programmes, and keeping only the longest follow-up, shapes which cohorts entered. Moss et al. (2010), one of the two general-population samples, follows NESARC respondents with an alcohol use disorder across the survey's two waves three years apart (Table 1), the same waves analysed by Vergés et al. (2012), and the other, Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), is a lifetime estimate from the same survey, so these sources overlap (editors' observation). One cohort entered here as a clinical sample, Moos and Moos (2007), is drawn from the source cohort that Mellor et al. (2019, pp. 64–66) treat as initially untreated people, seen after a single detox episode or at an information and referral centre.

exposure.measurement: The 'exposure' is having an SUD at baseline, as diagnosed in each cohort: DSM-III, DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, ICD-10, or study instruments and records (Alcohol Use Scale, Drinking Problem Index, Augmented Addiction Severity Index, Natural History Interview, screening interviews, clinical records) (Table 1, PDF pp. 5–6). The authors note that eight cohorts relied on self-reported SUD (PDF p. 11). 14 cohorts included any SUD (abuse and/or dependence), 7 dependence only (PDF p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Duration of the disorder before remission was reported by 8 cohorts (see key findings); the authors note that duration before entry was rarely recorded (PDF p. 11).
exposure.polysubstance: Five cohorts were classed as polysubstance. In two of them, separate substance-specific estimates were merged into one rate without a stated method: Hser et al. (2008), 0.33 heroin, 0.80 methamphetamine, 0.87 cocaine, entered as 0.660; Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), lifetime estimates for alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, entered as 0.957 (Fig. 4 notes, PDF p. 10). The authors note that cohorts rarely checked whether people in remission from one substance had moved to another (PDF p. 11).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Remission meant not meeting abuse or dependence criteria for at least six months at the final follow-up (PDF p. 1): minimum 6 months in 5 cohorts, 12 months in 12, 5 to 10 years in 4; 7 cohorts required abstinence and 14 accepted controlled use (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: None: a single-group meta-analysis of proportions. All comparisons are between cohorts (subgroups and meta-regressions), not within them.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Characteristics not tested as moderators, which the authors say could explain the heterogeneity: criminal activity, unemployment, social support, co-occurring mental disorders and treatment received over time (PDF p. 11); duration of the disorder before entry was rarely recorded (PDF p. 11).

outcomes.instruments: Each cohort's own remission assessment (Table 1). Two summary measures defined by the reviewers: the standard rate (people in continuous remission of more than six months at final follow-up, divided by those reaching final follow-up, excluding the dead, the lost and those no longer eligible) and the conservative rate (the same numerator divided by the whole baseline sample) (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.3.1). PEARR: the sample-size-weighted mean of −ln(1−b)/c across cohorts, where b is the remission proportion and c the years of follow-up (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.3.3); for the lifetime cohort, c was set at 40 years (Table 1 footnote n, PDF p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Included studies were 'critically appraised for inclusion' with questions adapted from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme; no study-level appraisal results are reported (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.2).
outcomes.operationalization: Remission is status at the final follow-up only: a person abstinent for most of the follow-up who relapsed in its last six months counts as not remitted, as the authors note (PDF p. 11). Remission definitions ranged from abstinence to controlled use, and minimum durations from 6 months to 10 years (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two pooled outcomes (standard and conservative rates), each tested in 5 subgroup comparisons and 4 univariate meta-regressions (18 moderator tests), at alpha 0.05 'given the exploratory nature' of the analyses (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently, with a third resolving disagreements (agreement 96% on a 10% sample); full texts were read and data extracted independently by two team members (PDF p. 3, Methods › 2.2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooling of proportions weighted by inverse variance (Comprehensive Meta-Analysis). Standard rate 54.4% (95% CI 42.1 to 66.2), study values 19.6% to 95.7%, weighted mean follow-up 17.9 years (SD 14.0), I2 99.4%, tau2 1.3, Q 3337.3 on 20 df; leave-one-out 50.1% to 56.4%; PEARR 9.1% (8.4 to 9.8). Conservative rate 35.0% (25.2 to 46.4) in the text (0.351, 0.252 to 0.464 in Fig. 4), study values 15.5% to 95.7%, weighted mean follow-up 16.9 years (SD 13.4), I2 99.5%, tau2 1.2, Q 3890.7 on 20 df; leave-one-out 30.9% to 36.3%; without the lifetime cohort 30.9% (26.1 to 36.1), I2 97.7%; PEARR 6.8% (6.3 to 7.4) (PDF p. 7; Fig. 4, PDF p. 10). No prediction intervals. Trim-and-fill: standard 0.60 (0.47 to 0.71), conservative 0.48 (0.38 to 0.59) (PDF p. 7). Editors' calculation: the PEARRs reproduce from Fig. 4 and Table 1 (9.1% weighting by final N, 6.8% by baseline N), but at a constant 9.1% or 6.8% per year cumulative remission after 17.9 years would be about 80% or 70%, whereas the pooled proportions imply about 4.4% and 2.6% per year (−ln(1−p)/t); the two summaries are not consistent under the constant-rate assumption the PEARR makes.
analysis.covariates: Univariate meta-regressions (follow-up duration, proportion male, age in 18 cohorts, retention in 20 cohorts) and subgroup analyses (substance, treatment at baseline, diagnosis, remission definition, remission duration), each tested separately; no multivariable model (PDF p. 3; Tables 2 and 3, PDF pp. 8, 10).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review states that it followed PRISMA (PDF p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: The funnel plots are not published ('available upon request', PDF p. 7); study-level appraisal results are not reported; the search strategy is described only by example keywords (PDF p. 2); how the substance-specific estimates of two cohorts were combined is not stated (Fig. 4 notes, PDF p. 10).
analysis.power: Not formally addressed; subgroups contain 4 to 15 cohorts and meta-regressions 18 to 21, and the authors say the small number of studies makes the non-significant moderator results hard to interpret (PDF p. 11).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 21 mostly treatment-recruited cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, between about a fifth and almost all participants were in remission at the last follow-up; pooled, 54% of those followed up (35% of everyone enrolled, counting deaths and losses as not remitted), with heterogeneity above 99%. Standard rates were higher in cohorts with longer follow-up and lower retention; no subgroup difference reached significance by substance, treatment at baseline (51% treated vs 62% not, standard rate), diagnosis, remission definition or remission duration.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion say the results support the view that SUDs are more likely to be 'chronic' or long-term disorders for a substantial number of people, that the PEARRs projected few cases of remission in any given year, and that treatment geared to chronicity such as assertive community treatment and intensive case management should be more available (PDF pp. 1, 12). Gaps: (1) a pooled proportion over follow-ups of 3 to 50 years describes no particular time point, and the review's own meta-regression shows the proportion rising with follow-up; (2) at the reported 6.8% to 9.1% a year, half of a cohort would remit in about 7.6 to 10.2 years (ln 2 divided by the rate; editors' calculation), which does not obviously mean 'few cases'; (3) 15 of 21 cohorts were clinical samples, whose course the authors expect to be worse than the population's (PDF p. 11), so the chronicity reading applies mainly to people who reached treatment; (4) the service recommendations are not tested by any analysis; (5) the Discussion restates 17.9 and 16.9 years of follow-up as years of substance use or consumption (PDF p. 7), and the conclusion that most people used for at least 14 years before remission (PDF p. 12) is not supported by the eight durations reported, several of which are under 10 years (Table 1; PDF p. 7). The limitations section is candid about heterogeneity, definitions and the small number of cohorts (PDF p. 11).

timeline.event: Calabria et al., systematic review of prospective studies of remission from amphetamine, cannabis, cocaine or opioid dependence; the source of this review's three-year minimum and annualized-rate method, cited here as reporting 5% (cocaine) to 22% (opioid) remission a year (PDF pp. 2–3, 7; General list #21; not read for this card).
White's analysis of 415 reports from 1868 to 2011, cited here as finding that about half of participants had remitted by the final follow-up (PDF p. 2; not read for this card).

Heyman, synthesis of national surveys, cited here as finding half of people with an alcohol use disorder in remission 16 years after onset and four years for cocaine (PDF p. 10; General list #23; not read for this card).
This review: the first systematic review and meta-analysis of remission across alcohol and illicit-drug use disorders, by the authors' account (PDF pp. 2, 11).

Mellor et al., systematic review of untreated remission from alcohol problems, showing how estimates depend on the starting sample and on definitions; it does not cite this review, and it treats the source cohort of Moos and Moos (2007) as initially untreated.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled figures are best cited as a range for long-term, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts: about a third (counting everyone enrolled) to about half (counting those followed up) were in remission at a last follow-up averaging 17 years. They are not an estimate of remission among all people with substance use disorders, among whom general-population cohorts, two of them here, are expected to show more remission; the primary cohorts should be cited for figures specific to a substance or time point.

funding.funder: Partly funded by a grant from the National Institute of Excellence in Health and Social Services, Quebec, Canada (Institut National d'Excellence en Santé et en Services Sociaux, INESSS); the funder had no role in study design or data collection for the review (PDF p. 12).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest, including financial interests or affiliations relevant to the manuscript (PDF p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from McGill University (Department of Psychiatry; Douglas Mental Health University Institute), Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières, Université Laval and three Quebec addiction rehabilitation centres; four of the seven authors are affiliated with addiction rehabilitation centres, and the review closes by recommending more chronic-care services. Recorded as a flag for closer reading of the recommendations, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: General-population cohorts that identify people when they first meet criteria, reassess them with a standard diagnostic interview at fixed intervals for ten years or more, record treatment as it happens and analyse time to first sustained remission and to relapse with survival methods that account for deaths and losses; or an individual-participant meta-analysis of existing cohorts using one remission definition and time-to-event methods, reporting treated and never-treated people separately.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with an SUD at baseline), outcome (remission of at least six months at final follow-up), minimum follow-up and designs are specified (PDF pp. 1–3).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA was followed (PDF p. 2).
Observational cohorts only; trials and studies of experimental or substitution treatment excluded because their selection favours atypical participants exposed to best practice (PDF p. 3).

Four databases, hand search of 19 journals and reference lists, search ending December 2015 for a paper received in March 2016; but the strategy is given only as example keywords, the English-or-French restriction is not justified, and grey literature and non-peer-reviewed reports were excluded (PDF pp. 2, 11). Judged 'no' under item 4 as written, as the project applies it to unjustified language limits (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Two reviewers screened independently with a third for disagreements (96% agreement on 10% of records), and two read the full texts (PDF p. 3).
Two team members extracted independently with a standardized form (PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives exclusion reasons with counts for the 98 excluded full texts, but no list of the excluded studies (PDF p. 4).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, N at baseline and follow-up, retention, age, sex, ethnicity, population, diagnosis, instruments, follow-up length, remission definition and duration of the disorder; treatment received during follow-up is not described (PDF pp. 5–6).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Studies were appraised only as a gate for inclusion with questions adapted from CASP; no domain-level judgments or results are reported, and confounding, selection and measurement were not assessed study by study (PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Inverse-variance random-effects pooling is a suitable technique, but combining was not justified for an outcome that depends on time: proportions observed after 3 to 50 years and a model-based lifetime probability (placed at 40 years) were pooled into one figure, the review's own meta-regression shows follow-up explaining part of the variation, two cohorts' substance-specific estimates were merged into one value by an unstated method, and no prediction interval is given despite I2 above 99% (PDF pp. 3, 6–7, 10).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No study-level risk of bias was assessed. The conservative-versus-standard comparison and the retention meta-regression address attrition only (PDF pp. 3, 7).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion weighs attrition (actual remission likely between the two rates), the predominance of clinical samples, self-reported SUD in eight cohorts and small final samples, and asks for caution (PDF pp. 7, 11).
Q, I2 and tau2 reported; subgroup analyses and meta-regressions explored sources; residual heterogeneity is acknowledged as unexplained (PDF pp. 7, 10–11).

Funnel plots and trim-and-fill, with impact discussed (PDF pp. 7, 11). The funnel plots are not published, and the limitations both say the adjusted estimates may be higher and that reporting bias seems unlikely; for single-group proportions the meaning of funnel asymmetry is uncertain.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and a no-conflict statement are printed (PDF p. 12).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are not met (2, 4, 7, 9 and 11), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The decisive weaknesses for the encyclopedia are not procedural: the headline proportions pool cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years and mostly recruited through treatment, the lifetime NESARC estimate sits beside observed proportions, and no study-level appraisal was done. The review may be cited for the range of remission proportions in long-term cohorts (about 20% to 96% among those followed up), for the effect of counting losses (35% vs 54%), for the finding that standard rates rose with follow-up length and fell with retention, for the absence of a detectable difference by substance, treatment at baseline or remission definition, and as a pointer to the primary cohorts. It should not be cited for a general remission rate, for an annual chance of remission, or for the claim that most people use for at least 14 years before remission.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: Medline, PubMed, EMBASE and PsycINFO, a hand search of 19 addiction journals and reference lists, for studies published January 2000 to December 2015 in OECD countries, in English or French; 8,855 records screened, 119 full texts assessed and 21 cohorts included (12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance). Of the 98 full texts excluded, 49 gave no remission data at final follow-up, 18 included people without an SUD at baseline, 15 had follow-up under three years, 4 were from outside the OECD, 4 defined remission over less than six months, 4 assessed interventions, 2 concerned special populations and 2 duplicated a cohort.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1 (PDF pp. 2–3); Results › 3.1, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Fig. 1 (PDF p. 4; an image, counts read on the rendered page)
key_findings.note: The Results text gives 8,885 records; the abstract and Fig. 1 give 8,855 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Included cohorts: follow-up 3 to 50 years (mean 17, median 13); baseline N 86 to 5,719 (mean 1,018, median 613); retention 21% to 96% counting deaths (mean 67%) and 47% to 98% excluding them (mean 80%); mean age 33 at baseline and 48 at last follow-up; on average 70% men in 16 cohorts and only men in 5; 14 cohorts any SUD and 7 dependence only; remission required for at least 6 months (5 cohorts), 12 months (12) or 5 to 10 years (4); 7 cohorts required abstinence, 14 accepted controlled use. 15 cohorts were clinical, 4 community and 2 general-population samples.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 3–4, figures on p. 4); Discussion, 7th paragraph (starting PDF p. 10; sample types on p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Standard remission rate (people in remission at final follow-up among those who reached it): study values 19.6% to 95.7%; pooled 54.4% (95% CI 42.1 to 66.2) after a weighted mean follow-up of 17.9 years (SD 14.0); I2 99.4%, tau2 1.3, Q 3337.3 (df 20); removing one cohort at a time gave 50.1% to 56.4%; annualized pooled rate (PEARR) 9.1% (8.4 to 9.8).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 1st paragraph; Fig. 4 (PDF p. 10)
key_findings.note: Editors' recalculation from the Fig. 4 study values (random effects on the logit scale, which reproduces the printed 0.544, 0.421 to 0.662): without the lifetime NESARC estimate (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011) the standard rate is about 0.501 (0.425 to 0.576), the lowest value of the printed leave-one-out range; the review prints the corresponding conservative figure (30.9%, key finding 3).

key_findings.finding: Conservative remission rate (same people in remission divided by everyone enrolled): study values 15.5% to 95.7%; pooled 35.0% (95% CI 25.2 to 46.4) after a weighted mean follow-up of 16.9 years (SD 13.4); I2 99.5%, tau2 1.2, Q 3890.7 (df 20); leave-one-out 30.9% to 36.3%; without the lifetime NESARC cohort (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011) 30.9% (26.1 to 36.1), I2 97.7%; PEARR 6.8% (6.3 to 7.4). The authors judge that actual remission probably lies between the two rates.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 4 (PDF p. 10)
key_findings.note: Fig. 4 prints the conservative pooled estimate as 0.351 (0.252 to 0.464).

key_findings.finding: Subgroups (Table 2), none significant. Standard rate: alcohol 0.517 (0.354 to 0.676), heroin 0.540 (0.269 to 0.789), polysubstance 0.609 (0.359 to 0.813), p 0.833; treatment at baseline 0.511 (15 cohorts) vs none 0.624 (6 cohorts), p 0.421; any SUD 0.464 (14) vs dependence only 0.695 (7), p 0.060; controlled use or abstinence 0.570 vs abstinence only 0.491, p 0.568; remission of 6 months 0.428, 12 months 0.597, 5 years or more 0.528, p 0.570. Conservative rate: alcohol 0.298, heroin 0.275, polysubstance 0.509 (p 0.157); treatment at baseline 0.382 vs none 0.279 (p 0.388); any SUD 0.289 vs dependence only 0.489 (p 0.081).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 7); Table 2 (PDF p. 8)
key_findings.note: Table 2 footnotes: 'treatment at baseline' means all or most people were in treatment at baseline; two of the six cohorts without treatment at baseline were population samples in which some people were in treatment. Treatment during follow-up was not analysed. Editors' reconstruction from Fig. 4 (AI readers 341 and 371, independently): the six cohorts without treatment at baseline are the two general-population and four community samples of Table 1 (Moss et al., 2010; Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011; Trim et al., 2013; Penick et al., 2010, drawn partly from municipal alcohol treatment clinics; Vaillant, 2003; Galai et al., 2003). With a common between-study variance the Fig. 4 standard rates reproduce Table 2 (0.511 and 0.624); the 0.624 includes the lifetime NESARC estimate (0.957), and without it the five remaining cohorts give about 0.48 to 0.49. The comparison is between cohorts by treatment status at entry and cannot show who remitted without treatment.

key_findings.finding: Univariate meta-regressions (Table 3): the standard rate was higher in cohorts with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, SE 0.016, 95% CI 0.014 to 0.08, R2 analog 0.30, p 0.004) and lower retention (B −1.975, SE 0.821, −3.583 to −0.367, R2 analog 0.06, p 0.016), and unrelated to proportion male (p 0.754) or age (18 cohorts, p 0.412). No characteristic predicted the conservative rate (follow-up p 0.235; retention p 0.060; male p 0.262; age p 0.446).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 7); Table 3 (PDF p. 10)
key_findings.note: The scale of B (probably the logit of the proportion) is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Funnel plots, not published, were described as asymmetric with more cohorts below the mean; trim-and-fill trimmed 3 cohorts for the standard rate (adjusted 0.60, 0.47 to 0.71) and 9 for the conservative rate (adjusted 0.48, 0.38 to 0.59).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Duration of the disorder before remission, reported by 8 cohorts: alcohol 9.6 (Gual), 11 (Mann), 13.6 (Penick) and 19 years (Vaillant); regular heroin use 22 years (Hser 2007); polysubstance median 27 years (Dennis); about 4 years of injecting before remission (Galai); in NESARC, half of people with alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted about 14, 6 and 5 years after onset (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, last column and footnote o (PDF pp. 5–6); Results › 3.2 (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Values as printed in Table 1. The text of 3.2 attributes the 11 years to Moos and Moos (2007), for whom Table 1 prints NA, and gives the NESARC medians as 6 years for alcohol and 14 for cannabis, the reverse of Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The lifetime NESARC cohort (5,719 people) entered both analyses as 0.957 (0.951 to 0.962); its components are given as 0.91 alcohol, 0.97 cannabis and 0.998 cocaine for the standard rate, and as 37%, 66% and 76% for the conservative rate; for the PEARR its follow-up was set at 40 years. The multi-sample cohort of Hser et al. (2008) entered as 0.660 from 0.33 heroin, 0.80 methamphetamine and 0.87 cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 footnote n (PDF p. 6); Fig. 4 and notes b to d (PDF p. 10; an image, values read at 300 dpi)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: few cohorts; trials, experimental studies and non-peer-reviewed reports excluded; OECD countries and English or French only, mostly US samples except for heroin; remission definitions from abstinence to controlled use and durations from 6 months to 10 years; status at final follow-up only, so people abstinent for most of the follow-up but relapsing near its end count as not remitted; eight cohorts used self-reported SUD; final samples of 41 to 129 people in a third of the cohorts; possible switching to another substance not checked.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (starting PDF p. 10; self-reported SUD and small final samples on p. 11) and 9th paragraph (substance switching, PDF p. 11); 4.1 Limitations (PDF p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: a third to a half of people with SUDs achieved remission after a mean follow-up of 17 years; annual remission of one person in ten to one in 15; the findings are said to support the view that SUDs are 'chronic' or long-term disorders for a significant number of people, and chronic-care management, assertive community treatment and intensive case management are recommended.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1); 4.2 Conclusion (PDF pp. 11–12)

reporting_issues.issue: The number of records screened is 8,855 in the abstract and Fig. 1 (171 + 10,921 − 2,237 duplicates) but 8,885 in the Results text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; Fig. 1's arithmetic supports 8,855.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion restates the weighted mean follow-up (17.9 and 16.9 years) as years of substance use or consumption, saying 54% were in remission after 18 years of use and 35% after 17 years of consumption.
reporting_issues.consequence: Follow-up time is not duration of use; the figures must not be quoted as years of use before remission.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.2 gives the NESARC times to half remission as 5 years (cocaine), 6 (alcohol) and 14 (cannabis); Table 1 footnote o gives 14 (alcohol), 6 (cannabis) and 5 (cocaine). Section 3.2 also attributes 11 years of active drinking before remission to Moos and Moos (2007), for whom Table 1 prints NA; Table 1 gives 11 years for Mann et al. (2005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Alcohol and cannabis are swapped in one of the two places, and one study attribution is wrong; the primary paper is needed before quoting substance-specific times to remission.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that the mean consumption period before remission was at least 14 years for most people (PDF p. 12), and the Discussion's 14 years for more than two thirds (PDF p. 9), cannot be derived from the eight durations reported (4 to 27 years, several under 10), which also measure different things (mean, median, years of injecting, time to half remission).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 14-year figure should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says cohorts of any SUD showed better standard remission than dependence-only cohorts (PDF p. 10); Table 2 shows the reverse (0.464 for any SUD vs 0.695 for dependence only).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the (non-significant) diagnosis difference is misreported in the text; use Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2, the conservative-rate subgroups by substance have narrow, non-overlapping intervals (alcohol 0.287 to 0.309; heroin 0.253 to 0.298; polysubstance 0.497 to 0.520), which by the Methods' own rule would indicate significant differences, yet Q is 3.707 (p 0.157) and the text reports no significant factor; the intervals are far narrower than the random-effects intervals elsewhere. The conservative 'treatment at baseline' row also gives 2 df for two groups, while its p value (0.388) corresponds to 1 df, and its two estimates (0.382 with treatment at baseline, 0.279 without) cannot be rebuilt from the Fig. 4 conservative study values with the grouping that reproduces the standard-rate subgroups (editors' reconstruction: about 0.32 and 0.44).
reporting_issues.consequence: The conservative-rate substance intervals appear to come from a different model or to be misprinted; they should not be cited, nor the conservative treatment-at-baseline contrast.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the subgroup estimates for alcohol, heroin and polysubstance as 51.7%, 54.0% and 60.0% (PDF p. 11); Table 2 gives 0.517, 0.540 and 0.609.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Table 2's 60.9% should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 4 shows 0.957 for the lifetime NESARC cohort in the conservative panel, but its footnote gives component rates of 37%, 66% and 76%, which cannot yield 0.957; how either panel's components were combined is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conservative value for the cohort with the largest single influence on that estimate cannot be verified.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints a retention of 79% for Delucchi et al. (2004), whose Ns are 1,599 at baseline and 1,094 at final follow-up, and NA for Cranford et al. (2014). By the editors' calculations, Delucchi's Ns give 68%, as does the ratio of its conservative to standard rate in Fig. 4 (0.183/0.268), and Cranford's Ns give 78%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the retention column cannot be relied on for single cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: Results 3.1 gives final follow-up samples of 45 to 1,797 people for the 20 prospective cohorts (PDF p. 4); Table 1 lists 41 for Vaillant (2003), as does the Discussion (41 to 129, PDF p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints Q 0.20 for proportion male (standard rate), where B and SE (0.506, 1.612) give about 0.10 and p 0.754 corresponds to that smaller value; the confidence-interval columns are both headed 'Lower limit'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor typesetting errors.

reporting_issues.issue: The index under Fig. 2 omits cohorts 6 (Noda et al., 2001) and 12 (Vaillant, 2003), which are plotted; Okruhlica et al. (2002) has an age range printed in reverse order (26.3 to 16.7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Fig. 3's index identifies the two cohorts.

reporting_issues.issue: The annualized rates (PEARRs) assume a constant yearly rate and weight cohorts by sample size, so large cohorts with short follow-up dominate. By the editors' calculation, at 9.1% or 6.8% a year cumulative remission after 17.9 years would be about 80% or 70%, far above the pooled 54% and 35%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The PEARRs and the pooled proportions are not mutually consistent; neither should be quoted as the yearly chance of remission.

design_detail: Short critical history (accepted manuscript of an article in a journal series that also revisited Robins's Vietnam studies, ref. 1) of the three 'Rat Park' experiments run by Bruce Alexander and colleagues at Simon Fraser University: Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway (1978), Hadaway et al. (1979) and Alexander et al. (1981). It describes the enclosure and the measurement methods, tabulates each study's group sizes, procedures and main findings (Table 1), lists design and reporting limitations, summarizes three independent housing studies (Hill & Powell 1976; Bozarth et al., dated 1987 in the text and 1989 in the reference list; Petrie 1996), and discusses how the popular account came to differ from the papers. No search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no formal appraisal and no new data. Every experimental finding it summarizes is in rats.
can_establish: What the three original Rat Park papers reported according to two independent readers (group sizes, measurement methods, the specific conditions under which housing differences appeared, the original authors' cautious conclusions), and how far the popular account has moved from those papers.
cannot_establish: Whether housing changes drug intake in rats in general, or anything about environment and addiction in people (no new data; the human arguments are cited, not tested); its summaries of the original papers and of the replication attempts are second-hand, and one of them (Petrie 1996, read for this round) is attributed to the wrong original study.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The Rat Park studies as tabulated (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10): 1978, 32 albino Wistar rats (isolated 4 females and 6 males; Rat Park 10 females and 12 males), 27 remaining after deaths; 1979, 36 rats (9 females and 9 males per housing condition); 1981, 32 rats in four groups of 4 females and 4 males (isolated throughout, Rat Park throughout, and the two groups switched at 65 days).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; the studies discussed were chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable to the review. For the 1978 study the text reports four deaths, but its own group counts (32 to 27 rats) and Table 1 give five (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own. The replication section names three studies with results in both directions; later animal work on enrichment and drug seeking is mentioned in one sentence without citations to specific drug studies, and choice studies offering rats a non-drug alternative are not discussed. Neither author is an author of the Rat Park papers (refs. 16–18).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable as a review. As summarized: oral morphine hydrochloride solution (with or without sucrose) offered beside water; isolated rats' bottles were weighed and corrected against a bottle on an empty cage, while Rat Park rats drank from a dispenser that released single drops, counted and filmed together with the drinking rat's identifying mark (PDF p. 2, The original 1978 study, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats, as tabulated (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10). 1978: housing from weaning; a limited-access period (fluid 7 h a day on a 3-day cycle, 9 cycles); 57 days with morphine solution as the only fluid (4 choice days); Nichols cycles (8 three-day cycles, 4 choice days); an abstinence period with choice days after 2 and 5 weeks. 1979: morphine-naive rats offered tap water against 0.5 mg/ml morphine hydrochloride with sucrose rising from 0 to 10%, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, 5 days per solution. 1981: a quinine bitter-sweet control, then 1, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml morphine hydrochloride in 10% sucrose, 5 days per solution.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (one drug, rats).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the 1978 study included an abstinence period with choice tests after 2 and 5 weeks without morphine (Table 1, PDF p. 8).

comparison.controls: Within the original studies: rats housed alone in 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages without sight of other rats, against the mixed-sex Rat Park colony in an L-shaped 8.8 m² enclosure with sawdust, open boxes, tubes, open-topped cages and a climbing pole (PDF p. 2).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the review; how rats were allocated to housing in the original studies is not described.

outcomes.instruments: As summarized: morphine solution and water intake per rat on choice days and in forced-access periods, with sex and housing effects tested by F tests (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review's central measurement criticism: intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions, so a systematic error in one (for example unrecorded leakage from the isolated cages' bottles) could create a group difference; the authors note that water intake did not show the same pattern, which offers some protection (PDF p. 3, Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: The original studies measured oral morphine intake; the review treats this as one behaviour under one manipulation (housing), not as a model of addiction (PDF p. 4, Legacy, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable to the review; the authors say the original studies made many comparisons in very small groups, raising the risk of false-positive results (PDF p. 3, Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph; PDF p. 5, Conclusion, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited from the original studies (Table 1, PDF pp. 8–10). 1978: limited-access data not presented because of measurement error; forced-access period, mean intake higher in Rat Park rats (18.6 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat) than in isolated rats (13.3 mg); Nichols cycles, isolated rats drank less on non-choice days but more on choice days (F=200.9, df 1/69, p<0.001); abstinence period, isolated rats drank more (F 26.38, df 1/23, p<0.001); females drank more than males (F 7.26, df 1/23, p<0.05; F=67.86, df 1/69, p<0.001; F=36.44, df 1/23, p<0.001). 1979: little evidence of a housing effect at high morphine and low sucrose; with 10% sucrose isolated rats drank more morphine solution, the largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml; sex differences inconsistent. 1981: rats living in Rat Park at testing drank less morphine solution than isolated rats regardless of early housing (F=33.64, p<0.0001, df not printed); no early-housing effect; weak evidence of an interaction; differences driven mainly by males. Amounts consumed are given only for the 1978 forced-access period.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a review. The table gives F tests and directions but, apart from the 1978 forced-access means, no amounts consumed, so the size of the housing effects cannot be judged from this source.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors call the group sizes very small even for an animal study (PDF p. 2, The original 1978 study, 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Three small rat experiments from one laboratory, with intake measured differently in the two housing conditions, found less oral morphine intake in colony-housed than in isolated rats under particular conditions (choice days after forced exposure, sweetened low-concentration solutions, housing at the time of testing), while Rat Park rats consumed more than isolated rats during forced access. The original authors drew cautious conclusions and did not link the findings to human addiction; independent housing studies gave mixed results.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The unlabelled summary paragraph at the head of the article (PDF p. 1) states the housing effect without qualification (enriched rats drank less whether pre-exposed, naive, or raised in either housing). The body qualifies it: in 1979 differences appeared only at high sweetness and low morphine (PDF p. 3), and overall only in very specific conditions (PDF p. 5); Table 1 shows the opposite direction during forced access. The authors' own conclusion, that the popular reading of Rat Park as a new understanding of addiction is overstated and that it models one manipulation on one behaviour (PDF p. 4), is argued from the literature, and they still call its core message (addiction is more than a biological response to a drug) hugely important (PDF p. 5). The replication section names the wrong original study for Petrie's attempt (see reporting issues).

timeline.event: Hill & Powell: rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake; enriched rats drank more cocaine solution (as summarized, PDF p. 4).
Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway: the original Rat Park study, 32 rats (as summarized, PDF p. 2 and Table 1).
Hadaway, Alexander, Coambs & Beyerstein: morphine-naive rats offered sweetened morphine solutions (as summarized, PDF p. 3 and Table 1).
Alexander, Beyerstein, Hadaway & Coambs: housing at testing, not early housing, went with intake; half the rats switched at 65 days (as summarized, PDF p. 3 and Table 1).
Bozarth, Murray & Wise: isolated rats acquired intravenous cocaine self-administration, socially housed rats not consistently (as summarized; dated 1987 in the text, PDF p. 4).
Petrie: two experiments did not reproduce lower intake in colony rats; designed as a replication of the 1981 study (read for this round).

replication.where_it_stands: Rat Park rests on three small experiments from one laboratory (1978–1981); the one published direct replication attempt read for this round (Petrie 1996) did not reproduce the housing effect, and the other housing studies summarized here point both ways. The popular version (rats in a rich environment refuse morphine) is not what the papers reported: Rat Park rats did drink morphine. All of it concerns oral morphine drinking in rats.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the accepted manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflict of interest: none (PDF p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychological Sciences, University of Liverpool (Gage) and Public Health Institute, Liverpool John Moores University (Sumnall). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered replication of colony versus isolated housing in rats of both sexes (housed so that pregnancies cannot occur), with the same automated individual intake measurement in both conditions, random allocation, blinded analysis and more than one strain or supplier; and, for people, longitudinal or natural-experiment studies of how housing, opportunity and social exclusion change the course of drug use.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the original papers and the replication attempts were chosen by the authors.

The original Rat Park studies are appraised in specific terms (measurement method, mixed-sex housing, group sizes, multiple comparisons), but the replication studies are summarized without any appraisal, and one is attributed to the wrong original study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the experiments discussed is the authors' own.

The body keeps the account of the studies apart from the authors' views, but the summary paragraph states the housing effect more generally than the body and Table 1 support, and statements about later enrichment research are made without the evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on housing and drug intake in animals
domains.note: The weaknesses of the original studies and the failed replication are set out in detail; later animal evidence that supports an environmental effect is mentioned in one sentence without citations to drug studies, so that side is the less documented one.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). This short history gives a specific, checkable account of what the Rat Park papers reported (Table 1), names concrete design problems, and its authors have no stake in the studies; but selection is unsystematic, its summaries of other studies are second-hand, one count is internally inconsistent and one replication is attributed to the wrong study. Cite it for the history of Rat Park, the design limits of the original experiments and the gap between the papers and the popular account, labelled as rat findings; cite Petrie 1996 directly for the replication; do not cite it for anything about environment and addiction in people.

key_findings.finding: The 1978 study used 32 albino Wistar rats: 4 females and 6 males housed alone in 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages without sight of other rats, and 10 females and 12 males in Rat Park, an L-shaped 8.8 m² enclosure with sawdust, open boxes, tubes, open-topped cages and a climbing pole. For three weeks before the experiment all rats had water and a morphine hydrochloride solution and drank almost only water, in both housing conditions.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1, 1978 study row, Number of rats column (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Intake was measured differently in the two housing conditions: isolated rats' bottles were weighed and corrected against a bottle on an empty cage for leakage and evaporation; Rat Park rats drank single drops from a dispenser whose counter and the drinking rat's mark were filmed. The authors point out that an error affecting only one method could produce a group difference where none existed; that water intake did not show the same pattern offers some protection.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 2nd paragraph (p. 2); Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: 1978 study as summarized: at the end, 2 isolated females, 6 isolated males, 7 Rat Park females and 12 Rat Park males remained; the isolated females (two rats) drank the most morphine in all periods; broadly, isolated rats drank more morphine than Rat Park rats and females more than males; across the choice days of the three-day cycle, intake rose in isolated rats and fell in Rat Park rats; Rat Park rats did drink morphine, contrary to some popular accounts.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text says four deaths; its own counts and Table 1 give five (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Table 1, 1978 study: limited-access data were not presented because of measurement error; in the forced-access period (morphine solution the only fluid for 57 days apart from 4 choice days), Rat Park rats consumed more on average than isolated rats (18.6 vs 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat); in the Nichols-cycle period, isolated rats drank less on non-choice days and more on choice days (F=200.9, df 1/69, p<0.001); in the abstinence period isolated rats drank more (F 26.38, df 1/23, p<0.001). Females drank more than males in the final forced-period choice days (F 7.26, df 1/23, p<0.05), the Nichols cycles (F=67.86, df 1/69, p<0.001) and abstinence (F=36.44, df 1/23, p<0.001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, 1978 study row (Main findings and Other findings columns)
key_findings.note: The amounts (18.6 and 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat) carry no time base (per day or per period) and no body-weight correction; cite them as tabulated. The abstinence result refers to the choice days after 2 and 5 weeks. On the df of the Nichols-cycle tests, see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The original authors' conclusions were cautious: sex and housing are important variables and theories ignoring them risk oversimplification. Nowhere in the three papers did they connect the findings to human addiction or to deprivation; after ending the animal work, Alexander used Rat Park to develop an adaptive model of drug use in lectures, writings and a popular book.
key_findings.locator: The original 1978 study, 4th paragraph (p. 2); Follow-up studies, 4th paragraph (pp. 3–4)

key_findings.finding: 1979 study (morphine-naive rats; 9 females and 9 males per housing condition): a choice between tap water and a morphine solution made sweeter and then weaker in 5-day steps; isolated rats drank more morphine solution than Rat Park rats only at high sweetness and low morphine concentration (with 10% sucrose; largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml), with little evidence of a housing effect at high morphine and low sucrose.
key_findings.locator: Follow-up studies, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, 1979 study row (p. 9)
key_findings.note: The text says females again drank more than males; Table 1 calls the 1979 sex differences inconsistent (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 1981 study (four groups of 4 females and 4 males: isolated or Rat Park from weaning, half of each switched at 65 days): rats living in Rat Park at the time of testing drank less morphine solution than isolated rats whatever their early housing (F=33.64, p<0.0001); no evidence that early housing mattered and weak evidence of an interaction; the housing difference was driven mainly by males.
key_findings.locator: Follow-up studies, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, 1981 study row (pp. 9–10)

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: different intake measurement in the two housing conditions; males and females housed together in Rat Park with no account in the papers of pregnancies or pups; competition and dominance in the colony; very small groups with complex designs and many possible analyses, raising the risk of false positives; and group differences that emerged only in specific conditions (rats pre-exposed to morphine, particular morphine and sucrose concentrations, certain stages of the experiments).
key_findings.locator: Follow-up studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 3); Conclusion, 1st paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Independent attempts gave mixed results: Hill & Powell (ref. 12, dated 1976 in the reference list) found no difference in morphine intake by rearing and more cocaine-solution drinking by enriched rats; Bozarth and colleagues found that isolated rats quickly learned to self-administer intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently; Petrie (1996), in two experiments with two colony measurement methods, found colony rats drinking about as much morphine solution as Rat Park's colony rats but isolated rats drinking much less than Rat Park's isolated rats, and pointed to a change in the Wistar stock.
key_findings.locator: Replication attempts and contemporaneous studies, 1st paragraph (p. 4); reference list, refs. 12, 25 and 26 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Second-hand summaries. Petrie (1996), read for this round (sc_petrie_1996), states it replicated Alexander et al. (1981), not the 1979 study named here. Bozarth et al. is dated 1987 here and 1989 in the reference list.

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the popular reading overstated: Rat Park models one manipulation (housing) on one behaviour (oral morphine intake) and was not particularly novel in its time; supply, availability and opportunity are proximal determinants of human drug use, and environment in human research also means access to services and social exclusion; most rodent self-administration studies still house animals individually; the story endured because policy advocacy needs a simple narrative.
key_findings.locator: Legacy, 2nd paragraph (pp. 4–5); Conclusion, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 1978 study had four deaths, but by the editors' count its own group sizes at the start and end (32 rats, then 2 + 6 + 7 + 12 = 27; isolated females 4 to 2, Rat Park females 10 to 7) imply five, and Table 1 lists five (two females in each housing condition during forced access, one Rat Park female during abstinence).
reporting_issues.consequence: Five fits the counts and the df of 1/23 in Table 1 (27 rats in a 2 × 2 design); cite five deaths, and note that the isolated-female group ended with two rats.

reporting_issues.issue: Petrie (1996) is said to have tried to replicate the 1979 study (ref. 17), but Petrie states in his General Discussion that his experiments were designed to replicate Alexander et al. (1981) (see sc_petrie_1996), and his procedure (a quinine bitter-sweet phase, then morphine falling from 1.0 mg/ml in 10% sucrose) is close to, though not identical with, the 1981 design in this paper's own Table 1 (quinine phase, then 1, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, 5 days each; Petrie used 4-day phases, 0.05 rather than 0.06 mg/ml quinine and 0.25 and 0.125 rather than 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml), and unlike the 1979 design (no quinine phase; 0.5 mg/ml with sucrose rising from 0 to 10%, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that Petrie's isolated rats drank much less than those in Rat Park compares them with the 1981 isolated rats; claims should name the 1981 study.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 1979 study again showed females drinking more morphine than males, but Table 1 calls that study's sex differences inconsistent (females drank less at 0.5 mg/ml with 1% sucrose and more at 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sex differences across the Rat Park studies should be described as inconsistent: females more in 1978, mixed in 1979, none in 1981 according to the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The unlabelled summary paragraph at the head of the article says enriched rats drank less morphine whether pre-exposed, naive or raised in either housing, without the body's qualification that differences appeared only in specific conditions; Table 1 shows Rat Park rats consuming more morphine than isolated rats during forced access (18.6 vs 13.3 mg per rat) and isolated rats drinking less on non-choice Nichols-cycle days.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim that Rat Park rats consumed less morphine must state the conditions: choice days, sweetened low-concentration solutions, and housing at the time of testing.

reporting_issues.issue: Bozarth et al. is dated 1987 in the text but 1989 in the reference list (ref. 25), whose title covers heroin as well as cocaine; only a cocaine result is summarized.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the date and the heroin results should be checked in the original before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical slips in the accepted manuscript: 'Robbins' for Robins (PDF p. 1); 'LHCl' for MHCl in Table 1 (PDF p. 9); the 1981 F statistic is printed without degrees of freedom (PDF p. 9).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the claims; the version of record may differ.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints df 1/69 for the Nichols-cycle housing and sex tests (F = 200.9 and 67.86), although at most 28 rats remained in that period (32 minus the four deaths of the forced period; df 1/23 elsewhere fits 27 rats in a 2 × 2 design), so the error term cannot be between rats; the review does not say how these tests were built.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the direction of the Nichols-cycle housing difference, not the size of its F, as evidence of a housing effect.

verification.source_read: Accepted manuscript PDF, 10 pages (text PDF pp. 1–5, references pp. 5–7, Table 1 pp. 8–10), all pages read on rendered pages and Table 1 checked at 150 dpi; pages differ from the version of record (Addiction 114(5):917–922, online 2018); no abstract heading in this version (the italic summary paragraph on PDF p. 1 serves as one); no supplement. Petrie 1996, the replication it summarizes, was read in the same session.
