design_detail: Two between-group experiments in rats, designed as a replication of Alexander et al. (1981), one of the 'Rat Park' studies (stated in the General Discussion, p. 398; the Introduction gives Experiment 1's aim as testing the new computer-controlled system by comparing colony and isolated rats, p. 392). The procedure is close to, not identical with, the 1981 study as Gage & Sumnall (2019) tabulate it (5-day phases, 0.06 mg/ml quinine, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml); this paper does not describe the 1981 procedure or give its intake figures, so its 'up to seven times' cannot be checked here. In each experiment 10 male and 10 female outbred Wistar rats (Charles River Canada) were raised from weaning (21 days) alone in standard cages and 10 males and 10 females together in an 8.8 m² colony box. From 113 to 142 days of age all rats had 24-h access to tap water and a second fluid in seven 4-day phases: 10% sucrose; 10% sucrose with 0.05 mg/ml quinine sulfate (a bitter-sweet control); morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose; 10% sucrose again. Experiment 1 recorded each colony rat's drinking with a computer-controlled, video-identified dispenser reached by climbing a pole; Experiment 2 removed the pole and the automated system and weighed communal reservoirs, so colony intake was known only as a group total. Isolated rats drank from weighed bottles in both experiments. Every finding is in rats.
can_establish: That in these two cohorts of Wistar rats from a later breeding stock, colony housing did not lower intake of sweetened morphine solution compared with isolation: in Experiment 1 colony rats drank slightly more at 1.0 mg/ml, with no significant differences at the lower concentrations (colony means numerically higher).
cannot_establish: Why the earlier result was not reproduced (the strain-change explanation was not tested: no rats from the earlier stock were run), the title's claim that environment matters less than other variables (genes were not manipulated), anything about individual colony rats in Experiment 2 (only reservoir totals), or anything about addiction in people.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory animals: outbred Wistar rats of Charles River Canada origin, raised from weaning (21 days) in their housing condition, tested from 113 to 142 days of age and killed at 143 days (p. 392, Experiment 1 › Method › Subjects; p. 393, Procedure; p. 396, Experiment 2 › Method › Subjects). Experiment 2 used a new set of rats (the first set was killed at the end of Experiment 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated.
sample.demographics: Equal numbers of males and females in every condition; body weights taken at 114 and 142 days but not reported.
sample.attrition: Not reported. The degrees of freedom of the Experiment 1 analyses fit 38 and then 37 rats rather than 40 (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: One supplier and stock; how rats were allocated to housing is not described; colony rats of both sexes lived together from weaning for about four months, and pregnancies or litters are not mentioned. The paper gives no dates for its experiments; the personal communications it cites are dated May 1985 (pp. 398–399) and it was accepted in January 1996 (p. 400).

exposure.measurement: Fluid weights. Isolated rats: two bottles fastened outside each cage, weighed, with bottles on two empty cages to correct for spillage and evaporation (p. 392). Colony, Experiment 1: a computer-controlled system weighed each of two fluids drunk at every visit (0.1 g resolution), identified the rat from a video of its hair-dye mark, and could be reached only by climbing a 41-cm pole (pp. 392–393). Colony, Experiment 2: two communal reservoirs weighed daily, with untouched control reservoirs for evaporation; individual intake unknown (p. 396).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats: oral, voluntary, 24-h choice beside tap water, 4 days per phase, bottle sides swapped every 2 days; morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose (16 days in all, in descending order), after a 10% sucrose phase and a quinine–sucrose phase and before a final sucrose phase (Table 1, p. 394; Procedure, p. 393). The quinine–sucrose solution was chosen because it tasted, to people, like the 0.25 mg/ml morphine solution (p. 393).
exposure.polysubstance: None: one drug, and the rats had no previous morphine exposure (p. 392).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: morphine-naive at the start; no withdrawal or abstinence tests.

comparison.controls: Isolated rats in standard 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages with sheet-metal walls preventing visual contact, against colony rats in an open-topped wooden box (8.8 m²) with cedar shavings and two open metal cages holding the feeders, in each experiment; sucrose-only phases (1 and 7) and the quinine phase (2) as taste controls (pp. 392–393).
comparison.matching: Same supplier, strain and age; equal sex numbers; shared lighting on one timer (p. 393).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure before housing began; allocation method not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Experiment 1: per phase, the proportion of experimental fluid to total fluid, mg of experimental substance per kg body weight, grams of experimental fluid, and total fluid in grams (p. 393, Results, 1st paragraph); means in Table 2 (p. 395). Experiment 2: group average daily grams of each fluid (Table 3, p. 397).
outcomes.validity_norms: The automated system was introduced because the older Rat Park apparatus was unreliable (eight days of data lost in Alexander et al. 1981, p. 392); its accuracy against weighed bottles is not reported here (it is said to be described in Petrie et al. 1985).
outcomes.operationalization: Morphine consumption = intake of sweetened morphine solution beside water; no measure of dependence, withdrawal or motivation.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Stated as two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs corrected for multiple comparisons, without naming the method, run separately for each of 7 phases and 4 measures (28 analyses, each testing housing, sex and their interaction), followed by Newman–Keuls comparisons; only p<.05 is reported (pp. 393–394). The count of 28 is the editors'. Experiment 2: no inferential test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; housing cannot be hidden from staff who weighed bottles and reservoirs.

analysis.effect_sizes: Average daily grams without SDs. Experiment 1 (Table 2, p. 395), experimental fluid, isolated vs colony: sucrose pretest 103.2 vs 108.3; quinine 33.4 vs 75.0; morphine 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6; 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3; 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3; 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8; sucrose posttest 81.4 vs 79.6. Colony more than isolated in the 1.0 mg/ml phase on all four measures (proportion F(1, 34)=55.2; grams F(1, 34)=80.98; total fluid F(1, 34)=11.4; mg/kg significant, statistic not printed); no housing difference at 0.5, 0.25 or 0.125 mg/ml (pp. 394–395). Females more than males in mg/kg in all four morphine phases (F 6.1, 12.1, 4.7 and 5.7, p<.05; p. 394). Experiment 2 (Table 3, p. 397), isolated vs colony: 1.0 mg/ml 0.3 vs 4.3; 0.5 mg/ml 9.4 vs 3.0; 0.25 mg/ml 17.4 vs 10.9; 0.125 mg/ml 44.4 vs 33.1; quinine 26.3 vs 10.4; no test. Editors' calculation (treating 1 g of solution as about 1 ml): mean daily morphine hydrochloride intake was 0 and 0.3 mg in isolated rats and 3.6 and 4.3 mg in colony rats at 1.0 mg/ml, between 0.25 and 4.7 mg across groups at 0.5 mg/ml, and between 2.7 and 5.6 mg in every group at 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml.
analysis.covariates: None; sex entered as a factor.
analysis.selective_reporting: mg/kg values and body weights are never shown, although mg/kg carries the sex differences and the Phase 3 housing difference; no SDs or individual data; non-significant effects are not reported with statistics.
analysis.power: Not reported; 10 rats per sex per housing condition in each experiment.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In two cohorts measured with different colony methods, colony housing did not reduce intake of sweetened morphine solution. Experiment 1 found colony rats drinking slightly more at 1.0 mg/ml (3.6 vs 0.0 g a day) and no significant difference at lower concentrations (colony means numerically higher). Experiment 2, without a test, showed colony rats drinking more at 1.0 mg/ml and less at 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, by margins smaller than the up-to-sevenfold differences the author cites for Alexander et al. (1981). Both groups drank far less of every morphine solution than of plain sucrose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says environment is not the most important variable in oral morphine consumption, and the summary attributes the non-replication to strain differences introduced when the supplier changed its breeding colony (p. 391); the conclusion calls the confounding factors most likely genetic (p. 399). Neither genes nor stock were tested: the evidence is a date (the 1981 study ran April–July 1979; the stock changed in November 1979), personal communications, and one study of amphetamine-induced activity in the two stocks (pp. 398–399). Experiment 2 is called consistent with Experiment 1 (p. 397), though in three of four morphine phases its isolated rats drank more, the direction of the original finding, and its quinine phase reversed Experiment 1's. The argument that rats drank for the sucrose rather than the morphine (p. 399) is not tested against the quinine control, which was meant for this: in Experiment 1 both groups drank less of the 0.25 mg/ml morphine solution than of the quinine solution said to taste the same (15.7 vs 33.4 g isolated; 18.3 vs 75.0 g colony), though the two phases differ in order.

timeline.event: Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway: isolated rats pretreated with unsweetened morphine drank more morphine solution than colony rats (as described, pp. 391–392).
Hadaway et al.: the same in morphine-naive rats offered progressively more palatable sucrose-morphine solutions (as described, p. 392).

Alexander et al. (published 1981) run April–July 1979 with the supplier's earlier Wistar stock; eight days of data lost to an apparatus fault; in November 1979 the supplier changed its breeding colonies (pp. 392, 398).
This study: two experiments with later-stock Wistar rats do not reproduce lower intake in colony rats.
Gage & Sumnall's critical history of Rat Park summarizes this study as a replication of the 1979 study, although it states it replicated the 1981 study.

replication.where_it_stands: The housing effect on oral morphine intake rests on three small studies from one laboratory and is contradicted by this non-replication; the other housing studies summarized by Gage & Sumnall (2019) point both ways. The strain explanation offered here has not been tested in any study read for this round.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, New Mexico Tech (p. 391). The author is a co-author, with Alexander and Beyerstein of the Rat Park group, of the 1985 chapter that describes the computer-controlled drinking system used in Experiment 1 (reference list, p. 400). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered replication run in parallel with rats from more than one stock or supplier, randomized to housing, with the same individual automated intake measurement in both housing conditions, sexes housed so that litters cannot confound intake, and prespecified analyses; that would test the housing effect and the strain explanation at once.

domains.note: How weanlings were assigned to isolation or the colony is not described.

Same supplier, stock, age and sex numbers; weights at 114 days were taken but not reported. Plain-sucrose intake in the pretest was similar (103.2 vs 108.3 g in Experiment 1; 116.2 vs 104.5 g in Experiment 2), but housing had already lasted three months.
Not reported.
Housing is the intervention itself; the placement of cages and colony box in the room is not reported, though both shared one lighting timer.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Housing cannot be hidden from staff, who weighed the isolated rats' bottles and, in Experiment 2, the colony reservoirs; nothing is said about limiting handling differences.
Every rat (or, in Experiment 2, the whole colony) was measured daily throughout.

Unblinded weighing, and in both experiments intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions (bottles against an automated dispenser or communal reservoirs), so measurement differences are built into the comparison.
The degrees of freedom imply that two and then three of 40 rats were missing from the Experiment 1 analyses; no reason or group is given.
No protocol (none would be expected at the time); significant effects only are reported with statistics, and mg/kg values, SDs and weights are not shown.

In Experiment 1 colony rats had to climb a 41-cm pole to drink, a cost isolated rats did not face; males and females shared the colony from weaning, with pregnancies not mentioned; Experiment 2 yields only colony totals, so no test was possible.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; this is the editors' summary, set to the most severe judgment among the items that bear on the housing comparison. Allocation is undescribed, weighing was unblinded and done by different methods in the two housing conditions in both experiments (the same weakness the original Rat Park studies are criticized for), colony rats faced an extra effort to drink in Experiment 1, two or three rats are missing from the analyses without explanation, and Experiment 2 could not be tested. Cite the paper for what it found in these two cohorts (no lower intake of sweetened morphine solution in colony-housed rats) and as the published non-replication of Alexander et al. (1981), labelled as a rat finding; do not cite it for the genetic explanation, for the title's claim about environment, or for anything about people.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rat; outbred Wistar from Charles River Canada (the supplier's later breeding stock, according to the author); 10 males and 10 females per housing condition in each of two experiments (80 rats); raised from weaning at 21 days; tested at 113–142 days of age.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Oral and voluntary: 24-h two-bottle choice between tap water and morphine hydrochloride in 10% sucrose at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, 4 days each in descending order (16 days of morphine availability), after sucrose and quinine–sucrose phases.
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given by the paper and none calculated here; intake was reported as grams of solution (mg/kg values not shown).
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No. Rats drank a sweetened oral solution with water always available, for 16 days in a fixed descending sequence; no escalation, dependence or withdrawal was measured; cage versus colony is a narrow stand-in for a human social environment.

key_findings.finding: Each experiment used 10 male and 10 female outbred Wistar rats in each housing condition, raised from weaning at 21 days either alone in 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages or together in an 8.8 m² box; from 113 to 142 days of age they chose for 24 h a day between tap water and, in seven 4-day phases, 10% sucrose, 10% sucrose with 0.05 mg/ml quinine sulfate, morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, and 10% sucrose again.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Method › Subjects and Apparatus (p. 392); Procedure, 1st–5th paragraphs (p. 393); Table 1 (p. 394); Experiment 2 › Method › Subjects (p. 396)

key_findings.finding: Intake was measured differently in the two housing conditions in both experiments: isolated rats drank from bottles weighed against bottles on two empty cages; in Experiment 1 colony rats climbed a 41-cm pole to a computer-controlled dispenser that weighed each visit's intake (0.1 g resolution) and identified the rat by video; in Experiment 2 the pole and the automated system were removed and two communal reservoirs were weighed daily against untouched control reservoirs, so individual colony intake was unknown.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Method › Apparatus (pp. 392–393); Experiment 2 › Method › Apparatus (p. 396)

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1: colony rats drank more of the experimental fluid relative to water than isolated rats in Phase 2 (quinine; F(1, 34)=32.6), Phase 3 (1.0 mg/ml morphine; F(1, 34)=55.2) and Phase 7 (sucrose; F(1, 33)=11.7); more grams in Phases 2 and 3 (F(1, 34)=18.8 and 80.98); more mg/kg in Phase 3 (statistic not printed); and more total fluid in Phases 2, 3 and 4 (F(1, 34)=6.3 and 11.4; F(1, 33)=17.5); all p<.05. There were no significant housing differences in morphine consumption in the 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml phases (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 395), where the colony means were numerically higher (Table 2); no SDs are given.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Results, 2nd to 5th paragraphs (p. 394; the Phase 3 mg/kg housing result is in the 3rd); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 395)
key_findings.note: Subscripts and some F values are garbled in the PDF's text layer; read on the rendered page at 300 dpi.

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1, average daily grams of experimental fluid, isolated vs colony: sucrose pretest 103.2 vs 108.3; quinine 33.4 vs 75.0; morphine 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6; 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3; 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3; 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8; sucrose posttest 81.4 vs 79.6. Water in the same phases: 2.5 vs 1.3, 26.3 vs 5.5, 39.5 vs 58.8, 44.5 vs 74.6, 33.9 vs 49.5, 23.2 vs 19.6, 8.8 vs 0.7.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: Means only, without SDs or n; checked at 300 dpi.

key_findings.finding: Experiment 1: females drank more mg/kg of experimental fluid than males in Phases 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 (F(1, 34)=15.8 and 6.1; F(1, 33)=12.1, 4.7, 5.7 and 14.5; p<.05), that is in all four morphine phases; in Phase 3 colony females drank more mg/kg than each other group, and colony males more than isolated males and females.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 1 › Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 394); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 395)
key_findings.note: Subscripts are garbled in the PDF's text layer; read on the rendered page at 300 dpi.

key_findings.finding: Experiment 2 (colony intake from communal reservoirs; no inferential test possible): average daily grams of morphine solution, colony vs isolated, 4.3 vs 0.3 at 1.0 mg/ml; isolated vs colony 9.4 vs 3.0 at 0.5 mg/ml, 17.4 vs 10.9 at 0.25 mg/ml and 44.4 vs 33.1 at 0.125 mg/ml. Quinine phase: isolated 26.3, colony 10.4; sucrose pretest 116.2 vs 104.5 and posttest 104.2 vs 94.9.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 2 › Results, 1st paragraph (p. 396); Table 3 (p. 397)
key_findings.note: The paper does not say how the colony's per-animal averages were derived from the reservoir totals.

key_findings.finding: The author states that the differences in Experiment 2 were never as large as in the rats kept in their original housing in Alexander et al. (1981), where continuously isolated rats drank up to seven times as much sucrose-morphine as continuously colony-housed rats; he concludes that neither experiment replicated the earlier housing research and that the second shows the non-replication was not due to the automated equipment.
key_findings.locator: Experiment 2 › Results, 2nd paragraph (pp. 396–397); Discussion (p. 397); General Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 397)

key_findings.finding: The author locates the difference in the isolated rats: they drank much less sucrose-morphine than the isolated rats of Alexander et al. (1981), whereas colony rats drank similar amounts in all three studies, although the 1981 rats drank less plain sucrose (Phases 1 and 7) than the present rats.
key_findings.locator: General Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposed explanation, not tested: the 1981 study was run April–July 1979, and in November 1979 the supplier changed its outbred Wistar breeding colonies, so the earlier rats were Old Colony and the present ones New Colony Wistars. Support offered: the supplier's reasons for the change (personal communication, May 1985), reports of lower voluntary alcohol intake in New Colony Wistars (two personal communications, May 1985), and one study (Ton et al. 1983) in which chronic naltrexone affected amphetamine-induced activity differently in Old and New Colony male rats. No Old Colony rats were tested.
key_findings.locator: General Discussion, 4th–9th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The author argues that, across all three studies, rats did not increase their morphine intake over time but drank more of the solution as its morphine content fell, consuming about the same absolute amount of morphine, and so drank it for the sucrose; he calls the data a strong disconfirmation of the natural-affinity hypothesis (Goldstein 1972, 1976).
key_findings.locator: General Discussion, 10th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Tables 2 and 3 (treating 1 g of solution as about 1 ml): mean daily morphine hydrochloride intake was 0 and 0.3 mg in isolated rats and 3.6 and 4.3 mg in colony rats at 1.0 mg/ml, 0.25 to 4.7 mg across groups at 0.5 mg/ml, and 2.7 to 5.6 mg in every group at 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml, so it was roughly constant only across the last two morphine phases; mg/kg values are not printed.

key_findings.finding: The drinking apparatus of the earlier studies was unreliable: in Alexander et al. (1981) an electronic fault lost eight days of data, so only three-quarters of the potential data could be analysed; the computer-controlled system was introduced for this reason, and no data were lost to equipment in Experiment 1.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 392); Experiment 1 › Procedure, 2nd paragraph (p. 393)

reporting_issues.issue: Experiment 1 had 20 isolated and 20 colony rats, but its ANOVAs report F with 1 and 34 df in Phases 1–3 and 1 and 33 df in Phases 4–7 (post hoc df 34 and 33 likewise); by the editors' calculation, 40 rats in a 2 (housing) × 2 (sex) design give 36 error df, so 38 and then 37 rats were analysed, and no death, loss or exclusion is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two or three rats were dropped from the analyses for unstated reasons and from unknown groups; with 10 rats per cell this could matter for the sex-by-housing comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: Experiment 2 is called consistent with Experiment 1, but in three of its four morphine phases its isolated rats drank more morphine solution than its colony rats (9.4 vs 3.0, 17.4 vs 10.9 and 44.4 vs 33.1 g), the direction of the original finding, whereas in Experiment 1 colony rats drank as much or more in every morphine phase; the quinine phase also reversed (colony 75.0 vs isolated 33.4 g in Experiment 1; colony 10.4 vs isolated 26.3 g in Experiment 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two experiments agree only in that neither shows a difference as large as the earlier study's; the reversal between colony measurement methods suggests that the method affected the results, which the paper does not discuss.

reporting_issues.issue: No standard deviations, individual data, body weights or mg/kg values are reported; the F statistic for the colony–isolated mg/kg difference in Phase 3 is not printed; and the method of the stated correction for multiple comparisons is not named.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes cannot be computed, and the claim about constant absolute morphine intake can be checked only roughly from grams of solution.

reporting_issues.issue: The General Discussion says rats kept consuming about the same absolute amount of morphine as the concentration fell, but by the editors' calculation from Tables 2 and 3 daily morphine intake was near zero in isolated rats at 1.0 mg/ml (0 and 0.3 mg) and below 1 mg in both Experiment 1 groups at 0.5 mg/ml, and about 2.7–5.6 mg in all groups only in the last two morphine phases.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sucrose-not-morphine reading rests on a pattern the tables show only at the lowest concentrations; avoidance of the stronger solutions fits the data at least as well.

reporting_issues.issue: The non-replication is attributed to a change of breeding stock in November 1979, but the paper gives no dates for its own experiments; the personal communications it cites are dated May 1985, and it was accepted in January 1996 (date printed at the foot of p. 400, absent from the PDF's text layer).
reporting_issues.consequence: When the experiments were run is unknown; claims should date the failed replication by its publication (1996), not by when the work was done.

disagreements.first_pass: Two between-group experiments in rats, designed as a replication of Alexander et al. (1981), one of the 'Rat Park' studies. In each experiment 10 male and 10 female outbred Wistar rats (Charles River Canada) were raised from weaning (21 days) alone in standard cages and 10 males and 10 females together in an 8.8 m² colony box. From 113 to 142 days of age all rats had 24-h access to tap water and a second fluid in seven 4-day phases: 10% sucrose; 10% sucrose with 0.05 mg/ml quinine sulfate (a bitter-sweet control); morphine hydrochloride at 1.0, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml in 10% sucrose; 10% sucrose again. Experiment 1 recorded each colony rat's drinking with a computer-controlled, video-identified dispenser reached by climbing a pole; Experiment 2 removed the pole and the automated system and weighed communal reservoirs, so colony intake was known only as a group total. Isolated rats drank from weighed bottles in both experiments. Every finding is in rats.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 342 (blind second reading): Missed items: Experiment 1's stated aim was to test the computerized system (p. 392, Introduction, 4th paragraph); the replication was close but not exact, and the 'up to seven times' and the comparison of isolated rats across studies cannot be checked from this paper.
disagreements.resolution: AI reader 371 (adjudication), 2026-11-12: Accepted; p. 392 and p. 398 checked on the rendered pages, the 1981 procedure in Gage & Sumnall's Table 1 (PDF pp. 9–10).

design_detail: Follow-up interview study of two random samples of US Army enlisted men and draftees who left Vietnam for the United States in September 1971: a 'general sample' of 470 drawn from about 13,760 returnees, and a 'drug-positive sample' of 495 drawn from about 1,400 whose urine at departure was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (22 men were in both; 943 selected). One structured interview 8 to 12 months after return (May to September 1972) asked about drug use before service, in Vietnam and since return; a urine specimen was taken at interview and military and Veterans Administration records were sought. Prevalence results are for the general sample (451 interviewed); predictor analyses combine both samples with the drug-positive sample weighted (automatic interaction detector and multiple classification analysis). The paper presents highlights; full methods and data are in a 1974 government monograph (ref. 1), not read.
can_establish: For US Army enlisted men leaving Vietnam in September 1971, the self-reported proportions who used narcotics and who met the study's own addiction criteria before service, in Vietnam and in the 8 to 12 months after return, and how few of the men addicted in Vietnam were addicted again in that first year home.
cannot_establish: Why remission was so common (the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change of social setting explains it, p. 960), whether it lasted beyond the first year, whether it happened without treatment (the departure screening was meant to hold men with a positive urine test for detoxification and treatment, and psychiatric treatment since return is tabulated, but how many men received drug treatment, before or after return, is not reported, nor how treatment related to remission), how it compares with remission in civilians addicted at home (the only comparison is another study's treated patients), whether it applies to women or to other places and times, or whether drug use caused the problems that went with it after return (no comparison group; one interview).

sample.recruitment: Random samples from military records: names of all Army enlisted men and draftees returning from Vietnam in September 1971 were supplied by the Department of Defense (general sample), and names of those with a positive departure urine test by the Surgeon General (drug-positive sample) (p. 956, Methods, 2nd paragraph). September 1971 was chosen as the first month with complete urine-test records and because those men's tours were thought to coincide with peak heroin use by US soldiers; one month's departures were taken so that the men had been exposed to drugs alike, had had comparable chances of treatment while in the military and had spent the same time back home (pp. 955–956, Methods, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Army enlisted men and draftees returning from Vietnam to the United States in September 1971. Drug-positive sample: departure urine positive for illicit drugs (narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) according to the Methods (p. 956); the abstract says positive for opiates (p. 955). No exclusions stated.
sample.demographics: General sample at arrival in Vietnam (tabulation, pp. 956–957; text p. 957): all men; draftees 46%, regular army 54%; age 24 or over 15%, 22–23 17%, 21 18%, 20 34%, 19 or under 16% (half under 21); white 80%, Black 13%, Spanish-American 5%, Oriental 1%, other 1%; 67% had at least a high-school diploma; single 68%, married 29%; 90% had held a full-time civilian job. Before service, 47% had tried an illicit drug (41% a cannabis derivative, and for 17% cannabis was the only one), 11% a narcotic (largely oral codeine or codeine cough syrup) and 2% heroin; one third had been drunk weekly in the year before induction and 4% had a history of 'problems' with alcohol.
sample.attrition: Single interview, no further waves in this paper. Of the 943 selected, 95% were interviewed (898), 92% gave a urine specimen and military records were obtained for 99% (p. 956, Methods, 3rd paragraph); 451 of the 470 in the general sample were interviewed (Table 1 footnote, p. 959; 96%, editors' calculation). The men not interviewed are not described.
sample.selection_effects: One month's returnees from one service at one point in the war: young enlisted men only, no women and no officers; men who did not return home that month are outside the frame by design. The drug-positive sample was selected on a positive urine test and enters the weighted predictor analyses and, unweighted, Table 2 and the Figure. The authors state, without data, that the general sample's drug experience before service did not differ from a national sample of comparable age (p. 957, citing ref. 3).

exposure.measurement: Self-report at one interview 8 to 12 months after return, covering use before service, in Vietnam and since return; interviewers did not know which men had used drugs or which sample they came from (p. 956). Checks: 97% of men whose military records showed heroin use in Vietnam reported it at interview; urine was taken at interview, but men's expectations matched their results poorly (16% of men with a positive specimen had expected it; 42% of those expecting a positive had one), which the authors attribute partly to question design (p. 956, Methods, 3rd paragraph). The share of interview specimens positive for opiates is not reported (the Comment calls it low, p. 961). Addiction was recorded by self-report and by the study's own criteria: three of four of more-than-weekly use for more than a month; at least two of chills, stomach cramps, insomnia and muscle pain on withdrawal; withdrawal lasting at least two days, or at least 12 hours if modified; believing oneself addicted (p. 957).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Among the 196 general-sample men who tried narcotics in Vietnam: fewer than 5 times 24%; 5 or more times but not more than weekly 9%; more than weekly for under 6 months 20%, for 6–8 months 23%, for 9 months or more 25% (p. 957, tabulation). Narcotics in Vietnam were mostly smoked; injection rose with prolonged use, and 40% of men using for nine months or more had injected (pp. 957–958). After return, injection was the preferred method of 63% of men using frequently, and heroin replaced codeine as the narcotic most used (p. 959). Amounts were not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Alongside narcotics in Vietnam: alcohol 92%, marijuana 69% (an estimate), amphetamines 25%, barbiturates 23%; use of all three of narcotics, amphetamines and barbiturates (18% of the general sample) was the rule among men using any of them (pp. 957–958). Other drug use was handled descriptively and by grouping men by the drug class used after return (Table 3, p. 960); one comparison of post-return problems held other drug use since return constant, with no data shown (p. 960).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable in the usual sense. Remission meant not being addicted again between return and interview, a window of 8 to 12 months (on average about ten months, p. 958); many men counted as remitted used narcotics after return (Table 2, p. 959: 33% to 50% of the previously addicted groups).

comparison.controls: No comparison group of the study's own for the remission estimates. The Figure and text set men first addicted in Vietnam beside a published series of 122 patients committed for treatment under the Narcotic Addict Rehabilitation Act (NARA), six months after release to aftercare (ref. 5), described in the text as young (under 30) patients treated at the Lexington and Fort Worth federal hospitals (Figure, p. 956; p. 958). Post-return problems are compared only among veterans grouped by drug use; with no nonveteran or non-Vietnam comparison, the authors say they cannot tell whether these problems were more frequent than expected (p. 959).
comparison.matching: None. The NARA series differs in setting (civilians committed for hospital treatment), in duration of addiction (the authors note that civilians usually reach treatment after several years, p. 961) and in follow-up interval (six months after release, against eight to ten months after return).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-service drug use, drinking, delinquency and family history were recalled at the same interview, one to several years later; only service status, age and education came from military records (p. 956). No pre-service psychiatric assessment.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable for the study (no external control group); not reported for the NARA series.

outcomes.instruments: Structured interview (not named; full presentation in the 1974 monograph, ref. 1), urine at interview, military records and Veterans Administration claims files (p. 956). Post-return outcomes: narcotic use graded as none, light, heavy or addiction (light and heavy are not defined in this paper); addiction by self-report and by the study's criteria; and, in Table 3, perceived drug-related problem, non-traffic arrest, psychiatric treatment, depressive syndrome, unemployment (men out of service six months or more), divorce (men ever married) and alcoholism (p. 960).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study-specific addiction criteria, not a standard diagnostic instrument; self-report checked against military records and urine (p. 956). Definitions of depressive syndrome and alcoholism are not given in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Remission: not addicted again between return and interview. Addiction: three of the four study criteria, or the man's own report (p. 957). 'Remission' therefore includes men who still used narcotics, lightly or heavily.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported. Seven post-return problems were compared across four drug-use groups in Table 3, with significance shown by symbols only and no test named; multivariate predictor analyses for narcotic use in Vietnam, narcotic use after return, heavy use after return and four post-return problems are described in words without statistics (pp. 958–960).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Interviewers did not know beforehand which men had used drugs or which sample they belonged to (p. 956).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only, without confidence intervals or test statistics. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals; general sample n=451, Table 1): narcotic use in Vietnam 43% (about 38.5% to 47.6%); self-reported addiction in Vietnam 20% (16.6% to 23.9%); narcotic use since return 10% (7.6% to 13.1%); addiction since return by the study's criteria 1% (0.4% to 2.4%), about 4 to 5 men, and by self-report 0.7%, about 3 men. In the combined Table 2 group still addicted at departure (n=134), readdiction 14% (9.1% to 20.9%). The statement that only 7% of men using narcotics after return became addicted rests on about 3 of about 45 men in the general sample (editors' calculation from Table 1: 0.7% and 10% of 451).
analysis.covariates: Predictor analyses used automatic interaction detector (AID) and multiple classification analysis (MCA) on the combined samples, with the drug-positive sample weighted to its share of the general sample (p. 958); one comparison held other drug use since return constant (p. 960). Results are given in words, without coefficients, except that pre-service variables together explained 10% of the variance in pre-service drug use (p. 960).
analysis.selective_reporting: The paper presents 'highlights' and refers to the 1974 monograph for the full data (p. 955). Several analyses are described without data: the AID and MCA results; the comparison of men who had and had not used narcotics in Vietnam among those not using narcotics after return (p. 960); and the urine results at interview, the main objective check on post-return use.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Key subgroups are small: 90 general-sample men first addicted in Vietnam (Figure), Table 3 groups of 33 to 71 men, and post-return addiction in the general sample amounting to a handful of men.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a random sample of 451 enlisted men interviewed 8 to 12 months after leaving Vietnam, 43% reported narcotic use and 20% reported addiction in Vietnam (21% met the study's criteria), against 11% narcotic use and 0.2% to 0.4% addiction before service; since return, 10% had used narcotics and 0.7% to 1% had been addicted (Table 1, p. 959). Of the men first addicted in Vietnam, a few percent were addicted again in that window (Figure: about 2% of the general sample's 90 and about 7% of the drug-positive sample's 341), while a third or more used narcotics again; among the 134 men still addicted at departure, 50% used narcotics after return and 14% were addicted again (Table 2). Heavy use of each drug class, injection and a preference for heroin over codeine were more common after return than before service (p. 959).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says usage and addiction essentially fell back to pre-Vietnam levels (p. 955), leaving out the rise in heavy use, injection and heroin preference that the results report (p. 959). The text calls the 95% remission rate one unheard of among treated US patients (p. 958), but the 95% is not tied to a stated sample or denominator, and the comparison is a different study of patients committed for treatment. The Comment concludes that, at least in certain circumstances, opiates are not so addictive that use necessarily leads to addiction or addiction to permanence (p. 961), and states the limits plainly: an atypical setting, a sample homogeneous in age, sex, occupation and period, a short tour, possible concealment and unknown generalizability (p. 961). For post-return problems the wording turns causal: the factors behind discontinuation "should probably be credited with preventing gross maladjustment" (p. 960), although the authors had just said they could not assume that drug use caused these problems (p. 959).

timeline.event: Robins, 'The Vietnam Drug User Returns' (Special Action Office monograph): the full methods and data of this study (ref. 1; on the General list as R3; not read for this card).
This paper: highlights of the first follow-up, 8 to 12 months after return.
A second follow-up about three years after return, with a matched nonveteran comparison group, is described as under way (p. 961).
Helzer, Robins & Davis, antecedents of narcotic use and addiction in the 898 veterans (Drug and Alcohol Dependence; _Dependence-epidemiology list #14; not read for this card).
Robins, on whether the veterans' rapid recovery from heroin addiction was a fluke or a normal expectation (Addiction; _Dependence-epidemiology list #11; not read for this card).
Price et al., 25-year follow-up of remission in the Vietnam cohort, with patterns of treatment use (American Journal of Public Health; General list #20; not read for this card).
Robins, the veterans three years after Vietnam and how the study changed the authors' view of heroin (American Journal on Addictions; _Dependence-epidemiology list #13; not read for this card).
Hall & Weier, methodological appraisal of Lee Robins' Vietnam studies (Addiction; _Dependence-epidemiology list #15; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: The circumstances (a relatively short tour of duty with inexpensive, relatively pure narcotics, then return home, p. 961) cannot be repeated, so the finding has later follow-ups of the same cohort and appraisals rather than independent replications; these are on the project's lists and were not read for this card. Within this paper, the findings concern young enlisted men within about a year of return; they cannot by themselves support statements about remission in people who come to treatment, about long-term remission, or about remission without treatment.

funding.funder: No funding statement or acknowledgement is printed. The introduction states that the White House Special Action Office for Drug Abuse Prevention (SAODAP) arranged for and assisted in the follow-up study (p. 955); the full report is a SAODAP monograph (ref. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Washington University School of Medicine, St Louis (p. 955). Completed interviews were sent to the Addiction Research Foundation in Canada under a link-file system so that no one could connect answers to names (p. 956). The study was set up by a White House drug-policy office to plan treatment for returning soldiers; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people identified when regular opioid use begins rather than when they reach treatment, followed for several years with a standard diagnostic interview, repeated biological testing and a record of any treatment, beside a matched comparison group and including people who leave the setting where their use began, would show how often, for how long and under what conditions opioid addiction remits without treatment.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The frame is the population the paper describes: all Army enlisted men and draftees returning from Vietnam in September 1971, from Department of Defense and Surgeon General lists (p. 956). How far this population stands for other people who use heroin is a question of indirectness, not of this item.

Random samples from complete lists; prevalence estimates come from the general sample, and the drug-positive sample is weighted in the predictor analyses (pp. 956, 958). Table 2 mixes the samples unweighted (see reporting issues).

451 interviews give headline prevalences to within about 4 to 5 percentage points (editors' calculation), but post-return addiction in the general sample rests on a handful of men, and remission estimates on 90 general-sample men first addicted in Vietnam.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Service status, age, race, education, marital status, work history and pre-service drug and alcohol use are tabulated for the general sample, and the setting is described (pp. 955–957).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 95% of the 943 men and 451 of the 470 in the general sample were interviewed (p. 956; Table 1 footnote, p. 959).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Addiction was defined by the study's own criteria, one of which is the man's belief that he was addicted, or by self-report alone; use before and in Vietnam was recalled one to several years later; light and heavy use are not defined in this paper. Self-report agreed well with military records of heroin use (97%), but the urine results at interview, the only biological check on post-return use, are not reported (pp. 956–957, 961).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same interview for all men, by interviewers who did not know their drug history or sample (p. 956).

Simple percentages from a random sample suit the descriptive aims, but no confidence intervals are given, significance is shown by symbols without tests, multivariate results have no coefficients, the 95% remission figure has no stated denominator, and Table 2 pools the two samples without weighting or saying so (pp. 958–960).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Interview completion 95% overall and about 96% in the general sample (p. 956; editors' calculation).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A random sample of a defined population, interviewed almost completely by interviewers blind to drug history, with record checks: strong features for 1975. The limits on its numbers come from self-reported, partly retrospective drug use judged by non-standard criteria, an unreported urine check after return, a short window of 8 to 12 months, and thin statistical reporting. The source may be cited for the proportions who used narcotics and met the study's addiction criteria before, in and after Vietnam in this population, and for the observation that few men addicted in Vietnam were addicted again in the first year home, many of them still using narcotics. It may not be cited for remission rates in general, for remission lasting beyond a year, for remission without treatment (how many men received drug treatment is not reported), or for effects of drug use on post-return problems, which rest on unadjusted, cross-sectional comparisons without a comparison group and would be at high risk of confounding under ROBINS-E.

key_findings.finding: Sampling: about 13,760 Army enlisted men returned from Vietnam to the United States in September 1971; a random 'general sample' of 470 was drawn from them, and a random 'drug-positive sample' of 495 from the about 1,400 whose departure urine was positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates; 22 men were in both samples, 943 in all. Between May and September 1972, 8 to 12 months after return, 95% were interviewed, 92% gave urine and military records were found for 99%.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Before service (general sample at arrival in Vietnam): 47% had tried an illicit drug, 41% a cannabis derivative (cannabis only, 17%), 11% a narcotic, mostly oral codeine or codeine cough syrup, and 2% heroin; under 1% had used any narcotic more than 25 times, and 13% had used any illicit drug more than a few times, almost always marijuana. Addiction to narcotics before Vietnam: 0.2% by self-report and 0.4% by the study's criteria (Table 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pre-Vietnam Profile, tabulation (pp. 956–957) and 2nd paragraph (p. 957); Table 1 (p. 959)

key_findings.finding: In Vietnam (interviewed general sample, N=451): alcohol 92%, marijuana 69% (estimated), any of narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates 46%, narcotics 43%, amphetamines 25%, barbiturates 23%; about one third tried heroin and about one third opium, and most who tried either tried both. Of the 196 men who tried narcotics, 24% used them fewer than 5 times, 9% five or more times but not more than weekly, and more than weekly 20% for under 6 months, 23% for 6–8 months and 25% for 9 months or more; 46% reported addiction and 47% met the study's criteria, which the authors translate into 20% of the whole general sample using more than weekly for at least six months, 20% reporting addiction and 21% meeting the criteria.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 1st to 3rd paragraphs and both tabulations
key_findings.note: The in-text tabulation gives 46% for any of the three drug classes and 16% for narcotics only, while Table 1 (p. 959), for the same 451 men, gives 45% and 15% (see reporting issues). Editors' arithmetic: 48% of the 196 used more than weekly for 6 months or more (23% + 25%).

key_findings.finding: The study's addiction criteria: three of four of more-than-weekly use for more than one month; at least two withdrawal symptoms among chills, stomach cramps, insomnia and muscle pain; withdrawal lasting at least two days unmodified or 12 hours modified; and the man's belief that he was addicted.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Narcotic use in Vietnam began early in the tour: one fifth of the men who used them started in the first week and three fifths within two months; only one fourth waited more than four months. The authors report no correlation between drug use and assignments, danger or death of friends (no statistics shown). Narcotics were mostly smoked; 40% of men using for nine months or more had injected.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 3rd paragraph (p. 957, continuing p. 958) and 5th paragraph (p. 958)

key_findings.finding: Pre-service predictors of narcotic use in Vietnam (both samples, weighted; AID and MCA, no coefficients printed): pre-service drug use, especially of several drugs, heavy drinking, arrests, not completing high school, growing up in a large city and being under 20 at arrival; first-term volunteers used drugs almost twice as often as draftees, also after controlling for the other predictors; being 24 or older best predicted avoiding drugs. No demographic characteristic predicted trying narcotics without heavy use; at least half of every group that tried narcotics used them heavily.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use in Vietnam, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: After return (Table 1, general sample, N=451, before / in / since Vietnam): narcotics 11% / 43% / 10%; addiction by self-report 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%; addiction by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%; amphetamines 24% / 25% / 19%; barbiturates 14% / 23% / 12%; marijuana 41% / 69% / 45%. About half of the men who used narcotics in Vietnam had become addicted, against 7% of those who used them after return; only 7% thought heroin use acceptable in Vietnam and 3% in the United States.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 1st paragraph (p. 958); Table 1 (p. 959)

key_findings.finding: Remission: the authors state an addiction remission rate of 95% for men who had been addicted in Vietnam and set it beside young patients treated at the Lexington and Fort Worth federal hospitals and re-examined six months later. In the Figure, narcotic use 8 to 10 months after return among men first addicted in Vietnam was, read approximately from the plotted points: general sample (N=90) about 65% no use, 21% light use, 12% heavy use, 2% addiction; drug-positive sample (N=341) about 61%, 22%, 10% and 7%; 122 NARA patients six months after release to aftercare (ref. 5) about 11%, 6%, 14% and 70%.
key_findings.locator: Figure (p. 956); Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 1st paragraph (p. 958)
key_findings.note: Figure values read from a 300-dpi rendering against 10-point gridlines; approximate to about 1 to 2 percentage points. Light and heavy use are not defined in this paper. An inset shows men with narcotic experience before Vietnam (N=106): about 44% no use, 33% light, 9% heavy and 12% addiction; which sample the inset uses is not stated. The 95% is not tied to either sample (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Table 2 (by use and addiction at departure; both samples combined, unweighted): still addicted, used at departure because they could not stop (n=134): 50% used any narcotic after return, 14% dependent; previously addicted and still using at departure (155): 35% and 5%; previously addicted, no use in the last 3 days (137): 33% and 5%; not addicted, still using (46): 17% and 0; not addicted, no use in the last 3 days (157): 10% and 2%; no narcotic use in Vietnam (269): 0.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 2nd paragraph (p. 958); Table 2 (p. 959)
key_findings.note: The row Ns sum to 898, all men interviewed in both samples, so the percentages mix the general and drug-positive samples without weighting (editors' arithmetic). Across the three previously addicted rows (426 men), about 8% were dependent and about 39% used any narcotic after return (editors' calculation, weighted by row N).

key_findings.finding: Timing and supply after return: men had been home on average ten months at interview; resumption of narcotics generally began within four months of return (median between the second and third month); 84% of men who used narcotics after return found a source within eight weeks, and men in all parts of the country reported ready availability; the deterrents cited most were expense, fear of addiction and fear of arrest.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 2nd paragraph (p. 958, continuing p. 959)

key_findings.finding: Heavy use did not fall back to pre-service levels: since return, 3% had had a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use, 6% regular amphetamine use, 3% regular barbiturate use and 25% heavy marijuana use, against under 0.5%, 3%, 2% and 12% before Vietnam. After return, injection became the preferred route of 63% of men using narcotics frequently, and heroin replaced codeine as the narcotic most used; the drug-positive sample showed the same trends.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Predictors of narcotic use after return (both samples combined): injecting narcotics in Vietnam raised the chance of later use from 9% overall to 32%, and injecting before service from 9% to 24%; weaker predictors were dependence in Vietnam or earlier in service, heavy barbiturate or amphetamine use in Vietnam, more than six months of narcotic use in Vietnam and low rank; pre-service predictors were weaker than in-service ones.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use After Vietnam, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Table 3 (general-sample men who used narcotics in Vietnam, N=196, by drug used after return: narcotic n=43 / amphetamine or barbiturate n=49 / marijuana only n=71 / none n=33): perceived drug-related problem 23% / 7% / 11% / 6%; non-traffic arrest 49 / 22 / 25 / 15; psychiatric treatment 26 / 12 / 6 / 12; depressive syndrome 16 / 14 / 10 / 3; unemployed (out of service 6 months or more) 38 / 14 / 19 / 10; divorced (ever married) 42 / 36 / 28 / 7; alcoholism 12 / 6 / 13 / 6. Symbols mark the narcotic group as significantly higher for drug-related problem, arrest, psychiatric treatment and unemployment, and men using any drug as higher than men using none for divorce.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and footnotes

key_findings.finding: Among men who used no narcotics after return, those who had used narcotics in Vietnam had more arrests than those who had not, but no other statistically significant ill effects, holding other drug use since return constant (no data shown). In the multivariate analysis, drug use in and before Vietnam was the strongest predictor of post-return arrests, depression, unemployment and divorce (no coefficients shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug Use and Post-Vietnam Adjustment, 3rd paragraph (p. 959, continuing p. 960) and 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Validity checks: 97% of men whose military records showed heroin use in Vietnam admitted it at interview; only 16% of men whose interview urine was positive had expected a positive result, and only 42% of those expecting one had it; 97% of men interviewed gave a urine specimen large enough to test. The proportion of positive specimens is not given.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors contrast their remission with earlier US follow-ups of hospitalized patients (relapse 80% to more than 90%, readdiction over 70%; refs 5–8), conclude that in certain circumstances people can use narcotics regularly and even become addicted yet stop in another social setting, and leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change of setting explains the remission. They list as limits the atypical setting, a sample homogeneous in age, sex, occupation and period, the short tour, possible concealment and unknown generalizability, and plan a three-year follow-up with a matched nonveteran group.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 960); 4th to 7th paragraphs (p. 961)

key_findings.finding: Pre-service characteristics associated with pre-service drug use (arrests, unemployment, race, early drunkenness, truancy, large city, age, parental problems) together explained only 10% of its variance.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Treatment context: from June 1971 servicemen due to leave Vietnam had mandatory urine screening, meant to identify men with recent illicit drug use and hold them for detoxification and treatment (the program whose positive results defined the drug-positive sample); the September 1971 cohort was chosen partly so that the men had had comparable chances of treatment while in the military. Psychiatric treatment since return is tabulated for general-sample men who used narcotics in Vietnam (Table 3: 26% of the 43 who used narcotics after return, 12% of the 33 who used no drugs; kind of treatment not stated), but the number of men who received drug treatment, before or after return, and its relation to remission are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 955); Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 955, continuing on p. 956); Table 3 (p. 960)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the drug-positive sample as men whose urine was positive for opiates at departure (p. 955); the Methods say it was drawn from men whose urine was positive for illicit drugs, defined as narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates (p. 956).
reporting_issues.consequence: The drug-positive sample may include men detected for amphetamines or barbiturates only; results for that sample (Figure, Table 2) should not be described as results for men who tested positive for opiates.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% remission rate for men addicted in Vietnam is given without its sample or denominator (p. 958). The Figure shows about 2% (general sample) and about 7% (drug-positive sample) addicted again, and the three previously addicted rows of Table 2 give about 8% dependent after return (editors' calculation). The Results open by saying that figures are for the general sample unless otherwise noted (p. 956), which would make the 95% a general-sample figure, yet the Figure implies about 98% remission in that sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 95% cannot be reproduced from the printed data; claims should give the sample-specific figures and say that 'remission' meant not being addicted again within 8 to 12 months, with many men still using narcotics.

reporting_issues.issue: Neither Table 2 nor its footnote says that it combines the general and drug-positive samples, and no weighting is mentioned; by the editors' arithmetic its row Ns (134, 155, 137, 46, 157, 269) sum to 898, the number interviewed in both samples (title, p. 955).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2 percentages over-represent men detected at departure; they describe groups defined by departure status, not the population of returnees.

reporting_issues.issue: For the same interviewed general sample (N=451), the in-text tabulation of drug use in Vietnam gives 46% for any of narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates and 16% for narcotics only (p. 957), while Table 1 gives 45% and 15% (p. 959).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one-point differences that do not change any conclusion, but a claim should cite one source and say which.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure is captioned as narcotic use eight to ten months after Vietnam (p. 956), while interviews took place 8 to 12 months after return (p. 956, Methods) and averaged about ten months (p. 958).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the window behind the Figure is not stated precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The pre-service profile tabulation is introduced as describing the general sample of 470 (p. 956), but only status, age and education came from military records; the drug-experience rows can only come from the 451 interviews.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the denominator for pre-service drug experience is probably 451, as in Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance in Table 3 is shown only by symbols, with no test, statistic or p value; the text says men who kept using narcotics after return exceeded the other men who had used narcotics in Vietnam in depression and divorce (p. 960), but Table 3 marks neither of these comparisons as significant, and the significant unemployment difference is not mentioned in that sentence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The depression and divorce differences between post-return narcotic use and other drug use should not be cited as statistically supported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment says the cohort was not preselected on any variable known to predispose to drug use (p. 961), which is true of the general sample but not of the drug-positive sample, selected on a positive urine test and used in the predictor analyses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Generalizability arguments for the predictor analyses rest on the weighting of the drug-positive sample, which is described only briefly (p. 958).

design_detail: Commentary (journal section 'Commentary') in Addiction by one author, Shane Darke (National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales), on Stam et al. (2019), the Australian study that compared a close review of coronial records of heroin-related deaths with official figures for the same period. Two pages, five references, no new data: it is evidence of a published comment, not of findings.
can_establish: That a published commentary endorsed Stam et al.'s finding that official figures under-report heroin-related deaths, restated two problems it presents as identified, in context by Stam et al. (deaths recorded as multiple drug toxicity, and heroin deaths recorded as morphine toxicity), adding its own statements that most heroin-related deaths are due to multiple drug toxicity and that 6MAM identifies only deaths after short survival, and argued that psychostimulant- and cannabis-related deaths are under-reported too.
cannot_establish: The size of any error in official counts (it repeats Stam et al.'s 32% without counts, period or denominator), whether its explanations account for the shortfall, whether some deaths are wrongly attributed to heroin, or anything about psychostimulant or cannabis deaths, for which it gives no data.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a commentary with no participants or data.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author without a search: five references, of which one is the target study and two are the author's own studies (Darke & Duflou 2016; Darke, Kaye & Duflou 2017).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable: no data were collected. The commentary discusses how heroin-related deaths are recorded in coronial records and then coded into official statistics.
exposure.polysubstance: Raised as an argument, without data: the commentary says most heroin-related deaths involve multiple drug toxicity, typically alcohol and/or benzodiazepines as well as heroin, and that deaths recorded as 'multiple drug toxicity' appear to be missed by official coders (PDF p. 1, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; the commentary does not define 'drug-related death', 'heroin-related death' or 'under-reporting'.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. It restates one figure from Stam et al.: 32% under-reporting in the official figures compared with the authors' review of coronial records (PDF p. 1, 1st paragraph), without counts, period, case definition or denominator.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a commentary.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results: the commentary restates Stam et al.'s 32% under-reporting figure and the problems it describes as identified (in context, by Stam et al.), adds its own elaborations, and extends the argument to psychostimulants and cannabis, supported by citations rather than data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: That there is good reason to believe official statistics substantially underestimate drug-related death (PDF p. 1, 1st paragraph); that the shortfall is not the result of a conspiracy but appears to be due to inadequate understanding of heroin-related death among those compiling the figures (2nd paragraph); that the problem is general, since there is no reason to believe it is local to Australia (2nd paragraph); and that official psychostimulant-related death counts are "absurdly low" compared with coronial records because deaths from cardiovascular disease, stroke, traumatic accident and suicide, which it calls attributable to psychostimulant use, are missed (3rd paragraph). The generalizations beyond one Australian heroin study, and the attribution of deaths from causes other than acute toxicity to psychostimulants, are asserted rather than shown; the opposite error, deaths wrongly attributed to a drug, is not considered.

timeline.event: Darke & Duflou: the toxicology of heroin-related death and estimated survival times; cited by the commentary for its statement that 6MAM identifies only deaths with survival under 30 minutes, which it says are a minority (as cited, PDF p. 1; not read).
Stam et al.: the study commented on, comparing a review of coronial records of heroin-related deaths with official figures (cited in the commentary as Addiction 2018, online).
Robertson, Bird & McAuley: letter calling this commentary insightful and arguing for a wider view of drug-related deaths, including late deaths among older people who use or used drugs.

replication.where_it_stands: A supportive comment by an author of earlier Australian studies of drug deaths. For the size and definition of the under-reporting, cite Stam et al. (2019) itself; the commentary adds explanations and a call for more studies of coronial records, not evidence.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declaration of interests: None (PDF p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Shane Darke, National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales, NSW, Australia. Two of the five references are his own studies, including the one behind the 30-minute 6MAM statement. Submitted 25 November 2018; final version accepted 30 November 2018 (PDF p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A study that re-codes a complete set of coronial records of drug deaths in several jurisdictions with explicit rules, compares them case by case with the official coded statistics in both directions (deaths missed and deaths wrongly included), and counts how many discrepancies arise from 'multiple drug toxicity' or 'morphine toxicity' certifications, testing the commentary's explanations directly.

domains.note: No search and no selection criteria: a two-page commentary citing five references chosen by the author.

Stam et al.'s method and figure are accepted without appraisal (for example, how the coronial-record review defined a heroin-related death and whether it could misclassify), and the cited studies are not appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of the five references are the author's own; the 30-minute 6MAM detection window, central to the second explanation, rests on his own study.

Much is hedged ('appears', 'likely'), but some statements are categorical and uncited (that it is well known most heroin-related deaths are due to multiple drug toxicity; that heroin itself is never detected in toxicology), and the global generalization and the psychostimulant attribution are asserted.

domains.domain: Balance of directions of counting error (undercounting versus overcounting)
domains.note: Only undercounting is argued. Deaths in which a drug was present but not the cause, and the limits of coronial records as the reference, are not discussed; overcounting is the under-represented side.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A single-author commentary without a search or appraisal, weighted to one direction of error; the overall rating cannot be milder than its worst domains. Cite it for: the existence of a published commentary in Addiction endorsing Stam et al.'s finding of under-reporting; its restatement of two problems as identified, in context by Stam et al. (deaths recorded as multiple drug toxicity, and heroin deaths recorded as morphine toxicity); its own additions (that most heroin-related deaths are due to multiple drug toxicity, and that 6MAM identifies only deaths after short survival) as the author's arguments; and its call for more studies of coronial records. Do not cite it for the size of the under-count (take that from Stam et al.), for claims about other countries, or for the attribution of psychostimulant- or cannabis-related deaths.

key_findings.finding: Type and author: a two-page Commentary in Addiction by Shane Darke (National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales) on Stam et al.; declaration of interests: none; submitted 25 November 2018, final version accepted 30 November 2018.
key_findings.locator: Title; author block; Declaration of interests (right column)

key_findings.finding: Stam et al.'s result as restated by the commentary: their close examination of coronial records of heroin-related death, compared with official figures for the same period, showed 32% under-reporting in the official figures. No counts, period, case definition or denominator are given.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 1st paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Why the shortfall: the commentary says it is not the result of a conspiracy but appears to be due to inadequate understanding of heroin-related death among those collecting official figures. It then describes two major problems as identified, without saying by whom (in context Stam et al., whose issues it later calls applicable globally). The first: it states as well known that most heroin-related deaths are due to multiple drug toxicity (typically involving alcohol and/or benzodiazepines as well as heroin); coronial records frequently give the cause in such cases as 'multiple drug toxicity', and these deaths appear to be systematically missed by official coders.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: The second problem: the complex metabolism of heroin is said to appear to cause coding errors. Heroin is described as a prodrug never detected in toxicology, rapidly metabolized to 6-monoacetylmorphine (6MAM) and then morphine; 6MAM, often used as the marker of a heroin overdose death, is said to identify only deaths with survival times under 30 minutes, a minority (citing the author's own study, Darke & Duflou 2016); coronial records frequently give 'morphine toxicity' as the cause, and it would appear that such deaths are often missed by those coding official statistics, who attribute them to morphine rather than heroin.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Generalization: the commentary states there is no reason to think the problem is local to Australia, as the issues apply globally; no data are offered.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph, last sentence (left column)

key_findings.finding: Extension to other drugs: official counts of psychostimulant-related deaths are said to be very low compared with coronial records because such deaths are mostly from causes other than acute toxicity (cardiovascular disease, stroke, traumatic accident, suicide), which the commentary calls attributable to psychostimulant use; a similar situation is said to be likely for cannabis, where no deaths from acute cannabis toxicity are documented and traumatic accident is the main contributor to mortality.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 3rd paragraph (starts in the left column, continues in the right)

key_findings.finding: Recommendations: official coders work as well as resources allow, but need more detailed knowledge of the causality, circumstances and toxicology of drug-related death; more studies of coronial records are needed, as few are done and many studies analyse official statistics only.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 4th paragraph (right column)

reporting_issues.issue: Stam et al.'s result is given only as a percentage (32% under-reporting in the official figures), with no counts, period, jurisdiction, case definition or denominator, so it is not clear whether 32% is a share of the coronial-record total or of the official count.
reporting_issues.consequence: The commentary cannot be cited for the size of the under-count; take the figure, its definition and its denominator from Stam et al. (2019).

reporting_issues.issue: Some factual statements are categorical and carry no citation: that it is well known most heroin-related deaths are due to multiple drug toxicity, and that heroin itself is never detected in toxicology.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are the commentator's statements, not evidence; claims that need them should cite primary studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that psychostimulant-related deaths are predominantly due to causes other than acute toxicity (cardiovascular disease, stroke, traumatic accident, suicide) is cited to references 2–4, but reference 2 (Darke & Duflou 2016) is, by its title, a study of survival times in heroin-related death.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only references 3 and 4 appear, from their titles, to concern psychostimulant deaths; the citation range may be an error, and the psychostimulant argument rests on at most two cited studies.

No supplement.
