design_detail: Retrospective agreement (test-accuracy) study in one US coroner/medical examiner office (Jefferson County Coroner/Medical Examiner Office, Alabama). Sixty deaths from 2017 that had a full autopsy, all autopsied by the first author, were selected by a method the paper does not describe; they included 38 accidental deaths from drug toxicity and 22 natural deaths. Three other forensic pathologists from the same office, all co-authors, independently assigned cause of death (COD) and manner of death (MOD) from written narratives of the history and scene investigation, the external examination and the toxicology report, without internal-examination or microscopic findings (the index classification). Their answers were compared with the COD and MOD in the original case file, certified after full autopsy (the reference). Statistics: percent agreement per reviewer, and Cohen's kappa for MOD against the case file and between reviewers. A 3-page original article.
can_establish: How often, in a selected set of clear-cut drug-toxicity and natural deaths from one office, three pathologists working without internal-examination findings reached the same cause and manner of death as the autopsy pathologist who had them.
cannot_establish: The error rate of certifying suspected drug deaths without autopsy in routine practice; how much of the disagreement comes from the missing internal examination rather than from differences between pathologists (no reviewer classified the cases with the full file); or in which direction the errors go (natural deaths called drug deaths, or drug deaths missed), which the paper does not report.

sample.recruitment: Records: the office's case management database. From 629 deaths in 2017 with a full autopsy (external and internal examination with microscopy), the authors excluded homicides, suicides and undetermined manners, and accidental deaths from motor vehicles, asphyxia, falls, fires, firearms and one envenomation (386 left); then the 277 cases autopsied by other pathologists, so that reviewers would not recognize their own cases (109 left, all autopsied by the first author); and cases with contributing factors. Sixty cases were then selected (pp. 99–100, Materials and Methods, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: 2017 deaths with full autopsy by the first author, case-file manner accident (drug toxicity) or natural, no contributing factors. Excluded: homicide, suicide, undetermined manner; accidents from motor vehicles, asphyxia, falls, fires, firearms and envenomation; other pathologists' cases. How the 60 were chosen from the 109, and how many cases were removed for contributing factors, is not stated.
sample.demographics: Decedents aged 21 to 77 years (mean 44); 44 men and 16 women (p. 100). Race, postmortem interval, decomposition and the drugs involved are not reported.
sample.attrition: None: all 60 cases were classified by all three reviewers and analysed.
sample.selection_effects: A deliberately simplified case mix: only accidental drug-toxicity deaths and natural deaths without contributing factors, from one pathologist's caseload in one office and one year, with drug deaths making up 38 of 60. Homicides, suicides, undetermined deaths and deaths with contributing factors, where an internal examination might matter most, were excluded, and the method of selecting the final 60 is not described. The results may not apply to other offices, other certifiers or the full range of suspected drug deaths.

exposure.measurement: Index classification: each reviewer's COD and MOD from a written narrative of the history and scene investigation, the external examination and the toxicology report, set as a series of questions designed by the first author; no internal or microscopic findings were given (p. 100, Materials and Methods, 2nd paragraph). The narratives stand in for an external examination: the reviewers did not examine the bodies. Reference: the COD and MOD in the original case file, decided by the first author after full autopsy, with the same investigation and toxicology plus internal examination and microscopy.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: no drug was given. Toxicology information was supplied for every test case, but the paper does not report which drugs were found, in which specimens, or the laboratory methods.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: no breakdown of the drugs found or of single- versus multiple-drug deaths among the 38 drug-toxicity deaths, and no description of toxicology findings in the 22 natural deaths.

comparison.controls: The reference is a single pathologist's full-autopsy determination (the first author's), which the authors treat as the correct answer. There was no control condition in which reviewers classified the same cases with the full case file, so disagreement between pathologists who have complete information is not measured; the reviewers' moderate agreement with each other (kappa 0.53 to 0.61) suggests it is not negligible.
comparison.matching: Same cases, and the same investigation and toxicology information, for index and reference; only internal and microscopic findings were withheld.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to decedents as such. Case features that could affect classification (postmortem interval, decomposition, drugs and concentrations found, the natural diseases found at autopsy) are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Percent agreement with the case file for COD and for MOD, per reviewer, for all 60 cases and in two subgroups; Cohen's ('simple') kappa for MOD against the case file and between reviewers (p. 100, Materials and Methods, 3rd paragraph; Results). Every reviewer classified every case; kappa was computed for MOD only.
outcomes.validity_norms: Kappa read on a conventional scale: 0 or below no agreement; 0.01 to 0.20 none to slight; 0.21 to 0.40 fair; 0.41 to 0.60 moderate; 0.61 to 0.80 substantial; 0.81 to 1.00 almost perfect (p. 100). Reviewers could choose among five manners (natural, accident, undetermined, homicide, suicide), while the reference set contained only accidents and natural deaths.
outcomes.operationalization: A classification counted as correct when it agreed with the case file. What counted as agreement on cause of death (identical wording, the same drug or drugs, or the same broad category) is not defined.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests, p values or confidence intervals are reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Reviewers had no internal or microscopic findings, had not autopsied these cases (pathologists in the office do not cosign one another's reports), and worked separately without discussing the cases (pp. 99–100). The questions were designed by the first author, who had performed the autopsies and knew the final COD and MOD; the reviewers are his colleagues and co-authors.

analysis.effect_sizes: COD agreement with the case file by reviewer: 71.6%, 66.6% and 80.0% (mean reported as 73%). MOD agreement: 85.0%, 70.0% and 85.0% (mean 80%). Kappa for MOD against the case file: 0.71, 0.46 and 0.69. Kappa between reviewers: 0.54, 0.61 and 0.53, pairs not identified (p. 100, Tables 1–3). No confidence intervals are given. Editors' calculation (counts implied by the percentages of 60: 43, 40 and 48 for COD; 51, 42 and 51 for MOD; Wilson 95% intervals): COD 59.2–81.5%, 54.1–77.3% and 68.2–88.2%; MOD 73.9–91.9%, 57.5–80.1% and 73.9–91.9%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is reported. The paper states a null hypothesis (that a full autopsy is not necessary to classify COD and MOD correctly) but sets no level of agreement in advance that would count as adequate, and reports no formal test of it (pp. 99, 101).
analysis.selective_reporting: No cross-tabulation of the reviewers' answers against the case file is given, so the paper does not show what the wrong answers were (a natural death called a drug death, a drug death called natural or undetermined, or a different drug named). The reviewer pairs behind the inter-reviewer kappas are not identified, and the tables do not print subgroup sizes (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not reported. With 60 cases, each reviewer's agreement has a 95% interval reaching roughly 7 to 13 percentage points either side of the estimate (editors' calculation above). With three reviewers, comparisons between reviewers, for example by experience, are anecdotal, as the authors say (p. 101).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Without internal-examination findings, three pathologists matched the autopsy pathologist's COD in 66.6% to 80.0% of 60 selected cases and the MOD in 70.0% to 85.0% (kappa 0.46 to 0.71), and agreed with each other only moderately (kappa 0.53 to 0.61). The design cannot say how much of the disagreement is due to the missing internal examination, and the paper does not report whether the errors would add drug deaths to the count or remove them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that a full postmortem examination is necessary to classify COD and MOD correctly in suspected drug toxicity (p. 99), and the last paragraph that the accuracy gained justifies autopsy for the authors' office and, "to our thinking, for the nation" (p. 101). The Discussion is less settled: it opens by saying that substantial agreement with the case file can be achieved without the internal examination (p. 100, Discussion, 2nd paragraph), says an internal examination may not be necessary when the investigation or history indicates drug use, and asks whether an office overwhelmed by deaths would accept 75% to 80% accuracy from a simple rule, and then whether it would need a forensic pathologist at all (p. 101, 4th and 5th paragraphs). No acceptable level of agreement was set in advance, the stated null hypothesis was not formally tested, the simple rule was not tested, and the 75% (COD) and 80% (MOD) given for cases with a drug history do not match the results reported for those cases (80% to 83% for COD; see reporting issues). That 73% to 80% agreement is not good enough is the authors' value judgment, reasonable but not a finding.

timeline.event: NAME Forensic Autopsy Performance Standards published (approved 2005); Standard B3.7 calls for a forensic autopsy when death is by apparent intoxication, later amended to allow an exception when a significant interval has passed and the medical findings and absence of trauma are well documented (as described in this paper, p. 99).

Gruszecki, Booth & Davis: predictive value of history and scene investigation for toxicology results in a medical examiner population; cited by the authors as showing that investigation alone predicts toxicology findings less well than investigation with autopsy and toxicology testing (as described here, p. 101; not read).
This study: 60 selected deaths in one Alabama office, three reviewers without internal-examination findings.
Hancock et al.: false-positive rate for suspected drug-related deaths following full autopsy; listed by the project to be read with this study; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: A small single-office study with no direct replication known to this card. Among selected cases, certification without the internal examination disagreed with the autopsy-based certification in about 20% to 33% of cases for cause and 15% to 30% for manner, but the paper does not show which way a death count would move. Hancock et al. (2024) is the later study the project pairs with it.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (p. 99).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Pathology (Dye, Atherton, McCleskey, Davis) and Department of Epidemiology (McGwin), University of Alabama at Birmingham. The first author designed the questions and performed all 60 reference autopsies; the three reviewers (Davis, Atherton, McCleskey) are co-authors who work in the same office, which autopsies all suspected intoxications under the NAME standards. The NAME position paper on certifying opioid deaths cited as ref. 5 is listed under Davis GG, the senior author's name. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of consecutive suspected drug deaths in several offices in which pathologists independent of the autopsy certify each case twice, once from the investigation, external examination and toxicology alone and once with the full autopsy, with a control group of pathologists given the full file and a consensus reference, reporting every discordant case by direction (drug deaths missed versus other deaths wrongly called drug deaths) and by drug.

domains.note: Not a consecutive or random series: 60 cases selected by an unstated method from the 109 left after excluding all manners other than accident and natural, accidents other than drug toxicity, other pathologists' cases and cases with contributing factors (pp. 99–100). The case mix is two-category and enriched for clear-cut cases.

Reviewers were blind to internal and microscopic findings and to the case-file result, and worked separately (p. 100), but the questions they answered were designed by the autopsy pathologist, who knew the final COD and MOD, so knowledge of the outcome could have shaped what the narratives included. No criterion for agreement on COD was defined.

The reference is one pathologist's full-autopsy certification, treated as correct, with no independent or consensus review. Inter-reviewer kappas of 0.53 to 0.61 (p. 100) show that certification varies between pathologists, so disagreement with one certifier is not the same as error. The reference also incorporates all the information the reviewers had.
Every case had the reference standard (full autopsy), and all 60 cases were classified by all three reviewers and analysed.
Clear-cut accidental drug-toxicity and natural deaths without contributing factors, from one pathologist in one office in one year: not the mix of cases an office would have to triage.
Reading a narrative summary is not the same as performing an external examination, and toxicology was available in every case.
Full autopsy is the accepted reference, but here one certifier's conclusions define it.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Patient selection and the single-certifier reference standard are at high risk of bias and the index test is unclear; QUADAS-2 has no overall algorithm, and the editors rate the study at high risk because two bias domains are high. The agreement figures are descriptive and imprecise (60 cases, three reviewers). Cite it for: in 60 selected deaths in one US office in 2017, three pathologists without internal-examination findings matched the autopsy pathologist's cause of death in 66.6% to 80.0% of cases and the manner in 70.0% to 85.0%, and agreed with each other only moderately; and for the authors' view that autopsy remains justified. Do not cite it for an error rate of certification without autopsy in routine practice, for the direction of error (overcounting or undercounting drug deaths), or for its subgroup figures, whose group definitions and sizes are inconsistent.

key_findings.finding: Case selection: from 629 deaths with full autopsy at the office in 2017, exclusions left 386 (no homicides, suicides or undetermined manners, and no accidents from motor vehicles, asphyxia, falls, fires, firearms or envenomation); the 277 cases of other pathologists were then excluded, leaving 109 autopsied by the first author; after excluding cases with contributing factors, 60 were selected: 38 accidental drug-toxicity deaths and 22 natural deaths, aged 21 to 77 (mean 44), 44 men and 16 women.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 1st paragraph (starts on p. 99, continues on p. 100)
key_findings.note: How the 60 were chosen from the 109, and how many cases were excluded for contributing factors, is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Index and reference: three board-certified forensic pathologists from the same office (25, 4 and 2 years in practice) each classified cause and manner of death from a narrative of the history and scene investigation, the external examination and the toxicology report, with no internal or microscopic findings, working separately; their answers were compared with the case-file cause and manner certified after full autopsy.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Subgroups by investigation findings: 43 decedents had a past medical history of illicit or prescription drug use or drug paraphernalia at the scene; 17 had neither.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cause of death agreed with the case file in 71.6%, 66.6% and 80.0% of the 60 cases for reviewers 1, 2 and 3 (mean reported as 73%; range given in the text as 66% to 80%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1, row 'All 60 cases'
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: implied counts 43, 40 and 48 of 60; Wilson 95% intervals 59.2–81.5%, 54.1–77.3% and 68.2–88.2%. The printed 71.6% and 66.6% are truncated rather than rounded (43/60 is 71.7%, 40/60 is 66.7%).

key_findings.finding: Manner of death agreed with the case file in 85.0%, 70.0% and 85.0% of cases (mean 80%); kappa against the case file was 0.71, 0.46 and 0.69, read by the authors, in the abstract, as substantial for two reviewers and moderate for one.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, 3rd paragraph (p. 99), for the authors' reading of the kappas; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Table 2 and Table 3, row 'All 60 cases' (p. 100), for the values
key_findings.note: The text lists the kappas as 0.71, 0.69 and 0.46; the card follows Table 3's order by reviewer. Editors' calculation: Wilson 95% intervals for agreement 73.9–91.9%, 57.5–80.1% and 73.9–91.9%.

key_findings.finding: Kappa for manner of death between reviewers was 0.54, 0.61 and 0.53, described by the authors as only moderate agreement; the Discussion opens its 2nd paragraph by saying that substantial agreement with the case file can be achieved without the internal examination, but that agreement between reviewers is inconsistent: one pathologist could get the correct cause and manner, but the result was not consistently reproducible with other pathologists.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (continues in the right column); Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The pairs behind the three values are not identified; 0.61 falls in the paper's own 'substantial' band (0.61 to 0.80).

key_findings.finding: By investigation findings (text): with a drug history or paraphernalia, cause-of-death agreement ranged from 80% to 83%; without, from 40% to 80%. Kappa for manner against the case file was 0.73, 0.39 and 0.28 with a drug history and 0.43, 0.25 and 0.75 without.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Tables 1–3, 2nd and 3rd rows
key_findings.note: Tables 1–3 print these values in rows labelled 'Overdose deaths' and 'Natural deaths': COD 82.5%, 80.0%, 80.0% and 50.0%, 40.0%, 80.0%; MOD 92.5%, 85.0%, 82.5% and 70.0%, 40.0%, 90.0%; kappa 0.73, 0.40, 0.29 and 0.43, 0.25, 0.75. Labels and group sizes are inconsistent (reporting issues 1 and 2).

key_findings.finding: Experience: the reviewer with the fewest years in practice had the highest cause-of-death agreement (80%), against 66.6% and 71.6% for the two more experienced reviewers; the authors note that three reviewers are too few for a confident conclusion.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (starts on p. 100, continues on p. 101)

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states that where the investigation or history indicates drug use, a pathologist could expect the correct cause of death from external examination alone in 75% of cases and the correct manner in 80%; it suggests that a simple rule (record the death as drug-related when the investigation suggests intoxication) could reach 75% to 80% accuracy, and asks whether an office would then need a forensic pathologist at all.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The 75% and 80% do not match the results reported for cases with a drug history (80% to 83% for cause), and the simple rule was not tested (reporting issue 3).

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the authors liken certification without autopsy in suspected intoxication to flipping a weighted coin, right more often than not but far from every time; they judge that the accuracy gained justifies full autopsy for their office and, in their view, for the country, and will keep autopsying suspected drug deaths under the NAME standards. The abstract states that a full postmortem examination is necessary.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, 3rd paragraph (p. 99); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 101)

key_findings.finding: Context: the office's caseload has grown by about 10% a year since 2012, mainly through suspected drug-related deaths, and all suspected intoxications there receive a full autopsy under the NAME standards; NAME Standard B3.7 requires a forensic autopsy for deaths by apparent intoxication, later amended to allow an exception after a significant interval when medical findings and the absence of trauma are well documented.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, 2nd paragraph; Introduction (unheaded), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Subgroup labels and sizes disagree. The Results text reports the subgroup values as cases with (43) and without (17) a drug history or paraphernalia, while Tables 1–3 label the same values 'Overdose deaths' and 'Natural deaths' (38 and 22 in the Methods). Editors' calculation: every subgroup percentage in Tables 1 and 2 is reproduced exactly by groups of 40 and 20 cases, whose counts also add up to each 'All 60 cases' value, but by neither 38 and 22 nor 43 and 17.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which cases the subgroup rows describe; the subgroup figures, including any contrast between drug and natural deaths, should not be cited until the group definitions are known.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives non-zero kappas within the rows labelled 'Overdose deaths' and 'Natural deaths'. If each row held a single case-file manner (accident or natural), kappa against the case file would be zero or undefined (editors' reasoning), so the labels cannot be literal; and two values differ between text and table (0.39 and 0.28 in the Results text, 0.40 and 0.29 in Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Supports reading the rows as the history-based groups described in the text, which then conflicts with the group sizes (issue 1); the 0.01 differences are minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives 75% (cause) and 80% (manner) as the accuracy to expect from external examination when the investigation indicates drug use, but the Results report 80% to 83% cause-of-death agreement in those cases (82.5% to 92.5% for manner in the corresponding table row); 73% and 80% are the all-case means.
reporting_issues.consequence: The practical figures in the Discussion cannot be traced to the subgroup results; cite the all-case values in Tables 1–3, not the Discussion's summary or the subgroup rows (see issue 1).

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the inter-reviewer kappas (0.54, 0.61, 0.53) only moderate, although 0.61 falls in the 'substantial' band of the scale the paper uses (0.61 to 0.80).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; agreement between pathologists was moderate at best either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe kappa as a measure of agreement between reviewers, but kappa is also reported for each reviewer against the case file; no kappa is given for cause of death and no confidence interval for any statistic.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers must estimate precision themselves (editors' intervals on this card).

reporting_issues.issue: The criterion for agreement on cause of death is not defined (for example, whether naming a different combination of drugs counted as disagreement), and discordant classifications are not tabulated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of error, drug deaths missed versus other deaths wrongly called drug deaths, cannot be read from the paper.

design_detail: Letter to the Editor in Addiction (one page, eight references) by Roy Robertson, Sheila M. Bird and Andrew McAuley (Edinburgh, Cambridge and Glasgow), responding to Stam et al. (2019) and to Darke's commentary on it. No new data: it is evidence of a published comment, not of findings.
can_establish: That a published letter from UK researchers supported Stam et al. and Darke's view that drug deaths are underestimated, pointed to definitions that differ between jurisdictions, and argued for a wider view that takes in deaths among older people who use or have used drugs, including late deaths from liver disease, measured with record linkage and cohort data.
cannot_establish: Whether, or by how much, official counts of drug deaths are too low; how many late deaths among people who use drugs are caused by drug use; or whether standardizing toxicology and pathology in Scotland improved accuracy. The letter gives no data of its own.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a letter with no participants or data.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Eight references chosen by the authors without a search: the target study and Darke's commentary; four reports by official bodies (National Records of Scotland, Public Health England, the Office for National Statistics, NHS National Services Scotland); an EMCDDA assessment co-authored by McAuley; and a study by Gao, Robertson and Bird.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable: no data. The letter discusses definitions of drug-related death, how information about a death reaches those who code its cause, and deaths among older people who use or used drugs.
exposure.polysubstance: Raised only as causes of death among older people who use or used drugs: liver disease and liver cancer linked to hepatitis C or alcohol, lung cancer and respiratory disease in heavy smokers, and co-dependency with alcohol (p. 1504, 3rd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; the letter does not define 'drug-related death' or the 'true impact' of drug use it calls for measuring.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The only number is in the title of a cited study: 3262 deaths in Scotland's methadone-prescription clients, 2009–2015 (ref. 5, p. 1504). The statement that Scotland's drug-related deaths are disproportionately high per head of population cites a National Records of Scotland report (ref. 3) without a figure.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a letter.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results: a short argument resting on official reports and two of the authors' own works.
interpretation_gap.claimed: That, as Darke suggests, deaths due to drugs are underestimated for further reasons, chiefly the problems of older people who use or used drugs: late deaths from end-stage liver disease and liver cancer linked to hepatitis C virus or alcohol, and other deaths adding to this group's burden of disease (early lung cancer and respiratory disease in heavy smokers, cardiovascular deaths, violence, trauma, suicide and co-dependency with alcohol) (p. 1504, 3rd paragraph); that record linkage and cohort data should be used to find the true impact of drug use (4th paragraph); and that standardizing toxicology and pathology across Scotland has helped accuracy (2nd paragraph). The letter does not separate deaths caused by drug use from deaths among people who use drugs: it attributes some of the causes it lists to smoking or alcohol, and the study it cites for older people (ref. 5) is titled as a study of non-drug-related and opioid-specific causes. The Scottish accuracy statement has no data or reference.

timeline.event: Stam et al.: the study the letter responds to (Addiction 114: 504–512, as cited in the letter).
Darke: the commentary on Stam et al. that the letter calls insightful and endorses.

replication.where_it_stands: A supportive letter that widens the question from how acute drug deaths are counted to the overall mortality of people who use or used drugs; it reports no data and does not dispute anything in Stam et al.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declaration of interests: None (p. 1504).
funding.affiliations_note: Roy Robertson, Usher Institute, Edinburgh University; Sheila M. Bird, Biostatistics Unit, University of Cambridge, and College of Medicine and Veterinary Medicine, University of Edinburgh; Andrew McAuley, School of Health and Life Sciences, Glasgow Caledonian University. Two of the eight references are the authors' own (refs 4 and 5).

what_would_settle_it: A record-linkage cohort of people who use drugs that classifies every death both under official drug-related-death definitions and by underlying cause, estimates how many deaths are attributable to drug use with smoking, alcohol and hepatitis C handled explicitly, and measures how many acute drug deaths the official statistics miss or wrongly include.

domains.note: No search and no selection criteria: a one-page letter citing eight references chosen by the authors.
Nothing cited is appraised; official reports are cited for statements without figures.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of the eight references are the authors' own (an EMCDDA assessment co-authored by McAuley; a study by Gao, Robertson and Bird), and the latter is the only study cited for the central argument about older people, beside a Public Health England report.

Mostly framed as recommendations, but the statement that standardization in Scotland helped accuracy and the list of further causes of death in older people carry no reference, and 'true impact' is not defined.

domains.domain: Balance of attribution (deaths caused by drug use versus deaths among people who use drugs) and of directions of error
domains.note: Only underestimation is argued. How to separate drug-attributable deaths from deaths with other causes such as smoking and alcohol, and the possibility of deaths wrongly attributed to drugs, are not discussed; attribution and overcounting are the under-represented side.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A one-page letter without a search or appraisal, weighted to one side of the attribution question; the overall rating cannot be milder than its worst domains. Cite it for: the existence of a published letter supporting Stam et al. and Darke; its points that definitions of drug-related death vary across jurisdictions and that there are problems in ascertaining information about a death, including its context, as provided by police, physicians, pathologists or coroners, and in its assimilation by those who code the cause of death; and its argument that deaths among older people who use or used drugs, including late deaths from liver disease, belong in a wider measure of drug-related mortality, best studied with record linkage and cohorts. Do not cite it as evidence that counts of drug deaths are too low or by how much, or that Scotland's standardization improved accuracy.

key_findings.finding: Type and authors: a Letter to the Editor in Addiction by Roy Robertson (Usher Institute, Edinburgh University), Sheila M. Bird (Biostatistics Unit, University of Cambridge, and College of Medicine and Veterinary Medicine, University of Edinburgh) and Andrew McAuley (School of Health and Life Sciences, Glasgow Caledonian University); declaration of interests: none.
key_findings.locator: Title; author block (right column); Declaration of interests (left column)

key_findings.finding: Response to Stam et al. and Darke: the letter says both resonate with concerns elsewhere in Europe, the UK and especially Scotland, where drug-related deaths remain disproportionately high per head of population (citing a National Records of Scotland report; no figure given).
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Definitions and information flow: definitions vary across jurisdictions, which makes data sets hard to compare (citing an EMCDDA assessment); there are problems in ascertaining information about a death, including contextual information, as provided by police, physician, pathologist and/or coroner, and in its subsequent assimilation by those who code the cause of death; attempts to standardize and coordinate toxicology and pathology across Scotland are said to have helped accuracy (no data or reference).
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Older people: agreeing with Darke that there are additional reasons why deaths due to drugs are underestimated, the letter points to the problems of older people who use or have used drugs, whose health it says yields additional insights (citing the authors' study of 3262 deaths in Scotland's methadone-prescription clients, 2009–2015); late deaths from end-stage liver disease and liver cancer linked to hepatitis C virus or alcohol remain a significant cause of mortality among them (citing a Public Health England report); and it lists early lung cancer and respiratory disease in heavy smokers, cardiovascular deaths, violence, trauma, suicide and co-dependency with alcohol as other deaths adding to this group's high burden of disease (no reference).
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph; references 5 and 6

key_findings.finding: Recommendation: record linkage studies and cohort data should be used to identify the true impact of drug use, and a more realistic assessment of that impact over time is urgently needed (citing the Office for National Statistics 'deep dive' into coroners' records and the Scottish National Drug Related Deaths Report); this might focus attention on early intervention in treatment and screening.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph; references 7 and 8

reporting_issues.issue: Deaths among older people who use or used drugs (late deaths from liver disease and liver cancer; other deaths from early lung cancer, respiratory and cardiovascular disease, violence, trauma and suicide) are offered as reasons why deaths due to drugs are underestimated, without distinguishing deaths caused by drug use from deaths among people who use drugs; smoking and alcohol are named as causes for some, and the study cited (ref. 5) is titled as a study of non-drug-related and opioid-specific causes of death.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the letter as an argument for wider measures of drug-related mortality, not as evidence that counts of drug deaths are too low or by how much.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that standardizing and coordinating toxicology and pathology across Scotland improved accuracy, and the list of further causes of death in older people, carry no reference or figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unsupported within the letter; not citable as evidence.

design_detail: Rats. Laboratory experiment in 32 albino rats of Wistar origin comparing oral intake of a morphine solution between rats housed singly since weaning in small metal cages (isolated: 4 females, 6 males at the start) and rats living together since weaning in an 8.8 m² open box (social: 10 females, 12 males), each kept in that housing throughout the experiment, with sex as a second factor. Four successive periods: limited access (about 7 h of fluid a day in 3-day cycles, one choice day per cycle), forced consumption (morphine hydrochloride solution 0.5 mg/ml as the only fluid for 57 days, with four 24-h choice days), Nichols cycles (eight 3-day cycles of no fluid, morphine only, water only, with four choice days) and abstinence (choice days after 2 and 5 weeks without morphine). Outcome: intake on 24-h morphine-or-water choice days. 27 rats analysed after five females died. The project's reading list calls it the Rat Park experiment; the paper itself does not use that name.
can_establish: Whether, in one small group of rats from one colony and one laboratory, rats raised and kept singly in small metal cages drank more of a bitter morphine solution when water was also available than rats raised and kept together in a large furnished box, after long forced exposure to the solution, and whether females drank more than males.
cannot_establish: Which feature of the housing made the difference (space, company, bedding, objects, the drinking apparatus and the way intake was measured all differed together), whether it arose from rearing after weaning or from housing at the time of testing (both differed since weaning), whether it reflects taste rather than the drug's effects (the solution was unsweetened and no taste control was run), or anything about people: these are rats, and the paper makes no claim about human addiction.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory rats: 32 albino rats of Wistar origin bought from the University of British Columbia colony (p. 175, Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond the description: 103–107 days old at the start; all had had continuous access to morphine solution and tap water for the 3 weeks before the experiment and drank water almost exclusively then (concentration not stated) (p. 175). How rats were assigned to isolated or social housing at weaning is not reported.
sample.demographics: Isolated group at the start 4 females and 6 males; social group 10 females and 12 males (p. 175). Body weights are not reported anywhere, although intake is analysed per kg of body weight.
sample.attrition: Five of the 14 females died and no male: two isolated and two social females during forced consumption, one more social female before the last abstinence choice day. Analysed: isolated females 2, isolated males 6, social females 7, social males 12 (p. 176). The authors write that the deaths seem to have been caused by extreme aversion to the morphine solution, leading to dehydration, in a few of the females, and that the differential mortality partly obscures the apparent sex difference among the survivors (p. 178). Half of the isolated females were lost.
sample.selection_effects: One small sample from one breeding colony and one laboratory. Groups were unequal in size (10 vs 22) and, after the deaths, in sex balance (25% vs 37% female). The isolated-female cell has 2 rats and carries the largest means and standard errors. All rats had an earlier 3-week exposure to morphine solution beside water before this experiment.

exposure.measurement: Housing (isolated vs social since weaning) is the experimental factor; morphine intake is the outcome. Intake was measured differently in the two conditions: isolated rats by weighing their bottles at the start and end of each choice day, corrected for spillage (1–3 g per bottle per day) measured on two control bottles on an empty cage; social rats by a drop counter on each of two dispensers at the end of a transparent runway (4.7 × 5.8 × 24 cm), with a camera triggered by each entry recording the counters and the rat's identifying mark. The sides of the two fluids were changed irregularly for both groups (pp. 175–176). Laboratory morphine hydrochloride solution of stated concentration; source not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Oral morphine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/ml in tap water. Limited access: about 7 h of fluid a day; a choice day followed by 2 days of morphine solution only, repeated nine times, then a final choice day. Forced consumption: morphine solution and no water for 57 days, except 24-h choice days on days 16, 38, 42 and 43. Nichols cycles: no fluid, then morphine only, then water only, each for 24 h, repeated eight times, with choice days after cycles 2, 4, 6 and 8. Abstinence: no morphine, food and water freely available; 24-h choice days after 2 and 5 weeks (p. 176). Mean forced intake after the first 2 weeks: 26.6 g of solution (13.3 mg morphine HCl) per isolated rat per day and 37.2 g (18.6 mg) per social rat (p. 176).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (laboratory rats given morphine only). Earlier exposure: 3 weeks of continuous access to morphine solution and water immediately before the experiment (p. 175).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Choice tests were run late in forced consumption, between Nichols cycles, and after 2 and 5 weeks without morphine (p. 176).

comparison.controls: Social rats: lived together since weaning in an open-topped plywood box with 8.8 m² of floor, a layer of sawdust, about a dozen small open-topped cages to explore and a 0.7 m climbing pole, and drank from two drop dispensers at the end of a runway (pp. 175–176). Isolated rats: housed singly since weaning in 18 × 25 × 18 cm metal cages whose sheet-metal sides prevented visual contact with neighbours, drinking from bottles fixed outside the cage (p. 175).
comparison.matching: Same colony and age; not matched on sex ratio or weight; allocation to housing not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Housing differed from weaning, so there is no measure taken before the groups diverged. Body weight, taste preference and activity were not reported; morphine preference in the earlier 3-week exposure is described only as water drunk almost exclusively, not by group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable: both groups followed the same morphine schedule.

outcomes.instruments: Fluid intake on 24-h choice days (water vs morphine solution), expressed as grams of morphine solution, proportion of morphine solution in total fluid, and mg morphine HCl per kg body weight; each converted to square roots and analysed by least-squares analysis of variance (environment × sex), with a repeated-measures analysis over the four Nichols choice days (p. 176).
outcomes.validity_norms: No calibration of drop counts against weight is reported for the social group, and measurement reliability on the limited-access choice days was described as not satisfactory for the social group (p. 176). Social females' total fluid on choice days (58.4–71.9 g) was 1.6 to 3.1 times that of isolated females (22.9–36.9 g), depending on the period (editors' calculation from Table 1, p. 177); whether this is real or a property of the measurement cannot be told.
outcomes.operationalization: Self-administration means voluntary oral intake of morphine solution on a day when water was also available, after forced exposure; mg/kg is the measure analysed in full.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three intake measures in each of three reported periods (nine analyses), each with environment, sex and interaction terms, plus a repeated-measures analysis; only the mg/kg analysis is reported in full, the authors stating that the other two gave the same direction and a very similar pattern of significance (p. 176).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; housing could not be concealed. Intake was recorded mechanically (bottle weights, drop counters).

analysis.effect_sizes: Untransformed means ± SE on choice days, mg morphine HCl/kg, in the order isolated females, isolated males, social females, social males (Table 1, p. 177): forced consumption 6.96 ± 4.1, 4.09 ± 1.9, 1.00 ± 0.2, 0.26 ± 0.1; Nichols cycles 19.7 ± 10.1, 6.4 ± 2.7, 2.3 ± 0.3, 0.8 ± 0.2; abstinence 6.2 ± 4.4, 1.5 ± 0.2, 1.5 ± 0.2, 0.07 ± 0.02. Editors' calculation from Table 1, isolated-to-social ratio of mean mg/kg within sex: forced consumption 7.0 (females) and 15.7 (males), Nichols cycles 8.6 and 8.0, abstinence 4.1 and 21.4; pooled over sex weighting by the analysed numbers (2, 6, 7, 12): 9.0, 7.2 and 4.5. The paper itself states no ratio. F tests on square-root mg/kg: forced consumption environment F = 21.46 and sex F = 7.26 (df 1/23); Nichols cycles environment F = 200.90, sex F = 67.86, interaction F = 6.95 (df 1/69); environment × trials F = 27.29 (df 3/69); abstinence environment F = 26.38 and sex F = 36.44 (df 1/23) (pp. 176–178). No confidence intervals.
analysis.covariates: None; two-way analysis of variance (environment × sex) on square-root-transformed values.
analysis.selective_reporting: Limited-access data are not presented (little morphine drunk; unreliable measurement in the social group; the authors state the trend was the same) (p. 176). Only the mg/kg analysis is given in full, and only the last two of the four forced-period choice days are shown. A significant decrease in sexual activity and fighting in the social group is asserted without method or data (p. 178). Body weights are never reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. One cell has 2 rats (isolated females) and the isolated group 8 in all.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 27 surviving rats from one colony, rats raised and kept singly drank more morphine solution on choice days than rats raised and kept together, in both sexes and in each reported period, by roughly 4 to 21 times depending on sex and period (editors' calculation from Table 1); females drank more than males; when morphine solution was the only fluid, the social rats drank more of it than the isolated rats (37.2 vs 26.6 g a day). The isolated-female means rest on 2 rats.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports the significant differences and the opposite trends of the two groups across the Nichols choice days, without the deaths of five females, the different measurement of the two groups or the social rats' larger intake when morphine was the only fluid (p. 175). The discussion says housing conditions appear to play an important role, proposes that morphine relieved the discomfort of confinement, isolation and stimulus deprivation in isolated rats and interfered with natural activity in social rats, and itself calls these explanations speculative because of the small number of rats, the many differences between the housing conditions, possible effects on taste, and the possibility that housing acted earlier in life (p. 178). It adds that a housing effect, if substantiated, would have to be explained by existing theories of addiction: a training procedure based on relief of withdrawal (Nichols, 1965) appeared to depend on the environment, since the social rats' intake fell across the Nichols choice days while the isolated rats' rose, and a neurochemical-change theory would also have to account for the effect; theories that leave out sex and housing risk oversimplification (p. 178). The paper makes no direct claim about people.

timeline.event: Hadaway, Alexander, Coambs & Beyerstein (Psychopharmacology 66: 87–91), on housing, sex and preference for morphine–sucrose solutions in rats not pretreated with morphine, cited by the 1981 paper as the second earlier experiment showing the housing effect (Alexander et al., 1981, pp. 571, 574); not in the library and not read.

Same laboratory, with early and later housing separated and sweetened morphine solutions offered without forced consumption: males living in the colony at the time of testing drank far less morphine–sucrose solution than caged males; females less conclusive; no sex difference, so the 1978 sex finding was not reproduced
Petrie: described in the project's reading list as a failed replication in Wistar rats; to be appraised from its own card
Gage & Sumnall: described in the project's reading list as a critical history of how Rat Park changed the narrative of addiction; to be appraised from its own card

replication.where_it_stands: This experiment and the 1981 one, both small and from one laboratory, found lower oral morphine intake in rats housed together than in rats housed singly; the 1978 sex difference was not seen in 1981. Whether independent laboratories reproduced the housing effect is for the Petrie (1996) card and the Gage & Sumnall (2019) review.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article; the acknowledgements thank eight named people for their contributions (p. 178).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors: Department of Psychology, Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, Canada (p. 175).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered experiment in rats of more than one strain and both sexes, randomly assigned to housing at weaning, with the same drinking apparatus and the same intake measurement in every housing condition, taste controls (a bitter non-drug solution or a tasteless opioid), body weights reported, social contact, space and enrichment varied separately, and repetition in an independent laboratory.

domains.note: How rats were assigned to isolated or social housing at weaning is not described; group sizes were unequal (10 vs 22).
Same colony and age, but sex composition differed (40% vs 45% female at the start, 25% vs 37% after the deaths); body weights and morphine preference before the groups diverged are not reported.
Not reported.

Housing is the factor studied, but it came with a different drinking apparatus (bottles on the cage vs a runway with drop dispensers shared by the colony), different intake measurement, and different space, bedding, objects and company all at once.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Not reported; housing could not be concealed from the investigators.
All surviving rats were measured over the same 24-h choice days.

Blinding of outcome assessment is not reported and housing could not be concealed, although intake was recorded mechanically; the larger detection problem is that intake was measured by different methods in the two groups (weighed bottles vs drop counts with camera identification), without reported calibration, and measurement in the social group was unreliable in the first period (p. 176).
5 of 32 rats died, all female, including 2 of the 4 isolated females; the dead rats were excluded from every analysis, and the authors say the deaths partly obscure the sex difference (p. 178).
Limited-access data withheld; only one of three intake measures analysed in full; only two of four forced-period choice days shown; behavioural changes asserted without data.

Between-group tests for the Nichols period use 69 error degrees of freedom instead of 23; one Table 1 cell is internally inconsistent; 2 rats in one cell; unsweetened bitter solution with no taste control.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE gives no overall score; the editors' summary is high risk of bias. The housing difference in intake is consistent across periods and sexes in Table 1, but housing came bundled with a different drinking apparatus and a different measurement method, allocation is not described, five females died (half of one four-rat cell), and the reporting is selective. Citable for: what this first experiment did and found in rats, with its numbers and limits. Not citable for: which aspect of the environment matters, for any effect in people, or as an independent replication of anything.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rats: albino, Wistar origin, University of British Columbia colony; 14 females and 18 males at the start; 103–107 days old at the start (p. 175).
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Oral morphine hydrochloride 0.5 mg/ml in tap water on the schedule given under exposure (study conditions only).
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given; the study is about how much rats chose to drink, not about dose effects.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No: 57 days of a bitter morphine solution as the only fluid, followed by laboratory choice tests; the paper does not compare its conditions with human use.

key_findings.finding: On the last two choice days of the forced-consumption period (days 42 and 43), isolated rats drank more morphine solution than social rats (F = 21.46, df 1/23, P < 0.001) and females more than males (F = 7.26, df 1/23, P < 0.05), with no environment × sex interaction (square-root mg/kg).
key_findings.locator: Results › Forced Consumption Period, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1; choice days listed in Procedure › Forced Consumption Period

key_findings.finding: When morphine solution was the only fluid (excluding the first 2 weeks), isolated rats drank a mean of 26.6 g a day (13.3 mg morphine HCl per rat) and social rats 37.2 g (18.6 mg per rat).
key_findings.locator: Results › Forced Consumption Period, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Sexes pooled; no variability, test or per-kg figure is given.

key_findings.finding: Mean morphine intake on choice days, mg morphine HCl/kg ± SE (isolated females n = 2, isolated males n = 6, social females n = 7, social males n = 12): forced consumption 6.96 ± 4.1, 4.09 ± 1.9, 1.00 ± 0.2, 0.26 ± 0.1; Nichols cycles 19.7 ± 10.1, 6.4 ± 2.7, 2.3 ± 0.3, 0.8 ± 0.2; abstinence 6.2 ± 4.4, 1.5 ± 0.2, 1.5 ± 0.2, 0.07 ± 0.02.
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: Untransformed means; the significance tests used square-root values. In the abstinence period isolated males and social females had the same mean, 1.5 mg/kg.

key_findings.finding: Proportion of choice-day fluid taken as morphine solution (same order): forced consumption 0.25, 0.16, 0.059, 0.01; Nichols cycles 0.44, 0.21, 0.041, 0.025; abstinence 0.12, 0.052, 0.027, 0.002. Total choice-day fluid (g): 22.9, 33.0, 71.9, 42.3; 33.6, 40.0, 58.4, 37.9; 36.9, 40.5, 59.8, 29.3.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: The paper states no “times more” figure. Editors' calculation from Table 1, ratio of isolated to social mean mg/kg within sex: forced consumption 7.0 (females) and 15.7 (males); Nichols cycles 8.6 and 8.0; abstinence 4.1 and 21.4. Pooled over sex, weighting by the analysed numbers (2, 6, 7, 12): 9.0, 7.2 and 4.5. For the proportion measure: 4.2 and 16; 10.7 and 8.4; 4.4 and 26.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (editors' calculation)
key_findings.note: The largest ratios involve social-male means of 0.26 and 0.07 mg/kg and proportions printed to one significant figure (0.01, 0.002), so they are imprecise; each isolated-female mean rests on 2 rats.

key_findings.finding: On the four Nichols-cycle choice days, isolated rats drank more morphine solution than social rats (F = 200.90, df 1/69, P < 0.001; the authors say there was virtually no overlap between the populations), females more than males (F = 67.86, df 1/69, P < 0.001), with a larger sex difference among isolated rats (interaction F = 6.95, df 1/69, P < 0.05). On the cycles' morphine-only days isolated rats drank less morphine solution than social rats, and on water-only days less water.
key_findings.locator: Results › Nichols Cycle Period, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The degrees of freedom of these between-group tests do not fit the design; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Across the four Nichols choice days the isolated rats' intake rose slightly and the social rats' fell (environment × trials F = 27.29, df 3/69, P < 0.001; sex × trials and the three-way interaction not significant).
key_findings.locator: Results › Nichols Cycle Period, 3rd paragraph (p. 177, continuing on p. 178); Fig. 2 (p. 177)
key_findings.note: Read approximately from Fig. 2 at 300 dpi (square root of mg/kg/day, choice days 1–4): isolated females 3.8, 4.2, 4.9, 4.1; isolated males 0.95, 2.7, 2.4, 2.55; social females 1.8, 1.55, 1.35, 1.15; social males 1.25, 0.9, 0.45, 0.1. The isolated rise is mostly the isolated males' jump between the first and second day, and on the first day their mean lay below both social groups'.

key_findings.finding: After 2 and 5 weeks without morphine, isolated rats again drank more morphine solution on the choice days than social rats (F = 26.38, df 1/23, P < 0.001) and females more than males (F = 36.44, df 1/23, P < 0.001); no interaction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Abstinence Period

key_findings.finding: Five females died and no male (two isolated and two social females during forced consumption, one more social female before the last choice day), leaving 2 isolated females, 6 isolated males, 7 social females and 12 social males. The authors write that the deaths seem to have been caused by extreme aversion to the morphine solution, leading to dehydration, in a few of the females.
key_findings.locator: Procedure › Forced Consumption Period and Abstinence Period, and the final-sample paragraph (p. 176); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 178)

key_findings.finding: Intake was measured differently by housing: weighed bottles corrected for 1–3 g/day spillage for isolated rats; drop counters at a 4.7 × 5.8 × 24 cm runway with camera identification for social rats.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Apparatus, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Procedure, paragraph on how consumption was determined (p. 176)

key_findings.finding: Little morphine was drunk on the limited-access choice days and measurement reliability was not satisfactory for the social group; these data are not presented, the authors stating that the trend was the same.
key_findings.locator: Results › Limited Access Period

key_findings.finding: The highest single-day intakes were 26.4 mg/kg (isolated females) and 8.7 mg/kg (isolated males), below the maximum of about 30 mg/kg/day reported in three earlier oral studies; the authors ask whether the housing effect would hold if procedures raised intake to that level.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors call their explanations (relief of confinement, isolation and stimulus deprivation in isolated rats; interference with natural activity in social rats) speculative, citing the small number of rats, the many differences between housing conditions, possible effects on taste preference or other psychophysiological parameters, and the possibility that housing acted earlier, perhaps in a post-weaning critical period.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The between-group F tests for the Nichols Cycle Period (environment, sex, interaction) are printed with 1/69 degrees of freedom, whereas the same tests in the other periods use 1/23. With 27 rats in four groups a between-rat test has 23 error degrees of freedom; 69 is the within-rat error term for four choice days (23 × 3), which fits the environment × trials test (3/69) but not a between-group test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-group tests for that period appear to have used the within-rat error term, overstating precision (editors' calculation: treating the four days as independent observations would give 92 to 104 error degrees of freedom, not 69); F = 200.90 cannot be taken at face value, although Table 1 leaves the direction of the difference clear.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the forced-consumption values for social females (total fluid 71.9 g, proportion 0.059, 1.00 mg/kg) do not fit together. Editors' calculation, using the paper's own conversion of 0.5 mg per g of solution (26.6 g = 13.3 mg, p. 176): 71.9 × 0.059 × 0.5 is about 2.1 mg morphine HCl per rat, which equals 1.00 mg/kg only at a body weight of about 2 kg; the same calculation gives 0.36–0.70 kg in the other cells (0.81 kg for social males in the forced period, whose proportion is printed to one significant figure). Means of ratios are not ratios of means, but even the largest negative covariance the printed standard errors allow leaves over 1.4 mg per rat.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the three values in that cell is misprinted or computed differently; the social-female forced-period ratio (7.0) is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The two housing groups' intake was measured by different methods (weighed bottles vs drop counts identified by camera), with no reported calibration of drops against weight; reliability in the social group was unsatisfactory in the first period, and social females' total choice-day fluid (58.4–71.9 g) was 1.6 to 3.1 times isolated females' (22.9–36.9 g), depending on the period (editors' calculation from Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of any difference in absolute amounts could come from measurement; the proportion measure is less exposed to this than grams or mg/kg.

reporting_issues.issue: Body weights are never reported, although mg/kg is the measure analysed in full; when and how often rats were weighed is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mg/kg values cannot be checked or reconverted, and differences in growth between housing conditions would enter the main measure unseen.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors state that the populations hardly overlapped in the Nichols period, but no individual values are shown, and Fig. 2 places the isolated males' mean on the first Nichols choice day below both social groups' means (editors' approximate reading, square-root scale: about 0.95 against 1.8 and 1.25).
reporting_issues.consequence: The no-overlap statement cannot be checked and does not hold for that day's means.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion reports a statistically significant decrease in several categories of sexual activity and fighting in the social group during forced consumption, with no method, data or test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be checked; the 1981 paper later cites this observation as one of three grounds for its preferred speculation (Alexander et al., 1981, p. 574).

reporting_issues.issue: Limited-access results are withheld, only the mg/kg analysis is reported in full, and only two of the four forced-period choice days are shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The consistency of the effect across measures and days rests on the authors' statement rather than on reported data.

reporting_issues.issue: Both sexes lived together in the social box from weaning (10 females and 12 males at the start), and the discussion refers to sexual activity in the social group (p. 178), but pregnancies, litters or any step to prevent them are not mentioned anywhere in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: Pregnancy or lactation could change fluid intake, body weight (and so mg/kg) and survival in the females concerned; it is one more possible reason, besides measurement, for social females' large total choice-day fluid (Table 1, p. 177), and its effect on the female results cannot be assessed.
