design_detail: Rats. Laboratory experiment in 32 albino rats of Wistar origin (16 male, 16 female) with a 2 × 2 housing design: isolated or colony housing from weaning to 65 days, crossed with isolated or colony housing from 65 days on, giving four conditions of 4 males and 4 females (II, CI, IC, CC; first letter early housing, second letter housing at testing). From 80 days of age, continuous 24-h choice between tap water and one sweetened solution per phase, in a fixed order: 10% sucrose (3 days), quinine in sucrose (5 days), morphine hydrochloride in 10% sucrose at 1.00, 0.50, 0.30 and 0.15 mg/ml (5 days each), sucrose again (3 days). No forced morphine period. The Rat Park follow-up in the project's reading list; the paper does not use that name.
can_establish: Whether, in a small group of rats from one laboratory, housing at the time of testing (a single wire cage or a shared furnished enclosure) or housing in early life was associated with how much sweetened morphine solution the rats chose to drink over water, and whether the housing groups differed in intake of sweet and bitter-sweet control solutions.
cannot_establish: Which feature of the colony mattered (space, company, cedar shavings, cans and boxes, height, the one-rat-at-a-time drinking tunnel and the measurement method all differed together), whether the difference lasts with longer exposure (it narrowed at the last concentration), whether taste explains the weaker female results, or anything about people: these are rats choosing a sweetened solution, and the authors draw conclusions for animal self-administration experiments only.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory rats: 16 male and 16 female albino rats of Wistar origin from the University of British Columbia breeding stock, obtained at weaning at 21 ± 2 days of age (p. 571, Method › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated. How rats were assigned to housing at weaning, and which half of each group was moved at 65 days, is not described (pp. 571–572).
sample.demographics: Eight males and eight females isolated and eight of each in the colony from weaning; at 65 days half of each group changed housing, giving four rats of each sex per condition (p. 571; Table 1, p. 572). All rats were weighed at 60 days; the weights are not reported.
sample.attrition: One CC female died after Phase 0.3 and one IC female after Phase 0.15, leaving 3 females in each of these conditions for the later analyses; no cause is given (p. 572). An electronic fault lost several days of colony data, and the same days were dropped for isolated rats: days 1, 2 and 4 of Phase Q, day 2 of Phase 1, days 1, 3 and 4 of Phase 0.5, and day 1 of Phase POST, so Phase 0.5 has 2 usable days of 5 (Table 1 and Apparatus and Procedure, 8th paragraph, p. 572).
sample.selection_effects: One small sample from one breeding stock and one laboratory, 4 rats per sex per condition. During testing the 16 colony rats (IC and CC) shared one drinking tunnel that admitted one adult rat at a time (pp. 571–572), whereas each isolated rat had its own bottles.

exposure.measurement: Housing at two stages is the experimental factor; intake is the outcome. Isolated rats: the two bottles on each cage were weighed daily, with an approximate correction for leakage and evaporation from two similar bottles on empty cages in the same rack. Colony rats: two dispensers (Lafayette Instruments 80201) at the end of a transparent tunnel (4.4 × 5.8 cm inside) released a drop each time a rat withdrew its head from a photoelectric beam; a camera triggered by each entry recorded the rat's dye mark and the counters; overflow was drawn off by a vacuum pump and the loss, usually under 10% of intake, was subtracted in proportion to each rat's intake for the day (pp. 571–572). Left–right positions of water and drug solution were reversed after each phase (p. 572).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Oral, 24-h access to tap water and one solution per phase (Table 1, p. 572): PRE water + 10% sucrose, 3 days; Q 0.06 mg/ml quinine sulfate in 10% sucrose, 5 days; Phases 1, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15, morphine hydrochloride 1.00, 0.50, 0.30 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, 5 days each, always in that descending order; POST 10% sucrose, 3 days. To the human palate the quinine solution tasted the same as the 0.3 mg/ml morphine solution, and in a pilot rats given 8 h with both drank about equal amounts (p. 572).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (laboratory rats; no other drug and no morphine before testing is described).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: rats were not given morphine before the first morphine phase.

comparison.controls: The four housing conditions are compared with each other. Colony: a large (8.8 m²) open-topped plywood enclosure with cedar shavings, empty canisters and small boxes for hiding and nesting. Isolated: standard wire-mesh cages, 18 × 25 × 18 cm. Both in the same large room, 12-h light–dark cycle, food freely available (pp. 571–572). Colony rats had 2 weeks after the move to learn the dispensers (p. 572).
comparison.matching: Same source and age; sexes balanced by design (4 + 4 per condition).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure before the groups diverged at weaning; body weights at 60 days and growth during testing not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Daily intake in each phase as grams of drug–sucrose solution, mg quinine sulfate or morphine HCl per kg body weight, and proportion of drug–sucrose solution in total fluid; repeated-measures analysis of variance for each phase (housing at testing × early housing), run for males, for females and for both sexes; comparisons based on 5-day totals; for females, analysis of covariance with the same measure in Phase Q as covariate (pp. 572–573).
outcomes.validity_norms: Measurement differed by housing (weighed bottles vs drop counts); drop size is not given; which body weight the mg/kg figures use is not stated (rats were weighed at 60 days and no later weighing is described).
outcomes.operationalization: Voluntary oral intake of a sweetened morphine solution when water is available; sucrose and quinine–sucrose phases serve as sweet and bitter-sweet taste controls.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 19 phase-by-measure combinations (two measures in PRE and POST, three in the other five phases), each tested for housing at testing, early housing and their interaction, separately in males and females, plus 76 tests of sex and its interactions; significance shown as stars from 0.05 to 0.0001 (Figs 1–2; p. 573).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; housing could not be concealed. Intake was recorded mechanically or by weighing.

analysis.effect_sizes: Few numerical results are printed. Males, Phases 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15: 8 of 9 F tests for housing at testing significant, 5 beyond 0.0001 (p. 572). The text gives the largest contrasts as ratios: isolated males drank 19 times (Phase 0.5) and 6 times (Phase 0.3) as much morphine solution as colony males, based on mg/kg (p. 572). Table 2 (Phase 0.3, males, mg/kg, p. 574): editors' calculation of condition means from the printed individual means, II 41.1, CI 58.5, IC 14.7, CC 2.4; isolated at testing 49.8 vs colony at testing 8.6, a ratio of 5.8; analysis of variance: housing at testing F = 33.64 (df 1, 12; P < 0.0001), early housing F = 0.13, interaction F = 4.32 (P = 0.06). Females: housing at testing significant for grams and mg/kg in Phase 0.3 and for the proportion measure in Phases 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15; after adjusting for Phase Q intake, significant only for proportion, F(1,11) = 5.53, F(1,11) = 8.91 and F(1,10) = 6.52, all P < 0.05; grams and mg/kg in Phase 0.3 F(1,11) = 3.71 and 3.65, P = 0.08 (p. 573). Sex: 1 of 76 F tests significant at 0.05 (p. 573). No confidence intervals or standardized effect sizes.
analysis.covariates: Females only: intake in Phase Q (same measure) as covariate in the analyses of covariance for Phases 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15.
analysis.selective_reporting: Individual data are given for one phase and one sex only (Phase 0.3, males), described as representative; other phases appear only in figures, and F values for males only as significance stars. The female analysis of covariance was added because of the control-phase trend (p. 573). The 19-fold figure for Phase 0.5 cannot be checked from printed numbers.
analysis.power: Not reported; 4 rats per sex per condition, 3 in two female conditions in the last phases.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With 4 rats per sex per condition, males living in the colony during testing drank much less sweetened morphine solution than caged males at 0.5 and 0.3 mg/ml (5.8-fold at 0.3 mg/ml, editors' calculation from Table 2), whatever their early housing; the difference narrowed at 0.15 mg/ml, when colony males that had been isolated until 65 days took almost all their fluid as the morphine solution (approximate figure reading). Early isolation raised colony males' intake only at 0.15 mg/ml. Females showed the same direction less consistently, with a possible taste confound. No sex difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says colony rats drank less morphine solution but did not drink less of the control solutions (p. 571), and the results and discussion say the same of males (pp. 572, 575); this rests on non-significant tests with 4 rats per sex per condition, while the results report a trend toward less quinine–sucrose intake in colony females (P = 0.134 and 0.143; p. 573), and in Fig. 1a CC males drank about 60 g of sucrose solution in Phase PRE against about 96–110 g in the other three conditions (editors' approximate reading; p. 573). The discussion says that these results and two earlier experiments suggest the housing effect is large and robust, in spite of the two qualifications it states itself (3 of 5 days lost in Phase 0.5; colony rats' rising intake suggesting a longer exposure might shrink the effect) (p. 574). Its second broad conclusion is that some attributes differing between the two environments “must affect a powerful control mechanism” for opiate self-administration; the attributes it lists (space, social contact, cedar shavings, cans and boxes, a high ceiling) leave out the different drinking arrangement and measurement, and the study is called a better controlled replication without weighing them (pp. 574–575). The result is described as compatible with the authors' speculation that colony rats avoid opiates because opiates interfere with complex species-specific behaviour, which this experiment did not measure (p. 574). The conclusions are drawn for animal self-administration experiments, not for people (p. 574).

timeline.event: Same laboratory, after 57 days of forced drinking of unsweetened morphine solution: isolated rats drank more morphine solution on choice days than social rats, and females more than males

Hadaway, Alexander, Coambs & Beyerstein (Psychopharmacology 66: 87–91), housing, sex and preference for morphine–sucrose solutions in rats not pretreated with morphine, cited here as the second earlier experiment (pp. 571, 574); not in the library and not read.
Petrie: described in the project's reading list as a failed replication in Wistar rats; to be appraised from its own card
Gage & Sumnall: described in the project's reading list as a critical history of the Rat Park narrative; to be appraised from its own card

replication.where_it_stands: Within this laboratory the lower intake of colony-housed rats was seen again, here in males with sweetened solutions and no forced exposure; the 1978 sex difference was not. The authors call this a better controlled replication, but it shares the 1978 design's main weakness (housing bundled with a different drinking apparatus and measurement). Independent replication is for the Petrie (1996) card and the Gage & Sumnall (2019) review.

funding.funder: Grants from the Health Promotion Directorate, Health and Welfare, Canada; the British Columbia Ministry of Labour; and the Steel Foundation, Simon Fraser University (p. 575, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors: Department of Psychology, Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, Canada (p. 571). The acknowledgements thank six named people for help and advice (p. 575).

what_would_settle_it: An adequately powered, preregistered experiment, repeated in an independent laboratory, with random assignment to housing, the same drinking device and measurement in every condition (or each colony rat's intake measured without competition for one tunnel), counterbalanced concentration order, a tasteless or taste-matched control solution, body weights reported, longer exposure at each concentration, and social contact, space and enrichment varied separately.

domains.note: Assignment to housing at weaning and to moving at 65 days is not described.
Same source and age, sexes balanced by design; weights at 60 days measured but not reported.
Not reported.

Both environments were in the same room on the same light cycle, but housing at testing came with a different drinking arrangement (own bottles vs one tunnel shared by 16 rats, one rat at a time) and different measurement.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Not reported; housing could not be concealed.
All rats were measured every day over the same 24-h periods.
Intake was measured by weighing for isolated rats and by drop counts with camera identification for colony rats; no calibration of drop size is reported.
Days lost to an electronic fault were dropped for all rats (balanced, reason given), but Phase 0.5 keeps 2 of 5 days; two females died, both in colony conditions, cause not given.
All measures appear in the figures, but numbers are given for one phase and one sex only, and the female analysis of covariance was added after the control-phase trend was seen.

Fixed descending order of concentrations (phase confounded with time and accumulated exposure); 4 rats per cell; the 19-fold figure is not reproducible from the printed data, and the figure and Table 2 disagree for Phase 0.3.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE gives no overall score; the editors' summary is high risk of bias. The early-versus-later housing design is an improvement on 1978, and Table 2 confirms a large difference in males at 0.3 mg/ml, but housing at testing is still bundled with a different drinking arrangement and measurement, allocation is not described, cells hold 4 rats, concentrations were not counterbalanced, and the headline 19-fold figure rests on 2 days and cannot be reproduced. Citable for: the direction and rough size of the housing difference in males in this experiment, the absence of a sex difference, and the narrowing at the lowest concentration. Not citable for: the 19-fold figure as an established quantity, which feature of the environment matters, or effects in people.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rats: albino, Wistar origin, University of British Columbia breeding stock; 16 males and 16 females obtained at weaning (21 ± 2 days); moved at 65 days; testing from 80 days of age (pp. 571–572).
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Oral; continuous 24-h choice between tap water and morphine hydrochloride 1.00, 0.50, 0.30 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose, 5 days each in a fixed descending order (study conditions only).
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given; the study is about how much rats chose to drink, not about dose effects.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No: a sweetened morphine solution offered beside water in cages or a laboratory enclosure; the authors draw conclusions for animal self-administration experiments, not for people (p. 574).

key_findings.finding: Four conditions of 4 males and 4 females (II, CI, IC, CC); rats were moved at 65 days and left undisturbed for 2 weeks before testing began at 80 days, so they had spent 44 days in the early and 15 days in the later housing when testing started.
key_findings.locator: Apparatus and Procedure, 5th and 6th paragraphs, and Table 1 (p. 572); Discussion, 1st paragraph (starting on p. 573; the 44 and 15 days are on p. 574)

key_findings.finding: Males living in the colony at the time of testing drank much less morphine–sucrose solution than isolated males in Phases 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 on all three measures; 8 of the 9 F tests for housing at testing were significant, 5 beyond 0.0001. No males drank much in Phase 1 (1 mg/ml), and, the authors state, colony males drank no less of the control solutions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effects: Males, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 1 (p. 573)
key_findings.note: The non-significant test is, judging from the stars in Fig. 1, the proportion measure in Phase 0.15. No F values for the control phases are printed. Approximate reading of Fig. 1a (600 dpi): in Phase PRE (sucrose only) CC males drank about 60 g against about 96–110 g in the other three conditions (on average about 108 g caged at testing vs 78 g colony at testing); Fig. 1 marks no significant difference in any control phase, with 4 rats per condition.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that in Phases 0.5 and 0.3 isolated males drank 19 times and 6 times as much morphine solution as colony males, based on the mg/kg data.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effects: Males, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Males only (8 vs 8). Phase 0.5 has 2 usable days of 5 (days 1, 3 and 4 lost; p. 572), and no Phase 0.5 means are printed. Editors' approximate pixel reading of Fig. 1b (600 dpi, against the axis ticks): CI about 58, II about 44, IC and CC about 4–5 mg/kg in Phase 0.5, a ratio near 11, but the figure's Phase 0.3 points also sit about 1.5–5 mg/kg above the Table 2 means, so the figure cannot test the 19-fold figure. The 6-fold figure for Phase 0.3 matches Table 2 (5.8, editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Phase 0.3, males, mg morphine HCl/kg (individual daily values and 5-day means): housing at testing F = 33.64 (df 1, 12; MS 34002, error MS 1011; P < 0.0001), early housing F = 0.13 (NS), interaction F = 4.32 (P = 0.06). Condition means, editors' calculation from the printed individual means: II 41.1, CI 58.5, IC 14.7, CC 2.4.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 15 of the 16 individual means reproduce from the daily values (one CI rat: printed 57.335, computed 57.339, immaterial), and the analysis of variance reproduces from the daily values (SS for housing at testing 34003, error MS 1011). Day-to-day values ranged from 0 to 131.5 mg/kg; individual means ranged 25.7–84.3 in the caged males and 1.4–24.0 in the colony males.

key_findings.finding: Early housing had no significant main effect in males; the early × later housing interaction was significant in Phase 0.15 for grams and mg/kg, colony males isolated until 65 days (IC) drinking more than colony males raised in the colony (CC); II and CI males did not differ consistently.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effects: Males, 3rd paragraph (p. 572, continuing on p. 573)

key_findings.finding: At the weakest concentration (0.15 mg/ml), the housing difference narrowed and most rats took most of their fluid as the morphine–sucrose solution. Editors' approximate reading of the figures, proportion of fluid taken as the solution: males II, CI and IC 0.98–1.0, CC 0.71; females II 1.0, CI 0.95, IC 0.90, CC 0.43; mg/kg: males CI 62, II 47, IC 34, CC 16 (isolated-to-colony ratio about 2.2); females II 68, CI 46, IC 46, CC 18 (about 1.8).
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1b–c (p. 573); Fig. 2b–c (p. 575); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 574) for the authors' remark
key_findings.note: Editors' approximate pixel readings of 600-dpi renderings; the paper gives no Phase 0.15 values in numbers. The authors note a trend for IC and, less so, CC rats to drink more across the 5 days of Phases 0.3 and 0.15, suggesting a longer exposure might reduce the housing effect (p. 574).

key_findings.finding: Females: colony females drank less morphine solution in Phases 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 on all three measures, but housing at testing was significant only for grams and mg/kg in Phase 0.3 and for the proportion measure in Phases 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15; IC females appeared to drink much more than CC females in Phase 0.15, the only significant test being early housing on the proportion measure.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effects: Females, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 (p. 575)
key_findings.note: Approximate reading of Fig. 2b for Phase 0.5: II about 89, CI 38, CC 32 and IC 11 mg/kg, so the CI (caged at testing) and CC (colony) females were close and the isolated-at-testing mean is carried by the II females.

key_findings.finding: In the quinine–sucrose control phase, colony females tended to drink less than isolated females: housing at testing F(1,12) = 2.45, P = 0.143 (grams) and F(1,12) = 2.58, P = 0.134 (mg/kg); the authors suggest the loss of 3 days of data increased within-group variance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effects: Females, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: With Phase Q intake as covariate, 3 of the 5 significant female housing effects remained, all on the proportion measure (Phase 0.5 F(1,11) = 5.53; Phase 0.3 F(1,11) = 8.91; Phase 0.15 F(1,10) = 6.52; all P < 0.05); grams and mg/kg in Phase 0.3 became F(1,11) = 3.71 and 3.65, P = 0.08. Three early × later interactions were significant in the adjusted analyses.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effects: Females, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Neither morphine nor control-solution intake differed by sex: 1 of 76 F tests for sex and its interactions with housing across the 7 phases was significant at 0.05.
key_findings.locator: Results › Gender Differences

key_findings.finding: The authors qualify the housing effect by the loss of 3 days of data in Phase 0.5 and by the colony rats' rising intake, yet write that these results and two earlier experiments suggest it is “both large and robust”; they call the study a better controlled replication, describe the result as compatible with their speculation that colony rats avoid opiates because opiates interfere with species-specific behaviour, and argue that relief of isolation stress is contradicted by studies of rats not physically dependent, while noting that the contrast with self-injection studies remains unexplained.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 574), 5th paragraph (pp. 574–575) and 6th paragraph (p. 575)

reporting_issues.issue: The headline figure that isolated males drank 19 times as much morphine as colony males in Phase 0.5 is given only in the text; Phase 0.5 kept 2 of 5 days, and no Phase 0.5 means are printed. In the editors' approximate reading of Fig. 1b the ratio is nearer 11 (about 51 vs 4.5 mg/kg).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 19-fold figure cannot be reproduced from what is printed and rests on 2 days of data in 8 vs 8 males; Table 2 supports about 6-fold in the next phase, and the figure suggests about 2-fold at the last concentration.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1b's Phase 0.3 points lie above the condition means computed from Table 2 for the same phase (editors' reading at 600 dpi and editors' calculation: CI about 62, II 46, IC 17, CC 4 mg/kg in the figure against 58.5, 41.1, 14.7 and 2.4 from the table, differences of about 1.5–5 mg/kg).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is not an exact plot of the tabulated data (perhaps hand-drawn); values read from the figures are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: Which body weight the mg/kg values use is not stated: rats were weighed at 60 days and no later weighing is described, while testing ran from 80 days for about a month.
reporting_issues.consequence: If 60-day weights were used, mg/kg would be overstated in growing rats, and any difference in growth between housing conditions would enter the main measure.

reporting_issues.issue: Intake was measured differently by housing (own bottles weighed daily vs drop counts from one tunnel shared by the 16 colony rats, one rat at a time), with no reported calibration of drop size and no discussion of competition for access.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of the lower absolute intake of colony rats could reflect the drinking arrangement or measurement rather than the housing; the proportion measure is less exposed to this.

reporting_issues.issue: Morphine concentrations were always given in descending order (1.00, 0.50, 0.30, 0.15 mg/ml), so concentration is confounded with time in the experiment and with accumulated exposure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The narrowing of the housing difference at 0.15 mg/ml cannot be separated from longer exposure or a less bitter solution.

reporting_issues.issue: The speculation the authors favour is said to have grown partly from the earlier experiment's report (reference 1 of this paper) that colony rats forced to drink morphine engaged in significantly less fighting and sexual behaviour, which that paper stated without method or data (see its card, sc_alexander_1978); the other grounds cited are reports that morphine reduces sexual behaviour and social cohesion in group-caged rats (refs 15, 17) and that species-specific behaviours are self-reinforcing (ref. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: This part of the behavioural basis of the authors' explanation cannot be checked from either paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says colony rats drank no less of the control solutions, while the results report a trend (P = 0.13–0.14) toward less quinine–sucrose intake in colony females.
reporting_issues.consequence: For females, a taste difference could explain part of the housing effect, as the authors acknowledge in the discussion (p. 575) but not in the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Both sexes lived together in the colony (8 males and 8 females from weaning, and again after the move at 65 days), and the introduction names mating among the behaviours that occur only in a colony (p. 571), but pregnancies, litters or any step to prevent them are not mentioned anywhere in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: Pregnancy or lactation could change fluid intake, body weight (and so mg/kg) and survival in the females concerned; whether this contributed to the less conclusive female results, or to the deaths of two colony females (cause not given, p. 572), cannot be assessed from the paper.

design_detail: Cross-sectional comparison of women and men within a treatment sample: 271 patients with current DSM-III-R cocaine, opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence entering inpatient or outpatient treatment at two Connecticut centres (156 women, 115 men). At treatment entry patients reported their ages at onset of regular use; the years between onset of regular use and entry into the current ('index') treatment were compared by gender within each dependence group, by ANCOVA adjusted for treatment setting, current age, number of previous treatments and other lifetime dependence diagnoses. ASI composite scores and SCID diagnoses were also compared.
can_establish: That in this treatment sample, women with opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence reported fewer years between onset of regular use and the current treatment than men, with similar reported ages of onset and similar dependence severity, while reporting more psychiatric and employment problems.
cannot_establish: That dependence progresses faster in women in general: everyone studied had entered treatment (time to treatment also reflects treatment-seeking and referral), the interval ends at the current rather than the first treatment, all timings were recalled at treatment entry, 'regular use' is not defined, and only 362 of 855 consecutive patients were recruited.

sample.recruitment: Treatment-seeking: 362 patients recruited from a consecutive series of 855 entering treatment at two Connecticut centres (two publicly supported outpatient units and an inpatient programme in a university hospital), paid for participation; the 271 with a current cocaine, opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence diagnosis were analysed and 91 without one were excluded (p. 266, Methods › 2.1 Subjects). Years of recruitment are not reported (the sample is described in Rounsaville et al., 1998).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Completed detoxification and remained in treatment at least 3 weeks (outpatient) or 3 days (inpatient); excluded if unable to read English, with lifetime DSM-III-R schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, or with current psychotic symptoms (p. 266).
sample.demographics: 156 women (57.6%); 56.0% European American, 34.0% African American, 10.0% Hispanic; mean age 32.5 (SD 7.9); education 11.9 years (SD 1.8); 58% unemployed; 14.0% married or cohabiting (pp. 266–267). Women were younger (31.4 vs 34.1), had less education (11.5 vs 12.4 years) and were more often unemployed (65.4% vs 48.7%) (Table 1, p. 267).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single assessment).
sample.selection_effects: A treatment sample, so the comparison is conditioned on having entered treatment, the very event that ends the measured interval; gender differences in treatment-seeking, referral and use of health services (discussed by the authors, pp. 266, 270) feed directly into the outcome. 362 of 855 consecutive patients were recruited, and the authors say many eligible patients declined (p. 270). Women were more often inpatients: 111 of 156 (71%) against 66 of 115 men (57%; editors' calculation) (p. 267).

exposure.measurement: The comparison is by gender (how recorded is not described). Ages at onset of regular use and of regular alcohol intoxication, and the pre-treatment years, were self-reported at treatment entry; the paper names the ASI and the SCID-I for DSM-III-R but not the items used, and does not define 'regular use' (pp. 266–267). The interval is described both as time elapsed from onset of regular use to entry into the index treatment (pp. 266–267) and as pre-treatment years of regular use (p. 268), without saying how it was computed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Days of use in the 30 days before treatment, women vs men: cocaine 14.0 vs 10.4; opioids 18.8 vs 17.3; cannabis 13.8 vs 11.6; alcohol 16.0 vs 16.6. Preferred route: cocaine smoked 63.0% vs 62.8%, intravenous 34.0% vs 27.9%, intranasal 3.0% vs 9.3%; opioids intravenous 65.7% vs 68.0%, intranasal 28.6% vs 28.0%. No gender difference was significant (Table 2, p. 268).
exposure.polysubstance: Patients could have several current diagnoses (mean 1.5 in women, 1.6 in men) and lifetime diagnoses (2.1 and 2.4) (Table 4, p. 269); each dependence group was analysed separately, so many patients appear in more than one comparison. Other lifetime dependence diagnoses were entered as factors (p. 267).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Assessed after detoxification and at least 3 weeks (outpatient) or 3 days (inpatient) of treatment (p. 266); how abstinence was verified is not described.

comparison.controls: Men in the same dependence group; no comparison with people outside treatment.
comparison.matching: None. ANCOVA with treatment setting entered before gender, current age, number of previous detoxification and rehabilitation treatments, and other lifetime dependence diagnoses (p. 267). Logistic models for diagnoses stepped in ethnicity, age and setting before gender.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Treatment-seeking propensity, referral route, childcare, health-service use, psychiatric history and trauma were not measured or not modelled (the authors discuss several as possible explanations, pp. 266, 270).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Men also had several diagnoses (mean 1.6 current, 2.4 lifetime; Table 4).

outcomes.instruments: Addiction Severity Index (seven composite severity scores, 0–1); Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID-I) for current (past-year) and lifetime dependence; eight interviewers (two at bachelor's, two at master's and four at doctoral level) (pp. 266–267).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments; inter-rater reliability not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Progression' = years between onset of regular use and entry into the index (current) treatment, used as a proxy for the overall progression of the disorder (p. 266); not the time to first treatment, although many patients had been treated before.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Editors' count of gender comparisons reported: 5 onset ages, 5 intervals, 4 frequencies of use, 6 route shares, 7 ASI scores and 10 diagnostic prevalences or counts.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; interviewers knew the patient's gender and recorded recalled histories.

analysis.effect_sizes: The main outcome is given only as F tests and as bars in Fig. 1 (mean ± standard error); no means are printed. Women reported fewer years from onset of regular use to the index treatment for opioids (F = 4.74, P = 0.03), cannabis (F = 7.28, P = 0.01) and regular drinking (F = 4.87, P = 0.03); regular intoxication P = 0.09; cocaine not significant (p. 268). Editors' reading of Fig. 1 by pixel measurement against the axis (approximate, about ±0.3 year), women vs men: cocaine 7.8 vs 8.8 years; opioids 8.1 vs 12.0; cannabis 12.8 vs 17.7; regular drinking 14.1 vs 18.7; regular intoxication 13.8 vs 17.8. Editors' calculation of standardized differences from F and group sizes (d ≈ √F × √(1/n1 + 1/n2)): about 0.47 (opioids), 0.88 (cannabis), 0.48 (regular drinking). ASI (Table 3, p. 269): psychiatric 0.36 vs 0.26 (F = 7.60, P = 0.006); employment 0.79 vs 0.66 (F = 11.75, P = 0.001); medical 0.30 vs 0.24 (F = 1.99, P = 0.15); alcohol 0.18 vs 0.23 and drug 0.19 vs 0.17, not different. Lifetime cannabis dependence 28.8% vs 47.0% (P < 0.001); the text gives OR 0.34 (95% CI 0.20–0.59) but labels it current cannabis dependence (p. 269); the unadjusted OR from the lifetime figures in Table 4 is 0.46 (0.28–0.76) (editors' calculation).
analysis.covariates: Treatment setting, current age, number of previous treatments and other lifetime dependence diagnoses in the ANCOVAs; ethnicity, age and setting in the logistic models (p. 267). Older patients reported longer intervals for every substance (for example cocaine F = 22.45, cannabis F = 103.68, P < 0.001), with no age × gender interaction (p. 269).
analysis.selective_reporting: No means or SDs for the main outcome; no statistics for the onset-age comparisons beyond a note that all were non-significant (Table 2); Pillai's statistic, promised in the Methods (p. 267), is not reported (p. 269).
analysis.power: Not reported. The cannabis comparison has 20 women and 18 men; the authors ask for caution (p. 269).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among patients entering treatment, women with opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence reported roughly 4–5 fewer years than men between onset of regular use and the current treatment (approximate, read from Fig. 1), with no difference for cocaine, no significant difference in reported age of onset, similar drug and alcohol severity, and higher psychiatric and employment severity scores. Women were also younger at treatment and more often inpatients.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports that women had more severe psychiatric, medical and employment complications (p. 265), but the medical difference was not significant (P = 0.15, p. 269), and concludes that there is a gender-based vulnerability to the adverse consequences of these disorders (p. 265); the summary says the shorter interval probably reflects a telescoped course of the disorders (p. 271) and supports earlier and more aggressive prevention among women at risk (p. 271). The Discussion argues that, because current age was controlled, the effects are not simply due to social and family pressures on women or to cohort (p. 270); adjusting for age does not address gender differences in treatment-seeking or referral, which act directly on time to treatment. It also presents the shorter interval as occurring although onset ages did not differ by gender (p. 269), but once current age is controlled, and if both sets of models hold the same covariates, a shorter interval and a later onset are arithmetically the same comparison (see reporting issues).

timeline.event: Lisansky: early description of a telescoped course in women with alcohol problems (cited by Hernandez-Avila et al., p. 265)
Piazza et al., on telescoping of alcohol problems in women, cited with Lisansky as where telescoping was first described (pp. 265–266)
Project MATCH treatment sample: as described by Hernandez-Avila et al. (p. 266), similar progression intervals in younger women and men with alcohol dependence but marked telescoping in older women

This study: shorter interval to treatment in women for opioids, cannabis and alcohol, not for cocaine, which the authors note conflicts with earlier cocaine studies (Griffin et al., 1989; White et al., 1996; Haas & Peters, 2000) (p. 269)
General-population test of telescoping in two US national surveys, listed in the project's reading list as the general-population counterpart; not appraised for this card
Critique of the origins of the telescoping concept, listed in the project's reading list; not appraised for this card

replication.where_it_stands: Within this paper the result is mixed across substances (opioids, cannabis and alcohol, but not cocaine), and the authors say their cocaine result conflicts with earlier treatment-sample studies (p. 269). Like the earlier work it cites, it rests on a treatment sample and recalled timings; general-population tests are on the project's reading list and are not appraised here.

funding.funder: NIH grants R01-DA05592, K05-DA00089 (B.J.R.), K24-AA13736 (H.R.K.) and T32-AA07290 (Acknowledgements, p. 271).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the University of Connecticut School of Medicine (Alcohol Research Center) and Yale University School of Medicine. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective general-population cohort that records, as they happen, the onset of regular use, the onset of dependence symptoms and the first treatment for women and men, analysed with survival methods that account for birth cohort and for people who never enter treatment.

domains.note: Gender is not caused by the usual confounders, but the comparison is entangled with age at treatment, cohort and treatment setting; the adjustment for current age makes the interval comparison equivalent to an onset-age comparison if the interval is age at treatment minus onset age and both sets of models hold the same covariates, and treatment pathways (referral, childcare, service use) were not measured.
Gender; recording not described but unlikely to be misclassified.
Only people who entered treatment, the event that ends the measured interval; 362 of 855 consecutive patients recruited, many eligible patients declined; women more often inpatients.
The interval runs to the current treatment, not the first; previous treatment histories may differ by gender (adjusted only as a count of previous treatments).
Missing data and their handling are not reported.

Onset of regular use recalled at treatment entry, on average about 8–19 years later (read from Fig. 1); 'regular use' undefined; the interval's computation not stated; interviewers aware of gender; recall may differ by gender.
Main-outcome means shown only in a figure; onset-age statistics and Pillai's statistic not reported; a mislabelled odds ratio; many comparisons without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The study reports what patients in treatment recalled, and its central contrast (time from regular use to the current treatment) is shaped by who enters treatment and when, by recall, and by an undefined measure whose adjusted comparison, on the simplest reading, is arithmetically tied to onset age. Cite it as a treatment-sample report of shorter recalled intervals to treatment in women with opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence (not cocaine), with similar severity at entry; not as evidence that dependence develops faster in women in the general population.

key_findings.finding: Of 855 consecutive patients entering treatment at two Connecticut centres, 362 were recruited; 271 with current DSM-III-R cocaine, opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence were analysed (91 excluded for no current dependence): 156 women and 115 men; 177 inpatients and 94 outpatients.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1 Subjects, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The number recruited is spelled out in the text (three hundred sixty-two).

key_findings.finding: Current dependence diagnoses: cocaine 167 (61.6%), opioids 93 (34.3%), alcohol 83 (30.6%), cannabis 38 (14.0%); by gender, cocaine 96 women and 71 men, opioids 58 and 35, cannabis 20 and 18, alcohol 41 and 42.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1 Subjects, 5th paragraph (p. 267); Table 2 column heads (p. 268)

key_findings.finding: Women were younger (31.4 vs 34.1 years; F = 8.25, P = 0.004), had less education (11.5 vs 12.4 years; F = 16.35, P < 0.001), were more often unemployed (65.4% vs 48.7%; χ2 = 7.58, P = 0.006) and more often inpatients (111 of 156, 71%; χ2 = 4.88, P = 0.02).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Demographic variables, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Mean age at onset of regular use, women vs men: cocaine 22.7 vs 23.4; opioids 23.7 vs 22.3; cannabis 15.6 vs 14.1; alcohol 20.3 vs 18.0 (regular intoxication 20.6 vs 19.0); none of the gender differences was significant (no test statistics given).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › 3.2, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Women reported fewer years between onset of regular use and entry into the index treatment for opioids (F = 4.74, P = 0.03), cannabis (F = 7.28, P = 0.01) and regular drinking (F = 4.87, P = 0.03); regular alcohol intoxication was a non-significant trend (F = 2.96, P = 0.09); there was no gender effect for cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Gender effects on progression to treatment entry, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Means are shown only as bars. Editors' reading of Fig. 1 by pixel measurement against the axis (approximate, about ±0.3 year), women vs men: cocaine 7.8 vs 8.8 years, opioids 8.1 vs 12.0, cannabis 12.8 vs 17.7, regular drinking 14.1 vs 18.7, regular intoxication 13.8 vs 17.8.

key_findings.finding: Older patients reported longer periods of regular use before treatment for every substance (cocaine F = 22.45, opioids F = 46.80, cannabis F = 103.68, alcohol F = 96.12, all P < 0.001), with no interaction between current age and gender; the number of previous treatments had no main or interactive effect (P > 0.10).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3, 4th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: If the interval is age at the index treatment minus onset age (the paper does not say; the implied ages in the reporting issues fit that reading), these age effects are largely built in, because current age is part of the interval; they are not separate evidence about progression (editors' reading).

key_findings.finding: Days of use in the 30 days before treatment and preferred routes did not differ by gender (for example cocaine 14.0 vs 10.4 days; cocaine smoked 63.0% vs 62.8%; opioids injected 65.7% vs 68.0%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 268); Results › 3.4, 1st paragraph (p. 269)

key_findings.finding: ASI scores at treatment entry, women vs men: alcohol 0.18 vs 0.23 and drug 0.19 vs 0.17 (no difference); psychiatric 0.36 vs 0.26 (F = 7.60, P = 0.006); employment 0.79 vs 0.66 (F = 11.75, P = 0.001); medical 0.30 vs 0.24 (F = 1.99, P = 0.15, not significant).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.5, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Lifetime cannabis dependence was less common in women (28.8% vs 47.0%, P < 0.001); no other current or lifetime dependence prevalence, and neither count of diagnoses, differed by gender. The text gives an OR of 0.34 (95% CI 0.20–0.59) for women but labels it current cannabis dependence.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.6, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Table 4 shows current cannabis dependence 13.5% vs 15.7% with no significance marker; see reporting issues. Per the Methods (p. 267), these comparisons used stepwise logistic models with ethnicity, age and setting entered before gender. Unadjusted, the Table 4 figures for current alcohol dependence (31.0% vs 43.5%) would differ (z ≈ 2.0–2.2, P ≈ 0.03–0.04), but the analysed group sizes in Table 2 (41 of 156 vs 42 of 115) give P ≈ 0.07 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations the retrospective design, reliance on self-reports open to recall bias, the many eligible patients who declined, and the larger share of women among inpatients.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The text says there was no gender difference in current cannabis dependence and, in the next sentence, that women were less likely to receive a diagnosis of current cannabis dependence (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.20–0.59); Table 4 shows current cannabis dependence 13.5% vs 15.7% without a marker and marks only lifetime cannabis dependence (28.8% vs 47.0%, P < 0.001), and the Discussion speaks of a lower lifetime risk.
reporting_issues.consequence: The odds ratio almost certainly refers to lifetime dependence; it should be cited as such, and as an adjusted estimate (the unadjusted OR from Table 4 is 0.46, 0.28–0.76; editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The current-dependence prevalences in Table 4 do not match the dependence groups analysed: 40.4% of 156 women and 34.0% of 115 men with current opioid dependence imply about 63 and 39 people (102), but the Methods and Table 2 give 93 (58 and 35); for alcohol, 31.0% and 43.5% imply about 48 and 50 (98) against 83 (41 and 42) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The prevalence table and the analysed groups do not describe the same patients, or one of them is in error; which patients formed each comparison cannot be confirmed.

reporting_issues.issue: With current age in every model (p. 267), a gender difference in the interval to treatment is arithmetically the same comparison as a gender difference in onset age, if the interval is age at the index treatment minus age at onset and both models hold the same covariates (the Methods list the number of previous treatments and other lifetime dependence diagnoses in the passage on the interval analyses, p. 267); the paper reports significant interval differences for opioids, cannabis and alcohol but no onset-age differences (Table 2). Combining Table 2 with the editors' reading of Fig. 1 gives implied mean ages at the index treatment of about 31.8 vs 34.3 years (opioids), 28.4 vs 31.8 (cannabis) and 34.4 vs 36.7 (alcohol; about the same for both alcohol intervals) for women vs men, consistent with the interval being computed that way.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the onset-age comparisons were not adjusted as stated, the two sets of models used different covariates, or the interval is something else (for example cumulative years of regular use), which the paper does not define. On the simplest reading, the women's shorter interval combines a younger age at treatment with a slightly later (non-significant) onset; with the same covariates, a significant interval difference alongside onset ages that did not differ could not both hold.

reporting_issues.issue: The F tests for the ANCOVAs are printed with denominator degrees of freedom equal to the group size minus one (for example d.f. = 1.92 for 93 opioid-dependent patients, 1.37 for 38 cannabis-dependent and 1.82 for 83 alcohol-dependent patients), although each model has several terms; the ASI tests use 1.264.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: with the correct error degrees of freedom the p-values barely change (for example F = 7.28 gives P = 0.010 with 37 and 0.011 with 30 degrees of freedom; editors' calculation), but the reported model cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: The main outcome's means and SDs are not printed (bars only, Fig. 1); the onset-age comparisons have no test statistics; and Pillai's statistic for the ASI MANCOVA, promised in the Methods, is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes for the central finding can only be estimated from the figure, and the omnibus test that should gate the univariate ASI tests cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that women reported more severe medical complications, but the medical severity difference was not significant (F = 1.99, P = 0.15); the abstract gives a mean age of 32.6 against 32.5 in the Methods (32.55 from Table 1; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates the medical finding; the age discrepancy is a rounding matter.
