design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis of 137 studies (142 latent class or latent profile analyses) of adult polysubstance use: at least three substance indicators and a mean sample age of 18 or older, in English-language peer-reviewed articles found in five databases (search dates not stated; latest included study 2022). The adult half of a two-part review registered on PROSPERO (registration details masked in the version read), whose adolescent half is Skandan et al. (2025). Study-level correlation and rank tests relate study features to the number of classes extracted. No appraisal of included studies and no pooled estimates.
can_establish: How adult latent class and latent profile studies of polysubstance use published up to 2022 were designed (samples, countries, indicators, scales, time frames and fit criteria), how many classes they extracted, and which of these study features went with extracting more classes.
cannot_establish: Which polysubstance patterns are common among adults or how many adults show them (each study's classes are listed in Table 2 but never synthesized, and nothing is pooled); whether the classes are valid or replicate across samples (no appraisal or validation was done); or that larger samples or more indicators reveal more real diversity, since these are unadjusted correlations between studies and, as the authors note, small samples are less able to detect rare classes.

sample.recruitment: Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO and Web of Science Core Collection (titles, abstracts and keywords), plus reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews and personal collections; the full strategy is in an online supplement that was not available, and no search dates are given in the text (PDF p. 7, 2.1). Sample types in the 137 studies: local or national samples 54, community samples of people with substance use disorders 27, sexual minorities 20, people in or entering treatment 19, partygoers 8, other 10 (Table 1, PDF p. 21; one study is counted in two groups, so the counts sum to 138).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: LCA or LPA with substance use variables as indicators of polysubstance classes; peer-reviewed; English; mean sample age 18 or older. Excluded: reports that were not peer reviewed (conference abstracts, theses, dissertations); samples that included people under 18; analyses not classifying polysubstance use; analyses with two substances as indicators or centred on one substance; papers not aiming to examine polysubstance patterns (PDF p. 7, 2.2). The authors state that the review focused on cross-sectional analyses (PDF p. 7, 2.3).
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 135 to 202,838 (mean 5382, median 1061); 113 studies (82.5%) published after 2014 (PDF p. 10, 3.2); the latest publication year in Tables 2 and 3 is 2022 (editors' check). Countries: US 76 (55.5%), Australia 16 (11.7%), Canada 6, Spain 5, UK 5, several countries 5, other 24 (Table 1, PDF p. 21). Participants' age and sex are not summarized. The total number of participants is not reported; 137 studies at the reported mean of 5,382 would give about 737,000 (editors' calculation, which counts overlapping survey samples twice and includes the 202,838 people whose deaths entered Culbreth et al., 2021).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed literature only, with no grey literature (both acknowledged, PDF p. 16); mostly US and Australian studies; many samples are of particular groups (people with substance use disorders or in treatment, people who inject drugs, sexual minorities, partygoers) alongside national surveys, so the class solutions describe those groups more than adults in general. Non-independence is not addressed: Beckham et al. (2022) and Coulter et al. (2019) report the same N (244) and the same three classes (48.4%, 21.3%, 30.3%) (Table 2, PDF pp. 24, 28); Harrell et al. (2012, 2014) appear to report two analyses of one sample of 552 (same N, population, indicators and software; PDF p. 34); and several studies draw on the same national surveys (for example NESARC, NSDUH and Australia's National Drug Strategy Household Survey; Table 2).

exposure.measurement: Self-report in 132 studies; objective testing (urinalysis, blood or other fluids, or toxicology) in 5 (PDF p. 9). Indicator scales: binary 98 (71.53%), ordinal 22 (16.06%), both 15 (10.95%), other 2 (Table 1, PDF p. 21). Time frames: within a month 46.72%, a period of months such as the past six months 10.95%, past year 29.93%, lifetime 14.60%, weekly 9.49%; a few studies used use at the last party attended, past-year diagnoses or urinalysis results (PDF pp. 9–10).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Most indicators were binary (any use in a period), which the authors say cannot capture quantity, frequency or cycles of use and abstinence (PDF p. 14, 4.1, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the review: polysubstance use is described as the co-use of multiple drugs, and the authors note there is no consensus on how to identify and classify it (PDF p. 2, Abstract). Substances used as indicators: stimulants in 91.97% of studies, cannabis 86.86%, opioids 73.32%, alcohol 67.15%, anxiolytics and sedative-hypnotics 45.99%, tranquilizers and anaesthetics 35.77%, hallucinogens 35.04%, inhalants or solvents 32.85%, tobacco or nicotine 32.85%, empathogens 31.39%, erectile dysfunction medicines 6.57%, and indicators covering a range of 'other drugs' 20.44%, sometimes single substances later collapsed into one category (PDF p. 9). A third of the studies did not include alcohol and two thirds did not include tobacco among their indicators, so their classes say nothing about how these substances combine with others (editors' observation).

comparison.controls: None. The review compares study features with the number of classes extracted, across studies.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. Predictors and covariates of class membership were extracted (PDF p. 8, 2.4, item 9) but are not reported anywhere in the review.

outcomes.instruments: Extracted per study: sample size and type, country, number, type, scale and time frame of indicators, number and description of classes, predictors and covariates, statistical methods and software (PDF p. 8, 2.4). Study-level tests: Spearman's rho (sample size; publication year), Pearson's r (number of indicators), Mann–Whitney U (self-report against objective measures; time frames; each fit criterion) and Kruskal–Wallis H (sample type) (PDF pp. 9–12).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of study quality or risk of bias is described or reported. Table 3 records which fit criteria each study used to choose its number of classes (PDF pp. 51–55).
outcomes.operationalization: The review's outcome is the number of classes each analysis extracted. Class content appears only as each study's own labels and proportions in Table 2 (PDF pp. 22–50).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The review reports at least ten study-level tests (three correlations, a self-report comparison, several time-frame comparisons, a sample-type comparison and a series of fit-criterion comparisons); the number in the two series is not stated. The single significant fit-criterion result (VLMR, p = 0.042) would not survive correction for any plausible number of tests, and the indicator correlation (p = .004) survives a Bonferroni correction only if 12 or fewer tests were run (editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles, abstracts and full texts were screened by two independent reviewers, with a third resolving disagreements; each study was extracted by one of three people, double-entered by another team member and cross-checked; inter-rater reliability was not calculated (PDF pp. 7–8, 16).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Classes per analysis 2 to 8, mean 3.85 (SD 1.10), median 4, mode 3, in 142 analyses across 137 studies; indicators per study 3 to 25, mean 8.69 (SD 3.78), median 8, mode 6 (PDF p. 9). Number of indicators and number of classes: Pearson r = .243, p = .004 (PDF p. 9). Sample size and number of classes: Spearman rho = .283, p < 0.001; publication year: rho = .004, p = .965 (PDF p. 10). Self-report against objective measures: Mann–Whitney Z = −1.876, p = 0.06 (PDF p. 9); time frames: all p > 0.108 (PDF p. 10); sample type: Kruskal–Wallis H = 5.81, p = 0.325 (PDF p. 11); VLMR, used by eight studies according to the text: fewer classes, Z = −2.03, p = 0.042; other fit criteria: no significant difference (PDF p. 12). No confidence intervals are given. By the editors' calculation, r = .243 and rho = .283 correspond to about 6% and 8% of the variation in class number between studies.
analysis.covariates: None. Each study feature was tested on its own; sample size and number of indicators were not analysed together, so their separate associations with class number are unknown.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registration on PROSPERO, as part of a two-part review, is stated in the abstract and methods, but the registration title and number are replaced by a placeholder in the manuscript version read (PDF pp. 2, 6), so the protocol could not be compared with the report. Deviations are not discussed; the report has no appraisal of included studies and does not synthesize two of its extracted items (class descriptions; predictors and covariates).
analysis.selective_reporting: Class descriptions and predictors or covariates of class membership were extracted (PDF p. 8, 2.4) but neither is synthesized in the text; class descriptions appear only study by study in Table 2. The PRISMA flow diagram cited as Figure 1 (PDF pp. 8, 15) is not in the manuscript PDF, so the reasons for excluding 293 full texts (484 reviewed, 191 kept; editors' arithmetic) are not available.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Some comparisons rest on few studies: 5 with objective measures, and 8 using the VLMR test according to the text (7 marked in Table 3). The authors cite a guide of upwards of 300 participants for most latent class analyses (PDF p. 13); the smallest included study had 135 (Jacka et al., 2021; PDF pp. 10, 35).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 137 adult studies, mostly from the US and Australia and often of particular groups, latent class analyses of polysubstance use extracted 2 to 8 classes (usually 3 or 4) from 3 to 25 indicators, mostly binary self-reports of use in the past month or year. Studies with larger samples and studies with more indicators extracted somewhat more classes (rho = .283; r = .243); time frame, sample type, self-report against testing, publication year and most fit criteria showed no detectable association. Which classes recur, and how large they are, is not summarized.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The results read the indicator correlation as meaning that studies including more substances found more diverse patterns of polysubstance use (PDF p. 9), and the discussion calls comprehensive indicator sets "essential to fully capturing substance use profiles" (PDF p. 14); an unadjusted between-study correlation of r = .243 does not show that the extra classes capture real patterns better rather than reflecting larger or more detailed studies. The conclusion that LCA/LPA "are effective tools for identifying previously unmeasured polysubstance use subgroups" (PDF p. 16) was not tested: the review did no validation, replication check or appraisal. The public significance statement says the work may aid the identification of polysubstance use profiles for clinical intervention (PDF pp. 2–3), but no profiles are synthesized. Right after reporting a significant VLMR effect, the results say the fit criteria used did not affect the number of classes, and the discussion repeats this (PDF p. 12). The abstract itself reports the two correlations and the heterogeneity without overstatement.

timeline.event: Tomczyk et al. review of 23 adolescent latent class studies, cited by this review among earlier reviews (PDF p. 5).

de Jonge et al. review of latent classes of substance use in young adults, and Karamouzian et al. review of latent polysubstance patterns among people who use opioids; both cited by this review as earlier reviews (PDF p. 5); not read.
Skandan et al., the adolescent half of this two-part review, to which 54 adolescent studies from the same search were assigned; cited as 2025 on PDF p. 6 and as under review on PDF p. 8; not read.
This review: 137 adult latent class studies.

replication.where_it_stands: The only review of adult latent class studies in the library. It is a review of methods: cite it for how adult polysubstance classes are built (which substances, scales and time frames), how many classes studies usually find and what that number depends on, and for the warning that class names are the researchers' choice. It cannot be cited for which adult patterns are common; that would need a coded tally of its Table 2 with duplicate samples removed, or the primary studies.

funding.funder: Listed on the manuscript cover page: 'Ashely Addiction Treatment' (as printed), the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse (PDF p. 1). The text has no funding statement describing the funders' role.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the manuscript version read; the version of record may contain one.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations are not given in the manuscript. One listed funder is a private addiction treatment provider: a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount. Table 2 includes Hochheimer et al. (2020) and Ellis et al. (2021), whose first authors share surnames with two of this review's authors, and the review's second author leads the companion adolescent review; the manuscript has no reference list for the 137 included studies, so the authorship of included studies cannot be checked from this file.

what_would_settle_it: A registered review of adult latent class studies that removes duplicate and overlapping samples, codes every study's classes against one scheme (for example no or low use; one main substance; alcohol, tobacco and cannabis; stimulant, opioid or party-drug clusters; wide-range use), reports how often each recurs and how large it is by population, and appraises study quality; or a joint re-analysis of the large national surveys with the same indicators, time frame and model-selection rules.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (samples with mean age 18 or older), method (LCA/LPA with substance indicators) and outcomes (study features and number of classes) are specified; a comparator does not apply.

Pre-registration on PROSPERO is stated (PDF pp. 2, 6), but the registration details are masked in the version read, so the protocol's contents cannot be checked, and no deviations are discussed although no appraisal of included studies was done.
The authors say they focused on cross-sectional analyses because this allowed comparable evaluation of methods and outcomes (PDF p. 7, 2.3).

Five databases, reference lists, relevant reviews and personal collections, with the full strategy in a supplement; but English only without a justification (the peer-review limit is given the reason of rigour), no grey literature, registries or experts, and no search dates in the text, so the 24-month currency the authors claim cannot be checked; the latest included study is from 2022. Item applied as written (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Two independent reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts in Covidence; a third resolved disagreements (PDF pp. 7–8, 2.3).

Each study was extracted by one of three people, double-entered by another team member and cross-checked, with discrepancies corrected (PDF p. 8, 2.4), which meets the item's consensus criterion; inter-rater reliability was not calculated (PDF p. 16).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded full texts; the PRISMA diagram (Figure 1) cited in the text is absent from the manuscript PDF, and the supplement is described as containing the search strategy.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives each study's N, sample description, indicators, scale and time frame, classes with proportions and software; country, design, age and sex are not given per study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal of included studies was done.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
Nothing pooled; the study-level correlation and rank tests describe study features and are not a meta-analysis of results.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Without an appraisal, the quality of the included studies plays no part in the interpretation.
Heterogeneity in methods and class solutions is the review's focus; sample size, indicators, scale, time frame, sample type and fit criteria are tested as sources and discussed (PDF pp. 9–15).
No meta-analysis; the authors note that the peer-review restriction may have contributed to publication bias (PDF p. 16).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funders are listed on the cover page, but the version read has no conflict-of-interest statement and no account of how potential conflicts were managed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (4: English only without a reason and no search dates; 7: no list of excluded studies, and the flow diagram is missing from this version; 9: no appraisal of included studies; 13: study quality therefore plays no part in interpretation), and item 2 is met only in part, which gives critically low confidence; items 11 and 15 do not apply because nothing was pooled. The review is a transparent catalogue of how adult latent class studies were done, with study-by-study tables that let readers check most counts; its study-level analyses are simple unadjusted tests. It may be cited for study features (indicators, scales, time frames, sample types, numbers of classes) and for the association of sample size and number of indicators with the number of classes; it should not be cited for which adult polysubstance patterns are common or how prevalent they are.

key_findings.finding: Of 2458 records, 2108 remained after removing 350 duplicates; 484 full texts were reviewed and 191 qualified for the two-part review; 54 adolescent studies went to the companion review, leaving 137 adult studies.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (PRISMA flow), cited here, is not in the manuscript PDF.

key_findings.finding: The search covered Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO and Web of Science Core Collection, with reference lists, relevant reviews and personal collections; studies had to be peer-reviewed, in English and with a mean sample age of 18 or older; analyses using two substances, centred on one substance or not aimed at polysubstance patterns were excluded. No search dates are given.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Search Strategy; 2.2 Eligibility Criteria

key_findings.finding: In 142 analyses across 137 studies, 2 to 8 classes were extracted (mean 3.85, SD 1.10, median 4, mode 3), from 3 to 25 indicators per study (mean 8.69, SD 3.78, median 8, mode 6).
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Latent Class Solutions, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Substances used as indicators: stimulants in 91.97% of studies, cannabis 86.86%, opioids 73.32%, alcohol 67.15%, anxiolytics and sedative-hypnotics 45.99%, tranquilizers and anaesthetics 35.77%, hallucinogens 35.04%, inhalants or solvents 32.85%, tobacco or nicotine 32.85%, empathogens 31.39%, erectile dysfunction medicines 6.57%; indicators covering a range of 'other drugs' in 20.44% (sometimes single substances later collapsed into one other-drug category).
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Latent Class Solutions, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 73.32% cannot be produced from 137 studies (100 of 137 is 72.99%, 101 of 137 is 73.72%; editors' arithmetic), probably a typing error; the intended count cannot be recovered.

key_findings.finding: The number of indicators correlated with the number of classes extracted (Pearson r = .243, p = .004).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (PDF p. 2); 3.1, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 9)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: r = .243 corresponds to about 6% of the between-study variation in class number. The correlation is not adjusted for sample size, and the indicator counts include some items that are not substance use (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Sample sizes ranged from 135 to 202,838 (mean 5382, median 1061); studies with larger samples extracted more classes (Spearman rho = .283, p < 0.001); publication year was not associated with the number of classes (rho = .004, p = .965); 113 studies (82.5%) were published after 2014.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (PDF p. 2); 3.2 Settings & Samples, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: 132 studies used self-report and 5 objective measures, with no significant difference in the number of classes (Mann–Whitney Z = −1.876, p = 0.06). Indicators were binary in 71.53% of studies, ordinal in 16.06% and both in 10.95%; time frames were within a month 46.72%, a period of months 10.95%, past year 29.93%, lifetime 14.60% and weekly 9.49%, with no difference in the number of classes by time frame (all p > 0.108).
key_findings.locator: 3.1, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 9, continuing on PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Studies that ran separate analyses for subgroups often found different solutions (Caravaca-Sánchez et al., 2022: 4 classes for men and 2 for women), while Armour et al. (2014) and El-Bassel et al. (2019), stratified by sex, and Stevens et al. (2021), stratified by survey wave, found identical solutions.
key_findings.locator: 3.2, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 10, continuing on PDF p. 11)

key_findings.finding: 55.47% of studies were from the US and 11.68% from Australia; samples were local or national (39.42%), community samples of people with substance use disorders (19.71%), sexual minorities (14.60%), people in or entering treatment (13.87%) and partygoers (5.84%); sample type was not associated with the number of classes (Kruskal–Wallis H = 5.81, p = 0.325).
key_findings.locator: 3.2, 2nd paragraph; counts in Table 1 (PDF p. 21)

key_findings.finding: Fit criteria used to choose the number of classes: BIC or adjusted BIC 94.20%, AIC or AICc 65.69%, LMR-LRT 37.23%, VLMR 5.8%, BLRT 23.36%, G2 7.97%, log-likelihood 21.90%, entropy over 56.2%; studies using the VLMR test extracted fewer classes (Mann–Whitney Z = −2.03, p = 0.042), while other criteria showed no significant difference.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Fit Indices for Latent Class Solutions
key_findings.note: The editors' count of the marks in Table 3 (PDF pp. 51–55) differs slightly: VLMR 7 studies (text: eight), LMR-LRT 53, AIC/AICc 91, log-likelihood 31, entropy 76, BIC/aBIC 129, G2 11.

key_findings.finding: The review includes no appraisal of the included studies, pools nothing and does not summarize which classes recur; each study's classes are listed with their proportions in Table 2.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Article Review & Synthesis and 2.4 Data Extraction & Outcomes (no appraisal step); Table 2

key_findings.finding: Table 2 shows what some adult polysubstance classes are built from: the largest sample, Culbreth et al. (2021, N = 202,838), used drugs present in toxicology reports at the time of violent death (classes: no or single substance 84.85%, alcohol and other substance 9.01%, marijuana and other substance 3.78%, opiates 2.35%); Agrawal et al. (2007, N = 43,093) used lifetime abuse or dependence diagnoses; Votaw et al. (2020) included sexually transmitted infection, deviant behaviours, arrest and suicidal ideation among its 15 indicators.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, rows Agrawal et al., 2007 (PDF p. 22); Culbreth et al., 2021 (PDF p. 29); Votaw et al., 2020 (PDF p. 48)

key_findings.finding: The authors cite a guide of upwards of 300 participants for most latent class analyses, especially when many subgroups are expected or classes are poorly separated, and say that small samples reduce the ability to detect rarer classes.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Methodological Considerations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors warn that class names are chosen by the researchers and can mislead (a naming fallacy), citing an included study that extracted both a cocaine, alcohol, marijuana and tobacco class and a separate cocaine polysubstance class; they recommend naming every substance with a high probability of use, quantifying terms such as high risk, and wording names probabilistically.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Methodological Considerations, the paragraph beginning 'Fourth'

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: English-only eligibility may have limited the pool of studies and their geographic diversity; including only peer-reviewed sources, without grey literature, may have contributed to publication bias; inter-rater reliability was not calculated when reconciling the double-entered data.
key_findings.locator: 4.2 Strengths & Limitations (continuing from PDF p. 15)

reporting_issues.issue: Beckham et al. (2022) and Coulter et al. (2019) report the same sample size (244), nine indicators and identical classes (48.4%, 21.3%, 30.3%), and Harrell et al. (2012, 2014) appear to be two analyses of one sample of 552 (same N, population, eight past-month indicators and software, yielding 3 and 5 classes); all four are counted as separate studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 137 studies include at least one, and probably two, repeats of the same sample, which inflates the counts slightly and gives these samples double weight in the study-level correlations; the review does not mention sample overlap, including the many studies drawn from the same national surveys.

reporting_issues.issue: The age criterion is not applied as stated: samples including people under 18 were to be excluded, but Guerras et al. (2021) studied men aged 16 to 64, and Steinhoff et al. (2021) used respondents surveyed at ages 13, 15, 17 and 20 without saying which age entered the analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: A few included samples are not strictly adult; in practice the boundary with the adolescent companion review is the mean age.

reporting_issues.issue: Some indicator sets include items that are not substance use, although eligibility required substance use variables as indicators: Votaw et al. (2020) used sexually transmitted infection, deviant behaviours, arrest and suicidal ideation among its 15 indicators; Fairgrieve et al. (2020) included addiction treatment (opioid agonist, inpatient or outpatient) in the past month among its 19 indicators.
reporting_issues.consequence: The indicator counts used in the correlation with the number of classes (r = .243) mix substance and non-substance items, and such classes are not pure substance use patterns.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the VLMR test was used in eight studies (5.8%) and gives percentages for the other fit criteria; by the editors' count of the marks in Table 3 (word positions in the PDF's text layer, checked on the rendered pages), VLMR is marked for 7 studies, LMR-LRT for 53 (the text's 37.23% is 51 of 137), AIC/AICc for 91 (65.69% is 90), log-likelihood for 31 (21.90% is 30) and entropy for 76 (over 56.2% is 77).
reporting_issues.consequence: The one significant fit-criterion result (VLMR, p = 0.042) rests on seven or eight studies; the fit-criterion percentages are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The opioid share of indicators is printed as 73.32%; by the editors' arithmetic no whole number of the 137 studies gives that figure (101 of 137 is 73.72%), while the other percentages match whole counts. The same paragraph prints 86.86.% and the sample-type paragraph 19.71 without a percent sign.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typing errors; the intended opioid share cannot be recovered, since 73.32% lies between 100 of 137 (72.99%) and 101 of 137 (73.72%) and is nearer the first.

reporting_issues.issue: The numbering and citation of the companion review are inconsistent: the methods call this review the second part and the adolescent review (Skandan et al., 2025) part one, while the results say the 54 adolescent studies went to part 2 and cite Skandan et al. as under review.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; affects only how the companion review is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The manuscript keeps masked placeholders for the PROSPERO registration and for the reviewers' initials, lacks the Figure 1 it cites, and has no reference list for the 137 included studies, which Tables 2 and 3 name only by author and year; several differ between the two tables (Banks et al. 2021 and 2020; Blow et al. 2011 and 2021; Noroozi et al. 2020 and 2022), and Caravaca-Sánchez is spelled Caracava-Sánchez in both tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: The registration, the flow of studies and the identity of some included studies cannot be checked from this version; the version of record (DOI 10.1037/pha0000791) may resolve them.

reporting_issues.issue: Immediately after reporting that studies using the VLMR test extracted fewer classes (p = 0.042), the results say the fit criteria used did not affect the number of classes, and the discussion repeats that fit criteria did not significantly influence it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor internal inconsistency; with many tests and no correction the VLMR result is weak in any case.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say the review concluded within 24 months of beginning the searches, as AMSTAR 2 recommends, but no search dates are given; by the editors' check of Tables 2 and 3 the latest included study is from 2022, while the article is from 2025.
reporting_issues.consequence: The currency of the search cannot be judged; studies from 2023 onward are absent.

reporting_issues.issue: The study-level correlation and rank tests do not say whether they used the 137 studies or the 142 analyses, although stratified analyses gave different numbers of classes within one study (for example 4 classes for men and 2 for women in Caravaca-Sánchez et al., 2022).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: which class count entered for stratified studies, and whether they were counted more than once, is unknown; the printed p-values fit either unit (editors' calculation).

design_detail: Prospective population birth cohort (Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, New Zealand; 1,037 children born April 1972 to March 1973) analysed with propensity-score matching. Exposure ('early exposure'): self-reported use of alcohol, cannabis, inhalants or other drugs on 'multiple occasions' in the past year at the age-13 or age-15 assessment (114 adolescents, mostly alcohol), against 813 without, matched 3 to 1 (342) on a score built from 13 childhood risk factors. Outcomes at 32: past-year substance dependence, herpes simplex type 2 serology, pregnancy before 21 (women only), no educational qualifications, and criminal convictions at 17–32. The analysis was repeated within two strata defined by an earlier conduct-problem trajectory (ages 7–13).
can_establish: That in this New Zealand birth cohort, adolescents who drank or used drugs repeatedly by 15 had higher rates of several adult problems at 32 than adolescents with similar measured childhood risk, including those with no history of childhood conduct problems.
cannot_establish: That early use caused these outcomes (no random assignment; peer substance use, parental monitoring, puberty timing, tobacco and inherited risk beyond a family-history score were not in the matching (parenting entered only through the maltreatment covariate), and no sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding is reported), what age at first use does (the exposure was repeated use by 15, not age at first use), which substance mattered (65 of the 114 used alcohol only), or whether the results hold for people born after 1973 or outside New Zealand.

sample.recruitment: Registry/population birth cohort: 1,037 children (52% male), 91% of the children born consecutively in Dunedin between April 1972 and March 1973, enrolled at age 3 and assessed at 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 26 and 32; 96% of living members took part at 32 (2003–2005) (p. 1038, Method › Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria beyond cohort membership are stated; 927 adolescents are in the analysis (Table 1 note, p. 1040). The paper does not say why the other 110 cohort members are not analysed or how missing data were handled.
sample.demographics: 52% male; families across the full socioeconomic range of New Zealand's South Island, primarily White (p. 1038). First exposures took place in 1984–1987 (p. 1043). Before matching, early-exposed and other adolescents were similar in sex (51.8% vs 50.6% male) and low SES (20.0% in both) (Table 1, p. 1040).
sample.attrition: 96% of living members assessed at 32 (p. 1038). Numbers with each outcome (blood sample for serology, pregnancy reports, interviews) are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A population cohort with high retention, so selection into the cohort is a small concern. But 110 of the 1,037 members are not in the analysis without explanation, and the prevalence of early exposure (11.2%, p. 1038) does not match 114 of the 927 analysed (12.3%); it would fit 114 of about 1,018 or about 116 of all 1,037 (editors' calculation), so prevalence and analysis appear to rest on different samples.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at the age-13 and age-15 assessments of past-year frequency (0 never, 1 once or twice, 2 multiple occasions) of sniffing glue, gasoline or other inhalants; smoking cannabis; using any other illegal drug; buying or drinking alcohol; and drinking alcohol during school. 'Early-exposed' = multiple occasions at 13, 15 or both (p. 1038, Method › Early Substance Exposure). Single informant; no amounts; no biological check. Recorded at the time, not recalled in adulthood. As described (past-year reports at 13 and at 15), use between the 13th and 14th birthdays was not asked about (editors' reading).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency only ('multiple occasions', number not defined); no quantities. 10% of members were exposed to alcohol before 15, 5% to cannabis, under 2% to inhalants or other drugs (p. 1038); 65 of the 114 early-exposed used alcohol only and 49 more than one substance (p. 1042); 1.2% of the cohort used only cannabis before 15 and under 1% only inhalants or other drugs (p. 1043).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol and drugs are combined in one exposure; specific drugs could not be separated because almost no one used them alone (p. 1043). Sensitivity analyses compared alcohol-only (n = 65) and more-than-one-substance (n = 49) adolescents with matched unexposed adolescents (pp. 1041–1042). Tobacco was not part of the exposure.

comparison.controls: Cohort members not exposed on multiple occasions before 15 (they may have used once or twice), matched 3 to 1 by nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching in PSMATCH2 (p. 1040, Statistical Analyses, 2nd paragraph). Whether matching was with replacement or within a caliper is not stated.
comparison.matching: Propensity score from a logistic regression on 13 covariates: family history of alcohol or drug disorder, conduct problems at 7, 9, 11 and 13, parental criminal conviction, low SES, maltreatment, low maternal IQ, low child IQ, undercontrolled temperament, ADHD and sex; c statistic .72 (95% CI .67–.77), scores .02 to .73 (p. 1040). Standardized bias across covariates ranged from −8% to 85% (average 17%) before matching and from −6% to 8% (average 0%) after (p. 1040; Table 1). Within the no-conduct-problem stratum the average fell from 2% to 1%, within the conduct-problem stratum from 11% to 0% (p. 1041).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not in the score: peer substance use, parental monitoring and drinking practices, puberty timing, early tobacco use, anxiety or depression, school engagement. Covariates were fixed (measured once), mostly before 13, but family history and parental conviction were collected in 2003–2006, ADHD used data from ages 5–15, maltreatment included retrospective self-reports, and conduct problems at 13 were measured at the same age as the first exposure report (p. 1039).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Matched adolescents could have used alcohol or drugs once or twice before 15; use after 15 is not reported for either group.

outcomes.instruments: Diagnostic Interview Schedule (DSM-IV) at 32 for past-year cannabis, other drug or alcohol dependence (tobacco not included); herpes simplex type 2 IgG by ELISA (HerpeSelect 2; cutoff 3.5, equivocal 0.9–3.5 resolved by Western blot) at 32; women's self-report of at least one pregnancy before 21; no educational qualifications by 32; number of convictions at 17–32 (violent and non-violent, traffic excluded) from the New Zealand Police database (p. 1039, Adult Outcomes).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments; covariate reliabilities all above .70 (p. 1039). Norms not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Binary outcomes as defined above; convictions as counts modelled with negative binomial regression (Table 2 note). The sensitivity analyses use a 'cumulative index of poor adult outcomes' whose construction is not described; for the alcohol-only analysis it is said to include dependence, herpes, no qualifications and convictions (p. 1042).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five outcomes estimated in the whole sample and in two strata (15 estimates), plus two sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Outcomes were collected 17 years after the exposure reports; serology and police records are objective.

analysis.effect_sizes: After matching (Table 2, p. 1041), early-exposed (n = 114) vs matched (n = 342): substance dependence at 32, 28.8% vs 14.7%, OR 2.25 (95% CI 1.35–3.73); herpes, 28.0% vs 16.1%, OR 2.02 (1.18–3.44); pregnancy before 21 (women), 44.7% vs 22.5%, OR 2.78 (1.38–5.57); no qualifications, 32.1% vs 19.3%, OR 1.97 (1.22–3.19); convictions at 17–32, mean 7.12 vs 1.74, IRR 3.95 (2.23–6.97). Before matching: ORs 3.25, 1.90, 3.65 and 2.74, IRR 5.35. Editors' calculation from the printed percentages: risk ratios after matching 1.96 (dependence), 1.74 (herpes), 1.99 (pregnancy) and 1.66 (qualifications); risk differences 14.1, 11.9, 22.2 and 12.8 percentage points. No-conduct-problem stratum (Table 3, p. 1042): dependence 23.2% vs 7.6%, OR 3.64 (1.57–8.45); herpes 32.7% vs 15.4%, OR 2.66 (1.26–5.60); pregnancy 34.4% vs 12.3%, OR 3.75 (1.45–9.69), labelled exploratory; no qualifications 14.2% vs 10.9%, OR 1.37 (0.56–3.34); convictions 1.59 vs 0.65, IRR 2.86 (1.2–6.6). Conduct-problem stratum: dependence 32.0% vs 15.3%, OR 2.60 (1.24–5.46); herpes 23.4% vs 20.5%, OR 1.18 (0.54–2.60); pregnancy 69.2% vs 35.9%, OR 4.02 (1.04–15.46); no qualifications 49.0% vs 28.7%, OR 2.38 (1.24–4.57); convictions 13.12 vs 2.52, IRR 4.96 (2.5–10.0). Sensitivity analyses give only Cohen's d for a composite whose construction is not described: alcohol only d = 0.51, more than one substance d = 1.15, both p < .01, no intervals (p. 1042).
analysis.covariates: The 13 matched covariates listed above, all fixed (no time-varying confounders after 15 were modelled; later use and schooling are potential mediators and were rightly not adjusted). Standard errors bootstrapped in PSMATCH2; sex-specific propensity scores for the pregnancy outcome (Table 2 notes, p. 1041).
analysis.selective_reporting: Five outcomes reported from a cohort that measures many; no protocol cited. The sensitivity analyses report d and p only, for a composite whose construction is not described. Differences between the two strata are described without a test of interaction.
analysis.power: Not reported. Each stratum has 55–56 early-exposed adolescents; the stratified pregnancy estimates rest on fewer than 50 early-exposed women each (Table 3 note, p. 1042).

interpretation_gap.results_show: After matching on 13 childhood risk factors, adolescents who reported repeated drinking or drug use at 13–15 (mostly alcohol) had about 1.7 to 2 times the risk of past-year substance dependence, herpes infection, pregnancy before 21 and no qualifications at 32, and about four times as many convictions, as matched adolescents; in the half with no childhood conduct problems the odds ratios for dependence, herpes and pregnancy (exploratory) were larger than in the whole sample and convictions were still raised (IRR 2.86), while the estimate for qualifications was small and imprecise.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that reducing or delaying early exposure may prevent a wide range of adult health problems (p. 1037), and the Discussion says the findings support a causal link and an independent risk (pp. 1042–1043). Three points go beyond the results. (1) The Results describe early-exposed adolescents as "approximately 2 to 3 times more likely" to have the outcomes (p. 1041), but these figures are odds ratios; the risk ratios are 1.7 to 2.0 (editors' calculation). (2) The abstract lists early pregnancy among the increased risks of adolescents without conduct problems without the Table 3 caveat that this estimate is exploratory (p. 1042), and the contrasts between strata (herpes raised only without conduct problems, qualifications only with them) are drawn without a test of interaction, although the intervals overlap widely. (3) The exposure is called exposure to illicit substances (p. 1038) or to drugs and alcohol, but 65 of the 114 early-exposed adolescents used alcohol only (p. 1042). The authors acknowledge that matching cannot replace random assignment (p. 1043) but report no analysis of how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to remove the effects.

timeline.event: Cross-sectional US survey: drinking before 15 statistically predicts adult alcohol disorders (cited by Odgers et al., p. 1037)
Prescott & Kendler, age at first drink and risk for alcoholism, subtitled 'a noncausal association'; cited by Odgers et al. among studies without consensus on cause (p. 1042)
Co-twin control study of early cannabis use, cited by Odgers et al. among studies without consensus on cause (p. 1042)
Wells, Horwood & Fergusson: links between adolescent drinking and later outcomes may reflect who drinks (cited by Odgers et al., p. 1042)

Australian twin study (age at first use recalled in adulthood): genetic overlap between earlier first use and use-disorder symptoms plus a residual unique-environmental correlation, read by its authors as consistent with a partly causal effect

replication.where_it_stands: The authors note that earlier work had not reached a consensus on whether early use is causal (p. 1042). Among the papers read in this round, a twin study with a different design (familial confounding modelled, adult recall) found both a shared familial liability and a residual association (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2016). No direct replication of this propensity-score analysis, and no randomized evidence on delaying first use, was among the papers read.

what_would_settle_it: A design that separates early use from the family and personal risk that comes with it: a prevention trial that delays first use at random and follows participants into adulthood, or within-family comparisons (siblings or co-twins discordant for early repeated use) with use recorded at the time and the same adult outcomes; any further propensity analysis should report how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to explain the results.

domains.note: Matching balanced 13 childhood factors well (standardized bias −6% to 8%), including conduct problems recorded prospectively by several informants, a real strength over cross-sectional studies. But peer substance use, parental monitoring and drinking practices, puberty timing, early tobacco use and anxiety or depression were not included; family history and parental conviction were collected decades later; no sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding is reported.

Recorded at the time (no adult recall), but single-informant, three-level frequency items without amounts; 'multiple occasions' is not defined, and as described the two past-year windows leave out the year between the 13th and 14th birthdays.

Population birth cohort with 96% participation at 32, but 110 of 1,037 members are not in the analysis without explanation, and 3 early-exposed adolescents are missing from the stratified analysis (56 + 55 of 114).
No intervention after exposure bears on the comparison; later use was not adjusted for, which suits an estimate of the total effect.

Handling of missing covariates and outcomes is not described; several covariate percentages among the 114 early-exposed (for example 31.8%, 10.0%, 7.2%) cannot arise from a denominator of 114, implying missing values (editors' calculation); numbers with serology and pregnancy data are not given.

Outcomes measured 17 years after exposure by structured interview, serology and police records; pregnancy and qualifications by self-report; blinding not stated but of little consequence for serology and records.

Five outcomes chosen from a cohort with many measures, no protocol; sensitivity analyses reported as d for a composite whose construction is not described, without intervals; stratum contrasts interpreted without interaction tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A strong observational design for this question (pre-exposure conduct problems recorded by several informants, exposure recorded at 13–15, objective outcomes at 32), but the causal reading the authors give depends on there being no important unmeasured confounding after matching on 13 factors, and several plausible confounders were not measured. Cite it for the associations after matching, their size (risk ratios about 2, not 2–3), and the finding that about half of early-exposed adolescents had no childhood conduct problems; not for a causal effect of early use, for effects of particular drugs (exposure was mostly alcohol), or for age at first use as such.

key_findings.finding: Of the cohort, 11.2% reported alcohol or drug use on multiple occasions in the past year at 13, 15 or both (the 'early-exposed'); alcohol was the most common (10% of members), cannabis 5%, inhalants or other drugs under 2%.
key_findings.locator: Method › Early Exposure and Conduct-Problem Measures › Early Substance Exposure, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Of the early-exposed adolescents, 65 used alcohol only and the remaining 49 more than one substance; only 1.2% of the whole cohort used cannabis alone before 15, and under 1% only inhalants or other drugs, so drug-specific effects could not be estimated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity Analyses, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 1041) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1042); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1043)

key_findings.finding: Childhood conduct problems predicted early exposure: 17.0% of adolescents with a conduct-problem history vs 9.1% without (OR 2.1, CI 1.4–3.1); 56 of the 114 early-exposed adolescents (about half) had no conduct-problem history.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that matching cannot substitute for random assignment, that the cohort first used substances in 1984–1987 (mainly alcohol and cannabis), that replication across ethnicities and cultures is needed, and that exposure should be measured with several informants and more precise timing and amounts.

reporting_issues.issue: The analysis sample is 927 (Table 1 note) of a cohort of 1,037, with no account of the 110 others; the early-exposure prevalence of 11.2% (p. 1038) does not match 114 of 927 (12.3%): it would fit 114 of about 1,018 members, or about 116 of all 1,037 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sample and the sample behind the prevalence figures differ in an unexplained way; whether the exclusions relate to exposure or outcomes cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 56 of the 114 early-exposed adolescents were in the no-conduct-problem stratum (p. 1041), which leaves 58 for the other stratum, but Table 3 shows 55.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three early-exposed adolescents are missing from the stratified analysis without explanation (perhaps no match was found); minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Several percentages for the 114 early-exposed adolescents in Table 1 (parental conviction 31.8%, low SES 20.0%, maltreatment 10.0%, low child IQ 15.2%, undercontrolled temperament 8.2%, ADHD 7.2%) cannot arise from a denominator of 114, and low maternal IQ in the same 114 is 18.1% before and 18.0% after matching (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Covariate data were partly missing, but the paper does not say how missing covariates entered the propensity model.

reporting_issues.issue: Effect sizes that cannot be reproduced from the printed figures: the matched OR for dependence (28.8% vs 14.7%) computes to 2.35, not 2.25; and none of the four conviction IRRs equals the ratio of the printed mean counts (before matching 5.35 vs 7.12/1.31 = 5.44; after matching 3.95 vs 4.09; no-conduct-problem stratum 2.86 vs 2.45; conduct-problem stratum 4.96 vs 5.21), the no-conduct-problem IRR differing most and in the other direction; all other ORs agree within about 0.03 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small; the models may have used weights or covariates that the paper does not describe.

reporting_issues.issue: The 49 early-exposed adolescents who were not alcohol-only are described as exposed to more than one substance (p. 1042), yet 1.2% of the cohort used only cannabis before 15 (p. 1043); whether those adolescents are among the early-exposed is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'more than one substance' group (d = 1.15) may include adolescents who used cannabis alone; the contrast with alcohol-only exposure is less clean than described.

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure is called exposure to illicit substances in the Introduction and Method (p. 1038), although it includes buying or drinking alcohol, and alcohol alone accounts for 65 of the 114 early-exposed adolescents (p. 1042).
reporting_issues.consequence: The study is mainly about repeated early drinking; citing it for early illicit drug use overstates what it measured.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity analyses use a 'cumulative index of poor adult outcomes' whose construction is not described (for the alcohol-only analysis the paper says it includes substance dependence, herpes infection, no educational qualifications and criminal convictions) and report Cohen's d without intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The alcohol-only and more-than-one-substance effects (d = 0.51 and 1.15) cannot be interpreted on the scale of the main outcomes or checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 3 note repeats the Table 2 statement that all findings remained statistically significant after bootstrapping of standard errors, but two Table 3 estimates carry no significance mark and have intervals that include 1 (herpes in the conduct-problem stratum, OR 1.18, 0.54–2.60; no qualifications in the no-conduct-problem stratum, OR 1.37, 0.56–3.34).
reporting_issues.consequence: The note cannot hold for every Table 3 estimate; significance should be read from the intervals and asterisks, which agree with the Results text (p. 1041).

design_detail: Classical twin study: biometric (ACE) modelling of 7,285 monozygotic and same-sex dizygotic twins from the Australian Twin Registry (Cohorts II and III), each interviewed once by telephone. Ages at first use of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis (recalled in adulthood, analysed as continuous) and lifetime DSM-IV symptom counts for nicotine dependence, alcohol use disorder and a restricted cannabis use disorder count were modelled as two latent factors (initiation and disorder), separately in men and women. The genetic (rG), shared-environmental (rC) and unique-environmental (rE) correlations between the two factors were estimated; a non-zero rE was read as a 'quasi-causal' signal. No explicit co-twin (discordant-pair) comparison was reported.
can_establish: How much of the association between earlier first use and more symptoms of use disorder in these Australian adults is shared with genetic and family-environmental influences, and that some association remained after modelling those familial influences.
cannot_establish: That earlier first use causes disorder: the remaining unique-environmental correlation also contains anything that differs between twins in a pair and affects both (for example conduct problems, peers or life events) and correlated reporting error from the same interview, and it shrank when correlated residuals were allowed; ages were recalled in adulthood; and the twin-model assumptions (such as equal environments for identical and fraternal twins) are not discussed in the paper.

sample.recruitment: Registry: Australian Twin Registry Cohort II (born 1964–1971, interviewed 1996–2000) and Cohort III (born 1972–1979, interviewed 2005–2009) (Table 1, p. 949). Participation rates are not given in this paper, which refers to earlier reports (p. 948).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Monozygotic and same-sex dizygotic twins who had ever used tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, or abstainers whose co-twin had (7,285 of 7,334). Opposite-sex pairs were excluded because the symptom counts were not measurement-invariant across sex and the structure of initiation differed by sex (p. 948, footnote 1; Table 1 note, p. 949).
sample.demographics: 40% men; mean age at interview 30.6 (range 24–40); Cohort II mean 29.9, Cohort III 31.8 (Table 1, p. 949). Largely Caucasian, with a very low alcohol abstinence rate (p. 957).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview). A retest subsample of 216 Cohort II twins was re-interviewed a mean 3.7 years later (range 1.1–4.3) (p. 948).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteer twin registry, largely Caucasian; only 0.8% had never drunk alcohol (p. 948). Abstainers from a substance contribute no age of first use or symptom count for it, so each association is estimated among people who had used the substance (p. 950). Response rates are not reported here.

exposure.measurement: Single retrospective interview based on the SSAGA (telephone in Cohort II, computer-assisted telephone interview in Cohort III) by trained lay interviewers blind to the co-twin's status (p. 948). The questions differed by cohort: age at the first cigarette tried (Cohort II) vs the first time even a puff was smoked (Cohort III); first time more than a sip vs a full drink of alcohol; first cannabis use. Reported ages below 5 were set to 5 for tobacco and alcohol. Test–retest correlations over about 3.7 years: tobacco .72, alcohol .82, cannabis .80; correlations between age at interview and reported age of first use −.01 to .08 (pp. 948, 957).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Age at first use only (continuous, reverse scored in the models); 'early' is not dichotomized. Mean ages: tobacco 13.7 (men) and 14.4 (women); alcohol 15.4 and 16.2; cannabis 18.7 and 19.2 in Cohort II, 17.6 and 18.1 in Cohort III (p. 948). In Cohort II, 69.5% of those who had smoked had smoked more than once or twice, 93.1% of those who drank became regular drinkers or got drunk, and 79.4% of those who used cannabis used it three or more times (p. 950).
exposure.polysubstance: Modelled jointly: the three substances are indicators of common initiation and disorder factors. 60.2% of the sample had used all three; the most common order was tobacco, then alcohol, then cannabis (46.6%), and 2.7% started all three at the same age (p. 951). The authors note that cannabis is often smoked with tobacco in Australia, which may inflate overlap between the two (p. 957). Other drugs were not considered.

comparison.controls: No external control group: the comparison is between the similarity of monozygotic and dizygotic twins, which partitions variation and covariation into additive genetic (A), shared environmental (C) and unique environmental (E) parts.
comparison.matching: Twins in a pair share age and family environment (and, for monozygotic pairs, genes); birth year was regressed out of all variables to adjust for cohort (p. 950).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measured confounders that differ within pairs (for example conduct problems, peer substance use, puberty timing, adversity affecting one twin); no prospective measures of any kind.

outcomes.instruments: Lifetime DSM-IV symptom counts from the SSAGA-based interview: nicotine dependence, 7 items (tolerance defined as ever smoking 20 or more cigarettes in a day); alcohol use disorder, 11 abuse and dependence items (log-transformed); cannabis use disorder, a restricted 6-item count (2 abuse, 4 dependence criteria) matching Cohort II's abbreviated assessment (log-transformed) (pp. 948–949). Cronbach's alpha .81, .77 and .84; test–retest .84, .64 and .82.
outcomes.validity_norms: Measurement invariance across sex was rejected for all three symptom counts, with differential item functioning (p. 949; supplement Tables S1–S3, not read). Lifetime prevalence: nicotine dependence 35.2% of men and 30.3% of women; DSM-IV alcohol abuse 40.0% and 18.6%; alcohol dependence 16.2% and 7.5%; one or more cannabis symptoms 38.1% and 25.5% (pp. 948–949; denominators not stated).
outcomes.operationalization: Disorder treated as continuous lifetime symptom counts (abstainers coded missing), not as diagnoses. In Cohort III, rerunning the analyses with the full 11-item cannabis count gave very comparable results (p. 957).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; models compared by the Satorra-Bentler scaled chi-square difference test and AIC.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Interviewers were blind to the co-twin's status (p. 948); exposure and outcome were recorded in the same interview by the same respondent.

analysis.effect_sizes: Phenotypic correlations between ages of first use and symptom counts: men −0.10 to −0.31, women −0.12 to −0.28 (p. 951). Univariate models, full sample (Table 3, p. 953): heritability of age at first use .27 (tobacco), .24 (alcohol), .19 (cannabis); shared environment .21, .20, .33; heritability of symptom counts .57 (nicotine), .43 (alcohol), .35 (cannabis); shared environment .02, .02, .11. Bivariate factor models (p. 952; Figures 4–5, pp. 955–956): men rG .55 (95% CI .38–.72), rC −.96 (−1.00 to 1.00), rE .42 (.06–.77); women rG .53 (.29–.76), rC .83 (.45–1.00), rE .23 (.04–.42). Editors' calculation from the standardized paths printed in Figures 4–5 (approximate, rounded inputs): the implied correlation between the initiation and disorder factors is about .37 in men (genetic part .31, shared-environmental −.04, unique-environmental .09) and about .50 in women (.20, .25 and .06), so the unique-environmental pathway carries roughly a quarter of the factor correlation in men and a tenth in women. When correlated residuals were allowed, rE was attenuated in both sexes; the values are not reported (p. 953).
analysis.covariates: Birth year regressed out of all variables (p. 950); family clustering handled in the phenotypic analyses; maximum likelihood with robust standard errors in Mplus 7, with full-information handling of missing data (p. 950). No other covariates.
analysis.selective_reporting: The common pathway model for disorder was retained although it fitted worse than the independent pathway model (Δχ2 = 17.47, df = 8, p = .03), for consistency and to make the bivariate model feasible (p. 952). The attenuated rE values after allowing correlated residuals are described but not given (p. 953). Univariate fits, independent-pathway estimates and variance proportions are in supplementary Tables S4–S9, not read.
analysis.power: Not reported. The authors note more power in women (60% of the sample), partly offset by the higher prevalence of disorder in men (p. 957). The men's rE interval is wide (.06–.77).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Earlier first use and more symptoms went together only modestly (r −0.10 to −0.31). The latent initiation and disorder factors shared genetic influences in both sexes (rG about .55) and family-environmental influences in women (rC .83, with a small and unstable shared-environment share of disorder). A residual unique-environmental correlation remained (men .42, CI .06–.77; women .23, CI .04–.42); it shrank, by an amount not reported, when correlated residuals were allowed, and by the editors' decomposition it carries roughly a quarter (men) to a tenth (women) of the factor correlation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the unique-environmental correlations indicate that the age at which several drugs are first used may directly increase risk (p. 946), and the Discussion that delaying first use may help directly reduce risk for disorder (p. 957). The text translates rE into a statement that an identical twin who starts earlier than the co-twin will be more likely to develop a disorder (p. 952), but no discordant-pair comparison or risk figure is reported, and rE also contains within-pair confounding and shared reporting error. The authors themselves state that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn (cross-sectional data, confounders that differ within pairs, common measurement error; p. 956) and that delaying first use would likely reduce only a small amount of the risk (p. 957); these caveats are not in the abstract.

timeline.event: Cross-sectional national survey: earlier drinking associated with alcohol disorder; cited as part of the robust association (p. 947)

Prescott & Kendler (behavioural genetic study): nearly all of the correlation between age at first drink and alcohol dependence explained by genetic sources (as summarized by Richmond-Rakerd et al., p. 947)

Co-twin control study: familial factors did not fully explain the link between early cannabis use and drug use disorders (as summarized by Richmond-Rakerd et al., p. 947); not independent of this paper: it drew on the same young-adult cohort as Cohort II here (born 1964–1971, interviewed 1996–2000, ages 24–36) and shares seven of its authors

Dunedin birth cohort (propensity-score matching, exposure recorded at 13–15): repeated early use, mostly alcohol, associated with adult dependence and other outcomes after matching on childhood risk; not cited by Richmond-Rakerd et al.
Sartor et al.: genetic correlation of 0.59 between timing of first alcohol use and alcohol dependence (as summarized by Richmond-Rakerd et al., p. 947)

replication.where_it_stands: The genetic overlap between age at first use and disorder agrees with the earlier single-substance twin studies the authors cite (p. 956). Whether a causal component remains is unsettled: the authors call the earlier evidence mixed (p. 956), and their own residual correlation is wide in men and attenuated, by an unreported amount, under a model with correlated residuals. The co-twin study of early cannabis use cited as earlier evidence (Lynskey et al., 2003) used the same cohort as Cohort II here (Table 1, p. 949; Lynskey et al., 2003, p. 428), so the two are not independent tests.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism grants AA023419 (LR), AA21235 (AA) and AA007728 (AH); US National Institute on Drug Abuse grants DA18267 (ML), DA32573 (AA) and DA23668 (AA) (author note, p. 946).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the University of Missouri, Washington University School of Medicine, King's College London, the University of the Sunshine Coast and QIMR Berghofer (Brisbane). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective, genetically informative cohort in which first use is recorded when it happens (not recalled), with measured within-pair confounders (conduct problems, peers) and an explicit comparison of identical twins discordant for age at first use; or a randomized prevention trial that delays first use and follows symptoms into adulthood.

domains.note: Genetic and shared family confounding are modelled by the twin design, a strength over ordinary surveys; but the quasi-causal estimate (rE) is directly biased by anything that differs between twins and affects both first use and disorder (for example conduct problems, peers), none of which was measured.
Ages recalled at a mean age of 30.6, with different question wording in the two cohorts and ages below 5 recoded; retest correlations .72–.82 and little relation to age at interview.
Volunteer, largely Caucasian twin registry; response rates not reported here; opposite-sex pairs excluded; each association estimated only among people who had used the substance.
No intervention after first use bears on the comparison.
Abstainers coded missing for that substance and handled by full-information maximum likelihood, which assumes data missing at random; abstention is not random.

Lifetime symptom counts from lay interviews in the same interview as the exposure (shared reporting error inflates rE, as the authors note); restricted cannabis count; alcohol retest .64; symptom counts not invariant across sex.
Common pathway model for disorder kept despite worse fit; attenuated rE values after allowing correlated residuals not reported; much model detail only in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The twin design gives a credible estimate of how much of the link between earlier first use and disorder is familial (genetic correlations about .55 in both sexes), but the causal reading rests on the residual unique-environmental correlation, which is wide in men, smaller in women, shrinks under a better-specified model and absorbs within-pair confounding and shared reporting error. Cite it for the familial overlap, the modest size of the phenotypic association and the authors' own view that delaying first use would remove only a small part of the risk; not as evidence that early first use causes disorder.

key_findings.finding: 7,285 Australian twins (2,941 men, 4,344 women; 3,122 complete pairs and 1,041 single twins), born 1964–1979 and interviewed 1996–2009 at a mean age of 30.6 (range 24–40).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Ages at first use were recalled in adulthood; retest correlations about 3.7 years later in 216 Cohort II twins were .72 (tobacco), .82 (alcohol) and .80 (cannabis), and correlations between age at interview and reported age of first use were −.01, .03 and .08.
key_findings.locator: Method › Procedure, 1st paragraph; Measures › Age of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis initiation

key_findings.finding: Mean ages at first use: tobacco 13.7 (men) and 14.4 (women); alcohol 15.4 and 16.2; cannabis 18.7 and 19.2 in Cohort II and 17.6 and 18.1 in Cohort III; never used: tobacco 11.9%, alcohol 0.8%, cannabis 37.5% of the sample.
key_findings.locator: Method › Measures › Age of tobacco, alcohol and cannabis initiation

key_findings.finding: Earlier first use and more symptoms were only modestly correlated: men r −0.10 to −0.31, women r −0.12 to −0.28.
key_findings.locator: Results › Descriptive Analyses, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Repeated in the Discussion (p. 957), where the authors conclude that delaying first use would likely reduce only a small amount of the risk.

key_findings.finding: Full sample, univariate models: heritability of age at first use .27 (tobacco), .24 (alcohol) and .19 (cannabis, CI −.004 to .39), shared environment .21, .20 and .33; heritability of symptom counts .57 (nicotine), .43 (alcohol) and .35 (cannabis), shared environment .02, .02 and .11 (not significant).
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Men, bivariate factor model: the initiation and disorder factors had a genetic correlation of .55 (95% CI .38–.72), a shared-environmental correlation of −.96 (−1.00 to 1.00; not significant) and a unique-environmental correlation of .42 (.06–.77).
key_findings.locator: Results › Biometric Model-Fitting: Bivariate Factor Model, 1st paragraph (p. 952); Figure 4 (p. 955)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the standardized paths in Figure 4: implied factor correlation about .37, of which about .09 runs through the unique environment.

key_findings.finding: Women, bivariate factor model: genetic correlation .53 (95% CI .29–.76), shared-environmental correlation .83 (.45–1.00), unique-environmental correlation .23 (.04–.42).
key_findings.locator: Results › Biometric Model-Fitting: Bivariate Factor Model, 1st paragraph (p. 952); Figure 5 (p. 956)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the standardized paths in Figure 5: implied factor correlation about .50, of which about .06 runs through the unique environment.

key_findings.finding: When the residual ACE components were allowed to correlate, the unique-environmental correlations were attenuated in both sexes while the genetic and shared-environmental correlations remained largely unchanged (the men's shared-environmental correlation, −.96 and called highly unreliable, became positive); no attenuated values are given, and the authors say this appeared to explain part, but not all, of the potentially direct association.
key_findings.locator: Results › Biometric Model-Fitting: Bivariate Factor Model, 2nd paragraph (begins on p. 952)

key_findings.finding: Ages of first use loaded on one common factor (common pathway model no worse than independent pathway: Δχ2 = 9.24, df = 8, p = .32), but the loadings differed by sex (alcohol .64 in men vs .50 in women; cannabis .62 in women vs .46 in men); for disorder the common pathway model fitted worse (Δχ2 = 17.47, df = 8, p = .03) but was retained.
key_findings.locator: Results › Biometric Model Fitting: Age of Substance Use Initiation › Multivariate models (p. 951); Biometric Model Fitting: Substance Use Disorder › Multivariate models (p. 952)

key_findings.finding: Shared-environment influences on disorder could be dropped in both sexes in the disorder-only models (best-fitting models without common or specific C), whereas the best initiation model for women kept common shared-environment influence and the men's kept the full model.
key_findings.locator: Tables 4 and 5 (bold rows)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn because the data are cross-sectional, confounders may differ within twin pairs, and shared measurement error may contribute to the unique-environmental correlation; they list a largely Caucasian sample, co-use of cannabis with tobacco, a restricted cannabis measure and adult recall as further limits.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Relation Between Initiation and Disorder, 2nd paragraph (p. 956); Discussion › Limitations (p. 957)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says shared environment explained 19% of the variation in disorder in women (p. 952), but the standardized shared-environment path to the disorder factor in Figure 5 is .41, about 17% of the factor's variance (.41 squared; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small; rounding cannot explain it (a path that rounds to .41 gives at most 17.2%), so the 19% may refer to another quantity, perhaps in supplementary Table S9 (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the shared-environment share of disorder in women nonsignificant (p. 956), while Figure 5 gives its path a 95% interval of .08 to .74; the nonsignificance matches the disorder-only models, in which shared environment could be dropped (Table 5, p. 954).
reporting_issues.consequence: The women's high shared-environmental correlation (.83) involves a variance component that the disorder-only models discard; it should be cited as uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The attenuation of the unique-environmental correlations after allowing correlated residuals is reported in words only, without estimates or intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the 'quasi-causal' residual under the better-specified model, the paper's key causal evidence, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says shared environment explained a significant proportion of the variation in age at first use of all three substances (pp. 951, 953), but in men the intervals for tobacco (.19, −.04 to .43) and alcohol (.15, −.09 to .39) include zero (Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement holds for the full sample and for women, not for men's tobacco and alcohol initiation; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4 the p-values for the women's Models IV and V (Δχ2 0.50 and 10.33) correspond to 4 df, i.e. tests against the full Model I, while in Table 5 the p-values for Models IV and V correspond to 3 df, tests against Model III; the reference model is not stated (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the choice of models; noted for anyone recomputing the tests.

reporting_issues.issue: For women, the initiation-only model comparison dropped the common genetic factor (Table 4, Model III without common A, Δχ2 = 1.88, df = 38, p = .17; best-fitting Model IV builds on it), yet the full bivariate model in Figure 5 estimates a common genetic path to initiation of .49 (95% CI .17–.82), on which the women's genetic correlation (.53) rests; the paper does not comment on the difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: As with the women's shared-environmental correlation, which involves a disorder component that the disorder-only models drop, the women's genetic correlation comes from the full bivariate model and involves a component that the best-fitting initiation model omits; cite it as model-dependent.
