design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis: a narrative synthesis, with one table of polysubstance classes (Table 2), of 23 studies that identified latent classes of substance use in adolescents aged 10–19 with latent class analysis (LCA), latent transition analysis (LTA) or related finite mixture models. Peer-reviewed articles to 30 June 2015 from three databases. Study quality scored with an adapted Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. No protocol or registration reported.
can_establish: Which kinds of latent substance use classes 23 mostly US school- and survey-based adolescent studies published to mid-2015 reported, how often each kind appeared and how large it was in each sample, and which predictors of membership in a polysubstance class those studies reported as significant.
cannot_establish: How common any pattern is among adolescents in general (nothing is pooled, and class sizes depend on each study's sample, indicators and time frame); that any predictor leads to polysubstance use (14 of the 23 studies are cross-sectional, and Table 1 lists only significant predictors); or how stable the class solutions are (fit statistics are missing for most studies and several analyses appear to share samples).

sample.recruitment: Searches of MEDLINE (via PubMed) and PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES (via EBSCOhost) for all years to 30 June 2015, plus reference lists and other reviews; peer-reviewed journals and human studies only (PDF pp. 2–3, 2.1). The search terms are in an online supplement that was not available. The included studies drew on school surveys, national household and youth surveys and cohorts; four studied youth in public service systems such as foster care or treatment, and one studied young gay and bisexual men in Chicago (PDF p. 14, last paragraph of 3.1 and 3.4.1; Table 1, PDF p. 10).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: children and adolescents aged 10–19 (wider age ranges only with separate analyses for this age group); observational, experimental, cross-sectional or longitudinal designs; peer-reviewed journals; measures of at least two substances over any time interval; latent classes of substance use, with studies excluded if non-substance variables such as deviant or violent behaviour were class indicators; class identification and analysis had to be described, but studies missing some of the three recommended kinds of fit information were kept and flagged in Table 1; English, German, Polish or French (PDF p. 3, 2.2). For longitudinal analyses only the baseline classes were extracted (PDF p. 3, 2.2(5)).
sample.demographics: Sample sizes from 450 to 419,698 (PDF pp. 1, 3). 19 studies from the US, one comparing the US with Puerto Rico, one from Argentina and two from Australia (PDF p. 3, 3.1; PDF p. 16, 4.2.1). One all-female and one all-male sample, two with no sex ratio reported, and a female share of 33% to 61% in the rest; mean age 13.13 to 18.9 years, with five studies giving only school grade or a point estimate (PDF p. 3, 3.1). The review gives no total number of participants: the 23 sample sizes in Table 1 sum to 892,991, of which 838,400 come from the two Gilreath et al. California analyses (editors' calculation).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Table 1 notes 30% dropout without analysis of attrition or missing data for Graham et al. (1991) (PDF p. 8).
sample.selection_effects: Mostly US school and household-survey samples, searched in three databases, peer-reviewed journals only, four languages, no grey literature. Several analyses appear to share data, which the review does not discuss: Gilreath et al. (2014, 2015), both California grades 7, 9 and 11 with N 419,698 and 418,702; Shin et al. (2010) and Shin (2012), both San Diego youth in public service systems with the same ethnic composition and mean age; Dierker et al. (2007) and Maldonado-Molina and Lanza (2010), both Add Health; Maldonado-Molina et al. (2007) and Lamont et al. (2014), both NLSY97 (Table 1, PDF pp. 6–12). The review's counts of studies may therefore count some samples, or parts of them, more than once (editors' observation).

exposure.measurement: All 23 studies used retrospective self-report at each measurement occasion (PDF p. 3, 3.1). The time frame of the class indicators varied: lifetime use only in 4 studies, lifetime with past-month use in 7, lifetime or past six months in 1, past year in 3, past six months in 1, past month in 1, last two weeks in 1, and past month with past year in 5, one of which also used lifetime use (PDF p. 13, text below Fig. 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Ten studies used several indicators for one substance (for example lifetime alcohol use, binge drinking and drunkenness), and five had time-sensitive indicators that separated occasional from frequent polysubstance use (PDF p. 14, 3.3 and 3.4.3).
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the review. Polysubstance use is described as use of at least two different psychoactive substances within a defined period, at the same time or separately (PDF p. 2, Introduction, 2nd paragraph). According to the text, all studies measured alcohol and cannabis and all but four measured tobacco; 15 also measured other drugs, which were often collapsed into one 'other drugs' indicator because of low cell frequencies (PDF p. 14, 3.3; PDF p. 16, 1st paragraph). Table 1 lists no cannabis indicator for Pilatti et al. (2013) (see reporting issues).

comparison.controls: No external comparison. For predictors, most primary studies compared their polysubstance classes with their no/low-use class by multinomial regression (PDF p. 14, 3.5, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Covariates differed across studies: most adjusted for age or gender and at least one other covariate, and four reported no statistical control (PDF pp. 3 and 13, 3.1). The authors note that poor school achievement may stand for low socio-economic status or for wider problem behaviour (PDF p. 16, 4.1, 3rd paragraph), which the review cannot separate.

outcomes.instruments: Latent class analysis or latent transition analysis on self-reported use indicators, as reported by each study (Table 1, PDF pp. 4–12). Study quality: the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale adapted for cross-sectional studies, giving more weight to statistical testing and less to ascertainment of exposure; Selection 0–4, Comparability 0–2 and Outcome 0–4 points; overall 9–10 points low, 7–8 average and below 7 high risk of bias (PDF p. 3, 2.4; Fig. 2, PDF p. 15).
outcomes.validity_norms: Fit reporting was incomplete: the last column of Table 1 lists missing likelihood tests, BIC or entropy for most studies (PDF pp. 4–12); only three studies mentioned local dependence between indicators, and two did not report class proportions (PDF p. 16, 4.2.2). The adapted scale scored reporting completeness as much as bias: the five high-risk studies were rated so mostly for missing information on participants' age, sex ratio or class proportions (PDF p. 14, 3.2).
outcomes.operationalization: A polysubstance class is any latent class combining at least two psychoactive substances (PDF p. 14, 3.4.3); Table 2 groups these classes by the substances combined (PDF p. 13). Predictors were summarized by counting studies that reported a significant association; Table 1 lists only significant predictors, meant to be those of classes with three or more substances against no/low-use classes (Table 1, footnote a, PDF p. 12).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: the review ran no statistical tests. Because Table 1 lists only significant predictors, the number of predictors tested in each primary study is not visible.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts were screened separately by two reviewers, with inconsistencies discussed and resolved; who scored study quality is not stated (PDF p. 3, 2.3–2.4).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled: the authors decided against summary measures because substances, time frames, sample sizes, populations and predictors varied, and present the results mostly as a narrative synthesis, with one summary table (PDF p. 3, 2.4, 2nd paragraph). Descriptive results: 3 to 7 classes per study, three or four in 17 of 23 (74%); a no/low-use class in 19 studies (17% to 77% of samples); a mainly-alcohol class in 16 (15% to 80%); at least one polysubstance class in all 23 (PDF pp. 1, 14). Table 2 (studies finding the class / studies that measured those substances; class size): alcohol and cannabis 8/23 (8–20%); alcohol and cigarettes 4/19 (1–23%); cigarettes and cannabis 2/19 (2–11%); alcohol and medication misuse 1/5 (8%); alcohol, cigarettes and cannabis 12/18 (6–29%); alcohol, cannabis and other drugs 4/15 (4–29%); alcohol, cigarettes and other drugs 3/11 (6–24%); alcohol, cigarettes, cannabis and other drugs 7/11 (2–13%) (PDF p. 13). Predictors, as counts of studies with significant results: higher age in 5, parental or peer substance use in 4 of the 4 said to examine it, poor grades in 2; gender and race/ethnicity inconsistent (PDF pp. 14–15). Study-level odds ratios are printed in Table 1 without intervals.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; covariates in the primary studies are listed per study in Table 1.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review states that it was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA statement (PDF p. 2, 2. Method).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists only significant predictors (footnote a, PDF p. 12), so null results for age, peer or parental use or school achievement in other studies cannot be seen, and the consistency of these predictors cannot be checked from the review. Only baseline classes of longitudinal studies were extracted (PDF p. 3, 2.2(5)).
analysis.power: Not addressed at review level. The authors note that some polysubstance classes were rather small, for example 24 of 822 adolescents in Snyder and Smith (2014), which may make class solutions unstable (PDF p. 15, 4. Discussion, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 23 adolescent latent class studies, mostly from the US and mostly cross-sectional, three or four classes were usual. A no/low-use class appeared in 19 studies and was the largest in most; a mainly-alcohol class appeared in 16; every study found at least one polysubstance class, most often alcohol, tobacco and cannabis together (12 of the 18 studies counted as measuring all three; 6–29% of samples), and classes that also took in other drugs were smaller (2–13% for the class with all four groups). Higher age (5 studies), parental or peer substance use (4 studies) and poor grades (2 studies) were the predictors reported consistently, by counting significant results only.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says polysubstance classes were "unanimously predicted by higher age, higher parental and peer substance use, and poor academic performance" (PDF p. 1). This rests on 5, 4 and 2 of the 23 studies, tabulated only when significant, mostly measured at the same time as use, and partly from overlapping samples; one of the four studies cited for parental and peer use (Kelly et al., 2015) has no predictor listed in Table 1. Table 1 also lists parental or peer substance use as a covariate in studies that are not counted (for example Chung et al., 2013; Snyder and Smith, 2014), lists academic failure for Kelly et al. (2015) without a result, and for one of the two studies cited for poor grades (Connell et al., 2009) shows grade in school, apparently the school year, not academic grades (PDF pp. 4–5, 8, 12). The abstract also says no/low-use classes were the largest and polysubstance classes the smallest; the results say this held in most studies, and Table 1 shows exceptions (Kelly et al., 2015: mainly alcohol 62%, no use 32%; Mitchell and Plunkett, 2000: predominantly alcohol 50%, abstaining 17%; Newcomb et al., 2014: alcohol and cannabis 70%). The conclusions call latent classes solid information and an ecologically valid approach, and say that numerous studies were well executed with low risk of bias (PDF pp. 1, 17), although the review did not test the validity or replicability of class solutions and Table 1 shows fit information missing for most studies. The implications that prevention aimed at families and schools seems particularly promising, and that classes including binge drinking go with more hazardous outcomes (PDF p. 17), were not examined in the results.

timeline.event: Connor et al. review of polysubstance use in the general population, which distinguished limited, moderate and extended ranges of use; this review could not reproduce that division in adolescent samples (PDF p. 15, 4. Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
This review: 23 adolescent latent class studies published to June 2015.
de Jonge et al. systematic review of latent classes of substance use in young adults (cited by LeComte et al., 2025; not read).
LeComte et al. systematic review of 137 adult latent class studies, which cites this review among the earlier adolescent reviews.
Skandan et al., the adolescent half of the LeComte et al. two-part review, to which 54 adolescent studies from that search were assigned (named in LeComte et al., 2025; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The adolescent review in the library; a later adolescent review from the LeComte group (Skandan et al., 2025) has not been read. Cite this review for the kinds of classes that recur in adolescent samples to 2015 (no or low use, mainly alcohol, alcohol with tobacco and cannabis, and smaller wide-range classes) and for the predictors that studies reported, not for prevalence or for causes.

funding.funder: No external funding (Role of funding source, PDF p. 17).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (Conflicts of interest, PDF p. 17).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the Institute for Therapy and Health Research, Kiel, Germany (PDF p. 1). The adaptation of the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale follows an earlier review that includes two of the authors (Suchert, Hanewinkel and Isensee, 2015; cited on PDF p. 3, reference list PDF p. 18).

what_would_settle_it: A registered review, or a pooled re-analysis of the main adolescent school and household surveys, that uses the same indicators, time frames and class-selection rules across samples, removes overlapping samples, reports class sizes with intervals and every predictor tested whether significant or not, and uses longitudinal waves to separate factors that come before polysubstance use from those that only accompany it.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (ages 10–19), the method (latent classes built from at least two substances), the outcomes (class structure and predictors) and the eligible designs are specified; a comparator does not apply to this descriptive question.
No protocol or registration is mentioned (PDF p. 2, 2. Method).
All designs were admitted, with the stated reason that finite mixture models serve many kinds of research question (PDF p. 2, Introduction, last paragraph; PDF p. 3, 2.2(2)).

Three databases for all years to June 2015, reference lists and other reviews, with search terms in a supplement; but limited to peer-reviewed journals and four languages without a stated reason, with no grey literature, registries or experts consulted. Item applied as written (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Titles and abstracts were evaluated separately by two reviewers, and inconsistencies were discussed and resolved (PDF p. 3, 2.3).

The methods do not describe data extraction; the contributors' statement says two authors were responsible for screening and data extraction (PDF p. 17), which does not show that two reviewers extracted or checked the same data. A close call.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives reasons with counts for the 34 excluded full texts (20 participants too old, 7 non-substance indicators, 7 no latent classes; PDF p. 13), but no list of the excluded studies; the article names only the search terms and the scoring scheme as supplement contents.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, place, N, ethnic composition, sex, age, covariates, indicators, classes with proportions, significant predictors and quality score for each study; years of data collection and follow-up periods are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: An adapted Newcastle–Ottawa Scale covering selection, comparability (confounding) and outcome was applied to the studies (PDF p. 3, 2.4; Fig. 2, PDF p. 15); it does not assess selective reporting, it largely scores completeness of reporting rather than bias in the latent class modelling, and Table 1 gives no score for Shin et al. (2010).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
Narrative synthesis; nothing pooled (PDF p. 3, 2.4, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The five high-risk studies are named only as failing to report statistical information (PDF p. 16, 4.2.2) and enter the class and predictor summaries like the others (Riehman et al., 2009, for example, is one of the five studies cited for age); the conclusion describes the studies as showing low risk of bias (PDF p. 17). The discussion does say that cross-sectional designs limit the predictor findings (PDF p. 16, 4.1).
Differences in indicators, time frames, populations and the number of indicators per substance are linked to differences in class labels and sizes (PDF p. 14, 3.4.2; PDF p. 16, 4.2.2).
No meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No external funding and no conflicts of interest (PDF p. 17).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item is not met: items 2 (no protocol), 4 (search limited to peer-reviewed journals in four languages without a reason), 7 (no list of excluded studies) and 13 (risk of bias not used in interpreting the results) are not met, and item 9 is met only in part; items 11 and 15 do not apply because nothing was pooled. The rating concerns how far the review's summaries can be trusted as complete and unbiased, not its usefulness: its Table 1 describes every included study and lets readers check most counts. It may be cited for the kinds of latent classes reported in adolescent samples up to 2015 and for which predictors studies reported as significant; it should not be cited for the prevalence of any pattern, for causes, or with the abstract's word 'unanimously'.

key_findings.finding: 23 studies were included: 963 records from the database search and 1 from reference lists; 300 duplicates removed; 664 titles and abstracts screened and 607 excluded; 57 full texts assessed and 34 excluded (20 with participants too old, 7 with indicators other than substance use, 7 without latent classes).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Fig. 1 (PDF p. 13)

key_findings.finding: The search covered MEDLINE (via PubMed), PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES (via EBSCOhost) for all years to 30 June 2015, with reference lists; eligibility required publication in a peer-reviewed journal in English, German, Polish or French.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Search strategy (PDF p. 2, continuing on PDF p. 3); 2.2 Eligibility criteria (3) and (6) (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Sample sizes ranged from 450 to 419,698. The studies were mostly from the US (19), with one comparing the US with Puerto Rico, one from Argentina and two from Australia; nine were longitudinal and fourteen cross-sectional; all used retrospective self-report.
key_findings.locator: 2.4, 2nd paragraph and 3.1 Sample and setting, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (PDF p. 3); 4.2.1 (PDF p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Studies extracted 3 to 7 classes: four in 10 studies, three in 6, four for girls and three for boys in Shin et al. (2010), five in 2, five (US) and six (Puerto Rico) in 1, six in 2 and seven in 1; the abstract gives 17 studies (74%) with three or four classes.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (PDF p. 1); 3.4 Latent classes of (poly) substance use, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 14)

key_findings.finding: A no/low-use class (low probabilities for every substance) was found in all but 4 studies (19 studies), made up 17% to 77% of the sample and was the largest class in most studies; the four without one were Newcomb et al. (2014), Riehman et al. (2009), Shin (2012) and White et al. (2013).
key_findings.locator: 3.4.1 No/low substance use classes (PDF p. 14); 4. Discussion, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 15)
key_findings.note: Table 1 shows a low-use class of 78% in Snyder and Smith (2014) (PDF p. 12), above the stated upper limit. The no/low-use class was not the largest in, for example, Kelly et al. (2015: no use 32%, mainly alcohol 62%; PDF p. 8) or Mitchell and Plunkett (2000: abstaining 17%, predominantly alcohol 50%; PDF p. 10).

key_findings.finding: Sixteen studies found at least one mainly-alcohol class (labelled alcohol experimenters, predominantly or mainly alcohol, alcohol only, or binge or heavy drinkers), making up 15% to 80% of the sample and usually the second-largest class; seven did not, four of them studies of youth in care settings or of young gay and bisexual men.
key_findings.locator: 3.4.2 Alcohol use classes

key_findings.finding: Polysubstance classes by substances combined (studies finding the class / studies measuring those substances; share of the sample): alcohol and cannabis 8/23 (8–20%; also found in five special-population studies at 29–70%); alcohol and cigarettes 4/19 (1–23%); cigarettes and cannabis 2/19 (2–11%); alcohol and medication misuse 1/5 (8%); alcohol, cigarettes and cannabis 12/18 (6–29%; also in two special-population studies at 4–5%); alcohol, cannabis and other drugs 4/15 (4–29%; found in every study without a separate tobacco indicator); alcohol, cigarettes and other drugs 3/11 (6–24%); alcohol, cigarettes, cannabis and other drugs 7/11 (2–13%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and its footnotes a-c

key_findings.finding: Every study found at least one polysubstance class; the most common combined alcohol, tobacco and cannabis, and classes that added other drugs were considerably smaller. In the five studies with time-sensitive indicators, occasional or experimental polysubstance classes made up 9–29% of the samples and frequent ones 7–18%.
key_findings.locator: 3.4.3 Polysubstance use classes, 1st-3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sixteen studies reported effect sizes for predictors, mostly comparing polysubstance classes with the no/low-use class. Higher age went with polysubstance class membership in 5 studies; all 4 studies said to examine parental or peer substance use found polysubstance class membership more likely among adolescents whose parents or peers used; 2 studies linked poor grades to polysubstance use; results for gender were mixed; for race/ethnicity, 3 studies found no association, 5 found African American adolescents less likely than White adolescents to be in polysubstance classes, and 3 found Hispanic adolescents more likely.
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Predictors of latent classes, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 14) to last paragraph (PDF p. 15)
key_findings.note: Counts of significant results only. Table 1 lists no predictor for Kelly et al. (2015), one of the four parental and peer studies (PDF p. 8), and lists significant peer substance use for Shin et al. (2010), which is not counted (PDF p. 11). For poor grades the text cites Connell et al. (2009), whose Table 1 entry is grade in school; the academic-grades result in Table 1 is for Connell et al. (2010) (PDF pp. 4–5; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Effect sizes behind the parental and peer finding vary widely in Table 1: Connell et al. (2010), peer substance use OR 26.13 (occasional) and 85.63 (frequent polysubstance class against non-use) and parental drinking OR 3.51 and 3.61; Cranford et al. (2013), parental substance use AOR 1.1; White et al. (2013), peer tobacco use RRR 3.84 and 6.17 and peer cannabis use RRR 3.52 and 11.07. No confidence intervals are given.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column 'Results—significant predictions', rows Connell et al. (2010) (PDF p. 5), Cranford et al. (2013) (PDF p. 6), White et al. (2013) (PDF p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (adapted Newcastle–Ottawa Scale): 11 studies low, 7 average and 5 high (Graham et al., 1991; Maldonado-Molina et al., 2007; Mitchell and Plunkett, 2000; Pilatti et al., 2013; Riehman et al., 2009), the high ratings mostly for missing information on age, sex ratio or class proportions.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Risk of bias (PDF p. 14); Fig. 2 (PDF p. 15)
key_findings.note: Table 1 gives no score for Shin et al. (2010) (PDF p. 11).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that most studies examined cross-sectional rather than longitudinal associations, which limits the predictor findings; that responses were often collapsed into one 'other drugs' indicator because of very low cell frequencies; that only three studies mentioned local dependence between indicators; and that two studies did not state class proportions.
key_findings.locator: 1st paragraph (continued from PDF p. 15); 4.1, 1st paragraph; 4.2.2, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The section on predictors cites Kelly et al. (2015) as one of the four studies in which parental or peer substance use predicted polysubstance class membership, but Table 1 lists no significant predictions for Kelly et al. (2015). Table 1 does list significant peer substance use for Shin et al. (2010) (OR 1.36 girls, 1.68 boys), which is not counted among the studies that examined parental or peer use. Parental or peer substance use is also listed as a covariate, with no result shown, for Chung et al. (2013) (peer use) and Snyder and Smith (2014) (parental substance problems), and Lamont et al. (2014) report significant antisocial-peer effects, with peers' alcohol or drug use given as examples; none of these is counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The four-of-four count cannot be reproduced from Table 1 and draws on a subset of the studies that examined parental or peer use; the parental and peer finding should be cited with the studies named in Table 1, not as a unanimous result.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives no risk-of-bias score for Shin et al. (2010), while Fig. 2 classifies all 23 studies (11 low, 7 average, 5 high). By the editors' arithmetic, the other 22 scores in Table 1 give 10 low, 7 average and 5 high, so the missing score must be 9 or 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one study's rating cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 says all studies measured at least alcohol and cannabis, and Table 2 counts 23 studies that measured alcohol and cannabis, but Table 1 lists no cannabis indicator for Pilatti et al. (2013) (alcohol, drunkenness, tobacco, other drugs). Table 2 also gives 19 studies that measured cigarettes and cannabis but 18 that measured alcohol, cigarettes and cannabis, which cannot both be right since every study measured alcohol (editors' observation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators in Table 2 are slightly inconsistent; the alcohol, tobacco and cannabis class may have been found in 12 of 19 rather than 12 of 18 studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The no/low-use classes are said to range from 17% to 77% of the samples, but Table 1 shows a low-use class of 78% in Snyder and Smith (2014).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the range should read 17% to 78%.

reporting_issues.issue: Several included analyses appear to draw on the same data, and the review neither notes this nor adjusts its counts: Gilreath et al. (2014, 2015), both California grades 7, 9 and 11; Shin et al. (2010) and Shin (2012), both San Diego youth in public service systems; Dierker et al. (2007) and Maldonado-Molina and Lanza (2010), both Add Health; Maldonado-Molina et al. (2007) and Lamont et al. (2014), both NLSY97.
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts of studies overstate the number of independent samples: for example, the five studies on African American adolescents and the three on Hispanic adolescents each include both Gilreath analyses, and the Gilreath pair supplies 838,400 of the 892,991 participants in Table 1 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table 1 says only significant predictors of classes with three or more substances against no/low-use classes are shown, but some entries compare other classes: Snyder and Smith (2014) report 2 vs 3, an alcohol-and-cannabis class against low use; Riehman et al. (2009) compare classes with a high-cigarettes-only class (1 vs 4, 2 vs 4); Lanza et al. (2010) compare a binge drinking and marijuana class (two substances) with the non-use class (4 vs 1) for every listed predictor, including school grades (OR 0.30). The age entry for Cranford et al. (2013) cannot be read as printed ('2 vs 1 AOR = 1.54 vs 1 AOR = 1.7').
reporting_issues.consequence: The predictor tabulation mixes different comparisons, and because only significant results are shown, the claimed consistency of predictors cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Eligibility was limited to ages 10–19 unless separate analyses were reported for that age group, but Newcomb et al. (2014) has a mean age of 18.9 (SD 1.3), so part of its sample was probably older than 19; the review does not say that a 10–19 subgroup was analysed (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one included sample probably extends into young adulthood.

reporting_issues.issue: The text twice cites Connell et al. (2009) and Lanza et al. (2010) as the two studies linking poor grades to polysubstance use (PDF p. 15, 3.5; PDF p. 16, 4.1), but in Table 1 the academic-grades result belongs to Connell et al. (2010) (OR 0.21 and 0.20, PDF p. 5), while Connell et al. (2009) show grade in school, listed with gender and race/ethnicity and apparently the school year (OR 1.39 and 1.38, PDF p. 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation of Connell et al. (2009) appears to be an error for Connell et al. (2010); the poor-grades finding rests on Connell et al. (2010) and Lanza et al. (2010), the latter comparing a two-substance class with the non-use class (see the issue on the comparisons in Table 1).

design_detail: Authors' reply (Addiction 101(4), pp. 474–476) by David M. Fergusson, Joseph M. Boden and L. John Horwood (Christchurch Health and Development Study) to the commentaries by Kandel et al., Hall and MacCoun on their 2006 Christchurch analysis, in three sections (model specification; contributions of animal studies; the political context) and a closing section on future directions; 6 references. It contains one new analysis of the same cohort: the main model of other illicit drug use re-estimated under four specifications (cannabis use in the same year or in the preceding year; with or without the lagged measure of prior other illicit drug use), each as a fixed- and a random-effects model, eight estimates in Table 1 (p. 475). The re-analysis is reported without its sample size, covariates, model family or age term. This card appraises the reply as a published argument with the editors' narrative-review checklist and records the re-analysis as data; in substance the re-analysis carries the risk of bias of the original study (sc_fergusson_2006, ROBINS-E).
can_establish: What the original authors conceded and rebutted in answer to the three commentaries, and that in their re-analysis of the same cohort the cannabis coefficient stayed similar in size and highly significant when cannabis use was taken from the preceding year and when the lagged outcome was dropped (fixed effects B 0.93 to 1.27; random effects 1.11 to 1.16; all P < 0.0001).
cannot_establish: That cannabis use causes other illicit drug use: the re-analysis addresses the order of the years and the lagged-outcome specification, not influences that change over time or with age, which the reply calls implausible without testing them; and because from age 16 the yearly reports were recalled at interviews two to four years apart (sc_fergusson_2006), taking cannabis use from the preceding year fixes the order of the years reported, not of the reports, and leaves shared recall error in place.

sample.recruitment: Re-analysis of the Christchurch Health and Development Study birth cohort, the data of the original paper (sc_fergusson_2006: children born in 1977 in the Christchurch urban region and followed to age 25). The reply does not give the number of people or person-years in the re-analysis.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported for the re-analysis.
sample.attrition: Not reported for the re-analysis; the original adjusted analyses used about 900 cohort members (sc_fergusson_2006).
sample.selection_effects: As in the original study (losses greater among disadvantaged families, sc_fergusson_2006); not restated in the reply.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported yearly frequency of cannabis use (the original four-level score, sc_fergusson_2006), entered for the same year as the outcome (models 1 and 3) or for the preceding year (models 2 and 4) (p. 474; Table 1, p. 475).
exposure.polysubstance: Prior other illicit drug use was a lagged covariate in models 1–2 and dropped in models 3–4; the other covariates are described only as covariate control (p. 475). In the original paper they included measures of tobacco and alcohol use (sc_fergusson_2006).

comparison.controls: Fixed effects compare each person's years with the same person's other years; random effects use differences both between and within people (as in the original paper).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Fixed effects remove stable influences whose effects are constant over time; influences that change with age or over time remain, a limitation the original paper states (sc_fergusson_2006) and the reply calls not particularly plausible without testing it (p. 475).

outcomes.instruments: Use of other illicit drugs within a given year, as in the original paper (p. 475). The original's other outcomes, DSM abuse/dependence and the number of drug classes used, were not re-analysed.
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report (sc_fergusson_2006).
outcomes.operationalization: Any use of other illicit drugs in a year (sc_fergusson_2006); the reply speaks of increasing risks of the use of illicit drugs within a given year (p. 475).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applied; all eight estimates have P < 0.0001.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report interviews).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (p. 475), cannabis coefficient B (SE), fixed effects then random effects, all P < 0.0001 by Wald χ² test: (1) same-year cannabis use with lagged other illicit drug use (the original model) 0.93 (0.07) and 1.12 (0.07); (2) preceding-year cannabis use with lagged other illicit drug use 1.27 (0.15) and 1.11 (0.13); (3) same-year cannabis use without the lagged term 0.97 (0.08) and 1.16 (0.07); (4) preceding-year cannabis use without the lagged term 1.11 (0.14) and 1.16 (0.14). Editors' calculation, 95% intervals as B ± 1.96 SE: fixed effects 0.79–1.07, 0.98–1.56, 0.81–1.13 and 0.84–1.38; random effects 0.98–1.26, 0.86–1.36, 1.02–1.30 and 0.89–1.43. Model 1 reproduces the adjusted estimates of the original paper's Table 3, which sc_fergusson_2006 records as log-odds of any other illicit drug use in a year per step of the four-level cannabis frequency score, at age 19–20 in models with a cannabis × age term. If every re-analysis kept that form (the reply does not say), the odds per frequency step are multiplied by about 2.5 (model 1) to 3.6 (model 2) in fixed-effects models and by about 3.0–3.2 in random-effects models (editors' calculation, exp(B)).
analysis.covariates: Described only as covariate control (p. 475). In the original paper (sc_fergusson_2006) the fixed-effects models adjusted for 18 time-varying factors and the random-effects models also for 23 fixed factors (editors' count recorded there), with a cannabis × age term.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a post hoc re-analysis presented in a reply.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the main outcome is re-analysed; the number of people and person-years, the covariates, the model family and the age term are not stated; the instrumental-variable approach named by Kandel et al. is not tried; no specification addressing confounding that changes over time is reported.
analysis.power: Not reported; precision is shown by the standard errors (0.07–0.15).

interpretation_gap.results_show: One re-analysis: four specifications, each fitted as fixed- and random-effects models, gave cannabis coefficients of 0.93–1.27 (fixed) and 1.11–1.16 (random), with P < 0.0001 in all eight. The fixed-effects estimate was larger, not smaller, when cannabis use was taken from the preceding year (1.27 and 1.11, against 0.93 and 0.97), with wider intervals. Everything else in the reply is argument.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The reply concludes from the stable estimates that the concerns of Kandel et al. about time order and lagged endogenous variables are no serious threat to its conclusions (pp. 474–475). That is supported for the two specifications tested, though the instrumental-variable method Kandel et al. named was not tried, and the lag orders the years reported rather than the reports, which were mostly given at the same interview (sc_fergusson_2006). The reply calls MacCoun's age-varying or interacting confounders possible but not particularly plausible and invokes Occam's razor for the simplest reading, that cannabis use increases the risk of illicit drug use (p. 475); but the original paper's own limitations name omitted time-varying confounders, and fixed confounders whose effects change with age, as possible sources of overestimation (sc_fergusson_2006), and parsimony is not evidence against them. Its twin argument treats discordant-twin and fixed-effects designs as sharing a logic, but each removes different influences (stable within-person ones; ones shared by co-twins), and its explanation of the conflicting twin results (limited data across ages) is offered without data. It quotes Hall without the words of residual confounding (p. 475), widening his conclusion. Its policy statements are hedged and fit the evidence: the policy significance is unclear, and neither prohibition nor liberalization has been shown clearly to break the link (p. 476).

timeline.event: Tsuang et al. (Archives of General Psychiatry): twin study cited by MacCoun and by the reply as conflicting with Lynskey et al. (references, p. 476); not in the library and not read.
Lynskey et al.: co-twin study whose conflict with Tsuang et al. the reply attributes to limited data on cannabis and other illicit drug use in populations of varying age (p. 475).

Reinarman, Cohen & Kaal (American Journal of Public Health 94: 836–842; printed in the reply as Reinaman, Cohen & Kaal, H. A.): the limited relevance of drug policy, cannabis in Amsterdam and San Francisco (title as printed in the reply's reference list), cited for the statement that neither prohibition nor liberalization has been shown clearly to break the link (p. 476); not in the library and not read.
Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: the Christchurch analysis defended here.
Kandel, Yamaguchi & Klein: commentary raising the outcome, lagged-outcome and time-order objections and arguing for animal models.
Hall: commentary judging the relationship in some sense causal and no longer an artefact of residual confounding; quoted in the reply without the words of residual confounding.
MacCoun: commentary arguing that fixed-effects models cannot rule out influences that change with age or interact with measured factors.

replication.where_it_stands: The reply settled two specification questions with data and accepted the onset objection as sound; the question that matters most for a causal reading, confounding that changes over time or with age, was answered by argument only and remains open, as the original paper's own limitations say.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement is printed with the reply (pp. 474–476). The original study was funded by New Zealand research grants (sc_fergusson_2006).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (no declaration of interests in the reply).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors: Christchurch Health and Development Study, Christchurch School of Medicine and Health Sciences, New Zealand (p. 476). The reply defends the authors' own study, and its only new evidence is a re-analysis of their own cohort. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: A re-analysis of this or a comparable cohort with estimators designed for a lagged outcome in panel data (or instrumental variables), exposure and outcome reported at separate interviews, year-by-year measures of access to drugs and of drug-using networks, and an explicit test of confounding whose effect changes with age (for example, genetically informed models in which genetic effects may change over adolescence); and, for the twin argument, co-twin and within-person estimates compared in the same sample.

domains.note: No search: 6 references (the three commentaries, the two twin studies MacCoun raised and one policy study), chosen to answer the comments.
The conflict between the two twin studies is explained away without data, and the policy study is cited for one conclusion without description.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The only new evidence is a re-analysis of the authors' own cohort, incompletely reported (no number of people, covariates or model family); expected in a reply, but unchecked by others.

The re-analysis is presented as evidence; the judgments that complex confounding is implausible and that the twin conflict has a good explanation are asserted as conclusions, with Occam's razor as the argument.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for the gateway association (a causal effect of cannabis versus common liability and time-varying confounding)
domains.note: MacCoun's evidence on the non-causal side (the common-factor model, exposure opportunity, genetic influences that grow with age) is not engaged, and confounding that the original paper lists among its own limitations is called implausible. Under-represented: common liability and time-varying confounding. On mechanism and policy, by contrast, the reply keeps pharmacological and social routes open.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a reply (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than its worst domains (no search; one-sided treatment of confounding). The re-analysis is data from the original cohort, and its risk of bias is that of the original study (sc_fergusson_2006, ROBINS-E: high for a causal reading) plus the reporting gaps listed here. Cite it for: the original authors' acceptance that their analysis does not strictly test the gateway hypothesis as stated; the eight re-estimated coefficients (robust to taking cannabis use from the preceding year and to dropping the lagged outcome); their argument against generalizing from animal studies; and their statement that the policy significance is unclear. Do not cite it as showing that time-varying or age-varying confounding has been excluded, or for Hall's conclusion as quoted here (cite Hall directly).

key_findings.finding: The authors group the comments under three issues: model specification, what animal studies can contribute, and the political context.
key_findings.locator: Reply, opening paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Concession: they call sound the criticism by Kandel et al. that the analysis is not a strict test of the gateway hypothesis but a test of the broader question of whether cannabis use raises a person's predisposition to use other illicit drugs, and reply that it still examines the central issue the hypothesis raises, whether cannabis use makes the use of other illicit drugs more likely.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Model specification, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Re-analysis: in answer to the points that including the previous year's other illicit drug use (a lagged endogenous variable) may make the estimates inconsistent, and that the models did not ensure cannabis use came before other illicit drug use within a year, they re-estimated both fixed- and random-effects models (a) with cannabis use in the preceding year in place of same-year use and (b) without the lagged measure of previous illicit drug use, giving eight estimates.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Model specification, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Table 1, cannabis coefficient B (SE), fixed effects then random effects, all P < 0.0001 (Wald χ² test): same-year cannabis use with lagged other illicit drug use (the original model) 0.93 (0.07) and 1.12 (0.07); preceding-year cannabis use with lagged other illicit drug use 1.27 (0.15) and 1.11 (0.13); same-year cannabis use without the lagged term 0.97 (0.08) and 1.16 (0.07); preceding-year cannabis use without the lagged term 1.11 (0.14) and 1.16 (0.14). Editors' calculation, 95% intervals as B ± 1.96 SE: fixed effects 0.79–1.07, 0.98–1.56, 0.81–1.13, 0.84–1.38; random effects 0.98–1.26, 0.86–1.36, 1.02–1.30, 0.89–1.43.
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: The scale is not stated. Model 1 matches the adjusted estimates of the original paper's Table 3, which sc_fergusson_2006 records as log-odds of any other illicit drug use in a year per step of a four-level cannabis frequency score, at age 19–20 in models with a cannabis × age term; if every model kept that form, the odds per frequency step are multiplied by about 2.5–3.6 (fixed effects) and 3.0–3.2 (random effects) (editors' calculation, exp(B)). The number of people or person-years and the covariates are not given. Checked on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Their reading: within each model type, changing the specification left the study's general conclusions unchanged; with covariates controlled, cannabis use stayed linked to a higher risk of illicit drug use in the same year, and because the result held across specifications, they judge that the concerns about time order and lagged endogenous variables “do not pose a major threat to the validity of the conclusions drawn”.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Model specification, 3rd paragraph (p. 474, right column, continuing on p. 475, left column)

key_findings.finding: Rebuttal to MacCoun on confounding: they restate his point as complex interplay between confounders, cannabis use and illicit drug use that their model does not capture, call it possible but “not particularly plausible”, see little or no reason to propose such models, and appeal to Occam's razor to prefer the simplest reading (that cannabis use increases the risk of illicit drug use) to MacCoun's untested, more complex alternatives.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Model specification, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Rebuttal on twin studies: the discordant-twin design works much like the fixed-effects model (it compares two people with the same genes and shared environment who differ in cannabis exposure, where fixed effects compare one person at times of different exposure), and both take account of unobserved genes and shared environment. They put the conflicting results of Lynskey et al. (2003) and Tsuang et al. (1998) down to both studies having little data on cannabis and other illicit drug use in samples of mixed ages, since the strength of the association changes with how much cannabis is used and with age, and stress the value of full data from adolescence into adulthood.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Model specification, 5th paragraph (p. 475, left column, ending at the top of the right column); references 3–4 (p. 476)

key_findings.finding: Rebuttal to Kandel et al. on animal studies: other things being equal, laboratory research gives firmer evidence than correlational research, but Kandel et al. overstate their case; whether processes seen in laboratory rats, mice and flies match those in people outside the laboratory would be much disputed, since animals lack the complex social and cultural experience of humans, and generalizing readily from them is, in the authors' phrase, “drawing a very long bow indeed”.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Contributions of animal studies (right column)

key_findings.finding: Political context: the authors say their research makes less plausible a past tendency to dismiss the gateway hypothesis as a statistical artefact of unobserved confounders, and quote Hall; but they call the policy significance unclear. A direct effect of cannabis on susceptibility would tend to support a prohibitionist approach, whereas a link through association with drug dealers, people who use drugs and a drug-using youth culture would suggest decriminalizing cannabis to break its ties to illicit drug markets; neither prohibition nor liberalization has been shown clearly to break the link (Reinarman et al. 2004, printed as Reinaman).
key_findings.locator: Reply › The political context (p. 475, right column, continuing on p. 476, left column); reference 6 (p. 476)

key_findings.finding: Future directions: two kinds of research are needed: laboratory studies of the neurophysiological routes by which cannabis might raise susceptibility to other illicit drugs (agreeing with Kandel et al.), and sociological and social-psychological research on how the social climate (laws, youth culture, contact with drug dealers) can set up situations in which cannabis use raises the risk of using other illicit drugs, which they see as perhaps the most promising way to learn how far gateway effects are social in origin.
key_findings.locator: Reply › Future directions (left column, continuing in the right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The quotation of Hall drops three words without marking the omission: the reply prints “an artefact with little or no policy significance”, where Hall wrote “an artefact of residual confounding with little or no policy significance” (p. 473).
reporting_issues.consequence: Hall's judgment concerned residual confounding specifically; the reply's version reads as a broader endorsement. Cite Hall from his commentary.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives no scale (log-odds or otherwise), no number of people or person-years, no list of covariates and no statement about the cannabis × age term; only the model 1 row can be matched to the original paper (its adjusted estimates, as recorded on sc_fergusson_2006). The original models also included previous cannabis use among their 18 time-dynamic covariates (original paper, Table 3 footnote 2, p. 563; Methods, p. 560); the reply does not say how that covariate was handled when cannabis use itself was taken from the preceding year (models 2 and 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The coefficients can be compared with one another, but turning them into odds ratios, or into effects at a given age, rests on assuming that the re-analyses kept the original model's form. If that covariate was the preceding year's cannabis use, models 2 and 4 could not have kept it unchanged; since the reply does not say what was done, the larger fixed-effects coefficient with preceding-year cannabis use (1.27 against 0.93) may reflect a change of covariates as well as of timing.

reporting_issues.issue: The reply restates MacCoun as saying that the analysis shows any simple version of the common-propensity account is incorrect; MacCoun wrote that it shows “any simple version is unlikely to be correct” (p. 473).
reporting_issues.consequence: A minor hardening of the critic's hedged judgment, in the original authors' favour; cite MacCoun's own wording.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 6 and its in-text citation print the first author as Reinaman, and the reference gives the third author's initials as H. A.; by its bibliographic record the article (American Journal of Public Health 2004, 94(5): 836–842) is by C. Reinarman, P. D. A. Cohen and H. L. Kaal.
reporting_issues.consequence: A search under the printed name may fail; trace the article by journal, volume and pages, or under Reinarman. The argument is unaffected.

All 7 pages read, the reply on pp. 474–476 and the three commentaries it answers on pp. 470–474; Table 1 and every page checked on renderings at 150 dpi; no supplement. The original study was not reread: statements about it, including the match of model 1 with its Table 3, come from its card, sc_fergusson_2006.
