design_detail: Rats. Between-group laboratory experiment from the Simon Fraser University group, the second of its three published housing experiments (after Alexander et al. 1978 and before Alexander et al. 1981; the series the project's reading list calls Rat Park, a name the paper does not use). 36 albino rats of Wistar origin (University of British Columbia breeding stock): 9 males and 9 females housed singly from weaning in 18 × 25 × 18 cm sheet-metal cages, and 9 males and 9 females housed together from weaning in one open-topped wooden box with 8.8 m² of floor, cedar shavings and 12 small open metal cages. From 85–87 days of age, with no prior morphine exposure and no forced-drinking phase, all rats had a continuous choice between tap water and: 5% sucrose (3-day pretest); then six 5-day phases of morphine hydrochloride solution made progressively more palatable (0.5 mg/ml unsweetened; 0.5 mg/ml with 1%, 5% and 10% sucrose; 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose); then 10% sucrose (5-day post-test). Isolated rats drank from weighed bottles; colony rats from two drop dispensers at the end of a one-rat tunnel, with each rat's intake taken from video and drop counters. Outcomes per phase: proportion of fluid taken as the test solution, mg morphine HCl per kg body weight (analysed as square roots) and total fluid in grams, with analyses of variance for housing, sex and their interaction. Every finding is in rats.
can_establish: Whether, in one group of 36 morphine-naive rats from one breeding stock and one laboratory, rats raised and kept singly drank more of a series of increasingly sweet and dilute morphine solutions offered beside water than rats raised and kept together in one large furnished enclosure, and whether females drank more than males, without any forced exposure to morphine.
cannot_establish: Which feature of the colony made the difference (company, space, bedding and objects, mixed-sex living with pregnancy and lactation, a different drinking device and a different measurement method all came together), whether the result holds beyond one colony (all 18 colony rats shared one enclosure, so housing was not replicated), whether the fixed order of solutions shaped the result, or anything about addiction in people.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory rats: albino, Wistar origin, University of British Columbia breeding stock; 9 males and 9 females in each housing group; 85–87 days old when the experiment began; no prior exposure to morphine (p. 87, Introduction, last paragraph, and Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated. How rats were assigned to housing at weaning, and the age at weaning, are not reported.
sample.demographics: Equal sex numbers by design. Rats were weighed before the pretest (p. 88), but no body weights are reported.
sample.attrition: One isolated male was accidentally killed, leaving 8 isolated males from Phase 0.5–1 on (p. 88). No other losses are reported.
sample.selection_effects: One breeding stock, one laboratory and one colony: all 18 colony rats lived in a single enclosure and drank from one shared tunnel, so the housing comparison rests on a single colony, and its rats are not independent observations, although the analyses treat them as such; the authors note that every colony rat had to receive the phases in the same order (p. 90). Both sexes lived together in the colony, and the Results suggest that gestation and lactation raised colony females' fluid needs (p. 89); pregnancies and litters are not otherwise reported.

exposure.measurement: Housing (isolated or colony, from weaning) is the experimental factor; intake is the outcome. Isolated rats: bottles fastened outside the cage, weighed daily and corrected for leakage and evaporation from two bottles on an empty cage. Colony rats: two drop dispensers (tap water; test solution) at the end of a transparent tunnel 25.4 cm long that admitted one rat at a time (inside 4.4 × 5.8 cm), each withdrawal of the head from a light beam releasing a drop; a camera triggered by each entry recorded the dye-marked rat and the counters showing the drops taken by the previous rat; spillage was collected and weighed daily (pp. 87–88). How drop counts were turned into grams is not described. Fluid sides were swapped at the end of each phase (p. 88).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats: oral, voluntary, 24-h two-fluid choice beside tap water; morphine hydrochloride at 0.5 mg/ml (unsweetened, then with 1%, 5% and 10% sucrose), 0.3 mg/ml and 0.15 mg/ml (both with 10% sucrose), 5 days each in that fixed order (30 days of morphine availability), after a 3-day 5% sucrose pretest and before a 5-day 10% sucrose post-test (Table 1 and Apparatus and Procedure, 5th paragraph, p. 88). The order was chosen to present morphine in increasingly palatable solutions, and order effects were not controlled (p. 88).
exposure.polysubstance: None: one drug, and the rats had no prior morphine exposure (p. 87).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: morphine-naive at the start; no withdrawal or abstinence tests.

comparison.controls: Isolated rats (single sheet-metal cages, no visual contact with neighbours, own bottles) against colony rats (one large enclosure, both sexes, bedding and objects, a shared tunnel with drop dispensers); the sucrose-only pretest and post-test serve as sugar-preference controls (pp. 87–88).
comparison.matching: Same stock, age and sex numbers.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure from before housing began; allocation not reported; body weights not reported.

outcomes.instruments: For each phase: proportion of fluid taken as the test solution; mg morphine HCl per kg body weight, square-root transformed for analysis to reduce heterogeneity of variance; total fluid in grams (p. 88). Analyses of variance for each phase with housing, sex and their interaction (the effects marked in Figs 1–3), plus an analysis of the first day of Phase 0.5–0 and analyses of absolute sucrose intake in the pretest and post-test (p. 90).
outcomes.validity_norms: Intake was measured by different methods in the two housing groups (weighed bottles against drop counts), with no calibration of drops reported; which body weight the mg/kg values use is not stated beyond a weighing before the pretest.
outcomes.operationalization: Morphine consumption = voluntary intake of the morphine (or morphine–sucrose) solution beside water, as a proportion of total fluid and as mg/kg; no measure of dependence, withdrawal or motivation.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 22 phase-by-measure analyses of variance (editors' count: proportion and total fluid in 8 phases each, mg/kg in the 6 morphine phases), each testing housing, sex and their interaction, plus the first-day and absolute-sucrose analyses; significance shown only as stars.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; housing could not be concealed. Intake was recorded by weighing or by drop counters and video transcription.

analysis.effect_sizes: Untransformed means ± SE are printed for one phase only (0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose; mg morphine HCl/kg): isolated females 36.64 ± 2.70, isolated males 24.09 ± 7.10, colony females 7.29 ± 2.70, colony males 1.46 ± 0.73; ratios 5:1 (females) and more than 16:1 (males) as printed (pp. 88–89). Other results appear only in Figs 1–3, with significance marked by stars and no test statistics except both F < 1.0 on the first day of Phase 0.5–0 (p. 90). Editors' approximate readings of Fig. 2 (proportion of fluid taken as the test solution; scan measured at 600 dpi against the axis ticks, about ±0.02): last morphine phase isolated females 0.78, isolated males 0.71, colony females 0.19, colony males 0.08; post-test (plain 10% sucrose) colony females 0.99, colony males 1.00, isolated females 0.93, isolated males 0.85.
analysis.covariates: None; housing and sex as factors.
analysis.preregistration_detail: None would be expected for a 1979 animal experiment.
analysis.selective_reporting: Numbers are printed only for the phase with the largest consumption, which supplies the abstract's five- and sixteen-fold figures; the other phases appear only as plotted square-root values, proportions and grams; no F statistics or degrees of freedom; body weights not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported; 9 rats per sex per housing group (8 isolated males from Phase 0.5–1 on), and one colony.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 36 morphine-naive rats, those housed singly drank more of the sweetened morphine solutions than those in the colony, and the gap widened as the solution became sweeter and weaker: in the last morphine phase, means of 36.64 against 7.29 mg/kg in females and 24.09 against 1.46 in males. By the editors' figure readings, colony rats then took about a fifth (females) and a twelfth (males) of their fluid as the morphine–sucrose solution, against about three quarters in isolated rats, yet took nearly all their fluid as plain 10% sucrose in the post-test. On the first day of unsweetened morphine there was no indication of a housing effect (both F < 1.0); the difference opened as the colony rats' intake fell over the following days. The housing main effect on mg/kg was not significant in two of the six morphine phases (0.5–1 and 0.5–5).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports the significant housing and sex differences and the five- and sixteen-fold differences from the phase with the greatest consumption, without the conditions behind them (one colony, a different drinking device and measurement, a fixed order) (p. 87); the introduction frames the question as whether the 1978 housing effect is general enough to change how self-administration studies are interpreted (p. 87). The discussion says the results confirm and extend the 1978 findings and concludes that it “now seems established, at least in one strain” that isolation favours morphine consumption far more than colony housing does and that females take more morphine than males (p. 90). That rests on one colony of 18 rats and the group's own earlier experiment, with housing bundled with a different drinking device and measurement and with mixed-sex living, and the sex conclusion passes over the authors' own suggestion that gestation and lactation raised colony females' fluid needs (p. 89). The explanation they think more likely, that morphine interfered with colony rats' species-typical behaviour (p. 89), was not measured here and leans on the 1978 report of less fighting and sexual behaviour under forced consumption. Their arguments against bitterness and caloric need use their own data (pp. 89–90); the argument against an effect of the drinking device says total fluid was similar in the two groups, which Fig. 3 does not bear out (p. 90). They note one negative study (Hill & Powell 1976) and the possibility of a strain-specific effect (p. 90). The paper makes no claim about people.

timeline.event: Alexander, Coambs & Hadaway (same laboratory and stock, different rats): rats pre-exposed to morphine and then made to drink unsweetened morphine solution as their only fluid for 57 days drank more on choice days when isolated than when housed socially, and females more than males (as recorded on sc_alexander_1978). This paper cites it as finding that colony-housed rats drank far less morphine solution (p. 87).
This experiment (received 8 December 1978): morphine-naive rats, progressively sweetened morphine solutions, no forced drinking; isolated rats drank more than colony rats and females more than males.

Alexander, Beyerstein, Hadaway & Coambs (same laboratory and stock; run April–July 1979 according to Petrie 1996): early and later housing crossed, morphine 1.0, 0.5, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml in 10% sucrose in descending order with a quinine–sucrose control; males living in the colony at testing drank far less, females less conclusively, and no sex difference was found (as recorded on sc_alexander_1981, which cites this paper as the second earlier experiment).

Petrie: two experiments with Wistar rats from the supplier's later breeding stock did not reproduce lower intake in colony rats; the strain explanation offered was not tested (as recorded on sc_petrie_1996).
Gage & Sumnall: critical history of how Rat Park changed the narrative of addiction (on the project's reading list; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: Lower oral morphine intake in colony-housed rats rests on three small experiments from one laboratory (1978, this one, 1981) and was not reproduced in the published replication attempt (Petrie 1996). This is the experiment without forced exposure and with sweetened solutions from the start; its sex difference (also reported in 1978) was not seen in 1981. All findings are in rats.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article; the acknowledgements thank six named people for their assistance (p. 90).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors: Department of Psychology, Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, Canada (p. 87), the laboratory of Alexander et al. (1978, 1981). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered experiment with rats randomly assigned to housing, several independent colonies (so that the colony, not the rat, is the unit of analysis), single-sex colonies or controlled breeding, the same drinking device and measurement in every condition, a counterbalanced order of solutions with taste controls, body weights reported, and repetition in an independent laboratory and in more than one strain.

domains.note: How weanlings were assigned to isolation or the colony is not described.

Same stock, age (85–87 days at the start) and sex numbers; body weights were taken but not reported, and housing had lasted since weaning, so there is no measure from before the groups diverged. In the pretest the proportion of sucrose taken did not differ significantly by housing (p. 90), but isolated rats drank more total fluid (p. 89).
Not reported.

Housing is the factor studied, but it came bundled with a different drinking device (own bottles against one shared drop-dispenser tunnel), different measurement, space, bedding and objects, company and mixed-sex living; all 18 colony rats were in one enclosure, so housing was not replicated.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Not reported; housing could not be concealed.
All rats were measured daily throughout.

Blinding is not reported and housing could not be concealed; the larger problem is that intake was measured by different methods in the two groups (weighed bottles against drop counts with video identification), with no calibration of drops reported.
One isolated male was accidentally killed and is missing from Phase 0.5–1 on; the reason is given and no other loss is reported.

No protocol (none would be expected at the time). All phases and measures appear in the figures, but numbers are printed only for the phase with the largest consumption, and no test statistics are given beyond F < 1.0 for one day.
One colony analysed as 18 independent rats; a mixed-sex colony with gestation and lactation mentioned but not reported; a fixed order of phases (acknowledged, p. 90); a misprinted significance key.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; this is the editors' summary, set to the most severe judgment among the items that bear on the housing comparison. Housing came bundled with a different drinking device and measurement, the colony was a single unit, allocation is not described, colony females may have been pregnant or nursing, and the order of phases was fixed. Cite it for what this experiment did and found in rats: morphine-naive rats, never forced to drink morphine, that were offered increasingly sweet and dilute morphine solutions drank more when housed alone than in the colony (last phase 36.64 against 7.29 mg/kg in females, 24.09 against 1.46 in males); there was no indication of a housing effect on the first day of unsweetened morphine (both F < 1.0); and colony rats, which took nearly all their fluid as plain sugar water, took little of the sugar water once morphine was in it (figure readings). Label every use as a rat finding from one colony in one laboratory. Do not cite it for which feature of the environment matters, for a sex difference independent of pregnancy and lactation, for anything about people, or as a replication independent of Alexander et al. (1978).

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rat; albino, Wistar origin, University of British Columbia breeding stock; 9 males and 9 females per housing group (36 rats; 8 isolated males from Phase 0.5–1 on); housed in their condition from weaning; 85–87 days old at the start (p. 87).
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Oral and voluntary: 24-h two-fluid choice between tap water and morphine hydrochloride solution, 0.5 mg/ml unsweetened and then with 1%, 5% and 10% sucrose, then 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose, 5 days each in a fixed order (30 days), between a 3-day 5% sucrose pretest and a 5-day 10% sucrose post-test (Table 1, p. 88). Study conditions only.
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given by the paper and none calculated here; the study is about how much rats chose to drink, not about dose effects.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: No: rats choosing a sweetened oral morphine solution beside water in a cage or a laboratory enclosure for 30 days; no escalation, dependence or withdrawal was measured, and cage versus colony is a narrow stand-in for a human social environment.

key_findings.finding: Subjects and housing: 9 male and 9 female albino rats of Wistar origin (University of British Columbia breeding stock) in each housing group, 85–87 days old at the start and never before exposed to morphine. Isolated rats were kept from weaning in standard 18 × 25 × 18 cm cages with sheet-metal walls, so they could not see their neighbours; colony rats shared, from weaning, one open-topped wooden enclosure with 8.8 m² of floor, a layer of cedar shavings and 12 small open metal cages to climb on and nest in.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (right column); Materials and Methods › Subjects; Apparatus and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Intake was measured differently in the two housing groups: isolated rats drank from bottles on the outside of the cage, weighed daily and corrected for leakage and evaporation using two bottles on an empty cage; colony rats drank from two drop dispensers (tap water and the test solution) at the end of a transparent tunnel 25.4 cm long that admitted one rat at a time (inside 4.4 × 5.8 cm), each withdrawal of the head from a light beam releasing a drop; a camera triggered by each entry recorded the dye-marked rat and the counters showing the previous rat's drops, and spillage was collected and weighed daily.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Apparatus and Procedure, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 87) and 4th paragraph (p. 88)

key_findings.finding: Procedure: after a 3-day pretest with water and 5% sucrose, all rats had 30 days of continuous choice between water and a series of morphine hydrochloride solutions, 5 days each in a fixed order: 0.5 mg/ml in water; 0.5 mg/ml with 1%, then 5%, then 10% sucrose; 0.3 mg/ml and then 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose; then a 5-day post-test with water and 10% sucrose. There was no forced-drinking phase. The order was designed to make the morphine solution progressively more palatable, order effects were not controlled, and fluid sides were swapped at the end of each phase.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Materials and Methods › Apparatus and Procedure, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Analysis: for each phase, analyses of variance on the proportion of test solution in total fluid, on mg morphine HCl per kg body weight (square-root transformed to reduce heterogeneity of variance) and on total fluid in grams. One isolated male was accidentally killed, leaving 8 isolated males from Phase 0.5–1 on.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Apparatus and Procedure, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the last morphine phase (0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose), untransformed means ± SE in mg morphine HCl/kg were: isolated females 36.64 ± 2.70 (n = 9), isolated males 24.09 ± 7.10 (n = 8), colony females 7.29 ± 2.70 (n = 9) and colony males 1.46 ± 0.73 (n = 9); the authors give the differences as 5:1 for females and more than 16:1 for males. These are the only intake means printed as numbers.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effect on Morphine Consumption, 3rd paragraph (p. 88, left column, continuing on p. 89, left column)
key_findings.note: The paper does not say whether these are daily means or totals for the 5-day phase, and the same SE (2.70) is printed for isolated and colony females. Editors' check of the printed ratios: 36.64/7.29 = 5.0 and 24.09/1.46 = 16.5. The group sizes are the editors' from the Method (one isolated male lost).

key_findings.finding: Isolated rats drank more morphine than colony rats on both measures, and the housing difference generally became larger and more significant from one morphine phase to the next, reaching well past P = 0.001 in Phase 0.15–10. The exception was Phase 0.5–1 (0.5 mg/ml with 1% sucrose), in which isolated females drank less morphine per kg than colony females while isolated males drank more than colony males, with a significant housing × sex interaction. By the figures' significance marks, the housing main effect was significant for mg/kg in Phases 0.5–0, 0.5–10, 0.3–10 and 0.15–10 but not in 0.5–1 or 0.5–5, and for proportion in every morphine phase except 0.5–0.
key_findings.locator: Results › Housing Effect on Morphine Consumption, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column); Figs 1 and 2 (significance marks under each phase, right column)
key_findings.note: Significance marks read on the rendered page at 300 dpi; the key printed under Fig. 1 is misprinted (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: On the first day of the first morphine phase (0.5 mg/ml, unsweetened), there was no indication of a housing effect on either measure (both F < 1.0); over the rest of that phase the colony rats' morphine consumption fell sharply while the isolated rats' stayed close to its first-day level.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Fig. 2 plots the proportion of each group's fluid taken as the test solution in every phase; the paper gives these values only in the figure. Editors' approximate readings (scan measured at 600 dpi against the axis ticks, about ±0.02): last morphine phase (0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose) isolated females 0.78, isolated males 0.71, colony females 0.19, colony males 0.08; post-test (plain 10% sucrose) colony females 0.99, colony males 1.00, isolated females 0.93, isolated males 0.85; pretest (5% sucrose) isolated females 0.79, isolated males 0.89, colony females 0.96, colony males 0.98; first morphine phase (unsweetened) isolated females 0.08, the other three groups about 0.03 or less.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 2 (right column)
key_findings.note: Values read from the figure, not printed. In the early morphine phases the colony markers overlap near zero and cannot be told apart.

key_findings.finding: Females generally drank more morphine solution than males: significant for both measures in Phases 0.5–5 and 0.3–10 and for mg/kg in Phases 0.5–0 and 0.15–10; in Phase 0.5–1 isolated females drank less than isolated males (housing × sex interaction significant). The authors offer no explanation for the sex difference and found no sign of a greater sugar preference in females.
key_findings.locator: Results › Gender Difference (p. 89, left column); Discussion, 11th paragraph (p. 90, right column)

key_findings.finding: All rats preferred the sucrose-only solutions to water. In the post-test, colony rats took a significantly higher proportion of their fluid as 10% sucrose than isolated rats, by a small margin; there was no significant housing effect on the proportion taken as sucrose in the pretest, nor on the absolute amount of sucrose solution drunk in either the pretest or the post-test, which the authors take as evidence against a greater caloric need in isolated rats.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sugar Preference (p. 89, left column); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 90, left column)

key_findings.finding: Total fluid: every group drank more when only sucrose and water were offered (pretest and post-test) than during the morphine phases; isolated rats drank more than colony rats in the pretest; in the morphine phases the housing and sex effects were qualified by significant housing × sex interactions, colony females drinking more than colony males (which the authors suggest may reflect greater fluid needs of gestation and lactation) and the sex difference running the other way in isolated rats except in the last two phases; in the post-test colony females drank about twice as much as colony males, with isolated rats in between. Editors' approximate readings of Fig. 3 (grams; time base not stated): pretest isolated rats about 117, colony females 93, colony males 85; morphine phases before the last, isolated females about 31–48, isolated males 39–45, colony females 53–65, colony males 39–52; last morphine phase isolated females 76, isolated males 71, colony females 66, colony males 47; post-test colony females 124, colony males 56, isolated females 93, isolated males 101.
key_findings.locator: Results › Total Fluid Consumption, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column) and 3rd paragraph (right column); Fig. 3 (left column)
key_findings.note: Figure readings from a 600-dpi measurement against the axis ticks, about ±2 g; where markers overlap, the value is that of the merged markers.

key_findings.finding: Explanations weighed by the authors: relief of anxiety from social and sensory deprivation (Khantzian 1974), argued against with studies in which rats avoided the pharmacological effects of opiates (Huidobro 1964; Wikler & Pescor 1967; Chipkin & Rosecrans 1978) and the authors' own unpublished quinine-versus-morphine tests before and after naltrexone; interference with colony rats' species-typical behaviour, which they believe more likely, citing the 1978 report of less fighting and sexual behaviour under forced consumption; isolated rats being less affected by morphine (evidence on both sides); stronger aversion to bitterness in colony rats (unlikely, since the gap was largest when the solution was least bitter and most sweetened); greater caloric need in isolated rats (remote, given the sucrose results); inhibition of drinking by the colony device (argued against because total fluid was similar and every colony rat learned the device on the first day); and the fixed order of phases (counterbalancing impossible in one colony; both groups had the same order, and the housing effect was significant in the first morphine phase).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd–9th paragraphs (p. 89, right column, to p. 90, left column)

key_findings.finding: Hill and Powell (1976) found no effect of social versus solitary housing on morphine intake; the authors note that neither of their groups drank appreciable amounts (greatest mean daily intake about 1.5 mg morphine sulphate/kg), probably rejecting the bitter unsweetened solution, and call the difference in methods the most parsimonious explanation, while saying that study leaves open the possibility that the housing effect is specific to one strain.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: whatever the cause, the authors write that it “now seems established, at least in one strain” that isolation favours morphine consumption far more than colony housing does and that females take more morphine than males, so that generalizations from self-administration studies should allow for housing and sex.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 12th (last) paragraph (right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The key to the significance marks, printed under Fig. 1 and used for all three figures, reads * P < 0.5 and ** P < 0.1 (with *** P < 0.001); editors' reading: presumably misprints for 0.05 and 0.01.
reporting_issues.consequence: One- and two-star results can be read only on that presumption; no test statistics are given to check them.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Fig. 1 gives morphine consumption as mg morphine HCl/kg body weight, but its axis is labelled in square-root units (√mg/kg), matching the transformation used for the analyses. Editors' reading of the last phase: about 5.4, 4.2, 2.3 and 0.9 on that axis (isolated females, isolated males, colony females, colony males), whose squares (about 29, 18, 5.4 and 0.8) lie below the printed untransformed means, as means of square roots must.
reporting_issues.consequence: Values read off Fig. 1 as mg/kg would understate intake several-fold; only the last phase has untransformed means in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The time base of intake is not stated: mg/kg and grams are given without saying whether they are daily means or totals per phase (the pretest lasted 3 days, the other phases 5), while the Discussion compares the results with another study's mean daily intake.
reporting_issues.consequence: Comparisons with other studies' daily intakes, including the 1978 and 1981 experiments, assume daily values.

reporting_issues.issue: How the colony rats' drop counts were converted into grams and mg/kg is not described, and no calibration of drop size is reported, while isolated rats' intake came from weighed bottles.
reporting_issues.consequence: Part of any difference in absolute amounts could come from the measurement method; the proportion measure is less exposed to this.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says total fluid consumption was similar in the two housing groups (its argument against inhibition of drinking by the colony device), but Fig. 3 marks a significant housing effect on total fluid in the pretest (isolated rats more) and in four of the six morphine phases, where the colony females drank the most.
reporting_issues.consequence: The device argument rests on a description the figure does not bear out, although in the morphine phases colony rats drank more, not less, total fluid; in the pretest they drank less.

reporting_issues.issue: Both sexes lived together in the colony. The Results suggest that colony females' greater fluid intake may reflect gestation and lactation, but the paper does not report how many females were pregnant or nursing, when, or whether litters shared the enclosure and the drinking tunnel.
reporting_issues.consequence: Pregnancy and lactation could change fluid intake, body weight (and so mg/kg) and drug intake in colony females; the conclusion that females consume more morphine than males (p. 90) does not take this into account.

reporting_issues.issue: Body weights are never reported, although mg/kg is a main measure; the only weighing described is before the pretest.
reporting_issues.consequence: If one starting weight was used across the 38-day experiment, mg/kg would drift with growth and with pregnancy, differently by housing and sex.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the housing effect was significant in the first morphine phase (used to argue that phase order did not create it) holds for mg/kg (Fig. 1) but not for the proportion measure, which has no significance mark in that phase (Fig. 2), and not for the first day of the phase (both F < 1.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: The order argument is weaker than stated; with a fixed order, the growth of the housing difference cannot be separated from time and accumulated exposure.

reporting_issues.issue: The same standard error (2.70) is printed for isolated females and for colony females in the last phase.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a coincidence or a transcription slip; it cannot be checked from the paper.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, a scan with an OCR text layer that spaces out some digits and garbles some words), pp. 87–91 (all 5 pages read on renderings at 150 dpi; Figs 1–3 and their significance marks checked at 300 dpi, and plotted values measured on 600-dpi renderings against the axis ticks, correcting for a slight rotation of the scan; no supplement).

disagreements.first_pass: Materials and Methods › Apparatus and Procedure, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 87) and 4th paragraph (p. 88)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 508 (round-2 check): wrong-location: text confirmed; locator should read Apparatus and Procedure, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 87) and 4th paragraph (p. 88); the bottles fastened outside each cage are in the 1st paragraph.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 87, Materials and Methods › Apparatus and Procedure: the 1st paragraph gives the bottles fastened outside each isolated rat's cage, the 2nd the colony tunnel and dispensers, the 3rd the camera and spillage; the weighing of bottles is in the 4th paragraph (p. 88). Locator corrected; finding unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: On the first day of the first morphine phase (0.5 mg/ml, unsweetened), there was no housing difference on either measure (both F < 1.0); over the rest of that phase the colony rats' morphine consumption fell sharply while the isolated rats' stayed close to its first-day level.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 508 (round-2 check): corrected: on the first day of the first morphine phase there was no indication of a housing effect on either measure (both F < 1.0), rather than no housing difference.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading p. 90, Discussion, 6th paragraph (left column): the paper says there was no indication of a housing effect (both F < 1.0), which reports a test with no detectable effect, not equal intake. Finding corrected, and the same day's result reworded to match in the interpretation gap and the risk-of-bias reasoning; no number changed.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 508 (round-2 check) and AI reader 522 (card adjudication)

design_detail: Commentary (Addiction 101(4), pp. 472–473; the second of three commentaries printed together with the original authors' reply) by Wayne Hall, Professor of Public Health Policy, School of Population Health, University of Queensland, on Fergusson, Boden & Horwood (2006), the Christchurch birth-cohort analysis of cannabis and other illicit drug use. Seven paragraphs and 8 references; no data and no search or selection method. It summarizes the gateway pattern and three explanations (one black market supplying both drugs; common causes; a pharmacological effect of cannabis), credits the fixed-effects analysis with answering the residual-confounding objection, sets out the opposite policy readings of the explanations (US prevention of cannabis initiation versus Dutch separation of markets) and lists the evidence that would decide between them. Evidence of a published argument, not new data.
can_establish: That a public-health policy researcher, co-author of an earlier review of these hypotheses, judged in 2006 that the Christchurch analysis made a good case for a relationship that is in some sense causal and that the relationship could no longer be regarded as an artefact of residual confounding, and named the evidence he thought would decide its mechanism.
cannot_establish: Which explanation is right (the commentary says that needs convergent evidence from several kinds of study), how large any effect is (no numbers are given), or whether fixed-effects control removes confounding that changes over time or with age, which the commentary does not discuss.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a commentary with no participants or data. Evidence pointed to (reference list, p. 473): Kandel & Yamaguchi (2002), on stages of drug involvement in the US population, for the gateway pattern; Hall & Lynskey (2005), the author's own review, for the three explanations and for evaluations of drug education; MacLeod et al. (2004), a systematic review of longitudinal general-population studies, for the critics' doubts about confounding; the original study; Polich et al. (1984) and de Kort & Cramer (1999) for the US and Dutch policy readings; Cadoni et al. (2001), on THC–morphine cross-sensitization in rats, and Lynskey et al. (2003), on twins discordant for early cannabis use, as examples of the evidence needed.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; references chosen by the author.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author without a search: 8 references, one of them his own review.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable: no data were collected. The commentary describes the original analysis as fixed-effects regression assessing how far the cannabis–other illicit drug relationship is explained by unmeasured as well as measured confounders (p. 472).
exposure.polysubstance: The pattern described: almost all adolescents who had tried cocaine and heroin had first used alcohol, tobacco and cannabis (p. 472).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The commentary reports critics' doubts that earlier longitudinal studies could adjust for all potential confounders, and credits fixed effects with addressing them (p. 472).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; the commentary uses the original study's framing (use of other illicit drugs) without defining it.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own and none quoted: the commentary says the relationship was weaker in fixed-effects than in random-effects regression but remained statistically significant, without numbers (p. 472).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a commentary.
analysis.selective_reporting: The limits of fixed-effects control (influences that change with age or over time, which the original paper lists among its own limitations, sc_fergusson_2006) are not mentioned.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results. The commentary restates the original finding qualitatively (weaker under fixed effects, still significant) and offers a framework of explanations, their policy implications and a list of the research needed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The judgment that the original authors make a good case for a relationship that is in some sense causal (p. 472) is hedged and fair. The concluding judgment, that it is “no longer possible to regard the relationship as an artefact of residual confounding” (p. 473), treats confounding as answered, whereas fixed effects remove only stable influences whose effects do not change over the years studied, as the original paper itself acknowledges (sc_fergusson_2006) and as MacCoun's commentary in the same issue argues (sc_maccoun_2006). The policy section is balanced: it shows the same pattern supporting opposite US and Dutch readings.

timeline.event: Lynskey et al.: study of twins discordant for early cannabis use, named by Hall as the kind of evidence needed (reference 8, p. 473).
Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: the Christchurch analysis commented on.
Kandel, Yamaguchi & Klein: commentary in the same issue, challenging the causal conclusion on three methodological grounds and proposing animal models.
MacCoun: commentary in the same issue, arguing that fixed-effects models cannot rule out influences that change with age or interact with measured factors.
Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: reply that quotes this commentary's conclusion without the words of residual confounding (p. 475) and calls the policy significance of the findings unclear.

replication.where_it_stands: Hall's research list (animal studies of mechanism, discordant twins, the effect of Dutch cannabis policy on the gateway pattern, evaluations of drug education interventions testing whether delaying cannabis use reduces other illicit drug use) names designs later used on this question; the project's reading list includes cross-national and common-liability studies of the gateway idea (Degenhardt et al. 2010; Vanyukov et al. 2012), not appraised here. His conclusion about residual confounding was disputed in the same issue by MacCoun and is not supported by the reply's re-analysis, which did not address confounding that changes over time.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement is printed with the commentary (pp. 472–473).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (no declaration of interests in the commentary).
funding.affiliations_note: Wayne Hall, Professor of Public Health Policy, School of Population Health, University of Queensland, Australia (p. 473). One of the 8 references is his own review with Lynskey (2005), the source of the three explanations. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: The designs Hall lists, done well: discordant-twin and other genetically informed studies tested against an explicit common-liability model; natural experiments in which access to cannabis changes without a change in access to other drugs (such as the Dutch separation of markets), with the gateway pattern measured before and after; and trials of programmes that delay cannabis use with later use of other illicit drugs as an outcome.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria: 8 references chosen by the author.
The fixed-effects approach is endorsed without stating what it leaves uncontrolled; the other studies are cited for their conclusions only.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 8 references is the author's own review, used for the framework of explanations and the research list; the argument rests mainly on others' work.
The policy section keeps the explanations apart from their implications, but the conclusion about residual confounding is stated as settled rather than as a judgment.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for the gateway association (a causal step from cannabis versus residual confounding)
domains.note: The three explanations and the two policy readings are presented evenly, but the residual-confounding side is closed without mention of confounding that changes over time. Under-represented: confounding that fixed effects cannot remove.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than its worst domain (no search). The commentary is short, even-handed on mechanism and policy, and firm on confounding. Cite it for: a 2006 judgment by a public-health policy researcher that the Christchurch analysis made a good case for a relationship that is in some sense causal; the three explanations and their opposite policy implications (US prevention of cannabis initiation versus Dutch separation of markets); and the list of evidence needed. Do not cite it as evidence that confounding has been excluded, or for any effect size.

key_findings.finding: The pattern, which Hall counts among the most robust findings of 30 years of research on adolescent drug use: nearly every adolescent who has tried cocaine and heroin used alcohol, tobacco and cannabis before them, and adolescents who use cannabis more regularly, or start it younger, are more likely to use other illicit drugs (cited to Kandel & Yamaguchi 2002, on the US population).
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 1st paragraph (p. 472, left column); reference 1 (p. 473)

key_findings.finding: Three explanations: (1) opportunity: one black market sells cannabis and other illicit drugs, so people who use cannabis have more chances to use them; (2) common causes: people who start cannabis young are more likely to use cannabis and other drugs regularly for reasons that have nothing to do with cannabis; (3) pharmacology: cannabis's effects make adolescents more likely to use other illicit drugs (cited to Hall & Lynskey 2005, the author's own review).
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 2nd paragraph (p. 472, right column); reference 2 (p. 473)

key_findings.finding: Longitudinal studies that adjusted statistically for characteristics present before cannabis use began usually found the relationship weakened but still present; critics doubted that such studies could measure and adjust for every potential confounder (MacLeod et al. 2004).
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 3rd paragraph (p. 472, right column); reference 4 (p. 473)

key_findings.finding: Fergusson et al. answered that criticism with fixed-effects regression, which tests how much of the relationship unmeasured as well as measured confounders explain; the relationship was weaker in fixed-effects than in random-effects regression but still statistically significant, and Hall offers the study as an illustration of what fixed-effects methods can add to epidemiological studies of adolescent drug use.
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Hall's judgment: the original authors make a good case for believing that the relationship is “in some sense, causal”, and point out carefully how hard it is to decide which causal explanation fits their data best, for example a pharmacological effect of cannabis use on the developing brain, drug markets and youth culture acting together on the chance of using other illicit drugs, or some combination of these.
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 5th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Policy: the explanations have very different implications. US policy analysts argued for preventing or delaying the start of cannabis use to reduce other illicit drug use (Polich et al. 1984); Dutch analysts attributed the pattern to cannabis and other illicit drugs being sold in the same black market and supported decriminalizing cannabis use and small retail sales to break that link (de Kort & Cramer 1999).
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 6th paragraph (p. 472, right column); references 5–6 (p. 473)

key_findings.finding: Evidence needed to decide between the pathways: animal studies testing whether a pharmacological mechanism is plausible (Cadoni et al. 2001), studies of twins who differ in cannabis use (Lynskey et al. 2003), studies of how Dutch cannabis policy has affected the gateway pattern, and evaluations of drug education testing whether delaying cannabis use lowers later use of other illicit drugs.
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 7th paragraph (left column); references 7–8

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: whatever later research shows about the causal explanation, the relationship can no longer be dismissed as “an artefact of residual confounding with little or no policy significance”.
key_findings.locator: Hall commentary, 7th paragraph, last sentence (left column)
key_findings.note: The original authors' reply quotes this sentence without the words of residual confounding and without marking the omission (sc_fergusson_2006b, p. 475); cite the wording from this page.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record): the journal's combined 7-page file of the three commentaries and the reply, Addiction 101(4): 470–476, read as PDFs/Cannabis/Fergusson_2006_ReplyToComments.pdf (the copy saved as Hall_2006_CommentFergusson.pdf and the two other copies have identical text and differ only in embedded title metadata). All 7 pages read, this commentary on pp. 472–473, with the other pieces read for context; every page checked on renderings at 150 dpi; no supplement. No internal inconsistency was found in this commentary. The original study was not reread: statements about it come from its card, sc_fergusson_2006.

design_detail: Commentary (Addiction 101(4), pp. 470–472; the first of three commentaries printed together with the original authors' reply) by Denise B. Kandel (Columbia University and New York State Psychiatric Institute), Kazuo Yamaguchi (University of Chicago) and Laura Cousino Klein (Pennsylvania State University) on Fergusson, Boden & Horwood (2006), the Christchurch birth-cohort analysis of cannabis and other illicit drug use. Seven paragraphs and 11 references; no data of its own and no search or selection method. It credits the study's fixed-effects analysis, challenges its causal conclusion on three grounds (the analysis concerns how often the two drug classes were used in the same period, not first use; fixed-effects models with a lagged outcome give inconsistent estimates; the order of cannabis and other drug use within the same 12 months was assumed, not modelled), states the authors' belief that enhanced sensitivity to drug reward is probably the mechanism, and proposes animal experiments as the route to causal tests. Kandel wrote the 1975 Science paper on stages of drug use that the commentary presents as the origin of the Gateway Hypothesis; Klein wrote one of the rat studies it cites. Evidence of a published argument, not new data.
can_establish: That three researchers on stages of drug use, led by the author of the 1975 stages paper, published three specific methodological objections to the Christchurch gateway analysis (outcome, model specification, time order) and argued for rodent experiments to test causation and mechanism.
cannot_establish: Whether the objections change the original estimates (the commentary contains no analysis; the original authors' re-analysis in their reply, sc_fergusson_2006b, found the estimates robust to the second and third objections), whether cannabis use causes other illicit drug use, or anything about people from the animal studies it cites (rats and worms).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a commentary with no participants or data. The evidence it points to (reference list, p. 472): the original cohort study; two methods texts (Hsiao 2003 on panel data; Heckman 2005 on causality); a chapter on sensitization as a process behind progression through gateway drugs (Schenk 2002, in a book edited by Kandel); a volume on adolescent brain development (Dahl & Spear 2004); and animal work: cross-sensitization between THC and morphine in adult rats (Cadoni et al. 2001), a review of animal models of periadolescent substance use (Smith 2003), adolescent-onset nicotine self-administration in female rats (Levin et al. 2003), adolescent nicotine exposure and later opioid consumption in rats (Klein 2001, by the third author), and natural variation in a receptor gene that decides whether the worm C. elegans feeds in groups or alone (de Bono & Bargmann 1998).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; references chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Apart from the study commented on and Kandel's own 1975 paper, no epidemiological study is cited, although the commentary says many studies have documented the cannabis–other illicit drug link (p. 470); co-twin, common-liability and exposure-opportunity studies are not mentioned. Three of the 11 references are the authors' own work or a chapter from Kandel's edited book.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable: no data. The commentary describes the original analysis as relating frequency of cannabis use to frequency of other illicit drug use, both measured over the same last 12-month period (pp. 470–471). By the original study's card (sc_fergusson_2006), the exposure was a four-level yearly cannabis frequency score and the main outcome was any use of other illicit drugs in a year, with DSM abuse/dependence and the number of drug classes used as further outcomes.
exposure.polysubstance: The commentary's framing covers the full sequence from drugs legal for adults (tobacco, alcohol) to heroin (p. 470); in its animal argument nicotine is the example of a substance that primes for another (cocaine; opioids) (p. 471).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The commentary's general point is that an observational study can never control all confounders, because a critic can always name an unmeasured one (p. 470).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: The commentary defines the Gateway Hypothesis as a claim about onset: starting a lower-stage drug raises the likelihood of starting a higher-stage one. A causal claim must show sequencing, association, and an association that persists after control for all possible confounders (p. 470).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own and none quoted: the commentary reports no estimate from the original study or from the animal studies it cites.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a commentary.
analysis.selective_reporting: The animal studies are cited for their conclusions only, without designs, sample sizes or limits. For the third author's study (Klein 2001), whose title names adult male and female rats, only a result in males is reported (pp. 471–472).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results. The commentary sets out three objections to the original analysis and a research programme. Its descriptions of the original study can be checked against that study's card (sc_fergusson_2006), and two of its objections were tested in the original authors' reply (sc_fergusson_2006b).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The critical claims are argued and largely sound: the original outcome is use in a year, not first use (the original study's card makes the same point), and exposure and outcome cover the same years. But the commentary misdescribes the outcome as frequency of other illicit drug use and the cohort as nationally representative (p. 470; the original is one city's birth cohort). Its positive claims go beyond its evidence: the authors' belief that heightened sensitivity to drug reward probably best explains the gateway pattern, and may explain why the association weakened with age (p. 471), rests on rodent sensitization and nicotine studies and on no human data; calling a developmental rodent model possibly the most direct test so far of the Gateway Hypothesis (p. 471), with the third author's rat study as the example, treats animal findings as tests of a hypothesis about people without discussing translation. The commentary does not test whether its specification objections change the estimates; the reply's re-analysis found that they did not (sc_fergusson_2006b).

timeline.event: Kandel: stages in adolescent involvement in drug use (Science), presented in this commentary as the article from which the Gateway Hypothesis stemmed (p. 470; reference 1, p. 472).
Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: the Christchurch analysis commented on.

Hall: commentary in the same issue, judging that the original authors make a good case for a relationship that is in some sense causal and that it can no longer be regarded as an artefact of residual confounding.
MacCoun: commentary in the same issue, keeping four explanations in play and calling twin and animal evidence not yet persuasive.

Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: reply accepting as sound the objection that the analysis is not a strict test of the gateway hypothesis, and re-estimating the model with cannabis use lagged a year and without the lagged outcome (estimates similar, all P < 0.0001); it rejects the claim that animal studies are the better route to causation.

replication.where_it_stands: The onset objection was accepted as sound by the original authors; the lagged-outcome and within-year-order objections were answered with a re-analysis that changed the estimates little (sc_fergusson_2006b), though not with the instrumental-variable approach the commentary named. The project's reading list includes a later paper by the first author combining mouse experiments with human epidemiology on nicotine as a gateway drug (Kandel & Kandel 2014; not in the library and not read here). Whether animal work of this kind bears on cannabis and on human sequences of drug use is not settled by this commentary.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement is printed with the commentary (pp. 470–472).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (no declaration of interests in the commentary).
funding.affiliations_note: Kandel: Division of Epidemiology of Substance Abuse, Columbia University and New York State Psychiatric Institute; Yamaguchi: University of Chicago; Klein: Department of Biobehavioral Health, Pennsylvania State University (p. 472). Kandel wrote the 1975 paper the commentary calls the origin of the Gateway Hypothesis and edited the book containing the cited sensitization chapter; Klein wrote the rat study given as the example of what the commentary calls perhaps the most direct test to date. Recorded as context for the reading, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: For the objections: an analysis of the first use of other illicit drugs (time-to-event models with cannabis exposure dated before that first use) in a cohort with precisely dated use, and estimators suited to a lagged outcome in panel data. For the proposal: animal experiments that vary the order and age of exposure to cannabinoids and other drugs and measure later self-administration rather than proxies such as locomotion, with a stated basis for applying the results to people.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria: 11 references chosen by the authors, most of them to support the case for animal models.
The original study is examined closely (three specific objections), but the animal studies offered as the way forward are cited for their conclusions only, without designs, sizes or limits.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The framing comes from Kandel's 1975 paper, the sensitization chapter from a book Kandel edited, and the example given for what the commentary calls perhaps the most direct test to date (a developmental rodent model) is the third author's study (Klein 2001).
Beliefs are flagged as such (we believe), but the preference for sensitization as the mechanism and for rodent models as the decisive test is not supported by the evidence cited.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for the gateway sequence (pharmacological effects of the first drug versus shared liability and social or market access)
domains.note: Social factors and availability are named only as questions animal models could resolve; shared-liability, co-twin and exposure-opportunity evidence is not mentioned. Under-represented: the non-pharmacological explanations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than its worst domain (no search). The critique of the original analysis is specific and checkable, and the original authors tested two of its three objections. Cite it for: the three published objections (the outcome is not first use; a lagged outcome in fixed-effects models; time order within the same 12 months) and as a statement of the animal-model research programme proposed in 2006. Do not cite it for: the mechanism of the gateway sequence, any effect size, the representativeness of the cohort (it calls it nationally representative; the cohort is from one city), or animal findings as evidence about people.

key_findings.finding: Who and what: a commentary by Kandel, Yamaguchi and Klein (Columbia University and New York State Psychiatric Institute; University of Chicago; Pennsylvania State University), the first of three printed with the original authors' reply. It traces the Gateway Hypothesis to a 1975 Science paper proposing developmental stages in drug use (reference 1, Kandel 1975) and calls the original authors' conclusion that cannabis use causes other illicit drug use a strong conclusion.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 1st paragraph (p. 470); author block and reference list (p. 472)

key_findings.finding: Three tests for a causal claim in epidemiological studies of the Gateway Hypothesis: sequencing (one drug consistently precedes the other), association (starting the first raises the risk of starting the second) and causation (the association persists after control for all possible confounders). The authors add that full control can never be achieved, because a critic can always invoke an unmeasured factor.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: What the commentary credits: for the first time, fixed-effects models controlling for unobserved heterogeneity and for selection into cannabis use were applied to the Gateway Hypothesis as a causal hypothesis, in a sample it describes as nationally representative and followed from birth to 25 years of age. It reports the original authors' conclusion that, even with control for unmeasured factors, the association between frequency of cannabis use and frequency of other illicit drug use remained significant, and says this appears to be a particularly strong result, especially because prior other illicit drug use was also controlled.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: The original paper describes a birth cohort of children born in the Christchurch urban region, not a national sample (sc_fergusson_2006, from that paper's Method); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: First objection: the analysis is “not truly a test of the Gateway Hypothesis”, which concerns onset (starting cannabis raising the likelihood of starting other illicit drugs), whereas the analysis looks at how often the two drug classes were used at one point in time, a different question, although the commentary grants that more frequent use of a lower-stage drug raises the likelihood of starting a high-stage drug. The authors suspect frequency was used because first use happens only once, and a fixed-effects model cannot be applied to a non-repeatable event.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Second objection: the fixed-effects models (linear, logit and Poisson, estimated by conditional likelihood in Stata release 8.0) are static models that assume all covariates exogenous; including the lagged outcome (prior other illicit drug use) makes them dynamic, which yields inconsistent estimates. An instrumental-variable method handles this for the linear model and was apparently not used; no satisfactory method exists for non-linear models.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 4th paragraph (p. 470, right column, continuing on p. 471, left column)

key_findings.finding: Third objection: cannabis frequency and other illicit drug frequency were measured over the same last 12 months, so a change in other drug use could sustain cannabis use as easily as the reverse; the time order should be built into the models, not assumed from the observation that cannabis use began first.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 4th paragraph, continued (left column)

key_findings.finding: On mechanism: the commentary disputes what it describes as the original authors' dismissal of the sensitivity hypothesis as bearing on continued use rather than on starting, calling the distinction between starting and continuing ambiguous at the very early stages of use. The authors say they believe enhanced sensitivity to drug reward is probably the most relevant interpretation underlying the Gateway Hypothesis and may also account for the age-related variations in the New Zealand cohort, while granting that such a causal hypothesis is very hard to test in a human population where the appropriate confounds cannot be controlled.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 5th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: Checked against the original paper (Fergusson, Boden & Horwood 2006, Addiction 101: 556–569, pp. 565–566, Discussion, item 1 Biochemical factors): it keeps biochemical mediation as a possibility, says increased sensitivity may perhaps explain the persistence of drug use but does little to explain why people seem to choose other drugs after, but not before, cannabis, or the age-related changes, and says which explanation, if any, applies is unclear (p. 566). The word dismiss overstates that position; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Animal evidence offered: reverse-sensitization studies are rare, one exception being cross-sensitization between morphine and cannabinoids in adult rats (Cadoni et al. 2001); several laboratories found that rodents starting nicotine in adolescence show stronger and longer-lasting effects on their adult nicotine intake than rodents starting as adults (reference: Levin et al. 2003, female rats); the commentary calls a developmental rodent model “perhaps the most direct test to date of the Gateway Hypothesis” and gives as its example the third author's finding that adolescent nicotine exposure increased later opioid consumption in adult male rats (Klein 2001); and a single-gene variant decides whether the worm C. elegans feeds in groups or alone (de Bono & Bargmann 1998), offered as a sign that social factors could be modelled in animals.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 6th paragraph (p. 471, left column, continuing in the right column); reference list (p. 472)

key_findings.finding: Proposal: the authors expect the next major progress to come from epidemiologists, behavioural pharmacologists and molecular biologists working together: causation would be tested by asking whether using one drug changes the threshold for using a second and whether age matters, and mechanism by molecular, biological and pharmacological work in genetically modified flies or mice.
key_findings.locator: Kandel et al. commentary, 7th paragraph (right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary describes the Christchurch cohort as a nationally representative sample of New Zealanders; the original study is a birth cohort of children born in one urban region (Christchurch), as recorded on sc_fergusson_2006 from that paper's Method.
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstates how far the findings can be generalized; describe the sample as the original paper does.

reporting_issues.issue: It describes the original analysis as relating frequency of cannabis use to frequency of other illicit drug use; by the original study's card, the outcomes were any use of other illicit drugs in a year, DSM abuse/dependence and the number of drug classes used, with cannabis frequency (four levels) as the exposure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The substance of the objection holds (the outcome mixes starting and continuing use and is not first use), but the description of the outcome is inaccurate; the reply accepts the objection as sound without correcting it (p. 474).

reporting_issues.issue: The third author's study (Klein 2001) is reported as showing increased opioid consumption in adult male rats; its title in the reference list names adult male and female rats, and the commentary does not say what was found in females.
reporting_issues.consequence: The animal evidence may be reported selectively; the primary study would need to be read before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary says the original authors dismiss the sensitivity hypothesis as relevant to maintenance rather than initiation; the original paper (Addiction 101: 556–569, pp. 565–566, Discussion, item 1 Biochemical factors) keeps such biochemical mediation as a possibility, says increased sensitivity may perhaps explain the persistence of drug use but does little to explain why people seem to choose other drugs after, but not before, cannabis or the age-related changes, and calls unclear which explanation, if any, applies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The maintenance-versus-initiation reading has a basis in the original, but dismiss overstates its authors' position; cite the original paper (sc_fergusson_2006), not this commentary, for that position.
