design_detail: Commentary (Addiction 101(4), pp. 473–474; the third of three commentaries printed together with the original authors' reply) by Robert J. MacCoun (Goldman School of Public Policy and Boalt Hall School of Law, University of California, Berkeley) on Fergusson, Boden & Horwood (2006), the Christchurch birth-cohort analysis of cannabis and other illicit drug use. Six paragraphs and 12 references; no data and no search or selection method. It scores the competing explanations of the cannabis–hard drug link (four of an earlier seven still in play), argues that the fixed-effects analysis makes any simple common-propensity account unlikely but cannot rule out influences that change with age or interact with measured factors, judges twin and animal evidence not yet persuasive, and argues that the policy debate turns on why the link is causal rather than whether it is. Evidence of a published argument, not new data.
can_establish: That a drug-policy researcher judged in 2006 that the Christchurch analysis made any simple common-propensity account unlikely without eliminating that account, which confounding structures he said fixed-effects models cannot exclude, and why he considered the twin and animal evidence of the time unpersuasive.
cannot_establish: Whether the confounding structures he describes operate in the cohort (they are offered as conceivable, not shown), or whether permitting retail cannabis sales in the Netherlands separated the soft and hard drug markets (asserted with a citation to his own book, without data).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a commentary with no participants or data. Evidence pointed to (reference list, p. 474): his own earlier scoring of seven interpretations (MacCoun 1998); the original study; a comparison of non-experimental and experimental estimates of earnings impacts (Glazerman et al. 2003); a developmental meta-analysis of twin studies (McCartney et al. 1990); a review of gene–environment interplay in antisocial behaviour (Moffitt 2005); a common-factor model of the gateway effect (Morral et al. 2002); analyses of exposure opportunity (Wagner & Anthony 2002); two twin studies with opposite conclusions (Lynskey et al. 2003, Australian Twin Register; Tsuang et al. 1998, Vietnam Era Twin Registry); rat studies of THC–morphine cross-sensitization (Cadoni et al. 2001) and of morphine self-administration after maternal THC exposure (Vela et al. 1998); and his book with Reuter on drug policy (MacCoun & Reuter 2001).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; references chosen by the author.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the author without a search: 12 references, two of them his own (the earlier scoring of explanations and the book cited for the Dutch market claim).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable: no data were collected.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed beyond the link between cannabis and hard drugs; hard drugs are not defined.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The commentary's point is that random- and fixed-effects controls probably rule out unobserved factors with a fixed shared influence on cannabis and hard drug use, but not influences that change with age or interact with the observed variables (p. 473).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own and none quoted.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a commentary.
analysis.selective_reporting: The evidence for a causal effect (twin and animal studies) is scrutinized; the evidence for common propensity and opportunity (the Morral et al. model; Wagner & Anthony) is cited for its conclusions without scrutiny.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No results. The commentary's assessment of the original analysis (it rules out simple fixed common propensity; it cannot rule out influences that change with age or interact with measured factors) matches limits the original authors themselves state (sc_fergusson_2006).
interpretation_gap.claimed: Most claims are hedged and labelled as the author's own scoring (four candidates still in the running; complex influences conceivable), and the title's no clear winner fits the argument. The one empirical claim about policy, that the Dutch decision to allow retail cannabis sales appears to have split the soft and hard drug markets (p. 474), is supported only by his own book, with no data in the commentary; the original authors' reply says neither prohibition nor liberalization has been shown clearly to break the link between cannabis and other illicit drug use (sc_fergusson_2006b).

timeline.event: Tsuang et al. (Archives of General Psychiatry): twin study of shared and drug-specific vulnerabilities across drugs in men of the Vietnam Era Twin Registry, cited as favouring a shared vulnerability over a causal marijuana gateway (p. 473); not in the library and not read.
Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: cited for showing that a drug-use propensity that goes with more chances to use drugs can produce a gateway effect that is not causal (p. 473).
Wagner & Anthony: cited for evidence that opportunities to use drugs differ with students' characteristics and histories (p. 473).

Lynskey et al.: twins discordant for early cannabis use in the Australian Twin Register, cited as reporting a raised risk of hard drug use with marijuana use among identical twins, with influences of the environment the twins did not share not ruled out (p. 473).
Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: the Christchurch analysis commented on.

Fergusson, Boden & Horwood: reply calling the complex confounding MacCoun describes possible but not particularly plausible and preferring the simplest causal reading by Occam's razor; it attributes the conflicting twin results to limited data across ages.

replication.where_it_stands: The confounding MacCoun describes (influences that change with age or interact with measured factors) was answered in the reply by argument, not by analysis (sc_fergusson_2006b); the original paper lists the same kinds of confounders among its limitations. The direct animal test he described as unclaimed, THC exposure changing a rat's own self-administration of opiates, is outside the papers read for this card.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement is printed with the commentary (pp. 473–474).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed (no declaration of interests in the commentary).
funding.affiliations_note: Robert J. MacCoun, Goldman School of Public Policy and Boalt Hall School of Law, University of California, Berkeley (p. 474). Two of the 12 references are his own (the 1998 scoring of interpretations; the 2001 book with Reuter on drug policy). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort or panel analysis that models influences that change over time and with age explicitly (for example, year-by-year measures of access to drugs and of drug-using networks, or genetically informed models that let genetic effects change with age), tested against a common-factor model of the Morral type; and, for the policy question, comparisons of the gateway pattern before and after changes in how cannabis is sold, with the markets for other drugs measured.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria: 12 references chosen by the author.

The twin and animal studies are appraised (conflicting twin results; sniffing, gnawing, licking and locomotion as very indirect proxies for drug consumption; maternal rather than the animal's own exposure), but the common-propensity and opportunity evidence and the Dutch market claim are cited without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The framework of seven, then four, explanations and the only support for the Dutch market claim are the author's own work.
Judgments are labelled as such (my scorecard; conceivable; does appear), and the evidence for each point is named.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for the gateway association (a causal effect of cannabis versus common propensity and opportunity)
domains.note: Scrutiny falls mostly on the evidence for a causal effect; the limits of the non-causal accounts (for example, whether the assumptions of the common-factor model fit real data) are not discussed. Under-represented: critique of the common-propensity side.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than its worst domain (no search). The commentary is careful and labels its judgments, but its selection is unsystematic and partly its author's own. Cite it for: the 2006 published argument that fixed-effects models cannot exclude confounding that changes with age or interacts with measured factors; the four explanations still in play; the critique of the animal evidence (indirect proxies; maternal exposure; no direct demonstration that THC exposure increases a rat's own opiate self-administration); and the point that US and Dutch policy differed on why, not whether, the link is causal. Do not cite it for the Dutch market-separation claim as a finding.

key_findings.finding: Scorecard: less than a decade earlier there were seven competing readings of the evidence for a gateway link between cannabis and hard drugs (MacCoun 1998, his own); by his count four are left: a shared propensity to use drugs that makes the link spurious; a biochemical effect of cannabis on the propensity to use other drugs; contact with subcultures that use hard drugs; and contact with people who sell them.
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 1st paragraph (p. 473, left column, continuing in the right column); reference 1 (p. 474)

key_findings.finding: Verdict on the original analysis: it leaves the common-propensity account standing, but shows that “any simple version is unlikely to be correct”.
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 1st paragraph, end (right column)

key_findings.finding: Limits of the method: in fields where randomized experiments and econometric analyses of observational data can be compared, the observational estimates are sometimes biased by unobserved confounders (Glazerman et al. 2003, on earnings impacts). He agrees with the original authors that their random- and fixed-effects controls probably remove unobserved factors that influence cannabis use and hard drug use alike and in a constant way, but notes that they cannot remove influences that change with age or that interact with the measured variables.
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 2nd paragraph (p. 473, right column); reference 3 (p. 474)

key_findings.finding: Such complex influences are conceivable: the genetic contribution to some traits grows with age (McCartney et al. 1990); genetic and neuropsychological deficits act together with the environment in antisocial behaviour (Moffitt 2005); circumstances and opportunities can magnify the effects of personal traits and histories; a drug-use propensity that goes together with more chances to use drugs can produce a gateway effect that is not causal (Morral et al. 2002); and young people's chances to use drugs differ with their characteristics and histories (Wagner & Anthony 2002).
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 3rd paragraph (p. 473, right column); references 4–7 (p. 474)

key_findings.finding: Twin studies are not yet persuasive: Lynskey et al. (2003), in the Australian Twin Register, report a raised risk of hard drug use with marijuana use among identical twins, whereas Tsuang et al. (1998), in the Vietnam Era Twin Registry, favoured a shared vulnerability over a causal marijuana gateway. Lynskey et al. acknowledge that their model cannot exclude influences of the environment the twins did not share, which MacCoun stresses because behavioural genetics finds such unshared influences usually outweigh those of a shared environment (McCartney et al. 1990).
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 4th paragraph (p. 473, right column); references 4, 8 and 9 (p. 474)

key_findings.finding: Animal findings are ambiguous: Cadoni et al. (2001) showed cross-sensitization between THC and morphine in rats, but measured sniffing, gnawing, licking and locomotion, which MacCoun calls “exceedingly indirect proxies” for actually taking drugs; Vela et al. (1998) showed changed morphine self-administration in female rats exposed to THC around birth, that is, through the mother's consumption rather than their own. Nobody had yet shown that a rat's own THC exposure changes how much opiate it self-administers.
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 5th paragraph (p. 473, right column); references 10–11 (p. 474)

key_findings.finding: Policy: MacCoun applauds the original authors for making clear that evidence against a common-factor account does not necessarily support a neurochemical account, and argues that the legalization debate may turn “less on whether the gateway effect is spurious than on why it is causal”. US officials hold that the effect is causal and favour tough measures against marijuana possession and sales; Dutch officials, who have long held that it is causal too, allowed retail cannabis sales, which, he says, does appear to have split the markets for soft and hard drugs (MacCoun & Reuter 2001, his own book). He calls for more empirical research on whether policy and market factors moderate the gateway association.
key_findings.locator: MacCoun commentary, 6th paragraph (left column); reference 12

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 9 (Tsuang et al. 1998) gives the volume of Archives of General Psychiatry as 5, while the reply's reference list gives 55 for the same article, with the same pages (967–972).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two printings disagree; trace the article by its authors, year and pages or by a DOI, not by the volume printed here.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record): the journal's combined 7-page file of the three commentaries and the reply, Addiction 101(4): 470–476, read as PDFs/Cannabis/Fergusson_2006_ReplyToComments.pdf (the copy saved as MacCoun_2006_CommentFergusson.pdf and the two other copies have identical text and differ only in embedded title metadata). All 7 pages read, this commentary on pp. 473–474, with the other pieces read for context; every page checked on renderings at 150 dpi; no supplement. The original study was not reread: statements about it come from its card, sc_fergusson_2006.

disagreements.first_pass: Policy: MacCoun credits the original authors for showing why ruling against a common-factor account does not by itself support a neurochemical one, and argues that the legalization debate may turn “less on whether the gateway effect is spurious than on why it is causal”. US officials treat the effect as causal and call for tough enforcement against marijuana possession and sale; Dutch officials, also treating it as causal, allowed retail cannabis sales, which he says appears to have split the soft and hard drug markets (MacCoun & Reuter 2001, his own book). He calls for research on how policy and market factors change the strength of the gateway association.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 508 (round-2 check): corrected: MacCoun applauds the original authors for clarifying why evidence against a common-factor account is not necessarily evidence for a neurochemical account; US officials believe the effect is causal; Dutch officials have long contended so and permitted retail sales, which does appear to have separated the markets; he calls for more empirical work on the potential moderating effects of policy and market factors.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted with changes (p. 474, 6th paragraph, left column): the checker's points are right (not necessarily evidence for; long contended; the firmer does appear; potential moderating effects rather than effects assumed to exist), but the checker's text copies long runs of the page unquoted; the finding gives those points in the editors' words, keeping its one quotation.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 508 (round-2 check) and AI reader 522 (card adjudication)

design_detail: Mixed-methods evaluation of a national policy: Portugal's decriminalization of the use and possession of all illicit drugs on 1 July 2001. Quantitative part: an ecological before-after description of Portuguese routine statistics and surveys (mostly 1998-2008), set beside Spain and/or Italy as comparison countries where EMCDDA data allowed, with no statistical modelling, tests or intervals. Qualitative part: semi-structured interviews with 13 purposively sampled key informants in late 2007 and late 2009, used to supplement and interrogate the documents (described here, not appraised). Filed as registry (routine national monitoring data), the nearest design the schema has, as for sc_zaychik_2024, and appraised with ROBINS-I as an evaluation of a policy, as the round brief directs. Read in the Advance Access version (published online 21 July 2010; pages numbered 1-24), whose pages differ from the version of record (Br J Criminol 50(6):999-1022); anchors give 'PDF p. N', which equals the printed Advance Access page.
can_establish: How Portugal's routinely reported indicators (self-reported drug use in adult and school surveys, estimated problem and injecting drug use, administrative referrals and arrests, prison figures, seizures, prices, recorded drug-related deaths, new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs, treatment numbers) moved from the late 1990s to 2008 around the July 2001 decriminalization, and how some of them compared with Spain and Italy, as reported by national agencies.
cannot_establish: Whether decriminalization caused any of these changes: a national drug strategy that expanded treatment and harm reduction began in 1999, the indicators are national aggregates without modelling or a defined counterfactual, Spain and Italy had already made drug use an administrative offence and differ in data and definitions, several series change definition or source at the reform (arrests, prices), and there is no adult survey before 2001; nor can it show what individual people referred to the commissions experienced afterwards (no follow-up data existed).

sample.recruitment: Quantitative data are national statistics, not participants: annual national reports of the Instituto da Droga e da Toxicodependencia (IDT, the government drug agency) 1998-2008 and the internal and external evaluations it carried out or commissioned, national general-population surveys of 2001 and 2007, ESPAD school surveys 1995-2007, problem-drug-use estimates, a 2004 police evaluation, Council of Europe prison statistics, a prison survey, the EMCDDA Statistical Bulletin 2009 and Spain's 2008 national report (PDF pp. 5, 8-17). Interviews: 13 key informants sampled purposively (the head of the IDT, IDT staff in research and in overseeing the commissions, representatives of non-governmental AIDS organizations and of organizations of people who use drugs, politicians of left and right, academics and EMCDDA representatives; a former police officer and an overseer of commission implementation; no member of the criminal justice system was willing or able to take part), 45-90 minutes, in English or Portuguese with a translator (PDF p. 5). IDT and EMCDDA staff assisted with recruitment and with interpretation of the results (Acknowledgements, PDF p. 20).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No stated criteria for which indicators, years or comparison data were reported; Spain and Italy were used 'subject to data availability' (PDF p. 5).
sample.demographics: Not applicable to aggregate data. People referred to the commissions: 94% male; 47% aged 16-24 and 31% aged 25-34 (PDF p. 6).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Data gaps named in the paper: no adult survey before 2001; drug-related crime not routinely collected; no data on later offending or drug use of people referred to the commissions; Spain's and Italy's survey figures lack heroin and any-drug prevalence; Italy's cocaine seizure data missing 1999-2004; no Spanish or Italian prison data (PDF pp. 7-9, 12-13).
sample.selection_effects: Indicators, years and comparators chosen by the authors without a stated protocol. The interviewees were purposively sampled, recruited partly with the help of the agency that ran the policy and produced most of the data; no serving police or criminal justice representative took part, and the authors say the sample did not reach data saturation (PDF pp. 5-6, 20).

exposure.measurement: The exposure is the policy. Under Law 30/2000, from 1 July 2001 acquisition, possession and use of any illicit drug for personal use, up to a legal threshold of ten days' supply, became an administrative instead of a criminal offence (previously punishable by up to one year in prison, with criminal conviction the norm); possession for supply stayed criminal. Police refer people to Commissions for the Dissuasion of Drug Addiction (CDTs), panels of three, supported by IDT staff, that judge whether a person is dependent and can recommend treatment or impose sanctions such as fines, community service or bans. The reform sat within Portugal's first national drug strategy, rolled out with expanded resources from May 1999 (prevention, harm reduction, treatment, social reintegration, supply reduction) (PDF pp. 3-5). Implementation varied: at times between 2005 and 2008 up to 38% of the commissions, including Lisbon's, were not operating (PDF p. 6).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. The legal threshold of ten days' supply is defined per drug in gram amounts listed in the paper (PDF p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable to a policy exposure. Indicators are reported drug by drug where the sources allow (survey prevalence, seizures, prices, share of deaths with opiates as the main substance).

comparison.controls: Portugal before and after July 2001, with no counterfactual Portugal, set beside Spain and/or Italy for some indicators (past-year prevalence 2001 and 2007, problem-drug-use estimates, school surveys for Italy, arrests and prices for Spain, seizures, deaths), chosen as neighbours in the same region. Italy (1990) and Spain (1992) had already introduced administrative sanctions for drug use and made no radical changes in the period (PDF p. 5).
comparison.matching: None. No adjustment, modelling or test of pre-reform trends; the comparison countries differ in size, survey methods and death definitions, which the paper does not discuss.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Concurrent changes in Portugal are named but not separated from decriminalization: the 1999 strategy's expansion of treatment and harm reduction, and the growth of low-threshold opiate substitution (whose roll-out footnote 14 dates to 1990); an ageing population of people who use heroin; commission staffing gaps; economic conditions (PDF pp. 6, 17-18). There is no adult survey before 2001, and the paper does not say whether the 2001 survey was fielded before or after July 2001 (PDF p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: National general-population surveys (lifetime and past-12-month use, ages 15-64; Tables 1-2); ESPAD school survey (lifetime use, ages 15-16; Figure 1); multiplier-method estimates of problem and injecting drug use per 1,000 aged 15-64 (Italy: multivariate indicator method); commission case statistics; police arrest statistics (Figures 2-3); a 2004 police evaluation of drug-linked crime; prison statistics and a prison survey; seizure amounts (Figures 4-6); average retail prices (Tables 5-6); recorded drug-related deaths (Figure 7); new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs; treatment numbers and ages of first-time clients; key-informant interviews.
outcomes.validity_norms: Most indicators are not defined. Drug-related deaths are not defined; the paper notes they depend on recording practice, and toxicological autopsies rose from 1,166 in 2002 to 2,805 in 2008 (PDF p. 16). After 1 July 2001 price data come from self-reports of traffickers and trafficker-consumers instead of street-level police data (footnote 13, PDF p. 16). Survey methods, sample sizes and response rates are not described.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Impact' is read as the direction of a national trend after 2001 and its similarity to or difference from Spain and Italy; 'net-widening' as the number of people in formal contact with police for drug offences; 'burden on the criminal justice system' as arrests, the share of drug-related offenders in prison and prison density.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: about 20 indicators are described and none is tested statistically.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to routine statistics; the interviews were conducted and interpreted by the authors with help from IDT and EMCDDA staff.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect estimates, intervals or tests; changes are given as raw figures, percentage-point differences or percentage changes. Editors' calculations from the printed figures: adult lifetime use of any illicit drug +4.4 points (+58% relative) from Table 1's 7.6% to 12.0%, or +4.2 points (+54%) from the text's 7.8%; past-year use +0.3 points (+9%, 3.4% to 3.7%); estimated injecting drug use -43% (3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000, 2000 to 2005); new HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs -71% (907 to 267) and AIDS cases -79% (506 to 108), 2000 to 2008; people in treatment +63% (23,654 to 38,532), 1998 to 2008; recorded drug-related deaths from 369 (1999) to about 152-157 a year in 2002-2004 (-57% to -59%) and about 340 in 2008 (-8% against 1999; the 2002-2008 values are editors' readings of Figure 7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; indicators, years and comparators chosen during the analysis.
analysis.selective_reporting: Baseline years differ by indicator and are sometimes peak years (2000 for arrests; 2001 for prices); lifetime-prevalence trends for Spain and Italy are asserted but not shown; Spain and Italy appear only for some indicators; no results of the interviews are reported systematically.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Around Portugal's 2001 decriminalization, self-reported drug use among adults rose modestly (lifetime 7.6% to 12.0% by Table 1, past-year 3.4% to 3.7%, 2001 to 2007); school students' lifetime use rose to 2003 and fell by 2007 to a level still above 1999 (about 12%, 18% and 14% in 1999, 2003 and 2007, editors' reading of Figure 1); estimated injecting drug use fell while the fall in total problem drug use lay within overlapping ranges; criminal drug arrests fell mainly because possession left the criminal system; the share of drug-related offenders in prison fell (44% to 21%); new HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell (907 to 267) and treatment grew (23,654 to 38,532); recorded drug-related deaths fell from 369 (1999) to about 150 a year (2002-2004), then rose to about 340 (2008) as toxicological autopsies more than doubled. Spain and Italy show some similar and some different trends.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the reform "did not lead to major increases in drug use" and that evidence indicates reductions in problematic use, drug-related harms and criminal justice overcrowding (PDF p. 1). The body is careful in places: it says it is impossible to attribute changes directly to decriminalization (PDF pp. 6, 19) and disputes the Cato report's attribution to decriminalization alone (PDF p. 18). Elsewhere it goes beyond its data: a decline in problem drug use that it calls not statistically significant (PDF p. 8) becomes strong evidence that harmful use did not increase (PDF p. 10); the Conclusion lists lower retail prices measured from 2001 (the heroin peak, just after the 2000 peaks for cocaine and hash) and across a change of data source at the reform (PDF pp. 15-16, 19); deaths are said to have fallen significantly without a test, and significant reductions in HCV and TB are asserted with no data shown (PDF p. 16). Two statements are accurate but easily misread: reduced use among adolescents at least since 2003 holds for ESPAD 2003-2007 (about 18% to 14%) but is measured from a post-reform peak, and 2007 is still above the 1999 level of about 12% (PDF pp. 10, 19); and the fall in criminal drug arrests from over 14,000 to 5,000-5,500 a year is mostly possession leaving the criminal count, which footnote 10 and the note to Figure 2 disclose (PDF pp. 10-11). A headline version (Portugal decriminalized all drugs and drug use did not rise while deaths and HIV fell) overstates on three counts: adult lifetime use did rise, the fall in recorded deaths had largely reversed by 2008 (which informants put down to more toxicological autopsies; the paper gives no autopsy numbers for the years of the earlier fall), and none of the falls can be attributed to decriminalization rather than the expansion of treatment and harm reduction that began in 1999, as the authors themselves say.

timeline.event: A government-appointed expert commission proposes decriminalizing illicit drugs for personal use and a first national drug strategy (as described, PDF p. 4).
May: the national strategy and expanded resources (prevention, harm reduction, treatment, reintegration) are rolled out, two years before decriminalization (PDF p. 4).
1 July: decriminalization under Law 30/2000 enters into force (PDF p. 4).

Internal (IDT) and external (Instituto Nacional de Administracao) evaluations; decriminalization and strategy extended (PDF p. 5). The authors' 2012 paper says these evaluations had little to say about the legislative reform.

Hughes and Stevens, Beckley Foundation briefing paper on the effects of decriminalization in Portugal; in this article the authors say the effects looked much less positive in those early years (PDF p. 19).
Greenwald, Cato Institute report; this article disputes its tendency to attribute positive changes to decriminalization alone (PDF p. 18).
This article (Advance Access, 21 July 2010).
The same authors re-examine the opposing 'resounding success' (Cato) and 'disastrous failure' (Pinto Coelho, Association for a Drug Free Portugal) accounts and add a physician-certified death series.

replication.where_it_stands: A single national natural experiment read in opposite ways by advocacy reports (Greenwald, 2009, for the Cato Institute; Pinto Coelho, 2010, for the Association for a Drug Free Portugal, as described in hughes_2012). No analysis with a modelled counterfactual was among the files. The authors' 2012 paper adds that physician-certified drug-induced deaths fell from about 76 in 2001 to about 20 in 2008, but that series starts in the reform year and does not remove the attribution problem.

funding.funder: The Beckley Foundation for some of the work; the Colonial Foundation to the Drug Policy Modelling Program (DPMP) (Funding, PDF p. 20).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Caitlin Elizabeth Hughes, Drug Policy Modelling Program, National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales (PDF p. 1); Alex Stevens's affiliation is not printed in this version (the 2012 paper gives the University of Kent). The authors had examined the reform for years (Hughes's earlier research, 2002-2006, in collaboration with the IDT; their 2007 briefing paper for the Beckley Foundation, which also funded some of this work), and IDT and EMCDDA staff assisted with recruitment and interpretation (PDF pp. 3, 5, 20). The IDT ran the policy and produced most of the data. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An interrupted-time-series or synthetic-control analysis, specified in advance, of harmonized annual indicators (physician-certified drug-induced deaths, HIV diagnoses among people who inject drugs, survey prevalence with consistent methods, treatment entries) for Portugal against a weighted set of European countries without a policy change in 2001, with the 1999 expansion of services modelled separately and with data sources that do not change at the reform.

domains.note: The national strategy that expanded treatment and harm reduction began in May 1999 and ran alongside the reform, and the roll-out of low-threshold opiate substitution, which the authors link to the fall in opiate-related deaths, is dated 1990 in footnote 14 (possibly a misprint); treatment numbers rose by about 63% from 1998 to 2008 (editors' calculation from 23,654 and 38,532), and the population of people who use heroin aged. No modelling of pre-reform trends and no adjustment; the comparison countries had already decriminalized use and are compared informally. The authors themselves say changes cannot be attributed directly to decriminalization.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Portugal is the only treated unit; Spain and Italy were chosen for geography and used where data existed, not for similar pre-reform trends; time windows differ by indicator.

The legal change is clearly dated, but it is bundled with the 1999 strategy, and what 'the reform' delivered changed over time (commissions closed, fewer treatment referrals and more punitive sanctions).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Up to 38% of commissions were not operating at times in 2005-2008 and the share of cases sanctioned fell from 75% to 48% (2003-2006), a fall the authors say has since been reversed, with all commissions but Vila Real operating again by mid-2008 (PDF p. 6); results describe the policy as implemented.
No adult survey before 2001; no follow-up of people referred; drug-related crime not routinely collected; several Spanish and Italian series missing or partial.

Several series change at the reform: possession arrests leave the criminal count in July 2001, and price data switch from street-level police data to traffickers' self-reports. Recorded deaths depend on the number of toxicological autopsies, which more than doubled 2002-2008, and are not defined; survey methods are undescribed; problem-drug-use estimates use different methods in Portugal and Italy; the agency running the policy produced most of the data.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol; indicators, baseline years (some at peaks: 2000 for arrests, 2001 for prices) and comparators were chosen by the authors; lifetime trends for Spain and Italy are asserted without data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I, because the paper evaluates the effects of a national policy without randomization (round brief). Its quantitative part is a before-after description of national series with an informal comparison to two neighbouring countries, with no modelling, and a co-intervention (the 1999 strategy and its expansion of treatment and harm reduction) that cannot be separated from the law: critical for any causal claim about decriminalization, as the authors acknowledge. The interview part (13 purposively sampled informants, recruitment helped by the agency that ran the policy, no saturation) is described, not appraised, and is citable only for informants' views. Citable for: what Portugal's routine indicators showed before and after 2001 as reported by national agencies, with their definitions and breaks; how the policy works and was implemented (commission caseloads, sanctions, staffing gaps); and the authors' own statement that changes cannot be attributed directly to decriminalization. Not citable for: decriminalization caused falls in deaths, HIV or problem drug use; drug use did not rise; prices fell because demand fell; criminal justice workload fell by the arrest figures quoted; or HCV and TB fell (asserted without data).

key_findings.finding: The policy: under Law 30/2000 (29 November 2000), from 1 July 2001 acquisition, possession and use of any illicit drug for personal use, up to ten days' supply, became an administrative offence instead of a crime punishable by up to one year in prison; possession for supply remained a crime. Police refer people to regional Commissions for the Dissuasion of Drug Addiction (panels of three, including lawyers, social workers and medical professionals) that can recommend treatment for people judged dependent or impose sanctions. The reform was part of Portugal's first national drug strategy, rolled out with expanded resources from May 1999.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph but one (begins on p. 2) and footnote 1 (p. 3); The Portuguese Decriminalization and Drug Action Plan, 3rd to 6th paragraphs and footnote 3 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The authors' own framing: the most important limitation is that there is no counterfactual Portugal; trends are compared with Spain and/or Italy (which had introduced administrative sanctions for drug use in 1990 and 1992 and made no radical change in the period) subject to data availability; and it is impossible to attribute changes directly to decriminalization, but the paper can, they say, test the hypothesis that decriminalization necessarily increases drug use and related harms.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 3rd paragraph (p. 5) and last paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Sources and interviews: IDT annual national reports 1998-2008 and the internal and external evaluations the IDT carried out or commissioned, supplemented by 13 key-informant interviews in late 2007 and late 2009 (45-90 minutes; purposive sample from government, non-governmental organizations, politics, academia and the EMCDDA; no serving criminal justice member took part); the authors say the interview sample did not reach saturation and is used to supplement and interrogate the documents.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 5) and 2nd paragraph of p. 6

key_findings.finding: Commission caseload: about 6,000 administrative processes a year since 2002 (6,543 in 2008), estimated at about 2.5% of the people who used an illicit drug in the past year (3.7% of 15-64-year-olds in 2007, about 261,968 people); 94% of those referred were male, 47% aged 16-24 and 31% aged 25-34. As fewer cases were decided, cases ending in a sanction fell from 75% (2003) to 48% (2006), a decline in decided cases that the paper, citing the IDT, links to commissions not operating (up to 38% at times in 2005-2008); the authors add that this trend has since been reversed, and by mid-2008 all commissions except Vila Real were operating again. Provisional suspension for people judged non-dependent was used in 59-68% of cases a year; provisional sanctions with treatment (for people judged dependent) fell from 31% (2002) to 18% (2008) and punitive sanctions rose from 3% to 15%; 5-6% of people were referred twice in a year, and no data were collected on prior or later offending or drug use.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 4th paragraph (the first on p. 6); Implementation of the Decriminalization, paragraphs 1-3 and 5 (pp. 6-7); footnote 5

key_findings.finding: Adult surveys (ages 15-64), 2001 and 2007: lifetime use of any illicit drug 7.6% and 12.0% in Table 1 (the text gives 7.8% for 2001); hashish 7.6 and 11.7; cocaine 0.9 and 1.9; ecstasy 0.7 and 1.3; amphetamines 0.5 and 0.9; heroin 0.7 and 1.1. Past-12-month use: any illicit drug 3.4% and 3.7%; hashish 3.3 and 3.6; cocaine 0.3 and 0.6; ecstasy 0.4 and 0.4; amphetamines 0.1 and 0.2; heroin 0.2 and 0.3. Increases were seen in all age groups above 19; there was no general-population survey before 2001.
key_findings.locator: p. 3, last paragraph; Trends Associated with the Decriminalization, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 8); Tables 1 and 2 (p. 9)
key_findings.note: Text (7.8%) and Table 1 (7.6%) disagree for 2001; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Comparison countries, past-12-month use 2001 and 2007 (EMCDDA data; heroin and any-drug figures not reported): Spain hashish 9.7% and 10.1%, cocaine 2.6 and 3.1, ecstasy 1.9 and 1.2, amphetamines 1.2 and 0.9; Italy hashish 6.2 and 14.6, cocaine 1.1 and 2.2, ecstasy 0.2 and 0.6, amphetamines 0.1 and 0.4. The authors say Portuguese trends largely mimicked these and that this congruity gives little evidence that the increases were directly attributable to decriminalization.
key_findings.locator: Trends Associated with the Decriminalization, 4th paragraph (p. 8); Tables 3 and 4 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: School students aged 15-16 (ESPAD): the authors write that reported lifetime use of most drugs rose in the lead-up to and just after decriminalization and then declined, very similar to Italy and the EU, the main differences being that the 2003-07 decline in reported use of any illicit drug appears more pronounced in Portugal and the decline in reported cannabis use appears less pronounced; ESPAD did not collect last-year use. Editors' reading of Figure 1 at 300 dpi (bars end at whole percentages): Portugal any illicit drug 8, 12, 18 and 14% in 1995, 1999, 2003 and 2007; cannabis 7, 9, 15 and 13%; ecstasy 1, 2, 4 and 2%; Italy any illicit drug 21, 26, 28 and 25%; EU 13, 18, 22 and 21%.
key_findings.locator: Trends Associated with the Decriminalization, 5th paragraph and footnote 7 (p. 8); Figure 1 (p. 10)
key_findings.note: Figure values are approximate readings (pixel measurement against the gridlines), not printed numbers. The 2007 Portuguese value (about 14%) is above the 1999 value (about 12%).

key_findings.finding: Problem drug use (multiplier method based on numbers in treatment): 7.6 per 1,000 aged 15-64 in 2000 and 6.8 in 2005, with overlapping ranges (6.8-8.5 and 6.2-7.4) that the authors say make the decline not statistically significant; injecting drug use 3.5 and 2.0 per 1,000 (ranges 2.3-4.6 and 1.8-2.2). In Italy the estimate rose from 6.0 to 8.6 per 1,000 between 2001 and 2007 (multivariate indicator method); in Spain the overall number may have risen with problem cocaine use. The authors call Portugal's decline in problem drug use strong evidence that decriminalization did not increase the most harmful forms of use.
key_findings.locator: Trends Associated with the Decriminalization, 6th-7th paragraphs (p. 8), continued on p. 9; summary paragraph (p. 10); footnote 9

key_findings.finding: Arrests: criminal drug arrests fell from over 14,000 people in 2000 to an average of 5,000-5,500 a year, but arrests before July 2001 include simple possession and later ones do not (footnote 10); people detected for administrative use or possession offences stayed at about 6,000 a year, which the authors read as no net-widening; in Spain detections, mostly administrative consumer offences, rose steeply from 1998. Editors' reading of Figures 2 and 3 at 300 dpi (approximate): in Portugal, arrests for trafficking and trafficking-consumption about 4,500 (1998), 5,000 (1999) and 6,300 (2000) against about 5,200-5,600 a year in 2001-2008; all police contacts for drug offences, criminal plus administrative, about 11,400, 13,000 and 14,300 in 1998-2000 against about 10,500-12,000 a year in 2001-2008; in Spain, detections about 80,000 in 1998 and 260,000 in 2007.
key_findings.locator: Burden on the criminal justice system, 1st-3rd paragraphs (pp. 10-11); Figure 2 (p. 11); footnote 10; Figure 3 (p. 12)
key_findings.note: Figure values are approximate readings of stacked bars; the comparison of 14,000 with 5,000-5,500 mixes categories (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Drug-linked crime: a 2004 police evaluation found crimes strongly linked to drugs (theft, robberies, public assaults, some fraud) up 9% between 1995-99 and 2000-04, with street robberies up 66%, theft from motor vehicles 30% and theft of motor vehicles 15%, while robberies of post offices fell 60% and thefts from homes and businesses 8% and 10%; the police did not attribute these changes to decriminalization, and such data were not routinely collected afterwards or in Spain and Italy.
key_findings.locator: Burden on the criminal justice system, 4th paragraph (p. 11, continued on p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Prisons: the share of prisoners whose offences were drug-related (committed under the influence of drugs or to fund drug use) fell from 44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008; prison density fell from 119 to 101.5 prisoners per 100 places (2001 to 2005); a prison survey found heroin use before prison down from 44% to 30% and in prison from 27% to 13% between 2001 and 2007, with less injecting and less HIV among prisoners; Spanish and Italian trends are not known.
key_findings.locator: Burden on the criminal justice system, last paragraph (p. 12, continued on p. 13)

key_findings.finding: Seizures: the number of seizures changed little from 1997 to 2008 except heroin (down from a 1999 peak to a steady level by 2004); quantities seized rose by 499% between 1995-99 and 2000-04 (cocaine 116%, hashish 134%, heroin 219%, ecstasy 1,526%), in spikes of different drugs in different years rather than steady growth, which the authors read as more law enforcement rather than domestic market growth, unlike Spain's near-linear growth in cocaine and hashish seizures.
key_findings.locator: Drug seizures and prices, paragraphs 1-4 (p. 13); Figures 4 and 5 (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Prices (Table 5, euros): heroin per gram 38.50 (1998), 31.33 (1999), 49.72 (2000), 50.27 (2001) and 33.25 (2008); cocaine per gram 45.63, 40.37, 60.31, 53.51 and 45.56; hash per gram 1.78, 1.09, 4.13, 4.06 and 3.28; ecstasy per tablet 11.70, 6.70, 5.98, 6.86 and 2.80. Since 1 July 2001 the criminal police no longer collect street-level prices, and price information is based on self-reports of traffickers and trafficker-consumers (footnote 13). Most Spanish prices were stable (heroin 63.96 and 62.69, cocaine 59.70 and 60.75 euros per gram, 2001 and 2007), the exception being hash (3.92 to 4.52). The authors write that the Portuguese falls may point to increased supply and to reduced demand and that, with school surveys giving some indication of reduced use of cannabis, cocaine and ecstasy, the price data suggest the reduced use reflected reduced demand rather than successful seizures; purity is unknown and more detailed studies would be needed.
key_findings.locator: Drug seizures and prices, 6th-8th paragraphs (p. 15); Tables 5 and 6 and footnote 13 (p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Deaths: drug-related deaths recorded in Portugal peaked at 369 in 1999 (57% more than in 1997) and, in the authors' words, reduced significantly between 1999 and 2002 (no test given); all three countries declined after their peaks (Italy 1996, Portugal and Spain 1999), more in Portugal and Italy than in Spain; Portugal alone rose again, which local informants attributed to more toxicological autopsies (1,166 in 2002, 2,805 in 2008); the share of deaths with opiates as the main substance fell from 95% (1999) to 59% (2008; 55% in 2007). The paper does not define a drug-related death. Editors' reading of Figure 7 at 300 dpi (approximate): Portugal about 234 (1997), 338 (1998), 370 (1999), 319 (2000), 280 (2001), 155 (2002), 152 (2003), 157 (2004), 219 (2005), 219 (2006), 314 (2007) and 340 (2008).
key_findings.locator: p. 3, last paragraph; Drug-related health harms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 16); Figure 7 (p. 17)
key_findings.note: The figure readings match the toxicology-positive (INML) series that the authors' 2012 paper plots and defines (hughes_2012, Figure 4): deaths with a positive post-mortem toxicological test for illicit drugs, not deaths judged to be caused by drugs.

key_findings.finding: Treatment and infections: people in drug treatment rose from 23,654 (1998) to 38,532 (2008); first-time treatment clients over 34 rose from 23% (2000) to 46% (2008). New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008) and AIDS cases from 506 to 108, a trend that, the paper says, has been attributed primarily to the expansion of harm-reduction services (it does not say by whom); in Spain drug-related AIDS cases fell from 5,085 (1994) to 639 (2007) after opiate substitution treatment was scaled up. The authors say falls in opiate-related deaths are likely to reflect the large increase in treatment, particularly low-threshold opiate substitution, and not simply decriminalization.
key_findings.locator: Drug-related health harms, 3rd-5th paragraphs (p. 17, continued on p. 18); footnote 14
key_findings.note: Footnote 14 dates the roll-out of low-threshold opiate substitution programmes to 1990, possibly a misprint (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Interviews (informants' views): informants generally agreed there had been small to moderate increases in reported adult drug use but disagreed on whether these were real, significant and attributable to the reform; most thought decriminalization reduced the burden on the criminal justice system and let police refocus on trafficking; they credited the commissions with earlier and broader intervention and more referrals to treatment and harm reduction, but said the reform's full potential had not been reached because of staffing gaps and a lack of interventions for young people who use drugs occasionally.
key_findings.locator: Implementation of the Decriminalization, 4th paragraph (p. 7); Trends, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Burden on the criminal justice system, 1st paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: The authors dispute Greenwald's (2009) tendency to attribute Portugal's positive changes to decriminalization alone, naming expanded treatment services and an ageing population of people who use heroin. The Conclusion lists seven changes that the indicators and interviews suggest occurred since July 2001 (small increases in reported adult use; reduced use among people with problem drug use and adolescents, at least since 2003; reduced burden on the criminal justice system; more treatment uptake; fewer opiate-related deaths and infections; more drugs seized; lower retail prices); says some trends clearly reflect regional shifts (such as the rise in adult use) or the expansion of services, while some effects appear specific to Portugal (the falls in problem drug use and in the criminal justice burden, unlike Spain and Italy, and no sign of mass market expansion); states that it is impossible to say any of them was the direct result of decriminalization; and says the evidence disconfirms the hypothesis that decriminalization necessarily increases the most harmful forms of drug use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 18); Conclusion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 19; the 3rd continues on p. 20) and 4th paragraph (p. 20)
key_findings.note: The contrast with Spain and Italy for the criminal justice burden rests on Spanish police data alone (Figure 3); the paper shows no Italian criminal justice data and says Spanish and Italian prison trends are not known (PDF pp. 11-13).

reporting_issues.issue: Lifetime use of any illicit drug in 2001 is 7.8% in the text but 7.6% in Table 1, where it equals the hashish row.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two is a transcription error; the authors' later paper plots about 7.8% for 2001 (hughes_2012, Figure 2; editors' reading). Cite 7.8% with the discrepancy noted, or both.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites Tables 3 and 4 for increases in lifetime prevalence of hashish, amphetamines and cocaine in all three countries, but those tables give only past-12-month prevalence for Spain and Italy, and in Spain past-year amphetamine (1.2% to 0.9%) and ecstasy (1.9% to 1.2%) use fell; Italy's past-year hashish rise (+8.4 points) dwarfs Portugal's (+0.3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that Portuguese trends largely mimicked Spain and Italy is not supported for lifetime use by any data shown, and for past-year use only in direction for hashish and cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives heroin and ecstasy prices with a dollar sign (50.27 and 33.25 per gram; 6.86 and 2.80 per tablet), while Table 5, from which they come, is in euros.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the values in euros from Table 5.

reporting_issues.issue: The price comparison starts in 2001, the peak year for heroin and close to the 2000 peak for cocaine and hash, and crosses a change of data source: from 1 July 2001 price information is based on self-reports of traffickers and trafficker-consumers instead of street-level police data (footnote 13). Against 1998-1999, 2008 prices were similar for heroin (38.50 and 31.33 against 33.25) and cocaine (45.63 and 40.37 against 45.56) and higher for hash (1.78 and 1.09 against 3.28).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Conclusion's 'reductions in the retail prices of drugs' and the inference of reduced demand depend on the baseline year and on a measurement break at the reform; only ecstasy fell steadily from 1998.

reporting_issues.issue: The fall in criminal drug arrests from over 14,000 (2000) to 5,000-5,500 a year compares all drug arrests, including simple possession, with criminal arrests after possession became administrative in July 2001 (footnote 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: Most of the fall is reclassification. Editors' reading of Figure 2 (approximate): trafficking-type arrests about 5,200-5,600 a year after 2001 against about 4,500-6,300 in 1998-2000, and all police contacts for drug offences about 10,500-12,000 a year after 2001 against about 11,400-14,300 before.

reporting_issues.issue: Quantities seized are said, from a 2004 police evaluation, to have risen 499% overall between 1995-99 and 2000-04, more than any single drug except ecstasy (1,526%); the paper does not give the evaluation's units, but its own Figure 4 counts ecstasy in pills and hashish and cocaine in kilograms, and how the overall figure combines drugs is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The overall 499% should not be cited; the drug-specific figures can be.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the analysis draws on independent evaluations, while the Methods describe the IDT's annual reports and the internal and external evaluations the IDT carried out or commissioned.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base is largely the policy agency's own reporting; the authors' 2012 paper adds that the available evaluations were part of wider strategy reviews with little to say about the legislative reform (hughes_2012, section on the evidence base).

reporting_issues.issue: The problem-drug-use comparison sets Portugal's estimates for 2000 and 2005 (multiplier method based on treatment numbers) against Italy's for 2001 and 2007 (multivariate indicator method).
reporting_issues.consequence: Different methods and periods; the contrast between Portugal and Italy is suggestive only. A treatment-based multiplier estimate also depends on how treatment numbers changed, and treatment expanded strongly over this period.

reporting_issues.issue: Drug-related deaths are not defined, the number of toxicological autopsies is given only for 2002 and 2008, and the Spanish and Italian counts come from a different source (EMCDDA) with national definitions that are not discussed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the sharp fall from 1999 to 2002 also reflects recording practice cannot be judged from the paper, and levels across countries are not comparable.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2001 adult survey serves as the baseline although decriminalization took effect on 1 July 2001; the paper does not say when in 2001 it was fielded, and there was no earlier survey.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2001-2007 adult changes are not a clean before-after contrast.

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote 14 dates the roll-out of low-threshold opiate substitution programmes, which the authors link to the fall in opiate-related deaths, to 1990, nine years before the May 1999 strategy that the paper otherwise credits with expanding treatment; the paper gives no other date, and 1990 may be a misprint.
reporting_issues.consequence: The timing of this co-intervention cannot be settled from the paper. On either date it precedes the July 2001 reform, so the confounding judgment is unchanged, but low-threshold substitution should not be described as part of the 1999 strategy on this paper's evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says there have been significant reductions in mortality, HIV, HCV and TB, and the Conclusion lists fewer infectious diseases, but the paper gives figures only for new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs; no HCV or TB data are shown and no test is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Reductions in HCV and TB are asserted, not shown; cite only the HIV and AIDS figures from this paper.

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded) [confounding note: The national strategy that expanded treatment, harm reduction and low-threshold substitution began in May 1999 and ran alongside the reform; treatment numbers rose by about 63% from 1998 to 2008 (editors' calculation from 23,654 and 38,532), and the population of people who use heroin aged.
