The authors themselves say changes cannot be attributed directly to decriminalization.] [unmeasured_premorbid: Concurrent changes in Portugal are named but not separated from decriminalization: the 1999 strategy's expansion of treatment and harm reduction, including low-threshold opiate substitution; an ageing population of people who use heroin; commission staffing gaps; economic conditions (PDF pp. 6, 17-18). There is no adult survey before 2001, and the paper does not say whether the 2001 survey was fielded before or after July 2001 (PDF p. 8).]
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 546 (round-2 check): footnote 14 dates the roll-out of low-threshold substitution programmes to 1990, before the 1999 strategy (possibly a misprint); relevant to the confounding timeline.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading PDF p. 17, footnote 14 (rendered): it says the 1990 roll-out. It matters because the card had tied low-threshold substitution to the 1999 strategy, which the paper does not say. New reporting issue; confounding note and unmeasured_premorbid reworded; judgment (critical) unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded) [reasoning ended: ...prices fell because demand fell; or criminal justice workload fell by the arrest figures quoted.]
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 546 (round-2 check): the text asserts significant reductions in HCV and TB (p. 16) but shows no HCV or TB data.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading PDF p. 16, Drug-related health harms, 1st paragraph (rendered), and searching the whole text: HCV and TB appear only there and on p. 3 (the 1990s rise); no figures. It matters for claims about infections. New reporting issue; added to the not-citable list and to the interpretation gap (entry below).

disagreements.first_pass: No effect estimates, intervals or tests; changes are given as raw figures, percentage-point differences or percentage changes. Editors' calculations from the printed figures: adult lifetime use of any illicit drug +4.4 points (+58% relative, 7.6% to 12.0% in Table 1); past-year use +0.3 points (+9%, 3.4% to 3.7%); estimated injecting drug use -43% (3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000, 2000 to 2005); new HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs -71% (907 to 267) and AIDS cases -79% (506 to 108), 2000 to 2008; people in treatment +63% (23,654 to 38,532), 1998 to 2008; recorded drug-related deaths from 369 (1999) to about 152-157 a year in 2002-2004 (-57% to -59%) and about 340 in 2008 (-8% against 1999; the 2002-2008 values are editors' readings of Figure 7).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 546 (round-2 check): effect_sizes computes adult lifetime use as +58% from Table 1's 7.6%; with the text's 7.8%, which reporting issue 0 advises citing, it is +54%.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted with changes (PDF pp. 3, 9): both baselines are printed, so both calculations are given: +4.4 points (+58%) from 7.6% and +4.2 points (+54%) from 7.8% (editors' calculation, 12.0/7.8 = 1.54).

disagreements.first_pass: Most indicators are not defined. Drug-related deaths are not defined; the paper notes they depend on recording practice, and toxicological autopsies rose from 1,166 in 2002 to 2,805 in 2008 (PDF p. 16). After 1 July 2001 price data come from self-reports of people arrested for trafficking instead of street-level police data (footnote 13, PDF p. 16). Survey methods, sample sizes and response rates are not described.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 546 (round-2 check): validity_norms repeats 'self-reports of people arrested for trafficking'; footnote 13 says only trafficker and trafficker-consumer self-reports.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after reading PDF p. 16, footnote 13 (rendered): no mention of arrest. Reworded.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract says the reform "did not lead to major increases in drug use" and that evidence indicates reductions in problematic use, drug-related harms and criminal justice overcrowding (PDF p. 1). The body is careful in places: it says it is impossible to attribute changes directly to decriminalization (PDF pp. 6, 19) and disputes the Cato report's attribution to decriminalization alone (PDF p. 18). Elsewhere it goes beyond its data: a decline in problem drug use that it calls not statistically significant (PDF p. 8) becomes "strong evidence" that harmful use did not increase (PDF p. 10); the Conclusion lists reduced drug use among adolescents since 2003 although the 2007 level remains above 1999, and lower retail prices measured from a 2001 price peak and across a change of data source at the reform (PDF pp. 15-16, 19); arrests are said to have fallen from over 14,000 to 5,000-5,500 a year, comparing all drug arrests including possession with criminal arrests excluding it (PDF pp. 10-11); deaths are said to have fallen significantly without a test (PDF p. 16). A headline version ('Portugal decriminalized all drugs and drug use did not rise while deaths and HIV fell') overstates on three counts: adult lifetime use did rise, the fall in recorded deaths had largely reversed by 2008 (which informants put down to more toxicological autopsies; the paper gives no autopsy numbers for the years of the earlier fall), and none of the falls can be attributed to decriminalization rather than the expansion of treatment and harm reduction that began in 1999, as the authors themselves say.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 546 (round-2 check): substantial agreed (strong evidence from a non-significant fall; a significant fall in deaths without a test; prices across a source break; the abstract's wording). Two listed overreaches are weak: reduced use among adolescents at least since 2003 matches ESPAD (18% to 14%), and footnote 10 discloses the arrest reclassification.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted with changes (PDF pp. 10-11, 19; Figure 1 and Figure 2 rendered): both statements are accurate as worded, so they move from the list of statements beyond the data to a list of accurate but easily misread statements (adolescent decline measured from a post-reform peak, 2007 above 1999; arrest fall disclosed as reclassification in footnote 10 and the Figure 2 note). HCV and TB assertion added (p. 16). Price clause made precise. Gap stays substantial.

design_detail: Harm Reduction Digest 44 in Drug and Alcohol Review, by Caitlin Elizabeth Hughes and Alex Stevens, with an introduction by the digest's co-editor Simon Lenton. A critical comparison of the two most divergent published accounts of Portugal's 2001 decriminalization, the Cato Institute report by Glenn Greenwald (2009, 'resounding success') and the reports of Manuel Pinto Coelho for the Associacao para uma Portugal Livre de Drogas (APLD, Association for a Drug Free Portugal, 2010, 'disastrous failure'), on three contested claims (drug use, drug-related deaths, Portugal compared with the rest of Europe), set against published national and international data that the authors re-present in three tables and five figures. No systematic search and no new data collection: evidence of an argument, with second-hand data. The authors are participants in the debate they examine (their 2007 Beckley Foundation report and their 2010 article, card sc_hughes_2010). Received 15 March 2011, accepted 18 September 2011. An erratum (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727, doi 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x) is on file and was read with the paper: it corrects only the statement that a US Office of National Drug Control Policy document could not be found on that office's website (p. 111).
can_establish: What each of the two advocacy accounts claimed about drug use, deaths and Portugal's place in Europe, which datasets and years each used or left out, and what the published Portuguese series showed when set side by side up to about 2008-2009, as compiled by two researchers who had published their own account.
cannot_establish: Whether decriminalization caused any change (no counterfactual analysis; the authors themselves find expanded services a more plausible explanation for falling deaths), whether the data compiled are complete (no systematic search), or whether any change was statistically significant (no tests).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (critical review). Data re-presented: four Portuguese school surveys (ESPAD 1995-2007, students aged 16; ECATD, ages 13-19; HBSC, grades 6, 8 and 10, 1998-2006; INME, grades 7-12, 2001 and 2006; Table 2, p. 104), the national general-population surveys of 2001 and 2007 (ages 15-64; Figures 2-3), two death series 2000-2008 (Figure 4), World Drug Report 2010 prevalence for 13 countries (Table 3), EMCDDA annual reports, and Factiva media counts 2001-2010 (Figure 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No stated criteria. The two accounts were chosen as the most prominent and divergent; data were chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Data selected without a stated search by two authors who are parties to the debate; the comparison of Portugal with Spain and Italy rests on their own 2010 article. The Cato and APLD reports are represented through the authors' summaries and short quotations; neither report was read for this card.

exposure.measurement: The policy (from July 2001, decriminalization of use, acquisition and possession of all illicit drugs for personal use, with sales still criminal) and the published accounts of its effects.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable; survey and death data are discussed by drug where the sources allow.

comparison.controls: The two advocacy accounts compared with each other and with the published data; for Europe, Portugal's place in cross-sectional rankings and, for trends, Spain and Italy as reported in the authors' 2010 article.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The authors note that many national factors besides policy (disposable income, leisure time, religiosity and other cultural norms; availability of treatment and harm reduction; health care and welfare) shape prevalence and harms (p. 110).

outcomes.instruments: Survey prevalence of drug use (lifetime, last 12 months, last 30 days); two death series: the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (INML) count of deaths with a positive post-mortem toxicological test for illicit substances, and the National Statistics Institute (INE) count of deaths that doctors determined under ICD protocols to be due to drugs; homicide statistics as reported by UNODC; HIV among people who inject drugs; cross-national prevalence rankings; media mentions.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors argue, citing UNODC, WHO and EMCDDA guidance, that recent and current use are better indicators of change in adults than lifetime use, and that physician-certified deaths are a better indicator of drug-attributable death than toxicology-positive deaths (pp. 105, 107). Survey methods and sample sizes are not described.
outcomes.operationalization: No formal criteria for 'success' or 'failure'; each claim is judged against the data the authors regard as more valid and against trends rather than rankings.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None estimated; percentage changes computed from published series, without intervals or tests. Statements about statistical significance (for example that most increases in adult lifetime use were unlikely to be significant) are given without tests (p. 105).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable: a critical review.
analysis.selective_reporting: The authors charge both accounts with selecting indicators, years and datasets. Their own re-presentation is broader but also partial: no data are shown for the 15-19 age group whose decline they say Pinto Coelho ignored, the INE death series starts only in 2001, and Spain and Italy are taken from their own article.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Each account rested on a partial dataset: Greenwald's fall in school students' use came from a survey first run in the reform year (INME 2001 and 2006), Pinto Coelho's rise from a survey spanning 1998-2002 (HBSC). The longest series (ESPAD) shows students' lifetime cannabis use rising 60% around the reform and falling slightly by 2007. Adults' lifetime use rose between 2001 and 2007 while past-year and past-month use changed little (about 3.4% to 3.7% and 2.5% to 2.5%, editors' reading of Figure 2), falling at ages 15-24 and rising at 25-34. Toxicology-positive deaths (INML) rose from 216 in 2006 to 314 in 2007 but stayed below 1999; physician-certified drug-induced deaths (INE) fell from about 76 in 2001 to about 9 in 2005 and were about 20 in 2008 (editors' reading of Figure 4). Pinto Coelho's 40% rise in drug-related homicides referred to all homicides; Greenwald's claim that Portugal had the EU's lowest lifetime cannabis prevalence was wrong; in 2008 Portugal had Europe's third-highest HIV rate among people who inject drugs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusion says the reform warrants neither the praise nor the condemnation it received and that its implications are nuanced "albeit largely positive" (p. 111); the Discussion finds clear proof of misuse of evidence by both accounts (p. 109); the authors write that more evidence-informed conclusions give ample indication of a successful reform (p. 111), that there was an overall positive net benefit for the Portuguese community (p. 105), and that a broader examination of EMCDDA reports and data shows post-reform Portugal performing, over time, similarly to or slightly better than most European countries (p. 109). They are explicit that falls in deaths are not attributable solely to the reform and that expanded services are the more plausible explanation (p. 108). Gaps: success, net benefit and better-than-Europe performance are judgments not tested against a counterfactual, and the European comparison rests on data that are not shown (p. 109). Three restatements of the authors' own 2010 article lean the same way: Portugal as the only one of three countries with declines in problem drug use drops that article's caveat that the decline was not statistically significant (p. 109); similar increases in lifetime and recent use in all three countries are not what its tables show (past-year data only for Spain and Italy, with Italy's cannabis rise far larger) (p. 109); and a reported fall in drug-related crime is not in it, since it reported a 9% rise in crimes strongly linked to drugs between 1995-99 and 2000-04 and a fall only in the share of prisoners held for drug-related offences (p. 108; hughes_2010, PDF pp. 11-13). The INE series begins in the reform year, so it cannot show a change from before to after the reform. A headline version (the data show decriminalization worked) would overstate a paper whose main finding, that both sides misused the data, is well supported by what it shows.

timeline.event: RAND report, 'Guidelines for implementing and evaluating the Portuguese drug policy' (Table 1, p. 102, as listed).
National evaluations by INA and IDT released (Table 1, p. 102).
Beckley Foundation report by Hughes and Stevens, 'The effects of decriminalization of drug use in Portugal' (Table 1, p. 102).

Cato Institute report by Glenn Greenwald launched on 2 April, with wide media coverage in April (Time, Scientific American, The Economist); the 2009 World Drug Report says the reform appeared to be working (Table 1, p. 102).
Hughes and Stevens, British Journal of Criminology article (July 2010).

Pinto Coelho's main report for the APLD, 'The resounding success of Portuguese drug policy: the power of an attractive fallacy', published on the World Federation Against Drugs website (August), after shorter pieces from September 2009; British Medical Journal commissioned piece by Portuguese officials (September) (Table 1, p. 102).
Global Commission on Drug Policy report acknowledges slight increases in overall drug use after the reform, as cited (p. 111).

July: erratum (Drug Alcohol Rev 31:727, doi 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x), read with the paper: it withdraws the statement that the ONDCP document was not on the ONDCP website and could be found only through Pinto Coelho, who had informed the journal that it is there; nothing else is corrected.

replication.where_it_stands: The most cited advocacy accounts of the Portuguese reform reached opposite conclusions from overlapping data; this re-examination by two authors who had published their own account finds selective use of evidence on both sides and argues for trends in recent use and physician-certified deaths rather than lifetime use, toxicology-positive deaths or rankings. It adds no counterfactual analysis, so the causal question remains open.

funding.funder: The Drug Policy Modelling Program (DPMP) is funded by the Colonial Foundation Trust (Funding, p. 111).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Caitlin Elizabeth Hughes, Research Fellow, Drug Policy Modelling Program, National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; Alex Stevens, Professor in Criminal Justice, School of Social Policy, Sociology and Social Research, University of Kent (p. 101). They describe themselves as two of the participants in the debate (p. 101); they wrote the 2007 Beckley Foundation report and the 2010 article, and Pinto Coelho named their accounts among those he called misleading (p. 110). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-specified comparative analysis of Portugal against a weighted set of European countries, using harmonized series that exist before and after 2001 (physician-certified drug-induced deaths, HIV among people who inject drugs, survey prevalence of recent use by age with consistent methods), with the 1999 expansion of services modelled separately from the 2001 law.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria; the two accounts are chosen as the most prominent and divergent and the data are chosen by the authors.

A strength of the paper is its appraisal of indicators (lifetime against recent use; toxicology-positive against physician-certified deaths; the scope of the homicide figure; rankings against trends). But the surveys are not appraised for method, sample size or comparability, and significance is asserted without tests.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors adjudicate a debate in which they are participants, and the comparison of Portugal with Spain and Italy rests on their own 2010 article, restated without its caveat on problem drug use and with its crime finding misstated (a 9% rise in crimes strongly linked to drugs restated as a fall; p. 108).

Causal explanations are labelled as plausible hypotheses (cocaine trafficking for homicides; services for deaths), but evaluative judgments ('successful reform', 'net benefit') are mixed with the data.

domains.domain: Balance of the two accounts and of evidence of benefit and harm
domains.note: Both accounts are criticized with specific errors on each side, and Pinto Coelho is credited where right (lifetime use rose); but the authors' own conclusion leans positive, and evidence of harm (the rise in lifetime use, Portugal's high HIV and opiate figures, the rebound in toxicology-positive deaths) gets less weight than evidence of benefit; the harm side is under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative critique (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain. The paper is valuable for setting the two most-cited advocacy accounts against the data and for explaining the indicator problems, but it has no systematic search, its authors are parties to the debate, and its comparison with Spain and Italy rests on their own article. Cite it for: what Greenwald and Pinto Coelho claimed and which datasets and years each used; the definitions of Portugal's two death series and their diverging trends; the specific errors identified (the homicide figure covered all homicides; the cannabis ranking); and survey figures as re-presented, with figure-read values marked approximate. Do not cite it as evidence that decriminalization reduced deaths, problem drug use, drug-related crime or drug use among young people, or for the statistical significance of any change.

key_findings.finding: Type and authors: Harm Reduction Digest 44 in Drug and Alcohol Review, by Caitlin Elizabeth Hughes (Research Fellow, Drug Policy Modelling Program, NDARC, University of New South Wales) and Alex Stevens (Professor in Criminal Justice, University of Kent), who describe themselves as two of the participants in the debate; received 15 March 2011, accepted 18 September 2011.
key_findings.locator: Title block; editor's introduction; Introduction, 1st paragraph; author footnote

key_findings.finding: Evidence base: only two internal and one external evaluation had been conducted, all as part of broader drug-strategy examinations and with little to say about the legislative reform; most accounts came from external stakeholders (RAND; the Beckley Foundation report written by the authors; the Cato Institute; the APLD). Greenwald, a constitutional lawyer, wrote the Cato report after a three-week visit, with interviews whose number and nature were not made public; Pinto Coelho is a Portuguese abstinence-based drug treatment provider and Chair of the APLD.
key_findings.locator: The Portuguese reform: The evidence base; The Cato report and the APLD report, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the right-column text after Table 1 continues the 1st); Table 1

key_findings.finding: The opposing claims on drug use: Greenwald cited INME school data with lifetime cannabis use falling from 10.4% to 6.6% in grades 7-9 (a 36% reduction) and from 25.6% to 18.7% in grades 10-12 (27%) between 2001 and 2006, and stressed a fall among 15-19-year-olds; for older groups he acknowledged a 'slight to mild' rise in lifetime use from 2001 to 2007, which he argued was inevitable through cohort effects. Pinto Coelho cited HBSC data showing an increase in every drug from 1998 to 2002, cannabis up 150% in his words, then a slight decrease to 2006 (for all drugs except heroin) to levels still much higher than before the reform, a 50% rise in lifetime prevalence among 20-24-year-olds between 2001 and 2007, and no drug whose lifetime prevalence among 15-64-year-olds had fallen since 2001.
key_findings.locator: Drug use: The 'resounding success' and The 'disastrous failure'

key_findings.finding: School data reconciled: four surveys exist (ESPAD, students aged 16, 1995, 1999, 2003 and 2007; ECATD, ages 13-19, 2003 and 2006 in Table 2; HBSC, grades 6, 8 and 10, 1998, 2002 and 2006; INME, grades 7-12, 2001 and 2006), and only HBSC and ESPAD were collected before and after the reform. By ESPAD, lifetime cannabis use rose 60% around the reform, not 142% as in Pinto Coelho's HBSC data; after the reform INME showed a 27-30% fall and the other datasets a 16% fall; last-30-day cannabis use fell 20-30% (INME) and 32% (HBSC). The authors read this as a moderate rise in lifetime use around the reform, mainly short-term experimental use, followed by a slight decline. Editors' reading of Figure 1 at 300 dpi (approximate): HBSC 3.8, 9.2 and 8.2% (1998, 2002, 2006); ESPAD 7.0, 9.4, 15.0 and 13.0% (1995 to 2007); INME 10.4 and 6.6% (grades 7-9) and 25.6 and 18.7% (grades 10-12).
key_findings.locator: Drug use: Accounts compared to the available evidence, 1st-3rd paragraphs (p. 103); Table 2 and Figure 1 (p. 104)
key_findings.note: The text's 27-30% and 16% falls cannot be reproduced from the values printed on p. 103 and plotted in Figure 1; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Adults (ages 15-64), 2001 and 2007: reported lifetime use rose for most age groups and substances, so Pinto Coelho was right that the Cato report was overly optimistic, but many increases were small (for example amphetamines 0.5% to 0.9%, which the authors judge unlikely to be significant, without a test); recent (last 12 months) and current (last 30 days) use changed minimally if at all, discontinuation rose, and recent and current use rose most among 25-34-year-olds (the text's maximum of 7% of any age group reporting recent use fits 2007; Figure 3 shows about 8.3% at ages 15-24 in 2001) and fell among 15-24-year-olds. Editors' reading of Figures 2 and 3 at 300 dpi (approximate): any illicit drug at ages 15-64, lifetime 7.8% and 12.0%, past year 3.4% and 3.7%, past month 2.5% and 2.5%; past-year use 8.3% and 7.0% at ages 15-24 and 4.9% and 7.0% at 25-34; past-month use 5.7% and 4.1% at 15-24 and 3.5% and 5.1% at 25-34.
key_findings.locator: Drug use, Accounts compared, 4th-6th paragraphs (p. 105); Figure 2 (p. 105); Figure 3 (p. 106)

key_findings.finding: The opposing claims on deaths: Greenwald reported a 10-fold rise in acute drug-related deaths before the reform and a fall in drug-related deaths from close to 400 in 1999 to 290 in 2006, despite more toxicological examinations, with deaths for every drug lower or constant compared with 2001; Pinto Coelho reported that deaths of people testing positive for drugs rose 45% from 216 (2006) to 314 (2007), the highest since 2001 (280), and that drug-related homicides rose 40% after July 2001.
key_findings.locator: Drug-related death: The 'resounding success' (p. 105, continued on p. 106) and The 'disastrous failure' (p. 106)

key_findings.finding: How Portugal counts drug deaths: deaths directly attributable to drug intoxication had not been reported historically, and overdose data became available only in November 2010. The main indicator, from the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (INML), counts deaths with a positive post-mortem toxicological test for illicit substances; it is the only series covering the years before and after the reform, it moves with the number of toxicological autopsies (which rose substantially from 2005 to 2009), and it shows that a drug was present, not that it caused the death. The National Statistics Institute (INE) series, backdated to 2001, counts deaths that doctors determined under ICD protocols to be due to drugs; it fell from 2001, rose slightly from 2005 to 2008/9 and stayed well below its level at decriminalization. The authors take this as support for the view that the INML rise was largely spurious, and say the decreases are not attributable solely to the reform, expanded services being a more plausible explanation, though the reform may have contributed by easing access to services. Editors' reading of Figure 4 at 300 dpi (approximate): INML 318, 280, 156, 152, 156, 219, 216, 314 and 338 (2000 to 2008); INE 76, 34, 23, 20, 9, 12, 14 and 20 (2001 to 2008).
key_findings.locator: Drug-related death: Accounts compared to the available evidence (pp. 106-108); Figure 4 (p. 107)
key_findings.note: The INML counts read from Figure 4 agree with the printed 280 (2001), 216 (2006) and 314 (2007). The INE series starts in 2001, the reform year, so it gives no comparison with the years before the reform; the INML series, which does, counts drug presence rather than cause.

key_findings.finding: Homicides: Pinto Coelho's 40% rise in drug-related homicides rested on a misattribution to the World Drug Report, whose figure covered all homicides (murder, manslaughter, euthanasia and infanticide); the 2009 report only speculated that the rise might be related to cocaine trafficking. The authors judge the claim of questionable validity and say it runs counter to the trend of reduced drug-related crime they reported earlier; their 2010 article in fact reported a 9% rise in crimes strongly linked to drugs between 1995-99 and 2000-04 and a fall in the share of prisoners held for drug-related offences, not a fall in drug-related crime.
key_findings.locator: Drug-related death: Accounts compared to the available evidence, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 108, left column)
key_findings.note: The restatement of the 2010 crime finding is incorrect (see reporting issues; hughes_2010, PDF pp. 11-13).

key_findings.finding: Europe: Greenwald's statement that Portugal had the absolute lowest lifetime cannabis prevalence in the EU (2001-2005) was wrong, since Bulgaria, Malta and Romania were lower; Pinto Coelho's statement that Portugal had eight times the European average of new HIV/AIDS cases related to injecting omitted that data were unavailable for Spain and Estonia. In 2008 Portugal had the third-highest rate of HIV among people who inject drugs in Europe (behind Spain and Latvia) and the fourth-highest incidence of new HIV cases; it has low past-year prevalence of cannabis and cocaine use but fares less well for opiates and problem drug use.
key_findings.locator: How Portugal compares to the rest of Europe: Accounts compared, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 108-109)

key_findings.finding: Past-year prevalence (% of 15-64-year-olds; World Drug Report 2010; cannabis, cocaine, opiates): Portugal 3.6, 0.6, 0.46; Spain 10.1, 3.0, 0.13; Italy 14.6, 2.2, 0.72; France 8.6, 0.6, 0.47; Netherlands 5.4, 0.6, 0.31; UK (England and Wales) 7.9, 3.0, 0.81; Australia 10.6, 1.9, 0.40; USA 12.5, 2.6, 0.58.
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Rankings against trends: the authors argue that rankings mislead because there is no direct cross-sectional link between national drug policies and prevalence of use, and that only by taking pre-reform rates, or preferably trends before and after the reform, into account can one examine how far Portugal's current position relative to Europe can be attributed to the reform; for trends they restate their 2010 article, including that Portugal was the only one of the three countries to show declines in problem drug use and the only one with a rise in drug-related mortality in 2007 and 2008, attributed to more toxicological autopsies and, they say, largely supported by the INE data.
key_findings.locator: How Portugal compares: Accounts compared, 3rd-5th paragraphs (p. 109); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 110)

key_findings.finding: Attention: media mentions of Portugal's reform numbered 415 in 2001-2010 (Factiva), 49% of them in 2009 and 2010, with the Cato report by far the most referred to, while the authors' earlier Beckley Foundation report drew little coverage. Editors' reading of Figure 5: about 60, 52, 24, 18, 7, 7, 19, 23, 81 and 124 mentions a year from 2001 to 2010, which sum to 415.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Figure 5

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: both accounts used evidence selectively (indicators, years, datasets) and left out other data; the reform warrants neither the praise of a resounding success nor the condemnation of a disastrous failure, and its implications are, in the authors' view, nuanced but largely positive; focusing on the law rather than the concurrent strategy that expanded services fostered overconfident claims; as a purported example of evidence being dismissed, the authors quote a US Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) document saying that drug legalization advocates' claims about Portugal had significantly exceeded the existing scientific basis; the paper said the document was not on the ONDCP website and could be found only through Pinto Coelho, which the erratum (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727) corrects: Pinto Coelho informed the journal that the document is on the ONDCP website, and the authors apologise for any confusion, saying they would not have cited it had they doubted it was a real ONDCP report; the Global Commission on Drug Policy acknowledged slight increases in overall drug use after the reform.
key_findings.locator: Discussion (pp. 109-111); Conclusion (p. 111); erratum (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Greenwald's INME data showed a 27-30% fall in lifetime cannabis use after the reform, but the INME figures it quotes on the same page (10.4% to 6.6% and 25.6% to 18.7%) are falls of 36% and 27%, as the page itself states.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 27-30% range is not reproducible; cite the grade-specific falls (36% and 27%) from the printed figures.

reporting_issues.issue: The fall of 16% attributed to all the other school datasets after the reform cannot be reproduced from Figure 1, and the ECATD years are 2003 and 2006 in Table 2 but 2003 and 2007 on the Figure 1 axis (where the survey is spelled ECTAD). Editors' calculation from Figure 1 readings: ESPAD about 13% (15.0 to 13.0), HBSC about 11% (9.2 to 8.2), ECATD from about 9% to 26% by age, with a small rise at age 13.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the dataset-specific values, not the pooled 16%; the ECATD survey year needs checking against its source.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper quotes Greenwald's drug-related deaths for 2006 as 290 and Pinto Coelho's as 216 without reconciling the two figures for the same year; nor does it set Greenwald's figure of close to 400 for 1999 against the 369 that the authors' own 2010 article reports for that year (hughes_2010, PDF p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The INML series in Figure 4 shows about 216 for 2006 (editors' reading), so Greenwald's 290 does not match it; its source is not identified, and neither it nor his close to 400 for 1999 should be cited as an INML count.

reporting_issues.issue: Pinto Coelho is quoted as describing a 150% rise in students' cannabis use (HBSC, 1998-2002), while the authors refer to the 142% suggested by his HBSC data.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor. Editors' calculation from the HBSC values in Figure 1 (about 3.8% to 9.2%) gives about 142%, so 142% is the figure the data support.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors say Pinto Coelho ignored notable reductions in the 15-19 age group, but no data for that age group are shown; the general-population figures use the age group 15-24.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 15-19 reduction is asserted, not shown; claims should use the 15-24 figures from Figure 3.

reporting_issues.issue: Names are spelled inconsistently: the HBSC survey (Health Behaviour in School-aged Children) appears as HSBC in the text and Table 2, ECATD appears as ECTAD in Figure 1, and Pinto Coelho appears once as Pinto Coehlo.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use HBSC, ECATD and Pinto Coelho when citing or searching.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says the homicide claim runs counter to the trend of reduced drug-related crime that the authors reported earlier (their 2010 article), but that article reported a 9% rise in crimes strongly linked to drugs between 1995-99 and 2000-04 (with falls in some more complex or violent categories), a fall in the share of prisoners held for drug-related offences (44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008), and no later crime trend, since such data were not routinely collected (hughes_2010, PDF pp. 11-13).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2010 article does not show a fall in drug-related crime; do not cite this paper for one. Its closest support, the prison share, was presented there as a reduced burden on the criminal justice system.

design_detail: Published critique (a For Debate article in Addiction) by three drug-policy analysts of the idea that drugs can be ranked on a single harm score and scheduled by rank, aimed chiefly at the ISCD multicriteria decision analysis (Nutt et al., 2010) and its 2007 predecessor. Argument only: no data collection, no literature search, no reanalysis; illustrative figures are taken from Nutt et al. (2010) and from UK prevalence sources.
can_establish: The conceptual and methodological objections to single-score drug-harm rankings as a basis for scheduling decisions, as argued by these authors in 2011, including specific points about how the 2010 ISCD composite score was built.
cannot_establish: Any new fact about the harms of particular drugs; how large the distortions it describes are in practice (no reanalysis of the ISCD scores is done); or whether harm matrices, its proposed alternative, would lead to better policy decisions.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (critique).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the authors address the 2007 and 2010 UK expert rankings and the general enterprise, citing 20 references of their choosing.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The authors chose what to engage with: the ISCD composite score, its weights and its policy use, but not the ISCD's correlations with outside data or its reported sensitivity analyses. Three of the 20 references are the authors' own work on drug markets and enforcement (refs 10, 15 and 18).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: The critique argues that rankings should reflect real use patterns, for example mephedrone taken with alcohol, and market-level substitution between drugs, which the ISCD scoring did not (p. 1888).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The critique contrasts the ISCD composite with its proposed alternative: harm matrices with one row per substance in a given policy context and one column per type of harm.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (argument). Figures used as illustrations: the ISCD overall scores for tobacco (26), GHB (19), crack (54) and powder cocaine (27); the ISCD part scores for tobacco and GHB (37 each for harm to the individual; 17 against 2 for harm to others); the ISCD weighting of the overall score (0.46 for harm to the individual, 0.54 for harm to others); the 80% weight of drug-specific relative to drug-related mortality; about 8.5 million people who smoke in the UK (Department of Health) and about 50 000 people who use GHB (British Crime Survey 2009/10, England and Wales, presented as UK).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Distinguishes harmfulness (harm per unit of use: the medical, laboratory or individual perspective) from aggregate harm (roughly harmfulness multiplied by extent of use), and argues that national policy should rest on aggregate outcomes and on the change in harm a scheduling decision would cause (pp. 1886–1888).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None (no data analysed). The one numerical illustration: on the ISCD ratio scale tobacco (26) scores about a third higher than GHB (19), although the UK has about 8.5 million people who smoke and about 50 000 who use GHB, because both drugs were judged similarly harmful to the individual (37 each) and tobacco's much larger prevalence enters only through the harm-to-others score (17 against 2) (p. 1887). Editors' check against Nutt et al. (2010): those part scores agree within about one point with the unweighted positions of tobacco and GHB in that paper's Figure 3 (re-measured at 300 dpi as about 37 and 17, and 38 and 2); 0.46 × 37 + 0.54 × 17 gives 26, but for GHB 0.46 × 37 + 0.54 × 2 gives about 18 against the printed 19, which the reading of 38 reproduces (18.6).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as a statistical concept. The critique does not discuss the evidence the ISCD paper offered for its scores (correlations with outside data and with other expert rankings) or the stability of its ranking under changes in the weights.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A reasoned argument with no data of its own. Its specific statements about the 2010 ISCD model check out against that paper: the overall score is a weighted sum with weights of 0.46 for harm to the individual and 0.54 for harm to others (Nutt et al., Figure 2 key); most harm-to-others criteria take account indirectly of the number of people using a drug (Nutt et al., p. 1558); the committee's weighting of drug-specific mortality at 80% of drug-related mortality is a valuation, not a count of deaths (Nutt et al., pp. 1559–1560); benefits were not scored (Nutt et al., p. 1564). The tobacco and GHB part scores it quotes are not printed as numbers by Nutt et al. but agree with their Figure 3 within about one point (GHB reads about 38, not 37, for harm to the individual).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The language is strong: hiding total harm's dependence on prevalence is called "analytical malpractice" (p. 1887) and single-number rankings "simplistic pseudo-scientific scores" (p. 1890); the abstract calls such efforts fundamentally flawed. Its central claims are logical rather than empirical: that even perfect ratings would not suffice for scheduling (policy chooses between decisions, not substances; decisions interact; consequences depend on context and on current prevalence) and that any composite is value-laden. These are arguments to weigh, not findings. The critique does not show that another method would rank drugs differently or lead to better policy, does not engage with the sensitivity analyses the ISCD reported, and rests several supporting points on uncited assertions.

timeline.event: Nutt, King, Saulsbury & Blakemore: nine-criteria UK expert rating, one of the critique's targets (cited as ref. 6).
Kalant: commentary on drug classification (ref. 11), cited for the point that weighting harms is a matter of judgement.
ACMD report on multicriteria decision analysis in drug-harm decision making (ref. 19), quoted for the distinction between harm and value (not read).
ISCD multicriteria decision analysis of 20 drugs, the critique's main target
This critique.
Rolles & Measham: second published critique of ranking drug harms (listed in the project's harm-rankings list; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: One of the published critiques that the project's harm-rankings list requires beside the Nutt rankings (list rows 2 to 4). Whether later multicriteria rankings answered its objections, for example by reporting harm to the individual and harm to others separately or by eliciting weights from other groups, is not settled here; those rankings have not been read.

funding.funder: No outside funding (Declarations of interest, p. 1890).
funding.declared_conflicts: None of the authors are connected to the tobacco, alcohol, pharmaceutical or gaming industries or any organization substantially funded by them (p. 1890).
funding.affiliations_note: Carnegie Mellon University Heinz College (Caulkins, Coulson) and University of Maryland School of Public Policy and Department of Criminology (Reuter); policy analysts of drug markets and enforcement. Three of the 20 references are their own work. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount the argument.

what_would_settle_it: A reanalysis of the ISCD scores that reports harm per person who uses each drug separately from total UK harm and shows how the ranking moves under weights elicited from different groups; and a test of whether policy makers shown harm matrices reach different, better-justified decisions than those shown composite rankings.

domains.note: No search; the critique addresses targets the authors chose (chiefly Nutt et al., 2010) and cites 20 sources of their choosing.

The target paper's construction is described accurately on the points checked (weights 0.46 and 0.54, the 80% mortality weight, benefits not scored, most harm-to-others criteria taking account indirectly of the number of people using a drug); its figure readings are close but not exact (GHB about 38 rather than 37 for harm to the individual in Nutt et al.'s Figure 3), its GHB prevalence comes from an England and Wales survey presented as UK, its validation correlations and sensitivity analyses are not discussed, and other sources are cited without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 3 of 20 references are the authors' own (drug prices, enforcement, Mexican trafficking revenues), used for supporting points rather than the core argument.

Openly argumentative, and the authors call the piece unambiguously sour on the enterprise; several empirical-sounding statements are uncited (alcohol prohibition in contemporary Saudi Arabia without gangland violence, heroin causing minimal organ damage), as is an expectation reasoned from market equilibria (legalizing marijuana changing use less than legalizing cocaine).

domains.domain: Balance of arguments for and against composite harm rankings
domains.note: The case for rankings is under-represented: the authors grant that a single harmfulness measure can inform an individual's choice and that evidence should inform policy, but they do not weigh the ISCD's reported stability under weight changes or its correlations with outside data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A narrative critique has no validated instrument (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist rates it high overall because, like any argument piece, it rests on an unsystematic selection. It is a published argument, not evidence about drug harms. Cite it for the objections it raises (mixing harm per person with prevalence-dependent harm to others; value-laden weights; benefits ignored; additivity requiring independence between criteria; harms that depend on legal status and context), noting that its statements about how the ISCD model was built check out and its readings of that paper's figure agree within about one point; do not cite it as evidence for its uncited empirical asides.

key_findings.finding: Argues that harm per unit of use (harmfulness) and aggregate harm to society are different quantities: aggregate harm is roughly harmfulness multiplied by the extent of use, and the extent of use itself depends on policy, so a legal drug causing more total harm than an illegal one does not imply that either should change legal status.
key_findings.locator: Individual- and aggregate-level perspectives should not be mingled, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Describes the ISCD overall harm score as a weighted sum, 0.46 × harm to the individual + 0.54 × harm to others, with the first part measured per person and the second mainly in aggregate; it therefore measures neither harm per unit of use nor aggregate harm but a weighted average of each. Used in policy debate, such scores imply that policy cannot change harm to the people who use a drug by changing the amount of use; hiding total harm's dependence on prevalence in this way is what the authors call analytical malpractice.
key_findings.locator: Individual- and aggregate-level perspectives should not be mingled, 6th and 7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The weights match the ISCD paper (Nutt et al., 2010, Figure 2 key: 46 and 54).

key_findings.finding: Illustration: tobacco scores 26 and GHB 19 on the ISCD ratio scale, about a third apart, although by the critique's figures about 8.5 million people in the UK smoke and about 50 000 use GHB; it explains that both were judged similarly harmful to the individual (37 each) and differ mainly on harm to others (17 against 2), so tobacco's far larger prevalence counts only through that term.
key_findings.locator: Individual- and aggregate-level perspectives should not be mingled, 8th paragraph (p. 1887); references 13 and 14 (p. 1890)
key_findings.note: The 37 and 17/2 part scores are not printed as numbers in Nutt et al. (2010). At 300 dpi that paper's Figure 3 places tobacco at about 37 and 17 and GHB at about 38 and 2 (editors' reading), so they agree within about one point. The GHB prevalence is cited to a survey of England and Wales (reporting_issues[4]).

key_findings.finding: Argues that even perfect harm ratings would not suffice for scheduling: societies choose between policies (a drug scheduled or not), not between drugs; decisions interact (on the ISCD scores any threshold between 27 and 54 would ban crack but allow the powder cocaine it is easily made from); drug combinations and cross-price effects matter (mephedrone taken with alcohol); and consequences depend on context and current prevalence (US alcohol prohibition in the 1920s against contemporary Saudi Arabia; firearm availability; syringe exchange).
key_findings.locator: Even perfect harm ratings would not be enough to create policy, 3rd to 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Argues that important harms (drug-related crime, environmental damage and the cost of police and prisons, all among the ISCD criteria) are not characteristics of a chemical but depend as well on legal status and on the programmes that implement laws, so that conflating the policy choice with the substance makes the whole assessment ill-defined; it says methamphetamine's environmental problems from production in small, technologically primitive laboratories would disappear if it were legal.
key_findings.locator: Even perfect harm ratings would not be enough to create policy, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: States that there is nothing conceptually wrong with a single harmfulness measure to inform an individual's choice of drug, or with evidence-informed policy that uses aggregate harm by substance; what it rejects is treating the lack of a direct link between such a measure and the strictness of prohibition as evidence of flawed policy.
key_findings.locator: Even perfect harm ratings would not be enough to create policy, 13th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Argues that weights are value judgements (the ISCD committee's decision to weight drug-specific mortality at 80% of drug-related mortality is a statement about valuation, not numbers of deaths); that policy gives weight to the pleasures of alcohol but ignores the benefits that people who use other drugs perceive, which an analytical exercise should not take as given; and that an additive score requires mutual preferential independence between criteria, which the authors argue does not always hold, notably between dependence liability and any attribute reflecting harm to the person using the drug. They add that this last criticism applies only to simpler models such as the linear additive form used by Nutt et al.; more complex models exist but are harder to elicit and interpret.
key_findings.locator: Is it even possible to create harm rankings?, 3rd to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposes harm matrices instead of rankings: a row for each substance in a given context (at least two rows per substance, under current and under alternative scheduling) and a column for each type of harm, as tools to educate policy makers rather than algorithms to replace their judgement. The authors call the idea not a silver bullet and grant that even harm matrices are not sufficient for guiding a scheduling decision, because values matter and decisions interact.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion: stress harm matrices, not harm rankings, 2nd to 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Gives, without a citation, the example that heroin kills many people directly through overdose while even chronic use does minimal organ damage, whereas few people die of nicotine overdose but smoking kills hundreds of thousands over time through lung cancer and heart disease.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion: stress harm matrices, not harm rankings, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: An uncited illustration; not evidence for either statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The tobacco and GHB part scores the critique quotes (37 each for harm to the individual; 17 against 2 for harm to others) are not printed as numbers in Nutt et al. (2010); they appear to be read from that paper's unweighted scatterplot (Figure 3), with which they agree within about one point: at 300 dpi Figure 3 places tobacco at about 37 and 17 and GHB at about 38 and 2 (editors' reading). With 37 and 2, GHB's weighted sum would be about 18 rather than the printed 19; 38 and 2 give 18.6 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite them as approximate values read from the figure in Nutt et al. (2010), not as published scores; GHB's position for harm to the individual is about 38.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 6 gives the 2007 Lancet rating the title "Developing a rational scale for assessing the risks of drugs of potential misuse", whereas Nutt et al. (2010, ref. 1) and the project's harm-rankings list (row 1) give "Development of a rational scale to assess the harm of drugs of potential misuse".
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor mis-citation; use the DOI from the project list.

reporting_issues.issue: Several factual premises are given without citation: alcohol prohibition in contemporary Saudi Arabia does not create gangland violence; violence from cocaine markets is greater in countries with more available firearms; heroin, even in chronic use, does minimal organ damage. The authors also state, as an expectation reasoned from market equilibria and without citation, that legalizing marijuana would change use less than legalizing cocaine.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are the authors' assertions and expectations; the paper cannot be cited as evidence for any of them.
