design_detail: Congressionally mandated evaluation of the US National Youth Anti-Drug Media Campaign (White House Office of National Drug Control Policy; nearly $1 billion appropriated 1998–2004) using the National Survey of Parents and Youth (NSPY): a household panel from a stratified 4-stage national probability sample (90 primary sampling units), three cohorts of youths aged 9–18 interviewed at home four times between November 1999 and June 2004 (8117, 6516, 5854 and 5126 youths in rounds 1–4). With no unexposed comparison area, effects were estimated from naturally occurring differences in individually recalled exposure, with propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders, in three analyses: trends 2000–2004; cross-sectional exposure-outcome associations; and lagged associations of exposure at one round with outcomes at the next, among youths aged 12.5–18 who had not used marijuana at the earlier round. Outcomes: self-reported marijuana use and marijuana-related intentions, beliefs, norms and self-efficacy.
can_establish: Whether US youths aged 12.5–18 in 1999–2004 who recalled more campaign advertising had different marijuana-related intentions, beliefs, norms and initiation at the next interview than those who recalled less, after weighting for measured confounders; and whether national prevalence and these cognitions changed over the campaign years.
cannot_establish: The effect of the campaign against no campaign (almost every youth was exposed and no area went without it); effects before the first survey round, which began with the full launch; effects on drugs other than marijuana, on reduction among youths already using, or on parents (reported separately); or, with confidence, a causal pro-marijuana effect, given recall-based exposure, possible residual confounding and many uncorrected tests.

sample.recruitment: Household (community) probability sample: 90 county-sized primary sampling units, then geographic segments, households, and 1 or 2 youths plus 1 parent per household. Interviews at home on laptops, with prerecorded questions over headphones and touch-screen answers for most of the interview, in English or Spanish (pp. 2229–2230).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Youths aged 9–18 at recruitment. Analyses were restricted to those aged 12.5–18 at outcome measurement, and to youths who had not used marijuana at the current round (cross-sectional analyses) or at the earlier round (lagged analyses) (p. 2232). The age limit was chosen for consistency, since few youths younger than 12.5 remained by round 4; the authors state that all conclusions were also supported by earlier analyses with the broader age range (ref. 18, not read; p. 2232).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated in the article; a supplement giving an overview of the cohorts (online only, not among the files read) is cited (p. 2230). Subgroup analyses by gender, age, race/ethnicity (White, African American, Hispanic) and marijuana-risk score (p. 2232).
sample.attrition: First-round youth response rate 65%; 86% to 93% of still-eligible youths were interviewed in later rounds. Numbers interviewed fell from 8117 to 5126 (63% of round 1, editors' arithmetic), partly because youths aged out. Longitudinal weights were adjusted for nonresponse using prior-round exposure and outcomes (pp. 2230, 2232).
sample.selection_effects: A 65% response rate at the first round of a household survey; survey weights adjusted for selection probabilities, nonresponse and undercoverage. The number of youths in each analysis (aged 12.5–18 and not having used marijuana) is not given in any table.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported recall. General exposure: how often in recent months the youth had seen or heard antidrug ads, asked for each medium (TV and radio, print, cinema or video, outdoor), worded after the Monitoring the Future survey. Specific exposure: prompted recall of up to 4 TV and 2 radio campaign ads aired in the 2 months before the interview, each played in full, with recall imputed for ads not shown. The authors cite validity evidence from comparisons with ads never broadcast and with the ratings points bought for each ad (p. 2230).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: 94% recalled general exposure to at least one antidrug message a month (median about 2 to 3 ads a week); 54% recalled at least weekly exposure to specific campaign TV ads; 15%, 31%, 38% and 16% recalled fewer than 1, 1 to under 4, 4 to under 12, and 12 or more campaign TV ads a month (p. 2232). The campaign planned for an average youth to see 2.5 targeted ads a week; 64% of the gross rating points bought were on TV and radio (p. 2229).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable as an exposure. Youths' earlier tobacco and alcohol use and parents' alcohol, tobacco and illicit drug use entered the confounder and risk scores. Outcomes were limited to marijuana because use of other drugs was too rare for adequate power (p. 2230).

comparison.controls: No unexposed group: comparisons are between youths recalling less and more exposure (general: under 4, 4–11, 12 or more a month; specific: under 1, 1–3, 4–11, 12 or more a month). Comparisons between areas were considered, but the advertising agency's buying plans did not forecast regional variation (p. 2231).
comparison.matching: Propensity-score weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders, including age, gender, race/ethnicity, survey wave, urban or rural residence, census neighbourhood characteristics, academic performance, family functioning, extracurricular activities, perceived parental supervision, antisocial peers, media consumption, household income, the parent's demographics, media use, substance use and involvement with the child, and an empirical marijuana-risk score; the lagged analyses also controlled for prior-round outcomes (pp. 2231–2232). The final models are described in a separate report (Orwin et al., 2006), not read.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Dispositions that could drive both ad recall and later attitudes (for example general attentiveness to advertising) are captured only indirectly, through media consumption, the risk score and prior-round outcomes.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Parents' substance use and youths' earlier tobacco and alcohol use entered the propensity and risk scores.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported lifetime, past-year and past-30-day marijuana use; intention (the answer "I definitely will not" use marijuana in the next 12 months, against any other answer); an antimarijuana attitudes and beliefs index (8 expected-outcome items and 2 attitude scales); a social norms index (5 items on friends' and peers' use and on disapproval); a self-efficacy index (5 items on confidence in refusing). The indices were weighted by regression on intention and scaled to 100 among youths aged 12–18 who had not used marijuana at wave 1. Lagged behaviour outcome: initiation of marijuana use by the next round (pp. 2230–2232).
outcomes.validity_norms: Intention predicted behaviour: among youths aged 12.5–18 who had never used marijuana, 9% of those answering "I definitely will not" and 39% of all others reported use 12–18 months later. Youths scoring above the median had relative odds of 21.7 (attitudes and beliefs), 17.4 (social norms) and 4.0 (self-efficacy) of giving that answer (pp. 2230–2231).
outcomes.operationalization: A campaign effect was an association between more recalled exposure and outcomes in the antidrug direction, expressed as Goodman and Kruskal's gamma (from −1 to 1). The team stipulated at the outset that it would claim an antimarijuana effect only if trends, cross-sectional associations and lagged associations all agreed (p. 2235).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Primary tests: 7 trend changes (Table 1), 8 cross-sectional gammas (Table 2) and 10 pooled lagged gammas (Table 3); further, 30 round-pair lagged gammas (Table 4) and 80 cross-sectional plus 80 lagged subgroup gammas reported as counts in the text. The authors treat 3 significant of 80 cross-sectional subgroup gammas as possibly chance, and 20 significant of 80 lagged subgroup gammas (19 in the pro-marijuana direction) as a pattern.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-administered audio interview).

analysis.effect_sizes: Trends among youths aged 12.5–18, 2000 to 2004 (Table 1, p. 2233): lifetime marijuana use 23.6% to 23.5% (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8); past year 17.1% to 16.7% (−0.4, −2.6 to 1.9); past 30 days 7.8% to 8.2% (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2); among youths who had not used marijuana, definitely not intending to use 86.7% to 87.5% (0.8, −1.0 to 2.6); self-efficacy index 102.6 to 105.0 (2.4, −3.3 to 8.2); social norms index 103.6 to 104.8 (1.2, −5.1 to 7.3); attitudes and beliefs index 105.1 to 111.4 (6.3, 0.4 to 12.2, the only significant change). Cross-sectional gammas (Table 2, p. 2233): general exposure −0.01 to 0.03, specific exposure −0.02 to 0.02, all intervals including zero. Pooled lagged gammas (Table 3, p. 2234): general exposure on intention −0.07 (−0.13 to −0.01) and specific exposure on social norms −0.05 (−0.08 to −0.02), both in the pro-marijuana direction; initiation, general exposure 0.07 (−0.01 to 0.15), specific exposure −0.02 (−0.13 to 0.08); the other six between −0.03 and 0.00, not significant. Round-pair gammas (Table 4, p. 2234): significant only in the pro-marijuana direction: round 1 to 2, general exposure on intention −0.16 (−0.27 to −0.06) and on social norms −0.06 (−0.12 to −0.01); specific exposure on social norms, round 2 to 3, −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.00), and round 3 to 4, −0.07 (−0.12 to −0.02); general exposure on initiation, round 3 to 4, 0.11 (0.00 to 0.22). Editors' count: 5 of 30 round-pair gammas significant, all pro-marijuana.
analysis.covariates: Propensity-score weights (see comparison); survey weights for selection probabilities, nonresponse and undercoverage; standard errors by jackknife replication allowing for the complex sample design (p. 2232).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not registered. The evaluation team stated a decision rule at the start: an antimarijuana effect would be claimed only if trends, cross-sectional and lagged associations agreed (p. 2235).
analysis.selective_reporting: The article summarizes a larger evaluation reported to the government by Westat (2003 and 2004 reports cited). Behaviour is analysed only as initiation in the lagged analyses; subgroup results appear only as counts; analytic sample sizes are not given; the authors' proposed mechanism for the unfavourable effects rests on data not shown.
analysis.power: Not reported for these analyses; the authors say the samples were too small to study drugs other than marijuana or reduction among youths already using occasionally (pp. 2230, 2232).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Exposure was high (94% recalled antidrug ads at least monthly). Marijuana use did not change between 2000 and 2004 (lifetime 23.6% to 23.5%; past 30 days 7.8% to 8.2%), and of four cognitions only the attitudes and beliefs index rose (6.3 index points, 95% CI 0.4 to 12.2). Youths recalling more exposure held no more antidrug views at the same interview. At the next interview, more exposure predicted fewer youths definitely intending not to use marijuana (γ −0.07) and weaker antidrug norms (γ −0.05); pooled initiation associations were not significant; initiation was significantly higher with more exposure only from round 3 to round 4 (γ 0.11, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.22). Every significant lagged association, overall and in subgroups bar one, was in the pro-marijuana direction.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the campaign is unlikely to have had favourable effects and "may have had delayed unfavorable effects" (p. 2229); the Discussion calls the support for pro-marijuana effects "tentative but not definitive" (p. 2235), noting that the pattern was absent cross-sectionally and showed more initiation in one round pair only. These conclusions are proportionate; the Results are worded more strongly, calling the lagged pattern an overriding one and the associations exposure effects (p. 2232), which the Discussion then tempers. A headline version, that anti-drug ads made teenagers more likely to start using marijuana, would overstate the paper: the initiation effect is one barely significant estimate among many uncorrected tests, the comparison is more against less recalled exposure rather than campaign against none, and the proposed mechanism (ads signalling that use is common) rests on data not shown. Conversely, the absence of favourable effects is limited by the lack of an unexposed comparison (effects spread through social networks would be missed, as the authors discuss) and by the first round starting with the full launch.

timeline.event: Congress begins appropriations for the campaign, nearly $1 billion over 1998–2004 (as described, p. 2229).
Full national launch in September 1999; NSPY round 1 begins in November 1999 (as described, p. 2229).
Palmgreen et al. (Am J Public Health): televised campaigns aimed at high-sensation-seeking adolescents and marijuana use, cited here among successful marijuana campaigns (ref. 29; not read).
The campaign introduces its Marijuana Initiative in late 2002 (as described, p. 2229).
Orwin et al.: Westat 2004 report of findings of the full evaluation, including effects on parents (ref. 4; not read).

Palmgreen et al.: effects of the Marijuana Initiative on high-sensation-seeking adolescents, reported as favourable in 2 medium-sized cities over one 6-month period (as described, p. 2235; ref. 41; not read).
This national evaluation: no favourable effects; lagged associations in the pro-marijuana direction.

replication.where_it_stands: The congressionally mandated national evaluation of the campaign, and by its authors' account the only source of lagged exposure-outcome data on it. It found no favourable effect and some evidence of delayed unfavourable effects, while a smaller study of the campaign's Marijuana Initiative (Palmgreen et al., 2007, not read) reported favourable effects in two cities over six months. Whether the unfavourable (boomerang) association has been replicated in another campaign is not known from the files read.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grants 3-N01-DA085063-002 and 1-R03-DA-020893-01 supported the research and preparation of the article. The evaluation was funded by Congress as part of the campaign's original appropriation; NIDA supervised the evaluation, Westat held the contract with the Annenberg School for Communication (University of Pennsylvania) as subcontractor, and the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy directly supervised the campaign (Acknowledgments, p. 2235).
funding.declared_conflicts: No separate conflict-of-interest statement. All authors were funded for this evaluation and other projects by NIDA; the views expressed are stated to be the authors' and not necessarily the sponsors' (p. 2235).
funding.affiliations_note: Annenberg School for Communication, University of Pennsylvania (Hornik, Jacobsohn) and Westat (Orwin, Piesse, Kalton). The evaluation was paid from the same federal appropriation as the campaign it evaluated; the findings were null to unfavourable. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A campaign evaluation with randomized or staggered rollout across media markets, so that some areas go without the campaign or receive it later, measuring marijuana initiation in household panels in both arms; and a pre-registered test of the lagged pro-marijuana association in another national youth campaign.

domains.note: Propensity weighting on more than 150 candidate confounders, with prior-round outcomes in the lagged analyses, covers the known domains; residual confounding by dispositions that drive both ad recall and later attitudes remains possible.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: National probability sample with a 65% first-round response rate; follow-up began only with the full launch, after earlier developmental phases of the campaign, so early effects could not be captured.

Exposure is self-reported recall (with imputation for ads not shown), with some validity evidence; in the lagged analyses it was measured before the outcome. Measurement error would bias towards no association.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Campaign content changed during the evaluation (Marijuana Initiative from late 2002; early-intervention ads in the final 6 months), and youths received much other antidrug messaging; pooled estimates mix campaign phases.

Interviews fell from 8117 to 5126 between rounds 1 and 4, partly by ageing out; 86% to 93% of still-eligible youths were reinterviewed and weights were adjusted for nonresponse; analytic sample sizes are not reported.
Self-reported marijuana use and cognitions, collected privately by audio self-interview; no biological verification.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: A decision rule was stated in advance and all three analysis types are reported, but many exposure-outcome-subgroup combinations were tested without correction, and the abstract highlights the significant unfavourable estimates.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-designed national panel with probability sampling, propensity weighting, lagged analyses and a pre-stated decision rule; but there is no unexposed comparison, exposure is recalled, outcomes are self-reported and dozens of tests were run without correction. The null result for favourable effects is the firmer finding. Cite it for: no detectable favourable effect of the campaign on marijuana use or cognitions among US youths in 1999–2004, and some evidence, weak and irregular, of delayed unfavourable associations; not for a proven boomerang effect.

key_findings.finding: NSPY household panel: three cohorts aged 9–18 from a national probability sample, interviewed four times between November 1999 and June 2004; 8117, 6516, 5854 and 5126 youths in rounds 1 to 4; first-round response rate 65%, then 86% to 93% of still-eligible youths.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods › Sample and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure was high: 94% of youths recalled at least one antidrug message a month (median about 2 to 3 ads a week) and 54% recalled at least weekly exposure to specific campaign TV ads; 15%, 31%, 38% and 16% recalled fewer than 1, 1 to under 4, 4 to under 12, and 12 or more campaign TV ads a month.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The 54% is spelled out in words in the text (fifty-four percent).

key_findings.finding: Among youths aged 12.5–18, marijuana use did not change from 2000 to 2004: lifetime use 23.6% to 23.5% (change −0.1 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 2.8), past-year use 17.1% to 16.7% (−0.4, −2.6 to 1.9), past-30-day use 7.8% to 8.2% (0.4, −1.4 to 2.2).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 2232); Table 1 (p. 2233)

key_findings.finding: Among youths who had not used marijuana, the share definitely not intending to use rose from 86.7% to 87.5% (0.8, −1.0 to 2.6; not significant); the attitudes and beliefs index rose 6.3 points (95% CI 0.4 to 12.2), while self-efficacy (2.4, −3.3 to 8.2) and social norms (1.2, −5.1 to 7.3) did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 2232); Table 1 (p. 2233)

key_findings.finding: Little evidence of a contemporaneous association, and none significant in the full sample: youths who had not used marijuana and recalled more exposure were no more likely to hold antidrug views (gammas −0.01 to 0.03 for general and −0.02 to 0.02 for specific exposure, all intervals including zero); 3 of 80 subgroup gammas were significant, which the authors say may easily be chance findings.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 2232); Table 2 (p. 2233)

key_findings.finding: Pooled lagged associations (exposure at one round, outcome at the next): more general exposure predicted fewer youths definitely intending not to use marijuana (82.3%, 78.2% and 78.4% across rising exposure; γ −0.07, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.01), and more specific exposure predicted weaker antidrug social norms (γ −0.05, −0.08 to −0.02); of the other 8 associations none was significant and 6 were in the unfavourable direction.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 2232); Table 3 (p. 2234)

key_findings.finding: Initiation of marijuana use by the next round was 10.7%, 11.2% and 12.5% across rising general exposure (γ 0.07, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.15, not significant) and 10.8%, 12.6%, 11.5% and 13.2% across specific-exposure levels (γ printed as −0.02, −0.13 to 0.08).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, last row
key_findings.note: Adjusted percentages; the printed sign of the specific-exposure gamma conflicts with these percentages and with Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: By round pair, no association was significant in the antidrug direction and each pair had at least one significant pro-marijuana association; general exposure at round 3 predicted initiation by round 4 (γ 0.11, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.22), described as barely significant; the strongest was general exposure on intention from round 1 to 2 (γ −0.16, −0.27 to −0.06).
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (p. 2232); Table 4 (p. 2234)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 4: 5 of 30 round-pair gammas significant, all pro-marijuana.

key_findings.finding: Of 80 lagged subgroup analyses (by gender, age, race/ethnicity and risk), 20 were significant, 19 of them in the pro-marijuana direction.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Intention predicted behaviour: among youths aged 12.5–18 who had never used marijuana, 9% of those answering that they definitely would not use it reported use 12–18 months later, against 39% of those giving any other answer.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures › Outcome measures, 4th paragraph (the intention measure)

key_findings.finding: Background messaging was already common: in 2000, youths reported in-school drug education (66%), conversations with friends about negative consequences of drug use (52%), two or more conversations with parents about drugs (54%) and weekly non-advertising media content about drugs (54%); campaign exposure was a median of once or twice a week, at most about one minute of messages a week.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Possible Reasons for Lack of Evidence of Success, 5th paragraph (p. 2234, continuing on p. 2235)

key_findings.finding: The team stipulated at the start that it would confidently claim an antimarijuana effect only if trends, cross-sectional and lagged associations all agreed; against those criteria the authors judge the claim of pro-marijuana effects to have tentative but not definitive support, and conclude that the evidence suggests the campaign had no favourable effects on youths' behaviour and may even have had an unintended and undesirable effect on drug cognitions and use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Conclusions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors offer two explanations for the unfavourable associations, which they call speculative and admit are somewhat at odds with their reasons for the lack of favourable effects: psychological reactance, not supported in analyses reported elsewhere; and an implicit message that drug use is common, consistent with evidence (data not shown) that more ad exposure went with believing that other youths used marijuana, a belief that predicted later initiation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Possible Reasons for Lack of Evidence of Success, 6th to 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors note the evaluation could miss effects spread through social networks (it compares more and less exposed youths) and effects before the first round, which began with the full launch; they argue that other national surveys found no significant decreases between 1998 and 2000.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Possible Reasons for Lack of Evidence of Success, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Some other surveys showed a downturn in youth marijuana use from 1999 to 2004 that the NSPY did not; the authors note even larger declines in tobacco and alcohol use in two school surveys, suggesting a general downward trend in substance use regardless of the campaign.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison of These Results With Other Relevant Evidence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The marijuana-risk score (a weighted sum of youth and parent risk factors, including age, sensation seeking, urbanicity, earlier cigarette and alcohol use, religious involvement, shared parenting and parents' marijuana, tobacco and alcohol use) strongly predicted initiation: among youths aged 12.5–18, 1 in 4 of those with a higher score (above 0.08 on a 0–1 scale) and 1 in 12 of those with a lower score reported initiation at the next interview. The score entered the propensity models as a confounder.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Measures › Potential confounder measures, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: For scale (editors' comparison): the adjusted initiation percentages across exposure levels in Table 3 span 10.7% to 13.2%.

key_findings.finding: Marijuana use and antimarijuana cognitions differed markedly between lower- and higher-risk youths and between younger and older youths, but minimally by gender or race/ethnicity; in most cases the changes from 2000 to 2004 for subgroups were broadly similar to those for all youths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Subgroup figures are in the Westat report (ref. 4), not read; the article gives no subgroup table.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled specific-exposure gamma for initiation in Table 3 is printed as −0.02 (−0.13 to 0.08), which conflicts with the adjusted percentages in the same row (10.8%, 12.6%, 11.5%, 13.2%, rising overall with exposure) and lies outside the range of the three round-pair estimates in Table 4 (0.02, 0.00 and 0.07). Editors' check: a gamma computed from those percentages is positive under plausible exposure distributions (about +0.03 with the shares of youths reported at each level of campaign TV ads, +0.05 with equal shares; the same method gives +0.03 to +0.08 for the general-exposure row, printed 0.07), while the printed interval is centred on −0.02, so a misprint would involve the interval too.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sign may be misprinted, together with its interval. The Results count of 6 unfavourable among 8 non-significant pooled associations depends on it (7 of 8 if the sign is positive). Not significant either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract presents the two significant pooled lagged estimates (γ −0.07 and −0.05) as occurring at one round, but they are the estimates pooled across all round pairs in Table 3, and they come from different exposure measures (general exposure for intention, specific exposure for norms).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the values as pooled lagged associations, naming the exposure measure for each.

reporting_issues.issue: The indices are said to be scaled so that the mean (and standard deviation) among youths aged 12–18 who had not used marijuana at wave 1 was set to 100; Tables 2 and 3 refer to this footnote but do not print it.
reporting_issues.consequence: If the standard deviation really is 100, the significant 6.3-point rise in attitudes and beliefs is about 0.06 standard deviations (editors' arithmetic); the sizes of index differences cannot be judged with confidence from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the cohorts were surveyed from September 1999, but the Methods date the first round from November 1999; September 1999 is when the campaign's full launch and ad buying began.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the survey began about two months after the launch.

reporting_issues.issue: No table gives the number of youths analysed (aged 12.5–18 and not having used marijuana) for any estimate, and subgroup results appear only as counts of significant tests.
reporting_issues.consequence: Precision can be judged only from the printed intervals; subgroup findings cannot be checked.

design_detail: Multicriteria decision analysis (MCDA) of 20 drugs relevant to the UK, scored by expert judgement at a one-day facilitated decision conference in June 2010 under the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs (ISCD): members of the ISCD expert committee plus two invited external specialists on legal highs (names and number only in a webappendix, not among the files read). The 16 harm criteria (9 harms to the individual who uses the drug, 7 harms to others, clustered as physical, psychological and social) had been chosen at a special 2009 meeting of the UK Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD). Each drug was scored 0–100 on each criterion in open group discussion (100 = the most harmful drug on that criterion, 0 = no harm); criteria were then swing-weighted within and across clusters, the weights normalized to sum to 1 (shown as 0–100), and scores combined additively in the Hiview program into two part scores (harm to individuals, harm to others) and an overall harm score. Sensitivity analyses varied the weights only. No new measurements: every input is the panel's judgement.
can_establish: How this panel of UK drug experts, using these 16 criteria, these swing weights and an additive model, judged the relative overall harm of 20 drugs in the UK in 2010; which criteria drove each drug's score; and how far the weights would have to move before the top ranks changed.
cannot_establish: That alcohol is more dangerous per use or per person than heroin or crack cocaine (the overall score blends harm to the individual with harm to others, and most harm-to-others criteria partly reflect how many people in the UK use a drug); any measured harm (the inputs are consensus judgements, of which only two criteria were compared quantitatively with outside data, for 5 to 12 drugs); how stable the scores themselves are (no uncertainty or between-panel analysis); the ranking in other countries, legal regimes, doses or patterns of use; benefits (not scored); or what drug law should be.

sample.recruitment: Expert panel formed from the ISCD expert committee, described as a new organisation of drug experts independent of government interference, plus two external experts with specialist knowledge of legal highs; their experience is described as spanning personal and social aspects of drug harm, many with substantial research expertise in addiction (pp. 1558–1559). The 20 drugs were chosen as representative drugs relevant to the UK spanning the range of potential harms and extent of use (p. 1558).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated for choosing experts or drugs beyond the descriptions above. The panel's names and size are in a webappendix (p. 1559) that was not among the files read.
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single one-day workshop).
sample.selection_effects: The panel came from one committee, described as independent of government, plus two invited experts; two of the three authors attended the decision conference (travel expenses declared; DJN designed and participated in the study, LAK participated; Contributors and Conflicts of interest, p. 1564). The number of scorers, their individual or initial scores, and any disagreement are not reported. The drug list, chosen by the organisers, mixes legal drugs (alcohol, tobacco), prescribed medicines (benzodiazepines, methadone, buprenorphine) and illegal drugs.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study. Each drug's harm on each criterion was scored by group judgement in open discussion, on a 0–100 ratio scale, with consistency checks of the relativities between drugs (p. 1559). The evidence the panel drew on for each score is neither cited nor listed.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not specified: each drug was scored as used in the UK, without stated doses, routes, forms or patterns of use. The authors list polydrug use, routes, patterns of use and context as issues not yet built into the model (Discussion, 10th paragraph, p. 1564).
exposure.polysubstance: Not modelled; named by the authors as an issue to explore (p. 1564).

comparison.controls: None within the study. Offered as external checks: the 2007 nine-criteria UK expert rating (15 drugs in common), the Dutch addiction-medicine expert ranking (van Amsterdam et al., 2010; 19 drugs, five criteria), the UK Misuse of Drugs Act classes, and outside data for two single criteria (pp. 1561–1563).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. The analogue is the evidence behind each score, which is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: 16 criteria defined in Panel 1 (p. 1560). Harms to individuals: drug-specific mortality, drug-related mortality, drug-specific damage, drug-related damage, dependence, drug-specific and drug-related impairment of mental functioning, loss of tangibles, loss of relationships. Harms to others: injury, crime, environmental damage, family adversities, international damage, economic cost, community. Normalized weights (Figure 4 key, p. 1563): economic cost 12.8, injury 11.5, crime 10.2, family adversities 8.9, drug-related mortality 6.4, dependence 5.7, drug-specific impairment of mental functioning 5.7, drug-related impairment of mental functioning 5.7, drug-specific mortality 5.1, loss of tangibles 4.5, loss of relationships 4.5, drug-specific damage 4.1, drug-related damage 4.1, environmental damage 3.8, international damage 3.8, community 3.2; cumulative weight 46 for harms to individuals and 54 for harms to others (Figure 2 key, p. 1561).
outcomes.validity_norms: Quantitative checks against outside data covered two criteria only: drug-specific mortality against the log10 safety ratio of Gable (2004), r=0.66 for 12 substances, and against mean fatality statistics for 2003–2007 (King & Corkery, 2010), r=0.98 and 0.99 for 5 substances; dependence against US lifetime dependence (Anthony et al., 1994), r=0.95 for 5 drugs (p. 1563). No harm-to-others criterion was compared quantitatively; for social harms the Discussion only points to outside estimates and police records, without comparing them with the scores (8th paragraph, pp. 1563–1564). The authors state that the weights cannot be cross-validated with objective data (p. 1564).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is what the 16 criterion definitions describe. By the paper's own account the harms-to-individuals criteria show the extent of individual harm, whereas most harms-to-others criteria take account indirectly of the numbers of people using the drug (p. 1558). Risk, in the sense of the probability of harm, was deliberately not considered (p. 1561), and benefits were not scored (p. 1564).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests. The model rests on 320 group judgements (16 criteria × 20 drugs, editors' arithmetic) plus the weights.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; scoring was open group discussion by people who knew the drugs and the earlier rankings.

analysis.effect_sizes: Overall weighted harm scores out of 100 (Figure 2, p. 1561; repeated in Figure 4, p. 1563): alcohol 72, heroin 55, crack cocaine 54, metamfetamine 33, cocaine 27, tobacco 26, amfetamine 23, cannabis 20, GHB 19, benzodiazepines 15, ketamine 15, methadone 14, mephedrone 13, butane 11, khat 9, anabolic steroids 10, ecstasy 9, LSD 7, buprenorphine 7, mushrooms 6. Weighted part scores: harm to individuals highest for crack cocaine 37, heroin 34 and metamfetamine 32; harm to others highest for alcohol 46, heroin 21 and crack cocaine 17 (Summary, p. 1558; Results, pp. 1560–1561). Alcohol's own harm-to-individuals part score is not printed; it is about 26 by subtraction (72 − 46, editors' arithmetic), fourth, as the Discussion says (p. 1562). Correlations of the overall scores: with the 2007 nine-criteria rating r=0.70 (15 drugs); with the Dutch expert ranking 0.80 (individual totals) and 0.84 (population totals); with the UK Misuse of Drugs Act classification 0.04 (pp. 1561–1562). No uncertainty interval is given for any score. Editors' check (Figure 3, read at 300 dpi, approximate): each overall score equals about 0.46 times the unweighted harm-to-individuals score plus 0.54 times the unweighted harm-to-others score (alcohol about 56 and 85, giving 72; heroin about 73 and 40, giving 55; tobacco about 37 and 17, giving 26). Conversely, the Figure 2 segments divided by 0.46 and 0.54 reproduce the Figure 3 positions within about half a point (for example GHB: about 17.5 / 0.46 = 38, against about 38 and 2 read from Figure 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The criteria were fixed by the ACMD in 2009, before the 2010 scoring (ACMD report cited, not read). No protocol for the scoring or the analysis is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the consensus result is shown, as bar charts and a scatterplot. The 320 criterion scores are not tabulated (they can be read only approximately from the stacked bars of Figure 4), individual or initial scores and any disagreement are not reported, and the sensitivity analyses, described as extensive, are summarized by three examples.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: One UK expert panel, in a one-day workshop, reached a consensus that put alcohol highest on a composite of 16 weighted harm criteria (72 of 100), followed by heroin (55) and crack cocaine (54). Alcohol's lead comes from harms to others (part score 46, against 21 for heroin and 17 for crack cocaine); on harms to the individual who uses the drug, crack cocaine (37), heroin (34) and metamfetamine (32) scored above alcohol (about 26 by subtraction). The harm-to-others criteria carry 54% of the weight and, by the paper's own description, most of them take account indirectly of the numbers of people using the drug. The ranking was stable to large changes in the weights, but the scores themselves were never varied, and only two criteria were compared quantitatively with outside data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary reports that overall alcohol was the most harmful drug and gives the part scores (p. 1558). The conclusion goes further: the findings are said to confirm that drug classification systems "have little relation to the evidence of harm" and to accord with expert reports that "aggressively targeting alcohol harms is a valid and necessary public health strategy" (p. 1564). This treats the panel's judgements as evidence of harm and moves from a composite that blends prevalence-dependent harm to others with harm per person to conclusions about legal classification and alcohol policy. A headline version, "alcohol is more dangerous than heroin or crack", overstates the paper: the ranking is of total UK harm to individuals and to others as judged by experts in 2010, not of the danger of a given amount of a drug to a given person, on which crack cocaine, heroin and metamfetamine were rated higher. In fairness, the authors state the limits plainly: only harms were scored, harms depend on availability and legal status, results may not apply to other countries, and a low score does not mean a drug is safe (p. 1564).

timeline.event: Nutt, King, Saulsbury & Blakemore: nine-criteria UK expert rating on four-point scales, averaged without weights; this paper reports r=0.70 with it for 15 drugs (as described, p. 1561).
Special ACMD meeting chooses the 16 harm criteria from first principles (as described, p. 1558).
van Amsterdam et al., Dutch addiction-medicine expert ranking (19 drugs, five criteria, four-point scales); r=0.80 and 0.84 with the ISCD scores (as described, p. 1562).
This ISCD multicriteria decision analysis.
Caulkins, Reuter & Coulson: published critique (mixing of individual and aggregate harm, value-laden weights, benefits ignored, additivity)
Rolles & Measham: second published critique of ranking drug harms (listed in the project's harm-rankings list; not read for this card).
van Amsterdam, Nutt, Phillips & van den Brink: European rating of drug harms (project list; not read).
Bonomo et al.: Australian drug harms ranking, with a corrigendum that alters reported values (project list; not read).
Broman et al.: US multicriteria decision analysis of drug harms (project list; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The source of the "alcohol is the most harmful drug" figure (project harm-rankings list, row 2), which the project's list says must never be cited without its published critiques (Caulkins et al., 2011, appraised in this round; Rolles & Measham, 2011, not read). Later multicriteria rankings in Europe, Australia and the US exist in the project's list but have not been read here, so this card cannot say whether other panels reproduce the order. As an expert-judgement model, its outputs are never measurements of harm.

funding.funder: Centre for Crime and Justice Studies (UK) (Summary, p. 1558; Acknowledgments, p. 1564). The sponsor is stated to have had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Role of the funding source, p. 1560).
funding.declared_conflicts: DJN and LAK received travel expenses to attend the decision conference. LAK is a consultant to the Department of Health and the EMCDDA. LDP is a director of Facilitations Limited, which paid him a consulting fee because it was the company engaged by the Centre for Crime and Justice Studies to run the study and analyse the data (p. 1564). Of the panel, the paper says all provided independent advice and no conflicts of interest were declared (p. 1559).
funding.affiliations_note: Imperial College London (DJN), EMCDDA expert adviser (LAK), London School of Economics (LDP). The paper calls the meeting's facilitator an independent specialist in decision analysis without naming him; LDP's company was engaged to run the study and analyse the data. Published on behalf of the ISCD, whose committee formed the panel. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeating the scoring with several independent panels (other countries, people who use drugs, members of the public, whom the authors propose for the weights), eliciting individual scores before discussion and reporting their spread; publishing the evidence behind each score; reporting harm per person who uses each drug separately from total population harm; and a probabilistic sensitivity analysis over the scores as well as the weights.

domains.note: No search for, or listing of, the evidence behind any of the 320 scores; experts scored from their own knowledge in open discussion; drugs and experts were chosen by the organisers without stated criteria.

No appraisal of the evidence underlying the scores. The post hoc quantitative checks cover 2 of 16 criteria for 5 to 12 drugs, and none of the harm-to-others criteria, which carry 54% of the weight; for social harms the paper only points, without any comparison, to outside estimates and police records (pp. 1563–1564).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two authors attended the decision conference; the validation leans partly on the first author's 2007 rating and on a fatal-toxicity index co-authored by LAK (King & Corkery, 2010, ref. 13), alongside independent comparisons (Gable, 2004; Anthony et al., 1994; the Dutch ranking).

The methods describe scores and weights as judgements and the discussion says the weights cannot be cross-validated, but the conclusion calls the results the evidence of harm and draws a policy conclusion on alcohol.

domains.domain: Balance of harms against benefits, and of whose values set the weights
domains.note: Benefits were not scored and harms caused by drug control were not separated from harms of use, both stated as limitations; the weights reflect one expert panel, with public and other panels deferred to future work.

domains.domain: Elicitation of scores and weights (decision-analysis domain added by the editors)
domains.note: Consensus scoring in open discussion in one day, with no reported number of scorers, individual scores or dispersion. The methods describe, as a general feature of the approach, that scores are often changed from those first suggested as participants share their experiences (p. 1559); the paper presents this as a strength and does not report how far scores moved at this conference, and open discussion also exposes the result to anchoring and dominant voices.

domains.domain: Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis (decision-analysis domain added by the editors)
domains.note: Weights were varied and three examples reported (p. 1564), but the scores were not, so the claim that the model is very stable covers the weights only.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for an expert-judgement decision analysis (METHODS 5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is applied as the brief requires, with two decision-analysis domains added. The model is transparent about its structure and weights, and its top ranks are stable to large changes in the weights, but every input is a group judgement without documented evidence, individual scores or uncertainty, and the composite mixes harm per person with prevalence-dependent harm to others. Cite it for what this panel judged in 2010, always with the part scores and weights and with Caulkins et al. (2011); never as a measurement of which drug is most dangerous.

key_findings.finding: Members of the ISCD expert committee plus two invited external specialists scored 20 drugs on 16 criteria (9 harms to the individual, 7 harms to others) at a one-day decision conference in June 2010. Scores were set in open group discussion on 0–100 scales (100 = the most harmful drug on that criterion, 0 = no harm) and the criteria were then swing-weighted. The criteria had been chosen at a special 2009 ACMD meeting; the number and names of the experts are given only in a webappendix.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Method; Methods › Study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Scoring of the drugs on the criteria, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Webappendix not among the files read; panel size unknown from the article.

key_findings.finding: Overall weighted harm scores (out of 100): alcohol 72, heroin 55, crack cocaine 54, metamfetamine 33, cocaine 27, tobacco 26, amfetamine 23, cannabis 20, GHB 19, benzodiazepines 15, ketamine 15, methadone 14, mephedrone 13, butane 11, khat 9, anabolic steroids 10, ecstasy 9, LSD 7, buprenorphine 7, mushrooms 6. Only eight drugs scored 20 or more.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (bar labels); Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Labels checked at 300 dpi and repeated in Figure 4 (p. 1563). Figure 2 places khat (9) before anabolic steroids (10), and the Discussion gives 5 for mushrooms (p. 1562); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Weighted part scores: for harm to the individual, crack cocaine 37, heroin 34, metamfetamine 32; for harm to others, alcohol 46, heroin 21, crack cocaine 17. Alcohol ranked fourth on harm to the individual and first on harm to others.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Findings (p. 1558); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 1560, continuing on p. 1561); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 1562)
key_findings.note: Alcohol's harm-to-individuals part score is not printed; by subtraction it is about 26 (72 − 46, editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Harms to others carried 54% of the total weight and harms to the individual 46%. The heaviest single criteria were economic cost (12.8), injury (11.5), crime (10.2) and family adversities (8.9); drug-related mortality carried 6.4 and drug-specific mortality 5.1.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 key and legend (p. 1561); Figure 4 key (p. 1563)

key_findings.finding: The paper states that the harms-to-individuals criteria show the extent of individual harm, whereas most harms-to-others criteria take account indirectly of the numbers of people using the drug.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' inference, not stated in the paper: because of this, the overall score partly reflects how many people use a drug; alcohol's 46 points for harm to others are most of its 72 (Figure 2, p. 1561).

key_findings.finding: Figure 3 plots the unweighted 0–100 scores for harm to the individual against harm to others; the authors note the two axes cannot be compared without the weights. Editors' reading of Figure 3 at 300 dpi (approximate): alcohol's harm-to-others score (about 85) is roughly twice the next highest (heroin, about 40), while its harm-to-individuals score (about 56) is below crack cocaine (about 80), heroin (about 73) and metamfetamine (about 69).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1561); Figure 3 (p. 1562)
key_findings.note: Positions read from the plot, not printed values (other readings: tobacco about 37 and 17, GHB about 38 and 2). Combined with the weights (0.46 and 0.54) they reproduce the printed overall scores, and the Figure 2 segments divided by the weights reproduce them within about half a point (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: Drug-specific mortality contributed substantially to the scores of alcohol, heroin, GHB, methadone and butane; economic cost contributed heavily to alcohol, heroin, tobacco and cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 4 (p. 1563)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analysis of the weights: heroin would displace alcohol only if the weight on either mortality criterion rose by more than 15 of 100 points; tobacco only if the weight on drug-specific damage rose from about 4% to slightly more than 70%; crack cocaine only if the weight on harm to the individual rose from 46% to nearly 70%. The authors call the model very stable; the scores were not varied.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the weights are judgements that cannot be cross-validated with objective data, and that data are not available for many criteria, so an expert-group approach is the best they can provide.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph (p. 1563, continuing on p. 1564) and 9th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quantitative checks against outside data covered two criteria: drug-specific mortality scores correlated r=0.66 with the log10 safety ratio of Gable (2004) for 12 substances, and r=0.98 and 0.99 with mean fatality statistics from 2003 to 2007 (King & Corkery, 2010) for 5 substances (heroin, cocaine, amfetamines, MDMA/ecstasy, cannabis; substances recorded among other mentions or as sole mentions on death certificates); dependence scores correlated r=0.95 with US lifetime dependence (Anthony et al., 1994) for 5 drugs (tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, heroin).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th to 7th paragraphs (p. 1563); references 12 to 14 (p. 1565)
key_findings.note: Correlations on 5 to 12 drugs; no harm-to-others criterion was compared quantitatively. For social harms the Discussion only points to outside estimates (accidents, drug-related violence, costs to provider countries) and police records, without comparing them with the scores (8th paragraph, pp. 1563–1564).

key_findings.finding: Overall scores correlated r=0.70 with the 2007 nine-criteria UK expert rating (15 drugs in common), 0.80 and 0.84 with the Dutch expert ranking's individual and population totals, and 0.04 with the UK Misuse of Drugs Act classification, which the authors describe as effectively no relation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 1561); 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 1562)

key_findings.finding: Unlike the 2007 rating, which used four-point ratings of risk averaged without weights, the ISCD scored harm, not risk (the probability of harm), on ratio scales; the authors attribute the wider spread of the new scores to this scaling.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: only harms were scored, not benefits; harms depend on availability and legal status, so results may not apply to countries with different laws and cultures; the model does not separate harms of drug use from harms of the control system; it does not cover prescribed use; polydrug use, routes, patterns of use and context were not modelled; and a low score does not mean a drug is not harmful.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Editors' reading of the Figure 2 stacked bars at 300 dpi: alcohol is the only one of the 20 drugs whose harm-to-others part (about 46) is larger than its harm-to-individuals part (about 26). For every other drug the harm-to-individuals part is the larger, for example heroin 34 against 21 and crack cocaine 37 against 17 (printed part scores), tobacco about 17 against 9 and cannabis about 12 against 8.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (stacked bars: segments for harm to individuals and harm to others)

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the lowest overall score as 5 for mushrooms and the highest-to-lowest ratio as about 14:1, while Figures 2 and 4 print 6 for mushrooms (a ratio of 12:1, editors' arithmetic). At 300 dpi the mushrooms bar measures about 5.5 in both figures (editors' reading; the Figure 3 point, about 12 and 0, gives the same), so 5 and 6 are probably both roundings of one value; on the bar the ratio is about 13:1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, a rounding difference rather than two results; give the lowest score as about 5.5 (6 in the figures, 5 in the text).

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2, titled as drugs ordered by overall harm score, places khat (label 9) before anabolic steroids (10) and ecstasy (9); Figure 4 repeats the order. At 300 dpi the labels match the bars (khat about 8.9, anabolic steroids about 9.7, ecstasy about 9.1, editors' reading of both figures), so the bars themselves are out of order and rounding does not explain it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the three scores lie within about one point of each other, but the figures' order of khat, anabolic steroids and ecstasy is not a ranking and should not be cited as one.

reporting_issues.issue: The worked example of weighting names the two mortality criteria the wrong way round: drug-related mortality is said to get the larger swing weight (100) and drug-specific mortality 80, but the next sentence says the scores on the drug-related mortality scale were multiplied by 0.8, so that heroin's weighted harm became 80 against its score of 100 on drug-specific mortality. The Figure 4 key (6.4 against 5.1) agrees with the first statement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weights in Figure 4 are presumably those used; anyone explaining how the weighting worked should follow the key, not the example.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text lists the drugs most harmful to others as alcohol (46), crack cocaine (17) and heroin (21), out of numerical order; the Summary orders them alcohol, heroin, crack cocaine. Both the Summary and the Results also list the drugs most harmful to the people who use them out of numerical order, as heroin (34), crack cocaine (37) and metamfetamine (32).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the numbers agree with each other and with Figure 2: crack cocaine is first on harm to individuals and heroin second on harm to others, so the order of these lists should not be read as a ranking.

reporting_issues.issue: On p. 1562 the Dutch expert ranking is cited as reference 2 (Murphy et al., 2007, a letter on drug-related harm), whereas on p. 1561 the same ranking is reference 8 (van Amsterdam et al., 2010); the committee is also misspelled ICSD once (p. 1563).
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; the correlations of 0.80 and 0.84 belong to van Amsterdam et al. (2010).

reporting_issues.issue: The number and names of the panel members, how many scored each criterion, and any individual or pre-discussion scores are not in the article (the webappendix was not among the files read).
reporting_issues.consequence: The breadth of expert opinion behind each score, and the extent of agreement, cannot be judged from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The criterion scores (16 for each of the 20 drugs) and the unweighted part scores are not tabulated; they can be read only approximately from Figures 3 and 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any single-criterion score (for example a drug's dependence score) cited from this paper is an approximate reading of a stacked bar.

design_detail: Meta-analysis of 11 controlled (experimental or quasi-experimental) outcome evaluations of the original Project D.A.R.E. school curriculum, published in peer-reviewed journals 1991–2002, pooling one effect size per study (r and Cohen's d) for substance-use behaviour (alcohol, tobacco and illicit drug use, combined) at follow-ups from immediately after the programme to 10 years. Searches of ERIC, MEDLINE and PsycINFO in late fall 2002 plus reference lists; roughly 40 articles reviewed. A 3-page brief report: no protocol, no appraisal of the primary studies, no heterogeneity statistics, and the pooling model not named.
can_establish: The average effect on self-reported substance use of the original D.A.R.E. curriculum across the 11 peer-reviewed controlled evaluations the authors found up to 2002: close to zero (d=0.023, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.08).
cannot_establish: The effect of the curriculum as revised from 2001 (no evaluation of it existed); effects on any single substance (outcomes were combined within each study); effects on knowledge or attitudes (excluded); a reliable upper bound on benefit (clustering within schools was ignored and four study effects were set to zero rather than computed); or whether the primary studies were at risk of bias (none was appraised).

sample.recruitment: Database searches (ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO) in late fall 2002 and the reference lists of retrieved articles (p. 1027). The primary studies sampled school students in grades 5 to 12, 236 to 2878 per study (Table 1, p. 1028). Table 1 gives no country: the article frames D.A.R.E. as a US programme (p. 1027) without stating where each study was done.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: (1) Published in a peer-reviewed journal (dissertations, theses, books and unpublished manuscripts excluded, as a filter for rigorous methods); (2) a control or comparison group (experimental or quasi-experimental design); (3) assessments before and after the intervention of at least one of alcohol use, illicit drug use or tobacco use. Only effect sizes on actual use were taken (p. 1027).
sample.demographics: From Table 1 (p. 1028): grades 5 and 6 (Ringwalt 1991, n=1270; Ahmed 2002, n=236), grade 5 (Becker 1992, n=2878; Harmon 1993, n=708), grades 7 and 8 (Ennett 1994, n=1334), grades 6 and 7 (Rosenbaum 1994, n=1584), grade 12 (Wysong 1994, n=619), grade 9 (Dukes 1996, n=849), grade 6 (Zagumny & Thompson 1997, n=395; Lynam 1999, n=1002), grades 5 through 10 (Thombs 2000, n=630). Sex and ethnicity are given for some studies only (for example 50% African American in Ringwalt 1991; 90.4% Anglo in Thombs 2000).
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level; the n listed for each study is not stated to be the analysed sample (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: Journal articles only, from three databases, with language limits not stated and no grey literature: the earlier meta-analysis (Ennett et al., 1994) had included reports produced for agencies associated with D.A.R.E., which this one excluded on purpose (p. 1027). The roughly 29 excluded articles are not listed (editors' arithmetic from roughly 40 reviewed).

exposure.measurement: Receipt of the original D.A.R.E. curriculum against each study's control or comparison condition; programme content, delivery and comparison conditions are not described.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol, tobacco and illicit drug use were combined into one effect per study; where a study gave two or more effect sizes in the same outcome category, their mean was used (p. 1027). How categories were combined within a study is not stated.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Follow-up ranged from immediately after the programme (4 studies) to 10 years (Lynam 1999) (Table 1; Figure 1, p. 1028).

comparison.controls: The control or comparison groups of each primary study, not described (no programme, another curriculum or usual health education is not stated).
comparison.matching: Not reported; randomized and quasi-experimental studies were pooled together without being distinguished.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline equivalence of D.A.R.E. and comparison groups is not reported for any study.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported alcohol, tobacco and illicit drug use as measured in each primary study (instruments not described). Effect sizes were calculated by Rosenthal's procedures from reported F, t and chi-square statistics or means and standard deviations, and expressed as r and as d (p. 1027).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not addressed.
outcomes.operationalization: Effectiveness meant a difference in substance-use behaviour between the D.A.R.E. and comparison groups; knowledge, attitudes and other mediating outcomes were excluded on purpose (p. 1027). Positive r and d favour D.A.R.E., negative values the comparison group (Table 1 note, p. 1028).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (one pooled estimate).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Duplicate screening or extraction is not described; the authors state that both contributed equally to design, analysis and writing (Contributors, p. 1029).

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled weighted effect: r=0.011, d=0.023, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.08 (the interval is on the d scale); cumulative significance test z=0.73, not significant (Results, p. 1028; abstract, p. 1027). Study effects (Table 1, p. 1028): from Becker 1992 (r=−0.058, d=−0.117, 95% CI −0.19 to −0.04, favouring the comparison group) to Ahmed 2002 (r=0.198, d=0.405, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.80, smoking only); Zagumny & Thompson 1997 d=0.376 (0.07 to 0.68); four studies entered as 0.000, footnoted as assumed effect sizes (Ennett 1994, Rosenbaum 1994, Wysong 1994, Lynam 1999). Editors' calculation from Table 1: a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects pooling of the printed d values, with standard errors taken from the printed intervals, reproduces the published estimate (d=0.023, 95% CI −0.039 to 0.085; z=0.74 against the printed 0.73), while a fixed-effect pooling gives d=−0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034); Cochran's Q=21.6 on 10 df (p about 0.02), I-squared about 54%. The paper names neither its model nor any heterogeneity statistic.
analysis.selective_reporting: No results by substance, design or follow-up period beyond a scatterplot of effect sizes against follow-up time (Figure 1, p. 1028).
analysis.power: Not addressed. The printed pooled interval excludes a d of 0.2 (Cohen's small effect), but because school clustering was ignored it is narrower than it should be.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 11 peer-reviewed controlled evaluations of the original D.A.R.E. curriculum (1991–2002), the pooled effect on substance-use behaviour was close to zero: d=0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08). Two small studies found benefits (one measured smoking only), the largest study found slightly more substance use in the D.A.R.E. group, and four studies were entered as zero effects; 9 of the 11 study intervals include zero or favour the comparison group (editors' count from Table 1). Study effects varied more than chance alone would predict (I-squared about 54%, editors' calculation).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the study supports earlier findings that "D.A.R.E. is ineffective" (p. 1027). For substance use after the original curriculum the data support this, the interval excluding effects as large as Cohen's small benchmark. Three overstatements: (1) the Discussion says the pooled effect would have needed to be "20 times larger to be considered even small" (p. 1028), whereas Cohen's small benchmarks (d=0.2, r=0.1) are about 9 times the pooled values (editors' calculation); (2) the conclusion is phrased about D.A.R.E. in general, although the authors note that the curriculum was revamped in 2001 and the new version had not been evaluated (p. 1029); (3) the pooled interval is narrower than it should be because many studies analysed students rather than schools, which the authors acknowledge but judge unlikely to matter (p. 1029). A headline version that D.A.R.E. made children more likely to use drugs is not supported: one study favoured the comparison group, two favoured D.A.R.E., and the pooled effect is zero.

timeline.event: Ennett, Tobler, Ringwalt & Flewelling: earlier meta-analysis of D.A.R.E. outcome evaluations (Am J Public Health), including non-peer-reviewed reports and immediate post-tests only: negligible positive effect sizes of 0.00 to 0.11 (as described in this paper, p. 1027; not read).
Lynam et al.: no effects of D.A.R.E. at 10-year follow-up (included here, entered as an assumed zero; not read).
D.A.R.E. curriculum substantially revamped, helped by a $13.6 million Robert Wood Johnson Foundation grant (the new D.A.R.E.; as described in this paper, p. 1029).
Ahmed et al.: smoking-only evaluation, the largest positive effect among the included studies (included here; not read).
This meta-analysis: pooled d=0.023 across 11 studies.

replication.where_it_stands: This brief meta-analysis and the earlier one by Ennett et al. (1994), as summarized here, agree that the original D.A.R.E. curriculum had no meaningful effect on substance use. The curriculum revised from 2001 is outside its scope, and later evaluations of it have not been read for this card. By current standards the meta-analysis is methodologically weak (no protocol, no appraisal of the studies, zeros imputed, clustering ignored), so its precision should not be over-read; its near-zero result holds under either pooling model (editors' calculation: fixed-effect d=−0.005, random-effects 0.023).

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article. Portions of the research were presented at the Eighth Annual Meeting of the Society for Prevention Research, June 2000 (Acknowledgments, p. 1029).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Rehabilitation Counseling, Virginia Commonwealth University (West) and Center for Developmental Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (O'Neal).

what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized trial of the current D.A.R.E. curriculum against an evidence-based alternative and against usual practice, analysed at the school level, with use of each substance followed into late adolescence; and, for the existing studies, a registered meta-analysis that computes rather than assumes every effect, adjusts for clustering, separates randomized from non-randomized studies and appraises risk of bias.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: All seven AMSTAR 2 critical items (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) are not met, which gives critically low confidence. The rating concerns how far the pooled number can be trusted, not the paper's value: it is a 3-page 2004 report that predates AMSTAR 2. Its near-zero result does not depend on the pooling model (editors' calculation: fixed-effect −0.005, random-effects 0.023) and agrees with the earlier meta-analysis; what cannot be trusted is its precision (clustering ignored, zeros imputed, no appraisal). Cite it for the absence of a meaningful pooled effect of the original curriculum on substance use, not for a precise bound.

key_findings.finding: Pooled effect of D.A.R.E. on substance-use behaviour across 11 studies: r=0.011, d=0.023 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.08), not significant (cumulative test z=0.73); positive values favour D.A.R.E.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1027); Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1028)

key_findings.finding: Of the 11 studies, four found no effect (entered as 0.000 and footnoted as assumed effect sizes), one found D.A.R.E. less effective than the comparison condition (Becker 1992: r=−0.058, d=−0.117, 95% CI −0.19 to −0.04, n=2878), and six found positive effects, mostly small; the largest (Ahmed 2002: r=0.198, d=0.405, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.80, n=236) examined smoking only.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Only two study intervals exclude zero in favour of D.A.R.E.: Zagumny & Thompson 1997 (6th graders, n=395, 4–5 years after D.A.R.E.; d=0.376, 0.07 to 0.68) and Ahmed 2002. Editors' count from Table 1: 9 of the 11 studies show no benefit distinguishable from chance (8 intervals include zero; 1 favours the comparison group).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: The four studies with an assumed zero effect are Ennett 1994 (n=1334, 2 years), Rosenbaum 1994 (n=1584, 1 year), Wysong 1994 (n=619, 5 years) and Lynam 1999 (n=1002, 10 years), including the longest follow-up (10 years) and a 5-year one. Editors' arithmetic: together 4539 of the 11,505 participants listed in Table 1 (39%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and footnote a
key_findings.note: Whether Wysong's 5 years is the second-longest follow-up depends on Thombs 2000, given in Table 1 as at least 1 to 6 years but plotted at 1 year in Figure 1 (reporting_issues[9]).

key_findings.finding: Follow-up ranged from immediately after the programme (Ringwalt 1991, Becker 1992, Harmon 1993, Ahmed 2002) through 1 year (Rosenbaum 1994), 2 years (Ennett 1994), 3 years (Dukes 1996, d=0.072), 4–5 years (Zagumny & Thompson 1997), 5 years (Wysong 1994) and at least 1 to 6 years (Thombs 2000, d=0.038) to 10 years (Lynam 1999). The authors note no noticeable effect in nearly half the reports, including the longest follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Figure 1; Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1028, continuing on p. 1029)

key_findings.finding: Searches of ERIC, MEDLINE and PsycINFO in late fall 2002 plus reference lists; roughly 40 articles reviewed; 11 studies published 1991–2002 met three criteria: peer-reviewed journal, a control or comparison group, and assessments before and after the intervention of alcohol, illicit drug or tobacco use. Only effects on actual use were taken; two or more effects in the same outcome category were averaged.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph and inclusion criteria 1 to 3; 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the pooled effect would have needed to be 20 times larger to be considered even small by Cohen's guidelines.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: Cohen's small effects (d=0.2, r=0.1) are about 8.7 and 9.1 times the pooled d and r, so about nine times, not 20; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that many included studies analysed individual students although students were nested in schools, which, citing Rosenbaum and Hanson (ref. 16), they say tends to overestimate effectiveness; they judge it unlikely to have changed the non-significant result.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Ignoring clustering mainly makes intervals too narrow, so the printed pooled interval overstates the precision of the null result.

key_findings.finding: All included evaluations were of the original (old) D.A.R.E. curriculum; the programme was substantially revamped in 2001, helped by a $13.6 million Robert Wood Johnson Foundation grant, and the authors found no major evaluation of the new model at the time of writing.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: D.A.R.E. is described as one of the most widely used US school-based prevention programmes and the largest single one by federal expenditure, with an average of about three quarters of a billion dollars a year spent on its provision (citing ref. 1).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A second-hand figure from McNeal & Hanson (1995, as printed in ref. 1), not a finding of this study.

key_findings.finding: The earlier meta-analysis of D.A.R.E. (Ennett et al., 1994) reported negligible positive effect sizes of 0.00 to 0.11 for outcomes immediately after the programme; it included non-peer-reviewed reports and only immediate post-tests, the two limitations this update set out to address.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 1027); reference 3 (p. 1029)

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from Table 1: random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) pooling of the printed d values, with standard errors from the printed intervals, reproduces the published estimate (d=0.023, 95% CI −0.039 to 0.085); fixed-effect pooling gives d=−0.005 (−0.043 to 0.034); Q=21.6 on 10 df, p about 0.02, I-squared about 54%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (editors' calculation)
key_findings.note: The paper names neither model nor heterogeneity; this reconstruction is the editors'. Its z (0.74) also matches the paper's test of cumulative significance (z=0.73), whereas an unweighted Stouffer combination of the study z values would give about 1.26 (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the pooled effect would have needed to be 20 times larger to count as small. Editors' calculation: Cohen's small benchmarks (d=0.2, r=0.1) are about 8.7 and 9.1 times the pooled d (0.023) and r (0.011).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 20-fold figure overstates how far the effect falls short of small; the accurate statement is about nine times smaller than Cohen's small effect.

reporting_issues.issue: Thombs (2000) has r=0.025 and d=0.038 in Table 1, but under the standard conversion the paper cites, r=0.025 corresponds to a d of at least 0.050 for any split of groups (editors' calculation); Ringwalt (1991), with the same r, has d=0.056.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values for Thombs is wrong; the effect on the pooled estimate is negligible.

reporting_issues.issue: For four studies (Zagumny & Thompson, n=395; Ahmed, n=236; Lynam, n=1002; Thombs, n=630) the printed 95% intervals are wider than the listed sample sizes would give, and group sizes and analysed samples are not reported. Editors' calculation under an equal-groups approximation, with the usual variance of d (including its d²/2N term): the intervals imply analysed samples of roughly 168, 100, 683 and 426, whereas the intervals of the other seven studies fit their listed n within rounding.
reporting_issues.consequence: The n column may give baseline or total samples rather than those analysed, so the total of 11,505 overstates the information behind the pooled estimate; the two largest positive effects come from the smallest analysed samples.

reporting_issues.issue: Four study effects are entered as 0.000 and footnoted only as assumed effect sizes, without saying why or how their intervals were derived.
reporting_issues.consequence: Imputing zeros pulls the pooled estimate towards zero, adds false precision and hides any non-significant effects those studies had in either direction.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says half of the included studies showed no benefit beyond chance (p. 1029), apparently counting the four zero effects and the one negative study; by the intervals in Table 1, 9 of the 11 studies show no benefit distinguishable from chance (editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper understates its own null pattern; use the Table 1 count.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives one effect per study, whereas the Methods describe averaging only within an outcome category (alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs); how categories were combined within studies, and which categories each study contributed, is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: No result for any single substance can be drawn from this meta-analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooling model and heterogeneity are not reported. Editors' calculation from Table 1: the published estimate is reproduced by a random-effects model, but not by a fixed-effect model (d=−0.005) or by sample-size-weighted (0.007) or unweighted (0.078) means of the printed d values; heterogeneity is moderate (I-squared about 54%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers cannot tell from the paper that the estimate depends on a random-effects model; the fixed-effect estimate is slightly below zero.

reporting_issues.issue: Thombs (2000) is described in Table 1 as 5th through 10th graders post-tested at least 1 to 6 years after D.A.R.E., while its reference (ref. 26) is titled as a retrospective study in undergraduates; a retrospective design would not obviously meet the criterion of assessments before and after the intervention.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unresolved without the primary paper; flag before citing the number of qualifying studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Two different Ennett et al. (1994) papers are cited: the earlier meta-analysis (ref. 3, Am J Public Health) and an included 2-year outcome study (ref. 21, Addictive Behaviors).
reporting_issues.consequence: Easy to confuse when citing; use the reference titles or DOIs.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 plots r, not d, against follow-up time and places the second point at r=0.025, which can only be Thombs (2000) since Ringwalt (1991) is plotted at 0, at 1 year, whereas Table 1 gives Thombs's follow-up as at least 1 to 6 years after D.A.R.E.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; Thombs's follow-up is uncertain, so only Lynam (1999, 10 years) can safely be called the longest follow-up; read the values in Figure 1 as r.
