design_detail: Cross-sectional online survey (the UK National Drug Survey, hosted at nationaldrugsurvey.org), launched on 21 July 2007 after a pilot with 50 people and advertised on internet sites, websites for people who use drugs, the BBC 'Horizon' website and by snowball e-mail; the closing date is not reported (p. 148). Respondents consented and confirmed they were over 18; 1501 UK residents completed it (p. 148). For each of 21 substances (the text says 20), respondents said whether they used it regularly, had used it, knew someone who had used it, or had no direct experience of it; everyone in the first three groups could rate the substance on the nine-parameter harm matrix of Nutt et al. (2007): acute, chronic and intravenous physical harm; intensity of pleasure, psychological and physical dependence; intoxication, social harms and health-service cost, each from 0 (no risk) to 3 (extreme risk); and on acute and chronic benefits, from 0 to 3 (p. 148). Mean ratings per substance were ranked and compared with each substance's class under the Misuse of Drugs Act (Kendall and Spearman rank correlations) and with the experts' ratings from Nutt et al. (2007), Table 3 (correlations across substances, overall and for each parameter, and one intra-class correlation per substance across the nine parameters) (pp. 148–151). Two of the authors were supported by an ESRC grant; D. J. Nutt, first author of the expert scale being tested, is a co-author.
can_establish: What a self-selected online sample of 1501 UK residents, recruited in 2007, rated as the harms and benefits of 21 substances on the nine-parameter scale of Nutt et al. (2007), and how closely the sample's mean ratings across substances tracked the experts' published ratings and the substances' legal class at the time.
cannot_establish: How harmful the substances actually are (the ratings are perceptions on an expert-designed matrix); whether people who use drugs in the UK in general hold these views (no sampling frame or response rate, a well-educated and mostly young sample, and for 12 of the 21 substances most of those able to rate it had not used it themselves); whether individual respondents' judgments agree with the experts' (only mean ratings per substance were correlated); or whether the agreement reflects independent knowledge rather than familiarity with the expert ranking, which the authors say had drawn wide government and media debate.

sample.recruitment: Advertisement (self-selected online survey): the website was launched on 21 July 2007 and advertised on various internet sites and websites for people who use drugs, on the BBC 'Horizon' website and through snowball e-mail (Method › Sample and Assessment, last paragraph, p. 148). Informed consent and confirmation of age over 18 were required before entry; a 'Withdraw' button discarded the respondent's data (1st paragraph, p. 148). 1501 individuals, all UK residents, completed the survey (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 148). Ethical approval: UCL Department of Psychology Ethics Committee (p. 153).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Over 18 and consenting (p. 148). The reported sample is all UK residents, but the paper does not say whether residence was an entry condition or a filter applied afterwards, how many started without completing, or whether repeat responses were checked. A substance could be rated by respondents who used it regularly, had used it, or knew someone who had used it (Method › Sample and Assessment, 1st paragraph, p. 148); the survey's format did not allow ratings to be separated by these levels of experience (p. 153).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (p. 149), percentages: age 18–24 34.9, 25–30 24.8, 31–40 22.7, 41–50 12.5, 51–60 5.1; education: no qualification 2.4, GCSE 12.5, AS/A level 25.3, degree 42.1, postgraduate degree 18.1, prefer not to say 0.01; employed 69.6, studying 21.9, unemployed 7.1, retired 1.2, prefer not to say 0.2; white 93.7, mixed Black/Asian 2.9, Black 0.9, Asian 1.7, Chinese/other 0.7; heterosexual 90.1, homosexual 4.8, bisexual 4.7; London 29.4, South 18.5, East Anglia/Midlands 16.1, North 17.1, Scotland/Wales/Northern Ireland 13.6, prefer not to say 5.3. Sex or gender is not reported anywhere in the paper.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). Not reported: how many people started the survey, and how many of those able to rate each substance actually rated it. The rows of Table 2 total 1384 (1385 for alcohol, cannabis and tobacco), so about 116 of the 1501 are not accounted for there (editors' calculation, p. 149).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected respondents reached through websites and e-mail chains: no sampling frame, no response rate and no weighting. The authors call the sample clearly self-selecting and largely well educated (60% with a university degree, which they think may have contributed to the high agreement with the experts), note its young age, and say minority and drug-dependent groups were not well represented (Discussion › Weaknesses of the survey, pp. 152–153). How many respondents had used any illegal drug is not reported; 1230 of the 1385 in the cannabis row of Table 2 had used cannabis (editors' sum, p. 149). Personal experience of the rated substance varied widely: of those able to rate a substance, the share who had used it themselves ranged from 99.5% for alcohol and 92.5% for cannabis to 22.6% for heroin (136 of 603), 22.9% for buprenorphine and 12.0% for anabolic steroids (editors' calculation from Table 2, p. 149). The survey was advertised on the BBC 'Horizon' website, and the authors note that the expert scale had stimulated considerable debate in government and the media (Introduction, p. 147), so respondents may have known the expert ranking.

exposure.measurement: Self-report: for each substance (listed with street names collected in pilot work as well as its actual name), one of four categories: regular use, having used it, knowing someone who had used it, or no direct experience or not heard of it (Method › Sample and Assessment, 1st paragraph, p. 148; Table 2, p. 149). 'Regular' is not defined. No amounts, frequency, recency, route, dependence or drug-related problems were asked; the authors list these as missing (p. 153).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured beyond the per-substance experience categories; combined use of different substances was not asked (Discussion › Weaknesses of the survey, p. 153).

comparison.controls: No control group. The main comparison is with the experts' ratings published by Nutt et al. (2007), taken from their Table 3 (Figure 2 caption, p. 150). This paper describes that expert work as two groups, 29 consultant psychiatrists specializing in addiction and a group of 8–16 professionals in various aspects of addiction, whose framework was developed by consensus (Introduction, p. 147); which group's ratings, or what combination, Table 3 of Nutt et al. holds is not stated here, and the experts' values are only plotted (Figure 2), not printed. The second comparison is each substance's class under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 at the time: A, B, C or unclassified (Figure 1, p. 150, where cannabis is shown as Class C).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. The same nine-parameter matrix and the same 0–3 scale as the experts (abstract and Method, pp. 147–148); respondents were also asked about benefits, which the experts had not rated.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as a premorbid baseline. Not measured: what respondents knew of the expert ranking or of the legal classes, where their views came from, and their own drug-related problems (p. 153).

outcomes.instruments: The nine-parameter matrix of Nutt et al. (2007), with detailed definitions as given in that paper (the survey's exact wording is said to be on the survey website; not read): physical harm (acute: harm after a single dose, such as the danger of overdose or permanent physical damage; chronic: harm from long-term or regular use; intravenous: the likelihood of intravenous use), dependence (intensity of pleasure from an acute dose, taken to relate to dependence-forming properties; psychological dependence; physical dependence) and social harm (intoxication: harm to property and others from a single dose; social harms: damage to the person's social network and achievement; health-service cost: overall cost, with respondents asked to take tax revenue into account for alcohol and tobacco), each rated 0 = no risk, 1 = some, 2 = moderate, 3 = extreme risk (Method › Sample and Assessment, p. 148). Benefits: acute (helping one relax, stay awake or socialize, or medical benefit) and chronic (long-term social or health benefit, or a positive change in one's perspective on the world), each 0 = no benefit to 3 = extreme benefit (p. 148).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the matrix for lay respondents and no reliability data are reported. Two parameters ask for judgments that are hard to make from personal experience: the health-service cost item asked respondents to weigh tax revenue against the overall cost to the economy for alcohol and tobacco (p. 148), and intensity of pleasure counts as a harm, which the authors suggest may have raised ecstasy's harm score (p. 152). The authors also note that weighting the nine parameters equally may misrepresent each substance's impact (p. 153). The intra-class correlation for each substance rests on its nine parameter means, so it partly reflects the general shape of the matrix (for example, intravenous use rated low for most substances) as well as agreement about that substance.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Harm' = mean rating of a parameter across all respondents able to rate the substance; category score = mean of its three parameters; overall harm = mean of all nine (p. 148). 'Agreement with the experts' = correlation across substances between the sample's means and the experts' ratings (overall and for each parameter), and an intra-class correlation for each substance between the two sets of nine parameter means (Results, pp. 148–149; Table 3, p. 151). 'Correspondence with the law' = rank correlation between legal class and the sample's harm ranking (p. 148).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. The alpha level for the correlations with the experts was Bonferroni-corrected to 0.005 (Results, 3rd paragraph, p. 148), which fits the overall correlation plus the nine parameter correlations. The 21 per-substance intra-class correlations were interpreted at p < 0.05 without correction (ten called significant, p. 149); at 0.005 four would remain (editors' count from Table 3, p. 151). Thirty-two tests in all: the legal-class correlation (two coefficients), 10 correlations with the experts and 21 intra-class correlations; the benefit ratings are descriptive only.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed online questionnaire).

analysis.effect_sizes: Legal class against the sample's harm ranking: Kendall 0.234 (p = 0.18), Spearman 0.301 (p = 0.19) (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 148); how the classes were coded is not described. Editors' check: coding the classes shown in Figure 1 from A = 3 to unclassified = 0 against the overall means computed from Table 3 gives Spearman 0.31 and Kendall 0.24 (p = 0.17) over 21 substances, and 0.23 and 0.18 over 20 without crack. Sample against experts across substances (the type of correlation is not named; Figure 2 plots mean ratings): overall r = 0.896 (p < 0.001), editors' 95% interval about 0.76 to 0.96 (Fisher z, 21 pairs); by parameter, acute 0.757, chronic 0.658 (p = 0.001), intravenous 0.716, psychological dependence 0.929, physical dependence 0.824, social harms 0.891 and health-service cost 0.880 (the others p < 0.001), while pleasure 0.559 (p = 0.008) and intoxication 0.508 (p = 0.019) missed the corrected 0.005 (Results, 3rd paragraph, pp. 148–149). Per-substance intra-class correlations across the nine parameters (Table 3, p. 151): alcohol 0.854, tobacco 0.85 and LSD 0.848 (each p = 0.001), heroin 0.769 (p = 0.002), cannabis 0.699 (0.013), khat 0.657 (0.01), street methadone 0.611 (0.034), GHB 0.605 (0.008), ecstasy 0.588 (0.02), amphetamines 0.574 (0.03), 4-MTA 0.569 (0.051), alkyl nitrates 0.439 (0.115), anabolic steroids 0.408 (0.086), benzodiazepines 0.103 (0.37); negative for ketamine −0.172 (0.699), cocaine −0.208 (0.708), solvents −0.291 (0.759), barbiturates −0.322 (0.988), buprenorphine −0.35 (0.809), methylphenidate −0.434 (0.853) and crack −0.453 (0.864). Overall harm means are shown only as bars in Figure 1; computed from Table 3 as the mean of the nine parameter means (editors' calculation) they run from 2.60 (heroin) and 2.34 (crack) to 0.83 (alkyl nitrates), in the same order as Table 3 and within about 0.02 of the bar heights. No standard deviations, confidence intervals or numbers of ratings are given for any mean.
analysis.covariates: None: no weighting and no adjustment. Ratings were not analysed by experience level (regular use, ever use, knowing someone), which the survey's format did not allow (p. 153).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration reported; ethical approval from the UCL Department of Psychology Ethics Committee (p. 153).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: the number of ratings behind each mean, any measure of spread, the benefit ratings as numbers (Figure 3 only) and the experts' values (only plotted, Figure 2). The type of correlation (overall and per parameter) and the intra-class correlation model are not named. Agreement within substances is summarized at an uncorrected threshold although a corrected one is stated for the correlations.
analysis.power: Not reported. The correlations across substances rest on 21 pairs of means; each intra-class correlation rests on nine pairs (one per parameter). The number of respondents able to rate a substance ranged from 89 (4-MTA) to 1381 (alcohol) (Table 2, p. 149).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2007, 1501 self-selected UK respondents (60% with a degree) gave mean harm ratings that ranked 21 substances much as the experts of Nutt et al. (2007) had (r = 0.896 across substance means; editors' interval about 0.76 to 0.96), agreeing on seven of the nine parameters but not significantly on pleasure (0.559) or intoxication (0.508). Within substances, the profile of the nine ratings agreed with the experts' at p < 0.05 for 10 of 21 substances (4 at p ≤ 0.005) and was below zero (a negative intra-class correlation, none significant) for 7, including crack and cocaine. The sample's harm ranking did not correlate significantly with legal class (Kendall 0.234, Spearman 0.301); alcohol, solvents and tobacco ranked 5th, 7th and 9th of 21. Ecstasy, cannabis and LSD had the highest mean benefit ratings, all below 2 (moderate) on the 0–3 scale (acute benefit about 1.8, 1.7 and 1.5; editors' reading of Figure 3). For heroin, crack, street methadone, GHB and eight other substances, most of those able to rate them had not used them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Abstract: a "remarkably high correlation" with the experts, implying that people who use drugs are "relatively well informed" about the harms of the drugs they use, and that the UK classification system is not acting to inform them of the harms (p. 147). Discussion: the findings support the scale of Nutt and colleagues and "demonstrate its utility with the general population" (p. 151); the classification has little bearing on whether people choose to use a substance, since ecstasy, a Class A drug, was the fourth most regularly used in the sample (p. 152); ecstasy's high benefit and low harm ratings question its Class A status (p. 152). Conclusions: a high agreement between experts and people who use drugs was demonstrated (p. 153). Gaps: (1) 'well informed' treats the experts' ratings, themselves consensus judgments, as the standard of truth, and the agreement could also reflect familiarity with the expert ranking, which the paper says had drawn wide debate (p. 147); (2) the sample is a self-selected, well-educated online sample, not the general population; (3) the abstract says that those with direct experience of a substance rated it, but people who only knew someone who had used a substance could rate it too, and they were the majority of those able to rate for 12 of 21 substances (Table 2, p. 149); (4) agreement holds for means across substances, while within substances it was negative for seven; (5) nothing measured why respondents chose to use a drug or what they knew of its legal class, so the statements about choice and about the law failing to inform rest on correlations of means and a count of regular use; (6) the 'high' benefits are means below the scale's 'moderate'.

timeline.event: Nutt, King, Saulsbury & Blakemore (Lancet 369:1047–1053): the expert ratings on the nine-parameter scale that this survey set out to test (cited from this paper's reference list; not read; no reference record).
This survey launched on 21 July 2007 (p. 148).
The authors report that they are collecting data on a revised version of the survey, at internationaldrugsurvey.org (Acknowledgements, p. 153); no results in this paper.

Nutt, King & Phillips: a later expert ranking of drug harms by the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs, reached in a decision conference (as described in the authors' 2011 reply; not read by this reader).
The authors' reply to six letters about the 2010 ranking (card sc_nutt_2011).

Reynaud et al. (J Psychopharmacol): damage-benefit ratings compared between the general population, people who use drugs and experts; on the project's General list (item 74); not read, no reference record.

replication.where_it_stands: No repeat of this comparison was among this reader's files, and none by an independent team or with a probability sample; Nutt is a co-author here and first author of the expert scale tested. The project's lists name later rankings and critiques of ranking drug harms (Caulkins et al., 2011; Rolles & Measham, 2011; Reynaud et al., 2013), not read by this reader.

funding.funder: As printed: "HVC & CJAM were supported by an ESRC grant (RES-000–23–0945)." (first-page footnote, p. 147).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: "The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare." (p. 153).
funding.affiliations_note: Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London (C. J. A. Morgan, L. Muetzelfeldt, M. Muetzelfeldt, H. V. Curran); Imperial College London, Division of Neurosciences and Mental Health (D. J. Nutt) (p. 147). Nutt is the first author of the expert scale this survey tested (Nutt et al., 2007, in the reference list, p. 153). By the contributions statement, Curran and Morgan designed the study, L. Muetzelfeldt, M. Muetzelfeldt and Morgan collected and analysed the data, and all authors contributed to, commented on and approved the paper (p. 153). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A survey with a sampling frame and known response (for example, people who use drugs identified within a general-population survey), recording each respondent's own experience of each substance and analysing ratings by experience, measuring whether respondents knew the published expert rankings, and reporting agreement with expert ratings at the level of individual respondents (with spread and numbers of ratings) rather than as correlations of group means.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: an open website advertised online and by snowball e-mail; the target population (people in the UK who use drugs) cannot be enumerated from it.
Self-selected volunteers; the authors call the sample clearly self-selecting (p. 152).

1501 overall, but those able to rate a substance ranged from 89 (4-MTA) and 140 (buprenorphine) to 1381 (alcohol), and the Results present these 'able to rate' counts (Table 2) as the numbers who rated, without a separate count of ratings given.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, education, employment, ethnicity, sexual orientation and region are given (Table 1), but not sex or gender, the closing date, how many started, or how residence was established.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: The rows of Table 2 account for 1384–1385 of the 1501; the number of ratings for each substance and parameter is not given apart from Table 2's 'able to rate' counts, which the Results present as the numbers rating.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The 'condition' is perceived harm, measured with the experts' own matrix and scale, which makes the comparison possible; but there is no validation for lay respondents, the question wording is not printed, and some items (health-service cost net of tax revenue) ask for judgments beyond personal experience.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online questions for all, but the raters' basis ranged from regular use to knowing someone who had used the substance and could not be separated (p. 153); no reliability data.

No spread or intervals, and no numbers of ratings beyond Table 2's 'able to rate' counts; correlations of means across substances with very unequal numbers of raters; correlation type and intra-class correlation model not named; agreement within substances summarized at an uncorrected threshold; substances counted as 20 in the text but analysed as 21.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Open web survey with no denominator: no response rate, no weighting and no comparison with a reference population is shown, although the Discussion says the sample broadly reflected UK prevalence of use by age and gender (pp. 152–153).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because the encyclopedia will use the survey's mean ratings, rankings and correlations. The figures describe what a self-selected, well-educated, mostly young and white UK online sample thought in 2007, many of them about substances they had not used, on a matrix designed by experts. The source may be cited for the sample's ratings and ranking of 21 substances, for the correlation of its mean ratings with the experts' ratings (r = 0.896 across substances, with the parameters and substances on which they did and did not agree), for the absence of a significant correlation with legal class at the time, and for the benefit ratings, each labelled as the perceptions of a self-selected online sample. It may not be cited for the actual harms of the substances, for the views of people who use drugs in the UK in general, for individual respondents' accuracy, for the claim that people who use drugs are well informed (the experts' ratings are judgments, not a criterion), or for any effect of the law on people's choices.

key_findings.finding: 1501 UK residents completed the online survey, which was launched on 21 July 2007 after a pilot with 50 people and advertised on internet sites, websites for people who use drugs, the BBC 'Horizon' website and by snowball e-mail; respondents consented and confirmed they were over 18.
key_findings.locator: Method › Sample and Assessment, 1st and last paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of the respondents, 34.9% were aged 18–24 and 5.1% were 51–60; 42.1% had a degree and 18.1% a postgraduate degree; 69.6% were employed and 21.9% studying; 93.7% were white; 29.4% lived in London. Sex or gender is not reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Anyone who used a substance regularly, had used it, or knew someone who had used it could rate it. Of the 603 able to rate heroin, 18 used it regularly, 118 had used it and 467 only knew someone who had; for crack 17, 143 and 428 of 588; for street methadone 17, 46 and 195 of 258; for alcohol 1180, 194 and 7 of 1381; for cannabis 508, 722 and 100 of 1330; for ecstasy 342, 541 and 305 of 1188.
key_findings.locator: Method › Sample and Assessment, 1st paragraph (p. 148); Table 2 (p. 149)
key_findings.note: For 12 of the 21 substances, most of those able to rate it had not used it themselves (editors' count from Table 2). The abstract says the raters were those with direct experience of a substance (p. 147).

key_findings.finding: Harms were rated on the nine parameters of Nutt et al. (2007), three each for physical harm (acute, chronic, intravenous), dependence (intensity of pleasure, psychological, physical) and social harm (intoxication, social harms, health-service cost), each from 0 (no risk) to 3 (extreme risk); a category score was the mean of its three parameters and the overall harm rating the mean of all nine. Acute and chronic benefits were rated from 0 (no benefit) to 3 (extreme benefit).
key_findings.locator: Method › Sample and Assessment, 2nd paragraph with its bullet lists, and 3rd and 4th paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Ranked by overall mean harm, the sample placed heroin first, then crack, cocaine, street methadone, alcohol, amphetamines, solvents, barbiturates and tobacco, with ecstasy 13th, LSD 16th, cannabis 18th, khat 20th and alkyl nitrates last (by the editors' count, Table 3 has 21 rows). Heroin, crack, cocaine and street methadone, all Class A, took the top four places, while three other Class A substances, ecstasy, LSD and 4-MTA, were in the lower half.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (p. 150); Table 3, order of rows (p. 151)
key_findings.note: The overall means are not printed. Computed from Table 3 as the mean of the nine parameter means (editors' calculation): heroin 2.60, crack 2.34, cocaine 2.07, street methadone 2.02, alcohol 1.92, amphetamines 1.71, solvents 1.59, barbiturates and tobacco 1.54, anabolic steroids 1.50, buprenorphine and ketamine 1.49, ecstasy and GHB 1.42, benzodiazepines 1.41, LSD 1.31, 4-MTA 1.30, cannabis 1.20, methylphenidate 1.16, khat 1.03, alkyl nitrates 0.83; these agree with the bar heights in Figure 1 to about 0.02 (Figure 1 places ketamine before buprenorphine). Classes as coloured in Figure 1.

key_findings.finding: The sample's harm ranking did not correlate significantly with the substances' class under the Misuse of Drugs Act (Kendall's rank correlation 0.234, p = 0.18; Spearman's 0.301, p = 0.19); alcohol, solvents and tobacco, all unclassified, were rated within the top ten.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: How the classes were coded is not described. Editors' check: coding the classes shown in Figure 1 as A = 3, B = 2, C = 1 and unclassified = 0 against the overall means computed from Table 3 reproduces Spearman 0.31 and Kendall 0.24 over 21 substances (0.23 and 0.18 over 20, without crack).

key_findings.finding: Across substances, the sample's overall mean ratings correlated with the experts' ratings from Nutt et al. (2007) at r = 0.896 (p < 0.001); the alpha level for these correlations was Bonferroni-corrected to 0.005.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 150)
key_findings.note: Editors' 95% interval about 0.76 to 0.96 (Fisher z, 21 pairs). The correlation is between group means across substances; it says nothing about agreement between individual respondents and the experts.

key_findings.finding: By parameter, the correlations with the experts were acute 0.757, chronic 0.658 (p = 0.001), intravenous 0.716, psychological dependence 0.929, physical dependence 0.824, social harms 0.891 and health-service cost 0.880 (the others p < 0.001), while pleasure (r = 0.559, p = 0.008) and intoxication (r = 0.508, p = 0.019) did not reach the corrected level.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 148, right column, continuing on p. 149, left column)
key_findings.note: The printed p values match 21 pairs rather than 20 (editors' calculation: pleasure gives p = 0.008 with 21 pairs and 0.010 with 20; intoxication 0.019 and 0.022; chronic 0.001 and 0.002).

key_findings.finding: Agreement between the sample's and the experts' profiles across the nine parameters (one intra-class correlation per substance) ranged from 0.854 for alcohol, 0.85 for tobacco and 0.848 for LSD (each p = 0.001) and 0.769 for heroin (p = 0.002) to negative values for seven substances: ketamine −0.172, cocaine −0.208, solvents −0.291, barbiturates −0.322, buprenorphine −0.35, methylphenidate −0.434 and crack −0.453 (p from 0.699 to 0.988).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, columns ICC and p
key_findings.note: The minus signs are printed on the page but are lost in a text extraction of the PDF (checked on the rendered page at 300 dpi).

key_findings.finding: The authors call agreement within substances significant for ten: alcohol, amphetamines, cannabis, ecstasy, GHB, heroin, LSD, khat, street methadone and tobacco.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (begins on p. 148; this sentence ends it, at the top of the right column of p. 149)
key_findings.note: These are the substances with p < 0.05 in Table 3 (p. 151); at the 0.005 level stated for the correlations, four remain: heroin, alcohol, tobacco and LSD (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: The authors describe heroin, cocaine and alcohol as rated consistently high and alkyl nitrates, cannabis, khat and methylphenidate as consistently low; tobacco's high overall place appeared, they say, to be driven by its dependence ratings (psychological 2.9, physical 2.8) and chronic physical harm (2.5); ecstasy had the highest pleasure rating (2.8) and LSD the fifth highest (2.2) while both were rated relatively low on harms; solvents were rated high on acute (2.1) and chronic (2.5) physical harm, and GHB was rated as having considerable acute physical harm (1.7).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 149, right column, continuing on p. 150); values from Table 3 (p. 151)

key_findings.finding: Acute benefits were rated higher than long-term benefits for every substance, and ecstasy, cannabis and LSD were rated highest on both.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th (last) paragraph (p. 150); Figure 3 (p. 151)
key_findings.note: The values appear only in Figure 3. Editors' reading against the gridlines (about ±0.02): acute benefit ecstasy 1.79, cannabis 1.67, LSD 1.49, then cocaine 1.48, methylphenidate 1.47 and benzodiazepines 1.46; chronic benefit LSD 1.16, ecstasy 1.08, cannabis 1.05, then methylphenidate 0.74; lowest acute benefit alkyl nitrates 0.64 and solvents 0.61. No substance's mean reached 2 (moderate benefit); no spread or test is given, so LSD's lead over cocaine, methylphenidate and benzodiazepines on acute benefit is a difference of about 0.01 to 0.03.

key_findings.finding: The experts had rated cannabis as more harmful than ecstasy, while the sample rated ecstasy as more harmful than cannabis; the authors suggest that ecstasy's high pleasure rating, counted as a harm in the matrix, may have raised its score, and name concerns about psychosis in vulnerable adolescents who use cannabis and negative media portrayal of ecstasy as other possible factors.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › The relationship between users' and experts' views, 3rd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 2 (p. 150): experts about 1.33 for cannabis and 1.1 for ecstasy; the sample 1.20 and 1.42 (means from Table 3).

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 plots the sample's overall rating against the experts' for each substance (by the editors' count, 21 points), with crack and cocaine at the same experts' value; off the diagonal, the sample rated barbiturates, benzodiazepines, ketamine and cocaine lower than the experts, and anabolic steroids, solvents, GHB, ecstasy and khat higher.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2
key_findings.note: Positions read by pixel against the axes (editors' reading, about ±0.03): crack and cocaine both at an experts' value of about 2.3; barbiturates about 2.06 (experts) against 1.54 (sample), benzodiazepines 1.73 against 1.41, solvents 1.27 against 1.59, anabolic steroids 1.18 against 1.50, ecstasy and GHB about 1.11 against 1.42, khat 0.80 against 1.03. LSD and 4-MTA overlap, as do ecstasy and GHB. Correlating these readings with the overall means from Table 3 gives r = 0.90 with crack and 0.89 without (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the close agreement suggests people who use drugs are relatively well informed about the harms of the substances they use, that the findings support the scale of Nutt and colleagues and show its utility with the general population, and that agreement was highest for alcohol, LSD, heroin and cannabis, with pleasure and intoxication the two parameters without agreement.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 151); Discussion › The relationship between users' and experts' views, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 152)

key_findings.finding: From the sample's ratings and the fact that ecstasy, a Class A substance, was the fourth most regularly used substance in the sample, the authors infer that legal classification has little bearing on whether people choose to use a substance, that the three-tier classification appears even less warranted than in Nutt et al. (2007), and that ecstasy's high benefit and low harm ratings question its Class A status; they add that the high benefit ratings for cannabis do not fit its move from Class C to Class B in 2008.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Implications for the Misuse of Drugs Act, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Perceived benefits of psychoactive substances, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Regular use in Table 2 (p. 149): alcohol 1180, tobacco 581, cannabis 508, ecstasy 342. Neither the reasons for using a substance nor knowledge of its legal class was measured.

key_findings.finding: The authors list as weaknesses a clearly self-selecting sample; a largely well-educated sample (60% with a university degree), which may have contributed to the high agreement with the experts; the young age of the sample, which limits judgments of long-term harm; poor representation of minority and drug-dependent groups; no data on drug-related difficulties, levels of use or combined use; and no way of separating ratings by level of experience. They add that it may be argued that weighting all harms equally, done to allow comparison with Nutt et al. (2007), misrepresents each substance's true impact.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Weaknesses of the survey, 1st paragraph (p. 152, right column, continuing on p. 153)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that respondents with direct experience of a substance rated its harms and benefits (p. 147), but the Method (p. 148) and Table 2 (p. 149) show that people who only knew someone who had used a substance could rate it too; they were the majority of those able to rate for 12 of 21 substances, for example 467 of 603 for heroin, 428 of 588 for crack and 287 of 326 for anabolic steroids, and the survey's format did not allow ratings to be separated by experience (p. 153).
reporting_issues.consequence: The ratings for heroin, crack, street methadone, GHB and the other eight such substances are largely the views of people without personal use; they cannot be cited as the views of people who use those substances.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (p. 147), the end of the Introduction (p. 148, which calls them the same 20 substances the experts rated), the Figure 2 caption (p. 150) and the Discussion (p. 152) speak of 20 substances, but Tables 2 and 3 and Figures 1 to 3 list 21, with crack and cocaine separately, and Figure 2 plots 21 points against experts' ratings, crack at the same experts' value as cocaine (about 2.3, editors' reading). The printed p values of the correlations fit 21 pairs, and the legal-class correlations can be reproduced over 21 substances but not over 20 (editors' calculations).
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparisons with the experts appear to include an experts' value for crack that the paper does not account for, possibly the cocaine value used twice; the correlations should be cited as computed over 21 substances, as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: 1501 people completed the survey (p. 148), but the rows of Table 2 do not add up to it (p. 149): by the editors' sums, each row totals 1384 (1385 for alcohol, cannabis and tobacco), leaving about 116 respondents unaccounted for. Table 2 counts those able to rate each substance, which the Results text presents as the numbers having experience and rating (p. 148); no count of ratings per parameter, and no separate count of completed ratings, is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators behind each mean rating are unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The alpha level for the correlations with the experts is Bonferroni-corrected to 0.005 (p. 148), but the per-substance intra-class correlations are called significant at p < 0.05 for ten substances (p. 149); at 0.005 four remain (Table 3, p. 151). The intra-class correlation model is not named, and the printed p values do not follow the order of the coefficients (for example GHB 0.605 with p = 0.008 against street methadone 0.611 with p = 0.034).
reporting_issues.consequence: Agreement within substances is weaker than the summary of ten significant substances suggests, and the two columns of Table 3 cannot be checked against each other.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion names alcohol, LSD, heroin and cannabis, in that order, as the substances with the highest agreement (p. 152); Table 3 places tobacco (ICC 0.85) second, between alcohol (0.854) and LSD (0.848) (p. 151).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the text omits tobacco.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the sample rated GHB as dangerous acutely but of much lower long-term risk, the reverse of tobacco (p. 152); Table 3 gives GHB 1.7 for acute and 2.0 for chronic physical harm (p. 151), and for every substance the sample rated chronic physical harm at least as high as acute.
reporting_issues.consequence: The GHB pattern holds only in relative terms: GHB ranks 5th of 21 on acute and 11th to 12th on chronic physical harm (editors' ranking from Table 3); it should not be cited as respondents judging GHB's long-term risk low.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the sample seemed broadly to reflect the prevalence of use in the UK across age and gender (pp. 152–153), but sex or gender is not reported anywhere (Table 1, p. 149) and no comparison with prevalence data is shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The representativeness statement cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The type of correlation behind r = 0.896 and the nine parameter correlations is not named; the abstract calls r = 0.896 a correlation between rankings (p. 147), while the Results and Figure 2 present it as agreement between mean ratings (pp. 148, 150).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite it as a correlation between mean ratings across substances, as plotted.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the 'prefer not to say' share for education is printed as 0.01%. By the editors' arithmetic, that is less than one person in 1501 (one person is 0.07%), and the education percentages sum to 100.4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one education figure is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper prints 'alkyl nitrates' (Tables 2 and 3) and 'Amyl nitrates/poppers' (Figure 2 legend) for the substances known as poppers, which the project files as alkyl nitrites; the legend of Figure 2 calls amphetamines 'Speed'; 4-MTA appears as 'flatliners' in Figures 2 and 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Names should follow the project's terms when citing (the project files poppers under alkyl nitrites); the paper's 'nitrates' should not be copied.

design_detail: Letter (Correspondence, The Lancet 377:555, 12 February 2011): the authors' reply by David Nutt, Larry Phillips and Les King to letters about their paper on the drug-harm scores of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs (ISCD). The reply calls it 'our paper' without a citation; the brief and the reference record identify it as Nutt, King & Phillips (2010). It answers six letters, naming their authors: John Britton and colleagues; Richard Peto and Jillian Boreham; Lee Claridge; Sheila Bird; Maria Viskaduraki and Diamanto Mamuneas; and Miles Hewstone. Its only data are one correlation the authors computed from figures in Bird's letter (r = 0.86 over five pairs); the rest is argument, statements about how the 2010 paper scored tobacco and how its scoring worked, and pointers to that paper's references 5 and 7. No reference list. Four paragraphs in the left column and the top of the middle column; the rest of the page holds two unrelated letters (not read).
can_establish: How the authors of the 2010 ISCD ranking answered the first published letters about it: what they conceded (that tobacco's total mortality is probably higher than that of all the other assessed drugs combined; that comparisons of harm scores can be misinterpreted), what they defended (the zero score for tobacco's drug-specific mortality, the decision conference as a way of limiting bias, the scoring of ties, and the validity of the scores), and how they say the scores treat the number of people using each drug.
cannot_establish: That the ISCD scores are valid or free of group bias: the one number offered is a correlation over five pairs from data the reply does not describe, the other correlations it invokes are not named, and the defence against group bias rests on the design of the method and on references not described in the reply, with no data on how individual scores changed during discussion.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The points answered were chosen by the authors from letters the journal published; each criticism is summarized in a clause or two. The letters themselves were not among this reader's files, so whether the reply represents them fairly cannot be checked here.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no individual data). The single number, r = 0.86, comes from the authors' correlation of five totals of male and female deaths in Sheila Bird's letter with the five corresponding ISCD scores for drug-specific mortality; which drugs, years and deaths the totals cover, and whether they are counts or rates, is not stated (3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (argument). The reply names ISCD criteria: drug-specific mortality, drug-related mortality, drug-specific damage, dependence and economic cost (1st paragraph); it distinguishes the scores for harms to the people who use a drug from the scores for harms to others (2nd paragraph); and it refers to scores out of 100, with ties allowed (4th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical analysis beyond one correlation).

analysis.effect_sizes: One statistic: r = 0.86 between five totals of male and female deaths (from Bird's letter) and the five corresponding ISCD scores for drug-specific mortality (3rd paragraph); no interval or test is given. Editors' calculation: with five pairs, two-sided p about 0.06 and 95% interval about −0.09 to 0.99 (Fisher z). Scores of the 2010 paper as the reply states them (not checked against that paper, which was not among this reader's files): tobacco zero for drug-specific mortality; the most harmful of all the drugs on drug-specific damage; second only to heroin for drug-related mortality; second to crack cocaine for dependence; second to alcohol for economic cost; and under 10 of 100 points on every other criterion (1st paragraph). Usually only one drug scored 100, and ties were allowed at any score (4th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: The 'high correlations' offered as validation despite national differences (4th paragraph) are given without values, data or source, and Bird's data are used without saying which drugs or deaths they cover.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the one correlation rests on five pairs.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A reply that concedes two points (tobacco's total mortality probably exceeds that of all the other assessed drugs combined; comparisons of harm scores can be misinterpreted), explains why tobacco scored zero for drug-specific mortality and how it scored on other criteria, says that the ISCD's scores for harm to the people who use each drug ignore how many people use it while its scores for harm to others take this into account, and offers one new number: a correlation of 0.86 over five pairs between Bird's death totals and the ISCD's drug-specific mortality scores.
interpretation_gap.claimed: That the five-pair correlation is "further validating our scores" (3rd paragraph); that the decision conference "is specifically designed to minimise bias", and that the three conditions under which an interacting group can outperform even its best member "were present in the ISCD decision conference" (4th paragraph); that despite national differences "the high correlations help to validate the ISCD's scores" (4th paragraph); and that the paper did not suggest reclassifying any drug but noted that the current classification is based on something other than harm (2nd paragraph). Gaps: (1) a correlation over five pairs has a 95% interval from about −0.09 to 0.99 and a two-sided p of about 0.06 (editors' calculation), and if Bird's totals are counts of deaths they mix how lethal a drug is with how many people use it, the very distinction the reply draws for the ISCD scores in its 2nd paragraph (it does not say whether drug-specific mortality is one of the scores for harm to the person); (2) the 'high correlations' are not specified; (3) the answer to the concern about group bias and more extreme ratings is a statement about the method's design and two references of the 2010 paper, not data such as individual scores before and after discussion; (4) the three conditions are not named. A summary saying the reply showed the ranking to be validated would overstate it.

timeline.event: Nutt, King & Phillips: the ISCD multicriteria ranking of drug harms that the reply defends (not among this reader's files).

Morgan et al., with Nutt as co-author: the mean ratings of 1501 self-selected UK respondents on the earlier expert scale of Nutt et al. (2007) correlated r = 0.896 with the experts' ratings across substances (card sc_morgan_2010c); not cited in the reply.

Letters in The Lancet by John Britton and colleagues, Richard Peto and Jillian Boreham, Lee Claridge, Sheila Bird, Maria Viskaduraki and Diamanto Mamuneas, and Miles Hewstone, as named in the reply (not among this reader's files; no reference records).
This reply (The Lancet 377:555, 12 February 2011).

Caulkins, Reuter & Coulson (Addiction), on basing drug scheduling decisions on rankings of harmfulness; listed on the project's harm-rankings list as one of the two principal critiques (not read by this reader).
Rolles & Measham (International Journal of Drug Policy), questioning the method and use of ranking drug harms in drug policy; listed likewise (not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: The reply answers by assertion what the letters raised about the method: whether the decision conference limited or introduced bias (no individual scores before and after discussion are reported here) and whether the scores are valid (one five-pair correlation and unnamed correlations). How far the ranking depends on its weights, and how the zero score for tobacco's drug-specific mortality affects tobacco's overall place, are not addressed. The project's General list records that its searches found no formal sensitivity analysis of the 2010 weights and no reply by the authors to the later critiques (section 10, known gaps); that is the list's statement, not checked by this reader.

Phillips); European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction, Lisbon (L. King). The authors are defending their own paper. what_would_settle_it: A repeat of the ranking by an independent panel using the same criteria and weights, recording each member's scores before and after discussion (to test the shift towards more extreme ratings that the letters raised), with a published sensitivity analysis of the weights and a test of the mortality scores against deaths per person using each drug, not total deaths, across more than five drugs.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies

domains.domain: Balance of the case for and against the ranking's method (the critics' arguments under-represented)
domains.note: Each letter's point is reduced to a clause; two points are conceded, but the concern about more extreme ratings after open discussion is answered only by a description of the method.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The reply is the authors' own answer to their critics. It may be cited for what the authors conceded and what they defended, for how they say tobacco scored on the ISCD criteria (labelled as the authors' statement), for their statement that the scores for harm to the person ignore how many people use each drug while the scores for harm to others take it into account, and for their statement that the paper did not propose reclassifying any drug. It is not evidence that the scores are valid or free of group bias: its one number rests on five pairs from undescribed data.

key_findings.finding: To John Britton and colleagues, and Richard Peto and Jillian Boreham, who say that mortality is higher for tobacco than for all the other assessed drugs combined, the reply concedes that this is probably true, but says tobacco was scored zero for drug-specific mortality because nobody dies directly from tobacco itself; that the authors judged tobacco the most harmful of all the drugs on drug-specific damage, second only to heroin for drug-related mortality, second to crack cocaine for dependence and second to alcohol for economic cost; and that on all the other criteria tobacco scored less than 10 points out of 100, because there is more to harm than deaths.

key_findings.finding: The reply states that the ISCD scores for harms to the people who use a drug do not take account of how many people use it, whereas the scores for harms to others do, and that this is why the overall rankings change depending on which of the two categories one looks at.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, end)

design_detail: Commentary (International Journal of Drug Policy 22:243–246; received 1 December 2010, revised 18 March 2011, accepted 26 April 2011) by S. Rolles (Transform Drug Policy Foundation, Bristol) and F. Measham (Lancaster University; a member of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs and of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs who attended both multicriteria decision analysis workshops). It questions the method and the policy use of single-figure drug-harm rankings, chiefly the ISCD analysis of Nutt et al. (2010). Argument with references to social-science, policy and some epidemiological sources; no data, no search, no reanalysis.
can_establish: The arguments, made in part from inside the expert process, that a single overall harm score does not practically capture how harm depends on dose, route, setting, polydrug use, individual vulnerability and the policy regime; that expert scoring without reported reliability is open to subjective error; and that rankings used to set criminal penalties rest on weak evidence.
cannot_establish: That the ISCD scores are wrong or that a different method would rank drugs differently: the commentary has no data or reanalysis, and several supporting examples are uncited or second-hand.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Sources chosen by the authors, mainly from sociology, criminology and drug policy. One author attended the workshops whose ranking is criticized (conflict statement, p. 246).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no data).
exposure.polysubstance: Argues that single-drug use, the model's focus, is the exception rather than the norm for many people who use drugs (EMCDDA, 2009, as cited) and that Nutt et al. mention polydrug use only in passing (p. 244).

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Contrasts two hypothetical people who inject heroin, one using illicit street heroin and one using prescribed pharmaceutical diamorphine under supervision, to argue that harm depends on the policy regime (pp. 244–245).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: None of its own. Discusses the ISCD model's 16 harm criteria (nine harms to the person using the drug, seven to others), with drug-specific mortality as the first criterion and dependence as the fifth (pp. 243–244).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm as scored by the ISCD panel; the commentary argues that even mortality and dependence, the most robust criteria, are arguably subject to a degree of social construction (p. 244).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical analysis).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The numbers given describe the ISCD model (criteria increased from nine to 16; twenty drugs ranked; alcohol most harmful) and MacCoun and Reuter's (2001) taxonomy of drug-related harms (forty-six harms in four categories; six groups who bear them; three primary sources of harm: use, illegal status and enforcement) (pp. 243, 245).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection; the ISCD's sensitivity analyses of the weights and the limitations the ISCD authors state themselves (companion card sc_nutt_2010, from Nutt et al., 2010, p. 1564) are not discussed.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A conceptual critique with seven strands: behavioural and contextual determinants of harm (dose, frequency, route, set and setting), individual vulnerability and polydrug use are not practically captured; mortality and dependence data are arguably subject to a degree of social construction; the overall index merges harms that do not move together (acute and chronic); expert value judgements, ratio scoring and swing weighting are used without reported inter-rater reliability; harms of use are not separated from harms of policy; in the UK, rankings serve to set criminal penalties, an approach with weak evidence; and benefits, including pleasure, are left out.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the delphic method highly vulnerable to subjective judgement and questions the utility of single-figure rankings (p. 243); the text also credits the Nutt papers with an "engaging and credible methodology" that usefully exposes flaws in UK classification (p. 243) and expects index rankings to keep a supporting role (p. 246). Gaps: (1) no evidence is offered that the ranking is wrong or would change under another method, and the commentary itself notes that ratings by people who use drugs gave similar results (Morgan et al., 2010, as cited, p. 244); (2) it describes two two-day workshops and a delphic method, whereas the companion card records Nutt et al. as describing a one-day decision conference with scores set in open group discussion (sc_nutt_2010, pp. 1558–1559); (3) several of its main points, polydrug use, routes and context, and the separation of drug harms from harms of control, are limitations Nutt et al. state themselves (companion card, p. 1564); (4) the near-zero overdose risk it gives for supervised prescribed diamorphine is uncited. A headline version, that drug-harm rankings have been discredited, would overstate it: the commentary argues the limits of one method and of its policy use, offers no alternative ranking, and expects rankings to keep a supporting role.

timeline.event: Nutt, King, Saulsbury & Blakemore (The Lancet): the nine-criteria rating that the 2010 model revised (as described, p. 243).
Beynon et al. question the accuracy of drug-related death data in the UK and Europe; cited for the social construction of mortality data (p. 244).
Nutt, King & Phillips: the ISCD multicriteria decision analysis of 20 drugs, the commentary's target (appraised on its own card).
Morgan et al. (J Psychopharmacol), harms rated by people who use drugs in the UK National Drug Survey, cited as giving results similar to the experts' (p. 244). Not read.
Nutt, King & Phillips, authors' reply in The Lancet (377:555), quoted for the decision conference being designed to minimize bias (p. 244). Not read.
Caulkins, Reuter & Coulson: the other principal published critique (appraised on its own card).

replication.where_it_stands: With Caulkins et al. (2011), one of the two published critiques the project's harm-rankings list requires beside the Nutt rankings. Both argue that a single overall score mixes different kinds of harm and that harm depends on legal status and policy; Rolles and Measham add behavioural and contextual determinants, the social construction of mortality and dependence data, the absence of reported inter-rater reliability, the problem of ignorance about new substances and the omission of benefits. Whether later rankings answered these points has not been read here.

funding.funder: Not reported (the acknowledgements thank anonymous referees only).
funding.declared_conflicts: Measham is a member of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs and of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs, attended both MCDA workshops and receives travel expenses only for these advisory roles; she writes in her capacity as Senior Lecturer in Criminology at Lancaster University, and the views are not those of the ACMD or ISCD (p. 246). No statement is made for Rolles.
funding.affiliations_note: S. Rolles: Transform Drug Policy Foundation, Bristol (p. 243); the commentary cites his 2010 BMJ article on alternatives to the war on drugs for policy alternatives (pp. 245–246). F. Measham took part in the expert workshops whose ranking she critiques. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the commentary.

what_would_settle_it: Rankings re-run by the same method under different policy regimes (for example illicit supply against prescribed, supervised supply), by different panels with inter-rater reliability reported, and separately for harm to the person and harm to others; and, for the policy argument, evaluations of whether classification by harm changes use or harm.

domains.note: No search or criteria; sources chosen by the authors.
Most points are referenced, but sources are not appraised; Rat Park is cited through a 2001 speech and the Vietnam veterans through a 1974 government report.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors' own works (Measham, 2004; Moore & Measham, 2011; Rolles, 2010) are cited for side points only.

Most claims are framed as arguments, but a few empirical statements are uncited (near-zero overdose risk with supervised prescribed diamorphine; the acute and chronic risk profiles of cigarettes and opiates).

domains.domain: Balance of the case for and against harm rankings (the case for rankings under-represented)
domains.note: Credits the method and notes that ratings by people who use drugs agree with the experts', but does not engage with the ISCD's sensitivity analyses or its stated limitations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. A reasoned critique without data or search, partly written from inside the expert process. It may be cited for its arguments, especially that harm depends on how, where and under what policy a drug is used and that a single score hides this; not for any claim that a particular drug is more or less harmful than the ranking says.

key_findings.finding: Summarizes the 2010 model: it raised the number of harm criteria from nine to 16 (nine harms to the self, seven to others), weighted each, and ranked twenty of the most commonly used legal and illegal drugs, with alcohol the most harmful; criteria and weights were decided by experts at two two-day workshops, held by the ACMD and then by the ISCD, both facilitated by Phillips.
key_findings.locator: Introductory paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: The companion card records Nutt et al. as describing a one-day decision conference in June 2010, with the criteria chosen at a special 2009 ACMD meeting (sc_nutt_2010, pp. 1558–1559); the two accounts differ. Measham attended both workshops (p. 246).

key_findings.finding: Credits Nutt et al. (2007, 2010) with an engaging and credible methodology that usefully highlights flaws in UK drug classification, notably the mismatch between scientific harm evaluations and the ABC classes of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and, for alcohol and tobacco, between harm and legal status.
key_findings.locator: Challenging ranking systems, 1st paragraph (right column, continuing on p. 244)

key_findings.finding: Argues that harm reflects pharmacology filtered through social, behavioural and environmental variables and the policy regime, from prohibition to legal regulation, a complexity that a single-figure index does not practically capture, nor is such an exercise necessarily useful for policy.
key_findings.locator: Challenging ranking systems, 2nd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Argues that ranking primarily by pharmacology misses behavioural determinants of risk (dose, frequency of use, preparation and route, set and setting), differences in vulnerability between individuals and subgroups, and polydrug use, which for many people who use drugs is the norm (EMCDDA, 2009, as cited), points Nutt et al. mention only briefly or in passing.
key_findings.locator: The social construction of drug-related harms, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: Argues that even pharmacological risks that are relatively easy to quantify, such as acute toxicity or propensity to induce dependence, are arguably subject to a degree of social construction. For drug-specific mortality, which it says the model positions as its first and most robust measure, it cites authors who question the accuracy of drug-related death data in the UK and Europe, suggesting that the data miss some deaths that could be attributed to drug use, such as from blood-borne viruses, yet include accidental and poisoning deaths of people without problem drug use (Corkery, 2008; Beynon et al., 2007, as cited), and Cruts (2000) for the potential subjectivity of attributing cause in drug-related deaths. Dependence, it says, has been seen as contingent on social factors (Rat Park, as described in a 2001 speech by Alexander; Vietnam veterans, most of whom stopped heroin use on returning to a less stressful environment, Robins, 1974; UK studies of occasional and regular heroin use).
key_findings.locator: The social construction of drug-related harms, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Argues that the overall harm index merges rankings of harms that do not agree, for example cigarettes with low acute but high chronic risk and most opiates arguably the reverse; the model allows this variation to be examined to a degree, but the overall index, which indicates one drug to be apparently more harmful than another, begins to lose its meaning in this context.
key_findings.locator: The social construction of drug-related harms, 5th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Argues that reliance on expert value judgements, magnified by ratio scoring and value-based swing weighting, leaves the model open to subjective error, and that no reliability indicators such as inter-rater reliability are reported; notes Cohen's (2010) question whether a different panel would change the ranking, and that ratings by people who use drugs gave similar results to the experts' (Morgan et al., 2010, as cited), while holding that evidence and value judgements remain intertwined.
key_findings.locator: The social construction of drug-related harms, 6th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Raises the problem of ignorance: for new psychoactive substances such as mephedrone and naphyrone the evidence base is negligible (ACMD, 2010b, 2010c, as cited).
key_findings.locator: The social construction of drug-related harms, 7th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Argues that the model largely fails to separate harms of use from harms of the policy environment, contrasting a person who injects street heroin of unknown strength and purity with possibly shared equipment, funds use through crime and has HIV, hepatitis C and a criminal record, with a person who injects prescribed pharmaceutical diamorphine of known strength in a supervised clinic with clean equipment, described as having near-zero risk of overdose death and no offending to fund use.
key_findings.locator: Disaggregating drug use harms from drug policy harms, 1st paragraph (p. 244, right column, continuing on p. 245)
key_findings.note: The near-zero overdose risk is the authors' assertion; no source is cited.

key_findings.finding: Proposes re-running the harm analysis for different policy contexts, since prescribed and supervised supply exists beside illicit supply, a suggestion the authors say Nutt welcomed in public debate in 2010; cites MacCoun and Reuter's (2001) taxonomy of forty-six harms in four categories, six groups who bear them and three primary sources of harm (use, illegal status, enforcement).
key_findings.locator: Disaggregating drug use harms from drug policy harms, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: Notes that the UK Government describes the classification system's purpose as setting criminal penalties with predominant reference to a drug's harm (HM Government, 2010), argues that evidence for the efficacy of this approach is weak and its evaluation systemically poor (House of Commons Public Accounts Committee, 2010), and that harms caused by policy, such as crime around the illegal trade and offending to fund dependence, are conflated with harms of use.
key_findings.locator: Relating rankings to drug policy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column, continuing in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Suggests that it could be argued that policy and personal decisions need to weigh harms against actual or potential benefits, which would theoretically need a parallel exercise for benefits, including pleasure, the money people are prepared to spend on drugs, the economic activity of drug markets and social benefits such as a sense of community in dance clubs; but adds that it could also be argued that attempts to quantify benefits are doomed, because cost–benefit analyses position the person who uses drugs as a rational actor and tend to overestimate rationality and underestimate the social and emotional nature of drug decisions.
key_findings.locator: The cost–benefit analysis, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Concludes that even refined single-index models are of limited use, likely to become increasingly so; that index rankings will continue to have a role, perhaps more to augment other forms of risk analysis, but seem likely to matter less as enforcement moves away from punitive responses to people who use drugs, or if harm assessments are decoupled from punishment, as the UK Parliamentary Science and Technology Select Committee recommended in 2006; that if analysis is to capture the complexity of drug use and its contexts, the various harm vectors must remain separate; and that government should review drug policy and law in the UK and, by implication, similar systems elsewhere, including the UN scheduling system.
key_findings.locator: Beyond rankings and classifications, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 245, right column, to p. 246, left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary describes two two-day expert workshops; the companion card records Nutt et al. (2010) as describing a one-day decision conference in June 2010, with the criteria set at an earlier ACMD meeting (sc_nutt_2010, pp. 1558–1559).
reporting_issues.consequence: Unresolved from the two papers; Measham attended both workshops (p. 246). Cite the process as Nutt et al. describe it and note the difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The method is called delphic (abstract, p. 243; p. 244), while per the companion card the ISCD scores were set in open group discussion at a decision conference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The word should not be read as the Delphi technique of anonymous, repeated rounds.

reporting_issues.issue: Several supporting points rest on secondary or non-peer-reviewed sources or on none: Rat Park through a 2001 speech, the Vietnam veterans through a 1974 government report, Nutt's welcome of policy-specific re-runs through a 2010 public lecture; Nutt's eagerness for participatory panels and the near-zero overdose risk with prescribed diamorphine are uncited.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the primary sources, not this commentary, for these facts.
