design_detail: Expert-judgement scoring exercise, published as a Health Policy article. The authors' matrix of nine harm parameters in three categories (physical harm: acute, chronic, intravenous harm; dependence: intensity of pleasure, psychological dependence, physical dependence; social harms: intoxication, other social harms, health-care costs) was scored on a four-point scale (0 no risk, 1 some, 2 moderate, 3 extreme risk) by two groups: 29 of 77 consultant psychiatrists on the Royal College of Psychiatrists' register of addiction specialists, by questionnaire, for 14 substances; and a multidisciplinary group (chemistry, pharmacology, forensic science, psychiatry and other medical specialties including epidemiology, legal and police services) in four delphic meetings of 8 to 16 members, for 20 substances. Scores were averaged across scorers with equal weights into category means and an overall mean of the nine parameters. The independent group's ranking was compared with the substances' classes under the UK Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 by rank correlation, and the two groups' overall means for 14 substances were plotted against each other. No harm was measured: every input is expert judgement (pp. 1049–1050).
can_establish: How two groups of UK experts, rating before January 2007 with the authors' nine-parameter matrix, a 0–3 scale and equal weights, judged the relative harm of 20 substances (14 for the psychiatrists), and how weakly that ranking tracked the substances' Misuse of Drugs Act classes at the time.
cannot_establish: That any substance is measurably more or less harmful than another (the scores are judgements, not validated against deaths, illness, dependence or costs); whether neighbouring substances differ at all (no spread, numbers of scorers or intervals are reported); how crack and powder cocaine compare (rated as one substance); harm at particular doses, routes or patterns of use, per person who uses a substance or across the population; the ranking under other weights, with other experts, in other countries or in later years; benefits (not rated); or what classes the law should use.

sample.recruitment: Psychiatrists: the national group of consultant psychiatrists on the Royal College of Psychiatrists' register as specialists in addiction; 77 were asked to rate 14 substances, and replies from 29 were received and analysed (Assessment of harm, 2nd paragraph, p. 1049). Independent group: experts with experience in one of the areas of addiction (chemistry, pharmacology, forensic science, psychiatry and other medical specialties including epidemiology, legal and police services), convened by the authors after the matrix had been found to work (Assessment of harm, 3rd paragraph, pp. 1049–1050); how they were identified or invited, how many took part in all, and who they were are not reported. Between 8 and 16 members scored at each of four meetings, the authors stating that the full range of expertise was kept at every assessment (p. 1050). The scoring procedure had first been piloted by members of the panel of the Independent Inquiry into the Misuse of Drugs Act (p. 1049; reference 13).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Experts: no criteria beyond those above are reported. Substances (Table 2, p. 1049): the psychiatrists' 14 (heroin, cocaine, alcohol, barbiturates, amphetamine, methadone, benzodiazepines, solvents, buprenorphine, tobacco, ecstasy, cannabis, LSD, anabolic steroids) plus, for the independent group, khat, 4-MTA, GHB, ketamine, methylphenidate and alkyl nitrites, added for completeness, some not illegal but each reported to be used non-medically (p. 1050). Five legal substances (alcohol, khat, solvents, alkyl nitrites, tobacco) and ketamine, uncontrolled when assessed, were included for reference (abstract, p. 1047); tobacco and alcohol as familiar benchmarks (p. 1049). Cocaine includes crack cocaine, heroin is crude diamorphine and street methadone is diverted prescribed methadone (Table 2).
sample.demographics: Not reported for either group: no professions by number, names, years of experience or interests. The psychiatrists who did not reply are not described.
sample.attrition: Psychiatrists: 29 of 77 replied (37.7%, editors' calculation). Independent group: attendance varied from 8 to 16 across the four meetings, each meeting covering only a few drugs; how many experts scored each drug, and how many individual scores were missing and ignored, are not reported (p. 1050).
sample.selection_effects: Neither group is a defined sample: the psychiatrists are a 38% response from one professional register, and the selection of the independent group is not described. The psychiatrists were on a UK register, and where the independent group's members worked is not stated; the listed areas of expertise do not include people who use drugs. Whether any author scored is not stated. Different drugs were scored at different meetings by different subsets of 8 to 16 members, so drugs rated at different meetings rest on different sets of experts. The independent group was given seven recent review articles (references 5–7 and 15–18), three of them by Nutt or King (references 5, 17 and 18; p. 1050 and p. 1053); who chose them, and on what basis, is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study: each substance is the unit of analysis, and its harm is the experts' rating on each of nine parameters (0 no risk, 1 some, 2 moderate, 3 extreme risk), given on an assessment questionnaire based on Table 1 with guidance notes, which are not given in the article (Assessment of harm, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, p. 1049).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not specified. Participants were asked to rate each drug in the form in which it is normally used (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 1052); no doses, frequencies, durations or patterns of use were defined. Route enters as a parameter (intravenous harm, parameter three): Table 3 gives 0 for the substances not injected and NA for alcohol (p. 1051). Crack and powder cocaine were not rated separately, nor were individual benzodiazepines (p. 1052).
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled. The authors note that cannabis is commonly smoked mixed with tobacco, which may have raised its physical-harm and dependence scores, and that polydrug use in the recreational group (GHB, ketamine, ecstasy, alcohol) adds uncertainty, because adverse effects may come mainly from one component of a mixture (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 1052).

comparison.controls: No control group. Two comparisons: the psychiatrists' and the independent group's overall means for the 14 substances rated by both (Figure 2, p. 1050; Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 1051), and the independent group's ranking against Misuse of Drugs Act class (A, B, C or not controlled) by Kendall's and Spearman's rank correlations (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1050).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to substances. The experts' prior views, professional interests and familiarity with each drug were neither measured nor reported.

outcomes.instruments: The authors' nine-parameter matrix (Table 1, p. 1049): physical harm (one, acute; two, chronic; three, intravenous harm), dependence (four, intensity of pleasure; five, psychological dependence; six, physical dependence) and social harms (seven, intoxication; eight, other social harms; nine, health-care costs), each scored on a four-point scale with verbal anchors only (0 no risk, 1 some, 2 moderate, 3 extreme risk). The procedure was piloted by members of the Independent Inquiry panel and then used as a questionnaire with guidance notes (p. 1049). The psychiatrists rated by questionnaire. The independent group scored independently, then each parameter's scores were shown to the whole group for discussion of the reasoning behind outlying scores, members could revise their scores, and a final mean was calculated; members were told in advance which drugs each meeting would cover and were given recent review articles (references 5–7 and 15–18) (pp. 1049–1050).
outcomes.validity_norms: No parameter, and no combined score, was checked against measured outcomes (deaths, illness, dependence, costs). The authors offer the similarity of the two groups' scores as a sign of some validity and robustness (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 1051), but agreement between groups using the same matrix and guidance is consistency, not validity. Correlations among the nine parameters and their principal components were deliberately not estimated, because the independent scores were few; the authors expect some redundancy (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 1052). The Physical section counts the risk of sudden death with injected drugs within acute harm (p. 1047), while parameter three scores the propensity for intravenous use again (Table 1; p. 1051), so route may be counted twice. Intensity of pleasure is scored as a harm parameter (Table 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm = the mean of experts' ratings on the 0–3 scale. A category score is the mean of its three parameters; the overall harm rating, the mean of all nine scores, was computed for the sake of discussion (Assessment of harm, 1st paragraph, p. 1049). Each parameter was weighted equally and individual scores were simply averaged (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 1052); missing individual scores were ignored, neither treated as zero nor interpolated (Assessment of harm, 5th paragraph, p. 1050). Table 3 prints parameter and category means for the independent group only; its overall means appear only as bars (Figure 1, p. 1050).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: one statistical comparison (the harm ranking against legal class), expressed by two rank coefficients, each with its P value (p. 1050). Agreement between the groups is shown without a test; everything else is descriptive.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable in the usual sense: raters necessarily knew which substance they were rating. In the delphic meetings, scores were discussed openly and could be revised after the discussion (p. 1050), so the independent group's final scores are not independent of one another.

analysis.effect_sizes: Comparison with legal class (independent group, 20 substances): Kendall's rank correlation −0.18 (P=0.25) and Spearman's −0.26 (P=0.26), reported as not significant (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1050). Agreement between the two groups: no statistic printed (Figure 2, p. 1050). Editors' calculations: overall means of the independent group, taken as the mean of the three printed category means (Table 3, p. 1051), heroin 2.77, cocaine 2.30, barbiturates 2.08, street methadone 1.94, alcohol 1.85, ketamine 1.74, benzodiazepines 1.70, amphetamine 1.66, tobacco 1.62, buprenorphine 1.58, cannabis 1.33, solvents 1.27, 4-MTA 1.27, LSD 1.23, methylphenidate 1.18, anabolic steroids 1.15, GHB 1.12, ecstasy 1.09, alkyl nitrites 0.92 and khat 0.80, each within 0.02 of its bar in Figure 1 measured on a 300-dpi render. From the psychiatrists' overall means read on a 300-dpi render of Figure 2 (approximate, about ±0.02), agreement with the independent group across the 14 substances: Pearson r about 0.89 (95% CI about 0.69 to 0.97), Spearman about 0.91. The psychiatrists' means span about 1.20 to 2.53, against 1.09 to 2.77 for the same 14 substances in the independent group; the mean absolute difference is about 0.20, and the largest differences are amphetamine (+0.51), alcohol (+0.49) and solvents (+0.43), rated higher by the psychiatrists, and heroin (−0.24), rated lower.
analysis.covariates: None: unweighted means of the experts' ratings.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. An early version of the paper appeared, unacknowledged, as Appendix 10 of the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee's 2006 report (Acknowledgments and reference 26, p. 1053); that version was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The independent group's scores are tabulated by parameter (Table 3, p. 1051) without any measure of spread, numbers of scorers per substance or counts of missing scores. The psychiatrists' scores appear only as 14 overall means plotted in Figure 2 (p. 1050), not by parameter or category. The independent group's overall means are only drawn (Figure 1). A sensitivity check excluding parameters three and nine is described without numbers (Results, 4th paragraph, p. 1051). The questionnaire, the guidance notes and the list of experts are not given in the article.
analysis.power: Not applicable to a descriptive exercise. For the comparison with legal class, 20 substances give little precision: a rank correlation of −0.26 has a 95% interval of roughly −0.64 to 0.22 (editors' calculation, Fisher z with the variance 1.06/(n−3), n=20), so the data fit anything from a moderate negative correlation to a weak positive one.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The independent group's averaged ratings put heroin and cocaine (crack included) highest (overall means about 2.8 and 2.3 on the 0–3 scale, editors' calculation), alcohol fifth, tobacco ninth, cannabis eleventh, LSD fourteenth and ecstasy eighteenth of 20, and khat lowest. The ranking correlated weakly and non-significantly with Misuse of Drugs Act class, in a direction that cannot be read because the coding is not stated. The psychiatrists' overall means for 14 substances tracked the independent group's closely in rank but over a narrower range, with differences of up to about half a point for single substances (editors' reading of Figure 2). No score was measured, and none comes with a measure of spread.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract describes the matrix and delphic procedure as assessing harms "in an evidence-based fashion" (p. 1047), and the Discussion calls the system "rigorous and transparent" (p. 1052); the evidence behind each score, the guidance notes, the experts' names, the independent group's size, and any spread of scores are not reported. (2) Figure 2 is said to suggest that the scores have some validity and that the process is robust (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 1051); agreement between two UK groups using the same matrix and guidance shows consistency, not validity, and no statistic is given. (3) The Discussion says that neither the rank order nor the grouping of drugs in the Misuse of Drugs Act is supported by the more complete assessment of harm described, and offers a possible re-banding with alcohol as the threshold for class A and cannabis for class C (pp. 1051–1052); without intervals, the differences between neighbouring substances on which such boundaries rest cannot be judged, and the comparison with legal class depends on a coding that is not stated. (4) The authors first state that the scores of tobacco and alcohol cannot be compared directly with those of the other drugs, because legality, through easier availability, could affect their harms (Assessment of harm, 2nd paragraph, p. 1049); the Discussion nevertheless compares them with class A and B drugs and calls their exclusion from the Act arbitrary from a scientific perspective (p. 1052). (5) The Discussion's own caveats (equal weighting cannot represent a drug that is extremely harmful in one respect; crack and powder cocaine and individual benzodiazepines were not rated separately; polydrug use; likely redundancy among the nine parameters; p. 1052) do not appear in the abstract (p. 1047).

timeline.event: An early version of this paper appeared, unacknowledged, as Appendix 10 of the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee's report Drug classification: making a hash of it? (Acknowledgments and reference 26, p. 1053); not read.

This paper: two UK expert groups rated 20 substances (14 for the psychiatrists) on the nine-parameter matrix; within the study, the psychiatrists' overall means for 14 substances agreed closely in rank with the independent group's, without a reported statistic (Figure 2). A Lancet Comment accompanied the paper (p. 972 of the same volume, signposted on p. 1047); it was not on file and was not read.

Successor exercise by multicriteria decision analysis: 20 drugs scored on 16 criteria (harms to the people who use them and harms to others) with swing weights, at a facilitated decision conference of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs; appraised on card sc_nutt_2010, and its ranking is not compared here.

Caulkins, Reuter and Coulson argue against basing drug scheduling on scientific rankings of harmfulness; the project's harm-rankings list names it the principal methodological critique of this paper and of Nutt et al. (2010); not read for this card.
Rolles and Measham question the method and utility of ranking drug harms in drug policy (the second critique in the project's harm-rankings list); not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: This is an early expert ranking of drug harm; the authors cite other risk-assessment systems, some numerical or delphic, and claim only that none covered as many parameters or drugs (p. 1052). Within the study, a second group of experts using the same matrix gave similar overall scores for 14 substances, which is agreement between two UK panels, not validation against measured harm. Later national rankings (Nutt et al., 2010, and, in the project's harm-rankings list, van Amsterdam et al., 2015, Bonomo et al., 2019, and Broman et al., 2025) used multicriteria decision analysis with other criteria and weights and are appraised on their own cards; no later study repeating this nine-parameter matrix with a new panel was among the sources read, and the published critiques (Caulkins et al., 2011; Rolles & Measham, 2011) have still to be read against it.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article (pp. 1052–1053).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflict of interest (Conflict of interest statement, p. 1053).
funding.affiliations_note: Nutt: Psychopharmacology Unit, University of Bristol; King: Forensic Science Service, London; Saulsbury: Police Foundation, London; Blakemore: Medical Research Council, London, and Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics, Oxford (p. 1047). Some of the ideas arose at workshops organised by the Beckley Foundation; David Spiegelhalter (MRC Biostatistics Unit) advised on statistics; an early version was requested by the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee (Acknowledgments, p. 1053). The scoring was piloted by members of the panel of the Independent Inquiry into the Misuse of Drugs Act, whose report the Police Foundation published (p. 1049; reference 13); three of the seven review articles given to the independent group were by Nutt or King (references 5, 17 and 18); whether any author scored is not stated. All authors contributed to the design, analysis and writing (Contributors, p. 1052). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Several independent, preregistered panels, including people who use drugs and experts outside the UK, scoring a published questionnaire from a shared, appraised evidence summary for each substance and parameter, with crack and powder cocaine rated separately; individual scores reported with their spread and intervals; sensitivity analyses for the weights; and each parameter checked against measured outcomes (deaths, hospital admissions, dependence per person exposed, costs) at stated doses and patterns of use.

domains.note: No search for the evidence behind the scores: the independent group received seven recent review articles (references 5–7 and 15–18, p. 1050) and the psychiatrists a questionnaire with guidance notes, with no stated basis for choosing them; the evidence behind each drug's score is not reported.

No appraisal of the evidence used, and scores are not linked to sources. Several background figures (shares of drug-related deaths and hospital illness attributed to tobacco and alcohol) carry no citation (pp. 1047, 1049).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The matrix is the authors' own; three of the seven review articles given to the independent group were by Nutt or King (references 5, 17 and 18); whether the authors took part in the scoring is not stated.

The abstract and Discussion present averaged expert ratings as an evidence-based, rigorous and transparent assessment, and the Discussion compares alcohol and tobacco with class A and B drugs after stating that such comparison is not possible (p. 1049 against p. 1052). The policy readings are hedged (one possible interpretation; raise questions) and the main limitations are listed in the Discussion (p. 1052).

domains.domain: Balance of harms against benefits, and of the expertise behind the scores
domains.note: Only harms were rated: medical uses and other benefits were not, and intensity of pleasure counts as a harm parameter (Table 1). The independent group spanned several disciplines, but people who use drugs are not among the listed areas; the authors note that legality, especially through easier availability, could affect the harms of the legal substances (p. 1049).

domains.domain: Selection and response of the expert panels (domain added by the editors)
domains.note: Psychiatrists: 29 of 77 (38%) replied, and the others are not described. Independent group: selection, total number, names, disciplines at each meeting and interests are not reported; attendance ranged from 8 to 16 per meeting, so different drugs were rated by different subsets (pp. 1049–1050).

domains.domain: Elicitation of scores (decision-analysis domain added by the editors)
domains.note: A coarse four-point scale with verbal anchors and guidance notes not given in the article; the psychiatrists rated alone by questionnaire, the independent group after open discussion focused on outlying scores, which can pull ratings together (p. 1050); equal weights and simple averaging, which the authors say would not give a valid indication for a drug with extreme acute toxicity (MPTP) and might not deal adequately with one extremely harmful in only one respect (tobacco) (p. 1052); route possibly counted twice (acute harm and parameter three); and alcohol's NA cell treated, by the editors' calculation, as zero without comment (Table 3, p. 1051).

domains.domain: Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis (decision-analysis domain added by the editors)
domains.note: No spread, intervals or agreement statistics for any score; no sensitivity analysis of the weights, although the authors note they could be varied (p. 1052); one sensitivity check (excluding parameters three and nine) reported only in words (p. 1051); agreement between the two groups shown only as a plot (Figure 2).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for expert-judgement rankings; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, as for the successor exercise (card sc_nutt_2010), with three domains added for expert elicitation. The scores are panels' opinions, gathered from a 38% response of one professional register and from a second group whose selection and membership are not reported, on a coarse scale with guidance notes not given in the article, averaged with equal weights and reported without any measure of spread or uncertainty. Cite it for: what these two UK expert groups judged, before 2007, about the relative harm of 20 substances (14 for the psychiatrists) on this matrix (in the independent group's ranking, heroin and cocaine, crack included, highest; alcohol fifth and tobacco ninth of 20; LSD fourteenth and ecstasy eighteenth; khat lowest), for the printed category scores, and for the weak, non-significant rank correlation between that ranking and the Misuse of Drugs Act classes (Kendall −0.18, Spearman −0.26). Do not cite it for: measured harm; any drug being more harmful than another beyond these experts' judgement; differences between neighbouring substances; crack versus powder cocaine; harm at particular doses or patterns of use; other countries or later years; or what the classification should be.

key_findings.finding: The scale: nine parameters in three categories (physical harm: acute, chronic, intravenous harm; dependence: intensity of pleasure, psychological dependence, physical dependence; social harms: intoxication, other social harms, health-care costs), each scored 0 (no risk), 1 (some), 2 (moderate) or 3 (extreme risk). A category score was the mean of its three parameters, and an overall harm rating, the mean of all nine scores, was computed for the sake of discussion.
key_findings.locator: Assessment of harm, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: First group: the national group of consultant psychiatrists on the Royal College of Psychiatrists' register as specialists in addiction; replies from 29 of the 77 asked were received and analysed. They rated 14 substances (heroin, cocaine, alcohol, barbiturates, amphetamine, methadone, benzodiazepines, solvents, buprenorphine, tobacco, ecstasy, cannabis, LSD, steroids) on an assessment questionnaire based on Table 1 with guidance notes, after the procedure had been piloted by members of the panel of the Independent Inquiry into the Misuse of Drugs Act.
key_findings.locator: Assessment of harm, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: A response of 37.7% (editors' calculation); those who did not reply are not described, and the questionnaire and guidance notes are not given in the article.

key_findings.finding: Second group: experts with a wider spread of expertise (chemistry, pharmacology, forensic science, psychiatry and other medical specialties including epidemiology, legal and police services) scored in meetings run on delphic principles. Each scored independently; each parameter's scores were shown to the whole group for discussion, with emphasis on the reasoning behind outlying scores; members could then revise their scores, and a final mean was calculated. Four meetings were needed, and 8 to 16 members scored at each; the authors state that the full range of expertise was kept at every assessment.
key_findings.locator: Assessment of harm, 3rd paragraph (starting on p. 1049, right column, and continuing on p. 1050)
key_findings.note: How the members were chosen, how many took part in all, who they were and whether any author scored are not reported.

key_findings.finding: The second group rated 20 substances: the psychiatrists' 14 plus, for completeness, khat, 4-MTA, GHB, ketamine, methylphenidate and alkyl nitrites. Members were told in advance which drugs each meeting would cover and were given recent review articles (references 5–7 and 15–18). Missing individual scores were ignored, neither treated as zero nor interpolated; the data were analysed in Microsoft Excel and S-plus.
key_findings.locator: Assessment of harm, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Status of the 20 substances under the Misuse of Drugs Act at the time: class A, ecstasy, 4-MTA, LSD, cocaine (including crack cocaine), heroin (crude diamorphine) and street methadone (diverted prescribed methadone); class B, amphetamine, methylphenidate and barbiturates; class C, buprenorphine, benzodiazepines, GHB, anabolic steroids and cannabis; not controlled, alcohol (for people over 18 years in the UK), alkyl nitrites, ketamine (uncontrolled when assessed, class C since January 2007), khat, solvents (sales restricted) and tobacco (for people over 16 years).
key_findings.locator: Table 2

key_findings.finding: Independent group, Table 3, in its rank order of overall score, with the printed mean scores for physical harm, dependence and social harm: heroin 2.78, 3.00, 2.54; cocaine 2.33, 2.39, 2.17; barbiturates 2.23, 2.01, 2.00; street methadone 1.86, 2.08, 1.87; alcohol 1.40, 1.93, 2.21; ketamine 2.00, 1.54, 1.69; benzodiazepines 1.63, 1.83, 1.65; amphetamine 1.81, 1.67, 1.50; tobacco 1.24, 2.21, 1.42; buprenorphine 1.60, 1.64, 1.49.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Mean columns of the three categories (first ten rows)

key_findings.finding: Table 3 continued, from the eleventh place down: cannabis 0.99, 1.51, 1.50; solvents 1.28, 1.01, 1.52; 4-MTA 1.44, 1.30, 1.06; LSD 1.13, 1.23, 1.32; methylphenidate 1.32, 1.25, 0.97; anabolic steroids 1.45, 0.88, 1.13; GHB 0.86, 1.19, 1.30; ecstasy 1.05, 1.13, 1.09; alkyl nitrites 0.93, 0.87, 0.97; khat 0.50, 1.04, 0.85.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Mean columns of the three categories (last ten rows)
key_findings.note: The order is the table's, which its caption says is by overall score; the overall scores are not printed (next finding). Solvents and 4-MTA are tied to two decimals by the editors' calculation.

key_findings.finding: The independent group's overall mean scores are shown only as bars in rank order, coloured by legal class, with no values printed; the two highest, heroin and cocaine, are class A. Editors' calculation from Table 3 (mean of the three category means): heroin 2.77, cocaine 2.30, barbiturates 2.08, street methadone 1.94, alcohol 1.85, ketamine 1.74, benzodiazepines 1.70, amphetamine 1.66, tobacco 1.62, buprenorphine 1.58, cannabis 1.33, solvents 1.27, 4-MTA 1.27, LSD 1.23, methylphenidate 1.18, anabolic steroids 1.15, GHB 1.12, ecstasy 1.09, alkyl nitrites 0.92, khat 0.80; each lies within 0.02 of the height of its bar measured on a 300-dpi render of Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 and Results, 1st paragraph (p. 1050); Table 3 (p. 1051)
key_findings.note: Bar heights were measured in pixels against the axis ticks; the figure itself carries no values. Because every category has three parameters, the mean of the category means equals the mean of the nine parameters when none is missing.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine was rated as one substance that includes crack cocaine and ranked second: physical harm 2.33 (acute 2.0, chronic 2.0, intravenous 3.0), dependence 2.39 (pleasure 3.0, psychological dependence 2.8, physical dependence 1.3) and social harm 2.17 (intoxication 1.8, social harm 2.5, health-care costs 2.3). The authors note that crack cocaine is generally deemed more dangerous than powdered cocaine but that the two were not considered separately.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 1049); Table 3 (p. 1051); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1052)

key_findings.finding: Heroin, cocaine, barbiturates and street methadone were in the top five places in all three categories, and khat, alkyl nitrites and ecstasy in the bottom five in all three. Some drugs differed across categories: cannabis low for physical harm (0.99) but higher for dependence (1.51) and social harm (1.50); anabolic steroids high for physical harm (1.45) but low for dependence (0.88); tobacco high for dependence (2.21) but lower for social harm (1.42, with intoxication 0.8), and modest for physical harm (1.24) despite a chronic-harm score of 2.9.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Legal class and harm score correlated poorly: among both the eight highest-scoring and the eight lowest-scoring substances, three were class A and two were unclassified; alcohol, ketamine, tobacco and solvents (all unclassified when assessed) were ranked above LSD, ecstasy and 4-MTA (all class A); and the correlation between class and harm rating was not significant (Kendall's rank correlation −0.18, P=0.25; Spearman's −0.26, P=0.26). Of the unclassified substances, alcohol and ketamine received especially high ratings.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: How the classes were coded, and whether the six uncontrolled substances entered as a fourth class, is not stated, so the sign of the coefficients cannot be read (see reporting issues). The editors confirmed the two counts of three class A and two unclassified substances from Tables 2 and 3.

key_findings.finding: The two groups' overall mean scores for the 14 substances rated by both are plotted against each other without a coefficient; the authors say the figure suggests that the scores have some validity and that the process is robust, giving similar results with rather different sets of experts. Editors' reading of Figure 2 on a 300-dpi render (approximate): the psychiatrists' means are heroin 2.53, cocaine 2.44, alcohol 2.33, barbiturates 2.20, amphetamine 2.17, methadone 2.11, benzodiazepines 1.85, solvents 1.70, buprenorphine 1.69, tobacco 1.52, ecstasy 1.32, cannabis 1.23, LSD 1.21 and steroids 1.20; Pearson r with the independent group about 0.89 (95% CI about 0.69 to 0.97), Spearman about 0.91.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (p. 1050); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1051)
key_findings.note: Circle centres were measured in pixels against the axis ticks; the horizontal coordinates recovered match the independent group's means from the editors' calculation within 0.015, so the psychiatrists' values should be within about 0.02. LSD's circle is partly hidden by its neighbours. The psychiatrists' scores by parameter or category are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Drugs that can be injected were generally ranked high; the authors state that this persisted when parameters three (propensity for intravenous use) and nine (health-care costs) were excluded, without giving the resulting scores. Editors' calculation from the parameter means of Table 3 without those two parameters: heroin and cocaine stay first and second and barbiturates and street methadone fourth and fifth, while alcohol rises to third and tobacco from ninth to sixth, and methylphenidate and anabolic steroids fall two places each.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column); Table 3
key_findings.note: The recalculation averages the seven remaining rounded parameter means; it checks the direction of the authors' statement and does not reproduce their analysis.

key_findings.finding: Tobacco and alcohol were included as familiar benchmarks, their extensive use having provided reliable data on their risks; the authors state that their scores cannot be compared directly with those of the other drugs, because legality could affect their harms in various ways, especially through easier availability.
key_findings.locator: Assessment of harm, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the results do not justify the sharp A, B and C divisions: Figure 1 shows only a hint of a transition, a small step between buprenorphine and cannabis; alcohol and tobacco are both in the top ten; and if three classes were kept, one possible reading would put drugs scoring as high as alcohol or higher in class A, cannabis and those below in class C and the rest in class B, which would give alcohol and tobacco harm ratings comparable with class A and class B drugs respectively.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (starting on p. 1051, right column, and continuing on p. 1052)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the overall means: the step between buprenorphine and cannabis (about 0.25) is the largest gap between neighbouring substances after the gap between heroin and cocaine (about 0.47); no interval is available to say whether it exceeds the experts' disagreement.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: drugs were rated in the form in which they are normally used, so harms could not always be separated from the style of use (cannabis smoked with tobacco may have raised its physical-harm and dependence scores); polydrug use in the recreational group (GHB, ketamine, ecstasy, alcohol) adds uncertainty; the benzodiazepine scores may lean towards the most misused, especially temazepam; correlations among the nine parameters were not estimated because the independent scores were few, nor were principal components extracted (too few data, and a reduced set might not be appropriate before further validation), and some redundancy is likely; and equal weights with simple averaging would not give a valid indication of harm for a drug with extreme acute toxicity (the MPTP example) and might not deal adequately with any substance extremely harmful in only one respect (the tobacco example), so the weights could be varied or multi-criteria decision analysis used.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that their findings raise questions about the validity of the Misuse of Drugs Act classification, that the discrepancies are especially striking for psychedelic-type drugs, that excluding alcohol and tobacco from the Act is arbitrary from a scientific perspective, that they saw no clear distinction between socially acceptable and illicit substances, and, in their stated belief, that a system like theirs, based on experts' scoring of harms on the basis of scientific evidence, has much to commend it and could be developed to aid decision-making by regulatory bodies such as the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs and the European Medicines Evaluation Agency.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol's physical-harm mean is printed as 1.40, with acute 1.9, chronic 2.4 and intravenous NA (Table 3, p. 1051), while the Methods say missing scores were ignored rather than treated as zero (Assessment of harm, 5th paragraph, p. 1050). By the editors' calculation, 1.40 matches the three values with NA counted as zero (1.43), not with NA left out (2.15); substances not injected are scored 0 for this parameter elsewhere in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither the table nor the Methods says how NA entered. Counting it as zero, as for the other substances not injected, gives alcohol an overall mean of about 1.85 (fifth); leaving it out would give about 2.10, above barbiturates (third) (editors' calculation). The bar for alcohol in Figure 1 matches the first value.

reporting_issues.issue: 4-MTA's dependence mean is printed as 1.30, although its three parameters are 1.0, 1.7 and 0.8; by the editors' calculation their mean is 1.17 and cannot exceed about 1.22 even allowing for rounding. All the other category means agree with their parameters within rounding, apart from alcohol's physical mean (previous issue).
reporting_issues.consequence: Perhaps the result of missing individual scores handled scorer by scorer, which the paper does not describe. The bar for 4-MTA in Figure 1 matches the printed 1.30; with 1.17, its overall mean would fall from about 1.27 to 1.22, below LSD (editors' calculation), so neighbouring ranks depend on such details.

reporting_issues.issue: No measure of spread is reported for any score: no standard deviations or ranges, no number of scorers per substance (attendance varied from 8 to 16 across meetings) and no count of missing scores; the psychiatrists' scores are given only as 14 points in Figure 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether neighbouring substances differ beyond the experts' disagreement, and so whether the class boundaries the Discussion proposes (at alcohol and at cannabis) mean anything, cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: Agreement between the two groups, which the abstract describes as roughly similar scores and rankings and the Results as a sign of some validity and of robustness, is shown only as a scatter plot without a coefficient, although the figure is titled as a correlation.
reporting_issues.consequence: It has to be estimated from the figure (editors' reading: Pearson r about 0.89 and Spearman about 0.91 across 14 substances, with the psychiatrists rating amphetamine, alcohol and solvents about 0.4 to 0.5 points higher); and agreement between two groups using the same matrix is consistency, not validity.

reporting_issues.issue: The coding of legal class for the rank correlations (which class was scored high, and whether the six uncontrolled substances entered as a fourth category or were left out) is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The signs of −0.18 and −0.26 cannot be interpreted. The printed P values fit the inclusion of all 20 substances (editors' calculation: two-sided P about 0.27 for both coefficients with 20 substances, about 0.37 with the 14 controlled ones).

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity check excluding parameters three and nine is reported only in words, with no scores or ranks (Results, 4th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The editors' recalculation from Table 3 broadly supports the statement for the highest-ranked drugs that can be injected (see key findings), but the authors' own figures cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The independent group's members are not identified: neither names, number, disciplines at each meeting, how they were selected, nor their interests are reported, although the Discussion calls the process transparent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The independence of this group from the authors and from the psychiatrists, and the balance of disciplines behind each drug's score, cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Background figures are given without a source or in two forms: tobacco and alcohol are said to account for about 90% of drug-related deaths in the UK (p. 1047), and tobacco for up to 40% of hospital illness and 60% of drug-related deaths (p. 1049), with no citation of their own; the loss of life expectancy from smoking is given as 10 years on average (p. 1047) and as up to 10 years on average for smoking beyond age 30 (p. 1052), both citing reference 9.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are background statements, not results of the study, and should not be cited from this paper.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), The Lancet 369:1047–1053, pp. 1047–1053 (all 7 pages); Tables 1–3 and Figures 1–2 checked on rendered pages, Table 3 and both figures at 300 dpi. The figures print no values: the overall means in Figure 1 and the psychiatrists' means in Figure 2 were read by pixel measurement on the 300-dpi render, as stated where used. No supplement. The Lancet Comment signposted on p. 1047 (p. 972 of the same volume) and the House of Commons committee report containing an early version (reference 26) were not on file and were not read.

disagreements.first_pass: No validated instrument exists for expert-judgement rankings; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, as for the successor exercise (card sc_nutt_2010), with three domains added for expert elicitation. The scores are panels' opinions, gathered from a 38% response of one professional register and from a second group whose selection and membership are not reported, on a coarse scale with unpublished guidance, averaged with equal weights and reported without any measure of spread or uncertainty. Cite it for: what these two UK expert groups judged, before 2007, about the relative harm of 20 substances on this matrix (heroin and cocaine, crack included, highest; alcohol fifth and tobacco ninth of 20; LSD fourteenth and ecstasy eighteenth; khat lowest), for the printed category scores, and for the weak, non-significant rank correlation between that ranking and the Misuse of Drugs Act classes (Kendall −0.18, Spearman −0.26). Do not cite it for: measured harm; any drug being more harmful than another beyond these experts' judgement; differences between neighbouring substances; crack versus powder cocaine; harm at particular doses or patterns of use; other countries or later years; or what the classification should be.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 635 (round-2 check): corrected at the source. The ranks of 20 are the independent group's; the psychiatrists rated 14 and not khat.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted by the AI co-editor (adjudication, 13 November 2026).

disagreements.first_pass: Two UK expert groups' averaged ratings put heroin and cocaine (crack included) clearly highest (overall means about 2.8 and 2.3 on the 0–3 scale, editors' calculation), alcohol fifth, tobacco ninth, cannabis eleventh, LSD fourteenth and ecstasy eighteenth of 20, and khat lowest. The ranking correlated weakly and non-significantly with Misuse of Drugs Act class, in a direction that cannot be read because the coding is not stated. The psychiatrists' overall means for 14 substances tracked the independent group's closely in rank but over a narrower range, with differences of up to about half a point for single substances (editors' reading of Figure 2). No score was measured, and none comes with a measure of spread.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 635 (round-2 check): corrected at the source. Ranks out of 20 come from the independent group only; 'clearly' sits badly with the card's own point that neighbouring differences cannot be judged (cocaine 2.30 against barbiturates 2.08).

disagreements.first_pass: (1) The abstract describes the matrix and delphic procedure as assessing harms "in an evidence-based fashion" (p. 1047), and the Discussion calls the system "rigorous and transparent" (p. 1052); the evidence behind each score, the guidance notes, the experts' names and number, and any spread of scores are not reported. (2) Figure 2 is said to suggest that the scores have some validity and that the process is robust (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 1051); agreement between two UK groups using the same matrix and guidance shows consistency, not validity, and no statistic is given. (3) The Discussion says that neither the rank order nor the grouping of drugs in the Misuse of Drugs Act is supported by the more complete assessment of harm described, and offers a possible re-banding with alcohol as the threshold for class A and cannabis for class C (pp. 1051–1052); without intervals, the differences between neighbouring substances on which such boundaries rest cannot be judged, and the comparison with legal class depends on a coding that is not stated. (4) The authors first state that the scores of tobacco and alcohol cannot be compared directly with those of the other drugs, because legality, through easier availability, could affect their harms (Assessment of harm, 2nd paragraph, p. 1049); the Discussion nevertheless compares them with class A and B drugs and calls their exclusion from the Act arbitrary from a scientific perspective (p. 1052). (5) The Discussion's own caveats (equal weighting cannot represent a drug that is extremely harmful in one respect; crack and powder cocaine and individual benzodiazepines were not rated separately; polydrug use; likely redundancy among the nine parameters; p. 1052) do not appear in the abstract (p. 1047).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 635 (round-2 check): corrected at the source. The psychiatrists' number (29) is reported.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted by the AI co-editor (adjudication, 13 November 2026).

disagreements.first_pass: This is the first of the expert rankings of drug harm. Within the study, a second group of experts using the same matrix gave similar overall scores for 14 substances, which is agreement between two UK panels, not validation against measured harm. Later national rankings (Nutt et al., 2010, and, in the project's harm-rankings list, van Amsterdam et al., 2015, Bonomo et al., 2019, and Broman et al., 2025) used multicriteria decision analysis with other criteria and weights and are appraised on their own cards; no later study repeating this nine-parameter matrix with a new panel was among the sources read, and the published critiques (Caulkins et al., 2011; Rolles & Measham, 2011) have still to be read against it.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 635 (round-2 check): corrected at the source. 'First' is not supported: the article cites earlier and concurrent systems (EMCDDA, Dutch CAM committee, delphic methods).

disagreements.first_pass: Neither group is a defined sample: the psychiatrists are a 38% response from one professional register, and the selection of the independent group is not described. Different drugs were scored at different meetings by different subsets of 8 to 16 members, so each drug's mean rests on a different set of experts. The independent group was given seven recent review articles (references 5–7 and 15–18), three of them by Nutt or King (references 5, 17 and 18; p. 1050 and p. 1053); who chose them, and on what basis, is not stated.

design_detail: Mini review (the authors' term; the format was chosen instead of a systematic review for concision and timeliness) of protective behavioural strategies (PBS: harm-reduction strategies used by the individual) for non-clinical use of classical psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin) and of MDMA and ketamine. Search: PubMed and Google Scholar, English, 2006 to 2023, four phrases combining psychedelic or hallucinogen with protective behavioral strategies or harm reduction, plus the reference lists of the articles found. No inclusion or exclusion criteria, no count of records screened or included, no appraisal of the cited studies and no quantitative synthesis. Strategies are arranged by time (before, during and after a psychedelic experience) in Table 1, which names 17 distinct sources (editors' count), followed by sections on measuring strategies and on associations with outcomes (four studies). 65 references.
can_establish: Which individual-level strategies for non-clinical use of psychedelics, MDMA and ketamine the authors found described in the literature from 2006 to 2023, arranged by before, during and after use, and how little outcome research they could find.
cannot_establish: Whether any strategy reduces harm or improves the experience (nothing is appraised, and the outcome evidence cited is one cross-sectional survey, one scale study, one ketamine study whose design the review does not state and one unreviewed preprint scoping review); how often strategies are used; or whether the catalogue is complete (four search phrases, no stated selection criteria, and the authors say articles may have been left out for space).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Literature found through PubMed and Google Scholar (English, 2006 to 2023; 2006 taken as the start of the 'psychedelic renaissance') with four search phrases and the reference lists of the articles found (Method, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated beyond language, years, non-clinical contexts and the drug classes covered (classical psychedelics, MDMA, ketamine). Books, a practitioner handbook and two preprints are cited alongside peer-reviewed studies.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Two search engines, one of them (Google Scholar) not reproducible; four narrow phrases, which the authors concede will miss studies describing the same strategies in other words (Limitations, 1st paragraph); no flow of records; selection by the authors without stated criteria, and the authors note pertinent articles may have been omitted for space. Much of the cited material is qualitative (open-ended survey questions, analyses of online forums and trip reports) or self-rated helpfulness.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The strategies come from the cited studies: qualitative interviews and open-ended questions, content analyses of an online forum (Reddit r/psychonaut) and of trip reports (Erowid), checklists in online surveys, a new scale (Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale) and a survey of callers to a peer-support helpline.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Table 1 names seven strategies concerning the amount taken, drug checking and combinations as strategies reported in the literature; the review tests none and gives no amounts, and this card reproduces none.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed only as a strategy category (care with, or avoidance of, some combinations) and as a reported practice (using cannabis alongside psychedelics was itself reported as a strategy in Carbonaro et al., 2016, as cited). Combinations are outside this card's scope and belong to the interactions page.

comparison.controls: None at review level. In the four outcome studies discussed, comparisons are between people reporting more or fewer strategies (Palmer and Maynard, 2022, a survey; Vidal Giné et al., 2016, design not stated in the review), across levels of a preparedness scale (McAlpine et al.), or within a preprint scoping review (Edwards et al., 2022), as summarized.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed. The review does not discuss that people who use more strategies may differ from people who use fewer in experience, intentions, setting, substance, amount or mental health, any of which could explain an association with outcomes.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: the Challenging Experience Questionnaire (26 items) and the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (6 items) in Palmer and Maynard (2022); unnamed mental-health and wellbeing measures after the experience in the Psychedelic Preparedness Scale study (McAlpine et al.); ketamine-related adverse outcomes and overall harm in Vidal Giné et al. (2016); perceived helpfulness in Carbonaro et al. (2016), McCartney et al. (2023) and the Fireside Project caller survey (Pleet et al., 2023).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; the review calls for the development and validation of measures of strategies and of outcomes (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Consequences', 'harm' and 'risk reduction' are not defined at review level and take whatever meaning each cited study gave them. Several of the cited findings are perceived effectiveness rated by the people who used the strategy.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled or computed. Second-hand figures only: 91% of respondents in Carbonaro et al. (2016) used at least one strategy during a challenging experience with psilocybin mushrooms and rated the strategies only modestly effective; 65.9% of surveyed Fireside Project callers (April 2021 to September 2022) found the helpline helpful in de-escalating distress; Palmer and Maynard (2022), n = 163, strategy use positively associated with emotional breakthrough and negatively with challenging experiences (no coefficients given in the review).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; the authors chose a mini-review format instead of a systematic one (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The summary of Palmer and Maynard (2022) omits that the association with challenging experiences was not statistically significant for the most recent experience and that the predictor was a score weighted by participants' importance ratings, not a count (see reporting issues). All MDMA strategy-outcome statements rest on a rapid scoping review posted as a preprint, which the review does not identify as unreviewed.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A catalogue of strategies described in mostly qualitative and self-report literature: sourcing, amounts, checking and combinations, mindset and intentions, the physical place and the company, telling a trusted person of one's plans, rest, exercise, water and a meal beforehand, calming, grounding, music, changing the setting and calling on others during difficult moments, a peer-support helpline, and integration afterwards. The review reports disagreement in the literature on the best place, on whom to be with, and on sober sitters. For outcomes it found one cross-sectional survey of classical psychedelic use (163 people), one preparedness-scale study (drug class not stated), one ketamine study (design not stated) and one preprint scoping review on MDMA; for perceived helpfulness, a mushroom survey (strategies rated modestly effective) and a helpline survey.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says emerging evidence suggests that psychedelic PBS use may be associated with decreased consequences, and the Implications say the review may give community members initial insights into risk mitigation. The wording is hedged and the conclusion asks for research on efficacy, but: (1) the 'emerging evidence' pools classical psychedelics with ketamine and MDMA, and for classical psychedelics rests on one retrospective cross-sectional survey and one scale study; (2) the introduction asserts the "efficacy of PBS in reducing consequences associated with alcohol and cannabis use" (Introduction, 3rd paragraph) on four references that, by their titles, are a scale-development paper, a review of measures and associated interventions, and two moderator studies, none a trial by title; (3) Table 1 presents the strategies as a list that can be read as recommendations, with only a table note saying that their support varies; (4) the summary of the main outcome study overstates its result (reporting issue 1). Against this, the authors mark their own inferences ('we posit'), state that few studies have examined outcomes, and name the limits of the mini-review format.

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms: 91% used strategies during the experience and rated them only modestly effective (as cited).
Vidal Giné et al. study of patterns of use, strategies and harms among people who use ketamine recreationally (as cited; the review does not state its design).
Palmer and Maynard cross-sectional survey of 163 people recalling their first and most recent psychedelic experiences: the review's main outcome study for classical psychedelics
Simonsson et al. survey of challenging experiences, cited for avoiding use after a major life event
Mian et al. develop the Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale (32 items, two factors), not yet tested against challenging experiences (as cited).
Pleet et al. survey of callers to the Fireside Project peer-support line: 65.9% found it helpful in de-escalating distress (as cited).
McAlpine et al. Psychedelic Preparedness Scale (dated 2023 in the review's text, 2024 in its reference list): higher preparedness went with better mental health and wellbeing afterwards (as cited).
This mini review.
Wood, McAlpine and Kamboj mixed-methods study of strategies for resolving challenging experiences (not cited by this review)
Dutton et al. scoping review of harm-reduction practices for people who use psychedelics (on this project's interactions list; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: A map of strategies named in the literature, not evidence that any of them works. No prospective or experimental test of a strategy for classical psychedelics is cited. Palmer and Maynard (2022) has its own card and should be cited directly instead of through this review; the MDMA statements should be checked against the published version of the Edwards et al. scoping review, if one exists; later reviews on this project's lists (Dutton et al., 2025) may supersede this one.

funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are from the Department of Psychology, Colorado State University. None of the studies cited for strategies or outcomes is by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people planning non-clinical psychedelic use that records the strategies planned and used before and during the experience, the substance, amount, place and company, and rates the experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, need for help, lasting difficulties) within days, with adjustment for prior experience and intentions; for a single strategy with plausible benefit, such as access to peer support or structured preparation material, a randomized offer of that support.

domains.note: Two engines (one not reproducible), four narrow phrases, English 2006 to 2023 and reference-list searching are stated; but there are no inclusion criteria, no record flow and no count of included studies, and the authors say relevant articles may be missing because of terminology and space.

No appraisal. Cross-sectional surveys, qualitative studies, forum and trip-report analyses, books, a handbook and two preprints are cited alike, and self-rated helpfulness is reported without saying that it is self-rated.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the cited strategy or outcome studies is by the authors.

The authors flag their own inferences and the Table 1 note says support varies, but the introduction asserts the efficacy of alcohol and cannabis strategies without trial evidence, and the main outcome study is summarized as fewer challenging experiences with more strategies.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether strategies help (null and unfavourable findings under-represented)
domains.note: Some caveats are given (false security from trusted sources; inexperienced sitters may harm the experience; ketamine testing and having a sober person present not associated with outcomes; supplements taken before or after MDMA poorly supported and possibly harmful), but the non-significant result for the most recent experience in Palmer and Maynard and the modest perceived effectiveness in Carbonaro et al. do not reach the abstract.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The search is described but narrow, selection is unstated and nothing is appraised; the overall judgment cannot be milder than the worst domain. Cite the review only as a map of the strategies named in the literature up to 2023 and for the observation that outcome research on them is scarce. Do not cite it for any strategy reducing harm or improving experiences: cite the primary studies (Palmer and Maynard, 2022, has its own card), and say that the MDMA statements come second-hand from an unreviewed preprint. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Method: PubMed and Google Scholar searched for English-language articles from 2006 to 2023 with four phrases combining psychedelic or hallucinogen with protective behavioral strategies or harm reduction, plus the reference lists of the articles found; classical psychedelics (LSD, psilocybin) and non-classical ones (MDMA, ketamine) in non-clinical contexts. A mini-review format was chosen instead of a systematic one for a concise, timely summary.
key_findings.locator: Method, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 4th paragraph; Abstract › Method

key_findings.finding: The authors found that most research on psychedelic protective strategies used qualitative methods (open-ended questions about harm-reduction practices, analyses of online drug forums) and describe a culture of harm reduction in psychedelic communities, illustrated by a content analysis of the Reddit r/psychonaut forum.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patterns of psychedelic PBS use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Table 1 arranges the strategies by time. Before use: drug acquisition (2 strategies), amounts, drug checking and combinations (7), set and setting (6: setting intentions, reflecting on motives, cultivating a positive mindset, avoiding use in negative or unstable moods, choosing the physical space, choosing the social setting), planning for challenging experiences (1: telling a trusted person of one's plans), bodily nourishment (4: rest, exercise, hydration, a nutritious meal). During use: working through challenging experiences (8: meditating, changing the physical or social setting, calming audio, calling on sitters or guides, grounding in nature, trying to calm the mind, moving the body, a peer-support helpline). After use: integration (4 examples). 17 distinct sources are named (editors' count). The table note says these are strategies proposed in the literature with varying support and some mixed findings.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and its note; Results › Patterns of psychedelic PBS use, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Drug acquisition: buying from reputable sources such as a trusted friend is described as one widely identified acquisition strategy; the review notes that it may give a false sense of security that leads people to skip testing, that cryptomarket purchasing was described as risk reduction in a field study of the Silk Road market, and that producing or foraging one's own supply is not feasible for every substance and carries more legal risk.
key_findings.locator: Results › Before the psychedelic experience: Preparation PBS › Drug acquisition, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Strategies about amounts, drug checking (reagent kits, fentanyl test strips), weighing and combinations are reported in the cited surveys and forum studies; the review notes that they vary by substance (adulterants more common in powders and tablets than in plant material, and mushroom weight varying with curing, as cited) and that using cannabis alongside psychedelics has itself been reported as a strategy (Carbonaro et al., 2016, as cited). No amounts are tested or given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Before the psychedelic experience: Preparation PBS › Dosing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Set and setting: mindset strategies centre on setting intentions (reflecting on motives, cultivating a positive mindset, avoiding use in negative or unstable moods) and also include meeting obligations first and choosing the timing, for example not after a major life event and keeping the next day free (citing Mian et al., 2023, and Simonsson et al., 2023). The review finds no consensus on the place (home versus a festival, for example) or the company (alone, a sitter, friends): spaces that feel comfortable and safe are generally recommended, and while some evidence stresses a sober sitter, inexperienced sitters can harm the experience through unsupportive behaviour (Engel et al., 2022, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Results › Curating an optimal set and setting › Mind set, Selecting a physical setting and Deciding who to trip with, one paragraph each

key_findings.finding: Planning and the body: people report telling a trusted person of their plans and asking them to be available if a challenging experience or emergency arises (Engel et al., 2022, as cited), and some researchers speculate that planning eases anxiety beforehand; preparation of the body includes rest, exercise, hydration and a nutritious meal before use, while fasting before some psychedelics is also discussed in the literature (Palmer and Maynard, 2022, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Results › Planning for challenging experiences, 1st paragraph; Bodily nourishment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: During use: in a thematic analysis of 22 Erowid trip reports covering ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin and LSD (McCartney et al., 2023), grounding in nature and listening to music were reported as ways to ease negative states during challenging experiences; perceived efficacy differed by substance (nature more for MDMA, music more for ketamine, more variable and dependent on the individual for psilocybin and LSD).
key_findings.locator: Results › During the psychedelic experience: PBS for working through challenging experiences, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In a survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms (Carbonaro et al., 2016), 91% of respondents used strategies to mitigate the experience (calming the mind, changing the physical setting, moving the body, changing the social environment, asking a friend for help, using cannabis or other drugs) and perceived them as only modestly effective.
key_findings.locator: Results › During the psychedelic experience: PBS for working through challenging experiences, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Fireside Project psychedelic peer-support line, set up in 2020: in a survey of callers between April 2021 and September 2022, 65.9% of respondents perceived it as helpful in de-escalating their distress (Pleet et al., 2023, as cited; response rate and denominator not given in the review).
key_findings.locator: Results › During the psychedelic experience: PBS for working through challenging experiences, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Integration after use is variably defined; Bathje et al. (2022) identified 14 integration themes in the literature. The review suggests that inadequate integration could contribute to extended difficulties such as derealization or panic attacks, citing a 2023 SSRN preprint (Evans et al.).
key_findings.locator: Results › After the psychedelic experience: Integration-related PBS, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measurement: the Protective Strategies for Psychedelics Scale (Mian et al., 2023) has 32 items in two factors (short-term and long-term strategies) from principal components analysis, showed convergent validity with alcohol and cannabis protective-strategy measures and a moderate association with lifetime psychedelic use, and had not been examined against challenging experiences when the review was written.
key_findings.locator: Results › Measuring psychedelic PBS use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Main outcome study for classical psychedelics, as summarized: Palmer and Maynard (2022), cross-sectional, n = 163, strategy use for the first and most recent experience from a list of 28; strategy use positively associated with Emotional Breakthrough Inventory scores and negatively with Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores, read by the review as more strategies going with more breakthroughs and fewer challenging experiences.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Checked against the source (PMC9310449; card sc_palmer_2022): the predictor was a sum of practices weighted by mean importance ratings, not a count; the CEQ correlation was significant for the first experience only (r = −0.21; most recent r = −0.15, p = 0.061); the size of the list is not stated in the source's main text.

key_findings.finding: McAlpine et al. (Psychedelic Preparedness Scale; subdomains Knowledge-Expectations, Intention-Preparation, Psychophysical-Readiness and Support-Planning): people with higher preparedness before a psychedelic experience scored significantly higher on mental health and wellbeing measures afterwards (as summarized; no figures, design or sample given in the review).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ketamine (Vidal Giné et al., 2016, as summarized): three strategies about how often and how much ketamine was used, and a fourth, avoiding mixing it with other drugs, were negatively associated with ketamine-related adverse outcomes, while testing the ketamine and having a sober person in the group were not; people who used strategies more often reported less harm overall.
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: MDMA, from a rapid scoping review posted as a preprint (Edwards et al., 2022): taking breaks to avoid overheating at dance events, keeping hydrated, avoiding certain combinations, moderating consumption and not using alone are described as associated with risk reduction; taking supplements or medicines before or after use to prevent unwanted effects ('pre-loading' and 'post-loading') was poorly supported and potentially harmful, with 5-HTP named as a possible serotonin-syndrome risk alongside MDMA (Silins et al., 2007, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Reference 48 is a Research Square preprint (DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-2178425/v1); these statements are second-hand from an unreviewed source.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the mini-review format simplifies issues and may omit pertinent articles for space; empirical studies are few; the search was limited to English-language articles from 2006 to 2023; and inconsistent terminology may have excluded relevant evidence.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: many people who use psychedelics employ protective strategies; research on the efficacy of specific strategies is needed so that harm-reduction recommendations are evidence-based, with attention to which strategies work for whom. The authors call for rigorous cross-sectional, longitudinal and experimental studies and for measures developed with people with lived experience.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The summary of Palmer and Maynard (2022) departs from the source in four ways: it says the practice list came from online forums and the literature, while the source names trusted online harm-reduction resources, the literature and discussion with colleagues; it gives the list as 28 strategies, a number not stated in the source's main text; it describes the source's example of an anecdotal myth (drinking orange juice) as aimed at enhancing the experience, while the source gives it as a belief that it lowers the chance of a bad trip; and it reads the result as more strategies going with fewer challenging experiences, while the source's predictor was an importance-weighted score and the challenging-experience correlation was not statistically significant for the most recent experience (r = −0.15, p = 0.061). Within the review itself, the CEQ is defined as a scale of distress during an experience, yet a lower score is read as 'fewer challenging experiences'.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 1st paragraph; checked against PMC9310449 (Methods › Measures › Harm reduction practices; Results › Experiences of first and most recent psychedelic experiences, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The review makes the only classical-psychedelic outcome study look stronger and more uniform than it is; claims must cite Palmer and Maynard directly (card sc_palmer_2022).

reporting_issues.issue: Inconsistent years for the same sources: Pestana et al. is 2020 in Table 1 and reference 26 but 2021 in the Drug acquisition text; Bathje et al. is 2023 in Table 1 and its note but 2022 in the integration text and reference 52; McAlpine et al. is 2023 in the text but 2024 in reference 57.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and note; Results › Drug acquisition, 2nd paragraph; Integration-related PBS, 1st paragraph; Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 2nd paragraph; references 26, 52, 57
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; match sources by reference number and DOI, not by author-year.

reporting_issues.issue: Two preprints are cited as evidence without being identified as such: Edwards et al. (2022), a rapid scoping review on Research Square (reference 48), is the only source for every MDMA strategy-outcome statement and appears in Table 1; Evans et al. (2023), an SSRN preprint (reference 53), supports the statement that poor integration could give rise to extended difficulties.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Associations between PBS use and outcomes, 4th paragraph; Integration-related PBS, 1st paragraph; references 48 and 53
reporting_issues.consequence: The MDMA findings are second-hand from an unreviewed source; the published versions, if any, must be read before these statements are used.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction states that protective strategies are efficacious in reducing consequences of alcohol and cannabis use, citing references 13, 16, 18 and 19, which by their titles are the development of a strategies survey (Martens et al., 2005), a review of strategy measures and associated PBS-related interventions (Peterson et al., 2021) and two studies of the independent and moderating effects of marijuana strategies (Pearson et al., 2019; Bravo et al., 2017); by title, none is a trial of a strategy.
reporting_issues.consequence: As cited, the efficacy statement is asserted rather than shown in this review; whether the review of interventions (reference 16) supports it would need that review to be read. For alcohol, Pearson (2013), a critical review on this round's list, is the source to check: it finds mixed evidence that strategies change drinking.
