design_detail: Theoretical, mathematical modelling paper with no new data, by mathematicians and computational neuroscientists. It asks whether the geometry of the simple geometric hallucinations that Klüver sorted into four classes of 'form constants' ((i) gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; (ii) cobwebs; (iii) tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; (iv) spirals) can be explained by the map from the retina to the primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex) and by V1's local and lateral circuits. Method: a continuum Wilson-Cowan-type model of V1 as a sheet of hypercolumns with every orientation preference represented at every point, local connections within a hypercolumn and weak anisotropic lateral connections that join only patches of the same orientation preference along the axis of that preference; a symmetry analysis showing that this connectivity is invariant under a new 'shift-twist' action of the Euclidean group E(2); linear stability analysis by Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory; the equivariant branching lemma to find the doubly periodic patterns ('planforms') that can emerge when the resting state becomes unstable, on square, rhombic and hexagonal lattices; cubic amplitude equations for their stability; and an inverse ('double') retinocortical map to draw what each pattern would look like in the visual field. Drug action enters only as a change of parameter that destabilizes the resting state (higher excitability or reduced inhibition). The output is compared by eye with published drawings of hallucinations. It extends the model of Ermentrout & Cowan (1979), co-authored by the corresponding author (pp. 299-330).
can_establish: That a V1-like network with this architecture and symmetry, when pushed past an instability, can produce activity patterns whose images in the visual field resemble each of Klüver's four classes of form constants, and which model assumptions (the spread of lateral connections, the strength of local inhibition) decide which patterns appear.
cannot_establish: That psychedelic or other geometric hallucinations are in fact generated this way in the human brain (no human data are analysed, and the comparison with hallucinations is by eye against a few redrawn images); how any drug produces the instability (hallucinogens appear only as an assumed change in excitability or inhibition, and the same mechanism is applied to flickering light and eye pressure); or anything about the complex, figurative visions people also report, several of which the authors say lie beyond the model.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: no participants. Inputs are published anatomical and physiological findings (cat, macaque, owl monkey and tree shrew V1, plus unpublished owl-monkey data cited as a personal communication; human estimates of V1 area and hypercolumn spacing) and published drawings and descriptions of hallucinations (Klüver, 1966; Knauer & Maloney, 1913; Oster, 1970; Siegel, 1977; Tyler, 1978; Patterson, 1992; Clottes & Lewis-Williams, 1998) (pp. 299-305).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The hallucination images used for comparison are a handful of illustrations redrawn by the authors from secondary sources (popular-science articles, a petroglyph, a book on prehistoric shamans' art), chosen without stated criteria; no systematic sample of what people see is used. The premise that all observers report seeing Klüver's form constants or variations (p. 301) and the figure of 30-40 repetitions of a pattern around the visual field (p. 317) are given without sources.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Hallucinogens are represented only abstractly: raising the coupling parameter, or equivalently the slope of the neurons' response function by a steady input, changes network excitability, which the authors describe as thought to be one of the possible effects of hallucinogens; an indirect reduction of inhibition is offered as another possibility (p. 311); the Discussion presumes the instability occurs shortly after hallucinogens act on brain-stem nuclei that control cortical excitability (p. 323). No receptor, drug or dose is modelled.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: No empirical comparison. The model is set against the earlier Ermentrout-Cowan model, which had no orientation preference and so could not produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, certain chequer-boards or cobwebs (p. 303), and, visually, against drawings of hallucinations (p. 317).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Mathematical analysis: eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the linearized model (pp. 309-312), planforms identified from the axial subgroups of the lattice symmetry groups (pp. 312-314), cubic amplitude equations for their selection and stability (pp. 318-323), and visual-field images obtained with single and double inverse retinocortical maps (pp. 314-320).
outcomes.validity_norms: No quantitative test against perceptual or physiological data. Resemblance to form constants is judged by eye (p. 317). Anatomical parameters come largely from other species and are scaled to human V1 with a hypercolumn spacing of about 1.33-2 mm taken from anatomical and psychophysical evidence (p. 304).
outcomes.operationalization: A geometric hallucination is identified with a spatially periodic pattern of V1 activity that branches off the uniform resting state when it becomes unstable. 'Contoured' patterns are lattices of locally oriented edges; 'non-contoured' patterns are contrasting regions of light and dark (pp. 312-314).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Not applicable (no statistical estimates). Quantities used or derived: retinocortical map constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 estimated from published data (Drasdo, 1977) (p. 302); human V1 about 3500 mm2 per hemisphere, a hypercolumn about 2.67 mm2, so about 1300 hypercolumns (p. 305); with a unit length of about 400 micrometres the critical pattern wavelength is given as about 2.66 mm (p. 311); commonly reported hallucinations show 30-40 repetitions around the visual field, corresponding to 2.4-3.2 mm in V1 (p. 317); contour-completing (even) patterns require lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees (theta0 > pi/4) from the axis of orientation preference (pp. 311, 324).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable. The authors defer a fuller stability analysis, including higher-order terms, to a separate paper (Bressloff et al., 2000b) (p. 319).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Mathematically, when the resting state of a V1-like sheet with local and weak anisotropic lateral connections loses stability, a finite set of doubly periodic patterns can arise; mapped back to the visual field, non-contoured patterns look like tunnels, funnels and spirals and contoured ones like honeycombs, chequer-boards, lattices and cobwebs. With the strict anisotropy suggested by anatomy, the contoured patterns that appear do not form continuous contours; contour-completing patterns needed lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees. Square patterns were unstable; rolls, hexagons and triangles could be stable. The resemblance to hallucinations is shown by comparing figures by eye.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion state that the planforms generate representatives of all the form constants and that all the Klüver form constants can now be obtained (pp. 299, 324), qualified in the abstract as resting on the authors' interpretation of the correspondence between V1 patterns and percepts and on the presumed action of hallucinogens. The Discussion concludes that V1 circuits normally involved in detecting oriented edges and processing contours 'are also responsible for the generation of the hallucinatory form constants' (p. 324), which goes beyond a model not tested against physiological or perceptual data, although the abstract frames the same point as an interesting possibility if the mechanism is sited mainly in V1 (p. 300). The authors list limits: continuity of the images across the midline and their stability in the visual field are deferred (p. 301); the restriction to doubly periodic solutions has no formal justification (p. 312); some reported images (a tunnel with reversed magnification, a lattice-tunnel, a complex image after LSD) cannot be understood with the simple model (pp. 325-326).

timeline.event: Klüver's classification of geometric hallucinations into four form constants, cited by this paper from Klüver (1966).

Ermentrout & Cowan: model in which hallucinogens destabilize a two-dimensional sheet of excitatory and inhibitory neurons so that stripes, hexagons or squares of activity form, which the retinocortical map turns into funnels, spirals and chequer-boards; without orientation it cannot produce lattices, honeycombs or cobwebs (as described, p. 303).
Wiener (1994, thesis) and Cowan (1997): preliminary accounts of the extension to orientation-selective cells (as described, p. 304).
This study.
Zweck & Williams (2001): basis functions with the same shift-twist symmetry, introduced for an algorithm of contour completion (as described, p. 325).

replication.where_it_stands: A theoretical account. Among the sources read for this card, no empirical test of its predictions (for example the double retinocortical map's predicted orientation changes near the horizontal meridian, detectable with optical imaging, p. 324) has been read. The card supports statements about what the model proposes, what it rests on and what it predicts, not about what happens in the brain during psychedelic use.

The corresponding author, J.D. Cowan, co-authored the earlier model this paper extends (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the work.

what_would_settle_it: Imaging of V1 activity at sufficient resolution during simple geometric hallucinations induced by a psychedelic or by flickering light, testing for the predicted stripe or lattice patterns with wavelengths of about 2.4-3.2 mm and for the predicted orientation structure, combined with systematic, quantitative reports from observers of which form constants they see and when.

domains.domain: Model assumptions and their empirical support
domains.note: The architecture rests on orientation maps and lateral-connection patterns from cat, macaque, owl monkey and tree shrew (partly unpublished data), scaled to human V1 by a hypercolumn spacing inferred from anatomical and psychophysical evidence; it assumes all orientations at every point, weak lateral connections, a continuum despite pattern wavelengths of about twice the hypercolumn spacing (p. 305), and doubly periodic solutions without formal justification (p. 312), each stated by the authors.

domains.domain: Comparison with the phenomenon it explains
domains.note: The only check against hallucinations is by eye, with a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources (pp. 300-302, 317, 325); there is no quantitative measure of fit and no systematic data on what people see; the repetition figure that sets the expected wavelength is uncited (p. 317).

Hallucinogens enter only as an assumed rise in excitability or fall in inhibition (p. 311); no receptor or pharmacology is modelled, and the same mechanism is applied to flickering light, eye pressure, anaesthetics and the edges of sleep, so nothing in the model is specific to psychedelics.

domains.domain: Sensitivity of the conclusions to parameter choices
domains.note: The abstract says the results are sensitive to the detailed specification of the lateral connectivity (p. 300); the contour-completing patterns that match seen form constants appear only when lateral connections spread more than 45 degrees from the axis of orientation preference, a departure from the strict anisotropy that motivated the model (pp. 311, 324).
Equations, parameter values for the plotted curves and derivations (Appendix A) are printed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own work
domains.note: Builds on the corresponding author's earlier model (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), a thesis and a preliminary account by authors (Wiener, 1994; Cowan, 1997) and the authors' own 2000 papers, with a fuller stability analysis deferred to one of them (p. 319).

Assumptions and interpretations are mostly flagged ('presumed action of hallucinogens', 'given our interpretation', 'intriguing possible scenarios'), but some premises are asserted (all observers see form constants, p. 301), and the Discussion's conclusion that V1 edge circuits are responsible for the form constants is firmer than the abstract's 'interesting possibility' (pp. 300, 324).

domains.domain: Balance (alternative explanations of the form constants)
domains.note: Alternatives are mentioned (filling in by higher areas, V2 for stabilization, dorsal MSTd for some tunnel images, an argument from continuity across the midline for higher levels) but no competing model is developed or compared; a retinal origin is set aside with a brief argument (images seen by blind subjects and in dark rooms, and moving with the eyes) (pp. 300-301, 312, 325-326).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for a theoretical model (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is applied with domains suited to modelling, as on other modelling cards. As mathematics the paper is careful and transparent, and it states its main assumptions. As evidence about psychedelic visuals it is weak: the drug appears only as an abstract parameter shared with flicker and eye pressure, the anatomy comes mainly from other species, and the fit to hallucinations is a visual resemblance to a few redrawn images. The card may be cited for what the model proposes and rests on: that the simple geometric patterns seen on psychedelics and in other conditions fall into Klüver's four classes, that the retina-to-cortex map turns tunnels, funnels and spirals into simple stripes of activity in V1, and that a V1-like network pushed past an instability can generate patterns resembling all four classes; and for its stated predictions. It should not be cited as showing that psychedelic visuals are produced this way, or as an account of how psychedelics act on the brain.

key_findings.finding: The paper takes Klüver's four classes of form constants as the phenomenon to explain ((i) gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; (ii) cobwebs; (iii) tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; (iv) spirals) and investigates mathematically the assumption that the retina-to-V1 map and V1's local and lateral circuits determine their geometry.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Geometric hallucinations are described as occurring after flickering light, certain anaesthetics, on waking or falling asleep, after deep pressure on the eyeballs and shortly after drugs such as LSD and marijuana; they are also seen by blind people and in sealed dark rooms, and they move with the eyes while keeping their positions relative to each other, which the authors take to mean they arise in the brain rather than the eyes; in the authors' view they are generated in V1 and stabilized by V2 and other areas.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (a) Form constants and visual imagery (p. 300, both columns; p. 301, left column, first paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Away from the fovea the retina-to-V1 map behaves like a complex logarithm (constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 estimated from Drasdo, 1977), so circles in the visual field become vertical lines in V1, rays become horizontal lines and logarithmic spirals become oblique lines: tunnel, funnel and spiral form constants correspond to stripes of neural activity at various angles in V1.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (b) The human retinocortical map (p. 302); (c) Form constants as spontaneous cortical patterns, 1st paragraph (p. 303); Figures 5-7

key_findings.finding: The earlier Ermentrout-Cowan model, in which a Turing-like instability makes stripes, hexagons or squares of activity form in a sheet of excitatory and inhibitory neurons, treats V1 as a 'cortical retina' without orientation preference and so cannot produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, certain chequer-boards or cobwebs, which, except the chequer-boards, look more like lattices of oriented edges than contrasting regions of light and dark.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (c), 2nd paragraph; (d) Orientation tuning in V1, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Anatomical basis of the new model: orientation preference repeats about every 300 micrometres in cat V1 and about every 0.5 mm in macaque V1; nearby cells connect roughly isotropically, while long horizontal axons in layers II-III link patches of similar orientation about every 0.5 mm, running along the axis of their orientation preference (owl monkey, tree shrew); these come almost entirely from excitatory cells, 20% ending on inhibitory cells; human V1 is estimated at about 3500 mm2 per hemisphere with a hypercolumn spacing of about 1.33-2 mm, about 1300 hypercolumns.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction › (d) Orientation tuning in V1, from the 2nd paragraph to the end of the subsection (pp. 303-304); Figures 8-10; 2(a) The model, left column (p. 305)

key_findings.finding: The drug enters only through the bifurcation parameter: raising global coupling, or equivalently the slope of the neurons' output function through a steady input, changes network excitability, which the authors describe as thought to be one of the possible effects of hallucinogens; hallucinogens might also act indirectly on the balance of inhibition, which could influence which patterns emerge.
key_findings.locator: 3. Linear stability analysis › (c) Marginal stability › (i) Choosing the bifurcation parameter

key_findings.finding: Two families of patterns: if inhibition between neighbouring orientation patches is weak, V1 behaves without intrinsic orientation tuning and, if the lateral interactions are still effective, non-contoured patterns (light and dark regions) arise, corresponding to tunnels, funnels and spirals; if it is strong, contoured patterns (lattices of oriented edges) arise, corresponding to honeycombs, chequer-boards and cobwebs (Discussion, p. 324). Elsewhere (pp. 303, 312) the paper groups chequer-boards with the light-and-dark patterns.
key_findings.locator: 3(d) The Ermentrout-Cowan model revisited (p. 312); 7. Discussion, item (i) of the second list, after the 3rd paragraph (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: With lateral connections strictly along the axis of orientation preference (and acting as inhibitory), the 'odd' contoured patterns are selected, and these do not form continuous contours; the contour-completing 'even' patterns, which recover the form constants missing from the earlier model, appear when lateral connections spread more than 45 degrees (theta0 > pi/4) from that axis.
key_findings.locator: 3(c), right-column paragraph beginning 'An interesting question' and Figure 17 (p. 311); 5(b) Planforms in the visual field, last paragraph (p. 317); 7. Discussion, item (ii) of the second list (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: Stability: on square or rhombic lattices rolls are stable and squares unstable (for contoured patterns on a rhombic lattice, rhombic patterns are stable when the lattice angle lies between 30 and 60 degrees); on hexagonal lattices stable hexagons appear first for even patterns, and hexagons or triangles for odd patterns; the authors note that hallucinations resembling square patterns exist and may be transitional forms.
key_findings.locator: 6. The selection and stability of patterns › (b) (p. 321); (c) and (d) (pp. 322-323); 7. Discussion, item (i) of the second list (p. 324)

key_findings.finding: Scale: commonly reported hallucinations have 30-40 repetitions of the pattern around the visual field, corresponding to 2.4-3.2 mm in V1, the range expected for the model's critical wavelength; with a unit length of about 400 micrometres the paper gives a critical wavelength of about 2.66 mm.
key_findings.locator: 3(c), last paragraph of the left column (p. 311); 5(b) Planforms in the visual field, right column, text after equation (45) (p. 317)
key_findings.note: The 30-40 repetitions figure is not referenced. On the 2.66 mm figure see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The match with hallucinations is shown by inviting the reader to compare figures: for example the pressure phosphene of Figure 1 with the model pattern of Figure 35a, and the cobweb petroglyph of Figure 4 with Figure 31a.
key_findings.locator: 5(b) Planforms in the visual field, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Prediction offered for testing: if V1 implements the double retinocortical map, cells tuned to the same relative angle should be preferentially connected, and orientation changes should be relatively large and detectable with optical imaging near the horizontal meridian (p. 324). Separately, the authors cite reports (Siegel & Jarvik, 1975) that after LSD and similar drugs many people see a bright white light at the centre of the visual field that explodes into a hallucination in about 3 s, which they say corresponds to activity spreading across V1 at about 2.4 cm per second and present as an 'actually observed' instance of a propagating-wave scenario consistent with their analysis, not as a prediction (pp. 324-325).
key_findings.locator: 7. Discussion, item (ii) of the first list, after the 2nd paragraph (p. 324); item (ii) of the second list (p. 324, continuing on p. 325)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: continuity of the images across the midline and their stability in the visual field are deferred; the restriction to doubly periodic solutions has as yet no formal justification, though they cite evidence from convecting fluids, reaction-diffusion systems and neural-net simulations that such systems tend to form doubly periodic patterns; many variants of the form constants have been described, some of which cannot be understood in terms of the simple model (a tunnel with reversed magnification, possibly involving circuits beyond V1 such as dorsal MSTd; a marijuana lattice-tunnel, for which they suggest a mismatch with a somewhat disordered cortical lattice and show a simulation; a complex image after LSD that may involve more than one length scale, beyond the model's scope).
key_findings.locator: 1(a), last paragraph (p. 301); 4. Doubly periodic planforms, 1st paragraph (p. 312); 7. Discussion, item (iv) of the second list (pp. 325-326)

reporting_issues.issue: The wavelength is given as 2 pi (0.400)/qc mm, 'ca. 2.66 mm at the critical wavenumber qc = 1'; at qc = 1 the expression gives 2.51 mm (editors' calculation). 2.66 mm corresponds to qc of about 0.94, close to the critical wavenumber marked in Figure 16a.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either value lies inside the 2.4-3.2 mm range the authors expect.

reporting_issues.issue: The model V1 domain is described as two pieces of 72 mm along x and 48 mm along y, and the cylindrical period in y is 96 mm (two hemifields of 48 mm), but the same paragraph says the y coordinate changes from -pi/2 to pi/2 'in 72 mm'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 48 mm fits the 96 mm period used in equation (43).

reporting_issues.issue: Two empirical premises carry no source: that all observers report seeing Klüver's form constants or variations (p. 301), and that commonly reported hallucination patterns have 30-40 repetitions around the visual field (p. 317), which fixes the expected cortical wavelength of 2.4-3.2 mm.
reporting_issues.consequence: The match in scale between model and hallucinations rests on an unreferenced figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The hallucination images against which the model's patterns are compared are redrawn by the authors from secondary sources (Oster, 1970; Siegel, 1977, both in Scientific American; a petroglyph; cave-art illustrations; Tyler, 1978), and one is a petroglyph whose hallucinatory origin is stated as possible ('patterns that may be hallucinatory'), not established.
reporting_issues.consequence: The visual comparison tests resemblance to selected illustrations, not to what people actually report seeing.

design_detail: Anonymous, unpaid, one-sitting online survey (Qualtrics; designed to take about 50 minutes) from the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, August 2020 to January 2021, of adults who said they had had changes in their beliefs that they attribute to a psychedelic experience. Respondents chose the single experience 'that you feel led to the greatest belief change' and, at the time of the survey, rated their agreement (-3 to +3) with ten statements about which entities can have conscious experience (self, other humans, non-human primates, four-legged animals, insects, fungi, plants, inanimate natural objects, inanimate man-made objects, the universe), five superstition or paranormal items and one free-will item, each for three time points: 'Before (e.g., a month)', 'After (e.g., a month)' and 'Now'; plus the MEQ30 for the remembered experience and ratings of challenge, personal meaning and insight. 1,606 analysed. Paired t-tests and McNemar tests, with differences counted as meaningful only if p < 1e-5 and d of at least 0.2 (means) or a difference of at least 10 percentage points (proportions); low vs high MEQ (median split); a linear mixed model with MEQ as a continuous predictor and listed covariates. All three time points, including 'before', were rated in one sitting a mean of 8.2 years after the experience (Materials and methods, pp. 2-3). Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as for the same group's similar surveys in the card set.
can_establish: What this self-selected group of 1,606 people, recruited because they attributed a belief change to a psychedelic experience, reported about their beliefs before, after and now, as percentages agreeing with each statement, and that those who rated the remembered experience as more mystical reported larger changes.
cannot_establish: That psychedelic experiences increase the attribution of consciousness (entry required a belief change attributed to a psychedelic, respondents described their most belief-changing experience, and 'before' beliefs were recalled years later, so the before-after difference may reflect selection and recall rather than change); how common such changes are among people who use psychedelics; whether the changes endure (the 'after' and 'now' ratings were made in the same sitting); or whether the beliefs are true, which the authors say the data neither support nor undermine (p. 6).

sample.recruitment: Internet postings on social media and relevant websites (for example Erowid) and email invitations to an anonymous survey for people who had taken a psychedelic that led to changes in their beliefs; the belief changes were intentionally described vaguely, inviting anyone who had had changes in beliefs that they attribute to a psychedelic experience (Materials and methods › Participant Recruitment, p. 2). No compensation (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over; able to read, write and speak fluent English; endorsing a belief-changing psychedelic experience with one of the listed classic psychedelics. After consent, sequential exclusions: no English fluency 170; no belief-changing psychedelic experience 264; failed one or more attention checks 38; a drug other than psilocybin mushrooms, LSD, ayahuasca, N,N-DMT, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline-containing cacti 76; multiple psychoactive drugs 633; age at the reference experience younger than age at first psychedelic use 11; did not complete 2,086; responses appearing to refer to several experiences 113 (Results › Survey Completion, pp. 3-4).
sample.demographics: Mean age 35.1 (SD 13.3); male 67%; White 89%, Hispanic 11%; United States 69%; bachelor's degree 32%, master's 17%, advanced professional degree 8%. Age at the reference experience 26.9 (SD 10.1); years since it 8.2 (SD 12.6); 25% within the past 12 months; for 44% it was their first belief-changing psychedelic experience; lifetime classic psychedelic uses 20.9 (SD 25.7). Substance at the reference experience: psilocybin mushrooms 49%, LSD 33%, ayahuasca 7%, N,N-DMT 6%, 5-MeO-DMT 3%, mescaline 2% (Table 1, p. 4).
sample.attrition: Of 11,281 who reached the landing page, 4,997 consented; 2,086 of those did not complete and 1,305 were excluded for the other reasons listed, leaving 1,606 (editors' arithmetic: 4,997 - 3,391). Non-completers were not compared with completers.
sample.selection_effects: Selection on the outcome: only people who attributed a belief change to a psychedelic were invited, and each described the experience that changed their beliefs most. Recruitment ran through psychedelic-interest websites and social media; people who had combined drugs (633) were excluded. The high rates of agreement 'after' therefore describe a group chosen for having changed, not people who use psychedelics in general.

exposure.measurement: Self-report of the substance (from a list), an estimated dose, other drugs taken, age at the experience and when it happened (p. 2); the MEQ30 rated retrospectively for the remembered experience (mean 74% of maximum, SD 20; 49% met the a priori criterion for a complete mystical experience) and psychological challenge on an 8-point scale (pp. 2-4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported in the article (an estimated dose was asked, p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Respondents who reported using multiple psychoactive drugs (633) were excluded (p. 4); other drug use is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. 'Before' ratings are each respondent's recollection at the time of the survey. The Discussion compares the 61% who agreed after the experience that plants can be conscious with 10% or 18% reported in general-population studies (Arico et al., 2011; Reggia et al., 2015), which used other samples and wording (p. 5).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Beliefs before the experience were not measured at the time; prior religious or spiritual commitments, interest in questions of consciousness and expectations are not reported in the article.

outcomes.instruments: Ten statements on the capacity of entities for conscious experience (nine entities in assumed descending likelihood, plus 'The universe is conscious'); three superstition items and two items judged a priori improbable (abominable snowman, Loch Ness monster) from the Revised Paranormal Belief Scale; one free-will item; each rated from strongly disagree (-3) to strongly agree (+3) for 'Before', 'After' and 'Now' (Materials and methods, pp. 2-3; Tables 2-3, pp. 5-6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study-made items without validation beyond internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.87 at all three time points for the consciousness items, p. 4); no norms; 'before' ratings are retrospective.
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement = a rating of +1 to +3. A meaningful change = p < 1e-5 and Cohen's d of at least 0.2 for mean ratings, or p < 1e-5 and a difference of at least 10 percentage points for proportions (McNemar tests) (Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, p. 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: No formal correction, but very strict thresholds (p < 1e-5 together with a minimum effect size or 10-point difference) for every comparison (p. 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (anonymous self-report).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages agreeing, Before to After to Now (Table 2, p. 5): self 80, 97, 98; other humans 78, 94, 95; non-human primates 63, 83, 85; four-legged animals 59, 79, 82; insects 33, 57, 60; fungi 21, 56, 62; plants 26, 61, 64; inanimate natural objects (for example rocks) 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects (for example chairs) 3, 15, 17; the universe is conscious 34, 80, 82. Every Before-After difference met the criteria (McNemar p < 1e-10 to < 1e-100); no After-Now difference did. Superstitions and free will (Table 3, p. 6): black cats 8, 4, 3; broken mirror 10, 5, 4; number 13 7, 3, 2; abominable snowman 6, 8, 8; Loch Ness monster 10, 10, 10; free will 74, 74, 73; no meaningful changes. Cohen's d values for the mean ratings are in Supplementary Table 2, not among the files (not extracted). Respondents with MEQ at or above the median reported higher 'after' ratings than those below it for every entity except other humans (Figure 2, p. 6); the mixed model with MEQ as a continuous variable is reported only in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).
analysis.covariates: Mixed model: age, age at the experience, sex, race, whether it was the first psychedelic experience, whether it occurred in the past year, number of lifetime psychedelic uses, which psychedelic was taken, and rated psychological challenge (nine variables listed in the Methods, p. 3; the Results speak of eight, p. 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. The data reported are a portion of a larger survey dataset to be reported separately (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Effect sizes and the mixed-model results are only in supplements (not read); the analyses by past-year and first experience are 'data not shown' (p. 4), as is the effect of MEQ on superstition and free-will ratings (p. 5); the sizes of the low- and high-MEQ groups are not given; the rest of the survey is to be reported elsewhere.
analysis.power: No power calculation; the sample is very large relative to the differences tested.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 1,606 people recruited because they attributed a belief change to a psychedelic experience, and describing their most belief-changing one, the shares who agreed that various entities can be conscious were higher for 'after' than for their recalled 'before', all rated in one sitting on average 8 years later: plants 26% to 61%, fungi 21% to 56%, insects 33% to 57%, rocks 8% to 26%, the universe 34% to 80%. 'Now' ratings were similar to 'after'. Superstition and free-will ratings did not change meaningfully (the three superstition items roughly halved from low levels). A more mystical remembered experience went with larger reported change.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says only that the experience is associated with increased attribution, which fits the design, but the abstract reports large increases, and the Discussion says the survey 'suggests that a single psychedelic experience can increase' these beliefs, that the increases occur soon after the experience and are 'enduring, being unchanged a mean of 8 years after the experience' (p. 5), and that the study demonstrates that attribution increases among people reporting belief-changing experiences (p. 6). Gaps: (1) all three time points were rated at once, years later, so 'soon after' and 'enduring' are recollections, not measurements; (2) recruiting on belief change and asking about the most belief-changing experience build the before-after difference into the sample; (3) a fifth of respondents recalled not agreeing before the experience that they themselves were capable of conscious experience (80% 'before'), which raises the question of how reliably earlier beliefs and the items were answered; (4) the comparison with 10-18% in the general population sets an 'after' figure from a selected sample against other surveys with other wording. The authors acknowledge the retrospective design, the restriction to people reporting belief change and possible demand effects, and call for prospective studies controlling for expectancy (pp. 6-7); their argument that unchanged free-will ratings show the findings are not just demand effects is indirect.

timeline.event: Griffiths et al.: the same group's retrospective online survey of 'God encounter' experiences, whose single-reference-experience method this survey follows (p. 2).
Davis et al.: the same group's retrospective survey of DMT entity encounters, using the same method (p. 2).

Timmermann et al.: prospective online cohort of psychedelic ceremony attendees; agreement with panpsychism and other non-physicalist statements was higher at 4 weeks and 6 months than a week before, among the 122 who answered both follow-ups; cited by this paper (pp. 2, 6).
This study.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction agrees with the one prospective study read for this card (Timmermann et al., 2021: a panpsychism item and related beliefs), which however lost about 85% of its baseline sample and had no comparison group. No prospective study that measured beliefs about which entities are conscious before a psychedelic experience, with a comparison group, has been read. The status is partial for that reason.

funding.funder: Support for SMN and RRG through the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research was provided by Tim Ferriss, Matt Mullenweg, Blake Mycoskie, Craig Nerenberg, and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation (Funding, p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: RRG is on the board of directors of the Heffter Research Institute; the remaining author declares no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest (Conflict of Interest, p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research (R.R. Griffiths also Department of Neuroscience). The funders are private donors and a foundation named in the Funding statement. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records beliefs about which entities are conscious before a planned psychedelic experience and again weeks and years later, in people not selected for having changed and in a comparison group who do not take a psychedelic, with dropouts followed; or a randomized trial with these beliefs as a pre-specified outcome and expectations measured beforehand.

domains.note: No frame: internet postings and email invitations.
Self-selected; eligibility required a belief change attributed to a psychedelic, which selects on the outcome.
1,606 respondents.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics and substances are detailed (Table 1), but the setting, amount and context of the experiences are not reported in the article.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Exclusions are documented step by step, but the 2,086 consenting non-completers (42% of those who consented) were not compared with completers.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Study-made items; 'before' beliefs recalled years later in the same sitting as 'after' and 'now'; the MEQ30 answered about a remembered experience on average 8 years old.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online items for all, with alpha 0.87; no test-retest reliability; retrospective framing.
Strict thresholds and an adjusted model, but effect sizes and model results only in supplements not read, a median split, group sizes not given, and error bars labelled as SDs that cannot be SDs.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: No denominator of people reached; 11,281 page visits, 4,997 consents, 1,606 analysed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because the encyclopedia will use the shares of respondents agreeing with each statement. The shares are precise but describe a self-selected group recruited for having changed its beliefs, reporting on its most belief-changing experience, with 'before' recalled years later. Cite for what these respondents reported, with the denominator and the selection stated (for example plants: 26% recalled agreeing before, 61% after), for the absence of change in superstition and free-will ratings, and for the association between remembered mystical intensity and reported change. Not for how often psychedelics change such beliefs, not as evidence that they cause the change, not for durability, and not for whether the beliefs are true.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment and flow: an anonymous online survey for people who attributed changes in their beliefs to a psychedelic experience, recruited through social media, websites such as Erowid and email, August 2020 to January 2021; 11,281 reached the landing page, 4,997 consented and 1,606 were analysed after exclusions (including 2,086 who did not complete and 633 who had used several drugs at the experience).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Participant Recruitment, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Results › Survey Completion, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Respondents (n = 1,606): mean age 35.1, 67% male, 89% White, 69% from the United States; the reference experience was on average 8.2 years (SD 12.6) before the survey, within the past 12 months for 25%, and the first belief-changing psychedelic experience for 44%; psilocybin mushrooms 49%, LSD 33%, ayahuasca 7%, N,N-DMT 6%, 5-MeO-DMT 3%, mescaline 2%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respondent Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: About 70% rated the experience among the five most personally meaningful and psychologically insightful of their lives; remembered MEQ30 scores averaged 74% of maximum (SD 20), and 49% met the a priori criterion for a complete mystical experience.
key_findings.locator: Results › Qualities of the Psychedelic Experience, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The 70% figure rests on Supplementary Table 1, which is not among the files.

key_findings.finding: Percentages agreeing that each entity can have conscious experience, Before to After to Now: self 80, 97, 98; other humans 78, 94, 95; non-human primates 63, 83, 85; four-legged animals 59, 79, 82; insects 33, 57, 60; fungi 21, 56, 62; plants 26, 61, 64; inanimate natural objects 8, 26, 29; inanimate man-made objects 3, 15, 17; the universe is conscious 34, 80, 82. All Before-After differences met the criteria (p < 1e-10 or smaller and at least 10 points); no After-Now difference did.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnote; Results › Changes in Attribution of Consciousness, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: All three columns were rated in one sitting. Figure 1 (p. 5) shows the mean ratings rising, for example plants from about -0.4 to about +0.8, fungi from about -0.3 to about +0.9 and insects from about 0 to about +0.8 on the -3 to +3 scale (read approximately by the editors from a 300-dpi crop).

key_findings.finding: The rise in attribution was reported to be unaffected by whether the experience occurred in the past year or was the respondent's first psychedelic experience (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in Attribution of Consciousness, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Respondents with MEQ scores at or above the median reported larger increases than those below it; 'before' ratings were similar in the two groups, and at 'after' the groups differed meaningfully for every entity except other humans. The relationship held with MEQ as a continuous variable after adjustment for demographic, psychedelic-use and other variables including psychological challenge. Note: group sizes are not given; the main text gives no statistics or location for the adjusted model (Supplementary Table 3, which it cites for the low/high MEQ comparison, was not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in Attribution of Consciousness, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Figure 2 and legend (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Group sizes are not given; the adjusted model is in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).

key_findings.finding: Superstitious beliefs and free will did not change meaningfully: black cats bring bad luck 8%, 4%, 3%; broken mirror 10%, 5%, 4%; 13 is unlucky 7%, 3%, 2%; the abominable snowman exists 6%, 8%, 8%; the Loch Ness monster exists 10%, 10%, 10%; people have free will 74%, 74%, 73% (Before, After, Now).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in Superstitious Beliefs and Freewill, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Table 3 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the 61% who agreed after the experience that plants can be conscious with 10% or 18% reported in the general population by other studies (Arico et al., 2011; Reggia et al., 2015).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: a retrospective design, a sample limited to people who endorsed a belief change they attributed to a psychedelic experience, and possible demand effects; they argue that unchanged free-will beliefs suggest the findings are not just an artefact of demand, and state that persistent beliefs after compelling experiences neither support nor undermine the epistemic validity of the beliefs.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (end) and 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors call for future prospective psychedelic drug administration studies that control for expectancies.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 6, continuing on p. 7); Abstract, Discussion

reporting_issues.issue: Figures 1 and 2 say the data are means plus or minus 1 SD, but the error bars span only about 0.07 scale points either side of the mean on a -3 to +3 scale (read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1), far too short for SDs of ratings on which, for example, 20% did not agree; their length fits standard errors or 95% confidence intervals of the mean in a sample of 1,606 (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures understate the spread of individual ratings; they should not be read as showing that respondents answered alike.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the income band 125,000-199,000 is printed as 0%, between bands of 10% and 9%, and the income rows sum to 89% (editors' arithmetic); the other categorical blocks with complete categories (marital status, education, substance) sum to 100%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misprint (about 11% may belong in that band); income composition cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list nine covariates for the mixed model (age, age at the experience, sex, race, first experience, past-year experience, lifetime uses, substance, psychological challenge), while the Results say the model controlled for eight variables.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; which model was run cannot be confirmed without the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the increased attributions did not decrease in those who completed the survey years after the experience, but the main text reports only that the effects did not depend on whether the experience was in the past year, with data not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The durability claim rests on an analysis that cannot be checked from the article, and on retrospective 'now' ratings.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor wording differences: the agreement category +1 is 'Somewhat agree' in the Methods and 'Slightly agree' in the table footnotes; the figure axes are labelled from -2 (Disagree), although the rating scale runs from -3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

design_detail: Two parts, from the Centre for Psychedelic Research at Imperial College London. (1) Prospective online cohort without a comparison group: adults who planned to attend a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD) signed up at psychedelicsurvey.com after online advertisements and answered a 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire written for the study (nine items form a 'Non-physicalist Beliefs' factor, NPB) and nine FAD-Plus items on free will and fatalistic determinism about one week before, and again 4 weeks and 6 months after, the ceremony; acute experience (one day after), absorption, peer conformity, identity fusion with the group and well-being were also measured. Analyses: Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests, tables of conversion between preferred positions, correlations of belief change with well-being change and an exploratory path model. (2) Secondary analysis of the phase 2 double-blind randomized trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram for major depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03429075): a 5-item short version of the questionnaire at baseline and week 6 in 30 and 29 patients, repeated-measures ANCOVA with one-tailed tests (pp. 8-11). Appraised as a cohort with ROBINS-E because the paper's headline claims rest on the uncontrolled cohort; the trial part is described in the notes.
can_establish: Whether, among people who chose to attend a psychedelic ceremony and answered the follow-up surveys, agreement with non-physicalist statements (other realms, a non-natural unifying principle, panpsychism, mind-body dualism) was higher 4 weeks and 6 months afterwards than a week before, and by how much on a standardized scale; and, in one randomized trial, whether patients given psilocybin therapy shifted more on a short version of the same questions than patients given escitalopram.
cannot_establish: That the psychedelic caused the shift in the ceremony cohort (no comparison group; the ceremony's setting, group, ritual, teachings and expectations come with the drug, and about 85% of baseline respondents are missing from the paired analyses); that the trial shows a difference between psilocybin and escitalopram at the usual two-sided level (one-tailed p = 0.041, two-sided equivalent about 0.08); whether the new beliefs are true, which the study does not address; or whether the shifts persist beyond 6 months.

sample.recruitment: Cohort: online advertisements inviting people planning to attend a ceremony with a plant medicine (for example an ayahuasca retreat) or another guided psychedelic experience to sign up at the study website; automated email links one week before, one day after and 4 weeks after the indicated date, with the 6-month survey named under Measures (Methods › Design and participants, p. 8; Measures, p. 10). Trial: 59 patients with major depression recruited through trial networks, social media and other sources (p. 9).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort: aged 18 or over, good comprehension of English, and the intention to take part in a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic (a 5-HT2A agonist such as psilocybin, DMT, mescaline or LSD); no exclusions stated (p. 8). Trial: HAM-D-17 above 17 at screening, aged 18-80; excluded personal or immediate family history of psychosis, medically significant conditions, serious suicide attempts, positive pregnancy test, MRI contraindications, current SSRIs or previous escitalopram (p. 9).
sample.demographics: Baseline cohort (Table 2, N = 819): age 44.4 (SD 12.6); 359 women (43.8%), 455 men (55.6%), 5 other; United States 43.8%, United Kingdom 19.5%; master's degree 33.6%, doctorate or professional degree 20.5%; White 90.7%; working full time 63.4%; median household income 9000 dollars a month (p. 9). Characteristics of the 122 analysed are in Supplementary Table 1, not among the files. Trial demographics are in the trial report (not read).
sample.attrition: Of 819 (Table 2) or 866 (Results) baseline respondents, 122 contributed paired NPB data at both 4 weeks and 6 months (t(121) at both time points; about 14-15%, editors' calculation); completers were not compared with dropouts. Other analyses used different, unstated samples: the r and p values in Figure 3 imply about 370 respondents at 4 weeks and about 140 at 6 months (editors' calculation), and a 0.8% cell in Figure 2 implies at least about 118 baseline dualists in the 4-week conversion analysis (editors' inference). Trial: 59 patients (30 and 29).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected attendees of psychedelic ceremonies and retreats, mostly from Western countries, highly educated and with high incomes, who already leaned towards non-physicalist positions at baseline (Figure 1b, p. 3: baseline means on the agree side for the transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism and dualism items and on the disagree side for materialism). Religious affiliation and interest in metaphysical questions were not recorded; the authors say the sample may be skewed towards people sensitive to these belief shifts (Discussion, 14th paragraph, p. 8). With about 85% missing from the paired analyses and no comparison of completers with dropouts, the results describe completers only; if people whose beliefs shifted were more inclined to keep answering, the shifts would be overstated.

exposure.measurement: Cohort: self-reported attendance at a psychedelic ceremony; the substance, amount and setting were participants' own choices and are not reported in this paper (study details in Kettner et al., 2021, not read). One day after: Mystical Experience Questionnaire, visual scales of the 11-dimension Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire and the Perceived Emotional Synchrony Scale; at baseline: absorption (MODTAS) and peer conformity (four items of the short suggestibility scale); identity fusion with the ceremony group (one pictorial item) shortly before the session. Where a respondent attended more than one ceremony and gave several reports, only the largest score on each scale was used (pp. 10-11).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cohort: not controlled and not reported. Trial (study conditions): psilocybin 25 mg on two dosing days plus 6 weeks of daily placebo, or psilocybin 1 mg on the two days plus daily escitalopram (p. 9).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported.

comparison.controls: Cohort: none; beliefs compared within person over time. A cross-sectional association with lifetime psychedelic use at baseline (Spearman r = 0.223). Trial: randomized comparison of psilocybin therapy with escitalopram, both with psychological support, on a 5-item short version of the questionnaire.
comparison.matching: Not applicable in the cohort. Trial: ANCOVA adjusted for baseline NPB (p. 11).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Religious affiliation, prior spiritual practice, interest in metaphysics, environmental susceptibilities, the beliefs of co-attendees, facilitators and trial staff, and the teachings offered at ceremonies were not measured; the authors call the failure to measure the cultural milieu an oversight (Discussion, 14th and 15th paragraphs, p. 8).

outcomes.instruments: Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire (MBQ): 13 agree-disagree statements, ten written for the study and three from earlier research; an exploratory factor analysis at baseline kept one factor of nine items with loadings above 0.4 in absolute value, labelled Non-physicalist Beliefs (NPB), Cronbach's alpha 0.86 (Table 1, p. 2). Nine items of the FAD-Plus free-will and fatalistic-determinism subscales. Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months. Trial: five MBQ items (ontological and supernatural transcendentalism, dualism, materialism, non-naturalism) and the Universality subscale of the Spiritual Transcendence Scale at baseline and week 6 (Methods › Measures, p. 10).
outcomes.validity_norms: The MBQ is new; its only psychometric evidence here is the baseline factor analysis and alpha, and the authors say the relationship between items and philosophical positions could be contested, so items are best treated at face value (p. 2). No norms. The 5-item trial version has no reported reliability.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Shift away from physicalism' = an increase in the NPB factor score. 'Conversion' = a change in which of three items (materialism, dualism, idealism) a respondent endorsed most, with ties or no positive endorsement classed as none/mixed; for panpsychism, believers, sceptics and neutral by one item (pp. 10-11).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The paper names two main outcome measures (the MBQ and the FAD-Plus items, p. 10); paired comparisons and item-level and conversion tests are Bonferroni-corrected, but there is no correction across scales, correlations or the path model. The trial analyses report one-tailed p values, justified by hypotheses derived from the survey data (p. 11).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for the online self-report cohort. Trial: double-blind allocation; whether patients could tell their treatment is not reported in this paper.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cohort, NPB, all respondents (n = 122): 4 weeks t(121) = 3.66, Bonferroni p = 0.001, d = 0.33; 6 months t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46 (printed 95% CIs [0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50]; editors' 95% CIs for d about 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65, see reporting issues). Psychedelic-naive (n = 53): d = 0.53 at 4 weeks and 0.73 at 6 months. Fatalistic determinism, all: d = 0.25 at 4 weeks (p = 0.012), no persisting change at 6 months; naive: d = 0.46 and 0.39 (p. 3). Baseline NPB and lifetime psychedelic use: Spearman r = 0.223, p < 0.0001; fatalism r = 0.186 (p. 3). Conversion (Figure 2, p. 4): of baseline 'hard materialists', 24.4% remained at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months (31.1% and 33.3% moved to dualism, 42.2% and 44.4% to none/mixed); of baseline dualists, 55.5% and 65.2% remained (37% and 23.9% moved to none/mixed); of respondents neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% and 54.5% became believers. Well-being: NPB change correlated with well-being change r = 0.2 (p = 0.0001) at 4 weeks and r = 0.18 (p = 0.033) at 6 months (Figure 3, p. 5). Path model, standardized betas to the 4-week NPB score: emotional synchrony 0.22, moderated by peer conformity (0.08); synchrony predicted by identity fusion 0.30, absorption 0.18, gender -0.17, age -0.12 and baseline NPB 0.13 (Figure 4, p. 5). Trial: drug by time interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed (editors' calculation: two-sided p = 0.082); psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45; escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2; psilocybin responders vs escitalopram responders Z = 1.74, p = 0.041, Hedges' g = 0.56, 90% CI -0.17 to 1.26; in the psilocybin arm NPB change correlated with change in spiritual universality r = 0.52, p = 0.003 (pp. 5-6; Figure 5).
analysis.covariates: None for the paired tests and correlations; the path model contained the variables listed above; the trial ANCOVA adjusted for baseline NPB.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan is mentioned for the cohort analyses. The trial is registered (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03429075, EudraCT 2017-000219-18; p. 10), but the paper does not say whether the belief items were a registered outcome; the registry was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The analytic sample of each analysis is not stated and differs between analyses; the path model kept only predictors with significant effects (mystical-type and visual scores were dropped for non-significance, p. 11); in the trial, psilocybin responders are compared with escitalopram responders rather than with non-responders, which is what the Discussion describes; the correlation with spiritual universality is not reported numerically for the escitalopram arm; supplementary results were not read.
analysis.power: No power calculation for either part.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 122 ceremony attendees who answered both follow-ups, agreement with non-physicalist statements was modestly higher 4 weeks (d = 0.33) and 6 months (d = 0.46) after the ceremony than a week before, more so in 53 respondents taking a psychedelic for the first time (d = 0.53 and 0.73); respondents already leaned this way at baseline. Fatalism rose at 4 weeks only. Positions shifted in both directions in the conversion tables (for example 17.6% of none/mixed respondents moved towards materialism at 4 weeks), but most baseline materialists moved away from materialism and many neutral respondents became panpsychist 'believers'. Belief change correlated weakly with well-being change (r about 0.2). In the trial, patients given psilocybin shifted on a 5-item version (d = 0.45) and patients given escitalopram less (d = 0.2), with a group difference significant only one-tailed (two-sided p about 0.08).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title states that psychedelics 'alter' metaphysical beliefs; the abstract that the findings 'imply that psychedelic-use may causally influence metaphysical beliefs' and that the shifts were consolidated by an independent controlled trial; the Discussion that psychedelic use may be a key 'casual' [sic] determinant of the shifts (p. 6). Gaps: (1) the cohort has no comparison group and ceremonies bundle the drug with group, ritual and teaching; the authors concede that views held by co-attendees and research staff may have transferred (p. 8); (2) the abstract calls the sample large, but the paired analyses rest on 122 of more than 800 baseline respondents; (3) the abstract says the changes were positively correlated with the extent of past psychedelic use, but the reported correlation is with baseline beliefs, a cross-sectional association, not with change; (4) in the trial the interaction is one-tailed (two-sided p about 0.08), the escitalopram arm moved in the same direction (d = 0.2), and the statement that belief change is specific to psychedelics rests on a correlation significant in one arm and not reported for the other; (5) the Discussion says the trial found belief shifts in psilocybin responders versus non-responders, whereas the Results compared psilocybin responders with escitalopram responders, with a 90% CI for g that includes zero; (6) the path model is exploratory, yet the Discussion says emotional synchrony 'strongly mediated' the shifts (beta 0.22, no indirect-effect test reported). The authors do decline to judge the value of the beliefs, note links between some non-physicalist beliefs and avoidant coping, and raise informed-consent implications (pp. 7-8).

timeline.event: Griffiths et al.: retrospective survey of 'God encounter' experiences, among the earlier retrospective evidence this paper cites (ref. 29).
Davis et al.: retrospective survey of entity encounters after inhaled DMT, one of the anecdotal, qualitative and retrospective reports this paper cites as hinting at belief change (p. 2).
Carhart-Harris et al.: phase 2 randomized trial of psilocybin therapy versus escitalopram for major depression, the source of this paper's trial data.
This study.

Nayak & Griffiths: retrospective survey of 1,606 people who attributed a belief change to a psychedelic experience; larger shares agreed after than (as recalled) before that animals, plants, fungi, objects and the universe can be conscious; cites this study.

replication.where_it_stands: Among the sources read for this card, this is the only prospective study of metaphysical belief change after psychedelic use, and its trial component the only randomized comparison; a retrospective survey reports shifts in the same direction for attributing consciousness to other entities (Nayak & Griffiths, 2022). The status is partial because the paper's own trial component points the same way but at one-tailed significance, and no independent prospective replication with a comparison group has been read.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study that measures metaphysical beliefs with a validated instrument before and after in people who take a psychedelic and in a comparison group attending similar retreats or ceremonies without one, records the teachings and the beliefs of facilitators and co-attendees, follows dropouts and pre-registers its analyses; and randomized trials with belief change as a pre-specified, two-sided outcome and a check on whether patients could tell their treatment.

domains.note: No comparison group in the cohort: the drug cannot be separated from the ceremony's setting, group, ritual and teachings, from expectations or from time. The trial part has randomization but a short, unvalidated version of the questionnaire and one-tailed tests.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Attendance is self-reported; the substance, amount and setting are not reported; for people attending more than one ceremony only the largest acute-experience score was used.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: Self-selected ceremony attendees who already leaned towards non-physicalist positions; entry did not depend on the outcome, but the sample is atypical.

Integration practices, further ceremonies and contact with psychedelic communities after the ceremony were not recorded; the authors suggest cultural reinforcement may consolidate such beliefs (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, pp. 6-7).
About 85% of baseline respondents are missing from the paired analyses, without a comparison of completers and dropouts; respondents whose beliefs shifted may have been more likely to keep answering.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: A new questionnaire with face-value items, self-reported in a context where the direction of expected change is culturally familiar; repeated administration.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration mentioned; analytic samples differ between analyses and are not stated; the path model kept significant predictors only; one-tailed tests in the trial; the responder comparison is described differently in the Results and the Discussion.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three domains are high, and each could by itself produce the reported pattern: confounding by the ceremony context without any comparison group, heavy unanalysed attrition, and selective, inconsistently reported analyses. ROBINS-E rates the result very high when several domains are high in ways that substantially lower confidence. The prospective measurement of beliefs before the ceremony is a real strength over retrospective surveys. The card may be cited for the observed modest shifts among the 122 completers (d = 0.33 at 4 weeks and 0.46 at 6 months), for respondents already leaning non-physicalist at baseline, for shifts occurring in both directions in the conversion tables, and for the trial's one-tailed result stated with its two-sided equivalent; it should not be cited as showing that psychedelics cause belief change, that the change is specific to psychedelics, or that the beliefs are true or false.

key_findings.finding: The 13-item Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire yielded one factor of nine items, Non-physicalist Beliefs (Cronbach's alpha 0.86): positive loadings for another realm that can be visited (0.790), supernatural transition to other realms (0.740), a unifying principle beyond scientific explanation (0.776), panpsychism (0.642), primacy of other realms (0.592), dualism (0.444) and solipsism or idealism (0.441); negative loadings for materialism (-0.727) and naturalism (-0.598).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Among respondents with paired data (t(121), that is 122 people by the editors' reading of the degrees of freedom), NPB scores shifted away from physicalism from a week before to 4 weeks after the ceremony (t(121) = 3.66, p = 0.001, d = 0.33) and to 6 months after (t(121) = 5.07, p < 0.0001, d = 0.46).
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 3rd paragraph (p. 2, continuing on p. 3); Figure 1a (p. 3)
key_findings.note: The printed 95% CIs ([0.12, 0.39] and [0.22, 0.50]) are not CIs of d; editors' 95% CIs for d are about 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65. 122 is about 15% of the 819 in Table 2 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Respondents having their first psychedelic experience (t(52), that is 53 people by the editors' reading of the degrees of freedom; the n is not printed) shifted more: d = 0.53 at 4 weeks (t(52) = 3.85, p = 0.001) and d = 0.73 at 6 months (t(52) = 5.32, p < 0.0001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 3rd paragraph (continued from p. 2)

key_findings.finding: At the item level, Figure 1b marks a significant change at 6 months (**) for ontological transcendentalism, supernatural transcendentalism, materialism (down), panpsychism and dualism, and at 4 weeks only (*) for non-naturalism and primacy of other realms; naturalism and solipsism or idealism carry no significance marker. At baseline the means already lay on the agree side for the transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism, primacy and dualism items and on the disagree side for materialism, naturalism and solipsism or idealism.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1b (left panel) and legend
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1b; the item axis runs from Disagree to Agree without numbers, so item changes cannot be given in scale units. The legend lists solipsism/idealism among items that changed, but the figure gives it no marker (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Fatalistic determinism rose at 4 weeks in all respondents (t(121) = 2.81, p = 0.012, d = 0.25) but not at 6 months; in psychedelic-naive respondents it rose at 4 weeks (d = 0.46, p = 0.003) and 6 months (d = 0.39, p = 0.012).
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatalism, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: At baseline, more lifetime psychedelic use went with stronger non-physicalist beliefs (Spearman r = 0.223, p < 0.0001) and with stronger fatalistic determinism (r = 0.186, p < 0.0001); in item terms with stronger panpsychist (r = 0.19) and weaker materialist views (r = -0.18). These are cross-sectional associations, not changes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs, 3rd paragraph and Fatalism, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Figure 1a (right panel); Figure 2e (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Conversion between preferred positions (Figure 2): of baseline 'hard materialists', 24.4% still held that position at 4 weeks and 22.2% at 6 months; 31.1% and 33.3% moved to dualism and 42.2% and 44.4% to none/mixed. Of baseline dualists, 55.5% and 65.2% remained; 37% and 23.9% moved to none/mixed. Shifts also ran towards materialism: 17.6% (4 weeks) and 15.2% (6 months) of none/mixed respondents moved there. Of respondents neutral on panpsychism, 57.3% (4 weeks) and 54.5% (6 months) became believers; 83.9% and 86.8% of baseline believers remained believers.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2a-d and legend; Results › Conversion of preferred metaphysical beliefs, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4)
key_findings.note: The group sizes behind the percentages are not printed; the chi-squared statistics are shown only as asterisks.

key_findings.finding: Shifts towards non-physicalist beliefs correlated weakly with increases in well-being (WEMWBS): r = 0.2, p = 0.0001 at 4 weeks and r = 0.18, p = 0.033 at 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Non-physicalist beliefs and well-being, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: These r and p values imply about 370 and about 140 respondents (editors' calculation), not the 122 of the paired analyses.

key_findings.finding: Exploratory path model (standardized betas): perceived emotional synchrony with the group during the session predicted the 4-week NPB score (0.22), moderated by baseline peer conformity (0.08); synchrony was predicted by identity fusion with the group shortly before the session (0.30), trait absorption (0.18), gender (-0.17), age (-0.12) and baseline NPB (0.13); baseline NPB predicted 4-week NPB with beta 0.75. Mystical-type and visual-effect scores were dropped from the model for non-significance.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4 and legend; Results › Process of change modelling, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Methods › Statistical analysis, path-analysis paragraph (p. 11)
key_findings.note: The coding of gender is not stated in the main text; model fit is in Supplementary Table 2 (not read).

key_findings.finding: Trial (psilocybin therapy n = 30, escitalopram n = 29, 5-item NPB at baseline and week 6): drug by time interaction F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 one-tailed; within-arm change psilocybin Z = 2.28, p = 0.02, d = 0.45, escitalopram Z = 0.24, p = 0.33, d = 0.2; psilocybin responders shifted more than escitalopram responders (Z = 1.74, p = 0.041, g = 0.56, 90% CI -0.17 to 1.26); in the psilocybin arm NPB change correlated with change in spiritual universality (r = 0.52, p = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Results › Validation with data from a controlled clinical trial, 1st paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6); Figure 5 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: F(1, 56) = 3.13 has a two-sided p of 0.082. See reporting issues on the escitalopram and responder statistics.

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: religious affiliation, environmental susceptibilities and interest in metaphysical beliefs were not collected; the sample may be skewed towards people sensitive to these shifts; both samples were largely Western and well educated; the two samples differ in size, distress and expectations; views held by co-attendees and trial staff, or the wider psychedelic culture, may have transferred to participants.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 14th and 15th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors say that services and studies offering psychedelic experiences may be ethically obliged to mention possible belief change in informed consent, and that it would be hasty to read the findings as showing that non-physicalist, panpsychist or fatalistic beliefs are of positive value, noting associations of some such beliefs with avoidant coping ('spiritual bypassing').
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 7) and 12th paragraph (p. 8)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say 866 respondents completed the belief survey at different time points, Table 2 gives 819 at baseline, and the paired analyses have 121 degrees of freedom (122 people) at both 4 weeks and 6 months; the abstract calls the sample large.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline belief shifts rest on about 15% of the baseline sample, and the main text does not say who the 122 were or how they compared with those who dropped out (Supplementary Table 1, cited for sample characteristics, was not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CIs printed next to the d values (d = 0.33 with [0.12, 0.39]; d = 0.46 with [0.22, 0.50]; d = 0.73 with [0.36, 0.80]) cannot be CIs of d: several sit asymmetrically around d or barely include it; editors' 95% CIs for d = 0.33 and 0.46 with n = 122 are about 0.15 to 0.51 and 0.27 to 0.65. They are probably CIs of the raw mean change, whose scale is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The intervals should not be quoted as uncertainty around the effect sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: Analytic samples differ between analyses and are not stated: in Figure 3, r = 0.2 with p = 0.0001 implies about 370 respondents at 4 weeks and r = 0.18 with p = 0.033 about 140 at 6 months (editors' calculation); in Figure 2, 0.8% of baseline dualists at 4 weeks implies at least about 118 dualists in that analysis, more than the 122 respondents of the paired analyses could supply alongside the other groups (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.consequence: The analyses do not describe one cohort; the well-being correlations and conversion tables cannot be linked to the paired belief changes.

reporting_issues.issue: The trial interaction is printed as F(56) = 3.13, p = 0.041 'one-tailed'; with 1 and 56 degrees of freedom this F gives p = 0.082 two-sided (editors' calculation). One-tailed testing is justified by hypotheses from the survey (p. 11).
reporting_issues.consequence: At the conventional two-sided level the psilocybin-escitalopram difference in belief change is not significant; the 'validation' is weaker than the abstract's word 'consolidated' suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: For the escitalopram arm, Z = 0.24 is printed with p = 0.33 and d = 0.2; Z = 0.24 corresponds to a one-tailed p of 0.41 (0.81 after the Bonferroni doubling applied to the psilocybin arm's Z = 2.28, p = 0.02), and a d of 0.2 in 29 patients would usually go with a larger Z (about 1.1 if d is the within-person standardized change; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the three escitalopram statistics is misprinted; the escitalopram change may be larger than 'no changes' suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The responder comparison is significant one-tailed (Z = 1.74, p = 0.041), yet its 90% CI for g (-0.17 to 1.26), the interval that matches a one-tailed 5% test, includes zero. The Methods describe a comparison of 'remitters', the Results of 'responders' (a fall of at least 50%), and the Discussion of psilocybin responders against non-responders.
reporting_issues.consequence: What was compared, and whether it is significant, is unclear; the number of responders per arm is not given.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the belief changes were positively correlated with the extent of past psychedelic use, but the Results report a correlation between lifetime use and baseline beliefs.
reporting_issues.consequence: A cross-sectional association is presented as if it concerned change.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor: in Table 2, 250 with a college diploma is printed as 30.1% (250 of 819 is 30.5%), and the ethnicity rows sum to 840 against a total of 819 (editors' arithmetic); the Figure 1 legend lists solipsism/idealism among items that changed, but the figure marks no significant change for it; the gender coding of the path model is not stated, although the Discussion says female gender predicted the shifts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; none changes the main findings.
