design_detail: National online survey (the Drug Policing Survey, late 2015) with an embedded randomized vignette experiment. 2115 Australians aged 18 or over who had attended an outdoor music festival and a licensed entertainment precinct in the past year, recruited online, were block-randomised to one of four written policing scenarios for a 30,000-person festival: high-visibility policing (over 200 uniformed and plain-clothes police inside and outside); riot policing (over 400 police including public order and riot squads and mounted police); three drug detection ('sniffer') dogs at the gates; or collaborative policing (police working with health organisations, first-aid tents and volunteers). Each participant also answered a no-police scenario (police said to have left before the band they want to see), and after each scenario said whether they would use, possess (carry drugs in), buy inside the grounds, give, or sell illicit drugs. Police presence against no police was compared within person (McNemar tests) and the strategies between blocks (logistic regression). The survey also asked about drug use, supply and police encounters at the last festival attended. The scenarios were built from 114 Australian police media releases and news articles (2002–2014) and focus-group tested. Only the festival half of a ten-scenario survey (the other half concerned licensed entertainment precincts) is reported.
can_establish: That among 2115 young Australian festival-goers recruited online, most of whom had used illicit drugs, stated intentions to use drugs and especially to carry them into a festival were lower in written scenarios with police (most with sniffer dogs) than without, while stated intentions to buy drugs inside the grounds were slightly higher, and that about two-thirds still said they would use drugs under every policing scenario.
cannot_establish: What people actually do when police or sniffer dogs are present (intentions in hypothetical scenarios, not behaviour); whether policing changes how much or which drugs people take, or leads people to swallow drugs to avoid detection (not studied in this paper); or how far the figures describe festival-goers in general (a self-selected online sample with unknown response rate).

sample.recruitment: Online, Australia-wide, mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media (e.g. Facebook), on drug-specific and other sites (p. 94, Methodology › Sample and recruitment). Of 4117 respondents, 2137 were asked about festivals; 18 were excluded for not consenting or being ineligible (e.g. aged 16) and 4 for invalid responses, leaving 2115.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or older, living in Australia, and attended at least one outdoor music festival and one licensed entertainment precinct in the last year (p. 94).
sample.demographics: Mean age 22.32 (SD 4.65); 54.9% male; 93.0% had completed year 12; 42.4% employed (29.9% full time); 71.3% metropolitan; 40.3% from New South Wales, 26.1% Victoria, 14.3% Queensland. Lifetime illicit drug use 89.1% and recent use 78.4%; cannabis and ecstasy used in the last 12 months by 68.6% and 62.4%. 47.0% had ever been stopped by Australian police, 21.9% searched (e.g. patted down or strip searched), 10.8% ever charged or arrested and 4.9% convicted (pp. 94–95; Table 2).
sample.attrition: The number who started but did not finish the survey is not reported; 22 of 2137 festival respondents were excluded.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected online sample recruited partly through drug forums, with very high rates of drug use (89% lifetime); no response rate can be computed. The authors report that demographics and drug use were broadly consistent with another national survey of festival-goers and with people who use ecstasy at least monthly (p. 95). Results describe this group, not festival-goers in general.

exposure.measurement: The exposure is the written scenario: the policing strategy described in a short vignette (Table 1, p. 93), randomly assigned between blocks, with every participant also answering the no-police scenario. Actual drug use, supply and police encounters at the last festival were self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Participants who said yes were asked which of nine drug categories and what quantity; these answers were collected but not reported in this paper (deferred to later work, p. 99).

comparison.controls: The no-police scenario, answered by every participant (the matched-pairs analysis implies this; the order in which the two scenarios were shown is not reported); in the regressions, the strategies were compared with collaborative policing.
comparison.matching: Randomized blocks were similar on measured characteristics except that the high-visibility block was about one year younger than the collaborative block (mean age 21.89 vs 22.81, p = 0.004) (p. 94; Table 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparison; scenario order, attention and seriousness of answers were not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same people answered the control scenario.

outcomes.instruments: Purpose-built online Drug Policing Survey: after each scenario, yes or no to using illicit drugs, possessing them (carrying or taking them into the grounds), buying inside the grounds, giving to a friend or acquaintance inside the grounds (social supply) and selling inside the grounds (for-profit supply); perceived likelihood of detection on a five-point scale; demographic, drug-use, criminal-justice and attitude items drawn from the National Drug Strategy Household Survey, Australian Institute of Criminology, US Bureau of Justice Statistics and EMCDDA instruments; last-festival drug use, supply and police encounters (pp. 93–94). The full instrument is online (p. 94).
outcomes.validity_norms: Scenarios focus-group tested; perceived detection differed between scenarios as intended (a manipulation check); validity of intentions argued from meta-analyses of intention–behaviour correlations (r 0.49–0.79) and from the similarity of stated and last-festival rates (pp. 93, 99). No validation of the survey items is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Deterrence as a lower proportion saying they would commit an offence under a policing scenario than under no police; any offending as any of the five behaviours.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Significance set at 0.001 to adjust for multiple comparisons (p. 94), but results with p = 0.003 to 0.041 are described or marked as significant in the text and tables (see reporting issues). Six offending outcomes were each tested for police against no police and across the four strategies, plus perceived detection and eleven candidate predictors.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed online survey); participants knew which scenario they were answering.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions saying they would offend (Table 4; any police vs no police): any offence 72.8% vs 77.4% (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6% vs 76.5% (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063); possess 52.6% vs 62.8% (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228); buy inside 39.5% vs 36.8% (+2.7); give 26.9% vs 28.9% (−2.0); sell 3.5% vs 5.1% (−1.6). By strategy (high-visibility, riot, dogs, collaborative): any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6% (p = 0.003); use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1% (p < 0.001); possess 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4% (p < 0.001); buy 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2% (p = 0.711); give 25.0, 26.3, 28.4, 27.9% (p = 0.029); sell 3.0, 3.0, 4.3, 3.6% (p = 0.029). Regression odds ratios against collaborative policing (Table 5): overall offending 2.687 (95% CI 1.495–4.832, high visibility), 2.259 (riot), 2.438 (dogs); possession 2.338, 2.692, 3.170; buying 1.315, 1.312, 1.341 (not significant). Editors' calculation from Table 4: the odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing are about 1.36, not 2.69, so the regression outcome must differ from the one described (see reporting issues). Absolute differences are a few percentage points.
analysis.covariates: Multivariate model (Table 6): policing strategy, festival frequency, lifetime drug use, age under 24, income, residence, ever encountering police, respect for police, perceived consequences of detection.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or pre-specified analysis plan is reported in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the festival half of the survey is reported; drug types and quantities were collected but deferred to later work (p. 99), so effects on how much or what people would take are not available.
analysis.power: Not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In written scenarios, any police presence lowered the share saying they would commit any drug offence from 77.4% to 72.8%, mostly through use and carrying drugs in; sniffer dogs lowered stated carrying from 62.8% to 47.1% and stated use from 76.5% to 66.3%, and stated buying inside the grounds rose from 36.8% to 39.5% with any police (43.8% with dogs, though the strategies did not differ significantly on buying). Collaborative policing gave rates close to no police. At their last festival, 65.3% of the sample said they had used illicit drugs, 22.5% had sold or given drugs, and 71.2% had seen police.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says police presence led to a 4.6-point reduction and that buying of drugs increased significantly within festival grounds (p. 91), describing hypothetical intentions as effects; it also says high-visibility policing most reduced overall offending, ‘including supply’ (p. 91), although it differs from drug detection dogs by 0.6 points without a test and the strategies did not differ on supply at the paper's own threshold (giving and selling p = 0.029, buying p = 0.711). The discussion says sniffer dogs lead to the highest rate of buying drugs inside festivals (p. 98), but the strategies did not differ significantly for buying (p = 0.711, Table 4). Statements resting on the regressions (odds 2.3–3.2 times higher than collaborative policing; police presence not the most significant predictor, Fig. 2) depend on models whose outcome is described inconsistently and whose statistics cannot all be reconciled (see reporting issues). The concerns about adulterated drugs bought inside festivals, switching to less detectable drugs, changing quantities or hasty consumption of pills to avoid police come from other sources or are speculation, not data from this survey. The authors state the central limitation, intended rather than actual behaviour (p. 99).

timeline.event: Hughes, Weatherburn and MacCoun (2015): the same team's 2014 pilot with three scenarios in 513 New South Wales festival patrons; police with drug detection dogs led to 9.5% fewer saying they would use illicit drugs than no police (as summarized on p. 92; not read here)
This study: national survey, four policing strategies, use, possession, buying and supply outcomes

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the pilot's finding on drug detection dogs and stated use was repeated here by the same team with the same method; both measure intentions in hypothetical scenarios. No study of actual behaviour is reported in this paper.

funding.funder: Australian Research Council Discovery Project DP150100910; the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre receives funding from the Commonwealth Australian Government; Alison Ritter holds a National Health and Medical Research Council Fellowship (APP1021988) (p. 99, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that there are no conflicts of interest (p. 99).
funding.affiliations_note: Drug Policy Modelling Program, National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research; Stanford Law School (p. 91). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study of actual behaviour at festivals with and without drug detection dogs or other policing, for example events or days with policing allocated at random, measuring drug use, carrying, buying inside, amounts taken at once and medical presentations, together with drug checking of what people buy inside the grounds.

domains.note: Block randomization is stated without method or concealment; blocks were similar except for a one-year age difference. For police against no police, each person answered both scenarios in an order that is not reported.
Participants answered the scenario allocated to them; perceived detection differed between scenarios as intended, suggesting the scenarios were read.
Break-offs in the online survey are not reported; 22 of 2137 exclusions are.

The outcome is a stated intention about a hypothetical festival, answered by participants who knew the scenario and had just answered a contrasting one; consistency and social-desirability effects are likely, and no behaviour was measured.

No registration; half the survey reported; quantities and drug types deferred; the stated significance threshold is not applied consistently; the regression outcome is unclear; p values differ between text and table.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized scenario design gives clean comparisons of what this sample said they would do, but the outcome is a hypothetical intention, not behaviour, and the reporting of significance and of the regressions is inconsistent. The paper may be cited for the sizes of the differences in stated intentions in Table 4 (for example carrying drugs in: 62.8% with no police, 47.1% with sniffer dogs; buying inside: 36.8% with no police, 39.5% with any police) and for the last-festival self-reports of this online sample (65.3% used illicit drugs, 22.5% sold or gave drugs, 71.2% saw police). It may not be cited for actual changes in behaviour, for effects on overdoses, drug quantities or swallowing drugs to avoid detection, for the regression odds ratios or predicted probabilities, or as representative of festival-goers.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 2115 people aged 18 or over who had been to an outdoor music festival in the past year, recruited online across Australia (mean age 22.32; 54.9% male); 89.1% had used an illicit drug in their lifetime and 78.4% recently; 47.0% had ever been stopped by Australian police and 21.9% searched.
key_findings.locator: Methodology › Sample and recruitment (p. 94); Results › Demographics and drug use characteristics of the sample (pp. 94–95); Table 2 (p. 94)

key_findings.finding: At the last festival attended: 65.3% of the sample said they had used illicit drugs (ecstasy most often), 22.5% had sold or given drugs to someone (mainly ecstasy), and 71.2% had seen or encountered police; among the types of police seen, drug detection dogs were reported by 43.5%, second to uniformed police (64.0%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug offending and police encounters at the last festival attended, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
key_findings.note: Table 3's drug-specific rows use an unstated denominator (ecstasy 85.1% is not a share of the whole sample, of whom 65.3% used any drug), and the denominator for types of police seen is not given (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Perceived chance of detection for use or possession was rated likely or very likely by 52.3% under sniffer dogs, 32.9% under riot policing, 26.5% under high-visibility policing, 14.9% under collaborative policing and 1.8% with no police; for supply offences 62.2%, 48%, 41.9%, 26.8% and 3.6%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Perceived likelihood of police detection under different policing vignettes; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 and this paragraph call the collaborative strategy community policing.

key_findings.finding: Any police presence against no police (stated intentions, Table 4): any drug offence 72.8% vs 77.4% (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6% vs 76.5% (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063, p < 0.001); carrying drugs in 62.8% with no police vs 52.6% with police (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228, p < 0.001); giving 26.9% vs 28.9% (−2.0) and selling 3.5% vs 5.1% (−1.6); buying inside the grounds rose from 36.8% to 39.5% (+2.7).
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Impacts of 'police presence' versus 'no police', both subsections
key_findings.note: The p values for buying, giving and selling differ between the text and Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: By strategy (Table 4; high-visibility, riot, sniffer dogs, collaborative, no police): would use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1 and 76.5%; would carry drugs in 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4 and 62.8%; would buy inside 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2 and 36.8%; any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6 and 77.4%. The p values compare the four strategies only (χ² with 3 degrees of freedom): use and carrying p < 0.001, buying p = 0.711 (no difference), any offence p = 0.003.
key_findings.locator: Table 4; Results › Impacts by policing strategy

key_findings.finding: Sniffer dogs produced the largest fall in stated carrying of drugs into the festival, from 62.8% with no police to 47.1% (15.7 points), against 59.4% with collaborative policing (3.4 points); collaborative policing produced no significant reduction in any offence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Impacts by policing strategy › Type of illicit drug offending (p. 96, right column); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 98)

key_findings.finding: Whatever the policing, about two-thirds said they would use illicit drugs and at least 25% said they would engage in some form of supply; the authors compare stated rates under the policing scenarios (use 66.3–69.2%; supply 25.0–28.4%) with those reported for the last festival (65.3% and 22.5%). [Table 4: use under collaborative policing was 75.1%, outside the authors' range, and 25.0–28.4% are the giving rates; no rate for any supply is reported.]
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 98, left column); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 99, left column)

key_findings.finding: People who had ever been stopped by police were less likely to be deterred (adjusted odds ratio 0.587, 95% CI 0.395–0.874); being deterred was more likely with lifetime drug use (3.894), rural residence (2.234), attending festivals only 1–2 times a year (3.403) and perceiving consequences of detection (2.205–2.603).
key_findings.locator: Results › Impacts of policing vis-a-vis other factors, 2nd paragraph (right column); Table 6
key_findings.note: The outcome of these models is described inconsistently and some statistics cannot be reconciled (see reporting issues); cite the direction only.

key_findings.finding: Drug types and quantities were collected but not analysed in this paper (to be examined in later work), so it contains no data on how much people would take, switching to less detectable drugs, or swallowing drugs to avoid police; the hasty-consumption concern in the introduction is attributed to other sources (Hickey et al., 2012, and media and advocacy reports).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, The challenge of policing outdoor music festivals, 3rd paragraph (p. 92); Methodology, 5th paragraph (p. 93); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 99)

reporting_issues.issue: Significance was set at 0.001 to adjust for multiple comparisons, yet results at p = 0.003 (strategy effect on any offence), 0.005, 0.009, 0.015, 0.017, 0.022 and 0.041 are called or marked significant in the text and Tables 4–6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under the paper's own threshold, the difference between strategies in overall offending and several predictors in the multivariate model would not be significant.

reporting_issues.issue: The p values for buying, giving and selling differ between text and Table 4: the text gives buying p = 0.001, giving p = 0.001 and selling p = 0.005, Table 4 gives buying < 0.001, giving 0.005 and selling 0.001; the chi-square for giving (11.57, printed with 2115 degrees of freedom) equals that for buying (11.572, 1 degree of freedom).
reporting_issues.consequence: The test results for the supply outcomes cannot be relied on; at least one value appears to have been copied.

reporting_issues.issue: The logistic regressions are described as models of offending (yes or no), but their odds ratios cannot be reproduced from the offending rates in Table 4 (editors' calculation: odds of not offending, high-visibility against collaborative policing, about 1.36 against the printed 2.687); the text calls the outcome being deterred, the multivariate model's 94.0% correct classification fits only a rare outcome such as changing one's answer between scenarios, and the predicted probabilities of deterrence in Fig. 2 (about 0.5 to 0.77) fit neither reading.
reporting_issues.consequence: The regression odds ratios and Fig. 2 should not be cited for magnitudes; the percentages in Table 4 are the interpretable result.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 and the text disagree on drug use at the last festival: the text says ecstasy was reported by 85.1% of the sample, although only 65.3% of the sample used any drug; hallucinogens are 10.2% in the text and 20.8% in Table 3; ecstasy supply (22.9%) exceeds any supply (22.5%). Denominators of the drug-specific rows are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-specific last-festival percentages cannot be cited as shares of the sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 53.2% attended a festival 1–2 times in the past year; Table 2 gives 58.4% overall, which matches its block values (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table value is internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors in Tables 5–6: a p printed as 0.35 for an odds ratio of 3.500 whose interval (1.093–11.209) excludes 1 (editors' calculation about 0.035); the giving comparison for dogs against collaborative policing printed as p = 0.035 although its interval (1.269–3.725) implies about 0.005; an upper limit printed as 3982; some intervals asymmetric around their estimates on the log scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: Individual regression statistics are unreliable; this adds to the concerns about the models.

reporting_issues.issue: The order of the two scenarios each person answered is not reported, and the no-police scenario differs from the others in more than policing (police said to have left before a late-afternoon band); the scenarios also differ in information source (friend, social media post, organisers' notice, hearsay) and, for collaborative policing, in the health services offered.
reporting_issues.consequence: Order and wording effects cannot be separated from the effect of policing on stated intentions.

design_detail: Parallel three-arm randomized trial (Study 1 of a 5-year project at the University of New Mexico, Albuquerque) in 130 concerned significant others (CSOs: spouses, partners, parents and other relatives living with a person with an alcohol problem who refused treatment). CSOs were randomized by urn randomization to Al-Anon facilitation therapy (n = 45; up to 12 one-hour sessions encouraging involvement in Al-Anon), a Johnson Institute intervention (n = 40; six sessions of about 2 hours preparing a confrontational family meeting) or community reinforcement and family training, CRAFT (n = 45; up to 12 one-hour sessions teaching behaviour-change and communication skills to use at home). All arms were manual-guided with about 12 hours of therapist contact, and therapists were nested within conditions. Primary outcome: the relative's entry into treatment within 6 months (at least the 4-hour assessment and one session), tracked to 12 months; CSO functioning measured at intake, 3 and 6 months. Relatives who agreed were offered free treatment in an embedded trial (Study 2), whose drinking outcomes are reported elsewhere.
can_establish: That, in this trial of mostly women family members of people with alcohol problems who refused treatment, being assigned to CRAFT led to treatment entry far more often within 6 and 12 months than being assigned to Al-Anon facilitation or a Johnson Institute intervention, as delivered by these therapists at this site.
cannot_establish: Whether CRAFT changes drinking or other outcomes for the relative (reported elsewhere); whether family members benefit from any of the three approaches compared with no help (all three groups improved equally and there was no untreated group); whether the advantage holds with other therapists, sites or drugs, for family members in less frequent contact, or where there is violence (excluded); or which parts of CRAFT do the work (skill use was not measured).

sample.recruitment: Community volunteers: CSOs seeking advice or help about the drinking of someone living with them, referred from various sources but mostly through announcements in local news media, living within 60 miles of the research site in Albuquerque, New Mexico (p. 688; p. 690).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: CSO living with a relative with a drinking problem who was a close relative (parent, child, grandchild, sibling), spouse or unmarried partner; contact on at least 40% of the past 90 days with no planned separation; both aged 18 or older; the relative described by the CSO, in a structured diagnostic interview (SCID), as meeting DSM-III-R criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence, refusing treatment, and untreated (other than detoxification) in the past 3 months. Excluded: CSO with a substance use disorder; unremitted psychosis or other severe psychiatric condition in either person; CSO planning more than 6 hours of other treatment in the next 3 months; relative with an illicit drug problem more severe than the alcohol problem, or any crack cocaine or injecting drug use; a Johnson intervention in the past 3 years; insufficient reading ability; relative with domestic violence or criminal assault in the past 2 years or a history of severe violence (p. 690). 50 cases excluded at screening: insufficient contact 17, the relative's violence 11, relative had not refused treatment 10, CSO unwilling 4, CSO alcohol dependent 3, relative with severe psychiatric disorder 3, relative not clearly meeting criteria 2 (p. 690).
sample.demographics: CSOs: 118 of 130 (91%) women; Hispanic 39%, White non-Hispanic 53%, Native American 6% (8), 1 African American, 1 other; age 21–81, mean 47; mean 14 years of education; 17% of family incomes below $15,000 and 53% below $30,000. Relationship to the relative: spouse 59%, parent 30%, boyfriend or girlfriend 8%, child 1.5%, grandparent 1.5%; mean relationship length 22 years (1–57); 58% had previously sought help through Al-Anon (p. 692). The relatives' own demographics are not reported.
sample.attrition: All 130 randomized CSOs were retained in the analyses (intention to treat, p. 692). Follow-up interviews: Al-Anon facilitation 44 of 45 at 3 and 6 months and 42 at 9 and 12; CRAFT 45 of 45 at 3, 6 and 9 months and 44 at 12; Johnson 39 of 40 at 3 and 6 months, 38 at 9 and 36 at 12; 94% of CSOs completed all four follow-ups (p. 693). The logistic regression used 120 CSOs with complete data (p. 694). The CSO-functioning analyses do not state their n; their error degrees of freedom (196 to 222) imply roughly 100 to 115 CSOs per measure (editors' inference).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers answering media announcements, nearly all women, in one US city with a large Hispanic population. CSOs had to see the relative on at least 40% of days, and relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use, or a more severe drug problem were excluded. The number of callers screened by telephone is not reported. The results concern family members of people with alcohol problems, not other drugs, and not families affected by violence.

exposure.measurement: Assigned intervention (randomized). Al-Anon facilitation: up to 12 sessions of 60 minutes (8 core), adapted from Project MATCH twelve-step facilitation, delivered by four counsellors with a mean of 14 years' twelve-step experience. Johnson Institute intervention: six sessions of about 2 hours (four preparatory sessions, the confrontation meeting with the relative, one review session), delivered by two counsellors with 27 and 17 years' experience from the local council on alcoholism, supervised by a psychiatrist experienced in the method. CRAFT: up to 12 one-hour individual sessions (awareness training, contingency management, communication skills, competing activities, outside activities, handling dangerous situations, suggesting counselling, functional analysis), delivered by five less experienced therapists (four with 0–3 years, one with 6 years) using a manual by R. J. Meyers, who developed the approach and supervised the condition (pp. 691–692). Weekly supervision and videotaped sessions, with randomly selected tapes reviewed for adherence; tapes were not coded for analysis (p. 692).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Sessions attended: Al-Anon facilitation 11.4 of 12 (95%), CRAFT 10.7 of 12 (89%), Johnson 3.18 of 6 two-hour sessions (53%), because 70% of Johnson-arm CSOs chose not to hold the confrontation (p. 692).
exposure.polysubstance: Relatives with a more severe illicit drug problem, or any crack cocaine or injecting drug use, were excluded, as were CSOs with their own substance use disorder (p. 690). The relatives' other drug use is not reported in this paper.

comparison.controls: Two active comparators: Al-Anon facilitation therapy, which the authors treat as a functional no-treatment control for engagement because changing the drinker is not an Al-Anon goal (p. 688), and the Johnson Institute confrontational intervention. No waiting-list or untreated group.
comparison.matching: Urn randomization balanced CSO gender, ethnicity, education, age, relationship type, lifetime DrInC score and lifetime Al-Anon meetings; 22 baseline comparisons (16 ANOVAs, 6 chi-squares) showed no significant differences, nor did CSO estimates of drinking, consequences or the relative's motivation (pp. 691–692).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a concern for the randomized comparison. The relatives' characteristics were known only through CSO report.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: the relative engaged in treatment within 6 months, defined as completing the initial 4-hour assessment and at least one session in the project's free treatment (Study 2), or at least two sessions of other treatment; tracked to 12 months (p. 693). CSO functioning: Beck Depression Inventory, State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory, Family Environment Scale (cohesion, conflict), Relationship Happiness Scale, at intake, 3 and 6 months (p. 694). Also collected at intake: State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, self-esteem, physical symptoms, Spouse Enabling and Sobriety Influence Inventories, Form 90, DrInC, Alcohol Dependence Scale, Dyadic Adjustment Scale and Conflict Tactics Scale (pp. 690–691).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments. Drinking data for relatives who did not enter treatment came only from CSOs; the 40% contact threshold was chosen because collateral and self-reports agreed only with frequent contact (r = .84 vs −.20 in Project MATCH data) (p. 691).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Engaged' is a low threshold (assessment plus one session); relatives who entered treatment stayed a median of 10.5 sessions (p. 693).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The primary outcome (engagement) was tested for Study 2 entry, the 6-month window and 12 months, each with a three-group test and two pairwise tests described as post hoc; five CSO measures (six F tests, state and trait anger separately) in one repeated-measures model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Follow-up interviews by independent research staff unaware of group assignment and of clinical procedures (p. 692). CSOs and therapists could not be blind. Entry into Study 2 treatment was recorded by the project; entry into other treatment came from CSO report.

analysis.effect_sizes: Engaged within 6 months (primary): CRAFT 29/45 (64%), Johnson 12/40 (30%), Al-Anon facilitation 6/45 (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001; CRAFT vs Johnson χ²(1, N = 85) = 10.29, p < .001 (Table 1; p. 693). Editors' calculation (Wald intervals): risk difference CRAFT minus Johnson 34 percentage points (95% CI about 14 to 54), CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51 points (34 to 68); about 3 and 2 families, respectively, trained in CRAFT for each additional relative engaged. Within 12 months: 67%, 35% and 20% (Table 1). Al-Anon facilitation vs Johnson not significant (6 months χ²(1, N = 85) = 3.56, p < .06). Condition remained associated with engagement after adjustment for drinking at intake, extra CSO therapy and relationship type: Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002 (p. 694). CSO functioning: no group × time interactions and no group main effects; time effects for depression F(2, 196) = 14.49, state anger F(2, 222) = 10.65, trait anger F(2, 214) = 8.48, family conflict F(2, 206) = 10.28, family cohesion F(2, 204) = 10.59, relationship happiness F(2, 198) = 9.00 (p. 694; Table 2).
analysis.covariates: Primary comparison unadjusted (chi-square tests, which the editors' recalculation shows are likelihood-ratio statistics). Logistic regression adjusted for the CSO-reported percentage of days abstinent at intake, the number of additional therapy sessions in months 1–3, and relationship type (p. 694). CSO outcomes adjusted for therapy received outside the project (p. 694).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration (published 1999) and no protocol cited; the primary outcome, engagement within 6 months, is named in the Results (p. 693).
analysis.selective_reporting: Drinking outcomes of the relatives are deferred to a later report of Study 2 (p. 696). Several intake measures (anxiety, self-esteem, physical symptoms, enabling, Dyadic Adjustment Scale, Conflict Tactics Scale) are not reported as outcomes.
analysis.power: Not reported. The CRAFT difference was large enough for this sample; the Al-Anon facilitation vs Johnson comparison (13% vs 30%) was not clearly resolved (p < .06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Family members trained in CRAFT got their relative into treatment within 6 months in 64% of cases, against 30% after the Johnson intervention and 13% after Al-Anon facilitation; at 12 months the figures were 67%, 35% and 20%. In the Johnson arm 70% of families did not hold the confrontation; of the 12 that did, 9 relatives entered treatment. Family members in all three arms reported less depression, anger and family conflict and more cohesion and relationship happiness over 6 months, to the same degree, whether or not the relative entered treatment. Parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% vs 32% at 6 months).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's and discussion's central claim, that CRAFT was more effective at engaging relatives in treatment, matches the results, and the discussion is careful that Al-Anon facilitation is not the same as a simple referral to Al-Anon and that no single trial is conclusive (pp. 695–696). Gaps: (1) the abstract says all three approaches were associated with similar improvement for family members; with no untreated group, that improvement cannot be credited to any of the interventions (time, regression to the mean and the act of seeking help are alternatives); (2) the discussion calls the Johnson and Al-Anon approaches 'comparatively ineffective' at starting treatment and says a majority of unmotivated relatives can be engaged through the family (p. 696), on the evidence of one site and one team, with therapists nested within conditions and the CRAFT condition supervised by its developer, a co-author; (3) 'more effective' refers to treatment entry only, not to drinking or wellbeing outcomes, which this report does not give.

timeline.event: Sisson and Azrin: 12 CSOs; 6 of 7 relatives entered treatment after community reinforcement training against none after an Al-Anon approach delivered by the same behaviour therapists, which the present authors call an unfair comparison (as described, p. 689).
Thomas et al.: unilateral family therapy with spouses; 8 of 13 treated cases (62%) entered treatment or cut drinking substantially (as described, pp. 689, 695).
This trial: CRAFT 64% vs Johnson 30% vs Al-Anon facilitation 13% engaged within 6 months.
Same group, CRAFT with CSOs of people who used illicit drugs: 74% engaged (Meyers, Miller, Hill & Tonigan, described as in press, p. 695; an uncontrolled study by the account of Roozen et al., 2010).
Meta-analysis of four RCTs including this one: CRAFT vs Al-Anon/Nar-Anon RR 3.25 (2.11–5.02); vs Johnson, this trial alone, RR 2.15

replication.where_it_stands: The engagement advantage of CRAFT over twelve-step family approaches was repeated in two later RCTs with families of people who use illicit drugs (Kirby et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2002, as summarized by Roozen et al., 2010), one of them from the same group; the comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on this trial alone. No trial in this set had an untreated control for family members' wellbeing.

funding.funder: Supported in part by Grant R01-AA09774 from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (author note, p. 688).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: R. J. Meyers, second and corresponding author, originally developed the approach that CRAFT extends, wrote the CRAFT manual and supervised the CRAFT condition (pp. 691–692). The authors nested therapists within conditions so that each approach was delivered by therapists committed to it (p. 692). Investigator allegiance is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A multi-site randomized trial run by teams independent of CRAFT's developers, with several therapists per condition (or therapists crossed with conditions), including family members of people who use drugs other than alcohol and those in less frequent contact, comparing CRAFT with usual care or a waiting list, and measuring treatment entry, the relative's substance use and safety, and family members' wellbeing for at least 12 months.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: Urn randomization balancing seven variables, and 22 baseline comparisons showed no differences; how allocation was concealed from the staff enrolling CSOs is not described.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Effect of assignment, analysed by intention to treat (all 130). CSOs and therapists knew the assignment, unavoidably; adherence was supervised by videotape. Not holding the confrontation (70%) is part of the Johnson approach as offered. Outside RoB 2's questions: therapists were nested within conditions, with less experienced therapists in CRAFT supervised by its developer, so method and therapist team cannot be separated (the two main CRAFT therapists engaged 50% and 91%).

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: Engagement status is known for all randomized CSOs, and 94% completed all follow-ups. (For the CSO-functioning outcomes, the analyses' degrees of freedom imply about 12% to 23% missing, editors' inference.)

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Entry into the project's treatment was recorded by the project; other treatment was reported by CSOs to interviewers unaware of assignment. (The CSO-functioning outcomes are self-reports by participants who knew their assignment.)

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registered protocol or analysis plan. Engagement is reported for three windows with three-group and post hoc pairwise tests, all in the same direction; the relatives' drinking outcomes are deferred to a later report.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged for the primary outcome, treatment entry. A well-conducted trial for its time: randomized with balance checks, intention to treat, follow-up interviewers unaware of assignment and 94% retention. The concerns (allocation concealment not described, no registered plan) are unlikely to explain a 34-point difference, but the comparison is of three therapist teams at one site, one led by the method's developer, which limits how far the size of the effect generalizes. For family members' own wellbeing the trial shows only equal improvement in all arms, without an untreated comparison, so it cannot show that any approach caused it. Citable for: CRAFT's advantage in getting relatives with alcohol problems into treatment over Al-Anon facilitation and the Johnson intervention; the Johnson intervention's 70% non-completion; not for drinking outcomes or for benefits to family members.

key_findings.finding: Who was studied: 130 family members (91% women; spouses 59%, parents 30%, partners 8%) living with a relative with an alcohol problem who refused treatment, in Albuquerque, New Mexico; randomized to Al-Anon facilitation (45), the Johnson Institute intervention (40) or CRAFT (45), and all retained in the analysis.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Within 6 months (primary outcome), the relative entered treatment in 29 of 45 CRAFT cases (64%), 12 of 40 Johnson cases (30%) and 6 of 45 Al-Anon facilitation cases (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Wald intervals): CRAFT minus Johnson 34 percentage points (95% CI about 14 to 54); CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51 points (34 to 68).

key_findings.finding: Within 12 months, engagement was 67% with CRAFT, 35% with the Johnson intervention and 20% with Al-Anon facilitation (χ²(2, N = 130) = 23.78, p < .0001); 74% of the relatives who entered treatment in the year had done so by the end of the family member's counselling (3 months) and 90% by 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: The Al-Anon 12-month figure is inconsistent within the paper (20% in Table 1, about 18% implied by the text and the test statistic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: CRAFT also beat the Johnson intervention alone: χ²(1, N = 85) = 15.66 for Study 2 entry, 10.29 at 6 months (p < .001) and 8.65 at 12 months (p < .003); Al-Anon facilitation and the Johnson intervention did not differ significantly (χ² 1.23, 3.56 and 3.29).
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the Johnson arm, 70% of family members decided not to go through with the confrontation. Of the 12 families that held it, 9 relatives (75%) entered treatment, all within 6 months; of the 28 that did not, 3 (11%) entered within 6 months and 5 (18%) within 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO Participation, 1st paragraph (p. 692); Treatment Engagement, 4th paragraph (p. 693)

key_findings.finding: Timing: median 47 days from the family member's first session to the relative's first treatment session; family members had completed a mean of 4.7 CRAFT sessions (median 4), 5.7 Al-Anon facilitation sessions (median 6) or 4.7 Johnson sessions (median 6) before the relative entered treatment; relatives who entered stayed a median of 10.5 sessions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Condition remained a significant predictor of engagement after adjusting for drinking at intake, extra therapy for the family member and relationship type (Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002). Relationship type also predicted engagement: across conditions, parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% vs 32% at 6 months; 56% vs 34% at 12 months).
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 6th paragraph (begins p. 693, continues p. 694)

key_findings.finding: Family members' own functioning improved over 6 months by similar amounts in all three arms, with no group × time interaction and no group effect: for example, Beck Depression Inventory means fell from 10.6–10.8 at intake to 7.0–7.5 at 6 months, and family conflict, anger, cohesion and relationship happiness changed in the same direction (time effects p < .001 to p < .002). Improvement did not depend on whether the relative entered treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO Improvement, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: There was no untreated group, so the improvement cannot be attributed to any of the three approaches. Table 2 gives no n per cell.

key_findings.finding: Attendance: family members completed 11.4 of 12 Al-Anon facilitation sessions (95%), 10.7 of 12 CRAFT sessions (89%) and 3.18 of 6 Johnson sessions (53%). In the 90 days after randomization, 75% in the Al-Anon facilitation arm attended Al-Anon against 18% in each other arm (N = 109), and they received more outside therapy sessions (mean 4.81 vs 2.03 and 2.62).
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO Participation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (2nd begins p. 692, continues p. 693)

key_findings.finding: Therapist differences: engagement rates per therapist ranged from 16% to 100% across the 11 therapists, and the lowest CRAFT therapist (50%) exceeded the highest in the other arms; the two CRAFT therapists with 10 or more cases differed (7/14, 50%, vs 10/11, 91%; χ²(1, N = 25) = 5.23, p < .02), whereas the pairs in the other arms did not (16% and 17%; 33% and 36%). CRAFT therapists had less experience than those in the other arms.
key_findings.locator: Method › Therapists, 2nd paragraph (p. 692); Results › Therapist Differences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 695)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the Al-Anon facilitation tested here, a structured 12-session individual therapy, cannot be equated with a simple referral to Al-Anon; that no trial, including this one, documented whether family members actually learned and used the skills taught; and that the 40% contact requirement leaves open whether less frequent contact would give similar results.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 695); 7th paragraph (p. 696)

reporting_issues.issue: The Al-Anon facilitation arm's 12-month engagement is inconsistent. Tables 1 and 3 give 9 of 45 relatives engaged by 12 months (20%), with 6 later engagements across arms (3, 2 and 1), but the text says 5 additional clients entered treatment in months 7–12. By the editors' recalculation, all nine reported chi-squares are likelihood-ratio statistics that reproduce from the Table 1 counts, except the two 12-month tests involving the Al-Anon arm (23.78 and 3.29), which reproduce only with 8 of 45 engaged (with 9 of 45 they would be 21.64 and 2.42). The statement that 90% of relatives were engaged by 6 months also fits 47 of 52 (90.4%) better than 47 of 53 (88.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Al-Anon facilitation 12-month rate was probably 18% (8 of 45) rather than 20%; the conclusions are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The 12-month comparison of Al-Anon facilitation with the Johnson intervention is printed as χ²(2, N = 85) = 3.29, with 2 degrees of freedom for a two-group comparison; the printed p < .07 corresponds to 1 degree of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the result is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The report says all randomized CSOs were retained for all analyses (intention to treat), but the F tests for the CSO-functioning measures have error degrees of freedom from 196 to 222, which by the editors' inference for a three-group repeated-measures model with one covariate implies roughly 100 to 115 CSOs per measure; Table 2 gives no n.
reporting_issues.consequence: The family-member outcomes may rest on 77% to 88% of the randomized sample, and the meta-analysis that pooled them (Roozen et al., 2010) used n = 45 for the CRAFT arm at both times.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 4.2.2) of randomized and controlled clinical trials comparing Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT) with Al-Anon/Nar-Anon-based approaches or the Johnson Institute intervention for concerned significant others (CSOs) of adults with substance use disorders who refused treatment. Five databases searched in November 2008; four RCTs included (Sisson & Azrin, 1986; Miller et al., 1999; Kirby et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2002), 264 CSOs. Outcomes: the relative's entry into treatment (at least one session), pooled as relative risk with numbers needed to treat; and CSO functioning, pooled as change from baseline to 6 months within the CRAFT arms of two trials. Evidence graded with a four-level rating system.
can_establish: The pooled relative chance that a relative who refused treatment entered it when the family member was trained in CRAFT rather than in a twelve-step family approach, across four small US trials published 1986–2002, three of them from CRAFT's originators.
cannot_establish: Whether CRAFT improves family members' own wellbeing compared with no help or with the other approaches (the CSO analysis pools before-and-after scores within CRAFT arms only); whether CRAFT beats the Johnson intervention beyond a single trial; effects on substance use, safety or violence (not synthesized); or effects outside the US and outside trials run by CRAFT's developers.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, PsycINFO, EMBASE, CINAHL and the Cochrane Library in November 2008, using the keywords of an earlier review by the first author plus CRAFT-related terms (Fig 1 legend), with reference checking and author consultation (pp. 1730–1731). Included trials: Sisson & Azrin (1986), 12 female CSOs of male drinkers, 3-month follow-up; Miller et al. (1999), 130 CSOs of people with alcohol problems, 6 months; Kirby et al. (1999), 32 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, mainly cocaine and heroin, 10 weeks; Meyers et al. (2002), 90 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, 6 months (Table 1, p. 1732).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: RCTs or controlled clinical trials comparing CRAFT with Al-Anon/Nar-Anon and/or the Johnson Institute intervention; CSOs of treatment-resistant people aged 18 or older with substance use disorders; therapists trained in the approach and supervised regularly; the primary goal of getting the relative to attend at least one treatment session (pp. 1730–1731). Of 218 records, 109 were excluded as not relevant and 105 as potentially relevant but ineligible (86 on the community reinforcement approach, 13 reviews or discussions, 2 CRAFT book discussions, 3 not RCTs or controlled trials, 1 with other outcome measures) (Fig 1, p. 1730). No language or date limits are stated.
sample.demographics: CSOs in the included trials were 88–100% women, aged 19–81; ethnicity reported for three trials (Anglo 48–75%; Hispanic 39–50% in the two New Mexico trials; African American 22% in Kirby et al.); relationships mostly partners or spouses, with 30–53% parents in three trials (Table 1, p. 1732).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition within the trials is not reported in the review.
sample.selection_effects: Four small US trials. Two (Miller et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2002) come from the group that developed CRAFT, and one (Sisson & Azrin, 1986) from the originators of the community reinforcement approach. Comparators differ (Al-Anon facilitation therapy; Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches) and follow-up ranges from 10 weeks to 6 months. Uncontrolled CRAFT studies discussed later in the review were not eligible. The authors thank three authors of included trials for assistance and supplementary data (Acknowledgements, p. 1737).

exposure.measurement: CRAFT (including its earlier form, community reinforcement training) delivered to family members by trained therapists, against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon-based approaches (four trials) or the Johnson Institute intervention (one trial). The content, number of sessions and delivery of each intervention are not described in the review.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (psychosocial intervention for family members). The review states that engagement typically followed four to six CRAFT sessions (p. 1735).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol and illicit-drug trials were pooled; the authors justify this by the overlap of alcohol and drug use and the absence of heterogeneity (Limitations, 2nd paragraph, p. 1735). Substance shares for relatives who did not enter treatment came from family members' reports (Table 1 note).

comparison.controls: Twelve-step family approaches (Sisson & Azrin: Al-Anon model; Miller et al.: Al-Anon facilitation therapy; Kirby et al. and Meyers et al.: Nar-Anon) and, in one trial, the Johnson Institute confrontational intervention. No included trial had an untreated group; the CSO-functioning analysis compares baseline with 6 months within CRAFT arms.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level (randomized trials).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level.

outcomes.instruments: Engagement: the relative attended at least one treatment session (inclusion criterion iv, p. 1731), as defined in each trial. CSO functioning: depression (Beck Depression Inventory), anger, family cohesion, relationship happiness and family conflict, as reported by the trials (p. 1733).
outcomes.validity_norms: Trial quality was scored by two reviewers independently on 11 internal-validity criteria adapted from Cochrane Back Review Group guidelines, 'high quality' meaning six or more criteria met; agreement 84% (κ = 0.65). The criteria and each trial's scores are not listed; all four trials scored six or more (pp. 1731).
outcomes.operationalization: Engagement as a binary outcome pooled as relative risk with numbers needed to treat; family-member 'improvement' as the weighted mean difference between baseline and 6-month scores in the CRAFT arms of two trials; strength of evidence graded on a four-level scale (strong: consistent findings in multiple high-quality RCTs; limited: one RCT) (p. 1731).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Seven pooled estimates: engagement against Al-Anon/Nar-Anon and against the Johnson intervention, and five family-member measures.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Whether study selection and data extraction were done in duplicate is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Engagement, CRAFT vs Al-Anon/Nar-Anon (4 trials; 125 vs 99 CSOs): 84 of 125 (67%; 95% CI 58.97–75.43) vs 18 of 99 (18%; 10.58–25.78); RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), P < 0.0001, NNT 2; Q = 3.09, df = 3, P = 0.38, I² = 2.9% (Fig 2, p. 1733). Trial RRs: Sisson & Azrin 9.75 (0.67–141.44), Miller et al. 4.83 (2.22–10.50), Kirby et al. 3.86 (1.28–11.64), Meyers et al. 2.34 (1.31–4.16). Without Sisson & Azrin: RR 3.21 (1.99–5.17), I² = 15.3% (p. 1736). CRAFT vs Johnson Institute (one trial): 64% (50.45–78.43) vs 30% (15.80–44.20); RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), P = 0.004, NNT 3 (p. 1733). Family-member change from baseline to 6 months in CRAFT arms (74 CSOs, two trials): depression WMD 3.60 (0.99–6.22), anger 3.39 (1.80–4.99), family cohesion −1.60 (−2.75 to −0.46), relationship happiness −1.28 (−2.16 to −0.39), family conflict 0.94 (0.21–1.67) (p. 1733; Fig 3, p. 1734). No prediction intervals.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The family-member analysis pools only CRAFT arms, and for Meyers et al. (2002) only one of the two CRAFT arms (n = 29), although both were combined for engagement; between-arm comparisons of family-member functioning, which the trials describe as similar, are not pooled. Publication bias is not discussed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The Johnson comparison rests on one trial of 85 CSOs; the pooled RR rests on 224 CSOs, with Meyers et al. (52.29% of the weight) and Miller et al. (29.97%) carrying most of it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across four small US trials, relatives whose family members were trained in CRAFT entered treatment about three times as often as when family members received a twelve-step family approach (67% vs 18%; RR 3.25, consistent across trials), and, in the one trial with a Johnson arm, about twice as often (64% vs 30%). Family members' depression, anger and family relationships improved from baseline to 6 months within CRAFT arms; the trials themselves report similar improvement in the comparison arms.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The engagement conclusion matches the pooled data, though 'strong evidence' rests on four small trials, three from CRAFT's originators, without any assessment of publication bias. The abstract says family members showed marked psychosocial and physical improvements whichever approach they received, and the review rates as strong (level 1) the evidence that CRAFT and Al-Anon/Nar-Anon improve family members' functioning (pp. 1729, 1733–1734); the pooled data are before-and-after changes within CRAFT arms with no untreated comparison, which cannot show that any approach caused the improvement, a limitation the authors themselves raise later (p. 1736), and physical symptoms were not pooled. The discussion calls CRAFT almost three times more effective than the Johnson intervention (p. 1736), against the RR of 2.15 on p. 1733. It suggests, without data, that partner violence may also have declined (p. 1735), although the largest alcohol trial excluded families with recent violence (Miller et al., 1999, p. 690). The recommendation that CRAFT be implemented in routine practice (p. 1736) rests on efficacy trials; the one routine-practice study cited engaged 55% (p. 1734).

timeline.event: Sisson and Azrin: 12 female CSOs of male drinkers; 6 of 7 relatives entered treatment with community reinforcement training vs 0 of 5 with the Al-Anon model; therapists crossed with conditions (as described in this review).
Three-arm trial with families of people with alcohol problems: CRAFT 64%, Johnson 30%, Al-Anon facilitation 13% engaged within 6 months
Kirby et al.: 32 CSOs of people using illicit drugs; CRAFT 64% vs Nar-Anon 17% at 10 weeks (as described in this review).
Meyers et al.: 90 CSOs of people using illicit drugs; CRAFT with or without aftercare 67% vs Nar-Anon 29% at 6 months (as described in this review).
Routine-practice effectiveness study of CRAFT: 55% engagement by intention to treat (Dutcher et al., 2009, as described in this review, p. 1734).
This review: CRAFT vs twelve-step family approaches RR 3.25 (2.11–5.02); vs Johnson RR 2.15 from one trial.

replication.where_it_stands: The pooled engagement advantage rests on four small US trials: two from CRAFT's developers, one from the originators of the parent approach, and one (Kirby et al., 1999) with no author in common with the others. Specific rates should be cited from the primary trials, and this review for the pooled relative risk with its limitations. Trials published after November 2008 are not included, and no included trial measured family members' wellbeing against an untreated group.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declarations of interest: none (p. 1737).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Erasmus University Medical Centre (Rotterdam) and two Dutch addiction services (Novadic-Kentron, Vught; Centrum Maliebaan, Utrecht). The acknowledgements thank R. J. Meyers, J. E. Smith and K. C. Kirby, authors of included trials, for assistance and supplementary data, and the reference list includes a 2009 paper on CRAFT co-written by the first author with Meyers (ref. 39). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: An updated, registered systematic review with duplicate screening and extraction, domain-level risk-of-bias assessment (including investigator allegiance and therapists nested within conditions), discussion of small-study effects, and between-arm rather than before-and-after analyses of family members' wellbeing; and new multi-site trials by independent groups, outside the US, with a usual-care or waiting-list arm.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (CSOs of treatment-resistant adults), intervention (CRAFT), comparators (Al-Anon/Nar-Anon, Johnson Institute) and outcomes (engagement, CSO functioning) are specified.
No protocol or registration mentioned.
RCTs and controlled clinical trials were eligible, without an explanation of the choice.

Five databases, keywords given by reference to an earlier review plus listed terms, reference checking and author consultation; no grey literature or trial registries, publication restrictions not stated, and the search is from November 2008.
Not described; only the quality assessment is stated to have been done by two reviewers.
Not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusions are given only as counts by category in the flow diagram (Fig 1); no list of excluded studies.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives sample size, CSO sex, age, ethnicity and relationship, substances, comparators, follow-up and results; intervention content, settings and recruitment are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: An 11-item internal-validity score (adapted from Cochrane Back Review Group guidelines) was applied by two reviewers independently, but the items and each trial's judgments are not reported, so it cannot be seen whether allocation concealment or blinding was assessed; results are given only as a summary score (all six or more).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

The engagement analysis (random-effects relative risk with heterogeneity tests) is appropriate, but the family-member analysis pools baseline against 6-month scores within CRAFT arms as if they were independent groups, ignoring both the within-person correlation and the randomized comparison arms; it cannot answer the review's own comparative question.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis omitting Sisson & Azrin (1986), the trial flagged for crossing therapists with conditions and for imprecision, left the RR unchanged (3.21); all other trials were rated high quality.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The conclusions call the evidence strong without discussing the trials' risks (unblinded family members, therapists nested within conditions, developers running most trials); the need for an untreated group is noted only in the discussion, while the abstract presents the family-member improvement as a result.
I² = 2.9% for the main analysis; pooling of alcohol and drug trials is discussed and justified by the low heterogeneity.
Not investigated or discussed (with four trials a funnel plot would not be informative, but the possibility is not mentioned).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no interests; funding for the review is not stated, and the acknowledged help from authors of the included trials is not discussed as a potential conflict.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence: five critical items are not met (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no reported domain-level risk-of-bias assessment, an inappropriate method for the family-member synthesis, risk of bias not used in interpretation) and publication bias is not considered. This judges how far the review's summaries can be trusted, not the trials themselves. The engagement meta-analysis is simple and checkable: its trial-level numbers match the primary trials (for example Miller et al., 1999: 29/45 vs 6/45), heterogeneity is low and the result survives removing the weakest trial. Citable for the pooled engagement relative risk against twelve-step family approaches, with its small, developer-dominated evidence base stated; not for claims that CRAFT or any other approach improves family members' own wellbeing, and not as independent support for the Johnson comparison, which is Miller et al. (1999) alone.

key_findings.finding: Five databases were searched in November 2008; of 245 records (218 after removing duplicates and adding 3), four RCTs met the criteria, with 264 family members in total; all four were rated high quality (six or more of 11 criteria), with 84% agreement between the two reviewers (κ = 0.65).
key_findings.locator: Fig 1 (p. 1730); Methods › Criteria for considering studies and search strategy, 1st paragraph (p. 1730); Methods › Methodological quality assessment (p. 1731, for the 11 criteria); Results › Study selection and methodological quality, 1st paragraph (p. 1731). [Fig 1 counts confirmed: 245 − 30 + 3 = 218; 218 − 105 − 109 = 4.]
key_findings.note: Record counts are printed only inside the Fig 1 flow diagram (image text, read on the rendered page): 32 + 62 + 94 + 32 + 25 = 245, minus 30 duplicates, plus 3 = 218.

key_findings.finding: Across four trials, relatives entered treatment in 84 of 125 CRAFT cases (67%) against 18 of 99 twelve-step family-approach cases (18%): RR 3.25 (95% CI 2.11–5.02), P < 0.0001, NNT 2, with little heterogeneity (Q = 3.09, df = 3, P = 0.38, I² = 2.9%); graded by the authors as strong evidence (level 1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effectiveness of CRAFT versus Al-Anon; Fig 2
key_findings.note: The arm totals (125 and 99) are printed only in the Fig 2 forest plot (image text, read on a rendered crop). The 67% and 18% are simple pooled proportions across trials: an editors' recalculation of Wald intervals from 84/125 and 18/99 reproduces the printed intervals (58.97–75.43 and 10.58–25.78).

key_findings.locator: Fig 2 (forest plot)
key_findings.note: Values read from the forest plot on a rendered, rotated 200-dpi crop.

key_findings.finding: Leaving out the smallest trial (Sisson & Azrin, 12 participants) hardly changed the pooled result: RR 3.21 (95% CI 1.99–5.17), NNT 2, I² = 15.3%.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 1735, continues p. 1736)

key_findings.finding: Only one trial (Miller et al., 1999) compared CRAFT with the Johnson Institute intervention: 64% (95% CI 50.45–78.43) vs 30% (15.80–44.20) engaged; RR 2.15 (1.28–3.62), P = 0.004, NNT 3; graded by the authors as limited evidence (level 3).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effectiveness of CRAFT versus Johnson Institute intervention

key_findings.finding: The included trials, as summarized: Sisson & Azrin (1986), 12 female CSOs of male drinkers, 86% vs 0% engaged at 3 months; Miller et al. (1999), 130 CSOs of people with alcohol problems, 64% vs 30% vs 13% at 6 months; Kirby et al. (1999), 32 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, 64% vs 17% at 10 weeks; Meyers et al. (2002), 90 CSOs of people using illicit drugs, two CRAFT arms combined 67% vs 29% at 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of included studies, 1st–4th paragraphs (p. 1731); Table 1 (p. 1732)

key_findings.finding: Family members' functioning: within the CRAFT arms of two trials (74 CSOs), scores improved from baseline to 6 months for depression (WMD 3.60, 95% CI 0.99–6.22), anger (3.39, 1.80–4.99), family cohesion (−1.60, −2.75 to −0.46), relationship happiness (−1.28, −2.16 to −0.39) and family conflict (0.94, 0.21–1.67); the review states that family members in the Al-Anon/Nar-Anon and Johnson arms improved similarly, whether or not the relative entered treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO improvements, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1733, continues p. 1734); Fig 3 (p. 1734)
key_findings.note: These are before-and-after changes within CRAFT arms, not comparisons between randomized arms; the authors later say a no-treatment group is needed to rule out change that would occur anyway (Limitations, 5th paragraph, p. 1736).

key_findings.finding: The authors summarize that CRAFT gets about two-thirds of relatives who refused treatment to attend it, and that engagement typically came after four to six CRAFT sessions with the family member.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Clinical implications, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Studies outside the meta-analysis, as cited by the review: an uncontrolled CRAFT study of 62 family members of people who used drugs, 74% engaged; a routine-practice effectiveness study, 55% engaged by intention to treat; parents of adolescents, 71% engaged; and unpublished data, as personal communications, of 40% engagement with a self-help book or self-directed treatment and 70% with a group format.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Clinical implications, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 1734–1735); Limitations, 6th paragraph (p. 1736)
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from studies not appraised here.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the quality assessment was not checked with the trial authors; alcohol and drug trials were pooled; the smallest trial was imprecise; which CRAFT components work is unknown; and an untreated comparison group is needed for the family-member outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st–3rd paragraphs (p. 1735), 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 1736)

reporting_issues.issue: The family-member meta-analysis (Fig 3) treats baseline and 6-month scores of the same CRAFT participants as two independent groups ('Favours baseline' against 'Favours 6 months'), ignores the randomized comparison arms, uses only one of the two CRAFT arms of Meyers et al. (n = 29) although both were combined for engagement, and assumes n = 45 at both times for Miller et al.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled 'improvements' describe change over time in CRAFT arms; they cannot be attributed to CRAFT, and their intervals do not account for the paired design. Miller et al. (1999, p. 694) report no difference between arms in these measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says CRAFT was found almost three times more effective than the Johnson Institute intervention (p. 1736), while the results report RR 2.15 and describe CRAFT as two times more effective (p. 1733).
reporting_issues.consequence: The discussion overstates the only comparison with the Johnson intervention.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says family members showed marked psychosocial and physical improvements in all three approaches, but no physical-symptom outcome was pooled, and the pooled analyses are within CRAFT arms only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract presents an untested, uncontrolled improvement as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says CRAFT encouraged about two-thirds of relatives to attend treatment 'typically for four to six CRAFT sessions', which reads as if the relatives attended four to six sessions; the body says engagement occurred after four to six CRAFT sessions with the family member (p. 1735).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the four to six sessions are the family member's, not the relative's.

reporting_issues.issue: The Fig 3 legend calls the depression measure the BDI-II, while Miller et al. (1999, p. 690) cite the original Beck Depression Inventory (Beck, Steer & Garbin, 1988).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the instrument version is mislabelled for at least one trial.
